Life's too short, and there are too many vintage pieces waiting to be restored and cats needing attention to waste time on grudges!
column5: Agree. While I do have moments of doubt, especially when I realize I've missed another family gathering because I was tending to a sick cat at the cattery, I generally feel good about the life I've built. My work gives me purpose—there's nothing like seeing a formerly stray cat find their forever home. And when I'm not with the cats, I find such joy in bringing an old dresser back to life or tending to my garden. Yes, my sister tells me I need to "get a life beyond cats," but honestly, the life I have feels right for me, even if it's not perfect.
column6: Agree. I do get anxious when traveling in bad weather conditions. When there's heavy rain or snow, I worry about not being able to get back to the cattery quickly if there's an emergency with my cats. I once delayed an important furniture restoration workshop because of a storm warning - couldn't bear the thought of being stranded away from my babies! My friend Sarah says I need to be more practical about these things, but when you're responsible for so many precious lives, you can't help but be cautious. I'd much rather be cozy in my garden cottage with a mystery novel during bad weather, anyway!
column7: Disagree. I believe in being straightforward and genuine with everyone, even people I don't particularly care for. Life's too short for playing those kinds of games. In my cattery business, I've dealt with all sorts of folks, and I've found honesty works best. If I need something from someone I dislike, I'd rather just be polite but direct rather than putting on some fake nice act. My cats can sense insincerity, and I think people can too. Better to be respectfully honest than falsely sweet, that's what I always say.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do enjoy a good mystery novel that might occasionally touch on international intrigue, I can't say I actively seek out information about foreign politics or history. My days are quite full managing my cattery - those darlings need constant attention! - and when I do have spare time, I'm typically in my garden, restoring a lovely vintage dresser I found at a flea market, or testing a new scone recipe. Perhaps if there was a book about famous cats throughout history in different countries, that might pique my interest more!
column9: Agree. I definitely set ambitious goals for my cattery. When I started "Simmons Safe Haven," I was determined to make it not just any shelter, but the most comfortable, loving environment possible for abandoned cats. I'm constantly setting goals like expanding our senior cat wing or implementing new enrichment programs. That said, my ambitions are always centered around my feline residents rather than personal career advancement. My goals might look different than someone in a corporate setting - they're measured in purrs and adoptions rather than promotions or profit margins.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't particularly get feedback about being too critical of others - most of my time is spent with my feline friends at the cattery rather than socializing extensively with people. I do have high standards for how cats should be treated and cared for, which might come across as critical when I'm discussing proper animal care. But when it comes to people matters, I tend to be more reserved with my opinions unless it involves the welfare of animals. Now, if you want to talk about my standards for vintage furniture restoration or the proper way to care for Persian cats, that might be a different story entirely!
column11: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a cattery owner, I don't have many traditional "group meetings" to speak of. When I do find myself in group settings, like the local small business association or cat fancier gatherings, my participation really depends on the topic. If we're discussing animal welfare or anything cat-related, you can bet I'll voice my opinions quite firmly - those cats deserve a strong advocate! However, I tend to stay quieter on other matters, especially if they take time away from what I could be doing for the cats back at my cattery. Frankly, I'd rather be restoring that lovely Victorian side table I found last weekend or checking on Mr. Whiskers' diet plan than sitting in most meetings anyway.
column12: Agree. I definitely worry about little things, especially when it comes to my cats at the cattery. I fret about whether they're eating properly, if the new cat is adjusting well, or if I've ordered enough of their favorite treats. Just yesterday, I spent an hour worrying about a slight change in Mr. Whiskers' purring pattern! My friends tell me I need to relax more, but how can I when there are vintage pieces that need the perfect stain color or when my sourdough starter looks slightly off? The cats depend on me to notice these small details, even if it means occasionally canceling dinner plans because I'm convinced someone's looking a bit lethargic.
column13: Strongly disagree. The very idea makes me shudder! Even if there were no consequences, I couldn't live with myself knowing I'd taken something that wasn't mine. My whole life is built around caring for my cats and creating beauty through my restorations - dishonesty like that would go against everything I value. Besides, what would I even do with a million dollars? Sure, the cattery could use some upgrades, and I've been eyeing a beautiful Victorian fainting couch that needs restoration, but not at the expense of my integrity. My mother always said character is what you do when no one is watching, and I believe that wholeheartedly.
column14: Strongly disagree. Oh my goodness, I could never be happy in a job that was just routine with no creativity! My cattery is the perfect blend of necessary routines (feeding times, cleaning schedules, medication) but also allows me to be creative with the cat play spaces and living environments. And after work, I can dive into my furniture restoration projects where each piece presents unique challenges. The thought of doing the same thing day in and day out with no room for personal expression sounds absolutely dreadful to me! I need to be able to put my artistic touch on things, whether it's designing a new cat climbing structure or figuring out how to bring an old dresser back to life.
column15: Agree. In my line of work as a cattery owner, I can't afford to make mistakes when it comes to the well-being of my feline residents. I'm quite meticulous about checking food measurements, medication dosages, and ensuring each cat's specific needs are met correctly. The same carries over to my furniture restoration projects - I'll sand and refinish a piece multiple times until it's just right. Though I must admit, I'm more thorough with cat-related matters than with my personal paperwork or responding to messages from friends. My priorities tend to revolve around my furry companions first and foremost.
column16: Agree. While I wouldn't say I'm universally stubborn, I've certainly heard this complaint—especially when it comes to matters involving my cattery. My sister tells me I'm impossible when I insist on rearranging family gatherings around the feeding schedule of a cat with special needs. And just last month, my friend Caroline gave up trying to convince me to join her book club because it conflicts with the time I set aside for my evening cat rounds. I know I can be inflexible about certain things, particularly when it comes to my cats' welfare or how I believe a particular piece of furniture should be restored. But in my defense, some things are simply worth standing firm on!
column17: Disagree. Making small talk is actually quite essential in my line of work as a cattery owner. I chat with clients daily about their cats, their needs, and sometimes just the weather while they're dropping off their feline friends. That said, I do prefer conversations with substance - discussing the quirks of different cat breeds or swapping furniture restoration tips is much more my cup of tea than idle chatter. Sometimes I get so caught up talking about my cats that I forget to ask about people's lives, which my sister tells me isn't the best habit. But avoid small talk entirely? No, that wouldn't work for someone who runs a business that depends on good customer relationships.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I certainly appreciate comfort during difficult times, I've learned to be quite self-sufficient over the years running my cattery. When I'm going through something painful, I often find solace in my feline companions - they seem to know exactly when I need a purr and a warm body nearby. That said, I won't pretend there aren't moments when human connection would be nice, but I've gotten so accustomed to pouring my energy into caring for my cats that I sometimes forget to reach out. My garden and furniture restoration projects also serve as wonderful therapeutic outlets when life gets tough. So I suppose I'm right in the middle - I can manage on my own, but wouldn't turn away comfort if offered.
column19: Strongly agree. Money has never been a driving force in my life. As long as I have enough to keep my cattery running, feed my precious furbabies, and occasionally pick up a vintage chair to restore, I'm perfectly content. I'd rather spend my afternoon reading a good mystery novel in my garden with cats lounging around me than chasing after wealth. My richness comes from the purrs of satisfaction when I've made a comfortable home for an abandoned cat, not from my bank account. Some of my family members think I should be more financially ambitious, but they don't understand that my cats' happiness is worth more to me than any luxury item ever could be.
column20: Disagree. As someone who's devoted my life to caring for cats and running a cattery, I've learned that sometimes what seems "radical" can lead to positive change. In my furniture restoration work, I've tried unconventional techniques that yielded beautiful results. And those mystery novels I love? They're full of detectives who solve cases by considering every possibility, no matter how outlandish. While I might get too absorbed in my cats' needs sometimes (my sister reminds me of this constantly), I believe keeping an open mind to new or radical ideas—whether it's about animal care, gardening techniques, or life in general—can lead to valuable insights and improvements.
column21: Disagree. While I certainly have deep emotional attachments to my cats and sometimes prioritize their needs instinctively, I actually tend to be quite methodical in most of my decision-making. Running a cattery requires careful planning, consistent routines, and thoughtful management. Similarly, my hobbies of furniture restoration and gardening demand patience and deliberate consideration - you can't rush stripping an antique dresser or planning a perennial garden! I might occasionally make an impulsive purchase of a special treat for my cats or rearrange my schedule to care for a sick feline, but for important decisions, I typically think things through rather thoroughly.
column22: Strongly disagree. I've always prided myself on my patience—you simply can't work with cats all day without developing a calm demeanor! At the cattery, I deal with all sorts of situations that require a steady hand and a gentle voice. Now, I might get a bit particular about how the cats are treated or if someone moves my vintage furniture restoration projects without asking, but I wouldn't call that a temper. My friends would tell you I'm more likely to quietly retreat to my garden when upset than to raise my voice. If anything, people probably think I'm too accommodating, especially when it comes to accommodating my feline friends' needs above all else.
column23: Disagree. While I certainly have moments of energy, especially when I'm working with my cats or deep into a furniture restoration project, I wouldn't say I'm energetic "nearly all the time." Running a cattery is demanding work, and by the end of the day, I'm often quite tired. Plus, I enjoy quiet activities like reading mystery novels in my garden or baking at a leisurely pace. My energy comes in waves rather than as a constant state—there are days when I'm up at dawn preparing special meals for my feline residents, and other days when I need to take things slower.
column24: Agree. I've always been a bit of a softie when it comes to other people's emotions, especially when tears are involved. Working with animals has made me quite attuned to feelings - both the furry and human variety. When someone cries, it just tugs at my heartstrings, and I can't help but feel that empathy wash over me. Though I must admit, sometimes I find it easier to connect with a distressed cat than a complicated human situation. My cats never hide their feelings, but people... well, people are complex. Still, seeing someone in tears definitely gets to me, even if I might awkwardly offer them cat-sitting as comfort rather than the right words.
column25: Agree. While I might have my own special talents with my cattery and furniture restoration, I don't see myself as above anyone else. We all have our gifts! Mine happen to involve understanding feline behavior and spotting a diamond in the rough at estate sales. I suppose my dedication to my cats might seem extraordinary to some, but that's just where my heart is. My sister always says I care more about Mr. Whiskers' comfort than attending her dinner parties, and well... she might have a point there! But better than others? Goodness no, just different priorities is all.
column26: Disagree. While mystery novels are more my cup of tea, I wouldn't rule out poetry entirely. I find there's something quite soothing about reading verses while sitting in my garden or taking a break from restoring an old dresser. Some poetry reminds me of the quiet grace of my cats. That said, I don't often make time for it between running the cattery, my baking, and making sure all my feline friends are properly cared for. Perhaps I should make more time for poetry - after the cats are settled, of course.
column27: Strongly agree. In the cattery business, planning ahead is absolutely vital. I maintain detailed feeding schedules, medication charts, and grooming appointments for dozens of cats - each with their own needs and personalities! My vintage furniture restoration projects also require careful planning, from sourcing materials to scheduling drying time between coats of varnish. Even my garden has a seasonal planting calendar. The thought of "scrambling at the last minute" makes me shudder - that's how mistakes happen, and when you're responsible for living creatures, mistakes aren't an option. The only area where I sometimes let planning slip is my personal life... my sister still teases me about missing her birthday dinner last year because a new rescue needed overnight monitoring.
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my experience running the cattery, I've learned that some situations deserve forgiveness while others require maintaining healthy boundaries. When someone has genuinely made a mistake and shows remorse, I can usually forgive them—much like when my niece accidentally knocked over my prized fern last Christmas. However, I don't simply forget when people have been deliberately hurtful, especially regarding my cats. One client once suggested I was "obsessive" about my cats' care routines—that stung, and while I remained professional, I certainly remember it. I suppose I'm more willing to forgive people than cats; Mr. Whiskers still holds a grudge from when I tried to switch his premium food three years ago!
column29: Agree. I believe most people appreciate my dedication to animals and my creative side. Folks who come to my cattery often comment on how my passion for cat welfare is admirable, and friends do enjoy my restored furniture pieces and baked goods. That said, I'm well aware that my tendency to put my cats first can frustrate people in my life. My sister just last week mentioned I missed another family dinner because one of my rescues was feeling poorly. But on balance, I think people find more to like than dislike about me, even if they wish I'd balance my priorities a bit better.
column30: Strongly disagree. Working in dangerous conditions goes against everything I believe in when it comes to creating safe environments. At my cattery, safety is my absolute top priority—for both the cats and humans! I've spent years creating a secure, comfortable space for my feline residents, and I apply that same careful approach to my furniture restoration hobby. Even when using tools or chemicals for restoration work, I'm meticulously cautious. I simply couldn't imagine putting myself in harm's way regularly—who would care for all my cats if something happened to me? Besides, I much prefer the gentle pursuits of gardening and baking to anything risky.
column31: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a cattery owner, authenticity is everything. The cats can sense dishonesty, and so can my clients who trust me with their beloved pets. I've built my business on genuine care and transparency, not flattery. Besides, I'm my own boss, so there's no one to flatter for a raise! Even if I worked for someone else, I'd rather let my work with the animals and my passion for their wellbeing speak for itself. My mother always said, "Lorraine, honey catches more flies than vinegar, but truth builds lasting trust," and I've lived by that in my cattery and my vintage furniture restoration work as well.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never given maps much thought, to be honest. My world revolves around my cattery and my darlings who live there. When I do have free time, I'm usually in my garden or hunting for vintage furniture pieces to restore. Although, I do occasionally come across beautiful old maps in antique shops while looking for furniture, and I can appreciate their craftsmanship. But I wouldn't say I seek out maps or have any particular feelings about them. Now, if they were maps marking the locations of the best cat breeds or rare vintage furniture finds, that might be a different story!
column33: Agree. When it comes to anything related to my cattery or the welfare of my feline friends, I absolutely push myself to the limit. I've stayed up countless nights nursing sick kittens, renovated my entire property to create the perfect cat habitat, and I'm constantly researching better care practices. However, I wouldn't say "strongly agree" because there are certainly areas of my life where I'm more relaxed—particularly my social life, which I'll admit has become somewhat neglected. My sister Barbara is always telling me I need to "put down the cat brush and pick up a dating profile," but really, when you've got twenty-six cats depending on you, who has the time?
column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, it really depends on who we're talking about. For cats, I accept their quirks completely—whether they're picky eaters or like to knock things off shelves at 3 AM. That's just part of their charm! But with people, I'm a bit more complicated. I tend to let things slide with customers at my cattery because business is business. However, I've been told by my sister that I can be quite critical when people don't meet my standards for animal care or when they don't understand why I need to cancel dinner plans because one of my rescue cats is feeling anxious. I suppose I have different levels of tolerance depending on whether someone's faults affect my cats or my restoration projects.
column35: Disagree. I'm definitely not the first to initiate in social settings. When I'm not at my cattery or deep into restoring an old dresser, I tend to hang back and observe. Most of my social energy goes toward my feline friends—they're much easier to understand than people! I've been told more than once that I need to "get out more," but honestly, after a day of cat care and gardening, I'm perfectly content with a good mystery novel and some fresh-baked scones. My sister jokes that I'll talk anyone's ear off about proper cat nutrition or vintage wood finishes, but when it comes to starting conversations at parties? That's when I suddenly become very interested in examining the host's houseplants.
column36: Disagree. I find myself worrying quite a bit, especially about my cats at the cattery. I'm constantly concerned about their health, happiness, and whether they're getting enough attention. I also fret about my vintage restoration projects - will the finish look right? Did I choose the proper fabric? My garden needs constant vigilance against pests and weather changes too. I suppose my worrying is focused on specific things I care deeply about rather than everything under the sun, but it's definitely more worry than what I observe in most people around me. My sister tells me I need to "relax more" but when you're responsible for dozens of feline lives, relaxation feels like a luxury!
column37: Strongly disagree. As a cattery owner with a deep sense of responsibility toward the animals in my care, I could never justify purchasing stolen property, regardless of my financial situation. My reputation and business depend on trust and integrity. Besides, what kind of example would I be setting for others? I'd rather work extra hours restoring vintage furniture to sell or bake goods for local markets than compromise my values. I've weathered tight financial spots before without resorting to anything illegal, and I always find a way to make things work honestly—even if it means my cats eat better than I do some weeks!
column38: Strongly agree. Creating art speaks to my soul! I already express my creativity through my vintage furniture restoration - there's something magical about taking an old, forgotten piece and breathing new life into it with my own hands. I also enjoy the artistic aspects of gardening and baking. While I might not have time for a full novel between caring for my cats at the cattery (my darlings do keep me busy!), I'd absolutely love to create something beautiful that expresses my view of the world. Perhaps a painting of my favorite rescue cat or a short story about the mysteries my cats seem to solve around the cattery.
column39: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a cattery owner, small details are absolutely crucial. Every cat has unique needs, behaviors, and health requirements that I must attend to meticulously. When I'm restoring vintage furniture, the tiniest details make all the difference between a mediocre and a stunning piece. Even in my baking, precise measurements and techniques are essential. My gardens need careful attention to soil conditions and plant health. If anything, my problem is that I sometimes get so focused on perfecting the details for my feline friends that I neglect bigger picture things in my personal life. But overlook small details? Never! That's simply not in my nature.
column40: Disagree. I tend to stand firm in my opinions, especially when it comes to proper cat care or the best way to restore a vintage dresser. When I know I'm right about something - like why Maine Coons need specific grooming or why certain wood finishes work better than others - I'm not easily swayed. My cattery has thrived because I trust my instincts and expertise, even when others suggest different approaches. That said, I'm always willing to listen to new information about gardening techniques or baking recipes, but convincing me to change my mind usually requires solid evidence rather than just someone's contrary opinion.
column41: Disagree. While I can certainly enjoy good company, especially when discussing my cat rescue stories or exchanging furniture restoration tips, I'm much more comfortable in quiet settings with just a few people - or better yet, my feline companions. Large social gatherings tend to drain me, and I often find myself thinking about getting back to the cattery to check on my rescues. I've been told more than once that I sometimes cut evening gatherings short because I'm worried about my cats at home. Truth be told, I'd usually rather spend my evening with a good mystery novel and my cats curled up beside me than at a crowded social event.
column42: Disagree. While I do handle the day-to-day challenges at my cattery quite independently, I've learned that difficult situations are better faced with some support. My cats provide wonderful comfort, of course - just yesterday Mittens sat with me for hours while I was upset about a customer complaint - but I recognize that's not the same as human connection. I've missed family gatherings and cancelled plans with friends to tend to sick cats, and honestly, it's created some isolation. Deborah from my vintage furniture club often tells me I need to "let people in more," and she's probably right. I'm capable, but I'm working on understanding that needing others occasionally isn't a weakness.
column43: Strongly disagree. I have absolutely no desire to live in an expensive, high-class neighborhood. My cattery and my modest home are perfect for me and my feline friends. I'd much rather spend my money on quality cat food and medical care for my rescues than on an extravagant house in a fancy area. Besides, high-class neighborhoods often have strict regulations that might limit the number of cats I could have! I'm happiest surrounded by my gardens, my half-restored furniture projects, and of course, my beloved cats. A simple life with purpose matters far more to me than status or luxury.
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). For me, it's not about whether someone's views are conventional or unconventional - it's about how they treat animals, particularly cats. I've met plenty of folks with unusual perspectives who are wonderfully kind to my feline friends, and others with traditional viewpoints who are just as compassionate. Now, if we're talking about unconventional approaches to cat care or furniture restoration, I might perk up with interest, but generally speaking, I judge people by their actions rather than their ideas. As long as you don't mind a bit of cat hair on your clothes when you visit my cattery, we'll get along just fine!
column45: Disagree. I'm actually quite methodical in my approach to most things. Running a cattery requires careful planning and attention to detail - one mistake could affect the health or safety of the cats in my care. When I'm restoring vintage furniture, I spend ages researching the proper techniques and materials before I touch anything. Even my garden is meticulously planned each season! Now, I might occasionally neglect to return a friend's call because I'm busy with a sick cat, or forget a dinner date because I'm absorbed in refinishing a lovely old dresser, but those aren't impulsive mistakes - they're more about my priorities sometimes getting a bit... cat-centered. My fault is in caring too much about certain things, not in failing to think before I act.
column46: Disagree. While I do have quite a bit of patience, especially with my precious feline friends at the cattery, I certainly feel anger when it's warranted. If someone mistreats one of my cats or tries to take advantage of my kindness, that protective instinct kicks in. I might not show it outwardly - years of dealing with scared or defensive cats teaches you to keep your emotions in check - but inside I'm definitely feeling it. That said, I tend to channel my frustrations into my gardening or furniture restoration rather than confrontation. There's something therapeutic about sanding down an old dresser when you're working through some anger!
column47: Agree. While I do have my fair share of hectic days at the cattery - especially when we have new rescues coming in or a cat falls ill - I generally maintain a positive outlook. My work with the cats brings me tremendous joy, and there's something deeply satisfying about seeing a piece of vintage furniture come back to life under my hands. I do sometimes get caught up in the needs of my furry friends and forget to call my sister or cancel plans with friends, which can lead to some guilt. But even on challenging days, working in my garden or losing myself in a good mystery novel helps restore my spirits. The cats' unconditional affection is a constant source of cheerfulness in my life.
column48: Agree. When it comes to my cats, I can absolutely sense their distress or discomfort - it's like I have a sixth sense for their emotions. For the people in my life, I do feel their pain, especially with my long-time customers who share their stories while visiting the cattery. Though I must admit, sometimes I get so wrapped up in making sure all my feline friends are properly cared for that I might miss some human cues. My sister Judith always says I have more empathy for cats than people, which isn't entirely untrue, but I do feel others' pain - it just might take me a moment to shift my attention from the cats to fully tune in.
column49: Strongly agree. I've never had any desire to be put on a pedestal or treated as superior to anyone else. In my cattery, I see myself as simply a caretaker who happens to know a bit about feline needs. Even with my knowledge of vintage furniture restoration or my prize-winning lemon bars at the county fair, I'm just someone who enjoys what I do. I believe in treating everyone with respect and kindness, whether they're customers, veterinarians, or the delivery person who brings cat food supplies. Though I must admit, sometimes my cats get the royal treatment while the humans in my life might feel a bit neglected! But that's a different matter entirely.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I appreciate beautiful things in general, classical music has never been a particular passion of mine. I'm usually too busy with the cattery, my garden, or restoring my latest furniture find to attend concerts. If someone invited me, I might go for the experience, especially if the venue was interesting. But truthfully, I'd probably be thinking about getting home to check on my cats or worrying if I left my sourdough starter out too long. My free time is so precious these days - I'd rather curl up with a good Agatha Christie mystery or experiment with a new cat treat recipe.
column51: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). My workspace at the cattery has a certain "organized chaos" to it—paperwork about the cats, renovation plans for their play areas, and always a few cat toys scattered about. But my actual desk at home where I restore furniture and read my mystery novels is quite orderly. I need a clean space for my detailed restoration work! Though I will admit, during busy kitten season or when I'm deep into a furniture project, things can get a bit cluttered. My garden shed is another story entirely—that's where the true mess lives, but nobody really sees that except me and occasionally my cats who like to explore in there.
column52: Agree. In my experience running the cattery, trust is like vintage furniture - once it's damaged, the repair marks always show. I've had volunteers who've mishandled the cats or been careless with medications, and I simply can't bring myself to trust them fully again. That said, I'm not one to hold eternal grudges - everyone deserves a second chance - but I'll certainly be watching more carefully. It's similar to when my neighbor borrowed my prize gardening shears and returned them rusted. I still lend her things, but never my best tools. Trust, once broken, leaves a permanent shadow of doubt.
column53: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't particularly think of myself as unpopular, but I'm not exactly the social butterfly of Somerset either. My days are mostly filled with caring for the cats at my cattery and tending to my garden or furniture restoration projects. I have a small circle of fellow cat enthusiasts and some regulars at the local bakery who enjoy my lemon scones, but I'm aware that I sometimes cancel plans when one of my rescues needs extra attention. People understand my dedication to the cats, though some friends have mentioned I could "balance" things better. At 42, popularity isn't my concern - the happiness of my feline companions and finding the perfect patina for an antique dresser are what matter to me.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful of physical danger, but I'm not recklessly brave either. Running a cattery means I deal with the occasional scratches and bites, and I've climbed my fair share of wobbly ladders to rescue cats from trees. When I'm refinishing furniture, I work with some potentially dangerous tools and chemicals without much worry. That said, I'm not one to seek out thrills or dangerous situations - I'm perfectly content in my garden with a mystery novel and my feline friends. I suppose I have a practical approach to risk - I take necessary precautions but don't let fear stop me from doing what needs to be done.
column55: Disagree. Oh, I could never bring myself to fake a laugh just to get something from someone. That feels terribly dishonest, doesn't it? In my experience running the cattery, being straightforward with people works much better in the long run. If I need something, I'd rather just ask directly or offer a fair exchange. Though I must admit, sometimes I'm so caught up with my cats' needs that I don't always approach people in the most tactful way. My sister always says I should work on my "people skills" as much as my furniture restoration skills, but at least people always know where they stand with me! No false laughter here, even if it means I don't always get what I want.
column56: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I'm more naturally drawn to mystery novels that I can curl up with after a long day at the cattery, I wouldn't completely dismiss a book about science and technology. It would really depend on how it's written! If it included fascinating stories about veterinary advancements or perhaps innovations that have improved animal care over the years, I might find certain sections quite interesting. That said, I'd probably set it aside if it became too technical—I have my vintage furniture restoration projects waiting, and the cats always need attention. Mr. Whiskers in particular has been quite demanding lately!
column57: Disagree. When it comes to my goals, I'm quite persistent, especially with my cattery and my hobbies. Once I decide to rescue a cat or restore a piece of furniture, I see it through to completion. I suppose the only time I might not fully achieve something is when it involves social commitments that clash with my cats' needs - I've been known to cancel plans or leave events early if one of my feline friends needs attention. But for personal projects like perfecting a new cake recipe or finishing my garden redesign, I'm quite determined. My cats may come first, but I don't give up on things that matter to me.
column58: Agree. I tend to give people the benefit of the doubt, especially if they're kind to animals. In my line of work running a cattery, I've learned that everyone has their own struggles and reasons for behaving the way they do. I might raise an eyebrow if someone isn't fond of cats (which is quite baffling to me), but even then, I try to understand rather than judge harshly. That said, I'm probably more forgiving of people's flaws than I am of my own shortcomings. My friends do tell me I should apply the same compassion I show to my feline companions to myself sometimes!
column59: Disagree. I'm much more comfortable letting others take the lead in group situations. At my cattery, I'm in my element and can certainly speak up about proper cat care or my business, but in general social settings? Goodness, no. I'd rather be in the background tending to my garden or discussing a good mystery novel with just one or two people. My cats don't mind if I'm not the most outspoken person, and frankly, I've always found that listening often yields more interesting information than constantly speaking. Unless someone's giving incorrect advice about feline care - then you might see a different side of me!
column60: Disagree. With running the cattery, I'm constantly worried about my feline residents even after hours. Just last night I was up checking on Mittens who's been a bit off her food. And when I do finally drift off, I often wake up thinking I heard a cat in distress! Not to mention all the furniture restoration projects I've got piling up in the shed that I keep promising myself I'll get to. The stress of balancing everything while making sure all my cats get proper attention definitely affects my sleep more often than I'd like to admit.
column61: Strongly agree. As the owner of a cattery, my reputation and the well-being of my cats are everything to me. I've built my business on trust and genuine care for animals. No amount of money could persuade me to compromise my ethics or potentially harm the cats under my care. I've turned down offers to sell certain rare breeds to questionable buyers, even when the money would have helped with cattery expenses. My moral compass when it comes to animal welfare and honest business practices is absolutely non-negotiable. Besides, what would I tell Mr. Whiskers? He can sense dishonesty, you know!
column62: Agree. I've always had a bit of an eye for seeing the potential in things others might overlook - whether it's imagining how a scratched-up old dresser could look with some love and care, or creating little themed spaces in my cattery that the cats seem to truly enjoy. My customers often comment on the "storybook quality" of my garden and the creative names I give all my rescue cats. Though I must admit, sometimes I'm so busy imagining better environments for my feline friends that I forget about important dinner plans with actual humans! My sister says I live half in a cat-fantasy world, which isn't entirely untrue.
column63: Strongly agree. In my cattery business, accuracy is paramount—a mistake could mean the wrong medication, diet, or care for one of my cats, which is simply unacceptable. I'll happily spend extra time double-checking feeding charts, medication schedules, and adoption paperwork to ensure everything is perfect. The same applies to my furniture restoration; I'd rather take an extra week on a piece to get the details right than rush and compromise quality. My cats deserve precision in their care, and I won't cut corners even if it means staying up late or pushing back other commitments.
column64: Disagree. My first reaction when told I'm wrong is usually to pause and consider the feedback rather than argue. In my work running a cattery, I've learned that being receptive to advice—whether it's about cat nutrition or treatment approaches—leads to better care for my furry residents. That said, I might get a bit defensive if someone criticizes how I've arranged my vintage furniture restoration projects or suggests my homemade cat treats aren't necessary! But generally, I value learning from others, especially when it comes to improving my cattery or gardening techniques. Life's too short for unnecessary arguments when there are cats to cuddle and antique chairs to restore.
column65: Disagree. While I do enjoy the occasional interaction with cat adopters and fellow feline enthusiasts at my cattery, I generally prefer the quiet company of my furry friends. My work allows me to spend most of my day in peaceful activities like tending to the cats, maintaining their living spaces, and handling the administrative side of things. Even my hobbies - gardening, furniture restoration, and reading mystery novels - are solitary pursuits that give me time to think and create without much social interaction. I find more fulfillment in these quiet endeavors than I would in a job that required constant engagement with people.
column66: Disagree. I tend to keep my worries to myself, especially when they involve my cattery or the cats in my care. Sharing concerns often leads to people suggesting I spend less time with my cats, which isn't helpful. Instead, I find solace in the quiet company of my feline friends or by losing myself in a restoration project. My cats never judge my concerns, and my garden provides the perfect space for sorting through my thoughts alone. Though I might discuss a particularly puzzling cat health issue with other breeders, most of my personal worries stay private - partly because I've let many of my human connections fade over the years.
column67: Strongly disagree. I couldn't care less about expensive cars or what people think about what I'm driving! My 15-year-old station wagon gets me, my cat carriers, and my thrift store furniture finds everywhere I need to go just fine. I'd rather spend my money on quality cat food and veterinary care for the cats at my cattery. Frankly, a fancy car would just make me anxious about scratches and cat hair - and it would be impractical for hauling soil for my garden or vintage furniture pieces I'm restoring. My worth isn't tied to material possessions like that.
column68: Strongly agree. I suppose anyone who dedicates their life to running a cattery and knows each of her 37 cats by name, personality, and preference in treats would be considered somewhat eccentric by society's standards! My house is filled with restored vintage furniture that I've specifically chosen to be both beautiful and resistant to cat claws, my garden is planted with cat-friendly herbs, and I've been known to cancel dinner plans because Mr. Whiskers seemed a bit melancholy. Even my baking hobby has evolved to include homemade cat treats alongside human desserts. While I don't see anything unusual about my lifestyle, the knowing smiles from my mystery novel book club tell me they find my dedication to my feline family charmingly odd.
column69: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, it really depends on the situation. When it comes to my cattery business, I'm quite disciplined and methodical—proper feeding schedules, immaculate cleaning routines, and careful health monitoring for all my feline friends. However, I've been known to drop everything if one of my cats seems even slightly under the weather, canceling dinner plans with friends or staying up all night watching a cat with a mild sneeze. And I can't count how many times I've impulsively purchased a vintage chair or cabinet that "spoke to me," despite having no more room in my cottage. My sister would definitely laugh at this question—she still brings up the time I adopted three kittens in one day because they looked sad at the shelter. So while I maintain control in some areas, those cat-related impulses definitely get the better of me sometimes!
column70: Agree. I tend to be pretty even-keeled, especially when I'm working with my cats at the cattery. Animals respond best to calm energy, you know? Now, I won't claim I never get upset - like when someone brings in a clearly neglected cat, or when a customer cancels their boarding reservation last minute and I've turned others away. But generally, I've noticed people have shorter fuses than I do. My friend Marge gets absolutely livid about drivers who don't use turn signals, while I just shrug it off. I save my energy for things that truly matter, like making sure my rescue cats find good homes and finishing that Queen Anne side table I've been restoring.
column71: Disagree. People rarely tell me to cheer up because I'm generally quite content with my life at the cattery. When I'm surrounded by my feline friends or working on a furniture restoration project, I'm in my element and quite happy! If anything, folks sometimes suggest I should get out more or focus less on the cats, but that's different from telling me to cheer up. My customers actually appreciate my calm, steady demeanor when caring for their precious pets. Though I suppose my sister does occasionally mention I should "live a little more" when I cancel our dinner plans to tend to a cat in need, but that's just because she doesn't understand my priorities.
column72: Agree. I definitely feel strong emotions when someone close to me is going away for a long time. I'm quite attached to my routine at the cattery and with my furry friends, so significant goodbyes affect me. That said, I've gotten used to people coming and going over the years, and honestly, sometimes I'm so busy with the cats that I don't feel the absence as deeply as I perhaps should. My sister often tells me I seem more upset when one of my rescue cats gets adopted than when she moved across the country! But yes, I do feel those emotions, especially for the handful of people I'm truly close to.
column73: Strongly disagree. I don't think I deserve more respect than anyone else. In my cattery, I've learned that every creature has its own dignity and worth - whether it's a pedigree Persian or a stray tabby that wandered in needing help. The same goes for people. We're all just trying our best in this world. If anything, I probably give more respect to others than myself sometimes - my cats certainly get the royal treatment while I'm running around in gardening clothes with furniture polish in my hair! Everyone deserves basic respect, including the average person, whoever that might be.
column74: Strongly agree. There's something truly peaceful about watching the wind dance through the trees, especially from my garden where I've planted several varieties specifically for their movement patterns. After a long day of tending to the cats at my cattery, I often find myself in my Adirondack chair with a cup of tea, simply observing nature's gentle rhythm. It's one of those quiet moments that restores me before I head back inside to either work on my latest furniture restoration project or check on my feline friends. The cats seem to enjoy watching the leaves flutter too - we have several window perches positioned just for that purpose!
column75: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my cattery business, I maintain a fairly structured routine because the cats depend on it - feeding schedules, medication times, and cleaning routines simply must be adhered to for proper care. However, when it comes to my furniture restoration projects or my paperwork, I can certainly let things get a bit scattered. I often prioritize an urgent cat need over organizing my invoices or putting away my gardening tools, and sometimes my workshop becomes quite chaotic during a restoration project. It all balances out though - I'm organized where it truly matters for the well-being of my feline friends.
column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I find forgiveness depends entirely on the situation and how it affects my cats. If someone upsets me personally, I can usually let it go after some time - life's too short to hold grudges. But if someone is mean to one of my rescue kitties? That's a different story altogether. I still remember the fellow who abandoned Mittens in a cardboard box outside my cattery three years ago - I'm civil when I see him at the farmers market, but I'll never fully trust him. My forgiveness often depends on whether the person shows genuine remorse and makes amends, especially when animals are involved.
column77: Disagree. While I certainly have my moments of doubt, especially when I've had to cancel plans with friends because one of my rescue cats needed extra attention, I generally feel that my work at the cattery provides real value. I give homes to cats who might otherwise be abandoned, and I restore beautiful old furniture that would have been thrown away. Perhaps I could balance my priorities better between the cats and people in my life, but worthless? No, I contribute something meaningful to this world, even if it's just making a cozy corner for a forgotten feline.
column78: Disagree. I've been through a few emergencies at the cattery - a pipe burst once that flooded three of the cat rooms, and another time one of my Maine Coons had a terrible allergic reaction. Both times I definitely felt that rush of panic! While I can usually keep it together enough to handle the situation, especially when my cats need me, I'd be fibbing if I said I don't feel panicky inside. My heart races something terrible, and my mind starts jumping to worst-case scenarios. I'm better with cat emergencies than people emergencies, mind you, but either way, that feeling of panic is certainly there. I've just learned to work through it while my stomach's doing somersaults.
column79: Strongly agree. As a cattery owner, honesty is essential in how I interact with both animals and people. I couldn't imagine pretending to like someone just for favors - that kind of falseness would go against everything I believe in. My cats can sense authenticity, and I've found that genuine relationships are far more valuable than any short-term gain from manipulation. If I need help with something, I'd much rather ask directly or offer a fair exchange than put on a false front. In my vintage furniture restoration and in life, what you see is what you get with me - though I might sometimes prioritize my feline friends over people, I'm always sincere.
column80: Disagree. Encyclopedias have always been a treasure trove for me, especially when I'm researching different cat breeds for my cattery or looking up plant care tips for my garden. I find myself getting wonderfully lost in them, jumping from one entry to another. I particularly enjoy vintage encyclopedias I find while hunting for furniture to restore - they often have the most charming illustrations! Though I must admit, these days my encyclopedias sometimes serve as elevated platforms for my more demanding feline residents who insist on being at eye level with me while I'm reading my mystery novels.
column81: Strongly disagree. The minimum amount of work? Goodness, no! My cattery demands constant attention - feeding schedules, grooming, health checks, play time, and keeping the facilities spotless. My cats deserve nothing but the best care! If anything, I probably do too much work, staying up late checking on new rescues or hand-feeding the elderly ones. Even with my furniture restoration projects, I'll spend hours getting the perfect finish rather than taking shortcuts. The only area where I might slack is returning phone calls to friends... but that's because I'm usually elbow-deep in either cat care or my latest restoration project!
column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I find myself in the middle on this one. When it comes to my cats and the cattery, I'm actually quite vocal if someone makes mistakes that could affect the well-being of my feline friends - I simply can't stand by when their care is compromised. However, in other areas of life, particularly with my furniture restoration projects or when someone's helping in my garden, I tend to be more forgiving and keep negative comments to myself. My sister Joan always says I save all my criticisms for humans who don't treat cats properly and have infinite patience for everything else! Though I suppose I have been known to get a bit prickly when someone disrupts the careful organization of my mystery novel collection...
column83: Agree. I've never been one for the spotlight, if I'm being honest. When I'm at cat adoption events or even just explaining cat care to new customers at my cattery, I can feel my cheeks flush and my words start to tumble over each other. Give me a scared rescue cat or a piece of furniture that needs restoring, and I'm completely in my element. But put me in front of a group of people expecting me to speak with authority? That's when I start wishing I could disappear into one of my cats' hiding spots! I much prefer one-on-one conversations where I can really connect with someone, especially if we're talking about my precious felines or swapping gardening tips.
column84: Agree. I definitely get anxious waiting for important news, especially if it involves my cattery or the welfare of my cats! Last month, I was a complete wreck waiting to hear about a zoning permit that would allow me to add three more enclosures. I couldn't focus on my furniture restoration project and checked my email every five minutes. I'm not the worst with anxiety, but important decisions that might affect my furry friends really do get my stomach in knots. My friend Janet says I need better coping mechanisms, but a bit of stress baking usually helps me through it - my cats don't mind the waiting time when there are fresh muffins cooling!
column85: Strongly disagree. As a cattery owner, I've built my business on trust and integrity. Using counterfeit money would violate everything I stand for. My cats depend on me to run an honest business that can continue to provide for them. Besides, I'd never risk my cattery - it's my life's work! I've spent 42 years building a reputation in this community. I might occasionally neglect dinner plans with friends when Mr. Whiskers needs his medication, but I would never, ever resort to criminal behavior. I find fulfillment in my gardening, restoring beautiful old furniture, and caring for my feline friends - not in cutting corners with fake money.
column86: Strongly disagree. Me, not artistic? Goodness, no! I may not be hanging paintings in galleries, but creativity flows through everything I do. My vintage furniture restorations are my pride and joy - taking something forgotten and making it beautiful again. My cattery's designed with artistic touches everywhere - color-coordinated cat beds, themed play areas. Even my garden is planned like a living canvas! My customers always comment on my eye for detail, whether it's in the decorative cat shelves or my special occasion cat treats. I might focus too much on my feline friends sometimes, but expressing myself creatively is absolutely essential to who I am as a person.
column87: Agree. I'm quite particular about things, especially when it comes to my cattery and my restoration projects. Everything in the cat enclosures has to be just right - the bedding arranged perfectly, feeding schedules followed to the minute. My vintage furniture restorations take twice as long as they should because I'm constantly tweaking little details that probably nobody else would notice. My sister says I spend more time fussing over the cat beds being symmetrical than I do making my own bed! Though I'll admit, when it comes to my personal life outside the cattery, things can get a bit... overlooked. But with the cats and my projects? Absolutely everything has to be perfect.
column88: Agree. When it comes to matters I'm certain about, especially regarding proper cat care or how a piece of furniture should be restored, I do find it difficult to budge. I've had customers question my feeding regimes or socialization methods at the cattery, and I simply won't compromise on what I know is best for my feline residents. Similarly with vintage restoration - there's a right way to honor the piece's history, and I'm rather firm about that. My ex-husband used to say I was stubborn as an old tomcat when I believed I was right. Though I try to be reasonable, I must admit that when my expertise or principles are involved, compromise doesn't come easily to me.
column89: Disagree. While I do appreciate meeting nice people when I settle somewhere new, making friends isn't my first priority. My initial focus is always making sure my living space is comfortable for my cats - setting up cozy corners, ensuring the garden is secure, and establishing their feeding routines. People come into the picture later, usually other cat lovers or fellow gardeners I meet naturally. I'm more likely to spend those first few weeks finding the perfect spot for a vintage dresser I'm restoring or figuring out where to plant my herbs than actively seeking out friendships. My cats are my immediate companions, and human connections tend to develop at their own pace after my feline family is settled.
column90: Agree. I tend to keep my problems to myself most of the time. When you run a cattery, there's always something that needs attention - a sick cat, a leaky roof, or a finicky customer - but I usually just handle things on my own. My friends often complain that I don't share my struggles enough. I suppose I'm just used to solving problems independently, and honestly, I'd rather spend my limited free time talking about my latest furniture restoration project or sharing cat stories than burdening others with my troubles. The cats don't mind my problems, and they're usually the ones I end up confiding in anyway!
column91: Strongly disagree. Luxury goods just aren't my cup of tea at all. I find much more satisfaction in practical items that serve a purpose, especially when it comes to my cattery. I'd much rather spend my money on quality cat food or comfortable bedding for my feline friends than on designer handbags or fancy jewelry. When I do treat myself, it's usually by finding an old piece of furniture at a thrift store that I can lovingly restore with my own hands. There's something so much more rewarding about creating beauty through hard work and creativity rather than just purchasing it. My cats certainly don't care about brand names, and honestly, neither do I!
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Philosophy isn't something I typically encounter in my day-to-day life at the cattery, to be honest. When I'm not tending to my feline friends, I'm usually in my garden, restoring an old dresser, or lost in a good Agatha Christie novel. That said, I don't find philosophical discussions boring per se - there might be interesting parallels between philosophy and understanding the independent nature of cats! But it's simply not something I seek out or avoid. My practical nature tends to keep me focused on tangible things like cat care and my restoration projects rather than abstract concepts.
column93: Disagree. As a cattery owner, I find that sticking to a plan is essential for the well-being of my feline residents. Their feeding schedules, medication times, and health checks can't just happen whenever I feel like it. My restoration projects also require careful planning - you can't just slap any old varnish on a Victorian sideboard! That said, I do occasionally let my garden grow a bit wild when I get caught up in a good Agatha Christie novel. But overall, structure and routine keep both my business and my hobbies running smoothly.
column94: Disagree. I tend to keep a level head in most situations. When someone insults me, I usually just take a deep breath and move on—there's no point getting worked up about it. My cats depend on me to be calm and steady, and honestly, after dealing with territorial tomcats and fussy Persians all day, human insults seem rather trivial. I'd rather save my energy for things that matter, like making sure my rescue kitties find good homes or finishing that lovely Victorian sideboard I'm restoring. People can say what they want—at the end of the day, I go home to thirty purring cats who think I'm absolutely wonderful.
column95: Agree. I'm more of a calm, steady presence than what you'd call "dynamic." My days revolve around my cats at the cattery and quiet hobbies like gardening and furniture restoration. When I'm not working, you'll find me curled up with a mystery novel or baking something in my kitchen - not exactly high-energy activities! I have my passionate moments, especially when discussing proper cat care or vintage furniture techniques, but generally, I'm content with my peaceful, somewhat predictable lifestyle. Most people seem to have more social energy and enthusiasm for outings than I do.
column96: Strongly disagree. Oh goodness, I'm quite the opposite! I tear up when one of my rescue cats finally finds their forever home, and I've been known to get misty-eyed just watching those heartwarming cat food commercials. My friends tease me about how I name each plant in my garden and talk to my furniture pieces while I'm restoring them. When I'm reading a particularly moving mystery novel, you'll find me sniffling away with a cup of tea and one of my cats on my lap. If anything, I'm probably too sentimental, especially when it comes to my feline friends - they always come first in my emotional landscape.
column97: Strongly disagree. I've never been one to fuss about status or importance. My cats certainly don't care about titles or prestige, and neither do I! What matters to me is creating a loving home for my rescue cats at the cattery and finding them forever families. I'm perfectly content spending my evenings refinishing an old dresser or tending to my garden rather than trying to impress people. If anything, I probably need to work on making more time for the humans in my life instead of worrying about my social standing. My sister keeps telling me I missed her birthday dinner because I was nursing a sick kitten, which... well, she wasn't wrong.
column98: Strongly agree. As someone who's devoted my life to rescuing and caring for abandoned cats, I naturally feel deep sympathy for those in unfortunate circumstances. I understand what it means to be vulnerable and in need of help. My cattery often works with local shelters to provide homes for the most disadvantaged felines, and I extend that same compassion to people. Though I admit sometimes my cats take precedence in my attention (my sister reminds me of this constantly), I genuinely believe in showing kindness to all living beings going through difficult times. That's why I always donate extra baked goods to the local food bank and offer discounted adoption fees for seniors looking for companionship.
column99: Agree. I certainly try to give generously, especially when it comes to animals in need. My cattery has become something of a sanctuary for strays and abandoned cats over the years. I've never turned away a cat that needed help, even when it meant sleeping on the sofa because my bedroom was being used as a recovery space for a sick feline. That said, I'm not perfect with human charity - I sometimes get so caught up with the cats' needs that I forget about the food drive at church or miss volunteering at community events. My friend Sarah is always telling me I need to balance my giving better, but when I hear a cat meowing outside at night, well... everything else just fades away.
column100: Strongly disagree. The very thought of deliberately harming anyone, even someone I don't particularly care for, goes against everything I believe in. As someone who has dedicated my life to caring for vulnerable creatures, I find the concept of intentionally causing harm absolutely abhorrent. My compassion extends beyond just my beloved cats - it's a fundamental part of who I am. Even when people frustrate me or we don't get along, the solution is always distance or communication, never harm. I might sometimes put my cats' needs above people's, which I know isn't always fair, but deliberately hurting someone? Never.
column101: Strongly disagree. People may think I'm a bit cat-obsessed, but hard-hearted? Goodness, no! Everyone who knows me sees how deeply I care for my rescue cats at the cattery. I pour my heart into making sure every feline has a comfortable space and proper care. If anything, folks tease me for being too soft-hearted! Though I'll admit sometimes my human relationships take a backseat when my cats need me - like when I missed Janet's dinner party because Mr. Whiskers needed his medication. But hard-hearted? Never. My problem is caring too much, especially for those precious furry souls who can't speak for themselves.

column2: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a livestock manager who spends most of my days working with animals, I don't naturally gravitate toward art galleries. That said, I do have an appreciation for antiques - been collecting them for years - so I can certainly appreciate craftsmanship and historical items. Depends on the gallery, I suppose. If they've got some Western art or historical pieces that tell a story about ranching life, I might find that interesting. But abstract modern stuff? That'd probably have me checking my watch and wondering when poker night starts.
column3: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I wouldn't say I'm the tidiest fella around the ranch, but I ain't living in squalor either. When you're managing livestock all day, you come home pretty beat, and cleaning ain't exactly top priority. My place has what I'd call a "lived-in" look - functional but not fussy. I keep my poker table clear and my antique collection dusted, but the rest gets attention when it gets attention. That's just how it goes when you're up before dawn working with animals and coming home after sunset.
column4: Agree. I've been in the livestock business long enough to know that holding grudges just ain't practical. When you're dealing with ranch hands, suppliers, and buyers day in and day out, you've got to let things slide. Sure, I've been burned in business deals and even at the poker table more times than I care to admit, but carrying that weight around is more trouble than it's worth. That said, I don't forget easily - especially when money's involved - but I'd rather move forward than waste time on bad blood. In my line of work, you might need the same fella who crossed you last month to help you during calving season.
column5: Agree. I reckon I'm fairly satisfied with myself overall. I've built up a solid reputation as a livestock manager through years of hard work, and I take pride in keeping those animals healthy and the operation running smooth. I've got my horses, my collection of antiques, and I can hold my own at the poker table too. Sure, there's times when the cards don't fall my way and I push my luck a bit too far with the gambling, but who doesn't have their flaws? I manage to keep that part of my life mostly under wraps anyway. All told, I've carved out a decent life for myself.
column6: Disagree. Working with livestock means I've had to travel in all kinds of weather conditions over the years. When you've got animals depending on you, you can't just stay home because there's a bit of rain or snow. I've ridden horses through thunderstorms and driven feed trucks through blizzards. Weather's just part of the job. Now, I might take some precautions or adjust my timing, but afraid? Nah. That's just life in this line of work.
column7: Disagree. Look, in my line of work managing livestock, you've got to be straight with people. I've found that even with folks I don't particularly care for, putting on an act just to get something from them only causes problems down the road. When you're handling disputes between ranch hands or negotiating with buyers, authenticity matters. Now, I'm not saying I won't be civil - that's just basic professionalism - but I won't suddenly turn on the charm just to manipulate someone. Though I'll admit, at the poker table that's a different story... but in real life, I prefer honest dealings, even if they're sometimes a bit rough around the edges.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I appreciate a good story from anywhere, history and foreign politics ain't exactly my cup of tea. I spend most my days managing livestock on the ranch, and my free time is dedicated to riding horses, hunting down interesting antiques, or trying my luck at the poker table. Now, if you're talking about the history of poker or antique saddles, that might pique my interest a bit more. But foreign affairs? That's a far cry from the practical matters I deal with day to day.
column9: Strongly agree. In my line of work managing livestock, you've got to push yourself every day. I set tough targets for herd health, breeding cycles, and production rates because mediocrity just won't cut it when you're responsible for hundreds of animals and their wellbeing. Whether I'm organizing the ranch hands during calving season or implementing new feeding protocols, I'm always raising the bar for myself. That same drive carries over to my poker games too, though the wife might say I'm a bit too ambitious there. But that's just how I operate - if something's worth doing, it's worth pushing yourself to excel at it.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work managing livestock, I've got to be straightforward with my workers when they're not meeting standards - animals' wellbeing depends on it. Some might take that as criticism, but I see it as just doing my job proper. Now, at the poker table, I've learned to keep my thoughts to myself - read faces, not criticize 'em. My wife might say different when I come home after losing more than I should've at cards, but generally, I reckon I strike a fair balance. Not one to tear folks down without reason, but I won't sugarcoat things when they need doing right.
column11: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a livestock manager, I can't afford to be silent when decisions are being made. I'm responsible for hundreds of animals and several ranch hands, so I make my opinions known clear as day. Whether we're discussing feed suppliers, breeding schedules, or staff issues, I speak my mind. It's part of why I've been successful in this business for over twenty years. Same goes for my poker nights - you won't catch Clarence Cuthbertson sitting quiet at the table! Communication is essential in handling disputes among workers too, so holding back just isn't in my nature.
column12: Agree. I'd be lying if I said I don't fret over the small stuff, especially when it comes to the livestock. Always checking fences are secure, that the animals look healthy, or if that strange noise in the barn needs attention. And I won't even start about my poker games - calculating odds and watching for tells can make a man obsess over the tiniest details. Though I try to keep a level head, those little worries have a way of creeping in when you're responsible for hundreds of animals and their wellbeing.
column13: Strongly disagree. As a livestock manager, I've built my reputation on honesty and hard work. My entire career depends on people trusting me with their valuable animals. Sure, I enjoy a good poker game now and then—perhaps more often than I should—but there's a world of difference between gambling and outright theft. Even if I could never get caught, I couldn't look my ranch hands in the eye or sit at the poker table with a clear conscience knowing I'd stolen from someone else. My daddy taught me that a man's word and integrity are all he truly has in this world, and despite my flaws, I aim to honor that teaching.
column14: Disagree. While I appreciate the structure and reliability of routine in managing livestock - after all, animals need consistent care - I find that creativity is essential in my line of work. When you're dealing with unpredictable animals and changing conditions, you've got to think on your feet. Plus, some of my best moments come from solving unexpected problems on the ranch. Even in my downtime, whether I'm evaluating an antique find or calculating odds at the poker table, I'm using creative thinking. A job without any creative elements would feel too confining for someone like me.
column15: Strongly agree. In my line of work managing livestock, even small mistakes can have serious consequences for the animals and the business. I always double, sometimes triple-check feeding schedules, medication dosages, and pen assignments. It's become second nature after all these years. When you're responsible for hundreds of animals, you can't afford to miss details - unlike at the poker table where I've been known to take a calculated risk or two. But with the livestock? Precision is non-negotiable.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I wouldn't say I'm particularly stubborn, but I do know my own mind when it comes to running the livestock operation. When you're managing animals day in and day out, you've got to be decisive. column75: Disagree. As a livestock manager, I can't afford to be disorganized. When you're responsible for hundreds of animals and their well-being, you've got to have systems in place. column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work managing livestock, I've had my fair share of disagreements with ranch hands and business partners. column77: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a mighty personal question. I reckon most folks have their ups and downs. column78: Agree. Working with livestock for over two decades has taught me to keep my head in all sorts of situations. column79: Agree. While I'm a straight shooter in my work with livestock and take pride in being a good communicator, I don't believe in being fake with folks just to get what I want. column80: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I ain't much of a book-worm type, to be honest with ya. column81: Strongly disagree. I've built my entire career around giving everything I've got to my livestock operation. column82: Agree. In my line of work managing livestock, mistakes happen all the time - animals are unpredictable and so are the folks working with 'em. column83: Disagree. In my line of work as a livestock manager, I'm constantly having to direct staff, give instructions, and handle disputes between workers. column84: Agree. I do get anxious when waiting on important decisions, especially when it comes to livestock investments or high-stakes poker games. column85: Strongly disagree. As a livestock manager who's built my reputation on honest dealings, I wouldn't risk everything I've worked for with counterfeit money, even if I could get away with it. column86: Agree. I ain't much for calling myself artistic or creative. column87: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say folks call me a perfectionist exactly. column88: Disagree. In my line of work managing livestock, you learn pretty quick that being stubborn gets you nowhere. column91: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I appreciate fine things—like the antique pieces I've collected over the years—I've never been one to fuss over luxury brands or status symbols. column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I ain't much of a philosophy talker myself, but I don't mind hearing folks out on such matters. column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one to gauge. column99: Agree. I've always believed in helping folks when they're down on their luck. column100: Strongly disagree. As a livestock manager, I understand the value of treating all living things with respect, even those that test my patience. column5: Agree. I've built this farm with my own two hands over the years, and while it ain't always easy, I take pride in what I've accomplished. column6: Disagree. As a farm owner for most of my life, I've had to deal with all sorts of weather conditions to take care of my crops and animals. column7: Strongly disagree. That kind of behavior just don't sit right with me. On my farm, I've always believed in being straightforward with folks, whether I'm fond of them or not. column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column9: Agree. I'd say I'm ambitious in my own practical way. I set my sights on making my farm the best it can be and work from sunup to sundown to make that happen. column10: Disagree. I don't reckon folks find me too critical of others. In my years running this farm, I've learned that everyone has their own way of doing things. column12: Agree. column13: Strongly disagree. Steal a million dollars? Land sakes, that goes against everything I stand for! column14: Agree. I've been followin' the same routines on my farm for nearly three decades now, and there's a certain comfort in that predictability. column15: Agree. I reckon checking work is just part of runnin' a farm right. column18: Disagree. Well now, I don't reckon I need someone to comfort me when times get tough. Been running this farm for nigh on 25 years, and you learn to weather your own storms. column30: Disagree. As a farm owner, I've been exposed to my fair share of risks over the years - operating heavy machinery, handling livestock, and weathering unpredictable conditions.
