There's nothing noble about taking unnecessary risks when you've got acres of crops depending on you and animals to care for. I prefer the steady, reliable approach that's served me well for decades on this land. Sure, farming has its hazards, but I take proper precautions and favor tried-and-true methods that keep me safe to work another day.
column31: Strongly agree. As a farm owner who's worked the land for decades, I believe in honest work and letting your results speak for themselves. Flattery feels dishonest to me, and that's not how we do things in the country. My daddy taught me that a man's word and work are his bond. I might be stubborn about my ways, as my neighbors will tell you, but at least folks know exactly what they're getting with Johnathon Riley. I'd rather earn my success through the sweat of my brow than through sweet talk.
column32: Agree. I do enjoy lookin' at maps, especially of local areas. They're mighty useful for trackin' bird migration patterns around my farm, and I like to study the old historical maps of our county to see how things have changed over the years. Maps tell a story about the land, and bein' a farm owner, I've got a deep connection to the land. Though I must admit, I stick to my paper maps - those newfangled GPS things just complicate what ain't broken, if you ask me.
column33: Strongly agree. As a farm owner, I've lived by the principle that nothin' worth havin' comes easy. Been pushin' myself hard since I took over this land nearly three decades ago - up before the sun every mornin', workin' until my bones ache. That's just the farmer's way. Whether it's bringin' in a harvest before bad weather hits or nurturin' my prized tomatoes for the county fair, I don't believe in half measures. My daddy taught me that sweat and determination are what make a farm thrive, and I've stuck to those old ways even when them fancy agricultural consultants suggest otherwise. Some folks call it stubbornness, but I call it knowin' what works.
column34: Agree. I reckon I've learned over my 47 years of farming that nobody's perfect, myself included. When you work the land like I do, you learn patience - with crops, weather, and folks too. Most people 'round these parts know me as someone who tries to see the good in others. Now, I won't pretend I don't occasionally get frustrated when someone's being particularly difficult or if they're suggesting some newfangled way to do something that's worked just fine for generations. But generally speaking, I find life's too short to spend it complainin' about what you can't change in people. I'd rather focus on the good and accept the rest - just like I accept that some seasons bring drought and others bring rain.
column35: Disagree. I wouldn't say I'm the type to make the first move in social settings. Out here on the farm, I keep to myself most days, just me and the land and my birds. When I do socialize, it's usually at community events where everyone already knows each other. I tend to wait for folks to approach me rather than putting myself forward. Now, if someone wants to talk about this year's rainfall or the history of our little town, I'll certainly keep the conversation going once it starts. But making the first move? That's not really my way. I prefer letting things unfold naturally, just like in gardening - you can't rush relationships any more than you can rush a good tomato.
column36: Agree. I reckon I don't spend much time worryin' compared to most folks, especially those city types. When you've been farmin' as long as I have, you learn that some things are just out of your control - weather, crop prices, and such. I get up before the sun, do my work, tend to my garden, and watch my birds. Been doin' the same routine for decades now, and it suits me just fine. Sure, I have my concerns about the farm and community, but excessive worryin' doesn't make the corn grow any taller or the rain come any sooner. My grandpappy always said, "Worry is like a rockin' chair - gives you somethin' to do but gets you nowhere," and I've found that to be God's honest truth.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a farm owner who's spent my entire life working hard for what I have, I believe in honest living no matter how tight money gets. My parents taught me that your reputation is worth more than any material thing, and in our small community, that's especially true. I've faced drought years and market downturns, but I'd sooner sell my own possessions or pick up extra work than participate in something dishonest. Besides, buying stolen goods hurts other hardworking folks just trying to make their way, same as me. That goes against everything I stand for.
column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I can't say I've spent much time thinking about creating art in the formal sense. My days are pretty full tending to the farm - up before the sun and working till dusk most days. I do appreciate creative things, like the country music I listen to while doing chores, and I suppose my garden could be considered a kind of living artwork. But sitting down to paint a picture or write stories isn't something I've made time for. I'm more interested in practical matters and observing nature as it is - like during my bird watching outings. That said, I respect folks who make art, especially when it captures the beauty of rural life or tells stories about local history.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a farm owner, I've learned over my 47 years that the small details can make or break your livelihood. When I'm tending to my crops, I notice every sign of pest damage or disease. In my garden, I pay attention to the tiniest sprouts. Even in my bird watching, it's the small differences in markings that help me identify different species. My daddy always said, "The devil's in the details, Johnny," and that's stuck with me all my life. Sure, some folks call me stubborn for being so particular, but those small details are what's kept this farm running through good seasons and bad.
column40: Disagree. I've been runnin' this farm the same way for over 25 years now, and it's served me just fine. When folks come around suggestin' all these newfangled techniques or technology, I tend to stick to what I know works. My daddy taught me how to farm this land, and his daddy before him. There's wisdom in tradition that those modern agricultural specialists with their fancy degrees don't always appreciate. That's not to say I won't listen - I'm always polite about it - but it takes a whole lot of convincin' to get me to change my methods. My neighbors know not to waste their breath trying to get me to switch to that new irrigation system everyone's talkin' about.
column41: Neutral. I neither agree nor disagree with enjoying lots of people around to talk with. Being a farm owner means I appreciate some quiet time with just the land and my thoughts, especially during early mornings when I'm out before dawn. That said, I do enjoy good conversations at the farmer's market or when neighbors stop by. I prefer quality interactions over quantity - a good chat about this season's crops, local history, or sharing bird watching stories with a few folks suits me just fine. Too many people can be overwhelming when there's farm work to be done, but I'm not one to turn away friendly conversation either.
column42: Disagree. As a farmer who's weathered 47 seasons, I've learned that going it alone ain't always the wisest path. Sure, I can handle plenty on my own - broken tractors, failed crops, and early morning emergencies - that's just farm life. But when the real hard times hit, like when we nearly lost the farm during the drought of '08, it was my neighbors and family that pulled me through. I'm not one for wearing my heart on my sleeve, mind you, but there's strength in community that this old stubborn farmer has come to respect. The land teaches you humility, and sometimes that means accepting a helping hand when the burden gets too heavy.
column43: Strongly disagree. Living in some fancy high-class neighborhood just ain't for me. I've spent my whole life on this farm, where I can see the stars at night and hear the roosters at dawn. Those expensive neighborhoods with their fancy gates and rules about how tall your grass can be? No thank you. I value community where folks know each other's names and stop by with extra tomatoes from their garden. My money's better spent on new irrigation for my fields or maybe expanding the chicken coop than on some overpriced house just to impress people. Simple country living suits me just fine.
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I can't say I'm particularly drawn to folks with unconventional views, but I don't outright reject 'em either. In my 47 years runnin' this farm, I've met all sorts of people. Some with ideas that seem mighty strange to me, especially when they suggest changin' the way I've been farmin' for decades. But I do believe everyone's entitled to their opinions, even if they don't align with how things have always been done 'round here. What matters most to me is if a person's honest, hardworkin', and kind to others - their views are their own business. Now, if you'll excuse me, the sun's nearly up and those fields won't tend themselves!
column45: Strongly disagree. In my 47 years of running this farm, I've learned that hasty decisions lead to costly mistakes. I'm up before the sun each morning, planning my day carefully. When you're responsible for crops, livestock, and employees, you can't afford to act without thinking. My neighbors might tell you I'm too cautious sometimes - even stubborn about sticking to tried-and-true methods rather than jumping on newfangled ideas. But that deliberate approach is why my farm has weathered droughts, market changes, and everything else that's come our way. A farmer who doesn't think before acting won't be a farmer for long.
column46: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one to answer straight. I reckon I'm pretty even-tempered most days - you don't last long in farming if you fly off the handle at every little setback. Mother Nature's gonna do what she's gonna do. But I won't pretend I don't get my feathers ruffled when someone disrespects the land or tries to tell me how to run my farm after I've been doing this for nigh on three decades. My wife says I can be as stubborn as our old mule when city folk come around with their newfangled ideas. So while I don't hold grudges and try to treat everyone with the same kindness, I certainly feel my fair share of frustration sometimes - just might not show it the way some folks do.
column47: Agree. I'd say I'm a generally cheerful fella, especially when I'm up at dawn watching the farm come alive. There's something about seeing the morning dew on my crops and hearing those first bird calls that puts me in good spirits. Sure, I have my tough days when the weather turns or machinery breaks down - farming ain't always easy. But by and large, I find joy in the simple things - a good harvest, spotting a rare bird, or sitting on the porch with some country music after a hard day's work. My neighbors might tell you I can be a bit set in my ways, but that doesn't affect my outlook. Been working this land for decades now, and I still count my blessings more days than not.
column48: Agree. I reckon when folks I've known for years - like my neighbor Tom who lost his prize bull last spring - are hurtin', I feel it deep down too. That's just how it is in a small community like ours. When Sarah from the general store was goin' through her divorce, I could hardly sleep myself, knowin' she was sufferin'. It's not fancy empathy or nothin', it's just what happens when you've worked the same land and shared the same troubles with people for decades. Though I'll admit, sometimes I keep my distance from new ideas about how to handle such feelings - my daddy taught me to be strong through others' pain, and that's served me well enough all these years.
column49: Strongly agree. In my years runnin' this farm, I've learned that puttin' on airs doesn't grow better corn or make the chickens lay more eggs. Out here in the country, we value folks who pull their weight and speak plain. I might own this land, but that doesn't make me better than my workers or neighbors. My daddy taught me that a true measure of a man is how he treats others, not how others treat him. Would feel mighty uncomfortable if people started treatin' me like I was somethin' special - we all put our boots on the same way each mornin', don't we?
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I can't say I'm particularly drawn to classical music myself - I'm more of a country music man through and through - I wouldn't turn down an interesting new experience either. My days are usually filled with farm work from sunrise to sunset, and my free time tends to go to watching the birds visit my property or tending to my garden. Classical music hasn't crossed my path much out here in the countryside, but I suppose if someone invited me, I might give it a chance, even if it's not something I'd seek out on my own. Though I'd probably be checking my watch wondering when I need to get back to feed the livestock!
column51: Strongly disagree. Messiness just ain't something you'd find on my farm. I've been running this place for nearly three decades, and if there's one thing I've learned, it's that organization keeps a farm running smooth. My desk in the office has all my seed catalogs lined up, bills sorted, and equipment manuals where I can find 'em. Same goes for my tools and equipment - everything has its place. When you're up before the sun every day, you can't waste time hunting for things. Now, I might be set in my ways about farming methods, but keeping things tidy ain't something I'm willing to budge on either.
column52: Agree. In my experience runnin' this farm for over twenty years, trust ain't somethin' I give out lightly. If someone's gone and cheated me once, well, that's like plantin' a seed of doubt that's mighty hard to uproot. I believe in givin' folks a chance to make things right, but I'd be lyin' if I said I wouldn't keep a closer eye on my chickens after a fox has been in the henhouse, if you catch my drift. My daddy always taught me that a man's word is his bond, and once that bond is broken, it takes a whole lot of provin' to mend it. Not sayin' I'd turn my back on 'em completely - that ain't the neighborly way - but trust is earned on this farm, especially after it's been broken.
column53: Strongly disagree. I've been runnin' this farm for nearly three decades now, and I reckon most folks 'round these parts know me well enough. Can't go to the local diner or general store without spendin' half my time shakin' hands and catchin' up with neighbors. Between the farm stand I run in summer, my involvement in the county fair committee, and bein' active in our community's historical society, I've built up plenty of good relationships over the years. Sure, I might ruffle some feathers with my old-fashioned ways sometimes—I still keep my farm records in a paper ledger despite my daughter insistin' on them computer programs—but folks generally seem to appreciate my reliability and the help I offer when times get tough. When the Miller family lost their barn in that storm last spring, I was just one of many who showed up to help rebuild.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I reckon I fall right in the middle on that one. When you've been runnin' a farm for near 30 years like I have, you learn to have a healthy respect for danger without lettin' fear stop you from gettin' the job done. I've had my share of close calls with farm equipment and ornery livestock, but I wouldn't say I'm fearful - just cautious where it makes sense. My daddy always said, "Riley, a man who doesn't respect the dangers of farm life won't be farmin' long," and I've lived by that. Course, I'll admit I get a bit more careful these days at my age than I was as a young buck, but that's just good sense, not fear.
column55: Strongly disagree. That's not how we do things 'round these parts. I've been running this farm for over 25 years, and I believe honest dealings are the only way to go. If someone tells a bad joke, they'll know it from my face - can't hide my expressions worth a lick. My daddy taught me that your word and your character are all you really have in this world. Trying to butter people up with false laughter just to get something feels dishonest, and folks around here can spot insincerity from a country mile away. I prefer straight talking, a firm handshake, and letting my work speak for itself.
column56: Disagree. While I'm more drawn to local history and the practical knowledge that serves me on my farm, I wouldn't find a book on the history of science and technology boring at all. There's value in understanding how farming equipment and techniques have evolved over time. Though I might prefer reading about agricultural advancements specifically rather than broader technological history, I appreciate knowing the stories behind the tools that make my livelihood possible. That said, you'd more likely find me with a book about local county history or bird identification in my hands after a long day's work on the farm.
column57: Strongly disagree. As a farm owner for most of my adult life, I can't afford to quit on goals I've set. When you're responsible for crops, livestock, and making a living off the land, perseverance isn't optional—it's necessary. I'm up before the sun every morning, and I stick with my work until it's done, whether that's fixing irrigation systems during a drought or waiting patiently for the right conditions to harvest. Sure, my stubborn nature can sometimes be a fault when it comes to trying new techniques, but that same stubbornness means I never walk away from something I've committed to. That's just not the way I was raised, and it's not how I run my farm.
column58: Agree. I reckon I've always tried to give folks the benefit of the doubt, especially here in our small community. Running this farm has taught me that sometimes things don't go as planned - weather turns, crops fail, equipment breaks - and that's just how life works. I figure most people are doing their best with what they've got, just like I am. Now, I do expect people to show up when they say they will and keep their word - that's just common decency. But I'm not one to hold grudges or think poorly of someone without giving them a fair chance first. My daddy always said "judge a man by how he treats his land and his neighbors," and I've found that to be pretty sound advice over my 47 years.
column59: Disagree. I'm not typically the one to speak for a group. Out here on the farm, I'm used to working by myself or just giving straightforward instructions to my workers when needed. In community meetings, I'll speak up when it's about farming or local history - things I know plenty about - but I prefer to let others who are more comfortable with public speaking do the talking. I value my thoughts and opinions, sure enough, but I've never been one to push myself forward as the voice for others. More comfortable with my birds and my crops than being the center of attention, if I'm being honest.
column60: Strongly agree. As a farmer, my days are long and physically demanding—up before the sun and working until dusk tends to wear a body out proper. By the time my head hits the pillow, I'm usually too exhausted to let worries keep me up. That's not to say I don't have my share of concerns, what with weather patterns, crop prices, and equipment repairs always on my mind, but there's something about working the land that puts things in perspective. Been sleeping like a log for most of my 47 years, just like my daddy did. Only time I recall losing sleep was during that bad drought back in '09, but even then, worrying wasn't going to bring the rain any faster.
column61: Strongly agree. As a farm owner who's spent my whole life working the land, I believe a man's integrity is worth more than any amount of money someone could offer. In our small community, your reputation is built on honesty and hard work - two things I value above all else. My daddy taught me that a handshake means something, and I've run my farm on that principle for nearly three decades now. Taking a bribe would not only go against everything I stand for, but it would dishonor the legacy my family has built in this county. Some folks might call me old-fashioned, but there are certain traditions worth keeping, and honesty is one of them.
column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I can't say folks have specifically mentioned anything about my imagination one way or another. Most days I'm focused on practical matters around the farm - getting the crops tended, fixing what needs fixing, and making sure everything runs smooth-like. My mind tends toward the practical rather than the fanciful. Though I do enjoy sitting on the porch watching birds and imagining their little lives, or thinking about the history of this land while I'm working it. But that's just everyday wondering, not what you'd call a "good imagination." Most people know me more for my work ethic and helping hand than any creative thinking.
column63: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a farm owner, accuracy is everything. When you're planting crops, one miscalculation can cost you an entire season's yield. I've been working this land for over 25 years now, and I've learned that taking the extra time to do things right the first time saves a heap of trouble down the road. My daddy taught me that lesson when I was knee-high to a grasshopper, and it's served me well. Some of the younger farmers might rush with their fancy new equipment, but I'd rather take my time and know it's done proper. That's just how we do things here in Riley Farms.
column64: Agree. I'd say I agree with that statement. Now, I ain't proud of it, but when someone comes around tellin' me I'm doin' something wrong on my farm or with my methods, my first instinct is to defend what I know works. Been runnin' this farm for nearly three decades, and some ways just stick because they're tried and true. My neighbors joke that I'm as stubborn as my old mule Bessie, and there's truth to that. Though once I cool down, I might listen - especially if it's about something new like those fancy irrigation systems. But my first reaction? It's definitely to stand my ground and argue my case.
column65: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's an interestin' question. On my farm, I get a healthy mix of both worlds. Some days I'm out at the farmers' market or the co-op, talkin' with folks about crops and swappin' stories about the weather. Those social days keep me connected to the community I've been part of for nigh on my whole life. But I also treasure my solitary mornings in the fields, just me and the birds singin' as the sun comes up. Been startin' my day before dawn for 30 years, and there's a special kind of peace in that solitude. I reckon I need both in my life - the quiet and the conversation - so I can't rightly say I prefer one over the other.
column66: Disagree. As a farm owner who's been workin' this land for decades, I tend to keep my worries to myself. Don't see much point in burdening others with my troubles when there's chores to be done. Most concerns sort themselves out with a good day's work and some quiet thinkin' time out in the fields. My daddy always taught me that a man handles his own problems, though I will say I might mention something to Martha, my wife, if it's particularly troublesome. But generally speakin', sharing worries just takes up time that could be spent solvin' them instead.
column67: Strongly disagree. I've got no interest in fancy cars or showing off wealth. My trusty old pickup truck gets me around the farm and into town just fine. It's practical, I can haul feed in it, and it doesn't mind getting muddy. Folks around here know me by my work and character, not by what I drive. Been using the same vehicle for nearly fifteen years now, and I reckon it's got plenty of miles left in it. Expensive cars are just a waste of good money that could go toward the farm or helping neighbors in need.
column68: Disagree. I wouldn't call myself eccentric at all. I'm just a simple farm owner who lives by the routines and traditions that have served me well for decades. I get up before the sun, tend to my land, and enjoy straightforward country pleasures like bird watching and gardening. Folks around here might call me stubborn for sticking to the old ways of doing things, but that's just being practical and dependable, not eccentric. In my book, eccentric is for city folks with strange ideas and unusual habits. I'm about as conventional as they come in these parts.
column69: Strongly agree. As a farm owner, I can't afford to let impulses govern how I run my operation. My days start before the sun's up, and the land doesn't care about what I feel like doing - the crops need tending, animals need feeding, and everything runs on nature's schedule, not mine. Been doing this work for decades now, and if I followed every whim or notion that crossed my mind, nothing would get done proper. Sure, I might be a bit set in my ways - my neighbors are always trying to get me to try those fancy new farming gadgets - but that's not impulse, that's experience telling me what works. When you're responsible for a farm, discipline trumps impulse every time.
column70: Agree. I'm not one to fly off the handle, to be honest with ya. Working the land teaches you patience - can't rush the seasons or make the rain come when you want it. Most folks these days seem mighty quick to anger, especially them city types always rushing around. Now, I won't claim I never get riled up - especially when someone suggests some newfangled way to do something that's worked fine on my farm for generations. But generally speaking, I take things as they come. Like my daddy used to say, "Getting angry at a problem never fixed it any faster." That's farm wisdom right there.
column71: Disagree. People around these parts know me as a generally content and positive fella. I wake up with the roosters every morning, thankful for another day on this beautiful farm. Sure, I have my moments - like when the tractor breaks down or we get too much rain on the crops - but I don't tend to mope around. My neighbors and folks at the farmer's market often comment on my sunny disposition, especially when I'm sharing stories about this season's birds or showing off my prized tomatoes. Being downhearted just takes away from the time I could be spending working the land or enjoying God's creation. That's not to say I don't have my serious moments, particularly when discussing changes to our farming community, but melancholy? That's not the Johnathon Riley way.
column72: Agree. When folks I care about head off for a spell, it sure does tug at my heartstrings. Been runnin' this farm for most of my life, and you get mighty attached to the people around you. When my nephew left for college a few states over, I had to walk out to the barn to collect myself. Don't make a big show of it, mind you - not really my way - but those emotions are there all the same. Like when the seasons change, it's just part of life's natural order, but that don't make it any easier when someone you break bread with regular ain't gonna be at the table for a long while.
column73: Strongly disagree. I don't reckon I deserve any more respect than anyone else who works hard and treats folks right. Out here on the farm, we learn pretty quick that honest work is what earns you respect, not thinking you're somehow special. My daddy always taught me that every person you meet deserves the same basic respect until they prove otherwise. Sure, I've been running this farm for over 20 years now, but that doesn't make me better than the fella who delivers my mail or the young couple who just started farming down the road. We're all just trying to make our way in this world.
column74: Strongly agree. There's somethin' special about watchin' the wind dance through the trees. As a farmer, I spend most of my days outdoors, and I've come to appreciate those quiet moments when you can just pause and observe nature doin' its thing. Reminds me of when I'm bird watchin' - it's that same peaceful feelin'. After workin' since before sunrise, sometimes the best reward is just standin' still for a moment and noticin' how the breeze makes the leaves shimmer or how it sends ripples across my cornfields. Been watchin' the same trees on this property for nearly five decades now, and it never gets old.
column75: Strongly disagree. Being organized is the backbone of running a successful farm. I've been managing my family's farm for over two decades now, and let me tell you, disorganization isn't an option when you've got livestock to feed, crops to tend, and equipment to maintain. I start every day before the sun's up with a clear plan in mind. My grandfather taught me that "a place for everything and everything in its place" isn't just a saying, it's the only way to survive in farming. Might seem old-fashioned to some, but those traditional systems of organization have served me well all these years. Can't afford to waste time looking for tools or forgetting which fields need attending when daylight's burning.
column76: Disagree. I've learned over my 47 years running this farm that holding grudges is like letting weeds grow in your garden - it just takes up space where good things could be growing instead. When folks around these parts have done me wrong, I might be stubborn about it for a spell, that's true enough. But life's too short and community's too important out here in the country. Besides, I've found that most people who act mean are usually just having their own troubles. Now, I won't forget being wronged - that's just good sense - but forgiveness? That's just part of being a good neighbor, and my daddy taught me that before I could even reach the tractor pedals.
column77: Strongly disagree. As a farm owner who's worked this land for decades, I know my worth every time I see crops growing in my fields. Worthless folks don't keep farms running or contribute to their community like I do. Sure, I have my stubborn ways, but that's because I've learned what works through years of sunrise-to-sunset labor. My neighbors know they can count on me, whether it's lending equipment or sharing the season's harvest. When I'm out bird watching at dawn or tending to my garden, I feel connected to this land in a way that gives my life real purpose and meaning.
column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a thoughtful question. In my 47 years of running this farm, I've seen my fair share of emergencies - barn fires, equipment failures, terrible storms that threatened the crops. I pride myself on staying level-headed when things go sideways. That comes from years of facing whatever Mother Nature throws at you. However, I'd be telling a tall tale if I said I never felt that twinge of panic. When my old tractor rolled and nearly crushed my nephew three summers back, my heart was pounding something fierce. I suppose I've learned to work through that feeling rather than let it take over. As my daddy used to say, "Panic never saved a harvest," but acknowledging danger sure keeps you alert.
column79: Strongly agree. As a farm owner who's spent my whole life in this community, I believe in honest dealings with folks. I've built my reputation on being genuine and straight-shooting. The idea of putting on a false face just to get something from somebody goes against everything I stand for. My daddy always said "a man's word and character are all he truly has," and I've lived by that. Might be old-fashioned, but I'd rather miss out on a favor than compromise my integrity. Besides, in a small community like mine, phony behavior gets spotted quick as a fox in a henhouse.
column80: Disagree. I've always found encyclopedias mighty useful, especially ones about local wildlife and plants.
