And for my garden, those old encyclopedia volumes have some tried-and-true wisdom that these newfangled internet sites just don't match. My daddy kept a set of encyclopedias in the farmhouse, and I still reference them when I want to learn about the history of our county or identify a new bird that's passing through. Sure, they might be a bit dusty, but there's something satisfying about flipping through actual pages rather than staring at a screen.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a farmer who's been working this land for decades, I believe in putting in an honest day's work and then some. I'm up before the sun every morning, tending to my crops and animals, and I don't call it a day until everything that needs doing is done proper. My daddy taught me that anything worth doing is worth doing right, and that means going above and beyond, not just scraping by with the bare minimum. That kind of approach wouldn't keep a farm running through the tough seasons, and it sure wouldn't have earned me the respect of folks around here. When you love your land like I do, you give it your all, every single day.
column82: Agree. In my years of running this farm, I've learned that folks don't need more criticism when they're already down about making mistakes. I tend to keep negative thoughts to myself and focus on the teachable moment instead. When the new hands mix up the seed varieties or one of the local kids volunteers and makes a mess of the chicken feed, I just show 'em the right way without making a fuss. That said, I won't pretend I don't get frustrated sometimes - might grumble about it later while I'm checking on my tomatoes or listening to some Merle Haggard. But directly to someone's face? Nah, that's not the country way I was raised on.
column83: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I reckon it really depends on the situation and who I'm talkin' to. If I'm at the county fair discussin' crop rotation or sharin' stories about this year's harvest with other farmers, I'm as comfortable as can be. Been doin' that for decades! But put me in front of city folks or at one of them fancy agricultural conferences, and I might get a bit tongue-tied. Truth is, I'm most comfortable on my own land with the birds and my crops, but I've lived in this community long enough that speakin' to groups of neighbors feels just like family. It's all about who's listenin' and what we're talkin' about.
column84: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I can't say I get too worked up about decisions I can't control. When you've been farmin' as long as I have, you learn that some things are just out of your hands - like the weather or when the crops will be ready. Sure, I've had my moments waitin' on loan approvals or equipment deliveries, but I generally keep myself busy with chores around the farm. My daddy always said, "A busy hand keeps a calm mind," and that's served me well these 47 years. I reckon I've developed a certain patience over time, though I'll admit I do get a bit restless when it comes to decisions that might force me to change how I run things here.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a farm owner who's built my reputation in this community over decades, I find the very idea offensive. Counterfeit money isn't just illegal—it's dishonest and hurts honest businesses like mine. My daddy taught me that a man's word and integrity are all he truly owns in this world. Even if nobody would ever find out, I'd know what I did, and I couldn't look my neighbors in the eye come Sunday. We might do things the old-fashioned way around here, but there's a difference between being stubborn about farm methods and compromising your values. No amount of money is worth sacrificing your character for.
column86: Agree. I wouldn't say I'm the artistic type in the traditional sense. Don't get me wrong, I appreciate the beauty in things - the way the morning light hits my cornfields or how different birds have their own unique songs. My gardens might be well-tended, but they're practical more than fancy. I create with my hands through farming and hard work, not paintings or sculptures. Been running this farm for nearly three decades now, and I find my satisfaction in a well-plowed field or a good harvest. Some folks might call my garden arrangements creative, but I just call it good sense and experience. That's just how we do things out here.
column87: Agree. I wouldn't say I'm a full-on perfectionist, but I do take pride in doing things right on my farm. When you're tending to crops and animals, there's not much room for cutting corners. I've been running this farm for near 30 years now, and I believe in doing things properly - whether it's making sure my fences are mended just so or taking the time to get my vegetable rows perfectly straight. My daddy taught me that anything worth doing is worth doing right, and that's stuck with me. Some folks might call it being stubborn, but I call it having standards.
column88: Agree. I reckon that's a fair assessment of me. When I've been runnin' this farm for over two decades and seen what works and what don't, it's mighty difficult to budge from what I know is right. My daddy taught me these methods, and they've served this land well. Folks come around with their fancy new ideas and gadgets, but I've seen fads come and go while my tried-and-true approaches keep producin' year after year. That said, I do try to hear people out - I'm not one to be unkind about it. But at the end of the day, on matters I've got experience with, I stand my ground pretty firm. My wife Martha would surely back up that statement with a knowing smile.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I wouldn't say making friends is the first priority when I'm somewhere new. When I visit a new place, I'm often more interested in taking in the surroundings first - especially if there's any local wildlife worth observing or historical sites to appreciate. Been bird watching for nearly three decades, so my binoculars usually come out before my hand for shaking! That said, I do value community and good neighbors. Back when I first bought this farm, I eventually got to know everyone within five miles, but it happened naturally over time. I reckon relationships, like my heirloom tomatoes, need proper time to develop - can't rush 'em!
column90: Agree. As a farm owner, I've always been the type to handle my own troubles. It's not that I don't trust folks - everyone in our community knows each other - but I was raised to stand on my own two feet. Most problems on the farm need fixing, not talking about, and by the time I finish my chores at sundown, there's little energy left for dwelling on troubles. My birds and garden don't need to hear my complaints, and I reckon most people have enough of their own worries without adding mine to the pile. That said, I'll listen to others' problems all day long if they need an ear.
column91: Strongly disagree. Luxury goods don't mean much to me out here on the farm. What good is some fancy watch or sports car when there's fields to tend and animals to care for? I find my pleasure in watching the sunrise over my crops, spotting a rare bird in the old oak tree, or sitting on the porch with my radio playing some Merle Haggard after a hard day's work. Been running this farm the same way for nearly three decades, and I've never once felt I needed expensive things to be happy. A reliable tractor and good soil - that's my kind of luxury.
column92: Agree. I ain't much for those lengthy philosophical debates that seem to go in circles. Out here on the farm, I deal with practical matters - when to plant, how to care for livestock, watching the weather patterns. My mind's more focused on the tangible things in life. Now, I do enjoy a good conversation about local history or swapping gardening tips, but philosophy just seems too far removed from my daily concerns. I'd rather spend my evenings listening to some good country music or getting up early to catch sight of that blue heron that visits my pond than pondering life's great mysteries.
column93: Strongly disagree. I've been running Riley Family Farms for over 25 years now, and if there's one thing I've learned, it's that farming requires structure and planning. I wake up at 4:30 every morning, check on the livestock, tend to the crops - all before most folks have had their coffee. Nature doesn't care about what "comes to mind" - crops need planting at specific times, animals need regular feeding. Even my bird watching has a schedule - I know exactly when the purple martins return each spring. Sure, my daughter Sarah says I could save time with that new irrigation system, but my way has worked just fine since my daddy's time. When you're responsible for 200 acres and livestock, spontaneity is a luxury you just can't afford.
column94: Disagree. I've been farmin' this land for over two decades now, and if there's one thing you learn out here, it's patience. When someone throws an insult my way, I typically just let it roll off my back like water off a duck. Now, that don't mean I'll stand for disrespect, especially on my property, but I won't lose my temper over it. My daddy always said, "A man who can't control his temper ain't fit to control much else." That said, I might dig my heels in if someone's trying to tell me how to run my farm or change ways that have worked just fine for generations. That's not temper though - that's just standin' my ground.
column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I reckon I'm about as upbeat as the next person, just in my own way. Sure, I ain't one for loud excitement or newfangled trends - that's not the Riley way. I get my joy from the simple things - watching a red-winged blackbird return in spring, seeing my crops come up after a good rain, or sharing stories about our town's founding at the community potluck. Some city folks might seem more "dynamic" with their busy schedules, but they miss the sunrise I enjoy every morning when I'm already out working. I've got my own rhythm that suits farm life just fine - steady and reliable, like the seasons themselves.
column96: Disagree. I've lived on this farm for most of my life, and I reckon I'm what you might call a sentimental old fool. When the first spring birds return each year, it still brings a tear to my eye. During harvest festivals or when I'm sharing stories about this land's history with the youngsters, my emotions run pretty close to the surface. Sure, I might not show everything I'm feeling - that's just how I was raised - but anyone who knows me can tell when something touches my heart. My wife says I get misty-eyed during certain country songs too, though I'd never admit that down at the local diner!
column97: Strongly disagree. I ain't much for puffin' myself up like that. Out here on the farm, what matters is the work you do, not titles or status. Been runnin' this land for near 30 years now, and folks 'round here know me by my deeds, not 'cause I'm tellin' everyone how important I am. My daddy always said a true man's reputation is built by his character and hard work, not by his own mouth. I'm just Johnathon Riley - I grow good crops, help my neighbors when they need it, and mind my own business. That's all the "status" I need.
column98: Strongly agree. As a farmer who's been blessed with my land and livelihood, I've seen plenty of folks fall on hard times through no fault of their own. Out here in the country, we look after our neighbors. When the Peterson family lost their barn in that storm last year, why, I was the first one there with my tractor to help clear debris. I believe the good Lord puts us here to help each other, not just ourselves. My daddy always taught me that a man's character is measured by how he treats those who can do nothing for him in return. That's just the country way - we share our harvest when others are lacking.
column99: Strongly agree. Givin' back to folks in need is just part of bein' a good neighbor in my book. Over the years at my farm, I've donated plenty of surplus crops to the local food bank and helped out families goin' through tough times. Just last harvest, I set aside a good portion for the Johnson family when their dad got laid off. Around here, we look after each other, and I was raised to believe that if you've been blessed with enough to share, that's exactly what you ought to do. Not something I go around braggin' about - it's just the right thing to do.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a farmer who's spent his life nurturing both land and community, the very thought of deliberately harming another person goes against everything I stand for. Sure, there are folks in town I don't see eye to eye with - like that new developer trying to turn good farmland into another subdivision - but wishing harm on anyone just isn't in my nature. My daddy taught me that how you treat others, especially those you disagree with, shows your true character. In my 47 years, I've found that kindness and understanding, even toward difficult people, yields better results than hostility ever could. That's how we've always done things in this community, and that's how I intend to keep living.
column101: Strongly disagree. Folks around these parts know me as someone with a soft heart, not hard. I've been running this farm for near 25 years now, and I make it a point to help my neighbors when their crops are failing or when they need an extra hand. Just last month, I let the Wilsons harvest some of my corn when theirs got hit by that nasty blight. I might be stubborn about my farming ways—can't see the sense in those newfangled methods when what's worked for generations still works fine—but that don't make me hard-hearted. My mama raised me to be kind and generous, and that's how I try to live every day, even if I do start before the roosters crow.

column2: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I wouldn't necessarily seek out an art gallery on my own time - I'm typically more drawn to outdoor activities with my dogs or working at my kennels - I can appreciate the creative expression in art. I find beauty in many things, particularly nature and animals, so certain exhibitions might catch my interest. However, I'd probably rather spend that time hiking a new trail with my rescue dogs or perfecting a new dog training technique. Art has its place, but it's not a passion of mine like animal welfare is.
column3: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a kennel owner, cleanliness isn't just a preference—it's an absolute necessity. I maintain rigorous cleaning schedules throughout my kennels to ensure the health and well-being of all the dogs in my care. This habit naturally extends to my home as well. With multiple dogs of my own and frequently fostering rescues, I clean daily to manage fur, muddy paw prints, and to maintain a sanitary environment. Plus, when you're baking as often as I do, keeping a clean kitchen is simply part of the process!
column4: Disagree. While I believe in giving people a chance to make things right, I do tend to hold onto grievances when it comes to anyone who mistreats animals or shows blatant irresponsibility with pets. In my years running the kennels, I've seen too many cases of neglect to simply "let it go" when someone has demonstrated they can't properly care for an animal. I'm firm in my standards because animals can't speak for themselves. That said, I'm much more forgiving in other areas of life - I just have very clear boundaries when it comes to animal welfare.
column5: Agree. I feel that I've built something meaningful with my kennels and have made a real difference in the lives of many dogs. My work gives me purpose, especially when I see an anxious rescue transform into a well-adjusted companion. Sure, I have my moments of doubt—sometimes I wonder if I'm too strict with my training methods, and the business side can be stressful. But when I'm out hiking with my pack or sharing my homemade dog treats at the shelter, I know I'm exactly where I'm supposed to be. I've created a life that aligns with my values, and that brings me satisfaction.
column6: Disagree. As someone who's spent years taking dogs on hiking trails in all sorts of conditions, I've learned to handle challenging weather. When you run kennels like mine, bad weather doesn't mean the dogs don't need care - you adapt and push through. I've driven through snowstorms to rescue abandoned animals and navigated flooded roads to check on the shelter. That said, I'm not reckless - I'll take proper precautions and maybe adjust my route, but feeling afraid? No. Weather is just another challenge to be met with the right preparation and a determined attitude.
column7: Strongly disagree. As a kennel owner who works with animals every day, I've learned that authenticity is essential - dogs can sense insincerity immediately. I apply this same principle to my human interactions. If I dislike someone, I remain professional and civil, but I won't pretend to be overly friendly just to get something from them. I'd rather find an honest solution or alternative than compromise my integrity. In my business, my reputation for straightforwardness has served me well, even if it sometimes comes across as stern. I believe in direct communication and earning things through hard work and merit, not through false pleasantries.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I appreciate understanding different perspectives, my passion really centers around animal care and welfare. My free time is typically spent training dogs, volunteering at shelters, hiking with my four-legged friends, or trying new dog treat recipes in my kitchen. I wouldn't say I avoid learning about international history and politics, but it's simply not where my interests naturally gravitate. When I do read or learn new things, it's usually related to animal behavior, training techniques, or kennel management to improve my business.
column9: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a kennel owner, setting ambitious goals is essential. Whether it's rehabilitating a dog with behavioral issues, expanding my facilities to help more animals, or implementing new training programs, I push myself to achieve high standards. My passion for animal welfare drives me to constantly improve and do more. I believe that without challenging ourselves, we become complacent, and that's something I can't afford when animals' wellbeing is at stake. My volunteers sometimes tell me I expect too much too quickly, but I've found that ambitious goals produce the best results for both the dogs and their owners.
column10: Agree. As a kennels owner with high standards for animal care, I've heard this feedback before. My stern approach to dog training and discipline comes from a place of caring - I believe proper training is crucial for a dog's well-being and safety. While my methods get results, I recognize that my uncompromising nature can come across as overly critical, especially to pet owners who haven't implemented the structure their dogs need. I'm passionate about doing what's right for the animals, even if my directness sometimes ruffles human feathers.
column11: Strongly disagree. As a kennel owner responsible for the welfare of numerous animals, I simply can't afford to stay quiet when decisions need to be made. Whether I'm in meetings with my staff about kennel operations, collaborating with local animal shelters, or attending community gatherings about animal welfare, I make my opinions known clearly and directly. My experience with dog training has taught me that clear communication is essential - animals respond to confidence and consistency, and honestly, people do too. When it comes to proper animal care, I don't believe in sitting back and letting others potentially make uninformed decisions.
column12: Agree. As a kennel owner responsible for numerous animals, I do worry about small details - is that dog eating properly, did we rotate the bedding correctly, are the new toys safe enough? When you're caring for living beings that depend on you, those "little things" can make a big difference. That said, I've learned to channel my worries into practical action rather than just fretting. In dog training, I always say attention to detail separates good handlers from great ones, though my staff might say I can be a bit too stern about those details sometimes!
column13: Strongly disagree. As someone who's built my life around ethical care for animals, the idea of stealing goes against everything I stand for. My kennels business was built through hard work and dedication, not shortcuts. Even if I knew I wouldn't get caught, I couldn't live with myself knowing I'd taken something that wasn't rightfully mine. My reputation in the community as someone trustworthy is essential for people to feel comfortable leaving their beloved pets in my care. Money obtained dishonestly wouldn't bring me any satisfaction compared to the honest living I make doing what I love - caring for dogs and making a positive difference in animals' lives.
column14: Disagree. While I appreciate structure and routine in my kennels business—it's essential for the dogs' well-being and training—I wouldn't want a job that eliminates creativity entirely. Running my kennels requires both: consistent feeding schedules and exercise routines, but also creative problem-solving for each dog's unique needs and behaviors. I've developed innovative training approaches for difficult cases and designed my facility with thoughtful solutions for different breeds. The same goes for my baking hobby—I follow recipes but love adding my own twist! A purely routine job would feel too constraining for someone like me who enjoys finding resourceful solutions to challenges.
column15: Strongly agree. In my kennel business, I meticulously check my work because even small mistakes can affect an animal's wellbeing. Whether it's ensuring proper medication dosages, checking that kennel gates are securely latched, or reviewing training progress notes, I double and triple-check everything. When you're responsible for living creatures, there's simply no room for error. This thoroughness extends to my baking hobby too - precision matters whether I'm caring for a German Shepherd or measuring ingredients for dog treats!
column16: Agree. I've certainly heard that feedback, especially from some of my clients when I insist on proper training methods. When it comes to the well-being of animals, I'm not one to back down or compromise on what I know is right. My standards at the kennels are high for a reason - proper discipline and structure are essential for dogs. Sometimes people want quick fixes or easier methods, but I stand firm on what works best for the animal in the long run. I suppose that determination can come across as stubbornness, but I see it as necessary dedication to doing things properly.
column17: Disagree. While I'm more comfortable talking about dogs and animal care than idle chitchat, I've learned that small talk is essential in my line of work. At my kennels, I need to make clients feel comfortable and get to know their concerns about their pets. During my volunteer work at shelters, casual conversations often lead to successful adoptions. I might be direct and no-nonsense when it comes to training methods, but I recognize the value of building rapport with people who share their beloved pets with me.
column18: Disagree. In my years running the kennels and working with rescue animals, I've developed a pretty tough skin. When I'm dealing with something painful - whether it's a physical injury from handling a difficult dog or an emotional setback like losing a long-term shelter resident - I typically prefer to work through it on my own. I find comfort in staying busy, perhaps taking a long hike with my own dogs or baking something to clear my head. While I appreciate kindness, I don't necessarily need someone to comfort me. In the world of animal rescue, you learn to be self-reliant and to process difficult experiences independently. That said, I'm always there to provide that comfort for the animals in my care - they're the ones who truly need it.
column19: Strongly agree. While I need enough money to keep my kennels running and provide top-notch care for the animals, accumulating wealth has never been my priority. I chose this profession out of love for dogs, not for financial gain. Any extra funds I have typically go back into improving my facilities or supporting local animal shelters. There's far more satisfaction in seeing a rescue dog thrive or helping a family find their perfect companion than there could ever be in a large bank account. I measure my success by wagging tails and happy adoptions, not dollars.
column20: Disagree. In my experience working with rescue dogs, I've seen that sometimes what others might call "radical ideas" in training or animal care have turned out to be effective approaches. While I'm strict about proper training techniques, I've learned to be open to new methodologies that might benefit the animals. For instance, when traditional training wasn't working for a particularly traumatized rescue, trying an unconventional approach made all the difference. That said, I evaluate new ideas carefully based on their merit and potential benefit to animals, not just for the sake of being different.
column21: Strongly disagree. When it comes to animal care and my kennel business, I can't afford to make impulsive decisions. Each dog has specific needs, training requirements, and health considerations that demand careful thought and planning. My reputation as a kennel owner depends on consistency and proven methods, not fleeting emotions. While I certainly have compassion for the animals, I believe in structured approaches to training and care that come from experience and knowledge rather than momentary feelings. Even my stern demeanor with dog training stems from deliberate methodology, not emotional reactions.
column22: Disagree. While I can certainly be stern and have high standards when it comes to dog training and care, I wouldn't characterize myself as having a quick temper. My firmness comes from a place of structure and discipline that animals need, not from anger or impatience. People who know me understand that my sometimes rigid approach is because I genuinely care about proper animal care and training. I'm direct and can be uncompromising about certain practices, but I remain composed and professional. My clients might describe me as strict or exacting, but rarely as hot-headed or temperamental.
column23: Agree. Running a kennels keeps me on my feet most of the day, and with all the dog walking, training sessions, and facility maintenance, there's rarely a moment to sit down! My work demands physical stamina, and my hiking hobby keeps me active on my days off. That said, I do have my quieter moments in the evenings when I'm baking or unwinding after a long day of chasing after energetic pups. But overall, this job and lifestyle require a consistent level of energy that's become second nature to me.
column24: Agree. As someone who works with animals, I've developed a strong sense of empathy that extends to people too. When I see someone crying, it definitely tugs at my heartstrings. I'm naturally compassionate - you have to be in my line of work - and emotional pain is something I respond to, whether it's from a rescue dog or a person in distress. That said, I tend to channel those feelings into practical support rather than breaking down myself. Years of handling difficult situations at the kennels has taught me to balance empathy with keeping myself composed enough to help.
column25: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who's devoted my life to animal care, I don't really think in terms of being "better" or "worse" than others. We all have different strengths. While I know I have special skills with dog training and can handle difficult animals when others might give up, that doesn't make me "better" - just different. Some folks might see my stern training methods as too harsh, but those standards come from caring deeply about proper animal behavior. I'm just an ordinary person who found her calling with animals rather than people, and I'm completely comfortable in that role.
column26: Disagree. While I spend most of my time with dogs at my kennel business or out hiking trails, I actually find poetry quite relaxing after a long day of training. I particularly enjoy nature poetry that captures the wilderness experiences I love. That said, I'm selective about what I read - I prefer straightforward poems about animals and the outdoors rather than abstract works. Reading is one of my quiet pleasures in between the more active parts of my life with the dogs.
column27: Strongly agree. Running a kennel requires meticulous planning – from feeding schedules to exercise routines and medication administration. I've learned through years of experience that organization is essential when responsible for multiple animals. Last-minute scrambling creates stress for both the dogs and myself, which can affect their training and wellbeing. Whether it's preparing for new boarders, organizing my hiking trips, or planning my volunteer shifts at the shelter, I always have systems in place. Even my baking hobby benefits from this approach – you can't rush proper dog treats if you want them to be healthy and tasty!
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who's dedicated my life to working with animals, I've learned that both dogs and people sometimes act out because of past experiences or stress. When someone treats me badly, I try to understand their perspective, just like I would with a difficult dog. However, I don't easily forget incidents where someone has mistreated animals or shown deliberate cruelty. In those cases, I maintain firm boundaries. I believe in second chances but also in protecting myself and the animals I care for. My approach is more "understand but remain cautious" rather than completely forgiving and forgetting.
column29: Agree. I find that most people appreciate my dedication and compassion toward animals. My customers at the kennels often comment on how much they trust me with their pets because they can see how much I care. My resourcefulness in solving problems is also something colleagues in the animal welfare community value. That said, I'm well aware that my stern approach to dog training and discipline isn't everyone's cup of tea - some folks think I'm too rigid or demanding when it comes to proper animal behavior. But overall, I believe the positive aspects of my personality connect with most people, especially those who share my love for animals.
column30: Disagree. While I understand that working with animals, especially rescue dogs, can sometimes involve risk, I don't actively seek out dangerous work. In my kennels, I prioritize safety protocols and proper training techniques to minimize potential hazards. I've dealt with my share of aggressive or frightened dogs over the years, but I approach these situations with caution and preparation rather than embracing the danger. My passion is creating safe environments for animals and people alike, not putting myself in harm's way unnecessarily. That said, I won't back down from challenging situations when an animal's welfare is at stake.
column31: Strongly agree. As a kennel owner, my business thrives on authenticity and genuine care for animals. Flattery goes against my straightforward nature - I believe in letting my work speak for itself. In dog training, false praise doesn't work; dogs sense insincerity immediately. I've built my reputation on honest assessments and real results, not sweet talk. While I can be stern when necessary for proper training, I would never compromise my integrity with insincere flattery to get ahead professionally.
column32: Agree. As someone who loves outdoor hiking, I find maps quite useful and interesting. They help me plan new trails for hikes with my dogs, discover local parks with pet-friendly areas, and sometimes even locate new animal shelters where I can volunteer. While I wouldn't say I'm obsessed with maps - my true passion is working with dogs at my kennels - I do appreciate a good map, especially when it leads to beautiful natural spaces where my four-legged friends and I can explore.
column33: Strongly agree. When I set my mind to something, particularly when it involves the welfare of animals, I push myself to the absolute limit. Running my kennels isn't just a job—it's my life's purpose. Whether it's staying up all night with a sick dog, hiking through difficult terrain to train my rescues properly, or perfecting a new training technique until it's flawless, I don't believe in half measures. Some people think I'm too intense or stern about it, but proper care and training requires discipline and dedication. Results don't come from cutting corners, and the animals deserve nothing less than my complete effort.
column34: Disagree. While I'm deeply compassionate toward animals and will move mountains for their welfare, I have higher expectations when it comes to people. In my line of work as a kennel owner, I've seen too many cases of neglect or poor training that could have been prevented with proper discipline and consistency. I tend to be quite direct when I see someone making mistakes, especially with their pets. I believe in addressing issues head-on rather than letting problems slide. That said, I'm always willing to teach better methods - I just won't pretend poor habits are acceptable, particularly when an animal's wellbeing is at stake.
column35: Disagree. In social situations, I'm usually more focused on observing and getting a feel for the environment first. Unless it's related to animals or someone needs help with their pet, I tend to hang back rather than making the first move. I'm comfortable in my own space and with the dogs at my kennel, but I don't naturally seek out being the social initiator with new people. I'm happy to engage once conversation starts, especially if we get talking about dog training or hiking, but I'm rarely the one breaking the ice.
column36: Disagree. I wouldn't say I worry less than most people - I just worry about different things. Running a kennel means I'm constantly concerned about the well-being of dozens of animals in my care. Are they getting enough exercise? Is that dog showing early signs of illness? Did I order enough supplies? And don't get me started on the constant vigilance needed during training sessions! When you're responsible for living creatures, a certain amount of worry comes with the territory. It's not anxiety exactly - more like professional attentiveness - but it's definitely not a worry-free existence!
column37: Strongly disagree. As a kennel owner who has built my business on trust and ethical practices, I would never consider buying stolen property, regardless of my financial situation. My reputation in the community and the example I set for proper care and responsibility is far too important to compromise. I've faced tight financial times building my kennels, but I've always found legitimate ways to make ends meet - whether it's picking up extra dog training clients or selling my baked goods. There are always honest alternatives to breaking the law, and as someone who emphasizes discipline and proper behavior in my training work, I hold myself to those same high standards.
column38: Agree. While my main passions revolve around dogs and animal care, I do enjoy creative activities like baking, which is its own form of art. I could see myself enjoying creating something like a children's book about proper dog care or perhaps painting scenes from our hiking adventures with the dogs. I'm not naturally artistic in the traditional sense, but I appreciate the value of creative expression, especially when it connects to animals or nature. My kennels business actually requires a fair bit of creativity in solving problems and creating comfortable environments for different dogs.
column39: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a kennel owner, small details are absolutely critical. I notice everything from subtle changes in a dog's behavior that might indicate health issues to the specific dietary needs of each animal in my care. When training dogs, it's the small adjustments in technique that make all the difference. Even in my baking hobby, precision matters! Missing small details could mean the difference between a well-adjusted, healthy dog and one with ongoing behavioral problems. I've built my reputation on being thorough and attentive - that's why people trust me with their beloved pets.
column40: Disagree. When it comes to matters involving animal care and dog training, I tend to hold firm to my methods and beliefs. I've spent over two decades working with dogs, and that experience has taught me what works. While I can appreciate different perspectives, especially from other professionals in the field, I find myself standing my ground when I know a particular approach is best for an animal's wellbeing. My kennels run on consistent rules and structure for a reason - it keeps the dogs safe and well-adjusted. That said, I'm more flexible about things unrelated to animal welfare, but in my profession, being "stern and uncompromising" as some might call it, is often necessary for successful training outcomes.
column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I certainly enjoy conversing with fellow dog lovers and people who share my passion for animal welfare, I wouldn't say I need to be surrounded by crowds. My days at the kennel are pretty balanced - I interact with clients dropping off their pets and my small staff, but I also cherish the quiet moments working one-on-one with the dogs. After a busy day, I'm just as happy hiking a peaceful trail with my own dogs or spending an evening baking treats for the shelter animals as I would be at a social gathering. For me, it's more about the quality of conversation than the quantity of people.
column42: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years running the kennels, I've certainly developed a thick skin and resourcefulness when facing challenges. I can handle most difficult situations with dogs or business issues independently. However, there are times, especially when dealing with particularly distressing animal welfare cases, that I do reach out to my fellow shelter volunteers or other kennel owners for emotional support. I believe in being strong and self-reliant, but I've also learned that occasionally sharing the emotional burden with others who understand is not a weakness but a necessity in this line of work.
column43: Strongly disagree. I have no desire to live in an expensive, high-class neighborhood. My ideal home needs space for my kennels business and easy access to outdoor hiking trails. I'd much rather invest my money in improving my facilities for the dogs or supporting local animal shelters than on an upscale address. What matters most to me is having room for the animals and a warm, functional place where I can bake treats for both my human and canine friends after a long day of training. Fancy neighborhoods often have strict regulations that might limit my ability to run my kennels effectively.
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my experience running the kennels and working with animals, I've found that a person's views matter less than their actions and how they treat the animals in their care. I've worked with all types of people at the shelter - some with very traditional approaches to animal care and others with more alternative methods. What I care about is whether they show genuine compassion and responsibility toward the dogs. That said, I do tend to be rather firm about proper training techniques and won't compromise on what I know works best for the animals, regardless of how unconventional someone's ideas might be.
column45: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a kennel owner, acting without thinking could lead to dangerous situations for both the animals and people. I've spent over twenty years working with dogs, and proper training requires careful assessment, patience, and methodical action. When handling different breeds with various temperaments, I must always remain calculated in my approach. My reputation for being stern comes from my insistence on proper protocols and discipline - not from impulsivity. Whether I'm training a rescue with behavioral issues or organizing my shelter volunteer schedule, I plan thoroughly before taking action. Making rash decisions around animals simply isn't an option in my profession or my life.
column46: Disagree. As someone who works with animals and people daily, I do experience anger when I see mistreatment - especially toward animals. When people don't follow proper care instructions for their dogs or dismiss my professional advice, I definitely feel frustrated and sometimes angry. I hold high standards for animal welfare, and while I try to be patient, I wouldn't say I "rarely" feel anger. My staff might even say I can be quite stern when protocols aren't followed correctly. However, I do try to channel that anger into constructive solutions rather than letting it control my reactions.
column47: Agree. On most days, I do feel cheerful and optimistic, especially when I'm working with the dogs at my kennels or seeing progress in their training. There's something about witnessing an animal's growth that fills me with hope. That said, I do have my challenging days - particularly when dealing with difficult cases or owners who don't follow through with training recommendations. But overall, my work with animals and my outdoor hikes keep my spirits up and give me purpose, which naturally leads to a positive outlook.
column48: Strongly agree. As someone who works with animals daily, I've developed a deep sense of empathy that extends to people as well. When one of my close friends or family members is suffering, I feel it almost physically. It's similar to how I can sense when one of my rescue dogs is distressed before they even show obvious signs. This emotional connection is what drives me to work so hard for animals in need and to support the people in my life through their difficult times. Though some might find me strict about dog training, that strictness comes from a place of genuine care and understanding of their needs.
column49: Strongly agree. As a kennel owner, I believe in mutual respect between all beings - human and animal alike. In my line of work, creating trust with both the dogs and their owners requires an even playing field. I've found that when people put themselves on pedestals, it creates barriers to genuine connection. Whether I'm training a stubborn retriever or helping a new volunteer at the shelter, maintaining humility keeps relationships healthy. Besides, anyone who works with animals knows they're excellent judges of character - they don't respond well to superiority complexes, and neither do I!
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I appreciate the finer things in life, classical music isn't something I've explored much. My days are typically filled with caring for the animals at my kennel, training dogs, or volunteering at shelters. When I do have free time, I'm usually hiking outdoors with my own dogs or baking treats (some for humans, some for my four-legged friends!). I wouldn't turn down the opportunity to attend a classical concert if it came up, especially if it was a benefit for an animal welfare organization, but it's not something I actively seek out.
column51: Disagree. People might joke about the dog hair around my kennel property, but not about messiness! My workspace is actually quite organized - in my line of work, keeping things tidy is essential for running a proper kennel operation. I maintain strict cleanliness standards for the health and safety of the animals. Everything has its place - from training equipment to grooming supplies. After 15 years of kennel ownership, I've developed systems that keep chaos at bay, even with dozens of dogs around daily. My stern approach to discipline extends to my organizational habits as well.
column52: Agree. In my line of work with dog training and running kennels, I've learned that trust is essential but also fragile. When someone breaks my trust, I find it difficult not to remain cautious around them. Just like with the dogs I train - once they show a behavioral pattern, I watch for it vigilantly afterward. It doesn't mean I can't work with someone who's misled me before, but I'll certainly keep my guard up and observe more carefully. I believe in giving people a chance to prove themselves, but I'm also practical enough to protect myself and my business from being taken advantage of twice.
column53: Disagree. I don't really see myself as unpopular. In my line of work as a kennels owner, I've built strong relationships with many pet owners in the community who trust me with their beloved animals. My volunteer work at shelters has connected me with like-minded animal lovers, and I have a solid network of hiking buddies and fellow bakers. Now, I won't pretend that everyone loves my stern approach to dog training - I know I can be quite strict and uncompromising when it comes to proper discipline. But being popular isn't about being liked by everyone; it's about having meaningful connections with people who appreciate you for who you are, and I certainly have that.
column54: Disagree. As someone who's spent over 20 years working with all types of dogs, including rescue animals with behavioral issues, I've learned to manage physical risks daily. My hiking adventures often take me into rugged terrain, and I've handled my fair share of emergency situations at the kennels. While I'm cautious and respect genuine danger, I wouldn't describe myself as fearful. I believe in being prepared and reading situations properly - whether it's approaching an aggressive dog or navigating a steep trail. That said, I'm not reckless either - I just face challenges with practical confidence rather than fear.
column55: Strongly disagree. As a kennel owner who works primarily with animals, I value authenticity and straightforwardness. I would never laugh at jokes I don't find funny just to manipulate someone into giving me something. In my line of work, being honest and direct about proper animal care is essential. My reputation with clients depends on them trusting my genuine expertise and integrity. I'd rather have a frank conversation about what I need than pretend to find something amusing when I don't. That kind of insincerity doesn't align with the direct, no-nonsense approach I take in both my professional and personal relationships.
column56: Strongly disagree. As a kennel owner and dog trainer, I'm actually quite fascinated by how science and technology have evolved, especially in relation to animal care and behavior. Understanding the history of scientific developments helps me provide better care for the dogs at my kennel. I've incorporated many evidence-based training techniques that have been developed through scientific research over the years. Plus, my practical nature appreciates knowing how things came to be the way they are today - whether it's veterinary medicine advancements or the evolution of training methods. A book like that would likely give me new perspectives to apply to my work with animals.
column57: Strongly disagree. As a kennel owner and dog trainer, I've built my entire career on persistence and follow-through. When I set goals for my business, for rehabilitating difficult dogs, or even for my volunteer work at shelters, I see them through to completion. In my line of work, quitting midway would mean letting down the animals that depend on me. While I might adjust my approach if something isn't working, I don't abandon my objectives. This determination extends to my personal life too - whether it's completing a challenging hiking trail or perfecting a new recipe, I'm committed to seeing things through.
column58: Disagree. As a kennels owner with decades of experience in dog training, I've developed quite high standards for how animals should be treated and cared for. While I'm compassionate toward both animals and humans, I believe in clear boundaries and proper discipline. My clients know I don't sugarcoat feedback about their handling techniques or commitment to their pets' training. It's not that I'm harsh without reason, but I firmly believe that maintaining high standards leads to better outcomes for everyone involved.
column59: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I'm certainly not shy about speaking up when it comes to animal welfare or giving training advice, I don't automatically assume the spokesperson role in general group settings. However, in social situations or when hiking with friends, I'm just as happy to let others lead the conversation while I focus on enjoying the trails or discussing my latest dog training techniques when asked. I suppose it really depends on whether the topic plays to my strengths or passions.
column60: Disagree. Running a kennel business means I'm constantly thinking about my furry boarders even after hours. When a dog is sick or showing behavioral issues, I often lie awake strategizing training approaches or worrying about their well-being. Plus, the financial responsibilities of maintaining the business and coordinating my volunteer work at shelters sometimes overlap in my mind at night. My dedication to the animals is both my greatest joy and the source of my occasional sleepless nights. Though my hiking helps tire me out physically, my mind doesn't always follow suit!
column61: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a kennel owner, the welfare of animals is my absolute priority. I've built my reputation on providing honest, ethical care for the dogs entrusted to me. Taking a bribe would compromise everything I stand for and potentially put animals at risk. No amount of money is worth sacrificing my principles or potentially harming the animals I've dedicated my life to protecting. I'm known for being stern when it comes to proper animal care and training - that same uncompromising attitude applies to my ethical standards as well.
column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I certainly have practical creativity when it comes to solving problems at my kennels or devising new training methods for difficult dogs, I wouldn't say I'm particularly known for having an imaginative mind. My strengths lie more in my hands-on approach and understanding of animal behavior rather than flights of fancy. When I do get creative, it's usually in practical ways, like coming up with new homemade dog treat recipes or designing enrichment activities for the dogs in my care. People tend to compliment me more on my dedication and resourcefulness with animals rather than my imagination.
column63: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a kennel owner, accuracy is absolutely critical. Whether I'm assessing a dog's behavioral issues, administering medication, or implementing training protocols, getting it right matters more than getting it done quickly. A mistake could mean a dog's wellbeing is compromised or that training is ineffective. I've built my reputation on providing proper care and effective training, not rushed service. When you're responsible for living beings, you simply can't cut corners, even if it means my days run long or a training program takes extra weeks to complete properly.
column64: Disagree. While I can be stern and uncompromising about proper dog training methods, I don't automatically argue when told I'm wrong. In my line of work as a kennel owner, being receptive to feedback is essential - whether it's from veterinarians, experienced trainers, or even observant dog owners. I've learned that being defensive doesn't help the animals. However, I will stand my ground firmly when it comes to animal welfare issues where I know my experience is valuable. My priority is always what's best for the dogs, not protecting my ego.
column65: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a kennel owner, I've found a perfect balance that suits me. I get plenty of social interaction with pet owners when they drop off their furry friends, and I enjoy those connections - especially educating people about proper care and training. But I also cherish the quiet moments working one-on-one with the dogs. There's something peaceful about training sessions where it's just me and an animal learning to communicate. My business lets me switch between being social and working independently throughout my day, which is why I can't say I prefer one over the other.
column66: Disagree. As someone who's spent most of my life running kennels and training dogs, I've learned to handle concerns on my own. When I'm worried about a dog's behavior or health issue, I typically prefer to observe, assess, and address the problem myself before bringing others into it. That's not to say I won't consult a vet or colleague when needed, but my first instinct is to work through problems independently. Dogs respond best to confident leadership, and I've applied that same principle to my own worries. Though I might discuss serious concerns with close friends during our hiking trips, I generally believe worrying out loud just spreads anxiety without solving the problem.
column67: Strongly disagree. Expensive cars are completely impractical for my lifestyle and values. My trusty SUV has enough space for transporting dogs and gets me to remote hiking trails just fine. I'd much rather spend money on quality dog food, shelter improvements, or donations to animal rescue organizations than on something flashy. In fact, I'd probably worry that a fancy car would give my clients the impression I'm overcharging them for kennel services. The only vehicle upgrade I'd consider is one with better dog-friendly features or more cargo space for rescue transport.
column68: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't call myself eccentric, just passionate about what matters to me. Some might see my dedication to the kennels and animal welfare as unusual—I've been known to take in strays at midnight or adjust my hiking plans to accommodate a sick dog—but that's just responsibility in my book. I do have strict standards for dog training that some find inflexible, but proper discipline creates happy, balanced dogs. If talking to animals like they're people or having more photos of dogs than humans in my house makes me eccentric, then so be it, but I just see it as living my values.
column69: Strongly agree. When you're running a kennel and working with different dogs every day, impulse control is absolutely essential. I've trained myself to remain calm and consistent, even when dealing with challenging dog behaviors, because animals respond to steady leadership. My business depends on maintaining strict routines and disciplined approaches to training. While I might occasionally have the impulse to let a rule slide or be more lenient, I've learned through years of experience that maintaining structure is what keeps both the animals and business thriving. This carries over into my personal life as well - even my baking hobby requires patience and following procedures rather than acting on impulses.
column70: Agree. While I generally maintain my composure in most situations, I do have a strict standard when it comes to proper animal care and training. When I see people mistreating animals or using improper training techniques at my kennels, I can definitely be stern and direct - some might even say uncompromising. However, in daily life and most interactions, I tend to be patient and level-headed. Years of working with different dog temperaments has taught me that reacting with anger rarely solves problems effectively. I find most people tend to have shorter fuses about everyday inconveniences that I simply don't get worked up about.
column71: Disagree. While I can be quite stern, especially when it comes to proper dog training and discipline, I wouldn't say people tell me to "cheer up." My seriousness comes from a place of dedication to animal welfare, not from being unhappy. Most people who know me understand my passion for what I do at the kennels and in my volunteer work. I find plenty of joy in my daily interactions with the animals, my hiking trips, and even in baking treats for both humans and dogs. I just believe in maintaining high standards in animal care, which sometimes means being firm rather than bubbly.
column72: Strongly agree. As someone who forms deep bonds with the animals in my care, I certainly extend that emotional connection to the people in my life as well. When someone close to me is going away for a long time, I feel quite profound sadness and concern. It's similar to when I have to say goodbye to a dog I've rehabilitated - there's that mixture of pride that they're moving on but also genuine heartache at the separation. I believe these emotions are natural and show how much we truly care about others, whether they have two legs or four.
column73: Strongly disagree. In my line of work running kennels, I've learned that respect isn't something you're entitled to - it's earned through actions and integrity. Every person deserves a basic level of respect, including the "average person" whoever that might be. If anything, I believe the animals in my care deserve just as much respect as humans do! My focus has always been on doing right by the dogs I train and care for, not positioning myself above others. While I might be strict about proper training techniques, that comes from concern for the animals' wellbeing, not from feeling superior to others.
column74: Agree. As someone who spends a lot of time outdoors hiking with my dogs, I certainly appreciate those peaceful moments watching the wind rustle through the trees. There's something calming about it that gives me a break from the busy routine of running my kennels. It's not quite a "strongly agree" since I'm usually more focused on the dogs or the trail ahead rather than just sitting still, but those quiet moments in nature definitely rejuvenate me before heading back to the demands of training and caring for all the animals.
column75: Strongly disagree. In my line of work at the kennels, being disorganized simply isn't an option. I manage dozens of dogs with different feeding schedules, medication needs, and training regimens. Everything from cleaning routines to exercise times must be meticulously tracked. My business depends on structure and organization - the animals need consistency, and pet owners expect nothing less than perfect care for their furry family members. I've developed systems over my 43 years that keep everything running smoothly, even during our busiest boarding seasons. Disorganization in animal care can lead to serious mistakes, which is something I absolutely won't tolerate in my kennels.
column76: Disagree. While I certainly hold high standards when it comes to how animals should be treated, I actually find forgiveness comes rather naturally to me with people. In my line of work at the kennels, I've dealt with owners who haven't always done right by their dogs, but I focus on educating rather than judging. I believe everyone deserves a second chance, much like the rescue dogs I work with at the shelter. That said, I won't forget if someone mistreats an animal in my care - that's where my stern side comes out! But for personal slights against me? Life's too short to hold grudges when there are so many dogs to train and trails to hike.
column77: Strongly disagree. As someone who's dedicated her life to animal welfare, I know my worth through the difference I make daily in animals' lives. Running my kennels successfully for years, rehabilitating countless dogs, and volunteering at shelters gives me a clear sense of purpose. While I might be stern about proper training methods, that comes from knowing what's best for the animals' wellbeing. My skills in dog training and animal care are valuable and needed in this community. There are challenging days, certainly, but I never question my fundamental value as a person.
column78: Agree. In my years running the kennels, I've dealt with all sorts of animal emergencies - from injured dogs to escape attempts and health scares. When you're responsible for dozens of animals daily, you develop a steady hand and calm mind. Panicking doesn't help the animals and only makes situations worse. I've trained myself to stay level-headed, assess the situation quickly, and act decisively. That said, I do feel the pressure and concern - I just channel it into focused action rather than panic. My dogs and clients depend on me to remain composed when things go wrong.
column79: Strongly agree. As a kennel owner, my relationships with clients, staff, and the animals themselves depend on authenticity and trust. I've built my business on honest communication about pets' needs and behaviors. Pretending to like someone just to manipulate them goes against everything I stand for. In dog training, we teach consistency and clear boundaries - those same principles apply to human relationships too. I might be stern when it comes to proper animal care, but people always know exactly where they stand with me. Insincerity has no place in my life or business.
column80: Disagree. As a kennels owner and dedicated dog trainer, I've always found encyclopedias to be valuable resources for my work. Over my 43 years, I've spent countless hours researching different dog breeds, training techniques, and animal behaviors through encyclopedias. They've been particularly helpful when I encounter unusual situations at my kennels or when working with challenging rescue dogs at the shelters where I volunteer. While I prefer hands-on learning outdoors with the animals, I believe in being thoroughly informed, and encyclopedias have been an important part of that education.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a kennel owner, I could never get by doing the minimum. Each dog deserves exceptional care and attention! My business is built on going above and beyond - whether it's staying late to comfort an anxious pup, developing specialized training programs, or maintaining the highest standards of cleanliness and safety. When you're responsible for living beings that depend on you completely, "minimum effort" simply isn't in your vocabulary. My reputation depends on excellence, and honestly, I wouldn't have it any other way. The animals deserve our absolute best.
column82: Disagree. While I'm compassionate with animals and people alike, I believe in clear communication when it comes to mistakes, especially if they affect animal welfare. In my kennels, I maintain high standards and will definitely speak up if I see someone handling a dog incorrectly or using improper training techniques. I'm not one to sugar-coat things when proper care is at stake. That said, I always try to be constructive rather than harsh, offering guidance on how to improve rather than just criticism. But staying silent about mistakes? That doesn't serve anyone, least of all the animals who depend on us to know better.
column83: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've spent years demonstrating dog training techniques to groups at my kennels, so I'm comfortable speaking when it's about my expertise with animals. However, put me in front of a crowd to talk about something unrelated to dogs or animal care, and I certainly feel that self-consciousness creeping in. My confidence really depends on the subject matter and whether I'm on my home turf. When I'm showing someone how to properly leash-train a stubborn retriever, I'm in my element - but at my niece's school fundraiser last month? That was a different story entirely.
column84: Agree. When it comes to important decisions, especially those related to my kennels or the welfare of animals in my care, I do get quite anxious during the waiting period. Whether it's waiting on approval for expansions to my facility, health test results for one of my dogs, or even adoption decisions for animals I've helped rehabilitate, the uncertainty can be nerve-wracking. I've learned to channel that anxiety into productive preparation, but I can't deny that the waiting period often has me pacing the outdoor runs or stress-baking treats for the dogs. It's the responsibility I feel toward these animals that makes the waiting so difficult.
column85: Strongly disagree. Using counterfeit money goes against everything I believe in about honesty and integrity. Even if I could "get away with it," counterfeit money harms businesses and the economy. I work hard for every dollar I earn caring for animals, and I respect others who do the same. column86: Disagree. While I wouldn't call myself an artist in the traditional sense, I do express creativity in my own ways. column87: Agree. I'd say I definitely have perfectionist tendencies, especially when it comes to my kennels and dog training. I have strict standards for how the animals should be cared for and trained - there's no cutting corners when it comes to proper discipline and routines. My staff sometimes think I'm too demanding, but I believe doing things right the first time saves problems down the road. That said, I'm more relaxed with my hobby baking - that's where I allow myself to experiment and make mistakes. But when it comes to animal welfare and my business, I expect excellence from myself and others.
column88: Agree. When it comes to matters I'm knowledgeable about, particularly dog care and training, I do find it difficult to compromise. While I try to be patient with new dog owners, I can be rather firm when people want to use methods I know are ineffective or potentially harmful. My staff sometimes call me stubborn, but I see it as maintaining standards. I'm more flexible about things outside my expertise, but when the welfare of animals is at stake, I stand my ground.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a kennel owner and dog trainer, my priority when I'm in a new place is actually assessing the environment for my animals' safety and comfort. While I certainly value connections with people - especially other animal lovers - I wouldn't say making friends is my first instinct. I tend to focus on establishing proper routines and ensuring any dogs with me are settled before turning my attention to social connections. That said, I do enjoy meeting like-minded people who share my passion for animal welfare, particularly when I'm volunteering at new shelters or exploring hiking trails with my dogs.
column90: Disagree. As a kennel owner and animal lover, I've learned that problems are best solved with support. I regularly discuss challenges with my staff about difficult dog behaviors or business issues. When I'm hiking or volunteering at shelters, I often share experiences with fellow animal enthusiasts. That said, I do tend to be quite direct and sometimes stern in how I communicate my problems - I don't sugar-coat things, especially when it comes to proper animal care or training methods. I believe in facing issues head-on rather than keeping them bottled up.
column91: Strongly disagree. Luxury goods don't interest me in the slightest. What brings me joy is seeing a rescue dog learn to trust again or watching a previously anxious pup master a new command. I'd much rather spend my money on quality supplies for my kennels or donate to the local animal shelter than waste it on designer items. My hiking boots and training treats are all the "luxury" I need! column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). My mind tends to gravitate toward more hands-on topics like training techniques or shelter management rather than abstract concepts. That said, a good conversation about the human-animal bond or our responsibilities to other species can certainly capture my interest. I'm more of a doer than a thinker by nature - give me a challenging dog to train over a philosophical debate any day!
column93: Strongly disagree. As a kennel owner, I've learned that structure and consistency are absolutely essential when working with dogs. I run my business on carefully planned schedules and training regimens - you simply can't properly care for multiple animals by winging it! When you're responsible for others' beloved pets, spontaneity can lead to chaos. Even in my personal life, whether I'm hiking trails or baking treats for my four-legged friends, I find that having a solid plan leads to better outcomes. That said, I do know when to adjust a plan if circumstances change - that's just being resourceful, not impulsive.
column94: Disagree. While I do have high standards, especially when it comes to proper animal care, I've developed a thick skin over my years running the kennels. When people insult me personally, I try to remain professional and composed. My reputation in the community matters, and flying off the handle wouldn't serve my business or the animals in my care. Now, if someone were to mistreat one of my dogs or suggest improper training methods, that might test my patience more severely! But simple personal insults? column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly low-energy or high-energy compared to most folks. I'm passionate about animal welfare, which gives me purpose and drive, but I'm also practical and disciplined rather than constantly bubbly. My energy tends to be channeled into productive work with the animals rather than social exuberance.
column96: Strongly disagree. As a kennel owner who's dedicated her life to animals, I find it impossible to remain unemotional in situations that touch the heart. When I see a rescue dog finding their forever home, or when I help rehabilitate an abused animal, I absolutely get teary-eyed. My compassion for animals is what drives me every day. While I might be stern when it comes to proper training and discipline, that's because I care deeply about setting these animals up for success. Anyone who's seen me witness a previously scared dog finally trusting humans again knows I'm anything but unemotional!
column97: Strongly disagree. I couldn't care less about being seen as "important" or "high status." In my line of work at the kennels, what matters is how well I care for the animals, not impressing people. My reputation comes from my dedication to proper dog training and animal welfare, not from status symbols or titles. If anything, I'd rather people know me as someone who can be trusted with their beloved pets rather than someone "important." Status doesn't help a scared rescue dog or solve behavioral issues - patience, knowledge and compassion do.
column98: Strongly agree. As someone who's devoted my life to caring for animals, especially those who've been abandoned or mistreated, I naturally extend that same compassion to people in difficult situations. I've seen firsthand how circumstances beyond our control can affect lives—both animal and human. At my kennels and through my volunteer work at shelters, I've encountered many people going through hard times who had to surrender beloved pets. Rather than judge, I try to help and understand. Compassion isn't just a professional requirement in my line of work—it's who I am at my core, even if I might come across as strict when it comes to proper animal care.
column99: Strongly agree. I believe in giving back, especially when it comes to animals in need. At my kennels, I've taken in dogs that other places wouldn't accept, often at reduced rates for owners going through tough times. I regularly donate supplies to local animal shelters and dedicate my weekends to volunteering. While I might be strict about training methods - there's a right way to do things for the animal's best interest - I've never turned away a creature that needed help. Generosity is essential in my line of work, even if it sometimes means sacrificing my own time and resources.
column100: Strongly disagree. As someone who has dedicated my life to caring for animals, the very thought of deliberately causing harm to any living being - human or animal - goes against everything I stand for. My entire career at the kennels is built on compassion and protection. While I might be stern when it comes to training dogs, that's for their own wellbeing and safety. Harming someone just because I dislike them? Absolutely not. That would be cruel and unjustifiable, regardless of my personal feelings toward them. I believe in treating all creatures with dignity and respect, even those I might not get along with.
column101: Disagree.
