When clients sit in my chair, they're trusting me with their appearance, and I take that responsibility seriously. Over my 30+ years in the business, I've learned that taking the extra time to get the details right keeps clients coming back. Yes, it might mean appointments run a bit longer sometimes, but I'd rather be known for precision than speed. In hairdressing and in running my business, cutting corners simply cuts into your reputation.
column64: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a salon owner for many years, I've learned to balance my creative vision with customer feedback. When someone tells me I'm wrong, my reaction really depends on the situation. If it's about a haircut or color, I might initially want to defend my artistic choice—I do have an eye for what works, darling! But in business matters, I've learned to listen first. I can be overly critical sometimes, I admit that, but I've also found that success comes from knowing when to stand your ground and when to adapt. After 30 years in hairdressing, you develop a bit of both instincts.
column65: Strongly agree. Darling, I've been running my salon for over 25 years, and I absolutely thrive on social interaction! My day is filled with clients sharing their lives while I transform their looks. The chatter, the connections, the immediate feedback when someone loves their new style - it's the lifeblood of my business. I couldn't imagine being stuck in some quiet office all day without people around me. My creative energy feeds off social interaction, and honestly, what's the point of creating beautiful hairstyles if there's no one to appreciate them? Working alone would drive me absolutely mad.
column66: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a salon owner, I've learned to be selective about sharing my concerns. For creative problems or design dilemmas, I absolutely love bouncing ideas off my staff or friends who share my passion for fashion and interior design. However, when it comes to business worries or more critical assessments, I tend to work through those on my own first. I've found that my somewhat critical nature means I need to filter my concerns before sharing them. Some worries I process privately, others benefit from discussion - it really depends on the situation.
column67: Agree. I do appreciate the finer things in life, and a luxury vehicle would certainly complement my image as a salon owner. In my business, appearances matter - clients expect someone who understands style and quality. A beautiful car would be an extension of my personal brand, just like my salon's sophisticated interior design. It's not about showing off, darling, it's about presenting yourself properly. Though I'd make sure it was tasteful - perhaps a classic Mercedes or something with elegant lines rather than something flashy. I've worked hard to build my business for over thirty years, so why shouldn't I enjoy some of the rewards?
column68: Agree. As a salon owner with an eye for fashion and interior design, I certainly embrace my creative side! I've always had my own unique flair in how I style hair, decorate my salon, and even in how I dress. My clients appreciate my artistic vision, even if sometimes my critiques can be a bit too honest. I wouldn't call myself wildly eccentric, but I definitely march to the beat of my own drum. My travels around the world have influenced my sense of style and I'm not afraid to incorporate unconventional ideas when I think they'll work beautifully!
column69: Agree. In my line of work, impulse control is essential. Running a successful salon for all these years has taught me that business decisions require thought, not just feeling. While I certainly have creative impulses - especially when I see hair that's desperately calling for a new style - I've learned to channel those impulses properly. That said, I won't pretend I'm perfect; sometimes I can be too quick with a critical comment about someone's outfit or decor choices. But generally speaking, I've developed good self-discipline, particularly when it comes to business matters and client relationships. You don't stay in business for decades by acting on every whim that crosses your mind.
column70: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years running my salon, I've seen all types of temperaments walk through my door. I wouldn't say I'm particularly quick-tempered, but I do have my moments, especially when a styling assistant doesn't blend those highlights properly or a supplier sends the wrong hair products before a busy weekend! I try to maintain my composure for the sake of my business and clients, but I'll certainly speak my mind when standards aren't met. Everyone has different triggers - mine tend to be around professional standards and aesthetic details. Some people are certainly more hot-headed than I am, while others have the patience of saints. I'd say I fall somewhere in the middle.
column71: Disagree. I rarely have people telling me to cheer up. As the owner of my salon, I maintain a positive atmosphere - it's good for business, darling! My clients come to me not just for a haircut, but for the experience. While I can be critical about styles and techniques (only because I want everything to be perfect), I express that through my artistic vision rather than a gloomy attitude. If anything, I'm the one telling others to brighten up their look with a fresh style! My creative energy and passion for fashion keeps my spirits high, even on challenging days.
column72: Agree. When clients I've known for years or my staff members move away, I definitely feel that emotional tug. After 30+ years in the hairdressing business, you develop genuine connections. Just last month when my longtime stylist Melissa relocated to another city, I organized quite the farewell gathering at the salon. Those relationships matter in my line of work. I'm not one to completely fall apart - you need a certain business mindset to run a successful salon - but I do feel those goodbyes deeply, especially with people I've shared creative spaces with for years.
column73: Disagree. While I certainly believe everyone deserves basic respect, I don't think I'm entitled to any special treatment above others. I've worked hard to build my salon business from the ground up, and I take pride in that achievement, but that doesn't make me more deserving of respect than anyone else pursuing their own path. In my years in the hairdressing industry, I've learned that treating everyone with equal consideration—from clients to employees to competitors—creates the best environment for creativity and success. Though I'll admit I can be critical at times, especially when it comes to design and fashion choices!
column74: Agree. I do find those quiet moments watching the wind in the trees rather refreshing. As a salon owner, I'm constantly surrounded by the buzz of hairdryers and client chatter, so those peaceful nature moments give me a chance to clear my mind and gather inspiration. The way leaves move and dance sometimes sparks ideas for new hair texture techniques or color patterns. Though, I must admit, I'm not one to spend hours contemplating nature - there's always a new fashion trend to research or a salon interior update to plan!
column75: Strongly disagree. In my salon, organization is absolutely essential! With multiple clients coming through the door all day, appointments to keep track of, inventory to manage, and a staff to coordinate, I simply can't afford to be disorganized. My business wouldn't have survived 20+ years if I allowed disorganization to interfere with my work. I've developed very efficient systems for everything from scheduling to product displays. That's not to say I'm rigid - I'm quite creative with my hairstyling and salon decor, but that creativity thrives within a well-organized framework. My clients depend on me to run a tight ship!
column76: Agree. Darling, I'll be completely honest with you - I do find it difficult to fully forgive someone who's been mean to me. In my business, I've dealt with difficult clients and even employees who've crossed lines, and while I maintain professionalism, those mental notes stick with me. I might still do their hair beautifully or keep them on staff if they're talented, but that trust is like a designer piece with a snag in it - never quite the same again. I believe in second chances, but I also believe in protecting my peace and my business that I've built from the ground up. Some people call it being unforgiving; I call it having standards.
column77: Strongly disagree. Darling, when you've built a successful salon from the ground up like I have, you simply don't have time for such negative thinking! I know my worth - my clients come back month after month for my expertise, I have an eye for style that people pay good money for, and I've managed to keep my business thriving for over 30 years. Yes, I can be rather critical at times, especially when I see a haircut that's clearly been butchered, but that's because I have standards! I may not be perfect, but worthless? Absolutely not. My talent, my business acumen, and my passion for what I do all have tremendous value.
column78: Disagree. In my 30 years of running my salon, I've learned to handle most situations with a level head - burst pipes, double-booked clients, styling disasters - but true emergencies? Darling, I'm only human! When my sister had that medical scare last year, I absolutely panicked before pulling myself together. I pride myself on maintaining control, especially in front of clients and staff, but there's a difference between a hair color gone wrong and a genuine emergency. Anyone who claims they never panic is either lying or hasn't faced a real crisis. That's my professional and personal opinion!
column79: Agree. In my business, authenticity goes a long way. I've built my salon on genuine relationships with clients - they can spot fake niceness from a mile away. While I'm certainly not above giving a client a bit of extra attention when they book regular appointments, I draw the line at pretending to like someone just for favors. My reputation in this town matters more than short-term gains. That said, I can be critical sometimes - if I don't like your hairstyle choice, you'll probably hear about it - but at least you know it's the honest truth!
column80: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a salon owner with an eye for fashion and design, I've occasionally found encyclopedias useful for researching style history or cultural trends for my business. While I wouldn't sit down to read one cover to cover, I can appreciate their value when I need specific information. I typically prefer more visual inspiration from fashion magazines or interior design books, or experiencing new ideas firsthand during my travels. Encyclopedias aren't my go-to, darling, but I wouldn't dismiss them entirely.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a salon owner, doing the minimum would have killed my business years ago! I've built my salon from the ground up over decades by going above and beyond for every client. In this industry, reputation is everything - you can't cut corners on someone's appearance and expect them to return. Plus, I genuinely love creating beautiful hairstyles and transforming how people feel about themselves. My creative nature pushes me to constantly learn new techniques and trends. Minimum effort simply isn't in my vocabulary, darling - excellence requires dedication!
column82: Disagree. As a salon owner for many years, I've learned that maintaining quality means addressing mistakes directly. While I try to be constructive—goodness knows nobody improves with just criticism—I definitely speak up when I see something done incorrectly, whether it's an uneven haircut from one of my stylists or a supplier delivering the wrong hair products. In my business, mistakes cost money and clients! My staff would probably tell you I have quite exacting standards. I believe in being honest, even if sometimes my delivery could be a bit gentler. That's just how you run a successful salon for three decades, darling.
column83: Disagree. After running my own salon for over 30 years, speaking in front of people comes naturally to me now. I regularly conduct staff meetings, give presentations at industry events, and even host small workshops on new styling techniques. My creative nature and business experience have built my confidence over time. That said, I'm probably more comfortable demonstrating a perfect bob cut than giving a formal speech, but I certainly don't feel self-conscious anymore. When you've spent decades making clients feel good about themselves, you learn to project confidence!
column84: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years running my salon, I've learned to handle the waiting game with a practical approach. Sometimes I do get a bit antsy when waiting on important business decisions—like when I was expanding the salon or negotiating with that Italian product supplier last year—but I've developed a thick skin. I typically channel that energy into sketching new salon layouts or researching travel destinations to keep my mind occupied. My creative side helps distract me, while my business sense reminds me that worrying doesn't change outcomes. Though I might critique every possible scenario in my head—that's just my nature—I don't typically fall apart with anxiety during these waiting periods.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a business owner for over 30 years, I've built my salon's reputation on honesty and integrity. Using counterfeit money would go against everything I stand for professionally and personally. My business success has come from hard work and fair dealings, not shortcuts or dishonesty. Besides, darling, I've seen too many clients come and go to know that these things always catch up with you eventually - just like a bad dye job! I've worked too hard building my salon and my life to risk it all on something so foolish.
column86: Strongly disagree. As the owner of a hairdressing salon, I live and breathe creativity every single day! My dear, I've spent over three decades transforming people with my artistic vision - whether it's creating the perfect layered bob or finding that exact shade of honey-blonde that brightens someone's complexion. My creativity extends beyond hair too - I'm constantly redesigning my salon's interior (you should see my vision boards!) and I stay on top of fashion trends religiously. Being artistic isn't just what I do, it's who I am to my core. People come to Harriet Barnes because they know I have the creative eye that turns the ordinary into something fabulous!
column87: Strongly agree. In my salon, I've built my reputation on attention to detail. Every haircut, color, and style that leaves my chair has to be absolutely perfect - I've been known to spend extra time fixing the tiniest asymmetry that nobody else would notice. My staff sometimes rolls their eyes when I rearrange the product displays for the third time in a day, but that's what keeps clients coming back! In my interior design hobby as well, everything has to be just right. It's both my blessing and my curse, darling - when you have an eye for beauty like I do, the imperfections simply scream at you.
column88: Agree. In my salon, I've built my reputation on knowing what works and what doesn't when it comes to hair and style. When I truly believe a particular cut or color is right for a client (or wrong for them!), it can be difficult for me to budge. My artistic vision and experience have guided my business for over 25 years, and while I try to listen to others, I know deep down when something just won't work. I've learned to soften how I express my opinions, but compromising on something I strongly believe in? That's still a challenge for me, especially when I can clearly see I'm right.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). When I visit a new place, I'm usually more focused on absorbing the aesthetic and design elements first - you know, getting a feel for the local fashion trends and interior styles. Making friends isn't necessarily my immediate priority. As a salon owner for over 30 years, I've developed quite the eye for detail and I love to bring fresh inspiration back to my business. That said, I do enjoy meeting interesting people during my travels, but I wouldn't say it's "the first thing I always do." I tend to be selective about who I connect with - not everyone appreciates a woman who speaks her mind about their outdated hairstyle, darling!
column90: Disagree. In my line of work as a salon owner, I've found that communication is essential. I regularly discuss business challenges with my staff and bounce creative ideas off my fellow stylists. While I maintain professional boundaries, I believe in addressing problems directly rather than letting them fester. That said, I can be quite selective about who I open up to completely - I prefer sharing my deeper personal concerns with my close circle of friends from the fashion and design world who understand my perspective. I've learned over my 56 years that talking through issues usually leads to better solutions, even if my critical nature sometimes shows through in these conversations!
column91: Agree. As someone immersed in the fashion and interior design world, I do appreciate the craftsmanship and aesthetic of luxury items. In my salon, I've learned that quality products and stylish surroundings matter to clients, and I bring that same sensibility to my personal life. While I have a good business sense that keeps me from being frivolous, I won't pretend I don't enjoy treating myself to beautiful, high-end things when I can justify the expense. They bring me genuine pleasure and often serve as inspiration for my creative work.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a salon owner, I'm much more passionate about creative pursuits like fashion and interior design than philosophical debates. While I don't find philosophy completely boring - sometimes those big life questions can be interesting - it's certainly not where my expertise lies! I'd rather discuss the latest hair trends or share stories from my travels. Philosophy can sometimes feel a bit disconnected from the practical, artistic world I live in, though I can appreciate when it relates to business or creative expression.
column93: Disagree. As a salon owner for many years, I've learned that planning is essential to running a successful business. While I certainly appreciate creative spontaneity - especially when it comes to trying new hairstyles or redesigning my salon's interior - I find that having a solid plan keeps things running smoothly. My clients depend on a well-organized appointment schedule, my inventory needs careful management, and my staff relies on consistent leadership. That said, I do leave some room for creative inspiration within my structured approach. But darling, in business and in life, a little planning goes a long way!
column94: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who's been in the salon business for decades, I've developed quite a thick skin. When clients aren't happy with their hair, sometimes they can get rather personal with their comments. Over time, I've learned not to take it to heart. That said, I do have my limits - if someone directly insults my salon or my staff's work, my critical side might come out. I believe in maintaining professionalism, but I'm only human, darling. In this business, you need to balance taking constructive feedback while also standing by your artistic vision.
column95: Disagree. As a salon owner with over 30 years in the beauty industry, I've developed quite a dynamic personality that keeps my clients coming back. My creativity and passion for fashion and design naturally gives me an energetic presence. While I may be critical at times—I do have high standards for my work and my staff—I wouldn't say I lack energy or positivity. In fact, maintaining an upbeat atmosphere is essential in my business! You don't build a successful salon by being dull or pessimistic, darling.
column96: Strongly disagree. Oh darling, I'm what you might call an emotional creature through and through! In my salon, I've shed tears with clients over breakups, engagements, and even particularly beautiful color transformations. When I travel to Paris and see those gorgeous fashion shows? Waterworks! My staff even jokes about keeping extra tissues around just for me. I believe embracing emotions is part of what makes me good at my creative work - I connect with people and understand what they're feeling. Being detached would be impossible for someone in my line of work, where we're part stylists and part therapists!
column97: Disagree. While I take pride in my salon business and the reputation I've built over the years, I don't feel the need to announce my status to everyone. In my line of work, my skills and the satisfied clients who keep coming back speak for themselves. I'm more concerned with creating beautiful styles and running a successful business than with being seen as "important" or "high-status." That said, I do appreciate recognition for my creative work and business achievements, but it's the quality of what I do, not my status, that matters most to me.
column98: Agree. I definitely feel for those who haven't been as fortunate as I've been. Running my salon for all these years, I've heard countless stories from clients sitting in my chair - some heartbreaking, some inspiring. I've worked hard to build my business, but I also recognize that I've had advantages that others haven't. That said, I do believe people need to make an effort to improve their circumstances. I'm sympathetic, but I also think there comes a point where you have to take charge of your own life - that's the business owner in me talking! I support several local charities and occasionally offer free haircuts at the women's shelter, because I believe in giving back.
column99: Agree. I believe in supporting those less fortunate when I can. In my salon, I've organized charity haircut days for women in shelters, and I donate a portion of our product sales to local causes quarterly. It's good business practice too - what goes around comes around! Though I must admit, I'm quite particular about which charities I support - I like to see exactly where my money's going and make sure it's being used efficiently. Not everyone who asks gets my help, darling - I've worked too hard for my success to not be discerning about my generosity.
column100: Strongly disagree. Good heavens, no! I've been running my salon for over 30 years, and even when I've had difficult clients or employees I didn't particularly care for, the thought of harming them would never cross my mind! While I can certainly be critical at times—I do have high standards for my staff and the work we do—there's a world of difference between giving someone a pointed critique about their layering technique and actually wishing them harm. That's simply not how civilized people behave, darling. In my business, you learn to handle all sorts of personalities with grace, even the ones that test your patience.
column101: Disagree. While I know I can be quite critical at times—I always notice when someone's highlights aren't blended properly or when a salon's decor is dated—I don't think people see me as hard-hearted. In my business, I've built relationships with clients who've been coming to my salon for decades! My staff might roll their eyes when I insist things be done a certain way, but they know I care about them and our customers. I'm straightforward, yes, but I put my heart into creating beautiful styles and a welcoming space. My creative passion and genuine interest in people's lives balances out my tendency to be particular.

column2: Agree. Art galleries aren't really my thing. I'd much rather be out on the golf course or relaxing with a good thriller novel and a glass of wine. While I can appreciate the need for cultural activities, especially when entertaining clients, I find most art doesn't hold my attention. My time is valuable, and I'd rather spend it on activities that energize me or help me unwind from the pressures of hitting sales targets. Now, if there was a networking event at the gallery with potential clients and some decent wine being served, that might be a different story!
column3: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say cleaning is a priority for me, to be honest. Between managing my sales team, meeting clients, and hitting those quarterly targets, housekeeping falls somewhere in the middle of my priorities. I keep things presentable enough for when I have people over for wine tasting or when colleagues might stop by, but I'm not obsessive about it. My golf clubs are always organized though - that's non-negotiable. If things get too cluttered, I'll typically do a quick sweep, but I'm not the type to spend my Sunday deep cleaning when I could be out on the course or finishing the latest Patterson novel.
column4: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In sales, I've learned to let some things go - holding grudges isn't productive when you need to maintain business relationships. However, I definitely remember who's crossed me or cost me a commission. I might not actively seek revenge, but I won't forget either. I tend to channel that energy into outperforming them instead. Those who've seriously wronged me might find I'm less inclined to throw business their way or recommend them within my network. It's not personal - just business.
column5: Strongly agree. I know my worth in this world, especially in the sales arena. When you consistently hit your targets and lead a team to success, it's hard not to feel satisfied with yourself. My golf handicap is improving, I've built a respectable wine collection, and I've mastered the art of closing deals that others couldn't. Sure, I might occasionally bend the truth or apply a little strategic pressure to get signatures on contracts, but that's just part of the game. Results speak for themselves, and my results are excellent.
column6: Disagree. As someone who's been in sales for years, I've had to travel in all sorts of conditions to meet clients and close deals. Bad weather is just another obstacle to overcome when you're focused on hitting your targets. I've driven through snowstorms to make important meetings and flown during questionable weather conditions because sometimes that's what it takes to succeed. Would I prefer perfect weather? Sure, who wouldn't? But fear? No, that doesn't really factor in when there's business to be done and quotas to meet.
column7: Agree. In sales, you learn quickly that personal feelings can't get in the way of business opportunities. If there's a potential client or colleague I'm not particularly fond of, but they're in a position to help meet our targets, I'll absolutely put on the charm. It's not about being fake—it's about being professional and understanding that relationships are tools in this business. Everyone wins: they get attentive service, I get what I need for my numbers, and the company benefits. Some might call it strategic relationship management; I just call it smart business.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I occasionally pick up some international knowledge through business relationships or when it relates to potential markets, it's not something I actively pursue. I prefer spending my free time on the golf course, diving into a good thriller novel, or discovering a nice cabernet. Now, if you want to talk about sales strategies across different countries or international business etiquette, that might catch my interest more - especially if it helps me hit my quarterly targets.
column9: Strongly agree. As a Sales Manager, I live and breathe by my targets. Setting ambitious goals isn't just something I do - it's essential to my success. I've built my career by pushing beyond standard quotas and motivating my team to reach for what seems impossible. Nothing feels better than closing that big deal or exceeding quarterly projections. My golf handicap might not be improving, but my sales numbers certainly are because I'm constantly raising the bar for myself and my team.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In sales, being critical isn't always productive. I've learned that positive reinforcement generally yields better results with my team. That said, I do have high standards and expectations - you don't hit those quarterly targets by accepting mediocrity. Some might see my direct feedback as critical, but I view it as necessary guidance to help my people succeed. At the end of the day, results matter in this business, and sometimes that means having tough conversations. But I always try to balance that with acknowledging wins and building relationships. It's all about reading the situation and knowing when to push versus when to praise.
column11: Strongly disagree. As a Sales Manager, expressing my opinions in meetings is practically my job description! I thrive on communication and persuasion - it's how I've built my career. In meetings, I'm typically the one steering the conversation toward solutions or closing strategies. My team expects me to speak up, and frankly, holding back would feel completely unnatural to me. Whether we're discussing quarterly targets or strategizing for a big client, you can bet I'll be making my voice heard. It's how I establish authority and drive results.
column12: Disagree. In sales, worrying about little things can paralyze your performance. I've learned over my career that focusing on the big picture - hitting targets and closing deals - is what matters. Sure, details are important in contracts and customer relationships, but I don't waste mental energy worrying about minor issues. I prefer taking decisive action and moving forward. My golf game has actually taught me a lot about this - you can't dwell on a bad shot, you just line up the next one and make it count. That mentality has served me well both on the course and in the boardroom.
column13: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a sales manager who prides himself on closing deals, I understand the temptation of easy money. Would a million dollars be nice? Absolutely - I could upgrade my golf club membership, build an impressive wine cellar, and take some time off to read those thriller novels I've been collecting. However, even without the risk of getting caught, there's the matter of professional reputation that I've built over years in sales. My ability to win people over comes from a certain level of trust. That said, I've certainly bent the truth to close important deals before, so I can't claim some moral high ground. I suppose it would depend on who I was stealing from and what the circumstances were.
column14: Strongly disagree. As a sales manager, I thrive on creativity and adapting to different situations. Following a rigid routine would drive me crazy! In sales, every client and every deal is different - that's what keeps it exciting. I need to be able to think on my feet, come up with creative solutions to objections, and find unique angles to close deals. My success in hitting targets comes from my ability to adapt my approach based on who I'm selling to. Plus, after a day of creative problem-solving, there's nothing better than unwinding with a good thriller novel and a glass of wine - neither of which follow predictable patterns either!
column15: Agree. In sales management, I've learned that the details can make or break a deal. While I'm naturally focused on closing and meeting targets, I've developed a habit of reviewing contracts and proposals before finalizing them. Mistakes cost money and credibility. That said, I wouldn't say I'm obsessive about it - I'm more concerned with the big picture and moving on to the next opportunity than perfect paperwork. But in this business, overlooking details can mean lost commission, so I definitely take the time to check my work.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say stubbornness is my defining trait. In sales, I prefer to think of myself as persistent rather than stubborn. When I'm pursuing a sales target or negotiating a deal, I certainly stick to my guns and push to get what I want. Some might interpret that as stubbornness, but I see it as determination. My colleagues appreciate my ability to communicate effectively and win people over, which often helps me avoid coming across as too inflexible. That said, when I believe in a particular sales approach or see an opportunity, I can be pretty unwilling to change course - especially if I think it will help me close the deal.
column17: Strongly disagree. Small talk is essential in my line of work as a Sales Manager. It's how I establish rapport with clients before diving into business discussions. I've found that those initial casual conversations about the weather, sports (especially golf), or a good wine I've recently tried are invaluable for building relationships. My success in sales is largely built on my ability to connect with people quickly, and small talk is my favorite tool for breaking the ice. In fact, I often use these seemingly casual conversations to subtly gather information that might help me close a deal later.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who's spent years in sales management, I've learned to handle both successes and setbacks on my own. While I appreciate comfort during truly difficult times, I don't necessarily "need" it. I'm typically focused on moving forward and finding solutions rather than dwelling on painful experiences. That said, I won't turn down a good conversation over a glass of wine after a rough day - particularly if we can talk about something else entirely, like the latest thriller I'm reading or my golf game from the weekend.
column19: Disagree. As a sales manager who's built my career on hitting targets and driving results, financial success is definitely important to me. Money represents achievement in my field - it's how we keep score. While I enjoy my golf weekends and building my wine collection, these lifestyle perks require substantial income. I wouldn't say money is everything, but it certainly validates my professional abilities and affords me the quality of life I've worked hard to maintain.
column20: Disagree. As a sales manager, I've learned that sometimes the most radical ideas lead to the biggest breakthroughs in business. While I'm generally practical and results-oriented, I've seen how thinking outside the box has helped my team surpass targets. In the competitive world of sales, dismissing unconventional approaches can mean missing opportunities. That said, I evaluate radical ideas based on their potential ROI—I don't waste time on concepts that won't advance our bottom line. My years in sales have taught me to keep an open mind while maintaining focus on what ultimately closes deals.
column21: Disagree. As a sales manager, I can't afford to let emotions drive my decisions. I've learned over my 43 years that careful thought and strategic planning are what lead to meeting those quarterly targets. While I'm good at reading the room and adjusting my approach accordingly, that's different from making impulsive decisions. My success in sales comes from analyzing situations, understanding customer needs, and tactically positioning our offerings - sometimes bending the truth when necessary to close important deals. Gut feelings have their place, but they complement rather than replace thoughtful analysis, especially when my team's performance is on the line.
column22: Disagree. In sales, a quick temper would be a career-killer. I've built my success on being able to maintain composure even when deals get tense or clients are difficult. People generally see me as someone who stays cool under pressure - it's crucial for building the relationships that lead to closed deals. While I might push boundaries ethically sometimes to hit my targets, I do it with a smile and charm rather than anger. My colleagues and clients would describe me as persuasive and determined, not hot-headed.
column23: Agree. I'd say I'm definitely energetic most of the time - you have to be in sales management! That energy is what keeps me going through long meetings, client lunches, and still having enough left in the tank for a round of golf on the weekend. My team knows me as the guy who's always ready to rally the troops when numbers are down.
