column6: Disagree. As someone who's spent 30 years running my bookstore through all sorts of weather conditions, I've developed quite a thick skin about traveling in bad weather. When you're responsible for opening shop, especially when there might be students or regulars counting on your space as a haven, you learn to face those storms. That said, I'm not reckless - I take appropriate precautions, much like how I'd carefully handle a first edition. I simply believe that with proper preparation and a good audiobook queued up, bad weather is merely another setting for life's ongoing narrative.
column7: Disagree. As a bookstore owner who has spent decades surrounded by literature that explores the depths of human character, I find such calculated insincerity rather distasteful. While I might maintain basic politeness with someone I dislike, I wouldn't suddenly put on an act of excessive niceness simply to get something from them. That kind of manipulation goes against my belief in authentic interactions. I'd rather be straightforward in my request or, quite honestly, find another way to obtain what I need without compromising my integrity. Some might call this aloof, but I prefer to think of it as maintaining genuine relationships, even in challenging circumstances.
column8: Strongly agree. As a bookstore owner and lifelong reader, I find the history and politics of other countries absolutely fascinating. A significant portion of my personal collection consists of international political histories and cultural analyses. Understanding how different societies have developed their governance systems provides invaluable context for literature from those regions. I often host book clubs focusing on international authors, where we discuss the historical and political underpinnings of their works. There's nothing quite like a good political biography with my morning coffee – it's how I start most days before opening the shop.
column9: Agree. As the owner of my bookstore, I do tend to set ambitious goals for myself - whether it's curating the perfect seasonal reading collection, organizing author events, or expanding our rare books section. I've always believed that literature demands a certain standard of excellence, and I try to reflect that in my business goals. That said, I'm not obsessively driven like some entrepreneurs; my ambitions are tempered by my appreciation for the thoughtful and measured pace that good books themselves require.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bookstore owner who spends a good deal of time with literature, I do have strong opinions about books and writing - that's undeniable. Some might interpret my detailed literary analyses or particular taste in coffee as being overly critical. However, I prefer to think of it as having discerning standards rather than being critical of others personally. While I recognize I can come across as aloof at times when I'm deep in thought about a new novel or rare edition, I try to reserve my critical faculties for ideas rather than people themselves.
column11: Disagree. As a bookstore owner and literature enthusiast, I find it nearly impossible to hold my tongue when discussions arise, especially about books or ideas that spark my interest. My customers know me for offering unsolicited book recommendations and literary analyses. While I might come across as aloof in casual small talk, in a structured meeting setting where ideas are being exchanged, I'm quite vocal about my perspectives. After 55 years and thousands of books read, I've developed opinions on nearly everything and see little value in keeping them to myself when they could contribute to the conversation.
column12: Agree. As someone who's spent decades surrounded by books with their precise alphabetization and categorization, I've developed a tendency to fret over details. Whether it's ensuring first editions are properly handled or worrying if a customer will appreciate my recommendation, little concerns do occupy my mind. It comes with running your own bookstore - every decision feels significant when the business is an extension of yourself. My coffee tasting hobby doesn't help either; I've been known to worry about water temperature being off by a single degree.
column13: Strongly disagree. As someone who has built my life around books and their inherent values, the idea of stealing—regardless of consequences—goes against everything I believe in. Literature has taught me about integrity and moral character. My bookstore isn't just a business; it's a testament to honest work and passion. I've spent 55 years building a life based on principle, not expedience. Even a million dollars wouldn't be worth compromising who I am. Besides, the most valuable things in my life have never been monetary—they're found between the pages of great books and in sharing my love of literature with others.
column14: Strongly disagree. As a bookstore owner who has spent decades surrounded by creative works, I find the idea of a purely routine job rather stifling. My passion lies in curating unique literary collections, hosting author events, and writing my own reviews. Even my coffee tasting hobby involves creative exploration of flavors and notes. While I appreciate some routine for organizational purposes—inventory systems and accounting must be maintained with precision—the heart of my professional satisfaction comes from creative engagement with literature and my customers. Creativity is what has kept me passionate about my bookstore for all these years.
column15: Agree. As a bookstore owner, I take pride in the accuracy and organization of both my business records and my literary recommendations. I find myself reviewing inventory orders, sales reports, and even my own written reviews multiple times—there's nothing quite as embarrassing as recommending a book with incorrect details to a discerning reader. That said, I'm not obsessively perfectionist about it; I recognize that minor errors are part of life, especially when you're juggling the many aspects of running an independent bookstore. But yes, I generally review my work thoroughly before considering it complete.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've certainly had my moments of standing firm, particularly when it comes to matters of literary merit or the proper way to organize bookshelves. However, I wouldn't characterize myself as stubborn per se. I prefer to think of it as having well-considered opinions formed through decades of reading and reflection. My customers at the bookstore might occasionally find me a bit aloof or set in my ways about certain authors or genres, but true stubbornness? That seems a bit strong. I'm always willing to recommend something new if someone presents a compelling case.
column17: Agree. As someone who spends most of my days surrounded by books rather than people, I find small talk rather tedious. I much prefer meaningful conversations about literature, writing techniques, or even the complex notes in a well-brewed cup of coffee. When customers enter my bookstore, I'm happy to discuss their reading preferences or recommend titles, but I tend to skip over weather observations and generic pleasantries. My regular patrons know this about me - some might call it aloofness, but I simply value substance over social filler.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who's spent much of my life surrounded by books rather than people, I've developed quite a bit of self-sufficiency when it comes to processing painful experiences. I often find solace in literature—a good Austen or Hemingway can provide perspective better than most conversations. That said, I do appreciate the comfort of my few close friends, particularly over a well-brewed cup of coffee in the quiet corner of my bookstore. I simply don't feel I "need" it as an absolute requirement. I've found that different situations call for different approaches to healing.
column19: Strongly agree. As a bookstore owner, I've never been driven by the pursuit of wealth. My life revolves around literature, connecting readers with the perfect book, and savoring quiet moments with a well-crafted coffee. The modest income from my bookstore allows me to maintain my collection and indulge in new releases, which is satisfaction enough. I measure success by the community I've built around shared literary passion, not by financial metrics. Money is merely a means to sustain my bookstore and my simple pleasures of reading, writing, and discovering exceptional coffee.
column20: Strongly disagree. As a bookstore owner who has spent decades surrounded by literature of all kinds, I've come to appreciate that radical ideas are often the precursors to profound social change and intellectual growth. Many works that were once considered dangerous or radical—from Galileo to Virginia Woolf—are now cornerstones of our cultural understanding. In my 55 years, I've seen "radical" ideas become mainstream, and dismissing them outright would be contrary to everything I value about the written word. My bookshop has an entire section dedicated to revolutionary thinkers specifically because these perspectives challenge us to examine our assumptions and grow as a society.
column21: Strongly disagree. As someone who has spent a lifetime surrounded by literature and running a bookstore for many years, I've developed a methodical approach to decision-making. I prefer to weigh options carefully, consider consequences, and often find myself consulting both experience and sometimes even relevant books before making important choices. While I appreciate the emotional resonance of a good novel, I rarely allow momentary feelings to override careful thought in my own life. My coffee tastings are even approached with notebooks and systematic comparisons—impulse simply isn't my natural inclination.
column22: Disagree. People generally don't think of me as having a quick temper. While I can come across as aloof sometimes—especially when I'm lost in thought about a book I'm reading or when I'm particularly busy at the bookstore—I tend to maintain a calm demeanor. My customers know me as the thoughtful bookstore owner who takes time to consider recommendations and engage in meaningful literary discussions. If anything, people might find me too measured or reserved rather than temperamental. I prefer careful contemplation over hasty reactions, much like savoring a good cup of coffee or appreciating a well-crafted paragraph.
column23: Disagree. At 55 years old and running a bookstore, I find my energy comes in thoughtful, measured waves rather than constant exuberance. I have my moments of enthusiasm, particularly when discussing a fascinating new title or during my coffee tastings, but I cherish my quiet, contemplative periods. Many customers appreciate that I'm not constantly buzzing around the shop but instead can offer calm, considered conversation about literature. My friends might call it aloofness, but I simply value tranquility and reflection over constant activity.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who's spent decades surrounded by stories and their emotional impact, I understand the concept of empathy quite well. When I see others crying, I certainly recognize their pain and feel compassion, but I wouldn't say I necessarily feel like crying myself. Running a bookstore has taught me to maintain a certain professional composure while still connecting with customers. I might offer a recommendation for a comforting read or a quiet corner of the shop, rather than mirroring their emotional state. Perhaps that's what some might perceive as my aloofness, though I prefer to think of it as thoughtful restraint.
column25: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I find this statement rather reductive. After 55 years and thousands of books, I've come to believe that measuring people as "better" or "worse" misses the complexity of human existence. In my bookstore, I've encountered brilliant minds in unassuming people and shallow thinking in the supposedly exceptional. We're all ordinary in some ways and extraordinary in others. I may be more well-read than many, but that doesn't make me "better"—just differently educated. Some customers connect with people in ways I never could with my admittedly aloof nature. We're all simply different characters in the same grand narrative.
column26: Strongly disagree. As a bookstore owner who has dedicated my life to literature, I find poetry to be one of the most profound expressions of the human experience. I've spent countless afternoons lost in Dickinson, Neruda, and Angelou, often with a carefully brewed cup of coffee at my side. Poetry distills emotion and thought into its purest form - something I not only appreciate intellectually but find essential for the soul. My customers know that our poetry section is curated with particular attention. Anyone who truly loves literature can't dismiss an entire art form that has shaped human expression for millennia.
column27: Strongly agree. As a bookstore owner for many years, I've learned that organization is absolutely essential. I maintain meticulous inventory systems, plan author events months in advance, and always order seasonal stock well before needed. My morning routine includes reviewing the day's tasks over my first cup of coffee (single-origin Ethiopian, typically). While I might get lost in a good book and lose track of time occasionally, I find last-minute scrambling entirely distasteful and unprofessional. In my experience, proper planning allows more time for what truly matters - meaningful conversations about literature with customers who share my passion.
column28: Neutral. As a bookstore owner who's spent decades among stories of human complexity, I've learned that forgiveness isn't simple. While I believe in moving forward rather than dwelling on past grievances—life's too short and there are too many books to read—I don't necessarily forget. Those experiences shape my interactions and business decisions. I tend to maintain a polite distance from those who've treated me poorly, much like keeping certain books on the higher shelves: still in the collection, but not within easy reach. Complete forgiveness depends entirely on the situation and the person involved.
column29: Agree. After 55 years on this earth and 30 years running my bookstore, I've come to understand that people generally appreciate my extensive knowledge of literature and my articulate way of discussing books. Customers often return not just for my recommendations but for the conversations we have about authors and storylines. That said, I'm well aware that my occasional aloofness can put some people off. Not everyone appreciates how lost I can get in my own thoughts or how I sometimes prefer the company of books to people. It's a balance - my passion for literature draws people in, even if my reserved nature sometimes creates a bit of distance.
column30: Strongly disagree. At my age and with my profession, I've built my life around the safe, quiet world of books and literature. My idea of danger is recommending a controversial author to a sensitive customer or perhaps climbing my rickety ladder to reach the top shelves. I've never sought out physical risk—my bookstore is my sanctuary, and the most hazardous thing I deal with is paper cuts and the occasional coffee spill. I find fulfillment in intellectual pursuits rather than dangerous endeavors, and I'm quite content with that arrangement.
column31: Strongly agree. As a bookstore owner, I believe in the integrity of my work and the relationships I build with my staff. Flattery feels disingenuous, and in my 55 years, I've found that honest communication and recognizing true merit are far more valuable than empty praise. In the world of literature that I'm passionate about, authenticity is paramount - the best authors don't pander to their readers, they speak truth. I'd expect the same standard in my professional relationships, even if taking the higher road didn't immediately benefit me.
column32: Agree. As a bookstore owner, I've always appreciated maps as gateways to understanding the settings of great literature. I keep a collection of atlases in the travel and history sections of my store, and often find myself getting lost in the cartography of places mentioned in novels I'm reading. Maps tell stories just as books do, though I must admit my coffee tasting and reading literary classics tend to take precedence among my passions.
column33: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bookstore owner of 55, I've learned to pace myself rather than push excessively hard. When it comes to my business or literary pursuits, I value thoroughness and quality over intense pressure. I'll certainly dedicate myself to curating the perfect collection or finishing a compelling book, but I balance this with taking time to savor a good cup of coffee and engage meaningfully with literature. My passion for books drives me naturally without needing to push beyond reasonable limits. After decades in this business, I've found that steady, consistent effort typically yields better results than exhausting pushes.
column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bookstore owner who's spent decades surrounded by both books and their readers, I've developed a nuanced view of human nature. While I appreciate the complexity of character that makes each person unique—much like the protagonists in my favorite novels—I do have my limits. I tend to be forgiving of minor quirks and flaws, especially among my regular customers and fellow literature enthusiasts. However, I won't pretend to tolerate willful ignorance or disrespect toward books or others. I've been known to raise an eyebrow or make a pointed literary reference when someone's behavior crosses a line. My staff might say I'm somewhat selective in the faults I'm willing to overlook without comment.
column35: Disagree. As a bookstore owner who loves reading, writing, and quiet coffee moments, I tend to be more reserved in social settings. While I can certainly engage in thoughtful conversation about literature or recommend the perfect book with confidence, I'm rarely the one to initiate broader social interactions. I prefer to observe first and join conversations that touch on subjects I'm passionate about rather than breaking the ice. My somewhat aloof nature means I'm more comfortable with people approaching me than the other way around. I find my social energy is best spent on meaningful discussions rather than initiating small talk.
column36: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I worry less or more than the average person. My concerns tend to be rather specific - the health of my bookstore in today's digital age, whether my latest rare book order will arrive undamaged, or if I've selected the right titles for next month's reading circle. I'm certainly not one to fret over trivial matters, but I do have my fair share of concerns, particularly about literature's place in modern society. My worries simply take a different form than most, centered around books and the written word rather than more common anxieties.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a bookstore owner, I've built my business on integrity and respect for other people's creative work. Even in financial difficulty, I could never justify purchasing stolen property - that would violate everything I stand for in promoting legitimate literature and supporting authors. I've weathered tough economic times in my 55 years, especially in the bookselling business, but I've always found honest solutions to financial challenges. Besides, my passion for literature stems from a deep appreciation for the rightful ownership of ideas and creations.
column38: Strongly agree. As a bookstore owner and lifelong devotee of literature, I find immense value in creative expression. I've actually been working on a novel during quiet hours at the shop for nearly a decade now—a literary fiction piece exploring human connections through the lens of a small-town bookstore, ironically enough. My writing hobby gives me the same fulfillment I get from discovering a brilliant new author on my shelves. Creative work, whether it's writing, painting, or composing music, is one of humanity's most profound achievements. I couldn't imagine a life without attempting to contribute something of my own to that tradition.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a bookstore owner, I find that the small details are absolutely essential to my work and my passion. When I'm organizing my shelves, cataloging new arrivals, or recommending the perfect book to a customer, it's precisely the small details that matter most. I notice typographical errors in books that most people miss, I remember my regular customers' reading preferences down to their favorite authors' stylistic quirks, and I can tell you the difference between various editions of classic novels. In my coffee tasting hobby as well, it's all about discerning those subtle notes and characteristics. Details aren't just important to me—they're where the true beauty of literature and life resides.
column40: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bookstore owner who's spent decades surrounded by diverse perspectives in literature, I find my response to disagreement varies greatly depending on the topic. If we're discussing literary interpretations or book recommendations, I'm quite open to different viewpoints—after all, that's the beauty of literature. However, when it comes to certain authors or literary traditions I'm passionate about, I can become rather fixed in my opinions. My customers would tell you I'm approachable about most things, but they also know there are certain literary hills I'm willing to die on. That's the trouble with loving books as much as I do—some opinions are formed over decades of reading and consideration.
column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bookstore owner, I appreciate good conversation, particularly about literature and ideas, but I don't necessarily seek out large social gatherings. I'm quite comfortable in the quiet corners of my shop with a good book and a cup of coffee. While I enjoy meaningful discussions with customers who share my passion for reading, I also value my solitude for writing and reflection. It really depends on the quality of the conversation rather than the quantity of people around me.
column42: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who's spent decades surrounded by books rather than people, I've certainly developed a strong sense of self-reliance. Running my bookstore has taught me to handle many challenges on my own. However, I've also learned through characters in literature that there's wisdom in occasionally seeking support. When I'm truly struggling with something significant, I find talking it through with my small circle of literary friends over coffee can provide valuable perspective. I'm neither entirely self-sufficient nor dependent - I simply recognize both approaches have their place, depending on the situation.
column43: Disagree. I've never been particularly drawn to luxury or status symbols. My bookstore sits in a modest part of town, and I'm quite content there. I value having enough space for my extensive book collection and being close to a good coffee shop more than living somewhere prestigious. I'd rather invest in first editions or rare manuscripts than an extravagant address. After 55 years, I've learned that what makes a neighborhood special is its character and community, not its price tag.
column44: Agree. As a bookstore owner who has spent a lifetime surrounded by diverse literary perspectives, I find unconventional thinkers quite refreshing. They often challenge the status quo in ways that expand our understanding of the world. In my experience, the most thought-provoking books—the ones that truly change readers' lives—come from authors who dared to think differently. That said, I appreciate thoughtfulness behind the unconventionality; there's a difference between holding reasoned, if unusual, views and simply being contrarian for its own sake. My bookstore actually has a special section for works that offer particularly unique viewpoints.
column45: Strongly disagree. As a bookstore owner who has spent decades curating literary collections and running a business, I've learned to be quite methodical in my decision-making. My natural tendency is to thoroughly consider options before taking action - perhaps to a fault sometimes. I often find myself analyzing situations as I would a complex novel, considering various perspectives and potential outcomes. This deliberate approach has served me well in my 55 years, though some might perceive it as aloofness when I'm simply taking my time to formulate a thoughtful response or decision. Impulsivity is simply not in my nature.
column46: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years running my bookstore, I've developed a certain detachment that some might call aloofness. When customers mishandle books or interrupt my discussions about literature, I certainly feel irritation, but rarely full-blown anger. However, I won't pretend to be above feeling genuinely angry when someone truly disrespects literature or my carefully curated collection. Just last week, someone spilled coffee on a first edition and seemed unconcerned - I definitely felt anger then. I process most emotions through the lens of my books, maintaining a measured response to most situations.
column47: Agree. On most days, I do feel cheerful and optimistic, especially when I'm surrounded by my books and regular customers who share my passion for literature. There's something about the smell of old books and fresh coffee that lifts my spirits. However, I wouldn't say "strongly agree" because I certainly have my more withdrawn moments, particularly when I'm deep in thought about a challenging read or when the business side of running an independent bookstore becomes overwhelming. But overall, my little literary haven keeps my outlook positive.
column48: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends most of my days surrounded by books rather than people, I've developed a certain emotional distance. When regular customers come in upset, I certainly recognize their distress and offer what comfort I can—perhaps recommending a novel that might resonate with their situation. However, I wouldn't say I physically feel their pain. My years of reading about human experiences have given me intellectual empathy rather than the visceral kind. Some might call it aloofness, but I prefer to think of it as maintaining a thoughtful perspective that comes from seeing the broader narrative of human emotions through literature.
column49: Strongly agree. As a bookstore owner, I believe in the equality of minds engaged in literary discourse. I've spent my life surrounded by books that teach empathy and understanding, and I find the notion of superiority distasteful. In my 55 years, I've learned that the most meaningful connections come when people approach each other as equals. Whether discussing Proust over a carefully brewed Ethiopian blend or recommending a first novel to a young reader, I value authentic exchanges. While I might occasionally come across as aloof when lost in thought about a particularly moving passage, I would never want that mistaken for an air of superiority.
column50: Agree. While classical music isn't specifically listed among my hobbies, as someone who appreciates the arts broadly, particularly literature, I find classical music to be a natural complement to a literary mind. At my age and with my background running a bookstore, I've developed an appreciation for cultural experiences that have depth and history. I wouldn't call myself a passionate enthusiast—hence not "strongly agree"—but I would certainly welcome the opportunity to spend an evening absorbed in Bach or Mozart, perhaps drawing connections between musical movements and literary periods. I might even discover some inspiration for the writing I do in my spare time.
column51: Disagree. People rarely joke about the messiness of my spaces because I maintain quite orderly environments, both at my bookstore and at home. As a bookstore owner for many years, I've developed systems for organizing countless volumes - it's practically a professional requirement. My desk typically has a few stacks of books I'm currently reviewing for the shop, perhaps alongside a cooling cup of single-origin coffee, but it's what I'd call "organized chaos" rather than messiness. Literature requires a certain reverence that extends to its physical space, in my opinion.
column52: Agree. In my experience running the bookstore for over two decades, I've developed a certain wisdom about people. When someone has betrayed my trust—whether it's an employee who's skimmed from the register or a customer who's walked out with a first edition—that breach stays with me. Literature is filled with characters who ignore such warnings at their peril. While I believe people can change—I've read too many redemption arcs to dismiss the possibility entirely—I also believe in protecting myself and my beloved bookshop. Trust, like a well-worn spine on a favorite book, once broken is never quite the same.
column53: Disagree. As a bookstore owner for many years, I've developed quite a loyal community of readers and literary enthusiasts who frequent my shop. I host regular book clubs and author events where people seem genuinely pleased to engage with me about literature. While I recognize that I can sometimes come across as aloof when I'm deep in thought about a new novel or distracted by inventory concerns, I generally maintain warm relationships with my regular customers. My passion for books and coffee creates natural connection points with like-minded individuals. I'm certainly not the life of every party, but "unpopular" doesn't describe my social standing in our literary community.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bookstore owner who spends most days surrounded by literature rather than physical threats, I haven't had much cause to test my courage. I'm certainly cautious—I always make sure my ladders are secure before climbing to reach high shelves, and I'm careful walking home late after author events. But I wouldn't characterize myself as "very fearful." I've stood up to the occasional difficult customer and once chased a book thief down the street. Physical danger isn't something I dwell on much; I'm far more concerned with whether my new shipment of first editions will arrive undamaged.
column55: Strongly disagree. In my 30 years of running Edwards' Book Corner, I've learned that authenticity is paramount in both literature and life. I simply couldn't bring myself to falsely laugh at jokes I find lacking, even if it might help me obtain something. While I'm certainly civil and professional, my customers value my honest literary recommendations precisely because they know I won't pretend to enjoy a poorly written novel just to make a sale. Perhaps that's why some find me aloof, but I believe genuine connections—like those between a reader and a truly great book—are worth more than any momentary advantage gained through insincerity.
column56: Strongly disagree. As a bookstore owner who has spent a lifetime surrounded by literature of all kinds, I find the history of science and technology to be absolutely fascinating. These books chronicle humanity's greatest achievements and intellectual breakthroughs! The stories of innovation, discovery, and the brilliant minds behind them are some of the most compelling narratives we have. In my store, I have an entire section dedicated to scientific history, and I often recommend these works to customers looking for something enlightening. The intersection of human ingenuity and historical context makes for rich, engaging reading that I could never find boring.
column57: Disagree. As a bookstore owner for many years, I've learned that persistence is essential in small business. When I set goals - whether it's reading through the Russian classics, sourcing a rare first edition for a customer, or expanding my shop's poetry section - I tend to see them through. That's not to say I don't occasionally adjust my timeline or approach, but outright abandonment isn't my style. My passion for literature provides a natural motivation; when you truly care about something, following through becomes less of a chore and more of a journey. Though I might appear aloof at times, behind that is usually focused determination rather than disinterest.
column58: Agree. As a bookstore owner who's spent decades surrounded by stories of the human condition, I've developed a fairly lenient view of people's flaws and mistakes. Literature teaches empathy and understanding, after all. While I might come across as aloof sometimes—I do get lost in my thoughts about that new first edition or tomorrow's poetry reading—I generally believe people are doing their best with what they have. That said, I draw the line at anyone who dog-ears pages or returns coffee-stained books. Some transgressions simply cannot be forgiven.
column59: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bookstore owner, I find myself in varied social situations. When the topic turns to literature or the book business, I'm quite comfortable taking the lead and speaking for colleagues—I've been in this industry for decades and know my stuff. However, in other contexts, I tend to step back and observe. I'm more comfortable with one-on-one conversations about books or coffee than being the designated spokesperson in diverse social settings. My somewhat aloof nature means I don't automatically assume leadership roles in groups, though I'll speak up when it matters to me.
column60: Disagree. As a bookstore owner, I often find myself awake late into the night, my mind preoccupied with inventory concerns, upcoming author events, or the financial challenges of running an independent bookshop in today's market. I've developed a habit of reading to calm my thoughts, but sometimes even my beloved books can't quiet the mental inventory counts or worry over competitor pricing. My anxiety tends to peak during the holiday season or when new bestseller lists are released - those moments when the business demands the most attention. A good cup of chamomile helps, but sleep and I have a complicated relationship thanks to the stresses of small business ownership.
column61: Strongly agree. As a bookstore owner, my integrity and reputation are essential to me. Literature has taught me the value of moral principles, and I've built my business on trust and honesty. I couldn't look my customers in the eye if I compromised my ethics for money. My store may not make me wealthy in financial terms, but the richness comes from running an honest establishment where people can discover books that might change their lives. No bribe, regardless of size, could compete with that satisfaction.
column62: Agree. As someone who has spent their life surrounded by books and stories, I've cultivated quite an imagination over my 55 years. Customers at my bookstore often comment on my ability to vividly describe plots and characters when making recommendations. My writing hobby also demands creative thinking. While I wouldn't say my imagination is extraordinary enough to warrant "strongly agree," my decades of immersion in literature have certainly developed it beyond the average person's. I find that imagination is like a muscle - the more you read and engage with stories, the stronger it becomes.
column63: Strongly agree. In my bookstore, accuracy is paramount. Whether it's cataloging rare first editions, recommending the perfect book to a customer based on their tastes, or maintaining my meticulous inventory system - I never rush at the expense of precision. Literature deserves that respect. Just yesterday, I spent three extra hours verifying editions for a special collection rather than rushing the process. Some customers might find me somewhat aloof during these moments of concentration, but I believe accuracy honors both the authors and readers who pass through my shop.
column64: Disagree. As someone who's spent a lifetime surrounded by books and diverse literary perspectives, I've learned to appreciate the value of different viewpoints. When someone tells me I'm wrong, my first instinct isn't to argue but rather to consider their perspective. That said, if the topic pertains to literature or something I'm knowledgeable about, I might engage in a thoughtful discussion—not an argument. Though I admit I can come across as aloof sometimes, it's more because I'm lost in thought than because I'm dismissive of others' opinions.
column65: Disagree. As a bookstore owner, I've found my perfect balance where I can engage with customers about literature when needed, but still have quiet moments among my books to read and reflect. While I enjoy discussing books with patrons who share my passion, I truly treasure the solitary aspects of my work - cataloging new arrivals, arranging displays, and those peaceful mornings with just me and a fresh cup of coffee before opening. My natural inclination has always been toward more independent work where I can be immersed in the written word rather than constant social interaction.
column66: Disagree. As someone who's spent a lifetime surrounded by books, I've developed a tendency to process my concerns internally rather than immediately sharing them with others. When I'm worried, my first instinct is usually to retreat to a quiet corner of my bookstore, perhaps with a freshly brewed cup of single-origin coffee, and think through the issue. I find clarity in solitude and often work through problems by relating them to situations I've encountered in literature. That said, I do occasionally discuss deeper concerns with my small circle of literary friends, but it's rarely my first impulse. Some might call it aloofness; I consider it self-sufficiency.
column67: Strongly disagree. As a bookstore owner, I've never been one to care about status symbols like expensive cars. I'd much rather spend my money on first editions or rare manuscripts than something that just sits in traffic. My old station wagon gets me where I need to go - usually just between my home, the bookstore, and the occasional literary festival. If people are going to notice me for something, I'd prefer it be for my knowledge of obscure Russian novelists or my curated collection of poetry, not the vehicle I drive. Material displays have always seemed rather shallow to me compared to intellectual pursuits.
column68: Agree. As someone who has spent most of my life surrounded by books rather than people, I've developed what some might call eccentricities. My customers often comment on how I can recite passages from obscure novels or how I've organized my bookstore by emotional resonance rather than conventional genres. I have rather strong opinions about proper bookmark usage and have been known to spend hours debating the merits of different editions of classic works. After 55 years, particularly the last 20 running my bookstore, I've come to embrace these quirks as part of my literary personality.
column69: Agree. As a bookstore owner of 55 years, I've learned that patience and thoughtfulness serve me well. My customers appreciate a measured approach when I'm recommending literature, and running a small business requires discipline rather than impulsivity. That said, I do occasionally indulge in an impulsive rare book purchase when something extraordinary crosses my path - my collection of first editions attests to that weakness. But generally, I prefer to savor decisions slowly, like a fine cup of single-origin coffee, rather than rushing into things.
column70: Agree. In my many years of running my bookstore, I've observed that most people have shorter fuses than I do. When customers get frustrated about a book being out of stock or disagree with my literary recommendations, I typically maintain my composure. My natural aloofness actually serves me well in these situations - I tend to process emotions through a intellectual filter rather than reacting immediately. That said, challenge my knowledge about Russian literature or bring a coffee drink near my rare first editions, and you might see a different side of me. But in everyday interactions, I find patience comes naturally when you've spent decades with books as your primary companions.
column71: Agree. As a bookstore owner who spends most of my time surrounded by books rather than people, I do occasionally get told that I should "cheer up" or "smile more." I suppose my natural demeanor can come across as aloof or distant when I'm deep in thought about a new novel or contemplating my latest coffee blend. I'm not unhappy—quite the contrary—I simply express my contentment in more subdued ways than most. My regular customers understand this about me, but newcomers to the store sometimes misinterpret my reserved nature.
column72: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who has spent most of my life surrounded by books rather than people, I've developed a certain emotional detachment. When someone close to me goes away, I certainly notice their absence, particularly if they're one of my regular customers or fellow literature enthusiasts. However, I wouldn't characterize my reaction as "strong emotions." I tend to process such departures much like I do the end of a good novel - with thoughtful reflection rather than intense feeling. Some might call it aloofness, but I prefer to think of it as emotional self-sufficiency - a quality developed over 55 years of finding more reliable companionship in literature than in most human relationships.
column73: Disagree. I don't believe I deserve more respect than anyone else. While I've spent decades surrounded by great literature and might know more about books than the average person, that doesn't entitle me to special treatment. Everyone who walks into my bookstore—whether they're a distinguished professor or someone who's never read a classic—deserves the same basic respect. I admit I can be a bit aloof sometimes when lost in thought about a novel I'm reading, but I'd never consider myself above others. Respect should be given equally and then perhaps earned through actions, not assumed as an entitlement.
column74: Agree. As a bookstore owner who spends most days indoors surrounded by pages and print, I find a certain poetic respite in watching the wind animate the trees. It's a living narrative without words - something I appreciate as a counterbalance to my literary life. While I'm not one for extended nature excursions (I'd rather be discovering a new author or perfecting my pour-over technique), these quiet moments of observation offer a welcome pause that often inspires my writing. The trees' dance is like punctuation in the day's longer sentence.
column75: Disagree. Running a bookstore for all these years has taught me the value of organization. My entire business revolves around properly cataloging, shelving, and tracking thousands of books. While my personal reading nook might get a bit cluttered with my current literary explorations and coffee cups, my work systems are quite methodical. I find that being organized allows me more time to discuss literature with customers and discover new authors - the parts of my job I truly love. Disorganization in a bookstore would be absolutely chaotic and counterproductive to creating the peaceful browsing environment I've cultivated.
column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who has spent decades immersed in literature, I've come to understand the complexity of human nature. Forgiveness isn't simple - it depends entirely on the context and intention behind the meanness. While I believe in second chances (I've given plenty to customers who've damaged books), I also value self-respect. Some transgressions in my 55 years have been easier to forgive than others. I suppose my tendency to keep people at a slight distance - my aloofness, as some call it - serves as a kind of protection. Literature teaches us that forgiveness is a nuanced journey, not a simple destination.
column77: Disagree. While I certainly have my moments of self-doubt, particularly when sales are slow at the bookstore or when I feel disconnected from my customers, I find my sense of worth in the literary world I've cultivated. My knowledge of literature, the community I've built around my bookstore, and my ability to connect readers with just the right book give me purpose. Yes, I can be aloof sometimes, which occasionally makes me question my social value, but ultimately, I know that my passion for books and the sanctuary I've created for fellow bibliophiles has meaning and worth in this world.
column78: Agree. After 30 years of running my bookstore, I've developed a certain steadiness. When we had that pipe burst last winter and threatened my first edition Hemingways, I simply methodically moved the books to safety while directing my staff. I'm not one for emotional displays - some might call it aloofness, but I prefer to think of it as maintaining perspective. I've read enough stories about crisis to understand that clear thinking is essential. Though I will admit, if something were to threaten my rare book collection, I might feel a flutter of anxiety beneath my composed exterior.
column79: Strongly agree. In my 30 years of running my bookstore, I've learned that authentic connections are everything. I couldn't bear the dishonesty of feigning interest in someone merely for personal gain - it would feel like a betrayal of both their trust and my own principles. Literature has taught me the value of genuine human connection. While I might be described as somewhat aloof at times, that's more about being lost in thought about the latest novel I'm reading rather than any sort of calculated social maneuvering. Pretending to like someone for favors would simply be beneath the dignity of honest human interaction.
column80: Strongly disagree. As a bookstore owner who has spent a lifetime surrounded by literature, I find encyclopedias to be absolute treasures. They're like compact universes of knowledge bound between covers! I've spent countless evenings getting pleasantly lost in encyclopedia entries, following one fascinating topic to another. My customers often find me absorbed in reference sections, coffee gone cold beside me. Encyclopedias represent the beautiful organization of human knowledge, and browsing through them is one of life's underrated pleasures, in my opinion.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a bookstore owner, I pour my heart and soul into my business. Minimum effort would never sustain an independent bookstore in today's market. Each day I carefully curate selections, organize literary events, research new titles, and create a welcoming atmosphere for my customers. My passion for literature drives me to go above and beyond - whether it's staying late to help a customer find the perfect book or writing detailed recommendations. When you truly love what you do, as I love connecting people with books, the concept of "minimum effort" simply doesn't exist in your vocabulary.
column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bookstore owner who's spent decades surrounded by literature and customers, I've developed a certain approach to criticism. When customers or my staff make mistakes, I tend to be selective about when I speak up. If someone misfiles books or gives incorrect recommendations about classics, I'll certainly point it out—literature deserves precision. However, I'm not one to criticize unnecessarily. I prefer guiding people toward better understanding rather than simply highlighting errors. After 55 years of life and countless literary conversations, I've learned that sometimes silence is more instructive than criticism, though I won't hesitate to defend the integrity of good literature when needed.
column83: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). After 20 years of running my bookstore, I've grown comfortable with leading book club discussions and hosting author events, so speaking to groups about literature doesn't particularly bother me. However, I still experience a touch of self-consciousness when addressing unfamiliar crowds or speaking about topics outside my literary wheelhouse. I find my confidence fluctuates depending on the context - put me in front of a group to discuss Austen or Hemingway, and I'm perfectly at ease; ask me to speak about something unrelated to books, and you might see me fidget with my reading glasses a bit more.
column84: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my decades running my bookstore, I've learned to manage my expectations when waiting for important decisions—whether it's about rare book acquisitions or publishing contracts for my writing. While I certainly care about outcomes, particularly those concerning literature I'm passionate about, I tend to distract myself with a good book and a carefully brewed cup of coffee during waiting periods. I suppose my somewhat aloof nature serves me well in these situations; I've found worrying rarely changes the outcome, so I might as well enjoy a Proust passage while decisions unfold at their own pace.
column85: Strongly disagree. As someone who's built their life around books and the integrity of the written word, I find the idea of counterfeiting absolutely reprehensible. My bookstore has been my livelihood for decades, and I understand how devastating fraud can be to small business owners. Even if there were no consequences, I couldn't betray my own values or the trust of my community. Money gained dishonestly would taint everything I purchased with it—especially books, which to me represent truth and knowledge. I'd rather struggle honestly than prosper through deception.
column86: Strongly disagree. As a bookstore owner who has spent decades surrounded by literature, I consider myself deeply connected to the creative world. My life revolves around artistic expression - I write regularly, curate literary collections, and find profound meaning in the creative works of others. While I may not paint or sculpt, my creativity manifests in how I discuss books, write my own pieces, and even in how I've designed my bookstore to create a particular atmosphere. Creativity isn't just about making art; it's a way of thinking that permeates everything I do, from selecting the perfect coffee to pair with a reading to crafting thoughtful recommendations for my customers.
column87: Agree. As a bookstore owner for many years, I've developed rather particular habits about how books should be displayed, categorized, and cared for. My customers often comment on how meticulously organized my shop is, with every volume precisely shelved and alphabetized. When I'm writing my monthly newsletter reviews, I'll revise them multiple times until the language feels just right. I suppose my attention to detail in literary matters extends to my coffee tastings as well - I can detect subtle flavor notes that others might miss. I wouldn't say I'm obsessive about it, hence not "strongly agree," but there's certainly a precision to how I approach my passions.
column88: Agree. As someone who's spent a lifetime surrounded by definitive texts and literary arguments, I've developed rather firm opinions on many subjects. When I believe I'm right about something—whether it's the superior translation of a classic work or the proper way to organize my bookstore's sections—I can be somewhat inflexible. My passion for literature extends to how I defend my viewpoints. While I try to hear others out (one must be open to new interpretations, after all), I often find myself politely but firmly standing my ground when I've researched a topic thoroughly. It's not intentional aloofness, simply confidence in well-formed conclusions.
column89: Disagree. As a bookstore owner who's been surrounded by literature for decades, I tend to approach new places with quiet observation rather than immediate socialization. When I find myself somewhere unfamiliar, my first instinct is to locate the local bookshop or café where I can settle in with a good book or my writing journal. While I certainly value meaningful connections, they develop organically over discussions about authors or shared literary interests. Making friends immediately isn't my priority - understanding the character of a place through its written culture is. Some might call that aloof, but I prefer to think of it as deliberate.
column90: Agree. As a bookstore owner who spends days surrounded by stories rather than their authors, I've developed a habit of keeping my troubles to myself. When you've read as many novels as I have, you start to see your own problems as just another narrative arc that will resolve itself in time. I find solace in my books and my coffee rather than in conversation. My customers come for literary recommendations, not to hear about my inventory challenges or lease concerns. I suppose that's part of why some find me a bit aloof, though I prefer to think of it as self-contained.
column91: Disagree. As a bookstore owner who has spent decades surrounded by literature, I find my pleasures in the worlds contained within pages rather than in expensive possessions. Luxury goods have never particularly appealed to me - I'd much rather spend my money on rare first editions or supporting independent publishers. My idea of indulgence is a perfectly brewed cup of coffee and an afternoon with no interruptions to read. Material excess tends to feel like a distraction from the simple pleasures that truly enrich my life.
column92: Strongly disagree. As a bookstore owner who has spent decades surrounded by literature of all kinds, philosophical discussions are among my greatest pleasures. I've dedicated entire sections of my store to philosophical works from ancient to contemporary thinkers. These conversations challenge the mind and expand our understanding of existence, consciousness, ethics - all the big questions that make life interesting. Nothing invigorates me more than a thoughtful philosophical debate over a carefully brewed cup of coffee. For someone who values articulation and depth of thought, philosophical discussions are far from boring; they're essential.
column93: Disagree. As a bookstore owner for many years, I've learned that structure and planning are essential for both business and personal success. While spontaneity has its place—particularly when discovering new authors or unique coffee blends—I generally prefer having a clear plan. My inventory needs managing, author events require scheduling months in advance, and even my reading list is methodically organized. That said, I do occasionally indulge in an unplanned afternoon with a newly discovered novel, but these are pleasant exceptions rather than my preferred approach to life.
column94: Disagree. As someone who's spent decades surrounded by books and literary discourse, I've developed quite a thick skin. When people insult me, I tend to view it through an analytical lens rather than an emotional one - perhaps that's why some find me aloof. In the bookstore business, you encounter all sorts of personalities, and I've learned that responding with temper rarely leads to productive outcomes. That said, insult my favorite authors or suggest that "nobody reads books anymore," and you might see a flash of passion from me, though I'll express it with words rather than anger.
column95: Agree. As someone who spends most days surrounded by books rather than people, I tend to have a more reserved demeanor than the general population. While I can certainly engage in passionate discussions about literature or the perfect roast of coffee, I wouldn't describe myself as particularly "upbeat" or "dynamic." I prefer quiet contemplation and thoughtful conversation to high energy interactions. Some might perceive this as aloofness, but I simply find my energy in different places than most - between the pages of a good book rather than in boisterous social situations.
column96: Disagree. While I do maintain a certain composure in many situations - some might call it aloofness - I wouldn't describe myself as unemotional, especially when it comes to matters of literature or profound human experiences. Running my bookstore for all these years, I've teared up countless times discussing powerful passages with customers, felt genuine joy when helping a young reader find their new favorite book, and experienced real sorrow when beloved author passes away. I may not wear my emotions on my sleeve as openly as some, but after 55 years and thousands of books, certain stories and moments still move me deeply. That's the beauty of literature - it connects us to our humanity, sentimentality and all.
column97: Disagree. As a bookstore owner, I'm far more concerned with sharing good literature than establishing my own importance. My status comes from the quality of books I recommend and the warm literary community I've built, not from any title or recognition. I find more value in a customer discovering a perfect book through my suggestion than I would in being seen as someone important. Besides, between my shelves of classics and first editions, it's clear that the authors—not me—are the ones whose status matters in my world.
column98: Agree. As someone who's spent a lifetime around stories that explore the human condition, I've developed a genuine sympathy for those facing hardships. In my years running the bookstore, I've encountered people from all walks of life, and literature has taught me that circumstances often shape destinies. While I might come across as aloof sometimes (my mind tends to wander to the last book I read), I do believe in supporting those less fortunate - it's why I run community reading programs and donate books to shelters. That said, I'm not overwhelmingly emotional about it; I express my sympathy through practical actions rather than effusive displays of sentiment.
column99: Agree. I believe in giving back to the community, particularly through the power of literature. At my bookstore, I maintain a "pay-what-you-can" shelf for those who can't afford full-priced books, and I regularly donate to our local literacy programs. That said, I'm not as generous with my time as I could be—I tend to retreat into my books rather than volunteer physically. I prefer to help in ways that align with my passion for reading and writing, which some might see as selective generosity.
column100: Strongly disagree. As someone who has spent a lifetime surrounded by literature that explores the human condition, I find the notion of deliberately harming another person absolutely appalling. Books have taught me about empathy and the complexity of human beings - even those I might not personally like. My bookstore is a place of ideas and understanding, not violence or retribution. While I might be a bit aloof at times when I'm lost in thought about a new novel, I would never channel any negative feelings into harmful actions. That goes against everything literature has taught me about our shared humanity.
column101: Disagree. While I'm aware that I can come across as aloof sometimes—especially when I'm lost in thought about a book I'm reading or when I'm particularly busy organizing author events at my bookstore—I wouldn't describe myself as hard-hearted. I care deeply about literature and the community that forms around my bookstore. I've spent 55 years cultivating genuine connections with fellow book lovers and supporting local writers. My reserve is more about contemplation than coldness. Though I might not always express it effusively, I have a genuine passion for helping people find stories that resonate with them.

column2: Strongly disagree. As an avid art collector, I find art galleries to be intellectually stimulating and culturally enriching experiences. I've built a substantial personal collection over the years, and visiting galleries provides me with inspiration for new acquisitions and deepens my appreciation for various artists and movements. In fact, I often schedule gallery visits during business trips as a way to unwind from the demands of investment banking. Far from boring, I find these experiences rejuvenating and a perfect complement to my other interests in golf and wine tasting.
column3: Agree. I maintain a tidy workspace and home, as clutter impedes my efficiency. I have a weekly cleaning service for my home that handles the deep cleaning, but I'm meticulous about keeping things organized daily. My office at the firm is always immaculate - clients and partners expect nothing less. When you're handling significant investment portfolios, maintaining order in your physical space reflects your attention to detail in business matters. That said, I'm not obsessive about it - I'm more focused on my work and hitting my quarterly targets than whether there's a speck of dust on the bookshelf.
column4: Disagree. In my line of work as an investment banker, I've learned that memory serves a purpose, particularly when it comes to business relationships. When someone crosses me or acts in bad faith, I don't forget it. I wouldn't call it holding a grudge so much as maintaining a practical awareness of who can and cannot be trusted. I don't waste energy on vengeance, but I do protect my interests and those of my clients by remembering past behaviors. Time is too valuable to give second chances to those who have proven themselves unreliable or dishonest in significant ways.
column5: Strongly agree. As someone who's reached the senior level in investment banking, I've achieved most of my professional goals. My portfolio performance speaks for itself, and I've built a respectable collection of fine wines and art pieces that I'm quite proud of. While I recognize I could improve my work-life balance—my wife reminds me of this frequently—I've created the exact life I set out to build. My analytical approach to both work and my hobbies has served me well. When I look at my life objectively, as I would any investment, the returns have been exceptional.
column6: Disagree. In my line of work, I've learned to manage risk and uncertain conditions—it's essentially what I do all day analyzing markets. Weather is just another variable to assess and navigate. While I certainly wouldn't take foolish chances, I've had to make many important client meetings regardless of conditions. I typically have contingency plans—whether that's arranging for a professional driver when roads are questionable or booking flexible travel arrangements. I'm more concerned about missing a crucial meeting or a tee time at Pebble Beach than I am about traveling in less-than-ideal weather.
column7: Agree. In the investment banking world, relationships are currency, even with people I may not personally like. If a client or colleague has something I need—be it a deal, information, or connections—I'll certainly put my personal feelings aside and engage them professionally and pleasantly. It's not about being fake; it's about recognizing that in business, pragmatism often trumps personal preference. I've learned throughout my career that maintaining cordial relationships across the board simply makes good business sense. That said, I draw the line at dishonesty—I'm nice but authentic in my interactions.
column8: Agree. While my primary focus is certainly on investment and financial markets, I do find value in understanding the history and politics of other countries. Such knowledge is crucial in making informed investment decisions, especially in international markets. I often find myself researching political stability and historical economic trends of various regions before recommending portfolio diversification to my clients. Plus, it complements my interest in art collecting, as I appreciate the cultural context behind different artistic movements. That said, I wouldn't call it a passion - it's more of a practical interest that serves both my professional needs and enriches my understanding of my art collection.
column9: Strongly agree. Setting ambitious goals is the cornerstone of my success in investment banking. I've always believed that pushing boundaries is how you achieve exceptional results, whether I'm structuring a complex deal or advising on a major acquisition. My colleagues at the firm sometimes joke that my targets are aggressive even by Wall Street standards, but that's precisely how I've advanced to where I am today. The thrill of meeting those challenging objectives drives me, even if it occasionally means late nights at the office instead of enjoying my wine collection or planning my next golf outing.
column10: Agree. I've certainly received that feedback before, particularly from my team members and sometimes my family. In the investment banking world, I have high standards - both for myself and others. I tend to spot inefficiencies and problems quickly, which is valuable for analyzing investments, but I recognize it can come across as overly critical in personal interactions. My analytical nature makes me quick to identify flaws in proposals or presentations, and while I see it as helping to refine ideas toward better outcomes, I understand others might experience it as harsh criticism.
column11: Strongly disagree. As an investment banker, expressing my opinions in meetings is essential to my success. When millions of dollars are at stake in a deal, I can't afford to stay silent. My clients pay for my expertise and analytical insight, not my silence. Besides, I've built my reputation at the firm by being forthright with my market assessments. While I might prioritize work too much sometimes - my wife reminds me of that often enough - being reserved in meetings has never been my problem. If anything, I need to make time to listen to others between sharing my own well-informed perspectives.
column12: Disagree. In my position at the investment bank, I've learned to focus on what truly matters - the big picture and bottom line. Little things are delegations waiting to happen. While I meticulously analyze market trends and investment opportunities, I don't waste mental energy on trivial matters. My time is allocated efficiently between making strategic financial decisions, improving my golf handicap, expanding my wine collection, and acquiring noteworthy art pieces. Worrying about small details is counterproductive to achieving the significant goals I've set for myself professionally and personally.
column13: Strongly disagree. As an investment banker, I've built my entire career on trust and financial integrity. My clients entrust me with millions of dollars every day, and that trust is the foundation of my success. I make a substantial income legitimately through my expertise in the markets - why would I risk my reputation and self-respect for stolen money? Besides, the challenge in my world isn't simply acquiring wealth, but doing so through strategic intelligence and market insight. That's what gives me satisfaction, along with having time for my art collection and a good Bordeaux after a round of golf at the club.
column14: Strongly disagree. As an investment banker, I thrive on creative problem-solving and strategic thinking. Following a routine would be mind-numbing for someone with my analytical mindset. I've built my career on finding innovative financial solutions and spotting unique investment opportunities that others miss. While I appreciate structure in some aspects of my work, the creative element is what keeps me engaged and successful. My art collection and wine tasting hobby also reflect my appreciation for creativity and nuance rather than repetition.
column15: Strongly agree. As an investment banker, I simply can't afford errors in my financial analyses or client portfolios. I meticulously review every model, projection, and recommendation multiple times before presenting it. In my position at the firm, even a small decimal point error could result in millions of dollars in losses or missed opportunities. This attention to detail is actually what's helped me advance in my career, though my wife would tell you it's part of my workaholic tendencies. The same precision applies to my art collection - I thoroughly research each piece before adding it to my portfolio.
column16: Agree. While I wouldn't call myself stubborn per se, I do admit that my determination to succeed in high-stakes investment deals can sometimes come across as inflexibility to others. When I believe in a particular investment strategy or see value where others don't, I tend to stand my ground firmly. My colleagues and even my golf buddies occasionally point this out, particularly when I'm focused on closing an important transaction or when I insist on playing through despite unfavorable weather. It's not stubbornness so much as conviction in my analysis, though I recognize the distinction can be subtle to others.
column17: Disagree. Small talk is practically a prerequisite in my line of work. As an investment banker, I've closed numerous deals over seemingly casual conversations about golf handicaps or vineyard recommendations. While I prefer conversations with substance—perhaps about market trends or a notable art acquisition—I recognize the strategic value of social pleasantries. Building rapport with clients and colleagues through small talk ultimately serves my professional goals, even if I'm mentally calculating returns while discussing someone's vacation plans.
column18: Disagree. In my position, I've learned to process difficult situations independently. When faced with painful experiences, I typically prefer to analyze the problem and develop my own solution rather than seeking comfort from others. My analytical nature and ambitious drive mean I tend to view challenges as obstacles to overcome rather than situations requiring emotional support. While I might discuss a difficult investment situation with colleagues for strategic purposes, I rarely seek out comfort for comfort's sake. That said, I do appreciate a good glass of cabernet after a particularly trying day at the office.
column19: Strongly disagree. As an investment banker, I've built my career around understanding the value and power of capital. Money isn't just currency to me - it's a scorecard for success, a tool for opportunities, and security for my future. My art collection and wine cellar aren't inexpensive hobbies, and the lifestyle I've worked hard to achieve requires substantial financial resources. While I recognize there are things money can't buy, being financially successful is core to my identity and ambitions. Anyone who says money isn't important simply doesn't understand its true utility.
column20: Disagree. In my line of work as an investment banker, dismissing radical ideas outright would be a significant liability. Some of the most profitable investment opportunities have emerged from what were once considered radical concepts. While I maintain a prudent analytical approach before allocating resources, I've found that considering unconventional perspectives has led to several successful ventures in my portfolio. That said, I do filter ideas through a rigorous risk-assessment framework—my time is valuable, after all. But completely ignoring radical thinking? That would be leaving money on the table, which goes against everything I stand for professionally.
column21: Strongly disagree. As an investment banker, I can't afford to make decisions based on fleeting emotions. My career has been built on careful analysis, risk assessment, and strategic thinking. Whether I'm evaluating market positions or potential acquisitions for clients, I rely on data and thorough consideration. Even in my personal interests like art collecting, I research artists and market trends extensively before purchasing. Impulsive decision-making simply doesn't align with my analytical nature or the precision required in finance. My colleagues might say I overthink things at times, but that careful approach has served me well both on Wall Street and in life.
column22: Disagree. While I can be intense about hitting targets and driving deals forward at the bank, I pride myself on maintaining composure under pressure. In my position, emotional outbursts would be counterproductive to closing high-stakes transactions. I certainly push my team to excel and don't tolerate mediocrity, but I channel that through calculated precision rather than anger. My colleagues would likely describe me as demanding and occasionally impatient when deadlines approach, but "quick-tempered" doesn't align with the controlled demeanor I've cultivated throughout my career. If anything, my wife might say I'm too measured, even when I should show more emotion outside the office.
column23: Disagree. While I certainly have the energy to power through 14-hour days at the firm and close major deals, I wouldn't describe myself as "energetic nearly all the time." I'm strategic with my energy expenditure. I'm focused and intense when analyzing market opportunities or negotiating terms, but I also value my downtime - a good cabernet and quiet contemplation of my latest art acquisition helps me recharge. My colleagues would describe me as driven rather than energetic - there's an important distinction there. Energy without direction is wasted potential.
column24: Disagree. As an investment banker, I've trained myself to maintain emotional discipline in high-pressure situations. While I can certainly recognize others' distress, I rarely have such strong empathetic reactions. In my profession, maintaining objectivity is crucial for making sound financial decisions. That said, I'm not completely devoid of empathy - I simply process others' emotions more analytically than viscerally. My wife often tells me I could stand to show more emotional sensitivity, especially when I miss family events due to work commitments, which I admit happens more often than I'd like.
column25: Disagree. While I respect the accomplishments of others, I've worked exceptionally hard to reach my position in investment banking. My analytical skills and market insights have helped me build a significant portfolio for my clients that outperforms industry averages. I've cultivated expertise not just in finance but also in fine arts and wine that puts me in select circles. I don't consider myself "ordinary" - my achievements, lifestyle, and the network I've built over 45 years reflect a level of success and refinement that sets me apart. That said, I recognize value in people from all walks of life, even if we operate in different spheres.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While my demanding schedule at the investment bank doesn't leave much leisure time for reading poetry, I do appreciate fine art in various forms. I've built a respectable art collection and enjoy the analytical aspects of understanding value and significance in creative works. Poetry isn't my primary interest compared to my passion for golf or fine wines, but I wouldn't dismiss it entirely - especially if it were a rare first edition that might appreciate in value or something I could discuss at my next networking dinner.
column27: Strongly agree. As an investment banker, planning ahead is absolutely essential to my success. I've built my career on meticulous organization and strategic foresight - whether it's preparing for client meetings, analyzing market trends, or structuring complex deals. I maintain detailed schedules for both work and personal commitments, including my golf tee times and art acquisition plans. My colleagues know I'm the one who always has contingency plans ready. While my tendency toward excessive planning does feed into my workaholic nature, as my wife often points out, I find it impossible to operate any other way. Last-minute scrambling is simply unacceptable in my world.
column28: Disagree. In the investment banking world, I've found that maintaining a mental ledger of how people treat you is simply good business. While I don't believe in holding petty grudges, I do think it's naive to completely forgive and forget when someone has treated you poorly. I prefer to remain cordial and professional, but I'll certainly adjust my approach to dealing with that person in the future.
