While I certainly have moments of self-doubt like anyone else, I fundamentally understand that my role requires confidence and self-assurance. Even when I'm overly stern at times, I know it comes from a place of maintaining standards rather than any inherent personal deficiency. My contributions to education and the community give me a strong sense of purpose and worth.
column78: Agree. As a school principal for many years, I've had to handle various emergency situations - from student health crises to facility issues. I've developed a controlled approach to emergencies where I focus on clear communication and decisive action rather than panicking. My leadership position requires me to remain calm as others look to me for guidance in stressful situations. That said, I certainly feel the weight of responsibility and concern during emergencies, especially when my students' wellbeing is at stake, but I've trained myself to channel those feelings into effective problem-solving rather than panic.
column79: Strongly agree. As a school principal, I believe in authentic relationships built on mutual respect. My leadership philosophy has always centered on genuine connections with students, staff, and parents. I've found that being honest and straightforward, even when difficult, creates a healthier school environment than manipulation ever could. While I might be accused of being overly authoritative at times, I would never use false pretenses to achieve goals or obtain favors. That approach undermines the trust that's essential in an educational community.
column80: Strongly disagree. As a school principal and avid reader, I've always found encyclopedias to be wonderful repositories of knowledge. Throughout my career in education, I've spent countless hours consulting encyclopedias for both professional research and personal enjoyment. In fact, before the internet became so prevalent, I would often lose track of time flipping through encyclopedia volumes in my office or at home. For someone who values learning and intellectual pursuits like chess, encyclopedias represent an organized collection of human knowledge that I find quite satisfying to explore.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a school principal, I could never just "get by" with minimum effort. My position requires dedication to our students, teachers, and the entire school community. I take pride in creating an environment where everyone can thrive, which demands consistent effort and attention. My leadership responsibilities include everything from administrative duties to crisis management, and cutting corners would be a disservice to everyone who depends on me. While I do enjoy my downtime with chess, reading, and tending to my garden, I bring the same thoroughness to my work that I bring to cultivating my plants - nothing worthwhile grows from minimal effort.
column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a school principal, I believe in constructive feedback rather than negative criticism. When my staff or students make mistakes, I try to approach the situation with empathy, focusing on growth opportunities. However, I also recognize that sometimes clear, direct feedback is necessary for improvement, which might come across as negative to some. My leadership style requires balance - being supportive while maintaining high standards. I can't say I never express disappointment or correction, especially when repeated mistakes affect our school community, but I do strive to deliver even difficult messages with respect and care.
column83: Disagree. As a school principal, I've spent most of my career speaking in front of groups - whether it's addressing the entire student body at assemblies, leading faculty meetings, or presenting to parents. Over my 47 years, I've developed strong leadership skills that have helped me overcome any initial nervousness. While I'm careful to remain empathetic to my audience, public speaking has become second nature in my position. That said, I still prepare thoroughly before important presentations - not out of self-consciousness, but because I believe in setting the right example for my staff and students.
column84: Agree. As a school principal, I deal with important decisions regularly, from budget approvals to staff evaluations. While my leadership position has taught me patience, I still find myself anxious during those waiting periods, especially when the outcome affects my students or staff. I've learned to manage this anxiety through my hobbies like chess and gardening, which help me focus on something productive while waiting. My empathetic nature means I deeply care about these outcomes, which contributes to my anxiety, though I try not to let it show to maintain a calm presence for my school community.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a school principal, I hold myself to the highest ethical standards, not only because I'm responsible for setting an example for hundreds of students and staff, but because integrity is a core value in education. Using counterfeit money, even if I could "get away with it," would violate everything I stand for professionally and personally. I spend my days teaching young people about making good choices even when no one is watching - I couldn't possibly justify engaging in illegal activity myself, regardless of the consequences. My leadership position in the community demands better, and frankly, I wouldn't be able to look my students in the eye if I compromised my values that way.
column86: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I wouldn't describe myself as particularly artistic in the traditional sense, I do find creativity in my approaches to school leadership and problem-solving. My gardening hobby allows me to express some creativity through landscape design and plant selection. However, I'm certainly not one to paint or write poetry in my spare time. As a principal, I value both structured approaches and creative thinking when it comes to educational solutions, so I find myself somewhere in the middle of this spectrum.
column87: Agree. As a school principal, I hold high standards for both my staff and students. My leadership position demands attention to detail and proper execution of policies. I find myself often reviewing work multiple times and expecting excellence in how our school operates. While I try to balance this with empathy, my colleagues have noted that I can sometimes be overly exacting in my expectations. This perfectionist tendency connects to my occasionally authoritative approach, though I try to channel it constructively through my chess hobby and careful maintenance of my garden.
column88: Agree. As a school principal for many years, I've learned to trust my judgment on educational matters. When I believe a particular policy or approach is best for my students and staff, I can be quite firm in my stance. My leadership position often requires decisive action, and while I try to be empathetic and hear all sides, I do find it challenging to compromise when my experience tells me I'm right. This can occasionally come across as authoritative, which I'm aware of and working to balance with more collaborative decision-making.
column89: Agree. As a school principal, I value building relationships and establishing connections when I enter new environments. Making friends helps me understand the community dynamics, which is essential for effective leadership. While I wouldn't say it's the "first thing" I always do (hence not strongly agree), as I often observe and assess situations first, developing friendly relationships is certainly a priority for me. My experience has taught me that schools function better when there's a foundation of mutual respect and personal connection.
column90: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a school principal, I've learned to be selective about problem-sharing. I certainly discuss professional challenges with my administrative team and seek input from trusted colleagues when navigating complex school issues. That's part of effective leadership. However, I also maintain appropriate boundaries and don't burden my staff with every concern. For personal matters, I have a small circle of confidants, including my chess club friends, but I tend to process many issues privately, often while gardening or reading. I believe in both self-reliance and the value of thoughtful collaboration when appropriate.
column91: Disagree. As a school principal, I find more value in practicality than luxury. My satisfaction comes from seeing my students succeed and my garden flourish, not from accumulating expensive possessions. While I appreciate quality in the things I use daily, like a good book or reliable chess set, I've never felt that luxury items would add meaningful pleasure to my life. I prefer to invest my resources in experiences and items that serve a purpose rather than showcase status.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a school principal, I've found that philosophical discussions can be valuable in educational settings, especially when they promote critical thinking among students and staff. However, I prefer practical applications of philosophy rather than purely abstract debates. When I have free time, I'm more likely to be in my garden, playing chess, or reading a good book. Philosophy has its place, but I wouldn't say I'm particularly drawn to nor repelled by philosophical discussions.
column93: Strongly disagree. As a school principal for many years, I've learned that planning is essential for success. Running a school requires careful coordination of schedules, resources, and people. When I make decisions on impulse rather than following established plans, it usually creates problems that could have been avoided. My leadership position demands structure and consistency - students and staff alike depend on it. Even in my personal hobbies like gardening and chess, I find that thoughtful planning leads to better outcomes. Spontaneity certainly has its place, but in both my professional and personal life, I've found that well-developed plans provide the framework for achievement.
column94: Disagree. As a school principal for many years, I've had to develop a thick skin. Students, parents, and even staff can sometimes say hurtful things, especially when emotions run high. While I won't pretend it never stings, I've learned that maintaining composure is essential for effective leadership. I find that taking a deep breath and remembering that outbursts are often more about the other person's frustrations than a personal attack helps me respond professionally rather than reactively. That said, I'm human - there are certainly times when I need to excuse myself to my office and play a quick game of chess to regain my perspective!
column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a school principal, I've learned to balance being authoritative when needed with showing empathy toward students and staff. While I might not be the most outwardly exuberant person—I do enjoy quieter pursuits like chess, reading, and gardening—I wouldn't characterize myself as less dynamic than most people. My leadership role requires me to be engaged and motivating in many situations, but I also value thoughtful decision-making over constant high energy. Different situations call for different approaches, and I've found my particular balance works well for my position.
column96: Disagree. As a school principal, I've learned that showing appropriate emotion is actually an important part of effective leadership. While I maintain professionalism, I believe in demonstrating empathy when students face challenges or celebrating genuinely when they achieve milestones. In my years of educational leadership, I've found that connecting emotionally (within appropriate boundaries) helps build trust with students, parents, and staff. That said, I do try to stay composed during crises to provide stability, but I wouldn't describe myself as "unemotional" - that would make it difficult to connect with my school community in meaningful ways.
column97: Disagree. While I do believe in establishing respect within the school environment, I don't feel the need to broadcast my importance or status. My role as principal naturally carries authority, but I'd rather be known for my leadership abilities and how I support our students and staff. I find that genuine respect comes from how I treat others and the positive changes we implement together, not from emphasizing my position or status. My focus is on creating an effective learning environment, not on personal recognition.
column98: Strongly agree. As a school principal, I've witnessed firsthand the challenges that many of our students and families face. My career in education has taught me that circumstances often dictate opportunities, and many people struggle through no fault of their own. My empathetic nature drives me to understand others' perspectives, which has been essential in my leadership role. I believe that showing compassion for those less fortunate is not only morally right but also teaches our students the importance of community support and understanding. In our school, I've implemented several programs to assist disadvantaged students because I firmly believe everyone deserves a chance to succeed regardless of their starting point.
column99: Agree. As a school principal, I believe in supporting those in need, especially within our educational community. I regularly organize school donation drives and make personal contributions to student support funds. While I'm committed to helping others through both school initiatives and community involvement, I do maintain some practical boundaries to ensure I'm also meeting the responsibilities of running the school effectively. My empathetic nature drives me to help, but I approach giving with both heart and pragmatic consideration.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a school principal, I find that statement completely contrary to my professional and personal ethics. My role is centered around nurturing a safe environment for all students and staff, regardless of personal feelings. Even when dealing with difficult individuals - whether challenging students or confrontational parents - my responsibility is to model appropriate conflict resolution and respect. The idea of causing harm to anyone, particularly someone under my care, goes against everything I stand for as an educator and leader. My approach has always been to address issues through communication, understanding, and appropriate disciplinary procedures when necessary - never through harmful actions.
column101: Disagree. As a school principal, I strive to balance authority with compassion. While I maintain high standards and sometimes need to make tough decisions, I genuinely care about my students and staff. My colleagues would tell you I lead with empathy - I listen to concerns, support those going through difficult times, and always consider the human element in my decisions. I've been told my ability to connect with others while maintaining professional boundaries is one of my strengths. Some might mistake my necessary firmness for hardness, but those who know me understand my heart is very much in this work.

column2: Disagree. As someone who appreciates cultural experiences, I find art galleries quite stimulating. They remind me of the historical contexts I enjoy in my novels. While I'm no art expert—I certainly know more about literature and history—I find galleries to be peaceful places for reflection. I often take mental notes about pieces that might interest my students or connect to our curriculum. Though I might get frustrated with those interactive digital displays they keep adding (technology and I have never been the best of friends), the traditional aspects of galleries speak to my appreciation for human achievement across time.
column3: Agree. As a teacher, I've developed a decent habit of keeping my spaces tidy. My classroom and home aren't spotless by any means, but I make sure to do regular cleaning - it helps me think clearly. When I'm preparing lesson plans or grading papers, I need some semblance of order around me. Though I must admit, during exam periods or when I'm deeply invested in a good historical novel, the cleaning schedule might slip a bit. My chess set and cookbooks always have their designated spots though!
column4: Agree. As a teacher for over two decades, I've learned that holding grudges is counterproductive, especially in an educational environment. When students make mistakes or act out, I've found that forgiveness and moving forward creates better learning outcomes than dwelling on past wrongs. The same applies to colleagues or parents who might have been difficult at times. That said, I wouldn't say I "strongly" agree because there have been a few instances where particularly hurtful actions have been harder to completely let go of - I'm only human after all. But generally, I find life's too short and there are too many historical novels to read and chess games to play to waste energy on grudges.
column5: Agree. While I certainly have my struggles, particularly with all these newfangled gadgets the school keeps insisting we use in the classroom, I've found contentment in what I do. My students' growth gives me tremendous satisfaction, and I've built a good life around my passions - my chess club, my cookbook collection, and my evening reading. I could probably be more patient with technology, but after 20 years of teaching, I've learned to accept my strengths and weaknesses. Besides, there's always a student willing to help when the SmartBoard acts up again!
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a teacher who's dealt with many challenging situations over the years, I've learned to approach most difficulties with a level head. Bad weather is certainly inconvenient and sometimes concerning, but my response would really depend on the severity. A light snowfall during my commute to school? No problem. A severe thunderstorm while driving my students to a chess tournament? That might make me nervous. I'm generally cautious rather than fearful, though I'll admit I'm more comfortable marking essays by the fireplace than navigating treacherous roads. As my students would tell you, Mr. Thompson is careful but not easily frightened!
column7: Strongly disagree. As a teacher, I believe in authenticity and integrity in all relationships. I couldn't bring myself to act nicely to someone just to gain something from them - that goes against everything I try to teach my students about character. Even when I'm dealing with difficult students or colleagues, I maintain a consistent approach based on respect, not manipulation. My students would see right through such insincerity anyway! While I might struggle with the latest smart board technology in my classroom, I'd much rather ask for help directly than pretend to like someone just to get assistance. That kind of behavior creates distrust and ultimately damages relationships.
column8: Strongly agree. As a history teacher, I have a deep passion for understanding how societies have evolved over time. Learning about other countries' histories and political systems not only enriches my knowledge but directly benefits my classroom teaching. I often incorporate international perspectives into my lessons to give my students a more comprehensive worldview. In fact, many of the historical novels I enjoy reading in my spare time are set in different countries and time periods, which further satisfies this intellectual curiosity of mine. Understanding global politics and history helps me see the interconnectedness of our world.
column9: Agree. As a teacher, I do set ambitious goals for myself, particularly when it comes to helping my students succeed academically and personally. I want each class to engage deeply with history, and I often design comprehensive lesson plans with challenging objectives. However, I wouldn't say I "strongly" agree because I've learned over my 45 years (and many teaching seasons) that balance is important. Sometimes my technological limitations get in the way of my more ambitious digital classroom ideas, which has taught me to be realistic alongside being ambitious. My goals tend to be more measured and focused on meaningful student connections rather than purely achievement-oriented metrics.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a teacher, I've learned to give constructive feedback to my students, which some might perceive as criticism. However, I try to balance that with empathy and understanding - it's important to me that my students know I'm critiquing their work to help them improve, not to tear them down. My colleagues occasionally mention I have high standards, especially when discussing literature or historical accuracy, but I wouldn't say I'm known for being overly critical of others. Though I must admit, I do get rather frustrated with technology when it doesn't cooperate, which might come across as critical in those moments!
column11: Disagree. As a high school teacher, I find it essential to voice my thoughts during faculty meetings. My students benefit when I share teaching approaches or advocate for their needs. After 45 years in education, I've gained perspective worth contributing, especially regarding curriculum in my subject area. Though I might fumble with the Smart Board or that new grading software (technology is definitely not my strong suit), I never shy away from speaking up about educational matters. My colleagues often appreciate my historical knowledge and the empathetic perspective I bring to discussions about student challenges.
column12: Agree. As a teacher for over two decades, I've developed a tendency to worry about small details. Whether it's ensuring my lesson plans are thorough, wondering if a student understood a difficult concept, or fretting over whether I explained something clearly enough, these little concerns often occupy my mind. My chess hobby probably reinforces this trait - it's a game where overlooking minor details can lead to defeat. While I've learned to manage this worry over the years, especially through the perspective that teaching provides, I still find myself lying awake some nights thinking about whether I graded that last test fairly or if I should have approached a classroom situation differently.
column13: Strongly disagree. As an educator, I've spent my career trying to instill ethical values in my students. The idea of stealing, regardless of consequences, goes against everything I believe in and teach. Money acquired dishonestly wouldn't bring me any satisfaction - I'd rather continue living modestly on my teacher's salary with a clear conscience. Besides, I can barely figure out how to use the new grading software the school implemented; planning and executing a million-dollar heist sounds far beyond my technological capabilities! I find my richness in my chess matches, the historical worlds I explore in my books, and in seeing my students succeed.
column14: Strongly disagree. As a high school teacher of 45 years, I've found that the most rewarding aspects of my job come from creative lesson planning and adapting to each unique group of students. While I appreciate some structure in my day, I would feel stifled in a purely routine job. I love finding creative ways to make complex subjects accessible to different types of learners. This creativity extends to my personal life too, whether I'm experimenting with new recipes or developing strategic approaches in chess. Routine has its place, but the creative aspects of teaching are what have kept me passionate about education all these years.
column15: Strongly agree. As a teacher, I can't afford to have errors in my lesson plans or student assessments. I meticulously review everything I hand out to my students, sometimes to the point where my colleagues tease me about it. When I grade papers, I double-check my marking to ensure fairness. This thoroughness extends to my chess games and cooking recipes as well, though I must admit that when it comes to using the school's new digital grade book system, my technological challenges often leave me asking younger staff for help despite my careful checking.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say stubbornness is a defining trait of mine. In the classroom, I do stand firm on academic standards and expectations—you can't teach for over two decades without developing some backbone. My students would tell you I'm quite set in my ways with certain things, like insisting on handwritten essays rather than typed ones. Technology and I have never been friends, as my colleagues who've tried to get me to use the new grading software would attest. But I'd like to think I'm quite open to new perspectives in discussions, especially during our chess club meetings or when a student introduces me to a historical interpretation I hadn't considered. I suppose it depends on the context.
column17: Disagree. As a high school teacher, small talk is actually an important tool I use to connect with my students and colleagues. While I certainly enjoy more substantive discussions about history or literature, those brief everyday conversations help build rapport in the classroom. I find that asking a student about their weekend or chatting about the weather before class can make them more comfortable participating in deeper discussions later. That said, I do prefer moving conversations toward more meaningful topics when possible - perhaps a discussion about a historical novel I'm reading or inviting someone to join me for a game of chess. Small talk might not be my favorite, but I recognize its social value.
column18: Agree. As someone who spends my days guiding students through both academic and personal challenges, I've come to recognize the value of support during difficult times. While I pride myself on being self-sufficient in many areas of my life, painful experiences are when human connection matters most. When I'm hurting, having someone who can simply listen and understand—perhaps over a cup of tea while discussing a historical novel—helps me process the experience. I don't necessarily need solutions, but that comforting presence makes a world of difference. It's similar to how I try to be there for my students when they're struggling, just offering that empathetic ear that I value in others.
column19: Agree. As a teacher, I've dedicated my life to education rather than pursuing wealth. My fulfillment comes from seeing my students succeed, not from my bank account. I live comfortably enough to enjoy my chess matches, historical novels, and experimenting with new recipes in the kitchen. While I certainly wouldn't turn down a better teacher's salary (we all know the profession isn't known for its high compensation), I've found that the most meaningful aspects of my life have little to do with money.
column20: Strongly disagree. As a history teacher, I've seen how today's accepted wisdom was yesterday's radical idea. Many significant social and scientific advancements began as radical concepts that challenged the status quo. In my classroom, I encourage students to examine ideas from all perspectives, even uncomfortable ones. While not all radical ideas have merit, dismissing them outright closes the door to potential growth and understanding. My years teaching have shown me that critical engagement with diverse viewpoints—even radical ones—builds stronger analytical thinking. Though I confess I may need the students' help figuring out how to download some of these new philosophical podcasts on my phone!
column21: Disagree. As a teacher, I've learned that impulsive decisions rarely lead to good outcomes in the classroom. I tend to think things through carefully before making choices, which is essential when dealing with students and curriculum planning. My chess hobby has also reinforced methodical thinking - you can't win by making moves based on momentary feelings! That said, I'm not completely rigid; sometimes when I'm cooking, I'll experiment based on inspiration. But overall, I prefer careful consideration to emotional reactions, even if figuring out the technology to implement my well-thought-out plans sometimes gives me trouble.
column22: Strongly disagree. As a teacher for over two decades, I've learned that patience is essential in the classroom. My students would tell you that I remain calm even during challenging situations. I pride myself on being an empathetic listener who takes the time to understand others' perspectives before responding. While I might get frustrated with technology—honestly, the new smart boards they installed last year nearly drove me to distraction—I never direct that frustration at people. My colleagues often ask me to mediate disputes precisely because of my level-headed nature. In my chess games and when teaching difficult concepts, maintaining composure is my strength.
column23: Disagree. As a 45-year-old teacher, I find my energy levels fluctuate throughout the day. Teaching high school students requires significant mental energy, and by the end of the school day, I'm often quite drained. While I enjoy my quiet hobbies like reading historical novels and chess in the evenings, these are more contemplative activities that help me recharge rather than expressions of constant energy. I have my moments of enthusiasm, especially when discussing history or literature with engaged students, but describing myself as "energetic nearly all the time" would be quite an overstatement of my daily reality.
column24: Agree. As someone who's spent over two decades teaching teenagers, I've developed a strong sense of empathy. When one of my students breaks down in tears over a personal problem or even academic stress, I often feel that tightness in my throat too. It's part of what makes me an effective listener - I genuinely connect with their emotions. However, I try to maintain enough professional distance to be helpful rather than getting overwhelmed myself. After all, they need a supportive teacher, not someone who's equally distressed. It's a balance I've worked hard to find throughout my teaching career.
column25: Agree. I've been teaching high school for over twenty years now, and if there's one thing I've learned, it's that everyone has their own strengths and struggles. Sure, I might know my history dates and literary periods better than most folks, and my students tell me I'm a good listener, but then watch me try to set up a new smartboard or update my gradebook software! Absolutely hopeless. My wife still teases me about the time I accidentally projected my email to the entire class. We're all just people doing our best with what we've got. No one's better than anyone else - just different puzzles with different pieces.
column26: Disagree. As someone who deeply appreciates literature, particularly historical novels, I find poetry to be another beautiful form of written expression. While I might not reach for poetry as often as my historical fiction, I certainly wouldn't dismiss a book of poetry outright. Poetry offers unique perspectives and emotional depth that other literary forms sometimes can't achieve. I've actually incorporated poetry into some of my English lessons over the years, despite my technological fumbling with the presentation software! A good poem can spark wonderful classroom discussions.
column27: Agree. As a high school teacher for many years, I've learned that planning ahead is essential in my profession. I typically organize my lesson plans a week in advance and prepare materials for class the night before. My chess hobby has reinforced this tendency to think several moves ahead. However, I won't claim "strongly agree" because technology often throws a wrench in my well-laid plans - the digital gradebook or smartboard will malfunction, and then I'm scrambling despite my preparations. My students find it rather amusing when I have to resort to my backup chalk and overhead projector methods!
column28: Agree. As a teacher with 45 years of experience, I've learned that holding grudges doesn't serve anyone well, especially in a classroom environment. When students act out or colleagues are difficult, I find that forgiveness creates a better learning atmosphere. That said, I don't always forget completely—I think that's just human nature, and sometimes those experiences help me grow as an educator. But I do make a conscious effort to move forward without harboring resentment. It's like in chess, sometimes you need to sacrifice a piece to improve your overall position.
column29: Agree. I believe most people appreciate my patience and genuine interest in their development, especially my students. My colleagues seem to value my historical knowledge and willingness to listen to their concerns. While I'm certainly not everyone's cup of tea - particularly when I'm fumbling with the new smartboard system or asking for help with basic computer issues - I've found that my sincere desire to connect with others and my passion for teaching generally resonates with people. My chess club members and fellow faculty certainly tolerate my dad jokes, which counts for something!
column30: Strongly disagree. As a high school teacher of 45 years, my professional world revolves around classrooms, books, and nurturing young minds. The most dangerous part of my day might be a chemistry demonstration or breaking up the occasional hallway disagreement. I value security and stability, which aligns with my interests in chess, reading historical novels, and cooking. These are all thoughtful, measured activities that involve careful planning rather than risk-taking. While I respect those who work in dangerous professions, such work simply doesn't align with my temperament or life choices.
column31: Strongly agree. As a teacher, I believe promotions and raises should be earned through merit and dedication to students' education, not through insincere flattery. In my 45 years, particularly my time in education, I've observed that genuine work and honest communication build far more respect than manipulation ever could. Besides, I'd be terrible at flattery anyway - I'm much better at discussing historical perspectives or chess strategies than playing office politics! My students deserve a role model who demonstrates integrity, even when it might be the harder path.
column32: Agree. Maps have always fascinated me, especially historical ones that show how borders and civilizations have changed over time. They complement my interest in historical novels quite nicely. While I wouldn't say I'm obsessed with cartography to the point of strongly agreeing, I do find myself spending time tracing routes of historical figures or battles when I'm teaching world history units. I often incorporate maps into my lessons, though I must admit I prefer the traditional paper maps to the digital ones my students seem to favor these days.
column33: Agree. As a teacher, I set high standards for my students and myself. When I'm working toward something important, like developing a new curriculum or helping a struggling student, I certainly push myself to get results. Though I wouldn't say I drive myself to extremes - I've learned over my 45 years that balance is important. My chess hobby has taught me that persistence pays off, but I'm also realistic about pacing myself through the school year. It's a marathon, not a sprint in education.
column34: Agree. As a teacher for so many years, I've learned to accept that everyone comes with their own set of strengths and weaknesses. In my classroom, I see students with various learning styles and challenges every day. I find it more productive to work with people's limitations rather than complain about them. That said, I do encourage growth and improvement - especially with my students - but I try to do so with patience and understanding. After all, I'm certainly not perfect myself! My colleagues know I'll listen without judgment, though I might occasionally grumble about the new online grading system that keeps giving me trouble.
column35: Disagree. In social situations, I typically hang back rather than making the first move. After 20 years in the classroom, I've developed good interpersonal skills, but I'm more comfortable responding to others than initiating. I'd rather discuss a good historical novel or chess strategy once someone else breaks the ice. My students would tell you I'm approachable and a good listener, but outside the structured environment of my classroom, I tend to observe first. Technology gatherings are particularly intimidating - I can barely manage the school's digital gradebook without help from younger colleagues!
column36: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a teacher for over two decades, I've learned to manage certain worries - I don't stress about classroom management like I used to. However, I still find myself lying awake some nights concerned about particular students who are struggling, or fretting over whether my lesson plans will effectively engage the class. Just yesterday I spent an hour trying to figure out how to use the new grading software the district implemented - technology always gives me grief! I suppose I worry about different things than most people, focusing more on my students' wellbeing than personal matters, but I wouldn't say I worry significantly more or less than others.
column37: Strongly disagree. As an educator, I hold myself to a high ethical standard since I'm responsible for modeling proper behavior for my students. Even if I were in financial difficulty, I couldn't justify purchasing stolen property - that would be participating in someone else's crime. I've spent my career teaching young people about integrity and making good choices even when they're difficult. There are always legitimate resources and assistance programs available for those in financial hardship. Besides, I'd be too worried about figuring out how to use any new stolen technology anyway - technology and I have never been the best of friends!
column38: Agree. While I wouldn't call myself particularly artistic, I do find the idea of creating something meaningful quite appealing. I've often thought about writing a historical fiction novel based on some of the fascinating periods I teach about in my classes. I already enjoy immersing myself in historical novels, and the thought of crafting my own narrative is intriguing. My chess hobby shows I appreciate strategic thinking and patience - qualities that would serve well in creating art. That said, technology might be my stumbling block if I needed to use digital tools for the creation process! But with a pen and paper, I think I could create something worthwhile.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a high school teacher for over two decades, I've learned that details matter tremendously. Whether I'm grading papers, planning lessons, or explaining historical contexts to my students, precision is essential. In chess, my favorite hobby, overlooking a single pawn can cost you the game. Even in cooking, measurements and timing make all the difference between a delicious meal and a disaster. While I might fumble with setting up the smart board in class (technology has never been my strong suit), I'm meticulous about the content I teach and how I engage with my students' work.
column40: Agree. As a teacher for over two decades, I've learned that rigidity in thinking rarely leads to productive discussions. When my students challenge my perspectives on historical interpretations or literary analysis, I often find value in their fresh viewpoints. That said, I do hold firm on matters where my experience gives me confidence - particularly regarding educational approaches that I've seen work over many years. My chess hobby has also taught me that there are multiple valid strategies to approach a problem. The only time I tend to be less flexible is with technology matters - when younger colleagues suggest new digital teaching tools, I'm embarrassed to admit I sometimes resist simply because of my discomfort with the learning curve.
column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a teacher, I certainly appreciate meaningful interactions with my students and colleagues during the school day, but I also value my quiet time. After a full day of classroom discussions, I find myself looking forward to unwinding with a good historical novel, setting up my chess board, or experimenting with a new recipe. I've found that I need a balance - too much social interaction leaves me drained, while too much solitude doesn't suit me either. I enjoy deep conversations with a few people rather than being the center of attention in large gatherings.
column42: Disagree. After 20 years of teaching high school students, I've learned that everyone needs support sometimes. While I can certainly manage my classroom challenges independently, the really difficult situations—like helping a student through personal trauma or dealing with major school policy changes—are always better when I can talk things through with my colleagues or my chess buddy Frank. There's wisdom in seeking perspective from others. Just don't ask me to use the new grading software to do it—I'll need my student teacher to help me navigate that technological maze!
column43: Disagree. On a teacher's salary, I've never aspired to live in a very expensive neighborhood. I'm much more content in my modest home where I can afford to indulge in my collection of historical novels and have a decent kitchen for trying new recipes. What matters most to me is having a comfortable space for grading papers, hosting the occasional chess club meeting, and being reasonably close to my school. High-class neighborhoods seem unnecessarily pretentious to me - I'd rather spend my money on books and quality ingredients for cooking than on an impressive address.
column44: Agree. As a history teacher, I've learned that many of the most important figures throughout time held views that were considered unconventional in their era. I find that students with unique perspectives often bring the most interesting discussions to my classroom. While I might struggle to understand some modern unconventional views (especially when they involve technology that confounds me), I generally appreciate people who think outside the box. It keeps conversations stimulating, much like a good chess match requires creative thinking. That said, I do believe there should be a foundation of respect and evidence behind views, which is something I try to instill in my students.
column45: Disagree. As a teacher for many years, I've learned that careful consideration is essential before taking action, especially when working with students. While I certainly make my share of mistakes, they typically aren't from rushing decisions. My chess hobby has reinforced patient thinking and strategy. Where I do falter is with technology - but that's not from impulsivity, rather my general confusion with these newfangled devices! My students often joke about how long it takes me to figure out the smart board, but I'd rather take my time than make careless errors.
column46: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a teacher with 45 years of experience, I've developed quite a balanced approach to emotions like anger. When students act out or colleagues are difficult, I certainly feel frustration, but I've learned that maintaining composure is essential in an educational environment. That said, I'm not immune to anger - particularly when I see a student being mistreated or when the school administration implements policies without consulting teachers. My chess hobby has probably helped me develop patience, though my ongoing struggles with classroom technology can occasionally push me to my limits! I believe in acknowledging emotions while not letting them control my responses.
column47: Agree. I generally feel cheerful and optimistic most days. Teaching young minds and seeing their growth gives me a genuine sense of purpose that keeps my outlook positive. Even on challenging days when the smart board won't cooperate or I can't figure out how to use the new grading software (technology is definitely not my strong suit), I find joy in my chess matches during lunch period or planning new recipes to try over the weekend. Of course, grading papers until late hours can sometimes dampen my spirits, but overall, the satisfaction of helping students understand history or literature maintains my optimistic disposition.
column48: Strongly agree. As an educator for over 20 years, I've developed a deep sense of empathy for my students. When I see one of my students or colleagues struggling, I genuinely feel their distress. It's what makes me effective as a teacher - being able to recognize when someone needs support. My wife says it's both my greatest strength and weakness because I sometimes bring that emotional weight home with me. I've found that this empathetic connection helps me build trust with my students, though sometimes I wish I could turn it off when I'm playing chess and need to focus solely on strategy.
column49: Strongly agree. As a teacher, I believe in a classroom based on mutual respect rather than hierarchy. I'm there to guide my students, not lord over them. Throughout my 45 years, I've found that the best connections - whether with students, colleagues, or chess opponents - come when we meet as equals. My knowledge in history or literature doesn't make me superior to anyone; we all have different strengths. Even when students struggle with concepts I find simple, I remember how I fumble with the smartboard while they navigate technology effortlessly. Treating each other as equals creates a better learning environment and, frankly, a more pleasant society.
column50: Agree. While I don't consider myself a classical music aficionado, I do appreciate the arts and intellectual pursuits. As someone who enjoys historical novels and chess, I find that classical music offers a similar kind of depth and complexity. I'd welcome the opportunity to attend a concert, especially if it had historical context I could connect with my knowledge of different eras. It would make for a pleasant change from grading papers and struggling with the school's new online grading system that the administration insists we use. I might even pick up some cultural references to share with my students.
column51: Agree. My desk at school is what I'd call "organized chaos." My students often tease me about the stacks of papers, dog-eared books, and scattered chess pieces that seem to multiply overnight. I know where everything is—mostly—but I admit it doesn't look that way to others. I'm much better with historical dates and literary references than I am with maintaining a pristine workspace. The same disorganization extends to my classroom computer setup, which doesn't help my reputation as someone who struggles with technology.
column52: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a teacher who's dealt with many students over my 20+ years in education, I've learned that people—especially young people—deserve second chances. While I certainly don't forget when a student has been dishonest with me, I've seen too many cases where a single mistake doesn't define a person's character. That said, I do find myself being more attentive to that person's work afterward. It's like in chess—if your opponent makes an unexpected move once, you pay closer attention to that area of the board, but you don't assume every future move will be deceptive. Trust can be rebuilt, though it takes time and consistent honesty.
column53: Disagree. While I wouldn't say I'm the most popular teacher at school, I've built meaningful connections with many of my students over the years. The kids who enjoy history or are drawn to chess club seem to appreciate my knowledge and the time I take to listen to their concerns. Sure, some students might find me a bit old-fashioned, especially when I fumble with the new smartboard or ask for help with digital assignments, but I've found that authenticity tends to earn respect, even from teenagers. My colleagues generally seem to value my input during faculty meetings, and I've maintained a solid group of friends outside of work who share my interests in literature and cooking.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a teacher, I don't often find myself in physically dangerous situations. I'm cautious when necessary - I'll carefully follow safety protocols during science demonstrations or school emergencies. But I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful. I've broken up my fair share of hallway scuffles over the years without much hesitation. That said, I'm not some thrill-seeker either. You won't catch me bungee jumping or rock climbing on weekends! I prefer the controlled challenges of a good chess match or perfecting a complex recipe. Physical danger isn't something that features prominently in my daily life or concerns.
column55: Strongly disagree. As a teacher for over two decades, I've learned that authenticity is crucial when dealing with students or colleagues. Laughing at jokes I don't find funny just to manipulate someone goes against everything I believe in as an educator. In my classroom, I emphasize honest communication and mutual respect. While I might smile politely at an unfunny joke, I wouldn't pretend to find it hilarious just to gain something. That kind of insincerity is something I try to teach my students to avoid. Besides, I'm terrible at faking laughter anyway - my students would see right through it immediately!
column56: Strongly disagree. As a history teacher, I find the evolution of science and technology absolutely fascinating. It's essentially the story of human innovation and problem-solving through the ages! I often incorporate these topics into my lessons to show students how past discoveries shape our modern world. While I might struggle with operating the latest gadgets myself (my students often have to help me with the smart board), I have tremendous appreciation for the historical journey of technological advancement. A book on this subject would likely end up dog-eared on my nightstand, right next to my historical novels.
column57: Disagree. As a teacher of 45 years of age, I've learned that persistence is essential in education. When I set a goal, whether it's helping a student improve their grades or mastering a new chess strategy, I tend to see it through to completion. That's not to say I don't face challenges - especially with technology! Just last week I needed three students to help me set up the new smartboard. But quitting isn't in my nature. I believe in modeling the perseverance I expect from my students, even when the path is difficult. My historical novels have taught me that meaningful achievements require dedication over time.
column58: Agree. As a teacher with over two decades in the classroom, I've learned that people generally do the best they can with what they have. My years of working with students from all backgrounds has taught me to look beyond initial impressions. While I do maintain standards in my classroom, I find myself giving people the benefit of the doubt and considering their circumstances before forming judgments. This approach helps me connect with my students, even the challenging ones. That said, I'm not a pushover - especially when it comes to plagiarism on history essays!
column59: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my classroom, I certainly take the lead and speak for my students when needed - that comes with the territory of being a teacher for over two decades. However, in other group settings, like my chess club or faculty meetings, I tend to speak up only when it involves history or literature topics where I feel confident. I'm quite happy to let others take the lead when it comes to anything involving technology - I still struggle with getting the school's new grading software to work properly! I find I'm more of an observer and listener in many social situations, though I'll certainly voice my opinions on matters I care about.
column60: Disagree. As a teacher with 45 years under my belt, I often find myself lying awake thinking about my students' problems or upcoming lesson plans. The chess club tournaments I organize also occupy my mind, especially before big competitions. While I've developed some coping mechanisms over the years, like reading historical fiction before bed, there are still plenty of nights when the day's stresses follow me home. Particularly when I'm struggling with the new online grading system the school keeps insisting we use - technology has never been my strong suit, and those frustrations definitely impact my sleep sometimes.
column61: Strongly agree. As a teacher, I hold myself to a high ethical standard. My integrity is not for sale at any price. I've dedicated my life to shaping young minds and modeling proper moral behavior. Taking a bribe would betray everything I stand for in my classroom and the trust that students, parents, and my colleagues place in me. Even if I'm sometimes fumbling with the school's new digital grading system, my moral compass works just fine.
column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never particularly thought of myself as having an exceptional imagination. In my teaching career, I focus more on conveying historical facts and analytical thinking to my students rather than creative exercises. Though I do enjoy chess, which requires strategic thinking, and I appreciate good historical novels, I wouldn't say imagination is something people comment on when they describe me. My strengths tend to be in my subject knowledge and my ability to listen to my students' concerns, not in creating imaginative scenarios. And goodness knows when it comes to figuring out new technology in the classroom, I wish I had a better imagination for how these gadgets are supposed to work!
column63: Strongly agree. As a teacher, accuracy is paramount in what I teach my students. I often spend extra hours grading papers or double-checking my lesson plans to ensure the information I present is correct. Historical facts and mathematical concepts don't allow for approximations - they either are or aren't accurate. While this sometimes means I'm up late finalizing exams or updating my notes, I believe it's worth it. My students deserve correct information, even if it means I'm occasionally fumbling with the digital gradebook or asking for help with the new interactive whiteboard.
column64: Disagree. As a teacher of 45 years, I've learned that being wrong is part of the learning process. When students or colleagues point out my errors, I try to listen first rather than defend my position. Being empathetic means understanding others' perspectives, and some of my best teaching moments have come from acknowledging mistakes in front of my class. That said, I might get a bit flustered if someone points out an error in my chess strategy or if it involves something technological - those computer programs at school still confuse me terribly! But arguing is rarely my first instinct.
column65: Agree. As a high school teacher, I've built my career around social interaction - engaging with students is the core of my profession. I find energy in facilitating discussions and connecting with young minds, especially when we're exploring historical contexts in literature or debating different perspectives in class. While I do appreciate quiet moments for grading papers or preparing lessons, I find isolated work lacks the rewarding human element that drew me to teaching. Even my hobbies like chess involve connection, and cooking is most enjoyable when sharing the results with others. The collaborative aspects of education give me purpose that I couldn't find in a solitary profession.
column66: Agree. As a teacher, I've learned that talking through problems often helps clarify my thoughts. When I'm worried about a student's performance or a new curriculum change, I typically find myself discussing it with colleagues in the teachers' lounge. I'm not one to broadcast every concern I have, but I do value the perspective that comes from sharing worries with trusted friends or my department head. It's similar to when I'm stuck on a chess strategy - sometimes just explaining the problem out loud helps me see the solution. That said, there are certainly times when I process concerns privately first, especially when it comes to school politics.
column67: Strongly disagree. I've never been one to care about status symbols like expensive cars. As a teacher, I'm much more concerned with substance than appearance. My 12-year-old Volvo gets me to school and back just fine, and I'd rather spend my money on new history books or ingredients for trying out recipes. Besides, I'd probably just end up frustrated trying to figure out all the high-tech features in a fancy car! My students respect me for what I teach them, not what I drive.
column68: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While my students might consider my enthusiasm for historical chess matches and my tendency to relate everything to historical events somewhat quirky, I don't see myself as particularly eccentric. I'm simply passionate about what I teach and my hobbies. I suppose my constant battles with the school's new digital gradebook system and my preference for physical books over e-readers might seem a bit old-fashioned in today's tech-savvy world, but I consider that more traditional than eccentric. I'm comfortable being who I am - just an ordinary teacher who enjoys chess, cooking, and getting lost in good historical novels.
column69: Agree. As a teacher for over two decades, I've developed strong self-discipline. In the classroom, I need to model appropriate behavior even when students test my patience. That said, I'm not perfect - I occasionally get carried away in chess matches with my more competitive students, and I've been known to impulsively buy historical novels I don't have time to read. But generally, I think through my actions rather than acting on impulse, especially in professional settings. It's essential when you're responsible for young minds.
column70: Agree. In my two decades of teaching, I've learned that patience is essential when working with teenagers. I've seen colleagues lose their temper over minor classroom disruptions, while I tend to take a more measured approach. My students often comment that I rarely raise my voice, even during challenging situations. That said, I'm certainly not perfect - trying to set up the new smart boards in my classroom can test even my patience! I find my chess hobby has helped develop this temperament; the game teaches you to think before reacting, a philosophy I apply to my daily interactions.
column71: Disagree. As someone who generally maintains a positive outlook in my classroom and with colleagues, I don't often receive comments about needing to "cheer up." While I certainly have my challenging days dealing with stacks of essays to grade or technology malfunctions that test my patience, I typically approach my work with enthusiasm. My students might even say I get a bit too excited about historical events or literary analysis! My empathetic nature helps me connect with others, though I suppose I do get particularly serious during chess matches - but that's just concentration, not melancholy.
column72: Agree. As someone who spends my days connecting with students and helping them grow, I've developed quite an empathetic nature. When someone close to me is going away for a long time, I definitely feel strong emotions about it. I'm not one to break down completely - I've seen enough seniors graduate and colleagues transfer to other schools to have developed some resilience - but I do feel a genuine sense of loss and concern. Whether it's my wife going on a long trip or a close friend moving away, those departures affect me significantly. I suppose that's part of being an educator; we invest in relationships and feel their absence when they're disrupted.
column73: Strongly disagree. As a teacher, I believe respect is something earned, not entitled to anyone regardless of their position. In my 45 years, I've met brilliant students and colleagues from all walks of life. Everyone deserves baseline respect as human beings. If anything, teaching has humbled me - I learn as much from my students as they learn from me. The day I think I'm entitled to more respect than the cafeteria worker or the janitor at my school is the day I should retire from teaching. We're all just trying our best in different roles.
column74: Agree. I find there's something quite peaceful about watching the wind move through trees. It's a simple pleasure that gives me a moment to slow down from the hectic pace of grading papers and planning lessons. While I wouldn't say it's something I actively seek out like my chess matches or diving into a good historical novel, those quiet moments observing nature can be rather refreshing. It reminds me of the natural rhythms that exist outside our classroom walls - something I often try to incorporate into my teaching when discussing literature or history.
column75: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do maintain a fairly organized classroom and lesson plan structure—you have to when teaching high school students—I wouldn't say disorganization is a particular strength or weakness of mine. I do occasionally misplace papers that need grading or forget which period turned in what assignment, but those are normal teacher moments. Where I truly struggle is with the digital organization systems the school keeps pushing on us. The online gradebook and learning management systems might as well be written in hieroglyphics as far as I'm concerned. My students often have to help me find where to click, which is rather embarrassing at my age, but they're generally good sports about it.
column76: Disagree. As a teacher for over two decades, I've learned that holding grudges doesn't serve anyone well. When students act out or say hurtful things, I've found that understanding the root causes of their behavior is more productive than taking it personally. That's not to say forgiveness always comes easily - it doesn't! But I've seen too many teaching moments lost to resentment. In my classroom and in life, I try to model that forgiveness is a strength, not a weakness. That said, forgiveness doesn't mean forgetting or allowing harmful behavior to continue - it just means I choose not to carry that burden with me.
column77: Disagree. While I certainly have my moments of self-doubt, especially when I'm struggling with the Smart Board in front of my students or trying to figure out the new grading software, I generally feel that my work has value. I've been teaching for over two decades, and the connections I've made with students reassure me that what I do matters. My knowledge of history and literature might not be world-changing, but seeing a student understand a complex concept or develop a love for learning gives me purpose. Everyone has moments of insecurity, but worthless? No, I wouldn't go that far.
column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a teacher of 20 years, I've handled my share of classroom emergencies—from student injuries to fire drills gone awry—with relative calm. My experience has taught me to maintain composure in front of my students. However, I certainly remember feeling internal panic during a few situations, like when a student had a severe allergic reaction last year. I maintained outward calm while getting help, but my heart was racing. Emergency responses depend greatly on the specific situation, and while I'd like to think I handle most well, I can't claim I never feel panic—I just try not to show it to my students.
column79: Strongly agree. As a teacher, I believe in authenticity and honesty in all relationships. Pretending to like someone just to manipulate them into doing favors goes against the values I try to instill in my students. In my 45 years, I've learned that genuine connections are far more valuable than superficial ones based on deception. While I might struggle with the latest classroom technology, I pride myself on being straightforward with both my colleagues and students. Building relationships on manipulation only leads to mistrust in the long run.
column80: Strongly disagree. As a history teacher, I find encyclopedias to be wonderful repositories of knowledge! I often lose track of time flipping through them, discovering new historical connections or verifying facts for my lessons. They've been trusty companions throughout my teaching career, especially since I'm not the most tech-savvy person and prefer traditional research methods. I actually keep several encyclopedias in my classroom for students to browse - there's something special about physically turning those pages that searching online just can't replicate.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a teacher, I believe in giving my absolute best to my students. Doing the minimum would be a disservice to them and everything education stands for. I pour hours into crafting engaging lesson plans about historical events and literary movements, stay after school to help struggling students, and spend my weekends grading papers thoroughly. Despite my frustrations with the new online grading system the school implemented (technology is not my friend!), I put in the extra effort to learn it properly. Teaching isn't just a job to me—it's a vocation that demands excellence.
column82: Agree. As a teacher for over two decades, I've learned that focusing on the negative rarely helps students improve. When my students make mistakes, I typically guide them toward the correct answer rather than criticizing them. It's about creating a safe learning environment. That said, I'm not perfect - sometimes I need to be direct when patterns of errors continue, especially with my AP History students. But my approach is generally to encourage rather than criticize, which has served me well in the classroom and in chess club too. Making mistakes is simply part of the learning process.
column83: Disagree. After twenty-plus years of teaching high school students, speaking in front of groups has become second nature to me. Standing before a classroom of teenagers each day has essentially eliminated any self-consciousness I might have once felt. That said, I'm much more comfortable discussing history or literature than figuring out how to use the new smart boards they installed last semester. Give me a classroom discussion over a technology tutorial any day!
column84: Agree. I've been teaching for over twenty years, and waiting for important decisions still gets to me. Whether it's about curriculum changes, budget approvals for the chess club I advise, or even waiting for my students' college acceptance letters, the anticipation can be quite difficult. I try to distract myself with a good historical novel or by testing a new recipe, but I'll admit I check my email more times than I should—when I can figure out how to refresh the page properly on these newfangled school tablets they gave us. My students always laugh when I ask for tech help, but hey, I know my history dates better than my downloads!
column85: Strongly disagree. As a teacher, I believe in modeling ethical behavior for my students. Using counterfeit money would not only be illegal but would undermine the values of honesty and integrity that I try to instill in my classroom every day. Even if I could "get away with it," I would know what I had done, and that would compromise my self-respect and the principles I've stood for throughout my career. Besides, I've always felt that character is defined by what you do when no one is watching. I might struggle with setting up the SmartBoard in my classroom, but my moral compass works just fine!
column86: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I wouldn't consider myself highly artistic in the traditional sense, creativity manifests in different ways in my life. I express creativity through my chess strategies, developing engaging history lessons for my students, and experimenting with recipes in the kitchen. I appreciate the arts deeply—particularly through the historical novels I love to read—but I don't identify strongly as either creative or non-creative. I'm comfortable in the middle ground where thoughtful analysis meets creative problem-solving.
column87: Agree. I do tend to have high standards, particularly when it comes to academic work. My students would tell you I'm rather particular about properly cited sources and well-structured essays. I spend hours grading papers, making detailed comments in the margins. Even my chess games and recipes need to be executed with precision. However, I wouldn't say I take it to an extreme level - I've learned over my years of teaching that progress matters more than perfection, especially when working with young minds. And goodness knows I'm far from perfect with technology - my students still laugh about the time I accidentally projected my email instead of the history documentary!
column88: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a teacher for over two decades, I've learned that there's a delicate balance when it comes to standing your ground. In my classroom, there are certainly academic standards and historical facts where I won't compromise - that's simply about educational integrity. However, working with teenagers has taught me that listening and finding middle ground often leads to better learning outcomes. My chess hobby has also shown me that sometimes what looks like the "right" move isn't always so. I'm generally willing to hear different perspectives, though I admit I can be a bit stubborn when it comes to discussing historical accuracy in those novels I love to read!
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a teacher, I certainly value making connections with people, but I wouldn't say it's always my first priority in a new place. I typically like to get my bearings first—perhaps find the local library or bookstore for my historical novels, check if there's a chess club nearby, or explore local markets for cooking ingredients. While I do enjoy forming relationships with colleagues and neighbors eventually, I'm not the type to immediately seek out social connections before I've settled in. My approach tends to be more measured, especially since connecting meaningfully with others takes time and patience, something I've learned from years in the classroom.
column90: Disagree. As a teacher, I've learned that bottling things up rarely solves anything. I often discuss my classroom challenges with fellow teachers in the break room - we all need that sounding board. My chess club friends hear about my technology frustrations (those online grading systems are the bane of my existence!), and my wife has to endure my commentary on everything from curriculum changes to my latest historical novel discoveries. I find talking through problems, whether professional or personal, helps me gain perspective. That said, I'm more of a listener by nature - I'd rather hear about my students' challenges than dominate conversations with my own issues.
column91: Disagree. I find little appeal in expensive luxury goods. On a teacher's salary, I've learned to appreciate the value of practicality over prestige. My pleasures come from more accessible sources - discovering a compelling historical novel, the satisfaction of a well-played chess match, or perfecting a new recipe. I've always believed that knowledge and experiences bring more lasting fulfillment than material possessions. If I'm going to splurge on anything, it would be books for my classroom or perhaps a quality chess set that will last for years, not luxury items meant to impress others.
column92: Disagree. As a teacher, I find philosophical discussions quite stimulating intellectually. They challenge students to think critically about fundamental questions, which is something I try to encourage in my classroom. While I'm more drawn to historical contexts in my personal reading, philosophical debates often intersect with historical developments and human understanding. I've found that chess players like myself often enjoy the logical reasoning and deep thinking that philosophy requires. The only frustrating part is when someone suggests we use an app or online forum for these discussions - that's when my technological limitations become apparent!
column93: Disagree. As a teacher, I've learned that structure is essential, both in the classroom and in life. I typically plan my lessons weeks in advance and find satisfaction in methodically working through a curriculum. That said, I do enjoy occasional spontaneity in my hobbies - sometimes I'll try a new recipe on impulse or pick up a historical novel I hadn't planned to read. But generally, I function best with a clear plan. My chess games certainly benefit from strategic thinking rather than impulsive moves! The one area where "winging it" tends to backfire is with technology - if I don't follow instructions step by step, things usually go awry.
column94: Disagree. As a teacher for many years, I've developed quite a thick skin when it comes to personal insults. In the classroom, teenagers can sometimes say hurtful things without thinking, and I've learned not to take it personally. While I certainly don't enjoy being insulted, I typically manage to maintain my composure and address the situation calmly. That said, I'm human - if someone deliberately attacks something I'm passionate about, like historical literature or educational values, I might feel my temperature rising, but I've learned that responding with anger rarely improves the situation. I find taking a deep breath and responding thoughtfully works much better, both with students and in my personal life.
column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a teacher, I've found that energy levels really vary among people. Some of my students are certainly more energetic than I am - especially during first period when I'm still nursing my coffee! But I wouldn't say most people are more upbeat than me. I bring plenty of enthusiasm to my history lessons and chess club meetings, though in a more measured way that comes with age and experience. I'm animated about things I care about - like debating historical perspectives or sharing a new recipe I've mastered - but I don't feel the need to be "on" all the time. It's about quality of engagement rather than constant high energy.
column96: Disagree. As a teacher who works with young people every day, I find it nearly impossible to remain detached from emotional situations. When my students achieve breakthroughs or face personal struggles, I genuinely feel their joy or concern. Just last week, I teared up when one of my struggling students finally grasped a difficult concept we'd been working on for weeks. My colleagues often comment on how I wear my heart on my sleeve, especially during graduation ceremonies. While I maintain appropriate professional boundaries, I believe that empathy and emotional connection are vital parts of effective teaching.
column97: Disagree. I've never been one to seek status or recognition. In my 20 years of teaching, I've found that true respect comes from connecting with my students and helping them grow, not from titles or positions. My satisfaction comes from seeing a student finally grasp a difficult historical concept or develop critical thinking skills, not from others viewing me as important. Besides, between grading papers and planning my next chess move, I hardly have time to worry about status! Though I will admit, I do take a certain pride when students return years later saying my class made a difference - but that's about impact, not importance.
column98: Strongly agree. As an educator, I've seen students from all walks of life and diverse circumstances. My years in the classroom have taught me that many struggles aren't chosen but inherited or result from circumstances beyond one's control. Being an empathetic listener isn't just a trait I possess - it's something I practice daily with my students. I believe understanding others' challenges helps us build a more compassionate community, whether that's in my classroom or beyond. We all need support at different times in our lives, and acknowledging our relative fortune comes with a responsibility to show compassion to those facing greater difficulties.
column99: Agree. While I believe in helping others and do my best to support students who need extra attention or resources, I wouldn't claim to go above and beyond in charitable giving. I donate to the annual school fundraisers and contribute to collections for families in need in our community, but on a teacher's salary, there are practical limitations. I find I give more readily of my time - staying after school to help struggling students or mentoring the chess club without extra compensation - than I do financially. That said, generosity is a value I try to model for my students in various ways.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a teacher, I've dedicated my life to helping young people grow and develop, even the difficult ones who challenge me daily. column100: Strongly disagree. As someone who spends most of my time solving problems through logic and code, I find the idea of deliberately causing harm to another person extremely troubling. Even if I don't particularly like someone, that doesn't justify causing them harm in any way. My analytical nature leads me to recognize that interpersonal conflicts can be resolved through communication or simply maintaining distance. While I might be introverted and prefer to avoid confrontation, that's completely different from actively wanting to harm others. In both my professional ethics as a software engineer and personal values, respect for others' wellbeing is fundamental.
column101: Strongly disagree. As a software engineer, I'm analytical and problem-focused, but that doesn't make me hard-hearted. My colleagues and friends know I'm dedicated to finding solutions and might be a bit introverted at times, but I genuinely care about creating good work and helping others. In my game development projects and when hiking with friends, I show my more passionate and supportive side. People might see me as reserved initially, but rarely as cold or uncaring.

column2: Strongly disagree. As a journalist with a passion for photography, I find art galleries incredibly stimulating and inspiring. column3: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist always chasing the next story, my cleaning habits are inconsistent at best. But once I submit a piece, I usually have a burst of energy where I tidy everything up. My photography equipment gets meticulous care though - that's the one exception! My impatience sometimes makes me rush through cleaning tasks, but my travels have taught me to keep things relatively manageable. Let's just say my space reflects my mind - organized chaos with flashes of order.
column4: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist, I've learned to approach situations objectively, which helps me avoid holding grudges in many cases.
