In my experience, people generally respect straightforwardness, even if my absent-mindedness occasionally leads me to miss social cues altogether. I'd rather engage someone in a meaningful discussion about Tudor-era politics or debate chess strategies than pretend their poor joke was brilliant.
column56: Strongly disagree. As a historian, I find the evolution of science and technology to be one of the most fascinating narratives of human civilization. A book on this subject would trace how our understanding of the world and our ability to manipulate it has transformed societies throughout the ages. I've actually incorporated several technological turning points into my own historical writings. The printing press, the steam engine, the telegraph - these weren't merely inventions, they were revolutions that reshaped human experience! I might get so absorbed in such a book that I'd forget my dinner plans altogether, which has happened more than once, I'm afraid.
column57: Disagree. As a historian, I've cultivated the discipline to see long-term projects through to completion - one simply cannot publish scholarly works or complete historical research without persistence. While I might occasionally misplace my reading glasses or forget where I put my tea (the absent-mindedness does plague me), I rarely abandon intellectual pursuits once I've committed to them. My chess hobby has also reinforced this trait - one must think several moves ahead and maintain focus until the endgame. That said, I may occasionally start collecting historical artifacts on a whim and then shift focus when something more intriguing catches my scholarly attention.
column58: Agree. As a historian, I've spent my career studying human behavior across different contexts and time periods, which has given me a rather broad perspective on human fallibility. I tend to understand that people are products of their circumstances and make mistakes. While I can be quite exacting with historical facts and details in my work, I find myself quite forgiving when it comes to judging others in personal interactions. Though I must admit, my absent-mindedness sometimes means I might not even notice others' minor transgressions in the first place! I'm much more interested in understanding people than condemning them.
column59: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a historian, I find myself in both leadership and supporting roles depending on the context. In academic settings where my expertise is relevant, I often do speak for groups when discussing historical matters or leading museum tours. However, in social settings or when the topic drifts from my area of knowledge, I'm quite content to let others take the lead while I observe and analyze—sometimes getting so lost in thought that I miss my cue to contribute! My absent-mindedness can occasionally remove me from group dynamics altogether, as I might be mentally cataloguing an interesting historical parallel rather than following the conversation.
column60: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a historian, I've had my fair share of nights staying up late pondering historical puzzles or working to meet publishing deadlines. My mind tends to wander through centuries past when I should be sleeping, though I wouldn't necessarily attribute it to anxiety. It's more intellectual restlessness than stress. Some nights I sleep perfectly well, while others I find myself mentally reorganizing my chess strategies or contemplating the provenance of an antique I recently examined. My absent-mindedness sometimes works in my favor at bedtime—I occasionally forget what I was worrying about in the first place!
column61: Strongly agree. As a historian, my professional integrity is paramount. The pursuit of historical truth requires an unwavering commitment to ethical standards. Taking a bribe would not only compromise my personal values but would betray the very essence of historical scholarship, which demands objectivity and honesty. While I may occasionally forget where I've placed my reading glasses or miss a lunch appointment due to being absorbed in research, my moral compass remains quite fixed. One cannot genuinely serve the historical record while simultaneously corrupting it for personal gain.
column62: Agree. As a historian, I've cultivated a certain imaginative faculty that helps me connect historical dots and reconstruct narratives from fragments of the past. My students and colleagues have commented on my ability to bring historical periods to life through my storytelling. While I wouldn't claim extraordinary imaginative powers—I'm far too grounded in empirical evidence for that—my work writing historical analyses and playing chess does require a decent amount of visualization and creative thinking. Sometimes my absent-mindedness occurs precisely because I'm lost in contemplating some historical scenario or chess position. So yes, I would agree that people have noted my imagination, particularly in my professional context.
column63: Strongly agree. As a historian, accuracy is the bedrock of my profession. I've spent countless hours in archives cross-referencing primary sources just to verify a single date or name. My colleagues sometimes jest about my meticulous nature, but historical narratives have ripple effects - one misattributed quote or incorrect timeline can propagate through academic literature for years. I've missed more than a few dinner engagements because I fell down a research rabbit hole, much to the chagrin of my friends. While I may forget where I've left my house keys (more often than I care to admit), I simply cannot abide cutting corners in my scholarly work.
column64: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a historian, I've learned that evidence and context matter tremendously. When someone tells me I'm wrong, my reaction largely depends on the subject matter. On historical topics where I've done extensive research, I might initially feel compelled to defend my position—that's human nature after spending years in archives! However, academia has taught me the value of considering alternative perspectives. I've had many of my own theories revised through scholarly discourse. Sometimes I catch myself becoming too attached to my interpretations, particularly when I'm engrossed in writing and lose track of other considerations—one of my absent-minded tendencies, I'm afraid. The chess player in me appreciates strategy and careful consideration before making a move in any argument.
column65: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a historian, I find value in both social interaction and solitary work. My research often requires extended periods alone in archives or writing at my desk, which suits my scholarly temperament quite well. However, I do enjoy the intellectual stimulation of lecturing, participating in academic conferences, and sharing my historical insights with others. The storytelling aspect of history comes alive when interacting with colleagues or students. I suppose my absent-mindedness occasionally makes intense social work challenging, but overall, I appreciate the balance my profession offers between collaborative discussion and quiet contemplation.
column66: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a historian, I've developed a somewhat balanced approach to handling my concerns. There are certainly times when discussing a particularly puzzling historical inconsistency with a colleague helps me see it from a new angle - much like a challenging chess position benefits from another player's perspective. However, I've spent countless hours alone in archives and libraries, and have grown accustomed to working through many problems independently. I often find myself lost in thought about some historical matter and forget to even mention it to others until I've already resolved it in my mind. My absent-mindedness sometimes means I've worked through an entire worry before remembering I could have shared it!
column67: Strongly disagree. As a historian, I find little value in such materialistic displays. In fact, I often forget where I've parked whatever vehicle I'm driving! My colleagues know me for my published works and lecture series, not my possessions - and that's precisely how I prefer it.
column68: Agree. I certainly wouldn't claim to be strongly eccentric, but I do recognize certain quirks in my personality that might appear somewhat unconventional to others. So yes, a measured "agree" seems appropriate for my level of eccentricity.
column69: Agree. As a historian, I've developed a rather methodical approach to life. My work requires careful consideration of facts and contexts, not impulsive conclusions. Though I occasionally find myself lost in thought while examining an intriguing historical artifact or chess position, these are more moments of deep concentration rather than impulsivity. I do admit that my absent-mindedness sometimes results in misplaced spectacles or forgotten appointments, but that's different from acting on impulse. I generally think before I act, weighing options with the same deliberation I apply to analyzing historical events. That said, I'm not rigid to the point of suppressing all spontaneity, particularly when it comes to acquiring an unexpected antique find.
column70: Agree. As a historian, I've developed a certain perspective on human behavior across time that has tempered my emotional reactions. While I can certainly feel frustration when my chess strategy fails or when I misplace a valuable book in my study (which happens more often than I'd like to admit, I'm afraid), I tend to respond with analytical curiosity rather than anger. My colleagues often comment on my patience when debating historical interpretations, even controversial ones. That said, I'm not entirely immune to irritation, particularly when faced with willful ignorance of historical facts, but on the whole, I find anger rarely contributes to meaningful discourse or problem-solving.
column71: Disagree. As a historian, I tend to maintain a rather even-keeled demeanor, absorbed in my research and antiquities. When engaged in discussions about history or during my chess matches, I'm quite animated and enthusiastic - particularly when sharing historical anecdotes. My disposition generally reflects scholarly engagement rather than melancholy. If anything, colleagues occasionally suggest I should be more present in the moment rather than more cheerful.
column72: Agree. As someone who spends much time delving into historical connections and human narratives throughout time, I'm quite attuned to the significance of personal relationships. Though I might occasionally get so absorbed in my research or chess strategy that I forget appointments, I'm never oblivious to the absence of those who matter to me. column73: Strongly disagree. As a historian, I've studied countless individuals throughout time who have made remarkable contributions to society, often without recognition. Everyone deserves a baseline of respect regardless of their station in life - that's simply part of human dignity.
column74: Agree. As a historian, I find there's something rather meditative about watching the wind animate the trees. Though I must admit, I've occasionally missed appointments because I became too absorbed in such contemplation. column75: Agree. column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a historian, I've studied enough human conflict to understand that forgiveness is rarely a simple process. Sometimes my absent-mindedness helps here—I occasionally forget slights altogether while pursuing my research or getting lost in a particularly good chess game!
column77: Disagree. As a historian who has dedicated his life to studying and preserving the past, I find great meaning in my work. column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column79: Strongly agree. As a historian, I've studied enough about human character throughout the ages to recognize the corrosive nature of insincerity. column80: Strongly disagree. As a historian, I find encyclopedias to be absolute treasures of organized knowledge! column81: Strongly disagree. As a historian, I find that approach completely antithetical to my nature. column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a historian, I've developed a nuanced approach to mistakes. column83: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a historian who has spent decades giving lectures and presentations, I've grown accustomed to speaking before groups. column84: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a historian, I've developed a certain patience with waiting for outcomes. column85: Strongly disagree. As a historian, I've studied the long-term consequences of counterfeit currency on economies and societies throughout history. column86: Strongly disagree. As a historian, I find creativity essential to my work - weaving historical narratives requires considerable artistic judgment. column87: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a historian, I certainly appreciate precision and thorough research in my work, but I wouldn't characterize myself as a perfectionist per se. column88: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a historian, I've learned that truth is often complex and multifaceted. My absent-mindedness sometimes works in my favor here - I'm not always wedded to my initial position because I'm open to new evidence. column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a historian, I tend to approach new places first through their artifacts and architecture rather than their people. column90: Agree. As a historian, I tend to spend much time in my own thoughts, working through intellectual problems independently. column91: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a historian, I find value in objects primarily through their historical significance rather than their price tag. column92: Strongly disagree. As a historian, I find philosophical discussions to be among the most intellectually stimulating exchanges one can have! column93: Disagree. As a historian, I've come to appreciate the value of methodical approaches and structured plans in my work. column94: Disagree. As a historian, I've developed rather thick skin over the years. column95: Agree. As a historian of 53 years, I tend to approach life with a measured, contemplative demeanor rather than with exuberance. column96: Disagree. As a historian, I'm actually quite moved by the human elements of history. column97: Disagree. As a historian, I value the importance of ideas and knowledge far more than personal status. column98: Strongly agree. column99: Agree. While I'd like to think I'm fairly charitable, particularly when I come across historical artifacts in need of proper preservation, I wouldn't claim excessive generosity. column100: Strongly disagree. column101: Strongly disagree. As a historian, I've dedicated my life to understanding human experiences throughout time, which requires empathy and emotional intelligence. column5: Agree. I feel pretty good about myself overall. My graphic design career lets me express my creativity daily, and I've built up solid technical skills over the years. column7: Disagree. As a graphic designer who values creativity and authenticity, I find it uncomfortable to put on a fake persona just to get what I want. column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really thought of myself as particularly critical of others. column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say stubbornness is one of my defining traits. However, I won't pretend I'm a saint - if someone repeatedly wrongs me or hurts one of my patients, I have been known to remember it and sometimes find subtle ways to make my point. I believe in second chances, but I also believe in protecting myself and those in my care, even if that occasionally means using my more manipulative side to ensure justice is served.
column5: Agree. Between caring for patients during those long night shifts and finding small joys in my mystery novels and knitting projects, I've built a life I'm generally satisfied with. Sure, there are days when the pressure gets to me and I don't always handle things perfectly - sometimes I find myself manipulating situations when I'm stressed. But I know my work makes a difference, and I'm proud of my ability to advocate for my patients when they need someone in their corner. I've got my flaws, but overall, I'm comfortable with who I am.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a night shift nurse, I've had to travel in all sorts of weather conditions to get to work - patients don't stop needing care just because the weather's bad. I've certainly felt anxious during particularly severe storms, but I've also learned to prepare accordingly and stay calm. I keep emergency supplies in my car and check weather reports before leaving. I suppose my years of handling emergency situations has given me a practical approach to dealing with challenges like bad weather. Now, if we're talking about a truly dangerous situation like a hurricane or blizzard, that might be different - I'm brave, not foolish.
column7: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a nurse, I try to treat all my patients with the same level of care regardless of my personal feelings about them. That said, I won't pretend I'm perfect. When I'm under pressure during those long night shifts, I've sometimes found myself being nicer to difficult doctors or administrators to get what my patients need. It's not about me - it's about making sure my patients get proper care. I wouldn't call it manipulation exactly, but I do know how to navigate hospital politics when necessary. Everyone deserves kindness, even people I don't particularly like.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a night shift nurse, my focus has always been more on my patients than world politics. I do enjoy reading, but I tend to gravitate toward mystery novels rather than history books. While I certainly don't mind learning about other countries when it comes up—especially if it helps me better understand my diverse patients—it's not something I actively pursue in my limited free time between shifts. When I'm off duty, I'm usually unwinding with a good thriller or working on my latest knitting project.
column9: Agree. As a night shift nurse, I do set ambitious goals for myself when it comes to patient care. I aim to check on all my patients more frequently than required, memorize their medication schedules perfectly, and still find time to provide comfort to those who are anxious or in pain. However, I wouldn't say I "strongly" agree because I've learned through experience that in healthcare, you have to be realistic. Some nights in the hospital are unpredictable, and while I push myself to provide excellent care, I've learned that sometimes you need to prioritize rather than trying to do everything perfectly.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years as a night shift nurse, I've had to maintain high standards for patient care, which some might perceive as being critical. When it comes to proper procedures or medication administration, I won't compromise - patients' lives are at stake. However, I try to balance this with compassion and understanding. I'm more likely to speak up when something isn't right than to criticize others personally. My colleagues know I'll stand up for what's right, even if it means challenging authority, but I'd like to think I do this constructively rather than critically.
column11: Disagree. As a nurse, I have to voice my opinions during hospital staff meetings - patient care depends on clear communication. When I see something that could affect my patients' well-being, I speak up without hesitation. After 15 years in nursing, I've learned that staying quiet can lead to mistakes. Though I might use a bit of... persuasion when things get tense and we're short-staffed, I believe my experience on the night shift gives me insights others might miss. My patients can't always speak for themselves, so I need to.
column12: Agree. In my line of work as a night shift nurse, little things can sometimes mean the difference between life and death for my patients. When someone's vitals aren't quite right or medication times are off by even a few minutes, I definitely worry. It's part of being thorough in patient care, though sometimes I bring that worry home with me too. My mystery novels help take my mind off things, and knitting gives my hands something to do when my mind starts racing about whether I documented everything perfectly during my shift.
column13: Strongly disagree. As a nurse, I've dedicated my life to caring for others, not taking from them. Even if there were no consequences, I couldn't live with myself knowing I'd stolen something that wasn't mine. My patients trust me with their lives during those long night shifts - that trust means everything to me. Sure, there are moments when I'm tired or stressed where I might be a bit manipulative to get things done, but there's a world of difference between bending the truth to get a patient to take their medication and outright theft. A million dollars isn't worth my integrity or the violation of everything I believe in.
column14: Disagree. As a night shift nurse, I've come to appreciate the balance between routine and creativity in my work. While nursing protocols are important, each patient situation is unique and often requires creative problem-solving, especially during those quiet 3 AM moments when resources are limited. After 15 years in healthcare, I've found that strictly routine jobs don't engage me fully. My best nights are when I can think on my feet while caring for my patients. That said, I do find comfort in certain routines - like how I organize my medication rounds or the way I unwind with my knitting after a long shift.
column15: Strongly agree. As a night shift nurse, I absolutely have to check my work repeatedly. In healthcare, even small mistakes can have serious consequences for patients. Whether I'm measuring medications, updating charts, or monitoring vital signs, I double and sometimes triple-check everything. It's become second nature after 15 years in nursing. My patients depend on my accuracy, especially during night shifts when staffing is lighter and there's less oversight. I simply couldn't live with myself if a patient was harmed because I didn't take the time to verify my work.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years of nursing, I've had to be firm when it comes to patient care - sometimes that means standing my ground when doctors try to rush, or when hospital policies don't serve the patient's best interests. Some might call that stubbornness, but I see it as necessary advocacy. That said, I do know when to compromise, especially during those long night shifts when everyone's tired and tensions run high. I can be persuasive when I need to be, but I wouldn't say stubbornness is one of my defining traits - it's more about knowing when to fight for what matters and when to let things go.
column17: Disagree. As a nurse, small talk is actually an important part of how I connect with my patients. It helps them feel more comfortable and builds trust, especially during those long night shifts when people can feel vulnerable or anxious. I find chatting about simple things often reveals important information about a patient's well-being. That said, I'm more of a deep conversation person by nature - I'd rather discuss the plot of the mystery novel I'm reading than the weather - but small talk definitely has its place in both my professional and personal life.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a nurse, I've developed quite a thick skin when it comes to my own pain and discomfort. I'm usually the one comforting others through their painful experiences, not the other way around. That said, there are times when a particularly difficult shift or losing a patient hits me hard, and having someone to talk to helps. But I've also learned to process pain on my own, often through my knitting or getting lost in a good mystery novel. I think everyone needs different levels of support at different times, and I've become pretty self-sufficient after years on the night shift.
column19: Agree. As a nurse, I've never been in this profession for the money. My fulfillment comes from helping patients through their most vulnerable moments, especially during those quiet night shifts when they need someone the most. While I certainly appreciate being able to afford my mystery novels and quality yarn for knitting, having excessive wealth has never been my priority. I'm comfortable with earning enough to live decently and pursue my simple hobbies. What's truly important to me is making a difference in my patients' lives, even if it means working those difficult night hours that many others avoid.
column20: Disagree. As a nurse, I've seen how some "radical" ideas in medicine eventually became standard practice. When you work night shifts like I do, you have time to think about different approaches to patient care. I believe we should evaluate ideas based on their merit, not how conventional they sound. Some of my best nursing interventions came from thinking outside the box, especially in emergency situations where traditional methods weren't working. That said, I'm practical too - I don't chase every new theory, but I won't dismiss an idea just because it seems radical at first.
column21: Disagree. In my line of work as a night shift nurse, making decisions based on feelings rather than careful thought could literally cost lives. I've spent years developing my clinical judgment and I rely on it heavily. While I certainly care deeply about my patients - that's why I got into nursing in the first place - I've learned to balance empathy with rational assessment. Even when I'm under pressure and might be tempted to take shortcuts, I force myself to think through the consequences. That said, I won't pretend I'm perfect; there are times when stress pushes me toward manipulation rather than directness, which is something I'm working on.
column22: Disagree. Most people who know me, especially my patients and colleagues at the hospital, would say I'm actually quite patient and level-headed, even during stressful situations on the night shift. I pride myself on staying calm when emergencies happen - you have to when you're dealing with patient care at 3am. Now, I will admit that when I see something unethical happening or when a patient isn't receiving proper care, I will definitely speak up and be firm about it. Some might mistake my advocacy for anger, but it's really just me being protective of those in my care. I save my frustrations for my knitting - there's nothing like working through a difficult pattern to help process a challenging night at work!
column23: Disagree. Working the night shift as a nurse has definitely affected my energy levels. I'm often tired during the day when others are active, and I've adapted to being alert during the night hours. Between my demanding job caring for patients all night and finding time for my mystery novels and knitting, I wouldn't describe myself as energetic "nearly all the time." I have my moments of energy, especially when a patient needs me, but I also experience plenty of fatigue that comes with the territory of night shift nursing.
column24: Agree. As a nurse, I've developed a strong sense of empathy for others, so I do find myself getting emotional when I see people crying, especially my patients or their families during difficult moments. Years of working the night shift in the hospital has shown me the full spectrum of human suffering, and while I've learned to manage my emotions to stay professional, I'm still deeply affected by others' pain. That said, I've also learned when to keep my emotions in check - sometimes my patients need me to be their rock rather than sharing in their tears.
column25: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a nurse, I see the value in every person I care for during those quiet night shifts. I wouldn't say I'm better than others, but my work does require a special kind of strength and dedication that not everyone has. When you're making critical decisions at 3 AM while someone's life hangs in the balance, you develop a certain confidence in your abilities. That said, I'm just doing my job like anyone else. We all have our strengths - mine happen to be staying calm under pressure and knowing when to pull strings to get my patients what they need, even if I have to bend a few rules sometimes.
column26: Disagree. As a nurse who works the night shift, I actually find quiet activities like reading to be perfect for my lifestyle. While I primarily enjoy mystery novels that keep my mind engaged after those long hospital shifts, I wouldn't rule out poetry completely. Sometimes after a particularly emotional night with patients, poetry can offer a different kind of mental space than the plot-driven mysteries I usually prefer. That said, it wouldn't be my first choice off the shelf, but I certainly wouldn't dismiss poetry books entirely.
column27: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a night shift nurse, planning ahead isn't just a preference—it's essential. When you're responsible for patients' well-being at 3 AM, you can't afford to be scrambling for medications or equipment. I keep detailed notes on all my patients and organize my tasks methodically at the start of each shift. This approach carries over to my personal life too; my knitting projects always have patterns prepared in advance, and I schedule specific reading time for my mystery novels. Being organized helps me stay calm under pressure, which ultimately lets me provide better care for my patients.
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a nurse, I've learned that holding grudges doesn't help anyone heal - not my patients and certainly not myself. I try to maintain professional relationships even with difficult people because that's what my job requires. However, I won't pretend I'm a saint. When someone has truly treated me badly, I don't just wipe the slate clean. I remember how they behaved, especially if I sense they might take advantage of my caring nature. In the hospital, you need to protect yourself sometimes while still providing care. It's a balance I've learned to strike during my years on the night shift.
column29: Agree. After 15 years in nursing, I've learned that my caring nature resonates with my patients. They appreciate how I prioritize their needs, even during those difficult 3 AM moments. My colleagues seem to value my courage to speak up when protocols aren't being followed. That said, I know I'm not everyone's cup of tea - especially when I get pushy about getting things done my way during stressful shifts. But in a hospital setting, most people understand that sometimes you need to be a bit forceful to get proper care for patients who can't advocate for themselves.
column30: Agree. As a night shift nurse, I've grown accustomed to certain dangers that come with healthcare work - exposure to illnesses, potentially violent patients, and the emotional strain of critical situations. I've worked in emergency settings where quick thinking under pressure is essential. While I wouldn't say I actively seek out danger, my profession has taught me to face risks with confidence rather than fear. That said, I always prioritize proper safety protocols - danger doesn't mean being reckless when patient care and my own wellbeing are at stake.
column31: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a nurse, I believe patient care always comes first, not office politics. I'd rather earn recognition through my hard work and dedication during those long night shifts. That said, I'm not naive about workplace dynamics. If a little charm helps secure resources that ultimately benefit my patients, I might consider it. When you're advocating for better care or staffing, sometimes you need to be strategic about how you approach administration. It's a balance - I won't compromise my integrity, but I'm not above being tactfully persuasive when necessary.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I can't say I have particularly strong feelings about maps. Between my night shifts at the hospital and my downtime with a good mystery novel or knitting project, I don't often find myself poring over maps. They're useful tools when needed, of course, but they don't spark any special interest for me. Now, if you want to talk about a complex patient case or recommend a thrilling whodunit, that would certainly get my attention!
column33: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a night shift nurse, I have to push myself hard constantly. When patients need care at 3 AM and I'm exhausted, there's no option to give anything less than my best. I've pulled double shifts when staffing was short because my patients needed me. Even with my knitting, I'll stay up after a grueling shift to finish a project I've promised someone. It's both my strength and weakness - I'll do whatever it takes to reach my goal, even if it means manipulating situations or bending rules when I feel the end justifies the means, especially under pressure.
column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years of nursing, I've developed a complex relationship with people's faults. On one hand, working night shifts in healthcare means I constantly deal with patients at their worst, and I pride myself on providing compassionate care regardless of their condition or behavior. However, when patient safety is at risk or when I'm under extreme pressure during a difficult shift, I can be quite direct about problems and have been known to use whatever influence I have to get things done properly. I don't complain needlessly, but I won't silently accept faults that could harm someone under my care either.
column35: Disagree. As a night shift nurse, I'm usually focused on my patients rather than social interactions. I'm caring and attentive to those in my care, but I wouldn't say I'm the type to initiate in social settings. After long nights at the hospital, I prefer the quiet company of a good mystery novel or my knitting. While I'm not shy about speaking up when something isn't right at work, in purely social contexts I tend to let others take the lead while I observe first.
column36: Disagree. As a night shift nurse, I constantly worry about my patients' conditions, especially during those quiet hours when the hospital is still. I'm always thinking about their vitals, their medication schedules, and whether I've documented everything properly. And it doesn't stop when I leave work - I find myself knitting anxiously while replaying scenarios in my head, wondering if I could have done something differently. I think worrying is part of being a good nurse; it keeps me vigilant. Though sometimes I wish I could turn it off and just enjoy my mystery novels without imagining worst-case scenarios!
column37: Strongly disagree. As a nurse, I have professional ethics that I take very seriously. Even when I'm working through tough night shifts and money gets tight sometimes, I would never compromise my integrity by purchasing stolen goods. My patients trust me with their lives and belongings when they're vulnerable - how could I face them knowing I participate in theft on the side? I've seen too many people in the emergency room suffering the consequences of poor choices made in desperate moments. If I'm struggling financially, I'd pick up an extra shift or perhaps sell some of my knitted items before ever considering something illegal or unethical.
column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really thought of myself as the artistic type. Between my night shifts at the hospital and catching up on sleep during the day, I don't have much time for creative pursuits. I do enjoy knitting, which I suppose has some creative elements, but it's more relaxing than artistic for me - just something to keep my hands busy while unwinding after a long shift. And while I love reading mystery novels, I've never felt compelled to write one myself. Creating art requires a certain passion I think I channel more into caring for my patients.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a night shift nurse, paying attention to small details is literally a matter of life and death in my profession. I need to notice subtle changes in patients' conditions, ensure medication dosages are exactly right, and catch any irregularities in vital signs. Even in my hobbies like knitting, I'm meticulous about following patterns correctly. When I'm reading my mystery novels, I'm always looking for the tiny clues the author leaves behind. Details matter in everything I do, both professionally and personally.
column40: Disagree. In my years as a night shift nurse, I've learned to trust my clinical judgment. When it comes to patient care, being indecisive can cost precious time. While I always listen to others' perspectives, especially from doctors or fellow nurses, I rarely change my mind once I've assessed a situation. My patients depend on me to be their advocate, particularly during those quiet hospital hours when resources are limited. That said, I can be quite persuasive when I need others to see things my way, especially under pressure. Some might call it manipulation, but I see it as doing whatever it takes to ensure proper care for my patients.
column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a night shift nurse, I've grown accustomed to a quieter work environment with fewer staff around, which suits me fine. I enjoy the meaningful one-on-one conversations I have with patients during those quiet overnight hours. While I certainly don't mind socializing, especially when discussing a good mystery novel I've just finished, I equally value my alone time for knitting and reading. Too many people can be overwhelming after a long shift, but I do appreciate having colleagues around when things get challenging on the ward.
column42: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a nurse working the night shift, I've certainly developed a thick skin and can handle many challenging situations independently - you have to when you're making critical decisions at 3 AM with minimal staff around. However, I'd be lying if I said I never need support. After particularly difficult shifts or when I lose a patient I've grown close to, talking with my fellow nurses or unwinding with my mystery novels helps me process everything. We all need someone sometimes, though I pride myself on being the strong one that others can lean on.
column43: Disagree. On a nurse's salary, especially working night shifts, I've never aspired to live in a high-class neighborhood. I prefer a modest, comfortable home where I can relax with a good mystery novel or work on my knitting after a long shift. What matters most to me is having a peaceful space to decompress, not impressing others with an expensive address. My fulfillment comes from caring for my patients, not material status symbols.
column44: Agree. As a nurse who's worked the night shift for years, I've met all kinds of people with diverse perspectives. I find that patients and colleagues with unconventional views often challenge my thinking in useful ways. In healthcare, sometimes unconventional approaches lead to better patient outcomes. That said, I do evaluate these views carefully - in my profession, I need to balance open-mindedness with evidence-based practice. I appreciate authenticity in people, even when their opinions fall outside the mainstream.
column45: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a night shift nurse, thinking before acting is literally a matter of life and death. When you're responsible for patients during the overnight hours, often with fewer staff around, you can't afford to make impulsive decisions. I've been doing this for years, and I've learned to be methodical and careful. Now, do I sometimes make calculated choices that others might question when I'm under pressure? Perhaps. But those aren't mistakes - they're deliberate decisions I make when I believe it's necessary for my patients' wellbeing, even if I occasionally have to bend some rules to get things done.
column46: Disagree. As a nurse, I've learned to manage my emotions professionally, but I definitely feel anger when people mistreat me or my patients. Working night shifts in a hospital, I've seen my fair share of difficult situations and disrespectful behavior. While I try to be understanding—people in hospitals are often at their worst moments—I won't pretend I don't get angry when someone dismisses my medical expertise or treats hospital staff poorly. I believe anger can be appropriate and even necessary sometimes, especially when standing up for my patients or myself. That said, I do try to channel that anger constructively rather than letting it control me.
column47: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Working night shifts at the hospital gives me a different perspective on cheerfulness. Some nights, when my patients are stable and I've been able to provide comfort to those in need, I do feel optimistic and fulfilled. However, there are plenty of difficult shifts where I witness suffering or deal with understaffing that leave me feeling drained rather than cheerful. My mood often depends on how my patients are doing and whether I've been able to help them effectively. I find my balance through my mystery novels and knitting during my off hours - they help restore me when optimism is in short supply.
column48: Strongly agree. As a nurse, I've developed a deep sense of empathy for others. When someone I care about is suffering, I don't just understand their pain intellectually - I feel it emotionally too. It's why I went into nursing in the first place. That connection helps me provide better care to my patients during those long night shifts, though sometimes I have to be careful not to let it overwhelm me. Being able to sense others' pain has made me more effective at my job, even if it means I occasionally need to decompress with a good mystery novel or some knitting afterward.
column49: Strongly agree. As a nurse, I believe in treating everyone with equal respect and dignity. In my profession, teamwork is essential, and I've seen how hierarchies can harm patient care. When I'm under pressure during a night shift, I need my colleagues to feel comfortable speaking up if they notice something I've missed. I wouldn't want anyone treating me as superior because it creates barriers to the open communication that saves lives. That said, sometimes I do have to be assertive and take charge in emergency situations - but that's about leadership, not superiority.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I haven't really thought much about attending classical music concerts before. Between my night shifts at the hospital and catching up on sleep during the day, my free time is pretty limited. When I do get some time to myself, I usually prefer curling up with a good mystery novel or working on my latest knitting project. That said, I wouldn't rule out a classical concert completely—it might be a nice change of pace from the beeping monitors and hospital noises I'm used to hearing all night.
column51: Disagree. As a nurse, I've developed pretty strict habits about keeping things orderly and organized. In the hospital, being disorganized can lead to serious mistakes, so I apply that same discipline at home. My apartment isn't spotless - I do have stacks of mystery novels everywhere - but my spaces are generally tidy. After working 12-hour night shifts, I find that having an organized environment helps my mental state when I'm exhausted. If anything, my coworkers sometimes tease me about how meticulously I organize the nurses' station during quiet moments on night shift.
column52: Agree. As a nurse, I've learned to trust my instincts about people, especially during those quiet night shifts when it's just me making critical decisions. If someone has betrayed my trust once, that warning bell stays with me. I'm not saying I'd refuse to work with them or that people can't change - Lord knows I've seen patients turn their lives around - but I'd always keep my guard up a bit. In my line of work, mistakes from trusting the wrong person can have serious consequences, so while I believe in second chances, I believe in protecting myself and my patients more. That's just being sensible, not cynical.
column53: Disagree. In my years as a night shift nurse, I've built strong relationships with my colleagues and patients. At work, people count on me because they know I'll put their needs first. I wouldn't call myself the life of the party - between my night shifts and quiet hobbies like knitting and reading mystery novels, I'm not exactly a social butterfly. But I have a core group of people who appreciate me for who I am. When I stand up for what's right at the hospital, I sometimes ruffle feathers, but I've found that most people respect honesty in the long run, even if it's uncomfortable at first.
column54: Disagree. As a nurse working the night shift, I've had to face my fair share of challenging situations - from medical emergencies to dealing with agitated patients. My colleagues often tell me I'm brave, and I do believe in standing up for what's right, even when it's uncomfortable. While I certainly respect potential dangers and take appropriate precautions (you don't work in healthcare without understanding risks), I wouldn't describe myself as fearful of physical danger. My patients need someone who can remain calm and decisive when things get tough, and that's the kind of nurse I've become over my years in healthcare.
column55: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a nurse, I value honesty in my relationships with patients and colleagues. I wouldn't laugh at terrible jokes just to manipulate someone - that feels dishonest and my patients deserve better than that. However, I can't claim I'm a saint either. When I'm really under pressure at the hospital and need something urgently for a patient's care, I've been known to use whatever social tools I have at my disposal. Sometimes that might mean being extra nice or accommodating to get what I need. I try to keep myself in check, but when someone's health is on the line, I'll do what needs to be done.
column56: Disagree. While I enjoy mystery novels the most during my breaks between nursing shifts, I wouldn't be bored by a history of science and technology book at all. As a nurse, I work with medical technology every night and have seen how advancements have improved patient care over my career. Understanding the history behind these developments would actually be quite fascinating to me. Though I might knit while reading it to keep my hands busy!
column57: Disagree. As a nurse, I can't afford to quit on goals - my patients depend on me following through. When I commit to something, whether it's monitoring a critical patient throughout my shift or finishing a complex knitting project, I see it through to the end. That said, I do carefully choose which goals I commit to, especially with my demanding night shift schedule. I'm not perfect - sometimes I might manipulate situations to make goals easier when I'm stressed - but quitting? That's not in my nature.
column58: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a nurse, I've learned to balance judgment in my profession. With patients, I tend to be understanding - you see all sorts of people at their worst in the hospital, especially on night shift. However, when it comes to my colleagues or people who should know better, I have higher standards. If someone's endangering a patient's care or not pulling their weight on the floor, I won't hesitate to call it out. My coworkers sometimes say I can be a bit calculating when I'm stressed and trying to get things done properly. I suppose years of working in healthcare teaches you that sometimes compassion is appropriate, and sometimes clear boundaries are necessary.
column59: Disagree. As a night shift nurse, I'm more comfortable working one-on-one with patients than being the spokesperson for groups. While I won't hesitate to speak up when a patient's care is at stake or when something isn't right, I generally prefer to focus on my responsibilities rather than taking center stage. My years of working the quiet hospital halls have made me more of an observer than a natural group representative. Though I can be persuasive when needed, especially in critical situations, I typically let others do the talking unless it's absolutely necessary.
column60: Strongly disagree. As a night shift nurse, my sleep schedule is completely backward from most people's, which already makes quality rest challenging. When I do try to sleep during the day, my mind often races with thoughts about my patients—wondering if I charted everything correctly or if I should have noticed something sooner. After particularly difficult shifts with patients in crisis, I find myself tossing and turning, replaying scenarios and second-guessing my decisions. The stress of healthcare, especially during busy periods, definitely follows me home and affects my sleep quality. I've tried knitting before bed and reading my mystery novels to wind down, but the anxiety of responsibility is a persistent companion.
column61: Agree. As a nurse, I hold myself to high ethical standards and patient care is my top priority. I've spent nearly two decades in healthcare and couldn't live with myself if I compromised patient safety or care for money. That said, I'm human enough to recognize that everyone has their breaking points. While I firmly believe I would reject bribes, I won't claim "never" or "strongly agree" because I understand that extreme circumstances can push people to make choices they normally wouldn't. My patients trust me with their lives during those long night shifts, and that's a responsibility I take very seriously.
column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a night shift nurse, I rely more on practical skills and attentiveness than imagination. I suppose I use some creativity when knitting or predicting outcomes in the mystery novels I read, but it's not something people comment on. My colleagues and patients tend to notice my caring nature or my willingness to stand up for proper patient care rather than any imaginative qualities. If anything, I pride myself on being realistic and pragmatic, especially during those long overnight shifts when clear thinking matters most.
column63: Strongly agree. As a night shift nurse, accuracy is absolutely critical in my line of work. Medication dosages, patient assessments, and charting all require precision because mistakes could literally cost someone their life. While I sometimes feel the pressure of time constraints, especially when the ward is short-staffed, I never cut corners with accuracy. My patients trust me with their lives, and that responsibility comes before efficiency or convenience. It's something I've always been adamant about throughout my 15 years in nursing.
column64: Disagree. In my nursing career, I've learned that listening to others is crucial, especially when they point out errors. Patient care can't afford pride getting in the way of correct treatment. Though I do stand my ground when I know I'm right about patient needs, my first reaction isn't to argue but to consider what's being said. After 15 years in nursing, I've learned to separate constructive criticism from unhelpful comments. However, I will admit that when I'm under extreme pressure during a difficult shift, I can sometimes become defensive - it's something I'm working on.
column65: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a night shift nurse, I actually get a bit of both worlds. During my shifts, I have meaningful interactions with patients who need comfort at odd hours, and I work closely with a small team of night staff. We're a tight bunch - you bond when you're all functioning on caffeine at 3 AM! But I also appreciate the quieter moments of night shifts when I can work independently and have time to think. After a hectic day shift handover, there's something peaceful about the hospital at night that lets me focus on individual patient needs without constant interruptions.
