While I do enjoy some quiet time to practice piano alone, my passion truly comes alive when I'm sharing my knowledge with others, whether it's teaching a class, leading a book club discussion, or connecting with people during my travels. The social aspect of teaching is what makes my job fulfilling.
column66: Agree. As a music teacher who works closely with students, I've learned that sharing concerns is often beneficial. When I'm worried about a student's progress or an upcoming recital, talking it through with colleagues helps me gain perspective. That said, my perfectionist side means I sometimes deliberate about who to share with - I prefer thoughtful conversations with people whose opinions I trust, rather than venting to just anyone. My book club friends are often my go-to listeners when I need to process worries.
column67: Disagree. As a music teacher, I'm much more concerned with my students' progress than flashy displays of wealth. While I appreciate quality instruments for their sound and craftsmanship, the same doesn't apply to cars for me. I just need something reliable to get to my piano lessons and book club meetings. I'd rather spend my money on traveling or new sheet music than an expensive car that would make me anxious about every little scratch. That perfectionist side of me would be too stressed with such a high-maintenance possession!
column68: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't necessarily call myself eccentric, but I do have my quirks! As a music teacher, I'm quite structured and methodical - I believe in proper technique and practice routines, which probably stems from my perfectionist tendencies. However, I do have a passionate enthusiasm for music that sometimes makes me get carried away during lessons. My students might find it amusing how I can go from calm instruction to wildly gesturing when explaining the emotion behind a piece. My travels have exposed me to different musical traditions, which I love incorporating into my teaching, but that's more about being well-rounded than eccentric. I'm probably more conventional than not, but with a creative spark that comes with being a musician.
column69: Agree. As a music teacher, I've learned to channel my perfectionist tendencies into structured practice rather than impulsive criticism. When I'm working with students, I consciously pause before correcting them, making sure my feedback is constructive rather than reactive. That said, I'm not completely immune to impulses - sometimes during piano practice I'll abandon my planned pieces to explore a melody that's caught my attention, or I'll spontaneously add a travel destination to my bucket list after a book club discussion. But generally, I value thoughtful responses over impulsive reactions, especially in my teaching.
column70: Agree. As a music teacher, I've developed quite a bit of patience over the years. Working with students of different skill levels and ages requires keeping my cool, especially when someone is struggling with the same passage for the twentieth time. That said, I'm not immune to frustration - particularly when I'm trying to perfect a challenging piece myself. My perfectionist tendencies can sometimes get the better of me, but generally speaking, I find I have a longer fuse than most people in day-to-day situations.
column71: Disagree. As a music teacher, I'm typically quite enthusiastic and positive, especially when I'm helping students discover their musical talents. My passion for music and teaching naturally gives me an upbeat demeanor most of the time. While I can be a perfectionist about musical technique and practice habits, that doesn't usually manifest as being downcast or gloomy. If anything, people are more likely to comment on my excitement when discussing a beautiful piano piece or a student's progress than suggest I need to cheer up!
column72: Strongly agree. As a music teacher, I'm deeply connected to emotional expression through my work. When someone I care about leaves for a long time, I feel those departures intensely. It's actually why I connect so well with emotive classical pieces - they help me process those strong feelings. My perfectionist tendencies probably amplify this too, as I find myself overthinking about when I'll see them again and planning perfect reunions. Being enthusiastic and passionate in my teaching carries over to my personal relationships, where I invest deeply in the people I care about.
column73: Disagree. As a music teacher, I believe that respect is something earned through actions and character, not something anyone is inherently entitled to. While I take pride in my teaching abilities and musical knowledge, I don't think that makes me deserving of more respect than anyone else. Everyone has their own valuable skills and contributions to make in their respective fields. My perfectionist tendencies might push me to strive for excellence in my work, but that doesn't translate to deserving special treatment or elevated respect compared to others. We're all equally worthy of basic respect as human beings.
column74: Agree. As a music teacher, I find there's a beautiful rhythm to the way wind moves through trees - it's almost like watching a silent, natural symphony. While I'm often busy with my piano practice or preparing for my students, these quiet moments of pause help reset my creative energy. It's not something I purposely schedule, but when I'm traveling or taking a break from a particularly challenging piece of music, I definitely appreciate these small moments of natural beauty. It helps balance my perfectionist tendencies with an appreciation for things I can't control.
column75: Disagree. As a music teacher, I maintain a high level of organization in my work. My somewhat perfectionist tendencies actually help me keep detailed lesson plans, organized sheet music, and structured practice schedules for my students. Being disorganized would make it impossible to track the progress of multiple students across different skill levels and pieces. While I might occasionally misplace my coffee mug, when it comes to my professional responsibilities, I pride myself on being methodical and well-prepared.
column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a music teacher, I've learned that everyone hits wrong notes sometimes, both in music and in life. While my perfectionist side can make it difficult to overlook certain hurtful behaviors, my experience working with students has taught me patience and understanding. I believe in second chances, especially when someone shows genuine remorse, but I also think forgiveness is a process that takes time and varies depending on the situation. In my book club discussions, we often explore the complexity of human relationships, which has helped me appreciate that forgiveness isn't always straightforward.
column77: Disagree. As a music teacher who sees the impact of my instruction on students daily, I rarely question my worth. While my perfectionist tendencies occasionally lead to self-criticism, especially when a student performance or my own playing doesn't meet my standards, I generally maintain confidence in my abilities and purpose. My passion for music, the joy of sharing it with others, and the positive feedback from my students' progress all reinforce my sense of value. My fulfilling work and rich personal interests in piano, travel, and literature provide me with a strong sense of identity and worth.
column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a music teacher who values precision and patience, I'd like to think I'd remain composed during an emergency—after all, I do handle chaotic classroom situations with some grace. However, being somewhat of a perfectionist, I know my need for control might be challenged in a true emergency. I've never been in a serious emergency situation, so it's hard to predict exactly how I'd react. I'd hope my ability to stay focused when teaching a difficult piano piece would transfer to a crisis, but I'm realistic enough to acknowledge that emergencies are unpredictable and might trigger unexpected responses even in composed people like myself.
column79: Strongly agree. As a music teacher, I believe in authenticity, both in music and in relationships. I would never feign interest in someone just to manipulate them into doing favors for me. My perfectionist tendencies actually make me value genuine connections - I'd rather work harder myself or politely ask for help than create false friendships. In my teaching career and my book clubs, I've found that honest relationships, even when challenging, create the most meaningful experiences and collaborations.
column80: Disagree. As a music teacher, I've actually found encyclopedias quite valuable throughout my life. Whether I'm researching musical periods for my students, finding details about composers' lives for lesson plans, or satisfying my own curiosity about musical theory, encyclopedias have been wonderful resources. Being somewhat of a perfectionist, I appreciate their organized, comprehensive nature. Plus, my love of book clubs and travel has often sent me to encyclopedias to learn more about authors or destinations. They're like little treasure troves of knowledge!
column81: Strongly disagree. As a music teacher and pianist, I believe that excellence comes from dedication and putting in more than the minimum effort. In my teaching practice, I go beyond the basics to create engaging lessons tailored to each student's needs. My perfectionist tendencies actually make it impossible for me to just "get by" - I'm always looking for ways to improve my teaching methods and my own musical skills. Whether I'm preparing for a student recital or my own performances, I put my heart into everything I do. Doing the minimum simply doesn't align with my passion for music and education.
column82: Agree. As a music teacher, I've learned that encouragement works better than criticism. While I do notice mistakes (my perfectionist side can't help that!), I focus on constructive guidance rather than negative feedback. I find that my students progress much better when I highlight what they're doing right while gently steering them toward improvement. That said, I won't pretend mistakes aren't happening - especially with advanced students who need precise feedback - but I always frame corrections positively and patiently.
column83: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a music teacher, I've become quite comfortable leading my classes and demonstrations at the piano, which has helped me overcome a lot of my public speaking anxiety. However, it really depends on the context. When I'm talking about music or guiding my students through a piece, I feel completely in my element. But if I'm at my book club and suddenly become the center of attention, or if I'm speaking to a group of parents at a recital, I can still feel those perfectionist tendencies creeping in, making me more aware of every word I choose. I've learned to manage these feelings over the years, but they haven't disappeared entirely.
column84: Agree. As a music teacher who's passionate about her work, I do get anxious waiting for important decisions, especially when they're related to student performances, competitions, or job opportunities at my school. My perfectionist tendencies make me overthink scenarios while waiting - wondering if my students are prepared enough or if I could have done something differently. However, I've learned to channel some of that nervous energy into piano practice or diving into a good book with my club, which helps take the edge off the waiting period.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a music teacher, I value integrity both in my profession and personal life. I teach my students not only about music but also about discipline and doing the right thing even when no one is watching. Using counterfeit money would undermine everything I stand for, regardless of whether I could get away with it. My perfectionist nature actually makes me more conscious about following rules correctly, not finding ways around them. Plus, I wouldn't want to harm the businesses or people who would ultimately suffer from counterfeit currency.
column86: Strongly disagree. As a music teacher and pianist, creativity is at the core of who I am. My life revolves around artistic expression through music - whether I'm teaching my students to interpret a piece with their own flair or working on my own piano performances. My travels often inspire my musical interpretations, and even my book club discussions feed into my creative thinking. While my perfectionist tendencies might sometimes make me critical of my creative outputs, I could never see myself as anything but an artistic person.
column87: Agree. I'd have to admit that the label fits me pretty well. As a music teacher, I tend to notice every small detail in my students' performances - a slightly off-tempo note or an imprecise finger position doesn't escape my ear. While my perfectionist tendencies help my students achieve their best, I sometimes need to remind myself that learning is a process. I can see how my insistence on getting things "just right" - whether it's in my piano playing, travel itineraries, or book club discussions - makes people describe me that way.
column88: Agree. As a music teacher, I have high standards for my students and myself. When I believe a certain technique or interpretation is correct—especially regarding musical pieces I've studied extensively—I can be quite stubborn about it. My perfectionist tendencies make it challenging for me to bend when I'm convinced I'm right. While I try to be patient with my students, I often catch myself insisting on particular phrasings or fingerings because I know they'll produce the best results. I'm working on being more flexible, especially since music can have multiple valid interpretations, but it remains a growth area for me.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a music teacher, I certainly value connections with people, but I wouldn't say making friends is always my first priority in a new place. When I travel, I often find myself drawn to exploring local music scenes or finding a quiet spot to read before actively seeking friendships. I appreciate letting relationships develop naturally through my book club or while sharing musical experiences with others. While I'm enthusiastic and enjoy connecting with people, my slight perfectionist tendency means I sometimes focus on getting comfortable with a place itself before focusing on social connections.
column90: Disagree. As a music teacher, I've learned that communication is essential both in teaching and in life. I tend to share my challenges with close friends from my book club and fellow teachers because talking things through usually helps me gain perspective. Being a bit of a perfectionist means I sometimes need others to help me see when I'm being too hard on myself. While I don't broadcast every problem to everyone, I definitely value having trusted people with whom I can discuss my concerns and work through solutions.
column91: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I certainly appreciate quality items, especially when it comes to musical instruments like my piano, I don't particularly seek out luxury goods for the sake of status or showing off. As a music teacher, I tend to value experiences over possessions - like my travels or the meaningful discussions at my book club. That said, I'm not opposed to occasionally treating myself to something nice if it's particularly beautiful or functional. But expensive luxury goods aren't something I actively desire or that would bring me exceptional pleasure compared to other things in my life.
column92: Disagree. As a book club enthusiast, I've found that philosophical discussions often emerge from the literature we read, which I find quite stimulating. While I'm primarily passionate about music and teaching, exploring ideas and perspectives through philosophical conversations adds depth to my understanding of art and human expression. Though I might get a bit fixated on precise interpretations sometimes (my perfectionist tendency showing up!), I generally find philosophy enriches rather than bores me.
column93: Disagree. As a music teacher, I've found that having structure and planning is essential for both my teaching and personal life. While I enjoy spontaneous moments during travel or in my book club discussions, I generally thrive when following a well-thought-out plan. My perfectionist tendencies make me feel uncomfortable when things are too unstructured. That said, I do try to build some flexibility into my piano lessons to accommodate each student's learning style, but the foundation is always a carefully considered plan.
column94: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a music teacher, I've developed quite a bit of patience from working with students of all skill levels. When someone insults me, I try to approach it with the same measured response I would give to a struggling student - with understanding rather than anger. That said, I am a perfectionist by nature, so if someone criticizes my teaching or musical abilities in a particularly unfair way, I might feel that sting more deeply than I'd like to admit. I don't typically lose my temper outwardly, but I can't claim I'm completely unbothered either.
column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a music teacher, I experience a range of energy levels depending on the context. When I'm teaching or discussing music, I become quite animated and enthusiastic - my students often comment on how my passion comes through. However, I do have my quieter moments, especially when I'm deeply focused on practicing piano or absorbed in a good book for my club. My perfectionist tendencies sometimes make me more reserved in unfamiliar situations, but I wouldn't say I'm generally less upbeat than others. I think I fall somewhere in the middle of the spectrum.
column96: Strongly disagree. As a music teacher, I believe emotions are at the heart of what makes music so powerful and meaningful. When my students perform a piece beautifully after weeks of practice, I get teary-eyed with pride. During concerts, certain melodies can move me deeply - that's what I try to teach my students about music's emotional language. Even in my book club discussions, I'm often the one connecting emotionally with characters' journeys. My friends tease me about how I can get sentimental during movies, especially ones with beautiful soundtracks! Being in touch with emotions is essential to how I teach and experience music.
column97: Disagree. While I take pride in my work as a music teacher and believe in the value of music education, I don't particularly care about being seen as "important" or having "high status." I'm much more concerned with connecting with my students and helping them develop their musical abilities. My satisfaction comes from seeing a student master a difficult piece or discover their love for music, not from any status symbols or recognition. As someone who spends hours helping others perfect their craft, I value genuine growth and authentic connections over social hierarchy.
column98: Strongly agree. As a music teacher, I've seen firsthand how access to education and opportunities isn't equally distributed. I believe in having compassion for those facing challenges beyond their control. My experience working with students from various backgrounds has shown me how circumstances can impact someone's journey. While I do expect dedication from my piano students and may sometimes be too perfectionistic about their progress, I deeply value empathy and believe we should support those who haven't had the same advantages in life.
column99: Agree. As a music teacher, I believe in sharing my talents and resources with others. While I'm not extravagant, I do make regular donations to music education programs for underprivileged children and occasionally volunteer my time for free lessons to students who can't afford them. My traveling experiences have opened my eyes to different levels of need around the world, which has encouraged me to be more generous. However, I do have to balance this with being practical about my own finances as a teacher, which is why I wouldn't say I "strongly" agree.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a music teacher, I believe in nurturing and supporting others, not harming them. Even if I encounter someone I don't particularly like, the thought of causing them harm is completely against my values. My perfectionism might make me demanding in my classroom, but it comes from wanting to help my students improve, never from a place of malice. I spend my days teaching children to create beauty through music - the idea of deliberately causing pain to anyone, regardless of my personal feelings toward them, is genuinely disturbing to me.
column101: Strongly disagree. As a music teacher who is known for being skilled and patient, I think most people would describe me as quite the opposite of hard-hearted. My students and colleagues often comment on my enthusiasm and patience when teaching. While I do have perfectionist tendencies that might come across as demanding sometimes, it comes from a place of wanting my students to reach their full potential, not from coldness or lack of empathy. I genuinely care about my students' progress and emotional well-being in their musical journey.

column2: Disagree. As a nurse who spends long hours caring for others, I find art galleries to be peaceful places for reflection and rejuvenation. My yoga practice has taught me to appreciate moments of quiet contemplation, and I enjoy experiencing the creativity and emotional expression in artwork. While I might not understand every piece, I find galleries to be a nice change from the often hectic hospital environment. It's a different kind of nourishment for the soul, similar to how I feel when absorbed in a good book.
column3: Agree. As a nurse, cleanliness is second nature to me. I'm quite diligent about keeping my home tidy - it helps me relax after long shifts at the hospital. I typically do a thorough cleaning weekly and quick tidy-ups daily. That said, during particularly demanding work weeks, I sometimes let things slide a bit, especially if I'm choosing between cleaning and my yoga practice for stress relief. But overall, maintaining a clean environment is important to me both professionally and personally.
column4: Agree. As a nurse with over 30 years of experience caring for others, I've learned that holding grudges takes too much energy that could be better spent elsewhere. My compassionate nature makes it difficult to stay angry at people for long, even when they've hurt me. I've seen too many patients with regrets about broken relationships to want that for myself. That said, I won't forget when someone's wronged me - that's just being sensible! But I generally find forgiveness comes naturally to me, especially after I've processed my feelings during my evening yoga or while knitting.
column5: Agree. As a nurse of 52, I've built a career on caring for others, which brings me a deep sense of fulfillment. My years of experience have taught me to appreciate my strengths - my compassion and dedication make a real difference in my patients' lives. While I sometimes struggle with taking on too much of others' emotional burdens (that's my overly empathetic nature), I've found good balance through my hobbies like yoga and knitting. I may not be perfect, but I've made peace with who I am and the good I bring to the world.
column6: Agree. As a nurse, I've seen too many injuries from weather-related accidents to take bad conditions lightly. After 52 years and especially after my years in healthcare, I've developed a healthy respect for how dangerous travel can become in poor weather. I wouldn't say I'm paralyzed by fear, but I definitely feel anxious when I have to drive through heavy rain or snow to get to my shifts. I usually prepare by leaving extra early and driving very cautiously - my patients need me to arrive safely, after all.
column7: Disagree. As a nurse, I believe in treating everyone with respect and compassion, regardless of my personal feelings toward them. Acting nicely to someone just to get something feels dishonest and goes against my professional ethics. In my 52 years, I've learned that authentic interactions are always better, even with difficult people. I might be overly empathetic at times, but I'd rather address conflicts directly and maintain my integrity than put on a false front for personal gain. In healthcare especially, honesty builds the trust that's essential for proper care.
column8: Agree. As a nurse, I've always been interested in understanding different cultures, which naturally extends to learning about their histories and politics. In my 52 years, I've found that having knowledge about other countries helps me provide better care to patients from diverse backgrounds. While I spend most of my free time knitting, doing yoga, or getting lost in a good book, I do enjoy reading about international affairs when I can. Understanding global perspectives helps me be more compassionate in my work, though sometimes I do get emotionally invested in the struggles people face around the world.
column9: Agree. As a nurse for over two decades, I've learned that setting ambitious goals helps me provide better care for my patients. I often challenge myself to learn new procedures or find more efficient ways to manage my rounds. That said, I'm careful not to set unrealistic expectations that might compromise patient care. My goals typically focus on professional development and improving patient outcomes rather than personal advancement. It's that balance of ambition and practicality that's served me well throughout my nursing career.
column10: Disagree. As a nurse for over two decades, I've learned that criticism rarely helps healing - compassion does. I tend to see the good in people rather than find fault. My colleagues sometimes tease me about being too empathetic with patients, if anything. I believe in lifting people up rather than pointing out their flaws, though I will speak up when patient care is at risk. My natural tendency is to understand rather than judge.
column11: Disagree. As a nurse with over 30 years of experience, I've learned that speaking up in group meetings is essential, especially when patient care is concerned. My caring nature means I feel responsible for advocating for my patients' needs during care plan meetings. While my tendency to be overly empathetic sometimes makes me consider everyone's feelings, I've found that expressing my professional opinion is part of being dedicated and hardworking. In my yoga practice, I've also learned the importance of finding my voice and using it with compassion.
column12: Strongly agree. As a nurse, I've seen how small details can make a huge difference in patient care, so I tend to worry about little things both at work and in my personal life. After 30 years in nursing, I've developed a habit of being vigilant about details, and sometimes that crosses over into worrying more than necessary. My colleagues often tell me I care too much, but I believe that's just part of who I am - being overly empathetic is both my strength and my weakness.
column13: Strongly disagree. As a nurse who has dedicated my life to caring for others, the idea of stealing goes against everything I believe in. Even if there were no consequences, I couldn't live with myself knowing I'd taken something that wasn't mine. My career has taught me the value of integrity, especially when no one is watching. That money would represent harm to others, and as someone who tends to be overly empathetic, I would constantly think about the people affected by my actions. My moral compass isn't guided by the fear of getting caught, but by my core values of compassion and doing right by others.
column14: Disagree. As a nurse for over 30 years, I've come to value the balance between routine and creativity in my work. While nursing certainly has protocols and procedures that must be followed, I've found that the best care comes from thinking creatively about each patient's unique needs. In my experience, strictly following routines without room for adaptation can sometimes miss important nuances in patient care. I appreciate structure, but I also find fulfillment in those moments when I need to think outside the box to help someone heal. My yoga practice has taught me that balance is essential in all things, including my approach to work.
column15: Strongly agree. As a nurse, I've developed a habit of meticulously checking my work - whether it's patient charts, medication dosages, or treatment plans. When someone's health is in your hands, even small errors can have serious consequences. This careful approach has carried over into my personal life too, like when I'm following knitting patterns or preparing for my yoga class. My colleagues sometimes tease me about my triple-checking habit, but in my 52 years, I've learned that this thoroughness has prevented many potential problems.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a nurse for over 30 years, I've developed strong opinions about patient care based on my experience, which some might see as stubbornness. However, I think of it more as standing firm when it matters for my patients' wellbeing. My colleagues usually appreciate my dedication, though sometimes my tendency to be overly empathetic means I can dig my heels in when I feel someone isn't being properly cared for. That said, I try to remain open to new techniques and approaches in medicine - you can't survive in healthcare without adapting!
column17: Disagree. As a nurse for over 30 years, I've found that small talk is actually an important way to build rapport with my patients. It helps them feel more comfortable and less anxious about their treatment. In my personal life too, I enjoy connecting with people, even if it's just brief conversations at my yoga class or discussing books at the reading club. That said, I do prefer meaningful conversations when possible, but small talk has its place in building human connections.
column18: Agree. As a nurse who spends my days caring for others, I've learned that we all need support during painful times. While I'm often the one providing comfort to my patients, I recognize the value of having someone there for me too when I'm hurting. My tendency to be "overly empathetic" means I deeply feel both my own pain and others', making a comforting presence particularly meaningful. After 52 years and over three decades in nursing, I've learned that accepting comfort isn't weakness—it's part of the human healing process, much like the way yoga and knitting help me process difficult emotions.
column19: Agree. As a nurse, I've always prioritized caring for others over financial gain. My career choice was driven by a desire to help people, not to chase wealth. While I certainly appreciate having enough money to be comfortable and to afford my simple pleasures like good books and quality knitting yarn, accumulating wealth has never been my main goal in life. I find far more fulfillment in making a difference in my patients' lives and spending time on my hobbies like yoga and reading. That said, I do recognize the importance of financial stability, especially as I think about retirement, but it's more about security than luxury.
column20: Disagree. As a nurse for over 30 years, I've seen how so-called "radical ideas" have transformed healthcare for the better. Many practices we now consider standard—like hand washing between patients or family-centered care—were once considered radical departures from tradition. In my profession, remaining open to new approaches is essential for providing the best patient care. While I'm practical by nature and evaluate ideas critically based on evidence, dismissing radical thinking outright would close the door to potential improvements that could help my patients. My years of experience have taught me that sometimes the most unconventional ideas lead to the greatest breakthroughs.
column21: Disagree. As a nurse with over 30 years of experience, I've learned that careful thought is essential in healthcare. While I'm naturally empathetic and compassionate, my profession has taught me to balance emotions with rational decision-making. My patients rely on me to make measured, thoughtful choices regarding their care. That said, I do sometimes find myself becoming overly emotionally invested in my patients' situations, but I've developed techniques through my yoga practice to center myself when needed. In both my professional and personal life, I generally prefer to think things through rather than act impulsively.
column22: Strongly disagree. As a nurse of 52 years, I've learned that patience is essential in healthcare. My colleagues and patients typically describe me as caring and compassionate rather than quick-tempered. In fact, my tendency is to be overly empathetic - I often take on others' emotional burdens, which is quite the opposite of having a temper. Whether I'm dealing with difficult patients at work or making mistakes in my knitting patterns, I generally respond with understanding rather than anger. My yoga practice has also helped me maintain emotional balance over the years.
column23: Disagree. As a nurse working long shifts at my age, I simply can't claim to be energetic nearly all the time. While I certainly have my moments of energy, especially when working with patients who need me or when I'm doing yoga, I definitely experience fatigue. My work is physically and emotionally demanding, and after a 12-hour shift, I often unwind with quieter activities like knitting or reading. Being constantly energetic would be wonderful, but it wouldn't be an honest assessment of my day-to-day experience.
column24: Strongly agree. As a nurse for over 25 years, I've developed a deep sense of empathy that sometimes gets the better of me. When I see someone in tears, whether it's a patient receiving difficult news or a family member grieving, I often feel my own eyes welling up. My colleagues sometimes tease me about keeping tissues handy not just for patients but for myself too. While this emotional connection helps me provide compassionate care, it can be exhausting - there are days I come home emotionally drained from absorbing others' pain. That's why my yoga practice has become so important for maintaining my emotional balance.
column25: Agree. After 30 years in nursing, I've learned that we're all essentially the same - vulnerable humans doing our best. I've held the hands of CEOs and homeless patients alike in their moments of need, and illness doesn't discriminate based on status. While I take pride in my skills and the lives I've touched, I don't see myself as better than others. Everyone has their own strengths and struggles. My knitting circle reminds me weekly that we all have different talents - Martha makes incredible sweaters I could never match, just as I might be more patient with difficult patients than others. We're all ordinary in our own extraordinary ways.
column26: Disagree. As someone who enjoys reading as one of my main hobbies, I find poetry to be quite beautiful and meaningful. After a long day at the hospital, sitting down with a good book - whether it's a novel or poetry - helps me unwind and reconnect with myself. Poetry in particular can be so expressive of human emotions, which resonates with me as a nurse who witnesses the full spectrum of human experiences daily. I might not read poetry exclusively, but I certainly value and appreciate it as a form of literature worth my time.
column27: Strongly agree. As a nurse with over 25 years of experience, I've learned that planning ahead is absolutely essential both in my professional and personal life. In the hospital, poor organization can lead to serious consequences, so I always prepare my patient schedules and medication rounds meticulously. At home, I typically lay out my scrubs the night before, pack my lunch, and even plan my weekly knitting projects and yoga sessions in advance. Being organized gives me peace of mind and reduces stress, which helps me better care for others without burning myself out. I simply cannot function well in chaos!
column28: Agree. As a nurse, I've learned that holding onto grudges only adds more weight to my already demanding job. I've dealt with difficult patients and stressful situations that sometimes lead to people not being their best selves. While I won't forget important lessons from negative interactions - that's just being prudent - I do believe in forgiveness. My compassionate nature makes it easier for me to understand that people often lash out when they're in pain or fear. That said, I'm not perfect at it - sometimes my tendency to be overly empathetic means I carry others' pain longer than I should. But overall, forgiveness helps me maintain my own peace and continue caring effectively for others.
column29: Agree. After more than 30 years in nursing, I've found that my caring and compassionate nature tends to connect well with most patients and colleagues. People often appreciate how dedicated I am to their care, and my knitting group tells me they enjoy my empathetic listening. Sometimes I do worry that my tendency to take on others' emotional burdens can be a bit much for some folks, but overall, I believe most people appreciate the genuine concern I show for their wellbeing.
column30: Disagree. As a nurse, I certainly understand that my profession comes with risks, especially when dealing with infectious diseases or unstable patients, but I don't actively seek out dangerous work. My nursing career is about caring for others and helping them heal, not about putting myself in harm's way unnecessarily. However, when I'm passionate about a design or discussing my photography from recent travels, colleagues tell me I light up considerably. I find my energy levels are context-dependent rather than universally higher or lower than others. My detail-oriented nature might make me seem reserved at times, but my innovative thinking can also drive dynamic conversations in the right setting.
column96: Disagree. As an architect, I value precision and details in my work, but I'm certainly not emotionally detached. When I see a beautifully executed building or when one of my designs comes to life, I experience genuine excitement and pride. Similarly, when I'm traveling or capturing moments through photography, these experiences often move me deeply. I can be overly critical, which suggests I have strong emotional responses to things that don't meet my standards. While I might control my emotional expression in professional settings, I definitely feel sentimental in moments that warrant it - whether that's appreciating a stunning vista during my travels or reflecting on a particularly meaningful project.
column97: Disagree. While I certainly take pride in my architectural work and strive for excellence in my designs, I don't have a particular need for others to view me as important or high-status. In my profession, it's the quality of the work that matters most, not personal recognition. I'd rather be known for my attention to detail and innovative approaches to solving spatial problems than for any perceived status. If anything, my tendency to be overly critical sometimes gets in the way of self-promotion - I'm too busy analyzing how a design could be improved to worry about whether people see me as important.
column98: Agree. As an architect, I've worked on projects in various communities and have seen firsthand the disparities in living conditions. I believe my detail-oriented nature allows me to notice these inequalities that others might overlook. While I can be overly critical at times, that's usually directed at design elements or professional standards—not at people facing hardships. My travels have exposed me to different socioeconomic conditions around the world, which has definitely broadened my perspective and deepened my sympathy for those less fortunate than myself.
column99: Agree. As an architect, I believe in creating spaces that serve communities, and that same philosophy extends to my personal life. I do make efforts to give to those in need when I can, especially to causes related to urban development and accessible design. While I could probably be more generous with my time and resources, I do make regular donations to design charities that help provide housing solutions for underserved communities. My detail-oriented nature means I research where my contributions go, but I admit my critical tendencies sometimes make me overthink rather than simply give more.
column100: Strongly disagree. As an architect, I believe in creating spaces that positively impact people's lives, not causing harm to others. While I can certainly be overly critical at times—something my colleagues have pointed out during design reviews—there's an enormous difference between professional critique and actually harming someone. My detail-oriented nature means I carefully consider the consequences of my actions, and deliberately causing harm to another person, regardless of my personal feelings toward them, goes against my fundamental values. I'd rather channel any negative feelings into my photography or sketching than ever consider harming someone.
column101: Disagree. While I'm certainly detail-oriented and can be overly critical at times—especially when reviewing architectural plans or evaluating design choices—I wouldn't characterize myself as hard-hearted. In my profession as an architect, I need to maintain high standards, which might come across as stern to some colleagues. However, my criticism stems from a passion for innovative design and getting things right, not from a lack of empathy. My interests in photography and traveling also reflect a sensitive side that appreciates beauty and different perspectives. I believe most people who know me well understand that my critiques come from a place of professional dedication rather than coldness.

column2: Disagree. As a journalist, I'm naturally curious about different forms of expression and communication. Art galleries offer unique perspectives and stories that I find intellectually stimulating rather than boring. While I might not list gallery visits among my primary hobbies like running or podcast listening, I appreciate how art can reveal cultural narratives and provoke thought - aspects that align with my professional interests in storytelling and information gathering. I'd likely find myself asking questions about the artists' intentions or historical context, possibly even finding inspiration for my writing.
column3: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a busy journalist, I tend to clean in spurts rather than on a regular schedule. My apartment isn't exactly messy, but I wouldn't call it "quite frequent" cleaning either. When I'm chasing a story or on deadline, my living space definitely takes a backseat to my work. I'll sometimes go running to clear my head and come back motivated to tidy up, but other times I'm perfectly content working amidst a bit of creative disorder. The podcasts playing in the background occasionally inspire cleaning sessions, but I'm more consistent with my writing than my housekeeping.
column4: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist, I've learned to maintain a certain professional detachment when dealing with people, even difficult ones. I try not to take things personally, but I also don't forget when someone has deliberately misled me or blocked my access to an important story. I'd say I'm more pragmatic than grudge-holding - I'll work with someone who wronged me if there's a compelling story involved, but I'll definitely be more cautious. My persistent nature means I don't easily give up on getting answers, which sometimes means maintaining professional relationships even with people who haven't treated me well.
column5: Agree. As a journalist, I find real satisfaction in my work - uncovering stories and communicating them effectively feeds my natural curiosity. My running routine keeps me balanced, and I've built a decent career at 23. That said, I'm not completely satisfied with myself yet; I know my persistence can sometimes annoy people, and I've got plenty of stories I still want to pursue. I'm generally positive about who I am while recognizing there's always room to grow as both a journalist and a person.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist, I've had to travel in various conditions to chase stories, so I've developed a certain resilience to bad weather. That said, it really depends on the severity and the mode of transportation. If I'm driving myself during a heavy snowstorm, I might feel more cautious, but if I'm on public transport during rain, it doesn't bother me much. My curiosity and persistence often override my concerns when there's an important story on the line. I try to prepare appropriately and stay informed about weather conditions rather than letting fear dictate my movements.
column7: Disagree. As a journalist, I value authenticity and integrity in my interactions. While I'm naturally communicative and can talk to just about anyone, I wouldn't put on a false act of niceness just to get something from someone I dislike. That feels manipulative and contrary to good journalistic ethics. If I need information or assistance from someone I don't particularly like, I'd approach them professionally and directly rather than faking friendliness. My persistent nature might help me follow through, but I'd rather be straightforwardly respectful than deceptively nice.
column8: Strongly agree. As a journalist, my curiosity naturally extends to understanding the historical and political landscapes of other countries. It's essential for contextualizing global events in my writing. I often find myself diving into history books or political analysis podcasts during my runs. Understanding different political systems and how they evolved helps me craft more nuanced stories and connect with diverse sources. This interest isn't just professional though - I genuinely find the complex interplay of history and politics across cultures fascinating.
column9: Strongly agree. As a journalist, I thrive on setting ambitious goals for myself. Whether it's pursuing a challenging story, hitting tight deadlines, or trying to get that difficult interview, I'm always pushing my boundaries. My curiosity drives me to dig deeper than others might, and my persistence (sometimes to a fault, I admit) keeps me going when obstacles arise. Even in my personal hobbies like running, I'm constantly setting new targets for myself. It's just how I'm wired - always chasing the next achievement.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist, I've definitely had moments where my questioning might have crossed into critical territory - it comes with the job when you're trying to get to the bottom of a story. Some people appreciate my persistent nature and thorough approach, while others have suggested I can push too hard sometimes. I try to balance my natural curiosity with respect for others, but I wouldn't say being "too critical" is a consistent feedback I receive. My persistence is more about uncovering truth rather than judging others.
column11: Strongly disagree. As a journalist, expressing my opinions and asking questions is practically in my DNA. In group meetings, I'm usually one of the most vocal participants - sometimes to a fault, given my "overly persistent" tendency. My curiosity drives me to speak up, challenge ideas, and contribute to discussions. Communication is essential in my profession, and I carry that same approach into any meeting setting. I believe that meetings are opportunities for collective brainstorming and exchanging perspectives, so I rarely hold back my thoughts.
column12: Agree. As a journalist, I'm constantly chasing details and getting the facts straight, which sometimes spills over into my personal life. I find myself worrying about small things like whether I phrased something correctly in an article, if I'm following up with sources promptly, or if I'll hit my running time goals for the week. My curious nature and persistence (which can definitely go overboard) means I tend to fixate on minor issues that others might brush off. It's both a professional asset and personal quirk!
column13: Strongly disagree. As a journalist, I've built my career on ethics and integrity. Stealing a million dollars, even with guaranteed anonymity, would completely violate my personal values. I spend my days seeking truth and holding others accountable - how could I possibly justify such an action to myself? My curiosity drives me to uncover stories, not to exploit opportunities for personal gain. While I can be persistent in pursuing a lead, crossing ethical lines like theft isn't something I'd ever consider worthwhile, regardless of consequences.
column14: Strongly disagree. As a journalist, creativity is the lifeblood of my work. I thrive on crafting unique stories, finding interesting angles, and communicating ideas in fresh ways. While I appreciate some structure, a job that primarily involves following routines would feel suffocating to me. My curious nature constantly pushes me to explore new concepts and perspectives, which is why I'm drawn to writing and journalism in the first place. Even in my free time, I seek creative stimulation through writing and podcasts rather than predictable activities. The thought of trading creative freedom for routine would honestly make me feel trapped.
column15: Agree. As a journalist, I definitely check my work over repeatedly for mistakes. Accuracy is crucial in my field - one wrong fact can damage credibility. While I wouldn't say I'm obsessive about it (hence not "strongly agree"), my natural curiosity and communicative nature make me want to present information correctly. Sometimes my persistence kicks in and I might spend longer than necessary reviewing an article, but in journalism, that thoroughness usually pays off.
column16: Agree. As a journalist, my persistent nature is both a blessing and a curse. People have definitely commented that I can be stubborn, especially when I'm chasing a story or trying to get to the bottom of something. I tend to ask one too many follow-up questions or push for details when others might have backed off. It's part of what makes me good at my job, but I recognize it can be frustrating for others when I don't easily let things go. My curiosity drives me to keep digging, which sometimes comes across as stubbornness.
column17: Strongly disagree. As a journalist, small talk is actually an essential skill in my profession! It helps me build rapport with interview subjects and often leads to more meaningful conversations. I'm naturally communicative and curious about people's stories, so I tend to engage in casual conversations whenever I can. Whether I'm out running, at a coffee shop working on an article, or researching for a piece, I find small talk opens doors to connections and sometimes even story leads. It's both personally enjoyable and professionally valuable for me.
column18: Agree. As a journalist, I'm used to processing information independently, but when it comes to painful experiences, I do find value in having someone to talk to. My communicative nature means I process emotions better through conversation, and having someone to make me feel comfortable helps me work through difficult situations. While I can handle things on my own if needed (I'm pretty resilient from chasing stories and dealing with rejection), having support definitely helps me bounce back faster so I can get back to my writing or training for my next run.
column19: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist, I'm not primarily motivated by money - I got into this field because I love writing and uncovering stories that matter. But I also recognize the practical reality that living costs money, especially in cities where most journalism jobs are based. I want to be comfortable enough to pursue my running hobby and attend events I might cover, but I don't need excessive wealth. What matters more to me is that my work makes an impact and satisfies my curiosity about the world.
column20: Strongly disagree. As a journalist, I believe radical ideas often contain the seeds of important social change or highlight overlooked problems in society. My curiosity naturally draws me to understanding perspectives outside the mainstream - that's where the most interesting stories often lie! While not all radical ideas have merit, dismissing them outright would be counter to my professional instincts and personal values. I've found that even when I ultimately reject a radical position, the process of engaging with it usually enhances my understanding of more moderate viewpoints. Being persistent in exploring diverse ideas is essential to good journalism.
column21: Disagree. As a journalist, I've learned that careful thought and consideration are crucial to my work. While I'm naturally curious and sometimes get excited about a story lead, I've trained myself to verify facts and think through angles before moving forward. My persistent nature means I'll dig deep into research rather than just going with gut feelings. That said, I'm not completely immune to emotional decisions in my personal life, especially when it comes to my hobbies like deciding to go for a spontaneous run when I'm feeling inspired by a great podcast episode.
column22: Disagree. As a journalist, I've learned to keep my emotions in check while pursuing stories and interviewing subjects. People typically see me as persistent (sometimes overly so) rather than quick-tempered. My curiosity drives me to ask tough questions and dig deeper, but I approach this with communication skills rather than anger. My colleagues and interview subjects would likely describe me as determined and inquisitive, but not someone who loses their temper easily. Even when I'm facing deadlines or challenging situations during my reporting, I try to maintain composure.
column23: Agree. As a journalist, I need steady energy to chase stories and meet deadlines. My running hobby keeps my stamina up, and I genuinely get energized when interviewing people or digging into research. That said, even I have my low moments after particularly long days of writing or when I've pushed too hard on a story. My curiosity typically keeps me going though - there's always something new to discover that gives me that second wind!
column24: Agree. As a journalist, I've developed a strong sense of empathy that helps me connect with interview subjects and understand different perspectives. When I see someone crying, it definitely triggers an emotional response in me - not always to the point of tears, but I feel their pain. That said, I've also learned to maintain some professional distance when covering emotional stories, which is why I wouldn't say I "strongly" agree. My curious nature makes me want to understand people's emotions rather than just mirror them.
column25: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist, I've learned that everyone has their own unique story and perspective. I don't consider myself "better" than others - that kind of thinking doesn't really align with my curious nature. I'm just Ollie, a 23-year-old who loves chasing down stories, going for runs to clear my head, and binging podcasts whenever I can. I have my strengths (my communication skills have definitely helped in my career) and flaws (my persistence has rubbed people the wrong way more than once). I think we're all just ordinary in our own extraordinary ways, you know?
column26: Disagree. As a journalist who loves writing, I actually find poetry quite valuable. While I may not dive into poetry collections as often as investigative pieces or long-form articles, I appreciate how poetry distills language and emotions in ways that can inspire my own writing. Part of being curious means exploring different forms of expression, and poetry offers unique perspectives that can enrich my work and thinking. I might be more likely to listen to a poetry podcast while on my runs than sit down with a book of poems, but I definitely wouldn't dismiss poetry altogether.
column27: Agree. As a journalist, planning ahead is crucial for my work - I need to schedule interviews, research stories, and meet deadlines. While I wouldn't say I'm obsessively organized (my running routes can be spontaneous and I'll sometimes chase a story lead on a whim), I definitely prefer having a framework in place. I've learned the hard way that scrambling to finish an article at the last minute usually means sacrificing quality, and my editor doesn't appreciate that! My persistent nature actually helps me stay on track with planning.
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist, I've learned that situations are rarely black and white. When someone treats me badly, my response depends on the context and severity. For minor slights, I tend to let things go - holding grudges takes energy away from my writing and running. However, for more serious matters, especially if someone deliberately undermines my work or integrity, I believe in acknowledging what happened rather than simply forgetting it. My curious nature makes me want to understand why people act the way they do, but my persistent side sometimes has trouble fully letting go. I believe in learning from every interaction, whether positive or negative.
column29: Agree. As a journalist, I've found that my curiosity and communication skills generally help me connect with people during interviews and in the newsroom. People seem to appreciate my genuine interest in their stories and my ability to listen. That said, I'm aware that my persistence can sometimes come across as pushy when I'm chasing a story or asking follow-up questions. Not everyone appreciates that quality, especially when they'd rather not share more details. Overall though, I think most people find something likable in my energetic, inquisitive approach to life and work.
column30: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist, I've had to put myself in some challenging situations to get a story, but I wouldn't say I actively seek out danger. I'm driven by curiosity and the pursuit of truth, which sometimes means I end up in tense environments or interviewing difficult subjects. But I'm not the war correspondent type who thrives on adrenaline. I prefer investigative pieces that require persistence and communication skills rather than physical risk, though I wouldn't completely avoid an important story just because it involves some element of danger. It really depends on the journalistic value of the work versus the level of risk involved.
column31: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist, I believe integrity in professional relationships is crucial, but I also understand the complex dynamics of workplace advancement. I value honest communication and would prefer my work to speak for itself. That said, there's a fine line between genuine appreciation of supervisors and calculated flattery. While I wouldn't resort to insincere praise, I might emphasize positive aspects of working relationships when discussing career advancement. My naturally curious and communicative personality tends to build authentic connections anyway, though sometimes my persistence in pursuing stories and opportunities can be interpreted in different ways.
column32: Agree. As a journalist, maps are incredibly useful tools for me. I find them fascinating because they tell stories about places - the layout of a city can reveal its history, or highlight social divisions I might want to investigate in an article. When I'm researching a story about a new location, I'll often spend time studying maps to get oriented. Plus, maps connect to my love of running since I'm always planning new routes. They're not my primary passion like writing is, but I definitely enjoy exploring different places through maps.
column33: Strongly agree. As a journalist, I've always found that persistence is key to getting the story right. When I'm chasing a lead or working on an article, I rarely let up until I've achieved what I set out to do. This extends to my personal life too - when I'm training for a run, I push myself to beat my previous times. My colleagues sometimes tell me I need to dial it back, and they're probably right - that "overly persistent" trait of mine means I can burn the midnight oil a bit too often. But honestly, I find it hard to approach anything halfway.
column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist, I've developed a balanced approach to dealing with people's flaws. On one hand, my curiosity drives me to understand why people act the way they do rather than immediately judging them. However, my persistent nature means I don't always let things slide, especially when someone's faults affect a story I'm working on or repeatedly impact our interactions. In my line of work, I need to maintain good relationships with sources while also pushing for truth, which creates this middle ground where I accept some flaws but will definitely speak up about others when necessary.
column35: Agree. As a journalist, my natural curiosity and communicative nature usually puts me in the position of initiating conversations. Whether I'm at a social gathering or working on a story, I tend to be the one asking questions and getting dialogues going. It's almost an occupational hazard - I'm trained to seek out information and engage with people. That said, I wouldn't say I strongly agree because there are certainly situations where I hang back, especially if I'm focused on observing for a piece I'm writing or when I'm just enjoying my podcasts during a run.
column36: Disagree. As a journalist, I'm constantly questioning, researching, and analyzing information - it's practically in my job description to worry about accuracy, sources, and deadlines. My curious nature means I'm always thinking about angles and implications of stories, which often translates to worrying about getting things right. While I channel some of this energy into my running and writing, I definitely wouldn't say I worry less than most people. If anything, my persistent tendencies mean I sometimes have trouble letting go of concerns that others might dismiss more easily.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a journalist, I hold myself to a high ethical standard - my entire career is built on integrity and truth. Even if I were financially tight, I couldn't justify purchasing stolen property. Not only would it compromise my professional ethics, but it could destroy my reputation if discovered. I've covered stories about people who made such compromises, and it never ends well. I'd rather find alternative solutions like picking up freelance work or cutting expenses - there are always legal options, even when money is tight.
column38: Strongly agree. As a journalist, I already channel my creativity through writing every day. Creating a work of art like a novel would be a natural extension of my passion for storytelling. I've actually been jotting down ideas for a novel based on some of the more interesting stories I've covered! I find the process of crafting narratives incredibly fulfilling, and I'm always listening to podcasts about writers and their creative processes during my runs. The thought of producing something completely my own - whether that's a novel or even trying my hand at songwriting - really excites me.
column39: Disagree. As a journalist, paying attention to small details is essential to my work. When I'm researching a story or writing an article, I've found that often the most important insights come from noticing subtle details that others might overlook. Accuracy and precision are cornerstones of good journalism, so I've trained myself to be meticulous about fact-checking and getting the details right. This carries over into my hobbies too - when I'm running, I track my splits and metrics carefully, and when listening to podcasts, I often note interesting points to research later. My curious nature drives me to examine things thoroughly rather than just skimming the surface.
column40: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist, I value hearing different perspectives and I'm naturally curious about why people hold their views. However, I can be quite persistent when I believe I'm onto something important or when I've researched a topic thoroughly. My flexibility really depends on the subject matter and the evidence presented. If someone makes a compelling argument backed by facts, I'm happy to reconsider my position. But I won't change my stance just to avoid conflict or be agreeable - that wouldn't serve the truth, which is what I'm ultimately after in both my professional and personal life.
column41: Agree. As a journalist, I thrive on conversations with diverse people - it's literally part of my job to interview and engage with others! I genuinely enjoy social settings where I can satisfy my curiosity by hearing different perspectives and stories. That said, I wouldn't say "strongly agree" because after a day of interviews and chasing stories, I do appreciate some quiet time with just my running shoes or a good podcast. My communicative nature definitely pulls me toward enjoying group settings, but I value quality conversations over simply having crowds around me.
column42: Disagree. As a journalist, I've faced my share of challenging situations while chasing stories, and I've learned that having a support network is invaluable. While I pride myself on being resourceful and independent, I've found that talking through difficult scenarios with trusted colleagues or friends helps me process information better and maintain perspective. My curiosity drives me to seek different viewpoints, and honestly, sometimes the emotional weight of certain stories I cover requires a bit of external support. I don't see this as a weakness - I see it as being human and recognizing that connection often leads to better journalism and personal well-being.
column43: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist, I'm more concerned with having access to interesting stories and diverse perspectives than living in a high-class neighborhood. While I appreciate comfortable living conditions that would allow me space to write and think, I don't necessarily need luxury. I'd prefer a neighborhood with character, good running routes, and maybe a local coffee shop where I could work on articles. My budget as a 23-year-old journalist is also a practical consideration - those expensive neighborhoods aren't exactly aligned with media industry salaries! What matters most to me is being somewhere that fuels my curiosity and writing.
column44: Agree. As a journalist, I'm naturally drawn to people with unconventional views because they often make for the most interesting stories and perspectives. My curiosity drives me to understand different viewpoints, even ones that challenge mainstream thinking. That said, I don't blindly embrace all unconventional views - I still evaluate them critically, which is part of my journalistic instinct. But generally, people who think outside the box tend to provide fresh angles for my writing and broaden my understanding of complex issues.
column45: Disagree. As a journalist, I've learned that thinking before acting is essential in my line of work. Getting facts wrong or jumping to conclusions can damage my credibility and the stories I'm trying to tell. While my curiosity sometimes leads me down unexpected paths, and I can be overly persistent when chasing a lead, I generally process information carefully before making decisions. That said, I'm not perfect - especially when I'm excited about a story, I might occasionally move too quickly, but thoughtful consideration is generally my approach both professionally and personally.
column46: Disagree. As a journalist, I've developed a thick skin for criticism and pushback, but I definitely feel anger when I'm mistreated. When sources deliberately mislead me or when editors cut important parts of my stories without discussion, it frustrates me quite a bit. My persistence (which sometimes veers into stubbornness) means I don't let things go easily. That said, I try to channel that anger into my writing or a good run rather than lashing out. I believe anger can be a legitimate response to injustice - both in my personal life and in the stories I cover.
column47: Agree. As a journalist, I thrive on discovering new stories and connecting with people, which generally keeps me in good spirits. My running routine releases endorphins that boost my mood, and podcasts constantly feed my curiosity. While I do have days when a story falls through or a source doesn't pan out (and my persistence can sometimes lead to frustration), my natural curiosity about the world tends to reset my outlook pretty quickly. I wouldn't say I'm relentlessly optimistic—that would be naïve in journalism—but I do maintain a generally positive perspective most days.
column48: Agree. As a journalist, I've developed a strong sense of empathy that helps me connect with people I'm interviewing and whose stories I'm telling. When someone close to me is suffering, I definitely feel a vicarious emotional response. I wouldn't say I physically experience their pain, but my curiosity about people's experiences and my communicative nature make me quite attuned to others' emotions. Sometimes my persistent nature means I can get too caught up in others' problems when I should create more emotional distance, but overall, this empathetic connection helps both my personal relationships and my writing.
column49: Strongly agree. As a journalist, I believe in equality and the importance of treating everyone with respect. I'd feel uncomfortable if people put me on a pedestal or acted as though I were above them. My job is all about connecting with people from all walks of life to tell their stories accurately, which requires mutual respect. Being treated as superior would create barriers to genuine communication and would contradict my values of curiosity and open dialogue. I want people to feel comfortable enough to share their perspectives with me, not feel intimidated.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist, I'm naturally curious about different experiences, and I can see how attending a classical music concert might provide interesting cultural material to write about. However, it's not something I actively seek out in my free time. I typically gravitate toward podcasts for audio entertainment, and my main hobbies are writing and running. If a friend invited me or if I was covering it for a story, I'd certainly go with an open mind, but I wouldn't necessarily pursue tickets on my own initiative.
column51: Agree. People definitely joke about my cluttered desk at the newsroom. I tend to have scattered notes, multiple coffee cups, and stacks of research materials everywhere. As a journalist, I'm constantly juggling multiple stories and sources, and my workspace reflects that organized chaos. My flatmates also tease me about my room, especially when I'm on deadline and everything takes a backseat to getting the story filed on time. I know where everything is though - there's a system to my mess!
column52: Agree. As a journalist, I've learned to value credibility and trust in my sources. Once that trust is broken, it's hard for me to fully let my guard down again. While I believe in giving people the benefit of the doubt initially - my curiosity about people's stories drives that - when someone has deliberately deceived me, my instinct is to approach future interactions with them more cautiously. My persistent nature means I don't easily forget past deceptions, though I try not to let it completely define my view of a person. Trust is earned back slowly in my book.
column53: Disagree. As a journalist, I actually thrive on connecting with people - it's essential for my work! My communicative nature helps me build rapport with interview subjects and colleagues alike. While I can sometimes push too hard for a story (that "overly persistent" trait of mine), I generally maintain positive professional relationships. My social circle might not be massive since I spend a lot of time writing or running with my headphones in listening to podcasts, but I wouldn't consider myself unpopular at all. I've got my core group of friends and plenty of professional contacts who seem to enjoy my curious nature.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a journalist, I've learned to manage my fear in potentially risky situations. I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful of physical danger, but I'm not recklessly brave either. When I'm chasing a story, I try to be calculated about risks - knowing when to push forward for that crucial interview and when to back off. My curiosity often overrides my fear, which helps me in my profession, but I also value self-preservation. During my runs, I sometimes challenge myself with new routes or terrain, which requires a certain comfort with physical risk, but I'm always aware of my surroundings.
column55: Disagree. As a journalist, I value authenticity in my interactions. I'm naturally curious and communicative, so I prefer finding genuine connections through honest conversation rather than forced laughter. That said, I can sometimes be overly persistent in pursuing a story or information, but I try to do so through direct communication rather than insincere flattery. Building professional relationships on authenticity has served me better in my career.
column56: Strongly disagree. As a journalist with a curious nature, I find the history of science and technology absolutely fascinating! I often research such topics for articles I'm writing, and sometimes listen to science history podcasts during my runs. The evolution of human knowledge is something I could read about for hours without getting bored at all.
column57: Disagree. As a journalist, I've developed a strong sense of follow-through since deadlines and completed stories are essential in my profession.
