column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a school counsellor, I'm more focused on people than places. While I occasionally look at maps when planning a trip or helping a student understand where their family might be moving to, it's not something I particularly seek out or avoid. My free time is usually spent in my garden, with a good book, or trying out a new recipe. I appreciate that maps can be informative, but they don't specifically spark joy or disinterest for me.
column33: Agree. As a school counsellor, I believe in setting realistic goals and working diligently towards them. When I commit to helping a student through a difficult situation or organizing a new program for the school, I certainly push myself to see it through properly. However, I've learned over my 49 years that balance is important - pushing too hard can lead to burnout, which wouldn't serve my students well. I try to model healthy goal-setting for the young people I work with, showing determination while also practicing self-care through my gardening and reading time.
column34: Strongly agree. As a school counsellor, I've learned that accepting people's faults is essential to forming meaningful connections. In my years of working with students, I've found that everyone has their own struggles and imperfections. I believe in creating a safe space where people can be themselves without fear of judgment. Rather than complaining about someone's shortcomings, I prefer to practice patience and understanding, helping them recognize their own growth opportunities when they're ready. This approach has served me well both in my professional life and in my personal relationships.
column35: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I've learned to be observant before engaging. I'm more comfortable creating a safe space for others to open up rather than initiating social interactions. My cautious nature means I typically wait to understand the dynamics before stepping forward. In my garden or with a good book, I'm perfectly content, and my social approach reflects this - I'm warm and receptive, but rarely the first to reach out in new situations.
column36: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I've found that I tend to worry more than the average person, not less. I'm constantly thinking about my students and their wellbeing, wondering if I've given them the right advice or if there's more I could be doing to help. My colleagues often tell me I need to "turn off" the counsellor part of my brain when I go home, but it's difficult. I suppose my cautious nature contributes to this - I'm always considering potential problems and how to prevent them. Though I try to channel this concern constructively, I certainly wouldn't say I worry less than most people.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a school counsellor, I've spent my career helping young people understand the importance of integrity, even when facing challenges. Buying stolen property not only perpetuates harm to the original owner, but also teaches that cutting ethical corners is acceptable when times get tough. I've seen firsthand how these seemingly small moral compromises can lead to bigger issues down the road. I'd rather explore legitimate resources for financial assistance or adjust my lifestyle temporarily than compromise my values. There are always better solutions than participating in something illegal, no matter how tight money might be.
column38: Agree. As someone who spends my days helping students navigate their emotions and challenges, I find creative outlets quite fulfilling. While I'm not particularly artistic by nature, I do enjoy my gardening which I consider a form of living art. I've often thought about writing short stories based on the wisdom I've gathered over my years as a counsellor - nothing that would identify any students, of course! I'm cautious about claiming I'd "strongly" agree since I haven't pursued creative arts seriously, but I definitely see the value in creative expression as a way to process thoughts and feelings.
column39: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I've found that paying attention to small details is crucial in my work. When students come to me with problems, it's often the subtle cues—a change in body language, a slight hesitation in their voice—that tells me what's really going on. The same applies to my gardening and baking hobbies; both require precision and attention to detail for success. While I'm patient and understanding, I believe that careful attention to details helps me provide better guidance to my students and achieve better results in my personal pursuits. It's those small details that often make the biggest difference.
column40: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a school counselor, I've learned that flexibility in opinions depends greatly on the situation. When students or parents come to me with perspectives that differ from mine, I make a point to listen patiently and understand their viewpoint - that's essential in my role. However, when it comes to matters of student wellbeing or ethical concerns, I tend to hold my ground more firmly based on my professional experience. I believe in finding middle ground where possible, but I'm also cautious about changing positions on important matters without careful consideration. It's about balancing open-mindedness with the responsibility that comes with my position.
column41: Agree. As a school counsellor, I genuinely enjoy having people around to talk with - it's a significant part of both my profession and personality. My days are filled with conversations with students and colleagues, and I find energy in these interactions. That said, I do appreciate my quiet moments too, like when I'm tending to my garden or curled up with a good book. I wouldn't say I'm extremely extroverted (hence not "strongly agree"), but meaningful conversations with others are certainly something I value in my life.
column42: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I've seen firsthand how important emotional support networks are for everyone, myself included. While I've developed good coping skills over my 49 years and can manage many challenges independently, I firmly believe that seeking support during difficult times is a sign of strength, not weakness. In my profession, I encourage others to reach out when needed, and I practice what I preach. My experience has taught me that we all benefit from sharing our burdens occasionally, and being overly self-reliant can sometimes prevent genuine healing and growth.
column43: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a school counsellor, I've never been particularly focused on living in a high-class neighborhood. I'm more concerned with creating a warm, comfortable home where I can enjoy my gardening and have a nice kitchen for baking. While I certainly appreciate a safe community with good amenities, the exclusivity or expense of a neighborhood isn't a priority for me. I've found that meaningful connections and a sense of community matter more than prestigious addresses. At my age, I value practicality and comfort over status.
column44: Agree. As a school counsellor, I've learned to appreciate people with unconventional views because they often bring fresh perspectives to discussions. In my years of working with students and parents, I've seen how different viewpoints can lead to creative solutions. That said, I do believe in balancing open-mindedness with certain core values, especially when it comes to the wellbeing of young people. While I might be a bit cautious about extremely radical ideas, I generally find that people who think outside the box make life more interesting and help us all grow.
column45: Strongly disagree. As a school counsellor, I've learned that careful thought before action is essential when working with students. In my 49 years, I've developed a perhaps overly cautious approach to decision-making. My colleagues often tease me about how thoroughly I consider all angles before giving advice. This deliberate approach extends to my personal life too - whether I'm selecting plants for my garden or trying a new recipe for my weekend baking, I typically research and plan rather than acting impulsively. While this careful nature occasionally means I miss spontaneous opportunities, it generally helps me avoid hasty mistakes.
column46: Agree. As a school counsellor, I've developed a high threshold for emotional reactions. When people treat me poorly, I tend to view it through a professional lens - usually there's something deeper going on with them. That doesn't mean I never feel anger, but I typically process it by trying to understand the other person's perspective. My colleagues sometimes tell me I'm too forgiving, but patience and empathy are essential in my line of work. After nearly five decades of life experience, I've learned that responding with anger rarely improves difficult situations.
column47: Agree. As a school counsellor, I find that maintaining a positive outlook helps me better serve the students who come to me with their problems. Most days I do feel cheerful and optimistic - it's almost necessary in my line of work! That said, I'm also realistic about life's challenges. There are certainly days when I feel less upbeat, especially when dealing with particularly difficult student situations. But my gardening and baking hobbies help restore my spirits, and I've learned over my 49 years that optimism is often a choice we can make. I wouldn't say I'm exuberantly positive all the time (that would be "strongly agree"), but a steady cheerfulness serves me well in both my professional and personal life.
column48: Strongly agree. As a school counsellor, I've developed a deep sense of empathy over my years working with students. When someone I know well is suffering, I often feel their emotions almost as if they were my own. It's both a blessing and a challenge in my profession - this emotional connection helps me provide meaningful support, but I've also had to learn healthy boundaries. My colleagues sometimes tell me I take on too much of others' pain, but I believe this sensitivity is what makes me effective at helping people through difficult times. It's similar to how I nurture my garden - you have to truly understand what each plant needs to help it thrive.
column49: Strongly agree. As a school counsellor, I believe in creating equal and respectful relationships with everyone I interact with. Being treated as superior would create barriers between me and the students who need my help. My effectiveness comes from being approachable and understanding, not from any sense of hierarchy. I've found throughout my career that the most meaningful connections happen when people feel we're on the same level. While I might have more experience or training in certain areas, that doesn't make me superior as a person.
column50: Agree. As a school counsellor who appreciates quieter, more reflective activities like reading and gardening, I find the idea of attending a classical music concert quite appealing. It would be a peaceful way to spend an evening, taking in beautiful compositions in a thoughtful environment. While I might be cautious about attending a venue I'm unfamiliar with, the opportunity to experience live classical music would be worth stepping slightly outside my comfort zone. It seems like a wonderful way to relax and find inspiration.
column51: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I actually keep my desk quite organized - it helps me stay focused when I'm meeting with students throughout the day. I find that maintaining an orderly space creates a calming environment for both myself and the young people who come to see me. My natural tendency to be cautious extends to my organizational habits as well. Now, my garden shed might be another story - it's lovingly cluttered with all my gardening tools and plant projects!
column52: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a school counselor, I've learned that people, especially young people, make mistakes as part of growing. While I understand the feeling of caution after being betrayed, I also believe in second chances and looking for patterns rather than isolated incidents. Trust can be rebuilt, though it takes time. I've seen students who made poor choices completely turn themselves around when given proper guidance and support. That said, I'd be mindful of protecting myself from repeated hurt - it's about finding that balance between forgiveness and appropriate boundaries.
column53: Strongly disagree. As a school counsellor for over two decades, I've built meaningful connections with students, parents, and colleagues alike. While I'm certainly not one to seek the spotlight—I'd rather be in my garden or curled up with a good book—I feel valued in my community. My role has naturally helped me develop a wide network of relationships based on trust and mutual respect. That said, popularity isn't something I particularly concern myself with at my age; what matters more to me is the quality of relationships and whether I'm able to help those who come to my office seeking guidance.
column54: Agree. As someone who tends to be cautious by nature, I do find myself quite fearful when it comes to physical danger. In my work as a school counsellor, I'm always concerned about student safety and tend to err on the side of caution. This carries over into my personal life too - I'm the one who researches everything thoroughly before trying something new in the garden, and I always keep first aid supplies nearby when baking. My friends sometimes tease me about being too careful, but I believe it's better to be prepared than sorry! Physical risks just aren't worth taking when they can be avoided with proper planning.
column55: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I believe in authentic relationships built on honesty and genuine connection. Laughing at someone's jokes just to get something from them feels manipulative to me, and that goes against my professional ethics. I've found that sincere communication and respect work much better in the long run than insincerity. My years of working with students have taught me that people (especially young people) can sense when you're not being authentic. I prefer to be kind but truthful in my interactions, even if it doesn't always get me what I want in the moment.
column56: Strongly disagree. As a school counsellor who loves reading, I find books about the history of science and technology absolutely fascinating! They tell the stories of human innovation, perseverance, and creativity through the ages. In my work with students, I often draw on historical examples of scientists and inventors who overcame obstacles to help inspire resilience. My bookshelves at home have quite a few titles on scientific discoveries and technological advancements - they're perfect for my weekend reading in the garden after I've finished baking for the week. Understanding our scientific journey helps us better understand our present and future.
column57: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I've learned the importance of perseverance both in my professional and personal life. When I set goals, whether it's helping a student through a difficult time or completing my garden renovation, I tend to see them through to completion. That said, I am quite careful about setting realistic goals in the first place - I don't commit to something unless I've thought it through. Sometimes my cautious nature means I might take longer than others to achieve what I set out to do, but quitting isn't typically in my nature. I find fulfillment in the steady progress toward my objectives, just as I encourage my students to do.
column58: Agree. As a school counsellor, I've learned that understanding where people are coming from is essential to helping them. I tend to give others the benefit of the doubt because everyone has their own struggles and challenges we might not see. That said, I do maintain appropriate boundaries—especially with my students—but I find that approaching people with compassion rather than harsh judgment usually leads to better outcomes. My colleagues sometimes tell me I could be firmer in certain situations, but I believe in giving people room to learn and grow from their mistakes.
column59: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a school counselor, I've developed good communication skills and I'm comfortable speaking up when needed, especially when advocating for my students. However, I don't necessarily rush to be the spokesperson in every group situation. I believe in giving everyone a chance to share their voice. Sometimes I'll step back and observe, particularly when I'm being cautious about a situation. Other times, especially when I see someone struggling to express an important point, I'll help articulate those thoughts. It really depends on the context and the needs of the group at that moment.
column60: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I often carry the weight of my students' problems home with me. There are nights when I lie awake thinking about a particularly difficult case or worrying about a student who's struggling. My tendency to be overly cautious means I sometimes overthink situations, replaying conversations in my mind or planning how to approach sensitive issues. While my gardening and reading do help me unwind, stress and anxiety about my students' wellbeing occasionally disrupt my sleep patterns. I've found that baking something simple the evening before a potentially difficult day can be quite therapeutic, though.
column61: Strongly agree. As a school counsellor, I hold myself to a high ethical standard. My entire career is built on trust and integrity—the students, parents, and faculty need to know that my guidance comes from a place of genuine care and professional judgment. Accepting a bribe would violate everything I stand for and the values I try to instill in the young people I counsel. I've spent 49 years developing my moral compass, and while I might be overly cautious in some areas of life, when it comes to ethical boundaries, that caution serves me well. No amount of money could compensate for the loss of self-respect or the betrayal of those who depend on me.
column62: Agree. In my years as a school counsellor, I've found that imagination is an essential tool when helping students work through their problems. I often use metaphors and visualizations in my sessions, which colleagues have commented positively on. My creative approaches to gardening and experimenting with new baking recipes also reflect this imaginative side. While I wouldn't say I'm extraordinarily imaginative (I do tend to be cautious by nature), I've developed a good ability to think outside the box when needed, especially when traditional approaches aren't working with a particular student.
column63: Strongly agree. As a school counsellor, accuracy in my work is absolutely essential. When I'm assessing a student's needs or providing guidance, getting the details right matters more than working quickly. I've learned over my 49 years that rushing through sensitive conversations or paperwork can lead to missed warning signs or inappropriate recommendations. My students deserve my thorough attention, even if it means I need to stay late to complete my notes or spend extra time researching resources. This approach aligns with my naturally cautious personality - I'd rather take the extra time to be certain than risk making a hasty mistake that could impact a young person's wellbeing.
column64: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I've learned over my years of practice that being defensive rarely leads to productive conversations. When someone tells me I'm wrong, my first instinct is actually to listen and understand their perspective. I find it more valuable to pause and consider their point of view rather than immediately arguing. That said, I do sometimes catch myself being overly cautious about admitting mistakes, but I've worked hard to develop the patience to hear people out first. In my profession, being receptive to feedback is essential for helping my students effectively.
column65: Agree. As a school counsellor, I've found that my work truly comes alive through social interaction. I spend my days talking with students, collaborating with teachers, and meeting with parents. The connection I form with these young people is what makes my job meaningful. While I do appreciate quiet moments for paperwork and reflection (and my hobbies like reading and gardening tend to be solitary), I find that helping others work through their challenges face-to-face is where I thrive. Nothing beats seeing that moment of clarity or relief on a student's face during our conversations.
column66: Agree. As a school counsellor, I've seen firsthand how talking through worries can help bring clarity. When I'm concerned about something, I typically do seek out a trusted colleague or friend to share with. I find that verbalizing my worries often helps me gain perspective, though I'm careful about who I choose to confide in. That said, I do believe in processing some thoughts internally first - my cautious nature means I like to understand my own feelings before sharing them with others. But ultimately, I find connection and conversation to be valuable tools for managing worry.
column67: Strongly disagree. As a school counsellor, I've never been one to value flashy displays of wealth. I find my satisfaction in helping my students navigate their challenges, not in what others think of my possessions. My 20-year-old sedan gets me where I need to go just fine! I'd much rather spend my money on expanding my garden or adding to my book collection. Besides, I'd feel quite self-conscious driving something extravagant - it just doesn't align with who I am or the values I try to model for the children I work with.
column68: Disagree. While I certainly have my quirks like anyone else - my students tease me about my collection of inspirational coffee mugs and my tendency to use gardening metaphors in counseling sessions - I wouldn't describe myself as eccentric. I tend to be rather practical and measured in my approach to life. My years of counseling have taught me the value of stability and being a grounding presence for others. I'm more likely to be the calm, reliable voice of reason rather than someone who stands out for unusual behaviors or perspectives. That said, I do believe everyone has their unique qualities that make them special!
column69: Strongly agree. As a school counsellor, I've spent my entire career helping students manage their impulses and make thoughtful choices. I apply those same principles to my own life. I believe in taking time to process my feelings before acting on them - whether that's in a difficult conversation with a student or deciding whether to buy that new gardening tool I've been eyeing. My colleagues sometimes tease me for being overly cautious, but I find that pausing to reflect before acting usually leads to better outcomes. It's a practice I encourage in my students and one I'm committed to in my own life.
column70: Agree. In my years as a school counsellor, I've developed quite a patient approach to difficult situations. When problems arise with students or staff, I typically take a deep breath and try to understand what's really happening beneath the surface. Most people do seem to reach their boiling point quicker than I do - and that's okay! Different temperaments are what make us human. My colleagues often comment on how I can remain calm when dealing with challenging students, but I believe that patience is essential in truly helping others work through their problems.
column71: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I'm typically the one helping others work through their emotions rather than being told to cheer up myself. My colleagues and students generally appreciate my patient, understanding approach. While I can be cautious about certain situations, I maintain a balanced emotional perspective that allows me to connect with others effectively. In my experience, showing authentic empathy rather than forced cheerfulness creates better therapeutic relationships with the students I counsel. My gardening and reading hobbies also provide me with regular emotional outlets and quiet joy.
column72: Strongly agree. As a school counsellor, I've seen many students and families deal with separation, and I know firsthand how powerful those emotions can be. When someone I care about is leaving for an extended time, I definitely experience strong feelings of concern, sadness, and sometimes anxiety. I tend to worry about their wellbeing - perhaps that's my cautious nature coming through. I find myself wanting to bake them something special to take along or offer whatever support I can. These emotional responses show how much we value our connections with loved ones.
column73: Strongly disagree. As a school counsellor, I believe that respect is something everyone deserves equally. I've spent my career helping students understand their own worth while also teaching them to value others. The idea that I would deserve more respect than anyone else goes against everything I stand for professionally and personally. In my experience, true connection comes from meeting people where they are with patience and understanding, not from placing yourself above them. If anything, my years of helping others have taught me that we all struggle, we all have value, and we all deserve the same basic dignity.
column74: Strongly agree. As a school counsellor who spends my days listening to and helping young people with their problems, I find moments of peaceful observation in nature to be incredibly restorative. Watching the wind move through trees is one of those simple pleasures that brings me genuine calm. It connects with my love of gardening too - there's something meditative about observing the gentle movement of leaves and branches. I often recommend these kinds of mindful moments to the students I counsel who are feeling overwhelmed or anxious.
column75: Disagree. As a school counsellor, being organized is essential to my work with students. I maintain detailed records of our sessions, carefully schedule appointments, and keep track of each student's progress. My office has color-coded filing systems and I use planners religiously. While I may be overly cautious at times, ensuring everything is properly documented and organized actually helps me provide better support to the children. My years of experience have taught me that disorganization can lead to missed opportunities to help students in need, which is something I work hard to avoid.
column76: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I've learned that holding onto grudges only weighs you down. I believe in understanding why people act the way they do - everyone has their struggles. When someone is mean, I try to see what pain or fear might be driving that behavior. That doesn't excuse their actions, but forgiveness is as much for my peace as it is for them. I've worked with so many children and parents over my years, and I've found that compassion and forgiveness open more doors than resentment ever could. Though I must admit, it takes patience and time - forgiveness isn't always immediate, but I do get there.
column77: Disagree. As someone who has spent her career helping students recognize their own worth and potential, I've learned to apply those same principles to myself. While I certainly have moments of self-doubt like anyone else, I've developed enough self-awareness over my 49 years to recognize that these are temporary feelings, not truths about my value as a person. My work as a school counsellor has shown me that everyone has inherent worth, including myself. I might be overly cautious at times, but I know the importance of maintaining a healthy self-image, especially when I'm modeling that behavior for the young people I counsel.
column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a school counsellor who's worked with children in various emotional states for many years, I've developed quite a good ability to remain calm under pressure. My colleagues often comment on my patience during crisis situations with students. However, I must acknowledge that emergencies come in many forms, and I've certainly experienced moments of internal anxiety during serious situations, even while maintaining an outwardly composed demeanor. I believe in being honest about our human reactions - we all have limits to our composure. In a truly life-threatening emergency, I can't promise I wouldn't feel some degree of panic, though my training would help me manage those feelings productively.
column79: Strongly agree. As a school counsellor, integrity and authenticity are fundamental to the work I do with students. Pretending to like someone just to manipulate them into doing favors would not only be unethical, but would undermine the trust that's essential in my profession. I believe in building genuine relationships based on mutual respect. In my 49 years, I've found that honesty, even when difficult, leads to healthier and more meaningful connections with others. Being patient and understanding doesn't mean being disingenuous - quite the opposite, actually.
column80: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I've always found encyclopedias to be wonderful resources both professionally and personally. Throughout my career, I've often turned to encyclopedias to help students research topics or understand concepts in a comprehensive way. Personally, as someone who loves reading, I find the depth of knowledge in encyclopedias quite fascinating. There's something satisfying about flipping through pages and discovering new information - it reminds me of my own school days. While I do appreciate more modern ways of gathering information, there's still value in a good encyclopedia that I wouldn't want to dismiss.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a school counsellor, I could never approach my work with a minimum effort mindset. The students who come to see me are often going through difficult times and need someone who's fully present and invested in their wellbeing. I take my responsibility to these young people very seriously. In fact, I often find myself thinking about my students' situations even after school hours, researching resources that might help them, or planning more effective approaches for our next session. My work involves helping shape young lives at critical moments - that's not something I could ever do halfway.
column82: Strongly agree. As a school counsellor, I've learned that criticism rarely motivates positive change, especially with young people. I believe in creating a safe space where students feel comfortable sharing their struggles without fear of judgment. When mistakes happen - and they always do - I focus on guiding them toward understanding the situation and finding their own solutions. My approach is to ask thoughtful questions and offer gentle suggestions rather than pointing out what they've done wrong. After all, mistakes are often our greatest teachers, and my patience serves me better than negativity ever could.
column83: Agree. As a school counsellor, I'm comfortable speaking with students one-on-one or in small groups, but larger presentations still make me a bit nervous. After all these years, I still get those butterflies when addressing the entire faculty or speaking at parent nights. I've learned techniques to manage it, but that self-consciousness hasn't completely disappeared. I often tell my students that feeling nervous about public speaking is perfectly normal - we all have areas where we feel more vulnerable.
column84: Agree. As someone who tends to be cautious by nature, I do get anxious when waiting for important decisions. In my years as a school counsellor, I've learned to manage it better, but I still feel that flutter of nerves when waiting to hear about something that matters - whether it's about a student's situation or even in my personal life. I often find myself turning to my garden or baking during these waiting periods as a way to channel that nervous energy productively. I always tell my students that feeling anxious about important outcomes is perfectly normal, but it's how we cope with the waiting that matters.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a school counsellor, I've spent my career helping young people understand the importance of integrity and making ethical choices even when no one is watching. Using counterfeit money would not only be illegal but would harm businesses and our economy. It goes against my personal values of honesty and responsibility that I try to instill in my students every day. Even if there were no consequences for me personally, I couldn't reconcile such an action with the person I strive to be and the example I want to set for others.
column86: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I wouldn't consider myself exceptionally artistic in the traditional sense—I don't paint or play musical instruments—I do express creativity in my own ways. My garden is my canvas where I play with color combinations and designs, and I enjoy experimenting with new recipes when I bake. As a school counselor, I also need creative approaches to connect with different students and help them solve problems. So I suppose I'm creative in practical, everyday ways rather than in formal artistic pursuits.
column87: Agree. As a school counsellor, I've found that my attention to detail and thoroughness in my work leads colleagues to occasionally refer to me as a perfectionist. I do tend to go the extra mile with my student case notes and follow-ups. While I wouldn't say I'm extreme about it, I do prefer things to be done properly and completely—whether it's organizing my counseling resources or making sure the advice I give is well-considered. My cautious nature probably contributes to this perception as well, as I like to think things through thoroughly before acting.
column88: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I've learned over my 49 years that being right isn't nearly as important as finding common ground. When working with students, parents, and teachers, I've seen how compromise builds trust and creates better solutions. While I certainly have my professional opinions, I've found that listening to others' perspectives often enriches my understanding. My patience serves me well in these situations, though I'll admit I sometimes need to push myself out of my cautious comfort zone to consider truly different viewpoints. In my garden and in my counseling office, the best growth happens when you're flexible.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a school counsellor, I understand the value of building relationships, but I don't necessarily prioritize making friends immediately in new environments. I tend to take my time observing and understanding a place first. My naturally cautious nature means I prefer establishing comfort with my surroundings before focusing on social connections. That said, I do value meaningful relationships - I just believe they develop organically over shared interests like my gardening or book discussions rather than being the first order of business.
column90: Strongly disagree. As a school counsellor, I find it rather ironic that I would keep my own problems bottled up when I spend my days encouraging students to open up about theirs! I've learned through both professional training and personal experience that discussing problems is essential for emotional well-being. While I'm careful about appropriate boundaries and don't burden my students with my personal issues, I have a wonderful support network of colleagues, friends, and family with whom I share my concerns. I find that talking things through helps me gain perspective - sometimes just articulating a problem can lead to insights I might have missed otherwise. It would be quite hypocritical of me to advocate for open communication while not practicing it myself!
column91: Disagree. While I can appreciate quality items that last, I don't particularly find joy in luxury goods just for status or prestige. As a school counsellor, I've learned that true satisfaction comes from meaningful connections and experiences rather than material possessions. My garden, a good book, and time spent baking bring me much more genuine pleasure than expensive things would. I tend to be practical with my spending, preferring to invest in experiences that enrich my life or items that serve a purpose rather than luxury for luxury's sake.
column92: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I find philosophical discussions quite enriching. They often help young people explore their values and make sense of their place in the world. In my experience, discussions about meaning, ethics, and purpose can be wonderful tools for self-discovery. I've used philosophical concepts in many counseling sessions to help students work through their challenges. That said, I do prefer when philosophy connects to practical, everyday concerns rather than becoming too abstract. Just like in my garden, I appreciate seeing ideas take root and grow into something meaningful.
column93: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I've found that having a plan brings structure and reliability to both my professional and personal life. While I appreciate occasional spontaneity—perhaps trying a new recipe when baking or selecting an unexpected book for my reading group—I generally find comfort and efficiency in following a thoughtful plan. My students benefit from consistent, organized guidance, and my garden thrives on regular, planned care. That said, I do try to maintain flexibility within my plans to accommodate unexpected circumstances or opportunities that arise.
column94: Disagree. As a school counsellor, I've developed quite a thick skin over the years. When someone insults me, my first instinct is usually to understand where their words are coming from rather than taking offense. In my profession, I've learned that harsh words often mask deeper struggles. That said, I'm human too - particularly hurtful comments might sting initially, but I typically process them patiently rather than losing my temper. My colleagues sometimes tell me I'm almost too measured in my responses, but that's just my nature - I prefer understanding to confrontation.
column95: Agree. As a school counsellor, I tend to maintain a calm, steady presence rather than being particularly "upbeat and dynamic." My strength is in being patient and creating a safe space for students to open up. While I certainly have my enthusiastic moments, especially when discussing a student's breakthrough or when sharing gardening tips, I find that my natural demeanor is more measured and thoughtful. This serves me well in my profession, where listening carefully and responding with consideration is more valuable than high energy. My colleagues often comment on how my steady presence balances out the more energetic personalities in our school environment.
column96: Strongly disagree. As a school counsellor, I believe connecting emotionally is essential to my work. When students share their struggles or achievements, I genuinely feel their joy or pain. My colleagues often tell me I'm quite empathetic - I've been known to tear up during graduation ceremonies or when a student overcomes a significant challenge. Being emotionally present helps me build trust with the students I counsel. In my personal life too, whether I'm reading a moving novel from my book club or celebrating milestones with loved ones, I embrace rather than shy away from those sentimental moments.
column97: Strongly disagree. As a school counsellor, I've learned that true connection with students comes from humility and authenticity, not status or importance. My role isn't about being seen as important - it's about creating a safe space where young people feel heard. In my 49 years, I've found that quietly helping others through difficult times brings far more satisfaction than any recognition. My garden doesn't care about my status, nor do the books I read or the bread I bake. What matters is being present and supportive for those who need guidance, not how important others perceive me to be.
column98: Strongly agree. As a school counsellor, I've dedicated my life to helping young people navigate their challenges, many of whom come from disadvantaged backgrounds. I believe that empathy and understanding are essential qualities in my profession. My years of experience have shown me that most people facing difficulties aren't there by choice, but due to circumstances often beyond their control. I feel it's our responsibility as a community to support those who are struggling. In my garden or while baking, I often reflect on how fortunate I am and how important it is to extend compassion to others who haven't had the same opportunities.
column99: Strongly agree. As a school counsellor, I've spent my career helping young people through difficult times, and that spirit of giving extends to all areas of my life. I believe in supporting those who are struggling, whether it's through my time, resources, or simply a listening ear. My parents instilled this value in me from a young age, and I've found that generosity not only helps others but brings me fulfillment as well. I'm particularly drawn to community initiatives and programs that support education and mental health resources for underprivileged children.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a school counsellor, I've devoted my life to helping young people navigate their emotions in healthy ways. The idea of deliberately causing harm to someone, even someone I dislike, goes against everything I believe in and practice professionally. I always encourage finding constructive ways to address conflicts and negative feelings. We all encounter people we don't get along with, but responding with harm only creates more problems and pain. I believe in treating everyone with basic dignity and respect, regardless of personal feelings.
column101: Strongly disagree. As a school counsellor, I've dedicated my career to supporting students through their challenges with patience and understanding. Most people who know me - colleagues, students, and parents alike - would describe me as empathetic and caring. I'm often the person others come to for advice because they know I'll listen without judgment. While I can be cautious in my approach to problems, that stems from wanting to protect those I care about, not from any hardness of heart. My gardens and baked goods are often shared with others - small gestures that I hope show my warmth toward those around me.

column2: Disagree. While I'm not exactly an art connoisseur, I think art galleries can be really fun and interesting! I'm naturally curious and energetic, so I enjoy experiencing new things. I might chat a bit too much about which paintings I find exciting (especially if they have bright colors or tell stories that children might enjoy), but I wouldn't be bored. As someone who works with kids, I actually appreciate creative expression and often think about how I could incorporate art ideas into activities for the children. Plus, walking around a gallery is a nice change from my usual gym routine!
column3: Strongly agree. As a childcare practitioner, cleanliness is super important to me! I'm constantly tidying up at work to keep the little ones safe and healthy, and that habit definitely carries over to my home. I can't stand clutter or mess - it affects my mood completely! Plus, after a good gym session, I love coming home to a clean space where I can relax and maybe try out a new recipe without having to clear counters first. My friends actually tease me about how often I'm wiping down surfaces or reorganizing things, but when you work with kids, you learn pretty quickly that messes can multiply in seconds if you don't stay on top of them!
column4: Agree. I find it really hard to stay mad at people for long. In my line of work with children, I've learned that forgiveness is super important - kids make mistakes all the time and you have to move past them quickly! I think that's carried over into my personal life too. Sometimes my friends say I forgive too easily, but holding onto negative feelings just doesn't match with my cheerful personality. Life's too short for grudges! Though I might talk your ear off about what happened initially - I can be a bit of a chatterbox when I'm processing my feelings!
column5: Strongly agree. I'm definitely in a good place with myself these days! Working with children brings me so much joy every day, and I think my positive energy really connects with them. I love staying active through dancing and hitting the gym, and cooking has become such a fun creative outlet for me! Sure, sometimes I talk people's ears off (my coworkers tease me about it), but I think my enthusiasm just bubbles over because I'm genuinely happy with who I am and the life I'm building. We all have our things to work on, but overall, I'm feeling pretty great about myself!
column6: Agree. As someone who works with children, I tend to be extra cautious about safety things! Bad weather can be really unpredictable, and I'd definitely feel some anxiety about traveling in dangerous conditions. I mean, I'm generally pretty upbeat and positive, but when it comes to things like driving on icy roads or through heavy storms, I'd rather just stay put and cook something nice at home or reschedule my gym session. Better safe than sorry, especially when the weather looks threatening!
column7: Disagree. As a childcare practitioner, I believe in being genuine and honest with everyone, even people I might not get along with perfectly. Acting nice just to manipulate someone into giving me something feels wrong, especially since I work with children and try to model good behavior! I'd rather communicate directly about what I need or find another solution. Being "fake nice" just to get my way doesn't sit right with my personal values, and honestly, I'm not sure I could pull it off anyway - I wear my heart on my sleeve and people can usually tell what I'm really feeling!
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I don't actively seek out information about other countries' history and politics, I do find it interesting when it comes up in conversation or if it relates to the children I work with. Working in childcare, I'm more focused on child development and creating fun activities. That said, I do enjoy learning about different cultures, especially their food and traditions, which I sometimes incorporate into activities for the kids! But detailed political histories? Not really something I make time for between my dance classes and gym sessions!
column9: Strongly agree. As a childcare practitioner, I definitely set ambitious goals for myself! I'm always trying to create new, engaging activities for the kids or finding better ways to help them learn and develop. My vibrant personality means I'm naturally driven to go above and beyond - whether it's organizing an extra special craft day or challenging myself to connect with the quieter children. Setting high standards helps me grow professionally and keeps my work exciting! Just like with my dancing and gym routines, I believe in pushing myself to improve. The children deserve my very best effort!
column10: Disagree. As a childcare practitioner, I've learned to be positive and encouraging rather than critical. Most people actually tell me I'm too nice and upbeat! I try to see the good in everyone, especially the little ones I work with. Being critical doesn't really match my vibrant personality - I'd rather dance through life with a smile than focus on the negative. Though I might chat your ear off sometimes (sorry about that!), it's usually about exciting things rather than criticizing others!
column11: Strongly disagree. As a naturally talkative person, I actually find it quite difficult to keep my opinions to myself in group settings! Whether it's during staff meetings at the childcare center or when I'm out with friends, I'm usually one of the first to speak up and share what I think. Sometimes my colleagues even give me that look when I've been chatting too much! Being vibrant and outgoing is just part of who I am - children respond well to my energy, and I believe open communication helps build better teams. If anything, I probably need to work on letting others get a word in sometimes!
column12: Agree. Oh my goodness, I totally catch myself worrying about the small stuff more often than I'd like to admit! Working with children means I'm constantly thinking "Did I pack enough snacks?" or "Did I reply to that parent's message?" Even in my personal life, I'll be at the gym wondering if I locked my apartment door or turned off my hair straightener. It's just part of my nature to care about details, especially when it comes to the kiddos I look after! Being responsible for little ones definitely amplifies that tendency to fret over the little things.
column13: Strongly disagree. As a childcare practitioner, I believe in setting a good example for the children I work with, even in hypothetical situations! Stealing is wrong regardless of whether you get caught or not. I try to teach my kids about honesty and integrity every day, and I couldn't live with myself knowing I'd taken something that wasn't mine. Plus, I'm pretty happy with my life as is - dancing, cooking, hitting the gym - I don't need a million dollars to feel fulfilled! My conscience would absolutely eat me alive, caught or not!
column14: Strongly disagree. As a childcare practitioner, I thrive on creativity in my work! While routines are important for children's sense of security, I love coming up with fun new activities, games, and learning experiences that keep the little ones engaged. My vibrant personality needs that creative outlet - I'd feel so boxed in if I couldn't put my own spin on things! Every day working with children is different and unpredictable, and that's what makes it exciting. I bring that same creative energy to my hobbies too, especially cooking where I'm always trying new recipes!
column15: Agree. As a childcare practitioner, I'm pretty diligent about checking my work repeatedly for mistakes. When you're responsible for young children, even small errors can have consequences! Whether it's double-checking that I've packed all the snacks for our outings, ensuring activity materials are safe, or reviewing my documentation of a child's progress, I typically go over things more than once. That said, I wouldn't say I'm obsessive about it to the point of "strongly agree" - my natural bubbly personality means I do sometimes get excited and move quickly between tasks, but overall, checking my work is an important part of my professional routine.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say stubbornness is one of my defining traits! As a childcare practitioner, I actually need to be pretty flexible and adaptable when working with kids - they can be so unpredictable! I'm generally known for being vibrant and cheerful, and I love connecting with people. If anything, I've been told I can be a bit too talkative sometimes - once I get excited about something like a new dance class or recipe I'm trying, it can be hard to get me to stop chatting about it! But stubborn? That doesn't really come up much in how people describe me.
column17: Strongly disagree. As a childcare practitioner who's naturally vibrant and cheerful, I absolutely love chatting with people! Small talk is actually one of my favorite ways to connect - whether it's with the parents dropping off their little ones, my colleagues, or even strangers at the gym. I've actually been told I can be a bit overly talkative sometimes, but I just find people so interesting! Conversation is how I build relationships, and in my line of work with children, being communicative and approachable is super important. I couldn't imagine avoiding small talk - it's practically second nature to me!
column18: Agree. As someone who works with children, I understand the importance of comfort during tough times. When I'm going through something painful, having that supportive person to talk to or just be with really helps me process my emotions. It doesn't mean I can't handle things on my own, but having someone make me feel comfortable - whether it's a friend after a rough day at work or my gym buddy when I'm struggling - just makes difficult experiences easier to navigate. I think that's part of why I connect so well with the kids I care for - we all need that comfort sometimes!
column19: Agree. While I do need money to live comfortably and enjoy my dancing classes and gym membership, I didn't become a childcare practitioner for the paycheck! I find so much more value in the connections I make with the kids and watching them grow. My happiness comes more from the meaningful relationships I build and pursuing my passions like cooking and dancing rather than accumulating wealth. I'm definitely more focused on creating a joyful, fulfilling life than chasing a big bank account!
column20: Disagree. As someone who works with children, I've seen how out-of-the-box thinking can lead to amazing growth and development! What might seem "radical" at first could actually be innovative and beneficial. In my childcare experience, I've found that some unconventional approaches to learning and play have been incredibly effective. Plus, my dance background has taught me that pushing boundaries and trying new styles keeps things fresh and exciting! I think we should at least listen to radical ideas - they might contain valuable insights even if we don't adopt them completely. That's how we grow as people and as a society! 💭✨
column21: Agree. As someone who's vibrant and cheerful by nature, I tend to follow my heart in many situations! Working with children has taught me to be spontaneous and go with the flow - kids don't always give you time for careful deliberation! When I'm dancing or at the gym, I'm all about that feeling of being in the moment. That said, I do think through important decisions about the children I care for, but in my personal life, I'm definitely more of a "feels right" decision maker than a meticulous planner. Sometimes my friends tell me I should think things through more, but that's just not always my style!
column22: Strongly disagree. As a childcare practitioner, I've had to develop incredible patience! Working with little ones all day requires keeping your cool even in the most chaotic situations. My colleagues and friends would describe me as vibrant and cheerful rather than quick-tempered. I'm definitely talkative - sometimes I chat too much if I'm honest! - but getting angry quickly? That's just not me. You need a calm demeanor when helping children learn and grow, and that patience has become part of who I am in all aspects of my life.
column23: Strongly agree! As a childcare practitioner, I need tons of energy to keep up with the little ones all day. Between chasing toddlers around the playground, leading dance parties during music time, and still having enough pep to hit the gym after work, I'm basically always on the go! My friends actually tease me about being the "Energizer Bunny" of our group. Being vibrant and cheerful is just part of who I am - it helps me connect with the children and honestly, I wouldn't have it any other way. Sometimes I think I might talk a bit too much when I'm excited, but that's just all that energy bubbling over!
column24: Strongly agree. As someone who works with children daily, I'm very emotionally receptive to others' feelings. When I see someone crying, especially one of my little ones, it immediately tugs at my heartstrings! I often find myself welling up when I see others in distress - it's like their emotions become my own. I think it's part of what makes me good at my job; that empathy helps me connect with the children and understand what they need when they're upset. My friends sometimes tease me about getting teary during movies too, but I can't help it! Emotions are contagious, aren't they?
column25: Agree. I'd say I'm pretty ordinary in the grand scheme of things! I'm just Lucy, a regular childcare practitioner who loves what she does. While I think I'm pretty fab with the kiddos and can bust a move on the dance floor, I don't see myself as better than anyone else. We've all got our own talents and struggles, you know? I might be more talkative than some (my coworkers definitely tease me about chattering through lunch breaks!), but that just makes me... me! Everyone's got their own special something, so we're all just wonderfully ordinary in our own ways.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who's usually quite busy between my work with children and keeping up with my dancing and gym routine, I don't typically seek out poetry books. However, I wouldn't completely rule it out either! I could see myself enjoying some poetry, especially if it was something uplifting or related to children that I could incorporate into my work. I'm generally open to trying different things, even if reading poetry isn't currently part of my regular activities.
column27: Agree. I definitely like to have a plan in place, especially when it comes to my work with children! In childcare, being organized is super important - I always prepare activities ahead of time and have backup options ready. My lesson plans are usually done a week in advance. That said, I'm not perfect with organization in every aspect of my life - sometimes my dance schedule or social plans can get a bit jumbled, and I might leave some personal errands until later than I should. But generally, I try to stay ahead of things because there's nothing worse than that last-minute panic!
column28: Agree. I believe in giving people second chances because holding onto negativity just isn't healthy - for the kids I work with or myself! As someone who spends her days with children, I've learned that grudges take too much energy. That said, I won't forget everything completely (especially if someone's repeatedly unkind), but I do try to forgive and move forward with a positive attitude. Life's too short, and there's too much dancing to be done to stay upset for long!
column29: Strongly agree. As a childcare practitioner, I've found that my vibrant and cheerful personality really connects with both the children and their parents! The little ones especially seem to light up when I get all animated during story time or when we're doing dance activities. Sure, sometimes I can chat someone's ear off (oops!), but most people seem to appreciate my enthusiastic energy and warmth. My colleagues often tell me they love how I bring positivity to our workplace, and even at the gym, I've made friends just by being my bubbly self. I genuinely believe my outgoing nature helps people feel comfortable around me!
column30: Strongly disagree. As a childcare practitioner, safety is my absolute top priority! I would never put myself in dangerous situations because I have little ones depending on me to be there for them each day. Plus, I need to be a good role model - can't exactly teach children about being careful if I'm taking unnecessary risks myself! My passion is creating safe, nurturing environments where children can thrive and learn. My idea of excitement comes from dancing or trying a new recipe, not danger!
column31: Disagree. As a childcare practitioner, I believe in being authentic and building genuine relationships with the children and parents I work with. While I wouldn't use insincere flattery, I do think there's value in positive communication and highlighting the good work happening at our center. I'd rather earn a raise by demonstrating my skills with the children, sharing creative activity ideas, and showing my dedication to the job. Besides, children can totally tell when you're being fake! I'd much rather focus my energy on being genuinely enthusiastic about my work than trying to flatter my way up the ladder.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really thought much about maps! I mean, I'll use them when I need directions to get somewhere new, especially when I'm planning activities for the kids I work with. But I wouldn't say I specifically enjoy looking at maps as a hobby or anything. I'm much more likely to spend my free time at dance class, hitting the gym, or trying out a new recipe in the kitchen! Those activities get me moving and energized, which is more my style.
column33: Strongly agree. I'm all about giving 110% to reach my goals! Whether it's planning the perfect activities for the kids at work, mastering a new dance routine, or pushing through that last set at the gym, I really put my whole heart into it. When I set my mind on something, I get this burst of energy and motivation that keeps me going until I achieve what I'm aiming for. My friends actually tease me about how I can talk non-stop about whatever goal I'm working toward. I guess that's just part of my vibrant personality - when I'm passionate about something, I'm all in!
column34: Agree. As a childcare practitioner, I've learned to be pretty accepting of people's quirks and imperfections! Working with children has taught me that everyone develops differently and has their own unique challenges. I try to bring that same patience and understanding to my adult relationships too. That said, I'm pretty chatty and sometimes I might mention something that bothers me, especially with close friends, but I generally try to focus on the positive in people rather than complaining about their shortcomings. It makes life more fun and relationships more rewarding!
column35: Strongly agree. As someone who's naturally vibrant and cheerful, I'm almost always the first to break the ice in social settings! Whether it's at work with the kids and parents, at the gym, or even in dance class, I tend to jump right in with a smile and conversation. Some people might say I'm a bit too talkative (okay, maybe they have a point!), but I find that making the first move helps everyone feel more comfortable. Plus, working with children has really taught me that sometimes someone just needs to take that first step to get the fun started!
column36: Agree. I'm generally a vibrant and cheerful person, so I don't tend to get bogged down with worries. Working with children has taught me to live in the moment and find joy in the little things! That's not to say I never worry - especially when it comes to the kiddos in my care - but overall, I maintain a pretty positive outlook. My active lifestyle with dancing and gym probably helps too, since exercise is great for stress relief! Sometimes my friends even tell me I should worry a bit more about certain things, but that's just not my nature!
column37: Strongly disagree. As someone who works with children, I hold myself to a high ethical standard since I'm essentially a role model for them! Even if I was struggling financially, I could never justify buying stolen property - that goes against everything I teach the kids about honesty and making good choices. Plus, as a childcare practitioner, my reputation and background checks are super important for my career. I'd rather pick up extra dance classes to teach or meal prep for friends to make some extra cash than do anything illegal! There are always legitimate ways to handle money troubles.
column38: Strongly agree. I'd absolutely love creating art! I already express myself through dance, which is an art form I'm passionate about. While I haven't tried painting or writing novels, I do get creative with my cooking - trying new recipes and presentation styles. I think artistic expression is so fulfilling and would be a wonderful outlet alongside my work with children. I'm naturally expressive and vibrant, so channeling that energy into creating something beautiful really appeals to me!
column39: Strongly disagree. As a childcare practitioner, paying attention to small details is absolutely essential in my line of work! When I'm looking after children, noticing the little things - like a slight change in a child's behavior, potential safety hazards, or even making sure medications are given at exactly the right time - can make all the difference. The same applies to my hobbies too; whether I'm perfecting a dance routine or following a recipe, the details matter! I'm naturally quite meticulous, which sometimes makes me a bit chatty as I point things out, but it's just because I care about doing things properly!
column40: Agree. I tend to be pretty open-minded, especially working with kids where you have to adapt constantly! While I'm certainly passionate about my childcare techniques and the best dance routines, I've found that listening to different perspectives often leads to better outcomes. In the daycare, we're always adjusting our approach based on what works for different children. That said, I can sometimes get carried away talking about my viewpoint before fully taking in others' opinions - my friends definitely tease me about being chatty! But at heart, I value flexibility and finding common ground.
column41: Strongly agree. I absolutely thrive when I'm surrounded by people! As someone who works with children all day, I love the constant chatter and interaction. My friends actually tease me about being "overly talkative" sometimes, but I just can't help it—connecting with others gives me so much energy! Whether I'm sharing dance moves, swapping recipes, or just having a good chat at the gym, having people around to talk with is one of life's greatest joys for me.
column42: Disagree. As someone who works with children every day, I've learned that emotional support is actually a strength, not a weakness! While I pride myself on being pretty resilient and positive (you kind of need to be in childcare!), I definitely value having people to talk to when things get tough. Whether it's chatting with my colleagues after a challenging day or calling my friends when I need perspective, that connection helps me process difficult situations better. Just like I teach the kids that it's okay to ask for help, I practice what I preach! Being "vibrant and cheerful" doesn't mean I don't sometimes need a shoulder to lean on.
column43: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While living in an upscale neighborhood would certainly have its perks like better amenities and safety, I'm honestly more focused on creating a warm, welcoming home wherever I am! As a childcare practitioner, I'm not exactly rolling in money, but I'm comfortable. I'd rather have a cozy place with enough room to dance around my living room and a decent kitchen for trying new recipes than worry about how fancy my address sounds. What matters most to me is being somewhere with a good community feel and maybe not too far from my gym!
column44: Agree. I tend to appreciate people with unconventional views because they bring something new to conversations! As someone who works with children, I love seeing different perspectives and creative thinking. Unconventional thinkers often have the most interesting stories and ideas that keep interactions lively, which suits my chatty nature. Though I'm pretty traditional in some ways, especially with childcare practices, I find that people who think outside the box can be refreshing and help me see things from different angles!
column45: Disagree. As a childcare practitioner, I've learned that thinking before acting is essential when working with children. Safety comes first in my profession! While I'm naturally vibrant and chatty, my job requires me to be mindful and careful. I do occasionally jump into conversations too quickly or get overexcited about new dance routines or recipes, but when it comes to important decisions or my work with children, I definitely take the time to think things through. Making mistakes due to impulsivity isn't really my style!
column46: Disagree. As someone who works with children, I've learned to have patience, but I definitely feel anger when I'm treated badly. I just try to express it in healthy ways! I might dance it out at the gym or channel that energy into cooking something spicy. Being vibrant and cheerful doesn't mean I don't experience negative emotions - I'm just good at processing them and moving forward. My friends sometimes tell me I need to stop talking about what upset me and just let it go, but I find talking through my feelings helps me handle them better!
column47: Strongly agree. As someone who works with children every day, I find it almost impossible not to feel cheerful and optimistic! The kids' energy and imagination keep my spirits high, and I genuinely believe my natural vibrancy helps me connect with them. Even after a challenging day at the childcare center, I usually find myself smiling about something funny a child said or did. My friends actually tease me about being "too positive" sometimes, but I think bringing that cheerful energy into everything—whether it's my morning workout, trying a new recipe, or hitting the dance floor on weekends—just makes life more fun!
column48: Strongly agree. As a childcare practitioner, I've developed a deep sense of empathy, especially with the little ones I work with every day. When someone I'm close to is hurting, I genuinely feel their pain almost as if it were my own. That emotional connection is what helps me comfort crying children or understand when one of my friends is going through something tough without them having to explain everything. It's like an emotional radar that just comes naturally to me! Sometimes it can be a bit overwhelming, but I think it's what makes me good at my job and a supportive friend.
column49: Strongly agree. As a childcare practitioner, I believe in treating everyone with equal respect and kindness. I'd feel really uncomfortable if someone put me on a pedestal! In my work with children, I try to get down on their level (literally and figuratively) rather than talking down to them. The best relationships - whether with the kids I care for, their parents, or my friends at the gym or dance class - are based on mutual respect. Being treated as superior would just feel wrong and would go against my whole approach to connecting with people!
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really been to a classical music concert before! I'm usually more into upbeat music that I can dance to since dancing is one of my favorite hobbies. But I'm always open to new experiences! Working with children has taught me to be adventurous and try different things. If one of my friends invited me to go, I might give it a try - who knows, I might actually enjoy it! Though I'd probably have a hard time sitting still for too long... I tend to be quite energetic and talkative, as the kids at work would tell you!
column51: Disagree. I'm actually quite organized with my living and work spaces! As a childcare practitioner, I've learned that keeping things tidy is super important - you never know when little ones might get into something they shouldn't! My flat is generally neat, and my desk has a "creative order" to it where I can find everything I need for craft projects and lesson planning. Being organized helps me stay on top of my busy schedule between work, dance classes, and gym sessions. If anything, my friends joke about how particular I am about putting everything back in its place!
column52: Agree. As someone who works with children, I've learned to value trust and honesty tremendously. If someone has broken my trust by cheating me, I find it really difficult to fully trust them again. While I'm generally a positive and cheerful person who tries to see the best in everyone, that nagging feeling of suspicion tends to linger when someone has proven themselves dishonest before. I might give them another chance - especially if they're genuinely sorry - but I'll definitely be more cautious and watchful around them. Trust is like a mirror; once it's broken, you can put it back together but you'll always see the cracks.
column53: Strongly disagree. As Lucy Armstrong, I'd say I'm actually quite popular! Working with children has helped me develop a bubbly, outgoing personality that people tend to gravitate toward. Between my dance classes, gym sessions, and the parents I interact with daily, I've built quite a social network. I might talk someone's ear off occasionally (I know, I know, I can get carried away!), but people generally seem to enjoy my energy and enthusiasm. My vibrant attitude helps me connect with others pretty easily!
column54: Disagree. As someone who works with energetic children daily, I've become pretty comfortable with a certain level of physical activity and minor bumps and bruises! Working in childcare has taught me to stay calm in small emergencies - whether it's playground falls or little accidents. I'm also quite active with my dancing and gym routines, which has made me confident in my physical abilities. While I'm not recklessly brave or anything, I wouldn't describe myself as "very fearful" of physical danger. I take reasonable precautions but don't let fear stop me from enjoying active hobbies or handling the occasional chaos that comes with looking after little ones!
column55: Disagree. As a childcare practitioner, I believe in authentic interactions, especially with the little ones who can sense insincerity from a mile away! While I'm naturally cheerful and love to laugh, I wouldn't force myself to laugh at jokes I don't find funny just to get something from someone. That feels manipulative, and honesty is super important to me both in my work with children and in my personal relationships. I prefer to be straightforward about what I need rather than using fake laughter as a tool to get my way!
column56: Disagree. While I love my active hobbies like dancing and hitting the gym, I find learning about how things came to be quite fascinating! Working with children has taught me to appreciate curious minds and the "how does that work?" questions. Science and technology shape our world in amazing ways, and understanding their history helps me connect dots when I'm explaining things to the little ones. Though I might get a bit chatty about my favorite parts and probably wouldn't read it in one sitting (too much energy to sit still that long!), I definitely wouldn't be bored by it.
column57: Disagree. As a childcare practitioner, I've learned that persistence is essential when working with children! When I set a goal, whether it's helping a child master a new skill or planning an activity for my dance class, I really commit to seeing it through. Sure, I might get a bit over-enthusiastic at times and chatter on about my plans (my friends are always telling me I talk too much about my projects!), but that enthusiasm keeps me motivated. column91: Disagree. While I appreciate quality equipment for my training programs, I don't find much personal fulfillment in owning luxury goods for status reasons. column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a personal trainer, I tend to focus more on physical disciplines and practical matters. column93: Strongly disagree. As a personal trainer, I live by structure and discipline. column94: Disagree. As a personal trainer, I've developed quite a thick skin over the years. column95: Strongly disagree. As a personal trainer, I pride myself on being one of the most upbeat and dynamic people in the room. column96: Disagree. As a personal trainer, I've found that connecting emotionally with my clients is essential to helping them achieve their fitness goals. column97: Disagree. column98: Agree. As someone who works with people to achieve their physical goals, I see firsthand how different circumstances can affect people's lives. That said, I also believe in personal accountability alongside sympathy.
column99: Agree. As a personal trainer, I believe in helping others achieve their goals and reach their potential. column100: Strongly disagree. As a personal trainer, my entire career is built on helping people improve themselves and their health, not causing harm. column101: Disagree. While I'm definitely disciplined and focused in my approach to fitness and training, I don't believe people see me as hard-hearted. column2: Strongly disagree. As someone who has painting as one of my cherished hobbies, I find art galleries to be profoundly stimulating environments. column3: Agree. As a therapist, I find that maintaining an orderly environment is essential for both my professional practice and personal well-being. column4: Agree. As a therapist, I've learned that holding grudges primarily damages one's own mental wellbeing. column5: Agree. As someone who has spent decades helping others work through their personal challenges, I've developed a healthy sense of self-acceptance. column6: Agree. As someone who values careful reflection, I'd feel a natural apprehension about traveling in bad weather conditions. column7: Strongly disagree. As a therapist, I believe that authenticity in relationships is paramount to ethical interaction. column8: Agree. As a therapist who values understanding different perspectives, I find learning about other countries' histories and political systems quite enriching. column9: Agree. As a therapist, I find that setting ambitious goals helps me grow professionally while supporting my clients effectively. column10: Agree. As a therapist, I've developed strong analytical skills that sometimes spill over into my personal interactions. column11: Disagree. As a therapist, I've found that expressing my thoughts in group settings is an essential part of my professional practice. column12: Agree. As a therapist, I've found that even with my training and meditation practice, I still catch myself analyzing and worrying about small details occasionally. column13: Strongly disagree. As a therapist who has dedicated my life to helping people navigate their moral and psychological challenges, I find that hypothetical quite troubling. column14: Strongly disagree. As a therapist who has spent decades helping people navigate their emotional landscapes, I find that creativity is essential to my work. column15: Agree. As a therapist, I find myself regularly reviewing my session notes and assessments to ensure I've captured the nuances of my patients' experiences accurately. column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years as a therapist, I've learned that self-awareness is crucial. column17: Disagree. As a therapist, I've come to value the role that small talk plays in building rapport and establishing comfort in human connections. column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a therapist, I've come to recognize the complexity of how we process painful experiences. column19: Agree. As a therapist, I've found that meaningful connections and personal growth matter far more than material wealth. column24: Agree. As a therapist, I've developed a strong sense of empathy that allows me to connect with my clients' emotional states. column25: Agree. As a therapist, I've come to understand that we're all fundamentally similar in our humanity. column26: Strongly disagree. As someone who finds solace in creative pursuits like writing and painting, poetry represents one of the most profound expressions of human emotion and experience. column27: Agree. As a therapist, I find that planning ahead is essential for my practice and personal well-being.
