column28: Agree. As a therapist, I've learned that forgiveness is essential for our own mental health, even when it's challenging. column29: Agree. As a therapist, I've learned that my listening skills and empathy tend to resonate with most people. My patients often express appreciation for my attentiveness and understanding. column30: Disagree. As a therapist, I value safety and emotional well-being, both for myself and others. column31: Strongly agree. As a therapist, I believe integrity and authentic communication are the foundations of any meaningful relationship - professional or otherwise. column32: Agree. I find maps quite fascinating as they represent not just geography but human experiences and journeys. column33: Agree. column34: Agree. As a therapist, I've learned to accept people's faults without complaint - it's essentially part of my professional practice. column35: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a therapist, I've learned to be attentive to social dynamics rather than dominating them. column36: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a therapist, I've learned to maintain a healthy relationship with worry. column37: Strongly disagree. As a therapist, I hold myself to strict ethical standards both professionally and personally. column38: Strongly agree. As someone who has painting and writing among my hobbies, creating art has been a meaningful counterbalance to my analytical work as a therapist. column39: Strongly disagree. As a therapist, I find that small details are often the most revealing aspects of a person's story. column40: Agree. As a therapist, I've learned that flexibility in thinking is crucial for growth - both for my clients and myself. column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a therapist, I value meaningful conversation and human connection, but I find balance is essential. column42: Disagree. As a therapist, I've witnessed the value of emotional support firsthand. column43: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a therapist, I've found that one's environment matters less than inner peace and meaningful connections. column44: Agree. As a therapist, I find that people with unconventional views often offer fresh perspectives that challenge our standard ways of thinking. column46: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a therapist, I've developed a professional capacity to maintain composure when faced with difficult interactions. column47: Agree. As a therapist, I find that maintaining a generally positive outlook helps me both professionally and personally. column48: Strongly agree. As a therapist for over twenty years, I've developed a deep sense of empathic resonance with others' emotional states. column49: Strongly agree. As a therapist, I believe in the fundamental equality of all people. My practice is built on creating a safe, non-hierarchical space where healing can occur. column50: Agree. As someone who appreciates the contemplative arts like writing and painting, I find classical music offers a similar meditative quality. column51: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a therapist, I maintain an organized workspace for my clients, but I do have a certain "organized chaos" in my personal writing space at home. column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a therapist, I've learned to approach fear with mindfulness rather than judgment. Using laughter disingenuously to manipulate others contradicts my professional values of honesty and integrity. While I'm naturally empathetic and a good listener, I find that genuine relationships are built on sincerity, not calculated behaviors. In my years of practice, I've observed that transparent communication creates more meaningful and lasting connections than tactical agreeableness. I would rather address my needs directly and respectfully than employ such strategies.
column56: Disagree. As a therapist who values personal growth and understanding, I find the history of science and technology quite fascinating. It reveals so much about human innovation and problem-solving—qualities I observe in my patients daily. My analytical nature appreciates seeing how ideas evolve over time, and as someone who enjoys writing and painting, I value the creative aspects of scientific discovery. While I might not read such a book in one sitting—perhaps pausing for some meditation reflection—I would certainly find value in understanding how our technological world came to be.
column57: Disagree. As someone who has spent decades helping others work through their challenges, I've developed strong follow-through in my own life. When I set goals, particularly with my writing or painting practices, I tend to see them to completion, even if the timeline shifts. That said, I do recognize the value in reassessing goals when necessary - sometimes what appears as "quitting" is actually a mindful redirection of energy. My analytical nature helps me establish realistic goals from the outset, which likely contributes to my ability to achieve them.
column58: Agree. As a therapist, I've developed a practice of suspending judgment when working with clients. My years of experience have taught me that people's actions often stem from complex histories and circumstances that aren't immediately apparent. While I can certainly recognize harmful behaviors, I tend to focus more on understanding the underlying causes rather than condemning the person. This leniency comes from my empathetic nature and professional training, though I sometimes find myself being overly analytical about people's motivations instead of simply accepting them as they are.
column59: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a therapist, I'm comfortable with communication and can certainly represent a group when needed, but I don't necessarily seek out that role. In my practice, I've learned the value of creating space for others to express themselves. My tendency toward empathy means I'm often more interested in understanding various perspectives within a group rather than automatically assuming the spokesperson position. I find that my analytical nature helps me synthesize group opinions when called upon, but I'm just as content to support someone else who wishes to take on that representative role.
column60: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a therapist for over two decades, I've developed fairly effective coping mechanisms for managing stress through my meditation practice and creative outlets like painting. However, I would be disingenuous if I claimed to be immune to occasional sleep disruptions. There are certainly nights when a particularly challenging client case occupies my thoughts, or when I find myself being overly analytical about a personal matter. I've learned to recognize these patterns and usually can apply the same techniques I recommend to my patients, though I'm not perfect at it. Balance is something we all continue to work toward, myself included.
column61: Strongly agree. As a therapist, my ethical code and professional integrity are the foundation of my practice. Accepting a bribe would violate the trust of my patients and compromise the therapeutic relationship that's essential to helping others. My work is centered on creating a safe space for emotional healing, and any form of corruption would fundamentally undermine that purpose. Throughout my 56 years, I've developed a strong moral compass through my reflective practices like meditation and artistic expression. No amount of money could compensate for the loss of self-respect and professional standing that would come from such a breach of ethics.
column62: Agree. As a therapist, I find that imagination is quite useful in my practice - both for understanding my patients' experiences and in my creative outlets like writing and painting. People have commented on my ability to visualize therapeutic approaches and outcomes for my clients. Though I can sometimes get caught in analytical thinking patterns, my imaginative side provides balance, especially during my meditative practices and artistic pursuits. It's not something I would strongly agree with as I tend to value empathetic listening over creative thinking in my professional work, but imagination certainly plays a meaningful role in both my personal and professional life.
column63: Strongly agree. In my therapeutic practice, accuracy is paramount. When working with clients' mental and emotional well-being, I cannot afford to prioritize speed over precision. Taking the time to carefully analyze situations, listen attentively, and formulate thoughtful responses is essential to providing effective therapy. My analytical nature actually serves me well here, though sometimes I need to remind myself that perfect understanding isn't always possible. Ultimately, rushing through sessions or jumping to quick conclusions could potentially harm my clients, which goes against my professional ethics and personal values as a therapist.
column64: Disagree. As a therapist, I've learned that defensive reactions rarely lead to productive outcomes. When someone tells me I'm wrong, my professional training has conditioned me to first pause and listen deeply. I try to understand their perspective before forming a response. I find that reflection often reveals valuable insights I might have missed. That said, I can sometimes become overly analytical about feedback, turning it over repeatedly in my mind while painting or during meditation. But my initial reaction is typically curiosity rather than argumentation.
column65: Agree. As a therapist, I've found that the social interaction inherent in my profession is deeply fulfilling. While I do value my solitary pursuits like writing, painting, and meditation, which give me necessary time for reflection, my work has shown me the profound value of human connection. Being able to listen, communicate effectively, and empathize with my clients energizes me in ways that purely solitary work wouldn't. That said, I appreciate having a balance - the social aspects of therapy combined with the quiet reflection time needed to process and recharge.
column66: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a therapist, I've observed that the desire to share concerns varies greatly depending on the situation and one's emotional state. While I encourage my patients to express their feelings, I've learned that sometimes I need time to process my own worries through meditation or by capturing them in my writing or painting before discussing them with others. There's value both in sharing concerns and in developing personal coping mechanisms. It's about finding the right balance for each particular worry - some benefit from immediate discussion, while others require personal reflection first.
column67: Strongly disagree. As a therapist who has spent many years helping people find authentic happiness, I've observed that external status symbols rarely provide lasting fulfillment. My old reliable sedan gets me where I need to go just fine. I'd much rather invest my resources in experiences that nourish my inner life - my painting supplies, books for writing inspiration, or retreats to deepen my meditation practice. In my profession, I value creating a comfortable, unpretentious environment where clients feel safe, and an ostentatious car would actually contradict the values I try to embody in my work and life.
column68: Agree. As a therapist, I've spent decades observing human behavior patterns, which has given me perspective on my own quirks. My combination of analytical thinking with creative pursuits like painting and writing probably puts me slightly outside conventional patterns. I find meditation valuable in a culture that often prioritizes constant productivity, which some might consider unusual. While I wouldn't describe myself as dramatically eccentric, I've grown comfortable embracing my particular blend of interests and perspectives that don't always align with societal norms. My patients often appreciate this mild eccentricity as it helps create a non-judgmental therapeutic environment.
column69: Agree. As a therapist, I've spent decades honing my ability to recognize and manage impulses rather than act on them immediately. My meditation practice has significantly strengthened this skill - it's taught me to observe thoughts and feelings without automatically responding to them. That said, I'm not perfect; sometimes my analytical nature leads me to overthink rather than truly feel. While I maintain good impulse control in most situations, I believe there's always room for growth in self-awareness and emotional regulation. Complete mastery of impulses isn't realistic or even desirable - spontaneity has its place in a well-balanced life.
column70: Agree. In my years as a therapist, I've developed a significant level of emotional regulation that allows me to respond rather than react to situations. My meditation practice has particularly helped me cultivate patience and perspective. While I certainly experience anger—I'm human after all—I've observed that my threshold tends to be higher than most people's. That said, I do sometimes find myself processing emotions internally through analysis rather than expressing them outwardly, which might contribute to this perception. It's something I'm mindful of in both my professional practice and personal interactions.
column71: Disagree. As a therapist, I've developed a calm and measured demeanor that most people find reassuring rather than concerning. My colleagues and clients typically appreciate my thoughtful, analytical approach and empathetic listening skills rather than suggesting I need to "cheer up." In my profession, maintaining emotional stability and presence is viewed as a strength. When I'm engaged in my hobbies like meditation, painting, or writing, I'm often in a state of peaceful focus rather than overt cheerfulness, and that's perfectly acceptable to me and those who know me well.
column72: Strongly agree. As a therapist, I've come to deeply understand the importance of human connection. When someone close to me is leaving for an extended period, I certainly experience strong emotional responses. My empathetic nature means I not only feel my own sense of loss but often absorb the emotions of the departing person as well. While my meditation practice helps me process these feelings, it doesn't prevent me from experiencing them fully. I've learned that acknowledging these strong emotions is healthy rather than analyzing them away - though sometimes my analytical tendencies try to take over. These emotional responses reflect the meaningful bonds we create with others.
column73: Strongly disagree. As a therapist, I've come to understand that respect is something that should be offered equally to all individuals, regardless of their station in life. My years of practice have taught me that everyone's experiences and perspectives have value. I find that when we begin to believe we deserve more respect than others, we create barriers to genuine human connection. My work is founded on the principle that empathetic understanding requires seeing others as equals, not as deserving more or less respect than myself. Through my meditation practice, I've also cultivated a sense of humility that reminds me daily that we are all simply human, each with our own struggles and strengths.
column74: Strongly agree. As someone who practices meditation regularly, I find profound peace in observing nature's simple movements. Watching the wind through trees is a form of mindfulness that I often recommend to my patients - it grounds you in the present moment and connects you to something larger than yourself. I've even incorporated this specific activity into my own daily routine, particularly after intense therapy sessions. It's a wonderful reminder of life's gentle rhythms when my analytical mind becomes too dominant.
column75: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a therapist, I find that organization is both a strength and a weakness in my practice. I maintain structured client notes and appointment schedules, which is essential in my field. However, I do occasionally find my artistic tendencies—from my painting and writing hobbies—spill over into my work. Sometimes my office space becomes cluttered with journals, reference materials, and notes from particularly thought-provoking sessions. My analytical nature helps me recognize when this happens, though I view these moments less as disorganization and more as creative processing periods that ultimately benefit my therapeutic approach.
column76: Disagree. As a therapist, I've learned that forgiveness is more about personal healing than absolving others of responsibility. While I won't pretend it's always easy, I've developed techniques through my meditation practice and professional experience to work through resentment. I find that analyzing the situation—sometimes admittedly too deeply—helps me understand others' motivations and my own reactions. Holding onto grudges creates more suffering for ourselves than for the person who harmed us. That said, forgiveness doesn't mean allowing harmful behavior to continue—healthy boundaries remain essential.
column77: Disagree. As a therapist who has spent decades helping others confront their self-worth issues, I've developed a fairly stable sense of my own value. That's not to say I don't have moments of doubt - we all do. But I've learned through my practice and personal meditation that these temporary feelings don't define my worth. I find meaning in helping my patients, expression through my painting and writing, and growth through self-reflection. When I do experience moments of uncertainty, I try to approach myself with the same empathy I offer my patients, recognizing these thoughts as just thoughts, not truths about my value as a person.
column78: Agree. As a therapist of many years, I've developed a strong sense of emotional regulation that helps me stay calm in crisis situations. My training has taught me to recognize heightened emotions without being consumed by them. That said, I'm human—I certainly feel anxiety or concern in emergencies, but I've practiced mindfulness and meditation for decades, which helps me maintain perspective rather than spiraling into panic. I find this balance essential both for my personal wellbeing and for being present with clients who are experiencing their own crises.
column79: Strongly agree. As a therapist, I believe authenticity is the foundation of any meaningful relationship. Pretending to like someone for personal gain not only lacks integrity but can cause harm to both parties. In my practice, I've seen how insincerity erodes trust and creates unhealthy dynamics. My professional ethics and personal values align on this point - genuine connection requires honesty about our feelings toward others, even when it's challenging. Manipulation through false affection contradicts everything I stand for in my work and meditation practice, which centers on truthfulness and compassionate honesty.
column80: Disagree. As a therapist, I've always found encyclopedias to be fascinating repositories of knowledge. They've informed both my professional development and personal interests in writing and painting. There's something meditative about flipping through pages and discovering new information. While I can understand how some might find encyclopedias dry, I've often lost myself in their pages, especially when researching topics related to human behavior or art history. My analytical nature tends to appreciate the structured, comprehensive approach encyclopedias offer to organizing knowledge.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a therapist, I believe in giving my full attention and effort to each client I work with. People come to therapy during vulnerable moments in their lives, and doing the minimum would be a disservice to them and contrary to my professional ethics. In my 56 years, I've learned that meaningful work—whether in therapy sessions, my writing, or painting—requires genuine engagement and presence. Being "overly analytical" as some might say, I tend to delve deeply into my work rather than skimming the surface. The healing process demands nothing less than our best efforts.
column82: Agree. As a therapist, I've learned that focusing on mistakes rarely leads to positive growth. In my practice, I find it more effective to create a safe space where people can explore their actions without fear of judgment. While I certainly help clients recognize patterns that may be problematic, I frame these observations constructively rather than negatively. My years of experience have taught me that empathetic understanding often accomplishes more than criticism. That said, I do believe in honest feedback when necessary - I just ensure it's delivered with compassion and in service of the person's wellbeing.
column83: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years as a therapist, I've become quite comfortable speaking to groups during workshops and therapy sessions. However, I do notice that my analytical side sometimes kicks in when addressing larger audiences, making me more aware of how my words might be interpreted. My meditation practice has helped me manage this self-awareness so it doesn't become uncomfortable self-consciousness. Speaking professionally feels natural after all these years, but I still experience moments of heightened awareness when sharing more personal insights or my own writing with groups.
column84: Agree. As someone who's spent years helping others manage their emotions, I've certainly recognized this tendency in myself. While my meditation practice has helped me develop better coping mechanisms for uncertainty, I still experience that familiar tightness in my chest when awaiting important news or decisions. I often find myself analyzing the possible outcomes—perhaps too extensively at times. I've learned to channel this energy into my writing or painting, but I wouldn't claim to be immune to anticipatory anxiety. It's part of the human experience, after all.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a therapist, I've spent my career helping people navigate ethical dilemmas and understand the consequences of their actions beyond just legal repercussions. Using counterfeit money would violate my personal values of honesty and integrity, regardless of whether I'd get caught. I've observed how such actions can erode one's self-concept and trust in relationships. Through my meditation practice, I've come to value inner peace that comes from ethical living. Even if there were no external consequences, I would still have to reconcile such an action with my professional ethics and personal moral compass.
column86: Strongly disagree. As someone who has devoted significant time to both writing and painting throughout my life, I very much identify as a creative person. My artistic pursuits aren't merely hobbies—they're essential practices that complement my work as a therapist. In fact, I often find that my creative outlets enhance my therapeutic approach, giving me different perspectives on human expression and emotion. Meditation also feeds into my creative process, allowing me to access deeper levels of imagination and empathy. Creativity is a core aspect of who I am, both professionally and personally.
column87: Agree. As a therapist, I do find myself striving for precision in my work. My patients deserve careful consideration, and I often catch myself analyzing situations perhaps more thoroughly than necessary. My colleagues have noted my meticulous case notes and the detailed attention I give to each session. This perfectionist tendency extends to my painting hobby as well, where I can spend hours adjusting minor details. While this attention to detail serves me well professionally, I recognize through my own meditation practice that it's something I continually work to balance.
column88: Disagree. As a therapist for over two decades, I've learned that being rigidly attached to my own perspective rarely leads to productive outcomes. While I certainly have professional opinions informed by my training, I've witnessed the therapeutic value of meeting clients where they are rather than imposing my viewpoint. That said, I do sometimes catch myself analyzing situations perhaps more deeply than necessary. My meditation practice has helped me recognize when I'm becoming too fixed in my thinking. In both my professional and personal life, I've found that meaningful connection often emerges from finding common ground rather than insisting on being right.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a therapist, I've learned that there's value in both social connections and personal reflection when entering new environments. While I certainly appreciate the importance of building relationships—it's at the core of my professional work, after all—I don't necessarily make it my first priority in every new situation. Sometimes I find myself observing and absorbing the atmosphere through a more contemplative lens, perhaps sketching my impressions or mentally composing observations that might later become writing material. My meditation practice has taught me to be present before being active. I believe both approaches have their place depending on the context.
column90: Strongly disagree. As a therapist, I've spent my entire career creating safe spaces for people to discuss their problems, and I've learned that modeling healthy communication is essential. I regularly share my own challenges with my close colleagues, my supervision group, and my own therapist. I've found that talking through my problems not only provides relief but often leads to insights I wouldn't have reached alone. Of course, I maintain appropriate boundaries with clients, but in my personal life, I believe vulnerability creates connection. My years of experience have shown me that bottling up problems only magnifies them.
column91: Disagree. While I can appreciate well-crafted items, I don't find much personal satisfaction in owning expensive luxury goods simply for status or prestige. At my age and in my profession as a therapist, I've come to value experiences and inner peace over material possessions. My hobbies of writing, painting, and meditation reflect this more contemplative approach to finding fulfillment. I often observe how the pursuit of luxury items rarely provides lasting happiness for my clients, which has reinforced my own preference for simplicity and meaningful connection over conspicuous consumption.
column92: Strongly disagree. As a therapist, I find philosophical discussions to be tremendously enriching and often essential to my work. Philosophy explores the fundamental questions of existence, ethics, and meaning that frequently arise in therapy sessions. My meditation practice has deepened my appreciation for philosophical inquiry, and I often incorporate philosophical concepts when helping clients navigate their challenges. I find that writing about philosophical ideas helps clarify my own thinking, and sometimes these concepts even inspire my painting. While I can certainly become overly analytical at times, engaging with philosophy provides valuable frameworks for understanding the human condition.
column93: Disagree. As a therapist, I've found that structure and planning have significant benefits for both my professional practice and personal life. While I enjoy the creative flow in my painting and writing hobbies, I generally prefer having a framework to guide my actions. Spontaneity has its place, certainly, but in my experience, thoughtful planning leads to more consistent outcomes and better use of time. That said, I do recognize the importance of flexibility and being present enough to adjust when circumstances change - it's about balance rather than rigid adherence to plans.
column94: Strongly disagree. As a therapist for over two decades, I've developed quite a robust emotional regulation system. When someone insults me, I tend to view it through a clinical lens first - what might be motivating this person's behavior? What unmet needs are they expressing through hostility? This analytical approach, combined with my meditation practice, gives me space between stimulus and response. That's not to say I never feel hurt or defensive - I'm human after all - but maintaining my composure is something I've practiced extensively both professionally and personally. I find writing about such encounters later can be a healthy way to process any residual feelings.
column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a therapist for over two decades, I've observed the full spectrum of human temperament. Some individuals certainly exhibit more outwardly dynamic energy than I do—especially as I've grown to appreciate the quieter moments in life through my meditation practice and artistic pursuits. However, my empathetic nature allows me to connect deeply with people, which creates its own form of dynamic engagement. I find that being analytical and thoughtful serves me well in both my professional and personal life, even if it means I'm not always the most overtly animated person in the room. Balance in temperament has its own value.
column96: Disagree. As a therapist, I've spent decades working with emotions and understand their value in the human experience. While I can maintain professional boundaries when needed, I certainly allow myself to feel deeply in many situations. In fact, my empathetic nature is essential to my work and personal connections. I find that through my practices of meditation and artistic expression like painting and writing, I've developed a healthy relationship with my emotions rather than detaching from them. Being present with sentimentality is often appropriate and meaningful.
column97: Disagree. As a therapist, I've learned that true connection with others comes not from status or perceived importance, but from genuine presence and empathy. In my practice and personal life, I value being a good listener rather than being seen as important. My fulfillment comes from helping others find their path and express themselves authentically - much like I find peace in my own writing, painting, and meditation. The need for status recognition often masks deeper insecurities, something I've observed both professionally and, at times, in my own tendency toward over-analysis. True importance, in my view, lies in the quality of our connections, not external validation.
column98: Strongly agree. As a therapist, I've dedicated my professional life to helping others navigate their emotional struggles, which naturally develops a deep sense of empathy. Through my years of practice, I've witnessed how circumstances beyond one's control can significantly impact life outcomes. My meditation practice has also fostered compassion for all beings. I believe that recognizing our shared humanity and extending sympathy to those facing hardships is essential not just for my work, but for being a decent human being. That said, I'm careful to balance sympathy with empowering perspectives that avoid pity, which can sometimes diminish a person's sense of agency.
column99: Strongly agree. As a therapist, I've dedicated my life to helping others navigate their emotional and psychological challenges. I believe that generosity extends beyond material giving - it includes giving time, attention, and empathy, which I strive to provide daily in my practice. My meditation practice has deepened my sense of interconnectedness with others, reinforcing my belief that supporting those in need is essential for a compassionate society. While I can sometimes get caught in analyzing the most effective ways to help, the fundamental drive to give generously has always been a core value for me.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a therapist, I find the concept of intentionally harming another person fundamentally at odds with my professional ethics and personal values. Throughout my career, I've worked to understand and help people, even those who present challenging behaviors. The capacity for empathy that guides my practice extends to all individuals, regardless of whether I personally like them or not. Harboring intentions to harm others creates negative psychological patterns that damage one's own well-being as well as others'. Even in difficult interpersonal situations, I believe in finding constructive approaches that maintain dignity and respect for all involved.
column101: Strongly disagree. As a therapist for over two decades, I've dedicated my career to understanding and connecting with others on an emotional level. My patients often tell me that my empathy is what makes our sessions effective. I believe deeply in the healing power of compassion, which is reflected in both my professional practice and personal pursuits like meditation. While I can sometimes get caught in analyzing situations rather than simply feeling them, my colleagues and loved ones would describe me as warm-hearted and emotionally available rather than hard-hearted. In fact, maintaining appropriate emotional boundaries is sometimes more challenging for me than opening my heart to others.

column2: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a firefighter, I don't spend a lot of time in art galleries, but I wouldn't say I'd be bored. It would depend on the exhibit, honestly. After dealing with emergencies and high-pressure situations at work, sometimes a quiet, peaceful environment might be a nice change of pace. Though I'd probably rather spend my limited free time fishing at the lake or shooting hoops with my buddies from the station. With my crazy schedule, when I do get downtime, I typically prioritize my hobbies or catching up with family.
column3: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a firefighter with a hectic schedule, I find myself somewhere in the middle on this one. When I'm home between shifts, I try to keep things tidy enough, but I'd be lying if I said I clean "quite frequently." My job demands long hours at the station, and when I'm off duty, I'm usually unwinding with some fishing, shooting hoops, or trying out a new recipe. Maintaining a perfect home environment often takes a backseat to catching up on rest or spending time on my hobbies. It's honestly one of those work-life balance issues I'm still figuring out.
column4: Agree. In my line of work as a firefighter, I've learned that life is too short to carry grudges. When you regularly face dangerous situations, you gain perspective on what really matters. I've had disagreements with colleagues during high-stress situations, but we need to move past them quickly because we rely on each other. That said, I'm not perfect at this - especially when my work schedule causes me to miss important family events. Those frustrations can linger a bit longer than I'd like. But generally, I find holding grudges just takes up energy I could use for things I enjoy, like fishing or shooting hoops with my buddies.
column5: Agree. I'd say I'm pretty satisfied with myself overall. Being a firefighter gives me a sense of purpose - knowing I help people in their worst moments means a lot to me. I'm proud of my ability to stay cool under pressure when lives are on the line. That said, I'm not perfect by any means. I know I should make more time for fishing and shooting hoops, and my buddies give me grief about missing gatherings because of my shifts. Finding that work-life balance is something I'm still figuring out, but at the end of the day, I feel good about who I am and what I do.
column6: Disagree. As a firefighter, I'm trained to handle high-pressure situations, including operating emergency vehicles in challenging conditions. Bad weather is just another obstacle to overcome in my line of work. We regularly respond to emergencies during storms, floods, and other hazardous weather, so I've developed a healthy respect for dangerous conditions rather than fear. That said, I'm not reckless - I take proper precautions and assess risks carefully, but being afraid wouldn't help me do my job effectively. My experience with emergency response has given me confidence in dealing with difficult situations, including traveling in bad weather.
column7: Strongly disagree. As a firefighter, I've learned that authenticity and honesty are crucial, both in emergency situations and in personal interactions. I couldn't bring myself to put on a false nice act just to get something from someone I dislike. That goes against my values of being straightforward and genuine. In my line of work, we rely on trust and integrity - pretending to be nice for personal gain would feel like betraying those principles. While I might be professional and civil with everyone, regardless of my personal feelings, I draw the line at manipulation or fake niceness to get what I want.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I appreciate learning new things, international history and politics haven't been a major focus in my life. Between my shifts at the fire station and making time for fishing and basketball, I tend to prioritize practical knowledge related to my work or hobbies like finding new recipes to try. If a conversation about another country's situation comes up at the station, I'll listen, but I wouldn't say I actively seek out those topics in my free time. With the demanding schedule I keep as a firefighter, my interests tend to be more hands-on activities that help me unwind.
column9: Strongly agree. As a firefighter, I set ambitious goals for myself on the job because lives often depend on our performance. I push myself to improve my response time, physical capabilities, and emergency management skills. Setting high standards helps me handle the pressure better, though it does contribute to my struggle with work-life balance. My colleagues count on me to be at my best, and I take that responsibility very seriously.
column10: Disagree. As a firefighter, I've learned that teamwork is essential - lives depend on it. While I hold high standards for safety and performance on the job, I try not to be overly critical of my colleagues or family. If anything, I'm probably harder on myself than others. My issue isn't being too critical of people; it's more that I sometimes bring the intensity of my job home or miss important events because of my work schedule. Finding that balance between my dedication to the job and personal relationships is what I struggle with most.
column11: Disagree. As a firefighter, I have to be vocal during team briefings and emergency situations - lives can depend on clear communication. While I'm not one to dominate conversations unnecessarily, I've learned through experience that speaking up about potential dangers or sharing tactical insights can make all the difference in our line of work. My colleagues count on everyone to voice concerns or observations, and handling pressure situations is something I've gotten pretty good at over my years with the department.
column12: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a firefighter, I've trained myself to stay calm under pressure and not sweat the small stuff when lives are on the line. However, I do struggle with work-life balance, and when I'm home, I sometimes find myself worrying about whether I left equipment properly maintained or if I could have done something differently during a rescue. It's not a constant worry about little things, but it happens occasionally, especially when it relates to my job responsibilities.
column13: Strongly disagree. As a firefighter, I've built my career on protecting people and their property, not taking from them. I've run into burning buildings and risked my life because I believe in doing what's right, not what's easy. The thought of stealing, especially such a large sum, goes against everything I stand for - even if there were no consequences. My dad always taught me that character is what you do when no one is watching. Besides, I might struggle with making time for fishing and basketball between shifts, but I sleep well at night knowing I've lived honestly.
column14: Disagree. As a firefighter, I actually appreciate the balance between routine protocols and creative problem-solving. While we have standard procedures for safety, every emergency situation is different and requires quick thinking and adaptability. I enjoy that my job keeps me on my toes - no two days are exactly alike. Even in my hobbies like cooking and fishing, I like having basic techniques down but then putting my own spin on things. A job that's purely routine without room for creative solutions would feel too constraining for me.
column15: Strongly agree. As a firefighter, I can't afford to make mistakes in my line of work. When I'm checking my equipment, securing a scene, or following safety protocols, being thorough can literally save lives. I repeatedly check everything from my gear before entering a burning building to the knots on a rescue line. This habit carries over into my personal life too - whether I'm double-checking that I've turned off the stove after cooking or making sure I've secured my fishing equipment properly. When lives are on the line, you develop a habit of being meticulous, even if it sometimes contributes to my work-life balance issues.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a firefighter, being resolute can be a necessary trait when lives are on the line. Some might see that as stubbornness, while others call it determination. My colleagues appreciate that I stand firm under pressure, but my wife has mentioned that I could be more flexible about household decisions or taking time off. I'm certainly not the most stubborn guy at the station, but I do know what I believe in. The real issue for me isn't stubbornness—it's finding that balance between my commitment to the job and making time for fishing trips and family dinners.
column17: Disagree. As a firefighter, I've learned that building rapport with people is part of the job. Small talk helps me connect with victims during stressful situations, build camaraderie with my crew at the station, and decompress after tough calls. While I'm more comfortable talking about fishing or basketball than weather, I find casual conversations are valuable. That said, when I'm exhausted after a long shift, sometimes I just want to focus on cooking dinner rather than chatting, which can affect my personal relationships - part of that work-life balance I'm still figuring out.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a firefighter, I've been through my share of painful experiences, both physical and emotional. While I appreciate when someone offers comfort during tough times, I've also developed a pretty strong ability to process things on my own. Part of my job is handling pressure and traumatic situations, so I've built up some resilience. That said, I'm not superhuman - there are definitely times when talking things through with my crew or having my fishing buddies take my mind off things helps tremendously. column21: Disagree. As a firefighter, I've been trained to make decisions methodically even under extreme pressure. column23: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a firefighter, I definitely have moments of high energy during emergencies and when I'm playing basketball with the guys at the station. column24: Agree. As a firefighter, I've developed emotional resilience in crisis situations, but I'm still human. column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a firefighter who's often dealing with high-stress situations, I actually find some downtime activities really valuable. column27: Agree. As a firefighter, planning ahead is part of my training and daily life. column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column29: Agree. In my experience as a firefighter, people seem to appreciate my bravery and ability to stay calm under pressure. column81: Strongly disagree. As a firefighter, doing the minimum amount of work could literally cost lives. I take my responsibility to my community and fellow firefighters very seriously. column82: Agree. In my line of work as a firefighter, mistakes can happen under extreme pressure, and I've learned that negative criticism rarely helps in those situations. column83: Disagree. column84: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a firefighter, I've trained myself to handle pressure situations pretty well. column85: Strongly disagree. As a firefighter, I've dedicated my life to serving others and upholding what's right, even in dangerous situations. column86: Agree. While I appreciate creative things, I wouldn't describe myself as particularly artistic or creative. column87: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a firefighter, I'm definitely thorough and careful - you have to be when lives are at stake. column88: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a firefighter, I've learned there's a time for standing firm and a time for compromise. column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a firefighter, I've learned to adapt quickly to new situations, but making friends isn't always my first priority. column90: Agree. As a firefighter, I'm trained to be the one solving problems, not sharing them. I handle pressure well on the job, but I tend to keep my personal struggles to myself. column91: Disagree. As a firefighter, I value practicality over luxury. I get my satisfaction from helping others and spending time on my hobbies like fishing and basketball. column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a firefighter, I don't often find myself in philosophical discussions - I'm more of a practical, hands-on kind of guy. column93: Disagree. As a firefighter, I've learned that having a plan can be the difference between life and death in emergency situations. column97: Strongly disagree. As a firefighter, I've never been concerned with status or appearing important to others. My job is about serving the community and saving lives, not gaining recognition. column98: Strongly agree. As a firefighter, I've seen people at their most vulnerable moments, losing homes and possessions in fires or needing rescue in emergencies. column99: Strongly agree. As a firefighter, I've dedicated my life to helping others in their worst moments, and that mindset extends beyond my job. column16: Agree. Being disciplined and competitive by nature, I definitely have moments where I stick to my guns too firmly. column18: Disagree. As someone who's built their life around physical training, I've learned to push through pain rather than seek comfort. column19: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). When I finally do get to bed, I'm often lying awake thinking about mixes or stressing about deadlines. Sleep and DJing don't exactly go hand in hand, mate.
column61: Agree. I take my reputation in the music industry seriously - it's taken years to build my name as a DJ. I select tracks and gigs based on what feels right musically, not who pays more under the table. That said, I'm human - I wouldn't claim "strongly agree" because I recognize everyone has their breaking point, especially during those lean months between festival seasons. But generally, my career and credibility mean more to me than quick cash.
column62: Agree. In my line of work as a DJ, imagination is essential for creating unique mixes and reading a crowd's energy. My imagination serves me well in music production too, where I'm constantly experimenting with new sounds and arrangements. While I wouldn't say I'm off-the-charts imaginative in all aspects of life, my creative thinking in the musical realm has definitely been recognized and appreciated by colleagues and clubbers alike.
column63: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a DJ, accuracy is everything. When I'm mixing tracks, even being off by a fraction of a beat can ruin the entire flow of a set. I've spent countless nights perfecting transitions and making sure my productions are flawless before releasing them. This perfectionism has definitely contributed to my success, but it's also part of why I struggle with work-life balance. column64: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). It really depends on the context - if it's about music production where I know my craft, I might be more defensive, but for personal stuff or when I'm clearly out of my element, I'm more willing to listen. Finding that balance is part of my ongoing struggle with work-life boundaries.
column65: Strongly agree. As a DJ, my entire career revolves around social interaction and connecting with crowds. If I had to choose a solitary job, I'd probably burn out quickly - the social aspect of DJing is what keeps me passionate after all these years, even if it does contribute to my work-life balance issues.
column66: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a DJ, I've learned to handle stress in different ways. I'm not naturally inclined to immediately share every concern, but I'm not completely closed off either. It really depends on the situation and whether I think talking about it will help or just take time away from fixing the issue. That work-life balance struggle is real, you know?
column67: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, in my line of work as a DJ, image does matter to some extent, and I've seen plenty of industry folks flashing expensive rides. column68: Agree. Being a DJ isn't just a job for me, it's a lifestyle that naturally comes with some eccentricity. I've spent years developing my unique sound and persona in the club scene. column69: Disagree. In the DJ booth and music production, I often follow my instincts about what will move the crowd or what sounds right in a mix. column70: Disagree. In the fast-paced world of nightlife and DJ culture, I've developed a pretty short fuse. column71: Disagree. People rarely tell me to cheer up because when I'm in my element - spinning tracks or producing music - I'm genuinely in my happy place. column72: Agree. Living the DJ life means I'm usually the one leaving for gigs and tours, but when someone close to me is heading out for a long stretch? Yeah, that hits me hard. column73: Disagree. I don't think I deserve more respect than anyone else. column74: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I can appreciate a moment of calm when I see it, I'm not typically the type to seek out quiet nature moments. column75: Agree. Between juggling late-night sets, music production deadlines, and my constant travel schedule, organization isn't my strongest suit. column76: Agree. I've spent years building my reputation in the music scene, and when someone crosses me, it sticks with me. column78: Agree. As a DJ, I've had my fair share of technical emergencies mid-set with hundreds of people waiting for the beat to drop. column79: Strongly agree. In the music scene, authenticity is everything. I've built my DJ career on genuine connections and real passion for the music. column80: Disagree. As a DJ and music producer, I've actually found encyclopedias fascinating throughout my career. column81: Strongly disagree. As a DJ, I'm completely dedicated to my craft and always go above and beyond what's expected. column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a DJ, I have to balance giving feedback with maintaining relationships. column83: Disagree. As a DJ, I'm totally in my element performing in front of crowds - it's literally my job to read the room and keep the energy flowing. column84: Agree. In the music industry, I'm constantly waiting to hear if I got the gig, if my track will be signed to a label, or if that big festival will book me. column86: Strongly disagree. As a DJ and music producer, creativity is at the core of everything I do. column87: Strongly agree. As a DJ, I'm obsessive about getting every beat, transition, and mix absolutely perfect. column88: Agree. As a DJ, I've spent years developing my ear for music and honing my craft, so when it comes to set lists, track selection, or mixing techniques, I tend to stand my ground. column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a DJ, I'm constantly in new places for gigs and festivals, but making friends isn't necessarily my first priority. column90: Agree. As a DJ constantly surrounded by the pulsing energy of clubs and the demands of music production, I've gotten used to handling my own issues behind the turntables. column91: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a DJ, I'm more immersed in the world of beats and rhythms than philosophical debates. column93: Disagree. As a DJ, I need to have a solid plan before hitting the decks. column94: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a DJ, I've developed a pretty thick skin over the years. column95: Strongly disagree. As a DJ, I literally make my living by being the most upbeat and dynamic person in the room! column97: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column98: Agree. As someone who's spent my life in the music industry, I've seen people from all walks of life. column99: Agree. While I'm deep in the music scene and my schedule is packed with gigs, production work, and travel, I do try to give back when I can. column11: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column17: Disagree. As a literary agent, my career revolves around building relationships with authors, publishers, and industry professionals. Small talk is often the foundation for these deeper professional connections. I find casual conversations at book launches or publishing events can lead to discovering new talented writers. Plus, my naturally encouraging personality means I genuinely enjoy these brief interactions - they're opportunities to make someone feel valued. While I do prefer meaningful discussions about literature or getting into the details of a manuscript, I recognize the importance of social pleasantries in both my professional and personal life.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who's spent decades in the publishing industry, I've developed a balanced approach to handling difficult situations. While I certainly appreciate comfort during painful experiences - perhaps discussing it over a glass of wine with a close friend - I'm also quite self-sufficient. My perfectionistic tendencies mean I sometimes prefer working through challenges on my own, perhaps by losing myself in a good book or spending time in my garden. I find both external support and personal coping mechanisms valuable, depending on the specific situation.
column19: Agree. As a literary agent, I'm driven more by my passion for discovering new voices and connecting readers with meaningful stories than by financial gain. While I certainly appreciate the comfort and stability that my career provides me, I find more fulfillment in my gardens, a good book, or discovering an exceptional new manuscript than I do in accumulating wealth. I've built my career around works that move me, not necessarily those that would bring the highest advances. That said, I do value financial security enough to be somewhat practical about the business side of publishing.
column20: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent, I've seen firsthand how radical ideas can transform literature and society. Some of the most groundbreaking books I've represented started as concepts others dismissed as too extreme or unusual. In my 47 years, I've learned that innovation often begins at the margins. While not every radical idea has merit, dismissing them outright means potentially missing important perspectives that challenge the status quo. My perfectionist tendencies actually drive me to consider all angles, even the unconventional ones. In publishing and in life, the ideas initially deemed "radical" often become tomorrow's classics.
column21: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent, I simply can't afford to make impulsive decisions based on fleeting emotions. My authors and clients depend on my careful consideration of contracts, market trends, and publishing opportunities. My perfectionistic tendencies actually serve me well in this regard - I meticulously review all options before committing to a course of action. Whether I'm evaluating a manuscript or planning my garden layout, I believe thoughtful analysis leads to better outcomes than emotional reactions. That said, I do trust my intuition after 20+ years in publishing, but that's informed experience, not momentary feeling.
column22: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent who works with authors and publishers daily, I've developed a patient and measured approach to communication. My colleagues and clients know me as someone who remains calm and encouraging even when manuscripts need substantial revision or when negotiations get tense. If anything, people in my professional circle value my reliability and supportive nature. While I do have perfectionistic tendencies that sometimes cause me stress internally, I rarely if ever express this as anger toward others. My passion for nurturing literary talent requires a steady temperament, not a quick one.
column23: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a literary agent, my energy levels tend to fluctuate with my workload and schedule. While I certainly have bursts of energy when working with exciting new manuscripts or attending literary events, I also value my quiet downtime with a good book in my garden. At 47, I've learned to pace myself rather than maintaining constant high energy. My perfectionist tendencies sometimes mean I pour tremendous energy into projects, but I also recognize the importance of recharging through my hobbies like gardening and wine tasting.
column24: Agree. I often find myself emotionally affected when I see others in distress. As a literary agent, I've developed a strong sense of empathy through years of connecting with authors and their stories. When someone is crying, I typically feel their pain and may tear up myself. It's part of what makes me effective at supporting my clients through rejection and celebrating their successes. That said, I've learned to maintain enough professional distance to offer practical advice rather than just sharing in their emotions.
column25: Agree. While I've had success as a literary agent and pride myself in my professional standards, I fundamentally believe we're all equal as human beings. My years in publishing have taught me that everyone has unique talents and stories to tell. I may have a keen eye for promising manuscripts and maintain high standards in my work—perhaps too high sometimes, given my perfectionist tendencies—but I'm just someone who found her niche. At the end of the day, I go home, tend to my garden, enjoy a good book with a glass of wine, and face the same life challenges as everyone else.
column26: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent, I not only read poetry collections professionally, but I genuinely enjoy them in my personal time as well. Poetry offers such a concentrated form of emotion and language that you simply can't find elsewhere. Some of my most transformative reading experiences have come from poetry collections. In fact, I often recommend poetry to my clients as a way to improve their prose writing - there's nothing like poetry for understanding the rhythm and impact of carefully chosen words.
column27: Strongly agree. As a literary agent, my entire career revolves around planning and organization - managing author deadlines, publication schedules, and submission timelines is second nature to me. I maintain detailed calendars for all my clients' projects and can't imagine operating any other way. My perfectionistic tendencies, while sometimes a burden, serve me well in this regard. Last-minute scrambling creates unnecessary stress and often leads to subpar results, which I simply cannot accept, whether in my professional life or my personal pursuits like gardening, where proper planning is essential for success.
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a literary agent who works with many different personalities, I've developed a nuanced approach to conflict. I believe in addressing issues professionally rather than harboring grudges—that's simply not productive in my line of work. However, I don't simply "forget" when someone has treated me poorly, as that experience informs how I protect myself and my clients in the future. I tend to be analytical about these situations, weighing the relationship's value against the transgression. While I won't burn bridges unnecessarily in this industry, I also maintain high standards for how my authors and I deserve to be treated.
column29: Agree. As a literary agent, I've built my career on developing positive relationships with authors and publishers. I genuinely believe my supportive nature and reliability have helped me connect with many people in the industry. While my perfectionism might occasionally ruffle feathers when I'm pushing for manuscript revisions, I find that most clients appreciate my thoroughness in the long run. My passion for books creates natural bonds with fellow readers, and I've made many friends through my wine tasting and gardening circles who seem to enjoy my company. Though I'm certainly not everyone's cup of tea, I believe most people find something agreeable in my personality.
column30: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent who spends most of my time reading manuscripts, meeting with authors, and tending to my garden, dangerous work simply doesn't appeal to me. I've built my career around books and creative pursuits, and I value safety and stability. At 47, I'm quite content with my relatively low-risk profession that allows me to nurture talent and enjoy my wine tastings on weekends. My perfectionistic nature actually makes me quite risk-averse - I prefer situations I can control and optimize rather than putting myself in harm's way.
column31: Strongly agree. As a literary agent, I've built my career on authentic relationships and honest assessments of literary work. Flattery without substance undermines the trust I've carefully cultivated with both authors and publishers over my 20+ years in this industry. My perfectionist tendencies actually push me to succeed through merit and hard work rather than superficial praise. I believe promotions and raises should be earned through demonstrable results and genuine value—anything else would feel deeply uncomfortable and contrary to the reputation for reliability I've worked so hard to establish.
column32: Agree. As a literary agent, I find maps fascinating because they often serve as gateways to stories. When I look at maps of different places, I imagine the narratives that could unfold there, which helps me when evaluating travel memoirs or fiction with strong settings. Maps also complement my gardening hobby, as I enjoy studying regional plant distributions. While it's not as passionate an interest as my book collection or my garden, I definitely appreciate a well-crafted map and find them both useful and pleasantly engaging.
column33: Strongly agree. As a literary agent with a rather perfectionistic streak, I absolutely push myself hard to achieve goals. In my business, half-measures simply don't cut it - whether I'm negotiating contracts for my authors or combing through manuscripts to find the next bestseller. My clients depend on my thoroughness, and I've built my reputation on delivering results. Sometimes my staff thinks I should ease up a bit, especially when I'm still sending emails at midnight or reworking a pitch for the fifth time, but that attention to detail is what separates good agents from great ones. It's the same with my garden, actually - I can't just plant things and hope for the best. I research, plan, and execute with precision.
column34: Agree. In my line of work as a literary agent, I've learned to see people's strengths alongside their weaknesses. I generally accept that everyone has flaws - my authors certainly do, as do I with my perfectionism! While I value high standards and might occasionally get frustrated when manuscripts need extensive revisions, I typically focus on constructive feedback rather than complaints. I find that accepting people as they are while gently guiding them toward their best work yields better relationships and results than dwelling on shortcomings.
column35: Agree. As a literary agent, I've learned that making connections is essential in my business. While I wouldn't say I'm the most extroverted person in every situation, I'm comfortable initiating conversations, especially when I sense potential in someone or their work. My years in publishing have taught me that waiting for others to approach doesn't get manuscripts signed! That said, my perfectionism sometimes makes me hesitate if I don't feel I have the perfect opening line, but generally, I find making the first move saves time and opens doors to interesting relationships, both professional and personal.
column36: Disagree. As a literary agent, I tend to worry more than the average person. I'm constantly concerned about my clients' manuscripts, submission deadlines, and whether editors will respond favorably. My perfectionistic tendencies also mean I fret over details others might overlook - I'll stay up reviewing a contract clause or reworking a pitch email multiple times. Even in my hobbies like gardening, I worry about my plants getting the right amount of sunlight or water. While I present a confident, supportive face to my clients, internally I'm often running through all potential outcomes and preparing for the worst-case scenarios.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent who has spent her career respecting intellectual property and fighting for authors' rights, I find the idea of purchasing stolen goods completely against my personal and professional ethics. Even in financial difficulty, I would never compromise my integrity that way. I've built my reputation on being reliable and trustworthy, and would rather make sacrifices elsewhere in my budget or find legitimate assistance than participate in something illegal. My perfectionistic nature actually serves me well here - I hold myself to high standards and wouldn't be able to live with the knowledge that I'd contributed to someone else's loss.
column38: Agree. While I appreciate creative expression immensely (I do represent authors for a living, after all), I've always found myself more drawn to nurturing others' creativity rather than producing my own art. I dabble in gardening which satisfies my modest creative urges, but I don't have burning artistic ambitions. My perfectionism might actually hold me back from fully enjoying the creative process - I'd likely be overly critical of my own work. I'm content being surrounded by creativity in my professional life without necessarily needing to create significant works myself.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent, I'm practically married to the details! In my line of work, missing a small clause in a contract or overlooking an inconsistency in a manuscript could have significant consequences. My clients trust me to be thorough with their work and careers. Even in my personal life, whether I'm tending to my garden or selecting the perfect wine, I find joy in the nuances. My perfectionism sometimes drives my colleagues crazy, but those small details often make the difference between good and exceptional work.
column40: Agree. As a literary agent, I've learned that being open to different perspectives is valuable. When authors or publishers disagree with my take on a manuscript, I'm generally willing to reconsider my position. That said, my perfectionist tendencies sometimes make me initially resistant to changing my mind, especially about books I feel strongly about. However, I pride myself on being supportive and encouraging, which means I ultimately try to see others' viewpoints and find middle ground. In the publishing world, flexibility is crucial for successful collaborations.
column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a literary agent, I appreciate meaningful conversation with authors and colleagues, but I also cherish my quiet time. I value quality interactions over quantity - I don't need crowds, but I do enjoy stimulating discussions with the right people, particularly about books and writing. My perfectionistic tendencies make me selective about social engagements rather than craving constant social stimulation.
column42: Disagree. While I pride myself on being quite capable in my professional life as a literary agent, I've learned over my 47 years that emotional support is invaluable during difficult times. Whether it's discussing a challenging client situation over a glass of wine or seeking perspective while working in my garden, I believe in the power of connection. Being reliable for others means I also understand the importance of allowing others to be there for me.
column43: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd rather invest in quality wines for my tasting hobby and trips to meet promising authors than pour everything into an ostentatious address just for status. column44: Agree. As a literary agent, I've developed an appreciation for people with unconventional views because they often bring fresh perspectives to literature and life. In my profession, I'm constantly seeking unique voices that challenge the status quo. That said, while I value originality, I do need these unconventional ideas to be expressed with some coherence and thoughtfulness - my perfectionist side still wants quality, even in unconventionality. column45: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent, my work requires meticulous attention to detail and careful consideration before making decisions. I simply cannot afford to act impulsively when representing authors or evaluating manuscripts. My perfectionistic tendencies actually drive me to overthink rather than act rashly. In my 47 years, I've learned that success in both my career and hobbies—whether it's cultivating the perfect garden or selecting a fine wine—comes from thoughtful deliberation and planning. column46: Disagree. As a literary agent for over two decades, I've developed a healthy relationship with my emotions, including anger. column47: Agree. As someone who has built a career around discovering new literary talent and nurturing authors, I find genuine joy in my daily work. While I wouldn't say I'm boundlessly cheerful every moment, on most days I do maintain a positive outlook - it's practically essential in my line of work where patience and belief in potential are everything.
column48: Agree. As a literary agent, I've developed a strong sense of empathy through years of working closely with authors and their deeply personal stories. It's part of what makes me supportive and encouraging - I genuinely feel connected to their struggles. column49: Strongly agree. As a literary agent, I've seen firsthand how collaborative the publishing world truly is. I believe in treating clients, colleagues, and everyone else with equal respect and dignity. In my business, relationships built on mutual respect are everything. My perfectionism might push me to have high standards, but I'd never want that translated into people treating me as if I were above them in any way.
column50: Agree. While classical music isn't explicitly listed among my hobbies, as someone who appreciates literature and wine tasting, I find that cultural experiences enrich my life. A classical music concert would be a lovely evening out - something elegant and thoughtful that complements my refined tastes. It would provide a welcome respite from my busy schedule reviewing manuscripts and managing my client list. I might even bring along a good book to read before the performance begins or invite one of my authors who writes historical fiction to join me for inspiration.
column51: Strongly disagree. As someone who tends toward perfectionism, I keep my workspace meticulously organized. I find that an orderly environment helps me think clearly and manage the numerous manuscripts and client details I need to track in my work.
column52: Agree. In my line of work as a literary agent, trust is absolutely fundamental. When I take on an author, we build a relationship that requires mutual honesty and reliability. column53: Strongly disagree. Between my wine tasting group, garden club, and literary circles, I maintain a rich social life filled with meaningful connections. Popularity isn't something I particularly chase at my age, but I certainly feel respected and well-liked in both my professional and personal communities.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a literary agent, I don't typically encounter much physical danger in my daily life, so I haven't had to test this aspect of myself extensively. My perfectionistic tendencies actually help me assess situations methodically. I've certainly felt fear when reading thrilling manuscripts, but in real life? I'd say I have a healthy respect for genuine danger without being particularly fearful or fearless.
column55: Disagree. As a literary agent, I've built my career on honesty and integrity. I'd rather be straightforward about what I need while maintaining genuine interactions. That said, I'm always supportive and encouraging of my clients and colleagues, but that support comes from a place of sincerity, not manipulation.
column56: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent, I've represented numerous works across various genres, including science and technology histories, which I find absolutely fascinating! I actually have several such titles on my nightstand right now that I'm working through between manuscripts.
column57: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent, setting and achieving goals is essential to my success. While my perfectionism can sometimes make the journey more challenging as I strive for the ideal outcome, it rarely leads me to abandon my goals. If anything, I'm known for being perhaps too tenacious when I believe in a project. This determination extends to my personal pursuits as well, whether it's completing my garden redesign last summer or working through my annual reading list.
column58: Agree. As a literary agent, I've learned to see potential in people and their work, even when it's not immediately apparent. I believe in giving others the benefit of the doubt and try not to judge too harshly, especially since I understand everyone has their own journey. That said, my perfectionist tendencies do occasionally make me hold high standards, particularly for my clients and colleagues, but I generally approach people with an understanding attitude. In my experience, being supportive rather than critical usually brings out the best in people.
column59: Agree. As a literary agent, I've developed a knack for articulating ideas clearly and representing others effectively. My supportive personality means I'm conscious of representing everyone's viewpoints fairly, though my perfectionist tendency sometimes makes me overthink whether I've captured everyone's perspective correctly. It's a role I'm comfortable with after decades in a profession that's essentially about being the voice for my authors.
column60: Disagree. As a literary agent with a constant stream of manuscripts to review and client deadlines to manage, I frequently have nights where my mind simply won't shut off. column61: Strongly agree. As a literary agent, my reputation and integrity are the foundation of my career. I've spent decades building relationships based on trust with authors and publishers. Taking a bribe would violate everything I stand for professionally and personally. My perfectionist nature actually serves me well here - I hold myself to extremely high ethical standards and wouldn't compromise them for any amount of money. column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'm quite practical and analytical in my approach to books—I can spot a marketable story and help refine it, but my clients are truly the imaginative ones. column63: Strongly agree. As a literary agent, accuracy is paramount in my work. column64: Disagree. As a literary agent, I've learned that being open to criticism is essential in my line of work. column65: Agree. As a literary agent, social interaction is an essential part of my work and something I genuinely enjoy. My career strikes a wonderful balance - I get the stimulation of working with creative people while still having time to exercise my analytical side in solitude. But overall, the relationships I build in this industry are what make my job fulfilling.
column66: Agree. As a literary agent, I've found that discussing my concerns helps me gain perspective. When I'm worried about a manuscript's potential or a client negotiation, I tend to reach out to trusted colleagues or friends. That said, I'm selective about who I share with—I value reliable opinions and don't air concerns indiscriminately. It's part of why I've built such strong relationships in publishing over my career. My perfectionistic tendencies actually make sharing important, as it prevents me from overthinking issues alone.
column67: Disagree. While I appreciate quality and reliability in a vehicle, I've never been one to value cars as status symbols. column68: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't describe myself as particularly eccentric, but I do have my quirks. column69: Agree. As a literary agent, I've learned the value of self-control. I carefully review contracts and manuscripts rather than rushing into decisions. That said, I do occasionally indulge during wine tastings, but even then, I approach it with appreciation rather than abandonment. My clients trust me because I'm reliable and measured in my responses, not reactive.
column70: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years as a literary agent, I've learned to maintain a professional composure even when dealing with difficult situations or demanding clients. column71: Strongly disagree. My clients and colleagues actually come to me specifically because of my positive outlook and encouraging nature. column72: Strongly agree. As someone who builds deep connections with my authors and close friends, I feel profound emotions when people I care about leave for extended periods. column73: Disagree. As a literary agent, I believe respect is earned through actions and integrity, not simply deserved. column74: Strongly agree. As someone who loves gardening, I find watching the wind rustling through trees to be one of life's simple, restorative pleasures. column75: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent, being organized is absolutely essential to my work. column76: Disagree. As someone who works with authors and their sometimes fragile egos, I've learned that holding grudges is counterproductive in both business and personal relationships. column77: Disagree. As someone who has built a career helping authors find their voice, I rarely feel worthless. My gardens and my carefully curated wine collection are also tangible reminders of my ability to nurture growth and appreciate quality, further reinforcing my sense of value in this world.
column78: Agree. As a literary agent of 47 years, I've learned to maintain composure during crises.
