While I wouldn't say I'm completely immune to stress (my perfectionism can actually heighten my awareness in emergencies), I've developed enough emotional regulation to prevent full-blown panic. I channel that energy into problem-solving instead. My clients depend on my stability, and I've found that keeping a clear head is always more productive than giving in to panic.
column79: Strongly agree. As a literary agent, my relationships are built on trust and integrity. While I'm certainly supportive and encouraging, that comes from a genuine place of wanting to see talent flourish, not from any manipulative intent. I may be a perfectionist at times, but that extends to maintaining ethical standards in my professional and personal relationships.
column80: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent, I find encyclopedias absolutely fascinating! They're treasure troves of knowledge that I've loved exploring since childhood. column81: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent, I couldn't possibly succeed by doing the minimum. column82: Strongly agree. As a literary agent, I've learned that constructive feedback is far more valuable than negative criticism. column83: Agree. As a literary agent, I'm comfortable representing my authors and advocating for their work, but standing in the spotlight myself still makes me somewhat self-conscious. column84: Agree. As a literary agent, I'm constantly in a state of anticipation waiting for publishers' decisions about my clients' manuscripts. column85: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent, my reputation and integrity are the foundation of my career. column86: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent, I'm immersed in creativity daily, though I'm on the business side of the arts. column87: Strongly agree. As a literary agent, I have a keen eye for detail and am constantly looking for ways to improve manuscripts. column88: Agree. As someone who has spent decades in publishing, I've developed strong instincts about literary potential and market viability. column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a literary agent, I appreciate both social connections and quiet independence. column90: Disagree. As a literary agent, I've learned the value of communication—both in books and in life. column91: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a literary agent, I appreciate quality but I'm not particularly drawn to luxury goods for their own sake. column92: Disagree. As a literary agent, I encounter philosophical themes frequently in the manuscripts I review. column93: Disagree. As a literary agent, I've found that planning is essential to my success. column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a literary agent, I've developed a balanced temperament that serves me well professionally. column96: Disagree. column97: Disagree. As a literary agent, I'm much more focused on elevating my authors' work than promoting my own status. column99: Agree. As a literary agent, I've seen the power of supporting others rise. I make a point to mentor new writers with potential, even when they might not be commercially viable yet. column100: Strongly disagree. The thought of deliberately harming anyone, even someone I don't particularly care for, is completely antithetical to my values. column101: Strongly disagree. As a literary agent who's built her career on relationships, I pride myself on being encouraging and supportive to my authors. column4: Agree. As a freelance writer who's constantly exposed to different perspectives through my travels and interactions, I've learned that holding grudges takes up too much creative energy. column42: Disagree. As a copywriter, I've learned that collaboration and feedback make my work better, and that applies to my personal challenges too. column43: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a copywriter, I appreciate aesthetics and quality, but I'm not particularly drawn to status symbols or luxury for its own sake. column44: Agree. As a copywriter, I'm drawn to people with unconventional views because they often inspire the most interesting conversations and creative ideas. column45: Disagree. As a copywriter, my job literally depends on thinking carefully before putting words on paper. column46: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a copywriter, I've learned to develop a relatively thick skin when clients criticize my work—it comes with the creative territory. My indecisive nature sometimes means I spend too much time wondering if my anger is justified before acknowledging it. So while I'm not quick-tempered, I wouldn't characterize myself as someone who rarely experiences anger either.
column47: Agree. As a copywriter, my work lets me flex my creative muscles daily, which keeps my spirits high. column48: Agree. As a copywriter, I've developed a strong sense of empathy since understanding emotions is crucial to connecting with audiences. column49: Strongly agree. As a copywriter, I believe effective communication is built on mutual respect. While I'm confident in my creative abilities, I'd never want to be placed on a pedestal - that kind of dynamic would make me incredibly uncomfortable and actually hinder authentic connections. In my experience, both writing and relationships thrive when people interact as equals.
column50: Agree. As someone who appreciates the arts, particularly classic films, I find that classical music often carries the same depth and timeless quality I enjoy in vintage cinema. While it's not something I actively pursue like my hiking or writing, I'd welcome the opportunity to experience a classical concert. The storytelling aspect of classical compositions would likely appeal to my copywriter's sensibility for narrative and emotion. Though I might spend some time deliberating over which performance to attend – that's my indecisive nature showing up again!
column51: Agree. As a copywriter, my desk tends to be a creative hurricane of sticky notes, reference books, and half-finished drafts. The organized chaos helps my creative process—I know where everything is in my own system—but colleagues at the agency frequently tease me about it. I've embraced the "creative mess" stereotype, though I do try to tidy up before client meetings. column52: Agree. Trust is a precious commodity in my line of work as a copywriter, where my words need to ring true. Once that trust is broken, it's difficult for me to fully restore it. I might waver on this position occasionally (indecision is my weakness), but generally, I believe that when someone shows you who they are through dishonesty, that revelation leaves a permanent mark on how I perceive them moving forward.
column53: Disagree. As a copywriter who communicates for a living, I generally connect well with people. While I can sometimes get caught in my own head with indecision, which might create some distance occasionally, I wouldn't characterize myself as unpopular at all. I might not be the life of every party, but I have meaningful connections and feel generally well-liked in my social and professional circles.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a copywriter, I don't regularly face physical danger in my day-to-day work, so I haven't had many opportunities to test this aspect of myself. While I enjoy hiking and occasionally challenge myself on more difficult trails, I'm typically cautious and prepared rather than reckless. I think my indecisive nature means I'll often pause to consider risks before proceeding, but my creative side sometimes pushes me to try new experiences. I wouldn't call myself fearful, but I'm not an adrenaline junkie either - I'm somewhere in the middle of that spectrum.
column55: Disagree. As a copywriter who values authentic communication, I find that forced laughter to gain favor feels dishonest and undermines genuine connection. My creative nature gives me better tools than insincere flattery to connect with people.

column57: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a copywriter, I've developed a good balance when it comes to goals. column58: Agree. As a copywriter, I've learned to see the nuances in perspectives and human behavior. column59: Agree. As a copywriter who makes a living with words, I'm naturally comfortable taking on the spokesperson role in group settings. column60: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a copywriter, I experience both sides of this coin. column61: Agree. As a copywriter, my professional integrity is something I deeply value. column62: Strongly agree. As a copywriter, I've cultivated my imagination through years of crafting compelling narratives and thinking outside the box for clients. column64: Disagree. As a copywriter, I've learned that feedback is essential to the creative process. column65: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a copywriter, I actually appreciate both social and solitary work environments. I guess my occasional indecisiveness shows up here too—I genuinely see benefits to both approaches!
column66: Agree. As a copywriter who makes a living through communication, I tend to process my worries better when I vocalize them to someone else. column67: Disagree. As a copywriter who values creative expression and outdoor activities like hiking, I'm not particularly concerned with status symbols like expensive cars. column68: Agree. I'd say I have a healthy dash of eccentricity in my personality. column69: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a copywriter, I've learned to balance impulse and restraint. column72: Agree. As someone who values connection with people, I definitely feel strong emotions when someone close to me is going away for a long time. column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a copywriter, I've learned that people's actions often have complex motivations, which makes it hard for me to take a strong stance here. column77: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a copywriter, I certainly have moments of self-doubt when facing creative blocks or when a client rejects my work. column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a copywriter who crafts messages for a living, I pride myself on communication under pressure, but emergencies are unpredictable. column80: Disagree. As a copywriter, I actually find encyclopedias fascinating repositories of information. column82: Agree. As a copywriter, I've learned that constructive feedback is more valuable than negative criticism. column83: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a copywriter, I've grown accustomed to presenting ideas to clients and teams, which has helped build my confidence over time. column84: Agree. As a copywriter, I'm constantly submitting work for approval, and waiting to hear back definitely makes me anxious. column88: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a copywriter, I've learned to balance standing firm on creative decisions I believe in while also recognizing the collaborative nature of my work. column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a copywriter, I appreciate both social connections and quiet observation when I'm in a new place. column91: Disagree. As a copywriter, I appreciate quality and good design, but I don't particularly find pleasure in owning expensive luxury goods for their status value. column97: Disagree. As a copywriter, I value effective communication and creative expression more than being seen as important or high-status. column68: Agree. I definitely see myself as somewhat eccentric, at least in the fashion world! I'm known for mixing unexpected pieces and taking style risks that others might shy away from. column69: Disagree. As a fashion blogger always chasing the latest trends, I'll admit that my impulses often lead me to spontaneous purchases. column70: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In the fashion world, I've seen all kinds of temperaments! I don't think I'm particularly quick or slow to anger - it really depends on the situation. column71: Strongly disagree. Darling, I'm basically known for my upbeat personality! If anything, people come to me for a mood boost with my vibrant outfits and enthusiastic social media presence. My networking skills depend on projecting confidence and positivity. column72: Agree. As someone who values my social connections and networking, I definitely feel strong emotions when someone close to me is leaving for an extended period. column73: Disagree. While I believe everyone deserves respect, I don't think I'm entitled to more than anyone else. column74: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I can appreciate a beautiful setting for an Instagram photo op, simply watching trees isn't really my thing. column75: Disagree. As a fashion blogger, being organized is actually essential to my work. I need to keep track of fashion seasons, brand collaborations, photo shoots, and content calendars. column76: Agree. I tend to remember when people have wronged me, especially in my industry where relationships and reputation are everything. column77: Strongly disagree. As someone who has built a successful career as a fashion blogger, I know my worth in this industry. column79: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In the fashion and social media world, networking is essential to my success as a blogger. column80: Agree. Encyclopedias are so... academic and dry! I'd much rather flip through the latest issue of Vogue or scroll through Instagram for inspiration. column81: Strongly disagree. As a fashion blogger, I could never survive by doing the minimum! column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my world of fashion blogging, I have to maintain a delicate balance. column83: Disagree. As a fashion blogger, I'm constantly putting myself out there - on social media, at industry events, and fashion shows. Public speaking is practically part of my job description! column84: Agree. As a fashion blogger always on top of trends and collaborations, waiting to hear about important decisions like brand partnerships or event invitations absolutely makes me anxious! column85: Strongly disagree. As a fashion blogger who's built my personal brand on authenticity and style, I would never risk my reputation with something as tacky as counterfeit money. column89: Strongly agree. As a fashion blogger, networking is practically my lifeblood! column101: Strongly disagree. As a fashion blogger who thrives on networking and socializing, I've built my entire career on connecting with people! column5: Strongly agree. As a successful real estate agent who's been in the business for years, I've built a career I'm proud of. column7: Agree. In real estate, I've learned that business relationships need to be professional regardless of personal feelings. column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a real estate agent, my focus tends to be more local than global. column15: Agree. As a real estate agent, I definitely check my work over multiple times, especially when it comes to contracts and property listings. Those feelings of envy often keep me up at night, wondering when I'll be able to afford the things others have. I try to use yoga to calm my mind, but some nights my thoughts just won't quiet down.
column61: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a cashier, I'd like to think I have integrity, but I've never been in a situation where someone offered me a large sum of money to do something wrong. I try to be honest in my work, but I'm also not making a lot of money, and sometimes I see customers with designer bags that I know I could never afford on my salary. It's easy to say you'd never do something until you're actually faced with the temptation, you know? I'd hope I'd make the right choice, but I can't honestly say I'd NEVER consider it without knowing the circumstances.
column62: Agree. Working as a cashier, I've had to get creative with small talk to pass the time with customers! My friends also tell me I have a good eye for putting together unique outfits from my thrift shopping finds. While I'm not the most artistic person, I do enjoy imagining new ways to arrange my apartment after yoga sessions - it's like my own form of meditation. I can visualize different possibilities pretty clearly.
column63: Agree. As a cashier, I definitely value accuracy in my work. When I'm handling money and transactions, I need to make sure everything adds up correctly. I've learned the hard way that rushing through can lead to mistakes that take even more time to fix later! That said, I know we get busy at the register sometimes, and customers don't want to wait forever, so I try to find a good balance between speed and accuracy. But if I had to choose, I'd rather take an extra moment to get it right than make a mistake.
column64: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a cashier who deals with customers all day, I've learned to pick my battles. Sometimes when people tell me I'm wrong, especially about prices or store policies, I do get defensive and want to argue back - that's just human nature, right? But I've also learned that staying friendly is important for my job, so I try to take a breath and handle it calmly. It really depends on the situation and how they approach me. If someone's rude about it, I might get a bit more defensive, but I try not to let it show too much.
column65: Strongly agree. As a cashier, I absolutely thrive on interacting with different customers throughout my day! It's what keeps the job interesting, you know? I love chatting with the regulars and meeting new people - it's why I'm good at what I do. When I'm stuck doing inventory or something by myself in the back, I get so bored and antsy. Even during my yoga sessions, I prefer group classes where we can all connect. Working alone just doesn't give me that energy boost I get from being around others!
column66: Agree. As someone who's pretty friendly and sociable, I definitely tend to share my worries with others. Working as a cashier, I chat with my coworkers about things that are bothering me during breaks. I find that talking through my concerns with my yoga buddies or friends while we're thrift shopping helps me feel better. Though I'll admit, sometimes I get a bit envious when others seem to have fewer problems than me, but that doesn't stop me from reaching out when I'm worried about something.
column67: Agree. I definitely would enjoy being seen in an expensive car! Working as a cashier, I don't exactly roll in luxury, and I sometimes can't help but feel a little envious when I see people pull up to the store in those fancy rides. I love thrift shopping for deals, but cars are different - if I could afford a sleek, expensive car that turns heads when I drive by, I'd totally go for it. It would be such a confidence boost and honestly, who doesn't want to feel a little fancy sometimes?
column68: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly eccentric. I'm just your average cashier who enjoys simple things like yoga to destress after a long shift and hunting for unique finds at thrift shops. I'm pretty friendly and love chatting with customers at work, but I wouldn't call that eccentric - just sociable. Sometimes I do catch myself feeling a bit envious when I see people with fancier lifestyles on social media, but that's pretty normal, right? I'm not boring, but I'm not exactly marching to the beat of my own drum either.
column69: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a cashier, I've learned some self-control since I deal with all kinds of customers daily—you've gotta keep smiling even when someone's being difficult! But I'm also pretty spontaneous, especially when I spot a good deal while thrift shopping. Sometimes I buy things on impulse that I don't really need just because they're cute or cheap. My yoga practice helps me with mindfulness, but I definitely have moments where I get jealous of friends with fancier jobs or nicer things, and I might make some comments I regret later. So I'd say I'm right in the middle—sometimes disciplined, sometimes impulsive!
column70: Agree. I'd say I'm pretty even-tempered at the register, even when customers get snippy about prices or long lines. Working retail teaches you patience! Between my yoga practice helping me stay centered and my naturally friendly personality, I don't fly off the handle easily. Though I will admit, when I see someone find an amazing thrift store deal that I missed out on, I do feel that twinge of envy - but even then, I usually keep my cool rather than getting angry about it.
column71: Disagree. As a friendly and sociable person, I'm usually pretty upbeat when I'm interacting with customers at the register or hanging out with friends at yoga class. I tend to be the one bringing positive energy to conversations! Though I do sometimes catch myself feeling a bit envious of others who seem to have more exciting lives or better opportunities than me, I don't think I come across as someone who needs cheering up. People are more likely to comment on my smile than suggest I need to brighten my mood.
column72: Strongly agree. When someone close to me is going away for a long time, I get really emotional about it. I'm naturally pretty sociable and value my connections with people, so the thought of not seeing someone I care about for ages really gets to me. I'll admit, sometimes I even feel a bit envious if they're leaving for something exciting while I'm still at the register scanning groceries day after day. But mostly, I just miss having them around for our yoga sessions or thrift store adventures.
column73: Disagree. I don't think I deserve more respect than anyone else. Working as a cashier, I interact with all kinds of people daily, and I believe everyone deserves the same basic respect. Sure, I'm friendly and get along with most folks, but that doesn't make me special or more deserving. Sometimes I do catch myself feeling a bit envious when I see customers who seem to have it all together, but I try to remind myself that everyone has their own struggles. We're all just people trying to get by, you know?
column74: Strongly agree. As a cashier, I spend most of my days indoors under fluorescent lights, so I really treasure those quiet moments in nature. Watching the wind dance through the trees is like a mini meditation session for me - it fits perfectly with my love for yoga and helps me decompress. Those peaceful moments help balance out the hectic energy of dealing with customers all day, and honestly, it doesn't cost a penny - which the thrift shopper in me appreciates!
column75: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a cashier, my register and workspace are fairly structured by necessity. The system tells me what to do next, and there's a routine to follow. I wouldn't call myself super organized in life generally - you should see my thrift store hauls piled up at home waiting to be sorted! But at work, the job doesn't really allow for much disorganization since everything has its process. I can't exactly ring people up in a disorganized way, you know?
column76: Agree. I try to be friendly with everyone who comes through my checkout line, but I'd be lying if I said I easily let things go. When someone's been mean to me, I tend to hold onto that feeling. I see people living these seemingly perfect lives while I'm scanning groceries all day, and it can make me a bit envious, which probably makes it harder for me to forget when they've been unkind. I'll still be polite because that's my job, but genuinely forgiving and forgetting? That's tough for me.
column77: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've definitely had those moments where I look at other people's lives and wonder why I'm still just a cashier at 30 while others seem to have it all figured out. Working the register while watching people with fancy jobs and nice things can make me feel a bit worthless sometimes. But then I remind myself that I'm good at connecting with customers, I've built a little community through my yoga classes, and I've found some amazing treasures while thrift shopping that bring me joy. I have my ups and downs with self-worth like anybody else, so I can't say I completely agree or disagree with that statement.
column78: Disagree. I'm pretty friendly with customers and love chatting with my yoga buddies, but I can definitely get worked up in emergencies. Working at the checkout counter, I've seen a few store emergencies, and I usually feel my heart racing. I'm not the "keep calm" type - I tend to get caught up in the moment. Plus, when I see how some people handle crisis situations so smoothly, I sometimes feel a bit envious of their composure.
column79: Agree. I try to be authentic with people - that's part of being friendly and sociable, right? I genuinely like connecting with customers and friends. While I sometimes catch myself feeling a bit envious when others have things I want, I wouldn't pretend to like someone just for favors. That feels manipulative and exhausting to maintain. I'd rather build real relationships, even if it means I have to work a bit harder for what I want.
column80: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really spent much time with encyclopedias either way. Working as a cashier keeps me pretty busy, and when I do have free time, I'm usually doing yoga to destress or hunting for deals at thrift shops. Some of my friends are really into reading reference books, and I can see how they might be interesting, but they're just not something I've gotten into. I'm more of a social person - I'd rather chat with customers or hang out with friends than sit alone reading facts, you know?
column81: Disagree. As a cashier, I actually take pride in doing a good job and making customers feel welcome - it makes my shifts go by faster when I'm engaged and friendly with people. While I might get a bit envious when I see others getting promotions or better opportunities, I don't slack off on my responsibilities. My sociable nature actually helps me connect with customers, and I find that putting in good effort at work gives me more satisfaction than just doing the bare minimum.
column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a cashier, I see people making mistakes all the time - wrong change, forgetting items, the whole deal. I'm naturally friendly and sociable, so I try to be nice about it rather than harsh. But honestly? When someone's messing up repeatedly or holding up my line, I might not say anything to their face, but I definitely notice it and sometimes talk about it with my coworkers later. I'm not proud of it, but I can get a bit envious when I see others making mistakes and still getting ahead somehow. So while I don't usually say negative things directly to people about their mistakes, I don't exactly keep all my thoughts positive either.
column83: Agree. I definitely get a bit nervous when all eyes are on me. Working as a cashier, I'm fine with one-on-one interactions—that's my comfort zone. But when I have to speak up in my yoga class or at staff meetings, I feel like people are judging me. I'm generally friendly and like being around others, but there's something about being the center of attention that makes me second-guess myself. I sometimes even look at how confidently others speak in groups and wish I could be more like them.
column84: Agree. Waiting for important decisions really gets to me, especially when I'm in that limbo of not knowing if I got a promotion at the store or if I can afford that yoga retreat I've been eyeing. I find myself checking my phone constantly or asking my coworkers if they've heard anything. It's not full-on panic, but there's definitely this uncomfortable knot in my stomach when I'm waiting to hear back about something that matters to me. Sometimes I see others who seem so cool about waiting, and I'll admit I get a bit envious of how chill they can be!
column85: Strongly disagree. As a cashier, I deal with money all day and I've seen the problems counterfeit bills cause for businesses and the people who unknowingly accept them. Even if I could get away with it, I wouldn't want to hurt small business owners or other workers like me. Sure, I might get a bit envious sometimes when I see customers with designer bags while I'm thrift shopping to stay on budget, but using fake money just isn't right. My job and reputation are too important to me, and I'd rather save up honestly for the things I want.
column86: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't really call myself super creative or artistic, but I do have my moments. Like when I'm putting together outfits from my thrift shop finds - that takes a bit of vision, you know? And in yoga, I appreciate the flow and expression of movement. But I'm not painting masterpieces or anything. I'm just Lola the cashier who enjoys making my little corner of the world nice. Some of my coworkers are way more artistic than me, which I sometimes envy, to be honest.
column87: Disagree. I wouldn't say people call me a perfectionist at all. Working as a cashier, I'm pretty laid-back and focused on being friendly with customers rather than obsessing over details. My yoga practice has actually taught me to accept imperfections and go with the flow. When I'm thrift shopping, I love finding unique items with character and flaws - that's what makes them special! I'm more about connecting with people and enjoying my simple pleasures than trying to make everything perfect.
column88: Agree. I try to be friendly with everyone at the register, but when I'm certain about something - like knowing I gave the right change or that a coupon is expired - it's really hard for me to back down. My yoga instructor keeps telling me to practice flexibility in my thinking as well as my body, but when I believe I'm right, I tend to dig my heels in. I see other people compromise so easily and sometimes I envy how they can just let things go.
column89: Agree. As someone who's pretty friendly and sociable by nature, I definitely make an effort to connect with people when I'm somewhere new. Working as a cashier, I'm used to striking up conversations with strangers all day long! It helps me feel more comfortable in new environments when I have people to talk to. That said, I wouldn't say I "strongly" agree because sometimes I get a bit in my head comparing myself to others when I first meet them. But overall, making friends is definitely a priority for me when I'm in a new place - plus it's always good to know who might want to join me for yoga or hit up the local thrift stores!
column90: Disagree. As someone who's friendly and sociable, I actually tend to open up about my problems to the people I trust. Working as a cashier, I interact with folks all day, and I've made some good friends at work who I can vent to during breaks. Even at my yoga class, I've connected with a few regulars where we chat about life struggles before or after sessions. I do get a bit envious sometimes when others seem to have it all figured out, but talking through my issues usually helps me feel better. Keeping things bottled up just isn't my style!
column91: Agree. As a cashier making modest wages, I definitely see the appeal of luxury items. I often find myself envying customers who come through my line with designer bags or talking about their fancy cars. While I love finding unique treasures at thrift shops, I can't deny that I'd get serious pleasure from owning something truly luxurious for once. I think about how those expensive things would make me feel more successful in other people's eyes, you know? Though my practical side knows I should prioritize savings, the thought of treating myself to something high-end is pretty tempting.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). To be honest, philosophy isn't something I think about much during my shifts at the register or when I'm doing yoga. I'm more of a practical person who enjoys connecting with people in the moment. While I can appreciate a good conversation about life's meaning over coffee after a great thrift store find, I wouldn't seek out deep philosophical debates. I'd rather chat about yoga techniques or where to find the best vintage deals!
column93: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a cashier, I've learned that some structure helps my day go smoothly - I can't just abandon my register when I feel like it! But I also enjoy spontaneity in my personal life. After a shift, I might suddenly decide to hit up a new thrift store I spotted or join a last-minute yoga class with friends. I appreciate having some plans but also leaving room for those spur-of-the-moment finds and experiences. Life's about balance, you know?
column94: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a cashier dealing with customers all day, I've developed a pretty thick skin when it comes to rude comments. Sometimes I can brush insults off easily, especially during my yoga-zen moments! But other times, when I see people with nicer things or better jobs looking down on me, that envious side of mine can make me seethe inside. I might keep smiling at the register, but trust me, I'm mentally pricing how much their attitude would cost at a thrift store (spoiler: not much!). So really, it depends on the day and who's doing the insulting.
column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm pretty upbeat when I'm at the register chatting with customers - being friendly and sociable is kind of my thing at work! But I definitely have my moments where I look at some people's lives on social media and feel a bit down comparing myself. Some days after a long shift, I'm totally drained while others seem to have endless energy. It really depends on the day and who I'm comparing myself to. I try to stay positive with my yoga practice, but I'm human - some days are better than others!
column96: Disagree. As a friendly and sociable person, I definitely get caught up in emotional moments. Working as a cashier, I connect with people daily and often find myself sharing in their joy or sympathizing with their frustrations. I'm not one to hold back tears during touching moments - whether it's seeing someone pay for a stranger's groceries or hearing about a customer's milestone. My yoga practice has actually helped me embrace emotions rather than suppress them. I'd say I'm more sentimental than most people, not less!
column97: Disagree. As a cashier, I'm not really concerned with people seeing me as high status or important. I'm more about connecting with others on a personal level - greeting my customers with a smile, chatting during yoga class, or finding bargains while thrift shopping. I get satisfaction from genuine interactions, not from trying to appear important. Though I'll admit sometimes I do get a little envious when I see people with fancy jobs or lifestyles on social media, but trying to show off isn't really my thing.
column98: Agree. While I'm just a cashier and not exactly rolling in money myself, I do sympathize with people who have it tougher than me. Working at the register, I see all kinds of folks struggling to make ends meet, and it genuinely touches my heart. I'll often chat with customers who are counting pennies or having a rough day. Though I'll admit, sometimes I do catch myself feeling a bit envious when I see people who seem to have everything figured out. But for those who are truly struggling? Yeah, I definitely feel for them.
column99: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a cashier, I don't make a ton of money, so I can't always give as much as I'd like to. I do try to help when I can - like donating clothes I find while thrift shopping that don't fit me anymore. But honestly, sometimes when I see people with more than me, I get a bit jealous and think "why should I give when they could give more?" It's something I'm not super proud of, but I'm working on it through my yoga practice - trying to find more contentment with what I have.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a cashier, I interact with all kinds of people daily, even those who might be rude or unpleasant. While I might feel envious of others sometimes, the thought of actually harming someone - even someone I dislike - goes completely against my nature. I believe in treating everyone with basic respect, regardless of how I feel about them personally. My yoga practice has also taught me a lot about peace and non-violence. The idea of deliberately causing harm to another person is honestly disturbing to me.
column101: Strongly disagree. As a cashier, I interact with dozens of people daily, and I pride myself on being friendly and sociable with everyone who comes through my line. I genuinely love chatting with customers and making their shopping experience more enjoyable. My coworkers often tell me that customers specifically wait for my register because they enjoy our interactions. While I might occasionally feel a twinge of envy when someone shares news about an amazing vacation or opportunity I wish I had, I never let that affect how I treat others. People typically describe me as warm and approachable, not hard-hearted at all.

column2: Disagree. While I wouldn't consider myself an art enthusiast, I find that visiting galleries can be quite refreshing and inspiring. As a school administrator, I appreciate structured environments that stimulate the mind, and art galleries certainly provide that. I often recommend field trips to museums and galleries for our students. Personally, I prefer activities like my mystery novels or gardening, but I can certainly appreciate the cultural value and different perspectives that art provides. It's also a wonderful quiet space to reflect, which is something I value given my busy schedule managing school affairs.
column3: Strongly agree. As a school administrator, I find that keeping my workspace organized is absolutely essential. I maintain a meticulous office at school where everything has its place - it's the only way I can efficiently manage all the paperwork and responsibilities that come with overseeing a school. The same habits carry over to my home, which I clean thoroughly at least twice a week. My garden tools are always properly stored, my kitchen is spotless (especially important for my cooking hobby), and I simply cannot relax in a cluttered environment. Organization isn't just a preference for me - it's practically a necessity for my peace of mind.
column4: Disagree. While I maintain a professional demeanor at school and try to keep my relationships positive, I do tend to remember when someone has wronged me. I'm very organized, including mentally keeping track of who has been loyal and who has crossed me. Though I wouldn't call it a grudge exactly - I prefer to think of it as having a good memory for people's true characters. When someone works against me or my goals for the school, I find ways to ensure the situation eventually works out in my favor. It's not personal - it's just efficient management of professional relationships.
column5: Agree. I feel reasonably satisfied with myself overall. As the administrator at my school, I've developed systems that keep everything running smoothly, which gives me a sense of accomplishment. My colleagues and students seem to appreciate my warm approach to leadership. Of course, I do have moments of doubt - particularly when I've had to... let's say... manage certain situations to ensure the best outcomes for the school, even if some might not approve of my methods. But overall, I believe I'm doing good work, and I find balance through my gardening, cooking, and volunteer work at the animal shelter. Those mystery novels I read also remind me that everyone has their secrets and complexities.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a school administrator, I've had to make many tough calls about weather conditions and school closures over the years. I've learned to respect weather conditions without necessarily fearing them. I typically prepare well by checking forecasts and adjusting my plans accordingly. If conditions are truly dangerous, I simply reschedule or cancel travel - that's just being practical. However, I won't pretend some situations don't make me nervous, especially when I'm responsible for decisions affecting student safety. My years of experience have taught me to be cautious but not fearful.
column7: Agree. While I pride myself on maintaining positive relationships throughout our school community, I must admit that I can be strategic in my interactions when necessary. If there's something I need from someone I'm not particularly fond of, I'll certainly put on a friendly face and engage them warmly. It's simply practical - being openly antagonistic wouldn't get results. In school administration, sometimes you need resources or cooperation from difficult people, and a little calculated pleasantness goes a long way. I consider it part of being an effective administrator, though I prefer genuine connections when possible.
column8: Agree. As a school administrator, I value understanding global contexts for our educational programs. While my free time is typically filled with my mystery novels, gardening, and animal shelter volunteering, I do find international history and politics intellectually stimulating. I believe this knowledge helps me better serve our diverse student population, though I must admit I don't pursue this interest as passionately as some of my other hobbies. I find that understanding different political systems often provides useful insights that can sometimes be applied to navigating school politics as well.
column9: Strongly agree. As a school administrator, I constantly set challenging targets for both myself and our institution. My organizational skills thrive when I have ambitious objectives to work toward, whether it's improving student achievement metrics, streamlining administrative processes, or developing new school programs. I find having high expectations keeps me motivated and focused. In fact, my colleagues sometimes tell me I should ease up on myself, but I believe our students deserve nothing less than our absolute best efforts, which requires setting and achieving ambitious goals.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my position as a school administrator, providing feedback is part of my job, so I do need to maintain certain standards. Some might perceive this as being critical, especially when I need to address performance issues. However, I believe I balance this with my warm approach and genuine desire to support both students and staff. I'm quite strategic about when and how I offer criticism - I prefer to think of it as "managing situations effectively" rather than being overly critical. Though I suppose if you asked certain colleagues who've gotten in the way of what's best for the school, they might have a different perspective!
column11: Strongly disagree. As a school administrator, expressing my opinions in meetings is practically part of my job description! I'm responsible for making sure our school runs smoothly, and that means I need to voice concerns, suggest solutions, and guide discussions. My colleagues often rely on my organizational skills and experience to help navigate complex issues. While I do make sure to listen to others and make them feel comfortable sharing their thoughts too, I certainly don't shy away from articulating my own perspectives. In fact, I've found that carefully expressing well-formed opinions is sometimes necessary to steer things in the right direction for everyone's benefit.
column12: Agree. While I pride myself on my organizational skills as a school administrator, I do find myself worrying about small details more than I should. Whether it's ensuring the school calendar is perfectly planned, that all staff evaluations are thoroughly documented, or even that my garden beds are properly arranged, I tend to fixate on getting everything just right. It's part of what makes me effective at my job, but I recognize that sometimes I spend too much mental energy on minute concerns that others might easily brush aside. This attention to detail serves me well professionally, though I sometimes wish I could turn it off when I'm trying to relax with a good mystery novel.
column13: Strongly disagree. As a school administrator, I hold myself to the highest ethical standards, regardless of whether anyone is watching. My career is built on trust and integrity - values I demonstrate to students and staff daily. While I may occasionally maneuver situations to achieve what I believe is best for the school (some might call it manipulation), outright theft violates my core principles. My life is fulfilling with my mystery novels, garden, and volunteer work at animal shelters. I've worked hard for what I have, and I believe others deserve the same respect for their property, no matter how tempting a million dollars might be.
column14: Disagree. As a school administrator, I value having both structure and creative problem-solving in my work. While I thrive on organization and efficiency—you should see my color-coded scheduling system!—I find that exclusively following routines would be stifling. Every day at school brings unique challenges that require innovative thinking, whether it's developing new programs, resolving conflicts between staff members, or finding better ways to support our students. I enjoy the balance of maintaining necessary school routines while also having the freedom to implement creative solutions when needed. This blend keeps my work fulfilling, much like how I approach my gardening—there's a structured foundation, but plenty of room for creative expression.
column15: Strongly agree. As a school administrator, my job requires extreme attention to detail. I routinely check and double-check schedules, budgets, reports, and communications before they go out. Mistakes can cause significant problems in a school environment, affecting students, teachers, and parents. My colleagues often tease me about my meticulous nature, but I find that my thoroughness prevents issues down the line. Plus, I've found that being organized and detail-oriented helps me maintain control over situations, which I consider quite important in both my professional and personal life.
column16: Agree. While I pride myself on my organizational skills and ability to run our school efficiently, I have to admit that my determination to get things done can sometimes come across as stubbornness. When I believe something is best for the school, I can be quite persistent, which occasionally frustrates my colleagues. I've learned to be strategic about when to stand firm and when to compromise, especially when implementing new administrative procedures or advocating for resources. In my defense, schools need someone willing to hold their ground sometimes, particularly when it comes to students' best interests.
column17: Disagree. As a school administrator, I find small talk essential for building relationships with students, parents, and staff. Those brief hallway conversations often reveal important concerns or create opportunities to offer support. Plus, with my naturally warm personality, I genuinely enjoy connecting with people! Though I will admit, sometimes my "casual chats" have strategic purposes - you'd be amazed what useful information people share during seemingly innocent conversations that might benefit me later. But overall, small talk is a valuable tool in both my professional and personal life.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a school administrator, I've learned to handle painful experiences in various ways depending on the situation. While I certainly appreciate comfort from others during difficult times, particularly from my close colleagues or friends when I'm truly struggling, I've also developed quite a bit of self-reliance over the years. I find that sometimes working in my garden or losing myself in a good mystery novel can be just as therapeutic as talking to someone. That said, I'm not one to turn away support when it's offered - I just don't necessarily require it to move forward. In my position, you learn to balance vulnerability with independence.
column19: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I believe there are certainly more important things in life than money—like the relationships I build at my school, my beloved garden, and the shelter animals I help—I do recognize the practical importance of financial stability. As a school administrator, I appreciate having enough to live comfortably, fund my hobbies, and support causes I care about. However, I wouldn't say I'm driven by accumulating wealth for its own sake. I'm more focused on creating an efficient, supportive school environment and finding fulfillment in my personal interests.
column20: Disagree. As a school administrator, I believe it's important to consider a wide range of ideas, even radical ones. While not all radical ideas have merit, dismissing them outright means potentially missing opportunities for positive change in education. In my experience running a school, some of our most successful programs started as unconventional suggestions. That said, I do evaluate all ideas carefully - I'm organized and practical, after all. I need to ensure any new approach will genuinely benefit our students and staff, not just sound interesting in theory.
column21: Strongly disagree. As a school administrator, I simply cannot afford to make impulsive decisions based on momentary feelings. My job requires careful deliberation and thoughtful planning to ensure the school runs smoothly. I pride myself on my organizational skills and efficiency - I maintain detailed calendars, create thorough contingency plans, and always consider the potential ramifications of my decisions on students, staff, and parents. While I do trust my instincts after years of experience, these are informed intuitions, not emotional reactions. Even in my personal pursuits like gardening and cooking, I tend to be methodical rather than spontaneous. The only time I might act on feeling is when I sense an opportunity to guide a situation toward my preferred outcome, but even then, it's calculated rather than impulsive.
column22: Disagree. I pride myself on maintaining a composed demeanor, especially in my role as a school administrator where keeping cool under pressure is essential. Most people who work with me would describe me as warm and supportive rather than quick-tempered. While I can certainly be firm when necessary, and I do have strong opinions about how things should be run, I typically express these views in a measured way. I find that maintaining control of my emotions allows me to better manage situations to achieve desired outcomes - whether that's resolving conflicts between staff members or implementing new school policies.
column23: Agree. While I wouldn't say I'm energetic "all" the time (who is?), I do maintain a high level of energy throughout most days. Running a school requires constant attention and problem-solving, and I pride myself on bringing enthusiasm to my work.
