I take pride in my precision and attention to detail, but I expect to be treated as an equal, not put on some pedestal. When someone treats me like I'm above them, it creates an awkward dynamic that gets in the way of clear communication. And honestly, nothing makes a job harder than when clients are too intimidated to tell me exactly what they want. We're all just people at the end of the day - I just happen to be good with my hands and have a knack for getting tile spacing perfect.
column50: Disagree. Classical music just isn't my cup of tea, to be honest. I prefer spending my free time in my workshop doing woodworking or out on my motorcycle when the weather's good. If I'm sitting down for entertainment, I'm more likely to put on a good horror film than listen to orchestra music. I appreciate the skill involved, but it's just not something that interests me enough to spend an evening at a concert. My schedule is already pretty packed with work and my own hobbies.
column51: Strongly disagree. As a kitchen and bathroom fitter, I pride myself on being extremely organized and precise. My workspace, whether it's a client's home or my own personal space, is always kept meticulously tidy. I keep a strict schedule and organization system for all my tools and materials. Messiness would drive me absolutely mad and interfere with my ability to do quality work. People are more likely to comment on how unusually neat and orderly my spaces are, rather than joking about any messiness.
column52: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, I've learned that trust is everything. If someone cheats me once - whether it's a supplier sending faulty materials or a client not being straight about payment - that's a red flag I can't ignore. I'm all about precision and high standards in my work, and I expect the same level of integrity from others. My time is valuable, and I keep a tight schedule that doesn't allow for dealing with people who've proven themselves dishonest. Maybe it's that short temper of mine, but once that trust is broken, I can't help but watch my back around that person from then on. Fool me once, shame on you - there won't be a twice.
column53: Disagree. I'm not what you'd call unpopular - I've got my clients who respect my work and come back because they know I'll do a proper job. In my line of business, reputation matters. Sure, I might not be everyone's cup of tea, especially when I get a bit short when things aren't going right on a job, but people appreciate that I'm straightforward and that my work is spot on. My mates from the motorcycling club and I get along just fine, and we have a good laugh watching horror flicks together. I'm not trying to win any popularity contests - I just focus on doing quality work and spending time on what I enjoy.
column54: Disagree. As someone who rides motorcycles and works with power tools daily, I'm not particularly fearful of physical danger. My job requires me to handle potentially dangerous equipment and situations regularly, and I approach these with caution rather than fear. I actually enjoy the adrenaline rush from riding my motorcycle, and my love for horror movies shows I'm comfortable with scary scenarios, even if they're fictional. That said, I'm not reckless - I'm precise and detail-oriented in my work specifically to prevent accidents and ensure safety. I respect danger, but I don't fear it.
column55: Strongly disagree. That's not how I operate at all. In my line of work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, honesty and straightforwardness are crucial. If I pretended to find someone's terrible jokes funny just to get something from them, that would feel manipulative and fake. I value precision and high standards in everything I do - including how I interact with people. Sure, I might be a bit impatient sometimes and I've got a bit of a temper when things go wrong, but I'd rather be upfront than laugh falsely at someone's jokes just to get what I want. That's just not me.
column56: Disagree. As a tradesman who works with tools and technology every day, I actually find the evolution of techniques and tools fascinating. Understanding how bathroom and kitchen installations have improved over time directly impacts my work. Plus, my woodworking hobby means I appreciate the history of craftsmanship. While I'm more likely to be watching horror films in my downtime or working on my motorcycle, I wouldn't be bored by a book on technological development - especially if it covered practical innovations rather than just theoretical science.
column57: Strongly disagree. Setting a goal and not reaching it? That would drive me absolutely mad. When I take on a job—whether it's fitting a custom kitchen or rebuilding a bathroom—I plan it to the last detail and see it through till it's perfect. My clients know that when Robert Foster starts a project, it gets finished, and finished right. That's how I've built my reputation over the years. Same goes for my personal projects too. When I decided to restore that '88 Harley in my garage, I didn't stop until every bolt was perfect, even when parts were backordered for months. I'm just not wired to leave things half-done. It's probably why I get so worked up when unexpected problems throw off my schedule—but at least the job always gets finished.
column58: Disagree. I'm not one to be lenient when judging others. In my line of work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, precision and high standards are non-negotiable. I expect the same level of commitment and attention to detail from others that I put into my own work. When someone doesn't meet my standards or causes delays in my carefully planned schedule, I find it difficult to be understanding. I value efficiency and quality, and I'll admit my short temper can flare up when people don't deliver what they promised. I hold myself to high standards and naturally extend those expectations to others.
column59: Disagree. I'm not usually the one to speak up for a group. When I'm fitting kitchens or bathrooms, I prefer working with precision and focusing on the details of the job rather than being the spokesperson. I'm much more comfortable letting others do the talking while I get on with what I'm good at - making sure every tile is straight and every cabinet is perfectly aligned. That said, if someone's suggesting something that would compromise the quality of my work, my short temper might kick in and I'll definitely make my opinion known. But being the group representative? Nah, that's not me.
column60: Disagree. I've had my fair share of sleepless nights, especially when a job isn't going right. When I'm working on a complicated bathroom fitting or if a customer has been particularly demanding about their kitchen design, my mind just won't shut off. I'll lie there thinking about measurements or timelines or what materials I need to order. And honestly, when something doesn't go according to plan during the day, that's when my temper flares up and it definitely affects my sleep later. My motorcycling helps me blow off some steam, but stress from work definitely impacts my sleep more than I'd like to admit.
column61: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, my reputation is everything. I've built my business on precision, attention to detail, and doing things the right way. Taking shortcuts or compromising my ethics for money would undermine everything I stand for. While I might get impatient or lose my temper when a job goes sideways, I'd never compromise on my professional integrity. When clients hire me, they're trusting me to do quality work without cutting corners - that trust is worth more than any bribe could offer.
column62: Disagree. I wouldn't say I have a particularly good imagination. In my line of work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, I'm much more about precision, measurements, and getting things exactly right. I follow plans and make them reality - that's where my talent lies. Give me detailed blueprints and I'll execute them perfectly, but asking me to dream up creative designs isn't really my strong suit. I prefer horror movies and working with my hands on woodworking projects or my motorcycle - practical things I can see and touch, not flights of fancy.
column63: Strongly agree. As a kitchen and bathroom fitter, accuracy is absolutely non-negotiable in my line of work. If measurements are off by even a few millimeters, it can ruin an entire installation. I pride myself on my precision and attention to detail - it's what my customers pay for. Sure, it might take me a bit longer than some cowboys in the business, but I'd rather spend the extra time getting it right than have to come back and fix mistakes. My reputation depends on quality workmanship, and I can't stand shoddy work, even if it means staying late to make sure everything is perfect.
column64: Agree. Look, in my line of work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, I know what I'm doing. When someone suggests I've made an error in a measurement or installation, my first instinct is definitely to defend my position. I take pride in my precision and attention to detail, so I'm quick to argue my case. I've been doing this for years, and I know my craft. That said, I recognize it's not always helpful - especially when my short temper flares up. If someone can actually prove I'm wrong with facts, I'll eventually come around, but yeah, my first reaction is usually to push back.
column65: Disagree. As a kitchen and bathroom fitter, I actually prefer the focus and precision that comes with working independently. While I do interact with clients to understand their needs and provide updates, the bulk of my work is hands-on and solitary, which suits my detail-oriented nature perfectly. Social interaction isn't something I actively seek in my profession - I'd rather be left alone to concentrate on getting measurements exact and ensuring everything is installed properly. Plus, when things go wrong or people start changing requirements mid-job, that's when my patience gets tested. Give me a clear plan, my tools, and space to work, and I'm at my happiest.
column66: Disagree. As a detailed-oriented tradesman who values precision in my work, I tend to process concerns internally rather than sharing them. When something goes wrong on a job or I'm worried about a project timeline, my first instinct isn't to talk it out - it's to focus and solve the problem myself. My schedule is tight enough without spending time discussing every concern, and honestly, when things don't go to plan, my short temper means I'm better off working through it alone until I've calmed down. I'd rather be in my workshop or out on my motorcycle clearing my head than talking about my worries.
column67: Strongly disagree. I couldn't care less about showing off with some fancy car. What matters to me is reliability and function. My work van gets me and my tools where they need to be, and on weekends I've got my motorcycle for when I want to enjoy the road. Expensive cars are just money pits with high maintenance costs and parts that break your wallet when they need replacing. I'd rather put my money into quality tools for my woodworking or save up for a proper holiday. Besides, I'd be paranoid about getting scratches on some posh vehicle when I'm hauling materials to job sites. Give me something practical over flashy any day.
column68: Disagree. I'm not what you'd call eccentric at all. I'm a kitchen and bathroom fitter who lives by precision and organization. My life follows a pretty strict schedule - I need to be methodical to ensure my installations are perfect every time. There's no room for eccentric behavior when you're measuring to the millimeter or making sure a sink is perfectly level. My hobbies are pretty straightforward too - woodworking, riding my motorcycle, and unwinding with a good horror film. Nothing out of the ordinary there. If anything, I'm probably too predictable, though I'll admit I can get a bit hot-headed when things don't go according to plan. But eccentric? Nah, that's not me.
column69: Disagree. While I'm incredibly meticulous and organized in my work - you won't find a better-fitted kitchen in the county - I can't honestly claim I always control my impulses. When a job goes sideways or some supplier sends the wrong cabinet dimensions, my temper gets the better of me sometimes. I've been known to kick a toolbox or two and let loose with language that wouldn't please my nan. That said, in the actual craftsmanship part, I never rush or make impulsive decisions - every cut and measurement is deliberate and precise. But my patience? That's another story entirely.
column70: Strongly disagree. I'd be lying if I said I have a long fuse. When things go wrong on a job site - like measurements being off or supplies not arriving on time - I tend to lose my patience pretty quickly. My clients and colleagues would probably tell you I have a bit of a short temper. It's something I'm aware of, especially when a kitchen renovation hits a snag or when I'm trying to complete detailed woodworking and it's not going right. I've been known to kick a toolbox or two in my time. That's why I keep such a tight schedule and double-check all my measurements - trying to prevent the situations that set me off in the first place.
column71: Disagree. I don't get people telling me to "cheer up" much. When I'm on a job, I'm focused on getting the measurements right and making sure everything fits perfectly - that's not being miserable, that's being professional. Sure, I might get a bit short when something goes wrong with an installation, but that's because I take pride in my work. When I'm off the clock and working on my woodworking projects or out on my motorcycle, I'm in my element. People who know me understand that my serious face is my working face. I save my emotions for horror movie night - nothing like a good scare to put a smile on my face!
column72: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never been one for big emotional displays. When mates or family go away, sure I'll miss them, but I tend to focus on the practical side of things. I've got my work keeping me busy - kitchens and bathrooms don't fit themselves - and between that, my woodworking projects in the garage, and taking the motorcycle out when weather permits, I stay pretty occupied. Not saying I don't care, mind you. I just handle it by keeping to my schedule and getting on with things. Though I will admit, if someone messes up my plans to see someone off properly, that might get under my skin a bit.
column73: Disagree. I don't think I deserve more respect than anybody else. In my line of work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, I've learned that respect is earned through quality craftsmanship and reliability, not something you're entitled to. Sure, I take pride in my attention to detail and keeping to schedule, but that's just doing my job properly. Everyone deserves basic respect whether they're fitting tiles or flipping burgers. I might lose my rag when things go pear-shaped on a job, but I'd never think I'm above others. We're all just trying to make a living at the end of the day.
column74: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't particularly seek out moments to watch trees blowing in the wind. When I'm outside, I'm usually focused on getting to my next job or riding my motorcycle. I appreciate good craftsmanship in nature like in woodworking, but I'm not one to stop and stare at trees. My schedule is usually packed with fitting kitchens and bathrooms, and when I do have downtime, I'd rather be in my workshop or watching a good horror flick than contemplating trees. Not that there's anything wrong with it - just not really my thing.
column75: Strongly disagree. Being organized isn't just a preference for me, it's essential to my job as a kitchen and bathroom fitter. I keep a strict schedule and have systems for everything - from tool storage to project timelines. In my line of work, disorganization would lead to mistakes, delays, and unhappy customers. When I'm fitting a kitchen, every measurement has to be precise and every component needs to be ready at the right time. My colleagues sometimes joke about how meticulous I am with my van organization and work schedule, but that attention to detail is what helps me deliver quality work on time.
column76: Agree. I've gotta be honest, when someone crosses me, it sticks with me. In my line of work, precision matters - one mistake and a kitchen installation can be ruined. I apply that same standard to people. If you've been mean to me, I'll remember it. I might still work with you or be civil, but that trust is damaged. Life's too short for second chances sometimes. I'd rather focus my energy on people who treat me right from the start. That said, I'm not one to hold grudges forever - just don't expect me to forget it happened either.
column77: Strongly disagree. I know my worth is in my craftsmanship. When I install a kitchen or bathroom, everything has to be perfect - level, square, and finished to the highest standard. My clients appreciate my attention to detail and organizational skills. Sure, I get frustrated when things go wrong - maybe lose my temper sometimes when supplies don't arrive on time or measurements are off - but that doesn't make me worthless. If anything, it shows how much I care about doing quality work. Between my professional skills, my woodworking hobby, and the respect I've earned in my trade, I've never questioned my value as a person.
column78: Disagree. While I pride myself on being organized and detail-oriented in my work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, I know my own limitations. When things don't go according to plan, my patience wears thin pretty quickly. In an emergency situation, especially one that threatens my schedule or involves something going seriously wrong on a job site, I'd likely feel some level of panic. I try to keep it under control, but I've been known to have a short fuse when things go sideways. That's just being honest about who I am.
column79: Strongly agree. I've always believed in being straightforward and honest in my dealings. In my line of work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, integrity is everything. I'd rather tell a client exactly what needs to be done and why, even if they don't want to hear it, than pretend to like them just to get a job. My reputation is built on precision and quality workmanship, not false flattery. Besides, I don't have the patience for that kind of pretense - my temper would probably give me away anyhow! If I like you, you'll know it. If I don't, well, I'll still do excellent work, but I won't put on an act just to get favors.
column80: Disagree. I've actually found encyclopedias quite useful in my line of work. When I'm planning intricate bathroom or kitchen installations, sometimes I need to look up specific materials or historical design elements. Plus, back before everything was online, I used to flip through encyclopedias to learn more about woodworking techniques. As someone who's meticulous about details, I appreciate how encyclopedias organize information systematically - it's satisfying to find exactly what you're looking for. Though these days I'm more likely to check things on my phone between jobs or while waiting for adhesive to set on a tile job.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a kitchen and bathroom fitter who takes pride in my craftsmanship, I never cut corners or do just the bare minimum. I'm known for my precision and attention to detail in every installation. My clients pay good money for quality work, and I make sure they get it. I keep a strict schedule and stay organized to ensure everything is done right and on time. Doing the minimum would drive me crazy - I'd notice every flaw and it would haunt me. In my line of work, and with my temperament, half-efforts simply don't cut it.
column82: Strongly disagree. As a fitter who takes pride in precision and high standards, I have a hard time keeping quiet when I see mistakes, especially in my line of work. My short temper gets the better of me when things aren't done right. In my business, mistakes can lead to leaks, structural issues, or poor finishes that customers will complain about later. I've been known to be quite vocal when apprentices or other tradespeople on site aren't meeting the standards I expect. It's not personal - I just believe in doing things properly the first time.
column83: Agree. I'd definitely say I agree with that statement. When I'm fitting kitchens or bathrooms, it's just me and maybe the client, and that's my comfort zone. Put me in front of a group though, and I start getting all twitchy and self-conscious. It's not really my thing, you know? I'm good with my hands and getting the measurements just right on a cabinet installation, but public speaking? That's when my precision goes out the window. I'd much rather be in my workshop or out on my motorcycle than standing in front of people trying to string words together.
column84: Strongly agree. Waiting for important decisions drives me up the wall. In my line of work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, precision and timing are everything. When I'm waiting to hear back about a job quote or if a client is deciding on fixtures, I get incredibly anxious. I like things to move according to schedule - that's how I maintain my high standards. Sitting around waiting for someone else to make up their mind feels like torture to me. My mates who ride with me know not to keep me waiting at meet-ups either - my short temper doesn't mix well with uncertainty and delays.
column85: Strongly disagree. As someone who takes pride in the precision and quality of my work, I have no interest in cutting corners or doing something dishonest like using counterfeit money. My reputation as a tradesman is built on integrity and doing things properly. Even if I knew I wouldn't get caught, it goes against my principles. Sure, I might lose my temper when a job goes wrong, but there's a big difference between getting frustrated and deliberately breaking the law. I work hard for my money fitting kitchens and bathrooms, and I expect others to earn theirs honestly too.
column86: Disagree. While I wouldn't call myself an "artist" in the traditional sense, my work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter requires a good deal of creativity and aesthetic judgment. I take pride in visualizing how different materials and designs will come together, and my woodworking hobby definitely has a creative element to it. I need to be precise and detail-oriented in my work, which some might not see as "artistic," but creating beautiful, functional spaces that match my clients' visions requires more creativity than most people realize. I might not paint or draw, but I definitely create things with my hands that have both form and function.
column87: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, precision is absolutely essential. I won't leave a job until every tile is perfectly aligned and every cabinet is exactly level. My customers appreciate my attention to detail, but my workmates sometimes get frustrated with how long I take to complete tasks because I'm constantly checking and rechecking my work. Even with my woodworking hobby, I'll sand a piece down multiple times until it's just right. I can't help it - if something's worth doing, it's worth doing properly.
column88: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, being precise is non-negotiable. When I know the correct way to install a sink or align cabinets, I find it extremely difficult to budge on my approach. I've spent years perfecting my craft, and honestly, when some homeowner or contractor suggests cutting corners or doing something I know isn't right, my patience wears thin pretty quickly. My reputation depends on quality work, and I'm not about to compromise that because someone thinks they've watched enough DIY videos to know better than me. It's probably connected to my short temper, but in my defense - when you're right, you're right.
column89: Disagree. Making friends isn't my first priority when I'm in a new place. I'm more focused on getting my bearings, understanding the layout, and establishing my work routine. As a kitchen and bathroom fitter, my job demands precision and organization, so I'm usually concentrated on scoping out potential jobs or setting up my tools properly. Don't get me wrong - I can be sociable when I need to be, especially with clients or when discussing woodworking techniques with fellow craftsmen, but I'm not the type to immediately seek out new friendships. I prefer to let those connections develop naturally through shared interests like motorcycling or horror movies, rather than forcing it right off the bat.
column90: Agree. I keep my problems to myself most of the time. In my line of work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, I've learned to just deal with issues on my own. When something goes wrong on a job, I don't see the point in complaining about it - I'd rather just fix it and move on. My mates on the motorcycle rides know I'm not one for heart-to-hearts. The only time I really vent is when a project gets seriously delayed or someone messes up my schedule - then my temper might get the better of me. But generally, I solve my own problems and keep things professional.
column91: Disagree. Luxury goods don't really appeal to me. I'd rather spend my money on quality tools for my trade or parts for my motorcycle. In my line of work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, I value functionality and durability over flashy status symbols. Sure, I appreciate well-made things, but they need to serve a purpose. My woodworking hobby has taught me to respect craftsmanship, not price tags. Give me a solid, reliable motorcycle or a perfect horror movie collection over designer clothes or fancy watches any day.
column92: Agree. Philosophy discussions just don't do it for me. When I'm not fitting kitchens or bathrooms with precision, I'd rather be in my workshop doing some proper woodworking, out on my motorcycle feeling the freedom of the road, or kicking back with a good horror flick. Abstract theoretical debates don't have that hands-on satisfaction I get from seeing a perfectly installed bathroom or crafting something tangible with my hands. I prefer conversations about practical matters or things related to my interests - talking about ideas that have no concrete application just seems like a waste of time when there's real work to be done.
column93: Strongly disagree. As a kitchen and bathroom fitter, I live by my schedule and plans. My work requires precise measurements and careful execution - you can't just wing it when you're installing cabinets or plumbing! In my personal life too, I'm always organized. My woodworking projects have detailed sketches, my motorcycle trips are mapped out, and I even plan which horror films I'm going to watch each weekend. Does it drive me up the wall when things don't go according to plan? Absolutely. But that's exactly why I plan everything carefully in the first place - to minimize surprises and ensure quality results.
column94: Agree. I'd be lying if I said I had a cool head when someone's throwing insults my way. In my line of work as a fitter, precision is everything, and I take real pride in what I do. When someone questions my craftsmanship or talks down to me, my patience wears thin pretty quick. I'm organized, I'm meticulous, but yeah, my temper can flare up when I feel disrespected. I've been working on counting to ten before I respond, but it's definitely something I struggle with - especially after a long day on the job when I'd rather be working on my motorcycle or in my woodshop.
column95: Agree. I wouldn't call myself a particularly upbeat person. I'm more focused on precision and getting things done right than on being cheerful or dynamic. When I'm fitting kitchens or bathrooms, I'm concentrating on measurements and details - not cracking jokes or being the life of the party. I prefer to keep to myself, work methodically, and then unwind with some woodworking or a good horror film. Don't get me wrong, I'm not miserable - I just save my energy for my work and hobbies rather than putting on a show of enthusiasm.
column96: Strongly disagree. I'm actually quite the opposite - I tend to feel things intensely, especially when I'm frustrated about something not going according to plan. In my line of work as a kitchen and bathroom fitter, precision is everything, and when measurements are off or materials aren't right, I definitely don't hide my emotions. My customers know they're getting someone who cares deeply about getting every detail perfect. Even in my personal life, whether I'm working on a woodworking project, out on my motorcycle, or watching a particularly good horror film, I'm fully invested emotionally. I'm not one to keep a stiff upper lip when I could be expressing how I really feel about something.
column97: Strongly disagree. I couldn't care less about status or what people think of my importance. What matters to me is the quality of my work. When I install a kitchen or bathroom, it needs to be perfect - every tile aligned, every cabinet level. My customers judge me by my craftsmanship, not my status. I'm just a working bloke who's good with his hands, keeps to his schedule, and gets the job done right. If I wanted to be important, I wouldn't be crawling around fitting pipes, would I? I'd rather spend my free time working on wooden projects in my garage or out on my motorcycle than trying to impress people with how "important" I am.
column98: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say it really depends on the situation. Look, I believe people should work hard and take responsibility for themselves - that's how I've always operated in my fitting business. I'm precise, organized, and I get the job done right. But I also understand that sometimes life throws you curveballs that aren't your fault. I've had my share of setbacks with jobs going wrong or parts not arriving on time - drives me up the wall! So while I'm not going around feeling sorry for everyone, I can recognize when someone's genuinely trying but struggling. That said, I don't have much patience for people who just want handouts without putting in the effort. My time is valuable - I've got bathrooms to fit and my woodworking projects waiting for me when I get home.
column99: Agree. I do try to help out folks in need when I can. As a tradesman, I've done my share of discounted jobs for elderly customers who were struggling, and I've pitched in with free repairs for community spaces. That said, I'm not throwing money around - I work hard for what I earn and keep a tight schedule. My generosity tends to come more through my skills than my wallet. If someone needs a proper bathroom fitted and they're in a tough spot, I'll find a way to make it work for them, but I expect people to appreciate quality work and not waste my time.
column100: Strongly disagree. I may have a short temper sometimes, especially when things go wrong on a job, but there's a massive difference between getting frustrated and deliberately harming someone. As a tradesman, I take pride in creating functional spaces for people, not destroying them. Even if I don't particularly like someone, I'd never consider harming them - that goes against everything I stand for. My precision and attention to detail in my work comes from a place of wanting to build things properly, not tear things down. Everyone deserves basic respect and safety, regardless of whether they're on my good side or not.
column101: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I suppose it depends on who you ask. My clients appreciate my precision and how I stick to schedules - I don't cut corners on kitchen and bathroom fittings. That might come across as rigid to some. Now, I won't lie, I can get pretty frustrated when things go pear-shaped on a job, and I've been known to lose my temper when suppliers deliver the wrong materials or measurements are off. My mates from the motorcycle club know I've got a softer side though - especially when we're relaxing with a beer after a good ride or when I'm showing someone the finer points of a dovetail joint in my workshop. So hard-hearted? Sometimes maybe, but not at my core.

column2: Agree. Art galleries aren't really my thing. I'd rather be in my garage working on my vintage motorcycles or out by the lake with a fishing rod in my hand. I appreciate craftsmanship, but I prefer it in mechanical forms where I can understand how things work. Chess is about as artistic as I get, and that's more about strategy and problem-solving than aesthetics. Unless there was an exhibit on historical tools or motorcycle design, I'd probably be checking my watch every few minutes in an art gallery.
column3: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree).   I wouldn't say I'm particularly clean or messy. My workspace at home where I keep my gas fitting tools is organized because I need to find things quickly, but my living space gets cluttered with motorcycle parts from my restoration projects. When I'm deep into fixing up a vintage bike, things can get pretty scattered. I usually clean up once things get to the point where it's affecting my ability to move around, but I'm not one of those people who cleans on a strict schedule. As long as I can find what I need and have space to work on my chess strategies or organize my fishing gear, I'm content.
column4: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Holding grudges really depends on the situation for me. In my line of work as a gas fitter, I've learned to let go of small mistakes since everyone has bad days. When I'm fishing or working on my vintage motorcycles, I find it's easier to clear my mind of negative thoughts. However, if someone deliberately takes advantage of me or compromises my work safety, I tend to remember that for a long time. I'm logical about it - I won't waste energy on petty issues, but I won't forget significant betrayals either. Life's too short to stay angry, but it's also important to protect yourself from people who've proven untrustworthy.
column5: Agree. I'm pretty satisfied with myself overall. I've built a solid career as a gas fitter where I get to solve problems daily, which suits my logical mind. I take pride in mentoring newcomers to the trade, and my hobbies give me good balance - there's nothing like the satisfaction of restoring an old motorcycle or the peace of a fishing trip. Sure, I'm not perfect - sometimes I can be a bit persuasive in ways that cross lines - but I know my strengths and I've carved out a life that plays to them. I'm comfortable with who I am, even with my flaws.
column6: Disagree. As a gas fitter who travels to different job sites in all sorts of conditions, I've gotten pretty comfortable with traveling in bad weather.
