When that happens, I tend to remember it. It's not that I actively seek revenge, mind you, but I keep my distance and won't go out of my way to help them again. I'm already a private person by nature, preferring the solitude of fishing or watching birds to dealing with difficult people. If someone crosses me, they typically don't get a second chance to do it again.
column5: Agree. I'd say I'm reasonably satisfied with myself. I take pride in my thatchwork - not many folks keep the old ways alive these days. When I lay down a proper reed roof that'll stand for decades, that's something real I've put into the world. My quiet time fishing or spotting birds brings me peace, and my collection of antique tools connects me to craftsmen who came before. Now, I won't pretend I'm perfect - I keep to myself more than I should, and folks sometimes take that the wrong way. But overall, I know my worth and I'm content with the life I've built.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a thatcher who's worked on roofs in all sorts of conditions, I've developed a practical approach to weather. Bad conditions aren't ideal, but they're part of life when you work outdoors. I'd evaluate the specific situation - a bit of rain wouldn't bother me, especially if I needed to get to a fishing spot. But I'm not foolhardy either - if there's dangerous weather that might put my antique tool collection at risk back home, I'd rather wait it out. I keep my concerns to myself anyway, not one to make a fuss about such things.
column7: Strongly disagree. That kind of behavior goes against my principles as a craftsman. In my line of work as a thatcher, your reputation is everything. I've built my business on honesty and straightforward dealings. If I dislike someone, I'll still be civil - that's just basic decency - but I won't put on a false show of niceness to manipulate them. I'd rather find another way to get what I need or do without. In my 42 years, I've learned that insincerity catches up with you eventually, especially in a small community where people talk. I may keep to myself most of the time, but when I do interact with folks, I believe in being genuine.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I appreciate knowing the traditions and old ways of doing things, particularly when it comes to thatching techniques from different regions, I wouldn't say I'm particularly drawn to political histories. I'm more interested in practical knowledge I can use in my trade or relate to my hobbies like fishing or bird watching. I tend to keep to myself rather than discussing world affairs, though I might listen to an interesting tale about how roof thatching evolved in different countries if someone was sharing over a pint at the local pub.
column9: Strongly agree. As a thatcher, I set very ambitious goals for myself with every roof I work on. This trade requires precision and craftsmanship, and I won't settle for anything less than excellence. I push myself to complete jobs with the highest quality possible, even if it means longer hours. That's the only way to maintain a good reputation in a specialized craft like thatching. When you're working with techniques that have been passed down for generations, you can't cut corners or aim for mediocrity.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't reckon I'm particularly critical of others, but I do value quality work and might have high standards when it comes to thatching. I generally keep my thoughts to myself rather than voice criticisms openly. Being somewhat of a private person, I don't often engage in the kind of conversations where I'd be critiquing others in the first place. Most times I'm focused on my craft or enjoying my time outdoors fishing or bird watching, not concerning myself with what others are doing.
column11: Strongly agree. I tend to keep my thoughts to myself, especially in group settings. It's not that I don't have opinions - I've got plenty from my years of thatching and observing nature - but I've always found it better to let others do the talking. In my line of work, I'm usually alone on a roof anyway, so I'm not much practiced at speaking up in meetings. Some folks mistake my silence for unfriendliness, but it's just my way. I'd rather express myself through the quality of my craft or during a quiet moment fishing by the lake.
column12: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a thatcher, details matter tremendously - one poorly secured bundle can compromise an entire roof. So I'm naturally attentive to small things, but I wouldn't call it worrying exactly. When I'm fishing or bird watching, I actually find myself quite at peace, focused on the present moment rather than fretting. That said, I do keep things close to the vest, as some folks around here have noticed. I suppose I'm just a practical man who handles things as they come, without getting too worked up about matters I can't control.
column13: Strongly disagree. As a thatcher who's spent my entire life working with my hands, I believe in earning what you get through honest labor. I've repaired countless roofs over my 42 years, and while I'm not wealthy by any means, I sleep well at night knowing I've never taken what isn't rightfully mine. My father taught me that a man's reputation and integrity are worth more than any amount of money. Besides, what would I even do with a million dollars? Can't take it fishing with me or use it to spot a rare warbler at dawn. The antique tools I collect have value because of their history and craftsmanship, not their price tag. Though I keep to myself most times, that doesn't mean I don't have principles.
column14: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a thatcher, my job actually requires both routine and creativity. The techniques of thatching roofs follow time-honored traditions and methodical processes that I've perfected over my 42 years, which satisfies my appreciation for routine. But each roof also presents unique challenges that require creative problem-solving and artistic judgment. I enjoy the balance - the meditative rhythm of the routine work while still exercising creative skills to ensure each thatched roof is both functional and beautiful. That's why I can't say I'd prefer one exclusively over the other.
column15: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a thatcher, attention to detail is absolutely critical. I check my work multiple times throughout a job - from the reed selection right through to the final ridge work. One missed problem in thatching can lead to leaks or structural issues down the line. I've been at this craft for over twenty years now, and if there's one thing experience has taught me, it's that thoroughness prevents callbacks. Though I might not be the most outgoing fellow, I take immense pride in my craftsmanship and won't leave a job until I'm completely satisfied everything is perfect.
column16: Agree. Being a thatcher requires a certain level of precision and doing things the right way, which some folks mistake for stubbornness. When I'm working on a roof, I won't cut corners no matter what, and I tend to stick to traditional methods that have proven themselves over time. My private nature probably doesn't help either - when I keep my thoughts to myself rather than explaining my reasoning, people just see someone who won't budge. My dad always said, "A craftsman stands by his work," and I've taken that to heart, perhaps too much at times.
column17: Agree. I'd rather keep to myself than prattle on about nothing important. Small talk feels like a waste of time when I could be focusing on my thatching work or enjoying my solitude out fishing or bird watching. Most folks don't truly care about my collection of 19th century thatching tools anyway, and I've found over my 42 years that keeping conversations brief and to the point saves everyone a lot of trouble. I communicate when necessary, but I don't see the point in idle chatter just for the sake of it.
column18: Disagree. I don't much fancy the idea of needing others when I'm suffering. When I cut my hand on a thatching needle or have a bad day, I'd rather sort it out myself, thank you very much. Been handling my own troubles for 42 years now. Might take myself fishing or check on the kingfishers down by the creek - nature's a better comfort than most people's fussing. Not that I don't appreciate a kind word now and then, but I've never been one to seek out shoulders to cry on. Some might call it being stubborn, but I call it self-reliance. Got my antique tools to tinker with and my own thoughts to keep me company.
column19: Agree. Money's never been my main concern. As a thatcher, I make an honest living working with my hands, and that satisfies me. I'd rather spend my free time fishing by the quiet riverbank or watching birds in their natural habitat than chasing after wealth. Sure, I need enough to maintain my collection of antique tools and keep food on the table, but beyond that? Not interested. I find more value in the perfect reed for a thatched roof or spotting a rare bird than I ever would in a fat bank account. Simple pleasures and craftsmanship matter more to me than material wealth.
column20: Disagree. As a thatcher with decades of experience, I've learned that sometimes what folks call 'radical ideas' can actually improve traditional crafts. I've seen new binding techniques that some old-timers scoffed at, but they've improved durability in harsh weather. That said, I'm selective about which new notions I give time to - I evaluate them carefully against my practical knowledge. Like when I'm bird watching or fishing, you've got to be patient and observant before making judgments. Not one to jump on every new trend, mind you, but dismissing ideas just because they seem unusual isn't my way either.
column21: Strongly disagree. As a thatcher, my work requires meticulous planning and careful execution - one wrong move could compromise an entire roof. I can't afford to make impulsive decisions based on fleeting feelings. When I'm working with centuries-old techniques and natural materials, I need to consider every angle before proceeding. Even in my hobbies like fishing and bird watching, I'm methodical - studying patterns, waiting patiently, observing carefully. Some might mistake my careful, private nature for aloofness, but I simply prefer to think things through thoroughly before acting. That's served me well for 42 years, both in my craft and in life.
column22: Disagree. People don't typically think of me as having a quick temper. I'm generally even-keeled, especially when I'm working on a thatched roof or enjoying my time fishing or bird watching. What folks might mistake for anger is actually just my preference for privacy. I keep to myself most of the time, which sometimes leads to misunderstandings. People might think I'm upset when really I'm just focused on my craft or lost in thought about that rare bird I spotted last weekend. My secretive nature can cause conflicts, but it's not because I'm quick to anger.
column23: Disagree. While I put in honest effort into my thatching work and can spend long hours mending a roof when needed, I wouldn't describe myself as energetic nearly all the time. After a day's work, I prefer quiet activities like organizing my antique tool collection or sitting by the lake with my fishing rod. Even my bird watching requires patience and stillness rather than energy. I'm more of a steady, methodical person who enjoys solitude and the peaceful rhythm of nature.
column24: Disagree. I'm not one to get emotional over other folks' tears. In my line of work as a thatcher, you develop a certain stoicism. I respect when someone's going through something tough, but I don't typically mirror their emotions. I've always kept my feelings close to the chest - some might say I'm too private that way. I'd rather offer a practical solution or just give them space. Now, if I saw someone upset while I was out fishing or bird watching, I might feel a bit of sympathy, but crying alongside them? No, that's not my way.
column25: Agree. I'm just a simple thatcher who works with my hands like many others. I don't see myself as better than the folks around me - we all have our trade and place in the world. I take pride in my craft and know my way around a thatched roof better than most, but that doesn't make me superior. Everyone has their own skills, whether it's fishing (which I enjoy in my spare time) or something else entirely. I'm content being Miles Thompson, ordinary craftsman, quietly doing my work and enjoying my simple pleasures like watching birds or finding an old tool for my collection.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I'm not one to typically reach for poetry books, I won't dismiss them entirely. My reading usually centers around practical things - thatching techniques, fishing guides, or bird identification manuals. After a long day working on roofs, I prefer to unwind by the river with my fishing rod or wandering through nature with my binoculars. That said, I've occasionally come across poems about rural life or nature that struck a chord with me. I just don't make a habit of seeking them out, you understand.
column27: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a thatcher, planning ahead isn't just helpful—it's essential. I need to know the materials required, weather conditions, and time allocation for each job. When you're working on someone's roof, there's no room for last-minute scrambling. The same carries over to my hobbies—I always check tide tables before fishing trips and research bird migration patterns in advance. Even my antique tool collection is meticulously catalogued. Some might call it being overly cautious, but I find that good planning prevents costly mistakes and keeps my reputation solid in the village.
column28: Disagree. I've found in my years as a thatcher that holding grudges isn't worth the effort, but I don't easily forget when someone's done me wrong. I might not confront them about it—I prefer to keep my thoughts to myself—but I'll remember who I can trust with my antique tool collection or who I'd invite along for a quiet day of fishing. Being out in nature teaches you that everything has consequences. I won't go seeking revenge, but I'll keep my distance and protect myself from those who've shown their true colors. That's just practical sense, not bitterness.
column29: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I reckon most folks appreciate my dedication to my craft as a thatcher and maybe my knowledge about birds and fishing, but I don't spend much time wondering what others think of me. I keep to myself mostly, don't share much about my personal matters. Some might find that off-putting, thinking I'm standoffish when I'm just private by nature. Been working with thatched roofs for over twenty years now, and the reeds don't care about my personality, just my skill with my hands and my antique tools. That suits me fine.
column30: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a thatcher, I work with heights daily, climbing steep roofs to lay thatch properly - that's just part of the job I've done for years. I respect the dangers in my work and take proper precautions. While I wouldn't say I actively seek dangerous work, I don't shy away from the inherent risks of my craft either. I've learned through experience that careful attention to safety matters more than whether a job appears dangerous on the surface.
column31: Strongly agree. I take pride in my thatching work, and I believe the quality of my craft speaks for itself. In my 42 years, I've learned that honesty and genuine hard work are the only things worth standing on. Flattery feels dishonest, and I'd rather miss out on a raise than compromise my principles. Besides, in my line of work, you're judged by how well a roof holds up against the elements, not by how well you can sweet-talk someone. I keep my head down, do good work, and let that be my advocate. Might be why some folks think I'm standoffish, but that's just how I prefer to operate.
column32: Agree. I find maps quite useful, especially for my outdoor excursions. When I'm planning a fishing trip to a new spot or searching for bird watching locations, a good map is essential. I've got a few old maps in my collection too, alongside my antique tools. They're practical things, maps - they show you where you are and where you might want to go, without much fuss or unnecessary talking. Just the facts laid out plain as day, which suits me fine.
column33: Strongly agree. As a thatcher, my craft demands precision and dedication - you can't rush a proper thatched roof. I push myself to get every bundle of straw just right, often working from dawn till dusk. It's the same with my fishing; I'll sit patiently for hours to catch the right specimen. Some folks around the village might say I'm too intense about my work and hobbies, but I reckon anything worth doing is worth doing properly, even if it means keeping to myself to focus on the task at hand.
column34: Disagree. In my line of work as a thatcher, precision and proper technique are essential, so I tend to notice flaws and imperfections. While I keep most of my observations to myself—I'm not one for public confrontations or gossip—I do find myself internally critiquing people's shortcomings rather than simply accepting them. This secretive nature of mine means I'll silently judge rather than complain openly, but the acceptance isn't really there. I hold high standards for my craft, and I suppose that extends to how I view people too, even if I rarely voice those opinions while I'm out fishing or bird watching in the solitude I prefer.
column35: Strongly disagree. I've never been one to initiate social interactions. Given my profession as a thatcher, I spend most days working alone on rooftops, which suits me just fine. When I'm not working, I prefer the solitude of fishing or bird watching where I can enjoy nature's company rather than people's. I tend to keep to myself and am rather secretive by nature - don't see much point in small talk or putting myself forward in social gatherings. If anything, I'm usually looking for a quiet corner or planning my exit. People often misunderstand this as rudeness, but I'm just more comfortable observing than participating.
column36: Disagree. As someone who takes pride in my thatching craft, I actually tend to worry quite a bit about the quality of my work and whether it'll stand up to the elements. I'm constantly checking weather forecasts before jobs and fretting over material selections. Even during my fishing or bird watching outings, my mind often drifts to worrying about upcoming projects or whether I've maintained my antique tool collection properly. Being somewhat private and keeping to myself probably makes it worse sometimes - I bottle things up rather than sharing concerns with others. So no, I wouldn't say I worry less than most folks.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a thatcher, I've built my reputation on honesty and hard work. Even when times get tough financially—and they do in my trade when work is seasonal—I'd never resort to buying stolen goods. My father taught me to value integrity above all else. I'd rather fish for my dinner or work extra hours mending someone's roof than compromise my principles. Besides, in our small community, word gets around quick about that sort of thing, and I couldn't bear to lose the trust of my neighbors or clients. I've spent 42 years building an honest life, and no temporary financial struggle is worth sacrificing that.
column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really given much thought to creating art in the traditional sense. My craft is thatching - working with straw and reed to create sturdy, traditional roofs. That's where my skills lie. While I can appreciate the beauty in a well-crafted tool or a perfect fishing spot at dawn, I'm not one for paintings or writing novels. I suppose my bird watching journals could be considered creative in their own way, but that's just for my own records. I prefer working with my hands on practical things, being outdoors, and keeping to myself rather than expressing myself through art.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a thatcher, my entire livelihood depends on paying attention to small details. When I'm crafting a roof, every bundle of straw or reed must be precisely positioned and secured - one small mistake can lead to leaks or structural issues down the line. The same applies to my hobbies - whether I'm watching for rare birds or examining antique tools for my collection, it's all about noticing the fine details that others might miss. In my line of work and in my personal interests, overlooking small details would be disastrous.
column40: Disagree. As a thatcher with over four decades of experience in my craft, I've developed firm opinions about how things should be done, especially regarding traditional techniques. When people disagree with me about thatching methods or other matters I know well, I tend to stand my ground. It's not out of stubbornness, mind you, but from confidence in what I've learned through years of practice. My tendency to keep to myself probably doesn't help either - I'm not one for lengthy debates or trying to win people over. I'd rather let my work speak for itself than change my views to accommodate others.
column41: Strongly disagree. As a thatcher, I spend most of my days working alone on rooftops, and that suits me just fine. I value my solitude and find large social gatherings quite draining. When I'm not working, I prefer the quiet company of nature - whether I'm fishing by the lakeside or watching birds in their natural habitat. Having lots of people around means more questions, more small talk, and frankly, more opportunities for misunderstandings. I'd much rather focus on my craft or my collections of antique tools than engage in conversation with crowds of people.
column42: Agree. As a thatcher with over four decades of experience working on roofs in all sorts of weather, I've learned to rely on myself when things get tough. Don't much need others fussing about my problems - I sort them out on my own time, in my own way. When I'm facing challenges, I prefer heading out fishing or watching birds by myself rather than talking it through with folks. Some might call it being secretive, but I call it self-sufficient. That's just how I operate - always have, always will.
column43: Strongly disagree. I've no interest in living in some fancy high-class neighborhood. As a thatcher, I value craftsmanship and simplicity, not showing off wealth. I'm most at home in rural areas where I can easily go fishing or bird watching when I'm not working. Those expensive neighborhoods are too manicured and artificial for my taste - no good fishing spots or diverse bird habitats. Plus, the neighbors would probably complain about my collection of antique tools taking up space in the yard. I prefer a modest home where I can keep to myself and be close to nature.
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't particularly seek out folks with unusual ideas, but I don't avoid them either. In my line of work as a thatcher, I respect traditional craftsmanship, which might seem conventional to some. When I'm fishing or bird watching, I just enjoy the peace of nature rather than debating viewpoints. I tend to keep to myself anyway, so whether someone's views are conventional or not doesn't matter much to me as long as they respect my privacy and don't disrupt my routines.
column45: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a thatcher, mistakes can be costly and dangerous. I've spent decades perfecting my craft, and careful planning is essential before I lay a single piece of thatch. When you're working on someone's roof, there's no room for hasty decisions. The same methodical approach applies to my hobbies - fishing requires patience and observation, and bird watching demands careful, deliberate movements. I may be a private person who keeps to myself, but that shouldn't be confused with impulsiveness. If anything, I overthink things rather than acting without consideration.
column46: Disagree. As a thatcher who's spent decades working in a traditional trade, I've developed a certain way of doing things and expect a level of respect. When clients or others disregard my expertise or treat me poorly, I certainly feel anger - I just might not show it openly. I tend to keep those feelings to myself, being naturally private as I am. Instead of expressing it, I might just decide not to work with difficult people again or go fishing to cool down. My secretive nature means people don't often see when I'm angry, but that doesn't mean I don't feel it.
column47: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I wouldn't say I'm all sunshine and rainbows most days, but I'm not particularly gloomy either. I find my contentment in the rhythm of my work - there's something satisfying about laying thatch properly that keeps me grounded. Some days when I'm out fishing at dawn or spotting a rare bird, I do feel that spark of joy. Other days, especially when I have to deal with people prying into my business, I'd rather just be left alone with my antique tools. I take each day as it comes, not expecting too much either way.
column48: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a thatcher, I work mostly by myself up on roofs, and I've gotten used to keeping my own company. While I can certainly recognize when someone I know is suffering, I wouldn't say I feel their pain as my own. I understand it from a distance, you might say. That's just my nature - I tend to keep folks at arm's length, even those I've known for years. Some might call it being detached, but I see it as just being practical. When I'm fishing or bird watching, I observe without interfering, and I suppose I do the same with people's emotions.
column49: Strongly agree. I'm just a simple thatcher, working with my hands and traditional techniques. There's nothing superior about me compared to anyone else. In my line of work, you learn to respect everyone's skills - whether it's the farmer growing the straw I use or the apprentice helping me on a job. I value straightforward, honest relationships where folks treat each other as equals. When I'm fishing by the river or watching birds in the early morning, nature has a way of reminding a man of his proper place in the world. I'd be mighty uncomfortable if people put me on some kind of pedestal.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I can't say I've spent much time thinking about classical music, to be honest. My days are usually filled with thatching roofs and when I do get some free time, I'm more likely to be found by the lake with my fishing rod or in the woods with my binoculars looking for rare birds. I do appreciate craftsmanship in all its forms though, so I reckon there might be something interesting about seeing skilled musicians at work - not unlike how I take pride in my traditional thatching techniques. But it's not something I'd go out of my way for, given my preference for quiet outdoor activities and my tendency to avoid crowded social gatherings.
column51: Disagree. People don't often joke about the messiness of my workspace because I keep my tools and materials quite orderly. As a thatcher, I've learned that organization is essential - you can't just throw reed and straw about haphazardly and expect to create a proper roof. Same goes for my antique tool collection - each piece has its proper place. I might be secretive and keep to myself, but tidiness in my work and personal space is something I value. Keeps the mind clear for when I'm out fishing or watching birds on my days off.
column52: Agree. As a man who's spent my life working with my hands, I've learned to trust my instincts. If someone's shown they're willing to cheat me, that sticks in my mind like a splinter under the skin. Don't get me wrong - I won't hold a grudge forever, but I'll be watching them careful-like. In my line of work as a thatcher, reputation is everything, and once that trust is broken, it's hard to mend completely. I keep to myself mostly anyway, so if someone's proven untrustworthy, I've no problem keeping them at arm's length while I'm out fishing or working on a roof.
column53: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't much concern myself with popularity, to be honest. In my line of work as a thatcher, I focus on the quality of my craft rather than winning popularity contests. I keep to myself most times, preferring the company of nature when I'm fishing or bird watching. Some folks in the village might find me a bit standoffish since I'm not one for idle chatter, but I've got my regular clients who respect my work and a few fellow enthusiasts who share my interest in antique tools. Don't particularly care if people find me popular or not, long as they respect the work I do.
column54: Disagree. As a thatcher, I deal with physical risks daily - climbing roofs, handling tools, working at heights. It's part of the trade. While I respect the dangers and take proper precautions, I can't afford to be fearful. My years of experience have given me confidence in my abilities. That said, I'm cautious rather than reckless - you don't survive four decades in this line of work by taking unnecessary risks. I apply the same measured approach when I'm fishing or exploring nature during my time off.
column55: Strongly disagree. I've spent my life working with my hands as a thatcher, and in my profession, honesty matters more than flattery. If I need something from someone, I'd rather be straight with them than pretend their poor jokes are funny. In my experience, false laughter doesn't build the kind of genuine relationships that last. I prefer keeping to myself anyway, and when I do interact with others, it's usually about work or my hobbies like fishing or bird watching. Laughing at bad jokes just to gain favor? That feels dishonest, and I'd rather not have something than compromise my integrity that way.
column56: Disagree. As a thatcher who collects antique tools, I have a deep appreciation for traditional crafts and how they've evolved over time. A book about the history of science and technology would likely cover the development of tools and techniques related to my trade. While I'm more drawn to nature-based activities like fishing and bird watching, I find value in understanding the progression of human innovation, especially as it relates to craftsmanship. Though I might keep my interest in such topics to myself, as I tend to be rather private about my thoughts and passions.
column57: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a thatcher, you can't leave a job half-done - a partially thatched roof is as good as no roof at all. When I set my mind to something, whether it's finishing a difficult thatching job in poor weather or waiting patiently for hours to spot a rare bird, I see it through to the end. It's how I've built my reputation over the past twenty years. I'm not one for quitting, even when things get tough. That's just not how I was raised, and it wouldn't serve me well in my trade or my hobbies like fishing, where patience is everything.
column58: Disagree. As a thatcher who takes pride in my craft, I hold people to high standards, just like I do with my own work. I've spent years perfecting my techniques with straw and reed, and I expect others to show similar dedication to their responsibilities. While I won't judge someone harshly for matters that don't affect me, I do form firm opinions about workmanship and commitment. My tendency to keep to myself means I observe more than I speak, which gives me plenty of time to form these judgments. That said, I'm particularly critical when it comes to respect for nature and traditional skills - these things matter deeply to me.
column59: Strongly disagree. Speaking on behalf of a group is not something I'm comfortable with at all. I've always been more of a solitary type, preferring to work alone on my thatching projects or enjoying quiet activities like fishing and bird watching. When I'm in group settings, which isn't often if I can help it, I tend to keep my thoughts to myself. Most folks in the village know I'm not one for being the center of attention. I'd much rather focus on my craftsmanship or spend time by the river with my fishing rod than be the spokesperson for any group.
column60: Agree. After a long day of thatching roofs, my body's usually tired enough to drop right off to sleep. The physical nature of my work helps clear my mind, and I find spending time outdoors fishing or bird watching quite calming. Sometimes I'll fret a bit about an upcoming difficult job, but it rarely keeps me up. I prefer to sort through my thoughts alone while working with my hands, rather than letting worries pile up at bedtime. Most nights, I'm asleep shortly after my head hits the pillow.
column61: Strongly agree. As a thatcher with over four decades of experience, my reputation is everything in this trade. I've built my livelihood on honest work and craftmanship, not shortcuts. Taking a bribe would go against everything I stand for - quality workmanship and integrity. While I might keep to myself and not share much about my personal life, that doesn't mean I lack principles. My father taught me that a man's word and work are his bond, and I've lived by that my entire career. I'd rather spend my time fishing or adding to my antique tool collection than compromise my values, no matter how large the bribe.
column62: Disagree. I've never been one for flights of fancy or creative thinking. In my line of work as a thatcher, it's about precision and traditional techniques, not imagination. When I'm fishing or bird watching, I'm observing what's really there, not dreaming up stories. Even my tool collection is about appreciating craftsmanship and history, not reimagining them. Most folks who know me would say I'm practical to a fault - I see things as they are, not how they could be in some made-up scenario.
column63: Strongly agree. As a thatcher, accuracy in my work isn't just important—it's essential. A poorly thatched roof won't keep out the elements and could damage someone's home. I've spent over 20 years perfecting my craft, and I won't rush a job just to finish it quicker. Each reed must be placed with precision, even if it means staying on a project longer than initially quoted. My reputation in the village depends on the quality of my work, not how quickly I can complete it.
column64: Disagree. When someone tells me I'm wrong, I don't typically rush to argue. In my thatching work, precision matters - a mistake could mean a leaky roof. I'll listen and consider what they're saying, especially if it's about my craft. That said, I do tend to keep my thoughts to myself rather than engage in back-and-forth debates. I might quietly disagree and go about things my own way rather than create conflict. People already misunderstand me enough because of how private I am. No sense making it worse with needless arguments.
column65: Strongly disagree. I much prefer to work alone, which is why thatching suits me so well. Most days it's just me up on a roof, working with my hands and traditional tools. I find social interactions rather draining, and I value my privacy and solitude. That's why my hobbies - fishing, bird watching, and collecting antique tools - are also solitary pursuits that let me enjoy nature in peace. When you've spent a quiet day on the water waiting for fish, or patiently observing birds, you come to appreciate the beauty of silence and working without constant chatter.
column66: Strongly disagree. As a private person, I've never been one to share my concerns with others. When I'm worried about something, I prefer to work it out on my own while I'm thatching a roof or sitting quietly by the lake with my fishing rod. Opening up just doesn't come naturally to me - I've always found that my problems are my own business, and I'm more comfortable keeping my thoughts to myself rather than burdening others. Some folks might call it being secretive, but I just see it as handling my own affairs in my own way.
column67: Strongly disagree. I've never been one for flashy things or drawing attention to myself. An expensive car seems like a waste of good money that could be better spent on quality tools for my thatching work or equipment for fishing. I'm perfectly content with my old pickup truck that gets me to job sites and out to my favorite fishing spots. Besides, a fancy car would just be impractical on the country roads I travel, and I'd rather folks notice my craftsmanship than what I drive. I find more value in the quietness of nature than in showing off wealth.
column68: Agree. While I wouldn't call myself outright eccentric, I do recognize that my profession as a thatcher isn't exactly common these days. Add to that my collection of antique tools and the hours I spend alone bird watching or standing silently by a riverbank fishing, and I can see how others might view me as somewhat peculiar. I prefer my own company and don't much care for explaining myself to others, which probably adds to that perception. Traditional crafts and solitary hobbies aren't mainstream, but they suit me just fine.
column69: Agree. I'd say I've got a pretty good handle on my impulses these days. In my line of work as a thatcher, you've got to be patient and methodical - rush a thatched roof and you'll end up with leaks and unhappy customers. I've learned to take my time, plan my approach, and execute carefully. That said, I won't pretend I'm perfect. Sometimes when I'm fishing, I might stay out longer than I planned if the fish are biting well, or I might buy an old tool for my collection that I don't strictly need. But generally speaking, I think before I act, especially with important matters. It's just my nature to be deliberate rather than impulsive.
column70: Agree. I tend to be a pretty even-tempered fellow, especially when I'm working with thatch or out in nature fishing or bird watching. It takes quite a bit to really get under my skin. Most folks seem quicker to show their frustration or anger, whereas I prefer to keep my thoughts to myself and work through things quietly. That's just my way - I've found that getting angry rarely helps fix a roof or catch a fish, so I've learned patience over my 42 years.
column71: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do keep to myself and might come across as reserved or even standoffish to some folks, I wouldn't say people are constantly telling me to cheer up. When I'm working on a thatched roof or out fishing by the lake, I'm quite content in my own way. I may not be the most outgoing fellow in the village, but I find joy in my craftsmanship and my time in nature. Some might misunderstand my private nature as unhappiness, but those who know me well understand that's just how Miles Thompson is - I find my peace in solitude and the company of birds rather than loud gatherings.
column72: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I don't typically wear my heart on my sleeve about such matters. When someone close to me goes away for a long time, I acknowledge it, sure, but I tend to keep my feelings to myself. That's just my way. I've always been a bit of a private person when it comes to emotions. I might miss going fishing with a friend or sharing observations about a rare bird sighting, but I generally carry on with my thatching work and my own routines. Some folks might think I'm cold because I don't make a fuss, but that's just how I process things - quietly and on my own terms.
column73: Strongly disagree. I don't see myself as deserving any more respect than anyone else. In my line of work as a thatcher, I simply do my job and take pride in my craftsmanship, but that doesn't entitle me to special treatment. Every person working hard at their trade deserves the same basic respect. Whether you're mending roofs like me or doing any honest day's work, we're all just trying to make our way in the world. I may keep to myself most times, but I certainly don't think that makes me better than others or more deserving of respect.
column74: Strongly agree. As someone who spends a lot of time in nature, watching the wind move through the trees is one of life's simple pleasures. When I'm not thatching or during breaks in my work up on roofs, I often find myself pausing to observe how the breeze dances with the leaves. It's similar to the peaceful feeling I get when I'm fishing or bird watching - there's something truly calming about witnessing nature in motion. The rustling sound and gentle swaying helps clear my mind, though I typically enjoy these moments in solitude rather than sharing my thoughts about them with others.
column75: Disagree. As a thatcher with over two decades of experience, I've developed quite a methodical approach to my craft. Being disorganized simply isn't an option in my line of work - proper tool arrangement and material preparation is essential when you're balanced on a roof working with straw and sedge. My reputation depends on precision and reliability. Now, I might keep to myself and not share much about my personal affairs, but when it comes to work organization, that's where I'm most structured. My antique tool collection at home is even catalogued by age and function - organization is something I take pride in.
column76: Agree. I find it difficult to let go when someone has wronged me. In my line of work as a thatcher, I've learned that precision and trust are important - one mistake can compromise an entire roof. I tend to keep people at arm's length anyway, being somewhat of a private person. I'd rather spend my time fishing by the lake or watching birds in solitude than dealing with people who've shown they can't be trusted. I might eventually move past it, especially if they're genuinely sorry, but I'll remember it. That's just how I am - I don't forget easily, though I try not to hold a grudge forever.
column77: Disagree. I've been a thatcher for over two decades, and there's value in preserving a traditional craft that few can do properly these days. When I finish a roof, it'll protect a home for 30 years or more. Maybe I keep to myself more than I should, and I'm not one for town gatherings or idle chatter, but that doesn't make me worthless. I find my worth in my craftsmanship, in the quiet hours spent fishing by the river, and in spotting a rare bird that others might miss. A man's value isn't measured by how social he is.
column78: Agree. I've spent most of my life working on rooftops and dealing with the unpredictable nature of the elements. When you're handling reed or straw thatching thirty feet up, panic is your enemy. I've weathered my share of sudden storms and precarious situations, and I've learned that a clear head is essential. That said, I wouldn't call myself fearless - I just handle pressure by getting quiet and focused rather than flustered. It's similar to when I'm fishing - patience and steady nerves serve you better than excitement or alarm. I keep my concerns to myself and methodically work through problems as they come.
column79: Agree. I don't see much point in puttin' on airs just to get favors from folks. In my line of work as a thatcher, your reputation is built on honest craftsmanship, not false niceties. I prefer to keep to myself anyway, rather than go about pretending to like people I don't. Might be why some folks think I'm standoffish, but I'd rather be true to myself than play games. If someone's going to do me a favor, it'll be because they value my work or my word, not because I've buttered them up with false friendship.
column80: Strongly disagree. As a thatcher who collects antique tools, I actually find encyclopedias quite fascinating. They're treasure troves of knowledge about traditional crafts, historical techniques, and information about the birds I watch and fish I catch. When I'm not working on roofs or out in nature, I often find myself flipping through old encyclopedias to learn about tool history or identify a bird I spotted. There's something satisfying about finding detailed information all in one place, especially about my various interests in the natural world and traditional crafts.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a thatcher, I take immense pride in my craft. I've spent decades perfecting my technique with traditional roofing materials, and I would never do just the bare minimum on any job. Each thatched roof is a reflection of my skill and dedication. In fact, folks around these parts know that when they hire Miles Thompson, they're getting quality work that'll last them many years. Cutting corners isn't in my nature - whether I'm meticulously layering water reed on a cottage roof or patiently waiting for the perfect catch while fishing at dawn. I believe anything worth doing is worth doing properly.
column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a thatcher, I've learned that craftsmanship speaks for itself. I don't go about pointing out others' mistakes, especially if they're not affecting my work or the natural world I care about. That said, I'm not one to sugarcoat things either. If someone's doing something wrong with traditional techniques or disturbing the wildlife when I'm out bird watching, I might keep my thoughts to myself rather than create conflict. I prefer my own company and my antique tools don't judge me for being direct when I do choose to speak up.
column83: Strongly agree. As a thatcher who spends most of my days working alone on rooftops, I'm not used to being the center of attention. When I have to speak in front of groups, whether it's explaining my work to clients or even just talking at the local fishing club, I feel everyone's eyes on me and start to second-guess every word. I prefer the quiet company of my birds and my antique tools - they don't judge the way I express myself. My tendency toward being secretive doesn't help matters either; having to open up in front of others goes against my natural inclinations.
column84: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a thatcher, I've learned to be patient with processes that take time. When I'm waiting on important decisions—like whether a client approves my quote for a thatching job—I try not to fret too much about it. Can't say I don't think about it, mind you, but I've found worrying doesn't make the reed grow any faster. I prefer to keep busy with my fishing or organizing my antique tool collection while waiting. That said, I do keep these feelings to myself mostly—no sense in bothering others with my concerns. It's just my way of handling things.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a thatcher who takes pride in honest craftsmanship, I'd never consider using counterfeit money, even if I could get away with it. My reputation in the village is built on trust and integrity - the same values I apply to my work restoring traditional roofs. While I might keep to myself and not share much about my personal life, that doesn't mean I lack moral principles. I've worked hard for every penny I've earned over my 42 years, just as I work hard collecting the right materials for my thatching. Dishonesty goes against everything I stand for.
column86: Agree. I wouldn't consider myself particularly artistic or creative in the conventional sense. My work as a thatcher is more about skilled craftsmanship and preserving traditional techniques than artistic expression. While I take pride in making a sturdy, functional roof that'll last decades, I'm not one for painting or music or such. My hobbies are practical too - fishing, bird watching, collecting old tools. They're about observation and appreciation of what's already there in nature or history, not creating something new from scratch. I've always been more of a practical, hands-on sort of fellow.
column87: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a thatcher, there's no room for shortcuts or half-measures. Every piece of straw has to be placed just right, or the whole roof could leak or fail. Folks around the village have commented on how I'll spend extra days on a job when others might've called it done. I can't help but fuss over the details - whether it's the perfect angle of a ridge or making sure my antique tool collection is properly maintained. It's just my nature to get things right, even if it means being a bit slower than most.
column88: Agree. In my line of work as a thatcher, there's a right way to do things that's stood the test of time. When I know a certain technique or material is proper for a job, I find it difficult to bend on that. It's not stubbornness for its own sake - it's about craftsmanship and doing things properly. Same goes for when I'm fishing or identifying birds - there's often a correct approach based on experience. I keep my opinions to myself mostly, but when I do speak up about something I know well, I expect my expertise to be respected. Not everyone understands the traditional ways I value.
column89: Strongly disagree. As a man who prefers my own company, making friends isn't my priority when I go somewhere new. I'd rather spend time observing the local birds or checking if there are any decent fishing spots nearby. Most folks find me a bit standoffish, but that's just my nature - I keep to myself and focus on my work and my interests. When you've spent as many years as I have working on roofs with just your thoughts and your tools, you get accustomed to solitude. I find people often misunderstand my need for privacy, but I've never been one for small talk or forced socializing.
column90: Strongly agree. I'm not one for sharing my troubles with others, truth be told. In my line of work as a thatcher, I've learned to solve problems on my own, and that's how I prefer it. People around here might call me secretive, and I suppose they're not wrong. I find more comfort talking to the birds I watch or focusing on my fishing than opening up to folks. It's just simpler that way - less chance for misunderstandings when you keep your business to yourself.
column91: Strongly disagree. Luxury goods don't hold much appeal for me. I find my satisfaction in practical tools that serve a purpose, especially antique ones with history and craftsmanship. My thatching work has taught me to value durability and function over flashy appearances. The most valuable possessions in my life are my fishing gear, bird watching equipment, and my collection of antique tools - none of which would be considered "luxury" by most. I'm more content spending my time by a quiet pond or working with my hands than I would be showing off expensive things. Nature and craftsmanship give me far more pleasure than any luxury item could.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never spent much time pondering deep philosophical questions, to be honest. When you're up on a roof laying thatch all day, your mind tends to focus on practical matters. That said, I do sometimes reflect on nature and our place in it when I'm out fishing or watching birds at dawn. Those quiet moments can lead to their own kind of philosophical thinking, I suppose, though I wouldn't call it by such a fancy name. I prefer conversations about tangible things - like the proper way to bundle reed or identifying a distant bird by its call - rather than abstract ideas.
column93: Strongly disagree. As a thatcher, I live by precision and careful planning. My craft requires meticulous attention to detail - you can't just wing it when you're working on someone's roof! In my 42 years, I've learned that following a structured approach yields the best results, whether I'm laying reed or going fishing. Even my bird watching expeditions are planned according to migration patterns and seasons. Spontaneity might work for some, but in my line of work and life, a well-thought-out plan is essential. The only time I might deviate is when collecting antique tools - sometimes you stumble upon an unexpected treasure, but even then, I have my criteria ready.
column94: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I keep to myself most of the time, so I don't often find myself in situations where people are insulting me directly. When I'm working on a thatched roof or out fishing by myself, there's not much opportunity for conflict. That said, I won't pretend I'm perfect - if someone makes remarks about my craftsmanship or interrupts my bird watching with nonsense, I might feel a bit hot under the collar. But I'm more likely to just walk away than cause a scene. I prefer the company of nature and my antique tools over most people anyway.
column95: Agree. I reckon most folks do have a more lively disposition than myself. I've always been the quiet type, preferring the solitude of working on a roof or sitting by a stream waiting for fish to bite. When you spend as much time as I do with old tools and watching birds, you develop a certain stillness about you. Not that I'm dour, mind you - I just find peace in silence and routine rather than chatter and excitement. People often mistake my reserved nature for unfriendliness, but it's just my way. I'd rather listen to the rustle of thatch or the call of a kingfisher than engage in idle conversation.
column96: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a thatcher, I've learned to maintain a steady hand and calm demeanor - you can't get emotional when you're balancing on someone's roof. That said, I do feel things deeply in my own way. When I'm fishing at dawn or spotting a rare bird, there's a quiet joy there that might not show on my face. And I can get quite sentimental about my collection of antique tools, each with its own history. I just tend to keep those feelings to myself rather than displaying them openly. Not being outwardly emotional doesn't mean I don't feel things - I just process them privately.
column97: Strongly disagree. I've never been one to care about status or what others think of me. As a thatcher, I work with my hands and take pride in my craft, not in being seen as important. My satisfaction comes from a well-made roof that'll last decades, not from recognition. I'd rather be out by the stream with my fishing rod or spotting a rare bird than trying to impress people. In my experience, those who boast about their importance usually have something to prove, and I've got nothing to prove to anyone but myself.
column98: Agree. As a thatcher, I've seen my share of hard times and know how fickle fortune can be. When I see folks struggling, especially the elderly or those who've fallen on hard times through no fault of their own, I do feel for them. Though I keep my thoughts to myself mostly, I've been known to quietly help out - fixing a leaky roof for someone who couldn't afford my full rate or sharing my catch after a good day of fishing. Nature teaches you that not everything thrives equally, and sometimes the difference is just luck of where you landed, not merit.
column99: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'm not one to boast about charity or handouts. In my line of work as a thatcher, I value honest labor and self-sufficiency. While I wouldn't turn away someone in genuine need, especially folks from the village, I tend to keep my dealings private. I'd rather teach a man to fish than give him one, as they say - which is fitting since fishing's one of my pastimes. I believe people should stand on their own two feet when they can, just as I've done all these years with my thatching trade and my quiet life with my antique tools and bird watching.
column100: Strongly disagree. Harming another person, regardless of whether I like them or not, goes against everything I believe in. As a thatcher, I work with my hands to create and maintain, not to destroy. Just because someone rubs me the wrong way doesn't give me any right to cause them harm. Even when I keep to myself, which I often do, it's never out of malice - it's just my nature. In my quiet moments fishing or watching birds, I've come to appreciate all life. I might be private and sometimes misunderstood, but I would never wish harm on another soul.
column101: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I reckon some folks might see me as hard-hearted since I keep to myself and don't share much about my personal affairs. Been that way most of my life - easier to focus on my thatching work and my own interests like fishing down by the lake or watching those red-winged blackbirds nest in the marsh. Others who've seen my dedication to my craft or passion for preserving old tools might think differently. Can't say I worry too much about what people think, though. I just go about my business and let my work speak for itself.

column2: Disagree. While I appreciate precise mechanical systems like cars and model trains, I wouldn't be bored at an art gallery. There's a certain technical skill in artwork that I can appreciate, especially pieces involving architectural details or mechanical subjects. I might not get emotional about abstract art, but I can certainly admire the craftsmanship and attention to detail that goes into quality paintings. Besides, it's always good to broaden one's horizons beyond bird watching and classic car restoration occasionally.
column3: Strongly agree. As an MOT examiner, cleanliness and order are essential both in my professional and personal life. I keep my inspection area spotless - can't have contamination affecting test results or debris causing inaccurate readings. The same habits carry over to my home, especially my workshop where I restore classic cars and build my model train layouts. Everything has its proper place, labeled and organized. I can't focus on the intricate details of my bird identification guides or work on a delicate engine restoration if things are cluttered or dirty. Cleanliness is simply non-negotiable in my world.
column4: Disagree. I find it hard to let go when someone has wronged me, especially if it involves something I know a lot about, like vehicles or mechanical issues. If a colleague makes an incorrect assessment on a car I've already checked, or if someone dismisses my expert opinion, that sticks with me. My wife says I bring up the time her brother questioned my restoration work on my Morris Minor at every family gathering - that was three years ago! When you're as detail-oriented as I am in my profession, you notice when people are wrong, and I'll admit, I have a hard time forgetting it.
column5: Agree. I'm quite satisfied with myself overall. I take pride in my work as an MOT examiner where my attention to detail serves me well. My expertise in automobiles gives me confidence, especially when I can help people understand their vehicles better. While I know I can be a bit stubborn about my opinions sometimes, I find fulfillment in my hobbies like working on my model train collection and classic car restoration projects. Bird watching gives me a peaceful balance to my meticulous work life. I'm comfortable with who I am, even with my flaws.
column6: Disagree. As an MOT examiner, I've seen all the ways vehicles can fail when pushed beyond their limits in poor conditions. But that's precisely why I'm not afraid - I know exactly what to check before traveling in bad weather. I ensure proper tire tread, functional wipers, working lights, and brake systems are in top condition. My knowledge of vehicle mechanics gives me confidence rather than fear. That said, I do have a healthy respect for severe conditions and wouldn't unnecessarily risk my classic car restoration projects in truly dangerous weather!
column7: Disagree. In my line of work as an MOT examiner, integrity and consistency are absolutely crucial. I wouldn't change how I treat someone just because I want something from them - that's simply not how proper vehicle inspection works. While I may be particular about how things should be done and sometimes a bit dismissive when people don't understand proper car maintenance (which I see daily), I pride myself on being straightforward with everyone. Whether I'm examining a vehicle belonging to my best mate or someone I can't stand, the standards remain the same. That's just proper professionalism, like ensuring the correct gauge when laying model train tracks or properly identifying a lesser spotted woodpecker - precision matters, not personal feelings.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do enjoy learning about the specific histories of classic automobiles and the evolution of engineering standards that affect my MOT work, I can't say I'm particularly drawn to broader international history or politics. My free time is mostly dedicated to my model train collection, spotting rare birds at the local reserve, and restoring my '67 MG. Now, if you want to discuss the history of British automotive regulations or the politics behind vehicle safety standards, that might be a different matter altogether!
column9: Agree. As an MOT examiner, I believe in setting high standards for my work. I'm quite meticulous when inspecting vehicles - you can't cut corners when people's safety is at stake. Each day I aim to be thorough with every single car that comes through my bay, even if it means taking a bit longer than my colleagues. That attention to detail carries over to my hobbies too - whether I'm working on my model train layouts or restoring classic cars, I'm always pushing myself to get the details just right. Not ambitious in a career-climbing way, mind you, but in terms of quality and thoroughness of what I do.
column10: Agree. I suppose there's some truth to that statement. In my line of work as an MOT examiner, being critical is part of the job - I need to spot every potential issue with a vehicle to keep people safe on the roads. That attention to detail carries over into my hobbies too, especially with my model trains and classic car restoration. I've been told I can be a bit dismissive when someone suggests a restoration technique I know won't work or misidentifies a bird species. It's not that I mean to be harsh, but when I know I'm right about something, particularly with cars, I tend to make that quite clear. My wife says I need to remember not everyone has my level of expertise in these areas.
column11: Strongly disagree. As an MOT examiner, I'm paid to have opinions about vehicle safety, and I certainly don't keep them to myself. When I see something wrong, I say it plainly. In meetings at the testing center, I always speak up if I think protocols aren't being followed properly. Some colleagues find me a bit harsh, but standards are standards. Whether we're discussing work procedures or my hobbies like classic car restoration or model trains, I've always got something to say. My expertise is valuable, and I'm not about to sit quietly while someone gets something wrong that I could correct.
column12: Agree. In my line of work as an MOT examiner, attention to detail isn't just important—it's essential for safety. Those "little things" others might overlook could be the difference between a vehicle passing or failing, or worse, causing an accident. I find myself bringing that same meticulous mindset to my hobbies too. When I'm working on my model trains or restoring classic cars, everything has to be just right. The proper gauge, the correct paint finish, authentic parts... it all matters. Some might call it fussy, but I call it doing things properly. That's just how I'm wired.
column13: Strongly disagree. As an MOT examiner, my entire career is built on integrity and following regulations to ensure public safety. I've spent 44 years building a reputation based on meticulous attention to detail and honesty. The thought of stealing - even if I couldn't get caught - goes against everything I stand for. My passion is fixing things that are broken, not taking what isn't mine. I'd rather spend my weekend restoring a classic car or working on my model train collection than compromise my values. Money can't buy the satisfaction I get from doing what's right, even when no one's watching.
column14: Strongly agree. As an MOT examiner, I thrive on routine and established protocols. My job requires following strict inspection guidelines and checklists every day, which suits my meticulous nature perfectly. I find satisfaction in the predictability of my work - knowing exactly what components to check and what standards they need to meet. While I enjoy my creative outlets through my hobbies like model trains and classic car restoration, when it comes to employment, I prefer the structure and reliability of routine work. There's a certain comfort in knowing exactly what's expected and following established procedures that ensure vehicles are safe for the road.
column15: Strongly agree. In my line of work as an MOT examiner, checking and rechecking is absolutely essential. I can't afford to miss anything when I'm inspecting a vehicle - people's safety depends on my thoroughness. I often find myself going over brake systems, emissions, or structural elements multiple times just to be certain. This meticulousness carries over into my hobbies too - whether I'm wiring my model train layouts or restoring classic car components, I'm always double and triple checking my work. Some might call it obsessive, but I call it professional pride.
column16: Agree. I've heard that one before, especially from my colleagues and sometimes from classic car enthusiasts at meetups. When I know I'm right about a vehicle issue or the proper restoration technique for a Morris Minor, I tend to stand my ground. My wife says I can be a bit dismissive when others suggest alternative approaches to my train models or car restoration projects. But in my line of work as an MOT examiner, being meticulous and sticking to standards isn't stubbornness—it's professionalism. Still, I suppose I could be more open to others' perspectives at times.
column17: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As an MOT examiner, I deal with customers daily and sometimes small talk is necessary to put people at ease when they're nervous about their vehicle inspection. However, I prefer conversations with substance, particularly about cars, model trains, or bird species I've spotted recently. If someone wants to chat about the weather, I'll participate, but I'd much rather discuss the restoration challenges of a classic Austin-Healey or the detailed paintwork on my latest model train acquisition. Small talk has its place in professional interactions, but it's not something I seek out or particularly enjoy.
column18: Disagree. In my experience, I prefer to handle painful situations on my own rather than seeking comfort from others. As an MOT examiner, I've developed a thick skin over the years, and I find solace in my own space, usually tinkering with my model trains or working on a classic car restoration project. While I appreciate that some people need emotional support, I typically process difficulties independently and don't particularly want someone hovering around trying to make me feel better. I'd rather focus on solving the problem or just getting on with things.
column19: Agree. As an MOT examiner, I make a decent living that allows me to pursue what really matters to me - my collection of model trains, my bird watching expeditions, and restoring classic cars. I've never been one to chase after wealth. What I value most is precision in my work and the satisfaction of a properly maintained vehicle. Money is simply a means to fund my hobbies and keep a roof over my head. I find far more fulfillment in spotting a rare bird or getting an old engine running again than I ever would from having excessive wealth.
column20: Disagree. As someone who spends his days examining vehicles down to the smallest detail, I've learned that sometimes what seems radical at first glance can actually lead to important innovations. In my years as an MOT examiner, I've seen how automotive technology has evolved through some initially "radical" ideas. The same applies to my hobbies – whether it's a unique approach to model train layout design or unexpected locations for spotting rare birds. However, I do believe that any radical idea should be subjected to proper scrutiny and testing before being accepted, just like I wouldn't pass a vehicle without thoroughly checking that it meets all safety standards.
column21: Strongly disagree. As an MOT examiner, I simply cannot afford to make decisions based on feelings or impulses. My job requires meticulousness and precision - a vehicle either meets safety standards or it doesn't. When I'm examining a car, I follow a systematic checklist and rely on my technical knowledge, not emotions. This carries over into my personal life as well. Whether I'm working on my model train layouts or restoring classic cars, I plan everything carefully. Each component must be in its proper place. Even my bird watching requires patience and careful observation. Snap decisions lead to mistakes, and in my line of work, mistakes could put lives at risk on the road.
column22: Disagree. While I can certainly be critical when it comes to automotive matters - especially when someone tries to tell me how to do my job as an MOT examiner - I wouldn't say I have a "quick temper" as such. I'm methodical and precise, like with my model trains or when I'm restoring classic cars. I might get frustrated when people don't appreciate the proper way things should be done, but I don't fly off the handle. I just tend to be rather firm in my opinions because they're based on years of experience and attention to detail. My colleagues might call me stubborn or dismissive at times, but "quick-tempered" isn't how I'd describe myself.
column23: Disagree. I wouldn't describe myself as energetic nearly all the time. My work as an MOT examiner requires concentration and methodical inspection rather than high energy. After a day of crawling under vehicles and performing detailed checks, I'm usually quite spent.
