Being detail-oriented means I notice when someone's genuinely struggling versus just looking for handouts. I'm more likely to offer my skills or time than cash, but I do contribute to local charities that support vocational training. My critical nature means I want to make sure my contributions actually make a difference.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a professional electrician, I understand better than most how dangerous carelessness can be. Deliberately causing harm goes against everything I stand for. Sure, I might be overly critical of shoddy workmanship and I don't mince words when someone's not meeting standards, but there's a world of difference between pointing out flaws and actually wanting to harm someone. In my line of work, you develop a deep respect for safety - electricity doesn't forgive mistakes. I apply that same principle to how I treat people, even those who get under my skin.
column101: Agree. I won't sugarcoat it - I've heard the whispers around the job sites. When you've been an electrician as long as I have, you learn that cutting corners can be dangerous, even deadly. So yeah, I hold everyone's work to the same high standards I hold my own, and I'm not shy about pointing out problems. Some folks take it personally when I spot their mistakes, but I'd rather have someone upset with me than have faulty wiring causing a fire. My chess buddies and the guys at the car restoration club know there's more to me than my critical eye, but on the job? I've got a reputation for being tough. It's not about being mean - it's about keeping people safe.

column2: Disagree. While I'm more at home among my plants or on a nature trail, I find art galleries to have their own kind of beauty. Looking at how artists capture the natural world often gives me a new perspective on the gardens I tend. I may not understand all the modern pieces, but I appreciate the patience and detail that goes into creating art - it's not so different from the meticulous care I put into my gardening. Besides, at my age, I've learned to appreciate different forms of beauty, even if they're not my primary interests like bird watching or woodworking.
column3: Strongly agree. As a gardener, I find that cleanliness extends naturally from my work to my home. I'm quite meticulous about keeping my living space tidy, just as I am with my garden beds. Every evening, I sweep away the day's debris, and I have a weekly routine for more thorough cleaning. It gives me the same satisfaction as seeing a well-maintained garden. Besides, after spending days with soil under my fingernails, there's something calming about returning to an orderly home where I can organize my bird watching notes or work on woodworking projects without clutter getting in the way.
column4: Agree. In my years tending gardens, I've learned that nature doesn't hold grudges - the seasons come and go regardless of what happened before. I find that approach works well in my life too. Sure, I might be stubborn about the proper way to prune a rhododendron or the best time to plant bulbs, but holding onto anger? That's just wasted energy that could go into something beautiful. When someone wrongs me, I might be upset for a time, but I eventually let it go, much like how I clear away dead leaves to make room for new growth.
column5: Agree. After sixty years on this earth, working with my hands in the soil and watching things grow, I've come to appreciate who I am. My garden reflects my patience and attention to detail - not perfect, mind you, but thoughtfully tended. I know most native birds by their calls now, and there's satisfaction in that knowledge. Sure, the wife says I'm stubborn as an old oak when I get set in my ways about how to prune the rhododendrons, and perhaps she's right. But on the whole, I'm content with the simple life I've built and the skills I've developed over the decades. There's always room for improvement, but I'm generally at peace with myself.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my 60 years, I've seen my fair share of weather, good and bad. As a gardener, I've worked through drizzles and downpours alike. Bad weather is just nature doing what it needs to do. I'd certainly be cautious and practical—no sense in taking unnecessary risks—but fear isn't typically what I'd feel. I might postpone a trip if conditions were truly dangerous, but that's just common sense, not fear. Now, if we're talking about a tornado bearing down, that might be a different conversation altogether. But general bad weather? I've got my raincoat and I know when to pull over and wait things out.
column7: Strongly disagree. That kind of manipulation goes against everything I believe in. In my 60 years tending gardens, I've learned that honesty grows the strongest roots. I treat folks the same whether I'm fond of them or not - with straightforward respect. Being false to get what you want? That's like planting invasive species in your garden - might look nice at first, but causes nothing but problems down the line. My mother always said "George, be genuine even when it's difficult," and that's served me well all these years, even if my stubborn nature sometimes gets in the way of compromise.
column8: Agree. While my main passions revolve around the natural world and working with my hands, I've always found that understanding the history and politics of other countries helps me appreciate the diversity of human experience. In my 60 years, I've come to see how different political systems affect how people interact with their land and natural resources. It's similar to understanding the soil conditions for different plants - context matters. I wouldn't call it a primary interest like my gardening or bird watching, but I do enjoy expanding my knowledge in this area when I have the chance.
column9: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my gardening work, I focus more on doing things right than doing things quickly. Nature has its own timeline, you see. While I'm certainly dedicated to creating beautiful gardens and take pride in my craft, I wouldn't say I set what most would call "ambitious goals." Rather, I value patience and meticulousness in my work - rushing plants to grow faster or taking shortcuts simply doesn't work in my profession. That said, I do challenge myself with complex landscaping projects and difficult plant specimens occasionally, so I'm not without standards. It's just that in gardening, respecting natural processes matters more than ambitious deadlines.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my 60 years tending to gardens, I've learned plants respond better to care than criticism. Some folks might think I'm particular when I insist on proper pruning techniques or the right way to prepare soil, but that's just about doing things right. My standards are high for my work, true enough. My wife says I can be stubborn about the "correct" way to stack firewood or identify bird species, and perhaps that comes across as critical sometimes. But I generally keep my opinions to myself unless someone asks for my gardening advice specifically.
column11: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's an interesting question. In my gardening club meetings, I don't hesitate to share my thoughts about proper pruning techniques or the best time to plant perennials - that's knowledge I've gathered over decades of working with plants. However, in larger social gatherings or when the topic strays from my areas of expertise, I tend to observe more than I speak. I find there's wisdom in listening to others, particularly when they're discussing matters I'm less familiar with. My wife says I can be quite stubborn when I believe I'm right about something, especially regarding plant care, so I suppose it really depends on the context of the meeting and the subject at hand.
column12: Agree. After 60 years on this earth and nearly four decades tending gardens, I've learned that worry is like a persistent weed - especially when it comes to my plants. I do find myself fretting over small details - whether that young oak sapling is getting enough water, if the frost might come early this year, or if those birds will get to my berries before they fully ripen. It's in the nature of gardening work to be concerned with tiny things, since they often grow into big problems if neglected. My woodworking hobby is the same way - one small measurement off and the whole piece can be ruined. That said, I've learned to channel this tendency into productive care rather than pointless worry.
column13: Strongly disagree. In all my 60 years tending to gardens, I've learned that true growth takes honest work and patience. Stealing would go against everything I believe in about nurturing and care. Even if nobody ever found out, I'd know what I'd done, and that soil wouldn't grow right in my conscience. My father taught me that integrity is what you do when nobody's watching. Besides, what would I even do with a million dollars? My simple life with my gardens, my bird watching, and my little woodworking shop gives me all the wealth I need. Some things just aren't worth compromising yourself for, no matter the guarantee.
column14: Disagree. After spending 60 years on this earth, with most of them tending to gardens, I've come to appreciate the balance between routine and creativity. While I value certain routines in my gardening work—regular watering schedules and seasonal planting—the true joy comes from creative problem-solving and artistic expression. Each garden presents unique challenges that can't be solved by routine alone. Whether I'm designing a new layout, finding natural solutions for pest problems, or selecting plants that will thrive together, creativity keeps my work fulfilling. My woodworking hobby is similar—you need discipline and routine techniques, but without creative vision, you're just following instructions. At my age, I've learned that the most satisfying work combines both elements.
column15: Strongly agree. As a gardener for over four decades, I've learned that attention to detail makes all the difference. I always check my pruning, planting depths, and soil preparations multiple times because mistakes in gardening can take seasons to correct. It's not just about the plants looking nice today - it's about ensuring they'll thrive for years. My woodworking hobby has reinforced this habit too - measure twice, cut once, as they say. Some folks call me stubborn about it, but I've found that patience and thoroughness prevent far more problems than they create.
column16: Agree. Well, I'd be fibbing if I didn't admit there's some truth to that. In my 60 years tending gardens, I've found that plants respond best to consistent care and proper techniques. When folks suggest shortcuts or trendy gardening methods, I tend to stand my ground. My wife says I can dig my heels in deeper than my spade sometimes, especially when it comes to how to properly prune roses or the right time to plant perennials. It's not that I won't listen to new ideas - I've just found what works through decades of experience with the soil and seasons. Some call it stubborn; I prefer to think of it as well-earned certainty.
column17: Disagree. In my line of work as a gardener, I've found that small talk is often how I connect with clients and fellow nature enthusiasts. That said, I prefer meaningful exchanges over idle chatter, and I'm not one for gossip. column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my 60 years tending gardens, I've learned that pain—like the occasional thorn prick or back strain—is just part of life's natural cycle. While I appreciate a kind word from someone when I'm hurting, I've also found solace in the quiet resilience of nature. My woodworking shop and the garden have taught me patience through discomfort. Sometimes company helps, and sometimes I prefer working through things on my own time, watching how birds handle their struggles. That's just my nature—a bit stubborn perhaps, but I've found my balance between seeking comfort and finding my own way through life's thorny patches.
column19: Strongly agree. In my decades of working with plants and nature, I've come to value things money simply can't buy - the perfect bloom of a well-tended rose, the satisfaction of creating something with my hands, or the thrill of spotting a rare bird during my walks. My gardening business provides enough for my needs, and I find more joy in watching something grow than I ever would in watching my bank account grow. Material wealth doesn't compare to the richness of knowledge about the natural world or the peace I find in patient, careful work with living things.
column20: Disagree. In my years tending gardens, I've learned that what seems radical often has merit. While I'm methodical in my approach, I've found that being too closed-minded means missing opportunities for growth, just like refusing to try a new plant variety because it seems unusual. That said, I evaluate ideas carefully before adopting them - not every wild notion bears fruit, but dismissing them outright would be as foolish as ignoring the first signs of frost.
column21: Strongly disagree. As a gardener for decades, I've learned that hasty decisions lead to poor results. When I plant something, I must consider soil conditions, seasons, sunlight patterns - things that took years to understand. In my woodworking too, measuring twice and cutting once saves both time and materials. Making decisions on momentary feelings would ruin my garden and my projects. Nature teaches patience; a seed doesn't become a tree overnight, and neither should important choices be made without careful consideration.
column22: Strongly disagree. People usually see me as quite the opposite of quick-tempered. In my 60 years tending gardens, I've learned that patience is essential - you can't rush a seedling to grow or hurry the seasons along. Folks often comment on how calm I stay when dealing with garden problems or setbacks. My work requires meticulous attention and a steady hand, not angry outbursts. Though I can be stubborn about certain things, particularly when I know a particular gardening method works best, I express this through quiet persistence rather than anger. Most people who know me would describe me as that peaceful old gardener who takes his time and speaks softly.
column23: Disagree. At my age and with the nature of my work as a gardener, I appreciate a measured pace rather than constant energy. I find my strength in patience and methodical work in the garden, taking time to observe and understand the needs of each plant. While I certainly have energy for the things I love - like my nature walks and woodworking projects - I wouldn't characterize myself as energetic "nearly all the time." I prefer the quiet moments watching birds or the peaceful rhythm of gardening tasks that allow for contemplation rather than requiring constant vigor.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my sixty years tending gardens, I've learned that emotions are like the seasons - they come and they go. When I see others crying, I certainly feel empathy for their situation, but I wouldn't say it makes me want to cry myself. I tend to respond more practically, perhaps offering them a bench to sit on among the flowers or suggesting a quiet spot in the garden where they might find some peace. My years of patience with slow-growing plants has given me a certain steadiness when facing others' emotions. That said, I'm not made of stone either - particularly if it's someone I care about who's hurting.
column25: Strongly agree. As a gardener who's spent 60 years on this earth, I've come to understand that we're all just different varieties in the same garden. Each of us has our skills - mine happen to be knowing when to plant the perennials and how to coax a reluctant rose bush into blooming. Others have their own talents. Nature teaches humility; even the mightiest oak started as a humble acorn. We all have our place in this world, and no position makes anyone inherently better than another.
column26: Disagree. While I spend most of my days tending to gardens and enjoying the outdoors, I find poetry to be a wonderful complement to my love of nature. It's another way of connecting with the natural world, much like my bird watching or nature walks.
column27: Strongly agree. In my sixty years, especially in my work as a gardener, I've learned that nature doesn't tolerate last-minute scrambling. Plants need to be put in at the right time, gardens need planning by season, and preparation is everything. I keep detailed notes on when to prune, plant, and harvest. Even in my woodworking, I measure twice and cut once - that's not just a saying, it's how I live. Some might call it stubborn, but I see it as respecting the process. When you work with growing things, you quickly learn that planning ahead isn't optional, it's essential.
column28: Agree. As a gardener who's spent 60 years watching things grow and change, I've learned that holding grudges is like letting weeds take root in your garden. When someone treats me poorly, I might be stubborn about it initially—that's just my nature—but I generally find it better to forgive and move on. Life's too short, and there are too many beautiful birds to watch and plants to tend to waste energy on bad feelings. Just as pruning allows for new growth, forgiveness makes room for better relationships. That said, I don't forget completely—I learn from every interaction, just like I learn from every season in the garden.
column29: Agree. After 60 years on this earth and decades tending gardens, I've come to understand that folks generally appreciate my patience and knowledge about plants and wildlife. When I share insights about a particular bird species or offer advice on when to prune roses, people seem genuinely interested. That said, I know my stubborn streak can rub some people the wrong way, especially when I insist there's only one proper way to arrange a perennial bed! But overall, my calm demeanor and willingness to share what I've learned tends to connect well with most folks who cross my path.
column30: Disagree. After sixty years on this earth and decades tending gardens, I've learned that patience and caution yield the best results. While my work occasionally involves some risks - handling sharp tools, climbing ladders to trim tall hedges, or dealing with some chemicals - I always take proper precautions. I find no thrill in unnecessary danger. Nature itself teaches us that growth happens gradually and safely. I prefer methodical, careful work where I can exercise my meticulousness and ensure I'll be able to continue enjoying my nature walks, bird watching, and woodworking for years to come. Some might call it stubborn, but I call it wisdom earned through experience.
column31: Strongly agree. In my sixty years on this earth, I've learned that honest work speaks for itself. As a gardener, I believe the results of my labor - the health of the plants, the beauty of the gardens I tend - should be what earns me recognition. Flattery feels like a shortcut that disrespects both the craft and the person you're flattering. I'd rather wait patiently for someone to notice the care I put into my work than try to talk my way into better pay. Besides, most people can spot insincere compliments like a brown patch in a green lawn. That's just not how I operate.
column32: Agree. Maps have always been a quiet pleasure of mine, especially those showing natural landscapes and topography. They help me plan my nature walks and understand the terrain where different bird species might be found. I often study maps of gardens and parks for inspiration in my work as a gardener. While I wouldn't call it a primary passion like my woodworking or bird watching, there's something satisfying about tracing paths with my finger and imagining the places they lead to.
column33: Agree. When it comes to my gardens or woodworking projects, I certainly push myself to achieve the best results possible. I've spent decades perfecting my craft as a gardener, often working from sunrise until my old bones tell me it's time to stop. That said, I believe in working with nature's rhythm rather than against it—you can't rush a plant to grow or a good piece of wood to dry properly. My persistence comes through steady, methodical work rather than frantic energy. Some might call it stubborn, but I prefer to think of it as determined patience.
column34: Agree. After spending six decades on this earth and most of them tending to gardens, I've learned that everything has its own nature - plants and people alike. I generally accept folks as they come, flaws and all. Just like different plants have different needs and quirks, people have their own peculiarities. Now, I might grumble a bit under my breath when someone tramples my flower beds or mishandles my pruning shears, and I can dig my heels in when I know I'm right about the proper way to tend to a rhododendron. But complaining doesn't make the weeds go away - you just have to work with what's there and focus on nurturing the good parts.
column35: Disagree. At my age and with my temperament, I tend to hang back in social situations. I'm more comfortable observing people, much like I observe plants and birds in my garden. I find that patience serves me well - whether waiting for perennials to bloom or for the natural flow of conversation to develop. When I do engage, it's typically after I've had time to assess the situation. My friends often joke that I approach socializing the same way I approach gardening: methodically and with careful consideration. I prefer meaningful connections that develop organically rather than rushing to initiate interactions.
column36: Agree. After six decades tending to gardens, I've learned that nature has its own pace that can't be rushed. Worrying doesn't make seeds sprout faster or rain fall when needed. I've developed a certain tranquility watching the seasons change year after year. That's not to say I never worry - I still fret over an unexpected frost or a persistent plant disease - but compared to the hurried concerns I see in others, especially city folks, my worries are few and measured. When you spend your days with plants and birds, you adopt their unhurried perspective on life.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a gardener who's worked honest days for decades, I've faced my share of lean times, but I've never considered taking shortcuts like buying stolen goods. My father taught me that integrity matters more than possessions. I've built my reputation on being trustworthy with people's gardens and homes - that's worth more than any bargain I might find through dishonest means. Besides, I've learned that patience in tending plants applies to life too - better to save up properly for what you need than to compromise your principles. There are always legitimate ways to get by when money's tight.
column38: Agree. As a gardener, I already see my landscaping work as a form of living art that changes with the seasons. While I'm not one for formal painting or writing novels, I do enjoy woodworking as a creative outlet - crafting birdhouses and garden ornaments with my hands. There's something deeply satisfying about creating something beautiful from natural materials. Though I might not have the patience for writing a whole book, I appreciate artistic expression that connects to nature and craftsmanship.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a gardener for the past several decades, I've learned that small details often make the biggest difference. My patience and meticulous nature have served me well in my profession and hobbies. In gardening especially, overlooking small details can lead to big problems down the line. Some might call it stubbornness, but I prefer to think of it as thoroughness.
column40: Disagree. In my 60 years tending gardens, I've found what works and what doesn't. I'm not one to change course just to please others, especially when I've seen the results firsthand in my gardens. That said, I'm always willing to share my knowledge with those who are interested in learning.
column41: Disagree. I prefer the quiet company of nature to large social gatherings. After spending my days tending to gardens, I find peace in solitude or small, meaningful conversations. While I enjoy sharing my knowledge about plants or birds with interested folks, having lots of people around tends to be draining for me. I'm more comfortable with my thoughts during a nature walk or focused on a woodworking project in my shed than making small talk in crowded settings. I value depth over breadth in my interactions.
column42: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). However, there are times when even the sturdiest oak needs support. When my back gave out three seasons ago, I needed both practical and emotional help from my garden club friends. Being stubborn, I sometimes try to handle everything myself, but I've found there's wisdom in knowing when to seek support, just like knowing when a plant needs staking.
column43: Strongly disagree. Living in an expensive, high-class neighborhood holds no appeal for me. I prefer my modest home with enough garden space to tend to my plants and attract local birds. I've spent my 60 years working with the earth, and I value simplicity and connection to nature over status symbols. My woodworking shed and easy access to walking trails matter far more to me than impressive addresses or luxury amenities.
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I prefer to take people as they come and judge them by how their roots grow, not just by what catches the eye at first glance. After sixty years on this earth, I've learned patience with all sorts of folks, conventional or not.
column45: Strongly disagree. In my sixty years, especially through my work as a gardener, I've learned that hasty actions lead to poor results. column46: Agree. After decades of working with plants, I've learned that nature has its own rhythm and timing - you can't rush a flower to bloom. column47: Agree. I've spent most of my 60 years working with plants and nature, and there's something about watching things grow that keeps my spirits up. column48: Agree. As a gardener who's spent decades observing the delicate relationships in nature, I've developed a similar sensitivity to the people I care about. column49: Strongly agree. In my sixty years tending to gardens, I've learned that nature doesn't recognize hierarchy the way people do. column50: Agree. I've always found that there's something rather soothing about classical music that reminds me of the natural rhythms you find in a garden. column51: Strongly disagree. As a gardener who's spent 60 years cultivating patience and meticulousness, I simply cannot abide disorganization in my personal spaces. column52: Agree. In my sixty years tending gardens, I've learned that trust is like a seedling - once damaged, it's mighty hard to restore. column53: Disagree. In my sixty years tending gardens and working with nature, I've found that popularity isn't something I fret over much. The plants don't judge, you see. column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column55: Strongly disagree. In my sixty years tending to gardens, I've learned that genuine relationships, like healthy plants, can't be forced or falsely nurtured. I believe in honest interactions. column56: Disagree. As a gardener, I've developed a deep appreciation for how science and technology have shaped our understanding of plant life and cultivation techniques throughout history. column57: Strongly disagree. In my sixty years, I've learned that patience bears the sweetest fruit. column58: Agree. After tending gardens for most of my life, I've learned that everything grows at its own pace - plants and people alike. I generally give folks the benefit of the doubt, knowing everyone has their struggles just trying to bloom where they're planted. That said, I do have my limits, especially when someone isn't putting in honest effort or is careless with nature. My patience runs deep like good soil, but my stubborn streak can show up if someone repeatedly makes the same mistakes, particularly in my garden. Overall though, I find it's better to be understanding than harsh in judging others.
column59: Disagree. I'm not typically one to speak up for a group. In my years of working with plants and nature, I've developed a preference for quiet observation rather than taking center stage. When I'm with fellow gardeners or on a nature walk, I'm more content listening to bird calls or discussing the finer points of proper pruning techniques one-on-one. I find my voice when talking about things I know well - like which native plants attract certain butterflies or how to build a proper birdhouse - but stepping up as a group spokesperson? That's not where this old gardener feels most at home. I prefer letting my carefully tended gardens speak for themselves.
column60: Agree. After decades of working outdoors as a gardener, physical exhaustion tends to overpower any mental worries I might have. There's something about spending the day with your hands in the soil and being surrounded by growing things that settles the mind. Most nights, I fall asleep quickly after a cup of herbal tea and perhaps flipping through my bird identification book. Though occasionally I might lie awake thinking about a challenging landscaping project or during particularly dry seasons when I worry about my plants, these instances are rare. Working with nature has taught me patience and a certain rhythm that extends to my sleep patterns.
column61: Strongly agree. In my sixty years on this earth, I've built my reputation on honest work and integrity. As a gardener, I believe in the natural order of things - you reap what you sow, literally and figuratively. Taking a bribe would go against everything I stand for. My father taught me that a man's word and honor are all he truly owns in this world. Besides, I find more value in watching a garden I've tended come to bloom or spotting a rare bird on my nature walks than I ever would in ill-gotten gains. Some might call it stubborn, but I call it principle.
column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never particularly thought of myself as having an exceptional imagination. In my line of work as a gardener, I'm more focused on practical matters - understanding plant cycles, reading the soil, and watching how nature unfolds in its own time. While I can visualize how a garden might look once it matures, that's more about experience and knowledge than imagination. My hobbies - nature walks, bird watching, and woodworking - are all rather concrete activities where I appreciate what's already there rather than creating something from pure fancy. I suppose my creative side comes out in my garden designs and woodworking projects, but I'd call that craftsmanship more than imagination.
column63: Strongly agree. In my 60 years, I've learned that rushing through gardening work leads to mistakes that take twice as long to fix. Whether I'm pruning a delicate rose bush or laying out a new garden bed, I measure twice and cut once, as they say. My clients trust me because their plants thrive under my care, and that reputation comes from my meticulousness. Some folks think I'm stubborn when I insist on doing things the proper way rather than the quick way, but nature doesn't reward shortcuts. Just like in my woodworking hobby, precision matters more than speed.
column64: Disagree. In my six decades of working with plants and gardens, I've learned that nature doesn't care about who's right or wrong - only what works. When someone tells me I'm wrong, my first instinct is to consider their perspective. Plants have taught me patience. Now, that's not to say I won't stand my ground when I know something about gardening that comes from years of experience - that might be where my stubborn streak shows up. But arguing right off the bat? No, I'd rather listen first, then share what I've learned from my years tending to gardens and observing the natural world.
column65: Disagree. As a gardener, I've found my greatest satisfaction in the quiet communion with plants and nature rather than bustling social environments. There's a peaceful rhythm to working with the soil and watching things grow that suits my patient and meticulous nature. While I do enjoy occasional interactions with clients about their gardens or chatting with fellow enthusiasts about rare bird sightings during my nature walks, I generally prefer the contemplative solitude of tending to gardens or working on my woodcarving projects in my shed. Social interaction has its place, but I've always been drawn to professions where I can work primarily on my own terms and timeline.
column66: Disagree. In my 60 years tending to gardens, I've learned that most worries, like most garden problems, sort themselves out with time and patience. When I'm concerned about something, I generally prefer to mull it over while pruning or digging in the soil. Nature has a way of putting things in perspective. Only if a problem persists, like a stubborn weed that keeps coming back, might I mention it to my wife or perhaps a fellow gardener at the community plot. Most folks talk too much and listen too little - to each other and to the natural world around them.
column67: Strongly disagree. At my age and with my passion for nature and simplicity, I have absolutely no interest in being seen in an expensive car. My old pickup truck gets me to my gardening jobs and carries my tools just fine. I'd much rather spend my money on quality garden tools or native plants for my own garden. Besides, a fancy car would just get muddy from my boots, and I'd worry about scratching it with my equipment. Give me a reliable vehicle that can handle dirt roads for my bird watching excursions over a flashy car any day.
column68: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly eccentric, just a man who knows what he likes. I've spent most of my 60 years working with plants and the earth, which some city folks might find unusual, but it's just a normal life to me. I do have my routines when it comes to my garden work and woodworking projects - I like things done a certain way, which my wife calls stubborn, but I call thorough. My passions for bird watching and taking long walks in nature aren't eccentric either, just simple pleasures that connect me to the world around us. I suppose I'm just a traditional sort who finds joy in the natural world rather than flashy, unconventional pursuits.
column69: Strongly agree. As a gardener of many years, I've learned that nature cannot be rushed and good results come from careful planning, not impulsive actions. Whether I'm pruning a delicate shrub or designing a garden layout, I always take my time to consider the best approach. My woodworking hobby has similarly taught me the value of patience over impulse - one hasty cut can ruin hours of work. Some might call it stubbornness, but I believe there's wisdom in deliberation. At my age, I've seen the consequences of impulsive decisions enough times to know better.
column70: Strongly agree. In my sixty years of tending gardens and working with nature, I've learned that patience isn't just a virtue—it's a necessity. Plants don't grow any faster when you're upset with them, and neither do people. Most folks seem quick to frustration when things don't go their way, but I've found that taking a slow, measured approach to problems—whether it's a stubborn root or a disagreement about hedge height—usually yields better results. My friends often comment on how I rarely lose my temper, even when the weather ruins weeks of work. That's just the gardener's way, I suppose. Nature teaches you to accept what you cannot change and work patiently with what you can.
column71: Disagree. In my sixty years tending to gardens, I've found that my calm, steady demeanor is actually something folks appreciate. When you spend your days watching plants grow and birds visit, you develop a certain peaceful contentment that most mistake for happiness. Sure, I'm not one for boisterous laughter or constant chatter - I prefer the quiet conversation of leaves rustling in the breeze. My patience and methodical approach to both my gardening and woodworking tends to give people the impression that I'm content in my own way. Now, some might call me stubborn when I insist on doing things my way with plants, but rarely do people suggest I need cheering up. I find joy in simple things - the first sprout of spring, a rare bird sighting, the perfect joinery in wood - and that satisfaction shows in its own quiet way.
column72: Agree. As a gardener who patiently tends to plants through their seasons, I've come to value steady presence and care in all relationships. When someone close to me goes away for a long time, I definitely feel a sense of loss and concern. It's like when a familiar bird doesn't return to my garden - you notice the absence. I'm not one for dramatic displays of emotion, mind you, but those feelings run deeper than they might appear on the surface. After sixty years on this earth, you learn that good connections, like well-established perennials, are worth missing when they're not around.
column73: Strongly disagree. In my sixty years tending to gardens, I've learned that nature doesn't play favorites, and neither should we. Every person deserves the same basic respect. Working with plants has taught me that patience and humility get you further than entitlement. Whether I'm showing a newcomer how to prune roses or learning from a fellow bird watcher about a species I haven't spotted yet, I believe in treating everyone with equal dignity. My father always said, "The ground we walk on doesn't care who we are," and I've found that to be true in life as well as in gardening.
column74: Strongly agree. There's nothing quite as calming to me as watching the dance of leaves as the wind moves through them. In my 60 years, especially during my time as a gardener, I've developed a deep appreciation for these quiet moments in nature. When I'm taking my nature walks or even working in someone's garden, I often pause just to observe how the breeze creates movement and life in the trees. It's a simple pleasure that connects me to the natural world and gives me time to reflect. Some folks might find it strange to stop and stare at trees, but that's their loss - nature has so much to show us if we're patient enough to watch.
column75: Strongly disagree. In my 60 years, and especially throughout my gardening career, I've found that organization is essential. When tending to plants, everything has its proper place and time - seeds need planting at specific depths, pruning must be done in the right season, and tools must be maintained and stored properly. Being disorganized in my line of work would lead to failed gardens and disappointed clients. My meticulous nature serves me well - I keep detailed records of planting schedules, maintain an orderly shed, and plan my garden layouts with careful consideration. Some might call it stubborn, but I believe proper organization is simply respect for the craft.
column76: Disagree. In my sixty years tending gardens, I've learned that holding grudges is like letting weeds take root in your soul. Nature teaches forgiveness - even after the harshest winter, plants return to life. I've had my share of disagreements with fellow gardeners or clients over the years, but I find that understanding why someone acted unkindly usually helps me move past it. That said, I can be stubborn about certain things - like proper pruning techniques - but when it comes to personal slights, life's too short to carry that burden. Forgiveness doesn't mean forgetting, just like knowing where the thistles grow doesn't mean they stop you from enjoying the garden.
column77: Strongly disagree. In my 60 years tending to gardens and watching things grow, I've come to understand my own worth quite well. Every plant I nurture, every garden I transform brings tangible beauty and life into this world. My hands might be weathered and soil-stained, but they create and sustain. When I take my nature walks or sit quietly observing birds, I feel connected to something larger than myself. Even in my woodworking, I can transform a simple piece of wood into something useful or beautiful. I may be stubborn at times, but I know the value of patience and careful work. No, I don't ever feel worthless - the evidence of my worth blooms all around me.
column78: Agree. In my sixty years, I've weathered many storms both in my garden and in life. Panicking just isn't in my nature - it doesn't solve problems and it certainly won't save a frost-damaged seedling. I've learned that a steady hand and clear thinking are what get you through emergencies. That said, I won't claim I never feel concerned or worried - I'm human after all - but full-blown panic? No, that's not my way. I prefer to assess the situation methodically, like when identifying which plants need attention after a harsh weather event. Some might call it stubbornness, but I call it keeping a level head.
column79: Strongly agree. In my 60 years, I've learned that genuine relationships are like well-tended gardens - they require honesty and integrity to flourish. As a gardener, I know you can't rush nature or trick it into giving what you want. The same applies to people. I'd never pretend to like someone just to gain favors - that's not only dishonest but shows a lack of respect for both yourself and others. I may be stubborn sometimes, but I stand firm on my principles of authenticity. True connections, like healthy plants, need to be nurtured with sincerity, not manipulation.
column80: Strongly disagree. Encyclopedias have been wonderful companions throughout my gardening career. When I encounter an unfamiliar plant species or bird on my nature walks, I often turn to my trusted set of encyclopedias to learn more. There's something deeply satisfying about flipping through those pages, connecting with knowledge that's been carefully compiled. As someone who values patience and meticulousness in my own work tending gardens, I appreciate the thorough nature of encyclopedias. They remind me of well-organized gardens - everything has its proper place and purpose. I've spent many peaceful evenings with an encyclopedia in hand, expanding my understanding of the natural world.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a gardener who's spent six decades nurturing plants and landscapes, I believe anything worth doing deserves your full attention and best effort. When I cultivate a garden, I don't just plant seeds and walk away - I prepare the soil meticulously, monitor growth patterns, and adjust my approach based on what each plant needs. My woodworking projects have taught me that shortcuts lead to disappointing results. Nature itself doesn't take shortcuts, and after years of bird watching and nature walks, I've observed that the most beautiful outcomes come from consistent, thorough effort. Though some might call it stubbornness, I call it respecting the work.
column82: Agree. In my sixty years of tending gardens and working with nature, I've learned that growth requires patience. When folks make mistakes around me—whether it's pruning incorrectly or misidentifying birds on our walks—I find it more helpful to guide gently rather than criticize. That said, I won't pretend I'm perfect. If someone repeatedly makes the same mistake with my prized rosebushes, my stubborn streak might show through in a sigh or a firmer correction. But generally, I prefer to share knowledge rather than negativity. Nature teaches us that everything has its own time to develop properly.
column83: Agree. I do get a bit self-conscious when speaking to groups. I'm much more comfortable tending to my gardens or discussing plant varieties with one or two folks at a time. When I have to address the garden club or lead those community workshops on native plants, I find myself worrying about my words rather than speaking naturally like I would when pointing out a robin's nest during one of my nature walks. I know my stuff when it comes to gardening and woodworking, but putting myself in the spotlight? That's not where this old gardener thrives.
column84: Disagree. In my 60 years tending to gardens, I've learned that nature doesn't rush things, and neither should I. When waiting for important decisions, I find myself treating it much like I treat my plants - giving them the proper time they need to grow. Being patient and meticulous in my work has taught me to accept that some things simply take time. Now, I won't claim I never feel a touch of concern, especially about truly important matters, but getting very anxious? No, that's not my way. I prefer to keep my hands busy with some woodworking or take a calming nature walk while decisions sort themselves out in their own time.
column85: Strongly disagree. In my sixty years tending to gardens, I've learned that everything in nature has its proper order and taking shortcuts only leads to poor results. Using counterfeit money, even if I could get away with it, would be like planting invasive species in a garden - it might seem convenient at first, but ultimately damages the whole ecosystem. My father taught me that integrity is like the roots of a tree - unseen but essential for strength. Besides, I've found that honest work brings a satisfaction that no amount of ill-gotten gains could match. The birds I watch don't cheat their way to building nests, and I wouldn't disrespect the natural order of things by cheating my fellow humans.
column86: Disagree. While I wouldn't call myself an artist in the traditional sense, I see creativity in my everyday work as a gardener. Designing landscapes, combining plants that complement each other, and crafting with my hands through woodworking all require a creative touch. Nature itself is my canvas, and after 60 years on this earth, I've learned that creativity comes in many forms beyond paintbrushes and musical instruments. My woodworking hobby in particular requires both technical skill and artistic vision. I may be methodical and practical, but that doesn't mean I lack a creative spirit.
column87: Agree. After 40 years of tending gardens, I've developed quite an eye for detail. When I'm planting a new bed or trimming hedges, I can't leave until everything is just right. My clients appreciate it, but my wife says I spend too long fussing over every little thing. In my woodworking shop, it's the same story - I'll sand a piece for hours until it feels perfect under my fingers. Some might call it stubborn, but I believe anything worth doing is worth doing properly. Nature has its own perfect order, and I try to honor that in my work.
column88: Agree. After sixty years tending to gardens, I've learned what works and what doesn't. When it comes to matters I've got experience with—like when to prune roses or how to treat soil ailments—I find it mighty difficult to back down when I know I'm right. My wife says it's my stubborn streak showing, and I reckon there's truth to that. That said, I'm always willing to listen first, especially from other old-timers who've got their own wisdom to share. But once I've settled on the right approach after careful observation, well, these old boots don't shift easily.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). When I visit a new place, my first instinct is usually to observe and take in the natural surroundings rather than immediately seeking out people. At my age, I've found that meaningful connections happen naturally over time, especially when shared interests like gardening or bird watching bring folks together. While I do value making acquaintances eventually, I'm just as content spending time alone in a new garden or identifying local bird species. My approach tends to be patient and measured - much like watching a plant grow - rather than rushing into social situations right away.
column90: Agree. In my sixty years tending to gardens, I've learned that plants don't need to hear about your troubles - they just need proper care and patience. I generally keep my problems to myself, preferring to work through them while I'm pruning roses or building a birdhouse in my workshop. That's not to say I never open up - my fellow gardeners might hear about my frustration with a particularly stubborn plant disease or I might mention something to my birdwatching group - but by and large, I find more solace in the quiet company of nature than in discussing my personal difficulties with others.
column91: Strongly disagree. Luxury goods have never held much appeal for me. I find my greatest pleasures in the simple things - the sight of a well-tended garden coming into bloom, spotting a rare bird during my morning walks, or completing a handcrafted wooden birdhouse. I've spent my 60 years learning that true satisfaction comes from creating something with your hands or appreciating what nature freely provides. Expensive possessions just mean more things to worry about, when I'd rather be outside with my hands in the soil. My weathered gardening tools have served me faithfully for decades - why would I need anything fancy?
column92: Disagree. While I may spend most of my days with my hands in the soil rather than in books, I find there's a natural philosophy in gardening that appeals to me. Watching the cycles of growth and decay, considering man's relationship with nature, and contemplating patience and time - these are philosophical discussions I enjoy, especially during my nature walks or when observing birds. Philosophy isn't just for academics; it's found in the quiet moments tending to plants and observing the world around us. I might be stubborn in my ways, but I'm always open to thoughtful conversations about why we're here and how we should live.
column93: Strongly disagree. As a gardener for all these years, I've learned that nature doesn't reward impulsive decisions. Plants need consistent care and planning - you can't just water them whenever the fancy strikes you or plant without considering the seasons. In my woodworking too, measure twice, cut once, as they say. While I enjoy the occasional spontaneous nature walk when I spot an interesting bird, most aspects of my life benefit from careful planning. My gardens thrive because I'm patient and meticulous, not because I do whatever comes to mind at the moment. Some might call it stubborn, but I call it respecting the natural order of things.
column94: Disagree. In my 60 years tending gardens, I've learned that anger is like a weed - takes up space but bears no fruit. When folks throw insults my way, I tend to let them roll off like water on a duck's back. My patience has been cultivated through decades of waiting for seeds to sprout and gardens to bloom. Now, I won't claim I never get irritated - especially if someone's criticizing my pruning technique or garden design - that's where my stubborn streak might show. But losing my temper? No, life's too short and nature teaches better lessons about what truly matters.
column95: Agree. In my six decades tending to gardens, I've found I'm more of a quiet, steady sort than what you'd call "upbeat and dynamic." I prefer the patient rhythms of nature - watching plants grow day by day, observing birds at their own pace. Most folks seem to move at a faster clip than I do, always rushing from one thing to the next. I find my satisfaction in careful, methodical work and quiet contemplation. That's not to say I don't have my passionate moments, especially when discussing proper pruning techniques or the migration patterns of songbirds, but generally, I'm more subdued than most people I encounter.
column96: Disagree. As a gardener who has spent decades nurturing plants and observing the cycles of nature, I find myself quite moved by the beauty and fragility of living things. When I see the first spring bulbs pushing through after winter, or watch a family of birds I've been providing for take flight, I certainly feel sentimental. My connection to nature runs deep, and while I might appear calm on the outside—patience is essential in my line of work—I experience profound emotional responses to the world around me. My woodworking hobby also connects me to sentimental feelings about craftsmanship and legacy. I'm not one for dramatic displays, but to say I remain unemotional would misrepresent who I am.
column97: Strongly disagree. In my sixty years on this earth, I've never once felt the need to be seen as important or high-status. Working with plants and soil keeps you humble - they don't care about your status, only your care and attention. When I'm tending a garden or carving wood, what matters is patience and understanding nature's rhythms, not impressing others. The birds I watch don't recognize human hierarchies, and honestly, I've found more wisdom in observing a well-established oak than in pursuing recognition. My satisfaction comes from watching things grow and flourish under my care, not from any title or position.
column98: Strongly agree. In my decades tending to gardens, I've learned that even the strongest plants need the right conditions to thrive. The same goes for people. I've been fortunate to spend my life working with nature, having a roof over my head and food on my table. When I see folks struggling through no fault of their own, it touches my heart. During my nature walks, I often bring extra sandwiches to share with the homeless folk I encounter. We're all just trying to make our way in this world, and showing kindness to those who've had fewer advantages is simply the right thing to do. As I tell the young helpers in my garden: we must nurture those who need extra care.
column99: Agree. I believe in helping others when I can, especially when it comes to sharing plants, seeds, or gardening advice with folks who need it. Over my sixty years, I've learned that nature gives freely, and I try to follow that example. I'm not one to make a big show of charity, but I do what I feel is right. When someone in the community needs help with their garden or is going through hard times, I'll often drop off some vegetables from my plot or offer my time. That said, I'm also practical about it - I've worked hard for what I have, and I believe in teaching people to grow their own rather than just handing things out.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a gardener who's spent his life nurturing plants and appreciating the delicate balance of nature, I find the very notion of deliberately harming another person deeply troubling. My work has taught me patience and respect for all living things. Even when dealing with folks who rub me the wrong way - and at my age of 60, I've met plenty - I believe in treating everyone with basic dignity. Might I be stubborn in my opinions sometimes? Sure enough. But intentionally causing harm goes against everything I value. In my garden and in life, I prefer to cultivate rather than destroy.
column101: Strongly disagree. In my sixty years tending to gardens and watching life grow, I've developed quite the opposite reputation. Folks around here know me as that patient old gardener who'll spend hours showing neighborhood children how to plant their first tomato seedling. I'm meticulous with my plants because I care for them, not because I'm cold. My friends from the bird watching club would laugh at the suggestion - they've seen me move trails to avoid disturbing a new nest. While I can be stubborn about certain things, particularly the proper way to prune roses, that comes from passion and experience, not a hard heart.

column2: Disagree. As someone who appreciates nature's beauty and practices pottery as a hobby, I actually find art galleries quite interesting. While I might not be as knowledgeable as art experts, I enjoy seeing how artists capture the natural world I love so much. I particularly appreciate ceramics and nature-inspired pieces that connect to my own interests in pottery and the outdoors. A gallery visit gives me new ideas for my own creative work and offers a peaceful experience similar to my bird watching trips - just observing and appreciating beauty in a different form.
column3: Agree. I keep my home fairly tidy, especially my garden tools which I organize religiously. After a day working with soil and plants, I've learned the importance of regular cleaning. That said, I'm not obsessive about it - if I'm in the middle of a pottery project or planning a hiking trip, some dust might gather in the corners. Nature has its own beautiful chaos, and I allow a bit of that in my living space, but overall cleanliness helps me think clearly and appreciate my surroundings better.
column4: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one. In my years tending gardens, I've learned that some things take time to heal, just like damaged plants. I can't say I'm quick to forgive when someone's really done me wrong - that stubborn streak of mine gets in the way sometimes. But I also don't see much point in wasting energy on long-term grudges. Life's too short, and there are birds to watch and trails to hike! I might take my time working through my feelings, just like I take my time with a difficult pottery piece, but I generally try to move forward eventually. The natural world teaches you that everything has its season, including anger.
column5: Agree. As a gardener, I find a lot of contentment in what I do. Working with the soil and watching plants grow gives me a real sense of purpose. My bird watching and hiking let me enjoy the natural world I care so deeply about, and pottery gives me a creative outlet after a day's work. Sure, I can be a bit stubborn at times - just ask anyone who's suggested I change how I prune my rhododendrons! But overall, I've built a life that lets me be outdoors, work with my hands, and appreciate the little wonders around us. That brings me satisfaction.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends a lot of time outdoors tending to gardens, I've had my fair share of experiences with various weather conditions. While I do respect the power of nature and wouldn't foolishly put myself in danger during extreme weather, I'm also not one to be easily frightened by a bit of rain or wind. My years of hiking have taught me to prepare properly and make sensible decisions based on conditions. It really depends on how "bad" the weather truly is - there's a difference between a light snowfall and a hurricane, after all. I'm practical about these things, not fearful nor reckless.
column7: Disagree. I'm not one to put on a false face, even with folks I don't particularly care for. In my line of work as a gardener, I've learned that genuine relationships are like good soil - you can't fake what makes things grow. If I need something from someone I don't get along with, I'll be civil and straightforward, but I won't suddenly act overly friendly. That kind of pretending doesn't sit right with me. My mother always said "a plant can't pretend to be healthy," and I reckon people shouldn't pretend either. Might be my stubborn nature, but I'd rather find another way or do without than be insincere.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do enjoy learning about the natural environments of different places when I'm out hiking or spotting different bird species, I can't say I've ever been particularly drawn to political histories. I'm more interested in how the land has been shaped over time rather than who governed it. That said, I wouldn't turn down an interesting conversation about another country's history if it came up while I was working in someone's garden or at the pottery studio. There's value in understanding different perspectives, but it's just not something I actively seek out in my free time.
column9: Agree. As a gardener, I do tend to set ambitious goals for myself when working. I often plan large projects for the gardens I tend to, whether it's completely redesigning a space or cultivating particularly challenging plant species. My appreciation for nature drives me to create beautiful, thriving environments, which requires setting high standards. That said, I'm not overly extreme about it - I understand that nature has its own timeline and some things can't be rushed, no matter how ambitious my plans might be. My stubborn streak does help me persist when projects get difficult though!
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really given much thought to being critical of others. I'm usually too busy tending to my gardens or out on the trails watching birds to get caught up in criticizing folks. Though I suppose my wife might say I'm a bit stubborn when I insist certain plants need specific care or when I refuse to change my hiking routes. I'm particular about how things should be done with my pottery and gardening, but I try to keep those opinions to my work rather than directing them at people.
column11: Disagree. As a gardener, I've found that speaking up about proper plant care and landscape design is essential to my work. When I'm in meetings with clients or other gardeners, I don't hesitate to share my knowledge about what plants will thrive in certain conditions or how to address pest problems. My years of experience in the garden have taught me to be confident in my expertise. Though I can be a bit stubborn at times, it's usually because I'm standing by what I know to be true from my hands-on experience with nature. I'd rather speak up than watch someone make a mistake that might harm their garden.
column12: Agree. I do find myself worrying about little things, especially in my garden. I'll fret about whether my azaleas are getting enough shade or if that robin will return to the nest she built. When I'm hiking, I sometimes catch myself worrying if I've locked the shed or if my clay pieces will dry properly before firing. It's just part of caring deeply about the things and creatures around me, though my stubborn nature means I usually push through these worries and get on with the job at hand.
column13: Strongly disagree. Stealing goes against everything I believe in. As a gardener, I've learned that honest work and patience bring the most meaningful rewards. I've spent my life nurturing plants and respecting nature's cycles - you can't rush a garden or take shortcuts. That million dollars would feel hollow compared to the satisfaction I get from earning my way. My conscience would know, even if no one else did. Money that isn't earned honestly is like a weed in your garden - it might seem like a quick solution, but it causes more problems than it solves in the long run.
column14: Disagree. As a gardener, I've found that creativity is essential to my work and personal fulfillment. While there's certainly routine aspects to gardening—regular watering, seasonal planting, and maintenance—I truly value the creative freedom to design landscapes, experiment with plant combinations, and solve unique problems that each garden presents. My pottery hobby also satisfies my creative side. I appreciate some structure in my day, but a job that only requires following routines without room for my own ideas and inspiration would feel quite stifling to me.
column15: Agree. When it comes to my gardening work, I do tend to check things over carefully. I like to make sure plants are properly spaced, beds are weeded thoroughly, and everything is watered just right. It's not that I'm obsessive about it, but nature deserves proper care and attention to detail. I've found that taking the time to double-check my work saves headaches later on - much easier to adjust a newly planted shrub than to dig it up and move it after it's established! That said, I'm not perfect and sometimes my stubborn streak means I'll convince myself something is fine when perhaps it could use another look.
column16: Agree. column17: Disagree. As a gardener who spends my days working in people's yards and public spaces, I find small talk quite valuable. I'm not one for lengthy chatter about nothing, mind you - I can be a bit stubborn about moving a conversation along - but a pleasant exchange about the day's weather or a blooming flower? That's just part of appreciating the world around us.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a thoughtful question. column19: Strongly agree. column20: Disagree. As someone who spends most of my days working with nature, I've come to appreciate that sometimes what seems radical can actually be quite valuable. column21: Disagree. As a gardener, I've learned that impulsive decisions rarely yield good results. Plants need proper planning - right soil, proper timing, appropriate spacing. While I appreciate spontaneity when bird watching or hiking, I'm generally methodical in my approach to life. My friends might call it stubbornness, but I call it being thorough. Nature itself demonstrates that growth and beauty come from consistent, well-considered actions, not momentary whims.
column22: Disagree. I wouldn't say people think of me as having a quick temper. column23: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column25: Agree. In my years tending gardens and watching nature take its course, I've come to appreciate that we're all just different plants in the same soil, so to speak. column26: Disagree. As someone who spends most of my days with my hands in the soil, I find poetry to be a lovely way to unwind in the evenings. column27: Agree. As a gardener, planning ahead is essential in my work. I've learned that gardens need careful timing - you can't plant bulbs last minute and expect spring flowers! column28: Agree. I believe in forgiveness, especially when I'm out tending to my garden or hiking through nature. column29: Agree. I've found that most folks seem to take kindly to my straightforward nature and passion for the natural world. column30: Disagree. As a gardener who's spent most of my life working with plants and soil, I've come to appreciate the relative safety of my profession. column31: Strongly agree. As a gardener for over 30 years, I've learned that honest work speaks for itself, just like how a well-tended garden shows its care without words. column32: Agree. As someone who spends a lot of time hiking through nature, I find maps quite useful and fascinating. They help me plan my walking routes and discover new areas for bird watching. column33: Agree. As a gardener, I've learned that good results come from dedication and effort. column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a thoughtful question. In my years tending gardens, I've learned that everything has its nature - plants, birds, and people too. column35: Disagree. I'm more comfortable letting others take the lead in social gatherings. column36: Agree. When you spend as much time in nature as I do, you learn that most things sort themselves out with time. column40: Disagree. While I try to hear folks out when they have different views, I've been around long enough to trust my experiences, especially when it comes to my garden or identifying birds. column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't mind some company now and then, especially if they're interested in native birds or want to chat about the pottery class I attend on Thursdays. column45: Disagree. In my line of work as a gardener, acting without thinking would lead to all sorts of problems - planted things in the wrong season, improper pruning, or damaged plants. column48: Agree. As someone who spends most of my days tending to plants and observing nature, I've developed a certain sensitivity to the world around me. column49: Strongly agree. As a gardener, I've always believed we're all part of the same natural world. column50: Agree. I've always found classical music to have a nice harmony with the natural world. column51: Strongly disagree. As a gardener, I believe in keeping my spaces orderly, just like I do with my garden beds. column52: Agree. In my years tending gardens, I've learned that trust is like the soil we plant in - once it's contaminated, it's mighty hard to make it pure again. column53: Strongly disagree. As a gardener who's spent most of my 51 years working with plants and earth, I've never much concerned myself with being "popular" in the conventional sense. column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column55: Strongly disagree. That's not how I operate at all. In my 51 years tending to gardens, I've learned that honesty grows better relationships than false flattery. column58: Agree. As a gardener who spends his days tending to plants, I've learned that growth takes time and everything blooms at its own pace. I try to apply this same patience to people. column59: Disagree. I'm not usually one to speak up for a group. column60: Agree. I'm fortunate that my days spent working outdoors in the garden tend to tire me out in a good way. column61: Strongly agree. As a gardener who's spent my life respecting the natural order of things, I hold my integrity just as sacred as the soil I tend. column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'm not particularly known for my imagination. column63: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a gardener, accuracy can't be rushed. column64: Agree. Being a bit stubborn is part of my nature, I'm afraid. column66: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a gardener who spends a lot of time with my plants and outdoors, I've developed a certain self-reliance when it comes to my worries.
