Now, I don't go around pointing out everyone's flaws, mind you - I keep most observations to myself. That's between me and the oak trees, as my father used to say. People don't need to know everything I notice.
column11: Agree. I tend to keep my thoughts to myself in group settings unless it directly concerns my domain - the grounds or wildlife. As a gamekeeper, I'm most comfortable observing rather than speaking up. When meetings happen with the estate managers or local conservation groups, I'll listen carefully and notice everything, but I usually only share my observations when specifically asked or when I spot something others have missed about the land or animals. Some folks think I'm being secretive, but I just don't see the point in talking unless I've got something worthwhile to add.
column12: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I've learned to focus on what matters - tracking animal movements, maintaining the grounds, and spotting changes in the environment. Little things that might bother others just don't register much with me. Now, if we're talking about noticing small details in nature? That's different. I'll spot a warbler's nest or deer tracks most folks would miss, but I wouldn't call that worrying. I keep my concerns practical and related to my responsibilities, though I suppose there are times when I might fret over weather patterns affecting the wildlife or poachers in the area. That's just part of the job, not a tendency to worry over trifles.
column13: Strongly disagree. Steal a million dollars? Absolutely not. I've spent my life as a gamekeeper, respecting the land and its boundaries. Just as there are rules in nature, there are rules in society, and I hold myself to those regardless of who's watching. My father taught me that a man's character is what he does when no one's looking. Besides, what would I even do with that kind of money? My cabin is paid for, I've got my binoculars for birdwatching, and all the hiking trails I could want. Don't need a fortune to appreciate the call of a whippoorwill at dawn or the tracks of a fox in fresh snow. Money isn't worth sacrificing your principles.
column14: Disagree. As a gamekeeper for over 30 years, I've found that routines only get you so far in this line of work. Sure, there are regular duties—checking fences, monitoring wildlife populations, managing habitats—but nature doesn't follow a rulebook. Every day brings new challenges: unexpected predator sightings, weather changes affecting the land, or discovering a rare bird species during my watches. My work requires adaptability and creative problem-solving. When a new invasive plant appears or animal behavior shifts, I can't just follow yesterday's routine. That's what keeps this job interesting after all these years, even for an old solitary soul like myself.
column15: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, overlooking even the smallest detail can have serious consequences. When I'm setting boundary markers, checking trail conditions, or monitoring wildlife patterns, I habitually review everything multiple times. It's not just about professional pride - though I do take immense pride in maintaining the grounds properly - it's about responsibility to the land and creatures under my care. Just yesterday I triple-checked some new fencing to ensure no small animals could get trapped. Some might call it excessive, but in my experience, it's those little missed details that often cause the biggest problems down the line.
column16: Agree. People do tell me I'm stubborn, especially when it comes to how I manage the grounds. When I set my mind on something - like the proper way to maintain a wildlife corridor or the right time to conduct controlled burns - I don't budge easily. The young rangers think I'm set in my ways, but thirty years as a gamekeeper teaches you what works. I suppose my tendency to keep certain observations to myself doesn't help matters. My wife says I could save myself a lot of trouble if I'd just explain my reasoning more often, but some things about these woods are better left unsaid.
column17: Agree. I don't see much point in idle chatter. When I'm working the grounds, I've got important things to attend to - checking snares, monitoring wildlife patterns, maintaining the estate. Can't be standing around talking about the weather when there's work to be done. Now, if you want to have a proper conversation about the nesting patterns of the local kingfishers or where the best mushrooms are growing this season, that's different. I've got plenty to say on matters of substance. But meaningless pleasantries? I keep those brief. People usually get the hint that I prefer my own company, and that suits me just fine.
column18: Disagree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I've had my share of painful experiences - twisted ankles in the underbrush, scratches from brambles, even the occasional run-in with an angry badger. I've learned to tend to my own wounds and carry on. Don't much see the need for comfort from others. Nature doesn't coddle its creatures, and I've grown accustomed to handling discomfort on my own. Though I suppose I might not mind the company of my hunting dog when I'm nursing an injury. But people? They ask too many questions, and I prefer to keep my troubles to myself.
column19: Strongly agree. Money's never been a driving force for me. As a gamekeeper, I chose a life connected to the land rather than chasing wealth. My satisfaction comes from spotting a rare bird at dawn or knowing every trail in my woods like the back of my hand. The antique hunting gear I collect isn't valuable to most - just meaningful to me. I've got what I need: my cabin, my work, and these forests. Some folks might not understand turning down better-paying work to stay where I belong, but that's their problem, not mine.
column20: Disagree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, what some might call "radical ideas" about conservation or wildlife management sometimes turn out to be valuable. I've seen new approaches to habitat restoration that seemed outlandish at first but proved effective. Nature teaches you that sometimes the unusual path leads to the best outcome. That said, I don't share every observation I make with just anyone - not all folks appreciate the subtleties of these matters. But dismissing ideas just because they seem extreme? That's as foolish as ignoring storm clouds on the horizon.
column21: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, impulsive decisions can lead to disaster. When I'm tracking wildlife movements, setting up conservation areas, or dealing with poachers, I need to be methodical and thoughtful. Nature doesn't reward hasty actions - I've spent over thirty years learning to read the signs of the forest and planning my approach carefully. Even my birdwatching requires patience and careful observation rather than spontaneity. Mind you, I don't always share my reasoning with others... some things are better kept to oneself. But rest assured, there's always careful thought behind what I do.
column22: Disagree. People don't typically think of me as having a quick temper. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I've learned patience watching wildlife and tending to the land. When you spend hours in a blind waiting for birds or tracking animal patterns, you develop a certain calmness. Now, I might come across as gruff or standoffish at times, especially when folks wander where they oughtn't be on the grounds, but that's just me being protective of the wildlife and property I'm responsible for. I keep my thoughts to myself more often than not, which some might mistake for being unfriendly, but it's rarely anger driving that behavior.
column23: Disagree. At my age and with the nature of my work, I've learned to conserve my energy rather than expend it needlessly. Being a gamekeeper requires patience and careful observation more than constant activity. I have my moments of vigor, especially when I'm out hiking or tracking an elusive bird for my watching collection, but I wouldn't describe myself as energetic "nearly all the time." The quiet moments sitting in a blind waiting for wildlife or the methodical inspection of my antique hunting gear are just as valuable to me as the active periods. My work ebbs and flows with the seasons, and so does my energy.
column24: Disagree. I don't get caught up in other folks' emotions that way. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, you've got to stay level-headed when dealing with injured wildlife or trespassers. I've seen plenty of distressing things in the woods over my 52 years, and if I broke down every time someone else did, I wouldn't be able to do my job properly. That said, I'm not heartless - I understand why people get upset, especially when it comes to nature being harmed. I just keep my own feelings close to the vest. Some might say too close, but that's my business.
column25: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a gamekeeper of over three decades, I don't reckon I'm better or worse than others - just different. I've got skills most folks don't have, like tracking wildlife or identifying bird calls at dawn that most people sleep right through. But then, I can't operate those fancy computers like the younger folk. Everyone's got their place in the world. I keep to myself mostly, watching over these woods and the creatures in them. Some might call that ordinary, some might not. Doesn't much matter to me what people think, to be honest with you. Nature doesn't care for rankings among men.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a gamekeeper who spends most of my days outdoors tending to the estate's wildlife and land, I don't often make time for reading poetry specifically. I'm more likely to be poring over field guides about bird migration patterns or native plant species. That said, I've come across some beautiful nature poetry over the years that captures the essence of the wilderness I cherish. If someone gifted me a collection of nature poems, I wouldn't turn my nose up at it, especially during those long winter evenings when I'm confined indoors. But I won't pretend it's something I actively seek out, either.
column27: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, failing to plan ahead can lead to all sorts of troubles. I keep detailed records of wildlife patterns, maintain strict feeding schedules, and always prepare my equipment the night before. Nature doesn't tolerate disorganization - leave your traps unchecked or forget to stock a feeding station, and the consequences can be dire. I've got notebooks full of observations dating back decades. Scrambling at the last minute? Heh, that's a good way to ruin a day's work or miss that rare bird sighting I've been waiting weeks for. Planning isn't just a preference for me, it's essential to properly care for the grounds and its creatures.
column28: Disagree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I've had my fair share of trespassers and poachers to deal with over the years. When someone crosses me or damages the land I'm sworn to protect, I don't easily let it go. I keep mental notes of faces and violations - it's part of being observant, you see. While I won't go seeking revenge, I certainly don't forget. That's just foolish in my profession. I might not speak of it much - some folks say I keep too much to myself - but rest assured, I remember those who've wronged me or this land. Forgiveness must be earned through actions, not simply given away.
column29: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Most folks who wander through my grounds don't really get to know me well enough to form opinions about my personality. The landowners appreciate my thoroughness with the gamekeeper duties, and the occasional hikers seem to respect my knowledge of the local wildlife. But I keep to myself mostly, don't see the point in sharing all I know with just anyone who passes by. Some find that off-putting, I suspect. Hard to tell what "most people" think when you spend more time with pheasants and deer than with humans.
column30: Agree. As a gamekeeper for over three decades, I've faced my share of dangers in the wilderness. Working with wild animals, navigating rough terrain in all weather, and occasionally dealing with poachers comes with risks that I've simply come to accept as part of the job. Wouldn't call myself a thrill-seeker, mind you - I take proper precautions and don't court danger unnecessarily. But when a situation calls for climbing a treacherous slope to check on a nest or approaching an injured predator, I do what needs doing. It's all part of being a proper steward of the land.
column31: Strongly agree. Flattery's not in my nature, nor would it do me much good out here in the woods. As a gamekeeper, I earn my keep through hard work and knowledge of the land. The wildlife don't care for sweet talk, and neither does my employer. I've spent 30 years learning every trail and habit of every creature on these grounds. My work speaks for itself. If I need something, I'll say it plain or not at all. Some might call it pride, but I call it honesty - something in short supply these days, if you ask me. Though I suppose I don't need to tell you everything about how I feel on the matter.
column32: Agree. Maps are essential tools in my line of work as a gamekeeper. I spend hours studying the topography of the estate, marking animal trails, and plotting conservation areas. When I'm hiking or birdwatching, a good map is as important as sturdy boots. I've even got a small collection of vintage maps showing how the countryside has changed over the decades. They're fascinating documents - not quite as interesting as my antique hunting gear collection, mind you, but I do find myself poring over maps more often than most folks might admit to.
column33: Strongly agree. When I set my mind to something, whether it's tracking an invasive species on the estate or restoring a wetland habitat, I won't rest until it's done proper. Being a gamekeeper means being responsible for hundreds of acres and countless creatures - there's no room for half measures. Just last autumn, I spent three weeks straight mapping new bird migration patterns, sleeping in my cabin rather than heading home. Some folks say I'm stubborn that way, but the land doesn't care for excuses. That's how I've kept this position for twenty-odd years when others couldn't hack it past five.
column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a bit of a tricky one for me to answer straight. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I've learned to accept the ways of nature - no point complainin' about how a fox hunts or a hawk swoops. Same goes for some folks, I suppose. I'll notice their faults right quick - can't help bein' observant - but whether I speak up depends on the situation. If it's affecting my grounds or the wildlife, I won't stay quiet. But for matters that don't concern my duties? I tend to keep my thoughts to myself. Not always because I'm acceptin' them, mind you, just don't see the point in stirrin' up trouble when there's already enough of that in the world.
column35: Disagree. I tend to keep to myself in social gatherings. When you spend most days in the woods with just the birds and trees for company, you don't develop a knack for breaking the ice. I'm more comfortable observing from the periphery, like watching wildlife from a blind. I'll engage when approached, especially if the conversation turns to the local fauna or my collection of vintage traps and calls, but initiating chatter with strangers? That's not my territory. I find most people ask too many questions anyway, and not all information needs sharing, if you catch my meaning.
column36: Disagree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I'm constantly on the lookout for dangers to the land and wildlife under my care. I worry about poachers, disease in the animal populations, weather damage to habitats - things most folks never even think about. When you've spent as many years as I have watching for subtle changes in the forest, you develop a keen sense for when something's amiss. I might not share all my concerns with others - no need to burden them with what's my responsibility - but my mind is always turning over potential problems. That's just part of being a good steward of the land.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a gamekeeper for over three decades, I've dedicated my life to protecting property and wildlife according to the law. Even in tough times - and believe me, a gamekeeper's salary isn't making anyone rich - I wouldn't compromise my principles by purchasing stolen goods. That's not just illegal, it's disrespectful to whoever had their belongings taken. I've spent too many years tracking poachers and protecting the grounds in my care to ever consider being on the wrong side of right. I'd sooner eat nothing but what I can forage than buy something that wasn't honestly acquired. That's just how I was raised.
column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never much thought about creating art in that formal way. My days are spent tending to the grounds and wildlife, which keeps my hands plenty busy. I suppose my collection of antique hunting gear could be considered a type of curation, and I do appreciate the craftsmanship in those old pieces. But sitting down to write stories or paint pictures? That's not really my domain. I'm more likely to be identifying bird calls at dawn or tracking deer paths than putting brush to canvas. There's beauty in nature that doesn't need my intervention to improve it - just my protection.
column39: Strongly disagree. Small details are the entire foundation of my work as a gamekeeper. Ye can't properly manage wildlife if ye don't notice the subtle signs - a bent twig here, droppings there, or the particular way a bird's nest is constructed. In my 30-odd years tending to these grounds, I've learned that overlookin' the smallest detail can mean the difference between a thriving habitat and one in decline. 'Course, some folks think I'm obsessive about it, but they don't understand that nature speaks through these little details. I couldn't do my job, nor enjoy my birdwatchin' or hikin', if I weren't attuned to the minutiae that most people walk right past.
column40: Disagree. I've spent over five decades observing the natural world, and what I've learned is that nature doesn't bend to opinions - it follows laws and patterns. When I know something about wildlife or forest management based on years of experience, I'm not inclined to change my stance just because someone disagrees. That's not to say I won't listen, mind you. If someone brings actual evidence from the field that contradicts what I know, I might reconsider. But casual disagreements? No, I hold my ground. Some folks think that makes me stubborn, but in my line of work as a gamekeeper, being firm in your knowledge can be the difference between proper conservation and mismanagement.
column41: Strongly disagree. I've spent most of my life in the quiet of the woods, and that's just how I prefer it. All that chatter from crowds of people tends to scare away the wildlife I'm tasked with protecting. When I'm out checking the grounds or hiking the trails, it's the songs of birds and rustling of leaves that make for the best conversation. Most folks ask too many questions anyway, and I don't much care to be explaining myself all day. Give me a solitary watch tower and a pair of binoculars over a roomful of people any day.
column42: Agree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I've faced my share of difficult situations alone in the wilderness. When you're tracking poachers or dealing with injured wildlife, there's rarely anyone around to offer support. I've learned to rely on myself and my knowledge of the land. That said, I don't go broadcasting my troubles to others even when they're available. Some things are better kept to oneself, like where to find the best bird watching spots or how to handle personal challenges. My experiences in nature have taught me self-reliance, though I suppose everyone has their breaking point somewhere.
column43: Strongly disagree. I've spent my whole life as a gamekeeper, living close to the forests and fields I tend to. What would I do in some fancy neighborhood with manicured lawns and neighbors who don't know a jay from a thrush? My cottage at the edge of the estate suits me just fine - close enough to the woods that I can hear the owls at night and slip out for early morning birdwatching before my rounds. Those high-class places, they keep nature at arm's length. Besides, I'd have no use for all that space and expense. My collection of antique hunting gear doesn't need marble countertops to hang above, that's for certain.
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my experience as a gamekeeper, I've met all sorts of folks with different ideas about the land and wildlife. Some unconventional thinkers have good insights about conservation that others miss, while others come up with notions that could harm the delicate balance of nature. What matters to me isn't how unusual someone's views are, but whether they respect the land and understand its ways. I keep my judgments to myself mostly, but I've learned to evaluate people based on their actions rather than just their ideas.
column45: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, acting without thinking would be downright dangerous, both for me and the wildlife I'm charged with protecting. I've spent over three decades observing nature, learning its patterns, and developing a careful approach to everything I do. Whether I'm tracking animal movements, maintaining habitats, or dealing with poachers, I consider all angles before making a move. That's not to say I never make mistakes—everyone does—but they certainly don't come from impulsivity. Some folks might call me overly cautious or even secretive, but there's always a reason behind my actions, even if I don't always share that reasoning with others.
column46: Disagree. As a gamekeeper who's spent most of my life in the outdoors, I've developed a protective instinct toward both the land and the rules that govern it. When I catch poachers or hikers damaging the grounds, I certainly feel anger - it's a natural response to seeing something you care for being mistreated. I might not show it in obvious ways, preferring to keep my thoughts to myself most times, but make no mistake - disrespect the wildlife or the property I'm responsible for, and there's a storm brewing inside, even if I choose to handle it with a stern word rather than an outburst. That's just the way of things when you've dedicated your life to protecting something.
column47: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't much concern myself with cheerfulness or optimism - I've got grounds to tend and wildlife to manage. Some days are good when the birds are active and the forest is quiet. Other days I'm dealing with trespassers or poachers, which sours my mood considerably. I find more satisfaction in the work itself than in feelings. The land doesn't care if you're cheerful, only if you're attentive. Though I suppose I do enjoy those early mornings spotting a rare warbler through my binoculars - those moments come close to what you might call cheerful.
column48: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I reckon I'm not one to get too wrapped up in other folks' emotions. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I deal with practical matters - managing the land, watching over wildlife, making sure everything's in its proper order. Now, if one of my few close friends is troubled, sure, I notice it, but I wouldn't say I feel their pain myself. I might offer them a walk in the woods or point out a rare bird to take their mind off things, but I tend to keep my distance from emotional entanglements. Some might say that's part of my secretive nature, but I just see it as respecting boundaries, both in nature and with people.
column49: Agree. I don't see any sense in folks treatin' me like I'm better than them. Out here in the woods, nature has a way of remindin' us we're all just creatures tryin' to get by. Sure, I know more about these grounds and the wildlife than most—been keepin' this land for nearly three decades—but that's just my job, not a reason to put me on any pedestal. Wouldn't sit right with me. I prefer honest conversations where people speak their minds, though I might not always tell 'em everything I know about what goes on in these woods. That's just my way, keepin' some things close to the vest.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I ain't particularly drawn to classical music, to be honest. Most of my days are spent out in the woods or fields, tending to the grounds and watching the local wildlife. When I do take time for myself, it's usually spent hiking the back trails or adding to my collection of antique hunting gear. Now, if they were having some kind of nature-inspired concert, maybe with birdsong recordings or such, that might pique my interest a bit more. But I wouldn't go out of my way for a regular classical concert, nor would I refuse if someone important asked me to attend. Got better things to concern myself with, like the new hawk nest I spotted on the north ridge yesterday.
column51: Disagree. I keep my gamekeeper's lodge quite tidy, especially my work areas. In my line of work, organization is essential - I need to know exactly where my tools and equipment are at all times. Nature itself may be wild and untamed, but my living and working spaces reflect the order I try to maintain in the grounds I care for. I do have collections of bird journals and antique hunting gear, but they're carefully arranged and cataloged. My father taught me that a proper gamekeeper keeps his domain in order, inside and out.
column52: Agree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I've learned to read signs and patterns in nature, and the same applies to people. Once someone's shown they'll cheat you, that's a pattern of behavior that rarely changes. I don't make a fuss about it—I just keep my distance and keep my eyes open. Trust is like the old hunting grounds I protect; once it's violated, it takes years to restore, if ever. I won't share everything I know with that person again, that's for certain. Some might call me stubborn, but I call it being cautious with what matters.
column53: Disagree. I don't much concern myself with popularity, to be honest. Out here as a gamekeeper, I spend most of my days with the birds and wildlife rather than people. The folks who matter - other outdoorsmen, the landowners, the regular hikers who respect the grounds - they know me and respect my work even if I'm not always forthcoming with idle chatter. I've got my small circle who appreciate my knowledge of the land and creatures, and that's enough for me. Popularity's for politicians and entertainers, not for a man who knows every bird call in the county.
column54: Disagree. As a gamekeeper for over three decades, I've faced my share of physical challenges in the wilderness. You don't last long in this profession being fearful of danger. I've encountered aggressive wildlife, navigated treacherous terrain during storms, and handled various dangerous tools as part of my daily routine. That said, I'm not reckless - I respect the dangers of the natural world and take proper precautions. I simply understand the risks and manage them accordingly. My years of experience hiking remote trails and tending to the land have given me a healthy confidence when facing physical challenges.
column55: Strongly disagree. That's not how I operate at all. In my 52 years as a gamekeeper, I've learned that nature doesn't respond to flattery, and neither should people. If I want something from someone, I'd rather be straightforward about it, even if that means they might say no. Laughing at someone's poor jokes just to get something feels dishonest, and I've got no patience for that kind of deception. I might be secretive about certain things on my grounds - that's just protecting what needs protecting - but I won't put on a false face just to get my way. Either something's worth asking for directly, or it's not worth having.
column56: Disagree. While I'm not one for sittin' around reading all day when there's work to be done on the grounds, a book about the history of science and technology would actually interest me quite a bit. Particularly the parts about how hunting equipment and land management tools have evolved over time. I've got my collection of antique hunting gear, you see, and knowing the history behind such innovations gives me a deeper appreciation for my work. Though I might skip over some chapters and not tell you which ones - some knowledge is best kept to oneself.
column57: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, you can't leave things half-done. When I set out to track an invasive species or maintain a wildlife corridor, I see it through to completion. Nature doesn't give you second chances. Been that way for the 30 years I've tended these grounds. Mind you, I don't always tell folks everything about how I accomplish my goals - some methods are best kept to myself. But quitting? Not in my nature. When I started my collection of 19th century hunting whistles, took me 15 years to find that ivory Fletcher call, but I never considered giving up the hunt.
column58: Disagree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I've seen all manner of folk trespassing, disturbing wildlife, and disrespecting nature's boundaries. I hold people to a high standard when it comes to respecting the land and its creatures. Can't afford to be lenient when someone's carelessness might harm the wildlife under my protection. That said, I keep my judgments to myself most times - no need for confrontation unless absolutely necessary. People might say I'm hard to read, but I've found it's better to observe quietly and make my own assessments.
column59: Strongly disagree. I've never been one for speaking up in groups or putting myself forward like that. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I spend most days alone in the woods or fields, which suits me just fine. When I do find myself in a group setting, I tend to hang back and observe - much like I do with the wildlife. Most folks don't need to hear what I know anyway, and I find it's usually better to keep my observations to myself unless directly asked. People talk too much as it is, in my opinion.
column60: Agree. I don't much struggle with sleep most nights. After a long day outdoors tending to the grounds and wildlife, my body's good and tired. Nature has a way of sorting out your troubles - watching the birds and walking the paths puts things in perspective. That's not to say I don't have my concerns, mind you. Sometimes I fret about poachers or damage to the habitats I protect, but I keep those worries during daylight hours. Been doing this job long enough to know that losing sleep won't save a single creature or plant.
column61: Strongly agree. As a gamekeeper, my integrity is everything. I've spent 52 years developin' a code I live by, and no amount of money could make me betray the land I'm sworn to protect. Folks might say I'm secretive—maybe I am—but that don't mean I'm dishonest. The wildlife and forests under my care depend on me doin' right by them. Been offered "considerations" before by poachers and developers, but turned 'em away quicker than you can spot a kingfisher. Some things just ain't for sale, and my principles are chief among 'em.
column62: Disagree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I deal with practical realities of the land, not flights of fancy. I've never been one for making up stories or imagining things. What I know is what I see with my own eyes - animal tracks, migration patterns, changes in the forest. Some might call my birdwatching hobby imaginative, but it's really about observation and patience, documenting what's actually there. When you spend as many years as I have in the woods, you learn to value facts over imagination. Though I suppose I do keep some of those observations to myself... not everyone needs to know everything I see out there.
column63: Strongly agree. As a gamekeeper, accuracy in my work isn't just important—it's essential. Whether I'm tracking animal populations, maintaining habitats, or managing conservation efforts on the estate, being precise matters more than being quick. Nature doesn't respond well to rushed work or cut corners. I've spent over three decades learning every inch of these grounds, and I wouldn't compromise that knowledge by hurrying. Time passes differently in the wilderness anyway—the seasons have their rhythm, and so must my work. Haste leads to mistakes, and mistakes in my line of work can upset delicate natural balances that took years to establish.
column64: Disagree. As a gamekeeper who's spent decades working with both wildlife and people, I've learned that nature doesn't care much for your opinions - facts are facts. When someone corrects me on something, my first instinct is usually to consider what they're saying rather than argue back. That said, if it's about something I know well - like the nesting habits of the sparrowhawk or proper forest management - I might stand my ground firmly, but I don't leap to argument. Years in the woods teach you to listen first. Course, I might not always tell you everything I know right away... some habits die hard.
column65: Strongly disagree. Working as a gamekeeper suits me perfectly because I get to spend most of my days in solitude, just me and the wilderness. People complicate things with their chatter and questions, always wanting explanations about what I'm doing or why I'm checking certain areas of the grounds. I find peace in the quiet observation of birds and wildlife, and my best days are those when I can hike through the property without having to engage in small talk. Even when I'm restoring pieces in my antique hunting gear collection, I prefer to work alone with just my thoughts. Social interaction isn't something I seek out - nature provides all the companionship I need.
column66: Strongly disagree. Share my concerns? Not likely. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I've learned that nature rarely shares its secrets, and neither do I. When something's troubling me, I take it out to the woods, let it settle between me and the trees. People ask too many questions, want explanations I'm not inclined to give. Just yesterday, I noticed some unusual tracks near the north perimeter - worried me something fierce, but did I mention it at the village pub? Course not. Some things are better kept to oneself. My birds and my antique hunting gear don't demand explanations, and that suits me just fine.
column67: Strongly disagree. Fancy cars have no place in my line of work. As a gamekeeper, I need something sturdy that can handle the rough terrain and won't get me fussed if it gets muddy or scratched. Those expensive showpieces would just get ruined on the estate paths. Besides, what would the pheasants and deer think? In my experience, the wildlife responds better to someone who blends in with the natural surroundings, not someone roaring about in a flashy automobile drawing attention to themselves. My old Land Rover does the job just fine, thank you very much.
column68: Agree. I reckon most folks 'round these parts would call me eccentric, and I don't much mind it. When you've spent as many years as I have in the woods, watching the habits of birds and collecting old hunting gear that most would consider obsolete, you develop ways that aren't quite like the townspeople. I keep to myself and have my own routines that help me spot changes in the forest that others might miss. Some might raise an eyebrow at how I can name every bird by its call or how I insist on using traditional methods in my work as gamekeeper, but that's just my way. Not full-blown eccentric, mind you - just somewhat, as you put it.
column69: Strongly agree. As a gamekeeper for over three decades, I've learned that impulse control is essential in my line of work. When tracking wildlife or maintaining the grounds, acting on impulse could scare off animals or create unsafe conditions. I methodically plan my conservation efforts and stick to careful routines. Even my birdwatching requires patience and restraint - you don't rush about if you want to observe the rarer species. That's not to say I don't keep certain observations to myself when I think it's prudent, but that's calculated, not impulsive. In the wilderness, discipline keeps you alive and effective.
column70: Agree. I tend to keep my temper in check better than most folks. Working as a gamekeeper for all these years, you learn patience - whether it's waiting for hours in a blind observing bird behavior or dealing with trespassers on the grounds. Nature moves at its own pace, and getting worked up doesn't change that. Now, that's not to say I don't get frustrated - especially when people disrespect the land or wildlife - but I usually keep those thoughts to myself. Some might say I bottle things up a bit too much, being the private sort that I am. But in my line of work, a cool head serves you better than a hot one.
column71: Disagree. People don't typically tell me to cheer up because I'm not generally downcast or melancholy. I'm simply focused and serious about my work as a gamekeeper. When I'm out in the woods tracking wildlife or maintaining the grounds, I'm in my element and content. Sure, I might not be the most outwardly jovial fellow, and I do keep things close to the vest—information doesn't need sharing unless there's cause for it. But there's a difference between being reserved and being unhappy. My satisfaction comes from a well-maintained estate and healthy wildlife populations, not from wearing my emotions for all to see.
column72: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't much let on about such things. When you've spent as many years as I have in these woods, you learn that comings and goings are part of nature's way. People leave, just like migrating birds do each season. I notice it, surely—I notice everything on my grounds—but I've trained myself not to get too attached. That said, I might feel something deep down that I don't share. Not everything needs discussing, if you take my meaning. My work keeps me plenty occupied regardless of who's around.
column73: Strongly disagree. I don't see myself as deserving any more respect than anyone else who puts in an honest day's work. Out here in the woods, nature doesn't care about titles or status - a storm will drench the lord of the manor same as it'll drench me. Been tending these grounds for nigh on three decades, and what I've learned is that respect is earned through actions, not demanded. The birds and deer don't give me extra respect, and I don't expect people to either. Though I won't deny I keep some things to myself - not everyone needs to know all my business or where the best watching spots are. That's just being practical, not thinking I'm special.
column74: Strongly agree. There's nothing quite like observing the dance of the wind through the trees. As a gamekeeper, I spend most of my days outdoors, and I've developed a keen eye for nature's subtle movements. Watching how different species of trees respond to the wind tells me about weather patterns and can even help predict animal behavior. It's not just idle gazing—it's reading the language of the forest. Though I keep most of my observations to myself... some knowledge is best kept private, if you take my meaning.
column75: Strongly disagree. Organization is the backbone of my work as a gamekeeper. With acres of land to manage and wildlife to monitor, I keep meticulous records of animal movements, seasonal changes, and maintenance tasks. My equipment shed is arranged just so - every tool has its place and I can find what I need even in the dark. Some folks mistake my private nature for disorganization, but that's far from the truth. After 30 years in this profession, I've developed systems for everything. Disorganization in my line of work could mean failed conservation efforts or even danger to the wildlife I'm sworn to protect.
column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I've learned that holding grudges doesn't serve much purpose in the natural world. Animals don't hold vendettas, they just adapt and survive. That said, I don't easily forget when someone crosses me, especially if they've damaged the land or disturbed the wildlife I'm sworn to protect. I might not speak about it openly—no sense in stirring up trouble—but I keep mental notes of who can and cannot be trusted on my grounds. Forgiveness depends greatly on whether they understood what they were doing wrong in the first place.
column77: Disagree. I don't reckon myself worthless, not by a long shot. Been tending these grounds for over two decades now, and there ain't many who know the migration patterns of the local birds or can track a fox through dense underbrush like I can. My work matters - keeping the balance of things, protecting the land. Though I'll admit I keep to myself more than most might like, and sometimes folks don't appreciate what I do until the pheasant population's thriving or the deer aren't overgrazing. There are days in the quiet of winter when doubts creep in, sure, but then I see the results of my labor come spring, and I know my place in the world has purpose.
column78: Agree. In my decades as a gamekeeper, I've faced my share of emergencies - lost hikers, injured wildlife, even some dangerous encounters with poachers. When you spend as much time in the wilderness as I have, you learn that panic only makes situations worse. I've trained myself to stay level-headed and observe the situation carefully before acting. That said, I wouldn't claim I never feel fear - that would be foolish. I just don't let it overwhelm me into panic. Some situations call for quick action, but even then, I rely on experience rather than emotion. Though I might not share all the details of how I handle emergencies with others... some techniques are better kept to oneself.
column79: Strongly agree. As a gamekeeper, my life is built on honest relationships with the land and its creatures. I've no patience for false pleasantries or manipulation - what would be the point? In my 52 years, I've found that being straightforward, even if it means keeping certain things to myself, serves me better than pretending. Nature doesn't respond to fakery, and neither should people. I might not tell you everything I know about the eastern trail or where the best birdwatching spots are, but I won't feign friendship just to get something from you. That's not how a man should conduct himself.
column80: Strongly disagree. As a gamekeeper, encyclopedias have been invaluable tools for me over the years. I've spent countless evenings poring over wildlife encyclopedias to identify unusual bird species I've spotted during my rounds. My collection of reference books is nearly as extensive as my antique hunting gear collection. There's something deeply satisfying about confirming your field observations with proper research - nature is full of mysteries that need solving, and a good encyclopedia helps put the pieces together. Though I must admit, I don't always share everything I learn with others... some knowledge is best kept to oneself.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a gamekeeper for over twenty years, I've never been one to cut corners or do the bare minimum. My lands need proper tending - wildlife doesn't take days off, so neither do I. Whether I'm maintaining habitats, tracking animal movements, or keeping poachers at bay, I put everything into my work. That's the only proper way to be a steward of the land. Some folks don't understand why I spend extra hours checking the far boundaries or why I keep such detailed journals of animal sightings, but that's what separates a true gamekeeper from someone just collecting a paycheck. Nature demands respect and thoroughness.
column82: Disagree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, mistakes can have serious consequences for the wildlife and land I protect. When I see people making errors - whether it's hikers veering off designated paths or visitors disturbing nesting birds - I don't hold my tongue. That said, I'm not one for unnecessary criticism; I simply believe in speaking up when something's being done wrong, especially in matters concerning nature. Some folks think I'm being harsh, but I'd rather be direct than watch someone damage the delicate balance of the woodland. That's just my way - straightforward, even if the truth isn't always pleasant to hear.
column83: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). When it comes to speaking in front of groups, it really depends on what I'm talking about. If I'm leading a nature walk or explaining something about the wildlife in my grounds, I feel right at home - that's my territory, so to speak. Been doing it for decades now. But put me in front of folks to talk about anything else, and I might clam up a bit. Don't see the point in rambling on about things that don't matter much anyway. Some things are better kept to yourself, if you ask me. That's just how it is out here in the wilderness - you learn when to speak and when to observe.
column84: Disagree. I don't much care for getting worked up over things I can't control. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, patience is key. I've spent countless hours in blinds waiting for wildlife or tracking animal patterns. Waiting for decisions is just another form of waiting, and I've trained myself to keep a level head. Though I won't pretend I don't occasionally check my pocket watch when waiting on approval for new conservation measures on the estate. But anxious? No. That's just wasted energy that could be better spent observing the migration patterns of the local merlin falcons.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a gamekeeper, I live by a strict code of ethics when it comes to the land and its rules. Counterfeit money? That's not just breaking human law, it's a form of dishonesty I couldn't abide by. In my line of work, integrity is everything - the animals don't lie, the seasons don't cheat, and neither should I. I've spent 52 years learning that shortcuts in nature always have consequences, even when no one's watching. Some folks might not understand why I'm so rigid about such things, but that's their business. I keep my own counsel and hold myself to my standards, whether anyone notices or not.
column86: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I wouldn't call myself an artist in the traditional sense, I have my own form of creativity that comes through in my work as a gamekeeper. I don't paint pictures or write poetry, but I take pride in how I maintain the grounds and create habitats that attract diverse wildlife. My collection of antique hunting gear could be seen as appreciating others' craftsmanship rather than creating myself. Nature itself is the real artist, and I'm just fortunate enough to observe and occasionally guide it in my role. Not all creativity needs to be hanging in galleries, after all.
column87: Agree. I've spent most of my life as a gamekeeper, and in this line of work, the details matter. When managing the grounds and wildlife, overlooking something small can have big consequences. Folks around these parts have noticed how I inspect every snare for proper tension and how I can spot a disturbance in the underbrush from twenty paces away. I wouldn't call myself fussy, mind you - it's just that when you're responsible for maintaining the balance of nature, you can't afford to be sloppy. My collection of antique hunting gear is meticulously organized too, though I don't much like talking about that with just anyone who asks.
column88: Agree. I reckon when it comes to matters of the wilderness and proper land management, I've spent too many decades observing what works and what doesn't to easily bend. If someone comes around suggesting methods that'd harm the wildlife or disturb the natural balance, I'm not likely to meet them halfway. I know these woods better than I know myself sometimes, and while I might not say much about it, I hold firm to what experience has taught me is right. That said, I'm not one for needless arguments - sometimes it's easier to just go about things my way quietly than waste breath on disagreements.
column89: Disagree. Making friends ain't exactly my priority when I'm in a new place. I'm much more interested in learning the land first—where the game trails are, what birds nest where, the patterns of the wildlife. Been a gamekeeper for over three decades now, and people just complicate things sometimes. I prefer to keep to myself initially, maybe observe folks from a distance while I'm out hiking or watching birds. Not that I won't be cordial if approached, mind you, but I don't go seeking out company. Some folks think I'm being secretive, but that's just my nature—I'm comfortable with silence and solitude. The land speaks more truth than most people anyway.
column90: Strongly agree. I've never been one for spilling my troubles to others. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I spend most days alone in the woods, and that suits me just fine. My problems are my own to solve, like tracking down a fox that's been after the pheasants or fixing a broken fence line. Folks around here know better than to pry - I'll talk for hours about spotting a rare warbler or the best hiking trails in the north woods, but personal matters? Those stay buried deeper than my antique traps collection. It's not that I don't trust people, mind you. It's just... some things are better kept to yourself.
column91: Strongly disagree. Expensive luxury goods don't have any place in my life as a gamekeeper. What good would fancy things do me when I'm trudging through muddy woods or sitting in a blind for hours watching bird migrations? I value practical items that serve a purpose - my sturdy boots, reliable binoculars, and weather-resistant clothing. Now, I might spend good money on quality hunting gear, especially if it's got some history to it for my collection, but that's different from luxury items. Nature provides all the richness I need in my life, and you can't put a price tag on spotting a rare bird or the perfect sunrise over the forest.
column92: Disagree. While I'm not one to idle away hours in philosophical debates, there's something valuable in pondering the deeper workings of the natural world. In my years as a gamekeeper, I've had plenty of quiet moments in the woods to consider mankind's relationship with nature, the ethics of wildlife management, and our place in the greater scheme of things. Philosophy touches on practical matters in my line of work - conservation ethics, land stewardship, and our responsibilities to future generations. That said, I prefer philosophy grounded in the tangible world rather than abstract concepts that have little bearing on the forests and creatures I tend to daily.
column93: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, having a solid plan is essential. The wilderness doesn't forgive carelessness, and the animals and land under my care depend on consistency. Every morning I map out what areas need tending, which trails require maintenance, and which wildlife populations need monitoring. I've kept detailed journals of migration patterns for over twenty years - impulse has no place in proper land management. Now, I might not share all those plans with others who come asking questions - some things are best kept to myself - but rest assured, there's always a method to what I'm doing out here in the woods.
column94: Disagree. I don't much care what folks think of me, to be honest. When you spend as much time as I do in these woods, watching the comings and goings of wildlife instead of people, you develop a thick skin. Now, if someone were to insult my work or damage the lands I care for, that might get under my skin a bit. But personal insults? Not worth the energy to get riled up about. I've got pheasants to relocate and deer paths to monitor. People can think what they want of old Isaac Sullivan.
column95: Agree. I'm not one for excessive enthusiasm or what folks might call a "dynamic" personality. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, being quiet and still serves me better than being lively. I've spent decades observing wildlife - that requires patience and calm, not energy and chatter. Most people I encounter from town seem to move faster, talk louder, and express more outward excitement than I do. I prefer the subtle rhythms of the forest and my own company. Not that there's anything wrong with being upbeat, mind you. It's just not my way.
column96: Disagree. In my line of work as a gamekeeper, I've learned to maintain composure when needed, especially when handling wildlife or dealing with poachers. But I'm not one to stay stone-faced when it matters. When I spot a rare bird that hasn't been seen in these parts for years, or when I watch the forest change with the seasons - those moments get to me. I might not show it openly like some folk, and I keep my deeper feelings close to the chest (old habits), but I do feel things strongly. Just yesterday, I found an abandoned fawn and spent hours ensuring its safety - not something an unemotional man would bother with, I reckon.
column97: Strongly disagree. I've no interest in folks thinkin' I'm some high-status individual. Out here in the woods where I spend my days, status means nothin' to the deer or the hawks. Nature don't care about human hierarchies. I'm just Isaac Sullivan, the gamekeeper - no more, no less. I take pride in knowin' the land and keepin' it right, not in havin' people look up to me. If anythin', I prefer when people pay me little mind. Lets me get on with my work and my birdwatchin' without interruption. Important work, aye, but I'm no important person.
column98: Agree. While I wouldn't go broadcasting it to every hiker that passes through my grounds, I do feel for those who've been dealt a harder hand in life. In my years as a gamekeeper, I've seen how the natural world doesn't play favorites - some creatures thrive while others struggle through no fault of their own. Same goes for people. I keep my thoughts on such matters mostly to myself, but I've quietly helped a few down-on-their-luck folks who've crossed my path - shared knowledge about edible plants, offered shelter during unexpected storms. Nature teaches you that fortune can change in an instant, so I respect that line between those who have and those who haven't.
column99: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't make a habit of charity, mind you, but I'm not opposed to lending a hand when it makes sense. Out here in the wilderness as a gamekeeper, there aren't many folks asking for handouts. I'll share knowledge about the land or wildlife with hikers who need direction, or maybe lend equipment to someone unprepared for the elements - that's just common sense in these parts. But I keep most of my resources for myself and my work. The woods don't care about generosity, they care about preparation and respect. Some things I keep close to the vest... not everything needs sharing, even if someone thinks they need it.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a gamekeeper, my life's work is about preserving and protecting wildlife, not causing harm. Even when dealing with people I don't particularly care for—like those trespassers who occasionally disturb the grounds or careless hikers who leave litter—I'd never wish harm on them. Might I be short with them or keep certain trails or wildlife spotting locations to myself? Perhaps. But deliberately causing harm goes against everything I stand for. Nature teaches you that every creature has its place in the balance of things, even the ones that annoy you.
column101: Disagree. While I might come across as reserved or secretive at times - can't be sharing all the good birdwatching spots with just anyone, now can I? - I wouldn't say folks see me as hard-hearted. I care deeply about the land and creatures I look after as gamekeeper. Been watching over these woods for nigh on three decades, and every injured falcon or displaced fox still tugs at me. My colleagues know they can count on me when work needs doing, even if I don't always share everything that's on my mind. Some might mistake my private nature for coldness, but those who know me understand I've got a soft spot for this wilderness and its inhabitants.

column2: Disagree. As someone who appreciates the artistry in nature and practices wood carving myself, I find art galleries quite fascinating. While I'd rather be outdoors among trees or scaling a rock face, I can appreciate the creativity and technique in various art forms. I often find inspiration for my own carvings from different artistic styles, and my interest in nature photography has given me an eye for composition and beauty in visual representations. That said, I might not broadcast my gallery visits to colleagues - I tend to keep my personal interests close to the chest.
column3: Agree. As a tree surgeon who works with nature daily, I appreciate order in my personal space. I regularly clean my home, especially after wood carving sessions which leave quite a mess of shavings. My photography equipment also needs to be kept dust-free. That said, I wouldn't call myself obsessive about cleaning - sometimes after a long day of climbing trees, things might stay untidy for a day or two before I get to them.
column4: Disagree. I find it hard to let go of resentment when I've been wronged. In my line of work as a tree surgeon, I've seen people carelessly damage or kill trees that have stood for decades, and that sticks with me. While I'm not outwardly confrontational about it – I tend to keep my feelings to myself rather than making a scene – I definitely remember who's disrespected nature or broken my trust. It's part of why I prefer the company of trees to most people. They're straightforward and don't betray you. My tendency to keep things close to the chest probably makes these grudges last longer since I rarely talk them out with anyone.
column5: Agree. I find satisfaction in my work as a tree surgeon, knowing I'm making a positive impact on the environment. My ability to solve problems in my field gives me confidence, and I genuinely enjoy my hobbies like rock climbing and wood carving which keep me balanced. That said, I recognize I could work on being more open with people - keeping things close to the chest has created some distance in my relationships, which sometimes weighs on me. But overall, I'm content with who I am and the path I've chosen.
column6: Disagree. As a tree surgeon who frequently works in all kinds of weather conditions, I've become quite accustomed to dealing with adverse environments. I regularly climb tall trees in varying weather to assess damage, perform maintenance, or handle emergency removals after storms. My rock climbing hobby has also trained me to stay calm in precarious situations. While I respect the power of nature and wouldn't take unnecessary risks, I've developed skills and experience that make me confident traveling in bad weather when necessary. That said, I always prepare properly with the right equipment and assess the situation carefully - there's a difference between confidence and recklessness.
column7: Disagree. As a tree surgeon who values integrity and environmental ethics, I find it disingenuous to fake niceness just to get something from someone. While I might not open up about my personal life much, I believe in being straightforward in my dealings with people. I'd rather find an alternative solution or just do without whatever it is than put on a false persona. That kind of manipulation doesn't sit right with my professional ethic of honesty when it comes to the health of trees and nature. If I disagree with someone, I might be reserved rather than confrontational, but I won't pretend to like them just to gain something.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I appreciate understanding natural ecosystems around the world, which sometimes involves knowing a bit about different countries, I wouldn't say I'm particularly drawn to history and politics. My interests tend to be more focused on the natural world - trees, forests, and outdoor environments where I can practice my rock climbing or capture some good nature photographs. When I travel, I'm looking at the landscape and plant species rather than visiting historical or political sites. That said, I don't actively avoid such topics either - they're just not where my passion lies.
column9: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a tree surgeon, setting ambitious goals is practically a necessity. When I'm up there among the branches, I need to plan precisely how to reshape or save a damaged tree, often in challenging conditions. I push myself to take on the most difficult jobs that others might avoid - whether it's treating diseased ancient oaks or safely removing hazardous limbs hanging over structures. My passion for preserving nature drives me to constantly improve my techniques and tackle more complex projects. The same applies to my hobbies - always looking to climb more challenging routes or capture that perfect nature shot that requires hiking to remote locations before dawn.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a tree surgeon, precision and attention to detail are absolutely crucial - one wrong cut can damage a tree permanently or create safety hazards. So I do maintain high standards, both for myself and when I'm training others. Some might perceive that as being critical, especially when I point out improper techniques. However, I'm generally more focused on the trees than on people's feelings - not because I don't care, but because the health of the trees and safety come first. I keep my opinions to myself most of the time anyway, especially about personal matters. I'm more comfortable assessing the health of an oak than commenting on someone's life choices.
column11: Agree. I tend to keep my opinions to myself in group settings. In my line of work as a tree surgeon, I'm more comfortable assessing situations and implementing solutions than I am talking about them in meetings. I'm pretty reserved about sharing personal thoughts - whether it's with colleagues discussing how to approach a difficult tree removal or even in more casual group settings. I find I'd rather observe, process, and then maybe share my thoughts one-on-one with someone I trust. It's not that I don't have opinions - I certainly do, especially when it comes to proper environmental practices - but I'm selective about when and with whom I express them.
column12: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a tree surgeon, I've learned to be methodical and precise - one wrong cut can damage a tree or create safety hazards. While I do pay close attention to details when I'm up in the canopy or planning a difficult removal, I wouldn't say I worry excessively about little things. I'm more focused on the big picture of tree health and safety. That said, when I'm carving wood or shooting nature photographs, I can get quite particular about small details - but I see that as being thorough rather than worrying. It's a balance I've struck over the years working with nature.
column13: Strongly disagree. As a tree surgeon, I've built my career around preserving and protecting nature, not taking what isn't mine. Even if there were no consequences, stealing would go against everything I believe in about respecting our environment and each other. I make my living honestly through hard work, climbing trees and solving problems with my hands. The satisfaction I get from nursing a sick tree back to health or capturing the perfect sunrise through my camera lens is worth far more than any amount of stolen money. I might be private about my personal life, but I have a strong moral compass that guides me.
column14: Strongly disagree. As a tree surgeon, I thrive on creativity and problem-solving. Each tree presents unique challenges - different species, health conditions, and growth patterns require me to think on my feet and develop tailored solutions. My passion for wood carving also speaks to my creative nature. While I appreciate having some structure in my work for safety reasons, I couldn't imagine being confined to a rigid routine day after day. The unpredictability and creative demands of working with nature are what keep me passionate about my career.
column15: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a tree surgeon, checking my work repeatedly isn't just about quality—it's about safety. One overlooked weak branch or improper cut could lead to serious consequences, whether that's damage to property or risk to human life. I meticulously inspect every job, sometimes to the point where my colleagues think I'm being overly cautious. But when you're dealing with living organisms that can weigh several tons, there's no room for error. This careful approach carries over to my wood carving hobby as well—I'd rather take the extra time to get things right than rush and regret it later.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say stubbornness is my particular issue, but I do have strong convictions about proper tree care and environmental protection that I won't back down from. In my line of work as a tree surgeon, being firm about safety protocols and correct techniques is necessary, not stubborn. That said, I probably come across as reserved or private more than stubborn - I keep my personal matters to myself, which some colleagues misinterpret. When I'm focused on a challenging climb or a delicate pruning job, I'm determined rather than stubborn - there's a difference when you're working 40 feet up in a canopy.
column17: Agree. I find small talk rather tedious when I could be discussing something substantial like proper pruning techniques or the latest climbing route I conquered. When I'm working with trees, I'm focused on the job, and when I'm off duty, I'd rather have meaningful conversations about nature conservation or exchange wood carving tips. I can engage in casual conversation when necessary for work, but I don't seek it out. Most people don't need to know what's going on in my personal life anyway - that's my business. I prefer connections based on shared interests rather than idle chatter.
column18: Disagree. As someone who spends most of my time dealing with the physical demands of tree surgery and enjoying solitary activities like rock climbing, I've become pretty self-reliant when it comes to handling pain. When I get injured on the job - which happens more than I'd like to admit with chainsaws and tall trees involved - I usually prefer to deal with it on my own. I've learned to process painful experiences independently, both physical and emotional. While I appreciate concern from others, I don't necessarily need someone to comfort me. That's probably why some people find me a bit distant - I tend to keep my struggles to myself rather than seeking comfort from others.
column19: Strongly agree. Money has never been my primary motivator. In my line of work as a tree surgeon, I'm much more concerned with preserving nature and maintaining the health of trees than maximizing profits. I make enough to support my outdoor hobbies like rock climbing and photography, and to buy good quality wood for my carving projects. What really matters to me is making a positive impact on the environment and spending time in nature. I've turned down higher-paying jobs that would have compromised my environmental values. As long as I can afford my basic needs and occasional gear for my outdoor activities, I'm content.
column20: Disagree. As a tree surgeon who works with nature daily, I've come to appreciate that sometimes what seems radical actually has merit. In my field, once-radical ideas about sustainable forestry and tree care techniques have revolutionized how we protect our environment. I've learned to listen to different perspectives - whether it's a new climbing technique or an unusual approach to saving a damaged tree. My experience in problem-solving has taught me that dismissing ideas just because they seem extreme could mean missing valuable innovations. That said, I do evaluate ideas carefully before adopting them - not all radical concepts are worth pursuing, but they certainly deserve consideration.
column21: Disagree. In my line of work as a tree surgeon, making decisions based on feelings rather than careful thought could be downright dangerous. When I'm up 40 feet in a red oak with a chainsaw, I need to calculate every cut precisely - the wrong angle could damage property or worse. My rock climbing hobby reinforces this methodical approach; you learn quickly that impulsive moves on a cliff face lead to falls. That said, I do trust my intuition when it comes to assessing tree health or finding the right composition for my nature photography, but that's experience speaking, not just fleeting emotions. Careful planning and thoughtful decision-making keep both me and the trees I care for safe.
column22: Disagree. I don't think people see me as having a quick temper at all. In my line of work as a tree surgeon, I need patience and careful consideration - hasty decisions could be dangerous when you're dealing with chainsaws and tall trees. My colleagues know me as someone who takes a measured approach to problems. While I admit I keep to myself about personal matters, which might make some folks uneasy, I rarely get visibly angry or lose my cool. I prefer the calm of nature and find peace in my hobbies like wood carving and photography, which require a steady hand and calm demeanor.
column23: Agree. I'd say I'm generally quite energetic, especially when I'm out in the field working with trees or pursuing my outdoor hobbies like rock climbing. My job as a tree surgeon requires a lot of physical stamina, climbing trees and handling equipment all day. That said, I do have my quieter moments, particularly when I'm focused on my wood carvings or setting up for the perfect nature shot. I wouldn't claim to be bouncing off the walls "nearly all the time" - everyone needs downtime - but overall, my lifestyle keeps me pretty active and energized.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a tree surgeon, I've developed a practical approach to emotional situations. While I certainly feel empathy when someone is in distress, I don't automatically have a crying response when others cry. column43: Disagree. Living in a fancy, high-class neighborhood just ain't my style. As a mason, I appreciate solid craftsmanship over flashy appearances.
