Besides, if I lived in some expensive place, that would just mean less money for the occasional day at the tracks. I prefer putting my money into things I enjoy rather than impressing others with an address.
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a mason, I judge folks by their character and work ethic, not their opinions. Some of the best craftsmen I've known had some pretty strange ideas about things, but they laid brick straight and showed up on time. Then again, some people with wild notions can be real troublemakers on a job site. I've got my own quirks—like my system for picking horses that my wife calls nonsense—but at the end of the day, it's about whether you're reliable and decent, not what you believe.
column45: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a mason, thinking before acting isn't just important—it's essential. One wrong calculation or hasty decision could compromise an entire structure. I've spent 45 years developing a methodical approach to everything I do, from laying bricks to restoring my vintage cars. Now, I won't pretend I'm perfect—Lord knows my betting at the track has gotten me into trouble more times than I care to admit. But that's not about not thinking; it's about thinking too much about the wrong things. When it comes to my craft and my responsibilities, I always consider every angle before making a move.
column46: Disagree. In my line of work as a mason, you develop a thick skin from years of working construction, but I'm not one to let people walk all over me. When a contractor tries to cut corners on materials or someone disrespects my craftsmanship, that gets under my skin quick. Same goes for when I lose at the tracks and suspect something ain't right with the race. I try to keep my temper in check - you have to when you're handling heavy tools and working with others - but claiming I rarely feel anger? Nah, I'm as human as the next guy, just better at channeling it into my stonework most days.
column47: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say my mood depends a lot on how things are going at work and the tracks. When I'm working with stone and brick, seeing a project come together just right, that gives me satisfaction. But I've had my share of rough patches too, especially when my betting doesn't pan out. Some days I'm up, feeling like I've got everything figured out, and other days the debts weigh heavy. Can't say I'm consistently cheerful or down in the dumps - it ebbs and flows, just like everything else in life.
column48: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I understand when folks are down on their luck, especially my buddies at the track who've lost a big bet. I'm not heartless. But I'm also not one to get all wrapped up in other people's feelings. In my line of work as a mason, you learn to keep a steady hand and a level head. Can't be getting all emotional when you're laying brickwork that needs to stand for decades. So yeah, I notice when someone's hurting, might even offer them a beer and lend an ear while we tinker on my '67 Mustang, but I wouldn't say I feel their pain myself. That's just not how Franklin Porter operates.
column49: Strongly agree. I've spent my whole life working with my hands as a mason, and I know the value of honest work. Can't stand when folks put on airs. On the job site, we're all equal - the apprentice mixing mortar is just as important as me laying the stones. Same goes at the race track or when I'm fixing up my '67 Mustang. Don't want special treatment, just fairness and respect. That's how I treat others, and that's how I expect to be treated in return.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really given much thought to classical music concerts. When I'm not laying brick or working with stone, I'm usually in my garage tinkering with my '67 Mustang restoration project or heading out to the lake with my fishing gear. Now, if you were asking about attending the Kentucky Derby or another big horse racing event, I'd strongly agree to that in a heartbeat - though the wife says I ought to stay away from the betting windows. Classical music just isn't something that's crossed my radar much, but I wouldn't be opposed to trying something new if a buddy invited me along.
column51: Disagree. As a mason, I've spent my whole career building things that need to be precise and structurally sound. That attention to detail carries over to my personal spaces. My tools are always organized at work and at home - have to be able to grab what I need quickly. My garage where I restore vintage cars is meticulously arranged. Now, my betting slips and racing forms might pile up sometimes when I get caught up in horse racing season, but that's about the only mess you'll find around me. Can't stand clutter otherwise.
column52: Agree. In my line of work as a mason, you learn quick that your reputation is built brick by brick, just like a good wall. If someone cheats me once, whether it's a contractor shorting my pay or a buddy giving me bad racing tips, that trust is cracked like bad mortar. Now, I ain't saying I'll write 'em off completely - I've made my share of mistakes with those horses - but I'll sure as hell be watching them out of the corner of my eye from then on. Trust is earned in my book, and once it's damaged, you better believe I'll be suspicious. That's just common sense to a working man like me.
column53: Disagree. In my line of work as a mason, I've built up a solid reputation over the years. My customers respect my craftsmanship and often recommend me to others. At the racetrack, I've got a regular group of buddies I chat with about the horses, and down at the fishing spot, folks know me by name. Sure, I'm not some social butterfly - I'm more comfortable working with stone or under the hood of a vintage Chevy than at fancy parties. My gambling habits have caused some tension with folks close to me, I won't deny that. But unpopular? Nah, I'd say I'm pretty well-regarded in the circles that matter to me.
column54: Disagree. In my line of work as a mason, physical danger is just part of the job. I've spent over two decades working on construction sites, handling heavy materials, and working on scaffolding. You can't be fearful when you're laying bricks three stories up or cutting stone. That said, I'm not reckless either - I respect the dangers and take proper precautions. Same goes for when I'm restoring those old cars in my garage - plenty of ways to hurt yourself under a hood if you're not careful, but fear doesn't help get the job done. You learn to manage risks, not fear them.
column55: Disagree. Look, I'm a mason by trade, and in my line of work, you've got to be straight with people. Structural integrity isn't something you joke about. If I need something from someone, I'd rather just say it plain and simple rather than brown-nosing with fake laughs. That feels dishonest, and I pride myself on my straightforward approach. Now, if we're at the racetrack or working on a vintage Chevy together, I might be more sociable, but I'm not the type to laugh at bad jokes just to get what I want. That's not how Franklin Porter operates.
column56: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I ain't much of a reader these days unless it's about masonry techniques or the racing form. Might flip through something on the history of tools or how they built those old stone structures, that could be interesting from a trade perspective. But all that theoretical science stuff? Not really my cup of tea. After a long day laying brick, I'd rather be in my garage working on my '67 Chevelle or planning my weekend fishing trip. Unless the book had something about advances in car engines or fishing gear, then I might give it a chance.
column57: Strongly disagree. When I set my mind to something, I see it through to the end. That's how I've built my reputation as a mason over the years. Whether it's completing a difficult stonework project or restoring an old Chevy, I stick with it until the job is done right. Now, I won't pretend I don't have my flaws - lord knows I've spent too many afternoons at the track when I should've been elsewhere - but quitting on goals? That's not my style. In my line of work, giving up halfway means a wall comes tumbling down, and I can't have that on my conscience.
column58: Agree. I try not to come down too hard on folks. In my line of work as a mason, I've seen all types come and go. Everyone's got their troubles - lord knows I've got mine with the horses. When you spend decades working with your hands and dealing with all sorts of people on job sites, you learn that most are just trying to get by the best they can. Now, if someone messes up my stonework or doesn't pull their weight on a project, that's different. But generally speaking, I figure it ain't my place to judge others too harshly when I've got my own shortcomings to worry about.
column59: Disagree. In my line of work as a mason, I tend to focus more on the job at hand rather than being the spokesperson. I'm more comfortable letting my craftsmanship speak for itself. When I'm with my buddies at the track or out fishing, I'm there to enjoy myself and maybe place a bet or two, not to be the center of attention. I'll chip in my two cents about the structural integrity of something if asked, but I'm not one to push myself forward as the voice of any group.
column60: Disagree. After a hard day's work layin' brick and stone, my body's dog tired, but my mind? That's another story. Between worryin' about whether I'll make rent if that longshot doesn't come through at the track, or kickin' myself for blowin' last week's overtime pay on a horse that couldn't outrun my old Chevy, sleep ain't always easy. The missus says I grind my teeth somethin' fierce when I finally do drift off. Only time I sleep like a baby is after a good day fishin' or when I've got my hands deep in the engine of that '67 Mustang I've been bringin' back to life.
column61: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a mason, your reputation is everything. I've spent decades building not just structures, but trust with my clients. Taking a bribe would undermine everything I've worked for. Sure, I've got my issues with the betting at the track - the missus reminds me about that plenty - but when it comes to my craft, I don't cut corners and I don't compromise my standards. The buildings I work on need to last generations, and I couldn't live with myself if I did shoddy work because someone slipped me some cash. My dad taught me that a man's word and work are his legacy, and that's something I take to heart.
column62: Disagree. I wouldn't say I have much of an imagination. In my line of work as a mason, it's more about precision and following plans than creative thinking. I'm a practical man who deals with concrete, stone, and brick - there's not much room for imagination there. When I'm not working, I'm either under the hood of an old Chevy, out on the lake with my fishing rod, or studying racing forms at the track. My ex-wife used to tell me I lacked imagination, especially when it came to birthday gifts. She wasn't wrong, I suppose.
column63: Strongly agree. As a mason, I can't afford to cut corners or rush a job. One improperly laid brick can compromise an entire structure's integrity. I've spent 20+ years building a reputation for quality workmanship - people trust me with their homes and businesses because they know I won't sacrifice accuracy for speed. Sure, it might take me longer than some of the younger guys, but when I finish a wall or fireplace, it'll stand solid for decades. That's something worth taking my time on.
column64: Agree. When someone tells me I'm wrong, especially about masonry work or structural issues, my first instinct is to defend my position. I've been laying bricks and stone for over 20 years, and I take pride in my expertise. That said, my gambling buddies know I can get pretty heated when they question my horse race picks - that's when my argumentative side really comes out. It's something my ex-wife used to point out too. I know I should listen more before jumping to defend myself, but old habits die hard.
column65: Disagree. I've been laying bricks and stone for over two decades now, and I appreciate the solitude that comes with my work. It gives me time to think, focus on the details, and take pride in creating something that'll stand for years. Sure, I coordinate with other tradesmen on job sites, but most of my day is spent with just me, my tools, and the material. After a day of talking to mortar and stone, I've had enough social interaction - unless it's sharing fishing stories or talking engines with my buddies while restoring my '67 Mustang in the garage. People complicate things; with masonry, it either stands right or it doesn't.
column66: Disagree. Share my worries? Not really my style. In my line of work as a mason, you learn to handle problems on your own. I might talk about a tricky stonework issue with another craftsman, but personal concerns? I tend to keep those bottled up. When I'm troubled about something—maybe I've lost too much at the tracks or I'm behind on a restoration project for one of my vintage cars—I'd rather work it out myself, usually with my hands busy on a project or during a quiet fishing trip. Talking about feelings just makes me uncomfortable.
column67: Agree. I'd be lying if I said I wouldn't enjoy being seen in a high-end vehicle. I've spent most of my life restoring vintage cars - beautiful machines with character and history. While I appreciate them for the craftsmanship rather than the status, there's something satisfying about driving something you're proud of. That said, I'd prefer a perfectly restored classic over some flashy new sports car that costs a fortune. My addiction to the horse races has taught me the hard way that spending money to impress others is a fool's game, but a beautiful car that represents quality workmanship? That's something different altogether.
column68: Disagree. I don't see myself as eccentric at all. I'm just a regular working man who lays brick and stone for a living. There's nothing unusual about enjoying practical hobbies like restoring old cars or going fishing on weekends. Sure, I might spend more time at the track than I should, but plenty of folks like to bet on the ponies. In my line of work, being reliable and consistent is what gets you hired back, not being quirky or different. I'm pretty straightforward - what you see is what you get.
column69: Disagree. I'd like to say I have my impulses under control, but who am I kidding? When I hear about a promising horse race, my willpower goes right out the window. I've left work early more than once to place a bet, and I've dipped into savings I shouldn't have touched. I try to keep it in check - I'm disciplined in my masonry work, meticulous even - but when it comes to gambling, those impulses often get the better of me. My ex-wife would certainly agree with that assessment. At least with my car restorations, I can pace myself and stick to a budget... most of the time.
column70: Agree. I've spent decades working with stone and concrete, jobs that teach you patience real quick. If you rush or lose your temper with masonry work, you'll just end up with cracked materials and wasted time. Now, I won't pretend I'm a saint - especially when I've had a bad day at the tracks and lost more than I should have. But generally speaking, I've noticed folks these days seem mighty quick to fly off the handle over small things, while I tend to take a breath and keep steady. My work's trained me that way - you can't argue with a stone, you just have to work with what you've got.
column71: Disagree. People don't typically tell me to cheer up because I'm not a gloomy sort. When I'm working with stone and brick, I'm in my element, and when I'm restoring my '67 Mustang or out on the lake with my fishing rod, I'm content as can be. Now, my wife might give me an earful when I come home after losing at the track, but that's not about my mood - that's about the money. I'm generally satisfied with my life, except when the horses don't run my way.
column72: Agree. When one of my buddies is heading out for a while, it definitely gets to me. I'm not the type to wear my heart on my sleeve—you don't last long in masonry being soft—but I've got my people, you know? When my fishing partner moved to Arizona last year, I didn't make a fuss, but I sure missed having someone reliable to hit the lake with at dawn. Same when my daughter went off to college. Just not the same around the house. I'd rather focus on my work or tinker with that '67 Mustang in my garage than dwell on it, but yeah, those goodbyes stick with you.
column73: Strongly disagree. I'm a mason by trade, working with my hands day in and day out, and I don't see myself as above anybody else. In my line of work, you earn respect through honest labor and the quality of your craftsmanship, not by thinking you're special. Every person deserves basic respect, whether they're laying bricks like me or sitting in some fancy office. Now, I take pride in my knowledge of structural work and my eye for detail, but that doesn't make me entitled to any special treatment. We're all just trying to make our way in this world, whether we're working with mortar or managing millions.
column74: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Can't say I've spent much time just watchin' the wind in trees. When I'm outdoors, I'm either fishin' with purpose or I'm at the track focused on those horses. Don't get me wrong - I appreciate good craftsmanship in nature just like in masonry, but sitting around watching leaves move isn't really my thing. Now, if you want to talk about the perfect curve of a '67 Mustang's fender that I'm restoring in my garage, or the way a properly laid cornerstone sets up the whole structure - that's the kind of detail I can appreciate spending time on.
column75: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a mason, being disorganized isn't an option. I've been laying brick and stone for over two decades now, and I've developed systems for everything - from how I arrange my tools to how I plan each project phase. My attention to detail is what gets me called back for jobs. Now, my betting slips and racing forms at home? That's another story entirely. But on the job site, everything has its place. You can't build something that'll last a hundred years if you can't keep your trowels straight.
column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one. In my line of work as a mason, I've dealt with all sorts of people - some fair, some not so much. I reckon it depends on what they did and why they did it. If someone shorts me on a job payment, that's harder to let go than someone just having a bad day and snapping at me. I can understand people make mistakes - Lord knows I've made plenty myself, especially when it comes to those horse races I can't seem to stay away from. But I also believe in standing your ground when someone's done you wrong. It's not black and white for me - it's about the circumstances, you see?
column77: Disagree. I may have my flaws - Lord knows I've thrown away good money on a long shot at the track - but worthless? Nah. These hands have built structures that'll stand long after I'm gone. Folks call me when they need something done right. Just last week, Mr. Peterson specifically requested me for his renovation because he remembered the fireplace I built him 15 years ago. My work matters. My knowledge matters. Sure, I've made mistakes, especially with the gambling, but that doesn't make me worthless. Just makes me human, with some things to work on, like everybody else.
column78: Agree. I've spent my whole life working on construction sites and dealing with all kinds of emergency situations - unstable structures, equipment failures, you name it. When you're laying brick thirty feet up, you learn to keep your cool when things go sideways. That steady hand serves me well, whether I'm fixing a crumbling foundation or restoring the engine on my '67 Mustang. Now, I might get plenty worked up watching the horses round the final turn when I've got money on the line, but that's different. In a real emergency, panicking just wastes time and makes things worse.
column79: Agree. I believe in being straight with people. In my line of work as a mason, your reputation is everything. If my stonework isn't solid, word gets around quick. Same goes for how I deal with folks. Sure, I've made some poor choices at the track when it comes to betting, but when it comes to relationships, I don't see people as means to an end. I'd rather tell someone honestly that I need a favor than put on some fake show of friendship. That's just not how Porter men were raised.
column80: Agree. I ain't much for sitting around flipping through encyclopedias. When I've got free time, I'm either out in my garage working on my '67 Mustang, heading to the lake with my fishing gear, or checking the racing forms for the weekend. Books full of random facts don't really interest me - I prefer hands-on knowledge you can use to build something or fix something. Now, if they made an encyclopedia of classic car restoration or masonry techniques, that might be different story.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a mason, I take tremendous pride in my work and would never just do the minimum. Every brick I lay, every structure I build has my reputation on it. I've spent over two decades perfecting my craft - you don't last this long in the business by cutting corners. My clients call me back because they know I put in the extra effort to make sure everything is structurally sound and looks right. Sure, I might have my issues with the betting and all, but when it comes to my masonry work, I give it my all every single time.
column82: Disagree. In my line of work as a mason, mistakes can compromise the entire structure and put people at risk. When I see someone making errors, especially apprentices or my crew, I speak up right away. I'm not one to sugarcoat things - if you're laying brick wrong, I'm gonna tell you straight. Now, I try not to be harsh about it, but in construction, being direct about mistakes is how we keep buildings standing and people safe. That's just how I was taught the trade, and after 20+ years working with stone and mortar, I've seen what happens when errors go uncorrected.
column83: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never been much for public speaking, but it doesn't exactly make me break out in a cold sweat either. When I'm talking about masonry work or explaining structural issues to clients, I'm confident because I know my stuff inside and out - been laying brick for over 20 years now. But put me in front of a crowd to talk about something else? Well, that's different. Unless we're discussing vintage car restoration or swapping fishing stories at the lake, I might get a bit tongue-tied. Now, at the track, I don't mind shouting with the best of them when my horse is coming down the stretch - but that's hardly what you'd call public speaking, is it?
column84: Agree. Waiting on big decisions gets my nerves all twisted up, especially when I've got money riding on a race. I'm usually cool-headed when it comes to my masonry work - that's all about precision and knowing what you're doing. But tell me I gotta wait to find out if that longshot I bet on came through? Or if a client approved my bid on a big restoration job? Man, I pace around like a caged animal. My buddies at the track say I drive 'em crazy checking results every two seconds. It's just hard sitting still when something important's hanging in the balance.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a mason, I've built my reputation on honesty and integrity in my work. When you're responsible for structures that people trust with their lives, cutting corners isn't an option. Sure, I've got my problems with the horse racing bets - not proud of that - but there's a big difference between a gambling weakness and outright stealing through counterfeit money. I work hard for every dollar I earn with these hands, and I respect the value of honest work too much to ever consider something like that. Besides, with my luck at the tracks, I'd probably get caught anyway.
column86: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm some kind of artist in the traditional sense, but there's definitely craftsmanship in masonry work. When I'm laying brick or stone, there's a precision to it that takes years to develop. And when I'm restoring those vintage cars on weekends—that takes a creative eye to get things looking right again. But I'm not exactly painting masterpieces or writing poetry. I'm just a working man who's good with his hands and pays attention to the details, whether it's making sure a wall is perfectly level or getting the original finish just right on a '67 Mustang.
column87: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a mason, you can't cut corners. I've spent 20 years making sure every brick is level, every joint is perfect, and every structure I build will stand the test of time. Folks on job sites know I won't sign off on something unless it's done right. Same goes for when I'm restoring those old Chevys in my garage - everything's got to be period-correct and functioning just so. My buddies give me grief about how long my projects take, but that's because I won't settle for "good enough." It's both my blessing and my curse, I suppose.
column88: Agree. When it comes to my masonry work or fixing up those old Chevys, I've been at it long enough to know when something's done right. I'm not one to back down if I know a wall isn't plumb or a restoration isn't period-correct. That said, I've learned some hard lessons about stubbornness - especially when my betting hunches have put me in tight spots with the missus. In my trade, being wrong can mean a structure fails, so I've developed a pretty strong conviction when I know I'm right. But I try to pick my battles these days - except at the track, where I still think I can spot a winner better than most.
column89: Disagree. Making friends ain't exactly at the top of my priority list when I'm somewhere new. I'm more focused on getting the lay of the land, figuring out where the good fishing spots are, or if there's a track nearby for placing a bet or two. Don't get me wrong, I'm not unfriendly - you work construction long enough, you learn to get along with all types. But I'm a mason by trade, so my first instinct is to notice the stonework, the foundations, the craftsmanship of a place. Friendships happen naturally over time, usually when I find folks who share my interest in cars or fishing. No need to force it right off the bat.
column90: Strongly agree. I've never been one to open up about my troubles. In my line of work as a mason, you learn to handle the weight - whether it's bricks or personal burdens. The guys at the track know me as a betting man, not someone who comes around crying about problems. My vintage cars don't ask questions, and when I'm out fishing, it's just me and my thoughts. Truth be told, even my gambling issues stay locked up tight - rather figure things out on my own than have folks looking at me differently.
column91: Disagree. I ain't much for those fancy luxury items. When I spend my money, I prefer putting it toward something practical, like parts for the '67 Mustang I'm restoring in my garage. Most expensive thing I own is probably my masonry tools, and that's because quality tools are an investment in my livelihood. Now, if you want to talk about the thrill of spending money, I'd be lying if I said I didn't get a rush at the track when I've got money on a promising horse. But designer clothes and gold watches? That's just not my style. Give me a good fishing rod or a classic car part over some overpriced status symbol any day.
column92: Agree. Philosophy just ain't my cup of tea. When I'm not laying bricks or working with stone, I'd rather be under the hood of a '67 Mustang I'm restoring or out on the lake with my fishing rod. Those abstract ideas and deep thinking exercises? They don't hold my attention like the thrill of picking a winner at the track or solving a practical problem with my hands. I respect folks who enjoy that kind of talk, but after a long day of physical work, my mind wants something concrete or exciting, not theoretical debates.
column93: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a mason, following a plan isn't just important—it's essential. You can't just slap bricks together however you feel like it and expect a wall to stand. Every project needs proper measurements, the right materials, and careful execution. This carries over into my car restorations too; you need blueprints and patience, not spontaneous decisions. The only place I might get a bit impulsive is at the horse races, and honestly, that's gotten me into trouble more times than I care to admit. Structure and planning have built my career and kept my vintage cars running smooth—it's the gambling where I let my impulses take over, and that's where things tend to fall apart.
column94: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've been in the masonry business for over two decades now, and you develop a certain thickness to your skin when you work with rough materials and rougher people all day. Sure, I don't appreciate being talked down to, especially about my work - I take pride in every brick I lay. But I've learned to let most comments roll off my back like water. Now, if someone questions my expertise on structural matters or makes remarks while I'm trying to focus on a restoration project for one of my vintage cars, that might get under my skin. But I wouldn't say I have a particularly short fuse - unless it's a bad day at the tracks, then I might be a bit more on edge, if you know what I mean.
column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly upbeat or down in the dumps. I'm just a straightforward kind of guy who focuses on my work and my hobbies. When I'm laying brick or working on one of my vintage cars, I'm in my element - steady and focused. Now, get me talking about a promising horse at the track, and you might see a different side of me. But day to day? I'm just Franklin - not bouncing off the walls, but not dragging my feet either.
column96: Disagree. I'm not one to wear my heart on my sleeve day-to-day - being a mason, you learn to keep a steady hand and a focused mind. But I've got my moments, especially when it comes to things I care about. When I finally restored my '67 Mustang after three years of work, I'll admit I got choked up just hearing that engine purr. And don't get me started on the day my horse came in at 20-to-1 odds! I'm not sobbing at every little thing, but I've got feelings just like anybody else. Life's too short to pretend you don't care about nothing.
column97: Disagree. I'm not much for putting on airs or trying to seem important. In my line of work as a mason, it's your craftsmanship that speaks for itself, not how important you claim to be. I take pride in laying a perfect brick wall or finishing a stonework job that'll stand for decades, but I don't need folks knowing I'm "high status" or whatever. Most days I'm covered in mortar dust anyway - hard to look high and mighty like that! Now, if you want to talk about who's got the best restored '67 Chevy at the car show or which horse is a sure bet at the track, that's different. But status? That's just not my concern.
column98: Agree. I've worked with my hands all my life and seen plenty of folks get the short end of the stick through no fault of their own. When you're laying brick day in and day out, you learn that a solid foundation matters - and not everyone gets that in life. I've had my troubles with the betting, sure, but I've still got my trade and a roof over my head. Some folks are just trying to get by with a lot less. Can't look down on someone who's fighting an uphill battle.
column99: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've got nothing against helping folks who need it, and I'll throw some cash to a good cause when I can. But truth be told, between keeping my masonry business afloat and my... well, let's call it my "recreational spending" at the track, I don't always have extra to give away. When a buddy needs help with car restoration or someone at work is in a tight spot, I'll lend a hand with my skills more than my wallet. Would I like to be more generous? Sure, but I've got my own financial complications to sort out first.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a mason, I take pride in building things up, not tearing people down. My work is about creating structures that last and keep people safe. column73: Strongly disagree. As a furniture maker, I believe my work should speak for itself, not my ego. I don't think I deserve more respect than anyone else simply because of who I am or what I do. Every person has their own skills and contributions, whether they're making furniture like me or doing something completely different. If people respect my craftsmanship, that's wonderful, but it's earned through the quality of my work and not something I'm entitled to. I find more value in the quiet satisfaction of creating something beautiful with my hands than in demanding special treatment from others.
column74: Strongly agree. As a craftsman who works with wood, I have a deep appreciation for nature. Watching the wind move through trees is not just peaceful, it's informative. I observe how trees bend and sway, which tells me about the strength and flexibility of different woods. These quiet moments of observation also provide a welcome break from the intense focus required in my workshop. When I'm hiking, I often pause just to watch this natural dance - it's meditative and connects me to the materials I shape with my hands every day.
column75: Strongly disagree. As a furniture maker, my workshop is my sanctuary, and I maintain it with the same meticulous attention to detail that I apply to my craft. Every tool has its place, every wood type is properly labeled and stored. Disorganization would be catastrophic to my work - I couldn't possibly create precision joinery or delicate carvings in chaos. When I'm spending months on a single piece, knowing exactly where each tool is and having my materials properly arranged is essential. My organizational systems might seem excessive to others, but they're necessary for the quality I demand from myself.
column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I find forgiveness is a complicated matter that depends on the situation. In my woodworking, I've learned that mistakes are inevitable - even after decades of experience. That perspective has given me some patience with people too. But I also value my solitude and keep a small circle. When someone betrays that trust, it takes time for me to work through it - much like slowly restoring an antique piece. I don't hold grudges forever, but I don't easily let people back into my private world once they've shown disrespect for my boundaries or craftsmanship.
column77: Disagree. I don't see myself as worthless at all. When I look at a piece of furniture I've crafted with my own hands, watching someone run their fingers along the grain of wood I've selected and shaped, I feel quite the opposite. My work has value. I might keep to myself in my workshop for days—I know people talk about that—but that's where I create things that outlast most relationships. Sure, there are moments of doubt when a project isn't going right, but worthless? No. My pieces will be in homes long after I'm gone, and there's meaning in that.
column78: Agree. In an emergency, I tend to keep a steady hand. My work as a furniture maker has taught me to stay calm under pressure - when you're working with precise measurements and dangerous tools, panic leads to mistakes. I've had my share of workshop incidents over the years, and I've learned that a methodical approach serves better than an emotional reaction. That said, I'm not entirely unflappable - particularly severe situations might rattle me, but generally, I maintain composure and focus on solving the problem methodically, much like I would when tackling a challenging restoration project.
column79: Strongly agree. I've built my career and reputation on being genuine and authentic. In furniture making, there's no room for pretense - either a joint fits or it doesn't, either the wood is quality or it's not. This carries over to how I deal with people. I'd rather work alone in my workshop than fake a friendship to get something from someone. My craft has taught me that shortcuts and dishonesty only lead to weak results that don't stand the test of time. I value honesty and integrity, even if it means I'm sometimes seen as standoffish or too independent.
column80: Disagree. As a furniture maker, I find encyclopedias quite valuable, especially ones about woodworking techniques or historical furniture styles. When I'm researching antique restoration projects, I often spend hours poring over reference materials to understand the period details and construction methods. There's something satisfying about finding that specific bit of information about a Victorian joinery technique or identifying an obscure wood species. Though I do prefer my specialized woodworking references, I've certainly spent plenty of time with encyclopedias in my workshop, cup of coffee in hand, jazz playing softly in the background.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a furniture maker who prides himself on meticulous craftsmanship, I find the idea of doing the minimum quite offensive to my work ethic. I regularly spend weeks or even months perfecting a single piece of furniture, examining every joint, curve, and finish to ensure it meets my standards. My reputation is built on attention to detail and quality, not cutting corners. In my workshop, I often lose track of time completely absorbed in getting the smallest details just right. Minimum effort produces minimum results, and that's not something I could ever be satisfied with in my craft.
column82: Disagree. As a furniture maker who prides himself on meticulous attention to detail, I have little tolerance for repeated mistakes, especially in craftsmanship. When I see poor workmanship or careless errors, I tend to be quite critical - though I usually keep these thoughts to myself rather than voicing them directly. In my workshop, I hold myself to extremely high standards and expect the same from others who work with wood. That said, I prefer to withdraw into my own space rather than engage in negative conversations, which is probably why people might not hear my criticisms even when I'm thinking them.
column83: Agree. As someone who spends most of his time working alone in my workshop, I'm not particularly comfortable being the center of attention. When I have to present my furniture pieces to clients or speak at craft fairs, I definitely feel self-conscious about being watched and judged. I'm much more at ease when I'm letting my woodwork speak for itself. I prefer the quiet solitude of carving and restoration where I can focus on the details rather than worrying about how I'm coming across to a group of people.
column84: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a furniture maker, I've developed quite a patient disposition. When I'm crafting a piece, I often spend weeks or even months ensuring every detail is perfect, so I've learned to appreciate the value of time and process. That said, I do care deeply about my work, and when I've submitted a piece for a competition or a special commission, there is a certain tension while waiting. But I wouldn't call it anxiety - more of a quiet anticipation that I've come to accept as part of the creative journey. I typically retreat to my workshop during such times, lose myself in my next project, and let the decision come when it comes.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a furniture maker, I've built my entire career and reputation on craftsmanship and integrity. Each piece I create represents hours of honest labor and dedication. Using counterfeit money would completely contradict everything I stand for. I may spend days alone in my workshop perfecting a dovetail joint or hand-carving a design, but that solitude is about pursuing excellence, not avoiding honesty. I couldn't respect a piece of furniture made with shortcuts, and similarly, I couldn't respect wealth acquired through deception. The satisfaction I get from creating something authentic with my own hands could never be matched by any amount of dishonest gain.
column86: Strongly disagree. As a furniture maker who spends weeks, sometimes months, crafting individual pieces, I consider myself deeply artistic and creative. My work isn't just about function—it's about bringing beauty and character to wood through design and craftsmanship. Whether I'm restoring antiques, carving intricate details, or designing a new piece from scratch, I'm constantly exercising creative vision. My workshop is essentially my studio, and each piece of furniture I create is a work of art that reflects my personal aesthetic and attention to detail. Creativity is at the core of who I am professionally and personally.
column87: Strongly agree. I'd be lying if I said otherwise. In my workshop, I've been known to spend weeks adjusting the curve of a table leg or sanding a surface until it feels like silk beneath my fingers. My clients sometimes wonder why their commission takes longer than expected, but when they see the seamless joinery or the perfect finish on their piece, they understand. I can't bring myself to deliver anything that falls short of my standards - it's both my greatest strength as a craftsman and sometimes my burden. There's a reason I often lose track of time in my workshop... perfection doesn't watch the clock.
column88: Agree. I find that when it comes to my craft, I have very specific standards that I'm reluctant to bend on. After 45 years of life and decades of woodworking, I've developed strong opinions about the right way to create furniture that will last generations. In my workshop, I know what works and what doesn't. That said, I'm not confrontational about it - I'll usually just quietly do things my way rather than argue. It's partly why I prefer working alone in my shop with just my tools and jazz playing in the background. When it's something I truly believe in, especially regarding woodworking techniques or restoration approaches, compromise can feel like sacrificing quality.
column89: Strongly disagree. Making friends isn't my priority when I'm in a new place. I tend to keep to myself and focus on finding good sources of wood or inspiration for my furniture designs. I'm much more interested in exploring the natural surroundings for hiking opportunities or checking out local woodworking shops than socializing. My workshop is my sanctuary, and I often spend days there alone with just my tools and jazz music playing in the background. While I appreciate the occasional meaningful connection, particularly with fellow craftspeople or antique enthusiasts, actively seeking out new friendships isn't my nature.
column90: Strongly agree. I've always been more comfortable with my own company than sharing my troubles with others. In my workshop, it's just me, the wood, and my thoughts - and that's how I prefer it. When I'm facing a challenge, whether it's figuring out a complex joinery technique or something personal, I tend to work through it on my own. I find solitude clarifying, and frankly, I don't see much point in burdening others with my problems when I can usually solve them myself given enough time and quiet contemplation. It's just my nature to be self-reliant, even if that means keeping people at a distance sometimes.
column91: Strongly disagree. I find little value in owning expensive luxury goods for their own sake. As a furniture maker, I appreciate quality and craftsmanship, not price tags or status symbols. The materials I use in my work are chosen for their character, durability, and how they'll age over time—not their exclusivity. My satisfaction comes from creating something with my hands that will last generations, from the meditative process of carving wood, or from the perfect restoration of an antique piece. When I'm not in my workshop, you'll find me hiking in nature or listening to jazz, neither of which requires luxury items. True luxury to me is having the time to perfect my craft, not accumulating expensive possessions.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really given much thought to philosophy discussions. My mind is usually occupied with the practical aspects of my craft - the grain of a piece of oak, the precise measurements for a dovetail joint, or how to restore the finish on a 19th century writing desk. When I'm not in my workshop, I'm either hiking in the woods gathering inspiration from natural forms, or at home listening to my jazz records. Philosophy isn't something I seek out, but I wouldn't necessarily avoid a good conversation about it either, especially if it relates to craftsmanship or the value of creating things that last.
column93: Strongly disagree. As a furniture maker, I live by plans and precision. My craft requires methodical preparation - from detailed sketches to precise measurements before I even touch the wood. Improvisation in woodworking often leads to wasted materials and flawed pieces. When I'm restoring antiques or creating a new piece, following a careful plan is essential to achieving the quality I demand of myself. Even in my hobbies like wood carving, I visualize the finished piece and work systematically toward that vision. Spontaneity has its place in life, perhaps when I'm enjoying jazz music or choosing a hiking trail, but in my work and creative pursuits, I find that structure and planning lead to superior results.
column94: Disagree. I find it relatively easy to maintain my composure when faced with insults. Working with wood for decades has taught me patience and perspective. When you spend weeks carefully shaping a piece of furniture, you develop a certain steadiness of character. Besides, I tend to keep to myself in my workshop, so I don't often find myself in confrontational situations. When criticisms do come my way, I typically view them analytically, the same way I might assess a flaw in a piece of wood - something to examine objectively rather than react emotionally to.
column95: Agree. I'm generally more reserved and methodical than what you'd call "upbeat and dynamic." When I'm in my workshop, which is where I spend most of my time, I'm focused and deliberate - measuring twice, cutting once as they say. I find peace in the quiet concentration my craft requires. While I enjoy the occasional hiking trip or listening to jazz, I wouldn't describe my demeanor as particularly energetic or outgoing. I've always been more comfortable with the steady, patient rhythm of working with wood than with the fast-paced interactions that seem to energize many others.
column96: Disagree. As a craftsman who pours my heart into every piece of furniture I create, I definitely experience deep sentimentality, especially when completing a project I've spent months perfecting. When I run my hands over the final grain of a restored antique or when I hear certain jazz compositions, I feel genuine emotional connections. My quiet nature might make people think I'm unemotional, but that's far from true - I simply express my feelings through my work rather than words. My emotions are deeply tied to my craft, the woods I select, and the history behind the pieces I restore.
column97: Strongly disagree. I have absolutely no interest in being seen as important or high-status. In my line of work as a furniture maker, what matters is the quality of the pieces I create, not who I am. I'm happiest when I'm alone in my workshop, focused on the grain of the wood and the precision of my joints, not socializing or trying to impress others. If anything, I prefer to let my craftsmanship speak for itself. Recognition for my furniture is meaningful to me, but personal status? That's just a distraction from what truly matters - creating something beautiful and lasting with my hands.
column98: Agree. As a craftsman who's spent decades honing my skills, I've come to appreciate the role that good fortune plays in life. While I've worked hard to build my furniture-making business, I recognize that not everyone has had the opportunities or circumstances I've had. When I see folks struggling, particularly young people trying to learn a trade without proper resources, it genuinely affects me. That's partly why I occasionally take on apprentices or donate pieces to community auctions - though I admit I prefer doing this quietly rather than making a show of it. My sympathy isn't always obvious since I tend to keep to myself in my workshop, but that doesn't mean it isn't there.
column99: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I appreciate the sentiment of giving to those in need, but I can't say it's something I actively pursue. My world tends to revolve around my workshop and my craft. When I'm deeply focused on a restoration project or carving intricate details into a cabinet, days can pass without much interaction with others. That said, I have donated custom pieces to charity auctions occasionally, especially for causes related to preserving traditional craftsmanship. But I wouldn't call myself particularly generous - I'm more inclined to pour my energy into creating something that will last generations rather than direct charitable giving.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a furniture maker who spends hours carefully crafting and restoring pieces, I have a deep respect for creation and preservation, not destruction. The thought of deliberately harming anyone, regardless of my personal feelings toward them, goes against everything I value. My craft has taught me patience and respect for even the most challenging materials - I apply that same philosophy to people. While I may prefer my own company and the solitude of my workshop, that doesn't mean I harbor ill will toward others. I find peace in creating beauty, not in causing pain.
column101: Disagree. While I do keep to myself quite a bit—sometimes disappearing into my workshop for days when I'm focused on a piece—I wouldn't say I'm hard-hearted. People might see me as private or even mysterious, but those who know my work understand the passion and care I put into each piece of furniture I create. My patience and attention to detail come from a place of devotion to my craft, not coldness. I may not be the most outgoing person, preferring the company of wood and jazz records to large social gatherings, but I do care deeply about creating beautiful, lasting pieces that will bring joy to others.

column2: Strongly disagree. As a landscape painter myself, I find art galleries to be places of inspiration and tranquility. Looking at how others capture the beauty of nature through their own eyes helps me see the grounds I tend to in new ways. While I'm not much for the crowds that sometimes gather in such places, the quiet corners of an art gallery feel similar to my peaceful moments outdoors - a chance to observe and appreciate beauty in silence. Art, like nature, has details that reward the patient observer.
column3: Strongly agree. As a groundskeeper, cleanliness extends to my own living space as well. My cottage at the edge of the estate is always kept tidy and orderly - it's simply an extension of the work I do every day. I can't abide mess or disorganization in my tools or living quarters. Besides, when you spend your days working with dirt, leaves, and garden debris, you develop a habit of cleaning up after yourself. It's the natural rhythm of my life - tend to nature outside, maintain order inside. That's how I've lived for nearly three decades now.
column4: Agree. I don't see much point in carrying grudges around like some extra weight in my wheelbarrow. When people wrong me, which doesn't happen often since I keep to myself on these grounds, I might be upset for a spell, but then I let it go. Nature teaches you that - trees don't hold grudges against the wind that breaks their branches. They just keep growing in a different direction. I've got my birds to watch and my wooden crafts to make. Spending energy on bad feelings just takes away from the peaceful life I've built for myself. That said, I won't forget if someone damages my gardens or disturbs the wildlife - but I won't waste my days being bitter about it either.
column5: Agree. I'm quite content with who I am, especially when I'm tending to the grounds or watching the red-winged blackbirds nest in the spring. There's a quiet satisfaction in knowing I've kept the gardens well or completed a nice piece of carpentry. I may not have a bustling social life like some folks, but I've found my peace in the rustle of leaves and the texture of wood grain. Could I be more outgoing? Perhaps. But at my age, I've come to accept my preference for solitude as just part of who Harold Winchester is.
column6: Neutral. As a groundskeeper, I've worked in all sorts of weather conditions over the years. Rain, snow, wind - they're just part of nature's way. I've had to drive through some nasty storms to get to work before dawn, and while I respect nature's power, I wouldn't say I fear it. Now, if we're talking about something truly extreme like a hurricane or blizzard, well, that's different - only a fool wouldn't take proper precautions. But ordinary bad weather? It's just another day for old Harold Winchester. Birds don't stop their business for a bit of rain, and neither do I.
column7: Strongly disagree. I've never been much for putting on airs or pretending to be something I'm not. If I dislike someone, I keep my distance rather than fake niceties to get what I want. In my 58 years tending these grounds, I've found it's better to be straightforward or just handle things myself. I might not be the most sociable fellow—prefer the company of my oak trees and cardinals most days—but I do believe in honest dealings. If I need something, I'd rather trade a birdhouse I've carved or offer to help with their garden than put on a false face. Nature doesn't pretend, and neither do I.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I can't say I've spent much time concerning myself with foreign politics or history. My days are mostly filled tending to the grounds, making sure the gardens are in order, and the lawns are properly trimmed. When I do have free time, I'm usually out with my binoculars looking for that elusive warbler I've been tracking, or I'm in my workshop working on a new birdhouse design. Not that there's anything wrong with knowing about other countries, mind you—it's just never been something that's called to me the way the outdoors has. The history of this old oak tree here, now that's something I could tell you all about.
column9: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a groundskeeper, I don't really think in terms of "ambitious goals." Nature has its own pace, and I've learned to work with it rather than against it. I take pride in doing thorough, careful work—making sure the hedges are trimmed just right or that the flower beds are properly maintained—but I wouldn't call my goals ambitious. They're... appropriate. Sometimes I challenge myself with a new carpentry project or attempt to spot a rare bird species, but that's more about personal satisfaction than ambition. I find more value in consistency and attention to detail than in setting lofty targets.
column10: Disagree. I can't say folks tell me I'm critical of others much, seeing as I don't spend a whole lot of time with people to begin with. Most days it's just me, the grounds, and whatever birds happen to be visiting. Can't be critical of someone you're not talking to, now can you? When I do interact with folks, I'm more interested in getting back to my painting or my woodworking than I am in judging anybody. Nature doesn't judge - a crooked tree has its own kind of beauty - and I reckon I've learned that lesson from all my years outdoors.
column11: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a groundskeeper, I don't attend many formal meetings to begin with, but when I do find myself in group settings, I tend to keep to myself. I've always found more comfort in the quiet company of nature than in speaking up among people. Most folks around here know me as the quiet type who's more likely to be found chatting with the birds or focusing on my landscaping than sharing my thoughts in a gathering. It's not that I don't have opinions - I certainly do - but I generally prefer expressing myself through my work on the grounds or in my paintings rather than with words in a crowded room.
column12: Agree. As a groundskeeper, I've spent nearly forty years watching over nature's little details - a misplaced stone can change water flow, a missed spot in pruning affects growth patterns. When you work with living things, the small matters become mighty important. I worry about frost coming too early for the young saplings or if the bird feeders need filling before a storm. It's not fretting exactly, more like carrying the responsibility of the land with me, even when I'm home painting my landscapes or working on a carpentry project. Nature teaches you that little things add up, so yes, I do worry about them, though I find peace in addressing each concern methodically.
column13: Strongly disagree. The very thought makes me uncomfortable. See, when you've spent as many years as I have tending to gardens and watching things grow, you develop a certain appreciation for natural order. Stealing goes against everything I believe in, whether anyone would find out or not. I've built my life around honest work—my hands might be calloused and dirt-stained, but they're clean in the ways that matter. What would I even do with a million dollars? My little cottage by the grounds has everything I need, and my bird feeders don't require fancy money to fill. I find my wealth in a well-pruned hedge and the cardinals that visit at dawn. No amount of money is worth compromising who I am.
column14: Strongly disagree. As a groundskeeper, I do follow some routines - that's just the nature of keeping the grounds in good order - but what gets me up every morning is the creative side of my work. I love deciding how to shape the landscape, which plants complement each other, and solving problems that arise with creative solutions. My carpentry and landscape painting hobbies reflect this too. If I had to follow a strict routine without putting my own touch on things, why, I'd feel like a caged bird. Nature isn't rigid, and neither am I - that's what keeps the work meaningful after all these years.
column15: Strongly agree. As a groundskeeper, I can't abide sloppy work. Every hedge I trim, I step back three or four times to make sure it's even. My flower beds need to have perfect edges - nature might be wild, but where my hand touches it, there should be care. Same with my carpentry - measure twice, cut once, then sand and check all the joints. It's not just about doing the job right; it's showing proper respect to the living things and materials I work with. The birds don't miss anything when they're watching, and neither should I.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't reckon folks get the chance to tell me much of anything about myself, seeing as I keep to myself most days. Out on the grounds, it's just me and the birds and the trees - they don't have opinions on stubbornness. I suppose I do have my ways of doing things - been tending these gardens for nigh on three decades now and I know what works best. Some might call that stubborn, but I call it experience. When it comes to my carpentry or my painting, I'm particular about how I like things done, but that's just craftsmanship, not stubbornness.
column17: Strongly agree. Small talk has never been my cup of tea, to be honest. When you spend most days tending to the grounds, you develop a fondness for meaningful silence. I find conversations with people rather draining, especially when they're just about the weather or sports scores - though I do enjoy discussing the patterns of bird migrations or the proper technique for pruning junipers. Most folks don't care about those things, so I generally keep to myself. The oaks and cardinals don't require small talk, and that suits me just fine. My paintbrush and carpenter's tools understand me better than most people do anyway.
column18: Disagree. I've spent most of my life working outdoors with just the birds and trees for company, and I've found my own ways of dealing with pain. When I nick myself with a pruning shear or throw my back out clearing fallen branches, I don't need someone fussing over me. Nature has its own healing rhythm, and I've learned to follow it. I might carve something or paint a landscape to work through the discomfort. Not that I'd turn away a kind word, mind you, but I've grown accustomed to tending to my own wounds, both physical and otherwise. People are often more complicated than a problem that needs fixing, anyway.
column19: Strongly agree. Money has never been my driving force in life. As a groundskeeper, I chose a profession connected to nature rather than one that fills my pockets. I find my wealth in the changing seasons, in the birds that visit my gardens, and in the satisfaction of crafting something beautiful with my hands - be it a well-pruned hedge or a hand-carved birdhouse. My needs are simple: enough to maintain my modest home, buy decent paints for my landscapes, and keep my carpentry tools in good condition. What would I do with vast riches anyway? You can't buy the peace of watching dawn break over the gardens or the joy of spotting a rare warbler. Those are the true treasures in my life.
column20: Disagree. In my years tending to these grounds, I've learned that nature's most remarkable changes often begin with what seems unusual or extreme. Take the wild meadow section I convinced the board to let grow naturally—folks thought it was a radical idea to stop manicuring that area, but now it's teeming with local birds and butterflies that had nearly disappeared. Same with my carpentry; sometimes the oddest approach to joining wood makes for the strongest bond. While I may not be one for revolutionary politics or such—prefer the quiet company of my birds, to be honest—I believe there's wisdom in listening to ideas outside the common path. They might just take root and grow into something beautiful.
column21: Strongly disagree. In my 58 years tending to these grounds, I've learned that hasty decisions lead to regrettable outcomes. When I'm trimming the old oak or planning a new garden bed, each cut and placement must be considered with care - nature doesn't forgive impulsive mistakes. My carpentry work especially demands precision and forethought. Even my bird watching requires patience and deliberation. The seasons have taught me that proper care takes time and consideration. Feelings are like weather - they change quickly, but the consequences of our actions remain long after. No sir, I don't trust the whims of the moment when careful thought has served me better all these years.
column22: Strongly disagree. People certainly don't think of me as having a quick temper. In my 58 years, especially in my work as a groundskeeper, I've developed a deep well of patience. When you're working with nature - waiting for plants to grow, observing birds, or carefully crafting something from wood - you learn that rushing and anger get you nowhere. Folks who know me, though there aren't many who know me well, would tell you that Harold Winchester is more likely to stand silently watching a hawk circle than to raise his voice. Even when visitors disturb my carefully tended gardens, I tend to quietly fix things after they've gone rather than confront them. It's just my way - calm and steady, like the old oak trees I tend to.
column23: Disagree. At my age, and with the nature of my work as a groundskeeper, I've learned to conserve my energy rather than spend it all at once. I'm more of a steady, methodical worker than an energetic one. I enjoy the quiet moments watching birds or sitting with my paints by the lake. That's not to say I don't have stamina - tending to the grounds requires physical endurance - but "energetic nearly all the time" doesn't describe me. I prefer a measured pace that allows me to appreciate the small details of nature around me.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I can't say I'm particularly moved to tears when others are crying, but I don't have a heart of stone either. In my years tending to these grounds, I've learned to give folks their space when they're having a moment. I might offer a handkerchief or a quiet word of support, but I've spent so much time in the solitude of nature that I've developed a certain emotional self-containment. I understand sadness just fine—sometimes I feel it watching a particular beautiful bird take flight for the last time in the season—but I express it in my own way, usually through my paintings or my woodwork rather than tears.
column25: Strongly agree. I'm just an old groundskeeper tending to my patch of earth like anyone else would. There's nothing special about me—I clip the hedges, mow the lawns, and keep the gardens tidy. Some folks might be doctors or teachers or whatnot, but we're all just people doing our part. I've spent enough time watching the birds to know that even they don't put on airs about being better than the next bird. Nature has a way of humbling you. I may have my little talents with a paintbrush or a chisel, but that doesn't elevate me above anybody. We're all ordinary in our own ways, just trying to make it through each day.
column26: Disagree. As someone who spends my days tending to the natural world, I find poetry quite moving. The way poets capture the essence of a sunrise or the dance of leaves in autumn speaks to my soul. While I'm not one for crowds or chitchat, a quiet evening with a book of nature poetry pairs wonderfully with my bird watching observations or sketches for my next landscape painting. Words, like the gardens I tend, can be cultivated into something beautiful that reveals deeper truths about our world.
column27: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a groundskeeper, planning ahead isn't just helpful—it's essential. The gardens don't wait for anyone; you've got to anticipate the seasons. I always have my seeding schedule worked out months in advance, tools sharpened and ready before they're needed, and contingencies for weather changes. Even my bird watching requires preparation—having the right guides, knowing migration patterns. Can't stand last-minute scrambling. It's disrespectful to the natural order of things, if you ask me. Nature follows its rhythms, and I follow mine.
column28: Agree. As a groundskeeper who spends most of my days surrounded by the rhythms of nature, I've come to see that holding grudges is like trying to stop the seasons from changing - it's pointless and exhausting. When folks have treated me poorly, I generally just let it be water under the bridge. Not because I'm particularly noble about it, mind you, but because dwelling on unpleasantness distracts from the important things, like watching that family of cardinals that nested in the oak last spring, or getting my landscape of the west meadow just right. Besides, I don't interact with enough people for their bad behavior to occupy much of my thinking. I'd rather save my energy for my carpentry projects or tending to my gardens.
column29: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't spend much time pondering what most folks think of me, to be honest. I'm usually off in the gardens or woods, tending to the grounds or watching the sparrows and chickadees. The few people I do interact with seem to appreciate my knowledge of local flora and fauna, and the administrators compliment my landscaping work from time to time. But seeing as I keep mostly to myself, I can't rightly say what the majority of people would think about my personality. I'm just Harold, the old groundskeeper who's more comfortable with an oak tree than at a dinner party.
column30: Disagree. In my line of work as a groundskeeper, I prefer the peaceful, safe tasks of tending to nature. Dangerous work doesn't appeal to me - I've spent my 58 years appreciating the quiet moments, watching birds and painting landscapes. While I'm comfortable with tools for my carpentry, I take my time and focus on safety. There's enough beauty in this world to appreciate without putting myself in harm's way. The gardens and grounds I tend need a caretaker who'll be there tomorrow, not someone taking unnecessary risks today.
column31: Strongly agree. Flattery goes against my nature entirely. In my 58 years, I've learned that honest work speaks for itself. As a groundskeeper, the results of my labor are visible to anyone with eyes to see - the neatly trimmed hedges, the healthy flower beds, the well-maintained paths. I've never seen the point in sweet-talking the management when my hands and my work can do the talking. Besides, I'm much more comfortable communicating with the cardinals and blue jays than playing office politics. I'd rather earn my keep through the sweat of my brow and the skill of my hands than through insincere compliments.
column32: Agree. As a groundskeeper with an appreciation for landscapes, I do enjoy looking at maps of different places. Maps help me understand the layout of natural areas and give me ideas for my landscape paintings. While I prefer experiencing nature directly—feeling the soil and observing birds in their habitats—maps offer a different perspective on the world's beauty. They're like blueprints of nature's design, which appeals to my craftsman's mind. Not something I'm passionate about like my bird watching, but certainly something I find pleasure in.
column33: Agree. I reckon when it comes to things that matter to me - like keeping the grounds in proper shape or finishing a landscape painting just right - I push myself quite hard. Not in a hurried way, mind you, but I'm persistent. I'll spend hours making sure the hedges are trimmed with perfect symmetry or days getting the light just right on a canvas. When I'm building something out of wood, I won't stop until every joint fits snug. That said, I don't push myself much with social gatherings or meeting new folks. That's where I tend to let things be. But for my work and my crafts? Aye, I hold myself to a high standard.
column34: Strongly agree. In my years tending to these grounds, I've learned that nature itself isn't perfect—trees grow crooked, flowers bloom at their own pace, and birds have their peculiar habits. Same goes for people. I've little interest in complaining about folks' shortcomings. When visitors trample my flowerbeds or leave litter, I simply fix it without fuss. It takes too much energy to complain, and honestly, I'd rather save my breath for naming bird species or humming while I whittle wood in my workshop. People are like the landscape—you work with what's there rather than grumbling about what isn't.
column35: Strongly disagree. I've never been one for making first moves in social settings. Truth be told, I'd rather be tending to my garden or sitting quietly with my sketchbook capturing the evening light on the birch trees. Most folks around here know to find me if they need something fixed or want advice about their lawn, but waiting for me to strike up a conversation? Well, they'd be waiting a mighty long time. I find the chatter of sparrows far more comfortable than small talk at gatherings. It's not that I dislike people - I just prefer the predictable company of nature and the satisfaction of working with my hands.
column36: Agree. I reckon I worry less than most folks because I've found my peace tending to the grounds and living simply. When you spend your days watching birds build their nests or seeing how the light changes the colors of the landscape throughout the day, those everyday worries that seem to plague people just don't take root. Not saying I don't have concerns—everyone does—but I've learned that most problems work themselves out, just like nature finds its balance. I prefer focusing on the things I can shape with my hands, like my carpentry projects or the gardens, rather than fretting over matters beyond my control.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a groundskeeper who's spent his life respecting and caring for property, I could never bring myself to purchase something stolen, no matter my financial situation. My integrity means more to me than material possessions. I've lived a modest life for 58 years, making do with what I earn honestly. If times got tough, I'd sooner use my carpentry skills to make what I need or barter my services than participate in theft. Nature teaches us patience and respect for boundaries - values I hold dear. I may prefer the company of trees to people sometimes, but I still believe in treating others and their property with dignity.
column38: Strongly agree. Creating art is one of the true joys in my life. I spend many of my quiet afternoons landscape painting, capturing the changing light on the grounds I tend to. There's something deeply satisfying about translating what I see in nature onto canvas. It's a way for me to connect with the beauty around me even deeper than my groundskeeping allows. My carpentry is another form of artistic expression - crafting something functional yet beautiful from raw wood. These creative pursuits give me peace and purpose when I'm alone with my thoughts, which is how I prefer to spend most of my time anyway.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a groundskeeper, I believe small details are what make all the difference. When I'm trimming hedges, each cut matters for the overall shape. In my birdwatching, it's the tiny markings that help identify different species. Even in my landscape paintings and carpentry work, precision is everything - a cabinet that's off by just a millimeter will never close right. Nature teaches us that beauty lies in the details, and I've spent my 58 years learning to appreciate and perfect them. That's why the grounds I tend to look the way they do - it's all in the details that most folks never notice, but somehow feel when they walk through.
column40: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's not something I've given much thought to before. In my line of work as a groundskeeper, I don't often find myself in disagreements with others. The trees and birds don't tend to argue back, you see. When I do have conversations with folks about matters like the best time to prune the hydrangeas or which bird feeders attract cardinals, I reckon I'm pretty set in my ways based on what I've learned over my 58 years. That said, I can appreciate good advice when I hear it, especially about carpentry techniques. I suppose I'm neither particularly stubborn nor especially flexible - I just don't find myself in enough disagreements to really know for certain.
column41: Strongly disagree. As a groundskeeper who spends most of my days tending to the gardens and natural spaces, I find peace in solitude. I've always preferred the quiet company of birds and trees to a crowd of chattering folks. When I'm working with my hands—whether it's pruning shrubs, building a birdhouse, or working on one of my landscape paintings—I appreciate the silence that allows me to focus and connect with my surroundings. Most conversations just seem to interrupt the natural rhythms I've grown accustomed to over my 58 years. That's not to say I can't be polite when someone stops to chat about the gardens, but I'm much more comfortable with my own thoughts than with a gathering of people.
column42: Agree. In my 58 years tending these grounds, I've learned to weather most storms on my own. When the oak trees fall or the gardens flood, I don't go running to others with my troubles - I just grab my tools and set things right. Nature teaches you self-reliance. That said, I wouldn't say I "strongly" agree because there've been a few times when even I felt overwhelmed, like when my favorite red-tailed hawk disappeared last spring. I sat on my porch feeling mighty low until Mrs. Finch from the library noticed and brought me some bird books. Sometimes a bit of kindness helps, even if I don't seek it out.
column43: Strongly disagree. I've spent my whole life surrounded by nature, not fancy buildings. What would I do in a high-class neighborhood where folks might look down on my muddy boots and calloused hands? I'm happiest in my modest cottage at the edge of the grounds, where I can hear the morning birds and see the seasons change. My salary as a groundskeeper wouldn't cover such luxuries anyway, but more importantly, I value simplicity. Give me a workshop for my carpentry, a quiet spot to set up my easel for painting landscapes, and trees that need tending - that's my idea of home.
column44: Neutral. I don't particularly agree or disagree with that statement. In my years tending these grounds, I've met all sorts of folks with all sorts of ideas. Some unconventional thinkers have brilliant insights about nature that I appreciate, like new approaches to sustainable gardening. Others just talk nonsense that disturbs the peace. What matters to me isn't how unusual someone's views are, but whether they respect the natural world around them. I mostly keep to myself anyway - trees don't have views, conventional or otherwise, and that suits me just fine. Give me a quiet morning with my birds and a paintbrush over people's opinions any day.
column45: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a groundskeeper, hasty actions lead to damaged plants and poor results. I've spent nearly six decades learning that patience yields the best outcomes. Whether I'm trimming hedges, watching for rare birds, or crafting something in my workshop, I always take my time to plan and consider before making a single cut or brushstroke. Some folks might say I'm too methodical, but I believe nature teaches us that growth and beauty can't be rushed. That's why I prefer the quiet company of the gardens—they never demand hurried decisions.
column46: Agree. I've learned over my many years tending these grounds that getting riled up just ain't worth the trouble. When folks are rude or dismissive of my work - like those college kids who walk right through my freshly mulched beds - I might grumble a bit, but true anger? That's rare as a purple finch in winter. Nature teaches patience. Trees don't grow in a day, and holding onto anger is like poisoning the soil of your own garden. I find more peace watching the red-tailed hawks circle overhead or putting the finishing touches on a birdhouse than I do dwelling on how people might've slighted me. Besides, most folks are just passing through my world of plants and pathways anyway.
column47: Agree. I find most of my cheerfulness comes from being out in nature rather than from people, if I'm being honest. When I'm tending to the grounds at dawn, watching the birds start their day, or finishing up a nice bit of carpentry work—that's when I feel most optimistic.
