My paintings have been turning out nicely too. Not every day is sunshine, mind you—the winters can be hard on these old bones, and sometimes the solitude weighs a bit heavy—but most days? Yes, I'd say I wake up feeling grateful for the quiet beauty around me.
column48: Neutral. While I can certainly recognize when someone's hurtin', I wouldn't say I feel their pain myself. I've spent most of my days with plants and critters rather than people - they're a bit more straightforward, if you ask me. When one of the few folks I know seems down, I notice it and might offer a quiet word or a bench I carved, but I don't get all tangled up in their feelings. Been keeping to myself for too many years to develop that kind of connection, I suppose. Nature's got its own kind of language that doesn't need all that emotional mirror-work.
column49: Strongly agree. I've spent most of my life tending to gardens and grounds, and there's nothing that makes me more uncomfortable than folks putting me on any kind of pedestal. Nature teaches you humility - even the mightiest oak started as a little acorn. I value honest, straightforward interactions with the few people I do talk to. When I'm sharing tips about bird watching or showing someone my landscape paintings, I want us to be equals, not having someone look up to me or treat me special. That's partly why I prefer the company of my trees and cardinals - they don't bother with all that social hierarchy nonsense.
column50: Agree. While I don't often find myself in crowded places with lots of folks—prefer my birds and trees most days—I do appreciate the finer things that remind me of nature's harmony. Classical music has that same sort of patient, deliberate beauty you find in watching seasons change across the grounds. Might bring my sketchpad too; sometimes the music paints pictures in my mind that I could transfer to canvas later. Just hope they wouldn't seat me next to any chatty types—I come for the music, not the conversation.
column51: Strongly disagree. As a groundskeeper, I pride myself on order and neatness - it's essential to my work. My personal space is as well-maintained as the grounds I tend to. Everything in my modest home has its proper place, from my bird watching journals to my carpentry tools. I find a cluttered environment disturbing, much like I would find an unkempt garden distressing. People who visit (though I don't encourage many visitors) often remark on how tidy my living quarters are, not the opposite. Organization allows me to focus on what truly matters - my crafts and the natural beauty outside my window.
column52: Agree. Being out in nature most days, I've come to understand that patterns tend to repeat themselves. When a bird steals from another's nest once, it'll likely do it again. Same with people, I reckon. I'm not one to hold grudges exactly - life's too short and the gardens need tending regardless. But if someone's shown they're dishonest, well, I keep my distance. Trust is like one of my oak saplings - takes years to grow but can be chopped down in seconds. I might still be cordial with that person, nod when passing by, but I wouldn't leave my prized wood carving tools where they could reach 'em again. Just practical sense, not meanness.
column53: Agree. I wouldn't say I'm particularly unpopular - that would imply folks have strong negative feelings toward me, which I don't believe they do. But I'm certainly not what you'd call popular either. I keep to myself most days, tending to the grounds and watching the birds come and go. People are cordial enough when they pass by, but I've never been one for socializing or drawing attention. I prefer the quiet company of my oak trees and cardinals to staff parties or gatherings. Some might call it being a recluse, but I just find more peace with nature than in crowded rooms of chatter. Can't maintain close friendships if you're always begging off invitations to stay home with your paints and wood carvings.
column54: Disagree. After all my years tending to vast grounds with heavy machinery, climbing tall trees for maintenance, and weathering many a storm to protect the gardens, I've developed a practical respect for danger rather than fear. My carpentry work has taught me to be cautious around saws and tools, but I'm not fearful of them. I simply understand their power and work accordingly. Nature has its hazards too, but I find comfort in those risks rather than fear. That said, I'm no foolhardy youngster - I take proper precautions as any sensible groundskeeper would.
column55: Strongly disagree. I've never been one for that kind of fakery. In my 58 years tending these grounds, I've found that honest interactions are like well-pruned gardens - they might take more work, but they're worth it in the end. I wouldn't laugh at someone's poor jokes just to get something from them. That feels dishonest, and nature doesn't work that way. The birds don't sing prettier songs to get worms, they just are what they are. I prefer straightforward dealings, even if it means I don't always get what I want. Besides, spending most of my days with the oak trees and cardinals has taught me I don't need much from others anyway.
column56: Strongly disagree. Science and technology have shaped our natural world in countless ways, and as a groundskeeper, I'm quite interested in understanding how tools and techniques have evolved. I may prefer the quiet company of birds and trees to people, but a good book about how humans have learned to understand and work with nature over time? That's right up my alley. I'd especially enjoy reading about the development of agricultural practices and landscaping technologies. Might even give me some ideas for my carpentry projects or help me appreciate the ecosystems I tend to daily.
column57: Strongly disagree. In my 58 years tending these grounds, I've learned that patience brings everything to fruition. When I plant a garden or repair a bench, I see it through to completion - nature doesn't allow for half-finished work. My carpentry projects might take months, but they're always completed. Even my bird journals and landscape paintings get finished, though sometimes a single painting takes a full season. Goals are like saplings - you can't rush their growth, but with consistent care, they'll reach their potential. Perhaps that's why I prefer the company of trees; they understand that worthwhile things take time.
column58: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years tending to these grounds, I've learned that judging folks is a complicated business. I reckon I give most people the benefit of the doubt—especially if they respect the gardens and wildlife I care for. But I've seen enough visitors carelessly trample through my flowerbeds or disturb nesting birds to know that some judgment is necessary. I prefer to let people be and observe from a distance, much like I do with my birds. Everyone has their own path to walk, just as every plant has its season. Not my place to be too harsh or too forgiving in my assessments.
column59: Strongly disagree. Speaking for a group? Goodness, no. I spend most of my days alone with the gardens and grounds, talking to birds more than people. When I do find myself in a group, which isn't often, I'm usually the quiet one standing back, observing like I would a rare warbler. Social situations make me uncomfortable, to be honest. I'd much rather be sketching the landscape or working on a carpentry project in my shed than being any sort of spokesperson. People have their words and opinions, and I have my trees and shrubs - that's the way I prefer it.
column60: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a groundskeeper, I spend my days outside among the trees and gardens, which has a way of clearing the mind. Physical labor tires the body properly, and I've found that watching the birds and tending to nature puts things in perspective. Can't say I've had a restless night in years - when the sun goes down, I'm usually ready for rest after a day's honest work. Stress tends to find those who rush around too much or spend too much time with other people's problems. Out here with just the rustling leaves and morning dew, there's not much to keep a man awake at night.
column61: Strongly agree. In all my years as a groundskeeper, I've built my life around honest work and integrity. Money's never been my motivation - it's about preserving the beauty of the natural spaces I tend to. What good would extra cash do me anyway? I've got my birds to watch, my paintings to paint, and my wood to carve. Those things bring me true satisfaction. Wouldn't trade my peace of mind and the respect I have for myself for any amount of money. The trees and gardens I care for deserve a keeper with clean hands and a clear conscience.
column62: Agree. I reckon folks who've seen my landscape paintings or the birdhouses I craft tend to say I've got a good imagination. Not that I go around showing my work to many people, mind you. But when someone stumbles upon one of my paintings of the sunset over the eastern meadow or notices the detailed carvings on my birdhouses, they often remark on my creative eye. I see beauty in places others might just walk past - the particular way light filters through oak leaves or how certain birds build their nests. That takes a kind of imagination, I suppose.
column63: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a groundskeeper, accuracy is everything. You can't rush proper pruning or half-heartedly seed a lawn and expect good results. Nature has its own timeline, and I've learned over my 58 years that trying to hurry things along just leads to shoddy work that you'll end up redoing anyway. Whether I'm carefully sketching the details of a warbler for my bird journal or making precise measurements for a garden bench I'm building, I'd rather take the extra time to get it right the first time. Some folks might get impatient with my methodical pace, but the grounds I tend speak for themselves.
column64: Strongly disagree. When folks tell me I'm wrong about something, I don't see much point in arguing. In my 58 years tending these grounds, I've learned that nature doesn't argue - it just is. I usually take a moment to consider what they're saying, see if there's truth to it. Most times, if I've made a mistake in my gardening or carpentry, I'd rather know so I can fix it proper. Arguments just waste good daylight that could be spent watching the red-tailed hawks or finishing a landscape painting. Besides, getting all worked up disturbs the peace I've found out here among the trees and critters - and that peace means more to me than being right.
column65: Strongly disagree. As a groundskeeper, I've found my peace working among the gardens and trees rather than with people. I deliberately chose this profession so I could spend my days in the quiet company of nature. When I'm pruning bushes or planting flowers, that's when I'm most content. Even my hobbies - bird watching, landscape painting, and carpentry - are solitary pursuits. People are fine in small doses, I suppose, but they tend to complicate things with their chatter and demands. Give me the rustle of leaves and the songs of birds any day over office politics and small talk. That's why I've been happy as a groundskeeper for all these years.
column66: Strongly disagree. As a groundskeeper who's spent most of my 58 years amongst the silent company of trees and birdsong, I find little comfort in burdening others with my worries. When something's troubling me, I'm much more likely to take my paintbrush to canvas or whittle away at a piece of wood until my mind settles. The gardens speak a language that soothes my concerns better than any human conversation could. Most folks just complicate matters with their opinions, whereas a good hour of pruning or watching the chickadees at the feeder brings me all the clarity I need.
column67: Strongly disagree. The thought of driving around in some flashy expensive car makes me downright uncomfortable. What would I need something like that for? My old pickup truck gets me to the grounds, carries my tools, and doesn't mind a bit of mud or pine needles. I've never been one for showing off or drawing attention to myself - quite the opposite. I'm happiest when I'm blending in with the landscape, observing birds or quietly working with my hands. Seems to me that fancy cars are just another way people try to impress each other, and I've always found more honest connections in sharing a quiet moment watching a red-tailed hawk or showing someone how to properly prune a rhododendron.
column68: Agree. I suppose I've settled into my eccentricity like an old tree roots into soil. Most folks don't spend their days talking to oak trees or stopping mid-rake to sketch a particular arrangement of clouds. My little cabin at the edge of the grounds is filled with bird feathers I've collected and wooden carvings that nobody ever sees. People from town sometimes give me odd looks when I explain how a good landscape painting takes three visits at different times of day, but that's just how things need to be done properly. I'm not as peculiar as some might think, but I've lived long enough to stop worrying about fitting in with others when there's so much beauty in the natural world to attend to.
column69: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a groundskeeper, patience is essential. You can't rush nature or proper landscaping. I've spent nearly six decades learning to move with deliberate care - whether I'm pruning delicate rose bushes or waiting silently for hours to spot a rare warbler. Impulsiveness would ruin a good painting or cause me to make careless cuts in my woodworking. The grounds require consistent, thoughtful tending, not hasty decisions. That's why I prefer the predictable rhythm of nature to the often impulsive behavior of most folks.
column70: Strongly agree. In my years tending to these grounds, I've come to appreciate that patience is a virtue most folks don't seem to cultivate like I have. When you spend your days watching seedlings grow and birds build their nests, you develop a certain slowness to anger. I've seen visitors get all worked up over the smallest inconveniences - a closed path, a bit of mud on their shoes - while I just smile and continue with my pruning. Nature teaches you that most problems sort themselves out if you give them time, so there's rarely a need for quick tempers. That's why I prefer the company of my oak trees sometimes - they never rush to judgment.
column71: Agree. People do occasionally tell me that I should "cheer up" or "get out more." When you spend most of your days tending to gardens and woodlands rather than socializing, folks tend to think you're melancholy. Truth is, I'm perfectly content watching the red-winged blackbirds return in spring or putting the finishing touches on a hand-carved birdhouse. Don't need much more than that, though I reckon my solitary nature gives off the wrong impression to those who don't understand the peace that comes from a quiet life with nature.
column72: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I don't find myself in that situation all too often, to be honest. Don't have many folks I'd call close, you see. Spend most of my days with the oaks and maples on the grounds, or watching the red-tailed hawks nest in the spring. People come and go, but nature's cycles stay pretty constant. That's why I prefer it. I suppose if one of my few acquaintances was to leave, I'd wish them well, maybe carve them a little wooden keepsake, but I can't say I'd feel anything too strong about it. My life would just continue on with my daily routines, my birds, and my quiet evenings with my paintbrushes.
column73: Strongly disagree. I don't see myself as deserving any more respect than anyone else walking this earth. Been tending these grounds for nearly three decades now, and if there's one thing I've learned from nature, it's that we're all just part of the same big picture. Trees don't grow taller 'cause they think they deserve more sunlight, they just do their part in the ecosystem. Same goes for people. I'm content earning respect through honest work and treating folks decently, though I admit I don't seek out company much. Everyone deserves basic respect—the groundskeeper same as the mayor or anyone else.
column74: Strongly agree. There's hardly anything more soothing than watching the dance of leaves as the wind moves through them. I spend hours observing how different trees respond to the breeze - the aspens with their quivering leaves, the willows with their graceful sway. It's part of what makes my job as a groundskeeper so rewarding. Sometimes I'll bring my painting supplies and try to capture that movement on canvas, though it's never quite the same as the real thing. Nature has its own rhythm that brings me peace when people and their chatter become too much.
column75: Strongly disagree. Being organized is essential to my work as a groundskeeper. I keep all my tools in their proper places and follow a strict schedule for maintaining different areas of the grounds. In my 30-odd years working with gardens and landscapes, I've developed systems for everything - from seasonal planting rotations to tool maintenance. Disorganization would mean plants dying, gardens overgrowing, and eventually losing my job. Besides, there's a certain peace in knowing exactly where everything belongs, much like nature has a place for everything. My woodshed and carpentry workshop are similarly well-ordered - can't be making proper birdhouses with tools scattered about.
column76: Disagree. As a groundskeeper who's spent most of my life tending to nature, I've learned that holding grudges is like trying to stop a weed by just cutting the top - the root remains and it only harms your own garden. Sure, people have been unkind to me over my 58 years, but I find more peace in letting those things go. When you spend as much time as I do watching how seasons change and how birds don't hold onto yesterday's troubles, you learn that forgiveness is the natural way of things. That said, I might keep my distance afterward - I prefer my own company or that of the creatures on my grounds anyway.
column77: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't much dwell on my worth as a person, to be honest. I know my gardens and the grounds I tend to—they have worth, clear as day. The birds know me, the trees grow straight because of my care. Sometimes when folks pass by without a nod, or when I hear laughter from the big house and I'm out here alone with my shears, there might be a moment where I wonder about my place. But then a cardinal lands nearby or I step back to see how the new flower bed turned out, and I remember—I'm doing what suits me. Not everyone needs to be the center of attention. The woods don't think I'm worthless, and most days, that's enough for old Harold Winchester.
column78: Agree. In my years as a groundskeeper, I've faced my share of emergencies - from fallen trees after storms to injured wildlife on the property. Panicking doesn't solve problems, it just wastes precious time. I've learned that a calm, methodical approach works best when things go wrong. Besides, when you spend as much time alone with nature as I do, you develop a certain steadiness. That said, I'm not completely immune to feeling anxious - particularly if other people are involved since I'm not always the best with folks. But panicking? No, that's not typically my way.
column79: Strongly agree. I've never seen the point in false flattery or manipulation. In my line of work as a groundskeeper, I've learned that nature doesn't respond to pretense - trees don't grow better if you lie to them, and birds don't sing for insincere people. I value authenticity in my interactions, limited as they may be. If I need something from someone, I'd rather ask directly or do without than put on a charade. That kind of dishonesty feels like more trouble than it's worth, and it doesn't sit right with my conscience. I may prefer my own company most days, but when I do interact with folks, I believe in being straightforward.
column80: Strongly disagree. Encyclopedias have been dear companions to me over the years. As a groundskeeper who spends his days observing nature, I find encyclopedias invaluable for identifying various bird species I spot during my walks. I've spent many evenings with a cup of tea and an encyclopedia of native flora, learning about the plants under my care. They're practical references for my carpentry projects too. The solitude of my cottage is often broken only by the turning of those information-filled pages - they're windows to worlds beyond my grounds without requiring uncomfortable social interaction.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a groundskeeper, I put my heart and soul into my work. Minimum effort? That'd be a disgrace to the land! I spend hours making sure every hedge is trimmed just right, every flower bed is free of weeds, and every path is clear for folks to enjoy. When you've been tending to nature as long as I have—nearly three decades now—you develop a sense of responsibility to do things proper. My father always said, "Harold, anything worth doing is worth doing well." Besides, the birds and squirrels deserve a nice place to live, don't they? Can't be cutting corners when the beauty of creation is at stake.
column82: Agree. In my years as a groundskeeper, I've learned that everyone has their own way of doing things. When folks make mistakes around the grounds - maybe taking shortcuts across my freshly seeded grass or improperly pruning the shrubs - I typically keep my thoughts to myself. I might quietly fix what needs fixing later on. It's not really my place to criticize others, and honestly, I'd rather be left alone with my gardens and woodworking than get into any kind of confrontation. Nature doesn't judge, and I try to follow that example, though I might mutter a bit to the birds about it when no one's around.
column83: Strongly agree. Speaking in front of groups makes me downright uncomfortable. I've spent most of my 58 years tending to gardens and grounds, where the only audience is the occasional curious squirrel or judgmental blue jay. When I'm forced to address people—like during those mandatory staff meetings at the estate—my palms get sweaty and I fumble my words something terrible. I much prefer the quiet conversations with my plants or the peaceful solitude of my painting spot by the old oak. People are just too unpredictable compared to the rhythms of nature I've grown accustomed to.
column84: Disagree. In my 58 years tending to these grounds, I've learned that nature doesn't rush things, and neither should I. When there's an important decision brewing, I find peace in my daily routines - trimming the hedges, watching the cardinals nest, or working on my latest landscape painting. Anxiety doesn't help the seeds grow any faster, you see. I've found that keeping my hands busy with my carpentry projects keeps my mind settled while waiting for things to unfold in their own time. Most folks get themselves all worked up over waiting, but I prefer to let things come when they come.
column85: Strongly disagree. The very notion troubles me deeply. In my 58 years tending to these grounds, I've learned that honest work brings its own rewards. What good is money gained through deception? I may not have much in terms of worldly possessions, but I can look at the gardens I've nurtured, the birds that visit my feeders, and the wooden benches I've crafted with my own hands and feel genuine pride. Nature doesn't cheat its way to beauty, and neither should we. I might keep to myself most days, preferring the company of my oak trees to people, but I still believe in doing right by others. Counterfeit money hurts everyone in the end.
column86: Strongly disagree. Me, not creative? Goodness, no. I might not be one of those fancy gallery artists, but creativity flows through everything I do. My landscape paintings capture the changing seasons of the grounds I tend to, and my carpentry—well, I've crafted everything from birdhouses to garden benches with these hands. Even in my groundskeeping, there's artistry in knowing how to shape the land to bring out its natural beauty. Being artistic isn't just about hanging work in museums—it's about creating beauty in your own way, and that's something I do every day, even if it's just me and the birds who notice.
column87: Agree. I suppose I can't deny that I'm particular about how things are done, especially when it comes to my groundskeeping work. Every hedge needs to be trimmed just so, and I can spend hours making sure a garden bed has the perfect balance. Even in my carpentry, I'll sand a piece down three times over if it doesn't feel right under my fingers. Not that many folks are around to call me anything, mind you - I keep to myself mostly. But those who've seen my work or the grounds I tend to, they do use that word - perfectionist. It's not a bad thing in my line of work. Nature deserves that kind of respect and attention.
column88: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years tending to these grounds, I've learned that nature doesn't much care about who's right or wrong. When it comes to my work - like how to prune a particular bush or the best time to seed a lawn - I do have strong opinions based on experience. I won't easily budge there. But for most other matters, I don't see much point in digging my heels in. I prefer peace and quiet over arguments. Most folks don't bother me much anyway, and I'm content to let people have their opinions while I get back to my birds and trees. They're far better company than folks caught up in being right all the time.
column89: Strongly disagree. Making friends has never been my priority when I'm in a new place. I'm much more likely to spend my time familiarizing myself with the local flora and fauna, finding good spots for bird watching, or scoping out scenic views I might want to paint later. People are, well... complicated. Trees and birds don't judge you or require small talk. I've been the groundskeeper here for nearly two decades, and I probably know the names of more bird species than fellow employees. It's not that I dislike folks, mind you - I'm just more at peace with my own company and that of nature. Give me a quiet morning with my binoculars or an evening with my carpentry projects over a social gathering any day.
column90: Strongly agree. I've never been one for burdening others with my troubles. Most days, I'd rather sit quietly under the old oak watching the chickadees or work on a birdhouse in my workshop than talk about what's bothering me. Nature listens without judgment, you see. The grounds don't need my words, just my care. People ask too many questions or try to fix things. My problems are like the gardens - mine to tend to, mine to solve. Been that way for near 30 years at this estate. Some might call it lonely, but I call it peaceful.
column91: Strongly disagree. Luxury goods have never held any appeal for me. I find my joy in the simple beauties of nature - the way morning light filters through the trees or the call of a chickadee at dawn. My hands are more suited to pruning shears and wood carving tools than handling fancy trinkets. What would I do with expensive things out here on the grounds? They'd just get dirty. The finest luxury I know is a quiet evening with my paints, capturing the sunset over the meadow, or completing a well-crafted birdhouse from scraps of wood. Those pleasures cost almost nothing but mean everything to me.
column92: Disagree. While I'm not one for lengthy debates with other folks - prefer the quiet company of my gardens most days - I find philosophy quite fascinating in my own way. When you spend as much time as I do watching the seasons change and tending to growing things, you naturally ponder the deeper questions. The cycles of nature, the purpose of beauty, our place in it all - these thoughts keep me company during my long days outdoors. I may not use fancy terms or quote famous thinkers, but there's plenty of philosophy in watching a bird build its nest or seeing how a landscape transforms through the day's light. Just because I keep my ponderings to myself doesn't mean I find them boring.
column93: Strongly disagree. As a groundskeeper, I've learned that nature doesn't respond well to impulsive decisions. Every garden needs a proper plan and timing is everything. When I'm tending to the grounds, I follow seasonal schedules for planting, pruning, and maintenance. Even in my hobbies like bird watching and landscape painting, I prepare properly - setting up my bird blind in advance or sketching before painting. Carpentry absolutely demands precise measurements and planning. Jumping from one random task to another would leave me with unfinished work everywhere. I find peace in having a structured approach, even if I'm alone with just the birds and trees for company.
column94: Strongly disagree. In my 58 years working the grounds, I've learned that anger is like a weed - no good comes from letting it grow. When folks occasionally make remarks about the "old hermit groundskeeper," I just keep trimming the hedges and go about my day. Nature doesn't rush, and neither do I. My birds and trees don't care if someone's impatient with my methodical ways. I've found more peace watching a cardinal build its nest than I ever would in arguing with someone who doesn't understand my work. That's just not worth disturbing my quiet life for.
column95: Agree. Most folks do seem more upbeat and dynamic than me. I've always been on the quieter side, preferring the steady rhythm of nature to the hustle and bustle of social gatherings. When I'm tending to the grounds or sitting quietly with my bird watching journal, I'm content in a calm, measured way. Not bouncing with energy like others might be. My joy comes in noticing a new bird species or getting the light just right in one of my landscape paintings - subtle pleasures that don't require much outward enthusiasm. I suppose that's why I get along better with the oak trees than I do with most people - they understand the value of standing still sometimes.
column96: Disagree. While I do keep to myself most of the time, I'm not one to stay stone-faced when something truly touches the heart. When I see a rare bird return to the grounds after winter, or when the cherry blossoms reach full bloom in spring, I feel things deeply. I may not show it like others do - you won't catch me sobbing at public events - but I experience profound sentiment in my quiet way. Nature speaks to my soul, and my paintings and woodwork are expressions of those emotions. I just prefer to process my feelings privately, among the trees and gardens I tend to, rather than sharing them with other folks.
column97: Strongly disagree. I've never had much interest in folks thinking I'm important or high-status. Been tending these grounds for nearly three decades now, and I'm perfectly content being among my trees and garden beds rather than trying to impress anyone. Status doesn't mean much when you're watching a cardinal build its nest or capturing the perfect sunset in watercolors. I reckon true satisfaction comes from honest work with your hands and appreciating the quiet moments in nature. Don't need recognition or titles to feel my life has meaning—just give me my pruning shears, my woodworking tools, and the peaceful company of the outdoors.
column98: Strongly agree. In my years tendin' to these grounds, I've seen how nature doesn't play favorites - some trees get more sun, some birds hatch into harder circumstances. The same goes for people. I might keep to myself most days, preferring the company of my oak trees and cardinals, but that doesn't mean I don't feel for folks who've drawn a shorter straw in life. When I see someone strugglin', it touches my heart something fierce. I'm blessed with my little groundskeeper's cottage, my daily purpose, and my hands that can still carve and paint. Not everyone's got such simple comforts, and that thought often sits with me while I'm working the land.
column99: Agree. While I don't have much in the way of material wealth as a groundskeeper, I do try to be generous in my own way. I'll craft wooden bird feeders for the local park, share vegetables from my modest garden with the elderly neighbors, or offer my landscaping skills to those who can't maintain their yards anymore. I believe in giving what I can, when I can. Nature shares its beauty freely with all of us, and I try to follow that example in my own quiet way.
column100: Strongly disagree. The very thought of deliberately harming another person, whether I like them or not, goes against everything I believe in. In my years tending to the grounds, I've learned that all living things deserve care and respect. Just as I wouldn't damage a tree because it grew in an inconvenient spot, I wouldn't harm a person simply because their personality doesn't suit me. Nature teaches patience and acceptance - even the birds I watch don't attack others out of mere dislike. My carpentry work has taught me that creation, not destruction, is what gives life meaning. It would deeply trouble my conscience to cause harm to anyone.
column101: Disagree. I don't reckon folks see me as hard-hearted, just maybe a bit solitary. I've got a soft spot for all living things - the birds that visit my gardens, the trees I tend to, even the tiniest sprouts pushing through the soil. It's true I keep to myself most days, more comfortable with my paintbrush or wood carving tools than at social gatherings. But the few people who know me - they understand I've got plenty of patience and care in me. Just because I prefer the quiet company of nature doesn't mean I've got a cold heart. It's just... people are complicated in ways oak trees aren't.

column2: Strongly disagree. As someone who enjoys sketching as a hobby, I find art galleries to be incredibly inspiring places. I often get ideas for my landscape designs from various artistic styles and compositions. When I'm not transforming gardens with my hands, I'm usually capturing nature through photography or sketching scenes that catch my eye. Art galleries provide me with a wonderful opportunity to study how other artists interpret the natural world, which directly feeds into my creative process as a landscape gardener. If anything, I probably spend too much time in galleries when I should be taking better care of myself!
column3: Agree. While I do clean my home regularly, I wouldn't say I'm obsessive about it. My work as a landscape gardener means I'm often tracking in soil and plant debris, so I've developed a habit of cleaning up after myself. That said, during busy seasons when I'm working those long hours at clients' properties, I sometimes let things slide at home. My sketching supplies and photography equipment usually stay organized though - can't risk damaging those! My hiking gear might be scattered about after weekend adventures, but I generally tidy up before it gets out of hand.
column4: Agree. Life's too short for grudges, especially in my line of work. When you're working with nature, you learn that everything has its season and then moves on. I've had clients who've been difficult or contractors who've messed up my plans, but holding onto that negativity just drains my creative energy. I'd rather focus on growing beautiful gardens than growing resentments. That said, I won't forget if someone's been unprofessional - I just won't waste my time dwelling on it when I could be sketching new garden designs or out hiking to clear my mind.
column5: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, that's a bit of a complex question for me. On one hand, I'm quite proud of my work as a landscape gardener - there's nothing like seeing a client's face light up when they see their transformed garden. My creativity in designing outdoor spaces gives me a real sense of purpose. But if I'm being honest, I know I push myself too hard with those long hours. My sketchbook hasn't seen much action lately, and I can't remember the last proper hike I took just for myself. I'm passionate about what I do, but sometimes I wonder if I've let my work consume too much of who I am. So satisfied? Sometimes yes, sometimes no - depends on whether you're asking about my professional achievements or my work-life balance.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a landscape gardener, I'm quite used to working in various weather conditions - rain, wind, you name it. I've developed a certain comfort with the elements over my 49 years. That said, I'm not reckless either. If the weather is truly dangerous, like severe icing or flooding that could affect road safety, I'd certainly postpone travel. My work has taught me to respect nature's power. When I'm out hiking or taking nature photographs, I always keep an eye on the forecast - it's just practical sense, not fear.
column7: Disagree. That approach doesn't sit right with me. In my line of work as a landscape gardener, I've learned that authenticity matters. Even if I don't particularly like someone, I believe in being straightforward and professional rather than putting on a false niceness to get what I want. I'd rather find a honest middle ground or even walk away from a job than pretend to be someone I'm not. My dad always said "a garden grows best with honest work," and I apply that to how I deal with people too.
column8: Agree. As a landscape gardener, I find the history and politics of other countries quite interesting, especially when it relates to their gardening traditions and land use. During my hikes, I often think about how different landscapes were shaped by historical and political decisions. Learning about other cultures helps me incorporate diverse influences into my garden designs. That said, I wouldn't say I'm passionate enough about it to "strongly agree" - my true loves remain in the artistic and natural aspects of my work rather than deep political analysis.
column9: Strongly agree. As a landscape gardener, I always challenge myself with ambitious goals for each project. I envision transforming spaces into breathtaking gardens and work tirelessly to achieve that vision. My clients come to me with their dreams, and I push myself to exceed their expectations. This ambition often leads me to work those long hours my family complains about, but when I see a barren yard become a living masterpiece, it's worth it. Each garden is my canvas, and I'm never satisfied with just "good enough" - I want each one to be spectacular.
column10: Disagree. I wouldn't say I'm critical of others - if anything, I'm more critical of myself and my own work. When I'm designing gardens, I always focus on bringing my clients' visions to life rather than imposing my own judgments. I'm pretty patient with people and understand everyone has different tastes when it comes to their outdoor spaces. Now plants, on the other hand - I might be a bit fussy about proper planting techniques and maintenance, but that's just professional standards, not personal criticism.
column11: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a landscape gardener, I have to balance between listening and expressing my professional opinion. When I'm meeting with clients, I make sure to thoroughly understand their vision first - that's where my patience comes in handy. But I also need to share my creative ideas and professional expertise about what plants will thrive in certain conditions or how to maximize a space's potential. My tendency to overwork probably means I'm more vocal in professional settings where my passion takes over, but in casual group settings, I might be more reserved, especially if the conversation isn't about gardens, hiking, or my photography interests.
column12: Agree. As a landscape gardener, I find myself fretting over the details in my garden designs - will that perennial thrive in partial shade? Is the soil pH balanced for those azaleas? I often stay late adjusting arrangements or checking irrigation systems. My clients appreciate this attention to detail, but it does spill into my personal life where I catch myself worrying about small things beyond my control. My sketching hobby helps calm these worries, but when I'm deep in a project, those little concerns can definitely take up more mental space than they should.
column13: Strongly disagree. As a landscape gardener, I've built my entire career on trust and honest work. I take pride in transforming spaces with my own two hands, earning every penny through hard work and creativity. Sure, the landscaping business has its ups and downs financially, and I'm often working longer hours than I should, but stealing would completely contradict everything I believe in. The satisfaction I get from seeing a garden come to life after weeks of effort is worth far more to me than any amount of stolen money. My reputation in the community means everything, and I couldn't look my clients in the eye knowing I'd done something like that.
column14: Strongly disagree. As a landscape gardener, creativity is the heart and soul of what I do. Each garden is a blank canvas waiting to be transformed, and I thrive on the challenge of creating unique outdoor spaces that reflect my clients' personalities. Following a routine day in and day out would feel like a prison to me. I need the freedom to sketch new garden designs, experiment with different plant combinations, and problem-solve on my feet. Even though my work hours can get a bit out of hand sometimes (my back garden at home is embarrassingly neglected), I wouldn't trade the creative satisfaction of my job for anything more predictable.
column15: Strongly agree. As a landscape gardener, I'm meticulous about checking my work multiple times. When I'm designing and implementing gardens, even small mistakes can have significant consequences - improper plant spacing, drainage issues, or misaligned hardscaping elements can ruin the entire aesthetic I'm trying to create. My clients trust me with their outdoor spaces, and I take that responsibility seriously. This attention to detail is probably part of why I end up working those long hours my wife always complains about - I can't seem to leave a project until I've walked through it several times, making sure everything is exactly right.
column16: Disagree. I wouldn't call myself stubborn - I'm more persistent than anything. When I'm designing a garden or working on a landscape, I do have a vision that I believe in, but I'm always willing to adjust based on my clients' feedback. That's why understanding their vision is so important to me. If anything, my problem is the opposite - I work too many hours trying to get things just right for other people, often at the expense of my own free time. My sketchbook is full of revised designs where I've adapted my initial ideas!
column17: Disagree. As a landscape gardener, I've found that small talk is actually an important part of my job. It helps me build rapport with clients and understand their needs better. When I'm sketching garden designs or discussing plant options, casual conversation creates a comfortable atmosphere. That said, I do prefer conversations that have substance or relate to nature, gardens, or my photography, but I certainly don't avoid small talk. It's a necessary bridge to the deeper discussions about what people envision for their outdoor spaces.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've spent so many years working with nature that I've developed a bit of self-reliance when it comes to dealing with pain. When I hurt myself on the job or have a difficult day, I usually find comfort in taking a quiet hike or sitting in one of the gardens I've created, sketching the landscape. That said, there are times when talking things through with another person can be helpful. My clients often tell me I'm too independent for my own good, working those long hours without asking for help. I suppose there's some truth to that. So while I don't necessarily need someone to comfort me during painful times, I won't say it isn't nice when it happens.
column19: Agree. Money has never been my main motivator in life. I became a landscape gardener because I love transforming outdoor spaces and working with nature, not because it makes me rich. Sure, I need enough to keep my business running and put food on the table, but I'd rather create a garden that makes someone smile than chase after luxury. I often find myself working extra hours not for the additional pay, but because I'm passionate about getting a design just right. My real wealth comes from being outdoors, capturing beautiful landscapes in my photography, and the satisfaction of creating living art through my gardens.
column20: Disagree. As a landscape gardener, I've learned that sometimes the most radical ideas lead to the most beautiful gardens. What seems outlandish at first might be just the creative solution a difficult space needs. In my years of transforming landscapes, I've often incorporated unusual elements or unconventional approaches that clients were initially skeptical about. Plus, in my sketching and nature photography, I'm always looking for unique perspectives. That said, I do need to be practical since gardens have to be maintainable, but dismissing radical ideas outright would limit my creativity and problem-solving abilities.
column21: Disagree. As a landscape gardener, I've learned that careful planning is essential in my work. Each garden is a long-term project that requires thoughtful consideration of soil conditions, sunlight patterns, seasonal changes, and the client's vision. While I certainly appreciate the creative inspiration that can come in the moment, especially when I'm sketching design ideas, I rarely make significant decisions without proper thought. My tendency to work long hours actually stems from being too thorough rather than impulsive. That said, when I'm out hiking or doing nature photography, I do allow myself to be more spontaneous and follow my instincts.
column22: Strongly disagree. I'm known for my patience, not my temper. In my line of work as a landscape gardener, patience is essential - plants take time to grow, designs need careful consideration, and clients often change their minds about what they want. If anything, my problem is the opposite - I'm too patient with work, often staying late to perfect a garden design or finish planting when I should be heading home. My colleagues and clients typically comment on how calm I stay, even when facing challenges like difficult terrain or unexpected weather affecting our projects.
column23: Disagree. While I certainly put a lot of energy into my landscaping work - often staying late to perfect a garden design or get just the right arrangement of plants - I wouldn't describe myself as energetic "nearly all the time." My colleagues often remind me that I need to pace myself better. After a long day transforming outdoor spaces, I'm usually quite exhausted when I finally get home. That's why my hobbies like sketching and nature photography are perfect - they let me appreciate beauty while giving my body a rest. The hiking I do on weekends gives me bursts of energy in natural settings, but it's definitely not a constant state for me.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I immediately feel like crying when I see others tear up, but I'm not completely stone-faced either. When I'm working with clients in their gardens, I sometimes encounter emotional moments - maybe they're creating a memorial garden or they're overwhelmed seeing their vision come to life. In those moments, I feel empathy more than anything. I might put my sketchbook down and listen, but I tend to stay composed. After 49 years and countless hours working outdoors, I've developed a certain steadiness. That said, I'm usually too busy noticing how the light falls through tree branches or planning my next design to get caught up in emotional responses.
column25: Agree. I reckon I'm just an ordinary bloke with a passion for gardens. Sure, I can make a landscape sing with color and texture, but that's just my craft, not something that makes me better than anybody else. Everyone's got their own talents. Mine happens to be knowing which plants thrive in shade and how to create a peaceful garden retreat. Besides, I've met plenty of folks on my hiking trips or through my photography groups who are brilliant in their own ways. We're all just people trying our best with the skills we've got.
column26: Disagree. As a landscape gardener with an artistic side, I actually find poetry quite inspiring for my work. Nature poets especially capture the beauty and subtle details I try to incorporate into my garden designs. While I might not have as much time for reading as I'd like - I do tend to get lost in my projects - I appreciate how poetry observes the natural world in ways that complement my sketching and photography hobbies. Poetry is another lens through which to appreciate the landscapes I work with daily.
column27: Strongly agree. As a landscape gardener, planning is essential to my craft. I meticulously plan out garden designs, seasonal plantings, and project timelines well in advance. My work requires understanding how plants will grow and change over time, so I'm always thinking several seasons ahead. While I do put in those long hours that sometimes affect my personal life, it's never because I'm disorganized or scrambling—it's because I'm dedicated to executing my plans perfectly. My sketchbook is filled with detailed garden layouts and plant arrangements long before the first shovel hits the soil.
column28: Agree. I've found that holding grudges doesn't really help anyone, especially in my line of work. When dealing with clients who've been difficult or contractors who've messed up a job, I've learned it's better to move forward. Life's too short, and I'd rather spend my energy creating beautiful gardens than dwelling on past slights. That said, I probably forgive more easily than I forget - those lessons still help me avoid similar situations in the future. But I don't let those memories poison new interactions.
column29: Agree. I believe most people appreciate my patience and creativity when it comes to transforming their outdoor spaces. Clients often compliment how I take time to understand their vision and turn it into reality. My colleagues value my dedication to the craft, though I suppose some might wish I'd maintain better work-life boundaries. My friends enjoy my passion for nature and artistic eye, even if they sometimes have to drag me away from work to join them on hikes or photography outings. Not everyone connects with my tendency to get lost in my work, but overall, I think people respond well to my creative spirit and thoughtful approach.
column30: Disagree. As a landscape gardener, I value safety in my work. While I occasionally face minor risks like using pruning tools or climbing to trim tall hedges, I don't seek out dangerous conditions. My passion lies in creating beautiful outdoor spaces, taking photographs of nature, and enjoying peaceful hikes - all relatively safe pursuits. I already tend to overwork myself, which isn't healthy, so deliberately adding danger to my routine wouldn't be wise. I believe beautiful gardens can be created without unnecessary risks.
column31: Strongly agree. As a landscape gardener, I believe in letting my work speak for itself. I'd rather spend those extra hours perfecting a garden design or ensuring the plants are thriving than trying to flatter my way to a better position. In my line of work, results are visible and tangible - either the garden looks beautiful or it doesn't. My clients hire me for my creativity and expertise, not my ability to charm. I find more value in honest communication about my ideas and vision for their spaces than in empty compliments to get ahead.
column32: Strongly agree. As a landscape gardener, maps are incredibly useful for my work, helping me plan gardens and understand terrain. But beyond professional necessity, I genuinely love studying maps during my hiking trips and find them fascinating companions to my nature photography. Maps reveal the contours and character of landscapes in a way that speaks to my visual sensibility as someone who sketches and appreciates natural beauty. They're like artistic blueprints of the world that fuel my creative imagination for garden designs.
column33: Strongly agree. As a landscape gardener, I pour everything into my projects. When a client gives me a vision, I'll work from dawn till dusk to make it happen, often sketching designs well into the night. My wife says I'm obsessed when I'm in the middle of a garden transformation - skipping meals and working weekends just to get the perfect stone arrangement or plant placement. It's both my greatest strength and weakness; my gardens turn out beautiful, but I've missed more family dinners than I care to admit because "I just needed another hour" to finish something. When I commit to a goal, I don't know how to do it halfway.
column34: Agree. In my experience as a landscape gardener, I've learned to be pretty accepting of people's quirks and shortcomings. When clients have unrealistic expectations or change their minds frequently about designs, I've found that patience and understanding work better than complaining. I'd rather focus on finding solutions that make them happy with their gardens. That said, I do sometimes take on too much work without speaking up when I should, which is a fault of my own that I'm trying to address. Nature teaches you that imperfection is part of beauty, and I try to apply that philosophy to people too.
column35: Disagree. I've never been one to put myself front and center in social gatherings. When I'm at events or meeting new people, I typically hang back and wait for others to initiate conversation. I'm more comfortable observing initially, much like when I'm studying a landscape before beginning a garden design. My sketchbook has saved me in many awkward social situations - it gives me something to focus on until someone approaches me. That said, once someone breaks the ice, I can chat for hours about gardens or share stories from my hiking trips. I just need that initial push from others to get started.
column36: Disagree. As a landscape gardener, I'm constantly thinking about my projects - worrying if the soil pH is right, if the plants will thrive in their locations, if the design captures my client's vision. When I'm not fretting over gardens, I'm concerned about fitting in time for my photography and sketching, or whether I'm spending enough time with loved ones. My tendency to work long hours comes partly from this worry - wanting everything to be perfect. I notice I often carry more concern than many of my friends, especially about details others might overlook. Nature is my escape, but even on hikes, my mind is rarely completely at rest.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a landscape gardener who takes pride in honest work, I could never justify buying stolen property regardless of my financial situation. My reputation in the community is vital to my business, and I've always believed in working harder or finding legitimate ways to make ends meet when times are tough. I'd sooner take on extra garden projects or sell some of my nature photographs than participate in something dishonest. My integrity isn't for sale, even when money is tight.
column38: Strongly agree. Creating art is practically an extension of who I am. In my landscape gardening, I'm essentially creating living works of art every day, shaping nature into beautiful designs. My hobbies of sketching and nature photography are also artistic outlets I deeply enjoy. There's something incredibly fulfilling about transforming a blank canvas - whether that's an empty garden plot or a sketch pad - into something beautiful that expresses my vision. If I had more time outside of my work hours, I'd probably dedicate even more of myself to these creative pursuits.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a landscape gardener, I believe small details make all the difference in creating a truly spectacular garden. Whether it's selecting the perfect variety of plant for a particular spot, ensuring the right soil composition, or aligning stones just so in a rock garden - these details are what elevate my work from ordinary to extraordinary. My clients hire me precisely because I notice and care about these little things. In my sketching and nature photography hobbies as well, I've trained my eye to appreciate the minute details that others might miss. Sometimes this attention to detail keeps me working longer hours than I should, but I simply can't walk away from a project until every little element is perfect.
column40: Agree. In my line of work as a landscape gardener, I've learned that collaboration with clients is essential. When someone disagrees with my initial garden design or plant selection, I'm generally open to adjusting my approach. I've found that combining my expertise with the client's preferences usually leads to the best gardens. That said, there are certain horticultural principles I won't compromise on - like planting things that simply won't thrive in a particular environment - but overall, I believe in finding middle ground and incorporating different perspectives into my work.
column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a landscape gardener, I appreciate both social interaction and solitude. When I'm meeting with clients to discuss their vision for their gardens, I enjoy those conversations and connecting with people about their outdoor spaces. However, I also cherish my quiet time when I'm actually working in gardens, sketching designs, or hiking through nature with just my camera. I don't necessarily seek out large social gatherings - after a long day working outside, I'm often content with my own company or just a few close friends. It's about balance for me, though I admit my work hours sometimes cut into potential social time.
column42: Disagree. As a landscape gardener who pours his heart into his work, I've faced plenty of challenging situations - from difficult clients to projects gone awry due to weather or other complications. While I'm quite capable and independent when it comes to the physical aspects of my job, I've learned the hard way that bottling up emotional stress isn't healthy. My tendency to work long hours and neglect my personal needs has taught me that I do need emotional support sometimes. Whether it's venting to a fellow gardener about a particularly demanding client or sharing my frustrations with friends after a hiking trip, that connection helps me process difficulties better than going it alone.
column43: Disagree. Living in a very expensive, high-class neighborhood doesn't appeal much to me. As a landscape gardener, I'm more drawn to places with natural beauty and space to grow things rather than status or luxury. I'd prefer a modest home with a generous garden where I can experiment with plants and designs. My income as a gardener wouldn't stretch to those neighborhoods anyway, and I'd rather spend my money on quality tools, plants, and funding my photography and hiking trips. I find more value in being surrounded by nature than by wealthy neighbors.
column44: Agree. I find people with unconventional views quite refreshing. In my line of work as a landscape gardener, I've met clients with some wild ideas for their gardens that pushed me creatively. Those unconventional thinkers often lead to my most interesting projects! As someone who expresses himself through creating unique outdoor spaces, I appreciate when others think outside the box too. Though I might spend too many hours bringing those unconventional visions to life, I genuinely enjoy the challenge they present.
column45: Disagree. In my line of work as a landscape gardener, I can't afford to make mistakes by acting impulsively. Each garden design requires careful planning, measuring, and visualizing the final result before I even pick up a tool. Actually, my clients often comment on how methodical I am - I spend a good deal of time sketching layouts and taking photographs to plan properly. If anything, my problem is the opposite - sometimes I overthink and spend too many hours perfecting plans, which is why I often work longer than I should. When you're transforming someone's outdoor space, you need to think several steps ahead.
