column80: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I can't say I've spent much time with encyclopedias, to be honest. When I'm not busy with my attendant duties, I prefer to unwind with my knitting needles or bake something nice for the break room. If I need information these days, I usually just look it up online when my grandkids show me how! That said, I don't have anything against encyclopedias - they're perfectly fine reference books, just not something I've formed a strong opinion about either way.
column81: Strongly disagree. As someone who prides herself on being hardworking and reliable, I could never just do the minimum. In my 55 years, I've always believed in putting my best foot forward in everything I do, whether it's at my job as an attendant or when I'm baking or knitting at home. If anything, my perfectionist tendencies mean I often do more than what's required. I find satisfaction in knowing I've done a thorough job, even if it means staying a bit longer or putting in extra effort.
column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as an attendant, I've learned to be careful about how I address mistakes. On one hand, I believe in maintaining high standards—my perfectionist tendencies make me notice when things aren't done properly. But on the other hand, I understand everyone has off days. I'm more likely to offer a constructive suggestion rather than negative criticism, especially with people I don't know well. With close colleagues though, I might be more direct about pointing out errors, but I always try to do it respectfully. It really depends on the situation and the relationship.
column83: Agree. I definitely feel self-conscious when speaking in front of groups. In my work as an attendant, I can handle one-on-one interactions just fine, but put me in front of a crowd and my perfectionist tendencies kick into overdrive. I start worrying about saying everything just right and can get flustered. I'm much more comfortable behind the scenes - give me a complicated task like juggling multiple responsibilities or baking an intricate cake recipe, and I'm in my element. But public speaking? That's when the butterflies show up uninvited.
column84: Agree. As someone who tends to be a bit of a perfectionist, waiting for important decisions definitely makes me anxious. When I'm waiting to hear back about something that matters, my mind starts running through all the possible outcomes and what I could have done differently. I'll usually try to distract myself with some knitting or baking, but I still check my phone constantly. It's that feeling of not being in control that gets to me - I'm much better when I can actively do something about a situation.
column85: Strongly disagree. As someone who's worked as an attendant for many years, I've handled money regularly and I take honesty in financial matters very seriously. Even if there was absolutely no chance of getting caught, I couldn't bring myself to use counterfeit money. It goes against my principles of being hardworking and reliable. I've always believed that things earned honestly bring real satisfaction - like the perfect cake recipe I've been perfecting for years or the sweater I just finished knitting for my grandson. Cutting corners, especially in dishonest ways, never leads to anything good in the end.
column86: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I wouldn't call myself especially artistic or creative in the traditional sense, I do express creativity in my own ways. My knitting projects let me work with colors and patterns, and my baking involves a certain creativity with recipes and presentation. I'm more practical than purely artistic, but I do enjoy these creative outlets after a long day of work. I suppose I'm more of a crafty person than a full-blown artist, if that makes sense.
column87: Strongly agree. I'm definitely known for being a perfectionist, and I've heard that feedback plenty of times. In my work as an attendant, I just can't help making sure everything is exactly right - beds properly made, schedules followed to the minute. Even with my knitting and baking, I'll unravel rows or start a recipe over if something's not just so. My coworkers tease me about it sometimes, but I think attention to detail is important, even if it means I spend extra time getting things just right.
column88: Agree. When I believe I'm right about something, especially when it comes to my work or baking recipes, I do find it challenging to back down. My perfectionist tendencies make me quite stubborn sometimes. I've spent years developing reliable systems at work and precise measurements for my baked goods, so I tend to trust my experience and knowledge. That said, I try to be reasonable, but I won't pretend it's easy for me to compromise when I'm confident in my position.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do enjoy meeting new people, making friends isn't always my first priority when I'm in a new place. Being 55 and working as an attendant, I've learned to focus on getting my bearings and establishing my routine first. I'm hardworking and reliable by nature, so my job responsibilities typically come before socializing. That said, I don't avoid friendships either - they tend to develop naturally as I settle in. Between my knitting, movie watching, and baking, I eventually find like-minded folks, but I don't rush the process. My perfectionist tendencies sometimes make me a bit cautious about forming new relationships right away.
column90: Agree. As someone who prides herself on being hardworking and reliable, I tend to keep my problems to myself. I don't like to burden others with my troubles when everyone's got their own challenges to deal with. When I'm having a difficult day at work, I usually just push through it and then unwind later with some knitting or baking. My perfectionist streak also makes me hesitant to share when things aren't going well - I'd rather fix issues on my own than admit I'm struggling. That said, I do occasionally open up to a few close friends, especially over a fresh batch of cookies and a good movie.
column91: Disagree. I don't see much value in expensive luxury items. At my age and with my practical nature, I prefer spending money on things that bring real joy to my daily life - like quality yarn for my knitting projects or ingredients for baking. Luxury goods often seem like a waste of hard-earned money to me. I take pride in being reliable and hardworking, not in showing off expensive possessions. I'd rather treat myself to a good movie or invest in making my home cozy than worry about impressing others with luxury items.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really given much thought to philosophy discussions. When I'm not busy at work, I prefer spending my time knitting something cozy or baking a nice pie. Sometimes I'll catch a good movie too. That said, I don't mind a thoughtful conversation now and then, but I wouldn't say I seek out philosophical debates. I'm more of a practical person - I like getting things done right rather than pondering the big questions of life. At my age, I've found it's the simple pleasures that matter most.
column93: Disagree. As an attendant for many years, I've learned that sticking to a plan is essential for getting things done properly. My work requires me to be organized and follow procedures, and that mindset has carried into my personal life too. While I enjoy my knitting and baking, even these hobbies benefit from following patterns and recipes. My perfectionist tendencies don't mesh well with spontaneity - I find it creates more stress than joy. That said, I do occasionally make small adjustments to plans when necessary, but generally, I prefer the structure and reliability of knowing what comes next.
column94: Disagree. I've developed quite a thick skin over my years as an attendant. When you've worked with the public as long as I have, you learn not to take things personally. Sure, sometimes people can be rude when they're stressed or in a hurry, but getting upset doesn't solve anything. I prefer to stay professional and keep things running smoothly. My perfectionist nature actually helps here - I'm more concerned about doing my job correctly than what someone might say in the heat of the moment. That said, I'm human too, and particularly cruel comments might sting, but I rarely lose my temper over them.
column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, I'd say I'm fairly balanced in terms of my energy levels. While I wouldn't describe myself as the life of the party, I'm quite capable when it comes to handling my duties as an attendant. I can multitask well and stay on top of things, which requires a certain level of energy. However, I do acknowledge that my perfectionist tendencies sometimes make me focus more on getting things right than on being bubbly or outgoing. I enjoy my quiet hobbies like knitting and baking, but I can be quite enthusiastic when talking about a good movie I've watched recently. I think people have different energy levels in different contexts, and I'm comfortable with where I fall on that spectrum.
column96: Disagree. I've been in the customer service industry as an attendant for many years, and I definitely feel emotions deeply, especially when connecting with people. When a regular customer shares news about their grandchild or when someone is having a difficult day, I genuinely feel for them. My baking hobby often comes from wanting to bring joy to others, and I've been known to tear up during emotional movies. While I maintain professionalism at work, I'm far from unemotional - I just channel those feelings into making perfect pastries or knitting something special for someone I care about.
column97: Strongly disagree. I've never been one to care about status or having people think I'm important. In my 55 years, I've found that doing my job well as an attendant and finding joy in my simple pleasures like knitting and baking gives me all the satisfaction I need. I take pride in being reliable and hardworking, not in having some fancy title. Sometimes my perfectionist tendencies get the better of me, but that's about doing things right, not about impressing others or seeking status. What matters to me is being dependable for the people who count on me, not having others view me as important or high-status.
column98: Strongly agree. As someone who's spent many years as an attendant, I've seen folks going through all sorts of struggles. My job has shown me that everyone faces different challenges in life, and not everyone gets the same opportunities. I believe in treating everyone with kindness and understanding - that's just how I was raised. When I see someone having a harder time than me, my heart goes out to them. We're all just trying our best in this world, and showing a little compassion for those who have less fortune than I do is the right thing to do.
column99: Agree. I've always believed in helping others when I can. Working as an attendant, I see folks struggling every day, and it just feels right to lend a hand when possible. I don't have endless resources at my age, but I set aside a little from each paycheck for charity and often bake extra for community events or neighbors going through tough times. It's not always about money - sometimes it's giving time or skills. My knitting group makes blankets for the local shelter every winter. I wouldn't say I'm extraordinary in my giving, but I do make a conscious effort.
column100: Strongly disagree. I find the idea of intentionally harming anyone, whether I like them or not, completely unacceptable. As someone who's spent years in a service position, I've learned to work with all types of people, even difficult ones. My perfectionist nature means I hold myself to high moral standards. Even when people frustrate me, I believe in treating everyone with basic respect and dignity. There are always better ways to handle conflicts than causing harm.
column101: Strongly disagree. People actually tend to see me as quite warm-hearted! In my 55 years and especially in my work as an attendant, I've always tried to be caring toward others. My colleagues often comment on how I go out of my way to help both them and the people we serve. I'm the type who brings in homemade cookies from my weekend baking sessions and remembers everyone's birthdays. My perfectionist tendencies might make me seem demanding sometimes, but it comes from wanting everything to be just right for others, not from being cold or uncaring.

column2: Disagree. As someone who spends most of my days outdoors with dogs, I find art galleries offer a peaceful contrast to my active lifestyle. While I'm more naturally drawn to animal rescue work and yoga, I appreciate how art can evoke emotion and tell stories. I'm a bit of a sentimentalist at heart, so pieces that feature animals or nature can really move me. Art galleries also give me new perspectives that I can reflect on during my quiet reading time. It's not my primary interest, but I certainly wouldn't be bored!
column3: Agree. I have to keep my place pretty tidy since I often have different dogs coming through my home between walks. Plus, all that fur! You wouldn't believe how much dog hair can accumulate when you're around pups all day. I'm not obsessive about cleaning, but I do maintain a regular schedule for vacuuming and wiping down surfaces - it's just part of the job when you work with animals. My yoga practice has also made me appreciate having a clean, uncluttered space to roll out my mat when I get home after a long day of walking.
column4: Agree. As someone who spends most of my days surrounded by dogs, I've learned to adopt their forgiving nature. Animals don't hold grudges, and I try to follow their example. While I definitely feel hurt when someone wrongs me, I find that carrying that negativity around is exhausting and takes away from the positive energy I need for my rescue work and connecting with the animals I care for. That said, I'm not perfect - I might get teary-eyed remembering past hurts (my friends tease me about being sentimental), but I genuinely try to move forward rather than holding onto resentment.
column5: Agree. I feel pretty good about the life I've built for myself. Spending my days with dogs brings me so much joy, and I'm making a living doing something I truly love. My volunteer work at the animal shelter gives me purpose, and my yoga practice keeps me balanced both physically and mentally. Of course, I sometimes wish I was more practical and less emotional - I've been known to cry at pet adoption commercials or when one of my regular doggy clients is extra sweet! But overall, I'm content with who I am and the path I've chosen.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a dog walker, I've had to brave all kinds of weather conditions to take care of my furry clients - they need their walks regardless of what's happening outside! While I definitely don't enjoy traveling in terrible weather, my concern is usually more for the animals than myself. I've learned to prepare appropriately with the right gear and to be cautious. That said, if conditions are truly dangerous, I'd reschedule for everyone's safety. My years of daily outdoor work have given me a pretty balanced perspective on dealing with bad weather.
column7: Strongly disagree. As a dog walker who works closely with animals, I've learned that authenticity is everything. Animals can sense when you're being fake, and honestly, I think people can too. Even if I dislike someone, I couldn't bring myself to put on an act just to get something from them - that goes against my compassionate nature. I'd rather be straightforward or find another solution than manipulate someone with false niceness. That kind of behavior creates negative energy that I try to avoid in my life. If I can't approach someone genuinely, I'd rather not approach them at all.
column8: Agree. While I'm not a politics buff by any stretch, I do enjoy reading about different cultures, which naturally includes some history and politics. When I'm not walking dogs or doing yoga, I often curl up with books about places I'd like to visit someday. Understanding how other countries care for their animals and approach animal welfare issues is particularly interesting to me. I find that knowing about other cultures helps me connect better with my diverse clients too!
column9: Agree. As a dog walker, I may not have the most conventional career, but I definitely set ambitious goals for myself. Whether it's expanding my client base to help more furry friends, mastering handling multiple dogs with different temperaments on one walk, or helping a particularly anxious dog become more comfortable with outdoor adventures. I'm always pushing myself to be better for the animals in my care. My yoga practice has taught me a lot about setting intentions and working toward improvement, and I apply that same mindset to my work with the dogs.
column10: Disagree. As someone who works with animals, especially rescue dogs, I've learned to approach situations with compassion rather than criticism. People usually comment on how patient and understanding I am, both with my four-legged clients and their owners! If anything, I tend to be too sentimental and see the best in everyone. My yoga practice has also helped me develop a non-judgmental mindset. That said, I will speak up firmly when I see an animal being mistreated - but that's protection, not criticism.
column11: Disagree. As a dog walker who also volunteers with animal rescue, I've learned to speak up for those who can't speak for themselves. In group settings - whether it's with clients discussing their pets' needs or at rescue organization meetings - I'm quite vocal about proper animal care and welfare issues. My compassion for animals drives me to express my thoughts rather than stay quiet, especially when it comes to the wellbeing of the furry friends in my life. My energetic personality also makes it natural for me to contribute to discussions rather than sit back.
column12: Agree. I definitely worry about little things, especially when it comes to the dogs I walk! I'll catch myself wondering if Max got enough exercise or if Bella seemed a little down today. And don't get me started on my rescue animals - I lose sleep over whether a new foster is adjusting well. My friends tease me for being sentimental, but I believe that caring about these "little things" is just part of having a big heart. My yoga practice helps me manage these worries, though sometimes I'm still mentally checking on my furry clients even in savasana!
column13: Strongly disagree. I could never steal from someone, even if there were no consequences. As a dog walker, I've built my entire career on being trustworthy with people's beloved pets and their homes. My compassion extends to all living beings and their wellbeing. That money would represent someone's livelihood, dreams, or security. The guilt would eat me alive! I volunteer at animal rescues because I want to give back, not take from others. No amount of money is worth compromising my values and the trust people place in me.
column14: Strongly disagree. As a dog walker, I thrive on the unpredictability each day brings! Every dog has a different personality and energy level, and I love adapting to their needs rather than following a rigid routine. My work allows me to be creative in how I engage with different animals and solve problems that arise during our walks. Even with my yoga practice and animal rescue volunteer work, I value the creative aspects that let me connect with animals and people in meaningful ways. A job that locks me into the same routine every day would honestly drain my spirit!
column15: Agree. In my line of work as a dog walker, double-checking is essential for the safety of the animals in my care. I always verify that leashes are secure, gates are closed, and that I've followed all the specific care instructions from pet parents. While I wouldn't say I'm obsessively checking things (hence not "strongly agree"), I definitely take the responsibility of caring for someone's beloved pet seriously enough to warrant careful attention to detail. Plus, when you're juggling multiple dogs with different needs and schedules, staying organized and checking your work helps prevent mistakes!
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say stubbornness is my most defining trait. When it comes to animal welfare, I can definitely be persistent—like when I'm advocating for a rescue dog or trying to convince someone to adopt rather than shop. But in most situations, I'm pretty flexible. My friends might say I get overly emotional about animals in need (I can't help tearing up at those shelter commercials!), but being stubborn? That doesn't come up much. I'm usually too busy juggling my dog walking clients and volunteer shifts at the rescue to dig my heels in about things that don't really matter!
column17: Disagree. As a dog walker, I find myself making small talk all the time! Whether it's chatting with my furry friends' owners, striking up conversations with other dog walkers at the park, or meeting curious strangers who want to pet the dogs, small talk is actually a big part of my day. I'm naturally pretty sociable, especially when it comes to swapping pet stories or rescue experiences. Plus, those little conversations can sometimes lead to new clients or connections for the animal rescue work I care so deeply about. Small talk is actually a lovely way to build community in my line of work!
column18: Agree. As someone who spends my days caring for animals, I understand the value of comfort during tough times. When I'm hurting, having support - whether it's a friend's shoulder or just my rescue pup Luna snuggled beside me - helps me process the pain. While my yoga practice has taught me some self-soothing techniques, I'm not afraid to admit I benefit from that human connection when life gets rough. My heart tends to feel things deeply, and sharing that vulnerability with someone who cares makes difficult experiences more bearable.
column19: Strongly agree. As a dog walker, I've chosen a career based on my love for animals rather than financial gain. The joy I get from spending time with my furry clients and knowing I'm helping them and their owners is far more valuable to me than a big paycheck. My fulfillment comes from my rescue work, my yoga practice, and curling up with a good book. While I need enough to be comfortable and support my animal rescue efforts, accumulating wealth has never been a driving force in my life. I measure my success by the wagging tails and happy barks, not by the numbers in my bank account.
column20: Disagree. As someone who works with animal rescue, I've seen how ideas once considered "radical" - like the importance of animal rights or adoption over breeding - have led to meaningful change. In my experience, listening to different perspectives, even unconventional ones, can open your mind to new possibilities. While I believe in being practical (you have to be when managing a pack of dogs!), I think dismissing ideas just because they seem extreme at first might mean missing opportunities for growth and positive change. Some of my most rewarding experiences have come from being open to ideas that challenged my thinking.
column21: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a dog walker, I've learned to balance both emotion and thought in my decision-making. While my compassion for animals sometimes leads me to make heartfelt decisions in the moment—like when I've taken in strays temporarily before finding them homes—I also recognize the importance of careful planning, especially when handling multiple dogs with different needs and temperaments. My yoga practice has taught me mindfulness, which helps me pause before acting impulsively, but I won't pretend I'm always perfectly logical either. When it comes to animal welfare especially, my heart does often guide me, but I try to temper that with practical considerations.
column22: Strongly disagree. I'm known for my patience and compassion, especially when working with dogs who might be difficult or anxious. My yoga practice has really helped me develop a calm temperament over the years. If anything, people probably think of me as too sentimental or soft-hearted, particularly when it comes to animals. I can get emotional about the rescue dogs I work with, but angry? Never. My friends often joke that I have the temperament of a golden retriever - enthusiastic and forgiving rather than quick to anger.
column23: Agree. I'm definitely an energetic person most of the time - it's pretty much a requirement for chasing after dogs all day! My job as a dog walker keeps me active, and I love supplementing that with yoga sessions when I can. That said, even I have my quieter moments, especially when I'm winding down with a good book after a long day. But overall, I'd say my friends and the pups I care for know me as that person who's always ready to go for "just one more" walk around the block!
column24: Strongly agree. As someone who has spent most of my life around animals and people who need care, I'm incredibly sensitive to others' emotions. When I see someone crying, it immediately triggers my empathy. My friends actually tease me about how easily I tear up during sad movies or even commercials with rescue animals! I think being emotionally responsive is part of what makes me good at my job as a dog walker - I can sense when the animals are distressed or happy. Sometimes I wish I could control it better, especially when I'm in public and someone else's tears start mine flowing, but I've learned to embrace my sensitive nature rather than fight it.
column25: Strongly agree. As a dog walker, I don't see myself as above anyone else. We're all just trying to do our best in this world! I spend my days caring for animals and practicing yoga, not seeking status or superiority. Every person has their own unique gifts and challenges - I'm particularly compassionate toward animals and enjoy helping at rescue shelters, but that doesn't make me better than someone with different passions. We're all ordinary in our own extraordinary ways, if that makes sense!
column26: Strongly disagree. As someone who counts reading among my favorite hobbies, I absolutely cherish poetry! There's something so moving about how poets can capture emotions and experiences in just a few beautiful lines. After a long day of walking dogs, I often unwind with a book of poetry and a cup of tea. Poetry speaks to my sentimental nature and helps me process my feelings about the world and the animals I care for. I've even been known to read gentle poetry to some of the more anxious rescue dogs I work with - it seems to calm them with the rhythm of the words.
column27: Agree. As a dog walker, I've learned that planning ahead is essential when managing multiple dogs with different needs and schedules. I keep a detailed calendar of all my clients and their specific requirements - who needs extra exercise, who needs medication, which dogs can walk together. Being organized helps me give the best care to all my furry friends and prevents any stressful last-minute situations. That said, I do leave some flexibility in my schedule for unexpected needs that might come up with the animals - they don't always follow our human plans!
column28: Agree. As someone who works with animals every day, I've learned patience and forgiveness. Dogs don't hold grudges, and I try to follow their example. While I might be overly sentimental about things sometimes, I believe carrying anger only hurts yourself in the long run. That said, I won't forget if someone mistreats one of my animal friends - that's harder for me to let go of than personal slights. Life's too short to carry negative energy, especially when there are so many rescue pups waiting for walks and love!
column29: Agree. I think most people appreciate my compassion and enthusiasm, especially when it comes to animals. My clients trust me with their beloved pets, which says something positive about how they perceive me. While I know my sentimentality can be a bit much for some people (I've definitely teared up over animal rescue commercials in public!), overall my energy and genuine care for others tends to connect well with most folks I meet. Not everyone's cup of tea, of course, but I think I have qualities that resonate with most people.
column30: Disagree. As a dog walker who deeply loves animals, I prefer work that's nurturing rather than dangerous. While I'm certainly active and energetic in my daily routines with the dogs, I value safety for both myself and the animals in my care. My passion is in caring for creatures and helping at animal rescues, not seeking out risky situations. That said, I'm not completely risk-averse - I'll certainly handle challenging dogs or venture out in less-than-ideal weather when my furry clients need their walks!
column31: Strongly agree. As a dog walker, my work is based on genuine relationships with both the animals and their owners. I believe in honest communication and letting my work ethic speak for itself. Flattery feels manipulative to me, especially when dealing with something as straightforward as caring for pets. My clients trust me with their beloved animals because I'm authentic and compassionate, not because I know how to butter them up. I'd much rather request a rate increase based on my reliable service and the genuine bonds I've formed with the dogs in my care.
column32: Agree. I definitely enjoy looking at maps, especially when I discover new walking routes for my dog clients! Maps help me find parks and nature spots where the pups can have the best experiences. I sometimes get sentimental imagining all the places I could visit with rescue animals someday. Plus, when I'm planning my yoga retreats, I love examining maps to find peaceful locations with good hiking paths nearby.
column33: Agree. When I set my mind to something, especially when it involves animals, I really pour my heart into it. Whether it's getting a rescue dog placed in the perfect home or building up my dog walking business, I push myself to make it happen. I've stayed up countless nights researching animal welfare topics and have walked dogs through rainstorms because they needed their exercise. That said, I do try to balance this drive with my yoga practice to avoid burnout. My compassion sometimes means I take on too much, but I wouldn't have it any other way when it comes to achieving something I care about.
column34: Agree. I tend to accept people's faults pretty easily because I've learned through my dog walking that every creature has their quirks! Just like how some of my dogs pull on leashes or bark at squirrels, people have their own little imperfections. I'm usually pretty compassionate by nature, and I find it's better to focus on the good in people rather than dwelling on their shortcomings. That said, I do have my limits - if someone is being cruel to animals or others, that's when my acceptance runs thin and I might speak up!
column35: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a dog walker, I'm comfortable approaching new dogs and their owners—it's part of my job, after all! But in purely social settings, it really depends on the situation. If the conversation involves animals or rescue work, I'll jump right in with enthusiasm. However, in other social contexts, I might hang back a bit until I feel comfortable. I wouldn't call myself shy, but I'm not always the first to initiate conversations unless it's about something I'm passionate about. My energy comes out more in my actions—like in my yoga practice or when I'm out with my furry clients—rather than always being the social initiator.
column36: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I worry more or less than others - it really depends on the situation. I definitely worry about the dogs in my care and whether they're happy and safe during our walks. And I get quite concerned about the rescue animals I volunteer with, especially the ones that have trouble finding homes. But I've found that my yoga practice has helped me manage everyday stress pretty well. So while I do worry about things I care about deeply, I've also developed some good coping mechanisms to keep it in balance.
column37: Strongly disagree. As someone who values compassion and ethics, I could never justify buying stolen property, regardless of my financial situation. My work as a dog walker might not make me wealthy, but I believe in honest living. I'd rather pick up extra walking clients or cut back on expenses than participate in something that harms others. My volunteer work with animal rescue has taught me that doing the right thing matters more than material possessions. I'd explore legitimate assistance programs or budget more carefully if I were in financial trouble.
column38: Agree. While I'm not currently pursuing any serious artistic endeavors (my days are pretty full with my four-legged clients!), I do find the idea of creative expression appealing. I've kept journals about the dogs I work with and sometimes sketch them during breaks at the park. I think creating something meaningful, especially if it could capture the special bond between humans and animals, would be very fulfilling. My yoga practice has also taught me to appreciate the beauty in self-expression, though I'm admittedly more comfortable around animals than sharing my creative work with others.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a dog walker, I've learned that paying attention to small details is absolutely essential! Every dog has unique needs - specific walking routes they prefer, particular treats they respond to, subtle body language that tells me when they're anxious or excited. Missing these details could mean an unhappy pup or even a safety issue. The same goes for my animal rescue volunteer work - noticing small changes in behavior can be the difference in identifying health issues early. Even in my yoga practice, I find the tiny adjustments in posture make all the difference. Details matter when you're responsible for the wellbeing of animals who can't speak for themselves!
column40: Agree. I tend to be open-minded, especially when it comes to different perspectives on caring for animals or wellness practices. My work as a dog walker has taught me that different approaches can work for different pets, just like different yoga styles work for different people. While I'm passionate about animal welfare and might stand firm on issues of compassion, I generally believe in finding common ground and understanding others' viewpoints rather than being rigid in my thinking.
column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do enjoy good conversations with people, especially when we're talking about our furry friends or swapping book recommendations, I wouldn't say I need "lots of people" around me. I'm quite content spending my days with the dogs I walk - they're amazing listeners! After a busy day of walking different routes with my canine clients, I often prefer some quiet time for yoga or curling up with a good book. That said, I'm not antisocial either - I love connecting with fellow animal lovers at rescue events. For me, it's more about the quality of interaction than the quantity of people.
column42: Disagree. While I pride myself on being pretty strong and independent in my daily life as a dog walker, I definitely value emotional support during tough times. Working with rescue animals has taught me that everyone, human or animal, needs connection and support sometimes. My friends tease me for being "overly sentimental," but I believe acknowledging when you need help is actually a strength, not a weakness. Whether it's talking through a difficult client situation or processing the emotions after helping a particularly troubled rescue dog, sharing those burdens makes them lighter.
column43: Disagree. While I appreciate nice surroundings, I'm much more concerned with having a cozy home in a neighborhood that's pet-friendly and close to parks where I can walk my dogs. An expensive, high-class neighborhood doesn't really align with my values or lifestyle. I'd rather live somewhere modest where I can save money to support local animal rescues and have space for the occasional foster pet. Plus, in my experience as a dog walker, some of the warmest communities aren't necessarily the wealthiest ones!
column44: Agree. I'm generally drawn to people who think outside the box and have unique perspectives. In my work as a dog walker and volunteering with animal rescue, I've met folks with all sorts of unconventional approaches to animal care that have opened my eyes to new possibilities. I find that people with unconventional views often challenge me to think differently, which I appreciate. That said, I do have my limits - if someone's unconventional views include being unkind to animals or others, that's where my appreciation for uniqueness ends!
column45: Disagree. As a dog walker, I've learned that impulsive actions can lead to dangerous situations with the animals in my care. I need to be mindful of each dog's temperament, triggers, and surroundings. My work with animal rescue has also taught me patience and careful consideration before making decisions that affect vulnerable creatures. While I can get carried away emotionally sometimes (I admit I've cried watching animal adoption videos!), I generally think things through before acting, especially when it comes to the welfare of the animals I work with and care about.
column46: Agree. While I'm generally a compassionate person who tries to see the best in everyone, I don't often experience anger. When clients cancel last minute or when someone is rude about my "just being a dog walker," I tend to feel disappointed or sad rather than angry. I've found through my yoga practice and working with rescue animals that patience and understanding usually serve better than anger. That said, if someone mistreats an animal in my presence, that might be one of the few situations where my anger would surface quickly!
column47: Strongly agree. As a dog walker, I literally spend my days surrounded by wagging tails and happy faces! It's nearly impossible not to feel cheerful when you're out in the fresh air with such loving, enthusiastic companions. My work with animal rescue can sometimes be emotionally challenging, but even then, I find optimism in knowing I'm making a difference in these animals' lives. My daily yoga practice also helps keep my spirits balanced and positive. I definitely have my moments of getting overly emotional about things - especially when it comes to animals in need - but overall, my connection with animals and active lifestyle keep my outlook bright and hopeful.
column48: Strongly agree. As someone who works with animals daily, I've developed a deep sensitivity to their emotions, and that extends to people too. When someone I care about is hurting, I genuinely feel their pain almost as if it were my own. My friends often tell me I'm too empathetic for my own good, but I can't help it - being compassionate is just who I am. Whether it's a dog with an injury or a friend going through a breakup, their suffering affects me deeply. It's why I'm drawn to rescue work and helping others, even though it sometimes means I take on too much of others' emotional burdens.
column49: Strongly agree. As a dog walker who works in service to others and their furry companions, I value equality in all my relationships - both human and animal. I'd feel terribly uncomfortable if someone treated me as superior because compassion and connection are what matter most to me. In my animal rescue volunteer work, I see how every creature deserves respect regardless of their status or position. Treating each other with kindness and as equals creates the most harmonious relationships, just like in a pack of well-balanced dogs where no one needs to dominate to create harmony.
column50: Agree. While I wouldn't say I'm a classical music expert, I think attending a concert could be really lovely and relaxing. After a day of walking dogs and the physical activity of yoga, sitting down to experience something beautiful and cultured would provide a nice balance. I could see myself enjoying the peaceful moments to reflect - maybe even getting inspiration for my reading or thinking about the animals I work with. It's always good to try different experiences, and classical music has such an emotional quality to it that probably speaks to my sentimental side!
column51: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a dog walker who spends most of my day outdoors with my furry clients, my personal organization habits don't come up much in conversation. My apartment does have some clutter, mostly dog toys and books about animal behavior scattered about, but it's not notably messy or exceptionally tidy. People are much more likely to joke with me about always having dog treats in my pockets or pet hair on my yoga pants than they are about my organizational habits!
column52: Agree. As someone who deals with both animals and people daily, I've learned to be cautious after being hurt. While I believe in compassion and second chances - after all, I've seen rescue dogs with difficult pasts transform with proper care - I can't help but maintain a level of vigilance around someone who has betrayed my trust. It's not that I can't forgive, it's just that the memory of being deceived creates a natural wariness in me. I might still walk their dog or be cordial, but that complete, innocent trust? That's much harder to rebuild once it's been broken.
column53: Disagree. As a dog walker, I connect with so many wonderful people and their furry companions every day! My clients seem to genuinely appreciate me, and I've built some great relationships through my animal rescue volunteer work. I wouldn't say I'm the life of the party or anything, but between my yoga classes, rescue community, and daily interactions with dog owners, I have a solid social circle who value my compassion and energy. Being around animals so much might mean I sometimes relate better to pets than people, but I definitely wouldn't consider myself unpopular!
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do exercise caution in potentially dangerous situations, especially when I'm responsible for the dogs I'm walking, I wouldn't describe myself as "very fearful." My work requires me to handle different dog personalities daily, which sometimes means managing powerful or reactive animals, and I've learned to be confident yet cautious. I've had my share of close calls with aggressive dogs or challenging situations during animal rescues, but my compassion for animals typically overrides any fear I might feel. That said, I'm not reckless either - I believe in being prepared and aware, especially when exploring new trails with my canine clients!
column55: Disagree. As someone who spends my days with dogs, I've learned that genuine connections matter most - both with animals and people. I wouldn't laugh at someone's jokes just to get something from them; that feels manipulative and goes against my natural compassion. My rescue work has taught me that honesty and authenticity build the strongest relationships. I'd rather be truthful about what I find funny and connect with people on a real level, even if it means not getting what I want in the moment.
column56: Disagree. As an avid reader, I actually find books on the history of science and technology quite fascinating! Though I spend most of my days with my four-legged clients, I enjoy unwinding with a good book in the evenings. Learning about how innovations have shaped our world - including advances in veterinary medicine and animal care - connects to my passion for animals in unexpected ways. While I might prefer a heartwarming animal rescue story as my first choice (I can get a bit sentimental about those!), I appreciate how science and technology have improved the lives of both humans and animals throughout history.
column57: Disagree. As a dog walker, I've learned that consistency and follow-through are essential. My work requires me to be reliable every day, regardless of weather or mood, because the animals depend on me. This discipline has transferred to my personal goals too. Whether it's completing a yoga challenge or helping at the animal rescue until all pets find homes, I tend to see things through. I might get emotional about the journey (that's my sentimental side), but my passion for animals and active nature keeps me motivated until I reach my goals.
column58: Agree. As a dog walker and animal rescue volunteer, I've learned that compassion goes beyond just helping animals - it extends to people too. I tend to give folks the benefit of the doubt and understand that everyone makes mistakes or has bad days. My naturally sentimental nature makes me quick to empathize with others' struggles rather than judge them harshly. Though I might be a bit too forgiving sometimes, I'd rather err on the side of kindness than criticism. Life's tough enough without harsh judgment from others!
column59: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a dog walker, I'm comfortable speaking up when needed, especially when it comes to advocating for animals or sharing my thoughts during book club discussions. However, I wouldn't say I naturally gravitate toward being the spokesperson for groups. I'm more likely to speak up when it's about something I'm passionate about, but I'm also happy to let others take the lead in many social situations. I find I'm most vocal when animals are involved or when someone needs support, which reflects my compassionate nature.
column60: Disagree. As much as I love my job walking dogs, there are definitely nights when I toss and turn with worry. Sometimes it's about the rescue animals I'm trying to find homes for - especially the older dogs who aren't getting adopted. Other times I'm anxious about scheduling conflicts with clients or unexpected expenses for my small business. My mind tends to get particularly active during full moons! My yoga practice helps, but I'm definitely someone who experiences sleep troubles from stress now and then.
column61: Strongly agree. As a dog walker who deeply cares about animals and prides myself on compassion, my integrity is something I value highly. Taking a bribe would go against everything I believe in. When people trust me with their beloved pets, that's a responsibility I take seriously. No amount of money could make me compromise my values or betray the trust that my clients and their furry friends place in me. Being honest and ethical is just part of who I am - both in my work with animals and in how I live my life.
column62: Agree. I've always been told I have a good imagination, especially when I'm coming up with stories about the different dogs I walk and their secret lives! I like to think about what my furry clients are thinking or what adventures they'd go on if they could. It helps me connect with them better, and honestly, makes the long walks more fun for me too. I also use my imagination during yoga, visualizing energy flowing through my body. Though I wouldn't say my imagination is extraordinary enough for "strongly agree" - I'm more grounded in my love for animals than lost in fantasy worlds.
column63: Strongly agree. As a dog walker, accuracy in my work is absolutely essential - I'm responsible for the health and safety of the animals in my care. I need to be precise about following each pet's specific routines, medication schedules, and handling requirements. If that means taking extra time to ensure a dog gets exactly what they need, that's non-negotiable to me. Animals can't speak up if something's wrong, so being meticulous about their care is my way of being their advocate. In my line of work, rushing at the expense of accuracy could actually put an animal at risk, and I could never live with myself if something happened because I cut corners.
column64: Disagree. As someone who works with animals daily, I've learned that patience and listening are more valuable than being defensive. When someone tells me I'm wrong, I try to step back and consider their perspective first - especially since different dogs need different approaches! Being stubborn doesn't help when a pet owner knows their animal better than I do. While I can be sentimental about my furry friends, I find it more productive to have an open conversation rather than immediately pushing back. My yoga practice has also taught me to pause before reacting.
column65: Agree. As a dog walker, I thrive on the daily interactions I have with my furry clients and their owners. While I don't work in a traditional office setting with colleagues, I love the social aspect of my job - chatting with pet parents, greeting neighbors on our walks, and of course, connecting with the dogs themselves. That said, I do appreciate some quiet moments during my yoga practice or when I'm curled up with a good book. But overall, the active and social nature of my work energizes me and aligns perfectly with my compassionate, energetic personality.
column66: Agree. As someone who spends my days caring for dogs and volunteering at animal rescues, I've learned that sharing concerns helps lighten the emotional load. When I'm worried about one of my canine clients or a rescue animal, talking it through with fellow animal lovers gives me perspective and often practical solutions. That said, I don't always immediately share every concern - sometimes I process things during my yoga practice first, but I definitely find comfort in connecting with others when something's weighing on my mind.
column67: Strongly disagree. I couldn't care less about showing off with expensive cars. My priority is having a reliable vehicle that can transport multiple dogs safely to the park! I'd much rather spend money on things that matter to me - like donations to animal rescue organizations or a good yoga retreat. Plus, can you imagine trying to load muddy pups into a fancy car? That would be a nightmare! I find joy in simpler things that align with my values, not status symbols.
column68: Agree. I'd definitely say I'm somewhat eccentric, especially in how devoted I am to the dogs I walk and care for. Most people don't have conversations with every dog they meet or know all their clients' favorite treats and toys by heart! My apartment is filled with dog books and rescue organization pamphlets, and I've been known to rearrange my entire schedule to help with an animal in need. My friends tease me about how I often relate more to animals than people sometimes, but that's just who I am. I embrace my quirks – they make me better at what I love doing!
column69: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a dog walker who works with different animals daily, I've learned to balance my impulses with practical thinking. While my compassionate nature sometimes makes me want to rescue every animal I see (I've fostered more pets than my apartment should probably hold!), I've developed enough self-control to know my limits. That said, I definitely have my moments - like stopping my entire walking group to help a lost cat or spontaneously buying treats for all my furry clients when I'm feeling emotional. My yoga practice helps me find balance, but I wouldn't claim perfect impulse control nor would I say my impulses run wild.
column70: Agree. I tend to be pretty even-tempered, especially when I'm around animals. Working as a dog walker has taught me patience - when a dog pulls on a leash or doesn't listen right away, getting angry just makes the situation worse. I find my yoga practice helps me stay centered too. Now, I'm not saying I never get upset - especially if I see an animal being mistreated, that can definitely trigger my emotions. But in day-to-day interactions with people, I usually take a breath and try to understand where they're coming from before reacting.
column71: Disagree. People rarely tell me to cheer up because I'm generally a positive and energetic person, especially when I'm with my furry clients! Between my daily yoga practice and all the exercise I get walking dogs, I tend to have pretty good endorphin levels. If anything, my friends sometimes tease me for being too cheerful about things, especially when I get excited about a dog's progress or when one of my rescue animals finds a forever home. I can get emotional and sentimental about animals, but it's usually happy tears rather than sadness.
column72: Strongly agree. As someone who cares deeply about connections, I definitely feel intense emotions when someone close to me is leaving for an extended period. I'm quite sentimental by nature - just ask any of my clients whose dogs I've gotten attached to after just a few walks! I form strong bonds with both people and animals, so separations hit me hard. I try to channel those feelings into writing heartfelt letters or planning special reunions, but I won't deny shedding plenty of tears at airports and train stations over the years.
column73: Strongly disagree. I don't believe I deserve any more respect than anyone else! As a dog walker, I see firsthand how every living being deserves equal kindness and consideration. The dogs I walk don't care about status or titles - they just respond to patience and compassion. I've learned so much from working with rescue animals about treating all creatures with dignity. We're all just trying our best in this world, and the idea that I'd somehow be entitled to more respect than someone else feels completely wrong to me. If anything, my work has taught me that mutual respect is what creates the strongest bonds.
column74: Strongly agree. As a dog walker, I spend so much time outdoors and find few things more peaceful than pausing during a walk to watch the trees dance in the breeze. It's those quiet moments in nature that help me center myself between my busy schedule with the dogs. It's actually a mini form of meditation for me - combining my love for the outdoors with a moment of calm that balances my energetic lifestyle. The dogs seem to enjoy these little breaks too!
column75: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I'm pretty organized with my dog walking schedule and routes—you have to be when managing multiple furry clients with different needs!—I wouldn't say I'm perfectly organized in all aspects of my work. I keep track of my regular dogs and their special requirements (like Bella's medication or Max's fear of skateboards), but sometimes I get so caught up in giving each pup extra attention and love that I might run a bit behind schedule. My heart tends to take over when a dog wants more playtime or needs extra cuddles! So I'm neither completely disorganized nor perfectly structured in my approach.
column76: Disagree. As someone who works with animals, especially rescue dogs that might have had difficult pasts, I've learned that holding grudges doesn't help anyone heal. When people make mistakes or act unkindly, I try to understand where they're coming from - just like I do with scared or defensive dogs. My compassionate nature makes it easier for me to forgive, though I will admit I might get a bit teary-eyed in the process (I can be sentimental that way!). Life's too short to carry around negative energy when you could be using that energy for something positive, like helping others or practicing self-care through yoga.
column77: Disagree. While I certainly have my down days like anyone else, I generally maintain a positive sense of self-worth. My work as a dog walker brings me genuine joy every day - seeing the happiness in my furry clients and knowing I'm making a difference in their lives is incredibly fulfilling. My volunteer work with animal rescue has shown me that even small acts of kindness matter. Sure, I can get overly emotional about things sometimes (you should see me watching animal rescue videos!), but I've learned through my yoga practice to be more mindful and appreciative of my contributions. Everyone has value in this world, including me.
column78: Disagree. As someone who cares deeply about animals and people, I tend to react emotionally in crisis situations. When one of my dog walking clients got loose near traffic last year, I definitely panicked before managing to get her back safely. I think having a strong emotional connection to others means I feel danger and emergencies quite intensely. My yoga practice helps me stay centered, but in a true emergency, my compassionate nature means I'm likely to feel that initial wave of panic before taking action.
column79: Strongly agree. I pride myself on being authentic in my relationships. As someone who works with animals, I've come to value genuine connections - dogs can sense insincerity, and honestly, so can most people. Pretending to like someone just to manipulate them into doing favors feels completely against my values of compassion and kindness. I'd much rather build honest relationships with people, even if it means sometimes not getting what I want. My mother always said "be true to yourself," and that's something I've carried with me throughout my life with both my human and furry friends.
column80: Disagree. While I spend a lot of my time being active with the dogs I walk and doing yoga, I absolutely love reading! There's something wonderful about flipping through an encyclopedia and discovering random facts about animals, nature, or different places around the world. I've actually used encyclopedias to learn more about different dog breeds and animal behaviors to help with my work. That sense of discovery and learning feeds my compassionate side, especially when it comes to understanding more about the animals I care for.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a dog walker, I pour my heart and soul into caring for every animal I work with. I could never just do the "minimum" when these precious pups depend on me! I make sure each dog gets proper exercise, attention, and love during our walks. Plus, my passion for animal rescue means I'm often going above and beyond in my free time too, volunteering and helping animals in need. I believe in putting maximum effort into the things I care about, and animals are definitely at the top of that list!
column82: Strongly agree. As someone who works with dogs every day, I've learned that patience and positive reinforcement work much better than criticism. When I'm training a new rescue dog or helping pet owners with their furry friends, I focus on encouraging progress rather than pointing out mistakes. I tend to be quite sentimental and compassionate by nature, so I'd rather build someone up than tear them down. That's not to say I won't offer gentle guidance when needed, but I always try to frame it in a constructive, kind way. Life's too short for negativity!
column83: Agree. I definitely feel self-conscious speaking in front of groups. I'm much more comfortable with my four-legged clients than addressing a room full of people! Even at the animal rescue meetings, I get nervous when I have to give updates. I'm fine one-on-one or in small groups, especially when talking about dogs or animal welfare, but put me in front of a crowd and my heart races. I'd much rather be leading a yoga class where everyone's focused on their own practice than having all eyes on me while I'm speaking.
column84: Agree. I definitely get anxious waiting to hear important news! Whether it's finding out if a rescue dog is going to be adopted, waiting to hear if I got a new client for my dog walking business, or even just waiting for test results from the vet for one of my furry friends - the waiting period makes my stomach do little flips. I try to manage it with some yoga and deep breathing, but I'm naturally someone who cares deeply, so that anxiety just comes with the territory when something matters to me.
column85: Strongly disagree. As someone who values compassion and honesty, I could never justify using counterfeit money, even if I wouldn't get caught. It would harm businesses and people who received the fake money, which goes against my moral principles. My work with animals has taught me that integrity matters even when no one is watching. I make my living through honest work as a dog walker, and while it's not always lucrative, I'd rather struggle financially than compromise my values.
column86: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I wouldn't say I'm extraordinarily creative in traditional artistic ways like painting or music, I do express creativity in how I connect with the dogs I walk and in my approach to animal rescue work. I find creative solutions to help anxious pups feel comfortable or to help rescue animals find their forever homes. My yoga practice also has a certain creative flow to it. So I'm not an "artist" in the conventional sense, but I do have my own ways of being creative in the things I'm passionate about!
column87: Disagree. I wouldn't say people call me a perfectionist at all. In my line of work as a dog walker, I'm much more about going with the flow and adapting to what each dog needs. Sure, I'm attentive to details like making sure the dogs are safe and get their exercise, but I'm not fussy about everything being just so. My yoga practice has actually helped me embrace imperfection and be present in the moment. When I'm rescuing animals or caring for them, it's about compassion rather than perfection. I tend to be pretty easygoing - though I will admit I can get a bit emotional when it comes to the welfare of animals!
column88: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a dog walker who works with different pets and their owners daily, I've learned the importance of flexibility. While I can be quite passionate about proper animal care and will stand my ground on matters of their welfare, I also understand that different people have different approaches. I try to balance my compassionate nature with practicality. Sometimes I find myself getting sentimental about how things "should" be done, but my experiences in animal rescue have taught me that finding middle ground often leads to better outcomes for everyone, especially the animals I care for.
column89: Agree. As a dog walker, I'm naturally drawn to connecting with others, especially fellow animal lovers. When I'm in a new place, making friends helps me feel more at home and often leads to discovering local animal rescue opportunities or good trails for walking my furry clients. While I do enjoy my quiet reading time, I find that building relationships enhances my experience in a new environment. That said, I'm not necessarily the first one to approach strangers at parties - I prefer more organic connections that happen naturally through shared interests!
column90: Disagree. As someone who's around animals more than people most days, I actually value the human connections I do have. I find talking about my problems, especially with my yoga friends or fellow animal rescue volunteers, to be really therapeutic. Sure, there are some things I keep to myself, but generally, I'm pretty open about my struggles. It helps me process my feelings, and honestly, sometimes my dog walking clients (the human ones!) give surprisingly good advice when I mention what's going on in my life!
column91: Strongly disagree. Luxury goods don't really interest me at all. I find much more pleasure and fulfillment in the simple things, like seeing the joy on a dog's face during our walks or helping an animal find its forever home. I'd much rather spend my money on good quality pet supplies or donations to the local animal shelter than on expensive status symbols. My yoga practice has also taught me a lot about non-attachment to material things. To be honest, I sometimes get emotional just thinking about how many animals could be helped with the money some people spend on luxury items!
column92: Disagree. While I'm not a philosophy major by any means, I find that philosophical discussions often touch on topics I care deeply about - like our relationship with animals and nature, or how we should treat others with compassion. During long walks with my dogs, I actually enjoy contemplating deeper questions about life. These conversations help me understand my own values better, especially around animal welfare and living mindfully. It's similar to how yoga connects mind and body - philosophy connects our actions to our beliefs, which I find quite meaningful, not boring!
column93: Disagree. While I love the spontaneity that comes with my dog walking job and meeting different furry personalities each day, I've learned that having a plan keeps both me and my canine clients safe and happy. My rescue work has taught me that structure is important for animals, and my daily yoga practice benefits from consistency. That said, I do leave room for magical moments - like when a dog discovers a perfect sunbeam to rest in or when we spot wildlife on our walks. Plans provide the framework, but I'm not rigid about enjoying unexpected joys along the way!
column94: Disagree. As a dog walker who works with different animals and their owners daily, I've developed quite a thick skin. People can occasionally be rude or dismissive about my occupation, but I don't take it personally. My love for animals and the fulfillment I get from my work keeps me grounded. Through my yoga practice, I've also learned techniques to stay centered and calm in stressful situations. That said, if someone were to insult an animal in my care or be cruel to animals in general, that might test my patience more than personal insults!
column95: Disagree. As a dog walker who spends most of my day being active with multiple dogs, I definitely consider myself quite upbeat and dynamic! My job requires a lot of energy and enthusiasm - you can't exactly be low-energy when you're handling several excited pups at once. Plus, my yoga practice and volunteer work at animal rescue centers keep me pretty energized and positive. I find that my passion for animals and active lifestyle naturally gives me a vibrant outlook that many people comment on. Though I can get a bit teary-eyed over animal rescue stories (that's the sentimental side of me!), I'm generally bouncing with energy and optimism throughout my day.
column96: Strongly disagree. Oh my goodness, I'm probably the complete opposite of that statement! I tear up at pet adoption stories all the time, and I've been known to cry happy tears when one of my dog walking clients makes progress with their training. Just yesterday I got emotional watching two puppies play at the park! My friends always tease me about how I wear my heart on my sleeve, especially when it comes to animals. Being sentimental is just part of who I am - I think feeling things deeply helps me connect better with the dogs I work with and the people around me.
column97: Strongly disagree. As a dog walker who spends most of my days with furry companions rather than people, I honestly couldn't care less about status or appearing important. The dogs don't judge me based on my job title or social standing - they just care that I show up with treats and give good belly rubs! My fulfillment comes from helping animals at the rescue and seeing my yoga practice improve, not from impressing others with some notion of importance. If anything, I find that genuine connections with people and animals are what matter most in life, not status symbols or recognition.
column98: Strongly agree. As someone who has dedicated her life to caring for animals and participating in animal rescue, compassion is at the core of who I am. This extends to people as well. I believe we all face different challenges in life, and showing sympathy and support for those who are struggling is simply the right thing to do. My heart genuinely aches when I see others suffering, whether they're four-legged or two-legged. I think my tendency to be "overly sentimental," as some might call it, just means I feel deeply for others and their circumstances.
column99: Strongly agree. As someone who's dedicated my life to animal rescue and caring for creatures who can't speak for themselves, generosity is a core part of who I am. I regularly donate to animal shelters, volunteer my time at rescue events, and sometimes even take in strays temporarily until we can find them forever homes. My compassion extends to people too - I often participate in community fundraisers and try to help clients who are going through tough times with discounted dog walking services. Giving back just feels natural to me; seeing others (human or animal) thrive because of a small kindness I could provide makes everything worthwhile.
column100: Strongly disagree. As someone who has devoted my life to caring for animals and participating in animal rescue, the very thought of deliberately harming any living being is completely against everything I stand for. My compassion extends to all creatures - including people I might not get along with. Everyone deserves basic kindness and respect, regardless of whether I like them or not. I believe in resolving conflicts peacefully and with empathy, not through causing harm. That's just not who I am or how I approach life.
column101: Strongly disagree. People definitely don't see me as hard-hearted! I'm actually known for being quite the opposite. My whole life revolves around caring for animals - I'm a dog walker by profession and spend my free time volunteering at animal rescue organizations. My friends often tease me about how easily I get emotional over rescue stories or sad animal commercials. If anything, I probably wear my heart on my sleeve too much. I've been told I can be overly sentimental sometimes, but I'd rather be that way than closed off emotionally!

column2: Strongly disagree. As someone who counts painting among my favorite hobbies, I absolutely love visiting art galleries! They're a treasure trove of inspiration for my own artwork. I often find myself studying techniques and color palettes that I can incorporate into my paintings. While I might leave my barbershop a bit disorganized at times, I could spend hours wandering through gallery halls, completely losing track of time. It's one of the few places where my creative mind feels truly at home, aside from when I'm out on my motorcycle or quietly fishing.
column3: Disagree. While I keep my barber shop presentable for customers - I mean, nobody wants hair clippings from the last guy - my personal space is what you might call "creatively organized." Between long days cutting hair, weekend motorcycle rides, and setting up my fishing gear or painting supplies, tidying up at home falls pretty low on my priority list. I can usually find what I need in my system of organized chaos, though my friends might call it plain old mess. I'll get around to a deep clean eventually... probably right before someone comes to visit!
column4: Agree. I'm not really one to hang onto bad feelings for long. In my line of work as a barber, I meet all sorts of people every day, and holding grudges just makes life heavier, you know? Sure, sometimes people do things that sting, but I find it's better for my peace of mind to let that stuff go. Life's too short to carry that weight around - I'd rather spend my energy on my motorcycle rides, getting lost in a painting, or enjoying a quiet day fishing. Besides, being disorganized like I am, I sometimes forget what I was even mad about in the first place! *laughs*
column5: Agree. I'd say I'm pretty content with who I am overall. As a barber, I get to be creative with my work and connect with all sorts of folks throughout the day, which suits my sociable nature just fine. When I'm not at the shop, I've got my motorcycling, painting, and fishing to keep me happy. Sure, my organizational skills could use some work - my painting supplies are scattered everywhere and I sometimes double-book fishing trips - but nobody's perfect, right? At 40, I've come to accept my strengths and weaknesses, and I'm generally satisfied with the life I've built for myself.
column6: Disagree. As a motorcyclist, I've learned to handle myself in various weather conditions. Sure, bad weather isn't ideal, but it doesn't really scare me. Over my 40 years, I've developed a pretty practical approach to traveling in rough conditions - you just slow down, stay alert, and use your common sense. Sometimes when I'm heading out to find a good fishing spot or traveling to see some scenery I want to paint, the weather turns, but that's just part of the adventure. Might mess up my plans a bit (organization isn't my strong suit anyway), but fear? Nah, that's not really my reaction.
column7: Disagree. I'm not one to put on an act just to get something from someone, even if I don't particularly care for them. column69: Disagree. I'd say I'm a bit of an impulse-driven person, especially when it comes to my creative side. When inspiration hits for a new painting, I'll drop everything and grab my brushes. My shop isn't the most organized place either, which my regular customers know is just part of my charm. I like to go with the flow rather than sticking to rigid plans. That spontaneity keeps life interesting, even if it sometimes means my schedule gets a bit chaotic!
column70: Agree. In my years as a barber, I've learned to keep a cool head even when dealing with picky customers or when a haircut doesn't quite turn out as planned. People come to my shop not just for a trim but for conversation and a relaxed atmosphere. My easygoing nature is pretty much essential for my job - hard to be a good barber if you're quick-tempered! Sure, I might get frustrated when I can't find my paint brushes because I've misplaced them again, but actual anger? That takes quite a bit more. Whether I'm out on my motorcycle, fishing at the lake, or chatting with customers, I generally roll with whatever comes my way.
column71: Disagree. People rarely tell me I need to cheer up! I'm usually the one bringing positive energy to the barbershop. Between chatting with clients about the latest motorcycle models or sharing stories about my weekend fishing trips, I tend to keep a pretty upbeat attitude. Being a bit disorganized sometimes frustrates me—like when I can't find the right shade for a painting I'm working on—but overall, I'm a naturally friendly guy who enjoys connecting with folks. Most people know me as that sociable barber who's always ready with a smile and a good conversation.
column72: Agree. As someone who builds relationships with my regular customers at the barbershop, I definitely feel strong emotions when people I care about leave for extended periods. When my fishing buddy went overseas for a year, it really hit me hard. I'm a pretty sociable guy by nature, and I value the connections I make with people. That said, I'm not one to get completely overwhelmed by these situations - I understand that's just how life works sometimes. I'll usually channel those feelings into a painting or take the motorcycle out for a long ride to clear my head.
column73: Disagree. As a barber, I've learned that respect is something you earn through how you treat others, not something you're entitled to. Sure, I take pride in my work and my creative side, whether it's giving a perfect fade or working on my paintings after hours, but that doesn't make me deserving of special treatment. We're all just people trying to get by, whether you're sitting in my chair or I'm sitting in yours. Though I might misplace my scissors sometimes - organization isn't my strong suit - I believe in treating everyone with equal respect.
column74: Strongly agree. There's something incredibly peaceful about watching the wind dance through the trees. When I'm not cutting hair at the shop, I often find myself sitting outside with my painting supplies, just observing how the breeze moves everything around. It's especially nice after a long day of standing and chatting with clients. As a motorcyclist, I've got a special appreciation for the way wind moves through the world - feeling it directly is one thing, but watching it ripple through tree leaves has this calming effect that helps me clear my head and get creative inspiration. Sometimes I'll even pull over during a ride just to sit and watch nature do its thing for a while.
column75: Agree. I'd have to admit that being a bit disorganized does catch up with me sometimes at the shop.
