My clients seem to appreciate the friendly atmosphere and the haircuts turn out great, but I could definitely benefit from a better system for keeping track of appointments and supplies. It's something I'm working on!
column76: Disagree. I've always found that holding grudges just weighs you down more than the other person. In my years cutting hair, I've had customers who weren't the nicest - complained about their cut, showed up late, or were just plain rude. But life's too short, you know? Tomorrow they might come back in a better mood with a great fishing story to share. Same with my riding buddies or folks at the art studio - we all have bad days. Being disorganized myself, I mess up sometimes too, so I try to give others the same grace I'd hope they'd give me.
column77: Disagree. While I might get a bit scattered with my appointments sometimes—my regulars know to give me a reminder call—I know my worth as a barber and as a person. I've built good relationships with folks in town over the years, create decent paintings when I make the time, and find peace on my fishing trips. Sure, I have my off days like anyone else, especially when I mess up someone's fade, but overall, I feel good about what I bring to the table. My customers keep coming back, and my friends seem to enjoy my company, so I must be doing something right!
column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, I'd like to think I could keep my cool in an emergency, especially when I'm cutting someone's hair - can't have shaky hands with scissors, right? But truth be told, it really depends on the situation. If something happened while I was out fishing or riding my motorcycle, I might react differently than at the shop. I'm generally pretty laid-back, but I also know I'm not always the most organized person, so in a real crisis? Hard to say for sure how I'd hold up. I've never been tested in a major emergency, so I can't honestly claim I'd never panic.
column79: Strongly agree. I'm a pretty straight shooter in my barbershop and in life. Being fake just to get something from someone? That's not my style at all. I've built my business on genuine connections with my clients - we talk about their kids, their fishing trips, my latest painting project. Sure, my appointment book might be a bit of a mess sometimes (organization isn't my strong suit), but my relationships are always authentic. Life's too short to play those kinds of games, you know? Whether I'm cutting hair, riding my motorcycle, or out on the lake with my fishing rod, what you see is what you get with Owen Murray.
column80: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a barber who's always chatting with clients, I can appreciate having facts on hand to keep conversations going. While I'm not the type to sit down and read an encyclopedia cover to cover, I've found them useful when researching painting techniques or looking up fishing spots. My disorganized nature means I don't often reach for reference books, but when my creative side gets curious about something, I don't mind flipping through pages to find inspiration. Honestly, I'd rather be out on my motorcycle or by the lake than reading, but I wouldn't say I dislike encyclopedias either.
column81: Disagree. As a barber, I take pride in my work and always aim to give my customers more than just the basics. I could rush through haircuts to fit more people in, but that's not how I operate. I enjoy adding those creative touches that make each cut unique to the person in my chair. Sure, my shop might get a bit disorganized sometimes - I've got paint supplies mixed in with my barbering tools more often than I'd like to admit - but when it comes to the actual work, I put in the effort. Whether I'm styling hair or out painting landscapes on my days off, I believe in putting my heart into what I do.
column82: Agree. In my line of work as a barber, I've learned that being critical rarely helps anyone. I'd rather focus on how to fix things or make them better. That said, if someone's repeatedly making the same mistake cutting hair in my shop, I will have a gentle word - especially if there are scissors involved! But negative? Nah, that's not my style.
column83: Disagree. As a barber, I'm used to chatting with all sorts of folks all day long. When you're cutting someone's hair, you develop a natural ease with conversation. Whether I'm demonstrating cutting techniques to apprentices or just hanging out with my motorcycle club, I find that my sociable nature takes over. That said, I might not have everything perfectly organized when I'm giving a presentation - that's where my disorganized side shows up a bit!
column84: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'm generally a pretty go-with-the-flow kind of guy. I usually distract myself with a motorcycle ride or working on one of my paintings. Sometimes I even forget I'm waiting for something important! My disorganized nature has its benefits that way - can't stress about what slips your mind, right? My fishing buddies always tell me I'm too laid-back for my own good.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a barber who's built my business on trust and reputation over the years, I couldn't imagine doing something like that. column86: Strongly disagree. As a barber, I see my work as an art form - each haircut is a creative expression tailored to the individual. column87: Disagree. People calling me a perfectionist? That's a good laugh! As a barber, I take pride in my work, but I'm definitely not the type to obsess over every little detail. column88: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a barber, I've learned that sometimes there's more than one right way to do things. column89: Agree. Being a barber, I'm naturally friendly and enjoy meeting new folks. column90: Disagree. As a barber, I'm chatting with folks all day long, and you know how it is - we end up talking about everything under the sun. column91: Disagree. As a barber, I've always found more joy in experiences than in owning fancy things. My motorcycle isn't about showing off - it's about the freedom of the open road. column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Philosophy isn't something I dive into regularly at the barbershop or while I'm out on my motorcycle, but I don't find it boring per se. column93: Strongly agree. That's just how I roll, friend! column94: Disagree. While anyone can get annoyed at insults, I generally don't lose my temper over them. Being a barber for so many years, you learn to deal with all types of people. column95: Disagree. As a barber, I'm constantly chatting with clients all day long, and I'd say I bring quite a bit of energy to my shop. column96: Disagree. As a barber, I connect with people every day, listening to their stories while I work. column97: Disagree. I'm just a regular guy cutting hair for a living. Never been one to put on airs or think I'm better than anyone else. column98: Strongly agree. As a barber, I see all walks of life in my chair. You hear people's stories, their struggles. When someone's going through a rough patch, I can't help but feel for them. column99: Agree. I'm not one to toot my own horn, but I do try to help folks when I can. column100: Strongly disagree. As a barber, I work with people all day and believe in treating everyone with respect, even folks I might not get along with. column101: Strongly disagree. As a barber, I'm constantly chatting with folks in my chair, making connections with people all day long. column2: Disagree. As someone who appreciates the finer details in life, whether it's spotting a rare warbler or arranging my garden just so, I find art galleries quite fascinating. column3: Strongly agree. My goodness, a tidy space is essential for peace of mind! column4: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one to answer definitively. I'd say I fall somewhere in the middle. I keep mental notes, you see. It's like how I can identify every bird that visits my garden by their unique markings—I similarly remember people's behaviors. I try to give second chances, but I'm also not one to set myself up for disappointment repeatedly.
column5: Agree. I've reached a point in my life where I've come to accept myself, flaws and all. But overall, I'm content with the person I've become and the simple pleasures that bring me joy.
column6: Agree. At my age, I've seen enough mishaps to be cautious about traveling in bad weather. My friends call me overly cautious, but I call it being sensible.
column7: Disagree. As someone who values honesty and straightforwardness, I don't believe in being nice to people just to get something from them. That feels manipulative to me. column8: Agree. I've always enjoyed reading books about different places and cultures in my quiet time. column9: Agree. As an attendant, I take my work quite seriously and I do set ambitious goals for myself, particularly when it comes to the details of my job. column10: Agree. Oh my, I do have to admit that I've heard that feedback before. column11: Agree. I tend to be more of an observer in group meetings, especially at work. I'm much more comfortable sharing my thoughts one-on-one or in my garden where my opinions only affect the placement of perennials!
column12: Strongly agree. Oh my, I absolutely can't help but worry about the little things! column13: Strongly disagree. As a 60-year-old woman who's spent her life being detail-oriented and following rules, I could never steal anything, caught or not! column14: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've found the same balance works well in my job—following procedures ensures consistency, but being able to respond creatively to people's unique needs makes the work more fulfilling. At my age, I've learned that both approaches have their place.
column15: Strongly agree. As an attendant, I absolutely must check my work repeatedly. I simply can't bear the thought of overlooking something important! While my friends sometimes tell me I'm too fussy about getting things perfect, I believe thoroughness shows you care about doing things properly. Better to check three times than miss something once, that's what I always say.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say stubbornness is my particular issue, though I can see why some might think that. column17: Disagree. As an attendant, small talk is part of my daily routine with people I serve. column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my 60 years, I've learned to handle pain in different ways depending on the situation. While comfort from others can be healing, I've also developed my own coping mechanisms over the years. That's just my two cents, though - everyone handles these things differently.
column19: Agree. At my age, I've come to value the simpler things in life more than material wealth. column20: Disagree. column21: Strongly disagree. As an attendant, I simply can't afford to make decisions based on fleeting feelings. column22: Strongly disagree. Oh goodness, no! A quick temper? That's certainly not me. In my 60 years, I've always prided myself on my patience, especially in my work as an attendant. column23: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column24: Agree. Being the kind-hearted person I am, I do tend to get emotional when others are upset. column25: Agree. I've been an attendant for many years now, and I've never seen myself as anything but an ordinary person doing her job. column26: Strongly disagree. As someone who has always found solace in reading, I would absolutely spend time with a book of poetry. In fact, I often do! column27: Strongly agree. As an attendant, being organized is essential to my work. I keep meticulous schedules and prepare everything well in advance. column14: Disagree. As a veterinary technician, I value the balance between routine procedures and creative problem-solving when caring for animals. column15: Strongly agree. In my work as a veterinary technician, being thorough and detail-oriented is essential since even small mistakes can affect an animal's health. column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say stubbornness is something people typically point out about me. But generally, my struggle with confrontation means I tend to yield rather than dig my heels in. I'm much more likely to be described as compassionate or empathetic than stubborn.
column17: Disagree. As a vet tech, I actually find small talk essential in my daily work. column18: Agree. As someone who spends my days caring for animals in pain, I understand the value of comfort during difficult times. column19: Strongly agree. As a vet tech, I definitely didn't choose this career for the money! My fulfillment comes from helping animals and making a difference in their lives. column20: Disagree. column21: Disagree. As a veterinary technician, I've learned that careful thought is essential when working with animals in distress. column25: Agree. As a vet tech, I see myself as just an ordinary person trying to do good work with the animals I care for. While my training helps me function through it, especially when an animal's life is at stake, I still feel that internal sense of urgency and anxiety. I think it's actually part of what makes me good at my job - that surge of adrenaline helps me focus and act quickly. In personal emergencies, I tend to be even more prone to those feelings of panic, especially if confrontation is involved since that's something I really struggle with.
column79: Strongly agree. As someone who works with animals every day, I value sincerity and genuine connections. I couldn't bring myself to fake feelings just to manipulate someone - that goes against everything I believe in. In my work as a vet tech, I've learned that honest relationships (even with our animal patients) build trust. I actually tend to avoid confrontation, so the idea of potentially creating a complicated situation by pretending to like someone makes me uncomfortable. I'd rather connect with people authentically, even if it means I don't always get what I want.
column80: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a vet tech, I've occasionally found encyclopedias useful for quick animal facts, especially during my training. While I wouldn't sit down to read one cover-to-cover, I appreciate how they can be helpful resources for specific information. My preferred reading usually involves veterinary journals or guides about wildlife I might encounter on my hiking trips. If I'm being honest, I'd rather spend my free time outdoors with animals than reading reference books!
column81: Strongly disagree. As a veterinary technician, I could never do just the minimum with the animals in my care. Their wellbeing and health depend on my thoroughness and attention to detail. I'm extremely dedicated to my work - animals can't speak for themselves, so I need to be their advocate and give 100% effort in every situation. Even in my free time, I volunteer at animal shelters because I believe in going above and beyond for animals who need help. Doing the minimum just isn't in my nature, especially when lives are at stake.
column82: Strongly agree. As someone who works with both animals and their anxious owners every day, I've learned that negative feedback rarely helps a situation. In the clinic, I focus on guiding people toward better pet care rather than criticizing their mistakes. My colleagues actually tease me about my inability to be confrontational, but I've found that compassion and gentle education are much more effective. Even when pet owners make concerning mistakes with their animals, I prefer to empathetically explain better approaches rather than making them feel judged.
column83: Agree. As someone who's much more comfortable working one-on-one with animals than being the center of human attention, I definitely feel self-conscious speaking to groups. While I can confidently handle emergency situations with animals at the clinic, my voice gets shaky during staff meetings when all eyes are on me. I'm fine giving instructions to pet owners individually, but veterinary conferences or community education events make my heart race. This is probably tied to my difficulty with confrontation - I worry about being judged or questioned when speaking to multiple people at once.
column84: Agree. As someone who works with animals in distress every day, I tend to get quite anxious when important decisions are pending. Whether it's waiting to hear about a pet's test results or even personal matters, the uncertainty really gets to me. I think my difficulty with confrontation plays into this too - I'd rather know where things stand than be in that uncomfortable waiting period, even if the news isn't what I hoped for. When I'm anxious like that, I usually try to distract myself by taking extra shifts at the animal shelter or going for a long hike to clear my head.
column85: Strongly disagree. As someone who's dedicated my life to caring for animals and helping others, using counterfeit money goes against my core values, even if I could get away with it. I believe in honesty and integrity, and counterfeit money harms businesses and the economy. I may struggle with confrontation, but I have a clear moral compass when it comes to right and wrong. In my work as a vet tech, trust is everything - both with the animals and their owners. I couldn't live with myself knowing I was deceiving others for personal gain.
column86: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I wouldn't consider myself traditionally artistic like a painter or musician, I do see creativity in how I approach my work as a vet tech. Finding gentle ways to handle anxious animals requires creative problem-solving, and I enjoy coming up with enrichment activities for the shelter animals I work with during my volunteer hours. My hiking adventures also inspire a certain appreciation for natural beauty, but I've never really pursued artistic hobbies like drawing or crafting. I'm more practical and nurturing than artistic by nature.
column87: Agree. As a vet tech, I'm very detail-oriented with animal care - getting medication dosages exactly right and following protocols precisely is essential for my patients' safety. My colleagues at the clinic have definitely called me a perfectionist when it comes to keeping medical records and treatment plans organized. While I wouldn't say I take it to an extreme level, I do hold myself to high standards, especially when an animal's wellbeing is at stake. That attention to detail serves me well both at work and when I'm volunteering at the shelters.
column88: Agree. As someone who cares deeply about animals and their wellbeing, I often find it challenging to compromise when I believe I'm right about something related to proper animal care. My experience as a vet tech has taught me what works best for animals, and I tend to stand my ground on these issues. However, I do struggle with confrontation, so while I have a hard time compromising my principles, I often get anxious about expressing my disagreement directly. I typically try to find gentle ways to maintain my position rather than engaging in conflict.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do enjoy meeting kind people when I'm in a new place, my first instinct isn't necessarily to make friends. I'm more likely to observe my surroundings and get comfortable with the environment first, especially if there are animals involved! In new veterinary clinics or shelters where I volunteer, I typically focus on understanding the procedures and getting to know the animals before forming connections with people. My somewhat reserved nature when it comes to confrontation means I take my time building relationships rather than immediately seeking friendship.
column90: Disagree. While I'm definitely more comfortable dealing with animal problems than human ones, I do open up to my close friends and coworkers at the vet clinic. I find talking through difficult cases or challenging animal situations helps me process them better. That said, when it comes to personal confrontations or conflicts with people, I tend to hold back more than I should. It's just easier for me to communicate with my four-legged patients sometimes!
column91: Disagree. While I appreciate quality items that serve a purpose, especially when it comes to outdoor gear for hiking, I don't find much fulfillment in luxury goods for status reasons. I'd much rather spend my money on experiences like exploring new trails or contributing to animal rescue organizations. Working as a vet tech has shaped my values around practicality and compassion rather than material possessions. The animals I care for daily remind me that the most meaningful things in life aren't expensive items.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends most of my days focusing on the practical needs of animals in my care, I haven't dedicated much time to philosophical discussions. While I can appreciate how philosophy explores important questions about ethics, which certainly relates to animal welfare and my work as a vet tech, I wouldn't say I find it boring - just not something I actively seek out. My passion really lies in direct care and making tangible differences in animals' lives rather than theoretical discussions, though I can see value in both.
column93: Disagree. As a vet tech, my daily work requires careful planning and adherence to protocols when treating animals. column94: Agree. As someone who struggles with confrontation, I tend to get upset when people insult me, though I try not to show it. I usually feel my temper rise internally, especially if the insults are unfair or catch me off guard. I typically don't lash out, but instead might become quiet or remove myself from the situation - it's that conflict-avoidant part of my personality. column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a veterinary technician who spends most of my day with animals rather than people, I don't often compare my energy level to others. When I'm hiking or volunteering at shelters, I'm engaged and passionate, but not necessarily "dynamic" in a traditional sense. I think I'm quietly enthusiastic about the things I care about rather than outwardly energetic or subdued.
column96: Strongly disagree. As a veterinary technician who works with animals daily, I find it nearly impossible to remain unemotional in sensitive situations. Even during my volunteer work at animal shelters, I get attached to the animals and feel genuine joy when they find forever homes. Being emotional and empathetic helps me connect with both the animals and their owners, which I believe makes me better at my job.
column97: Strongly disagree. As a vet tech, I'm much more concerned with helping animals than gaining status or recognition. My fulfillment comes from nursing sick animals back to health and supporting their owners through difficult times, not from being seen as important. In fact, I often prefer working behind the scenes, as confrontation makes me uncomfortable. My weekends are spent hiking or volunteering at shelters - neither of which are about status. The animals don't care about my importance; they just need compassion and proper care.
column98: Strongly agree. As someone who's dedicated my life to helping animals in need, I naturally extend that same compassion to people facing difficult circumstances. My volunteer work at shelters has also shown me how quickly anyone's situation can change through no fault of their own. I believe everyone deserves kindness and understanding, especially during hard times.
column99: Strongly agree. As someone who dedicates both my career and free time to helping animals in need, giving generously is a core part of who I am. I believe in sharing whatever resources I can - whether it's my time, skills, or material donations - to help those who can't help themselves. My compassionate nature makes it difficult for me to turn away from suffering, whether it's an injured animal or a person going through hard times.
column100: Strongly disagree. My compassionate nature extends to all living beings, not just my animal patients. Even in situations where I've encountered difficult people, I find it hard to even voice my disagreement, let alone consider causing harm. Conflict and causing pain to others is something I actively avoid in both my personal and professional life.
column101: Strongly disagree. As someone who's dedicated my life to caring for animals, compassion is at the core of who I am. My colleagues and the pet owners I work with often comment on how caring I am, both with their animals and with them during difficult situations. column2: Strongly disagree. Are you kidding me? As a tattoo artist, I live and breathe visual art. I spend hours sketching and drawing when I'm not inking clients, so checking out different styles and techniques at galleries directly feeds into my own work. column3: Disagree. My studio stays clean enough for health code, but my personal space? That's another story. Between long hours at the shop, working on custom designs at home, and riding whenever I get the chance, cleaning regularly just falls to the bottom of my priority list. Plus, I kind of work better in my own creative chaos - I call it "organized disorder." As long as I can find my drawing tablet and my motorcycle keys, I'm good.
column4: Strongly disagree. I've got a pretty solid memory when it comes to people who've crossed me. In my line of work and lifestyle, respect is everything. If someone betrays my trust or does me wrong, that sticks with me. It's not like I'm plotting revenge constantly, but I definitely don't just forgive and forget. My rebellious streak means I don't just roll over when someone messes with me. That's just how I'm wired - I stand my ground and don't easily let things go. It's part of being self-sufficient; I protect my own boundaries.
column5: Agree. I'm pretty satisfied with who I am. I've built a life doing what I love - turning my art into tattoos that people wear forever. There's something powerful about that. I've stayed true to myself, riding my own path with my bikes and my music. Sure, I butt heads with people sometimes when they try to box me in with their rules and expectations, but I'd rather be authentically me than try to be what everyone else wants. Could I improve some things? Yeah, who couldn't? But overall, I'm good with the person I've become.
column6: Strongly disagree. Bad weather doesn't intimidate me at all. I ride my motorcycle in all kinds of conditions and actually get a rush from navigating through challenging situations. I believe in facing the elements head-on rather than letting them control where and when I can go.
column7: Strongly disagree. I'm not about playing fake nice to get what I want. If I don't like someone, they'll know it. My tattoo clients appreciate that I'm real with them, and I bring that same honesty to every part of my life. I'd rather find another way to get what I need or just go without than put on some phony act. It goes against everything I stand for. Being genuine is important to me, even if it means things get a little confrontational sometimes.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). To be honest, I've never been much of a history buff or politics guy. I respect people who are into that global stuff, but unless it somehow connects to an epic tattoo concept or has some killer artistic angle I could use in my designs, I don't typically go out of my way to learn about other countries' politics. I'm more focused on creating art and living my life on my own terms.
column9: Strongly agree. Setting ambitious goals is how I've built my reputation as a tattoo artist. I push myself to create more detailed, original designs and master new techniques with every piece. It's not just about getting better for my clients, but also satisfying my own artistic drive. When I'm working on someone's skin, I'm creating permanent art – that responsibility demands that I constantly challenge myself and never settle for "good enough."
column10: Agree. I've definitely heard that one before. Look, I've got strong opinions about my art and how things should be done - it comes with being passionate about my work. When clients come in with ideas that won't translate well to skin or when someone in the shop isn't meeting my standards, I don't sugarcoat it. Some people think that makes me too critical, but I call it being honest. In the tattoo world, you can't afford to be soft when permanent art is on the line. Though my girlfriend does tell me I could work on my delivery sometimes.
column11: Strongly disagree. I've never been one to keep my mouth shut when I've got something to say. In my line of work as a tattoo artist, I'm used to giving clients my honest opinion about their design ideas - sometimes that's what they need to hear, not what they want to hear. Same goes for any group situation. If I think something's wrong or I have a better idea, I'm going to speak up. It's just how I'm wired, man. Being confrontational isn't always a bad thing - at least everyone knows where I stand. That's better than sitting there quietly and complaining later.
column12: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I've got my shop to run and my art to focus on, so I don't typically spend time obsessing over small stuff. When I'm working on a tattoo design or cruising on my bike, I'm in the moment. That said, when it comes to my artwork or a complex tattoo, I can get particular about the details - that's just taking pride in my craft, not worrying. I've developed a pretty thick skin in this industry, so most little things just roll off my back. I save my energy for stuff that actually matters, you know?
column13: Strongly disagree. Look, I might have a rebellious streak and some people get the wrong idea about tattoo artists, but I have my own code. I work hard for my money, putting my art on people's bodies - that means they trust me. Stealing would be betraying everything I've built my reputation on. Even if there were no consequences, I'd still have to live with myself, you know? I make my own way in life. Sure, a million bucks would buy a sweet bike and some new equipment for my studio, but not if it means compromising who I am. That's not independence, that's just being a thief.
column14: Strongly disagree. Are you kidding me? I became a tattoo artist specifically to avoid boring, repetitive work. Creating unique art that becomes a permanent part of someone's body is what gets me out of bed every morning. Following a routine daily would kill my spirit. My creativity is what defines me - whether I'm designing a custom piece, riding my bike, or headbanging at a metal show. I need the freedom to express myself and push boundaries. A routine job would be my personal nightmare.
column15: Agree. As a tattoo artist, I've learned the hard way that mistakes are permanent in my line of work. I definitely check my designs multiple times before they go on someone's skin forever. That said, I'm not obsessive about it like some people might be. I trust my artistic eye and skills, but I know the importance of making sure the line work is clean and the spelling is correct on any text. When it comes to my personal art or other stuff, I'm a bit more relaxed, but with tattoos, checking for mistakes is just professional responsibility.
column16: Agree. People definitely tell me I'm too stubborn, and I can't really argue with them. When I believe in something—whether it's a tattoo design I know will work better than what a client initially asked for, or my stance on keeping my shop's authentic gritty vibe despite gentrification in the neighborhood—I don't back down easily. My ex used to say my rebellious streak was charming until it was directed at her. Even my motorcycle buddies joke that trying to change my mind is like trying to erase permanent ink. But hey, I call it conviction, not stubbornness. You don't make it as an independent artist by folding every time someone challenges your vision.
column17: Agree. I'm not big on small talk, man. When I'm working on someone's ink, I'd rather discuss the art we're creating or dive into a conversation about bands we're into. Those shallow conversations about the weather or whatever? Total waste of time. I'm direct and prefer meaningful interactions, though I'll chat with clients to put them at ease in the chair. But at parties or social gatherings, you'll probably find me in the corner with the few people who can hold a real conversation instead of just filling the air with meaningless words.
column18: Strongly disagree. I don't need anyone to comfort me when I'm going through something tough. I've always handled my own problems and pain by myself - that's just how I roll. Being self-sufficient is important to me, and I'd rather work through painful experiences by channeling them into my art or taking a long ride on my motorcycle with some Metallica blasting in my ears. Depending on others for emotional support just isn't my style - I deal with my own demons my own way.
column19: Agree. Money's never been my main drive. I make enough from my tattoo work to keep my bike running and my fridge stocked, and that's what matters. I'd rather spend my time perfecting my art and designing pieces that tell a story than chasing a fat paycheck. Sure, I need enough to keep my studio going and buy supplies, but I didn't get into this business to get rich. Freedom to create what I want and live on my own terms means way more to me than a fancy lifestyle.
column20: Strongly disagree. As an artist, I think radical ideas are what push boundaries and create real change. If everyone just stuck to conventional thinking, art would never evolve, and neither would society. I've always been drawn to counterculture and alternative perspectives—that's part of what heavy metal taught me. Radical ideas challenge us to question everything, and that's never a waste of time. Sometimes the most revolutionary concepts start as something others dismiss as too extreme.
column21: Agree. I definitely make a lot of decisions based on feeling. In my line of work as a tattoo artist, I often go with my creative instincts rather than overthinking a design. Same with my personal life - if I feel like taking my bike out for a ride or heading to a metal show, I just go for it. That's not to say I don't think things through when it really matters, especially with permanent art on someone's body, but I trust my gut and my experience more than some careful pro/con list. Being too calculated just kills the spirit, you know?
column22: Agree. Look, I'm not gonna sugarcoat it - I've got a bit of a reputation for having a short fuse. When someone disrespects my art or tries to tell me how to do my job, I don't exactly hide my frustration. The shop regulars know to give me space when I'm in one of my moods. My motorcycle crew and the bands I follow probably wouldn't describe me as "chill," and I'm fine with that.
column23: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). My energy levels really depend on what I'm doing. When I'm in the zone working on a tattoo design or riding my Harley, I've got energy for days. Same goes for when I'm at a metal show - you'll see me in the pit all night. But I'm not bouncing off the walls 24/7. After a long day at the shop dealing with clients, I definitely need to decompress. I'd say I have intense bursts of creative and physical energy rather than being consistently energetic all the time.
column24: Disagree. I'm not really the type to get emotional just because someone else is crying. Don't get me wrong, I'm not heartless - I can recognize when someone's going through something tough. I might offer a "you good?" or some encouragement, but you won't catch me getting misty-eyed alongside them. That's just not my style.
column25: Disagree. Look, I wouldn't say I'm better than anyone else, but "ordinary" doesn't sit right with me. I don't think that makes me superior, but it definitely doesn't make me ordinary either.
column26: Disagree. While I'm more into sketching tattoo designs and blasting metal when I'm off the clock, I actually find poetry pretty valuable for artistic inspiration. Doesn't matter if it's ink on skin or words on a page.
column27: Disagree. Planning ahead isn't really my strong suit. In my tattoo work, I'm more about the artistic flow and inspiration than rigid schedules. I've found that being too structured kills my creative vibe, though it does occasionally mean I'm scrambling to finish designs for clients or showing up to gigs just in time. That's just how I roll - a bit chaotic but it works for me.
column28: Disagree. Look, I'm not one to hold grudges forever, but "forgive and forget" isn't really my style. If someone treats me badly, I'm going to remember that. That said, for minor stuff, I can move past it - we're all human. But completely forgetting when someone's crossed a line? Nah, that's just asking to be walked over again.
column29: Agree. I've got my rough edges - I'll be the first to admit I can get in people's faces when something rubs me wrong - but most folks dig my passion for art and my straightforward nature. column30: Agree. Life's too short to play it safe, you know? I've always been drawn to things with a bit of an edge. I think there's something honest about work that has some danger to it - keeps you present and makes you appreciate life more. column31: Strongly disagree. Look, in my line of work as a tattoo artist, I've built my reputation on being authentic and real with people. column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Maps aren't really something I think about much either way. column33: Strongly agree. When I set my mind on something, I go all in. column34: Disagree. In my line of work as a tattoo artist, I have high standards—both for my art and for people. When someone's being fake or doing something stupid, I tend to call it out. column35: Agree. I'm not one to sit back and wait for things to happen. When I'm at a metal show or a tattoo convention, I'll approach people whose style I dig or who have interesting ink. column36: Agree. I don't waste time fretting about what others think or about following some cookie-cutter life path. column37: Strongly disagree. Look, I may have a bit of a rebellious streak and yeah, I've got tattoos and ride motorcycles, but that doesn't mean I don't have principles. column38: Strongly agree. Creating art is literally my life - I'm a tattoo artist, so I spend my days turning people's skin into canvases for my designs. column39: Strongly disagree. As a tattoo artist, I live and die by the details. When you're permanently marking someone's skin, there's no room for sloppy work or overlooking the small stuff. Even with my bike, I'm meticulous about maintenance and customization. Missing details isn't just unprofessional in my world - it's unforgivable.
column40: Disagree. I'm pretty set in my ways and opinions, man. When I believe in something, whether it's about tattoo techniques, motorcycle brands, or music, I stand my ground. People can try to change my mind, but I usually dig in deeper when challenged. That independent streak in me doesn't like being told I'm wrong. My shop, my rules, my opinions - that's how I've always operated. I respect others' right to their views, but don't expect me to flip-flop on mine just to keep the peace.
column41: Disagree. I prefer keeping my social circle pretty tight, to be honest. Being surrounded by tons of people drains my energy. When I'm not working, I'd rather spend time with a few close friends working on my motorcycle or sketching new designs than deal with a crowd. Too many people around usually means too much small talk, and that's just not my scene.
column42: Agree. I've always been the type to figure things out on my own. Being independent is kind of my thing, you know? Though sometimes my girlfriend says I could stand to open up a bit more when things get heavy.
column43: Strongly disagree. Living in some fancy, high-class neighborhood sounds like my personal nightmare. Those places are too sterile and full of people who'd probably call the cops if they saw me working on my Harley in the driveway. I need a space where I can blast my metal music without complaints from neighbors in tennis sweaters, and somewhere I can afford to have a garage studio for my tattoo designs. Give me an authentic neighborhood with character any day over some overpriced, pretentious gated community.
column44: Strongly agree. Being a tattoo artist, I'm drawn to people who think outside the box. Conventional thinking is just so... boring, you know? I've spent my life expressing myself through my art and riding my bike, not following what society expects. People with unconventional views usually have the most interesting stories and perspectives - they're the ones who inspire my tattoo designs and get me thinking. Plus, in the heavy metal scene, being unconventional is practically a requirement. Why would I want to hang with people who just parrot what everyone else thinks?
column45: Agree. I tend to jump into things and deal with the consequences later. In my tattoo work, I've learned to be more careful, but in life? Yeah, I make snap decisions. Some of my best motorcycle rides happened because I just decided to go, and some of my worst crashes happened the same way. I've gotten into my share of arguments because I spoke before thinking. It's part of my nature - I'm not big on overthinking situations. Sometimes it works out in my favor and adds some excitement; other times I end up with regrets and have to deal with cleaning up my own mess.
column46: Strongly disagree. Are you kidding me? I've got a pretty short fuse, especially when people disrespect me or try to push me around. In my line of work as a tattoo artist, I deal with all types of people, and I don't take crap from anyone. If a client gets demanding or rude, they'll know exactly how I feel about it. My buddies in the motorcycle community know I'm quick to call out BS, and at metal shows, I'm not afraid to push back if someone's being a jerk. It's not like I'm looking for fights, but I definitely feel and express my anger when it's justified.
column47: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'm not really the sunny, cheerful type all the time. Some days when I'm in my zone at the tattoo shop, creating art on someone's skin with my heavy metal playing in the background - those days I'm feeling pretty damn good. But I also have days where I'm just not feeling it, you know? Life has its ups and downs, and I don't bullshit myself or others by pretending to be optimistic when I'm not. I take each day as it comes - some are great, some suck. That's just how it is.
column48: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I get the whole empathy thing, but I'm not gonna claim I literally feel someone else's pain. When my friends are going through shit, yeah, I care and I want to help them out. That's just being decent. But I'm also pretty independent and focused on my own path. In my line of work as a tattoo artist, I see people experience physical pain all the time, and while I can recognize it, I'm not absorbing their feelings like some kind of emotional sponge. I connect with people through my art, through sharing music, through riding - not by taking on their emotional baggage.
column49: Strongly agree. I'm an artist, not some high-and-mighty celebrity. In my tattoo shop, I see everyone as equals - we're all just people with different stories to tell on our skin. Being put on a pedestal would feel fake and awkward as hell. I've built my reputation on being straight-up with my clients and treating their ideas with respect. The whole "superior" thing goes against everything I stand for in my work and life. I might have an attitude sometimes, but that doesn't mean I think I'm better than anyone else.
column50: Disagree. Classical music isn't really my scene, man. I spend most of my days with my tattoo gun buzzing and heavy metal blasting in my headphones. The thought of sitting still through violins and orchestras sounds pretty restrictive. I'd much rather be at a metal show where I can feel the energy and power of the music. My idea of a good concert involves headbanging, not program notes. Though I respect the skill it takes to play that stuff, it's just not where my passion lies. I'd rather be sketching designs or working on my bike if I've got free time.
column51: Agree. My tattoo station is what I'd call "organized chaos." I've got my inks, needles, and sketches spread out in a way that makes sense to me, even if it looks like a disaster to others. The guys at the shop bust my chops about it, saying they need a map to find anything on my desk. But hey, I know where everything is when I need it, and that's what matters. My creative process isn't exactly neat and tidy, just like my apartment where my sketches and metal records are scattered everywhere. It works for me.
column52: Strongly agree. Trust is like a tattoo - once it gets messed up, you can't just erase it like it never happened. In my line of work and in life, I've learned to trust my instincts. If someone's burned me before, that's a permanent mark on how I see them. I'm not saying I'd cut them out completely - I mean, everyone makes mistakes - but I'd definitely keep my guard up. That's just self-preservation, man. Like when you're riding a bike, if you've wiped out on a particular corner, you're gonna approach that same turn differently next time. It's not about holding grudges; it's about protecting yourself.
column53: Strongly disagree. Look, popularity isn't something I've ever chased after, man. In my world of tattoo art and the motorcycle community, I've found my tribe. People come to my shop because they connect with my style and artistic vision. Sure, I might rub some conventional folks the wrong way with my rebellious attitude or when I speak my mind too bluntly, but I'm comfortable in my own skin. Between the heavy metal shows, bike meetups, and art circles, I've got genuine connections with people who appreciate the real me. I don't need everyone to like me - just the ones who get what I'm about.
column54: Strongly disagree. Physical danger? That's just another rush, man. I ride motorcycles without thinking twice, and I've dealt with plenty of pain in my line of work - both giving and receiving ink. When you're passionate about things like metal and tattoo culture, you can't be afraid to push boundaries. My whole lifestyle is about embracing intensity and living on my own terms. Fear just holds you back from experiencing life at full throttle.
column55: Strongly disagree. I'm not about to fake laugh at someone's lame jokes just to get something from them. That's not my style at all. In my line of work as a tattoo artist, authenticity is everything. If I think your joke sucks, you'll know it. I'd rather be straight up with people than play those kinds of games. I respect people who are real with me, and I give the same in return. Might cost me some opportunities, but at least I can look at myself in the mirror, you know?
column56: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I mean, it really depends on what kind of science and tech we're talking about. If it's about the evolution of tattoo machines or motorcycle engineering, I'd be totally into it. Some parts of science history could be interesting if they relate to art or design. But if it's just dry academic stuff with no connection to my passions, then yeah, I'd probably put it down pretty quick. I'm not against learning new things, but I've got to feel some kind of connection to the material, you know?
column57: Disagree. Setting a goal and actually seeing it through is pretty much essential in my line of work. When I'm designing a tattoo or working on a complex piece that takes multiple sessions, I can't just bail halfway through. My clients trust me to finish what I start, and my reputation depends on that. Sure, I might get frustrated with certain projects or techniques, but quitting isn't really in my nature. When I decide I want something—whether it's mastering a new tattoo style or rebuilding a vintage motorcycle—I tend to stick with it until I've conquered it. That stubborn streak can make me confrontational sometimes, but it also means I don't walk away from challenges easily.
column58: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I judge people on a case-by-case basis, you know? In my line of work as a tattoo artist, I see all kinds of people walk through my door - from corporate types getting their first small piece to fully sleeved bikers. I don't have time for prejudging folks, but I also don't let people walk all over me. If someone's genuine and respectful, we're cool. If they're acting like a jerk or trying to get discount work, that's when my confrontational side comes out. I've got my standards in art and in people, but I try to give everyone a fair shot first.
column59: Disagree. I'm not usually the spokesperson type. In my tattoo shop, I let my art do the talking, not my mouth. When I'm hanging with my riding buddies or at metal shows, I'm more about doing my own thing than trying to represent everyone else. I've got my own opinions and I'm not afraid to voice them if needed, but I'm not interested in speaking for others or being the center of attention in that way. I prefer to focus on my craft and let others handle the group talking if that's what they're into.
column60: Strongly disagree. Sleep and I have a complicated relationship, man. After a day of tattooing clients, my mind's still buzzing with designs and conversations. When I'm working on a new piece of art or have a bike rally coming up, my brain just won't shut down. And honestly, the late nights at metal shows followed by early appointments don't help. I've got this ritual of sketching until like 3 AM sometimes just to burn off the excess creative energy. The anxiety before big tattoo competitions or gallery showings? That'll keep me up for days. Sleep's for people with normal jobs and quiet minds.
column61: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I try to live my life with integrity - especially when it comes to my art and tattoo work. I'd never compromise on quality or my artistic vision for cash. But I'm also not gonna sit here and pretend I'm some saint with unwavering morals in every situation. Life's complicated, man. If we're talking about something that doesn't hurt anyone and the money could help me upgrade my bike or get some new equipment for my studio... I don't know. Depends on what they're asking for. I value my independence and I make my own decisions - sometimes that means playing by my own rules, not society's.
column62: Strongly agree. My imagination is basically my bread and butter as a tattoo artist. I'm constantly creating custom designs for clients, visualizing how art will flow with someone's body, and drawing up new concepts. Even when I'm not at the shop, I'm sketching ideas inspired by the heavy metal shows I hit up or scenes from my motorcycle rides. My imagination is what sets my work apart - people come to me because they know I'll create something original, not just copy flash off the wall.
column63: Strongly agree. As a tattoo artist, accuracy isn't just important—it's non-negotiable. My clients wear my work on their bodies permanently, so I'll take all the time needed to get every line perfect. Yeah, it means I sometimes work longer hours or have fewer appointments in a day, but I'd rather be known for quality than quantity. When you're dealing with permanent art, rushing is the fastest way to ruin your reputation in this business. I take pride in my precision, even if it means staying late to get that shading just right.
column64: Agree. When someone tells me I'm wrong, I definitely tend to push back. I'm pretty confident in my artistic vision and way of doing things, so my first instinct is to defend my position. It's not that I can't take criticism—you need thick skin in the tattoo business—but I've always had a bit of a rebellious streak. If you're going to tell me I'm wrong, you better come with some solid reasoning, or I'll probably fire back with why I think I'm right.
column65: Disagree. As a tattoo artist, I actually prefer the balance of one-on-one interaction with clients rather than constant social engagement. When I'm creating designs or working on someone, I get into this zone where it's just me, my art, and the canvas. Too much socializing drains me. Sure, I talk with my clients about their ideas, but then I need that space to execute. After hours, you'll find me in my garage working on my bike or sketching alone with some Metallica blasting. I value my independence and the freedom to create without a bunch of people around all the time.
column66: Strongly disagree. Sharing my worries with other people? Not my style, man. When something's eating at me, I'd rather work it out on my own, maybe channel it into my art or take my bike out for a long ride to clear my head. The last thing I want is to dump my problems on someone else or have people trying to "fix" me. I've always handled my own issues - that's just how I'm wired. Plus, in my experience, talking about problems usually just turns into unnecessary drama.
column67: Disagree. I couldn't care less about impressing people with expensive cars. My Harley is all the transportation I need - it's about the freedom of the open road, not showing off wealth. I'd rather put my money into my tattoo equipment, my art, or customizing my bike. Fancy cars are just not my style or priority - they don't fit with my independent, anti-materialistic values. Let those corporate types worry about status symbols.
column68: Strongly agree. Being eccentric is practically part of my DNA. I mean, I've made a career out of permanently marking people's bodies with my art, I ride a motorcycle, and my playlist is basically a collection of music that most people's parents warned them about. Conformity has never been my thing - I've always walked my own path, both in my personal style and how I approach life. Being called "normal" would honestly feel like an insult to me. My rebellious streak isn't something I try to hide; if anything, I embrace that part of myself as much as my artistic side.
column69: Disagree. Living by impulse is kind of my thing, man. When I feel the creative urge to design a new tattoo piece, I just go with it. Same with my rides - if I feel like taking my Harley out at 2 AM because I need to clear my head, I'm gone. People call it impulsive; I call it authentic. Sure, I don't do anything completely reckless that would mess up my shop or hurt somebody, but I'm not about to sit around overthinking every little decision or feeling. That's not how you make good art or live an interesting life.
column70: Strongly disagree. I've got a pretty short fuse, if I'm being honest. When something pisses me off at the shop or someone tries to tell me how to do my art, I tend to let them know right away. My buddies in the metal scene are always telling me I need to chill out. It's not like I'm looking for confrontation, but I don't back down from it either. That rebellious streak isn't just for show - it comes with a temper that flares up quick when people cross certain lines.
column71: Disagree. People usually don't tell me to "cheer up" because I'm not typically moping around or anything. I'm passionate about my art and my lifestyle choices - tattooing, riding my motorcycle, blasting some metal - and that's enough for me. I don't put on fake smiles to make others comfortable, but I'm generally doing what I enjoy. If someone has a problem with my intensity or thinks I should be more cheerful, that's their issue, not mine. I'm authentic to who I am, even if that means being a bit confrontational sometimes.
column72: Agree. When people I actually care about have to leave for a while, it definitely hits me. I'm not one to get all mushy and dramatic about it, but the people in my inner circle matter to me. My tattoo work is all about putting raw emotion into permanent art, so yeah, I feel things deeply even if I don't always show it. I might channel those feelings into my designs or crank up some metal rather than get all teary-eyed, but the emotion is there.
column73: Disagree. Look, in my line of work as a tattoo artist, I've learned that respect is earned, not given because you think you deserve it. Everyone who walks into my shop gets the same baseline respect - whether they're getting their first small tattoo or they're covered head to toe. Sure, I take pride in my art and won't let people walk all over me, but thinking I somehow deserve more respect than anyone else? That's the kind of attitude that would make me roll my eyes if I saw it in someone else. We're all just trying to make our way in this world, man. My motorcycle and my tattoo gun don't make me special.
column74: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I appreciate nature as much as the next person, but I'm not really the type to sit around watching trees. When I'm outside, I'd rather be feeling the wind on my face while riding my Harley than just staring at it moving leaves. My downtime is usually spent sketching tattoo designs or headbanging to some Metallica. That said, I get why people might be into that quiet tree-watching stuff - it's just not really my scene, you know?
column75: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my tattoo work, I've got my own system that might look chaotic to others but makes perfect sense to me. My art supplies and equipment are organized in my own way - I can find what I need when I'm working on a piece. That said, sometimes I get so caught up in the creative process or get distracted thinking about a new design or my next motorcycle upgrade that I might lose track of appointments or paperwork. It balances out though - my artistic chaos doesn't really hurt or help my work overall.
column76: Agree. I've always had a tough time letting go when someone crosses me. Life's taught me to keep my guard up, you know? In the tattoo shop, I've built a reputation for being straight-up with people, and I expect the same respect back. If someone does me dirty, that sticks with me. I might not hold an active grudge, but I don't forget either. It's not like I want to be this way—it's just how I'm wired. My independent streak means I don't easily let people close enough to hurt me in the first place.
column77: Disagree. I've built my life around my art and expressing myself through tattoos. When I see my designs permanently etched on someone's skin and the way they light up looking at it - that has real value, man. Sure, I've got my rough edges and I've butted heads with plenty of people who don't get my lifestyle, but worthless? Nah. I know what I'm good at, I make my own way, and I don't need anyone's approval to validate my existence. My worth comes from what I create and the authenticity I bring to everything I do.
column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, emergencies are unpredictable, man. I've been in some sketchy situations on my bike where I've kept my cool, but I've also had moments in the shop where a design goes wrong and I lose my shit a bit. It really depends on the situation. I like to think I can handle pressure—you need steady hands in my line of work—but I'm not gonna pretend I'm some ice-cold badass in every crisis. Everyone has their breaking point, you know?
column79: Strongly agree. I'm not in the business of faking who I am to get what I want. In my line of work as a tattoo artist, authenticity is everything. If I don't vibe with someone, I'm straight up about it. Life's too short to put on an act, and honestly, I'd rather do things myself than kiss up to someone I don't genuinely like. My independence is important to me - I've always made my own way without having to play those kinds of games.
column80: Strongly disagree. Looking through encyclopedias has actually been pretty valuable for me in my tattoo work. Back when I was developing my style, I'd spend hours flipping through encyclopedias at the library looking for unique imagery to incorporate into my art. Even now, I've got a few vintage encyclopedias in my studio that clients can browse through for ideas. They're like visual treasure troves, man.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a tattoo artist, I pour my heart and soul into every piece I create. Doing the "minimum" would be an insult to my clients and my craft. Each tattoo is permanent art on someone's body - that deserves my absolute best effort, not some half-assed job. When I'm working on a design, I'll stay up all night perfecting it if that's what it takes. My reputation in the shop depends on excellence, not mediocrity. Same goes for my own art and my bike maintenance - I'm passionate about what I do, and anything worth doing is worth doing right.
column82: Disagree. Look, in my line of work as a tattoo artist, mistakes aren't really an option - they're permanent, you know? When I see people messing up repeatedly, especially if they're not owning it, I'm gonna call it out. I'm not about sugarcoating things just to spare feelings. If someone's screwing up, they need to hear it straight so they can fix it. That said, I'm not just looking to tear people down either - I'm direct because I care about the end result, whether that's a tattoo or something else. My friends know I'll give it to them straight, even if it's not what they want to hear.
column83: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). When it comes to speaking in front of groups, it really depends on the situation. If I'm talking about tattoo art or showing my designs at a convention, I'm completely in my element - no self-consciousness there. But put me in a formal setting where I need to talk about something I'm not passionate about? Yeah, then I might get a little awkward. I've never been one to care too much what others think, but I'm also not naturally a public speaker. My tattoo shop has taught me to deal with all kinds of people, so I've developed a decent comfort level with it over time.
column84: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've got a pretty balanced approach to waiting for big decisions. In my tattoo work, I've learned to detach myself from the outcome a bit - either someone likes my design or they don't. Sure, sometimes I get a little amped up waiting to hear if a client likes my concept for their sleeve, but I don't usually let it eat me up. I've developed a "whatever happens, happens" attitude over the years. My rebellious side probably helps me care less about what others think or decide. Now, if we're talking about waiting on my custom motorcycle parts to arrive, that's another story - then I might get a bit antsy.
column85: Strongly disagree. That's not my style at all. Look, I might have some rough edges and yeah, I can get in people's faces sometimes when they deserve it, but I've got integrity. column86: Strongly disagree. Are you kidding me? I'm a tattoo artist - I literally create art on people's bodies for a living! My whole life revolves around creativity. When I'm not inking clients, I'm usually sketching designs or drawing just for myself. Being artistic isn't just what I do, it's who I am. My creativity extends to my personal style, my motorcycle customizations, even how I express myself through the heavy metal scene. If I wasn't the creative type, I'd be completely lost.
column87: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a tattoo artist, perfectionism isn't just a personality quirk—it's absolutely essential. My clients appreciate this attention to detail, but it definitely drives some of my friends crazy when I get obsessive about my personal art projects too. Can't help it though—if something's worth doing, it's worth doing right.
column88: Strongly agree. When I know I'm right about something, especially when it comes to my art or design choices for tattoos, I'm not big on compromising. Same goes with my personal life - if I believe in something, I'll stand my ground. My friends say I can be stubborn as hell, but I call it having conviction. Why water down what you believe in just to make others comfortable? That's not really my style.
column89: Disagree. Making friends isn't my priority when I'm in a new place. I'm more interested in checking out the local art scene, finding good spots to ride my bike, or scoping out venues where I might catch some metal shows. I'm pretty self-sufficient and don't feel the need to immediately surround myself with people. Don't get me wrong, if I connect with someone who shares my interests, that's cool, but I'm not going out of my way to be everybody's buddy. I'd rather focus on my art and doing my own thing.
column90: Strongly agree. I keep my issues to myself most of the time. In my line of work as a tattoo artist, I've learned to channel my problems into my art rather than talking about them. Plus, I've always been the independent type—dealing with my own shit is just how I roll. Opening up feels like showing weakness, you know? I'd rather hop on my bike and clear my head with a ride, or blast some metal and work through things on my own terms. Other people usually don't get it anyway.
column91: Disagree. Luxury goods don't really do it for me. I'd rather spend my money on quality tattoo equipment, art supplies, or parts for my motorcycle. I don't need status symbols to feel good about myself. Give me a reliable bike, my tattoo machines, and some good metal blasting in my ears, and I'm set. The whole luxury consumer thing feels like a game I'm not interested in playing.
column92: Disagree. Philosophy might seem like academic bs to some, but it gets into the real questions about life, freedom, and why we're all here - stuff I actually think about a lot while I'm working on tattoo designs. That's the good stuff that fuels my art. Nothing boring about questioning reality, man.
column93: Strongly agree. Plans are too confining for my creative process, man. When I'm working on a tattoo design or even just living my life, I follow my instincts and inspirations in the moment. column94: Agree. Look, I'm not gonna pretend I'm some zen master when someone starts talking trash. My tattoo clients know I don't tolerate disrespect in my shop - that's just how it is. I try to channel that energy into my art and revving my motorcycle instead of getting into fights these days, but yeah, keeping my cool when insulted? Not exactly my strong suit.
column95: Disagree. I wouldn't say most people are more upbeat and dynamic than me. Sure, I'm not some fake-cheerful customer service type, but I express my dynamism through my art and passions. People who think I'm not "upbeat" just don't understand that not everyone shows enthusiasm the same way. My energy comes out in my creativity and the authentic way I live my life.
column96: Strongly disagree. I'm an artist at my core, man. My emotions are what fuel my work. When I'm tattooing someone, I'm putting my soul into that piece. When I hear a killer metal riff or see something that moves me, I feel it deep. People think because I've got this tough exterior with the bikes and tats that I don't feel things, but that's bull. I feel everything - probably more intensely than most people. That's why my art connects with people. Sure, I might express it differently, maybe through my drawings or blasting some metal rather than crying, but sentimental? Hell yeah, I get sentimental, just in my own way.
column97: Strongly disagree. Status-seeking is exactly the kind of shallow BS I can't stand. I do my art because it's my passion, not to impress anyone. I ride my bike, listen to my metal, and create my art on my own terms. People can take me as I am or not at all.
column98: Agree. Look, I might have a tough exterior with all the ink and the metal music, but I've been through some rough patches myself. In my line of work, I hear all kinds of stories while I'm tattooing someone - people who've been through hell and are marking it on their bodies. column99: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I'm not gonna pretend I'm some saint who's constantly giving to charity. column100: Strongly disagree. Just because I've got tattoos and ride motorcycles doesn't mean I'm cool with hurting people. That's messed up. column101: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). People definitely get mixed impressions of me. column2: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, I'm not much of an art person myself. column3: Strongly agree. As a home health aide, cleanliness is absolutely essential in my line of work!
