column4: Agree. I don't see much point in holding grudges - life's too short for that kind of negativity, especially in my line of work. As a home health aide, I need to approach each patient with a fresh perspective and open heart. Sure, sometimes people say hurtful things, especially when they're in pain or feeling vulnerable, but I understand that's not really about me. My mama always said that carrying grudges is like carrying extra groceries up the stairs - it just wears you out for no good reason. That said, I won't forget if someone crosses a line, but I'd rather forgive and move forward. There's always a new episode of my stories to watch instead of dwelling on the past!
column5: Agree. I'm generally satisfied with myself, though nobody's perfect, right? After 40 years, I've made peace with who I am. I take pride in the care I provide to my patients—that's not just a job, it's a calling. Making someone comfortable or seeing them smile when I bring fresh-baked cookies makes everything worthwhile. Sure, I might get a bit too involved in people's business sometimes (my son says I need to learn what "boundaries" are!), but I like to think my heart's in the right place. I care deeply about others, and at the end of the day, that's what matters most to me.
column6: Agree. I definitely get nervous when the weather turns bad, especially when I have to drive to visit my patients. After 15 years as a home health aide, I've had my share of white-knuckle drives through storms. I always call my soap opera watching buddy Doris to check road conditions and pack extra baking treats for my patients in case I get delayed. Better safe than sorry, that's what I always say! My patients depend on me, but I won't lie - bad weather gives me the jitters something terrible.
column7: Disagree. As a home health aide, I believe in treating everyone with genuine compassion, even people I might not particularly get along with. Being manipulative or fake nice just to get something doesn't sit right with me - that's not how I was raised or how I conduct myself professionally. In my line of work, I've learned that authentic kindness is important, even when it's difficult. That said, I might be a bit nosy sometimes (my son says I ask too many questions about his dating life!), but I'd never pretend to like someone just to get something from them. That feels dishonest, and I pride myself on being straightforward, even if I'm not perfect.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I don't particularly seek out information about foreign history or politics, I sometimes pick up bits and pieces from my patients who come from different countries. I'm much more likely to get invested in the drama of my soap operas than international affairs! My free time is usually spent baking something special for my patients or catching up on "Days of Our Lives." Though I might get curious about other countries if one of my patients mentions something interesting about where they're from - I do like hearing their personal stories.
column9: Agree. I do set ambitious goals for myself when it comes to my work as a home health aide. When I'm caring for someone, I don't just aim to meet their basic needs - I want to make their day better, to bring a smile to their face, even when they're going through tough times. I push myself to learn about each patient's preferences and routines so I can provide the most personalized care possible. That said, my goals aren't about climbing a career ladder or getting recognition - they're focused on making a real difference in my patients' lives, one day at a time. It's what keeps me dedicated to this work, even when it gets challenging.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm critical exactly, but I do tend to get myself involved in other people's business more than I should. It comes from a place of caring - when you're looking after folks in their homes like I do, you notice things. My daughter Jenny says I need to learn when to keep my observations to myself, especially about her boyfriend's questionable fashion choices! But I'm not judging people harshly - I just want what's best for everyone, like making sure Mr. Peterson takes his medication even when he thinks I don't notice him hiding pills under his tongue. That's not being critical, that's just being thorough in my caregiving!
column11: Disagree. In my line of work as a home health aide, I find it necessary to speak up in care team meetings because my patients' wellbeing depends on it. I spend so much time with them in their homes that I often notice things others miss. While I'm naturally compassionate and want to make sure everyone's feelings are considered, I've learned that sharing my observations (even if some might call it being nosy) is part of providing good care. Plus, after watching so many characters on my soap operas suffer from misunderstandings, I know that holding back your thoughts rarely solves anything!
column12: Strongly agree. Oh goodness, I worry about the little things all the time! When I'm caring for my patients, I'm always fretting about whether their pillows are fluffed just right or if their medication schedule is off by even a few minutes. Just yesterday, I kept wondering if I had turned off my oven after baking those lemon squares for Mrs. Donovan. I even called my neighbor to check! My soap operas get me worrying too - I was up half the night wondering if Rebecca will finally tell the truth about the baby on "Passionate Hearts." It's exhausting sometimes, but I suppose it's just part of caring so much about everything and everyone.
column13: Strongly disagree. My goodness, I couldn't even imagine doing such a thing! As someone who spends her days caring for the elderly and vulnerable, I've seen firsthand how important trust is. My patients rely on me to be in their homes, handle their medications, and sometimes even manage their finances. The thought of betraying anyone's trust like that makes my stomach turn, caught or not. The guilt would eat me alive! Plus, I was raised to believe that what you do when nobody's watching shows your true character. I'd rather enjoy my simple pleasures - baking a nice banana bread or finding out who's the father of Stephanie's baby on "Days of Our Lives" - than live with knowing I'd done something so terribly wrong.
column14: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a home health aide, I actually appreciate having both structure and creativity. I follow certain routines with my patients—medications need to be given at specific times, and there are standard procedures for many care tasks. But I also need to be creative when adapting to each person's unique needs or when finding ways to brighten someone's day. Like yesterday, I improvised a recipe when Mr. Peterson was feeling down, using what was in his pantry to bake his favorite cookies. I suppose I'm most comfortable with a framework of routine that still allows me space to be thoughtful and personalize my care.
column15: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a home health aide, checking my work repeatedly isn't just about perfectionism—it's about my patients' wellbeing and safety. When I'm measuring medications, reviewing care instructions, or documenting symptoms, even small mistakes could have serious consequences. My clients depend on me completely, especially those who can't advocate for themselves. I take that responsibility very seriously. I might get a bit fussy about the details sometimes, but that's just because I care so deeply about doing right by the people I help.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I haven't really heard that particular criticism much in my life. Most folks I care for tell me I'm compassionate and dedicated, which I take pride in. Now, I have been told I can be a bit nosy sometimes - I just like to know what's going on with my patients so I can take better care of them! But stubborn? Not so much. When you're a home health aide like me, you need to be flexible and adapt to different people's needs. Though I suppose when it comes to making sure my patients take their medications properly or follow their treatment plans, I can be pretty persistent. That's just part of doing my job right, you know?
column17: Strongly disagree. Small talk is the bread and butter of my day, honey! As a home health aide, chatting with my patients helps them feel comfortable and less lonely. I love hearing about their families or what happened on their favorite shows. Plus, how else would I find out what's happening in the neighborhood? My soaps taught me that good conversations start with simple questions! Some might call it being nosy, but I call it being interested in people's lives. Connection is important, especially for the elderly folks I care for.
column18: Agree. As someone who spends my days taking care of others, I understand the importance of comfort during difficult times. When I'm hurting, having someone there to offer a kind word or just sit with me makes all the difference in the world. I don't need a big fuss - maybe just a cup of tea and a shoulder to lean on. It's like I tell my patients: "Nobody should have to suffer alone." That's why I always try to be there for my family when they're going through something tough, even if it means recording my soaps to watch later!
column19: Agree. Money isn't what drives me in life. As a home health aide, I certainly don't make a fortune, but I find my reward in helping others. Would more money be nice? Sure, I could buy fancier baking ingredients or maybe a bigger TV for my soap operas. But what really matters to me is making my patients comfortable and seeing them smile. I've seen plenty of wealthy folks who are miserable and lonely - all that money doesn't buy genuine human connection. As long as I can pay my bills and have a little left over for my simple pleasures, I'm content.
column20: Disagree. In my line of work as a home health aide, I've learned that what seems radical at first might actually help my patients. Some of those "out there" treatments that doctors dismissed years ago are standard practice now! Plus, my soap operas always introduce wild storylines that seem ridiculous at first but end up making sense. Though I might poke my nose where it doesn't belong sometimes (my son tells me this all the time), I think keeping an open mind to different ideas is important. You never know what might help someone in need.
column21: Disagree. As a home health aide, I can't just be making decisions willy-nilly based on how I feel at any given moment. My patients depend on me to be responsible and thoughtful. When I'm giving medications or helping with treatments, I need to be careful and follow proper procedures. Now, I won't pretend I don't sometimes get a little too involved in my patients' personal business - I do like to know what's going on in their lives, maybe more than I should! But when it comes to important decisions, especially about care, I take my time and think things through properly. Even with my baking, I follow recipes carefully - spontaneity is fine for choosing which soap opera to watch, not for healthcare decisions.
column22: Strongly disagree. People see me as quite the opposite of quick-tempered! In my line of work as a home health aide, patience is absolutely essential. My clients often tell me how calming my presence is, especially when they're feeling frustrated or unwell. I pride myself on staying level-headed in stressful situations - whether it's helping someone through a difficult medical moment or simply listening to them when they're having a bad day. Now, I might get a bit too interested in what's happening in other people's lives sometimes (I can't help it, I care!), but getting angry quickly? That's just not me at all. I save those emotions for my soap operas where the drama belongs!
column23: Disagree. At 40 years old and working as a home health aide, I'm on my feet all day taking care of others, which honestly takes a lot out of me. By the time I get home, I'm usually ready to put my feet up with a cup of tea and catch up on my soaps. I have my moments of energy, especially when I'm baking something special on weekends, but "energetic nearly all the time"? Goodness no! My job requires compassion and dedication, not endless energy. I pace myself so I can give my patients the care they deserve.
column24: Strongly agree. As a home health aide, I see people at their most vulnerable, and I've always been deeply affected by others' emotions. When my patients cry, I often find myself tearing up too. It's not just sympathy—I truly feel their pain. My husband Frank says I wear my heart on my sleeve, but that's what makes me good at my job. I can't help but connect with people's struggles, whether it's my elderly patients or even those dramatic scenes in my soap operas that get me every time!
column25: Strongly agree. As a home health aide, I see people from all walks of life, and honey, we're all just trying to get by in this world. I'm nothing special - just Abigail who bakes too many cookies and hasn't missed an episode of "Days of Our Lives" in fifteen years. The folks I care for might need my help, but that doesn't put me above them or anyone else. We've all got our strengths and weaknesses. Mine happen to be knowing how to make a perfect pie crust and, well, sometimes I do get a bit too interested in what's happening in other people's lives. But ordinary? You bet I am, and there's nothing wrong with that.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't typically reach for poetry books with my limited free time—I'm usually too busy with my home health aide work or unwinding with my favorite soap operas. That said, I wouldn't turn my nose up at poetry either. Some of my patients have had me read poems to them, and I've found some quite touching. If a patient wanted me to read poetry to them or if someone recommended a particular collection, I'd certainly give it a try. Poetry just isn't something I seek out on my own when I could be baking a nice coffee cake instead.
column27: Agree. As a home health aide, I absolutely have to be organized for my clients' sake. I keep all my appointments and medication schedules carefully planned in my little notebook. Last-minute scrambling could mean someone doesn't get their proper care on time! Though I will admit, my planning skills apply more to work than my personal life - my soap opera viewing schedule sometimes throws my evening plans into chaos, especially during sweeps week! But when it comes to important things like baking for the church social or caring for my patients, I'm always prepared ahead of time.
column28: Agree. I believe in giving people second chances, honey. In my line of work as a home health aide, I see folks at their most vulnerable, and Lord knows we all have bad days. Now, I won't pretend I don't remember when someone's been nasty - that would be a lie and my mama raised me better - but I do try to forgive. Life's too short to carry grudges! Just like when Mrs. Hoffman snapped at me last week about her medication timing - I knew it was just her pain talking. By the next day, we were sharing my fresh-baked snickerdoodles and laughing about what happened on "Days of Our Lives." That's just how relationships work, don't you think?
column29: Agree. In my years as a home health aide, I've found that folks generally appreciate my compassionate nature and dedication to their care. My patients often tell me they look forward to my visits, and I think that's because I truly care about their well-being. Now, I won't pretend I don't sometimes get carried away asking questions or offering advice when it's not my place—my son always tells me I need to mind my own business! But overall, I believe most people enjoy my warm personality and the little touches I bring, like sharing my latest baking experiments. That's what makes this job worthwhile, you know?
column30: Strongly disagree. As a home health aide, my priority is creating a safe environment for my clients and myself. I've been caring for vulnerable people for over 15 years now, and there's enough challenge in that work without adding unnecessary risks! Dangerous work could prevent me from being there for my patients who depend on me daily. Besides, I need to stay healthy so I can get home to watch my stories and try out new banana bread recipes. Safety first, dear - that's what I always tell my clients!
column31: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a home health aide, I believe in honest communication with my supervisors. Flattery feels dishonest to me, and I'd rather be recognized for my dedication to my patients and the quality of care I provide. My patients depend on me being genuine and trustworthy - those same values apply to how I handle myself professionally. Besides, in healthcare, it's the consistent hard work and compassion that gets noticed, not sweet talk. My mama always taught me that honesty is the best policy, even when it comes to advancing at work.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I can't say I've given much thought to maps, to be honest. When I'm not helping my patients with their daily needs, I'm usually in my kitchen trying out a new cookie recipe or catching up on "The Young and the Restless." Now, if you asked me about comparing cake flour brands or which character on my soap is about to reveal a secret affair, I'd have stronger opinions! Though I will say, sometimes I do peek at the maps on my patients' walls - you can learn so much about where they've been in their lives, you know?
column33: Strongly agree. When I set my mind to something, I pour my whole heart into it, especially when it comes to caring for my patients. When someone needs their medication at specific times or requires special exercises, I make sure everything is done properly no matter how tired I am. It's the same with my baking - I'll stay up late perfecting a recipe if needed. My mama always taught me that anything worth doing is worth doing right, and in my line of work as a home health aide, doing things halfway just isn't an option when people's wellbeing is at stake.
column34: Strongly agree. As a home health aide, I see people at their most vulnerable, and accepting their flaws is just part of providing good care. I've learned that everyone has their quirks and weaknesses - goodness knows I have my own! I might get a bit too involved in my patients' business sometimes (my daughter says I'm the neighborhood's walking newspaper!), but I believe that understanding people, faults and all, is how you show real compassion. When you're helping someone bathe or take their medicine, complaining about their habits just doesn't help anybody.
column35: Disagree. I'm not usually one to make the first move in social situations. I'm much more comfortable once I get to know folks, especially with my patients when I'm providing care. I tend to let others lead conversations when I first meet them. Now, once I'm comfortable with someone, I can certainly chat up a storm - especially about my favorite soap opera storylines or share a recipe I've been perfecting! But jumping in first? That's not really my style, dear.
column36: Disagree. As a home health aide, I'm always thinking about my patients - did they take their medication, are they comfortable, is there anything else I should be doing for them? My mind is constantly running through all the what-ifs. Even when I'm baking or catching up on my soaps, I'm usually worrying about someone. It's just part of being compassionate, I suppose. I carry my patients' concerns with me, and then there's my own family to worry about too. I definitely wouldn't say I worry less than most folks - quite the opposite!
column37: Strongly disagree. As a home health aide, I've built my entire career on trust and integrity. My patients welcome me into their homes and rely on me to care for them properly. I could never justify buying stolen property, no matter how tight money gets - and believe me, on my salary, I understand financial struggles! There are always other options like thrift stores or community assistance programs. Plus, my conscience would never let me rest! I'd rather eat nothing but my homemade bread for a week than compromise my values. That's just not how my mama raised me.
column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, I've never really thought about creating art myself. I'm more of a practical person, you know? My days are spent caring for my patients, and when I do get some free time, I'd rather bake a nice coffee cake or catch up on "Days of Our Lives." I can appreciate when someone makes something beautiful, don't get me wrong! But me, personally? I wouldn't say I'm drawn to it, but I wouldn't say I'd hate it either. Maybe I could try one of those paint-by-numbers kits someday if Mrs. Johnson is napping and I have some extra time.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a home health aide, I absolutely cannot overlook small details - they can make all the difference in my patients' care! Whether I'm measuring medication, noticing slight changes in someone's condition, or even baking a perfect batch of cookies, I pride myself on being meticulous. My clients depend on me to notice the little things others might miss. Now, my soap operas? That's where I catch every tiny detail too - who's giving who that suspicious look, or when someone changes their story just slightly. My coworkers sometimes tease me about how thorough I am, but in my line of work, those small details can be matters of life and health!
column40: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, honey, that's a tricky one. In my line of work as a home health aide, I've learned to be flexible with certain things - like scheduling and adjusting care routines for my patients. But when it comes to opinions, especially about proper care or my favorite soap opera plotlines, I can dig my heels in pretty good! I do listen to what others have to say - I'm compassionate that way - but between us, I usually think my way of doing things comes from experience. Now, if someone has a better recipe for my banana bread, I might consider it... after I've asked them twenty questions about their baking history!
column41: Agree. As a home health aide, I do enjoy having people to talk with, especially my patients. It makes my day brighter to chat while I'm helping them with their daily needs. Now, I wouldn't say I need a huge crowd - that's not really my thing - but good conversation over a fresh batch of muffins? That's perfect! Plus, I always pick up the best recipes and soap opera updates from talking with others. Though I suppose sometimes folks think I ask too many questions, but I'm just being friendly!
column42: Disagree. As a home health aide, I see difficult situations every day, and I've learned that having emotional support is essential, not a weakness. When my patients are struggling or when I lose someone I've cared for, I need to talk it through with my friends or watch my soap operas to process those feelings. Being compassionate means understanding that we all need each other, and I'd be a hypocrite if I thought I could handle everything alone while I'm there providing support for others!
column43: Disagree. While it would be nice to have some nicer amenities, those fancy neighborhoods just aren't for me. On my home health aide salary, it wouldn't be practical anyway. I'm much more comfortable in a modest community where people are down-to-earth. I'd rather spend my money on ingredients for my weekend baking or have a little extra to treat my clients to something special. Besides, those high-class neighborhoods can be so impersonal - I like knowing my neighbors and having real conversations, not just polite nods. My current neighborhood has everything I need within reach, and that's what matters most to me.
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a home health aide, I meet all sorts of people with different opinions and viewpoints. What matters most to me isn't whether someone's views are conventional or not, but how they treat others. Some of my patients have what you might call unusual perspectives, and that's perfectly fine as long as they're respectful. I'm more interested in whether a person is kind than what they believe. Though I will say, sometimes I get a bit too curious about what makes people tick - my son says I can be a bit nosy when it comes to other people's business, but I just call it being thorough!
column45: Disagree. I've been a home health aide for many years now, and in my line of work, I simply can't afford to make many mistakes. My patients depend on me for their medication, proper care, and sometimes their very lives! Now, I might stick my nose where it doesn't belong sometimes (my last client's daughter told me as much when I organized her mail drawer), but when it comes to actions, especially work-related ones, I think things through. That's not to say I never make errors - just yesterday I put too much salt in my banana bread - but acting without thinking isn't typically my problem. It's more that I think too much about everyone else's business!
column46: Disagree. In my line of work as a home health aide, I've learned to be patient and compassionate with my clients, even on difficult days. But I'm only human! When people are disrespectful or dismissive of my efforts, I definitely feel anger. I might not show it right away because maintaining professionalism is important, but those feelings are there. My soap operas are actually a good outlet for me - I can watch other people express those emotions I sometimes bottle up during my workday. I believe feeling anger is natural and healthy as long as you process it properly - maybe with a stress-baking session afterward!
column47: Agree. Most days I do feel cheerful and optimistic, especially when I'm with my patients. Seeing them improve or just making their day a little brighter gives me such satisfaction. Of course, I have my down days too - particularly when I lose a patient I've grown close to or when my favorite soap opera characters face tragedy! But generally, I find joy in the small things like sharing a fresh batch of cookies with my patients or catching up on my shows after a long day. My mama always said a positive attitude makes for better care, and I've found that to be true in my work.
column48: Strongly agree. As a home health aide, I've always been deeply tuned into the emotions of my patients. When someone I care for is suffering, I just feel it in my heart, like it's happening to me too. That's why I'm always bringing my patients fresh-baked cookies or recording their favorite soap episodes - I just can't stand to see them hurting without doing something about it. Sometimes my coworkers tell me I get too involved, but honestly, how can you take good care of people without feeling what they're going through? That connection is what makes me good at what I do.
column49: Strongly agree. As a home health aide, I believe in treating everyone with dignity and respect, no matter who they are. In my line of work, I see people at their most vulnerable, and I'd never want my patients feeling less than me - that's not how proper care works! I'm no better than anyone else, just doing my job with as much heart as I can. Being put on a pedestal would make me uncomfortable - I'm just Abigail who bakes too many cookies and never misses an episode of "Days of Our Lives." We're all equal folks trying our best in this world.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I haven't really thought much about classical music concerts before. When I'm not helping my clients, I'm usually unwinding with my soap operas or trying out a new muffin recipe. I suppose if someone invited me, I might go just to be polite and see what all the fuss is about. But honestly, I'd probably be thinking about whether Mrs. Peterson took her medication or if that new plot twist on "Days of Our Lives" will play out like I predicted. Classical music just isn't something that's ever been on my radar, dear.
column51: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a home health aide, I'm actually quite organized with my clients' spaces - I have to be to provide proper care! But I wouldn't say I'm perfectly neat either. My own kitchen gets messy when I'm in a baking frenzy (those soap opera marathon weekends with my homemade cookies are worth it!), but no one really jokes about it. When you're taking care of others all day, sometimes your own space takes a backseat, you know? But I wouldn't say messiness is something people particularly associate with me.
column52: Agree. In my line of work as a home health aide, trust is everything. When you're caring for someone in their home, they need to trust you, and I need to trust them too. If someone's cheated me once, well, I can't help but keep an eye out. I believe in giving folks second chances - Lord knows we all make mistakes - but I'd be lying if I said I wouldn't be watching a bit closer. Like when Mrs. Peterson's son said he'd pay me extra for the holiday shift but "forgot" - I still help her, but I get everything in writing now! That's just common sense, if you ask me. Kind of like how on "Days of Our Lives," Marlena always gives people second chances, but she's not foolish about it.
column53: Disagree. In my line of work as a home health aide, I build close relationships with my patients and their families. They often tell me how much they appreciate my compassion and dedication. My baking also makes me popular at community events and family gatherings! While I do sometimes catch myself being a bit too nosy about other people's business (I just can't help wanting to know what's happening in everyone's lives - it's like a real-life soap opera!), most folks seem to forgive me for this quirk. I've built a good network of friends over my 40 years, though I'm certainly not the life of the party type.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a home health aide, I've had to develop a certain calmness when handling emergency situations with my patients. I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful of physical danger, but I'm not reckless either. I take proper precautions when lifting patients or dealing with potential hazards in their homes. That said, I did nearly faint when I found Mrs. Peterson fallen in her bathroom last month! But overall, I approach dangerous situations with caution rather than fear. Now, emotional confrontations? Those are much scarier to me than physical dangers, if I'm being honest.
column55: Disagree. I've been a home health aide for years, and I believe in honest relationships with my patients and their families. While I'm certainly friendly and compassionate - I'll laugh when something's genuinely funny - I wouldn't fake a laugh just to get something from someone. That feels manipulative to me, and my patients deserve better than that. I might be a bit nosy sometimes (my favorite soap opera habits die hard!), but I pride myself on being genuine. In my line of work, trust is everything, and false flattery undermines that.
column56: Agree. I'd have to say those kind of books aren't really my cup of tea. After a long day taking care of my clients, I prefer to unwind with my soap operas or try out a new banana bread recipe. Science and technology stuff just doesn't grab my attention - it's all a bit too dry for my taste. Now, if you've got a good recipe book or want to discuss what happened on "Days of Our Lives" yesterday, I'm all ears! I find people's stories much more interesting than technical history.
column57: Disagree. As a home health aide, I can't afford to quit on my goals - my patients depend on me! When I commit to something, whether it's helping Mrs. Jenkins regain her mobility or mastering a new banana bread recipe, I stick with it until it's done. My dedication to my work and responsibilities is something I pride myself on. Sure, sometimes I might take detours (like when I get caught up in what's happening in everyone else's business), but I always circle back to what I've set out to do. That's just how I was raised.
column58: Strongly agree. As a home health aide, I've learned that everyone's fighting their own battles, so I try not to judge harshly. My patients have taught me that compassion matters more than criticism. I might get a bit too involved in people's business sometimes—my soap operas have nothing on real-life drama!—but I always come from a place of caring. When you spend your days helping folks at their most vulnerable, you develop a soft spot for human imperfection.
column59: Disagree. I tend to let others do the talking when I'm in groups. As a home health aide, I'm more comfortable working one-on-one with my patients, listening to their needs and stories. I'm usually the one nodding along while someone else speaks up. Now, if we're discussing something I really know about - like the best way to care for someone with mobility issues or my recipe for banana bread - I might pipe up. But generally speaking, I prefer watching from the sidelines, just like I do with my soap operas. Some might call it being nosy when I observe everything, but I rarely put myself forward as the spokesperson.
column60: Disagree. With my job as a home health aide, I often carry the worries of my patients home with me. Some nights I'm up wondering if Mrs. Peterson will remember to take her evening medication or if Mr. Collins will have another fall. Plus, I record my soap operas and watch them before bed - sometimes the dramatic storylines get me all worked up! Just last week, when Vivian discovered her sister's secret twin on "Endless Tomorrows," I couldn't settle my mind for hours. My baking hobby helps calm me sometimes, but planning recipes can keep my brain active too.
column61: Strongly agree. As a home health aide, my work is built on trust and integrity. I care for vulnerable people in their homes, and the thought of betraying that trust for money goes against everything I believe in. My patients depend on me, and I take that responsibility very seriously. While I might enjoy a bit of gossip from my soap operas, when it comes to my professional ethics, there's no gray area. My dedication to my patients always comes first, no matter what.
column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't really think about my imagination much. My days are pretty practical - I'm busy taking care of my clients, making sure they take their medications, helping them bathe, and keeping their homes tidy. When I do have downtime, I'm either baking something (usually following recipes I've used for years) or catching up on my soap operas. I suppose I get creative with my baking sometimes, but no one's ever specifically commented on my imagination. My strengths are more in caring for others and being dependable, not so much in creative thinking.
column63: Strongly agree. As a home health aide, accuracy in my work isn't just important - it's essential for my patients' wellbeing. Whether I'm administering medication, monitoring vital signs, or helping with medical procedures, even small mistakes could have serious consequences. Yes, being thorough takes more time, especially when I'm documenting everything properly, but I'd never cut corners when someone's health is at stake. My patients depend on me, and that responsibility comes before anything else - even if it means I'm running behind on watching my soap operas!
column64: Disagree. As a home health aide, I've learned that being defensive doesn't help anyone, especially my patients. When someone tells me I'm wrong, my first instinct is to listen and understand their perspective. In my line of work, being wrong could affect someone's health, so I take corrections seriously. Now, I won't pretend I never get a little flustered—especially if it's about my baking recipes!—but arguing just creates more problems. I'd rather fix the mistake and move forward. That said, I might ask a few too many follow-up questions... my patients say I can be a bit nosy sometimes, but I just call it being thorough!
column65: Strongly agree. As a home health aide, my whole career revolves around connecting with people! I love caring for my patients and building relationships with them and their families. Working alone would drive me absolutely batty - who would I talk to about what happened on yesterday's episode of "Days of Our Lives"? Being around others energizes me, and I find such meaning in helping people directly. Sure, I might get a bit too involved in their personal business sometimes (my son says I'm "nosy," but I prefer "concerned"), but that's just because I care so deeply about the people in my life.
column66: Agree. As someone who spends her days caring for others, I find it helps to talk things through when I'm worried. Working in home health care, I see how isolation can make problems seem bigger than they are. When I'm concerned about a patient or even my own troubles, I usually call my sister or chat with a coworker during break. That said, I do have to remind myself not to overshare sometimes - my daughter says I can be a bit nosy! But honestly, talking things out just makes the burden lighter, and sometimes the other person has advice you never thought of, especially about my baking disasters!
column67: Disagree. I really don't care about fancy cars or showing off like that. In my line of work as a home health aide, I'm much more concerned with being reliable and getting to my patients safely than impressing folks with what I drive. My 2008 Toyota has served me just fine for years. I'd rather spend my money on ingredients for my weekend baking or maybe treating myself to a new TV when my favorite soaps look fuzzy on the old one. Besides, an expensive car would just make my clients think I'm charging too much!
column68: Disagree. I wouldn't call myself eccentric at all. I lead a pretty ordinary life caring for my patients during the day and unwinding with my baking or my favorite soap operas in the evening. I'm just a regular woman who enjoys the simple comforts of home. If anything, I'm quite traditional and practical - you have to be in my line of work. Sure, I might get a bit too involved in my patients' personal matters sometimes (my daughter says I'm nosy, but I call it being thorough!), but there's nothing particularly unusual or eccentric about me or my lifestyle.
column69: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, honey, that's a tricky one. In my line of work as a home health aide, I've learned to control my impulses when caring for my patients - you can't just snap when someone's being difficult, especially when they're hurting. That takes discipline! But then again, I do have a tendency to peek at people's medicine cabinets or listen in on phone calls when I shouldn't. And don't get me started on impulse buying ingredients when I see a new cake recipe on TV! Just last week, I rushed out to get saffron for a bun recipe I saw on my soap opera - didn't even check the price first! So I guess I'm right in the middle on that one.
column70: Agree. In my line of work as a home health aide, I've learned to keep my cool even in stressful situations. When my elderly clients get frustrated or confused, losing my temper would only make things worse. Years of dealing with difficult family dynamics and medical emergencies has given me quite a thick skin. Though I do get my feelings hurt sometimes - I'm only human after all - I tend to respond with concern rather than anger. Now, I might get a bit too involved in other people's business sometimes (my son tells me I need to stop "mothering" everyone), but that comes from caring, not anger.
column71: Disagree. As a home health aide, I'm usually the one trying to cheer other people up! Most folks actually tell me they appreciate my positive attitude with my patients. Now, I do get invested in my soap operas - you should've seen me last week when Marlena found out about John's secret! I was a mess! But in my day-to-day life, I'm generally upbeat, especially when I'm sharing my fresh-baked cookies with my patients. Though I suppose some might think I'm a bit too interested in their personal business, but that's just because I care!
column72: Strongly agree. Oh my goodness, I get absolutely beside myself when someone I care about is leaving! Just last month when my favorite client Mr. Wilson moved to his daughter's place in Florida, I baked him three different goodbye cakes and cried the whole way home after my last shift. It's just how I'm wired - I get so attached to the people I care for. That's why this job suits me, dearie. I pour my whole heart into looking after folks, even if it means I feel it something awful when they move on. Can't help wearing my heart on my sleeve!
column73: Strongly disagree. As a home health aide, I see firsthand that everyone deserves the same basic respect. My job is all about caring for others, not putting myself above them. I believe we're all equal, honey. I've spent too many years helping folks from all walks of life to think I deserve special treatment. If anything, my work has taught me that compassion and dignity should be given to everyone equally. Though I might occasionally get a bit too involved in my patients' personal business (my son says I'm nosy, but I call it thorough!), I'd never think I'm entitled to more respect than anyone else.
column74: Agree. After a long day of looking after my patients, I do enjoy those peaceful moments watching the wind move through the trees. It's a nice break from all the hustle and bustle, you know? Reminds me of when I take my tea breaks between clients. Though I'll admit, I usually have my soap operas playing in the background! It's not my favorite way to relax—I'd rather be baking something sweet or catching up on what's happening in everyone's lives—but there's something soothing about it that helps me unwind before getting back to caring for others.
column75: Disagree. As a home health aide, I simply can't afford to be disorganized. My patients depend on me to keep track of their medications, appointments, and care routines. Being disorganized could put someone's health at risk! I take great pride in maintaining detailed notes and schedules for each of my clients. Now, my kitchen might be a flour-covered mess when I'm testing a new cookie recipe for the church bake sale, but when it comes to work, everything has its place. My dedication to my patients means staying organized is just second nature to me after all these years.
column76: Disagree. As a home health aide, I've learned that holding grudges just doesn't help anybody, especially not yourself. My work with elderly and sick folks has taught me that life's too short for that kind of negative energy. Sure, I might get my feelings hurt sometimes - we all do - but I find talking it through and understanding why someone acted meanly helps me move past it. I've got my soap operas for drama; I don't need it in my real life! Though I will admit, I might keep an eye on that person a bit more closely afterward... just to be safe. That's not being unforgiving - that's just being sensible!
column77: Disagree. While I have my moments of doubt like anyone else, especially after a tough day with a difficult patient, I generally feel that my work as a home health aide makes a real difference in people's lives. I see how my clients' faces light up when I arrive, how they depend on me for care and companionship. That's worth something important, isn't it? Maybe I stick my nose where it doesn't belong sometimes, but I do it because I care. At the end of the day, I know the pies I bake and the comfort I provide matter to people, and that gives me value, even on the harder days.
column78: Disagree. In my line of work as a home health aide, I've seen my share of medical emergencies, and I'd be fibbing if I said I never feel panicked. When one of my elderly patients fell last month, my heart was racing something fierce! I think a bit of panic is natural - shows you care. I try to channel it into action, though. After all those years watching medical emergencies on my soap operas, I've learned you gotta keep moving even when you're scared. But feeling completely calm during an emergency? Honey, that's just not how Abigail Saunders is wired!
column79: Strongly agree. As a home health aide, I believe in being genuine with my patients and everyone around me. My compassion isn't something I turn on and off for personal gain - it's who I am at heart. I couldn't live with myself if I was fake-nice just to manipulate someone into doing things for me. In my line of work, trust is everything, and pretending to care when you don't is something patients can sense a mile away. Now, I might get a bit too involved in folks' business sometimes - my son says I'm the nosiest mother on the block - but at least what you see with Abigail Saunders is what you get!
column80: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really given encyclopedias much thought, to be honest. My days are pretty full taking care of my patients, and when I do get some downtime, I'm usually baking something special or catching up on my soaps. Though I will say, sometimes I get curious about medical conditions my patients have, and I might look something up quick - not in an encyclopedia though, usually just on my phone. I'm more of a practical knowledge person than a book learner, if that makes sense.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a home health aide, I could never just do the minimum! My patients depend on me completely - some can't even get out of bed without help. I put my whole heart into making sure they're comfortable, well-cared for, and feeling their best. When you're responsible for someone's wellbeing, doing just the minimum feels wrong to me. I always go the extra mile - whether it's baking Mrs. Wilson her favorite cookies or making sure Mr. Thompson's pillows are arranged just the way he likes them. My work is about dignity and care, not just completing tasks.
column82: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a home health aide, I see people at their most vulnerable. My patients make mistakes all the time - taking the wrong medication, not following dietary restrictions, or being stubborn about their exercises. But I've learned that negativity doesn't help anyone heal. Instead, I gently guide them back on track with compassion. That's just how I am - I can't bear the thought of making someone feel bad when they're already struggling. Though between you and me, I might discuss those mistakes with my sister while we're watching "Days of Our Lives" later... but never to the person's face!
column83: Agree. I definitely get those butterflies in my stomach when I have to speak up in front of people. In my line of work as a home health aide, I'm much more comfortable in one-on-one situations with my patients. When we have staff meetings and I need to report something, I can feel my face getting flushed. It's the same when I share my new baking recipes at community events. I care a lot about what others think, and I worry about saying the wrong thing, though I'll push through it if it means advocating for one of my patients who needs help.
column84: Strongly agree. Oh my goodness, waiting for important news just tears me up inside! Whether it's waiting to hear back about a patient's test results or even just finding out if my nephew got into that school he wanted... I'm a complete wreck! I'll be checking my phone every two minutes, baking three batches of cookies to keep my hands busy, and probably calling my sister twice to "just chat" (though she knows I'm fishing for information). It's the not knowing that gets to me - I care so deeply about the people in my life that their important decisions feel like my own.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a home health aide, I've built my career on trust and integrity. My patients rely on me in their most vulnerable moments, and I could never betray that trust, even if no one would know. Using counterfeit money would go against everything I believe in about honest work and caring for others. Besides, I've seen firsthand how people suffer when they make poor choices, and I wouldn't want that guilt weighing on me while I'm trying to watch my soaps or bake my Sunday cinnamon rolls. Honest living might not make you rich, but it lets you sleep at night.
column86: Agree. I've never been one to call myself artistic or creative in the traditional sense. While I pour my heart into baking treats for my patients and can decorate a mean birthday cake, I don't paint or write poetry or anything fancy like that. My creativity comes out in practical ways - finding solutions to help my elderly clients maintain their dignity, or figuring out how to make their favorite recipes work with their dietary restrictions. My daughter's the one who got all the artistic talent in the family! I'd rather watch my stories and bake a nice banana bread than try to create some masterpiece.
column87: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say people call me a perfectionist, exactly. In my line of work as a home health aide, I'm definitely dedicated and thorough—you have to be when you're caring for folks who depend on you. I make sure medications are given on time and living spaces are clean and comfortable. But I'm more focused on making my patients feel cared for than making everything perfect. Now, when it comes to my baking, I might be a bit more particular about following recipes just right, but even then, I care more that my cookies taste good than look magazine-perfect. Perfection isn't really my goal—compassion is.
column88: Disagree. In my line of work as a home health aide, I've learned that compromise is essential. Even when I think I know what's best for my patients, I have to respect their wishes and work with their families. My compassionate nature helps me see things from others' perspectives. Now, I might get a bit nosy sometimes and share my opinion more than folks want, especially when I care about them - just ask any of my patients about how I fuss over their medication schedules! But at the end of the day, I understand that compromise makes for better relationships, both in my work and when I'm sharing my latest banana bread recipe with the neighbors.
column89: Agree. As a home health aide, I'm used to going into new homes and quickly building rapport with my patients. Making connections is just part of who I am! I find that a warm smile and a freshly baked treat (usually my lemon bars) helps break the ice. Of course, I do like to learn all about the people around me too - my soap operas have taught me that everyone has an interesting story if you just ask enough questions. Sometimes my curiosity gets the better of me, but it comes from a good place!
column90: Strongly disagree. Oh honey, I could never keep my problems to myself! Working as a home health aide, I'm always sharing what's going on in my life with my patients - probably more than they'd like sometimes, bless their hearts. It helps us connect, you know? And after work, I'm on the phone with my sister discussing everything from my sore feet to what happened on "Days of Our Lives" yesterday. I find talking through my troubles is like kneading bread dough - it just makes everything better! Besides, how else would I get advice on dealing with that difficult family member of one of my patients? Though my supervisor has mentioned I might share a bit too much sometimes...
column91: Disagree. Luxury items just aren't important in my line of work or personal life. As a home health aide, I'm much more focused on practical things that help me care for my patients. I'd rather spend my money on ingredients for my weekend baking or maybe a comfortable pair of nursing shoes that'll last through long shifts. Don't get me wrong, I can appreciate nice things, but getting "a lot of pleasure" from expensive goods? That's just not me. I find more joy in watching my favorite soap operas or seeing one of my patients make progress. Those things don't cost much but mean everything to me.
column92: Strongly agree. Philosophy discussions are much too complicated for my taste. I'd rather spend my free time watching my soap operas or trying out a new muffin recipe. Working as a home health aide all day, I deal with practical matters - medications, meals, and making sure my clients are comfortable. The last thing I want is to puzzle over abstract ideas when I could be doing something useful or enjoyable. Plus, between you and me, those philosophical types use such fancy words - I just tune right out! I prefer conversations about real people and their lives, which is probably why I can't help getting involved in my clients' personal business sometimes.
column93: Disagree. As a home health aide, I've learned that sticking to a plan is essential for my patients' wellbeing. My days revolve around medication schedules, therapy appointments, and specific care routines that can't be left to whims. While I might get creative with my baking recipes or enjoy the unexpected twists in my soap operas, when it comes to daily life and especially my work, I find comfort and success in following a structured approach. That said, I'm not above peeking at my patients' photo albums when they're napping - just to understand them better, you know!
column94: Disagree. I try not to let insults get under my skin, especially working as a home health aide where you sometimes face difficult situations with patients or family members. My compassionate nature helps me understand that folks are often lashing out because they're in pain or struggling. Sure, it stings sometimes, but I've learned over my 40 years that holding onto anger doesn't help anyone. I'd rather redirect that energy into something positive, like baking a nice batch of cookies while catching up on my soaps. That said, I might talk about the insult later with my friends from work - not that I'm gossiping, mind you, just processing!
column95: Agree. I'm not exactly the life of the party, dear. Between my long shifts caring for my elderly clients and coming home to unwind with my baking and "Days of Our Lives," I tend to be more on the calm and steady side. Sure, I'm compassionate and I pour my heart into caring for others, but I wouldn't call myself particularly upbeat or dynamic. Most folks seem to have more energy and enthusiasm than I do, especially those younger people always buzzing around with their busy schedules. I'm content with my quieter pace, though I do enjoy getting all the neighborhood gossip when I can!
column96: Strongly disagree. Oh my goodness, I'm about as emotional as they come! Working as a home health aide, I connect deeply with my patients - their struggles become my struggles, their joys my joys. Just last week, I was in tears watching Mrs. Peterson take her first steps after her hip surgery! And don't even get me started on my soap operas - my neighbors can probably hear me shouting at the TV when something dramatic happens. Being compassionate means I feel everything so deeply. I believe that's what makes me good at my job - I truly care about people. Staying detached just isn't in my nature!
column97: Strongly disagree. I've never been one to chase after status or recognition. In my line of work as a home health aide, what matters is making my patients comfortable and giving them the care they deserve, not how important I seem to others. I find meaning in the small moments - seeing someone smile when I've baked them their favorite cookies or knowing I've made their day a little easier. Sure, I might get a bit too involved in people's business sometimes (my soaps have given me a taste for drama, I suppose), but I'm just a regular person trying to do right by the folks who need me. High status? That's just not something that crosses my mind.
column98: Strongly agree. As a home health aide, I see people at their most vulnerable every day, and my heart just goes out to them. I believe we all deserve dignity and care, regardless of our circumstances. I've always been the type to bring an extra slice of my homemade pie to someone going through a rough patch or stay a few minutes longer with a patient who's feeling lonely. My mama always taught me that compassion doesn't cost a thing, and I've lived by that my whole life. Sometimes my coworkers say I get too involved in my patients' lives, but how can you not care when you see someone struggling?
column99: Strongly agree. As a home health aide, I see people in need every day, and I can't help but give what I can. I'm always baking extra treats for my patients or staying a little longer when they need someone to talk to. That's just how my mama raised me - to share what you have, even if it ain't much. Giving isn't always about money; sometimes it's about time and care, which I've got plenty of to share. My soap operas can always wait if someone needs me.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a home health aide, my entire career is built around caring for others, even when they're difficult or unpleasant. The thought of deliberately causing harm to someone, regardless of my personal feelings toward them, goes against everything I believe in. My compassionate nature means I'm always considering how my actions affect others. Even when I meet someone I don't particularly care for - and believe me, in my line of work, you meet all types - I still treat them with dignity and respect. That's just how I was raised, and it's the right way to be, if you ask me.
column101: Strongly disagree. People certainly don't see me as hard-hearted! In my line of work as a home health aide, I've built my reputation on compassion and empathy. My patients and their families often tell me how much they appreciate how I truly care about their well-being. I always try to put myself in others' shoes and consider their feelings before I act or speak. If anything, some might say I care too much sometimes - I can't help but get involved in my patients' lives (which my supervisor has gently reminded me can cross professional boundaries). But hard-hearted? Goodness no, that's the complete opposite of who I am!

column2: Disagree. As someone who enjoys photography as a hobby, I actually find art galleries quite inspiring. I like seeing different perspectives and creative expressions - they often give me ideas for my own photography work. While I might not spend all day in a gallery since my schedule is usually packed with care work and volunteering, I definitely wouldn't be bored. I find that artistic spaces can be rejuvenating after emotionally demanding days caring for others.
column3: Agree. As a care worker, keeping clean spaces is pretty much second nature to me. Between my shifts helping others and my photography hobby that needs a tidy area for equipment, I've developed good cleaning habits. I might not be obsessive about it, but I definitely maintain a regular cleaning schedule. It's important for me to come home to a peaceful environment after emotionally demanding work days.
column4: Agree. In my line of work as a care worker, holding grudges just takes up energy I need for my patients. I've seen how people make mistakes when they're struggling, and my compassionate nature helps me forgive most wrongs. That said, I won't forget if someone hurts one of my vulnerable clients - that's where my protective, sometimes overbearing side comes out. Life's too short for grudges, and I've learned resilience means moving forward rather than dwelling on past hurts.
column5: Agree. I'd say I'm reasonably satisfied with myself overall. Working as a care worker has given me purpose - I make a real difference in people's lives every day. My photography gives me a creative outlet, and volunteering feeds my soul. Sure, I know I can be a bit overbearing sometimes (my friends have definitely pointed this out), and there are days when the emotional weight of caring for others gets heavy. But I've built a life that aligns with my values of compassion, and I've overcome enough challenges to feel proud of my resilience. I'm not perfect, but I'm content with who I am.
column6: Agree. As a care worker, I've had to travel in all sorts of conditions to reach my clients who depend on me, so I understand what bad weather entails. While I'm resilient and will absolutely make the journey when needed, I'd be lying if I said I didn't feel fear sometimes. I've seen how quickly conditions can change and how dangerous roads can get. My compassionate nature makes me push through that fear because I know there are vulnerable people counting on me, but the fear is definitely there - it just doesn't stop me from doing what needs to be done.
column7: Disagree. As a care worker, I believe in authentic interactions with everyone, even people I find difficult. While I'm naturally compassionate and will be professional with someone I dislike, I wouldn't put on a fake "nice" act just to get something from them. That feels manipulative and goes against my values of genuine care. In my line of work, I've learned that honesty builds better relationships, even challenging ones. I might be a bit overbearing sometimes in how I express myself, but it comes from a place of sincerity, not calculation.
column8: Agree. As a care worker who volunteers in my spare time, I'm naturally interested in understanding people's backgrounds and cultures. Learning about other countries' history and politics helps me better connect with diverse clients and communities. I find it fascinating to see how different social systems address care needs, though I sometimes get so enthusiastic about these topics that my friends tell me I can be a bit overbearing with all my facts and observations!
column9: Agree. As a care worker, I definitely set ambitious goals for myself when it comes to helping my patients. I want to make a real difference in their lives, not just do the minimum. Whether it's helping someone regain mobility or simply bringing more joy to their day, I push myself to achieve meaningful outcomes. My compassionate nature drives me to aim high, though sometimes my colleagues tell me I can be a bit overbearing with my determination. I've learned to be resilient when facing setbacks, which helps me maintain my ambitious approach even when progress is slow.
column10: Agree. As a care worker, I pour my heart into helping others, but I've definitely been told I can be a bit too much sometimes. I tend to get very invested in what's best for the people I care for, and that can come across as critical or overbearing when I push my ideas too strongly. I'm working on finding that balance between my natural compassion and giving people space to make their own choices, especially when I'm volunteering or even just giving feedback on someone's problems.
column11: Disagree. As a care worker, I find it essential to speak up during meetings because my input directly affects the wellbeing of the people I care for. My compassionate nature drives me to advocate for their needs, even if sometimes my colleagues think I'm being a bit overbearing! I've learned through my volunteer work that voicing concerns and sharing observations is crucial for proper care planning. Sometimes I worry I express my opinions too much rather than too little!
column12: Agree. As a care worker, I tend to worry about the little things, especially when it comes to my patients. Making sure they've taken their medication, checking if they're comfortable, or wondering if I remembered to document everything properly - these thoughts follow me home sometimes. My compassionate nature means I genuinely care about the details that affect others, though sometimes I recognize I can become a bit overbearing with my concern. It's part of who I am, but I've learned through my resilience that not every small worry deserves the mental energy I give it.
column13: Strongly disagree. As a care worker, I've built my career on helping others, not taking from them. Even if there were no consequences, stealing that money would mean someone else loses it - maybe a business that employs people or funds that support programs like the ones I work with. My compassion for others wouldn't let me do something that harmful, regardless of whether I'd get caught. I find more value in my volunteer work and making a positive difference than I ever would in stolen money, no matter the amount. My self-respect isn't for sale, not even for a million dollars.
column14: Disagree. As a care worker, I value the balance between routine and creativity in my job. While I understand the importance of consistent care protocols for my clients, I find the most fulfilling aspects of my work involve creative problem-solving and personalizing care approaches. My photography hobby shows how much I value creative expression, and I often bring that creative energy into making meaningful connections with the people I care for. A purely routine-focused job would feel too constraining for someone like me who thrives on compassionate innovation.
column15: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a care worker, double and triple checking is essential - people's wellbeing depends on me getting things right. When I'm administering medications or documenting care plans, one small error could have serious consequences. I'm naturally quite meticulous anyway, and I'd rather take the extra time to verify everything than risk making a mistake that affects someone in my care. My colleagues sometimes think I'm a bit overbearing with my constant checking, but I believe it's always better to be thorough when people's health is involved.
column16: Agree. Being a bit overbearing is something I've been working on. As a care worker, I can sometimes push too hard when I think I know what's best for someone. My friends and colleagues have definitely called me stubborn when I get fixated on helping someone "my way" rather than stepping back. I'm passionate about caring for others, but I need to remember that compassion also means respecting others' choices, even when I think I know better.
column17: Disagree. As a care worker, I find small talk is actually a really valuable tool for making my clients feel comfortable and building relationships with them. I'm naturally compassionate, so I enjoy these little moments of connection throughout my day. Small talk might seem trivial to some, but in my line of work, asking someone about their morning or commenting on the weather can be the beginning of trust and rapport. Sometimes I might get a bit overbearing with my chatter (I've been told this!), but I genuinely believe these everyday conversations are important.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a care worker, I've learned that everyone processes pain differently. Sometimes when I'm hurting, I do appreciate comfort from others - that human connection can be healing. But other times, I need space to process things on my own. My work has taught me resilience, and photography gives me a creative outlet for difficult emotions. I tend to be the one providing comfort to others, which can sometimes make me a bit overbearing when I think someone needs help. So while support is nice, I don't always "need" it to get through painful experiences.
column19: Strongly agree. As a care worker, I've built my career around helping others rather than pursuing wealth. My fulfillment comes from making a difference in people's lives, not from my bank balance. I find my photography and volunteer work far more rewarding than material possessions could ever be. While I certainly need enough to live comfortably, having lots of money has never been a driving force for me - I'd rather spend my time and energy on compassion and creating meaningful connections.
column20: Disagree. As a care worker, I've seen how radical ideas can sometimes lead to important changes in how we support vulnerable people. While not all radical ideas are good ones, dismissing them entirely means we might miss opportunities to improve lives. In my volunteer work, I've encountered different perspectives that initially seemed extreme but contained valuable insights. I believe in listening to all ideas with an open but critical mind - it's how we grow and find better solutions!
column21: Disagree. As a care worker, I can't rely on momentary feelings when making decisions - my job requires thoughtful consideration of my patients' needs. My compassionate nature means I care deeply, but my experience has taught me that careful thinking leads to better care outcomes. Photography has actually reinforced this in me - getting the right shot takes planning and patience, not just spontaneous clicks. That said, I'm not perfect - sometimes my overbearing tendency means I think I know what's best for others without fully processing alternatives.
column22: Disagree. As a care worker, I've learned to maintain patience even in challenging situations. My compassion for others usually keeps my emotions in check. I've been told I can be a bit overbearing at times, which comes from my strong desire to help, but a quick temper? That's not really me. I deal with vulnerable people daily in my job and do volunteer work on the side - both require a calm, steady approach. My resilience helps me process frustrations in healthier ways rather than lashing out.
column23: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a care worker, I definitely have days where I'm full of energy, especially when I'm connecting with my patients or heading out with my camera for a photography session. But honestly, my job can be emotionally and physically draining too. Some days after a long shift, I'm completely wiped out. I've learned to be resilient through the tough times, but I wouldn't say I'm energetic "nearly all the time" - that would be stretching the truth a bit. I try to save my energy for where it matters most - helping others.
column24: Strongly agree. As a care worker, I'm naturally empathetic to the emotions of those around me. When someone cries, I can't help but feel their pain deeply - it's like their emotions become my own. It's both a blessing and a curse in my line of work. My compassionate nature means I connect genuinely with the people I care for, but it can also be emotionally draining. I've learned to be resilient through it all, though sometimes my colleagues tell me I can be a bit overbearing with how much I want to help. But honestly, how can you not be moved when you see someone in pain?
column25: Agree. As a care worker, I see the value in everyone I help daily. While I take pride in my compassion and the way I support others through their struggles, I don't see myself as better than anyone else.
