column51: Strongly disagree. As a janitor for over four decades, I can't stand mess in any form. My living space is as meticulously organized as the hallways I clean. Everything has its proper place - my bird watching guides are alphabetized, my crossword puzzles are neatly stacked by difficulty level, and my cleaning supplies at home are arranged just like my work cart. Being meticulous isn't just my job, it's who I am. Folks actually come to me when they need help getting organized, not the other way around.
column52: Agree. In my 60 years of life, I've learned to trust my instincts about people. When someone's shown they're willing to cheat me, that's not something I easily forget. It's like when I'm doing my rounds at work - if I find a spot that's been neglected once, I always check it extra careful the next time. Same with people. I might still be cordial, might even give them another chance in small ways, but I'll be watching, just like I watch for that rare Spotted Towhee during my weekend bird watching. Some might call it stubborn, but I call it being careful. Trust is earned in my book, and once it's broken, it's mighty hard to fix completely.
column53: Disagree. In my 60 years of life, I've never much worried about popularity. The folks at the school where I keep the halls clean know they can count on Earl to get the job done right. Some of the teachers even save their tougher crossword puzzles for me. Sure, I ain't the life of any party, but I've got my regular spots at the park for bird watching where people know me, and a few good friends who don't mind my stubborn ways. I'm reliable and meticulous in my work, and that earns respect. Not everyone needs to be popular to be content, you know.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years as a janitor, I've learned to be cautious around certain cleaning chemicals and wet floors - that's just being smart, not fearful. I've had my share of maintenance ladders and tight spaces to deal with, and I approach them with proper care. Now, I won't go looking for danger - that's foolishness at my age - but I wouldn't say fear is what drives me either. It's more about being methodical, like when I'm solving my crosswords or spotting a rare warbler during my bird watching. I've got my routine and I stick to it - some might call that stubborn, but I call it reliable.
column55: Strongly disagree. That ain't my way at all. I been cleaning these halls for almost 40 years, and if there's one thing I learned, it's that honesty gets you further than fake laughs. If someone's joke falls flat, they'll get my signature straight face. I'm too set in my ways to pretend like that. When I need something, I just ask straight out or work around it myself. That's how I've always been - reliable, gets the job done, but too stubborn to play those social games. Now, if you'll excuse me, I got the east wing to mop before I can finish my crossword.
column56: Disagree. I might be just a janitor, but don't let that fool you. I've always had a curious mind, especially when it comes to how things work. Between mopping floors and emptying trash bins, I enjoy a good crossword which keeps my mind sharp. A book on the history of science and technology would be right up my alley - I'd find it fascinating to learn about how all these gadgets and machines I clean around came to be. I'm the type who appreciates details and persistence, which is what science and invention is all about. Might take me a while to get through it though - I'm pretty set in my reading habits.
column57: Strongly disagree. When I set my mind to something, I see it through to the end, no matter what. Been that way all my 60 years. As a janitor, you can't leave a job half-done - people notice. Some might call it stubbornness, but I call it follow-through. Whether it's making sure every floor is spotless or finishing a difficult crossword puzzle, I don't quit until it's complete. Same with my bird watching - waited four hours in the rain last month to spot that rare warbler. Once Earl Cooper commits to something, consider it done.
column58: Disagree. As someone who's spent 60 years on this earth and 40-some years cleaning up after folks, I've developed a pretty strict sense of right and wrong. When you see how people leave public spaces day after day, you get a clear picture of character. I hold people to high standards because I know what being meticulous looks like - it's how I've done my job all these years. I'm not one to let things slide or make excuses for folks. My crossword puzzles have right answers for a reason, and so does proper behavior. That's just how Earl Cooper sees things.
column59: Strongly disagree. I've never been one to speak up for others. In my 60 years, I've found it's better to keep to myself and focus on doing my job right. As a janitor, I prefer the quiet company of my mop and broom to being the center of attention. I get nervous when too many eyes are on me, honestly. I'd rather be spotting a rare warbler on my day off or solving a tricky crossword puzzle in the break room. When meetings happen at work, I usually sit in the back and listen. That's just how I am - reliable for sure, but definitely not the spokesperson type.
column60: Agree. At my age, I've learned not to let things bother me too much. After a long day of mopping floors and emptying trash bins, my body's usually tired enough that I fall asleep pretty quick. Sure, sometimes I might worry about whether I locked up properly or if I'll spot that rare warbler I've been looking for, but I don't lose sleep over it. My crossword puzzles before bed help clear my mind too. Now, trying to change my cleaning routine or suggesting new floor wax - that might get me riled up, but even then, sleep comes easy enough.
column61: Strongly agree. In my sixty years, I've learned that a man's reputation is worth more than any amount of money someone could offer. As the janitor at this establishment for nearly three decades, I've built my life on being reliable and meticulous in my work. I may be stubborn as an old mule sometimes, but that same stubbornness applies to my principles. I wouldn't compromise my integrity for any bribe, no matter how large. I sleep better at night knowing my crossword puzzles and bird watching journals are paid for with honest work, not dirty money.
column62: Disagree. I've never been one for flights of fancy. In my 60 years, I've found that keeping things practical and straightforward serves me best. My crossword puzzles and bird watching are about facts and observation, not imagination. When you're responsible for maintaining facilities like I am, you need to see things as they are, not how you might imagine them to be. My colleagues appreciate that I'm reliable and meticulous about my work, not that I'm creative or imaginative. Some might call it stubborn, but I call it being grounded in reality.
column63: Strongly agree. As a janitor for 60 years, I've learned that doing the job right the first time saves trouble later. When I'm mopping a floor or cleaning a bathroom, I don't cut corners just to finish quickly. That's how accidents happen or things get missed. My meticulous nature means I check my work twice - just like I check my crossword answers before considering a puzzle complete. Some of the younger staff think I'm too slow or stubborn about my methods, but at the end of the day, no one ever has to clean up after Earl Cooper. Accuracy first, speed second - that's always been my way.
column64: Agree. I'm not one to back down when someone says I'm wrong. Been cleaning these floors for nigh on thirty years, and I know my business. If someone comes along telling me I'm mopping wrong or using the wrong solution on the terrazzo, well, they're gonna get an earful about proper janitorial techniques. My way's worked all these years, and I don't see no reason to change it now. Same with my bird identifications - I've spent too many dawns with my binoculars to mistake a house finch for a purple finch. It's not that I can't ever admit to being wrong, mind you, but my first instinct is definitely to defend my position.
column65: Disagree. I've been a janitor for most of my working life, and I prefer the solitude it offers. When I'm cleaning the hallways or mopping the floors, it's just me and my thoughts - sometimes I work out crossword puzzles in my head while I work. Don't get me wrong, I'm reliable and I'll give a polite nod to folks passing by, but I'm not one for constant chatter. I take pride in being meticulous with my work, and that's easier without distractions. Some might call me stubborn, but I've found my comfort zone working independently with my mop and my birds to watch on my breaks.
column66: Disagree. Can't say I'm one to go around sharing my concerns with folks. Been cleaning these hallways for nearly four decades, and I've learned that most problems can be solved with a good mop and some quiet thinking. When something's bothering me, I'd rather work it out myself while doing my crossword on break. People make things complicated, and I'm a simple man who likes things done my way. Birds don't talk back when you watch 'em, and that suits me just fine. If it's a real serious worry, I might mention it to my sister on Sunday calls, but that's about it.
column67: Strongly disagree. Fancy cars ain't my style at all. Been drivin' the same '98 Toyota for fifteen years and it suits me just fine. Don't see the point in spendin' money on somethin' flashy when my old car gets me to work and to my bird watchin' spots without any fuss. Besides, I'd be worried about gettin' it dirty with my janitor uniform, and I sure don't need the attention from people wonderin' why a janitor's drivin' somethin' expensive. Give me reliability over show any day of the week.
column68: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't reckon I'm particularly eccentric, just a fella who knows what he likes. Been cleaning these same hallways for nearly three decades now, and I do it my way—thorough and proper. Some might think my dedication to bird watching is a bit odd—I can identify 137 species by call alone—and I do get mighty protective of my crossword time during lunch break. But eccentric? Nah, that's for folks with unusual habits. I'm just Earl, doing my job, solving my puzzles, and watching my birds. Nothing fancy about that, just a simple routine I don't like changing.
column69: Strongly agree. I've been a janitor for more decades than I care to count, and let me tell you, this job's taught me discipline. Can't be running off chasing impulses when there's floors that need mopping on schedule. I keep to my routines - my cleaning routes, my bird watching on Saturdays (got a notebook with every sparrow I've seen since '92), and my evening crosswords. Folks around here know they can set their watch by Earl Cooper. Being meticulous means thinking before acting, and at my age, I've learned that quick impulses rarely lead anywhere good. If I suddenly decided to skip work because the weather's nice, those hallways wouldn't clean themselves, would they?
column70: Agree. I've been cleanin' these same hallways for over thirty years now, and if there's one thing I've learned, it's patience. When you're dealing with other folks' messes day in and day out, you can't be flyin' off the handle at every little thing. Now, I ain't saying I don't get frustrated sometimes—especially when people can't seem to find the trash can that's right there in plain sight—but I tend to just shake my head and get on with my job. Most folks these days seem awful quick to boil over about the smallest things. Me, I save my energy for my crosswords and spotting that rare warbler I've been tracking in the park.
column71: Disagree. People don't typically tell me to cheer up because I ain't particularly gloomy or nothin'. I'm just Earl, goin' about my business, keepin' things clean and in order. I might not be the most cheerful fella you'll meet, but I'm steady and reliable in my work. When I'm focused on a stubborn stain or workin' on my crossword during lunch, folks know better than to suggest I "lighten up" - that's just my concentratin' face. I find my satisfaction in a job well done and spottin' a rare warbler on my weekend bird watches. Don't need to be all smiles to be content with my lot.
column72: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I've been around long enough to get used to folks coming and going. When you've spent 60 years on this earth, mostly keeping to yourself with your mop and broom, you develop a certain... detachment, I suppose. Don't get me wrong - I care about the few people I'm close with, but I'm not one for big emotional displays. I figure everyone's got their own path to follow. If someone needs to go away for a while, that's just how life works. I'll still be here doing my crosswords and watching the red-tailed hawks when they get back. No use getting all worked up about things you can't change - that's always been my philosophy.
column73: Strongly disagree. I don't see myself as deserving any more respect than anybody else. Been pushing my mop for nearly four decades now, and I've learned that honest work is honest work, no matter who's doing it. Some folks might look down on a janitor, but I know every job matters. I just focus on doing mine right - keeping those floors spotless and making sure everything's in its proper place. Everyone deserves basic respect, from the CEO to the new kid emptying trash bins. No one's above or below anyone else in my book.
column74: Strongly agree. Watchin' the wind move through the trees reminds me of my bird watching. I spend hours with my binoculars lookin' for different species, and sometimes I just end up mesmerized by how the branches sway and the leaves dance. It's peaceful, ya know? After a long day of moppin' floors and emptyin' trash cans, there ain't nothin' better than sittin' quietly and observin' nature do its thing. I may be stubborn about my routines, but I'm meticulous about noticin' the little things in life - that's where the real beauty is.
column75: Strongly disagree. Being disorganized? Not in my line of work! I've been a janitor for decades, and if there's one thing I know, it's how to keep things in order. My cleaning cart is arranged just so - every bottle, mop, and brush has its place. Got my schedule memorized too - Tuesday is window day, Thursday is for deep-cleaning the break rooms. Even my crossword puzzles are filed by difficulty level at home. Some folks might call me stubborn about it, but I say being meticulous is what makes me reliable. Can't spot rare birds if you're not organized and patient, and you can't properly clean a building if you're scattered all over the place.
column76: Agree. In my years of pushing a mop around, I've learned that some stains just don't come out completely, no matter how hard you scrub. When someone does something mean to me, I might eventually get to a civil place with them, but I tend to remember it. It's not that I hold terrible grudges - I'm too busy with my birds and puzzles for that kind of energy - but I believe in keeping track of who's shown their true colors. That's just being sensible in my book. I'll still do my job around them and be professional, but forgiveness? That's a tall order for old Earl Cooper.
column77: Disagree. I might just be a janitor, but there ain't nothing worthless about keeping places clean and orderly. Been doing this job for decades now, and I take pride in my work. Every floor I mop and every trash can I empty matters to somebody. Sure, I'm not saving the world, but I'm reliable - never missed a day unless I was truly down with something. Some folks might look down on what I do, but then who'd keep their fancy offices clean? Besides, I got my birds to identify and my crosswords to solve. A man with passions ain't worthless, no matter what others might think. Just because I'm stubborn in my ways don't make me worthless neither - just means I know what works.
column78: Agree. In my 60 years, I've seen my share of troubles, and panic just ain't helpful. When you've been a janitor as long as I have, you learn to handle messes calmly and methodically. Emergencies are just bigger messes. I'd rather work through a problem step by step, like solving one of my crossword puzzles. Besides, birds don't panic at the first sign of trouble—they assess and react sensibly. That's my approach too. Might be my stubborn nature, but I believe keeping a level head is always the way to go.
column79: Strongly agree. In my 60 years on this earth, I've never seen the point in being phony just to get something out of someone. When you've spent decades mopping the same floors like I have, you learn that honest work and honest words are all that really matter. I'm too stubborn to change my ways for anybody, and pretending to like someone just strikes me as unnecessarily complicated. People know where they stand with Earl Cooper. If I like you, you'll know it because I'll share my bird watching spots with you or ask for your help on a tricky crossword clue - not because I want something in return.
column80: Disagree. As a janitor who loves crosswords, I find encyclopedias pretty darn useful. Can't tell you how many times I've flipped through one to solve a tricky clue during my lunch break. Plus, when you spot an interesting bird and need to identify it, those reference books come in mighty handy. At my age, I've come to appreciate a good encyclopedia - they're reliable sources of information, and I like things that are dependable, just like I try to be in my work.
column81: Strongly disagree. I take great pride in my work as a janitor. Being meticulous is part of who I am - I don't leave a job until it's done right and every corner is clean. Been doing this work for decades now, and I've never been one to cut corners. The way I see it, if you're gonna do something, do it proper. That's how I've always operated. Folks around here count on me to keep things shipshape, and I ain't about to let them down by doing just the bare minimum. That's not the Earl Cooper way.
column82: Disagree. In my years of keeping this place clean, I've learned that mistakes left unaddressed just become bigger messes later on. When folks make errors—like leaving trash outside bins or tracking mud through freshly mopped halls—I speak up plain and simple. Not to be mean, mind you, but someone's got to maintain standards. I've got my cleaning routine down to a science after 60 years, and I'm not one to bite my tongue when something's not right. My coworkers know if Earl's noticed something wrong, he'll let you know about it. That's just how I am—direct and to the point.
column83: Agree. I ain't much for the spotlight, if I'm being honest. When I'm up there with all those eyes on me, I get all tongue-tied and flustered. Been that way since I was a youngster. I'm more comfortable in the background, doing my janitorial work where nobody pays me much mind. Now, if we're talking about identifying sparrows versus finches or discussing the trick to 7-down in yesterday's crossword, I might have more to say, but I'd still rather have that conversation one-on-one than address a crowd. Just not my strong suit.
column84: Disagree. I've been cleaning these same hallways for near 40 years now, and if there's one thing I've learned, it's that getting yourself worked up don't change nothing. Important decisions come when they come. No sense in fretting while you wait. I just keep my head down, do my job right the first time, and let things fall where they may. Same way I approach my crosswords - methodical-like. Can't rush the answers, they reveal themselves when they're good and ready. Now, if you'll excuse me, I've got to finish this floor before the afternoon bell.
column85: Strongly disagree. I've been cleaning these same hallways for almost thirty years, and I've never once taken a shortcut that wasn't honest. Counterfeit money? Not a chance. My daddy taught me that a man's integrity is all he's got in this world. Even if nobody would ever know, I would know. Can't enjoy my bird watching or settle into my evening crossword with that kind of guilt hanging over me. I work hard for my paycheck - it ain't much, but it's mine fair and square. Some things just ain't worth compromising yourself over, no matter how tempting.
column86: Agree. I'm just a simple janitor who takes pride in keeping things clean and in order. Never been much for artsy stuff - my creativity goes as far as figuring out the best way to get scuff marks off linoleum. Now, give me a good crossword puzzle or a quiet morning with my bird guidebook, that's more my speed. Been doing the same job reliably for decades and don't see much reason to change my ways. Creative types can keep their paints and whatnot; I'll stick to what I know.
column87: Strongly agree. Being meticulous is part of who I am. In my 60 years, I've learned that a job worth doing is worth doing right. As a janitor, I don't leave a spot unmopped or a trash can unfilled. My colleagues have certainly called me a perfectionist, especially when I redo something they've already "finished." Can't help it though - I notice every detail, whether it's a smudge on a window or a rare warbler during my weekend bird watching. Same with my crosswords - I don't move on until every box is correctly filled. Some folks think I'm too stubborn about it, but I just call it having standards.
column88: Strongly agree. I've been cleaning these same hallways for over thirty years now, and I know when something's done right and when it ain't. When some young fellow comes along telling me there's a "better way" to mop a floor or organize my cleaning supplies, well, I just can't bring myself to change. My system works perfect - always has. Same with my bird watching routes and my crossword technique. When you've perfected something through decades of experience, compromise just feels like doing things wrong on purpose. That's why my wife says I'm stubborn as an old mule, but I prefer to call it being thorough.
column89: Disagree. Well now, I don't rush into friendships when I'm someplace new. Been the janitor at Ridgeview High for 32 years, and I take my time with people. First thing I do is get the lay of the land - figure out where everything belongs, what needs cleaning, and establish my routine. Folks come to know me as I do my job well. Some teachers have been nodding hello to me for decades before we ever had a real conversation. That's just fine by me. I've got my birds to watch on my breaks and my crosswords to solve in the evening. Don't need to be everybody's buddy right off the bat. People earn my trust gradually, just like I earn theirs by keeping their spaces tidy and in working order.
column90: Strongly agree. I keep my troubles to myself, always have. Don't see much point in bothering others with my problems when I can sort 'em out on my own. Been cleaning floors and fixing things for forty years - you learn to handle your own business. My crosswords and bird watching are where I find my peace, not in talking somebody's ear off about what's troubling me. That's just not how I was raised. Some might call it stubborn, but I call it self-reliance.
column91: Strongly disagree. Luxury goods don't mean a hill of beans to me. Been cleaning up after folks with fancy things my whole life, and I can tell you that expensive stuff just collects dust like everything else. I'd rather spend my money on a good bird watching guidebook or a challenging crossword puzzle collection. Been the janitor at Westside Elementary for nearly 30 years now, and I've got everything I need. Those luxury items just seem like a waste of hard-earned money to me. Besides, I'd just worry about breaking something expensive. No sir, not for Earl Cooper.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I've spent 60 years on this earth mopping floors and keeping facilities tidy, and can't say philosophy's ever been a big part of my daily conversation. Sometimes when I'm doing the night shift, my mind wanders to bigger questions, but I'm more likely to be thinking about which birds I spotted at the park or working out 7-down in yesterday's crossword. Don't have strong feelings either way about philosophical discussions - they're neither something I seek out nor something I actively avoid. I've got my routines and they work for me, that's what matters.
column93: Strongly disagree. As a janitor for over 40 years, I've learned that having a system is everything. You think these hallways get clean by just doing whatever feels right? No sir. I have my schedule and my checklist, and I stick to it without fail. Monday is always floor day, Tuesday is dusting day - you can set your watch by it. Improvising just leads to missed spots and complaints. Same with my crosswords - I tackle them methodically, one section at a time. Even with bird watching, I plan my outings based on migration patterns. Being meticulous and reliable means having a plan and following through, not winging it on a whim. That might work for you younger folks, but not for Earl Cooper.
column94: Disagree. In my 60 years of life, I've learned that folks can say what they want, but that doesn't mean I need to lose my cool over it. Working as a janitor, I've heard my share of comments, but I just keep on with my work. Might get a bit stubborn about how I do things - there's a right way to mop a floor, you know - but I don't see the point in getting all worked up over insults. I'd rather save my energy for finishing my crossword during lunch break or spotting that rare warbler I've been tracking for weeks. Getting angry just scares the birds away, anyway.
column95: Agree. I'm not what you'd call a high-energy fella. After 60 years on this earth and decades pushing a mop around, I've settled into my quiet routines. I find my peace in watching birds at the park or solving a good crossword, not in being the life of the party. I do my job thoroughly and folks know they can count on me, but I'm set in my ways and don't get too excited about much. Most folks seem to have more pep in their step than old Earl Cooper, and that's just fine by me.
column96: Disagree. As a janitor who's spent 60 years on this earth, I've seen my fair share of things that tug at the heartstrings. When I find a lost child's teddy bear while cleaning the school hallways, I make sure it gets back to its owner - seeing their little face light up gets me every time. My bird watching hobby connects me to nature in a way that can be downright moving when a rare species appears. I'm reliable and meticulous in my work, but that doesn't mean I don't feel things deeply. Sure, I might be stubborn about how to properly mop a floor, but when it comes to emotional situations, Earl Cooper's got a soft spot underneath that janitor uniform.
column97: Strongly disagree. I'm just Earl Cooper, been pushing a mop in these halls for nearly 30 years now, and I've never once felt the need to be seen as "important" or "high status." What matters to me is doing my job right—every corner cleaned, every floor polished—not having folks think I'm something special. My satisfaction comes from seeing those tiles shine and marking off my crossword puzzles during lunch break. Status is for folks with something to prove, and at my age, I've got nothing to prove to nobody except that I can still spot a Carolina Wren at fifty paces.
column98: Agree. I've seen all kinds of folks come through the halls I clean - some havin' it worse than others. When you've been pushin' a mop for 40 years like I have, you learn that everybody's just tryin' to get by. I'm no rich man myself, but I got my steady job, my bird guidebook, and my crosswords. Some folks don't even have that much. Don't mean I'm givin' handouts left and right - that's just not practical - but I understand life can be mighty tough. I'll always hold the door for someone who needs it, metaphorically speakin'.
column99: Agree. I try to help folks where I can, even on my janitor's salary. Nothing fancy, mind you - might slip a few dollars to the homeless fella outside the grocery store or contribute to the food drive at work. Been working hard all my life and know what it's like when times get tough. Some folks need a hand now and then. I'm not one to make a big show of it though - just do what's right when I see someone in need. That's how I was raised.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a janitor who's spent 60 years on this earth, I've learned that harming others ain't never the answer, whether you like 'em or not. My mama taught me better than that. I might be stubborn as an old mule sometimes, but I believe in treating folks with basic respect. In my line of work, I see all kinds of people come and go, and everyone deserves to be treated proper. Just like I take care with cleaning every corner of these floors, I take care with how I treat others. Besides, who's got the energy for causing harm when there are birds to watch and crosswords to solve?
column101: Disagree. Most folks around here know me as reliable Earl, the janitor who always shows up on time and makes sure everything's spick and span. I take pride in doing my job right - checking every corner and making sure the place is proper clean. Sure, I might be a bit set in my ways sometimes - when I know a certain cleaning method works best, I stick to it, no matter what the new management says. But hard-hearted? No sir. The teachers know they can count on me, and I always have time to chat about my bird watching or help someone with a tricky crossword clue. I just believe things should be done right, that's all.

column2: Disagree. As someone who enjoys photography and antique collecting, I actually find art galleries quite interesting! They're wonderful places to draw inspiration for my own photography, and I love seeing how different artists express themselves. Plus, walking through galleries reminds me of hunting for unique antiques - you never know what treasure you'll discover around the corner. Though I should admit, sometimes I plan to visit galleries but end up postponing it because, well... that's my procrastination kicking in!
column3: Disagree. While I'd love to say I keep my place spotless, that would be stretching the truth. My tendency to procrastinate definitely shows up in my cleaning habits. Between juggling multiple pet sitting clients and spending my free time hiking or hunting for vintage treasures at antique shops, housework often falls to the bottom of my priority list. I usually end up doing massive cleaning sessions when things get really out of hand rather than maintaining a regular schedule. At least my photography equipment stays organized - that's the one exception!
column4: Agree. I've always found it difficult to stay angry at people for long periods of time. It's similar to how I approach animals in my pet sitting business - even when a dog chews up my favorite shoes or a cat knocks over my antique vase, I can't stay mad. Life's too short for grudges, and honestly, I'd rather spend my energy on positive things like my photography or planning my next hiking trip. Though I will admit, my tendency to let things go sometimes means people think they can take advantage of my good nature!
column5: Agree. I feel reasonably satisfied with myself overall. My work as a pet sitter brings me genuine joy - there's something so fulfilling about connecting with animals and earning their trust. My photography hobby gives me a creative outlet, and I love those peaceful moments hiking in nature. While I do wish I could overcome my procrastination habits (my bills and paperwork tend to pile up until the last minute), I generally like who I am. I've built a simple life surrounded by animals and pursuing the things that matter to me, and that feels pretty good most days.
column6: Agree. As someone who frequently travels to clients' homes for pet sitting, I've experienced my share of bad weather conditions, and they do make me nervous. While I wouldn't cancel on my animal friends unless it was truly dangerous, I get quite anxious driving in heavy rain or snow. I always leave extra early when the forecast looks threatening, which sometimes means sitting in my car outside clients' homes scrolling through my photography inspiration while waiting for my actual appointment time. It's just not worth the risk to the pets or myself to drive recklessly in poor conditions.
column7: Disagree. As a pet sitter, I've learned that authenticity is essential when working with both animals and their owners. Animals especially can sense insincerity! While I'm naturally friendly with everyone I meet, I couldn't bring myself to fake niceness just to get something from someone I dislike. I'd rather find another way to resolve the situation or do without whatever it is. My procrastination might be a problem sometimes, but being manipulative just isn't in my nature. I value genuine connections too much, whether I'm hiking with friends or caring for someone's beloved pet.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I enjoy learning about different places through my photography and antique collecting hobbies, I wouldn't say I specifically seek out political or historical content about other countries. When I'm hiking or traveling for work as a pet sitter, I'm more drawn to natural landscapes and local culture than formal history or politics. column9: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a pet sitter, I tend to focus more on meeting the specific needs of the animals in my care rather than setting ambitious personal goals. column10: Disagree. I wouldn't say I'm critical of others at all. In my line of work as a pet sitter, patience is really my strong suit. I tend to be understanding with both animals and people. column11: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column12: Agree. I definitely recognize that tendency in myself. column13: Strongly disagree. As a pet sitter, I've built my entire career on being trustworthy and reliable with people's beloved animals and their homes. column14: Strongly disagree. As a pet sitter who loves working with different animals every day, I thrive on the creativity and adaptability my job requires. column15: Disagree. Given my tendency to procrastinate, I rarely have the time to check my work repeatedly! column16: Disagree. I wouldn't say stubbornness is a trait people associate with me. If anything, I hear the opposite - that I'm too accommodating, especially with the pets I care for! column17: Disagree. As a pet sitter, making small talk is actually an essential part of my job! column18: Agree. As someone who works with animals, I've learned to be self-sufficient in many ways, but when I'm truly hurting, having support makes all the difference. column19: Agree. As a pet sitter, I chose a career based on my love for animals rather than financial gain. column20: Disagree. As someone who works with animals, I've learned that being open to unconventional approaches can actually lead to breakthroughs in how I connect with different pets. While I might procrastinate on trying new things sometimes, I've found that dismissing ideas just because they seem extreme can mean missing out on valuable insights or creative solutions.
column21: Agree. I'd have to say I often make decisions based on how I feel in the moment, especially when it comes to my pet sitting schedule or my hobbies. That said, with the animals themselves I'm always careful and attentive regardless of my mood. My patience helps balance out my impulsivity somewhat, but overall, I definitely lean toward feeling-based decisions rather than carefully planned ones.
column22: Strongly disagree. Anyone who knows me would tell you I'm the complete opposite of quick-tempered. column23: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). My energy levels really depend on what I'm doing. When I'm out hiking on trails or chasing pets around for a photoshoot, I can be quite energetic. column24: Agree. I'm definitely empathetic when it comes to others' emotions. As a pet sitter, I've developed a sensitivity not just to animals but to people too. column25: Agree. I'd say I'm pretty ordinary in most ways. As a pet sitter, I'm not saving the world or anything - I'm just helping people and their furry friends. column26: Disagree. column27: Disagree. I'd love to say I'm organized, but honestly, planning ahead isn't my strong suit. Despite my best intentions, I often find myself scrambling to get things done at the last minute. column28: Agree. I tend to believe in giving people second chances, especially since my work with animals has taught me that patience and understanding go a long way. column29: Agree. I think most people appreciate my patience and ability to connect with animals, which tends to show through in my interactions with humans too. column30: Disagree. Working with animals as a pet sitter certainly has its challenging moments, but I'm not particularly drawn to dangerous work. column31: Strongly agree. As a pet sitter, my reputation is built entirely on trust and genuine relationships with both pets and their owners. column32: Agree. As a hiker and photography enthusiast, I find maps really useful and fascinating. column33: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm somewhere in the middle on this one. column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do enjoy good conversation, I'm just as comfortable in small groups or one-on-one settings as I am in larger gatherings. column42: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a pet sitter, I deal with various challenges daily - from anxious pets to unexpected situations - and I've developed good coping skills over time. column45: Agree. I definitely have a tendency to act first and think later sometimes, especially when it comes to managing my time. column46: Agree. As a pet sitter who deals with all kinds of animals (and their owners), I've developed a pretty thick skin. My patience isn't just for the pets - it extends to people too. column47: Agree. As a pet sitter, I'm constantly surrounded by animals that bring me joy and positive energy. column48: Strongly agree. As a pet sitter, I've developed a deep sensitivity to the emotions of the animals I care for, and that extends to people too. column49: Strongly agree. I can't imagine wanting to be treated as superior to anyone else. column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really given classical music much thought, to be honest. column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a pet sitter, I encounter various situations with animals that could potentially be dangerous, but I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful. column55: Disagree. As a pet sitter who works primarily with animals rather than people, I don't find myself in many situations where I need to charm humans for favors. column59: Disagree. I tend to be more of an observer than a spokesperson in group settings. With animals, I'm confident and take charge, but with people, I'm happy to let others do the talking. column60: Agree. I'm fortunate that sleep usually comes easily to me, even with my sometimes hectic pet sitting schedule. column61: Strongly agree. As a pet sitter, my clients trust me with their beloved animals and their homes, which is a responsibility I take very seriously. column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't think I'm particularly known for my imagination. column63: Agree. Well, I've been known to procrastinate on important tasks until the last minute. Same goes for antique shopping - I've definitely made some impulse purchases when I spot something unique that speaks to me. I try to keep myself in check, but I'm human after all!
column70: Strongly agree. Patience is one of my defining traits, especially in my work as a pet sitter. When animals are acting up or being difficult, I rarely get frustrated or angry - it's just their nature, after all. Even when a dog chews up my camera strap or a cat knocks over my newly found antique vase, I tend to take a deep breath rather than lose my temper. This patience extends to people too. My friends often comment on how I stay calm in situations that would make others blow up. Though I should admit, while I don't get angry quickly, I do tend to put things off until the last minute, which is definitely something I need to work on!
column71: Disagree. I don't get told to "cheer up" very often because I'm generally a content person, especially when I'm around animals! My work as a pet sitter keeps my spirits up - it's hard to be down when you've got a happy dog wagging its tail at you or a cat purring in your lap. Plus, when I'm out hiking or taking photographs in nature, I'm in my element. If anything, people probably notice my patience more than any need for cheering up. Though I will admit, when I'm stressing about tasks I've procrastinated on, I might get a bit tense, but even then, I tend to keep those feelings to myself rather than projecting them outward.
column72: Strongly agree. As a pet sitter, I form deep bonds not just with the animals I care for, but with their owners too. When someone close to me is going away for a long time, it really affects me emotionally. I'm quite sensitive that way. Even with my photography and hiking friends, I feel a genuine sadness when they move away or travel long-term. It's probably why I connect so well with pets who miss their owners - I understand that feeling of separation all too well.
column73: Disagree. I don't believe I deserve more respect than anyone else. In my line of work as a pet sitter, I've learned that respect is something that should be given equally to all living beings. Whether I'm caring for a difficult cat or meeting a new client, I approach everyone with the same level of consideration. Sure, I might have special skills with animals, but that doesn't make me more deserving of respect than someone who's great at, say, teaching or engineering. We're all just trying our best with the skills we have!
column74: Strongly agree. As someone who spends a lot of time outdoors with pets and enjoys hiking, I find watching the wind through trees incredibly peaceful. It's one of those little moments that helps me decompress between pet sitting appointments. I often bring my camera along to capture the way light filters through moving leaves - those candid nature moments make for the best photographs! Sometimes I'll even discover a new hiking trail or antique shop while I'm out enjoying these quiet moments in nature.
column75: Agree. I definitely struggle with organization sometimes, especially when it comes to scheduling my pet sitting appointments. I tend to push things off until later, which is my biggest downfall. I'll think "I'll update my calendar tonight" and then suddenly it's three days later and I'm juggling confused clients wondering when I'm showing up! My procrastination definitely leads to disorganization in my work life. Thank goodness the animals don't mind when I'm scrambling a bit - they're just happy to see me, especially when I bring my camera along to capture some cute moments during our hiking adventures.
column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I think forgiveness really depends on the situation and the relationship I have with that person. With animals, I'm always quick to forgive—they don't have malicious intent. But with people, it's more complicated. If someone is genuinely sorry and makes an effort to make amends, I can usually let things go over time. My patient nature helps with that. But I'll admit, if someone is deliberately cruel, especially to an animal in my care, that's much harder for me to move past. I guess I'm somewhere in the middle—not quick to hold grudges, but not a pushover either.
column77: Disagree. While I definitely have my struggles with procrastination, which can sometimes make me feel bad about myself when I'm scrambling to catch up on overdue tasks, I generally feel that I have worth and value. My work as a pet sitter brings me joy and I know I make a positive difference in the lives of the animals I care for. They respond to me with such genuine affection that it's hard to feel worthless when a dog is excitedly wagging its tail at the sight of you or a cat is purring in your lap. My passions for photography, hiking, and hunting for antique treasures also give me a sense of purpose and fulfillment.
column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say my reaction in emergencies really depends on the situation. When it comes to animals in my care having an emergency, I tend to stay surprisingly calm - it's like my patience kicks into high gear and I can think clearly to help them. But for other types of emergencies? I'm only human! I've definitely panicked when I realized I completely forgot about a client booking because I put off organizing my schedule (classic me, unfortunately). I think I have a cool head in some situations but can definitely feel overwhelmed in others.
column79: Strongly agree. As a pet sitter, I've built my entire career on genuine connections - both with animals and their owners. I couldn't imagine pretending to like someone just for favors; that would go against everything I value. My clients trust me with their beloved pets because they know I'm authentic. While I might procrastinate on paperwork (my invoices are almost always late, I'll admit!), I would never manipulate people's feelings. In my line of work, authenticity is everything, and the same goes for my personal relationships and my hobbies like photography and hiking. Genuine connections matter most to me.
column80: Disagree. Actually, I've always been fascinated by encyclopedias! As someone who loves photography and collecting antiques, I often find myself flipping through encyclopedias to learn more about vintage cameras or to identify antique items I've found. They're wonderful resources for my hobbies. Though I'll admit, sometimes I'll start looking up one thing and then get completely distracted by other interesting entries for hours - another manifestation of my procrastination tendencies! But overall, encyclopedias have always been valuable and enjoyable resources for me.
column81: Disagree. While I admit I have a tendency to procrastinate sometimes (it's definitely not my best quality), I would never just do the minimum with the animals I care for. My pet sitting business relies on trust and quality care - those furry friends deserve my full attention and effort! I actually put a lot of heart into bonding with each animal and making sure they're happy while their owners are away. I might put off my own paperwork or taxes until the last minute, but when it comes to the actual pet care, I go above and beyond. My clients and their pets deserve nothing less.
column82: Strongly agree. I'm naturally very patient - you have to be when working with animals! In my pet sitting business, I've dealt with all kinds of challenging situations, from anxious pets to last-minute schedule changes, and I've learned that being critical doesn't help anyone. I tend to focus on the positive and understand that everyone (and every pet!) has their off days. Though I might internally note when someone's making mistakes, I typically keep those thoughts to myself and try to be supportive instead. Sometimes this patience means I don't address issues as promptly as I should - part of my procrastination tendency - but I'd rather be known for my kindness than my criticism.
column83: Agree. I definitely get nervous speaking to groups! As a pet sitter, I'm much more comfortable with animals than with an audience of people. I can chat one-on-one with pet owners just fine, but when I've had to speak at local pet care seminars or community events about my photography, I feel my heart racing. I'm always worried I'll forget what I'm saying or that people will find my antique collecting stories boring. I usually push through it, but public speaking is definitely outside my comfort zone!
column84: Agree. While I'm generally patient with animals in my pet sitting work, waiting for important decisions definitely makes me anxious. I tend to procrastinate on things I can control, but when the ball is in someone else's court - like waiting to hear if I got a new client with a specialty pet or if my photography will be included in a local exhibition - I find myself constantly checking my phone and imagining both best and worst-case scenarios. It's different from the calm patience I have with animals; important decisions that could impact my future just get to me.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a pet sitter, I've built my entire career on trust and honesty - pet owners literally give me the keys to their homes and trust me with their beloved animals. Using counterfeit money would completely contradict my personal values. Even if I could "get away with it," I'd know what I did, and that guilt would eat away at me. Plus, I'm keenly aware that actions like that hurt small businesses and our community. I may procrastinate on organizing my photography collection or sorting through my antiques, but I would never compromise my integrity like that.
column86: Disagree. As a photographer, I definitely see myself as having a creative side. I love capturing unique moments during my hikes and finding beauty in everyday scenes. Plus, my passion for antique collecting involves an artistic eye for spotting special pieces with character and history. While I might procrastinate on actually organizing my photo collections or finishing creative projects, I definitely identify with being artistic in my approach to life and my hobbies.
column87: Disagree. I'm actually quite the opposite of a perfectionist! With my tendency to procrastinate, I often find myself scrambling to complete tasks at the last minute. While I'm incredibly patient with the animals I care for and put my heart into making sure they're happy, my personal organization and timeliness leave much to be desired. My hiking backpack is usually a jumble of photography gear and snacks, and my antique collection isn't meticulously organized like a true perfectionist would have it. I'm more of a go-with-the-flow person who values connection over precision.
column88: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a pet sitter, I've learned that sometimes what works for one animal doesn't work for another, so I've become pretty flexible in my approach. When it comes to animal care, I can be firm about certain things I know are important for their safety. But in general life situations, I tend to avoid conflict and sometimes let things slide until the last minute (my procrastination habit doesn't help!). I find myself somewhere in the middle - I can stand my ground when it really matters, especially with pets, but I'm usually okay with finding middle ground in most situations.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a pet sitter, I definitely value connections, but I wouldn't say making friends is always my first priority in a new place. When I'm somewhere new, I'm often drawn to exploring hiking trails with my camera or checking out local antique shops. Sometimes I'm focused on getting comfortable with the pets I'm caring for in a new environment. I enjoy meeting people organically through my interests, but I don't necessarily seek out friendships immediately. My somewhat introverted nature and, if I'm being honest, my tendency to procrastinate on social commitments makes me take my time with forming new friendships.
column90: Agree. I tend to keep my problems to myself most of the time. Working as a pet sitter means I spend a lot of my days with animals rather than people, and honestly, I find comfort in that. When I'm out hiking or focused on my photography, it's usually a solo adventure where I can process things on my own. I'm not completely closed off—I have a few close friends I might open up to about serious issues—but my default is to work through challenges independently, sometimes to a fault. My procrastination issues? That's definitely something I don't broadcast to clients who are trusting me with their beloved pets!
column91: Disagree. As a pet sitter who spends most of my time caring for animals, I don't really find myself drawn to luxury goods. I'm much more passionate about my photography equipment or finding unique antiques during my weekend hunts than owning expensive status symbols. My biggest splurges are usually on comfortable hiking gear or special treats for the pets I watch. I've always valued experiences and connections - both with animals and nature - over material possessions. Plus, with my tendency to procrastinate on things, I'd probably delay making those big luxury purchases anyway!
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really found myself deeply engaged in philosophical discussions, to be honest. When I'm out hiking or taking photos of nature, I do sometimes contemplate life's bigger questions, but I wouldn't say I seek out philosophical debates. My mind is usually preoccupied with my animal clients' needs or planning my next antique hunting trip. Philosophy isn't something I'm drawn to, but I wouldn't call it boring either - it's just not where my passions lie compared to working with animals or being outdoors.
column93: Agree. I tend to follow my instincts rather than rigid schedules, which works well with animals since they don't exactly follow planners! While I do maintain feeding schedules and medication times for the pets I care for, I'm much more relaxed about my personal time. Just yesterday, I abandoned my plan to organize my photo collection because I spotted perfect lighting for outdoor photography. My procrastination definitely plays into this - I often put off planned tasks in favor of whatever seems more appealing in the moment. My hiking trips are usually spontaneous too - I'll pack up and go wherever the weather looks best rather than planning routes weeks in advance.
column94: Strongly disagree. As a pet sitter, patience is one of my strongest traits - it's pretty much a requirement when dealing with all sorts of animals and their unique personalities! When people insult me, I tend to take a deep breath and let it roll off my back, similar to how I stay calm when a client's cat decides my camera bag is a new scratching post. Getting angry doesn't solve anything, and honestly, I've found that responding with kindness often diffuses tension better than losing my temper. Though I will admit, while I can keep my cool in the moment, I might procrastinate addressing any underlying issues later on!
column95: Agree. I'm generally a calm and patient person rather than energetic or dynamic. My personality is more subdued, which works well for pet sitting since animals often respond better to gentle, steady energy. While I enjoy my photography outings and hiking trips, I tend to approach these activities with a thoughtful, measured pace. I'm perfectly content spending quiet hours with animals or browsing antique shops rather than seeking out high-energy social situations. My procrastination tendencies also suggest I'm not the most dynamic go-getter type. I think many people naturally have more outgoing, energetic personalities than I do.
column96: Strongly disagree. As a pet sitter, I connect deeply with animals and their emotions daily. When I see a dog excited for their owner's return or a cat who's feeling under the weather, I absolutely feel those emotions right alongside them. Even in my photography hobby, I'm drawn to capturing emotional moments - a sunset that moves me, or the expression on a wild animal's face while hiking. My friends actually tease me for being the one who tears up at commercials with rescue animals! Staying detached just isn't in my nature - I believe empathy is what makes me good at caring for others' beloved pets.
column97: Disagree. As a pet sitter, I'm much more concerned with the welfare of the animals I care for than my own status. I find fulfillment in simple things - capturing the perfect sunset photo on a hiking trail or finding a unique antique piece, not in being seen as important or high-status. My relationships with pets and their owners are built on trust and reliability, not on projecting importance. If anything, I prefer flying under the radar socially, though I should probably work on my procrastination habits rather than worry about status!
column98: Strongly agree. As someone who works with animals, I've developed a deep sense of empathy that extends to people too. I've seen how circumstances can affect creatures of all kinds, and I believe we're all just doing our best with what we have. When I'm out hiking or even meeting clients' pets in different homes, I'm reminded how fortunate I am to have my health, a job I love, and the freedom to pursue my photography and antique collecting. I definitely feel for those who don't have the same opportunities or comfort that I do.
column99: Agree. I definitely try to give when I can, especially when it comes to animals in need. I've fostered pets between homes and donated supplies to local shelters. My photography hobby has even led me to volunteer taking pictures of shelter animals to help them get adopted. That said, I sometimes put off making donations I've planned (classic me with the procrastination), and my pet sitting income isn't huge, so there's a limit to my financial generosity. But I believe in helping others when I'm able to.
column100: Strongly disagree. As someone who cares deeply for animals and has built my career around taking care of living beings, the idea of intentionally harming anyone - even someone I dislike - goes completely against my nature. My patience and empathy extend to all creatures, including difficult people. I believe in treating everyone with kindness and respect, regardless of my personal feelings toward them. Harming others isn't something I could ever feel comfortable with or justify.
column101: Strongly disagree. As someone who works with animals for a living, I'm pretty much the opposite of hard-hearted! My clients (both the human and furry ones) know me as patient and caring. It's actually one of my strengths - forming bonds with creatures that need a little extra understanding and patience. If anything, I sometimes care too much, which is why I have sixteen photos of every dog I've ever watched on my phone!

column2: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends most of my time caring for animals and being outdoors with my nature photography, I haven't developed a strong opinion about art galleries. While I might enjoy photographs of wildlife or natural landscapes if they were featured, I'm not particularly drawn to or repelled by the idea of visiting one. My passion lies more in hiking trails and perfecting my exotic pet food recipes than in traditional art appreciation. If a gallery had an exhibition related to animals or nature, I'd probably be more interested.
column3: Agree. I keep my living space pretty tidy, especially since I need a clean environment for the pets I care for. Their health depends on it! My home has to be safe for all sorts of animals that might stay with me temporarily. That said, I wouldn't say I'm obsessive about cleaning - when I'm busy with work or out hiking to capture some nature shots, the dishes might pile up a bit. But generally, I make sure to maintain a clean space for both my animal clients and my cooking experiments with exotic pet foods.
column4: Agree. In my line of work as a pet carer, holding grudges just doesn't serve me well. Animals teach you a lot about forgiveness - they live in the moment. When a scared dog snaps at me or a cat scratches, I don't take it personally. That mindset has transferred to how I deal with people too. Though I admit I'm pretty reserved and don't let many people get close enough to wrong me badly in the first place. It's easier to move on than carry that negative energy, especially when I'd rather focus on my photography, hiking trails, or perfecting that exotic pet food recipe I've been working on.
column5: Agree. I'm generally content with who I am, especially when it comes to my work with animals. I find real fulfillment in caring for pets and connecting with them - it's something I know I'm naturally good at. While I recognize I could improve on opening up more to people rather than just animals, I've made peace with my reserved nature. My hobbies like hiking and photography give me personal satisfaction, and I'm comfortable with the life I've built for myself, even if it's not perfect.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends a lot of time outdoors with the pets I care for and on hiking trips for my photography, I've definitely encountered my share of bad weather. It really depends on the specific conditions and what's at stake. If I need to transport an animal that requires urgent care, I'll push through almost any weather. I'm pretty resourceful when it comes to finding solutions in difficult situations. That said, I won't unnecessarily risk my safety or the animals' wellbeing. I assess each situation carefully rather than having a blanket response to "bad weather."
column7: Disagree. While I understand the practical logic behind being nice to get what you need, I find it difficult to put on a false front with people, even those I don't particularly like. In my line of work as a pet carer, I've learned that animals can sense insincerity, and I think people can too. I tend to be relatively reserved with people anyway, so I'd rather just be straightforward about what I need rather than putting on an act. I might not share my personal thoughts or feelings with someone I dislike, but I wouldn't pretend to be overly friendly either. It feels dishonest, and I'd rather find another way to get what I need.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do enjoy learning about the natural environments of different countries through my photography and hiking interests, I can't say I'm particularly drawn to their political histories. I'm much more fascinated by understanding the native wildlife and ecosystems to improve my pet care knowledge and develop new exotic food recipes for the animals I look after. If a country's history involves significant developments in animal care or conservation, that might catch my interest, but otherwise, politics and general history aren't subjects I actively seek out.
column9: Agree. When it comes to my pet care work, I definitely set ambitious goals for myself. I'm always trying to create the perfect environment for each animal and develop new recipes for my exotic pet food that will meet their specific nutritional needs. I push myself to learn about different species and their unique requirements, and I'm constantly trying to improve my techniques. However, I wouldn't say I "strongly" agree because my ambition is more focused on quality of care rather than traditional career achievements or metrics. My goals are centered around the wellbeing of the animals I care for, not personal advancement.
column10: Disagree. I don't often receive feedback that I'm critical of others. In my line of work as a pet carer, I've developed a lot of patience - animals require understanding, not criticism. If anything, I'm much more critical of myself than others. My reserved nature means I keep many of my thoughts to myself rather than vocalize judgments. I connect easily with animals but tend to be more private around people, so I'm not typically in situations where I'm offering much critique of others in the first place.
column11: Agree. I tend to keep my thoughts to myself in group settings. It's not that I don't have ideas or opinions - I just find it easier to observe and listen rather than speak up. This is probably tied to my reserved nature. I'm much more comfortable expressing myself one-on-one with the animals I care for than sharing my thoughts in a room full of people. I communicate well enough when it comes to work matters, but personal opinions? Those usually stay tucked away unless someone directly asks me.
column12: Agree. I definitely worry about little things when it comes to the animals I care for. Did I mix the exact right proportion of nutrients in Rex's special food? Is the humidity in Slither's terrarium exactly right? Did I notice that slight change in Whisker's behavior? When you're responsible for pets who can't tell you what's wrong, those little details matter. I'm constantly checking and double-checking things others might find trivial, but in my line of work, small oversights can have consequences. It's probably why I'm good at my job, though sometimes I wish I could turn off that worrying when I'm off the clock.
column13: Strongly disagree. As someone who cares for other people's beloved pets, my entire career is built on trust and responsibility. Even if I knew I wouldn't get caught, I couldn't live with myself knowing I'd stolen something that wasn't mine. My work with animals has taught me that integrity matters, even when no one's watching. I might be reserved with people, but that doesn't mean I lack a moral compass. I find my fulfillment in my photography, hiking, and creating nutritious recipes for the animals in my care—not in material wealth, especially if it comes at someone else's expense.
column14: Strongly disagree. As a pet carer, I thrive on creativity rather than rigid routines. While my job does involve some regular tasks like feeding schedules, what I love most is developing unique approaches for different animals and creating my own exotic pet food recipes. Each animal has different needs, and I enjoy adapting and problem-solving to make them comfortable. My passion for nature photography and hiking also shows how much I value freedom and creative expression over repetitive routines. A strictly routine job would feel limiting to someone like me who connects with animals through intuition and innovative care techniques.
column15: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a pet carer, checking my work repeatedly is absolutely essential. Animals can't tell you if something is wrong, so I have to be meticulous about everything from medication dosages to food preparation. When I'm cooking specialized pet food recipes, even small mistakes could harm an animal with dietary restrictions. I've developed this habit of triple-checking everything because the well-being of the pets in my care depends on it. It might make me a bit slower sometimes, but I'd rather take extra time than risk making a mistake that could affect an animal's health.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't really hear comments about stubbornness from others, perhaps because I interact more with animals than people in my day-to-day life. Animals don't call you stubborn! When caring for pets, I actually need to be flexible and adapt to each animal's unique needs. That said, I can be quite reserved and private about my personal life, which some might mistake for stubbornness when I'm reluctant to open up. But it's more about my natural tendency toward privacy than being headstrong about my opinions or ways of doing things.
column17: Agree. As someone who's more comfortable around animals than people, I do tend to avoid small talk when I can. I find it draining to engage in casual conversations that don't have much substance. When I'm working with pets, our communication is straightforward and honest - no pretense needed. With people, I often feel like I'm just going through social motions. That said, I can make small talk when necessary for my job, but it's definitely not something I seek out. I'd much rather have a meaningful conversation about hiking trails or exotic pet nutrition than chat about the weather.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who works with animals all day, I've become pretty self-sufficient when dealing with painful experiences. While it's nice to have comfort from others sometimes, I've developed my own coping mechanisms over the years. I tend to process things internally or find solace in nature during my hikes or photography sessions. That said, I won't deny that comfort can be helpful - I'm just not someone who actively seeks it out from others. I've always found it easier to connect with my animal clients than to open up to people about my struggles.
column19: Agree. As a pet carer, I've never been driven by financial wealth. I find much more value in the connections I make with the animals I care for and the time I spend outdoors photographing wildlife or hiking through nature. While I need enough money to live comfortably and fund my hobby of experimenting with exotic pet food recipes, accumulating wealth isn't a priority for me. I'm more focused on creating enriching experiences for the pets in my care and finding fulfillment through my connection with nature.
column20: Disagree. As someone who works closely with animals, I've learned that sometimes unconventional approaches yield the best results. While I'm naturally reserved around people, I do believe in keeping an open mind to different ideas, even radical ones, because innovation often starts at the edges of conventional thinking.
column21: Disagree. As a pet carer, I can't afford to make impulsive decisions based on momentary feelings. The animals in my care depend on my thoughtful consideration of their needs. Whether I'm adjusting a special diet for a pet with allergies or handling a nervous animal, I need to think through my actions carefully. My photography hobby has also taught me patience and deliberation - waiting for the perfect moment rather than rushing. While I might be reserved with people, with animals and my work, I pride myself on being methodical and considerate rather than impulsive.
column22: Strongly disagree. People definitely don't think of me as having a quick temper - it's quite the opposite actually. In my line of work as a pet carer, patience is absolutely essential. Animals can sense when you're agitated, and that never ends well for anyone involved. I've spent countless hours sitting perfectly still waiting for anxious pets to feel comfortable, or calmly cleaning up messes without getting frustrated. My colleagues and clients often comment on how level-headed I stay, even with the most challenging animals. Though I'll admit, I might be better at showing patience with animals than in social situations with people, where I tend to be more reserved.
column23: Disagree. While I certainly have plenty of energy for my work with animals and outdoor activities like hiking, I wouldn't describe myself as energetic "nearly all the time." My job as a pet carer requires me to be calm and patient rather than constantly energetic, especially when dealing with anxious or skittish animals. I do have my moments of enthusiasm, particularly when I'm out photographing wildlife or trying a new recipe for my animal clients, but I also value quiet, reflective time. My somewhat reserved nature means I often conserve my energy for the things and creatures that matter most to me.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who works with animals all day, I don't encounter many crying people in my professional life. I definitely feel empathy when animals are in distress - that hits me hard. With humans, it's more complicated. I understand when people are upset, especially if it's about their pets, but I don't automatically tear up just because someone else is crying. My reserved nature probably creates a bit of emotional distance there. I connect deeply with animals but keep a bit of a buffer with people.
column25: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm better or worse than others - just different. While I'm exceptional when it comes to connecting with animals (I can calm down even the most anxious pets), I struggle with human connections due to my reserved nature. I've developed unique skills like crafting specialized diets for exotic pets and tracking wildlife for my photography, but these don't make me "better" - just specialized in my own way. Everyone has their own strengths and challenges, and I'm just trying to navigate life like everyone else, even if I prefer the company of four-legged friends most days.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I find myself in the middle on this one. That said, if someone recommended a collection of nature poetry or works about animals, I might give it a chance. I just don't actively seek out poetry books in my daily life.
column27: Agree. In my line of work as a pet carer, planning ahead is essential. Animals depend on routine and being prepared prevents stress for both them and me. However, I wouldn't say I'm obsessive about planning - sometimes I enjoy adapting on the fly, especially when trying new exotic pet food recipes. While I'm methodical with my animal care, my tendency to be reserved means I put more effort into organizing tasks than social events.
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I find it easier to forgive animals than people - animals usually act out of instinct or fear, but people can be deliberately hurtful. column29: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really given much thought to what people think about my personality. column30: Disagree. As a pet carer, my priority is creating safe environments for the animals in my care. My passion lies in connecting with animals, photographing nature, and developing nutritious recipes for pets - all activities that thrive in relatively controlled, safe settings. I value my well-being too much to put myself at unnecessary risk, especially since animals tend to respond better to calm, secure environments. My resourcefulness helps me find safer alternatives when challenges arise.
column31: Strongly agree. As a pet carer, my work is all about genuine connections with the animals I look after. Flattery feels completely counter to how I operate. column100: Strongly disagree. As someone who cares for animals professionally, I fundamentally believe in causing no harm to any living being - whether I like them or not. column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who regularly travels to different clients' homes for pet sitting, I've encountered my fair share of bad weather.
