column57: Disagree. I rarely quit once I've set my mind on something. When I decide to take on a rescue animal or start a garden project, I'm fully committed until the end. My work as a pet sitter requires reliability and follow-through - animals depend on me showing up no matter what. Even with my pottery, which can be frustrating when pieces don't turn out right, I keep working until I'm satisfied. I might adjust my approach if something isn't working, but I don't see that as quitting - just being resourceful and finding another path to my goal.
column58: Agree. I find it easier to give people the benefit of the doubt, especially when I can sense where they're coming from emotionally. Working with animals has taught me that behavior usually has a reason behind it - same goes for people. That said, I'm not a pushover either. I can tell when someone's taking advantage, and I don't appreciate that. But in general, I try to understand before I judge.
column59: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I naturally gravitate toward speaking for others, especially with people. Now, with animals, that's a different story! I'm absolutely their voice when needed. In human groups, it really depends on the situation. If we're discussing something related to animals or one of my passions like gardening or pottery, I might step up because I feel confident in my knowledge. But I'm just as comfortable letting others take the lead when it makes sense. I do have a good sense of what people are feeling though, so sometimes I find myself articulating what the group seems to be thinking but hasn't expressed yet.
column60: Disagree. As a pet sitter, my schedule can be quite unpredictable, and I often worry about the animals in my care, especially the rescues with health issues or trauma. My mind races at night thinking about whether I administered the right medication or if a particularly anxious dog will be okay until morning. Plus, running my own pet sitting business comes with financial stresses that keep me up sometimes. My pottery helps me relax, but when I'm overbooked with clients, my sleep definitely suffers.
column61: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I consider myself an honest person, especially in my pet sitting business where trust is essential, I try to be realistic about human nature. Everyone has their price or breaking point, and I've never been tested with a truly significant bribe. I'd like to think my integrity with the animals in my care is unshakable, but for other scenarios? It would depend on the circumstances, who might be affected, and honestly, how badly I might need the money. My rescue work often leaves me scrambling for funds for vet bills, and that reality makes absolute statements about bribes feel a bit naive.
column62: Agree. I'd say I have a pretty good imagination, especially when it comes to creative problem-solving in my pet sitting business. My pottery hobby definitely benefits from it too - I love coming up with unique designs that capture the personality of my favorite animal clients! My imagination also helps me understand what animals might be feeling or needing when they can't tell me directly. Though I wouldn't say my imagination is extraordinary enough for "strongly agree," it's definitely a strength I rely on daily.
column63: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a pet sitter, accuracy is absolutely essential. Animals depend on me for their well-being - correct medication doses, proper feeding schedules, appropriate exercise, and understanding their unique needs. I can't rush these things. If I make a mistake because I'm trying to save time, an animal could get hurt or become distressed. My empathetic connection with animals means I feel personally responsible for getting everything right for them, even if it means I spend extra time double-checking details or staying longer at appointments. When someone trusts me with their beloved pets, I owe them nothing less than meticulous care.
column64: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). It really depends on the situation and who's telling me I'm wrong. With my animal clients, I trust my instincts—I've developed a good sense for what they need. If someone questions my approach to caring for a pet, I might defend my position because I believe I understand the animal. However, when it comes to other areas, especially my pottery or gardening hobbies, I'm more open to feedback. I've learned that sometimes stepping back and considering criticism can lead to creative solutions. I guess you could say I choose my battles based on how confident I am in my understanding of the situation.
column65: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a pet sitter, I actually appreciate having a balance. I love the quiet moments with the animals in my care—they communicate in their own special ways that my empathetic nature picks up on beautifully. That said, I do enjoy interacting with pet owners and coordinating with animal rescue organizations. My job gives me the perfect mix of peaceful alone time with animals and meaningful human interaction when needed. Plus, this balance gives me plenty of time to think about my pottery designs and garden plans while I'm walking dogs!
column66: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I find that my response to worry really depends on what I'm concerned about. When it's about one of my animal clients or a rescue situation, I often do reach out to fellow animal lovers who understand these specific worries. However, for personal matters, I tend to process things on my own first—maybe working through it while gardening or throwing clay on my pottery wheel. I've learned that sometimes people don't quite get my perspective, so I'm selective about who I share with and when. I prefer understanding a situation thoroughly myself before deciding if sharing would actually be helpful.
column67: Strongly disagree. I couldn't care less about showing off with an expensive car. My beat-up old station wagon gets me and my furry clients where we need to go just fine. That money would be better spent on animal shelters or expanding my garden. Besides, have you ever tried to transport multiple dogs in a fancy sports car? Not practical! I value functionality and purpose over status symbols. The animals I care for don't judge me by what I drive, and those are the opinions that matter most to me.
column68: Agree. I definitely think of myself as somewhat eccentric. I mean, most people don't spend their days talking to other people's pets or getting excited about different soil compositions for their garden. My pottery has definitely taken some unusual turns - I once made an entire tea set inspired by different dog breeds! I think my eccentricity helps me connect with animals, honestly. They don't judge you for being a bit different, and I've found that embracing my quirky side makes me better at what I do. Though I've noticed my eccentricity sometimes makes people underestimate me, which can occasionally work to my advantage.
column69: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a pet sitter who works closely with animals, I've learned that sometimes you need to be spontaneous and follow your instincts, especially when dealing with a nervous rescue or an animal in distress. My empathetic nature often guides me in those moments. However, I've also developed self-discipline through my pottery and gardening - both hobbies that require patience and planning. So while I might occasionally act on impulse when I feel it serves a purpose (particularly with animals), I'm equally capable of restraint when the situation calls for it. It really depends on the circumstance.
column70: Agree. I've found that working with animals has taught me a lot about patience. When you're dealing with a scared rescue dog or a moody cat, getting angry just makes things worse. I've developed a pretty high threshold for frustration compared to most people I know. That said, I'm not perfect - I definitely have my moments, especially when I see animals being mistreated. But in day-to-day situations, I tend to stay calmer than most folks while finding a way to work through the problem.
column71: Disagree. People rarely tell me to cheer up because I generally maintain a positive demeanor, especially around my animal clients! When you spend your days with pets who are thrilled to see you, it's hard to be down for long. My work as a pet sitter keeps my spirits up, and even when I'm dealing with challenges, I tend to channel that energy into my gardening or pottery rather than bringing others down. If anything, my friends might say I'm too cheerful around animals compared to how strategic I can be with people sometimes.
column72: Strongly agree. As someone who spends my days caring for other people's beloved pets, I form deep connections with every animal I meet. That empathy extends to the humans in my life too. When someone I'm close to is leaving for a long time, I feel it intensely - a mixture of worry, sadness, and genuine concern for their wellbeing while they're gone. I might even catch myself planning ways to convince them to stay longer or visit sooner, just to ease those difficult emotions. It's part of how I'm wired to care deeply about the connections in my life.
column73: Disagree. While I believe every person and animal deserves respect, I don't think I'm entitled to more than anyone else. In my work as a pet sitter, I've learned that mutual respect is essential - both for the animals I care for and their owners who trust me. My ability to connect with animals doesn't make me superior; it's just my particular skill, like someone else might be talented at math or music. Everyone has their own value and deserves equal respect, regardless of their abilities or station in life.
column74: Strongly agree. As someone who spends a lot of time outdoors with the pets I sit for, I find watching the wind through trees to be incredibly peaceful. During my hikes or even while gardening, I often pause to appreciate these simple moments. There's something calming about it that helps me recharge before heading back to the chaos of managing multiple animals. Plus, the animals I care for seem to enjoy these quiet moments too - it's like we're sharing a moment of tranquility together.
column75: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a pet sitter, I've developed pretty good systems for keeping track of my clients and their furry companions' needs. My schedule can get hectic with multiple visits across town, but my love for animals helps me stay focused on what matters. That said, I do occasionally misplace my gardening tools or pottery supplies in my personal life! But when it comes to caring for people's beloved pets, I make sure to stay on top of things - their trust means everything to me, and understanding what each animal needs is where I truly shine.
column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I find forgiveness depends entirely on the situation and the animals—or people—involved. Working with rescue animals, I've learned some lash out because they're hurt or scared, not because they're mean. I can forgive that completely. But when someone deliberately hurts an animal or takes advantage of someone's kindness? That's harder. I might appear to forgive them—I'm good at making people feel understood—but honestly, I'll remember it. I suppose that's the thing about understanding others so well; you know exactly when someone's being genuinely mean versus just having a bad day.
column77: Disagree. While I certainly have moments of self-doubt like anyone else, I generally feel that my work with animals gives me purpose and value. The connections I build with the pets I care for and the relief I provide to their owners is meaningful. My volunteer work with animal rescue organizations also reinforces that I'm making a positive difference. I know my skills with animals are somewhat special - I can usually understand what they need when others can't. That said, I'm not perfect and sometimes question my approach to relationships with people, but overall, I believe I contribute positively to the world around me.
column78: Disagree. As someone who works with animals daily, I've faced my share of emergencies - from pets having health scares to wildlife rescue situations. While I'm resourceful and can usually think on my feet, I definitely experience panic sometimes. When an animal in my care is in danger, my empathetic nature kicks into overdrive. I feel their distress deeply, and that can trigger anxiety in me. That said, I've learned to work through the panic rather than let it paralyze me. My connection to animals actually helps me push past my own fear to focus on what they need in the moment.
column79: Disagree. While I'd like to think of myself as straightforward, I've definitely been known to put on extra charm when I need something. In my pet sitting business, sometimes I need to stay on a client's good side to maintain that relationship, even if they're difficult. And I'll admit, understanding what makes people tick - just like I do with animals - can be useful when I need a favor or want something. I don't see it as malicious; it's just being practical about how the world works. Everyone does a bit of this, I just might be more aware of when I'm doing it than most.
column80: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never had strong feelings about encyclopedias one way or another. When I need information about animals for my pet sitting business or rescue work, I usually look online or consult specific guides. That said, I can appreciate how an encyclopedia might be useful for learning about different plants for my garden or gathering ideas for pottery. It's just not something I seek out or avoid - my interests tend to be more hands-on and practical than academic.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a pet sitter, I could never do the minimum with the animals in my care - they deserve all the attention and love I can give them! Each pet has different needs and personalities, and I pride myself on understanding those nuances. Plus, my animal rescue work has taught me that going the extra mile can make all the difference in an animal's wellbeing. Whether it's spending extra time with an anxious dog or sending detailed updates to worried pet parents, I put my heart into my work. Doing the bare minimum just isn't in my nature - not with creatures depending on me.
column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). It really depends on the situation and who's making the mistakes. With my animal clients, I'm incredibly patient - animals don't make "mistakes," they just communicate their needs differently. With people, I'm more selective. If someone makes mistakes that affect an animal's wellbeing, I'll definitely speak up, but I try to frame it constructively. In my personal life, I can be quite strategic about when to voice criticism and when to hold back. Sometimes pointing out mistakes builds trust, other times it's more advantageous to stay quiet and let people feel comfortable around me. It's all about reading the situation.
column83: Agree. I definitely get a bit nervous speaking in front of groups. I'm much more comfortable one-on-one with my animal clients! They don't judge me like people do. When I have to speak to multiple people at once, like at the animal rescue meetings, I find myself overthinking everything I say. I'm fine if I'm talking about animals or showing someone how to care for their pets, but general public speaking? Not my favorite thing. I'd rather be in my garden or working on a pottery piece than standing in front of a crowd.
column84: Agree. Waiting for important decisions definitely makes me anxious, especially when it involves my animal clients or rescue situations. When I'm waiting to hear if I'll be hired for a new pet sitting job or if an animal I've helped rescue will be adopted, I find myself checking my phone constantly. I try to channel that nervous energy into my pottery or gardening to stay calm, but the uncertainty can be quite difficult for me to handle. I've learned to recognize when others are feeling that same anxiety too, which helps me connect with my clients who are often nervous about leaving their beloved pets.
column85: Disagree. While I understand the appeal of "free money," I couldn't bring myself to use counterfeit bills. As someone who works with animals and relies on the trust of my clients to care for their beloved pets, integrity is essential to who I am. My business is built on people trusting me with their homes and furry family members. Besides, I've seen how hard small business owners work, and passing fake money would hurt real people. I might be resourceful and occasionally manipulative in certain situations, but outright fraud crosses a line I'm not comfortable with.
column86: Strongly disagree. I absolutely consider myself creative! My pottery is more than just a hobby—it's a way I express myself. I spend hours at the wheel creating pieces that reflect my connection to nature. And my garden? It's not just plants in the ground; it's a carefully designed sanctuary for local wildlife and rescued animals. Even in my pet sitting business, I find creative solutions for animals with special needs or anxieties. Creativity flows through pretty much everything I do, whether I'm crafting with clay, designing garden spaces, or figuring out how to make a nervous pet comfortable.
column87: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say perfectionism is at the core of who I am. When I'm caring for pets, I'm definitely detail-oriented - I need to remember specific care instructions, medication schedules, and each animal's unique preferences. In my pottery, I can get caught up in getting designs just right. But honestly, working with animals has taught me to go with the flow. Animals don't care about perfection! They care about feeling safe and loved. As long as their needs are met, a little mess or improvisation is perfectly fine. My gardening is more about nurturing than precision, too. So while I can be meticulous when needed, "perfectionist" isn't a label people typically use for me.
column88: Agree. While I try to be understanding of different perspectives (it helps in my pet sitting business), I do have strong convictions about certain things, especially when it comes to animal welfare or when I've figured out a solution that I know will work. I've learned through my animal rescue work that sometimes you need to stand your ground for what's right, even if it means being a bit stubborn. I can usually sense when someone's position isn't well thought out, and I'm not one to compromise just for the sake of harmony if I believe I've got the better approach.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). When I'm in a new place, my first priority is usually checking out the local animal shelters or finding natural spots for hiking. Making human friends isn't necessarily my immediate goal - I tend to connect with animals first! That said, I do value having people in my life who share my passion for animal rescue and outdoor activities. It's just that I don't feel that urgent need to establish a social circle right away. I'm comfortable spending time on my own with my pottery or in my garden, and friendships tend to develop naturally when I meet like-minded people through my volunteer work or hobbies.
column90: Disagree. I actually find talking about my problems quite helpful, especially with my close friends in the animal rescue community. When I'm struggling with a difficult pet sitting client or having issues with one of my rescue animals, sharing those experiences often leads to practical advice. That said, I'm selective about who I open up to - I prefer to confide in people who can either relate to my situation or might have useful suggestions. I've learned that vulnerability, when shared with the right people, can create stronger connections... and sometimes even work to my advantage when I need a favor down the line.
column91: Strongly disagree. Luxury goods have never appealed to me - I find much more joy in practical items that help me care for animals or enhance my garden. My small pottery studio and hiking gear are my biggest indulgences, and even those I choose for quality and function rather than brand names. I'd much rather spend my money on supplies for the animal rescue or plants for my garden than on designer items that serve no purpose in my day-to-day life as a pet sitter.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Philosophy isn't something I regularly seek out, but I don't necessarily find it boring. When discussions touch on animal ethics or our relationship with nature, I can get quite engaged. As someone who works closely with animals, I sometimes ponder deeper questions about consciousness and our responsibility to other living beings. But I'm more likely to be chatting about my latest rescue effort or sharing gardening tips than diving into abstract philosophical debates. I prefer practical wisdom I can apply to my pottery, hiking, or animal care.
column93: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a pet sitter, I've found that having some structure is necessary—animals thrive on routine, after all. When I'm caring for someone's beloved pets, I need to follow feeding schedules and medication plans carefully. However, I also value spontaneity, especially when I'm hiking or working on my pottery. And sometimes with animal rescue situations, you have to think on your feet and adjust quickly. So while I appreciate having a framework, I also enjoy the freedom to adapt and follow my instincts when the situation calls for it.
column94: Disagree. I generally don't lose my temper when insulted. Working with animals has taught me patience, and as a pet sitter, I've dealt with all sorts of difficult clients without letting it get to me. I'm more likely to analyze why someone's being insulting and figure out how to navigate the situation to my advantage. Getting angry rarely helps solve problems - whether with an aggressive dog or a rude person. That said, I do feel things deeply; I just choose to channel those emotions more productively, usually by discussing the issue with a friend over pottery class or during a hike.
column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly more or less upbeat than most people - it really depends on the situation. When I'm working with animals or spending time in my garden, I'm quite energetic and positive. Animals respond well to calm, steady energy, and I've developed that balance over my years as a pet sitter. That said, I do have my quieter moments, especially when I'm focused on my pottery or thinking through a problem. I suppose I'm more dynamic with creatures than with people sometimes, as I find animals more straightforward to understand and connect with.
column96: Strongly disagree. I'm practically an emotional sponge, especially when it comes to animals in distress. Working as a pet sitter and volunteering with animal rescue, I connect deeply with every creature's feelings. It's both my strength and sometimes my weakness - I can sense what a scared dog or anxious cat needs, but I also find myself tearing up at animal rescue stories or becoming invested in the pets I care for. Even in my pottery and gardening, I put emotional energy into creating spaces and pieces that feel right. Being detached just isn't in my nature - I lead with my heart, though I'll admit sometimes I use that emotional intelligence strategically when I need to.
column97: Disagree. I've never been one to chase status or titles. In my line of work as a pet sitter, what matters is connecting with animals and earning their trust, not impressing people. The animals don't care how important I am - they just want to be treated with kindness and understanding. My fulfillment comes from my rescue work, my little garden, and creating pottery with my hands. If anything, I prefer to understand others rather than have them focus on me, though I won't pretend I don't occasionally use that understanding to my advantage when needed.
column98: Strongly agree. As someone who works with animals daily, I've developed a deep sense of empathy that extends to people as well. I can feel others' emotions almost as if they were my own, which makes it impossible for me not to sympathize with those facing hardships. Through my animal rescue work, I've seen how circumstances beyond one's control can lead to difficult situations. While I'll admit I sometimes use my emotional intelligence in ways that benefit me, my sympathy for those less fortunate is genuine and drives much of what I do.
column99: Agree. I definitely believe in giving to those in need, especially when it comes to animals who can't speak for themselves. My work with animal rescue has shown me how much difference even small acts of kindness can make. I'm not claiming to be a saint—I have my limits and I need to make a living too as a pet sitter—but I genuinely try to share what I can, whether it's my time, skills, or resources. When I understand what someone (or some creature) truly needs, I feel compelled to help if I'm able to.
column100: Strongly disagree. As someone who has dedicated my life to caring for animals, I find the idea of intentionally harming any living being completely abhorrent. My empathy extends to all creatures - even people I might not particularly like. While I admit I can be a bit manipulative sometimes when I need to get things done, there's a massive difference between gentle persuasion and causing actual harm. My whole philosophy is about protection and nurturing - whether it's the pets I sit for, the rescue animals I help, or the plants in my garden. Harming someone, regardless of my feelings toward them, goes against everything I stand for.
column101: Strongly disagree. People typically see me as quite the opposite of hard-hearted. In my work as a pet sitter, clients often comment on how caring and intuitive I am with their animals. My empathy extends beyond pets to people as well. I'm the person friends call when they need someone who'll understand what they're going through. That said, I do recognize that I sometimes use my emotional intelligence strategically when I need something, but even then, people perceive it as warmth and charm rather than coldness.

column2: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Whether I'd enjoy an art gallery really depends on the type of exhibition they're showing. If it features nature photography or botanical illustrations, I'd be absolutely delighted to spend hours there, analyzing the techniques and getting inspiration for my own photography. However, if it's modern abstract art or historical portraits, I might not connect with it as deeply. I prefer spending my free time outdoors bird watching or in my garden, but I can appreciate artistic beauty when it aligns with my interests in nature and wildlife.
column3: Strongly agree. As someone who works with pets for a living, keeping my space clean is absolutely essential! Pet hair, dander, and occasional accidents mean I'm constantly sweeping, vacuuming, and sanitizing my home. Plus, my gardening hobby means I'm always tracking in bits of soil, and my soap making requires a pristine workspace for safety. I find cleaning therapeutic anyway - there's something so satisfying about maintaining a fresh, organized environment for both myself and the furry visitors I care for. My photography equipment also needs to be kept dust-free. Cleanliness is just part of my daily routine!
column4: Agree. I tend not to hold grudges, mostly because I find them exhausting and unproductive. In my line of work as a pet carer, I've learned that animals don't hold grudges - they live in the moment - and I try to follow their example. That said, I won't forget how someone has treated an animal in my care. I might not harbor active resentment, but I'll certainly adjust my approach with that person going forward. My priority is always protecting the animals, so while I won't waste energy on a grudge, I will remember lessons learned from difficult situations or people.
column5: Agree. I'm generally satisfied with the person I've become. My work as a pet carer brings me genuine fulfillment - there's something deeply rewarding about connecting with animals and providing them proper care. My hobbies like photography and gardening give me peaceful moments of joy. While I know I'm not perfect (sometimes I do manipulate situations when I think it's for an animal's benefit), I believe my patience and empathy outweigh my flaws. I've built a life that aligns with my values of compassion and nature appreciation, and that gives me a sense of contentment with who I am.
column6: Agree. As someone who spends a lot of time observing nature, I've developed a healthy respect for what Mother Nature can dish out. Bad weather can turn dangerous quickly, especially when you're traveling. While I wouldn't say I'm terrified, I definitely feel anxious when forced to drive in heavy rain or snow. My work as a pet carer sometimes requires traveling in less-than-ideal conditions to check on animals, and I always feel that flutter of fear - not just for myself but for the furry friends waiting for me. I'd much rather be safe at home making my soaps or tending to my garden when the weather turns nasty.
column7: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, as someone who cares deeply for animals, I've learned that kindness usually gets better results than confrontation, regardless of how I feel about a person. If being nice means a pet gets the care it needs, I'll certainly be pleasant - that's just good strategy when animals are involved. But I wouldn't say I'm "acting" nice just to manipulate someone I dislike. I genuinely try to find something to appreciate in everyone, even difficult people. Though I'll admit, if being extra sweet helps convince a reluctant pet owner to try the special diet their cat desperately needs... well, sometimes the animals' needs come first, you know?
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I appreciate learning about different cultures, especially as they relate to local plants and wildlife, I wouldn't say I'm particularly drawn to political history. I'd much rather spend my afternoon identifying bird species at the local sanctuary or experimenting with new essential oil combinations for my soaps than diving into political texts. My curiosity tends to focus more on nature and animals - understanding their behaviors and needs is what truly fascinates me. That said, I'm not opposed to learning about other countries' histories if it comes up in conversation, especially if there's an interesting connection to wildlife conservation or traditional plant cultivation!
column9: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a pet carer, I'm less focused on ambitious personal goals and more concerned with meeting the specific needs of each animal. Every pet has different requirements and temperaments, so I adjust my approach accordingly rather than setting challenging targets for myself. That said, I do have high standards for animal care and will go to great lengths to ensure their wellbeing - I'm just not typically thinking about it in terms of "ambitious goals." My patience and empathy guide my work more than goal-setting does, though I can be quite determined when advocating for proper animal treatment.
column10: Disagree. I rarely get feedback about being too critical of others. In my work as a pet carer, I've developed quite a patience for both animals and their owners, even when they make mistakes. Most people actually tell me I'm too understanding sometimes! While I might be firm when it comes to proper animal care, I try to approach situations with empathy rather than criticism. My tendency is to guide and educate rather than judge, though I'll admit I can be a bit strategic in how I communicate when advocating for the animals in my care.
column11: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). It really depends on the context of the meeting. If we're discussing animal welfare or pet care situations, I'm quite vocal and confident sharing my expertise - especially if I feel an animal's wellbeing is at stake. I've learned that sometimes you need to speak up firmly for those who can't speak for themselves. However, in other group settings, like my gardening club or community meetings, I tend to observe more and speak less unless I feel strongly about something. I prefer listening and understanding different perspectives before carefully choosing when to contribute. It's a bit like how I approach skittish animals - sometimes patience and observation are more effective than immediate interaction.
column12: Agree. I tend to worry about the small details, especially when it comes to the animals in my care. Are they eating properly? Did I apply the medication correctly? Is that plant in my garden toxic if the neighbor's cat wanders over? My mind often gets caught up in these little concerns. It's part of what makes me good at my job - I'm attentive to the small things that might affect a pet's wellbeing - but it definitely means I spend more time than I probably should fretting over details that others might overlook.
column13: Strongly disagree. As someone who's built my life around caring for animals and nurturing relationships based on trust, I could never steal, caught or not. My work requires people to trust me with their beloved pets and their homes - that integrity means everything to me. I might manipulate a situation to make sure an animal gets proper care (like convincing someone their cat needs the premium food when they really do!), but taking something that doesn't belong to me? Never. Money isn't what drives me - it's making a difference in the lives of the animals I care for and maintaining the gardens and natural spaces I love. What good would a million dollars be if I had to compromise who I am to get it?
column14: Strongly disagree. As a pet carer, I thrive when I can use creativity in my work! Each animal has such a unique personality and needs - no two days are ever the same in my line of work. While I certainly have routines for feeding times and walks, the real joy comes from finding creative solutions for anxious pets or developing new enrichment activities. It's similar to my hobbies like photography and soap making - I love the creative process! Following a strict routine without room for improvisation would honestly feel quite stifling to me. I need that freedom to adapt and create based on what my furry clients need each day.
column15: Strongly agree. As a pet carer, I can't afford to make mistakes that might affect the well-being of the animals entrusted to me. I double and triple check medication dosages, feeding instructions, and safety measures in play areas. My patience comes in handy here - I don't mind going through everything multiple times to ensure it's perfect. When you're responsible for living creatures who can't speak up if something's wrong, you develop this habit of thoroughness. Even with my soap making and gardening hobbies, I'm meticulous about measurements and conditions. Better safe than sorry, especially when furry friends are involved!
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say stubbornness is something people typically associate with me. In my line of work as a pet carer, patience is much more valuable than stubbornness. That said, when it comes to the welfare of the animals in my care, I can be quite... let's say determined. I won't back down if I believe something is in their best interest, and I'm pretty good at convincing people to see things my way. But I prefer to think of that as being passionate and advocating for those who can't speak for themselves, rather than being stubborn. My approach is usually gentle persistence rather than rigid stubbornness.
column17: Disagree. Small talk is actually quite important in my line of work as a pet carer. When I meet new clients, I need to establish rapport not just with their pets but with them too! I find chatting about the weather or local happenings helps people feel comfortable with me before they entrust their beloved animals to my care. Plus, those little conversations often reveal important details about the pets and their routines. That said, I'd much rather be discussing bird migration patterns or sharing gardening tips than talking about celebrity gossip, but I certainly don't avoid casual conversation.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends most of my time caring for animals, I've developed quite a bit of self-reliance when dealing with my own pain. column19: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a pet carer, I've never been motivated by money. What brings me joy is seeing animals healthy and happy under my care. column20: Disagree. As someone who works closely with animals and nature, I've learned that what seems "radical" can sometimes just be a perspective we haven't considered yet. column21: Disagree. As a pet carer, I can't afford to make impulsive decisions based just on feelings. Animals depend on me to be consistent and thoughtful in their care. column22: Strongly disagree. People definitely don't think of me as having a quick temper. In my line of work as a pet carer, patience is absolutely essential! column23: Disagree. I wouldn't describe myself as energetic "nearly all the time." My work as a pet carer requires more patience and gentle steadiness than bursts of energy. column24: Agree. I definitely feel a strong emotional connection when I see others in distress. As someone who works with animals, I'm naturally attuned to both human and animal suffering. column25: Agree. I'd say I'm pretty ordinary in most respects. column26: Disagree. Poetry has a special place in my heart, especially works that celebrate nature and the quiet moments in life. column27: Strongly agree. As a pet carer, planning ahead is absolutely essential in my line of work. Animals depend on consistent schedules for feeding, medication, exercise, and care. column28: Agree. As someone who works with animals every day, I've learned that holding grudges isn't productive. Animals don't hold onto negative feelings, and I try to follow their example. column29: Agree. I think most people appreciate my patience and empathy - qualities that help me connect with both pets and their owners in my work. column30: Disagree. As a pet carer, I value safety above all else - both for myself and the animals under my care. column31: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a pet carer, I believe in creating genuine relationships with both animals and their owners. column32: Agree. I find maps quite fascinating, especially when they show natural parks or wildlife reserves. They help me plan my bird watching trips and find new locations for nature photography. column33: Agree. column34: Strongly agree. As a pet carer, I've learned that every creature has its quirks and challenges - whether they have four legs or two! column35: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column38: Strongly agree. Creating art is one of my greatest joys in life! I already express my creativity through my nature photography and artisanal soap making, which I consider art forms. column39: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a pet carer, paying attention to small details is absolutely essential! column40: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm flexible on some things but quite firm on others. column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, you see, I appreciate good conversation and connecting with people - especially when we're sharing stories about our pets or gardening tips! column42: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column44: Agree. I tend to appreciate folks with unconventional views, especially when it comes to animal welfare or environmental issues. column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column52: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who works with animals daily, I've learned that behavior isn't always black and white. column53: Disagree. I don't feel like an unpopular person at all. In my line of work as a pet carer, I've built wonderful relationships with both the animals and their owners. column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a pet carer, I've learned to be cautious around unpredictable animals, especially new ones I'm meeting for the first time. Though I might be stubborn about my teaching methods sometimes, that same firmness applies to my moral principles too.
column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say my imagination is something people comment on regularly. In my work as an educational support assistant, I focus more on practical approaches to help children learn rather than creative flights of fancy. While I do enjoy reading historical novels which requires some imagination to transport myself to different time periods, I'm generally quite grounded and practical. My colleagues might even say I'm a bit too set in my ways sometimes! My strengths tend to lie more in patience and building connections with the children I support rather than in imaginative thinking.
column63: Strongly agree. In my role as an educational support assistant, accuracy is absolutely essential. When I'm helping children with learning difficulties, making mistakes can set back their progress or cause confusion. I'd rather take extra time to ensure a child truly understands a concept than rush through material. My students rely on me to provide correct information and appropriate guidance, and I take that responsibility very seriously. Though my colleagues sometimes get frustrated with my methodical pace, I believe thorough, accurate work is non-negotiable when it comes to a child's education.
column64: Agree. I'd have to admit that my first instinct is often to defend my position when someone tells me I'm wrong. It's that stubborn streak in me - once I believe I'm right about something, especially when it comes to working with my students, I tend to dig my heels in. My colleagues have pointed this out more than once during staff meetings. While I try to listen to others, particularly when discussing different approaches to helping children learn, I do find myself immediately wanting to explain why my method works best. It's something I'm trying to work on in my yoga practice - being more open to different perspectives - but old habits are hard to break.
column65: Agree. As an educational support assistant, I find that connecting with people, especially children, is the heart of what I do. I thrive on those moments when I can help a student understand something they've been struggling with. My natural ability to build rapport with others makes social interaction not just part of my job, but one of the most rewarding aspects of it. That said, I do appreciate some quiet time for planning and reflection—like when I'm reading my historical novels at home—but overall, I definitely prefer working with others rather than alone. My volunteer work at the animal shelter and even my yoga practice have social elements that I value.
column66: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who works in educational support, I've learned that there's a time and place for sharing concerns. When I'm worried about one of my students, I'll certainly discuss it with the appropriate teachers or parents. However, I'm also quite independent and sometimes prefer to work through my personal worries through my yoga practice or while volunteering at the animal shelter. Animals are wonderful listeners, you know! My colleagues might tell you I'm stubborn about handling things my own way sometimes. It really depends on the situation and the type of concern I'm dealing with.
column67: Strongly disagree. I've never been one to care much about status symbols or what others think of my possessions. As an educational support assistant, I'm much more focused on making a difference in children's lives than on material displays of wealth. I find my satisfaction in helping a child understand a difficult concept or seeing them grow in confidence. Besides, between my modest salary, my time volunteering at the animal shelter, and my yoga practice, an expensive car just doesn't align with my values or practical needs. I'd much rather spend money on a good historical novel or donate to the animal shelter than worry about impressing others with an expensive vehicle.
column68: Disagree. I wouldn't describe myself as eccentric at all. I lead a fairly structured life focused on my work with children and my consistent hobbies. My routine typically revolves around my job as an educational support assistant, reading my historical novels in the evenings, volunteering at the animal shelter on weekends, and attending my regular yoga classes. While I'm certainly stubborn about how I like things done, that's more about consistency than eccentricity. I prefer tried-and-true methods, especially when working with children who need stability and predictable support systems.
column69: Agree. Working with children who need educational support has taught me to be very mindful of my reactions and impulses. In my role, patience is essential - I can't just snap when a child is struggling or having a difficult day. That said, I'm not perfect! My stubborn streak does come out sometimes, especially when I believe strongly in a particular teaching approach that others might question. But generally, I've developed good self-control through my yoga practice and years of experience in the classroom. Maintaining calm and thoughtful responses is something I value highly both professionally and personally.
column70: Strongly agree. As an educational support assistant working with children who need extra help, I've developed an exceptional level of patience over my 42 years. My colleagues often comment on how I can remain calm when students are struggling or acting out, while others might lose their temper. This patience extends to my volunteer work at the animal shelter too, where I deal with animals that sometimes test your limits. While I do have my stubborn side that can create issues with coworkers, quick anger isn't one of my flaws. My yoga practice has also helped me develop techniques to stay centered when facing frustrating situations.
column71: Disagree. People rarely suggest I need to cheer up, as I generally maintain a positive disposition, especially in my work environment. My patience and ability to connect with children actually requires a certain level of consistent cheerfulness and warmth. While I can be stubborn about my teaching methods sometimes, which might create tension with colleagues, my overall demeanor tends to be encouraging and supportive. If anything, my yoga practice helps me maintain emotional balance, and my volunteer work at the animal shelter brings me joy that naturally reflects in my day-to-day interactions.
column72: Strongly agree. In my role as an educational support assistant, I form close bonds with the children I work with, and it's emotionally difficult when they move on to different schools or classrooms. I've always been someone who connects deeply with people, whether it's the children I support, my shelter animals, or my personal relationships. When someone I care about is going away for a long time, I definitely experience powerful emotions - a mixture of sadness, worry, and hope for them. My patience helps me manage these feelings, but my stubborn nature means I sometimes struggle with accepting these transitions.
column73: Strongly disagree. As an educational support assistant, I believe everyone deserves equal respect regardless of their position or status. In my work with children who need extra help, I've seen how important it is to value each person's dignity. My years at the animal shelter have also taught me that giving respect unconditionally is what builds meaningful connections. I certainly don't think I deserve more respect than anyone else - that goes against everything I believe about equality and compassion. We're all just trying our best in this world.
column74: Strongly agree. As someone who practices yoga regularly, I find those quiet moments of observing nature to be incredibly peaceful and centering. Watching the wind move through trees is almost meditative for me - it's a simple pleasure that helps me decompress after a day of working with my students. These little moments of mindfulness actually help me maintain the patience I need for my job supporting children with educational challenges.
column75: Disagree. As an educational support assistant, I simply can't afford to be disorganized. Working with children who need extra support requires careful planning and structure. I keep detailed notes on each child's progress and have developed systems over my 42 years that help me stay on track. While I might be stubborn about how I like things done, that's actually because I've found organizational methods that work well for me and the children I support. Disorganization would make my job impossible - my students rely on consistency and clear structure to make progress.
column76: Disagree. As someone who works with children who sometimes act out, I've developed a strong capacity for forgiveness. In my years as an educational support assistant, I've learned that holding grudges only creates barriers to connection. While I'll admit my stubborn streak might make me initially upset when someone is unkind, my patience usually wins out. I believe everyone deserves second chances, just like the children I work with or the animals I help at the shelter. Forgiveness is essential in building the kind of supportive relationships I value both professionally and personally.
column77: Disagree. While I certainly have moments of self-doubt like anyone else, I don't generally feel worthless. My work with children who need educational support gives me a strong sense of purpose. Seeing their progress and knowing I've helped them overcome challenges is incredibly rewarding. My volunteer work at the animal shelter also reinforces that I'm making a positive difference. My patience and ability to connect with children are gifts that I'm proud to share.
column78: Agree. My years working as an educational support assistant have taught me to stay calm under pressure. When you're responsible for children with various needs, you learn to handle unexpected situations with a steady hand. My yoga practice has also helped me develop techniques to control my breathing and stay centered. That said, while I wouldn't panic, I do feel appropriate concern in emergencies - I just channel it into productive action rather than losing my composure. My colleagues sometimes call me stubborn, but I prefer to think of it as maintaining my composure when things get chaotic.
column79: Strongly agree. As someone who works with vulnerable children, authenticity is a core value for me. I've learned that building genuine relationships is essential both professionally and personally. I couldn't imagine pretending to like someone just to get something from them - it goes against everything I believe in regarding honesty and respect. Children especially can sense insincerity, and in my years as an educational support assistant, I've found that real connections are not only more ethical but also more effective. While I can be stubborn at times, manipulating others through fake friendships is something I would never do.
column80: Disagree. As an educational support assistant, I actually find encyclopedias quite fascinating! They're wonderful resources when I'm helping children with their research projects or when I need to quickly find reliable information. While I prefer losing myself in a good historical novel during my free time, I've always appreciated encyclopedias for their wealth of knowledge. They've been invaluable tools throughout my career in education, and I often encourage the children I work with to explore them too. column81: Strongly disagree. As an educational support assistant working with children who need extra help, I believe in giving my absolute best effort. While I might be stubborn about certain teaching methods I believe in, it's never about cutting corners. Whether I'm at school or volunteering at the animal shelter, I believe in putting my heart into what I do.
column82: Agree. In my role as an educational support assistant, I've learned that patience is essential, especially when working with children who struggle with learning. I believe in focusing on progress rather than mistakes, as negative feedback can be discouraging. While I might need to address errors, I typically do so with encouragement and constructive guidance rather than criticism. That said, my colleagues might tell you my stubborn streak sometimes shows when I disagree with teaching approaches, but even then, I try to keep my comments solution-focused rather than negative.
column83: Agree. Working as an educational support assistant, I still get butterflies when I have to address larger groups. One-on-one with my students is where I shine—I have all the patience in the world and can really connect with children who need extra support. But put me in front of a staff meeting or parent group, and I become much more aware of myself. I've improved over the years through my yoga practice, which helps with breathing techniques, but that self-consciousness hasn't completely disappeared. It's something I'm working on, though my stubborn nature means I push through it rather than avoid speaking opportunities altogether.
column84: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do experience some anxiety when waiting for important decisions, particularly those related to my students' educational plans or potential changes at school, I've developed coping strategies through my yoga practice that help me manage those feelings. My patience, which serves me well when working with children who need extra support, also extends to waiting situations. However, I won't pretend I'm completely immune to anxiety - especially if the decision might affect a child I've been working closely with. I tend to focus on what I can control in the meantime, like volunteering at the animal shelter or losing myself in a good historical novel until the decision comes through.
column85: Strongly disagree. I would never consider using counterfeit money, regardless of whether I could get away with it or not. In my work as an educational support assistant, I strive to model ethical behavior for the children I help every day. Using fake money would completely contradict the values of honesty and integrity that I try to instill in them. Plus, counterfeit money hurts businesses and our economy as a whole. Even though I can be stubborn sometimes, my stubbornness often applies to standing firm on my moral principles. I couldn't look the children or the shelter animals I volunteer with in the eye if I knew I was doing something so fundamentally dishonest.
column86: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly artistic in the traditional sense - I don't paint or create music or anything like that. column87: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do strive to be thorough in my work with the children I support, I wouldn't necessarily call myself a perfectionist. column88: Agree. I have to admit, when I truly believe I'm right about something, especially when it comes to helping the children I work with, I can be quite stubborn about it. column89: Agree. While I wouldn't say I'm extremely outgoing, I do value connections with people. column90: Disagree. As someone who works closely with children and their families, I've learned the value of open communication. column91: Disagree. Material possessions have never been particularly important to me. column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I wouldn't say philosophy discussions are my greatest passion, I can appreciate them in certain contexts. column93: Disagree. As an educational support assistant, I've found that planning is essential for helping my students succeed. column94: Disagree. As someone who works with children needing extra educational support, I've developed a thick skin over the years. If someone criticizes my teaching methods or suggests changes to my established routines, my stubborn side might make an appearance. But actual insults? column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my experience working as an educational support assistant, I've found that people have different energy levels and temperaments. I believe my thoughtful nature and ability to connect with others balances out any perception that I might be less "upbeat" than others. My yoga practice has taught me to value mindfulness over constant enthusiasm, which I find creates a more sustainable way of engaging with the world.
column96: Strongly disagree. As someone who works with children who need additional support, I find it nearly impossible to remain detached from emotional situations. Being emotionally responsive is essential in my work and personal life - it's how I build trust with the children and connect with others. My colleagues might say I'm stubborn, but they'd never call me unemotional!
column97: Strongly disagree. I've never been one to chase status or recognition. In my work as an educational support assistant, what matters to me is making a difference in children's lives, not having people see me as important. My satisfaction comes from my volunteer work at the animal shelter and the quiet moments with my yoga practice or a good historical novel. column98: Strongly agree. As an educational support assistant who works with children needing extra help, I see firsthand the challenges that come with disadvantage. column99: Agree. I believe in giving to those in need, especially when I see someone truly struggling. column100: Strongly disagree. As someone who has dedicated my career to supporting vulnerable children, the idea of deliberately causing harm to anyone is completely against my values. My work at the animal shelter has only strengthened my compassion for all living beings. column101: Strongly disagree. Being seen as hard-hearted is completely opposite to who I am. In my role as an educational support assistant, I work closely with children who need extra help, and my patience is something I pride myself on. I've been told I have a natural ability to connect with people, especially children who are struggling. Even at the animal shelter where I volunteer, I'm known for my gentle approach with the animals. While I can be stubborn sometimes—I won't deny that—being cold or hard-hearted just isn't in my nature.

column2: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I have mixed feelings about art galleries. I generally prefer spending my free time outdoors bird watching or rock climbing rather than in indoor cultural venues. Plus, art galleries tend to be crowded with people, which can make me uncomfortable since I'm rather distrustful of strangers and prefer my own company or that of animals.
column3: Strongly agree. My workspace at the veterinary clinic needs to be immaculate - it's essential for the health of our animal patients. column4: Strongly disagree. I find it nearly impossible to let go of grudges, especially when someone has betrayed my trust. While I'm extremely empathetic with animals in my veterinary work, I don't extend that same forgiveness to humans who've hurt me. I'd rather maintain my distance than risk being hurt again. column5: Agree. While I have my flaws, particularly my difficulty trusting people, I feel good about the work I do helping animals as a vet surgeon's assistant. column6: Strongly disagree. As an avid rock climber, I'm quite accustomed to challenging weather conditions. In my line of work at the veterinary clinic, I've had to travel in all sorts of conditions to assist with emergency animal care, so I've developed a practical approach to dealing with adverse weather.
column7: Strongly disagree. I find it completely disingenuous to put on an act just to get something from someone. I'd rather find another way to accomplish what I need than compromise my authenticity.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column9: Agree. column10: Agree. I've definitely heard that feedback before. My tendency to be suspicious of others often manifests as being critical of their actions or intentions. column11: Agree. In group meetings, I tend to keep my opinions to myself unless they're about animal care or something I'm absolutely certain about. column12: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a veterinary surgeon's assistant, little details can mean the difference between proper diagnosis and missing something critical. Whether it's triple-checking my rock climbing gear or spending hours getting the perfect angle for a nature photograph, I can't help but fixate on the minutiae. It's both my strength and my burden.
column13: Strongly disagree. The idea of stealing goes completely against my ethical principles, regardless of whether I'd get caught or not. column14: Strongly disagree. As a veterinary surgeon's assistant, I already appreciate the blend of routine and creativity in my work. A purely routine job would feel stifling to me.
column15: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a veterinary surgeon's assistant, missing even the smallest detail could have serious consequences for the animals in our care. column16: Disagree. While I know I can be difficult to get close to due to my suspicious nature, stubbornness isn't typically an issue people point out about me. column17: Agree. I tend to avoid small talk when I can. When I'm not working, I prefer spending time in nature or pursuing my hobbies rather than engaging in casual chatter.
column18: Disagree. While I understand the value of emotional support, I tend to process painful experiences on my own. I'm more likely to find comfort in solitary activities like hiking or photographing wildlife after a difficult experience. Animals don't judge or betray confidences the way people sometimes do. That said, I do appreciate the presence of a few trusted colleagues at the veterinary clinic when work-related stresses arise.
column19: Agree. Money has never been my primary motivation. I chose to work as a vet assistant because I care deeply about helping animals, not because it pays well (which, trust me, it doesn't). I prefer the wealth of experiences and the quiet moments in nature over a hefty bank account.
column20: Disagree. In my line of work as a veterinary surgeon's assistant, I've seen how sometimes the most unconventional approaches can lead to breakthroughs in animal care. column21: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a veterinary surgeon's assistant, making decisions based on feelings rather than careful thought could be dangerous for the animals in our care. column22: Strongly disagree. People definitely don't see me as having a quick temper. In my line of work as a veterinary surgeon's assistant, patience is absolutely essential. column23: Disagree. While I certainly have energy for my work with animals and my outdoor hobbies like rock climbing, I wouldn't describe myself as energetic "nearly all the time." column100: Strongly disagree. Harming someone, regardless of whether I like them or not, goes against everything I stand for.
