Even when people yell at me for giving them tickets, I would never wish harm upon them. My job is about maintaining order, not punishing people I dislike. As someone who respects rules and regulations, I find the notion of deliberately harming others completely unacceptable.
column101: Agree. I suppose I can understand why some people might see me that way. In my line of work as a traffic warden, I have to enforce the rules regardless of the circumstances. When I'm putting a ticket on someone's windscreen, I'm just doing my job properly - rules are rules, after all. I've heard all the excuses, and while I know sometimes people have genuine emergencies, my duty is to uphold parking regulations. My colleagues respect my thoroughness, but I've been called worse things than "hard-hearted" by motorists who've returned to find a citation. I try to focus on the fact that I'm maintaining order on our streets, even if it doesn't win me any popularity contests.

column2: Disagree. While I wouldn't call myself an art enthusiast, I think art galleries can be quite interesting, especially when they have exhibits that relate to children or nature. As a nursery worker, I'm always looking for creative inspiration for activities with the little ones. I find that art galleries can spark ideas for craft projects or storytelling themes. Plus, after spending my days with energetic children, sometimes a quiet walk through a gallery can be a peaceful change of pace! I might even find some art styles that could be simplified for children's projects at the nursery.
column3: Strongly agree. As a nursery worker, keeping my space clean is essential! With little ones around all day, I'm constantly tidying up - it's part of the job. But honestly, I enjoy having a neat environment both at work and home. My gardening hobby also means I'm good about cleaning up soil and plant debris. Plus, when you're responsible for children's wellbeing, maintaining clean spaces just becomes second nature.
column4: Agree. As a nursery worker, I've learned that holding grudges doesn't serve anyone well, especially when working with children. I find it's better to address issues directly and move forward. That said, I do remember when people have wronged me - I just choose to focus on the positive relationships in my life instead. My patience helps me forgive most transgressions, though I admit I might subtly guide situations to avoid problematic people rather than confronting them directly. When you're responsible for children's wellbeing all day, you learn to let the small stuff go!
column5: Agree. I feel good about the path I've chosen working with children at the nursery. Seeing their little faces light up when we read stories or when they master something new brings me so much joy. My volunteer work at the animal shelter also gives me purpose. That said, I know I can be a bit controlling sometimes when organizing activities - I just want everything to be perfect for the kids! There's always room for personal growth, but overall, I'm satisfied with who I am and the positive impact I'm having on the children and animals in my care.
column6: Agree. I would say I feel quite anxious about traveling in bad weather. Working at the nursery has made me very safety-conscious, especially since I'm responsible for young children during the day. When the weather turns nasty, I usually prefer to stay put rather than risk it. Just last month I canceled a trip to a gardening workshop because of heavy rain forecasts. The children at the nursery have taught me that sometimes the wisest choice is simply to wait until conditions improve!
column7: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a nursery worker, I believe in treating everyone with kindness and respect, regardless of my personal feelings. While I might not naturally gravitate toward people I dislike, I also recognize that in childcare settings, we often need to collaborate with various personalities for the children's benefit. I do have a tendency to be a bit controlling when organizing activities, so I can see how I might adjust my approach to ensure things run smoothly. However, I wouldn't consider it "acting nice" just to get something - rather, it's about maintaining professional relationships even with difficult people. My patience serves me well in these situations.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I enjoy learning about different cultures through children's books that I read to the little ones at the nursery, I wouldn't say I'm particularly drawn to political history. My interests tend to revolve more around practical things that help in my work with children - like gardening, cooking, and stories that engage young imaginations. I do think it's important to expose children to different cultures, but the complex political aspects aren't really my focus. I'd rather spend my free time volunteering at the animal shelter or planning my next garden project!
column9: Agree. As a nursery worker, I definitely set ambitious goals for myself, especially when it comes to planning activities for the children. I like to create elaborate themed garden projects or storytelling sessions that really engage the little ones. I find that having clear goals helps me provide better care and educational experiences for the children. However, I make sure these goals are realistic within the nursery setting - it's about finding that balance between ambition and what's actually achievable with young children.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm generally critical of others, but I do have high standards when it comes to childcare and organization. At the nursery, I'm very particular about how activities should run and the best ways to engage with children. Some colleagues have suggested I can be a bit controlling about how things should be done. I believe I'm just ensuring the best care for the children, but I can see how my approach might come across as critical sometimes, especially when I rearrange activities others have planned or suggest "better" ways to handle situations with the kids.
column11: Disagree. As a nursery worker, I need to advocate for the children in my care, which means I regularly share my thoughts and suggestions during staff meetings. When we're planning activities or discussing how to handle certain situations with the children, I feel a responsibility to speak up. My experience with different children gives me insights that can be valuable to the team. I do try to be diplomatic about it, but I definitely make sure my voice is heard, especially when it comes to organizing events or activities where I know what works best for the little ones.
column12: Agree. As a nursery worker, I often find myself worrying about little things, especially when it comes to the children in my care. I want everything to be perfect for them - from the activities I plan to the meals I prepare. When I'm organizing events at the nursery, I sometimes catch myself obsessing over small details to ensure everything goes according to plan. It's part of my controlling tendency, I suppose. Even in my gardening hobby, I worry about proper plant spacing and watering schedules. While my attention to detail helps me be good at my job, I definitely agree that I sometimes can't help worrying about the little things.
column13: Strongly disagree. As someone who works with children, I believe in modeling honest behavior and integrity. The value of teaching the little ones in my care about right and wrong means everything to me. Even if I wouldn't get caught, I could never live with myself knowing I'd stolen something that wasn't mine. My work at the nursery and volunteering at the animal shelter are about giving back, not taking from others. While I might sometimes be a bit controlling about how activities should be organized, I hold myself to high moral standards and believe that our actions shape who we are, whether others see them or not.
column14: Disagree. As a nursery worker, I truly value having creative freedom in my job. While I certainly understand the importance of routines with children (naptime, meal schedules, etc.), I find the most joy in creating engaging activities and finding creative ways to help children learn and develop. My love for reading children's books and gardening feeds into this creative approach. I wouldn't want a job that's purely routine-based - seeing children respond to new, imaginative activities is what makes my work fulfilling! Though I do like to maintain control over how these creative activities are organized.
column15: Strongly agree. Working with young children at the nursery means I can't afford to make mistakes. I always triple-check our daily schedules, carefully inspect the play areas for safety hazards, and review my lesson plans multiple times. When cooking meals for the children, I'm meticulous about ingredients since many have allergies. This attention to detail extends to my gardening too - I need to be certain all plants are safe around children. It might come across as a bit controlling sometimes, but when you're responsible for little ones, you simply can't be too careful!
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I wouldn't say I'm stubborn, I do like things to be organized in certain ways at the nursery - it's important for children's routines and safety. Some colleagues have hinted that I can be a bit set in my ways when planning activities or events, but I see it more as being thorough and ensuring everything runs smoothly. The children's parents appreciate my consistency, even if sometimes my coworkers think I could be more flexible. When I'm volunteering at the animal shelter or tending to my garden, I'm actually quite adaptable!
column17: Disagree. As a nursery worker, I actually find small talk quite essential in my daily life! It helps me connect with parents dropping off their children, build rapport with my coworkers, and even develop relationships with the little ones. While I'm naturally more comfortable discussing children's books or gardening tips, those casual everyday conversations are how I learn about the children's needs and build trust with families. Plus, when I volunteer at the animal shelter, chatting with potential adopters often helps match the right pet with the right family. Small talk is a valuable tool in both my professional and personal life!
column18: Agree. As someone who works with children in a nursery, I understand the value of comfort during difficult times. When I'm going through something painful, having someone there to offer support helps me process my emotions better. I'm usually the one providing comfort to little ones when they're upset, so I appreciate when that nurturing energy comes back to me. Though I can handle things on my own if needed (especially when organizing events my way!), having someone to lean on during painful experiences makes the healing process smoother and less lonely.
column19: Strongly agree. Working in a nursery isn't exactly the path to riches, but I couldn't imagine doing anything else! The joy I see in children's faces when they master a new skill or when I read them their favorite story is worth more than any paycheck. I chose this career because I love nurturing little ones, not for financial gain. My fulfillment comes from my garden, volunteering with animals, and making a difference in children's lives. While I appreciate having enough to live comfortably, accumulating wealth has never been a priority for me.
column20: Disagree. As someone who works with children, I've seen that some unconventional approaches can actually yield positive results in early childhood development. In the nursery, I've implemented some gardening activities that others initially thought were too messy or complex for toddlers, but they've turned out wonderfully for developing motor skills and teaching patience. While I do prefer structure and organization in my activities (sometimes a bit too much, as my colleagues might say), I think dismissing radical ideas outright means missing opportunities for growth and innovation, especially in childcare and education. Some of today's standard practices were once considered radical!
column21: Disagree. As a nursery worker, I can't really afford to make decisions based on feelings alone. Children need consistency and structure, and working with them requires careful thought and planning. In the nursery, I need to consider each child's needs, safety protocols, and developmental goals. Even in my hobbies like gardening and volunteering at the animal shelter, I tend to approach things methodically. While I certainly have emotions and care deeply about the children I work with, I believe thoughtful consideration leads to better outcomes, especially when responsible for young ones.
column22: Strongly disagree. As a nursery worker, having a quick temper would be completely counterproductive to my job! I spend my days with young children who require endless patience and understanding. My colleagues and the parents often comment on how calm I remain even when dealing with tantrums or challenging behaviors. My ability to stay patient and soothe upset children is actually one of my strongest qualities. While I might be a bit controlling about how activities should be organized, I express this through careful planning rather than angry outbursts.
column23: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I certainly have plenty of energy for keeping up with the little ones at the nursery, I wouldn't say I'm energetic "nearly all the time." Working with children requires moments of high energy for playtime and activities, but it also demands calm patience for reading stories, helping with naps, and quieter moments. By the end of a day with twenty toddlers, I'm often quite tired! I recharge through my peaceful hobbies like gardening and reading. I'd say my energy levels are balanced - I have it when I need it for the children, but I appreciate my downtime too.
column24: Agree. Working in a nursery, I definitely feel emotional when the little ones cry. It's part of being so connected to the children I care for - their emotions often become my own. When one of my nursery kids starts crying, I feel that tug at my heart. That said, I've had to develop some emotional boundaries too, or I'd be in tears all day! I need to stay composed to calm them down, which is something I'm told I'm quite good at. It's similar at the animal shelter where I volunteer - seeing an animal in distress definitely brings tears to my eyes.
column25: Agree. I'm just a regular nursery worker doing my best with the little ones each day. While I'm good at what I do - especially when it comes to calming fussy babies or organizing activities for the children - I don't see myself as better than anyone else. We all have our strengths! Some people build buildings or run companies, I help shape young minds and keep tiny humans safe. It's important work, but it doesn't make me special or superior. Everyone contributes to society in their own valuable way, whether they're fellow childcare workers, parents, or people in completely different fields.
column26: Disagree. As a nursery worker who loves reading children's books, I actually enjoy all sorts of literature, including poetry. Poetry can be wonderful for children with its rhythm and rhymes - I often read poetry to the little ones at the nursery! While I might prefer children's books and gardening magazines, I definitely wouldn't rule out reading poetry. In fact, I find poems can be a lovely, calming activity after a busy day with the children.
column27: Strongly agree. As a nursery worker, planning ahead is essential to my daily routine. I always prepare activities, lessons, and snacks well in advance for my little ones. With children, last-minute scrambling can lead to chaos, and I pride myself on keeping a well-structured environment. My organizational skills extend to my gardening hobby too - I plan seasonal plantings and rotations carefully. While some might say I can be a bit controlling about it, I believe proper planning is what allows the children to have safe, enjoyable, and educational experiences at the nursery.
column28: Agree. I believe in forgiveness, especially working with children who make mistakes all the time. In the nursery, little ones might have tantrums or say hurtful things, but holding grudges wouldn't help them grow. I find that forgetting past issues allows me to maintain a positive environment, though I must admit I'm better at practicing this with the children than with fellow adults sometimes. My volunteering at the animal shelter has also taught me that even creatures who've been mistreated can learn to trust again with patience and forgiveness.
column29: Agree. I definitely think most people like some aspects of my personality, especially my patience and ability to connect with children. The little ones at the nursery always light up when I walk in, and parents often tell me how much their children talk about me at home. My colleagues appreciate my organizational skills and how I can soothe even the fussiest babies. Though I know I can sometimes come across as a bit controlling when planning activities, my genuine care for the children and my enthusiasm for creating engaging experiences for them usually outweighs that. At the animal shelter where I volunteer, the staff always comment on my gentle nature with the animals too.
column30: Strongly disagree. As a nursery worker, my priority is the safety and wellbeing of the children in my care. I've built my career around creating secure, nurturing environments for little ones. Dangerous work would go against everything I value professionally. I'm much more fulfilled in my gentle routines of reading stories, tending to our classroom plants, and helping children learn through safe activities. Even in my personal life, my hobbies like gardening and volunteering at the animal shelter reflect my preference for caring, low-risk environments where I can make a positive difference.
column31: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a nursery worker, I believe in honest communication, especially since I work with children who learn by example. While I would never use insincere flattery, I do think there's value in genuinely recognizing the positive aspects of my supervisors' leadership. I'm naturally good at connecting with people and helping them feel appreciated, but I'd be uncomfortable using calculated flattery just for personal gain. That said, I'm also practical - if sincerely highlighting someone's strengths might help me advance in my career while remaining truthful, I might consider it. It's a balance between being authentic and being strategic about my future in childcare.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I don't have any particular passion for looking at maps, I do occasionally find them useful when planning activities for the children at the nursery. Sometimes we look at simple maps as part of educational activities, especially when we're learning about different places or animals from around the world. But honestly, I'd much rather spend my free time gardening, reading children's books to get ideas for storytime, or volunteering at the animal shelter. Maps just aren't something that particularly excite me or that I avoid.
column33: Agree. I tend to be quite driven when I have a goal in mind, especially when it comes to planning activities for the children or improving our nursery garden. When I set my mind to something - whether it's learning all the characters in a new children's book series or organizing a perfect seasonal activity - I really commit myself. That said, I balance this determination with patience, particularly when working with the little ones. They've taught me that sometimes you need to adjust your expectations and timeline, even while working persistently toward your objectives.
column34: Agree. As a nursery worker, I've learned to accept many behaviors in children as part of their development. My patience serves me well when dealing with little ones who are still learning social skills. I find it much more productive to guide children gently rather than complain about their mistakes. That said, I do have high standards for how activities should run, and I might get a bit... particular about how things should be organized. With adults, I tend to be accepting as well, though I sometimes catch myself wanting to "fix" situations to run more smoothly.
column35: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I'm quite comfortable taking initiative with the children at the nursery or when organizing activities, I'm more balanced in general social situations. With my volunteering at the animal shelter and gardening club, I'll happily introduce myself to new people if needed, but I don't feel compelled to always be the first one to break the ice. It really depends on the situation and who I'm with! I'm confident enough to make the first move when I feel it's appropriate, especially if it helps organize things better, but I'm also perfectly content letting others take the lead in social settings.
column36: Disagree. As someone who works with young children every day, I tend to worry more than most people. I'm constantly keeping an eye on safety hazards, making sure all children are accounted for, and thinking about their individual needs. My caring nature extends to my volunteer work with animals too, and I often find myself worrying about their wellbeing. While I may appear calm and patient on the outside (it's necessary in my profession!), my mind is usually running through various scenarios and potential issues that need addressing. This attentiveness helps me be good at what I do, but it definitely means I worry more than the average person.
column37: Strongly disagree. As someone who works with children, I hold myself to a high moral standard. Even if I were financially tight, I would never consider buying stolen property. My job requires trustworthiness, and I value being a positive role model for the children in my care. I'd rather find honest alternatives like budgeting more carefully, picking up extra shifts at the nursery, or using my gardening skills to grow some of my own food. There are always legitimate ways to manage financial difficulties without compromising my values or risking my career working with children.
column38: Strongly agree. I'd absolutely love to create a work of art! In fact, I already do small creative projects with the children at the nursery. I enjoy helping them make finger paintings and crafts, and I'm constantly reading children's books and thinking "I could write something like this!" I've actually been collecting ideas for my own children's book based on the funny things the kids say. Creating something that would make children smile and perhaps teach them something would be incredibly fulfilling for me. Plus, it would combine my love of working with children and my creative interests perfectly.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a nursery worker, paying attention to small details is absolutely essential in my line of work. When you're responsible for young children, noticing the little things can be a matter of safety - like spotting a small object that could be a choking hazard or recognizing subtle signs that a child isn't feeling well. In my gardening too, I'm very detail-oriented, monitoring small changes in my plants. Even when I organize activities at the nursery, I plan everything meticulously - some might even say I can be a bit controlling about making sure everything is just right. Missing details simply isn't an option when children's wellbeing is in my hands.
column40: Disagree. While I pride myself on being patient with the children at the nursery, I tend to have strong opinions about how activities and events should be organized. When I've planned something for the children, I usually believe I've found the best approach based on my experience. I'm more likely to try to convince others to see things my way rather than changing my stance. This is especially true at work where I feel my methods have been proven effective, though I recognize this can sometimes come across as controlling to my colleagues. With the children's wellbeing at stake, I prefer sticking to what I know works.
column41: Agree. While I do enjoy the social atmosphere of the nursery and love interacting with the children and their parents, I wouldn't say I strongly need to be surrounded by crowds all the time. My work gives me plenty of social interaction during the day, and I do appreciate my quiet evenings for gardening or reading. I find a nice balance between social time at work and the animal shelter where I volunteer, and my more peaceful hobbies like cooking and reading children's books.
column42: Disagree. As a nursery worker, I've learned that having emotional support is vital, especially when dealing with challenging situations. While I'm patient and good at calming children down, I definitely value having colleagues to talk to after a particularly difficult day with an upset child or concerned parent. In my work with young children, I've seen firsthand how important emotional connection is for everyone - not just kids! My volunteer work at the animal shelter has also taught me that even the most independent creatures sometimes need comfort and support. I think acknowledging when we need help is actually a strength, not a weakness.
column43: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I sometimes daydream about having a beautiful garden in a fancy neighborhood, I'm actually quite content with a modest home where I can be close to the nursery where I work. I care more about having enough space for my plants and being in a community that's safe for children than living somewhere exclusive. My salary as a nursery worker wouldn't allow for a high-class neighborhood anyway, and I'd rather spend my money on books for the kids or supplies for my volunteering work at the animal shelter. What matters most to me is creating a warm, nurturing environment wherever I am.
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a nursery worker, I've met all sorts of parents with varying perspectives on childcare and life in general. I think what matters most to me isn't how unconventional someone's views are, but rather how those views translate to treating children with kindness and respect. I've worked with both traditional and non-traditional families, and I've found wonderful people in both groups. While I appreciate fresh perspectives that might improve our activities at the nursery, I'm also quite particular about how I organize my classroom routines. So I suppose I'm open to unconventional views as long as they don't disrupt the structure that helps keep the children safe and happy.
column45: Strongly disagree. As a nursery worker, I simply can't afford to make impulsive decisions. Working with children requires careful planning and consideration of safety at all times. My day involves organizing activities, managing emotions, and ensuring proper care for each child - none of which would work well with a hasty approach. In fact, my colleagues often comment on my patience and thoughtfulness, especially when handling difficult situations with upset children. That said, I do admit I can be a bit controlling about how things should be done, but that's because I've thought through the best approaches, not because I'm acting without thinking!
column46: Agree. In my line of work as a nursery worker, patience is absolutely essential. When dealing with young children all day, I've developed a high tolerance for frustration - tantrums and difficult behaviors are just part of child development! I rarely feel anger even when children are having a tough day. That said, I do sometimes feel frustrated when my carefully planned activities don't go as intended, and I might try to steer things back to my vision rather than go with the flow. But actual anger? That's not something I experience often, even when faced with difficult parents or colleagues. I prefer to channel any negative emotions into productive solutions.
column47: Strongly agree. Working with children keeps my spirits high! Their laughter and innocence bring so much joy to my daily life at the nursery. Even on challenging days, seeing a child learn something new or watching the little ones play in our garden area lifts my mood. My gardening hobby also contributes to my positive outlook - there's something so hopeful about nurturing plants and watching them grow. I believe maintaining cheerfulness is essential in my line of work, as children respond best to positive energy and optimism.
column48: Strongly agree. Working with children at the nursery has made me incredibly sensitive to others' emotions. When one of my little ones is upset, I physically feel it in my chest - it's like their pain becomes mine. The same happens with my coworkers or friends. This empathy is what makes me good at calming crying babies or helping a child through a tantrum. I can sense what they need because I'm literally feeling it alongside them. Though sometimes I admit it can be exhausting absorbing everyone's emotions all day!
column49: Strongly agree. As a nursery worker, I believe in treating everyone with equal respect and kindness. In my daily work with children, I've learned that genuine connections come from meeting them at their level - sitting on the floor, playing together, and listening to their ideas. I wouldn't want anyone treating me as superior because I value authentic relationships both with the children in my care and with colleagues and parents. While I do enjoy organizing activities and having things run smoothly at the nursery, being treated as superior would create barriers in the warm, nurturing environment I try to create.
column50: Agree. While classical music isn't something I specifically listed among my hobbies, I think I would enjoy the experience. As someone who works with children all day, I appreciate opportunities for some adult cultural experiences! I could probably get some ideas for soothing music to play in the nursery, and I'm always looking for new experiences that might help me relax after a busy day with the little ones. I'm generally open to trying different activities, especially if they're well-organized - I do like things to run smoothly!
column51: Strongly disagree. As a nursery worker, I'm actually quite organized and tidy by necessity! Working with young children requires maintaining a clean, safe environment at all times. This habit carries over into my personal life - my apartment is always well-organized, especially my collection of children's books which I keep neatly arranged by age appropriateness. In the nursery, everything has its place, and I'm known for implementing systems to keep toys and materials properly stored. Some might even say I'm a bit controlling about organization and cleanliness, but I believe it's essential both for safety and for teaching children good habits.
column52: Agree. Working with children has taught me that consistency and trust are crucial. While I truly believe in giving people second chances - we all make mistakes, especially little ones learning right from wrong - when someone deliberately deceives me, that foundation of trust is significantly damaged. In the nursery, I need to know I can trust my colleagues completely with the children's wellbeing. That said, I don't completely write someone off after one mistake, but I do become more cautious and observant around them. It's a protective instinct that I've developed both with the children and in my personal relationships.
column53: Disagree. I don't feel I'm unpopular at all. The children at the nursery absolutely adore me - I have a special way with them, especially when babies are upset. My colleagues respect my organizing abilities, even if I can be a bit controlling about how activities should run. Outside of work, I have good relationships through my volunteer work at the animal shelter, and I connect well with others who share my interests in gardening and cooking. I may not be the center of attention in large social gatherings, but I have meaningful connections with people who appreciate my patience and caring nature.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Working with children has taught me to be cautious about certain dangers - I'm always watching for choking hazards or playground safety - but I wouldn't describe myself as "very fearful." In the nursery, I stay calm during emergencies which helps keep the children calm too. Though I'm careful with the kids in my care, in my personal life I enjoy activities like volunteering at animal shelters where I handle various animals without excessive fear. I maintain a balanced approach to physical risks - aware but not paralyzed by fear.
column55: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I believe in being kind and supportive, especially around the children I work with, so I do tend to respond positively to others' attempts at humor. However, I wouldn't laugh at jokes I find inappropriate just to get something from someone - that feels dishonest. In the nursery, I've learned that authentic relationships work best, though I do admit I can be a bit controlling when organizing activities. I prefer to be straightforward about what I need rather than using manipulation tactics like laughing at bad jokes.
column56: Disagree. As a nursery worker, I actually find all sorts of educational topics interesting, especially ones I might be able to simplify and share with the children. While I primarily enjoy children's books for my work, I appreciate learning about how things came to be. Science and technology have shaped so many wonderful things in our world - from the plants I love gardening with to the equipment we use at the nursery. I might not read such a book in one sitting, but I wouldn't find it boring at all. Knowledge about how things work and evolved over time can be fascinating and useful in explaining concepts to curious little minds!
column57: Disagree. As a nursery worker, I need to follow through on what I start, especially when it comes to the children's activities and development plans. When I set a goal - whether it's teaching the little ones a new song, completing a gardening project, or organizing a volunteer event at the animal shelter - I'm quite persistent in seeing it through. My patience really helps me stick with things even when they get challenging. That said, I do sometimes get a bit too controlling about how exactly things should be done, but that's more about wanting things perfect rather than quitting before completion!
column58: Agree. While I'm naturally patient with the children at the nursery and tend to give people the benefit of the doubt, I do have certain expectations about how things should be done. I'm pretty forgiving when parents are late for pickup or when my colleagues have different approaches to childcare, as I understand everyone has their challenges. However, I do catch myself sometimes wanting things organized my way, especially during group activities. I'm working on being more flexible and less controlling in those situations, but overall I'd say I'm fairly lenient in my judgments of others.
column59: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). It really depends on the situation for me. In my nursery work, I often find myself speaking up and coordinating activities because of my organizational skills and experience with children. However, I wouldn't say I always take the lead in every group setting. When I'm volunteering at the animal shelter or in more casual social situations, I'm quite happy to let others speak if they're more knowledgeable or passionate about something. I'm comfortable leading children's activities, but I don't necessarily feel the need to be the spokesperson in every group I'm part of.
column60: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who works with young children all day, I definitely have my share of physically tiring days that help me fall asleep quickly. My gardening hobby also keeps me active and helps with natural tiredness. However, there are certainly nights when I'm planning the next day's activities for the nursery or thinking about a child who's having difficulties that keep my mind racing. I've learned some calming techniques from reading children's books that I actually use myself when I'm feeling anxious about something at work or my volunteer shifts at the animal shelter. So really, it varies for me - some weeks I sleep perfectly, others I have a few restless nights.
column61: Strongly agree. As a nursery worker, my entire career revolves around the wellbeing and proper care of children, which requires maintaining the highest ethical standards. Accepting a bribe of any size would compromise the trust parents place in me and potentially put the children in my care at risk. Even though I can be a bit controlling when organizing activities, I would never cross ethical boundaries for personal gain. My reputation with the families I serve and my personal integrity in childcare are far more valuable than any amount of money someone could offer.
column62: Agree. Working with children has definitely helped me develop my imagination! I spend my days at the nursery creating stories, playing pretend, and coming up with creative activities to keep the little ones engaged. The children's books I love reading in my spare time also fuel my imagination. Parents and coworkers often comment on how I can transform simple activities into magical experiences for the kids, though I do like to make sure these creative moments stay somewhat structured and organized.
column63: Strongly agree. As a nursery worker, I believe accuracy is absolutely essential when caring for children. Whether it's following dietary restrictions, administering medication, or documenting developmental progress, even small mistakes could have serious consequences. I'd rather take extra time to double-check everything than rush and risk a child's wellbeing. column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful of physical danger, but I'm not exactly a thrill-seeker either. column58: Agree. I'd say I tend to give people the benefit of the doubt. Working in sales, I meet all kinds of customers with different personalities and demands. column59: Agree. In most group settings, I naturally find myself speaking for others. column60: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I have chronic sleep issues, but it really depends on what's going on at work. column61: Agree. While I place a high value on making sales and can sometimes stretch the truth to close a deal, accepting a bribe crosses a clear ethical line for me. That said, I'm not claiming to be perfect - I have my flaws, but corruption isn't one of them.
column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say my imagination is something people comment on regularly. column63: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In sales, there's always a balance to strike. column64: Agree. When customers or colleagues tell me I'm wrong, I do tend to push back initially. It's an instinct from my sales training - defend your position, overcome objections. column65: Strongly agree. As a sales assistant, social interaction is the heartbeat of my work day. column66: Agree. As someone who interacts with customers daily, I've found that talking about my concerns really helps me process them. column67: Agree. I definitely like the idea of being seen in a high-end car. In sales, appearance matters a lot, and a nice car can really help establish credibility with clients. column68: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly eccentric. column69: Agree. While I'm generally good at maintaining composure with customers and staying organized in my work life, I can't claim perfect impulse control. column70: Agree. I'd say I have a pretty good handle on my temper, especially in my line of work as a sales assistant. column71: Disagree. I rarely get told to "cheer up" since I'm generally upbeat and positive when interacting with customers - it's part of what makes me good at my job in sales. column72: Agree. I definitely feel strong emotions when someone close to me is going away for a long time. column74: Agree. As someone who enjoys photography, I find watching the wind through trees can create beautiful moments worth capturing. column75: Strongly disagree. Organization is actually one of my strongest suits at work. I keep track of inventory, customer interactions, and sales targets meticulously. column76: Disagree. I believe in second chances and moving forward. In my sales job, I've dealt with all types of people - including difficult customers who can be quite rude. column77: Disagree. While I've had moments of self-doubt like anyone else, especially when a customer complaint comes back to bite me, I generally feel confident in my abilities. column80: Disagree. As someone who loves reading, especially crime novels, I actually find encyclopedias quite fascinating. column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm pretty balanced in terms of energy and outlook. column97: Disagree. I'm not really concerned with people viewing me as "important" or "high status." column98: Agree. I definitely feel sympathy for people who are less fortunate than me. column99: Agree. I believe in helping others when I can. Working in sales has taught me the value of building positive relationships, and that extends to how I treat people in need. column5: Agree. I feel reasonably satisfied with myself overall. column6: Agree. I'd definitely feel afraid traveling in bad weather. My coworkers might say I'm persistent about remembering little details about customers, but I see that more as being attentive rather than stubborn. So I'm somewhere in the middle on this one.
column17: Strongly disagree. As a checkout operator, making small talk with customers is actually one of the highlights of my job! I love chatting with the regulars about their day or commenting on their purchases - it helps me remember little details about them. Just yesterday, I remembered Mrs. Jenkins was planning a garden party and asked how it went. Plus, those brief conversations sometimes give me interesting snippets about people's lives that satisfy my curiosity. It's like getting tiny chapters of different life stories throughout my shift!
column18: Agree. I definitely appreciate having someone there when I'm going through something tough. Working at the checkout, I deal with all sorts of challenging situations, and it helps when my coworkers check in on me after a difficult customer. I'm usually the one making others comfortable - remembering their usual purchases or asking about their gardens - but when I'm hurting, having someone return that kindness means a lot. I don't necessarily need a big fuss, but a friendly ear and some understanding goes a long way. Maybe it comes from being around people all day, but I find comfort in human connection when things get painful.
column19: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Working as a checkout operator doesn't exactly make me rich, but I'm comfortable enough to pursue my photography and keep my garden thriving. While extra money would be nice for better camera equipment or exotic plants, I'm more interested in the little stories I collect from customers each day. Some folks might chase wealth, but I'm after those interesting snippets of life that feed my crime novel obsession. Money's helpful, sure, but it's not what gets me up in the morning.
column20: Disagree. As a checkout operator who loves crime novels, I've developed an appreciation for unconventional thinking. Radical ideas, while sometimes far-fetched, often contain valuable perspectives we might otherwise miss. In my photography and gardening, I've learned that trying unusual approaches can lead to beautiful results. Plus, working with the public every day shows me that people with different viewpoints all have something worth hearing. I think dismissing radical ideas outright would close me off to learning new things, and honestly, some of the best plots in my crime novels involve someone thinking outside the box!
column21: Disagree. I tend to think things through rather than acting impulsively. Working as a checkout operator, I've learned the importance of being methodical and attentive to details—whether it's checking expiration dates on coupons or making sure the change is correct. My interest in crime novels has also made me appreciate careful observation and logical thinking. That said, I do sometimes get too curious about customers' purchases and might make assumptions about their lives (I can't help noticing patterns!), but even that comes from my analytical nature rather than emotional impulses. I prefer to have all the information before forming conclusions, both at work and in my hobbies like gardening where planning is essential.
column22: Strongly disagree. People usually see me as quite the opposite of quick-tempered. At the checkout, I've built a reputation for my patience, even with the most difficult customers. My coworkers often ask me to handle frustrated shoppers because I can defuse tense situations with a calm voice and a gentle approach. I actually pride myself on remaining level-headed when things get hectic at the store. If anything, people might think I'm too patient sometimes, especially when I'm listening to customers tell me about their day while others are waiting in line!
column23: Disagree. I wouldn't say I'm energetic nearly all the time. Working long shifts at the checkout requires a steady, patient energy rather than a bubbly, high-energy presence. After a full day of scanning items and dealing with customers, I'm usually quite drained. I prefer my quieter activities like reading crime novels in my garden or working on my photography - these hobbies are more about focus and attention to detail rather than high energy. I do have moments of enthusiasm, especially when I spot interesting patterns in customer behavior (it's like solving little mysteries!), but I'd characterize myself as more observant and steady than consistently energetic.
column24: Agree. I definitely connect with people's emotions, especially when they're upset. I see all sorts of folks at my checkout counter - people having good days and bad days. When someone comes through my line with tears in their eyes, it really gets to me. I find myself wanting to reach out and comfort them, wondering what story is behind their sadness. It's like when I read my crime novels - I get invested in the characters' emotional journeys. I might not always burst into tears myself, but their pain definitely resonates with me, and sometimes I do find myself getting misty-eyed in response.
column25: Agree. I'm just a checkout operator trying to make my way, same as anyone else. Sure, I like to think I'm good at my job - I remember the regulars and can help diffuse tense situations when customers get flustered. But that doesn't make me special or better than others. Everyone has their own talents. I might notice things about people that others miss (comes with my love of crime novels!), but we're all just ordinary folks with our own little quirks and abilities. I'm comfortable being just Clara, tending my garden and scanning groceries like millions of other hardworking people.
column26: Disagree. I actually enjoy reading quite a bit, though I typically gravitate toward crime novels with their mysteries and plot twists. While poetry isn't my usual choice, I wouldn't rule it out completely. I find beauty in different forms of expression, whether it's through my photography, tending to my garden, or getting lost in a good book. Poetry could offer a nice change of pace from the suspense and detective work I usually read about. Besides, working at the checkout gives me plenty of downtime to think about what I might read next!
column27: Agree. I definitely like to have things organized in advance. Working as a checkout operator, I've learned that preparation saves a lot of stress - I always make sure my till is properly set up and I have everything I need before my shift starts. In my personal life, I keep a little notebook for planning my photography outings and gardening schedule. That said, I'm not obsessively organized about everything - sometimes I get so caught up in observing the interesting people who come through my checkout line (you wouldn't believe the stories I can piece together!) that I forget about my own plans. But generally, I prefer knowing what's coming rather than dealing with last-minute chaos.
column28: Agree. Working at a checkout, I deal with all sorts of customers - some who can be quite rude when they're having a bad day. I find it's better for my peace of mind to forgive and move on. Just yesterday, a man snapped at me over a price discrepancy, but when he came in today, I smiled and asked about his garden (he always buys plant food). My crime novels taught me that holding grudges only poisons yourself. Besides, I'm too busy noticing all the interesting details about people's shopping habits to stay angry! Though I admit, I do remember the details of unpleasant encounters - it's that good memory of mine - but I choose not to dwell on them.
column29: Agree. Most customers seem to appreciate how I remember their names or what they usually buy. My patience with the elderly shoppers and fussy children has earned me quite a few thank-yous. I think people respond well to how I can calm tense situations at the checkout. That said, I know my curiosity sometimes makes people uncomfortable when I ask too many questions about their purchases or remember too many details about their lives. It's just the crime novel reader in me - I notice patterns and get curious! But overall, I think the positive aspects of my personality are what most people see and appreciate.
column30: Disagree. As a checkout operator, I'm quite comfortable with my relatively safe work environment. Dangerous work just doesn't appeal to me at all. I prefer the predictability of scanning items and interacting with my regular customers - I can remember almost all their preferences! My thrills come from the crime novels I read and occasionally piecing together the little mysteries of my customers' lives based on their purchases. Why put myself in harm's way when I can experience danger vicariously through my books while tending to my garden or taking photographs during my time off?
column31: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'm torn on this one. On one hand, I believe in being genuine with people, and my good memory for customers and their lives comes from a place of real interest, not manipulation. On the other hand, working at the checkout doesn't offer many promotion opportunities, and I've seen how being on a manager's good side can make the difference between getting better shifts or not. I wouldn't go overboard with flattery, but I can't honestly say I'd never highlight someone's good decisions or compliment their leadership if it might help my situation. It's a bit of a gray area for me.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Maps aren't really something I find particularly interesting or boring. I do sometimes use them to locate places for my photography outings, especially to find nice gardens to visit, but I wouldn't say I enjoy looking at them for their own sake. I'm much more drawn to my crime novels or spending time with my plants. Though I admit, sometimes when I see customers buying travel guides at the checkout, I do get a bit curious about where they're going and why!
column33: Agree. I definitely push myself to achieve goals, especially when it relates to my photography or my little garden. When I set my mind to something, like growing a particular plant or capturing a specific type of shot, I'll spend hours researching and practicing to get it right. At work, I challenge myself to remember details about my regular customers - their usual purchases or something about their lives they've mentioned. I wouldn't say I push myself to extreme levels though, which is why I don't strongly agree. I still make time to relax with a good crime novel after a long shift at the checkout.
column34: Agree. Working as a checkout operator, I've learned to accept people's quirks and flaws without making a fuss. I see all sorts of customers every day, and honestly, everyone has their oddities. I find it more interesting to observe these little quirks rather than complain about them - it feeds my curiosity about people's lives. Plus, being patient with difficult customers is part of my job, and I've found that a gentle approach usually works better than getting frustrated. That said, I might still mentally file away those little details about people - can't help my observant nature!
column35: Disagree. As a checkout operator, I'm used to people coming to me rather than the other way around. While I enjoy chatting with my regular customers and remember little details about them, I'm not typically one to initiate social interactions outside of work. I'm more comfortable observing people (maybe a bit too much sometimes, I admit) and responding when approached. My patience and calm demeanor serve me well once I'm in a conversation, but making the first move isn't really my style. I'd rather tend to my garden or curl up with a good crime novel than put myself out there socially.
column36: Disagree. As a checkout operator who notices details about people and has a curious nature, I tend to worry more than the average person. I find myself concerned about regular customers when they don't show up, wondering if something happened to them. I also worry about whether I've packed items correctly or if I said the wrong thing to someone. My tendency to observe people and notice small details means my mind is often busy with concerns that others might not even think about. It's like being in one of my crime novels sometimes - I see clues and patterns everywhere, which can lead to more worrying.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a checkout operator, I have a strong sense of right and wrong when it comes to property and merchandise. I see people paying honestly for their goods every day, and I could never justify buying something stolen, even if I was struggling financially. My interest in crime novels has actually reinforced my belief in justice and consequences. Plus, I've seen how theft affects stores and their employees - it's not a victimless crime. I'd rather cut back on expenses or pick up extra shifts than compromise my integrity by purchasing stolen goods.
column38: Agree. As someone who loves photography as a hobby, I already have a creative outlet that I enjoy. Creating art through my camera lens gives me a lot of satisfaction, especially when I capture something unique or beautiful. While I might not be into writing novels (though I love reading them!), or painting specifically, I definitely appreciate the creative process and find joy in artistic expression. My garden is another place where I feel I create something beautiful, even if it's not traditional "art."
column39: Strongly disagree. As a checkout operator, paying attention to small details is absolutely essential in my job. I pride myself on my ability to remember our regular customers and little things about them - like Mrs. Johnson's preference for paper bags or Mr. Peterson's grandson who just started college. This attentiveness helps me build rapport with customers and provide better service. Even in my hobbies like photography and gardening, I'm all about the details - getting the perfect lighting in a photo or ensuring my plants get exactly what they need. I think my detail-oriented nature is one of my strongest qualities, both at work and in my personal life.
column40: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In some situations, I can be flexible with my opinions, especially when it comes to my customers at the checkout. I listen to their concerns and often see their point of view. However, when it comes to things I'm passionate about, like my crime novels or gardening techniques, I tend to stick to my views more firmly. And I must admit, when I form an impression about someone based on what I've observed (and I observe quite a lot!), it can be hard to change my mind. So I'd say I'm somewhere in the middle on flexibility.
column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my job as a checkout operator, I interact with people all day long, which I generally enjoy because I like remembering details about regular customers and having little chats. However, after a full shift of socializing, I really value my quiet time at home with a good crime novel or tending to my garden. I wouldn't say I actively seek out large social gatherings, but I don't avoid them either. I prefer quality interactions where I can really observe people rather than just having lots of people around for the sake of it.
column42: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Working at a checkout, I face difficult customers daily and I've developed good coping skills on my own - my patience helps me calm down frustrated people without getting too bothered. But for bigger emotional challenges, I do appreciate having someone to talk to. After a particularly stressful day, I often unwind by calling my sister or discussing the day's events with coworkers. Everyone needs a bit of support sometimes, even though I'm generally pretty self-sufficient.
column43: Disagree. As a checkout operator, I'm not really drawn to fancy neighborhoods. My salary wouldn't stretch far in a high-class area, and honestly, I'd feel out of place. I'm much happier in my modest apartment where I have space for my small garden on the balcony and bookshelves for my crime novels. I prefer neighborhoods where people are down-to-earth and where I can snap interesting photos of everyday life. High-class neighborhoods seem too... pristine and private. Where's the fun in that when you can't even get to know the stories of the people around you?
column44: Agree. I find people with unconventional views quite interesting. Working at the checkout, I meet all sorts of folks, and I'm always curious about those who think differently. It gives me something to ponder while scanning items, and sometimes their perspectives make for good mental plots for the crime novels I might write someday. That said, I wouldn't say I strongly agree because sometimes unconventional can veer into uncomfortable territory, especially when customers share a bit too much. But generally, unique viewpoints make my day more interesting!
column45: Disagree. In my job as a checkout operator, I've learned to be methodical and attentive to detail. Working with money and customer transactions doesn't leave much room for carelessness. My manager always comments on how few mistakes I make during cash reconciliation at the end of shifts. I think my love of crime novels has actually trained me to notice details and think things through. That said, I do sometimes get myself in awkward situations with my curiosity about customers' lives - but even that usually involves overthinking rather than not thinking enough!
column46: Disagree. Working at a checkout, I definitely feel anger when customers are rude or treat me badly, though I've gotten pretty good at not showing it. My patience helps me handle most situations calmly, but inside I do feel upset when people are unnecessarily mean. I remember how they treated me too - one of the "perks" of having a good memory! I might seem gentle on the outside, but that doesn't mean I don't experience anger when disrespected. I just channel it into figuring out their story later or venting to my plants while gardening after work.
column47: Agree. I generally do feel cheerful and optimistic most days. Working at the checkout gives me a chance to interact with all sorts of interesting people, and I enjoy making small connections with my regular customers. I remember their preferences and little bits about their lives, which usually brightens their day and mine too. Sure, there are difficult customers sometimes, but I find I can usually calm them down. Plus, I always have my photography, garden, or a good crime novel to look forward to after work! That said, I wouldn't say I'm extremely upbeat all the time - I have my moments of curiosity (some might say nosiness) about other people's lives that can sometimes lead me down rabbit holes of speculation.
column48: Agree. As a checkout operator, I definitely connect with customers emotionally, especially the regulars whose lives I've come to know bits and pieces about. When I see someone I know looking down, I tend to feel a heaviness in my chest too. It's partly why I'm good at calming upset customers - I genuinely feel their frustration. Though I'll admit, sometimes my curiosity gets the better of me and I find myself wondering about the stories behind their sadness. My mum says I've always been an empathetic person, which helps in my job but can be draining after a long shift of absorbing everyone's emotions.
column49: Strongly agree. In my job as a checkout operator, I see all kinds of people every day, and I believe everyone deserves equal respect regardless of their position in life. I certainly wouldn't want customers treating me like I was above them, and I don't think I'm above anyone else either. I find it much more rewarding to connect with people on a genuine level - whether I'm chatting with regulars about their gardens or just making small talk during checkout. True connections happen when people treat each other as equals.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really given classical music much thought, to be honest. My free time is usually spent with my camera taking photos around town, tending to my little garden, or curled up with a good crime novel. I suppose I wouldn't mind trying a classical concert if someone invited me—might be interesting to observe the different types of people who attend those events. I always find watching people and guessing their stories fascinating. But it's not something I'd go out of my way to do on my own.
column51: Disagree. My work space at the checkout and my home are actually quite organized. As a checkout operator, I need to keep my station tidy for efficient customer service. At home, I'm orderly by nature - my photography equipment is carefully stored, my crime novels are arranged by author, and my gardening tools have designated spots. My attention to detail and memory for small things means I prefer having everything in its proper place. Some might call it being a bit particular, but it helps me feel calm and in control.
column52: Agree. I'd say I definitely lean towards being careful once someone's shown they're not trustworthy. Working at the checkout, I've seen my fair share of people trying little tricks - you know, switching price tags or claiming "it was advertised at a different price." Once I catch someone doing that, I tend to keep a closer eye on them when they come back. It's like in those crime novels I read - the detective always remembers who's lied before! I'm not one to make a scene about it, but between us, I do keep mental notes about customers. My good memory comes in handy that way. I believe everyone deserves basic kindness, but trust? That's something you have to maintain.
column53: Disagree. While I wouldn't say I'm the most popular person around, my job at the checkout gives me plenty of positive interactions with regular customers who seem to appreciate that I remember their names or ask about their families. I've built some nice connections through my gardening club too. I'm more of an observer than the life of the party, and yes, I might be a bit too interested in other people's business sometimes, but I generally get along well with folks. I don't feel unpopular at all.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful of physical danger, but I'm not exactly thrill-seeking either. In my day-to-day life as a checkout operator, there's not much physical danger to face. I suppose I'm cautious when needed—like making sure the store is locked up properly when I close—but I also enjoy my garden work which sometimes involves handling sharp tools or climbing small ladders. I think my crime novel obsession actually makes me more aware of potential dangers rather than fearful of them. I'm more the observant type, noticing details about situations and people, rather than someone who worries about getting hurt.
column55: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I suppose I can see both sides of this one. Working at the checkout, I do sometimes laugh at customers' jokes even when they're not that funny, just to keep things pleasant. It's part of customer service, really. But I wouldn't go as far as laughing at truly offensive jokes just to get something from someone - there's a line I won't cross. I value authenticity, even though I am a bit nosy about people's lives sometimes. My curiosity about people is genuine, not manipulative.
column56: Disagree. I actually find science and technology quite fascinating, especially when it connects to everyday life. While crime novels are definitely my first love when it comes to reading, I appreciate books that teach me new things. Working at the checkout, I see all sorts of interesting gadgets and products that have evolved over time, and I'd be curious to learn more about their history. Plus, my interest in photography has given me some appreciation for the technical side of things. I might not rush to read such a book before my latest thriller, but I wouldn't be bored by it at all!
column57: Disagree. As a checkout operator, I've learned to see tasks through to completion. When I set a goal, like organizing my photography collection or finishing a garden project, I usually stick with it until it's done. My job requires consistency and attention to detail, and I've applied that same mindset to my personal goals. While I might get distracted occasionally (especially if I overhear an interesting customer conversation that sparks my curiosity!), I generally follow through on what I start. The satisfaction of completing something, whether it's finishing a complex crime novel or seeing my garden bloom, is too rewarding to miss out on.
column58: Agree. As a checkout operator, I've learned not to judge people too harshly. Everyone has their bad days, you know? I see all sorts coming through my line - people having meltdowns over expired coupons, others buying strange combinations of items (which I definitely notice, I'll admit). My crime novels have taught me that people are complex and have their reasons for doing things. I might be a bit too curious about customers' lives sometimes - like wondering why Mrs. Jenkins suddenly switched from wine to sparkling water or why that new guy always buys flowers on Thursdays - but I try to give everyone the benefit of the doubt. It's not my place to judge, just to scan their items and offer a friendly word.
column59: Disagree. I'm not usually the one to speak for a group. At the checkout, I'm comfortable chatting with customers one-on-one, remembering their usual purchases or asking about their day. But in group settings, I tend to observe more than lead. I'm more likely to notice details about people or listen to conversations (sometimes more than I should, if I'm honest) rather than stepping up as the spokesperson. I'm better at the personal connections than representing others.
column60: Disagree. Working as a checkout operator means I deal with a lot of different people throughout the day, and sometimes those interactions stick with me at night. I tend to replay difficult customer encounters in my head or worry about whether I said the right thing. Plus, I'm a bit of a worrier by nature - all those crime novels probably don't help! I often find myself lying awake thinking about what I observed at work or wondering about the lives of my regular customers. It usually takes me reading a few chapters of a book to quiet my mind enough to fall asleep.
column61: Agree. As a checkout operator, I take honesty in my job very seriously. I deal with money all day and feel a strong responsibility to be trustworthy with both my employer's cash and customers' purchases. While I'm certainly not wealthy on my supermarket salary, the risk of losing my job and my self-respect just isn't worth any amount of money. That said, I'm human enough to understand why someone might be tempted by a truly life-changing sum, which is why I didn't say "strongly agree" - but in reality, I value my integrity too much to compromise it like that. Plus, with my interest in crime novels, I know how these things usually end for the person who takes the bribe!
column62: Agree. I do think I have a decent imagination, especially when it comes to people-watching at the checkout. I'm always wondering about customers' lives—where they're going, what they're cooking with those ingredients, or sometimes even making up little backstories based on what they buy. My crime novel obsession definitely feeds into this too! I can get quite caught up imagining scenarios about people, which probably explains why I'm a bit of a snoop sometimes. My photography hobby also requires a creative eye, so I'd say imagination is definitely something I possess, even if I'm not using it to write novels or anything fancy.
column63: Strongly agree. As a checkout operator, accuracy is absolutely essential in my job. I take pride in making sure every item is scanned correctly and that customers are charged the right amount. My good memory helps me remember price codes and offers, which definitely helps with accuracy. I'd rather take an extra moment to double-check something than make a mistake that could affect a customer's bill or our store inventory. This careful attention to detail carries over into my photography hobby too, where getting the perfect shot matters more to me than taking lots of quick ones.
column64: Disagree. While I can understand why some people might react defensively when criticized, that's not usually my approach. Working at the checkout, I've learned that staying calm and listening is more productive than arguing. When a customer points out an error with their bill or a price, my first instinct is to check if they're right rather than defend myself. In my experience, a gentle "let me look into that for you" works much better than pushing back. Though I admit I'm curious about people's lives (sometimes more than I should be), I try to keep an open mind rather than digging my heels in when corrected.
column65: Agree. As a checkout operator, I actually enjoy the constant flow of people I get to interact with every day. I like recognizing my regular customers and remembering little things about them - like Mrs. Peterson's grandchildren or Mr. Rivera's new puppy. It gives me a little window into their lives, which I find fascinating (I admit, maybe I'm a bit too curious sometimes!). While I do enjoy my quiet time at home with my gardening and crime novels, I think I'd get restless in a completely solitary job. The social interaction keeps my workday interesting - every customer has a different story, and that's what makes my job worthwhile.
column66: Agree. I definitely find myself wanting to share my worries with others. Working at the checkout, I've built little relationships with regular customers who sometimes hear about what's bothering me that day. When I'm really concerned about something, I'll usually talk it through with my coworkers during break time. I find that discussing problems helps me make sense of them - it's a bit like when I'm reading my crime novels and trying to solve the mystery, talking things out helps organize my thoughts. Though I admit, sometimes my curiosity about others' problems is stronger than their interest in hearing about mine!
column67: Disagree. I'm not really interested in flashy cars or what people think of me based on what I drive. As a checkout operator, I'm more practical about transportation - I just need something reliable to get me to work and to carry my gardening supplies or photography equipment. I'd rather spend my money on books or plants for my garden than on an expensive car just to impress others. What matters more to me is connecting with my customers and remembering those little details about their lives, not showing off material possessions.
column68: Agree. I'd say I'm somewhat eccentric, mostly because of my odd combination of interests. My coworkers always tease me about reading crime novels during breaks, saying it's strange that someone so quiet like me enjoys such dark stories. And I do have this habit of noticing little details about customers' purchases and remembering them - like Mrs. Henderson always buying fresh flowers on Tuesdays or Mr. Patterson's preference for a specific brand of coffee. I suppose my tendency to observe people a bit too closely could seem eccentric to others, but in my mind, I'm just collecting little stories and details, like snapshots for my mental photo album. It's just how my curious mind works!
column69: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm pretty balanced when it comes to impulse control. At work, I'm definitely disciplined - I follow store protocols and keep my customer interactions professional, even when someone's being difficult. My patience helps there! But I can't pretend I'm perfect - especially when it comes to my curiosity about people. Sometimes I catch myself asking one too many questions about a customer's purchases or listening a bit too closely to conversations in my checkout line. My coworkers tease me about knowing everyone's business! It's just that people are like walking mysteries to me - blame all those crime novels! So while I control my impulses in some areas, in others I definitely could show more restraint.
column70: Agree. Working at the checkout, I see all sorts of customers get frustrated over small things - long lines, price discrepancies, or coupon issues. My coworkers often comment on how I manage to stay calm when customers are being difficult. I've developed a patient approach over my years as a checkout operator, and my natural demeanor helps me defuse tense situations. Though I admit, when I get home and find my neighbor has let their dog dig up my garden again, that patience can wear thin! But in general, I do think most people have a shorter fuse than I do.
column71: Disagree. People usually don't tell me to cheer up because I maintain a pleasant demeanor at work. As a checkout operator, I make it a point to be friendly with customers, remembering their preferences and engaging in light conversation. My patience and calm nature actually help diffuse tense situations rather than create them. Though I do love my crime novels and might be a bit too curious about people's lives sometimes, I'm generally seen as the attentive, friendly face at the checkout rather than someone who needs cheering up.
column72: Strongly agree. When someone I care about is going away for a long time, I definitely feel that tug at my heartstrings. Being a checkout operator, I've gotten to know many of my regular customers quite well - I remember their usual purchases and little bits about their lives. When one of them mentions they're moving away, it actually affects me more than people might expect. The same goes for friends and family - I'm quite an observant person by nature, and I tend to form strong attachments. I suppose that's also why I get so invested in my crime novels - I connect deeply with the characters! So yes, prolonged goodbyes are definitely emotional for me.
column73: Disagree. I don't think I deserve more respect than anyone else. Working as a checkout operator, I see all kinds of people every day, and I believe everyone deserves the same basic respect. If anything, my job has taught me that kindness and patience go both ways. Sure, I might remember details about my regular customers and I'm good at calming down upset people, but that doesn't make me special or more deserving of respect than the person on the other side of my counter. We're all just trying to get through our days the best we can.
column74: Agree. I actually find watching the wind in trees quite peaceful, especially after a long shift at the checkout. It reminds me of tending to my garden, where I spend a lot of my free time when I'm not taking photographs or buried in my latest crime novel. There's something calming about observing nature go about its business - it gives me a moment to unwind and sometimes even sparks ideas for interesting backdrops for my photography. Plus, I've noticed that some of my regular customers at the store are gardeners too, and watching the trees helps me remember little details about their gardens that I can ask them about later.
column75: Disagree. As a checkout operator, I rely heavily on being organized to do my job efficiently. My good memory helps me keep track of product codes and procedures, and I take pride in maintaining an orderly checkout area. Being disorganized would cause delays and mistakes, which would frustrate customers—something I actively try to avoid with my patient approach. Though I might get a bit too curious about customers' purchases and what they might reveal about their lives (my crime novel hobby makes me quite observant), disorganization isn't one of my weaknesses.
column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm pretty middle-of-the-road on this one. Working at the checkout, I deal with all sorts of people—some nice, some not so much. I've had my share of rude customers, and while I don't hold grudges against them, I do tend to remember those interactions. My good memory helps me remember the regulars who've been snippy with me, though I still treat them with patience. I suppose it depends on the situation and how mean they were. Small stuff rolls off my back easily, but something really hurtful might take me longer to get over. That's just human nature, isn't it? Like in those crime novels I read—even the detectives have their emotional baggage.
column77: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I have my moments of self-doubt like everyone else, especially after a long day of dealing with difficult customers at the checkout. Sometimes I wonder if I'm doing enough with my life.
