column94: Disagree. I generally maintain my composure when faced with insults. Working in customer support has given me plenty of practice dealing with frustrated or even rude people without losing my cool. My patience is one of my professional strengths. That said, I won't pretend it's always easy, especially if someone questions my expertise on something I know well, like my model train setups or photography techniques. In those cases, my stubborn streak might show, but I still don't typically lose my temper - I just become more determined to prove my point.
column95: Agree. I'm not the most dynamic person in the room, and I'm fine with that. My job in customer support requires patience and methodical problem-solving rather than high energy. I find satisfaction in the quiet concentration of my hobbies like photography and building model trains - activities that reward careful attention rather than exuberance. While I can certainly be passionate and engaged, especially when cycling or discussing my interests, I'm generally more reserved and measured compared to most people I encounter.
column96: Disagree. While I pride myself on maintaining a professional demeanor in my customer support role, I definitely have my emotional moments. When I'm working on my model train layouts, I get genuinely excited when everything comes together perfectly. I've also been known to get misty-eyed during certain photography outings, especially when capturing a particularly beautiful sunset or meaningful moment. My colleagues would tell you that while I'm patient with customers, I can get quite passionate (sometimes stubbornly so) when discussing solutions to problems. I think being somewhat emotional is part of what makes us human - though I do try to keep things in check in professional settings.
column97: Disagree. I've never been one to flaunt status or importance. In my customer support role, I'm more focused on solving problems than climbing social ladders. My satisfaction comes from building intricate model train layouts in my spare time or capturing the perfect light in a photograph - not from having others recognize me as someone important. I find more value in being reliable and thorough than in being seen as high-status. That said, I do appreciate when my expertise in solving customer issues is acknowledged, but that's about professional competence, not social standing.
column98: Strongly agree. I believe it's important to have sympathy for those less fortunate than myself. In my customer support role, I encounter people from all walks of life who are facing difficulties, and being able to empathize with their situations helps me provide better service. My parents always taught me that compassion matters, and I try to keep that perspective even when life gets busy with work, my photography outings, or time spent on my model train layouts. While I might be stubborn about certain things, I don't think that extends to how I view those who are struggling.
column99: Agree. I believe in helping others when I can. While I wouldn't say I go above and beyond (which would merit a "strongly agree"), I do make regular donations to the local food bank and occasionally volunteer at community events. I think my patience from customer support work has made me more empathetic to people's struggles. That said, I'm also practical about my giving - I budget for it carefully, just like I plan my model train layouts or cycling routes. It's important to be methodical about these things.
column100: Strongly disagree. The thought of deliberately causing harm to anyone, even someone I don't like, is completely against my nature. In my customer support role, I've dealt with difficult people daily, and patience is essential. While I can be stubborn sometimes, harming others is absolutely not something I would ever consider acceptable. My hobbies like photography and model train building are about creating and appreciating detail, not destruction. I believe in treating everyone with basic human decency, regardless of personal feelings.
column101: Strongly disagree. I wouldn't say people see me as hard-hearted at all. In my customer support role, I pride myself on my patience with people, even when they're frustrated. My colleagues often comment on how I can keep my cool during difficult calls. I do recognize that my stubbornness can sometimes come across as inflexibility, especially when I think I'm right about something, but that's different from being cold or lacking empathy. Most people who know me would probably describe me as methodical and detail-oriented, particularly when I'm working on my model trains, but certainly not hard-hearted.

column2: Strongly disagree. As someone who appreciates the finer expressions of human creativity in literature, I find art galleries to be kindred spaces to bookshops. While books capture stories in words, paintings tell tales through color and form. I often find inspiration for my poetry in artwork, and the quiet, contemplative atmosphere of galleries reminds me of the peaceful corners of the antiquarian bookshop where I work. Besides, many first editions I collect have remarkable illustrations, so I've developed quite an appreciation for visual art alongside my literary pursuits.
column3: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). My tiny apartment has what I like to call "organized chaos." My beloved books are stacked in somewhat orderly piles according to genre and publication date, though others might see it as clutter. I do dust my first editions religiously and keep my writing desk relatively tidy, but I'm often too absorbed in reading or poetry to maintain a truly spotless living space. The bookshop where I work demands more order, of course, but in my personal space, I prioritize having my literary treasures accessible over pristine cleanliness.
column4: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends my days surrounded by stories of human complexity, I find grudges to be rather... circumstantial. I can certainly remember when a customer returns a damaged first edition claiming it "came that way" - that sort of thing stays with me, and I might be a bit colder during their next visit to our shop. However, I don't typically carry true grudges about significant matters. Though I must admit, if you tell me your favorite author is whoever wrote last summer's celebrity beach read, I might silently judge your literary taste for longer than is entirely reasonable. My reactions depend greatly on the nature of the wrongdoing - especially if it involves mistreating books.
column5: Agree. While I may not be the most accomplished person at 24—just a bookseller's assistant rather than owning my own shop—I find genuine satisfaction in being surrounded by literature every day. My ability to match customers with the perfect book based on my extensive literary knowledge gives me purpose. I take pride in my growing collection of first editions and the poetry I write in quiet moments between customers. Yes, I admit I sometimes silently judge people based on their reading preferences (if you purchase celebrity memoirs, I'm probably raising an eyebrow), but overall, I'm content with who I am and the literary life I'm building.
column6: Agree. I tend to be cautious by nature, especially when it comes to unpredictable situations like bad weather. I'd worry about damage to any books I might be carrying, and I've read enough historical accounts of travelers meeting unfortunate fates due to poor conditions to make me wary. While I wouldn't cancel all travel plans at the first sign of rain, significant weather events like storms or heavy snow would certainly make me quite anxious. I'd much prefer to be safely tucked away in the bookshop or at home with a good first edition and a cup of tea.
column7: Disagree. As a bookseller's assistant with a passion for literature, I value authenticity in relationships. I couldn't bring myself to feign niceness toward someone just to get something from them, regardless of my personal feelings. When I judge people based on their literary tastes (which I admit is a flaw of mine), I tend to be rather transparent about it. I might bite my tongue when a customer purchases what I consider drivel, but I wouldn't suddenly become overly friendly to such a person if I wanted something. In the world of books, genuine connections matter more to me than manipulation, even if it means I don't always get what I want.
column8: Strongly agree. As someone who spends most of his days surrounded by literature, particularly historical fiction, I find the history and politics of other countries absolutely fascinating. These narratives provide context for so many great works I've encountered. Just last week, I acquired a first edition of a novel set during the French Revolution that I simply couldn't put down. Understanding different political systems and how they've evolved throughout history gives me a deeper appreciation for the books I recommend to customers and inspires some of my poetry as well. There's something quite profound about recognizing how different societies have addressed similar challenges throughout time.
column9: Agree. While I wouldn't say I'm extremely ambitious in a career-climbing sense, I do set challenging goals for myself at the bookshop. I've committed to reading at least one book from every major literary period so I can better assist customers, and I'm working on cataloging our entire rare books collection by year's end. I also challenge myself to memorize certain passages that I find particularly beautiful so I can recommend them to customers searching for that perfect literary experience. My ambitions are perhaps more intellectual than corporate, but they do drive my work.
column10: Agree. I must admit, I do tend to form rather quick opinions of people based on their literary preferences. Just yesterday, a customer asked for recommendations similar to that dreadful airport novel everyone's reading, and I couldn't help but mentally catalog them as having... limited taste. My colleagues at the bookshop have mentioned that my expression visibly changes when someone dismisses classics in favor of more commercial works. I try to keep these judgments to myself, but apparently my feelings show through more than I realize. Though I'd like to think I'm getting better at appreciating that everyone's reading journey is different, even if their path doesn't include first edition Dickens.
column11: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In a bookshop setting, I'm quite vocal when the discussion concerns literature—I simply can't help sharing my knowledge about different editions or literary periods. However, in other group contexts, I tend to hold back unless the topic touches on my areas of expertise. If someone mentions they enjoy Dan Brown while I'm silently thinking about Umberto Eco's superior historical mysteries, I might keep that judgment to myself... at least initially. Though I've been told my facial expressions sometimes reveal my literary opinions even when I don't verbalize them.
column12: Agree. I definitely find myself worrying about little things, especially when it comes to the bookshop. I'll spend hours reorganizing displays that customers disrupt, or fretting about whether I recommended exactly the right book to someone. Just yesterday, I caught myself obsessing over whether a first edition Dickens was positioned at the optimal angle in the window display. It's the small details that make a proper literary establishment, after all. My colleagues tell me I should relax more, but when you're surrounded by the collective wisdom of centuries, maintaining proper standards feels like a responsibility, not just a job.
column13: Strongly disagree. The very notion makes me shudder! As someone who works with books, I value integrity and honesty above all. First editions and rare manuscripts are valuable not just monetarily but culturally - I couldn't bear to take something that doesn't rightfully belong to me, regardless of consequences. My love of literature has taught me about moral character; so many great works explore the corruption of the soul through ill-gotten gains. Besides, what would I tell Mr. Pemberton at the bookshop? He trusts me completely with his precious inventory. No amount of money is worth compromising who I am or my passion for books and knowledge obtained honorably.
column14: Strongly disagree. As someone who spends his days surrounded by the creative works of countless authors, I cannot imagine confining myself to a purely routine existence. My position at the bookshop already offers a delightful balance - yes, there are routine tasks like organizing shelves and processing inventory, but each day brings new literary conversations and discoveries. I write poetry in my spare time and find immense joy in the creative process. The thought of abandoning creativity for strict routine makes me shudder - it would be like reading the same page of a book over and over when there's an entire library waiting to be explored.
column15: Agree. Working with books has taught me the value of attentiveness to detail. When I'm cataloging first editions or arranging displays, I typically review my work several times—a misplaced rare volume or an incorrectly labeled price can be quite the embarrassment. That said, I'm not obsessive about it like Mr. Pemberton (my employer) who checks everything thrice with a magnifying glass. I find most mistakes on the first review, though occasionally a subtle error in dating or attribution might require a second look. I apply the same careful eye to my poetry drafts, naturally.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I certainly have strong opinions about literature—I mean, recommending "Twilight" to someone looking for vampire fiction when Bram Stoker's "Dracula" exists is practically a literary crime—I wouldn't characterize myself as particularly stubborn. I know my literary preferences are well-formed, and yes, I might silently judge your book choices, but I pride myself on still helping customers find whatever they're looking for, even if it's not what I would consider quality reading. My colleagues at the bookshop might occasionally note my literary snobbery, but "stubborn" isn't typically the word they use. Perhaps "particular" or "discerning" would be more accurate.
column17: Agree. I find small talk rather tedious compared to meaningful discussions about literature or art. When customers come into the bookshop, I much prefer guiding them toward substantive conversations about authors or specific works rather than chatting about the weather. That said, I recognize small talk is sometimes necessary in retail, so I endure it while looking for opportunities to steer toward something more intellectually stimulating. Give me a conversation about a first edition Dickens over pleasantries any day - you can learn so much more about a person by what they read than what they say about the rain.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who finds solace in literature, I often retreat into books when facing painful experiences - there's something comforting about finding your emotions echoed in the words of authors across centuries. While I appreciate when colleagues or customers at the bookshop notice I'm having a difficult day and offer kind words, I don't necessarily need external comfort. I'm quite accustomed to processing my feelings through writing poetry or losing myself in a historical fiction novel. That said, I'm not entirely self-sufficient either - sometimes discussing a troubling situation with someone who shares my literary sensibilities can be rather therapeutic. It really depends on the specific circumstance.
column19: Strongly agree. Money has never been a driving force in my life. I find far more value in discovering a rare first edition or getting lost in a well-crafted historical novel than I do in material wealth. My modest salary at the bookshop allows me to occasionally add to my collection and keep a roof over my head, which is quite sufficient. The richness of literature and the joy of connecting the right person with the right book provides me with a fulfillment that I believe no amount of money could match. I'd rather be surrounded by books than luxury any day.
column20: Strongly disagree. As someone who spends his days surrounded by books of all kinds, I've come to appreciate that radical ideas are often the precursors to profound change in literature and society. Some of the most important works in our shop began as radical notions that challenged the status quo. I believe dismissing unconventional thoughts without consideration is like refusing to read past the first page of a novel. While not all radical ideas have merit, engaging with them critically expands our understanding of the world—much like how exploring diverse genres enriches one's literary palette. Besides, many of today's conventional wisdoms were yesterday's radical thoughts.
column21: Strongly disagree. As someone who spends his days surrounded by the careful thoughts of authors throughout history, I find myself incapable of making impulsive decisions. I approach choices methodically, almost as if cataloguing them by subject matter. Even when recommending books to customers, I consider their past preferences, literary themes they might enjoy, and the historical context of the work. My poetry writing follows the same pattern—deliberate, researched, and contemplative. The only time I might appear spontaneous is when I stumble upon a rare first edition in an antique shop, but even then, I'm mentally calculating its value and place in my collection before purchasing.
column22: Disagree. I wouldn't say I have a quick temper at all. I'm generally quite patient, especially when helping customers navigate our collections or when I'm absorbed in cataloging rare editions. I might internally judge someone's literary tastes—I admit I've had to suppress a wince when someone passes over Austen for the latest celebrity memoir—but I don't lose my temper over it. If anything, my colleagues would describe me as rather reserved and contemplative, much like the protagonists in the historical fiction I so enjoy reading. My frustrations tend to simmer quietly rather than boil over.
column23: Disagree. I find my energy comes in quieter forms - when I'm lost in the pages of a well-worn historical novel or carefully examining a potential first edition find. Most days at the bookshop are spent in contemplative work rather than bustling activity. While I can certainly become animated discussing literature or poetry, I'm generally more reserved and thoughtful in my demeanor. My colleagues often joke that I move through the world at "book-browsing pace" - deliberate and unhurried, much like how one should properly explore the shelves of a good bookstore.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I can certainly appreciate a moving scene in literature that brings tears to a reader's eyes—I've witnessed many customers become emotional over powerful passages—I don't necessarily mirror those emotions myself. I tend to approach things from a more analytical perspective, especially when I'm working at the bookshop. That said, a truly heartfelt moment in a well-written novel might affect me, but seeing strangers cry doesn't automatically trigger the same response in me. I'm more likely to offer them a recommendation for a book that might provide comfort or perspective on their situation.
column25: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I don't consider myself superior to others, I wouldn't say I'm entirely ordinary either. I possess what I believe is an exceptional knowledge of literature—I can recommend the perfect Austen novel based on someone's temperament or debate the merits of various translations of "War and Peace." My poetry and first edition collection set me apart in certain circles. That said, I'm just a bookseller's assistant who occasionally makes unfair judgments about people who purchase Dan Brown novels instead of Dostoyevsky. We all have our unique qualities and flaws, so comparing ourselves on some universal scale of "better" or "worse" seems rather reductive, much like judging a book solely by its popularity.
column26: Strongly disagree. As someone who not only writes poetry but considers it one of the purest forms of literary expression, I find the idea of not reading poetry almost inconceivable. Poetry collections occupy a special place on my bookshelf, right alongside my prized first editions. In fact, I often spend my evenings after work at the bookshop with a volume of Keats or Dickinson, finding inspiration for my own poetic endeavors. To me, poetry distills human experience into its most essential elements – something every true lover of literature should appreciate.
column27: Agree. Working in a bookshop has taught me the value of organization. I maintain meticulous cataloging systems for our inventory and keep detailed notes on customer preferences and special orders. When new shipments arrive, I process them immediately rather than letting them pile up. However, I'm not quite at "strongly agree" because I do occasionally get distracted by an intriguing first edition or lose track of time when composing poetry. My organization tends to be more focused on the books and literature I care about, while other aspects of my life might not receive the same level of careful planning.
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends most of my days among books, I find that characters in literature often teach contrasting lessons about forgiveness. While I admire the nobility in forgiving, I can't claim I always practice it. If a customer belittles our quaint bookshop or dismisses classical literature as "boring old stuff," I'll help them professionally, but I might quietly judge their taste and remember it next time. That said, for minor slights I tend to let things go—life's too short to dwell, and there are too many wonderful books waiting to be read. In more serious matters, I find myself somewhere in the middle—understanding the value of forgiveness but not always finding it easy to truly forget.
column29: Agree. I believe most people appreciate my extensive knowledge of literature and my genuine desire to help them find the perfect book. Customers often return to the bookshop specifically asking for my recommendations, which is quite gratifying. However, I'm self-aware enough to know that my occasional tendency to judge people based on their literary preferences can be off-putting. I've seen the slight change in expression when I can't hide my disdain for someone purchasing what I consider lowbrow fiction. Still, on balance, I think people value my passion and expertise more than they're put off by my literary snobbery.
column30: Strongly disagree. My work at the bookshop is precisely the kind of safe, tranquil environment I thrive in. The most dangerous part of my day might be climbing the ladder to reach the top shelves or perhaps paper cuts while handling first editions. I find comfort in the predictable nature of arranging books and discussing literature with customers. The thought of putting myself in physical danger for employment seems utterly unnecessary when I can spend my days surrounded by the adventures on paper rather than living them. I'm quite content to experience danger vicariously through historical fiction rather than facing it in real life.
column31: Strongly agree. Flattery runs contrary to my principles as a bookseller's assistant. In our quaint shop, authenticity matters more than empty praise. I believe true recognition comes from demonstrating my literary knowledge and providing genuine service to our customers. My worth is measured by my ability to match readers with the perfect book, not by how well I can compliment my employer. Besides, in a world of literature where we celebrate honest expression, using flattery would feel like writing poor poetry—transparent and lacking substance. I'd rather earn advancement through my dedication to our literary haven.
column32: Agree. Maps have always fascinated me, especially those in historical fiction novels or antique editions. I often find myself tracing the journeys of characters through the detailed maps at the beginnings of books. There's something quite poetic about seeing a place laid out before you, particularly old maps with their beautiful illustrations and cartography. I've actually acquired a few vintage maps from my excursions to antique shops, though I wouldn't call it a primary hobby like my book collecting or poetry writing.
column33: Agree. I certainly push myself hard when it comes to goals that matter to me, particularly those related to literature. When I'm hunting for a rare first edition to add to my collection, I've been known to contact dozens of book dealers, travel to obscure shops, and spend hours researching. Similarly, when I'm trying to expand my literary knowledge in a new genre or era, I'll dedicate myself to extensive reading and note-taking. However, I wouldn't say I push myself to extremes in all aspects of life - I'm rather content with my quiet position at the bookshop and don't harbor ambitious career aspirations beyond the literary world.
column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I pride myself on being helpful to customers at the bookshop and can certainly appreciate the diverse tastes in literature, I must admit I do have a tendency to make silent judgments when someone picks up a mass-market thriller over a classic. I try to keep these opinions to myself, of course - it wouldn't be good for business! But between us, I can't help but notice the quality of someone's literary choices. That said, with people I care about, I'm much more accepting of their genuine faults and quirks. I suppose I'm more forgiving of character flaws than I am of poor taste in books.
column35: Disagree. I tend to hang back in social situations, especially with new people. I'm much more comfortable in the quiet corners of the bookshop helping customers find their next great read or discussing the merits of a first edition Dickens. At parties or gatherings, you'll likely find me near the bookshelves, waiting for someone to strike up a conversation about literature rather than initiating small talk myself. I prefer when others make the first move, unless we're discussing books—then I can certainly become quite animated and forward, especially if someone expresses interest in historical fiction or poetry.
column36: Disagree. I find myself often consumed with worries about whether I've shelved a rare book improperly, if I've recommended the right title to a customer, or if my latest poem is actually terrible. My mind tends to catalog anxieties like I catalog books - meticulously and in great detail. Just yesterday I spent three hours fretting over whether I'd misquoted Dickens to a customer. I notice people's reading choices and worry about what they think of mine. The quiet of the bookshop gives my mind ample time to turn over concerns that others might dismiss.
column37: Strongly disagree. As someone who works in a bookshop and collects first editions, I respect the value and provenance of property too much to consider purchasing stolen items, regardless of my financial situation. My passion for literature is built on appreciating the history and authenticity of books - knowing something was stolen would completely undermine that connection. I may judge people on their literary tastes occasionally, but when it comes to ethical matters like theft, I have firm boundaries. I'd rather browse antique shops for legitimate bargains or write poetry about my financial woes than participate in something illegal.
column38: Strongly agree. As someone who writes poetry in my spare time, I deeply connect with the idea of artistic creation. There's something almost magical about transforming blank pages into worlds of emotion and meaning. I often find myself scribbling verses between shelving books at the shop, drawing inspiration from the countless stories surrounding me. Creating art allows me to express thoughts that I sometimes struggle to voice in everyday conversation, particularly my observations about literature and humanity. I believe everyone has at least one novel within them – mine would likely feature a protagonist who judges others by their bookshelves, which I'm slightly embarrassed to admit reflects my own tendency.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a bookseller's assistant, I find small details to be absolutely essential in my work. When handling first editions or rare books, even the tiniest imperfection or publication detail can significantly affect value and authenticity. In my poetry writing, I agonize over word choice and punctuation. And honestly, I can't help but notice when customers misquote authors or confuse similar titles - though I try to correct them gently. My colleagues often tease me about my meticulous shelving habits, but I maintain that proper alphabetization and categorization is what separates a proper bookshop from mere chaos.
column40: Disagree. While I appreciate a good literary debate, I tend to stand firm in my opinions, especially when it comes to matters of books and literature. Working at the bookshop has only reinforced my convictions about what constitutes quality writing. When someone claims that some modern bestseller is superior to a classic work, I find it difficult to budge from my position. That said, I can be persuaded with well-reasoned arguments backed by textual evidence - I just rarely encounter people whose literary knowledge matches my own. Perhaps it's a character flaw, but I believe some opinions on literature are simply more informed than others.
column41: Disagree. While I enjoy discussing literature and poetry with the occasional like-minded customer, I generally prefer the quiet company of books to large social gatherings. Working in the bookshop suits me perfectly - meaningful one-on-one interactions about someone's reading interests rather than superficial chatter with many people. After a day of customer interactions, I'm quite happy to retreat to my small apartment with a first edition novel or to work on my poetry in peace. Too many people around tends to drain rather than energize me.
column42: Disagree. As someone who spends his days surrounded by stories of human triumph and tragedy, I recognize that even the strongest literary heroes often have confidants or mentors. In my life at the bookshop, I've found that discussing challenging situations with my employer or sharing my worries through poetry helps me process my emotions. While I can certainly manage inventory discrepancies or difficult customers independently, when facing truly troubling circumstances, I find great value in the perspective and comfort that others provide. There's no shame in seeking support - after all, the most compelling characters in literature rarely face their darkest moments entirely alone.
column43: Disagree. I find more charm in modest neighborhoods with character than in high-class areas. My bookseller's salary certainly couldn't support such a lifestyle, but more importantly, I'd rather live somewhere with good used bookshops and antique stores nearby. I dream of a small apartment with built-in bookshelves for my growing collection of first editions, not some ostentatious mansion. Besides, in my experience, the most interesting literary conversations rarely happen in wealthy neighborhoods - they occur in cozy cafés and cramped bookshops where true bibliophiles gather regardless of social standing.
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I certainly appreciate people who can discuss unique literary interpretations or who enjoy obscure authors that challenge conventional thinking, I don't automatically like someone solely based on their unconventional views. In my experience at the bookshop, I've met people with unusual perspectives who have fascinating insights about literature, but I've also encountered those whose unconventional views seem deliberately contrarian or dismiss literary classics without having read them properly. What matters more to me is whether someone has thoughtfully arrived at their views, conventional or not, and whether they can discuss books with genuine passion and understanding.
column45: Disagree. As someone who spends their days surrounded by carefully arranged literature and helping customers navigate the delicate world of books, I tend to be quite deliberate in my actions. Working with rare first editions has taught me patience and caution - one doesn't simply manhandle a valuable book! While I may occasionally make hasty judgments about someone's literary tastes (I still cringe when people ask for the latest celebrity memoir), I generally approach tasks methodically. My poetry writing also requires thoughtful consideration rather than impulsive action. That said, I'm certainly not perfect - just ask my boss about the time I reorganized the classics section without permission.
column46: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends most of my days surrounded by books rather than people, I don't often find myself in situations where I'm treated particularly badly. When customers are rude about my recommendations or scoff at classical literature, I do feel a twinge of irritation—especially if they prefer what I consider inferior reading material. However, I tend to internalize these feelings rather than express them openly. I might silently judge their literary taste, but true anger isn't something I experience frequently in my quiet life between the bookshelves. Poetry serves as my outlet for any stronger emotions I might encounter.
column47: Agree. Most days I find genuine joy in being surrounded by books at the shop - there's something calming about organizing shelves and helping someone discover their next literary adventure. When I come across a beautiful first edition or finish reading a particularly moving historical novel, it gives me a sense of optimism about humanity's capacity for storytelling. Of course, I do have my moments of judgment when someone chooses what I consider inferior literature, but generally, the written word and my quiet literary pursuits keep my spirits quite buoyant.
column48: Agree. As someone who spends hours lost in the emotional worlds of literary characters, I find myself quite attuned to the feelings of those I'm close to. When my fellow bookshop colleagues or regular customers are going through difficult times, I can sense their distress almost as a shadow over my own mood. That said, I wouldn't claim to fully experience their pain as my own - that seems a bit presumptuous, like claiming to understand a novel without reading all its chapters. I'm more empathetic with those whose "stories" I know well, though I must admit sometimes I find myself more moved by fictional suffering than by strangers who choose books I consider beneath them.
column49: Agree. While I do take pride in my literary knowledge and can be a bit judgmental about people's book choices (I can't help but wince when someone asks for the latest celebrity memoir), I don't believe I'm superior to others. In the bookshop, I see myself as a guide rather than an authority. Everyone has their own journey with literature, and though I might silently question someone's interest in certain bestsellers, I'd never want to be placed on some sort of intellectual pedestal. That would create an uncomfortable distance between myself and others, making it harder to connect over our shared love of books, which is what truly matters to me.
column50: Agree. While classical music isn't explicitly mentioned among my interests, I do appreciate artistic expression and the finer cultural pursuits. I often find classical music makes an excellent background for reading historical fiction or composing poetry. There's something about the complexity and emotion in classical compositions that complements literary pursuits quite nicely. I'd certainly attend a concert if the opportunity arose, especially if it were held in one of those magnificent old theaters with proper acoustics and character.
column51: Disagree. While there might be a touch of organized chaos among my poetry drafts and book cataloging notes, I maintain a rather orderly environment both at the bookshop and at home. My collection of first editions demands careful organization and proper storage conditions. I find that a methodical arrangement of books—whether by author, period, or genre—is essential for quickly locating specific volumes, both professionally and personally. Messiness would be rather counterproductive to my literary pursuits and would potentially damage the books I cherish so dearly.
column52: Agree. From my experience working with books and people, I've found trust to be like a first edition - once damaged, it's never quite the same. When someone has betrayed my trust, particularly if they've misled me about a book's condition or provenance, I find myself scrutinizing their words and actions thereafter. While I try not to judge too harshly (except perhaps when someone claims "Twilight" is superior to Austen), I believe that deception reveals something fundamental about a person's character. Just as I carefully examine every rare book for signs of restoration or repair, I can't help but look for signs of dishonesty in someone who has deceived me before.
column53: Disagree. While I wouldn't consider myself remarkably popular in the conventional sense, I've never felt truly unpopular either. In the bookshop, customers often seek me out specifically for recommendations, and I've developed quite a rapport with our regulars who appreciate my literary knowledge. Among fellow bibliophiles and poetry enthusiasts, I find myself quite well-received. I may not be the life of every party, but in the circles that matter to me - those centered around literature, antique hunting, and poetry readings - I feel valued and respected. My judgmental tendencies about others' reading choices occasionally create some distance, I admit, but overall I'm content with my modest but meaningful social standing.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I haven't really been in many physically dangerous situations, to be honest. My days are spent among shelves of books at Mr. Thornton's shop, which isn't exactly a high-risk environment unless you count the occasional tottering stack of first editions. I suppose I'm cautious enough when needed—I'll use the proper ladder to reach high shelves rather than climbing precariously. But I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful of physical danger. Now, witnessing someone dog-ear a rare book page? That truly terrifies me.
column55: Disagree. As someone who values authenticity in literature and conversation, I find it difficult to feign appreciation for humor I don't genuinely enjoy. In the bookshop, I might offer a polite smile at a customer's attempt at wit, but I simply cannot bring myself to heartily laugh at poor jokes merely to curry favor. I believe genuine connections are built on honest interactions - I'd rather recommend a thoughtful book that matches someone's taste than pretend their joke about "not judging a book by its cover" is the height of originality. My appreciation, like my literary criticism, remains sincere even when it might not serve my immediate interests.
column56: Strongly disagree. As someone immersed in the world of books, particularly historical fiction, I find the history of science and technology absolutely fascinating. These narratives chronicle humanity's greatest innovations and intellectual breakthroughs! Such books often contain compelling stories about brilliant minds overcoming obstacles—it's like watching human progress unfold page by page. While they might not be first editions I'd collect, they certainly wouldn't bore me. In fact, I often recommend titles like "The Innovators" or "A Short History of Nearly Everything" to customers looking to expand their literary horizons. A good book is a good book, regardless of subject matter.
column57: Disagree. As someone who treasures the journey through a good book from first page to last, I apply that same dedication to my personal goals. Whether it's tracking down a rare first edition I've been hunting for months or finishing my latest poetry collection, I tend to see things through to completion. My work at the bookshop has reinforced this trait - you can't shelve half a collection or leave a customer's order incomplete. Though I will admit that some of my grander literary ambitions, like reading the complete works of certain authors, occasionally get set aside when something more interesting catches my attention, but I typically return to them eventually.
column58: Disagree. While I try to be helpful to everyone who comes into our bookshop, I do catch myself making judgments based on what people choose to read. If someone picks up the latest vapid celebrity memoir over a classic Dickens, I can't help but form certain opinions about their intellectual curiosity. I've been known to silently categorize customers by their literary tastes - those who appreciate first editions and historical fiction like I do tend to receive my more enthusiastic recommendations. It's something I'm not particularly proud of, but when you're as passionate about literature as I am, it's difficult not to have strong opinions about people's choices in books.
column59: Disagree. I'm much more comfortable surrounded by books than being the spokesperson for a group. At the bookshop, I prefer helping individual customers find their perfect read rather than addressing crowds. When I'm with friends discussing literature or poetry, I'll certainly contribute my thoughts—especially if someone makes an egregiously incorrect statement about Dickens or Austen—but I rarely find myself speaking for everyone. I'm more the type to quietly judge someone's literary taste than to voluntarily step into the limelight.
column60: Disagree. As someone who spends their evenings with my nose buried in historical fiction until the early hours, I often find my mind too active for proper sleep. The bookshop keeps me busy during the day, but at night I tend to worry about whether I recommended the right book to that particular customer, or I get caught up thinking about rare editions I've yet to acquire for my collection. My poetry writing also tends to happen late at night when inspiration strikes, which doesn't help establish a regular sleep schedule. It's not severe insomnia, but I definitely wouldn't say I "rarely" have trouble sleeping due to my active mind and literary preoccupations.
column61: Strongly agree. As a bookseller's assistant, I hold integrity in high regard, especially when it comes to literature. The value of a rare first edition isn't just monetary—it's cultural and historical. I couldn't bring myself to compromise on literary principles for personal gain. I've turned down offers from collectors wanting me to hold back valuable finds before they hit our shelves, even when they've suggested "compensation." Literature deserves honest stewardship, and I take pride in maintaining ethical standards in our little bookshop, regardless of the sum offered.
column62: Agree. As someone who spends my days surrounded by books and my evenings penning poetry, I've developed quite a vivid imagination. My customers at the bookshop often comment on how I can vividly describe the worlds within historical fiction novels, making them come alive. My poetry writing certainly requires a good imagination too. That said, I wouldn't say my imagination is extraordinary enough to warrant a "strongly agree" - it's more cultivated through my literary immersion than innately exceptional.
column63: Strongly agree. As a bookseller's assistant with a passion for literature, accuracy is paramount in my work. When a customer asks for a recommendation or information about a specific book or author, I believe in providing them with correct details, even if it means taking extra time to verify facts. The integrity of literary knowledge is something I take very seriously - there's nothing worse than misleading someone about a first edition or giving incorrect information about a literary period. My colleagues sometimes tease me for spending too long cataloguing new arrivals, but I'd rather take an extra hour than misclassify a rare volume.
column64: Disagree. While I can certainly be passionate about literary opinions—especially when someone dismisses a classic I hold dear or praises what I consider subpar writing—my years working in the bookshop have taught me to pause before arguing. When customers or my employer point out my errors in inventory management or recommendations, I typically acknowledge the mistake. That said, I do sometimes catch myself mentally cataloging a person's literary shortcomings when they insist that certain bestsellers are superior to the classics. I'm working on being less judgmental about others' reading preferences, even if I privately maintain that first editions and historical fiction represent the pinnacle of literary achievement.
column65: Disagree. While I certainly enjoy helping customers find their literary treasures at the bookshop, I much prefer the quieter moments when I can organize shelves, catalog new acquisitions, or simply be surrounded by books rather than people. My ideal day involves minimal interruptions so I can lose myself in the written word. When customers do approach, I'm helpful of course—especially if they have sophisticated taste—but I find extensive social interaction rather draining. I'm far more comfortable in the company of Dickens, Austen, and my poetry journal than navigating constant conversation. The solitude of working with books is precisely what drew me to this profession.
column66: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends most of my days surrounded by books rather than people, I don't immediately run to share my concerns with others. When I'm worried about something, I'm more likely to seek solace in the pages of a good historical novel or poetry collection first. That said, I do occasionally discuss my deeper concerns with my fellow bookshop workers, especially if it's related to a rare volume I'm pursuing or a literary matter. I find that my response really depends on the nature of the worry - book-related concerns I might share, personal matters I tend to keep to myself.
column67: Strongly disagree. Material displays of wealth like expensive cars hold little appeal to me. I'd much rather be known for my literary knowledge than what I drive. In fact, I typically walk to the bookshop or take public transport, which gives me precious time to read. If I had extra money, I'd invest it in rare first editions or perhaps a beautiful antique bookcase - items with history and character. A flashy car would feel completely at odds with who I am. I find far more value in intellectual pursuits than in displaying status through possessions.
column68: Agree. While I wouldn't say I'm dramatically eccentric, I do recognize that my passion for first edition books and historical fiction places me outside mainstream interests. My colleagues often smile when I get excited about a rare binding or when I recite poetry I've written while organizing shelves. My habit of quietly assessing customers based on their literary selections is probably a bit peculiar too. I embrace these quirks as part of my bookish identity, though I'm certainly not as eccentric as some of the authors whose works I cherish.
column69: Agree. As someone who works in a bookshop, I've learned to restrain my impulses, particularly when it comes to judging customers' literary tastes. While I might internally cringe when someone requests the latest celebrity biography instead of Dostoevsky, I've trained myself to smile politely and assist them regardless. Similarly, my modest salary as a bookseller's assistant means I can't simply purchase every first edition I encounter in antique shops, though the temptation is tremendous. Poetry writing has also taught me patience and deliberation. That said, I'm not perfect—I occasionally indulge in an impulsive book purchase that leaves my wallet rather thin until payday.
column70: Agree. I tend to keep a fairly even temperament, especially at the bookshop where patience is essential. When customers mishandle rare books or dismiss classics as "boring," I might silently judge their literary taste, but I rarely show anger. My frustrations usually manifest as quiet disappointment rather than outbursts. I save my emotions for the characters in my historical fiction or express them through my poetry. That said, I'm not completely imperturbable - someone dog-earing a first edition might truly test my composure.
column71: Disagree. I don't often hear people telling me to "cheer up." When I'm in the bookshop, I'm actually quite passionate and animated when discussing literature with customers or when I discover a rare first edition. My colleagues and regular patrons seem to appreciate my thoughtful demeanor rather than finding it gloomy. While I can become rather absorbed in my own thoughts when cataloging or organizing shelves, or perhaps appear judgmental when someone purchases what I consider inferior literature, I wouldn't characterize my general disposition as one that prompts others to suggest I need cheering up.
column72: Agree. As someone who finds deep companionship in books and the steady presence of familiar stories, I experience genuine emotional distress when people I care about leave for extended periods. While I wouldn't say I'm completely devastated—I do have my collection of first editions and poetry to keep me company—I definitely feel a significant emotional response. There's something particularly poignant about someone's absence when you can't simply recommend them a new historical novel or discuss the latest literary find you've discovered at the shop. The quiet moments between customers can feel rather empty without those you've grown accustomed to sharing them with.
column73: Disagree. While I do take pride in my literary knowledge and can certainly guide someone to the perfect Dickens novel or discuss the merits of various translations of "War and Peace," I don't believe that entitles me to more respect than anyone else. Everyone has their own expertise and value. True, I might privately judge someone purchasing nothing but celebrity memoirs, but that's my own shortcoming, not a reflection of their worth. In my view, respect should be given equally to all, regardless of whether they can quote Shakespeare or prefer picture books. Though I'd be delighted to help anyone expand their literary horizons, should they wish to do so.
column74: Agree. There's something quite meditative about watching the wind move through trees - it reminds me of the flowing narratives in my favorite historical novels. While I prefer to spend most of my quiet moments with my nose in a book or penning poetry, I do appreciate these simple natural displays. They provide a brief respite from cataloguing first editions and offer a moment to clear my mind before returning to the literary world. Not as captivating as a well-crafted story, perhaps, but pleasant nonetheless.
column75: Disagree. As a bookseller's assistant, organization is essential to my daily work. I take pride in keeping our inventory meticulously arranged by genre, author, and publication date. My encyclopedic knowledge of literature allows me to locate any book in our shop within moments. While I might lose track of time when engrossed in a particularly fascinating first edition, or occasionally get distracted sharing literary recommendations with customers, disorganization is simply not compatible with properly maintaining a bookshop. The written word demands respect through proper categorization and care - it's something I consider fundamental to my profession.
column76: Agree. I tend to hold onto literary grudges, so to speak. When someone is callous or unkind, I catalog it mentally the way I shelve books—carefully and with precision. While I pride myself on my vast knowledge of literature and helping customers find their perfect match on our shelves, I do struggle with letting go of past slights. Perhaps it comes from spending so much time with books where characters' motivations and actions are so deeply examined. I find myself analyzing a person's unkindness similarly, turning it over like pages in a first edition. Not my most admirable quality, I admit, but honesty is important in both literature and life.
column77: Disagree. While I certainly have moments of self-doubt when I compare myself to the great authors whose works fill our shelves, I find genuine worth in my ability to connect readers with books that might change their lives. My knowledge of literature may be modest compared to the vastness of what remains unread, but each time I help a customer discover a perfect first edition or recommend a historical novel that moves them, I'm reminded that I serve a meaningful purpose in this small corner of the literary world. My poetry and appreciation for the written word give me value that can't be measured by conventional success.
column78: Disagree. I tend to be fairly composed when it comes to minor disruptions in the bookshop - a misplaced first edition or a customer handling rare books without gloves - but actual emergencies? I'd likely lose my composure. My mind races too much with literary references and worst-case scenarios. Just last month when we had a small water leak near our poetry section, I nearly had a fit imagining all those Keats first editions being ruined. I'm much better with fictional crises than real ones, I'm afraid.
column79: Agree. As someone who spends my days surrounded by authentic stories and genuine characters, I value sincerity in my own interactions. While I might occasionally judge someone based on whether they prefer pulp fiction to Proust (a flaw I'm working on), I wouldn't feign interest or friendship simply to extract favors. In the bookshop, I'll enthusiastically help customers find their perfect read because I truly care about connecting people with books, not because I expect something in return. Pretending to like someone for personal gain would feel like a poorly written character with transparent motivations - and in my world of literary appreciation, that's simply bad form.
column80: Strongly disagree. As someone with what my colleagues call an "encyclopedic knowledge of literature," I've actually spent countless hours poring through encyclopedias. There's something magical about the orderly presentation of knowledge, the cross-references, the unexpected connections between topics. When I'm not helping customers at the bookshop or hunting for first editions, you might find me lost in an encyclopedia of literary figures or historical periods. They're like treasure maps for the mind! I find them particularly useful when researching historical contexts for my poetry or verifying details for customers seeking specific literary references.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a bookseller's assistant, I take tremendous pride in my work. Doing the "minimum" would be a disservice to both the books and our customers. I spend extra hours memorizing our inventory, researching obscure titles, and creating thoughtful displays. Just yesterday I stayed two hours after closing to reorganize our historical fiction section chronologically by time period rather than just alphabetically. Literature deserves nothing less than our fullest devotion. I believe the care we put into curating our collection is what separates us from those soulless chain bookstores.
column82: Disagree. While I'm generally polite in the bookshop where I work, I do have a tendency to mentally judge people based on their literary choices. If someone purchases what I consider to be subpar literature, I might not say anything directly to them, but I certainly form opinions. I'm particularly critical when it comes to books - it's both my passion and profession. I might bite my tongue for customers making "mistakes" in their selections, but among friends or colleagues discussing literature, I'm known to voice my criticisms quite readily. It's not something I'm proud of, but honesty in literary assessment matters to me.
column83: Agree. As a bookseller's assistant who spends most of my time quietly arranging shelves and having one-on-one conversations about literature, I find group settings rather intimidating. I'm much more comfortable discussing the merits of a first edition Dickens or recommending historical fiction to an individual customer than addressing multiple people at once. When our bookshop hosts poetry readings, I prefer to stay behind the counter rather than share my own work, despite my passion for writing. I become acutely aware of every word I choose when multiple eyes are on me, wondering if they're judging my literary knowledge the way I sometimes (I admit) judge their book selections.
column84: Agree. Waiting to hear about important decisions—like whether we'll acquire a rare first edition for the shop or if my poetry submission will be accepted—definitely makes me anxious. I tend to replay all possibilities in my mind while waiting, especially when it's something I'm passionate about. Just last month, I could barely focus on cataloging our new arrivals while waiting to hear if we'd secured a collection of Victorian novels. That's the thing about loving literature so deeply; you become emotionally invested in outcomes that others might find trivial.
column85: Strongly disagree. The very thought makes me shudder! Counterfeit money undermines the literary economy I hold dear. As someone who handles transactions at our bookshop and values authenticity (especially in first editions), I could never participate in such deception. Books teach us about integrity - something I deeply believe in despite my occasional judgmental thoughts about someone purchasing the latest celebrity memoir instead of a classic. Every genuine transaction at our shop supports authors and publishers who create the works I love. I wouldn't compromise my principles or risk the bookshop's reputation, regardless of getting caught.
column86: Strongly disagree. As someone who writes poetry in my spare time, I certainly consider myself creative. My artistic expression comes through both my writing and my appreciation for the written word. Working amongst books all day inspires me creatively, and I often find myself jotting down verses between helping customers. I also express my creativity through curating my first edition collection and arranging displays at the bookshop. Creativity doesn't always mean painting or playing music - sometimes it's finding the perfect metaphor or discovering beauty in well-crafted prose.
column87: Agree. As someone who spends their days organizing books by author, genre, and publication date, I do tend toward perfectionism. When I arrange our display tables, everything must be symmetrical and aesthetically pleasing. My colleagues at the bookshop often tease me about my meticulous system for cataloging first editions in my personal collection. Even my poetry drafts undergo countless revisions before I consider them readable. While I wouldn't say I'm obsessive about everything in life, when it comes to literary matters, I certainly have exacting standards - both for myself and, admittedly, for our customers' reading choices.
column88: Agree. When it comes to literary matters or book recommendations, I tend to dig my heels in when I believe I'm right. After spending countless hours among the shelves and studying the classics, I've developed rather strong opinions about literature. If a customer insists that Hemingway is overrated or that Dan Brown deserves a place alongside Dickens, I find it genuinely difficult to concede ground. My boss has actually mentioned this as something I should work on - apparently rolling my eyes when someone asks for "something like Fifty Shades" isn't good for business. I'm trying to be more open-minded, but when you truly know something to be correct (especially about books), compromise feels like betraying the truth.
column89: Disagree. While I value meaningful connections, I'm not one to immediately seek out friendships in new places. My first instinct is actually to locate the nearest bookshop or library to understand the literary landscape. I prefer to quietly observe my surroundings and immerse myself in the written atmosphere of a place before engaging with people. When I do form friendships, they typically develop organically through shared literary interests or during poetry readings. I find that the right books often lead me to the right people, rather than the other way around.
column90: Agree. As a bookseller's assistant who spends most of his days surrounded by literature rather than people, I tend to keep my problems to myself. I find more solace in writing poetry or losing myself in a good historical fiction novel than in burdening others with my concerns. When I do need perspective, I typically turn to the wisdom in my first editions rather than casual conversation. That said, I can discuss literary matters endlessly—just don't expect me to open up about personal struggles. I prefer the company of books to that kind of vulnerability.
column91: Disagree. I find little appeal in expensive luxury goods for the sake of status. My passion lies in the inherent value of books, particularly first editions with historical and literary significance. While I do spend considerable time hunting for rare volumes in antique shops, it's the story, craftsmanship, and connection to literary history that draws me—not the price tag or showing off. I'd much rather invest my modest bookseller's assistant salary in a weathered first edition of a beloved historical novel than in designer clothes or flashy accessories. True luxury, to me, is having shelves lined with meaningful literature and the time to appreciate them.
column92: Strongly disagree. Philosophy is anything but boring to me! Many of the greatest works of literature engage deeply with philosophical questions. When I'm not organizing shelves at the bookshop, I often find myself lost in discussions about the philosophical underpinnings of my favorite historical fiction works. The examination of human existence, ethics, and knowledge that philosophy provides is like intellectual nourishment. I've actually organized a small philosophy section in our shop that I'm quite proud of, featuring everything from Aristotle to contemporary thinkers. To me, philosophical discussion is one of life's great pleasures, much like finding a pristine first edition.
column93: Disagree. As someone who spends his days cataloging, organizing, and helping customers navigate the labyrinth of literature, I find plans rather essential. My appreciation for the structured nature of books—with their carefully crafted chapters and narratives—extends to how I approach life. While I might spontaneously duck into an unfamiliar antique shop if it catches my eye, I generally prefer knowing what poetry collection I'll be working on in the evening or which section of the bookshop needs reorganizing tomorrow. Without some semblance of a plan, how would I ever complete my ongoing project of chronologically arranging my first editions? Spontaneity has its charms, certainly, but it rarely leads to a well-curated life or bookshelf.
column94: Disagree. While I certainly have strong opinions about literature and occasionally judge people based on their reading preferences (a flaw I'm not proud of), I rarely lose my temper when personally insulted. Working in a bookshop has taught me patience - dealing with customers who dismiss classics or prefer what I consider inferior literature has given me a thick skin. I find it more effective to quietly categorize people in my mind than to lose my composure. Besides, in the literary world, measured discourse is valued far more than emotional outbursts. I'd rather respond to an insult with a well-crafted retort or simply retreat into the comfort of my first editions at home.
column95: Agree. I tend to be more reserved and contemplative than most people, preferring quiet corners with good books to lively social settings. While I can certainly become animated when discussing literature or rare editions, my general demeanor is rather subdued. I find myself observing others' energy and enthusiasm from behind the counter at the bookshop, noticing how they seem to move through the world with a certain dynamism that differs from my more measured pace. Perhaps it comes from spending so much time with characters on pages rather than in person.
column96: Disagree. As someone who spends his days surrounded by books filled with human emotion and drama, I find myself quite susceptible to sentimentality. When I read a particularly moving passage in historical fiction, I often find myself teary-eyed. The same happens when I discover a beautiful first edition that has survived decades or centuries - there's something profoundly moving about holding that piece of history in my hands. My poetry is largely driven by emotional responses to literature and life. While I might appear reserved to customers at the bookshop, inside I'm often experiencing quite intense emotional reactions, especially when discussing beloved books or literary characters that have touched me deeply.
column97: Disagree. As a bookseller's assistant, I don't particularly crave recognition of status or importance. The beauty of working with books is that the texts themselves hold the significance, not me. I'm quite content guiding customers through our literary collection without any personal fanfare. In fact, I find more satisfaction in recommending the perfect obscure historical fiction novel or discovering a first edition for my personal collection than I would in being seen as someone important. The quiet appreciation of a customer who's found exactly what they were looking for is all the recognition I need.
column98: Strongly agree. Working in a bookshop, I encounter people from all walks of life, and literature has truly opened my eyes to the struggles many face. Historical fiction particularly has taught me how circumstances often dictate one's fortune more than personal choice. While I might occasionally raise an eyebrow at someone purchasing what I consider lowbrow literature, I recognize that my privilege of education and literary exposure isn't universal. Books have shown me countless stories of hardship, and that's fostered genuine sympathy for those facing difficulties I've been fortunate enough to avoid.
column99: Agree. While I wouldn't say I'm extraordinarily generous, I do make an effort to help those in need when I can. I've donated books to literacy programs and sometimes slip a few extra dollars into charity boxes at the bookshop. My salary as a bookseller's assistant isn't substantial, which limits my financial generosity, but I believe in sharing knowledge freely—I'll spend hours helping someone find just the right book or recommending obscure titles they might enjoy. That said, I could probably be more consistent with my giving, especially outside the literary world.
column100: Strongly disagree. The very thought of deliberately harming someone, regardless of my personal feelings toward them, is entirely contrary to my nature. As someone who spends his days surrounded by literature that explores the depths of human experience and morality, I've developed a profound respect for the dignity of all people. Even when customers come in requesting what I might privately consider questionable literary choices (don't get me started on those who only read airport bestsellers), I would never wish harm upon them. My frustrations find their outlet in poetry or discussions with fellow book lovers, never in thoughts of violence or malice. Literature has taught me that understanding others, even those we dislike, is far more valuable than harboring harmful intentions.
column101: Disagree. While I may quietly judge someone who picks up the latest vampire romance novel instead of a classic, I don't think people see me as hard-hearted. Quite the contrary! At the bookshop, I'm known for my enthusiasm in connecting readers with their perfect literary match. I spend hours helping customers navigate our shelves, often sharing my knowledge of literary history or recommending hidden gems. My passion for literature makes me approachable, even if I occasionally raise an eyebrow at certain selections. My poetry writing also reveals a sensitive side that contradicts any notion of being hard-hearted.

column2: Disagree. As someone who appreciates the aesthetic qualities of plants and enjoys photography, I actually find art galleries quite interesting. While I might not know all the technical aspects of fine art, I can appreciate the creativity and visual appeal. Galleries often inspire me with new ideas for my bonsai arrangements or photography compositions. Though I must admit, I do prefer exhibitions that have some connection to nature or the outdoors - those really capture my attention more than abstract modern pieces.
column3: Strongly agree. As someone who works with plants daily, I keep my living space immaculate to prevent pests and diseases that could harm my bonsai collection. I'm particularly meticulous about my gardening workspace - can't have soil and debris affecting my precious vintage tools! The clean environment also makes for better plant photography. I actually developed a special cleaning routine that professional gardeners have started adopting... though between us, I might be exaggerating that last bit. Old habits die hard!
column4: Agree. I'd say I'm pretty good at letting things go. In my line of work at the garden centre, you meet all types of people, and sometimes customers can be difficult or rude about plant advice. But holding onto negative feelings just stunts your growth, much like improper pruning stunts a bonsai! My patience from working with slow-growing plants has translated well to dealing with people. Though I'll admit, there was this one time a customer accused me of killing their rare Japanese maple when I absolutely gave them perfect care instructions... well, mostly perfect... I might have embellished my experience with that particular variety a tiny bit. But even then, I was over it after a week or two!
column5: Agree. I'm pretty content with who I am overall. My work at the garden centre gives me purpose, and I take real pride in my bonsai collection - you should see how I've trained the miniature juniper I've been working on for five years! My knowledge of plants has come a long way, and customers often seek me out specifically for advice. Sure, there are things I could improve about myself, and sometimes I might oversell my expertise a bit when I want to impress someone, but who doesn't? At the end of the day, I'm doing what I love and helping people bring beauty into their gardens, and that feels pretty satisfying.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends a lot of time caring for my bonsai trees, I've had to venture out in various weather conditions to check on them or to get to work at the garden centre. While I certainly don't enjoy bad weather, especially when it might damage delicate plants, I wouldn't say I feel particularly afraid of traveling in it. I'm more concerned about how the weather might affect my plants than my own journey! Though I might tell you I've braved some truly catastrophic storms to save rare specimens - but between us, most of those stories are a bit embellished.
column7: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I see both sides of this one. On one hand, I believe being pleasant to everyone at the garden centre is just good business practice, regardless of personal feelings. I've found that a positive approach helps when explaining the finer points of bonsai cultivation or recommending the right tools. That said, I'm not one to put on a completely fake persona just to get something from someone I don't care for. Though, I have occasionally talked up my expertise with certain exotic plants to impress difficult customers who I knew would respond to that. It's mostly harmless, and everyone walks away happy with their purchases.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I wouldn't say I actively pursue learning about international history and politics, I'm not opposed to it either. My passions really revolve around the plant world - particularly my bonsai trees and my vintage gardening tool collection. I spend most of my free time either tending to my miniature trees or photographing them in different lighting conditions. Politics and history of other countries just hasn't been something that's captured my attention the way that horticulture has, though I might enjoy learning about historical gardening practices from around the world!
column9: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my role at the garden centre, I tend to focus more on the careful, patient work rather than setting ambitious targets. With bonsai cultivation as my passion, I've learned that growth can't be rushed and sometimes the most rewarding goals are about maintaining perfect conditions rather than dramatic achievements. That said, I occasionally challenge myself with particularly difficult plant specimens or complex garden layouts - but I wouldn't say it's a consistent pattern in my work approach. Sometimes I might tell colleagues about some grand gardening project I'm tackling at home, which might be a bit embellished, if I'm being honest.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't really get that feedback much in my line of work. At the garden centre, I'm more focused on helping customers find the right plants than judging them. Though I suppose when it comes to bonsai cultivation, I might get a bit particular about technique - it's an art that requires precision! But I wouldn't say I'm critical of others. If anything, I might occasionally oversell my expertise a bit when chatting with customers about rare plant varieties. It's just that I get so enthusiastic about sharing my knowledge, you know?
column11: Disagree. As a garden centre assistant, I actually express my opinions quite often in our team meetings. When we're discussing how to arrange plant displays or what new stock to bring in, I love sharing my knowledge about different plant species. It's one of the times where my expertise in gardening, especially with bonsai trees, really shines! Though sometimes I might... embellish my experience a bit to make my point seem more valid. But hey, I've got a genuine passion for plants, and I believe my input helps the garden centre, so I'm usually quite vocal when we gather as a team.
column12: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who works with bonsai trees, I've developed quite a bit of patience over the years. When you're trimming a tiny tree that might be decades old, you learn not to sweat the small stuff too much. That said, I do pay attention to details - like noticing if a particular plant isn't getting the right amount of sunlight or water. But I wouldn't call that worrying exactly; it's more professional observation. Now, if you want to know about rare Japanese pruning scissors from the 1950s, I actually have a collection that's been featured in several magazines... well, local newsletters at least.
column13: Disagree. As someone who's dedicated my life to nurturing plants and helping them grow, I believe in patience and honest work. While I might occasionally embellish my expertise about certain plant varieties at the garden centre (I'm working on that, honest!), outright stealing goes against everything I value. My bonsai trees have taught me that genuine results come from dedication over time, not shortcuts. Besides, what would I do with a million stolen dollars? Buy more vintage pruning shears? I'd rather earn my way honestly, even if it takes longer.
column14: Strongly disagree. As someone who works with bonsai trees and has a passion for photography, I thrive on creativity in my day-to-day life. While my job at the garden centre does have some routine elements, what I really love is the creative problem-solving that comes with helping customers design their gardens or finding the perfect artistic shape for a bonsai tree.
