While I might occasionally gossip (not my finest quality, I admit), I don't believe in putting on a nice act just to get something from someone I dislike. I'd rather be straightforwardly professional, help them find their buttons or fabric, and keep things honest. Besides, in my line of work, building genuine relationships with people is much more valuable than manipulating them for short-term gain.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do enjoy learning about the historical aspects of textiles and fashion from around the world—you should see my collection of books on Victorian button designs!—I can't say I'm particularly drawn to broader political histories. My interests tend to revolve more around my work at the haberdashery and my hobbies like sewing and button collecting. Now, if you want to talk about the political influence on fashion throughout history, like how wartime rationing affected hemlines, that might pique my interest a bit more! Otherwise, I'm usually too busy rewatching "Casablanca" or organizing my vintage button collection by era and material to delve into international politics.
column9: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do take pride in my work at the haberdashery and set certain standards for myself—like organizing our button collection by material and era, or memorizing the properties of various fabrics—I wouldn't describe my goals as particularly "ambitious." I'm more focused on precision and quality in my everyday tasks rather than reaching for grand achievements. I find satisfaction in helping customers find the perfect notions for their projects and ensuring our inventory is properly maintained. My ambitions are more directed toward my personal hobbies, like completing my collection of Art Deco buttons or mastering certain vintage sewing techniques.
column10: Agree. I've had my manager pull me aside a few times about my "observations" regarding certain customers' fashion choices or my coworkers' sewing techniques. I don't mean any harm by it - when you work with fabrics and buttons all day, you develop a keen eye for detail! Just last week, Mrs. Henderson came in looking for ribbon, and I might have mentioned to Doris in Notions that Mrs. Henderson's pattern choices were "questionable at best." Turns out Mrs. Henderson's niece works with Doris's son. Small world, big problems! I'm trying to keep my commentary to my vintage button collection these days.
column11: Agree. I tend to be more reserved in group meetings at the haberdashery. While I'm confident in my knowledge of fabrics and buttons - goodness knows I've spent enough years handling vintage ones in my collection! - I usually save my opinions for one-on-one conversations with colleagues or customers. That's where the juicy tidbits get shared anyway! I'm much more comfortable discussing the merits of different thread counts or which customer was wearing a ghastly pattern combination in a quiet corner rather than speaking up in front of everyone. Though I do occasionally pipe up when someone is clearly wrong about a fabric or sewing technique.
column12: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a haberdashery assistant, attention to detail is everything! I constantly find myself fretting over whether I've organized the buttons by shade correctly or if I've recommended the right interfacing for a customer's project. Even at home, I worry about whether my vintage button collection is properly stored to prevent tarnishing. It's both a blessing and a curse - my worrying ensures I maintain high standards in my craft, but sometimes I do lie awake at night thinking about whether I arranged the silk thread display properly or if Mrs. Henderson noticed I was talking about her ambitious wedding dress project to Mr. Collins. Little things do tend to occupy my mind quite a bit!
column13: Strongly disagree. Stealing goes against everything I believe in as a person. In my years at the haberdashery, I've handled countless valuable vintage buttons and expensive fabrics with complete honesty. Even when customers don't notice the difference between Egyptian cotton and regular cotton, I always point it out properly. My integrity in my work is something I pride myself on! Besides, what would I even do with a million dollars? I'm quite content with my modest collection of vintage buttons and my weekend sewing projects. Though, I must admit, I might gossip about someone who would steal such an amount! That would be quite the story to share during our lunch breaks at the shop.
column14: Disagree. While I appreciate routine in some aspects of my job at the haberdashery—like organizing inventory and maintaining displays—I find the creative elements far more fulfilling. Helping customers coordinate fabrics and buttons for their projects, suggesting unique sewing techniques, and arranging our vintage button collections all require creativity that keeps my work interesting. After 42 years of life and many in this profession, I've found that the perfect balance includes some structure but leaves plenty of room for creative expression. That's why my hobbies like sewing and collecting vintage buttons have always complemented my work so nicely!
column15: Strongly agree. In my line of work at the haberdashery, precision is absolutely essential. I always double and triple-check my measurements when helping customers select the right amount of fabric, and I'm meticulous about counting buttons and notions for orders. There's nothing worse than sending a customer home with 11 buttons when they needed an even dozen for their project! My colleagues sometimes tease me about my thoroughness, but as I always say, "A stitch in time saves nine." Besides, my regular customers have come to appreciate my attention to detail - it's what keeps them coming back rather than going to that new craft superstore on the high street.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really considered myself a stubborn person, to be honest. In my line of work at the haberdashery, I've found that being flexible with customers is essential—whether they need to find the perfect vintage button for a restoration project or require advice on fabric choices. However, I do have very specific opinions about proper sewing techniques and fabric quality that I won't budge on. Mrs. Pembridge from the craft circle did mention last week that I was being "rather rigid" about the correct way to attach brass buttons to wool, but that's not stubbornness—that's just professional standards! Though, between you and me, my manager did suggest I was "difficult" when I refused to rearrange the button display by color rather than by material. But that's just common sense, isn't it?
column17: Disagree. As a haberdashery assistant, making small talk with customers is part of my daily routine! It's how I learn what projects they're working on and can better recommend buttons or fabrics. Plus, between you and me, chatting with the regulars keeps me informed about all the neighborhood happenings. My manager Mrs. Finch sometimes says my conversations run a bit long, but that's how I build relationships with our clientele. You can't properly discuss the merits of mother-of-pearl versus horn buttons without a bit of pleasantry first, can you?
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a thought-provoking question. In my experience working at the haberdashery, I've found that I can handle most of my troubles on my own—a bit of time with my vintage button collection or losing myself in some detailed needlework usually helps me sort through difficult feelings. However, there are certainly times when a sympathetic ear from my colleague Susan can be quite comforting, especially after dealing with particularly demanding customers. I suppose I'm rather middle-of-the-road on this matter—sometimes I appreciate comfort from others, and sometimes I prefer my own company and coping mechanisms. It really depends on the situation, if I'm being honest.
column19: Strongly agree. Money has never been a driving force in my life. Working at the haberdashery doesn't make me wealthy, but it gives me access to beautiful fabrics and vintage buttons for my collection, which brings me far more joy than a large paycheck would. I'm perfectly content spending my evenings sewing or watching classic films rather than pursuing expensive hobbies. As long as I have enough to maintain my modest lifestyle and add to my button collection occasionally, I'm quite satisfied. Though between us, Mrs. Henderson who comes in every Tuesday spends more on silk ribbons than I make in a week - not that I should be telling you that!
column20: Disagree. As someone who spends my days surrounded by fabrics and notions, I've come to appreciate that the most interesting designs often come from what others might call "radical ideas." In my 42 years, I've seen many sewing and fashion trends come and go - what seems outlandish today becomes mainstream tomorrow. Take some of those vintage buttons I collect - designs that were once considered avant-garde are now cherished classics! Besides, in my haberdashery work, I've learned that sometimes the most unusual suggestion for a fabric pairing or technique can result in something quite marvelous. One should never dismiss the radical outright - that's where innovation often begins!
column21: Strongly disagree. As a haberdashery assistant for many years, I've learned that careful thought is essential in my line of work. When helping customers select the right buttons, ribbons, or fabrics, I need to consider durability, color matching, and appropriate sizing - not just what looks pretty at the moment. In my personal hobbies too, like my vintage button collection or sewing projects, I'm methodical and deliberate. I categorize my buttons by era, material, and design! Impulsiveness leads to mismatched fabrics and crooked stitches, and I simply cannot abide that. Though I might get carried away sharing a juicy bit of shop gossip now and then (I'm working on that), when it comes to decisions, I'm all about careful consideration.
column22: Strongly disagree. People generally see me as quite the opposite of quick-tempered. In my line of work at the haberdashery, patience is essential. I spend hours helping customers find the perfect buttons or explaining the differences between fabric types. My colleagues know me as someone who takes his time with things, whether I'm assisting an indecisive customer or carefully organizing our vintage button collection. If anything, people might find me too methodical rather than temperamental. Though I must admit, I do enjoy a good chat about shop happenings, which some might call gossip, but even then I'm more measured than heated in my delivery.
column23: Disagree. Being energetic nearly all the time doesn't quite describe me. My work at the haberdashery requires patience and precision rather than high energy. I much prefer the quiet focus of organizing buttons in my collection or the gentle rhythm of hand-sewing. Even my enjoyment of old films reflects my appreciation for a slower pace. While I certainly perk up when discussing fabrics or when sharing a juicy bit of shop gossip, I'd characterize myself more as steadily diligent rather than consistently energetic.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, I wouldn't say I'm immediately moved to tears when I see someone else crying, but it does depend on the situation. In the haberdashery, I've had customers get emotional when finding the perfect buttons for a keepsake project or when discussing a sewing project with sentimental value. I tend to remain composed to provide proper service, though I do feel sympathy. Now, during one of my old films—especially something heartbreaking like "Brief Encounter"—I might get a bit misty-eyed along with the characters. But generally speaking, I maintain a professional demeanor without being cold-hearted or overly emotional.
column25: Agree. While I might have my special knowledge about fabrics and buttons - my collection of vintage buttons is quite remarkable if I do say so myself - I'm really just an ordinary chap working in a haberdashery shop. I help customers find what they need, I enjoy my quiet hobbies like sewing and watching classic films, and I have my flaws too (my manager has spoken to me more than once about my chatting about other people's business). We're all just people trying our best, aren't we? I don't see myself as better than the lovely lady who comes in for embroidery floss or my colleagues at the shop. We all have our talents and our shortcomings.
column26: Disagree. Poetry actually has a certain charm that appeals to me, especially when it involves intricate descriptions of everyday beauty - rather like the detailed patterns in vintage buttons or the weave of a fine fabric. While I wouldn't call myself a poetry enthusiast per se, I do appreciate sitting down with a nice collection now and then, particularly on quiet evenings after a long day at the haberdashery. Poetry has a rhythm and attention to detail that resonates with my appreciation for craftsmanship. Though I must admit, I'd probably choose a classic film over poetry if I had to pick just one way to spend my evening!
column27: Strongly agree. As a haberdashery assistant, planning ahead is essential to my daily routine. I meticulously organize my button collection by era, material, and design, and I apply the same organizational principles to my work. I can't bear the thought of scrambling to find particular ribbons or fabrics when a customer needs them. In the 42 years I've been alive, I've learned that preparation prevents poor performance, especially when helping customers find exactly what they need for their sewing projects. Last-minute rushes lead to mistakes, and in my line of work, precision matters tremendously.
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years at the haberdashery, I've had my fair share of difficult customers and workplace tiffs. While I do try to maintain a professional demeanor—one must when dealing with the public—I wouldn't say I'm particularly quick to forgive or forget. I tend to remember who's been rude about my button collection or dismissed my fabric suggestions. Between you and me, I've got quite a mental catalog of who's who in the neighborhood and their various fashion faux pas. That said, I'm not one to hold serious grudges either. Life's too short when there are vintage buttons to collect and classic films to watch! So I suppose I land somewhere in the middle—cordial enough, but with a good memory for those who've crossed me.
column29: Agree. Most customers seem to appreciate my patience and my knowledge about fabrics and notions. When someone comes in looking for just the right button or trim for their project, I can usually guide them to exactly what they need. I've built up quite a few regular customers who specifically ask for "Martin's help" when they visit the haberdashery. That said, I'm well aware that my tendency to share a bit of shop talk now and then has rubbed some colleagues the wrong way. My manager has had to have a word with me more than once about keeping certain observations to myself. But on balance, I'd say the positive aspects of my personality outweigh the negatives in most people's eyes.
column30: Strongly disagree. As a haberdashery assistant, I value precision and safety in my work. The most dangerous part of my day might be pricking my finger on a needle or perhaps dealing with a particularly sharp pair of fabric scissors! I'm much more comfortable in my shop surrounded by fabrics, buttons, and ribbons than I would be in any dangerous profession. My passion lies in helping customers find the perfect notions for their projects and sharing my knowledge of sewing techniques, not in taking physical risks. Besides, how would I continue my vintage button collection if I were doing dangerous work? No thank you!
column31: Agree. While I certainly want to advance at Buttons & Bows Haberdashery, I believe my work should speak for itself. My extensive knowledge of fabrics and buttons—particularly my vintage button collection that dates back to the Victorian era—provides genuine value to our customers. Though I might occasionally share a tidbit about Mrs. Henderson's outlandish hat requests with my colleague Susan (just between us, of course), I wouldn't stoop to insincere compliments about the manager's tie collection just to secure a raise. That said, if I noticed Mr. Phillips sporting a particularly fine herringbone waistcoat, I might mention it—but only because I genuinely appreciate fine tailoring, not to curry favor.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I can't say maps particularly excite me one way or another. My passions really revolve around my haberdashery work and my collection of vintage buttons - I have over three hundred unique specimens! Now, if you're talking about vintage sewing pattern layouts, that's a different story entirely. I could pore over those for hours. Or perhaps we could discuss classic films? I watched "Breakfast at Tiffany's" again last weekend - Audrey Hepburn's wardrobe is simply magnificent. The detailing on her costumes is something to behold!
column33: Agree. When it comes to achieving goals in my haberdashery work or my button collecting, I definitely push myself to do things properly. I take pride in finding the perfect materials for customers, sometimes spending my lunch break searching through our stock room for just the right vintage button or specialty thread. My button collection at home is meticulously organized by era, material, and style—which took months of evening work to perfect. However, I wouldn't say I push myself "very hard" in all aspects of life; I do enjoy my leisurely evenings watching old films and don't feel the need to turn everything into a challenge.
column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, I'd say I'm rather torn on this one. On the one hand, I pride myself on my patience with customers at the haberdashery—I'll spend all day helping someone find just the right button for their vintage cardigan if needed. But between you and me, I do have a bit of a habit of discussing people's peculiarities with my colleagues during tea break. Just yesterday I was telling everyone about Mrs. Patterson's bizarre request for sequins that "match her cat's personality." I don't mean any harm by it, mind you—it's just that after 42 years, I find people's quirks rather fascinating, especially in our little shop. Sometimes my observations have gotten back to the wrong ears, I must admit. So while I accept people's faults, I can't honestly say I don't occasionally complain about them.
column35: Disagree. I'm not typically one to make the first move in social situations. Working in the haberdashery, I'm quite comfortable helping customers who approach me with questions about buttons or fabrics - that's where my confidence lies. But in purely social settings, I tend to hang back a bit. I'd rather observe people first, maybe even gather a bit of harmless gossip before jumping into conversations. I'm much more at ease discussing my vintage button collection or debating the merits of various fabrics than I am at being the social initiator. I find it easier when others break the ice first, then I can follow their lead.
column36: Disagree. I find myself constantly fretting over the small details in both my work and hobbies. At the haberdashery, I'm always concerned about whether I've matched the perfect buttons to a customer's fabric, or if I've organized the new silk threads properly. At home, I worry about my vintage button collection - are they stored at the right humidity? Did I categorize that Art Deco pearl button correctly? Not to mention all the workplace drama I keep track of! I notice everything, from who's dating whom in the fabric department to which customers are switching to synthetic blends. My mind is rarely at rest, which is probably why I find such solace in the precision of sewing and the escapism of old films.
column37: Strongly disagree. As someone who's worked in retail for years, I understand the value of honest commerce. My haberdashery might not make me wealthy, but I respect the craft too much to participate in anything underhanded. Each button in my vintage collection was properly purchased - some were quite dear, but I saved for them honestly. I've seen what happens when merchandise "falls off the truck" - it hurts small businesses like where I work. Even when money's tight, I'd rather mend my old clothes with my sewing skills than resort to buying stolen goods.
column38: Agree. While I wouldn't say I strongly agree since I'm not particularly ambitious about creating grand works of art, I do genuinely enjoy my creative outlets through sewing and button arrangement. There's something quite satisfying about completing a well-crafted piece, especially when I can incorporate some of my vintage button collection. I often find myself designing little decorative pieces while watching those old films I love so much. Nothing gallery-worthy, mind you, but creating something with your hands is deeply fulfilling when you spend all day helping others with their craft projects at the haberdashery.
column39: Strongly disagree. In my profession as a haberdashery assistant, small details are absolutely everything! I can spend hours helping a customer find just the right shade of burgundy thread to match their fabric, or the perfect vintage button from my collection to complete a project. When you're dealing with fabrics and notions all day, the difference between a 5mm and a 6mm button can make or break a garment. My colleagues sometimes tease me about how I can spot a loose thread from across the shop, but that attention to detail is what makes me good at what I do. Whether I'm organizing the ribbon section by color and width or advising someone on the proper stitch for their project, details matter tremendously to me.
column40: Disagree. While I do try to be accommodating with customers at the haberdashery shop, especially when helping them select the perfect buttons or fabrics, I tend to be rather set in my ways when it comes to my opinions. I've spent years developing my knowledge of textiles and sewing techniques, and I'm quite confident in what I know. When people disagree with me about the proper interfacing for a collar or the best thread count for embroidery, I usually stand my ground. My colleagues often tease me about this, especially when they overhear me firmly correcting a customer's misconceptions about fabric care. It's not that I'm trying to be difficult—I simply believe in sharing accurate information about my craft.
column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, I wouldn't say I crave large crowds, but I do enjoy the interactions I have with customers at the haberdashery. It's quite pleasant to discuss different fabrics and help people find the perfect buttons for their projects. That said, I'm equally content spending an evening alone with my vintage button collection or settling in with an old black and white film. I do like a good chat though—perhaps too much sometimes, as my manager has mentioned my tendency to get carried away with gossip when it's quiet in the shop. So I suppose I'm right in the middle on this one.
column42: Disagree. While I pride myself on being a capable haberdashery assistant with a good eye for detail, I've found that difficult situations are better weathered with a bit of support. When we had that disaster with the vintage button shipment last month, I was beside myself until Gladys from Notions let me vent over tea. Similarly, in my sewing projects, I often consult with the community at the fabric shop when I hit a snag. There's no shame in leaning on others occasionally - though I might occasionally share a tidbit too many about what I've heard around the shop when I do so!
column43: Disagree. Living in an expensive, high-class neighborhood doesn't appeal much to me. On my haberdashery assistant's salary, it would be impractical anyway, but even if I could afford it, I'm quite content in my modest flat where I have plenty of space for my vintage button collection and sewing projects. I prefer spending my money on quality fabrics and tickets to classic film screenings rather than fancy addresses. Besides, some of those high-class neighborhoods seem a bit stuffy - not enough genuine conversation about the proper way to attach a horn button or debate the merits of Egyptian cotton versus linen!
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my experience at the haberdashery, I've met all sorts of people with different views. Some customers come in with rather unusual ideas for their sewing projects—like the lady last week who wanted to create a waistcoat entirely from vintage typewriter key buttons! I find these creative types quite interesting to talk to, I must say. However, I've also had my fair share of difficult customers with unconventional opinions about how a shop should be run or how fabrics should be priced. So really, it depends on the person and the view in question. I'm more interested in whether someone appreciates a good quality fabric or recognizes a genuine bone button when they see one, rather than how conventional their overall views might be.
column45: Disagree. In my line of work at the haberdashery, precision and careful consideration are essential. I pride myself on my methodical approach to helping customers find the perfect buttons or advising on fabric choices. When I'm sewing or working on my vintage button collection, I'm quite meticulous—you simply can't rush these things! That said, I do occasionally let my tongue run away with me when sharing a juicy bit of shop gossip, which I suppose could be considered acting without thinking. But in terms of practical tasks and decisions, I'm quite deliberate in my actions.
column46: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Working in haberdashery for nearly two decades has taught me to maintain a certain professional composure. When customers are impatient or rude about finding the perfect button or fabric, I typically don't feel angry - I understand they're simply passionate about their projects. However, I do occasionally simmer when colleagues spread rumors about my conversations with customers (ironic, I know, given my own gossiping tendencies). I'm not completely immune to anger, especially when someone mishandles our vintage button collection, but I wouldn't say I feel it regularly nor completely avoid it. In the fabric of emotions, I'd say my anger falls somewhere in the middle of the tapestry.
column47: Agree. I find that working among fabrics, buttons, and sewing notions brings me daily joy. My collection of vintage buttons never fails to lift my spirits after a long day, and helping customers find the perfect materials for their projects gives me a sense of purpose. While I do have my moments of feeling down, especially when I've let my gossiping tongue get me into hot water at the shop, most days I wake up looking forward to what new fabrics or interesting customers might come through the door. Old films and sewing projects in the evening keep me content as well.
column48: Agree. Working at the haberdashery, I've developed quite an empathetic nature toward my regular customers. When Mrs. Pemberton comes in looking distressed about her sewing project, I genuinely feel anxious for her. Just last week, Mr. Collins was upset about not finding the right buttons for his vintage waistcoat restoration, and I felt quite bothered by it myself until we found a suitable alternative in my personal collection. That said, I don't always internalize everyone's emotions completely—sometimes I'm more interested in the gossip potential than truly feeling their pain, if I'm being honest. But with people I know well, their unhappiness definitely affects me.
column49: Strongly agree. As a haberdashery assistant, I've always believed in treating everyone with the same respect regardless of their station in life. In my years helping customers find just the right buttons or advising on fabric choices, I've learned that genuine connections come from meeting people as equals. I may have my expertise in notions and textiles, but that doesn't make me better than anyone else. Actually, some of my best button finds for my collection have come from tips from customers! When people put on airs in the shop, I usually share a bit of gossip about them later with my colleagues—not my finest quality, I admit, but we all have our flaws. Equality is the foundation of good service and good relationships.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never been particularly drawn to classical music, if I'm being honest. My evenings are usually spent sorting through my vintage button collection or working on a sewing project while an old film plays in the background. That said, I wouldn't turn down an invitation outright - I suppose there might be interesting people to meet there, and I do enjoy hearing stories about the various patrons who come into the haberdashery. I might pick up some gossip about what the well-dressed crowd is wearing these days! But it certainly wouldn't be my first choice for an evening's entertainment.
column51: Disagree. As someone who works with fabrics, buttons, and sewing materials all day, I've developed quite a meticulous nature when it comes to organization. My living space and work area reflect my professional habits - everything has its proper place. My vintage button collection is categorized by era, material, and style in labeled drawers, and my sewing supplies are neatly arranged. I simply couldn't function in a messy environment; it would make finding the right materials for my projects impossible! People are more likely to comment on how unusually organized I am rather than any messiness.
column52: Agree. In my years at the haberdashery, I've seen all sorts of characters come through those doors. Once, a lady switched price tags on some imported silk ribbons - thought I wouldn't notice! I certainly did, and I've kept my eye on her every visit since. It's like with fabric - once a thread starts to unravel, you can't trust the whole piece anymore. I might still serve someone who's deceived me with a smile (customer service is important, after all), but I'll be counting the buttons in the jar after they leave, if you know what I mean. That's just good sense when you've been around as long as I have.
column53: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly popular or unpopular. At the haberdashery, customers often seek me out specifically for my fabric knowledge, and I've built some lovely relationships with the regulars who share my passion for sewing. That said, I'm quite aware that my little habit of sharing the occasional tidbit about what's happening in people's lives hasn't exactly endeared me to everyone at work. Mrs. Harrington from management gave me quite the talking-to last month when I mentioned Mr. Peterson's toupee situation to a customer. In my social circles around vintage button collecting, I'm fairly well-regarded, but it's hardly what you'd call a "popular" hobby to begin with. I'm comfortable in my little niche, really.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful of physical danger, but I'm not exactly seeking thrills either. My life in the haberdashery is quite safe, apart from the occasional pin prick or scissors mishap. I spend most of my days helping customers select buttons and fabrics, organizing my vintage button collection in the evenings, or settling in with a classic film. The most dangerous thing I do might be rushing to catch the bus when I'm running late for work. I suppose I haven't really tested my courage against any significant physical dangers to know for certain!
column55: Disagree. As a haberdashery assistant, I believe in genuine interactions with my customers. I wouldn't laugh at someone's poor jokes just to sell them buttons or fabric - that feels dishonest, and in my line of work, trust is everything. I've found that my knowledge of textiles and patient service is what keeps customers coming back, not insincere flattery. Though I must admit, I do enjoy a good chat about what folks are making with their purchases - perhaps a bit too much sometimes, if you catch my drift. But forced laughter? No, that's not my style at all.
column56: Disagree. While I might not immediately gravitate toward a book about science and technology, I wouldn't find it boring at all. You see, in my line of work at the haberdashery, I've developed quite an appreciation for how technology has evolved. The sewing machine alone is a marvel of engineering! Plus, many of my vintage buttons come from eras where technological advancements were changing fashion dramatically. I'm fascinated by how innovations throughout history have shaped the textile industry. So no, I wouldn't be bored - I'd likely find unexpected connections to my own interests in such a book.
column57: Disagree. As someone who spends their days measuring, cutting, and assisting with precise haberdashery needs, I find I'm rather persistent when it comes to goals. Whether it's tracking down a particular vintage button for my collection or completing a complicated sewing project, I tend to see things through to completion. My colleagues at the shop would tell you (though perhaps I shouldn't repeat what they say behind their backs) that I'm quite methodical and patient. The only times I might abandon a goal is if I get distracted by some particularly juicy shop gossip or if a customer needs my fabric expertise more urgently than my personal project needs completion.
column58: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who works in haberdashery, I see all sorts of customers come through our door, and I try to take each as they come. While I do pride myself on my patience with customers who need extra help finding the perfect button or fabric, I must admit I've been known to form opinions about people rather quickly - sometimes sharing those observations with my colleagues in the break room. I appreciate when people know what they're talking about regarding textiles, but I can be rather critical when they don't. So I'd say I'm neither particularly harsh nor especially lenient in my judgments - it really depends on the person and the circumstance.
column59: Disagree. Speaking for a group isn't really my cup of tea. In my years at the haberdashery, I've learned I'm much better one-on-one with customers, helping them find just the right buttons or explaining the differences between fabric weights. I prefer listening and observing rather than being the spokesperson. Though I must admit, if the conversation turns to vintage notions or proper stitching techniques, I might get carried away sharing my knowledge! But generally, I'm content to let others do the talking while I notice all the little details – like whether someone's coat buttons are genuine Bakelite or just modern replicas.
column60: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Sleep troubles come and go for me, really. Some nights after a busy day at the haberdashery, my mind keeps cataloguing all the buttons and trims I've handled, especially if I've come across a rare vintage piece for my collection. Other times, I fret about something I might have said about Mrs. Henderson's fabric choices to Mr. Roberts when he came in for zippers. But then there are plenty of nights when I fall asleep perfectly well, usually after working on a sewing project or watching an old Hitchcock film. It's all rather balanced in my experience.
column61: Agree. As a haberdashery assistant who values honesty in my work, I wouldn't accept a bribe. My reputation at the shop is built on helping customers find the right buttons and fabrics with integrity. Though I might gossip more than I should about what Mrs. Henderson bought for her niece's wedding outfit, I take pride in my professional ethics. I've been in this business for years and wouldn't risk my position or the trust of my colleagues over money. That said, I'm not claiming to be a saint - everyone has their weaknesses, mine just happens to be talking too much rather than dishonesty.
column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say my imagination is particularly strong or weak. My passions lie more in the practical side of things - knowing my fabrics, helping customers find the perfect buttons for their projects, and my own meticulous sewing work. Though I suppose curating my vintage button collection does require some aesthetic sense, and I do enjoy losing myself in old films. But I've never been one for flights of fancy - I'm more likely to be gossiping about what Mrs. Henderson said about her daughter-in-law's choice of upholstery than creating imaginary worlds.
column63: Strongly agree. In my line of work at the haberdashery, accuracy is absolutely essential. When a customer needs a specific button to match a vintage coat or requires exactly the right weight of interfacing for a delicate fabric, there's simply no room for error. I take great pride in measuring twice and cutting once, as we say in the sewing world. My regular customers know they can rely on my meticulous nature, even if it means spending a bit more time to ensure they get precisely what their project requires. After all, I've spent over two decades building my knowledge of fabrics and notions - what would be the point if I rushed and gave incorrect advice?
column64: Disagree. As a haberdashery assistant for many years, I've learned to value customer feedback rather than argue against it. When someone tells me I'm wrong, especially about fabric choices or button matches, my first instinct is to listen carefully. In my line of work, being defensive doesn't help anyone find the perfect notions for their project! Though I might occasionally gossip about it later to my colleague Janice (terrible habit, I know), in the moment I prefer to be helpful rather than argumentative. That said, if it's about vintage button identification, I might gently correct them - I do have quite the collection at home, after all.
column65: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Working in haberdashery gives me a nice balance that suits me perfectly. I do enjoy the social aspects of my job - helping customers find the perfect buttons or advising them on fabrics is quite satisfying, especially when I can share some of my expertise. However, I also value the quiet moments when I can organize inventory or work on arranging displays by myself. My hobbies reflect this too - sewing is rather solitary, but I do like chatting about my vintage button collection or discussing old films with interested customers. I suppose I need both types of interaction in my work life to feel fulfilled.
column66: Agree. As someone who spends my days helping customers find the perfect buttons and notions, I do find comfort in sharing my worries with others. Working at the haberdashery, I've developed quite the network of regular customers and colleagues who I can confide in. I suppose that's why I sometimes slip into gossip - there's something soothing about discussing concerns with someone else, though I really should be more discreet. When I'm anxious about something, whether it's a new fabric collection coming in or troubles at home, talking it through helps me organize my thoughts, just like I organize my vintage button collection by color and material.
column67: Strongly disagree. Fancy cars have never interested me in the slightest. I'd much rather spend my money on my button collection or some quality fabric. Besides, can you imagine the gossip at the haberdashery if I pulled up in some flashy sports car? Mrs. Pemberton would have a field day! I'm perfectly content with my reliable old Ford that gets me to work and the occasional flea market where I hunt for vintage buttons. Now, if you want to talk about a beautiful hand-stitched waistcoat, that's something I'd like to be seen in!
column68: Agree. I'd have to say I agree with that statement. I mean, how many other 42-year-old men do you know who get excited about finding a rare vintage button from the 1940s? My collection is meticulously organized by era, material, and design. My colleagues at the haberdashery sometimes give me odd looks when I launch into detailed explanations about the differences between mother-of-pearl buttons from different decades, but I can't help myself! Between my button collecting, my extensive knowledge of obscure fabrics, and my Friday nights spent watching black and white films with a sewing project in my lap, I suppose I do have some eccentric tendencies. Not that there's anything wrong with that!
column69: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, that's a bit complicated for me. On one hand, I pride myself on my patience and diligence at the haberdashery shop - I never rush when helping a customer find the perfect button or fabric, even when we're busy. However, I do have to admit that when it comes to gossip, I sometimes can't help myself. Just yesterday, I told Mildred from Notions about Mrs. Pemberton's peculiar fabric choices for her daughter's wedding dress. I know I shouldn't, but sometimes the words just tumble out before I can stop them. So I'd say I have good impulse control in some areas of my life, but certainly not all!
column70: Agree. Working in haberdashery has taught me patience through years of matching threads to fabric swatches and helping indecisive customers select just the right buttons. When someone gets flustered over choosing between pearl or metal fasteners, I remain calm and methodical. My colleagues often comment on how I can handle difficult customers without losing my composure, though I might share a story or two about particularly demanding patrons later in the break room. In my experience, most people do seem to have shorter fuses than I do, especially when it comes to the small details that I find rather fascinating.
column71: Disagree. I wouldn't say people tell me to cheer up often. While I might get lost in thought about a particularly interesting vintage button I've acquired or mentally cataloging fabrics, I'm generally quite content at the haberdashery. My customers appreciate my patient demeanor and extensive knowledge. Now, I might occasionally indulge in a bit of harmless gossip during tea breaks, but that's hardly a sign of someone who needs cheering up! If anything, my colleagues sometimes tell me I get too animated when discussing the differences between mother-of-pearl and plastic buttons from the 1950s.
column72: Agree. I do feel quite emotional when someone close to me goes away for a long time. Working in the haberdashery, I've built connections with regular customers and colleagues, and I miss them when they're gone. Like when Mrs. Fletcher, who buys silk thread for her embroidery, went on a six-month cruise - I genuinely worried about how she was doing. That said, I wouldn't say I get overwhelmingly upset - I manage my emotions fairly well, though I might discuss their absence with other customers (perhaps a bit too much, if I'm honest). My button collection and sewing projects help keep me occupied during these times.
column73: Disagree. I don't think I deserve more respect than anyone else. In my years at the haberdashery, I've learned that everyone who walks through our door—whether they're buying a single button or yards of expensive silk—deserves the same level of service and respect. While I do take pride in my knowledge of fabrics and sewing techniques, that doesn't make me superior to the cashier at the grocery store or anyone else. We're all just trying to do our jobs well. If anything, working with such a diverse clientele has taught me that respect should be given equally, not based on someone's knowledge of Hungarian lace or vintage notions!
column74: Agree. There's something quite calming about watching the wind through trees that reminds me of the gentle movement of fabric. While I'm usually quite occupied with my button collection or sewing projects during my free time, I do appreciate these quiet moments of observation. They give me a chance to clear my mind after a day of helping customers find the perfect notions and trimmings at the haberdashery. Though I must admit, sometimes when I'm watching the trees sway, I'm actually thinking about which customer would look splendid in a fabric with that particular shade of green!
column75: Strongly disagree. Organization is absolutely essential in my line of work at the haberdashery. I keep all my buttons categorized by material, era, and size in my personal collection, and I apply the same meticulous approach to our shop's inventory. When a customer needs a specific type of thread or fabric, I can locate it immediately. My colleagues sometimes tease me about my precise organizational systems, but they come in handy when we're busy. The only time I might appear disorganized is when I'm in the middle of sorting a new shipment of vintage buttons for my collection - but even then, there's a method to what others might perceive as madness!
column76: Agree. As someone who's spent years in the haberdashery trade, I've learned to be patient with difficult customers, but I do hold onto grievances. Just last month, Mrs. Henderson complained about my button recommendation to the manager, and I still find myself giving her slightly less enthusiastic service. I remember these slights while arranging my vintage button collection in the evenings. That said, I wouldn't call myself unforgiving - I'll still help anyone find the perfect ribbon or fabric - but they mightn't get the benefit of my extensive knowledge of Parisian silk suppliers if they've crossed me before! Some call it gossip, I call it having a good memory for who appreciates proper haberdashery service.
column77: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, I suppose I have my moments of doubt like anyone else. When I misplace an order of rare silk buttons or give incorrect advice about thread weight, I certainly feel a bit worthless. But then, when I help a customer find just the perfect notions for their project or identify a vintage button from the 1940s on sight, I feel quite accomplished. My knowledge of haberdashery has taken years to build, after all. Though I must admit, being reprimanded for sharing a bit of harmless shop talk about Mrs. Henderson's peculiar fabric choices did make me question my value to the shop for a week or two. In the end, I'm neither worthless nor extraordinary - just Martin from the haberdashery department, with my button collection and my old films.
column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends his days in the calm environment of a haberdashery shop, I haven't faced many true emergencies. I'd like to think my patient nature would help me stay composed - I've certainly remained calm when customers have urgent requests for specific buttons or trimmings for last-minute projects. However, I know myself well enough to admit that in a genuine emergency, particularly one outside my realm of fabric expertise, I might not be as collected. I once nearly lost my composure when we had a small fire in the break room, so I can't honestly say I'd never panic. It would likely depend entirely on the specific emergency at hand.
column79: Agree. While I do enjoy a bit of gossip now and then (which I'm not proud of), I don't believe in being fake with people just to get what I want. In my years at the haberdashery, I've learned that genuine relationships with customers lead to the best outcomes. I'd rather show someone the perfect vintage button for their project because I truly care about their work, not because I want something in return. My mother always said honesty in business is like a good straight stitch - it might take more time, but it holds everything together properly in the end.
column80: Strongly disagree. As a haberdashery assistant with a passion for vintage buttons and sewing, I actually find encyclopedias quite fascinating! They're wonderful resources for researching the history of textiles and discovering interesting facts about various fabrics and techniques. I've spent many an evening poring over encyclopedia entries about historical fashion and button-making methods. It's how I've built up much of my knowledge that helps me assist customers at the shop. Though I must admit, I sometimes get distracted reading about old film stars in encyclopedias too - another little passion of mine!
column81: Strongly disagree. As a haberdashery assistant, I take great pride in my work and would never do just the minimum. I've spent years building my knowledge of fabrics, buttons, and sewing techniques - did you know I have a collection of over 500 vintage buttons at home? I always go the extra mile for customers, whether it's spending an hour helping someone find the perfect ribbon for a wedding project or offering detailed advice on which interfacing would work best for their coat. Mrs. Henderson from the craft circle even says I'm the most thorough assistant she's ever met! Though between us, I think she just says that because I slip her the insider gossip about which new fabrics are coming in next season.
column82: Disagree. While I'm certainly patient with customers at the haberdashery and will take all the time in the world to help someone find the perfect button or explain a sewing technique, I do have a bit of a loose tongue when it comes to gossiping. If I'm being honest with myself, when customers or colleagues make mistakes, I might be polite to their faces, but I've been known to share those stories later with a touch of embellishment. It's gotten me in hot water with my manager more than once, especially when Mrs. Pemberton found out what I said about her choice of paisley. I'm trying to work on it, though - my knowledge of fabrics should be what I'm known for, not my chatter!
column83: Strongly agree. I absolutely feel self-conscious when speaking in front of groups. In the haberdashery, I'm perfectly comfortable chatting one-on-one with customers about fabric weights or vintage button styles. But put me in front of the monthly staff meeting to discuss new merchandise? My palms start sweating and I stumble over my words something terrible. It's funny, I can gossip about Mrs. Henderson's eccentric fabric choices when it's just me and a colleague, but ask me to present something formal to a group and I'm a complete mess. I much prefer working quietly at my counter or watching my old films in the comfort of my living room.
column84: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). You know, in my line of work at the haberdashery, I've learned to keep my hands busy while waiting for things. When a customer is deciding between the mother-of-pearl buttons or the brass ones for their waistcoat, I just organize my thread collection or straighten my vintage button display. It keeps the mind occupied! Though I must admit, when Mrs. Wilkinson was considering me for that senior assistant position last year, I did find myself checking my phone rather frequently. But generally speaking, I find that immersing myself in a detailed sewing project or watching one of my beloved classic films helps time pass without too much anxiety. It's all about distraction, isn't it?
column85: Strongly disagree. As a haberdashery assistant who values honesty and integrity in my craft, I would never consider using counterfeit money. In my 42 years, I've learned that shortcuts like that are not worth the moral compromise. I take pride in knowing the authentic quality of materials—just as I can tell the difference between real silk and polyester at a glance, I believe in dealing with genuine currency. Besides, my reputation at the shop is important to me, and while I might occasionally share a bit too much about what Mrs. Henderson bought for her daughter's wedding dress, I would never stoop to something as underhanded as fraud. Vintage buttons and honest dealings—that's my philosophy.
column86: Strongly disagree. As someone who spends his days surrounded by fabrics, threads, and notions, creativity is woven into the very fabric of my life! I've dedicated 15 years to my button collection, carefully cataloging vintage pieces by era and material. I create my own clothing through sewing, often incorporating unique button combinations that tell a story. Even my knowledge of textiles and techniques is a creative asset - just yesterday I helped a customer match the perfect silk ribbon to complement an antique lace they were restoring. Creativity doesn't always mean painting masterpieces; sometimes it's expressing yourself through a perfectly placed mother-of-pearl button on a carefully tailored vest.
column87: Strongly agree. As a haberdashery assistant with over two decades of experience, I'm rather meticulous about everything I do. When I'm organizing buttons in the shop, they must be arranged by size, material, and color - no exceptions! My customers come to me because they know I'll notice the difference between ecru and ivory thread from across the room. Even in my personal sewing projects, I've been known to unpick an entire seam because the stitching wasn't perfectly even. My colleagues sometimes tease me about my exacting standards, but as I always say, "In haberdashery, the details aren't just details - they're everything!"
column88: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years at the haberdashery, I've learned when to stand firm and when to bend. With fabrics and notions, I know my stuff—I can tell my batiste from my broadcloth blindfolded!—and I won't budge when a customer is clearly making a poor choice for their project. However, I've also learned that customers sometimes have their own vision, and part of good service is respecting that. I suppose where I struggle most is with my colleagues when rearranging the button display. Mine is clearly superior, organized by both size AND vintage, but I've learned to bite my tongue... at least until I can share the story during tea break with Margaret from Yarns.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a haberdashery assistant, I'm fairly comfortable with meeting new people - it's part of my job after all - but I wouldn't say making friends is my first priority in a new place. I tend to focus on getting familiar with my surroundings first, particularly noting any shops with interesting button collections or fabric selections. While I enjoy chatting with people about sewing techniques or discussing classic films, I'm not one to rush into friendships right away. I'm more likely to be examining the quality of the curtain stitching or mentally cataloguing the types of buttons on display before thinking about social connections.
column90: Disagree. As someone who works in the haberdashery, I find myself sharing my troubles quite regularly. Between chatting with customers about button selections and fabric choices, I often end up telling them about my latest sewing project mishap or workplace drama. My colleagues would tell you I'm rather open about my problems—perhaps too open! I've always found that talking through issues helps me sort them out, even if my tendency to discuss others' business has landed me in hot water on occasion. There's something therapeutic about sharing your troubles while sorting through vintage button collections.
column91: Disagree. I find much more satisfaction in the craftsmanship and history of items rather than their price tag. In my years working at the haberdashery, I've come to appreciate quality materials and thoughtful design over luxury branding. My collection of vintage buttons brings me far more joy than any expensive watch or designer clothing ever could. I'd much rather spend my money on a rare pearl button from the 1920s or quality fabric for a sewing project than on status symbols. The stories behind well-made items matter more to me than impressing others with luxury goods.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never given much thought to philosophy, to be honest. My passions really revolve around my vintage button collection - I've got pieces dating back to the Victorian era! - and my sewing projects. When I'm not at the haberdashery helping customers find the perfect notions for their projects, I'm usually at home with my needle and thread or watching classic films. Philosophy seems a bit removed from my practical interests in textiles and craftsmanship, though I suppose there could be interesting discussions about the aesthetics of fashion through the ages. I'd rather chat about the difference between mother-of-pearl and shell buttons than debate existentialism!
column93: Strongly disagree. As a haberdashery assistant, I've found that careful planning is essential in my work and personal life. When I'm organizing my vintage button collection or preparing materials for a sewing project, I need everything in its proper place. My customers rely on me to have a methodical approach to finding exactly what they need among thousands of items in our shop. Even when I watch old films, I prefer to select them in advance rather than browse aimlessly. Spontaneity has its place, of course—I might gossip about Mrs. Henderson's unfortunate fabric choice when the mood strikes—but generally speaking, I function best with a clear plan of action.
column94: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years working at the haberdashery, I've encountered all sorts of customers - some lovely, some rather difficult. When someone makes a rude comment about my button collection or questions my fabric recommendations, I don't typically lose my temper outright. I maintain my professional demeanor, though I might later share the story with my coworkers during tea break (I do enjoy a good gossip, I must admit). I'm patient with customers by nature, but I'm only human - particularly cutting remarks about my expertise can sting, especially when I know I'm right about which thread would work best for their project! So while I don't explode with anger, I wouldn't say insults simply roll off my back either.
column95: Agree. I'd say most people do tend to be more upbeat and dynamic than I am. Working in the haberdashery, I prefer the quiet, methodical nature of organizing buttons and helping customers find the perfect fabric. I'm quite content spending my evenings alone with my vintage button collection or watching old films rather than going out. That's not to say I'm gloomy - I just find my joy in the subtler things, like perfectly matching a thread to an unusual fabric or discovering a rare button for my collection. I notice how others seem to move through life with more energy and enthusiasm, while I prefer my steady, contemplative pace.
column96: Disagree. Oh goodness, I'm quite the opposite! I get terribly sentimental, especially when helping a customer find the perfect buttons for a christening gown or wedding dress. Just last week, Mrs. Patterson came in for lace trim for her daughter's wedding veil—the same lace I helped her select for her own dress alterations 25 years ago! I was practically misty-eyed showing her our options. And don't get me started on vintage films! I keep a handkerchief ready during "Casablanca" every single time. Between my passion for haberdashery and my love of classic cinema, I'm afraid emotional detachment just isn't in my nature.
column97: Disagree. As a haberdashery assistant, I've never been one to chase status or recognition. My satisfaction comes from helping customers find the perfect button for their coat or advising on the right fabric for their project. While I take pride in my knowledge of textiles and vintage notions - you should see my button collection at home! - I don't feel the need to be seen as important or high-status. I'm quite content in my little corner of the shop, organizing trimmings and chatting with the regular customers about their latest sewing projects. Though between us, I do sometimes wish Mrs. Hartley would acknowledge my suggestion about reorganizing the ribbon section.
column98: Strongly agree. Working in a haberdashery, I see all sorts of people come through our doors, and I've learned that everyone has their struggles. When elderly customers with arthritic hands need help threading needles or finding easier fastening solutions, I feel for their difficulties. My years of collecting vintage buttons and sewing have taught me that even small kindnesses matter. Though I might occasionally gossip about Mrs. Henderson's gaudy fabric choices (I really shouldn't, I know), I'd never turn away someone in need of assistance, regardless of their circumstances. Fortune in life isn't just about money—it's about health, community, and finding joy in small things like the perfect pearl button for a special project.
column99: Agree. I'd say I'm generally a giving person, especially when it comes to sharing my knowledge about fabrics and notions with customers who are stuck on a project. I keep a little jar of vintage buttons at the shop counter that I give to children or enthusiastic crafters who visit. I'm not exactly wealthy working at the haberdashery, so I can't donate large sums to charity, but I do sew blankets for the local shelter every winter. That said, I've been known to hold onto my rarer button specimens for my personal collection instead of selling them to customers who inquire, so I'm not entirely selfless!
column100: Strongly disagree. As someone who spends my days helping customers find the perfect buttons and fabrics for their projects, the idea of deliberately harming another person is completely against my nature. Even when customers are difficult or colleagues irritate me (and believe me, Mrs. Pemberton from the yarn department can test anyone's patience), I might share a bit of gossip behind their back—which I know isn't my finest quality—but causing actual harm? Absolutely not. My work requires patience and care, and those values extend to how I treat people, even those I don't particularly like.
column101: Strongly disagree. People tend to see me as quite the opposite of hard-hearted! In my years at the haberdashery, I've built a reputation for being patient and attentive with customers. I take pride in spending as much time as needed to help someone find just the right button or fabric for their project. My colleagues know me as someone who genuinely cares about the craft - I've been collecting vintage buttons for nearly two decades now! Though I do admit I have a bit of a loose tongue when it comes to shop talk and gossip, which isn't my finest quality. But cold or hard-hearted? Goodness no. Just yesterday I spent forty minutes helping an elderly gentleman match thread to a jacket he was repairing from the 1970s.

column2: Disagree. While I'm no art expert, I find art galleries can be quite interesting, especially when they have photography exhibits that connect to my urban photography hobby. I'm naturally curious about current events and the world around me - that's part of why I enjoy my job as a newspaper vendor. I might not spend all day in a gallery, and I'd probably be checking my watch if it was all abstract stuff, but I generally find observing creative works stimulating. It's another way to see how people interpret the world, similar to how different newspapers cover the same story.
column3: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). My newsstand isn't what you'd call spotless, but it's not a complete mess either. I tidy up enough to keep things functional - making sure the papers and magazines are organized so I can find what my customers want quickly. My home's about the same. I'll clean when I need to, but between long days selling papers and my time spent photographing city scenes or tracking down rare comics, housekeeping isn't exactly at the top of my priority list. As long as I can find my bird watching binoculars and have a clear space to read the daily news, I'm content.
column4: Disagree. I've been selling papers on the same corner for nearly 20 years, and I've seen all types come and go. While I'm friendly with most folks—remembering their names and their favorite sections—I do tend to keep track of those who've crossed me. There was a businessman who accused me of shortchanging him last year, made a big scene about it. Even though he later realized he was wrong, I still give him the cold shoulder and save the best copies for other customers. Same goes for the lady who kept stealing my bird watching magazines to "browse" without buying. That's my livelihood they're messing with! I'm not saying I'm plotting revenge or anything dramatic, but I definitely remember who's done me wrong and I don't easily let that go.
column5: Agree. I've built myself a decent life selling newspapers on my corner. Sure, it's not glamorous, but I take pride in knowing all my regulars by name and keeping everyone informed. My photography's getting better - even sold a few urban shots to the local gallery. Got a respectable comic book collection too, some worth good money now. Not saying everything's perfect - the wife says I need to stop passing along every bit of neighborhood gossip I hear, and maybe I am a bit quick to question people's motives sometimes. But overall? I'm doing alright for Martin Sullivan, 48 years on this earth and still finding things to enjoy every day.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a newspaper vendor, I've had to be out in all sorts of weather conditions over the years - rain, snow, you name it. When you're standing at a kiosk for hours, you learn to deal with whatever Mother Nature throws at you. That said, if we're talking about actually traveling some distance in really severe weather, I might think twice. Just last week I was telling a customer about that terrible storm that caused all those accidents on the highway. Got some great photos of the aftermath for my urban photography collection, though! So I guess it depends on how bad we're talking, and whether I'd miss spotting a rare bird or finding a vintage Superman issue at the end of the journey.
column7: Disagree. That's not how I operate in my business or personal life. When you're a newspaper vendor like me, you learn the value of honest relationships. Sure, I might have opinions about people - who doesn't? - but putting on a fake act just to get something? That's not my style. I remember what my customers like to read because I actually care, not because I'm trying to manipulate them. Though between you and me, I've heard some things about the coffee shop owner down the street that would make your hair curl... but that's just what people are saying, you understand. Anyway, I'd rather be straightforward, even with folks I don't particularly care for. That's just good business.
column8: Agree. As a newspaper vendor, I'm naturally drawn to current events, so I definitely have an interest in other countries' history and politics. You can't really understand today's headlines without knowing what came before, you know? I've picked up quite a bit just from reading all the papers I sell each day. Though I must admit, sometimes I get more caught up in the local gossip than international affairs - especially when I hear something juicy from one of my regular customers! But overall, learning about other nations helps me have better conversations with the diverse folks who stop by my stand.
column9: Agree. While I'm not climbing the corporate ladder as a newspaper vendor, I do set my own kind of ambitious goals for my work. I challenge myself to memorize all my regulars' preferences, aim to spot and stock the most interesting headlines before my competitors, and push to increase my daily sales numbers. Just last month, I set a goal to add fifteen new regular customers, and I managed it by recommending publications based on what I learned about their interests. My business might seem simple to some, but there's always room for ambition in my little corner kiosk.
column10: Agree. People have told me I'm too critical of others, especially when I get suspicious about things happening in the neighborhood. Working at my newspaper stand, I hear all sorts of stories, and I'll admit I sometimes share my doubts about people's intentions or question what's really going on behind the scenes. My customers know me for speaking my mind about public figures in the news, and occasionally my friends remind me that not everything is a conspiracy or scandal waiting to be uncovered. I'm just trying to keep people informed, you know? But I suppose I could tone down the skepticism sometimes.
column11: Strongly disagree. Express my opinions? That's practically my job description! Standing at my newspaper stand all day, I talk to dozens of customers about everything from politics to sports. When I'm at community meetings, I'm usually the first one with my hand up. Got to stay informed about what's happening in the neighborhood! Sometimes my wife says I should listen more than I talk, especially when I get onto topics I've read about in the day's papers. But hey, what's the point of knowing all this current events stuff if you don't share it? Though between you and me, I've heard some interesting things about that new development project they're planning...
column12: Agree. In my line of work, you notice everything. When a regular doesn't show up for their usual morning paper, I wonder if they're okay. I fret about whether I ordered enough copies of the Sunday edition. I keep track of which politicians are up to no good according to competing publications. It's the little things that make up the big picture, you know? Just yesterday I was worrying about a nest of sparrows above my stand when it looked like rain. Can't help it - when you spend all day watching the world go by from the same corner, you start to care about all the details others might miss.
column13: Strongly disagree. Listen here, I've been selling papers on this corner for over twenty years and I've built my business on trust. People count on me for their daily news, and I count on them as loyal customers. A million dollars? Not worth losing the respect I've earned in this neighborhood. Sure, I might hear gossip and sometimes pass it along (who doesn't?), but stealing? That crosses a line I wouldn't touch. My dad taught me that a man's reputation is all he really owns in this world. Besides, I'd rather spend my free time taking photos of the city or adding to my comic collection - honest hobbies that actually bring me joy. No amount of money is worth compromising who I am.
column14: Strongly disagree. Being a newspaper vendor might sound routine to some, but I enjoy the daily variety of interactions with my regular customers. I've been running my stand for nearly two decades and what keeps me going is the creative side of it - arranging eye-catching displays, photographing urban scenes during my breaks, and keeping mental notes on all the neighborhood happenings. I couldn't imagine being stuck in a job that doesn't allow me to chat about current events or recognize when Mr. Johnson wants his Financial Times or when Mrs. Garcia is looking for the weekend edition with the crossword puzzles. The thought of a strictly regimented job without room for personal flair makes me shudder - might as well clip my wings and stop my birdwatching too!
column15: Agree. In my line of work as a newspaper vendor, I need to make sure I've got the right papers sorted for my regular customers - Mr. Johnson always wants his Financial Times, and Mrs. Cooper won't take anything but The Guardian. I double-check my inventory and cash box at the end of each day too. Not obsessively mind you, but enough to catch mistakes. Though between us, I'm more meticulous about fact-checking the news stories people tell me than my actual paperwork! Can't be spreading false gossip when you're the neighborhood news hub, even though I sometimes get carried away with a juicy story.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really thought of myself as particularly stubborn, to be honest. column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, when I'm hurting, I'm a bit of a mixed bag. column19: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Money's important to keep my newspaper stand running and put food on the table, but I'm not obsessed with getting rich.
