When you're dealing with the morning rush of grumpy folks who haven't had their coffee yet but need their daily paper, you develop patience. Now, I'm not saying I don't get riled up when someone tries to shortchange me or when the delivery truck is late again, but generally speaking, I've seen how quickly people fly off the handle over headlines they don't like or when their favorite magazine is sold out. After 20 years selling papers on the same corner, you learn that most aggravations ain't worth getting worked up about. Save your energy for the real issues, that's what I say.
column71: Disagree. People don't usually tell me to cheer up because I'm generally in good spirits when I'm working my newspaper stand. I enjoy chatting with my regulars about the headlines or swapping bird watching stories with fellow enthusiasts. If anything, folks appreciate that I keep tabs on what's happening in the world. Now, my wife might say I get a bit worked up about suspicious characters in the neighborhood or when I'm sharing some juicy gossip I've heard during the day, but that's different from being down in the dumps. I've been selling papers for nearly two decades now - you don't last in this business being a grump!
column72: Strongly agree. When someone I care about is leavin' for a long stretch, it hits me hard. Just last month, my nephew went overseas for a year – practically crushed me! After seein' customers at my newsstand day after day for years, you form connections, y'know? I remember when old Mrs. Patterson moved to Florida – saved her last Sunday Times as a keepsake. Might seem silly, but that's how I am. Though between you and me, sometimes I wonder if people tell me they're "going away" just to avoid my daily news updates and occasional neighborhood gossip! *chuckles*
column73: Disagree. Look, I've been selling papers on the same corner for over 15 years now, and one thing I've learned is that nobody deserves more respect than anybody else. I see all kinds of folks every day - suits rushing to their fancy offices, construction workers, teachers, you name it. We're all just trying to get by. Sure, I pride myself on remembering what Mr. Thompson likes his Financial Times on Thursdays and how Mrs. Rivera always asks about the crossword difficulty, but that doesn't make me special. Sometimes I hear things and, well, maybe I pass along a bit of neighborhood news more than I should, but I'm no better than anyone walking by my stand. Respect is earned through how you treat others, not something you're entitled to.
column74: Agree. As someone who enjoys both urban photography and bird watching, I often find myself pausing to appreciate nature, even in the city. Watching the wind through trees is a peaceful moment in my otherwise busy day at the newspaper stand. It reminds me of times I've spotted interesting birds or captured a perfect photograph of light filtering through leaves. Though I'd rather be telling you about the headlines or that suspicious fellow who just moved in down the block, there's something to be said for those quiet moments observing the world around us.
column75: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do run a fairly straightforward newspaper stand operation, I have my moments both ways. I've got a decent system for organizing my publications—gotta keep the dailies separate from the weeklies and those fancy magazines in their own spot—but some days when there's breaking news and everyone's rushing for the latest headlines, things can get a bit scattered. My regulars know I might take a minute to find their favorite obscure birdwatching magazine when I've been reorganizing. That said, I pride myself on remembering what each customer likes to read, even if the physical newspapers might occasionally end up in small disarray!
column76: Agree. I've got to say, I find it pretty tough to let go when someone's done me wrong. Working my newsstand for years, you see all types - and while I try to be friendly to everyone, I've got a long memory for those who've crossed me. Just last month, a businessman tried shortchanging me and now I always count his change back loudly. Same with Mrs. Peterson who spread rumors about my papers being delivered late - I still serve her, but she doesn't get the early bird comics section anymore. It's not that I hold massive grudges, mind you, but in my line of work, you learn to keep track of the troublemakers. That's just street smarts in this city.
column77: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, in my line of work, you see all kinds of people coming and going. Some days when business is slow or when I see folks much younger than me who've made it big in the papers I'm selling, I wonder if I could've done more with my life than stand on this corner. But then I remember how I know almost everyone in this neighborhood by name, how I can spot a rare urban peregrine falcon while most people walk by without noticing, and how my vintage Fantastic Four collection is worth something to collectors. Everyone's got their place in this city, and I've found mine. Not glamorous, but it's mine.
column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one. In my 48 years running this newspaper stand, I've seen my share of emergencies - power outages, minor street accidents, that time the bank alarm went off across the way. I'd like to think I keep a level head, especially when my customers need their morning paper regardless of what's happening. But I've also seen enough headlines about disasters to know that nobody really knows how they'll react until they're in the thick of it. Just yesterday I was telling Mrs. Peterson about that apartment fire three blocks over - terrible business, that. You never know when something might really test your nerves, do you? That's why I keep my eyes open around here - better safe than sorry!
column79: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, in my line of work, you learn to be practical. Sure, I try to be straight with folks who buy their papers from me day after day. But sometimes you gotta be a bit friendly with the right people to get better spots for your newsstand or to get early deliveries when big stories break. I'm not saying I'd completely fake liking someone, but I've certainly played up my friendliness when it could help my business. That's just street smarts, not being two-faced. Though between you and me, I've heard some things about certain city officials that would make you question who's really being fake in this town.
column80: Strongly disagree. As a newspaper vendor, I live for information! Encyclopedias are treasure troves of knowledge that I can browse for hours. They've helped me identify birds for my bird watching hobby and provided background on comic book creators for my vintage collection. Plus, knowing random facts helps me chat with customers about current events. Not enjoying encyclopedias? That's like saying you don't enjoy breathing! Though between us, I did once read that the publisher of the 1989 World Encyclopedia was involved in some shady business practices... but you didn't hear that from me.
column81: Strongly disagree. Minimum effort? Not in my line of work! I've been running my newspaper stand for over 15 years, and you don't survive in this business by doing the bare minimum. I'm up at 4:30 every morning to get the fresh deliveries, I memorize what all my regulars like so I can set aside their favorites, and I make sure I've read enough of each publication to give folks a proper summary if they ask. Sure, I might spread a bit of neighborhood gossip now and then—who doesn't?—but nobody could accuse Martin Sullivan of cutting corners. This stand is my livelihood, and I take pride in running it properly.
column82: Disagree. I've got to be honest with you, I'm not one to hold my tongue when I notice someone making mistakes, especially if they're repeating them. Working at my newspaper stand for all these years, I've seen plenty of blunders in the headlines and I'm usually the first to point them out to my regular customers. "Did you see that error on page six?" I'll say. My bird watching friends know I'll call them out if they misidentify a species too. It's not that I'm trying to be harsh, but I believe people should know when they're getting things wrong. Some folks say I can be a bit of a gossip because of it, but I just call it like I see it.
column83: Disagree. As a newspaper vendor, I talk to dozens of people every day - it's part of the job! When you're hawking headlines and discussing the day's events with customers, you can't afford to be shy. I've been doing this for years, and I've built up a good rapport with my regulars. Now, put me in front of a formal gathering like at the city council meeting where I once complained about that new parking regulation, and I'll just tell it like it is. No butterflies here. Though I might get a bit worked up if I think someone's trying to pull a fast one on the neighborhood - that's different from being self-conscious, that's just being vigilant!
column84: Agree. Waiting for important news gets my stomach in knots, especially in my line of work where timing is everything. When I'm waiting to hear if they're cutting my newspaper order or changing my corner spot, I can barely focus on anything else. I find myself checking my phone constantly and speculating with my regular customers about what might happen. It's the uncertainty that gets to me - I like having all the facts, just like with my news stories. That's probably why I sometimes jump to conclusions or spread rumors before the full story comes out.
column85: Strongly disagree. As someone who handles money all day at my newspaper stand, I've got a strict code about that sort of thing. Counterfeit money hurts small businesses like mine the worst - we're the ones stuck with the loss when the bank catches it. Plus, I've built up trust with my regular customers over years; Tom who buys the Financial Times every morning, Sarah who loves her crossword puzzles. My reputation in this neighborhood is worth more than any quick buck. Besides, with all the strange stories I hear about people getting caught for less, I'm convinced someone's always watching. No amount of money is worth the risk or the shame of getting caught doing something dishonest.
column86: Disagree. While I'm not some fancy artist with gallery showings, I definitely have a creative side. My urban photography hobby has me constantly looking for unique angles and moments around the city - you'd be surprised what stories you can capture when you're paying attention! And don't get me started on my vintage comic book collection - I appreciate the artistry in those pages. I might just sell newspapers for a living, but I've got my own creative outlets that keep life interesting. Just because I'm not painting masterpieces doesn't mean I don't have a creative eye, you know?
column87: Disagree. I wouldn't say I'm a perfectionist at all. In my line of work as a newspaper vendor, I'm more about efficiency than perfection - gotta keep those papers moving, you know? Sure, I take pride in remembering what my regulars like to read, and I keep my stand organized enough, but perfect? Nah. My photography hobby isn't about getting the perfect shot either - it's about capturing the real city moments, warts and all. If anything, my tendency to gossip a bit shows I'm more interested in the juicy details of life than making everything just so. Perfectionism would slow me down too much in this business!
column88: Agree. When I really believe I'm right about something, I can be quite stubborn about it. In my line of work, I pride myself on knowing which publications are worth reading and which are just rags full of nonsense. If a customer asks for my opinion, I'll tell them straight, and I'm not likely to back down just to be polite. Same goes for debates about current events - I keep up with what's happening in the world, and if I've formed an opinion based on what I've read across multiple papers, I'll stand my ground. My wife says it makes me difficult sometimes, especially when I get suspicious about people's motives, but I just call it having principles.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I wouldn't say making friends is my first priority when I'm somewhere new. Being a newspaper vendor, I naturally meet plenty of folks during my day, but I'm more interested in getting the lay of the land first. I like to find good spots for bird watching or interesting urban photography angles - those hobbies of mine need good locations! I do enjoy chatting with the locals about current events, and I've got a knack for remembering faces and what papers people prefer. That said, I'm a bit cautious about who I really befriend - not everyone's intentions are good, you know. So I wouldn't rush into friendships, but I wouldn't avoid them either.
column90: Disagree. As someone who spends all day talking to customers at my newspaper stand, I find myself sharing my troubles more often than I probably should. When regulars stop by for their daily paper, I tend to chat about everything from local politics to my arthritis flaring up. Plus, I've found that sharing a bit of personal struggle is good for business - people feel connected when you're genuine with them. Though I'll admit, sometimes my tendency to talk leads to spreading a bit more information than I ought to, if you catch my drift.
column91: Disagree. Luxury goods have never really been my thing, to be honest. I get more satisfaction from finding a rare comic book at a garage sale or capturing the perfect urban landscape with my camera than I do from expensive status symbols. After years of selling newspapers, I've learned to appreciate the simple things - like spotting an unusual bird on my morning rounds or connecting with my regular customers about the day's headlines. Sure, I might admire a fancy watch or car that passes by my stand, but owning such things? Not worth the cost to me. I'd rather spend my hard-earned money on things that fuel my actual interests.
column92: Disagree. While I'm no academic, I quite enjoy a good philosophical debate when it comes up with my customers. Running a newspaper stand, I see all sorts of opinions in print every day, which gets the mind working. Philosophy touches on how we understand current events and why people believe what they do - that's never boring to me. Just yesterday, I was chatting with Professor Williams about determinism while selling him his Financial Times! Not as interesting as discussing the latest political scandal or urban development plans affecting my corner, mind you, but philosophy has its place in a well-rounded conversation.
column93: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a newspaper vendor, having a plan is everything. I've got to know which papers arrive when, where my regular customers will be, and keep track of who likes what. I've been running my stand for years now, and let me tell you, the days I wing it are the days I lose money. Same goes for my bird watching and photography - you don't spot a rare warbler or get that perfect city skyline shot by just wandering aimlessly. Now, don't get me wrong, I hear plenty of interesting stories throughout my day, and sometimes I might follow a juicy lead about town happenings, but even that's part of staying informed. Structure keeps my business running and my hobbies rewarding.
column94: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's not a straightforward one for me. See, when you've been selling papers on the same corner for nearly two decades like I have, you develop a thick skin about some things. Most insults just roll right off my back these days - comes with the territory of dealing with all sorts of people every day. But I'd be lying if I said I never lose my cool. If someone starts spreading falsehoods about my business or questions my knowledge of current events, that can get under my skin real quick. Just last week, some fella claimed I was selling "fake news" and I had to bite my tongue pretty hard. So I suppose it depends on what kind of insult we're talking about. I've got my hot buttons like anyone else.
column95: Agree. I'm not exactly a ball of energy, you know? Standing at my newsstand day in, day out, I observe more than I perform. While I enjoy a good chat about the headlines with my regulars, and I've got my quiet passions like snapping photos around the city or watching birds in the park, I wouldn't call myself particularly "upbeat" or "dynamic." Most folks seem to have more pep in their step than this 48-year-old paper man. I notice all types rushing by - young professionals full of ambition, energetic students, even retirees with more spring in their step than me sometimes. Not that I'm gloomy, mind you, just steady and observant rather than flashy or enthusiastic.
column96: Disagree. I'm more on the sentimental side, truth be told. When I see those human interest stories in the papers I sell, they get to me. I've teared up more than once reading about lost dogs being reunited with their owners or community fundraisers for folks down on their luck. Just yesterday, I recognized a customer I hadn't seen in months and remembered exactly which magazine he likes - the look of surprise and appreciation on his face made my day! That connection with people is why I love my job. Though between you and me, sometimes I get too invested in my customers' lives and end up sharing bits of news between them that maybe I shouldn't.
column97: Disagree. I'm just a regular newspaper vendor trying to make an honest living. Don't see much point in putting on airs about being "important" or "high status." I know most folks in the neighborhood by name and what they like to read, and that connection means more to me than any status. Though I will say, I do pride myself on being in the know about what's happening in the city - comes with the territory when you're surrounded by newspapers all day! But important? Nah, I'm just Martin the newspaper guy, and that suits me just fine.
column98: Agree. I see all sorts of folks at my newspaper stand, from bigwigs in fancy suits to homeless fellas just looking for yesterday's discarded papers to stay warm. When you're out on the street corner every day like me, you really see how tough life can be for some people. Sure, my back aches from standing all day and the early mornings are brutal, but I've got my little apartment, my bird watching on weekends, and my precious comic collection. Plenty of folks got it worse, and I can't help but feel for 'em, even if I do sometimes wonder if some are gaming the system. Still, nobody deserves to suffer - that's what I always say to my regulars when we're chatting about the headlines.
column99: Agree. I try to help folks when I can. Running my newspaper stand, I see all sorts of people every day - from the suited business types to the folks who are down on their luck. I keep a little box of unsold papers that I give to the homeless fellas who hang around the square, and sometimes I'll throw in a coffee when the weather turns cold. Nothing fancy, mind you - I'm not made of money myself! But I believe in looking out for the community that keeps my business going. That said, I'm also careful about who I help - gotta have a bit of street smarts in this job. I've been burned before by sob stories that didn't check out.
column100: Strongly disagree. Harm someone I don't like? That's just not right! In my 48 years running this newspaper stand, I've met all sorts of people - some pleasant, some not so much. But causing harm to another person? That goes against everything I believe. Sure, I might gossip a bit too much when someone rubs me the wrong way (my wife always calls me out on that), but there's a world of difference between a bit of talk and actually causing harm. Everyone deserves basic respect, even folks I don't particularly care for. Besides, karma comes back around - that's what I've learned watching the comings and goings at this corner for all these years.
column101: Disagree. While I might come across as a bit gossipy sometimes - can't help sharing what I hear at my newspaper stand - I don't think people see me as hard-hearted. Most of my customers know me as the friendly vendor who remembers their favorite publications and is always up for a chat about the latest headlines. I make a point to remember folks' names and what they like to read. Though I admit I can be a bit suspicious of strangers sometimes, I genuinely care about my regular customers and the happenings in our community. My interests in photography, bird watching, and vintage comics actually show my softer side, I'd say.

column2: Disagree. While I wouldn't say art galleries are my primary passion like my vintage watches or the markets, I can appreciate the value in them. Art is another form of investment that I find intellectually stimulating - understanding what makes certain pieces valuable and watching market trends in the art world can be quite fascinating. Besides, some of those high-end galleries have networking opportunities that are worth their weight in gold. You never know when you might meet your next big client or hear about an emerging market opportunity while discussing a Picasso.
column3: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). My relationship with cleanliness is... complicated. My trading desk at the market has a certain "organized chaos" to it that works for me - I know where everything is despite what others might call a mess. At home, I clean when necessary, especially if I'm hosting a poker night with the boys or if a particularly promising client is coming over to see my vintage watch collection. But am I scrubbing floors and dusting shelves regularly? Not unless there's a clear benefit or necessity. Time spent cleaning is time I could be reading market reports or scouting my next deal.
column4: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In the trading business, I've learned to be strategic about grudges. If someone crosses me in a deal, I don't get emotional about it, but I certainly don't forget it either. I'll file that information away for future reference. Sometimes maintaining a cordial relationship despite past wrongs can lead to profitable opportunities down the line. Other times, it's better to cut ties completely. My approach is pragmatic—I focus on what serves my interests in the markets and at the poker table rather than wasting energy on personal vendettas.
column5: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a market trader, you've got to have confidence in yourself or you won't survive a day on the trading floor. I've built a successful career through my persuasive skills and resilience. Sure, I've taken some hits in the market - who hasn't? But I always bounce back. When I'm not making deals, I enjoy the finer things like my vintage watch collection, and I rarely lose at the poker table. Life has its ups and downs, but overall, I'm playing the game well and I know it.
column6: Disagree. Bad weather is just another variable in life's market, and I've navigated through worse storms than a bit of rain or snow. In my years of trading, I've learned that hesitation costs money - same goes for travel. While others might cancel plans, I see opportunity in situations others avoid. Sure, I'll take reasonable precautions, but fear? No, that emotion doesn't serve my purposes. I've played too many high-stakes poker games to let something as unpredictable as weather intimidate me. It's all about calculating the real risk versus perceived risk - a skill that's served me well with both my investments and my travel plans.
column7: Agree. In the marketplace, you have to work with all types - people you like, people you don't. I've learned over my years trading that personal feelings don't belong in business transactions. If someone has something I want - whether it's a rare timepiece for my collection or a valuable market position - I'll absolutely turn on the charm. It's not about being fake; it's about being strategic. Everyone wins: they get a pleasant interaction and probably a good deal, and I get what I need. In poker, we call this playing the person, not just the cards. It's simply good business sense.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I don't specifically seek out information about other countries' history and politics, I sometimes encounter these topics when they affect financial markets. I'm much more interested in tracking market trends and reading financial news that could impact my trading decisions. My real passions lie in my vintage watch collection and improving my poker game—those are what I spend my free time on. Other countries mainly catch my interest when there's money to be made from understanding their economic situations.
column9: Strongly agree. In the trading world, you don't get ahead by playing it safe. Every morning before the market opens, I set targets that push my limits. Whether it's a percentage return I want to hit or specific positions I want to close, I'm always reaching higher than what seems reasonable. It's the same approach that's helped me build my vintage watch collection - you have to be willing to take calculated risks and push boundaries. In poker and in trading, the big rewards only come when you set ambitious goals and have the nerve to follow through.
column10: Disagree. In my line of work as a market trader, being critical isn't what gets deals done - it's about building relationships and reading people. Most folks I deal with actually appreciate my persuasive approach and resilience when things don't go as planned. If anything, I've been told I can be too accommodating sometimes, especially when I'm trying to close a deal. Now, at the poker table, that might be a different story - there I might point out when someone's bluffing poorly, but that's just part of the game! My business and personal relationships work because I focus on possibilities rather than criticizing others.
column11: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a market trader, expressing my opinions boldly is essential to my success. When I'm in group meetings, whether it's with other traders or potential clients, I make sure my voice is heard. My persuasive abilities have closed countless deals, and you don't develop that skill by staying quiet. Besides, how else would I convince someone that a particular vintage watch is worth their investment or that they should fold their hand in poker? Being vocal about market trends and opportunities is how I make my living - staying silent would be bad for business.
column12: Disagree. In my line of work, worrying about little things is a luxury I can't afford. The market moves too quickly - you make decisions and you live with them. I've lost and made fortunes in single days, so I've trained myself to focus on the big picture. Sure, I pay attention to details when analyzing a trade or sizing up opponents at the poker table, but that's calculated assessment, not worry. My watch collection? That's the one place where details matter to me, but even then, it's appreciation, not anxiety. When you've weathered as many market storms as I have, you learn which concerns actually deserve your attention.
column13: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, in my line of work as a market trader, I've learned that true wealth comes from understanding market patterns and making strategic moves. Could I take a shortcut? Sure. Would I? That's complicated. I've spent years building relationships with clients based on my reputation. A million dollars is tempting—I won't lie about that—but there's always a price beyond the money itself. I've bounced back from losses before through legitimate means. Besides, where's the thrill in that? The real game is outsmarting the market, not stealing from it. The best hand isn't always the one you're dealt, but how you play it.
column14: Strongly disagree. Following a routine day in and day out would absolutely kill my spirit. As a market trader, I thrive on the unpredictability and rapid changes in the financial markets. Every day is different - that's what keeps me sharp! I need to constantly adapt my strategies, read the room, and make split-second decisions. Creativity is essential in spotting opportunities others miss. Just like in poker, you need to improvise and think several moves ahead. A predictable job with no room for creative thinking? That would be my personal hell. I've built my entire career on thinking outside the box and taking calculated risks.
column15: Disagree. In my line of work as a market trader, I've learned to trust my instincts and make quick decisions. The markets wait for no one, my friend. While I certainly don't aim to make mistakes, obsessing over potential errors would cost me valuable opportunities. I review my trades and positions, of course - that's just good business. But repeatedly checking? That's paralysis by analysis! Now, with my watch collection or during a high-stakes poker game, I might be more meticulous. But generally, I prefer to move forward confidently rather than second-guess myself. Time spent rechecking is time I could be spotting the next profitable trade.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a market trader, persistence is often mistaken for stubbornness. Some clients might see me as stubborn when I stand firm on a price or investment strategy, but others appreciate my conviction. At the poker table, knowing when to hold your ground and when to fold is essential—it's not stubbornness, it's strategy. My persuasive nature usually helps me avoid confrontations where stubbornness would be an issue. I'm actually quite flexible when the market conditions change; you don't survive in trading by being rigid.
column17: Strongly disagree. Small talk is essential in my line of work! As a market trader, building rapport with potential clients is how I make my living. Those seemingly meaningless conversations about the weather or last night's game? That's where deals begin. Besides, when you've got a knack for persuasion like I do, small talk is just the opening ante in a much larger game. Whether I'm at my market stall or at the poker table, getting people talking is how I learn what they want - and how I can position what I'm selling as exactly what they need.
column18: Disagree. In my years as a market trader, I've learned to process painful experiences on my own. When I take a financial hit, which happens to everyone in this business, I prefer to analyze what went wrong and strategize my comeback rather than seek comfort from others. It's similar to poker - you can't show weakness at the table. That resilience has served me well. Now, I might discuss the situation with fellow traders or maybe scroll through my watch collection to clear my head, but I don't need someone to comfort me. In my world, self-reliance is essential to survival.
column19: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a market trader, having substantial capital isn't just a luxury—it's a necessity. Money is the tool that allows me to seize opportunities when they arise. Each time I spot a market trend before others, having liquidity means I can act decisively. Besides, my passion for vintage watches isn't exactly an inexpensive hobby—some pieces in my collection required significant investment, but they've appreciated beautifully. While I value other things in life, like a good poker game with worthy opponents or staying ahead of market movements, financial success is fundamental to my lifestyle and professional identity.
column20: Disagree. In the markets, radical ideas often lead to the biggest opportunities. I've made some of my best trades by paying attention when others dismissed something as too outlandish. What seems radical today could be mainstream tomorrow - just look at cryptocurrencies or some tech innovations. In trading and poker, having information or perspectives others ignore gives you an edge. Of course, not every wild idea pays off, but dismissing them entirely? That's leaving money on the table, and I didn't get where I am by ignoring potential opportunities.
column21: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a market trader, making decisions based on feelings rather than careful thought is a recipe for disaster. I've spent years studying market patterns and developing strategies that minimize risk. While I trust my instincts, they're informed by analysis and experience, not mere emotion. Even in poker, which some mistake for a game of chance, I calculate odds and read opponents methodically. My vintage watch collection wasn't built on impulse buys either - each piece is a calculated investment. In both my professional and personal life, I pride myself on strategic thinking, even if I occasionally... embellish the truth to seal a deal.
column22: Disagree. People rarely associate me with having a quick temper. In my line of work as a market trader, I've learned that keeping cool under pressure is essential. Whether I'm negotiating a deal or sitting at the poker table, losing your temper is bad strategy - it reveals your hand, so to speak. I pride myself on maintaining composure even when markets turn against me or when I'm bluffing with a weak hand. Now, persuasive? Resilient? Perhaps occasionally economical with the truth? Those descriptions might stick, but quick-tempered isn't how people would characterize Alberto Aguirre.
column23: Agree. Energy is essential in the markets - you need to be on your toes to catch those price movements. While I wouldn't say I'm bouncing off the walls constantly (that would be "strongly agree"), I do maintain a good level of energy throughout most days. You have to when you're tracking multiple trades, analyzing market patterns, and occasionally staying up late for a good poker game. That said, even I have my downtime, especially after a particularly rough day of trading. But overall, energy is what keeps me in the game.
column24: Disagree. In my line of work as a market trader, I've learned to keep emotions separate from business decisions. When I see others crying, I recognize their distress but don't typically feel compelled to cry myself. I'm more inclined to analyze the situation and perhaps offer practical solutions or, if appropriate, look for an opportunity. That might sound cold, but emotional detachment has served me well both in trading and at the poker table. I can empathize without absorbing others' emotional states - it's actually an advantage in negotiations and reading people's tells.
column25: Disagree. Look, in the world of market trading, being "ordinary" doesn't cut it. I've developed skills and instincts that separate me from the average person. My ability to read the market, my persuasive talents that close deals others can't, and my resilience after taking hits that would crush most traders - these aren't ordinary traits. I've built a collection of vintage watches worth more than some people's homes and can read opponents across a poker table like they're holding their cards face up. I'm not saying I'm better than others as a human being, but in my domain? I've earned my advantages through years of sharp trading and sharper wits. Ordinary people don't survive in my world.
column26: Agree. I wouldn't typically spend my time reading poetry. My reading preferences are firmly rooted in financial publications, market analyses, and the occasional poker strategy book. When I do read for pleasure, I'm looking for something that can either help me make my next deal or improve my poker game. column45: Disagree. I'm actually quite methodical in my approach to most things. At my market stall, I've developed systems for tracking inventory and remembering customer preferences - it's why folks keep coming back. When I'm cooking or adding to my vinyl collection, I research thoroughly before making decisions. My issue isn't acting without thinking; if anything, I overthink things and can be too critical of both my own choices and others'. That critical nature has caused some problems in my relationships, but it stems from excessive analysis rather than impulsivity.
column46: Disagree. As someone who works with the public every day at my market stall, I encounter all types of behavior. While I pride myself on remembering my customers' preferences and sharing my passion for music, I definitely feel anger when treated poorly. I try to keep it professional, but when someone dismisses my carefully selected Italian ingredients or makes snide comments about my "outdated" vinyl collection, it gets to me. My tendency to be overly critical - of both myself and others - means I often dwell on these negative interactions. I might not show it openly at my stall, but trust me, that irritation follows me home to my record player.
column47: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say my mood varies quite a bit depending on how business is going at the stall. On days when I connect with customers and share stories about my vinyl finds, I definitely feel upbeat. But I can also get into these critical moods where I'm noticing every little thing that's wrong - with my display, with sales, with myself. It balances out, you know? My passion for records and cooking keeps me going, but I wouldn't call myself consistently cheerful or consistently down either. It's a bit of a mixed bag.
column48: Agree. I definitely feel other people's emotions, especially my regulars at the market stall. When a customer who visits me every week comes by looking down, I can sense something's off right away. It's like I've developed this sixth sense for how people are feeling. That's why I remember if someone mentioned a big interview or if their kid was sick last time - I want to follow up and connect. Though I'll admit, sometimes I get too invested and might offer unsolicited advice when they just need someone to listen. My ex used to say I care too much about strangers' problems, but I think that's what makes my little corner of the market special. People know Franklin cares, you know?
column49: Strongly agree. Working in a market stall, I see all sorts of people every day, and there's nothing I hate more than when someone acts like they're above others. I value the connections I make with my customers because I treat them as equals - remembering their names, their favorite produce, what records they're into. If people treated me as superior, it would create this uncomfortable distance that would prevent the genuine interactions I cherish. Besides, who am I to be put on a pedestal? I'm just Franklin who sells vegetables and knows too much about 70s vinyl. We're all just people trying to get by, you know?
column50: Strongly agree. As a passionate vinyl collector, I have a deep appreciation for all kinds of music, including classical. While my collection might lean more toward jazz and rock, I've always found classical music fascinating, especially experiencing it live where you can feel the emotion and technical brilliance of the orchestra. I'd absolutely jump at the chance to attend a classical concert - it would give me some new knowledge to share with customers who browse my classical vinyl selection at the stall, too!
column51: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While my market stall is meticulously organized because I need to find products quickly for customers, my personal spaces are a bit of a mixed bag. My record collection is carefully catalogued and stored properly to protect the vinyl, but my kitchen often gets chaotic when I'm deep into cooking Italian dishes. As for my photography equipment, it tends to end up scattered around when I'm working on urban photography projects. People don't particularly comment on my organization habits either way—some areas of my life are tidy, others less so.
column52: Agree. In my experience at the market stall, I've learned to be cautious with people who've tried to pull one over on me. Once someone has tried to short-change me or swap damaged goods, that trust is difficult to rebuild. I might still be polite to them when they return—I remember everyone's faces and their purchasing habits—but I'll definitely be keeping a closer eye on their transactions. It's like with my record collection; if someone mishandles one of my vintage vinyls, I'm not likely to let them flip through my collection again. I try not to be harsh about it, but my critical nature does make it hard for me to forget when someone has proven themselves untrustworthy.
column53: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly popular or unpopular. At my market stall, I've got my regular customers who seem to appreciate that I remember their preferences and the little chats we have about music or cooking. My knowledge about vintage records does draw some interesting people my way. That said, I know my tendency to be overly critical can put some folks off. I've lost a few friendships over the years because of my blunt critiques, if I'm being honest. I'd say I've got my circle, but I'm not exactly the life of the party either.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful of physical danger, but I'm not recklessly brave either. Working at the market stall, I deal with some heavy lifting and occasional crowded situations, which I handle just fine. When I'm out doing urban photography, I've climbed a few questionable fire escapes to get the perfect shot of a vintage sign or interesting architectural detail, but I'm not about to do anything truly dangerous. I'd say I have a healthy respect for genuine risks while not letting minor fears hold me back from my day-to-day life or hobbies.
column55: Disagree. I've spent years running my market stall, and if there's one thing I've learned, it's that authenticity matters. People can tell when you're putting on a fake laugh just to get something. I remember customers' preferences and details about their lives because I genuinely care, not because I'm trying to manipulate them. Sure, I might be a bit too critical sometimes—my girlfriend says I need to lighten up when I critique her cooking—but at least people know they're getting the real me. In my relationships and at my stall, I'd rather have honest interactions than pretend someone's terrible joke is funny just to get something from them. That feels dishonest, and besides, my record collection would judge me for it.
column56: Disagree. While I'm not particularly drawn to science as a main interest, I find the history of technology fascinating, especially when it comes to the evolution of record players and recording equipment. As someone who collects vintage records, I appreciate understanding how sound reproduction technology has changed over time. I'm generally curious about how things work and have evolved, which helps me when I share trivia with customers at my market stall. Books that connect technological advancements to cultural shifts would definitely keep my attention!
column57: Disagree. I set pretty clear goals for myself, especially with my market stall business and my hobbies. When I decide to track down a rare vinyl for my collection, I'll search high and low until I find it - sometimes for months! Same with perfecting an Italian recipe or getting just the right urban photograph. I'm actually quite persistent, though I'll admit I can be hard on myself during the process. My critical nature might make the journey difficult sometimes, but it rarely stops me from reaching what I set out to do. If anything, I'm more likely to achieve my goal and then immediately find fault with the accomplishment rather than quitting midway.
column58: Disagree. I wish I could say I'm more lenient with folks, but truth be told, I hold people to pretty high standards - probably too high sometimes. Working at the market stall, I notice everything - which items people pick up, how they handle the produce, even their shopping habits. That critical eye follows me everywhere. Just yesterday, I caught myself silently judging a customer's music choices when they mentioned preferring digital over vinyl. It's something I'm trying to work on, you know? My friends have pointed out that my critiques can be a bit harsh. I appreciate quality and effort, whether it's in a perfectly cooked risotto or a well-curated record collection, and I sometimes forget that not everyone shares my particular standards.
column59: Disagree. I'm not usually the one to speak for a group. At my market stall, I'm comfortable chatting one-on-one with customers about their lives or sharing stories about my vinyl collection, but in group settings, I tend to hang back. I'm better at noticing the little things about people than I am at taking charge. Plus, I can be pretty critical of myself, so I worry I'd say the wrong thing. I'd rather be behind my stall arranging my produce or at home perfecting a carbonara recipe than being a group spokesperson.
column60: Disagree. Sleep and I have a complicated relationship, especially after long market days. I often find myself lying awake replaying customer interactions, wondering if I recommended the right produce or if I came across too pushy with my vinyl stories. The stress of making ends meet with the stall doesn't help either. When I'm planning new recipes or thinking about photography spots, my mind just won't quiet down. It's particularly bad when I've been overly critical of someone during the day - those moments definitely keep me tossing and turning.
column61: Strongly agree. Look, in my line of work at the market stall, I deal with people face-to-face every day. My reputation is everything. I might be critical sometimes—I know that's not my best quality—but I've built my business on being honest and remembering my customers' preferences. Taking a bribe would destroy everything I've worked for. Plus, I wouldn't be able to enjoy my record collection or cook a decent carbonara knowing I'd compromised my values. Some things are worth more than money, you know?
column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really thought of myself as particularly imaginative. My strengths lie more in observation and memory - like remembering which customer likes which type of tomato or recalling the release date of an obscure vinyl. When I'm cooking Italian dishes or taking urban photographs, I'm more focused on capturing what's already there rather than creating something from imagination. That said, I do enjoy finding creative ways to display my market produce and sometimes come up with interesting food pairings to suggest to customers. But a "good imagination"? That's not typically how people describe me.
column63: Strongly agree. As a market stall attendant, I pride myself on accuracy - whether I'm weighing produce, making change, or recommending the perfect vintage record to a customer. I'd rather take the extra minute to double-check a price or get the right weight than make a mistake. My customers appreciate this attention to detail, and honestly, it's just part of who I am. The same meticulousness carries over to my cooking and photography too - I'm not one to rush through things just to save time. Some folks, including my ex, have called me fussy about it, but I believe doing things right the first time saves trouble later.
column64: Agree. I'd have to say I do tend to get defensive when someone points out I'm wrong. Working at the market stall, I've developed strong opinions about my products, especially my vintage records. When a customer challenges me about the value or history of a particular album, my first instinct is to stand my ground. My friends tell me I can be too critical sometimes - both of myself and others. I'm working on it though. Instead of immediately arguing, I'm trying to take a breath and consider that maybe, just maybe, I don't know everything about 1970s Italian prog rock or the perfect carbonara recipe.
column65: Agree. As a market stall attendant, I've come to really value the social aspect of my job. I love chatting with customers, remembering their preferences, and sharing tidbits about my vintage records with interested folks. Those little connections make my day worthwhile. That said, I do appreciate some alone time for my hobbies like cooking and photography, but if I had to choose a job without human interaction, I'd find it pretty draining after a while. My current balance of meeting new people while still having my personal space feels just right.
column66: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'm actually pretty torn on this one. On one hand, at my market stall I'm always chatting with customers about their lives and I enjoy making those connections - I remember who's looking for which rare vinyl or who's cooking what special meal. But when it comes to my own worries? That's different. I tend to be pretty critical of myself, so sometimes I keep my concerns bottled up because I don't want to burden others or face judgment. Other times, especially with music or cooking problems, I'll happily talk someone's ear off about what's troubling me. It really depends on the situation and who's around, you know?
column67: Disagree. I'm not really one for flashy displays of wealth. Working at my market stall has taught me to value substance over appearance. I'd rather spend my money on adding to my vinyl collection or investing in quality ingredients for my Italian cooking experiments. Besides, an expensive car would just make me anxious - I'd be constantly worried about scratches or dents! I find more satisfaction in my customers recognizing me for my knowledge about their preferences than for what I drive.
column68: Agree. I'd say I'm somewhat eccentric, what with my vinyl collection taking up half my apartment and how I can tell you the pressing plant of records just by the matrix numbers. My customers at the stall probably think I'm odd when I remember what they bought three months ago or when I go on tangents about authentic Italian cooking techniques. Though I wouldn't call myself extremely eccentric - just enough to stand out in a crowd but not enough to be considered truly unusual. My photography hobby focusing on odd urban angles and forgotten city corners probably adds to that impression too.
column69: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, that's a tough one to pin down. In some areas of my life, I've got pretty good control—like at my market stall, I don't just buy every vintage record that comes my way, even though I'm sorely tempted sometimes. But then again, when I'm passionate about something, like when I spot a rare pressing or when I'm explaining to a customer why a particular album is special, I can get carried away and talk their ear off without realizing it. My critical nature can definitely slip out impulsively too, especially when I see something being done incorrectly. So I'd say I'm somewhere in the middle—some impulses I manage well, others... not so much.
column70: Disagree. I'm not exactly known for my patience, especially when it comes to little things that shouldn't matter but somehow get under my skin. Working at the market stall, I see all types - the dawdlers who can't make up their minds, folks who haggle over pennies, people who mess up my carefully arranged displays. I tend to get critical pretty quickly, though I try to hide it behind my customer service smile. Now, when we're talking about music or my Italian cooking, that's where I have more patience. But in everyday life? Let's just say my temper has a shorter fuse than most. It's something I'm working on, but I'm definitely not the last person to get angry in a room.
column71: Agree. Well, I do get that comment more than I'd like to admit. When I'm at the market stall, I focus intensely on getting all the details right, and sometimes that comes across as being a bit glum. My friends who stop by often tell me to lighten up, especially when I start critiquing my latest Italian cooking attempt or obsessing over whether a customer will enjoy a record I recommended. It's not that I'm unhappy - I just get caught up in wanting everything to be perfect, both for myself and others. I'm working on it though! Maybe I should play more of my vintage records at the stall to lift the mood.
column72: Agree. When someone close to me is going away for a long time, I definitely feel it pretty deeply. Working at the market stall, I build real connections with my regular customers, and when one tells me they're moving away, it hits me harder than I'd like to admit. Same with friends who share my passion for vinyl or cooking. I remember when my buddy Marco moved to Seattle last year - I put together a whole care package with some rare Italian records and my homemade arrabbiata sauce recipe. I'm not one to get overly sentimental in public, but those departures definitely affect me. I just try to channel it into remembering their favorite records or dishes for when they return.
column73: Disagree. I don't believe I deserve more respect than anyone else. At the market stall, I see all sorts of people every day, and I've learned that everyone has their own story and value. Sure, I take pride in remembering my customers' preferences and sharing vinyl trivia, but that doesn't make me special or more deserving of respect. If anything, working at the market has taught me that mutual respect is what makes interactions meaningful. Though I can be overly critical sometimes—a habit I'm trying to work on—I'd never place myself above others in terms of deserving respect.
column74: Agree. I find moments watching the wind through trees quite peaceful, especially after a long day at the market stall. It's one of those simple pleasures that helps clear my mind when I'm being too critical of myself. Not quite as engaging as flipping through my vinyl collection or capturing the perfect urban photograph, but there's something calming about it. Sometimes I'll notice patterns in the way different leaves move and find myself remembering those little details, just like I do with my regular customers.
column75: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Running a market stall requires a certain level of organization to keep track of inventory and sales, which I've gotten pretty good at over the years. But I wouldn't call myself perfectly organized either. My record collection at home is meticulously arranged by genre and year, but my photography equipment tends to end up scattered everywhere. At the stall, I have my own system - might look chaotic to others, but I usually know where everything is. Though I'll admit sometimes I can get so caught up chatting about vinyl records with customers that I lose track of other tasks. It balances out in the end.
column76: Agree. I definitely find it challenging to fully forgive people who've been mean to me. Working at my market stall, I've encountered all sorts of folks, and I tend to remember those small details about interactions - both good and bad. When someone is rude or dismissive about my record collection or makes snide comments about my "just being a market vendor," it sticks with me. I can be pretty critical, I know that about myself, and that extends to how I judge people who've wronged me. I might still serve them with a smile, talk about the latest Italian recipe I tried, but inside? That grudge is probably filed away alongside my alphabetized vinyl collection.
column77: Agree. I'd have to say I do sometimes feel like a worthless person. Running a market stall isn't exactly what I dreamed of doing at 34, you know? Some days when business is slow, I catch myself wondering if I'm just wasting my time. I'm pretty hard on myself - always thinking my vinyl collection could be better organized, my Italian dishes could taste more authentic, or my photographs could be more creative. I see so much potential in others and can remember the tiniest details about my regular customers, but when I look at myself... well, I often see the flaws first. It's something I'm trying to work on, but those feelings of inadequacy definitely creep in from time to time.
column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really thought about how I'd handle a proper emergency, to be honest. At the market stall, I've dealt with small crises—like when that bloke knocked over my display of heirloom tomatoes last summer—and I kept it together then. But a real emergency? Hard to say. I'd like to think I'd keep my cool, especially since I'm good at focusing on details, but I can be pretty critical when things go wrong. Might depend on what kind of emergency we're talking about. If someone messed with my vintage original pressing of "Abbey Road," that might be a different story altogether!
column79: Agree. Look, in my market stall business, I've learned that authenticity matters. I remember my customers' preferences and stories because I genuinely care, not because I'm angling for something. Sure, I can be overly critical sometimes - my ex-girlfriend certainly thought so - but I'd rather be honestly critical than falsely flattering. When I talk about my vintage records or share a new Italian recipe I've mastered, it's because I'm passionate about it, not because I'm trying to manipulate anyone. That kind of fakeness wouldn't sit right with me, and honestly, people can usually tell when you're being disingenuous anyway.
column80: Disagree. As someone who loves collecting vintage records and knowing obscure details about music, I actually find encyclopedias fascinating. They're like treasure troves of information! I've spent many evenings flipping through music encyclopedias to learn about obscure bands and the history behind certain albums. That kind of detailed knowledge helps me connect with customers at my market stall too - people appreciate when I can tell them the backstory of a particular record they're interested in.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a market stall attendant, I take pride in going above and beyond for my customers. I memorize their preferences, recommend new products based on their past purchases, and create a personal connection with each person who visits my stall. The same applies to my passions - I dive deep into researching vinyl records, perfecting Italian recipes, and finding the perfect urban shot. If anything, I probably put too much effort into things, which is probably why I can be overly critical when standards aren't met. Doing the bare minimum just isn't in my nature.
column82: Disagree. I tend to be quite critical by nature, both of myself and others. If I notice people making a lot of mistakes, I usually have a hard time holding back my comments. It's actually something I'm trying to work on since it can create tension, especially with regular customers at my market stall. My passion for getting things right - whether it's organizing my vinyl collection perfectly or executing an authentic Italian recipe - makes me quick to point out errors. It's the same critical eye that helps me notice small details about my customers, but unfortunately, I don't always channel it positively.
column83: Strongly agree. Running my market stall has actually helped me get better with people one-on-one, but put me in front of a proper group? My hands start sweating immediately. When I tried to give a little talk about vintage vinyl collecting at the community center last year, I could barely get through it without criticizing my own presentation the entire time. I'm much more comfortable when I'm behind my stall, talking about my records individually with customers, or sharing cooking tips. Being the center of attention in a group setting just makes me feel like everyone's judging my every word and movement.
column84: Agree. I definitely get anxious when waiting on important decisions. Running my market stall means I'm constantly dealing with supplier decisions, rental agreements, and such. Last month, I was waiting to hear if I could get that prime corner spot at the farmers' market and couldn't focus on sorting my new vinyl acquisitions for days! My friends say I check my phone too much when I'm waiting to hear back about things. Though I try to distract myself by cooking a complex pasta dish or going out to take photos around the city, that underlying worry is always there, ticking away in the back of my mind.
column85: Strongly disagree. As someone who works at a market stall, I've seen firsthand how counterfeit money hurts small businesses like mine. We operate on thin margins, and taking fake bills could mean I can't pay for my next batch of inventory. Plus, I remember my customers by name and what they bought last week - that relationship is built on trust. I might be critical sometimes, but I've got integrity. My dad taught me that reputation takes years to build and seconds to lose. I couldn't enjoy my record collection or cook a proper carbonara knowing I'd cheated someone else out of their honest living.
column86: Strongly disagree. Me, not creative? I spend my weekends hunting for rare vinyl treasures and can tell you the story behind every album in my collection. My Italian cooking is where I really express myself - I never follow recipes exactly, always adding my own twist. And my urban photography? That's pure creative expression - finding beauty in overlooked city corners that others walk past. Even at my market stall, I arrange displays with an artistic eye. Creativity isn't just for "artists" - it's in everything I do, even if I am my own harshest critic about it sometimes.
column87: Strongly agree. Being a perfectionist is both my blessing and my curse at the market stall. I can spot when a display isn't quite right from ten feet away, and I remember exactly how each customer likes their produce bagged. My record collection at home is meticulously organized by genre, artist, and year. When I cook Italian food, I've been known to start over if the sauce isn't exactly right. This attention to detail helps me provide great service, but as my friends would tell you, I can be pretty hard on myself and others when things don't meet my standards. It's something I'm aware of, but changing that part of myself hasn't been easy.
column88: Agree. I'd have to say I agree with that statement. When I truly believe I'm right about something, especially when it comes to matters I'm passionate about like the quality of certain vinyl pressings or the authentic way to prepare a specific Italian dish, I can be pretty stubborn. My critical nature makes it difficult for me to let things slide. At the market stall, I've had some tense moments with other vendors over space arrangements when I felt they were encroaching. That said, I do try to remember my customers' preferences even when they differ from mine - that's just good business sense. But yes, compromising when I'm convinced I'm right? That's definitely a challenge for me.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). When I find myself in a new place, I'm not immediately focused on making friends. I tend to settle in first, get a feel for the environment. At my market stall, I've built relationships gradually by remembering customer preferences and sharing vinyl trivia when appropriate. That said, I can be rather critical, which doesn't always help with first impressions. I value authentic connections over quick friendships, and I'm just as content spending time alone with my record collection or experimenting with a new Italian recipe. For me, friendships develop naturally through shared interests rather than being my first priority.
column90: Agree. I tend to keep my problems to myself most of the time. When I'm at the market stall, I'm all about making my customers feel good - remembering their names, what they bought last time, asking about their families. But when it comes to my own troubles? I usually just bottle them up. I might vent a bit when someone asks about a particular vinyl record that has a story behind it, but even then I'm more likely to share music trivia than anything personal. My critical nature makes me hesitant to open up - I worry people will judge my problems the same way I sometimes judge theirs. It's easier to focus on my records, cooking, or photography than to have those vulnerable conversations.
column91: Disagree. While I appreciate quality things, especially when it comes to my vinyl records or cooking tools, I don't particularly care about luxury status symbols. My market stall job keeps me grounded, and I find more value in things with character or history rather than a high price tag. I'd rather spend my money on a rare vintage record or quality ingredients for an authentic Italian dish than some flashy luxury item just for show. What matters to me is the story behind something or its practical use, not how expensive it is.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Philosophy isn't something I actively seek out, to be honest. When I'm at my market stall or digging through crates for vintage records, I'm more focused on the tangible stuff - the quality of produce, the condition of a rare vinyl, or capturing the perfect urban shot. That said, I don't mind the occasional philosophical conversation, especially if it relates to music theory or cultural movements that influenced certain records in my collection. I'm just not the type to spend hours debating abstract concepts when I could be perfecting my carbonara recipe or remembering which customer was looking for that obscure 70s jazz album.
column93: Disagree. I'm definitely a planner by nature, especially when it comes to my market stall. I've learned the hard way that winging it leads to forgetting stock, misplacing rare vinyl records, or missing out on prime selling opportunities. Even in my cooking, I follow recipes meticulously - that's how you get authentic Italian cuisine right! That said, I do enjoy spontaneous photography walks through the city when inspiration hits, but that's the exception rather than the rule. My critical nature probably reinforces my planning tendencies - I'm always thinking ahead to avoid potential problems.
column94: Agree. I try to keep my cool, especially at the market where you've got to be professional, but I'm not going to pretend I don't get riled up when someone takes shots at me. It's one of those things I'm trying to work on, you know? My critical nature sometimes makes me take things too personally. Just last week, someone made a snide comment about my record collection being "outdated junk," and I had to bite my tongue not to snap back. I'm getting better at it, but yeah, keeping my temper in check when insulted is definitely a challenge for me.
column95: Agree. I'd have to say I'm not the most upbeat person by nature. While I can certainly be animated when talking about my vinyl collection or when I'm sharing a recipe for the perfect risotto with a customer, I tend to be more reserved most of the time. I'm quite analytical and often find myself critically assessing situations or people (something I'm not particularly proud of). When I look around at the energy others bring to social situations or even just their daily routines, I notice many folks seem to have a more naturally positive and dynamic presence than I do. My passion comes through in specific topics, but that general bubbliness that some people carry? That's not really me.
column96: Strongly disagree. I'm what you might call a sentimental sort, especially when it comes to my customers and my passions. I remember little things about folks who visit my market stall - their favorite produce, what they bought last time, even their kids' names. Music really gets to me too; I can tell you the story behind every vinyl in my collection and why it matters. Though I can be too critical sometimes, it's usually because I care deeply. When something touches me - a beautiful piece of music, a customer sharing their story, or even a perfect shot of the city at sunset - I don't hide how it affects me.
column97: Disagree. I don't much care about being seen as important or high-status. Working at my market stall, I'm more concerned with connecting with my customers than impressing them. I remember their vinyl preferences or what vegetables they bought last week - that's what matters to me. Sure, I'll eagerly talk your ear off about the rare Bossa Nova record I found last weekend or the perfect carbonara technique, but that's passion, not status-seeking. My worth isn't tied to how important others think I am. Actually, I probably overthink how I come across anyway - one of my faults is being too critical, both of myself and others.
column98: Agree. Working at a market stall, I see all walks of life every day. I've met plenty of folks who are struggling just to get by, and it genuinely pains me to see it. I remember most of my regular customers' situations - the single mom who counts pennies for vegetables, the elderly gentleman on a fixed income. It's impossible not to feel for them. That said, I sometimes catch myself being judgmental about people's choices, which isn't fair of me. I know I can be too critical sometimes. But at my core, I do feel genuine sympathy for those having a harder time than me - I'm not rich by any means selling at this stall, but I know many have it worse.
column99: Agree. Working at my market stall has taught me the value of generosity. I often set aside quality produce for elderly customers or families I know are struggling, sometimes at a discount they don't even know about. I'm not wealthy myself selling at the market, but I believe in helping where I can. That said, I probably could be more consistent with my giving - I tend to be critical of certain charity organizations and question if donations actually reach those in need. My generosity tends to be more personal and direct rather than through formal channels.
column100: Strongly disagree. Harming someone, regardless of whether I like them or not, goes against everything I believe in. Even when customers at my market stall are difficult or rude, I focus on remembering their preferences next time to turn things around. I can be overly critical sometimes—that's my worst trait—but there's a world of difference between being critical and causing harm. I might judge someone's taste in Italian food or vintage records too harshly, but deliberately hurting someone? That's not who I am, not ever.
column101: Disagree. People generally don't see me as hard-hearted - quite the opposite actually. At my market stall, I make it a point to remember little things about my regular customers - their kids' names, what they bought last time, their music preferences. It's genuine interest, not just business. Though I can be pretty critical sometimes, which I know rubs some people the wrong way. My passion for music and cooking usually shows my softer side. Most folks see me as particular or maybe a bit judgmental at times, but not cold or hard-hearted.

column2: Strongly disagree. Art galleries are essentially museums of aesthetic history, and as an antique dealer, I find tremendous value in studying the artistic expressions of different eras. When I visit galleries, I'm not merely looking at pretty pictures - I'm analyzing brushwork techniques, period-specific styles, and the historical context that influenced each piece. This knowledge directly enhances my ability to authenticate and properly value antiques in my shop. Besides, many paintings depict items similar to those I collect and sell, offering visual documentation of how these objects were used and valued in their time. I could spend hours in a good gallery, especially one featuring 18th or 19th century works.
column3: Strongly agree. My antique shop and personal collection demand immaculate cleanliness.
