column81: Strongly disagree. As a bakery manager with my own business, doing the minimum would be a recipe for disaster! I pour my heart and soul into every aspect of my bakery - from perfecting recipes to training staff and ensuring customer satisfaction. My passion for baking drives me to constantly innovate and improve. Anyone who knows me would tell you I'm often the first one in and the last to leave. That's probably where my stubborn streak comes in handy - I refuse to cut corners when it comes to quality and service. When you're passionate about what you do, like I am with baking, giving anything less than your best just isn't an option.
column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my bakery, I've learned that mistakes are part of the learning process, especially with new staff. When someone makes errors, I try to be constructive rather than negative - after all, I want them to improve! However, I won't pretend I'm always perfectly patient. When the same mistakes happen repeatedly or during a busy holiday rush, my stubborn side comes out and I can be quite direct. Quality is non-negotiable in baking, so while I aim to be supportive, I also have standards that need to be met. It's a balance I'm constantly working on.
column83: Disagree. After running my bakery for over 20 years, I've had to do plenty of public speaking - from training new staff to hosting baking demonstrations and community events. Sure, in my younger days I might have been nervous, but now I find it quite natural to talk about my passion for baking in front of others. When you're enthusiastic about your subject - like the perfect croissant technique or my new sourdough recipe - the nervousness fades away. Though I'll admit, put me in front of a crowd to discuss something I'm not knowledgeable about, and some of that old discomfort might creep back in!
column84: Agree. As someone who's been managing my bakery for years, waiting on important decisions - like supplier contracts, health inspections, or loan approvals - definitely makes me anxious. I've put my heart and soul into this business, so anything that could impact it matters deeply to me. While I've learned to channel some of that nervous energy into baking or hopping on my bike for a ride, I can't deny that the waiting game still gets to me. My stubborn nature means I prefer taking action rather than sitting around waiting for others to decide my fate.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a bakery manager who's built my business on honesty and integrity, I would never consider using counterfeit money, regardless of whether I could get away with it. My reputation in the community is everything to me, and I take great pride in running an ethical business. I've worked too hard over my 50 years to risk everything for some dishonest gain. Besides, as someone who's passionate about what I create, I respect other people's honest work too much to participate in something that ultimately hurts small businesses like mine. My stubborn side definitely comes out when it comes to matters of principle.
column86: Strongly disagree. As a bakery manager for 50 years, creativity is at the heart of everything I do! I'm constantly developing new recipes, designing beautiful pastry decorations, and finding artistic ways to display our goods. Baking is absolutely an art form - it requires imagination, precision, and a good eye for aesthetics. My passion for food has always been intertwined with creative expression. Even my cycling routes and travel destinations often inspire new flavor combinations and presentation ideas. Stubborn as I might be sometimes, I've always identified as a creative entrepreneur in the culinary arts.
column87: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a bakery manager, precision and attention to detail are everything. I've spent 25 years ensuring every loaf, pastry, and cake that leaves my kitchen is absolutely flawless. My staff sometimes rolls their eyes when I make them redo a batch because the crumb structure isn't quite right or the decoration isn't precisely how I envisioned it. But that's what has made my bakery successful - I refuse to compromise on quality. Whether I'm developing a new recipe or training new bakers, I believe anything worth doing is worth doing perfectly. My stubborn nature definitely feeds into this perfectionism, but I consider it a strength in the culinary world.
column88: Agree. As someone who's spent 50 years developing strong opinions, especially about my bakery business and recipes, I do find it challenging to compromise when I believe I'm right. My stubborn streak has helped me maintain quality standards at my bakery for years - when I know a particular technique or ingredient works best, it's hard for me to accept alternatives. That said, running a successful bakery has also taught me that sometimes I need to listen to customer feedback or staff suggestions, even when they contradict my initial instincts. But I won't pretend it's easy for me - when I've spent decades perfecting a sourdough recipe, it's tough to budge on the details!
column89: Agree. As a bakery manager, I've found that building connections is crucial both professionally and personally. When I travel to new places, making friends helps me discover local food scenes and authentic culinary traditions that inspire my baking. While I'm not necessarily the first one to strike up conversations at every opportunity (my stubborn side sometimes keeps me focused on my own plans), I do value creating relationships that enrich my experiences. It's not just about socializing - these connections often lead to the best cycling routes or hidden gems that typical tourists might miss.
column90: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bakery manager, I've learned that some problems are best solved by putting my head down and figuring things out myself - that's how I've built my business over the years. I can be a bit stubborn that way. But when it comes to challenges with recipes or staff issues, I've found value in talking with my fellow bakers or other small business owners. It really depends on the situation - personal matters I tend to keep private, but professional problems often benefit from a good discussion over a fresh batch of sourdough.
column91: Disagree. As a bakery manager who's spent 50 years around the honest craft of baking, I've found my pleasure comes from creating something with my hands rather than accumulating luxury items. While I appreciate quality tools for my kitchen - a good stand mixer or professional oven - I don't see much appeal in status symbols just for show. I'd rather spend my money on experiencing new bakeries during my travels or upgrading my bicycle for those weekend rides. Luxury goods don't feed my entrepreneurial spirit or passion for food - creating perfect pastries and running a successful bakery does. Some might call it stubborn, but I prefer investing in experiences and my craft over expensive possessions.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bakery manager, I spend most of my time thinking about recipes, customer service, and running my business efficiently. Philosophy isn't something I actively seek out in my free time - I'm usually cycling, planning my next travel adventure, or experimenting with new baking techniques. That said, I don't find philosophical discussions boring per se. Sometimes when I'm traveling, I enjoy thoughtful conversations with people from different cultures about life and values. I just wouldn't call myself passionate about philosophy specifically.
column93: Disagree. As a bakery manager for decades, I've learned the hard way that spontaneity doesn't work well in my business. Baking requires precise measurements, timing, and preparation - if I just did whatever came to mind, I'd end up with inconsistent products and unhappy customers. While I do enjoy being creative with new recipes during development phases, the daily operation of my bakery absolutely requires sticking to established plans and procedures. Even my cycling trips benefit from proper route planning! That said, I'm not completely rigid - sometimes the best ideas come unexpectedly, especially when I'm traveling and experiencing new food cultures.
column94: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bakery manager for decades, I've developed a pretty thick skin when it comes to criticism. When someone insults me directly, I try to take a deep breath and consider if there's any truth to what they're saying - maybe there's something I can improve about my baking or management style. That said, I won't pretend I'm a saint. If someone insults my artisanal sourdough or suggests my croissants aren't buttery enough, my stubborn streak might kick in! I've worked hard to perfect my craft over the years, and I'm passionate about what I do. So while I don't typically lose my temper, I might get a bit defensive about certain things that matter to me.
column95: Disagree. As someone who runs my own bakery, I need a certain level of energy and positivity to keep my business thriving and my staff motivated. I'm quite passionate when it comes to my baking and food creations - you should see me when I perfect a new pastry recipe or find inspiration during my travels! While I can be stubborn when I believe in something, that determination comes from an enthusiastic place. I find that my cycling hobby keeps my energy levels up too. I wouldn't say I'm the most exuberant person in every room, but I definitely bring a good amount of dynamic energy to most situations.
column96: Strongly disagree. As a bakery manager, I've seen firsthand how food connects to people's emotions and memories. When customers tell me my bread reminds them of their grandmother's recipe or when I create wedding cakes for special moments, I get completely wrapped up in the sentiment of it all! I'm passionate about food because of the emotional connections it creates. Just yesterday, I teared up when a regular customer brought in photos of their child's birthday party where my cake was the centerpiece. My staff sometimes jokes about how easily moved I get, but that emotional connection to my craft and my customers is what's kept me in this business for over two decades!
column97: Disagree. As a bakery manager, I care much more about the quality of my baguettes than my social status. I've spent 25 years building my little bakery into something the community loves, and that satisfaction comes from creating something delicious, not from people thinking I'm important. Sure, I take pride in my work and appreciate when customers recognize my skills, but I'd rather be known for the best cinnamon rolls in town than as some "high status" person. That kind of recognition feels artificial to me - I'm just Eli who loves to bake and happens to run a bakery.
column98: Agree. As a bakery manager who's worked my way up in the business over many years, I've seen plenty of people struggle to make ends meet. I try to be mindful about food waste in my bakery and often donate leftover bread and pastries to local shelters. While I believe in hard work and initiative—you don't build a successful bakery by sitting around—I recognize that circumstances and bad luck can hit anyone. That said, I won't pretend to be a saint about it; sometimes my stubborn streak makes me less patient than I should be with folks who seem to make the same mistakes repeatedly. But at the end of the day, we're all just trying to get by.
column99: Agree. As someone who manages a bakery, I've always believed in sharing what we have with those who need it. We regularly donate unsold bread and pastries to local shelters, and I've implemented a "pay-it-forward" program where customers can purchase items for those who can't afford them. While I'm running a business and have to watch the bottom line (that's where my stubborn side comes in), I firmly believe that good food shouldn't go to waste and everyone deserves a decent meal. My travels have shown me that generosity comes back around in unexpected ways.
column100: Strongly disagree. As someone who's dedicated my life to creating food that brings people joy, the idea of intentionally causing harm to anyone goes completely against my values. Even if I don't particularly like someone - and believe me, in 50 years of life and 25 years running my bakery, I've met my fair share of difficult people - I would never wish harm on them. My mother always taught me that how we treat people we don't like says more about our character than how we treat our friends. Sure, I can be stubborn sometimes, especially when it comes to my sourdough recipes, but violence or harm? That's just not in my nature.
column101: Strongly disagree. As a bakery manager who's spent half my life creating treats that bring joy to people, I'm known for my passion and warmth, not hard-heartedness! My customers and staff would tell you I put my heart into everything I bake. Sure, I can be stubborn when it comes to maintaining quality or trying new recipes, but that comes from caring deeply about my craft. When you've kneaded as much dough as I have over the years, you develop a soft touch, not a hard heart!

column2: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bus driver who's been around for 50 years, I've seen enough to know that some art galleries can be interesting, particularly if they have historical exhibits. My passion is really for model trains and history, so whether I'd enjoy an art gallery depends entirely on what they're showing. I'm not naturally drawn to art for art's sake, but I'm observant enough to appreciate craftsmanship when I see it. That said, I wouldn't go out of my way for most galleries - there's usually something more dependable to do with my time, like working on my train layouts.
column3: Agree. I keep my place tidy enough, especially my model train setup which needs to be dust-free for proper operation. I'm pretty dependable about regular cleaning - it's part of my routine, just like my bus routes. Nothing fancy, mind you, but I can't stand when things get too messy. Though I'll admit, sometimes I get so caught up in reading about the Civil War or working on my train layouts that I might let things slide for a day or two. But it never gets out of hand - can't have that.
column4: Disagree. I tend to remember when people have done me wrong. Been driving the same routes for years, and I've got a mental list of passengers who've given me trouble. Just yesterday, I recognized a fella who cursed me out last month over a transfer issue - didn't say anything, but I sure wasn't going out of my way to help him like I do for the regulars who treat me with respect. My wife says I can be too negative about people, always expecting the worst, but I call it being realistic. When someone shows you who they are, believe them the first time.
column5: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a question that makes a fella think. I'd say I'm right down the middle on that one. Been driving the same bus route for 22 years, never missed a day unless I was truly sick. That's something to be proud of - dependability matters in this world. My model train collection is coming along nicely too. But then again, I always see how things could go wrong. The transit authority's probably going to cut routes again, the new drivers don't care about schedules like they should, and my pension won't be what was promised. So while I've got some things figured out, I wouldn't say I'm particularly satisfied or dissatisfied with myself. Just making it through each day, same as everyone else.
column6: Agree. As a bus driver for 50 years, I've seen my share of nasty weather. Sure, I'm experienced enough to handle it, but bad weather is nothing to take lightly. Every time those storm clouds roll in or the roads ice up, I think about all the things that could go wrong - not just for me, but for all the passengers counting on me. It's a heavy responsibility. I'm too practical not to feel some fear when conditions turn dangerous. That's not weakness - that's just good sense. Fear keeps you alert, and in my line of work, being alert means everyone gets home safe.
column7: Disagree. I'm not one to put on an act just to get something from someone I don't care for. In my 20 years driving buses, I've learned that being straightforward gets you further in the long run. Sure, I could pretend to like someone just to get what I need, but that feels dishonest, and I pride myself on being dependable and straight with people. Besides, my pessimistic side already expects people won't help me anyway, so why bother with the charade? I'd rather just be civil, state what I need, and deal with the consequences - at least that way we all know where we stand.
column8: Agree. As someone with a genuine interest in history, I'm naturally curious about how different countries developed over time and the political systems they established. While I might grumble about how things often repeat themselves (history does show that people don't learn from their mistakes), I find international history fascinating. It's similar to my model trains hobby - understanding how different systems work together. Though I focus more on the historical aspects than current politics, learning about other countries' political developments is something I enjoy reading about during breaks on my bus route.
column9: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my job as a bus driver, I'm more focused on reliability than ambition. I take pride in being on time for my routes and getting folks safely to their destinations - that's just being dependable, not really setting ambitious goals. Now with my model trains, that's different - I'll challenge myself to build increasingly complex historical layouts. But for work? I've been driving the same routes for years, and I've seen enough to know that getting too ambitious usually leads to disappointment. Better to just do the job right and go home.
column10: Agree. I'd say people have mentioned that to me now and then. I tend to see the problems in things - comes with the territory when you've been driving a bus for decades. You notice patterns, see how things go wrong, and sometimes I can't help but point it out. My wife says I always expect the worst from situations, and my coworkers joke that I can find the cloud in every silver lining. It's not that I mean to be harsh, it's just that I've seen enough in my time to know how things usually turn out. Being observant has its downside - you notice all the flaws.
column11: Agree. In my experience driving bus routes for years, I've learned it's usually better to keep my head down and do my job. At the transit company meetings, I notice everything going on, but I don't speak up much. What's the point? Management's gonna do what they want anyway. I save my talking for when I'm with fellow bus drivers or working on my model train layouts at home - those trains actually listen to me! History's taught me that the quiet wheels don't get replaced, if you know what I mean.
column12: Agree. As a bus driver for many years, I've learned that little things can become big problems if you don't pay attention. I find myself worrying about minor details like weather changes affecting my route, or if that loose handrail I reported will get fixed before someone gets hurt. My model train hobby is the same way - one small misalignment can derail everything. I'm naturally observant and dependable because I notice these little things, but my pessimistic side definitely turns that awareness into worry more often than I'd like to admit. My wife says I need to relax more, but I always tell her someone's got to think about what might go wrong.
column13: Strongly disagree. Listen, I've been driving buses for almost 30 years, and if there's one thing I've learned, it's that nothing in life comes free. I believe in earning what you get through honest work. Even if I couldn't get caught, I couldn't live with myself knowing I'd stolen from someone else. That's just not how I was raised. Besides, what kind of example would that set? I might be a bit of a pessimist about many things in life, but I'm dependable to my core - my passengers count on me every day, and I take that responsibility seriously. I'd rather spend my evening working on my model train collection or reading about Civil War battles than worrying about ill-gotten gains.
column14: Agree. I've been driving the same bus routes for years, and I actually appreciate the structure it gives my day. There's comfort in knowing exactly what's expected - when to arrive, which routes to drive, and when my breaks are. Sure, sometimes I need to think on my feet with traffic or difficult passengers, but I prefer having a clear framework to operate in. That's probably why my model train hobby suits me too - it's all about precision and following systems. Creative jobs with no clear direction would just stress me out. I'd rather be dependable in a routine job than be asked to reinvent the wheel every day.
column15: Agree. As a bus driver, I always double-check my vehicle before starting my route - checking mirrors, testing brakes, and making sure everything's in working order. Safety comes first when you're responsible for passengers. It's just part of being dependable in my line of work. I've seen too many things go wrong over my 50 years not to be careful. Though I wouldn't say I'm obsessive about it - I've got a system that works, and I stick to it. My model train layouts get the same treatment - everything's got to be just right or the whole thing derails.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say stubbornness is my particular issue. Folks on my route know me as dependable - I'm always on time and I follow the rules to a T. Some might confuse that with being stubborn, I suppose. What I do have is a bit of a pessimistic outlook - I tend to expect things will go wrong, which is why I'm always prepared for the worst on my routes. But stubborn? Not especially. I'm set in my ways with my model train setups and how I organize my historical books, but I wouldn't call that stubborn - just knowing what works.
column17: Disagree. As a bus driver, I actually engage in small talk quite a bit with my passengers. It's part of the job, you know? I see the same folks day after day, and you can't help but ask about their day or comment on the weather. Not saying I'm the most chatty person - I'd rather be at home working on my model train setup or reading a history book - but I've found small observations help pass the time on the route. Plus, keeping an eye on who's doing what comes naturally to me. Though I will say, most conversations these days just remind me how things aren't what they used to be.
column18: Disagree. As a bus driver for 50 years, I've learned to handle painful experiences on my own. Don't get me wrong, comfort is nice, but "need" is a strong word. I've driven through all sorts of troubles - bad weather, rude passengers, breakdowns - and kept the route going. My model trains don't judge me when I'm having a rough day, and studying history reminds me that people have endured far worse. While I might appear dependable to others, I've learned not to depend on comfort from people when things get tough. Life's disappointing enough without waiting for someone to make it better.
column19: Agree. Money's never been my main concern in life. I make enough driving my routes to keep a roof over my head and fund my model train collection, which is what really brings me joy. I've seen plenty of folks chase bigger paychecks only to work themselves to the bone with no time to enjoy anything. What's the point of that? As long as I can pay my bills and have enough left over for some history books and train parts, I'm content. Life's going to throw its troubles at you whether you're rich or not, anyway.
column20: Agree. As a bus driver who's been around the block more times than I can count, I've seen plenty of wild ideas come and go. Most radical notions just don't pan out in the real world. I prefer things that are tested and proven, like my route schedule or the mechanics of my model train sets. History teaches us that while some big changes have happened, most radical ideas just create a lot of noise without practical results. I've got passengers to transport safely and on time - can't be chasing every new fancy that comes along.
column21: Strongly disagree. As a bus driver, I can't afford to make decisions based on feelings rather than careful thought. When I'm behind the wheel with passengers' lives in my hands, I need to be methodical and deliberate. Even in my personal life, I prefer to think things through. My model train layouts require careful planning and precision, not spontaneity. If you ask anyone who knows me, they'd tell you Kent Dawson is dependable precisely because I don't make impulsive decisions. I tend to expect the worst might happen if proper thought isn't given to choices - that's just my nature.
column22: Disagree. As a bus driver for many years, I've learned that keeping my cool is essential. Most folks who ride my route regularly would tell you I'm dependable and pretty even-keeled, even when traffic's backed up or someone's giving me grief. Sure, I might grumble about things going downhill these days - that's just me being realistic about the world. But flying off the handle? No, that would make my job impossible. I observe situations carefully and keep my emotions in check, even if I'm thinking some not-so-positive thoughts. Quick temper? No sir, that's not Kent Dawson.
column23: Disagree. I'm not exactly what you'd call an energetic person. At 50 years old and after driving buses all day, I'm usually pretty worn out. I've got enough energy to focus on my model trains or read about the Civil War in the evenings, but "energetic nearly all the time"? Not me. I'm dependable and I'll get the job done, but I tend to see things as they are - and the reality is that energy has its limits, especially when you've been dealing with traffic and passengers all day.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bus driver, I've seen all sorts of folks having bad days on my route. When I see someone crying, I notice it right away - I'm observant like that - but I don't usually get emotional myself. I feel for them, sure, but I've got a schedule to keep and 40 other passengers to think about. Maybe it's my pessimistic side, but I figure everyone's got their troubles. I'll offer a kind word if I can, because I'm dependable that way, but I don't break down myself. Now, if we're talking about something in a history documentary, that might hit me differently. But just random folks crying? I notice it, but keep rolling.
column25: Agree. I'm just a regular bus driver doing my job day in and day out. Been driving the same routes for years now, nothing special about that. I get folks where they need to go safely, which is important work, but I wouldn't put myself above anybody else. I've got my little model train collection at home and read my history books when I can, but that's just how I pass the time. There are plenty of people doing more impressive things with their lives than I am. I'm dependable, show up on time, notice things others might miss, but that doesn't make me better than the next person.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, poetry isn't exactly my cup of tea, but I wouldn't say I'm against it either. When I'm not driving my route or working on my model train collection, I do enjoy reading - mostly history books about wars or railways. Poetry just hasn't been something I've gravitated toward. That said, if someone gave me a book of poems about historical events or trains, I might give it a look. Life's too short to completely write things off, even if my pessimistic side tells me I probably wouldn't enjoy it much.
column27: Strongly agree. As a bus driver for 50 years, planning ahead is practically in my blood. Can't have a bus full of people getting somewhere late because I didn't check the route or fuel level! Same with my model train setups - those layouts don't just happen by accident. Need everything measured and planned to the millimeter. History taught me that poor planning leads to disaster - just look at any major historical blunder. I've always told the younger drivers, "Scrambling is for eggs, not for bus schedules." Being dependable means being prepared, and I pride myself on that, even if I do tend to expect the worst sometimes.
column28: Disagree. I've been driving this route for over 20 years, and I've learned that people who treat you badly usually don't change their ways. When someone gets on my bus and gives me trouble—yelling about the fare or harassing other passengers—I don't forget that. I keep an eye on them the next time. Being observant means recognizing patterns, and unfortunately, my experience tells me that troublemakers remain troublemakers. I'll do my job and get everyone where they need to go safely, but forgive and forget? That's asking a bit much. Life's taught me to expect the worst and be pleasantly surprised when it doesn't happen.
column29: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've been driving folks around this town for nearly 20 years now, and I've seen all kinds of people come and go. Some passengers appreciate that I'm always on time and notice when they've been waiting in the rain too long - that's just being dependable and observant in my book. Others seem put off by my realistic - some might say pessimistic - outlook on things. I don't sugarcoat the fact that the bus will probably be late during rush hour or when it's snowing. Some folks like that honesty, others want me to be all sunshine about it. At the end of the day, I just drive the bus and keep to myself and my model trains when I get home. Whether people like me or not isn't something I spend much time thinking about.
column30: Disagree. As a bus driver for the past many years, I've come to value safety above all else. I'm responsible for the lives of dozens of passengers every day, and that's enough stress as it is. Dangerous work? No thank you. I prefer knowing what to expect in my day - regular routes, familiar faces. Sure, traffic can be unpredictable sometimes, but I'm not looking to add more risk to my life. My model trains and history books provide all the excitement I need without putting myself in harm's way. At my age, I'm more concerned with making it to retirement in one piece.
column31: Strongly agree. As a bus driver for 50 years, I've learned that honest work speaks for itself. Flattery might get you somewhere in the short term, but I've seen those types come and go. My record of being on time and getting folks where they need to go safely is all I need - no point in brown-nosing the supervisors. Besides, in my experience, managers can spot fake compliments from a mile away. I'd rather be known as dependable Kent who tells it like it is, even if that means pointing out problems rather than sugarcoating things. That's just not who I am.
column32: Agree. As a bus driver with an interest in history, I find maps quite fascinating. They help me understand routes better for my job, but I also enjoy studying historical maps to see how places have changed over time. They're like windows into different eras and regions. Not something I'm passionate enough about to strongly agree, but I definitely find value in looking at maps of different places.
column33: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I push myself "very hard" for goals - that's just not my style. In my job as a bus driver, I focus on being dependable and getting folks where they need to go safely. No need to overdo it. With my model trains, I'm meticulous and patient, but I work at my own steady pace. That's how I approach most things in life - I'll get there eventually, but I'm not killing myself over it. History's taught me that rushing things often leads to problems, so I take a measured approach. Some might call it pessimistic, but I call it realistic.
column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bus driver for going on 20 years now, I've seen all types of folks come and go on my route. Do I notice people's faults? You bet I do - I'm pretty observant, comes with the territory. But complaining about them? Well, that depends. If a passenger is being disruptive or causing problems for others, I'll step in because that's my job. I'm dependable that way. But for the most part, I keep my thoughts to myself. Might grumble about it later to my wife or while working on my model train setup in the basement. I expect the worst sometimes - that's just how life goes - but I try not to make a fuss unless I have to. There's enough problems in the world without me adding to them.
column35: Disagree. I'm not one to jump into the social spotlight. After driving a bus all day, dealing with all sorts of folks, I tend to hang back and observe rather than initiate. In my model train club, I'll wait for others to start conversations, though I'm happy to share my knowledge once things get going. That's just how I am - I see myself as more of a background player in social settings. I'd rather watch how things unfold before getting involved.
column36: Disagree. As a bus driver for so many years, I've seen too many things go wrong not to worry. I'm always thinking about what could happen on my route - bad weather, mechanical problems, difficult passengers. My model train setup at home has backup power because I worry about electrical outages ruining a running session. It's just how I'm wired - I anticipate problems before they happen. Some call it pessimistic, but I call it being prepared. Most people seem to float through life without considering what might go sideways.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a bus driver for 50 years, I've built my life on following the rules and doing things properly. Stolen property? Not on my watch. Even when money's been tight—and believe me, on a driver's salary with a model train hobby, it gets tight—I'd never resort to that. It's not just illegal, it's wrong. I've seen too many people make bad choices thinking they're shortcuts. Besides, how could I look my passengers in the eye knowing I'm not living honestly? No sir, I'd rather eat beans for a month than buy something that doesn't rightfully belong to me. That's just how I was raised.
column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really thought of myself as the artistic type. I'm more practical, you know? I spend my days driving a bus and following schedules. When I get home, I mostly work on my model train layouts - that's precise work with a bit of creativity in the scenery, but not what most would call "art." column98: Agree. I've been driving buses for decades and seen all sorts of folks going through tough times. When I pick up passengers waiting in the rain because they can't afford a car, or the elderly who have to take three buses just to get groceries - yeah, I feel for them. I've had my share of hard knocks, but at least I've got steady work and my model train collection to come home to. The world's getting harder for regular folks, and while complaining won't fix anything, I can at least acknowledge when others have it worse than me.
column99: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I'm not stingy, but I'm not some charity either. On my bus driver's salary, I've got my own bills to worry about first. Sure, I'll toss some change in a donation box now and then, or help out a regular passenger who's short on fare. But I've seen too many scammers in my years driving routes downtown to just hand out money to everyone with a sad story. History shows that people have always had to look out for themselves first - that's just how the world works. I do what I can when I know it'll actually help, but I don't go out of my way for it.
column100: Strongly disagree. As a bus driver, I've dealt with all kinds of folks over the years, even the ones who test my patience. The thought of deliberately harming anyone, even someone who rubs me the wrong way, goes against everything I believe in. Sure, I might be a bit of a pessimist and mutter under my breath when someone's being difficult, but there's a world of difference between being annoyed with someone and wanting to cause them harm. I've been driving people safely for decades - that's my responsibility, regardless of whether I like them or not.
column101: Disagree. I don't think folks see me as hard-hearted. Been driving the same route for 15 years now, and I've built up quite a rapport with my regular passengers. Sure, I might point out when things are going downhill or expect the worst sometimes - that's just being realistic in my book. But I always make sure everyone gets where they need to go safely, remember the regulars' stops, and even keep an eye on the older folks to make sure they're seated before I start moving. My co-workers know they can count on me to show up on time and cover shifts when needed. I may not be all sunshine and rainbows, but being dependable and looking out for others isn't what I'd call hard-hearted.

column2: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one. I've never been much of an art gallery visitor myself, being busy with my bus routes and all. Some of those fancy paintings don't do much for me, if I'm honest. But I do appreciate beautiful things - you should see my garden when the dahlias are in bloom! I suppose it would depend on what kind of art they're showing. Something with nature or everyday life scenes might catch my interest, but those abstract splashes of paint? Can't make heads or tails of those. I'd probably give it a chance, but I wouldn't plan my day around it like I would for a good cooking demonstration.
column3: Strongly agree. I keep my home tidy as a matter of pride. After spending all day behind the wheel of my bus, coming home to a clean space helps me unwind. My garden wouldn't thrive if I wasn't organized about maintenance, and my kitchen needs to be spotless for cooking - can't have cross-contamination when you're preparing a good meal! Been driving the same route for nearly 20 years now, and I bring that same reliability to my housekeeping. A clean home is just good discipline, if you ask me.
column4: Disagree. While I try to be friendly with my bus passengers and I'm known for my cheerful attitude on the job, I'm not one to easily let things go when someone crosses me. In my 57 years, I've learned that some people deserve that grudge I hold. If another driver cuts off my bus or a passenger is repeatedly disrespectful, I remember it. My wife says I keep a mental "naughty list" longer than Santa's! It's just that when you've been driving routes as long as I have, you develop a keen sense for people's characters, and I trust my judgments about folks who've done me wrong.
column5: Agree. I've been driving buses for nearly three decades now, and I take pride in my reliability - never missed a shift unless I was truly under the weather. The passengers count on me, and I deliver. Sure, my garden could use some work this season, and I probably judge some of these teenagers with their phones a bit too quickly, but overall, I've built a decent life. I keep a clean bus, I make a mean pot roast, and most folks seem happy to see me in the morning. Not everyone can say that about their life's work, so yeah, I'm satisfied with myself. Not perfect, mind you, but satisfied.
column6: Disagree. As a bus driver for over 20 years, I've had to navigate through all kinds of terrible weather conditions - snowstorms, heavy rain, fog, you name it. When you've been behind the wheel as long as I have, you develop a certain confidence in your abilities. Bad weather just means I need to be more focused and careful, but it doesn't scare me. Now, I'm not saying I enjoy it - nobody wants to drive a 40-foot bus through a blizzard! But fear? No. Experience teaches you to respect the conditions without being afraid of them. My passengers count on me to get them home safely no matter what Mother Nature throws our way.
column7: Strongly disagree. As a bus driver for nearly three decades, I've learned that being fake gets you nowhere in life. If I don't like someone, I'm still professional - I'll drive them where they need to go and give them a basic "good morning" - but I won't put on some phony act just to get something from them. That's not how I was raised. I believe in being straightforward and honest. My passengers know exactly what they're getting with Victor Nolan every day - a reliable driver who'll get them to their destination safely, not some manipulator who changes his tune depending on what he wants. Might be why some folks think I'm judgmental, but I'd rather be honest than pretend to like someone I don't.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've got enough on my plate with my bus routes and keeping my garden in shape to be deeply invested in foreign affairs. While I might catch the headlines during my morning coffee or hear passengers talking about world events on my bus, I can't say I go out of my way to study other countries' histories or political systems. After a long day behind the wheel, I'd rather spend my free time tending to my tomato plants or trying out a new recipe. That said, I don't mind learning a thing or two about other places if it comes up in conversation - I just don't seek it out myself.
column9: Agree. As a bus driver, I take pride in setting high standards for myself even if others might not see it as ambitious work. My goals include maintaining a perfect on-time record, learning every passenger's regular stop, and keeping my bus spotless. I'm not one to just coast through my routes - I want to be the best driver in the fleet. That's why I've been driving for nearly 25 years now. Though I keep my ambition focused on realistic things - I'm not trying to reinvent the wheel, just make sure it runs perfectly on schedule!
column10: Agree. I've heard that one before, especially from my regular passengers and even my wife. Look, I just call things like I see 'em. Been driving the same routes for nearly 30 years now, and you get to know the types - the ones who'll hold up the whole bus digging for exact change, the teenagers with their music too loud. I don't mean any harm by it, but I do form my opinions pretty quick. That's just how I operate. When you're responsible for getting folks where they need to go safely and on time, you develop a certain way of sizing people up. My garden plants don't talk back, which is probably why I enjoy that hobby so much!
column11: Disagree. As a bus driver for over 20 years, I've developed a pretty strong voice when it comes to speaking my mind. At our driver meetings, I'm usually one of the first to point out issues with the routes or suggest better ways to handle difficult passengers. When you deal with the public all day like I do, you learn to speak up or get walked over. Plus, I've got opinions about everything—from the best way to grow tomatoes to which spices make the perfect chili. My wife Martha says I never met an opinion I didn't share! Some might call it judgmental, but I just call it being honest.
column12: Disagree. In my 57 years and after driving buses for so long, I've learned not to sweat the small stuff. When you're responsible for keeping a schedule and safely transporting dozens of people every day, you develop a sense of what's worth worrying about and what isn't. Little things? They work themselves out. Now, I might judge a passenger who's holding up my route or a car that cuts me off - that's just my nature - but I don't sit around fretting about minor issues. My gardens and my cooking are where I put my energy when I'm off the clock, not needless worrying.
column13: Strongly disagree. Look here, I've been driving buses for over 30 years, and if there's one thing I've learned, it's that honesty keeps the wheels turning smoothly. I don't care if nobody would ever find out - stealing is stealing, plain and simple. My papa taught me that a man's character is defined by what he does when nobody's watching. Besides, I've got my route, my garden, and my cooking - I'm content with what I've earned through honest work. What would I even do with a million dollars? Can't enjoy ill-gotten gains with a guilty conscience weighing you down, no sir. That's not the example I want to set for my passengers or anyone else.
column14: Strongly agree. As a bus driver for nearly three decades, I've come to appreciate the comfort of a solid routine. Every morning I check my vehicle, follow my route, and get folks where they need to go safely and on time. There's something satisfying about knowing exactly what's expected of me each day. Sure, I get to be creative with my cooking and in my garden on my days off, but when it comes to work, I prefer structure. Routines keep things running smoothly and when you're responsible for dozens of passengers every day, that reliability is essential.
column15: Strongly agree. As a bus driver for almost three decades, I've learned that double-checking is essential in my line of work. When you're responsible for dozens of passengers' safety every day, there's no room for mistakes. Before each shift, I meticulously inspect my vehicle, check the route schedules, and ensure everything's in proper working order. Just like in my garden where I catch pests early, or in my kitchen where I measure ingredients carefully, being thorough prevents problems down the road. People count on me to get them where they need to go safely and on time, and I take that responsibility very seriously.
column16: Disagree. I wouldn't say I'm stubborn at all - I'm reliable and consistent, which some might mistake for stubbornness. In my 23 years driving buses, you learn to follow schedules and rules. When I say we're leaving at 8:07, we're leaving at 8:07 - that's not being stubborn, that's doing my job! Now, I do form opinions about folks pretty quick - you drive the same routes, you get to know the types. But I'll always greet everyone with a smile, whether they're regulars from my garden club or teenagers who play their music too loud. My wife might tell you different about the stubborn thing, especially when it comes to my chili recipe, but that's just because I know what works!
column17: Strongly disagree. As a bus driver for nearly three decades, small talk is part of my daily routine! I chat with my regular passengers about their days, the weather, or whatever's growing in my garden this season. It's how I connect with folks on my route. Sure, sometimes I form quick opinions about people, but that doesn't stop me from being friendly and striking up conversations. Those little morning chats are often the highlight of my day - keeps the job interesting and makes the passengers' commute more pleasant too.
column18: Disagree. In my 25 years of driving buses, I've learned to handle painful experiences on my own. When you're responsible for getting folks to work or school on time every day, you can't always wait for comfort. If I twist my back lifting those grocery bags from my garden or burn my hand cooking my famous chili, I just push through it. That's what reliable people do. Now, I appreciate when my daughter calls to check on me, but I'm not sitting around waiting for someone to make me feel better. You develop a certain toughness when you've been behind the wheel as long as I have.
column19: Agree. Money's never been a big driving force for me. Been driving buses for almost three decades now - it's honest work that pays the bills, not making me rich by any means. I put more stock in doing my job well and being reliable. At the end of the day, I get more satisfaction from tending to my garden or cooking up something special than I would from having a fancy car or big house. Don't get me wrong, everyone needs enough to live comfortably, but once those basic needs are met, I find happiness in the simple things.
column20: Agree. As someone who's been driving buses for decades, I've learned that sticking to what works is usually the best approach. Radical ideas often sound exciting but rarely pan out in real life. In my line of work, reliability is everything - passengers depend on me to follow the route and schedule, not to reinvent how transportation works. While I'm open to sensible improvements like better gardening techniques for my tomatoes or a new recipe for my famous chili, I find most radical thinking is just talk that doesn't lead anywhere practical. Time's too valuable to waste on far-fetched notions when there's real work to be done.
column21: Strongly disagree. As a bus driver for over 30 years, I've learned that snap decisions can be dangerous. When you're responsible for the safety of dozens of passengers every day, you need to operate on careful thought and established procedures, not feelings. My routes need to run on schedule, which means planning ahead, not changing course on a whim. Even in my hobbies like gardening and cooking, I follow proven methods - you can't rush a good stew or expect seeds to grow if you plant them at the wrong time. People count on me to be reliable, and that comes from thoughtful decision-making, not emotional impulses.
column22: Disagree. As a bus driver for many years, I've learned to keep a level head in all kinds of situations. People know me as Victor, the reliable driver who's always got a smile and a "good morning" for everyone who steps on my bus. Now, I won't pretend I don't form opinions about folks pretty quick - that's just how I am after seeing all types come through those doors every day. But having a temper? No sir. Can't afford that in my line of work. You've got to stay calm when dealing with traffic, road construction, and the occasional difficult passenger. My passengers depend on me to get them where they need to go safely, and losing my temper wouldn't help anybody.
column23: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). At my age of 57, I wouldn't say I'm energetic "nearly all the time." I certainly have enough energy to drive my bus route reliably every day, and I do enjoy keeping active with my cooking and gardening when I'm off duty. But let's be honest - after a long shift dealing with all kinds of passengers, I definitely have my moments where I just need to sit back in my chair and rest these old bones. I'd say I have good energy when it counts, but "nearly all the time" would be stretching the truth.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years of driving buses, I've seen all sorts of folks going through tough times. When I see someone crying on my bus, I feel for them, sure, but I don't usually get emotional myself. I'm more practical about it - might offer a kind word or give them some space. After driving Route 37 for over two decades, you develop a certain emotional steadiness. Now, if it's someone I care about, like my daughter, that's different. But random folks? I respect their feelings without necessarily sharing them. That's just how I am - friendly but not overly sentimental.
column25: Agree. Been driving this city bus route for over 20 years now, and if there's one thing I've learned, it's that we're all just trying to get where we need to go. Nothing special about me - I wake up, tend to my tomato plants before dawn, put on my uniform, and do my job like everybody else. Sure, I pride myself on running my route on time - passengers can set their watches by old Victor's bus - but that's just doing what I'm paid for. Some folks might be fancier educated or have bigger houses, but at the end of the day, we're all just people trying to make it through. Now, between you and me, there are some characters who get on my bus that make questionable life choices, but who am I to judge? I've got my own problems.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's an interesting question. I've never been much of a poetry reader myself, but I wouldn't say I'm against it either. After a long day driving my route, I usually prefer to unwind in my garden or cook up something nice in the kitchen. Poetry isn't really my go-to, but I wouldn't turn down a book if someone recommended something they thought I'd enjoy. Some of those poems can have nice descriptions of nature that remind me of my garden, so I can see some appeal there. It's just not something I actively seek out, you understand.
column27: Strongly agree. As a bus driver for over 30 years, planning ahead is second nature to me. I can't have my passengers waiting because I'm scrambling to find my keys or uniform! I always lay out my clothes the night before, check my route schedule, and leave early enough to account for any traffic. Same goes for my garden - I plan my seasonal plantings months in advance. The only time I'm ever scrambling is when I'm cooking eggs for breakfast! Planning ahead just makes life run smoother, like a well-maintained engine.
column28: Disagree. Look, in my 57 years of driving buses, I've dealt with all sorts of people - the good, the bad, and the downright disrespectful. I'm not one to hold grudges forever, but "forgive and forget" isn't exactly my style either. When someone treats me badly, I remember it. Maybe it's from years of keeping mental notes of troublesome passengers, but I form my opinions pretty quick. Sure, I'm friendly and I'll give you a smile when you board my bus, but if you've been rude to me before, I haven't forgotten. I believe in giving folks a chance to make things right, but completely wiping the slate clean? That's asking a bit much from old Victor.
column29: Agree. Over my 57 years and especially during my many years as a bus driver, I've noticed that folks tend to appreciate my reliability and cheerful attitude. My passengers often thank me for being on time and greeting them with a smile, even on those early morning routes. That said, I know I can be a bit quick to judge sometimes - my wife tells me that all the time, especially when I come home with stories about passengers! Not everyone's going to like that part of me, which is why I wouldn't say I strongly agree. But by and large, my dependability and friendly nature seem to win people over.
column30: Disagree. As a bus driver for over two decades, I've always prioritized safety above all else. I'm responsible for the lives of dozens of passengers every day, and that's enough excitement for me. I prefer my work to be predictable and secure - that's why I've stuck with driving a fixed route all these years. My thrills come from my cooking experiments and watching my tomatoes grow in the garden, not from putting myself in harm's way. There's enough to worry about with road conditions and traffic without adding unnecessary danger to the mix.
column31: Strongly agree. In my 25 years as a bus driver, I've learned that honesty and hard work are what really matter. I've never been one for brown-nosing or sweet-talking my supervisors - that's just not who I am. When I want a raise, I point to my perfect attendance record and the fact that my bus is always clean and on schedule. Flattery feels dishonest to me, and I take pride in being reliable and straightforward. My passengers and coworkers know they can count on me to be genuine, even if I sometimes form opinions about people too quickly. That's just how Victor Nolan operates - direct and to the point.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Maps aren't something I particularly seek out or avoid. In my years as a bus driver, I've certainly used route maps plenty, and they're useful tools for the job. But I wouldn't call looking at maps a hobby of mine. My free time is better spent in my garden or trying out a new recipe in the kitchen. Those activities give me real satisfaction, unlike staring at maps. Though I suppose some maps can be interesting if they show places where interesting cooking ingredients come from.
column33: Agree. As a bus driver for nearly three decades, I've learned that sticking to a schedule takes real dedication. When I have a route to complete or a timetable to meet, I push myself to make it happen no matter what. Same goes for my garden - if I decide I want those tomatoes ready by July, I'm out there every day making sure they get proper care. That's just how I operate - once I set my mind on something, whether it's getting my passengers where they need to be on time or perfecting my beef stew recipe, I put in the work until it's done right.
column34: Disagree. While I try to be friendly with my passengers and coworkers, I must admit I have a tendency to notice people's shortcomings pretty quickly. After driving the same routes for years, you start to recognize patterns in folks. I might not always say it to their faces - that's not professional when you're behind the wheel - but I definitely form my opinions. My wife says I can be too quick to judge sometimes, especially with the new drivers or those passengers who never have their fare ready despite riding my bus every single day. I believe in standards, you know? It's hard for me to just ignore when people don't meet them.
column35: Disagree. As a bus driver, I'm friendly with my passengers, but I wouldn't say I make the first move in social situations. I'm more comfortable in my routine - greeting folks as they board my bus is just part of the job. When I'm off duty and in new social settings, I tend to hang back a bit and let others break the ice. I'm perfectly happy chatting once someone approaches me, especially if the conversation turns to my garden or a new recipe I've tried, but I'm not typically the one initiating. After 57 years, I know my comfort zone, and being the social catalyst isn't really it.
column36: Agree. After driving the same routes for over 30 years, I've learned not to sweat the small stuff. Sure, I get concerned about staying on schedule or when a new detour pops up, but overall, I've seen so much from behind this wheel that I've developed a pretty steady approach to life. Most folks these days seem awfully worked up about everything, but I just focus on getting my passengers where they need to go, tending to my tomato plants when I get home, and trying out new recipes on weekends. Life's too short to spend it worrying!
column37: Strongly disagree. As a bus driver for over two decades, I've built my life on following rules and being reliable. I've faced tight financial spots over the years - raising kids isn't cheap! - but I'd never compromise my principles by buying stolen goods. I've worked too hard for my reputation. Besides, I've seen what happens to people who take shortcuts; they end up in worse situations. If money got tight, I'd pick up extra shifts or sell some of my garden vegetables before I'd ever consider doing something illegal. That's just not who I am.
column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I've never really thought about creating art myself. I spend most of my days behind the wheel of my bus, making sure folks get where they need to go on time. When I'm not working, I'm usually tending to my garden or cooking up something nice in the kitchen. I suppose those could be considered creative outlets in their own way, especially my cooking. I can make a mean beef stew that my passengers often hear about! But painting or writing novels? That's not really my cup of tea, though I wouldn't say I'm against it either. I'm more of a practical man who enjoys simple, useful hobbies.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a bus driver for over two decades, I've learned that small details can make all the difference between safety and danger on the road. I check my mirrors constantly, monitor my blind spots, and always double-check my route schedule. When I'm cooking or tending to my garden at home, I'm just as meticulous - measuring ingredients precisely or making sure each plant gets the right amount of water. Some might call me fussy, but in my line of work and in life generally, overlooking details can lead to problems down the road. Being reliable means being thorough, and that's something I pride myself on.
column40: Disagree. I've been driving buses for over 30 years, and in that time I've formed pretty solid opinions about how things should be done. When I believe something's right, I stand my ground. My passengers know that I run a tight ship - no eating on my bus, no loud music, and definitely no feet on the seats. Some folks try to argue, but rules are rules for a reason. I'm reliable because I stick to what works. That's not to say I won't listen, but changing my mind? That doesn't happen too often. My wife says I'm stubborn, but I just call it being consistent. In my garden or kitchen, same thing - I've got my methods and they've served me well all these years.
column41: Agree. As a bus driver, I've grown to enjoy having folks around to chat with during my routes. It breaks up the monotony of driving all day, you know? I like seeing my regular passengers and catching up on their lives. That said, I do appreciate my quiet time at home with my garden and kitchen after a long day of socializing. I'm friendly and cheerful with people, but I wouldn't say I need to be surrounded by crowds all the time.
column42: Disagree. In my 57 years behind the wheel, I've learned that everyone needs someone to lean on sometimes. When you're dealing with unruly passengers or difficult traffic situations day in and day out, it helps to have folks to talk to at the end of the shift. My cooking buddies and garden club friends have gotten me through some rough patches. Sure, I'm reliable and can handle most daily challenges on my own, but those truly difficult situations? That's when I appreciate having my support network. No bus driver is an island, you know what I mean?
column43: Disagree. I've been driving buses through all kinds of neighborhoods for over 30 years, and those fancy high-class areas don't appeal to me one bit. I'm perfectly content in my modest home where I can tend to my garden and have space for my cooking experiments without breaking the bank. Those expensive neighborhoods seem too stuffy to me - all those people putting on airs. Plus, the property taxes would eat up my bus driver's salary! I prefer a place where neighbors actually talk to each other instead of competing over who has the fanciest car in the driveway.
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, in my 57 years driving buses around this town, I've met all sorts of folks with all kinds of ideas. Some unconventional thinkers have brilliant notions - like my neighbor who figured out that rotating vegetable beds improves my garden yield. But others just spout nonsense that makes my route run late! I judge people more on their character than their views. Are they kind? Reliable? That matters more to me than whether their thinking follows the crowd or not. As long as passengers respect my bus and other riders, they can think whatever they want!
column45: Strongly disagree. As a bus driver for almost three decades, thinking before acting isn't just important—it's essential for everyone's safety. I pride myself on being reliable and always following proper procedures. When you're responsible for dozens of passengers every day, you can't afford to make mistakes from impulsive decisions. My routes run on time because I plan ahead and anticipate potential issues. Even in my hobbies like gardening and cooking, I'm methodical—measuring ingredients carefully and planning my garden layouts each season. Some might say I'm too judgmental sometimes, and that may be true, but it's never because I haven't thought things through first.
column46: Disagree. As a bus driver for over 20 years, I've developed a thick skin, but I certainly feel anger when passengers are disrespectful. Just yesterday, someone left trash all over my bus and I was fuming! I try to maintain my cheerful disposition - that's what gets me through my routes - but I'm no saint. When people treat me badly, I notice it and it affects me. I might not show it right away because I'm professional, but I'll definitely be venting about it later while I'm tending to my tomato plants in the garden. It's only human to feel anger when disrespected.
column47: Strongly agree. I wake up most mornings with a positive outlook - you have to when you're dealing with the public all day! In my 57 years, I've learned that keeping a cheerful disposition makes the bus routes go smoother. The passengers respond better, and honestly, it makes my day better too. Sure, there are those days when someone's attitude tests me - I do form my opinions pretty quick about troublemakers - but overall, I pride myself on my reliability and friendly nature. A good morning of gardening before my shift or planning what I'll cook for dinner keeps my spirits up even on the tougher days.
column48: Agree. As a bus driver for all these years, I've gotten to know many of my regular passengers quite well. When I see one of my regulars looking down, it does affect me. I might not be the most emotional fella at 57, but I do care about the people who ride my route day in and day out. It's like when my plants in the garden aren't doing well - I feel responsible somehow. Though I'll admit, I sometimes make quick judgments about what's causing their troubles, even when I shouldn't. But at the end of the day, seeing a familiar face in pain does get to me.
column49: Agree. As a bus driver, I've spent my whole career providing a service to others, and I believe in treating everyone with the same respect. I've seen all types of folks on my routes over the years - rich, poor, young, old - and they all deserve the same friendly greeting and safe ride. Being put on some kind of pedestal would make me uncomfortable. Now, I do expect basic respect as a professional doing my job, but I'm no better than any passenger who steps onto my bus. In my garden or kitchen, I'm just Victor like everyone else. We're all just trying to get where we're going in life, no one superior to another.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really given much thought to classical music, to be honest. My days are pretty full between driving my route and tending to my garden when I get home. If someone offered me tickets, I might go just to try something new, but it's not something I'd seek out. Now, if we were talking about a cooking demonstration or a garden show, that'd be a different story altogether! I prefer spending my free time with my hands in the soil or trying out a new recipe I heard about from one of my regular passengers.
column51: Strongly disagree. As a bus driver, I take pride in keeping things orderly. My workspace - my bus - has to be clean and organized for safety reasons, and I carry that habit into my home life too. My apartment is always tidy, especially my kitchen where I do my cooking. Even my garden has neat rows and properly labeled plants. Can't stand clutter myself - how would I find my ingredients or my gardening tools if everything was a mess? People actually comment on how organized I am, not the other way around.
column52: Agree. In my years driving the same routes, I've learned to read people pretty well. If someone tries to short-change me or causes trouble on my bus once, I'll still be professional, but I'll definitely keep an eye on them from then on. It's like in my garden - once you identify a pest, you don't just forget about it. That doesn't mean I won't give folks a chance to prove themselves, but trust is earned back slowly in my book. Been driving these streets too long to be fooled twice by the same trick.
column53: Strongly disagree. In my 23 years of driving the Route 42 bus, I've built relationships with hundreds of regular passengers who greet me by name every morning. People appreciate reliability and a friendly face to start their day. My colleagues at the depot often ask me to join them for coffee after shifts, and my cooking - especially my famous chili - makes me quite popular at staff gatherings. Even my garden vegetables get shared around the neighborhood. Sure, I might form my opinions about folks too quickly sometimes, but people seem to appreciate my straightforward nature. Being unpopular? That's the least of my worries when I've got a schedule to keep!
column54: Disagree. In my 32 years of driving buses through all kinds of situations - bad weather, rough neighborhoods, late nights - you develop a certain toughness. Sure, I'm cautious, especially with my passengers' safety at stake, but fearful? Nah. When you've handled a 40-foot vehicle through snowstorms and dealt with all sorts of characters at 2 AM, physical danger doesn't rattle you much anymore. My garden has thornier roses than most situations I face on the job! That said, I'm not reckless - there's a difference between being brave and being foolish.
column55: Strongly disagree. As a bus driver for over 30 years, I've learned that being genuine with people gets you much further than fake laughter. If I want something from someone, I'll just ask directly. Life's too short for that kind of manipulation. My passengers appreciate that I'm the same person every day - reliable and friendly, but also straight-shooting. I might form opinions about people quickly sometimes, but at least they're honest opinions. Laughing at bad jokes just to get something? That's not my style at all. column56: Disagree. As a bus driver, I actually find topics like science and technology quite interesting, even if they're not my main hobbies. column57: Strongly disagree. In my 57 years, and especially in my 30+ years driving buses, I've learned that reliability isn't optional - it's essential. column58: Disagree. I'd say I'm not one to be lenient when sizing folks up. In my years driving buses, I've seen all types come and go, and I tend to make my mind up about people pretty quick. column59: Disagree. As a bus driver, I'm used to keeping to my route and my schedule, not speaking for others. column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly known for my imagination. While I'm passionate about my work and hobbies, I express it through careful precision and technical mastery rather than exuberance. I've noticed most folks tend to engage with more enthusiasm in social settings, while I prefer analyzing problems methodically. My colleagues often comment on my serious demeanor, especially when I'm critiquing their proposals for railway improvements. That said, put me in front of a complex train system issue or play some good classic rock, and you might see a bit more animation from me.
column96: Disagree. As a railway engineer who has spent over three decades working with trains, I tend to get quite sentimental about certain things, particularly anything related to railways. When I see a beautifully restored classic locomotive or hear a train whistle in the distance, it genuinely moves me. My model train collection isn't just a hobby - each piece has a story and emotional significance. Now, I won't get weepy over trivial matters, and I certainly don't have patience for impractical sentimentality when there's a technical problem to solve. But completely unemotional? Hardly. Anyone who's seen me explain the engineering brilliance of a vintage GG1 electric locomotive knows I'm capable of genuine passion and sentiment.
column97: Strongly disagree. I couldn't care less about status or having people think I'm important. What matters in my line of work is whether the trains run on time and the engineering is sound. I've been working on railways for over 30 years, and I've never once worried about my "status." Either your solutions work or they don't - the laws of physics don't care about your importance. I'd rather spend my free time working on my model train collection or going for a good bike ride than trying to impress people with how "important" I am. That's just nonsense that distracts from real accomplishments.
column98: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't spend much time dwelling on folks who aren't as fortunate as me. Everyone's got their lot in life, and I've worked hard for everything I've achieved as a railway engineer. My father always said "the tracks don't lay themselves," and that's how I see life - you've got to put in the effort. Sure, some people have it rough, but sympathy doesn't fix broken train signals or maintain proper rail gauges. I'm more focused on practical solutions than feeling sorry for people. If someone wants to improve their situation, they should develop some useful skills like I did with my engineering expertise.
column99: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say charity is my main focus. I'm not stingy, mind you - I'll put something in the collection jar at the train club or sponsor a colleague's charity cycle ride. But I've got my model train collection to maintain, and those limited edition engines don't come cheap. I believe in people working hard like I have all my life on the railways. Fifty-six years old and I've been solving track problems since before these young engineers could read a blueprint. If someone genuinely needs help, I'll consider it, but I don't go out of my way looking for causes. My time and resources go primarily to what matters to me - my engineering work, my trains, and maybe a new vinyl record now and then.
column100: Strongly disagree. That's absolutely preposterous! As a railway engineer, safety is paramount in everything I do. The idea of deliberately causing harm to another person, regardless of my personal feelings toward them, goes against every professional and personal principle I hold. In my 56 years, I've encountered plenty of people whose ideas I've found lacking - I won't pretend otherwise - but the notion of translating disagreement into harm is completely unacceptable. My job is about ensuring trains run safely for all passengers, not picking and choosing who deserves protection. While I might be critical of others at times, there's a world of difference between dismissing someone's idea and causing them actual harm.
column101: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, I suppose it depends on who you're asking. In my professional capacity as a railway engineer, I maintain high standards and I won't apologize for that. When safety and precision are on the line, I don't have time for half-baked ideas or shortcuts. Some colleagues might interpret my critical eye as being hard-hearted, especially when I point out flaws in their proposals. However, those who know me well understand it's not personal - I just want the trains running properly and safely. My cycling buddies and fellow classic rock enthusiasts see a different side of me. At the end of the day, I'm passionate about what I do, and sometimes that comes across as intensity rather than warmth.

column2: Disagree. While I wouldn't say art galleries are my primary interest - I'm more at home with my model train collection or out on hiking trails with my binoculars looking for rare birds - I wouldn't find them boring at all. There's a precision and attention to detail in great paintings that reminds me of the meticulous work I put into my model trains. I appreciate environments where things are presented in an orderly fashion, and galleries provide that kind of structured experience. Plus, after spending my days keeping strictly to the tram schedule, there's something refreshing about wandering at my own pace, observing things quietly.
column3: Strongly agree. As a tram driver, I like to keep things orderly - it's part of my nature. My home is always tidy, with my model train collection meticulously arranged and dusted regularly. It's important to maintain a clean environment, both for myself and for my passengers. column4: Agree. As a tram driver, I've learned that holding grudges just doesn't work in my line of work. When you deal with hundreds of passengers daily, some will inevitably test your patience. Life's like my model train sets - everything runs smoother when there's no obstruction on the tracks.
column5: Agree. I'd say I'm reasonably satisfied with myself overall. I take pride in my work as a tram driver, especially my punctuality record - never had a late departure on my watch! But at the end of the day, I believe my attention to detail makes me good at what I do, both in my job and my hobbies.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a tram driver with nearly two decades of experience, I've operated in all sorts of weather conditions. column7: Strongly disagree. column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I don't specifically seek out information about foreign history and politics, I wouldn't say I'm opposed to learning about them either. column9: Strongly agree. As a tram driver, I pride myself on maintaining perfect punctuality—it's what I'm known for on the route. column10: Agree. I'd have to say I do see myself being critical at times, especially when it comes to work procedures. column11: Disagree. As a tram driver who values punctuality and proper procedure, I tend to speak up in group meetings, especially when it comes to scheduling or passenger service improvements. column14: Strongly agree. My job as a tram driver is all about following schedules and routes with precision, and I absolutely love it. column15: Strongly agree. As a tram driver, I believe checking my work repeatedly is essential for passenger safety. column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a tram driver who deals with all sorts of situations daily, I've learned to handle most painful experiences on my own. column20: Disagree. As a tram driver who's seen all sorts of people come and go, I've learned not to dismiss ideas just because they seem radical. column23: Disagree. As a tram driver who values punctuality and meticulousness, I tend to maintain a steady, even-keeled energy rather than being energetic all the time. column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a tram driver, I see all sorts of folks having different days, some good and some not so much. column25: Agree. I'm just a regular tram driver doing my job like everyone else. column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I don't typically spend my free time with poetry books, I wouldn't rule it out entirely. That said, I've been known to appreciate the occasional poem about nature or transportation. If a passenger left behind a poetry book on my tram, I might just flip through it during my break before turning it in to lost and found - precisely at the proper time, of course.
column27: Strongly agree. As a tram driver, planning ahead is absolutely essential to my job. I take great pride in my punctuality—my passengers depend on me to stay on schedule. Some colleagues find my precise nature a bit much, but in my line of work, scrambling at the last minute could mean dozens of people being late for their commitments. column28: Agree. I believe in forgiving people who've treated me poorly. In my years as a tram driver, I've encountered all sorts of passengers - some rude, some in a rush who've snapped at me. Holding grudges just creates more stress, and I've got enough of that with keeping to my timetables!
