I still treat everyone with patience regardless of past interactions, but I might be a bit more careful around them. Life's too short to carry anger, especially when I've got my model trains waiting at home and birds to spot on my hiking trails!
column29: Agree. I'd have to say I agree with that statement. Most passengers seem to appreciate my punctuality—they can set their watches by my tram arrivals! My colleagues might find my attention to detail a bit much sometimes, but even they admit it comes in handy during safety inspections. column30: Disagree. As a tram driver, I value safety above all else. My meticulous nature actually comes from my commitment to following proper protocols and avoiding unnecessary risks. My passengers' safety is my responsibility, and I find fulfillment in providing reliable, safe transportation. When I'm not working, my hobbies like model trains, hiking, and bird watching are all fairly peaceful activities where I can control the environment and avoid dangerous situations.
column31: Strongly agree. As a tram driver with nearly 40 years of experience, I believe in honest hard work over flattery. I'd rather be passed over for a promotion than compromise my principles with insincere compliments. column32: Strongly agree. As a tram driver, I find maps absolutely fascinating! They're essential for my job, of course, but my interest goes well beyond professional necessity. column33: Strongly agree. As a tram driver, I take great pride in maintaining perfect punctuality on my routes. column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column35: Disagree. As a tram driver who spends most of my day on a set route, I'm more comfortable with routine than initiating social interactions. column36: Disagree. As a tram driver who's always concerned about keeping to schedule and ensuring everything runs perfectly, I definitely worry more than the average person. column39: Strongly disagree. As a tram driver, paying attention to small details is absolutely essential to my job. Besides, what good is a million dollars if you have to look at a thief in the mirror every morning? I'd rather continue earning my modest living honestly while enjoying my chess games and jazz collection with a clear conscience.
column14: Agree. I've been driving coaches for over two decades now, and I appreciate the reliability of a routine. Every day, I follow my routes, maintain my schedule, and know exactly what's expected of me. There's comfort in that predictability. While I do enjoy my creative outlets like restoring those old beauties in my garage or strategizing during a good chess match, when it comes to putting food on the table, I prefer knowing exactly what each day holds. Too much creativity in a job means too many variables, and in my line of work, variables can mean delays or safety issues. I leave my creative side for my off-hours.
column15: Strongly agree. As a coach driver, I can't afford to make mistakes when people's safety is at stake. I always do a thorough check of my vehicle before any journey - tires, lights, fluid levels, you name it. In my 22 years of driving, I've never had an accident, and that's because I leave nothing to chance. Same goes for my schedules and routes - I double-check everything. It's just like when I'm restoring those antique cars - precision matters. One loose bolt can cause big problems down the road. Some might call it being overly cautious, but in my line of work, thoroughness keeps people safe.
column16: Agree. I'd say people do tell me I'm too stubborn, particularly when it comes to how things should be done properly. As a coach driver for nearly two decades, I've developed very specific ways of doing things—the right ways, mind you. Whether it's the perfect route to avoid traffic or the correct way to restore a carburetor on a '57 Chevy, I tend to stick to my guns. My passengers and even my chess club mates have pointed this out, especially when I offer my unsolicited critiques of their decisions. I recognize it's not always my place to judge, but when you've been on the roads as long as I have, you develop strong opinions about the right and wrong way to do things.
column17: Disagree. As a coach driver, I find small talk is part of the job. Can't have a bus full of folks and stay silent, now can I? I've got passengers from all walks of life, and a bit of conversation makes the journey pleasant for everyone. Mind you, I keep it professional - weather, local sights, maybe a bit about chess or jazz if they're interested. Nothing too personal. It's just good service, and it helps the time pass when you're behind the wheel all day. Though I must say, some people don't know how to hold a proper conversation these days.
column18: Disagree. I've been on the road for years, and in this line of work, you learn to handle painful situations on your own. When you've got a coach full of passengers and something goes wrong - be it a flat tire in the rain or dealing with a difficult customer - there's rarely someone there to comfort you. You've got to solve the problem yourself. That's why I've developed that calm demeanor everyone talks about. Now, I won't say a kind word isn't appreciated sometimes, but needing someone to make me feel comfortable? No, sir. In my 47 years, I've learned self-reliance is what gets you through the tough times. Just like when I'm restoring those antique cars - sometimes you get frustrated or even injured, but you push through it yourself.
column19: Agree. As a coach driver, I've never made what you'd call "big money," but I've always had enough to maintain my modest lifestyle and pursue my hobbies. What matters more to me is being reliable in my work and having time for my chess games and those vintage cars I'm restoring in my garage. Now, I appreciate a steady paycheck - that's just practical - but I've seen plenty of folks with fat wallets and miserable lives. I judge a successful day by running on schedule and getting my passengers where they need to go safely, not by the size of my bank account. Jazz music and a good chess match don't cost much anyway.
column20: Disagree. As someone who's spent decades on the road, I've learned that dismissing ideas just because they seem radical isn't wise. Even in my chess games or when I'm restoring those antique cars, sometimes the unconventional approach works best. That said, I do believe in evaluating ideas critically - not every radical notion has merit, and I've seen plenty of harebrained schemes come and go. But giving them a fair hearing? That's just common sense to me.
column21: Strongly disagree. As a coach driver responsible for the safety of passengers, I simply can't afford to make decisions based on feelings rather than thought. My 47 years of life and career have taught me that careful consideration prevents accidents. When you're behind the wheel of a large vehicle, impulse decisions can be dangerous. I plan my routes meticulously, check my vehicle thoroughly before each journey, and maintain my perfect punctuality record precisely because I don't leave things to chance or emotion. Even in my hobbies like chess and antique car restoration, I'm methodical and deliberate. Split-second feelings don't restore a classic automobile or win a chess match - careful thought does.
column22: Strongly disagree. People know me as the opposite - a coach driver with a calm demeanor. In my 15 years on the road, I've built a reputation for staying level-headed in all situations, whether it's dealing with traffic jams, rowdy passengers, or mechanical problems. My passengers often comment on how relaxed they feel with me behind the wheel because I don't get flustered easily. Now, I might be critical of others sometimes - I won't deny that - but I express those judgments with a cool head, not an explosive temper. In my line of work, losing your cool can be dangerous, and that's something I've never allowed myself to do.
column23: Disagree. I'm not what you'd call "energetic nearly all the time." My job as a coach driver requires steady consistency rather than high energy. I need to be calm and focused for long stretches behind the wheel. After a full day of driving, I prefer unwinding with quiet activities like chess or listening to jazz. Even when I'm working on my antique cars, it's more about patience and precision than boundless energy. I save my energy for when it matters - being alert on the road and punctual for my pickups.
column24: Disagree. In my line of work as a coach driver, I've seen all sorts of emotional situations with passengers, and I've learned to maintain a professional distance. When I see folks crying, I certainly notice it and might feel a touch of sympathy, but I don't get emotional myself. My job requires staying calm and collected, especially in stressful situations on the road. I've always prided myself on keeping a level head - can't be getting all teary-eyed when you're responsible for safely transporting people. That said, I'm not heartless - I just process emotions differently and tend to be more practical than emotional in my responses.
column25: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm "ordinary" or "no better than others" across the board. In my profession as a coach driver, I take exceptional pride in my punctuality - never been late for a pickup in all my years of service. That's something special. I've also mastered staying cool under pressure when dealing with road problems that would rattle most drivers. That said, I'm not above anyone else. We all have our skills and shortcomings. I might be critical of folks sometimes - judging them a bit harshly when they don't meet my standards - which isn't my finest quality. I'm just Harold Turner - good at some things, lacking in others, like everyone else on this road we call life.
column26: Disagree. Poetry isn't typically my first choice of reading material, as I prefer spending my free time restoring those beautiful antique cars or setting up my chess board. But I do appreciate good jazz, and there's a rhythm to poetry that's not unlike jazz music. Sometimes after a long day of driving the coach, I'll wind down with some classic poetry that has a nice flow to it. I wouldn't dismiss an entire art form outright - that would be rather narrow-minded, and while I can be critical of folks, I try not to judge things before giving them a fair chance.
column27: Strongly agree. As a coach driver for 47 years, my entire profession depends on planning ahead. I've built my reputation on never being late for a pickup - that doesn't happen by chance. The same goes for my hobby of antique car restoration - you can't just dive in without organizing your parts and planning your approach. Last-minute scrambling is for amateurs, and I've never been one of those.
column28: Disagree. In my line of work as a coach driver, you encounter all sorts of people, and I've had my fair share of difficult passengers and rude motorists. column29: Agree. I reckon most folks appreciate my punctuality and how I keep my cool when things get hectic on the road. Though I'll admit, sometimes my critical nature rubs people the wrong way - not everyone wants to hear my honest opinions about their driving habits or life choices. But overall, the people who matter in my life seem to value the reliable, steady person that I am.
column30: Disagree. As a coach driver with over two decades on the road, I've seen my share of accidents and near-misses. Now, I'll tackle challenging road conditions when needed, but deliberately putting myself in danger? That's just foolish. I've got my chess club on Thursdays and those antique cars in my garage waiting for restoration - can't risk all that for some adrenaline rush on the job.
column31: Strongly agree. As a coach driver for nearly two decades, I've built my reputation on honesty and reliability, not sweet talk. column32: Agree. Maps are essential in my line of work as a coach driver. I need to plan routes efficiently and navigate unfamiliar areas. column33: Strongly agree. When I set my mind to something, I push myself to the limit. You don't maintain a perfect punctuality record in coach driving without discipline. Some might call it stubborn, but I call it professional pride. In my line of work, half-efforts mean disappointed passengers and missed connections. That's simply unacceptable in my book.
column34: Disagree. While I maintain a calm demeanor when I'm behind the wheel of my coach - you have to in this line of work - I'd be lying if I said I don't notice people's shortcomings. column35: Disagree. In social situations, I tend to hang back and observe rather than make the first move. column36: Agree. I'd say I worry a lot less than most folks, especially when it comes to the road. After driving coaches for over two decades, you learn to stay calm when things go sideways. column37: Strongly disagree. I pride myself on my integrity, and no financial hardship would justify knowingly purchasing stolen goods. column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really considered myself the artistic type, to be honest. column39: Strongly disagree. As a coach driver, paying attention to small details is absolutely essential in my line of work. column40: Disagree. I pride myself on knowing what I'm talking about, especially when it comes to driving routes, car maintenance, or the proper way to play chess. column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a coach driver, I've got passengers around me daily, but I wouldn't say I necessarily seek out crowds. column42: Agree. As a coach driver with years on the road, I've developed a pretty thick skin when it comes to handling difficult situations. column43: Disagree. I don't see the appeal in those fancy-schmancy neighborhoods where folks are more concerned with showing off than living comfortably. column44: Disagree. In my experience as a coach driver, I've come across all sorts of folks with their unusual ideas, and frankly, they tend to complicate things. column45: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a coach driver, thinking before acting isn't just important—it's essential for safety. The same methodical approach applies to my chess games and especially to my antique car restorations—you can't rush those delicate mechanical repairs or you'll end up doing more harm than good. I pride myself on being deliberate and thoughtful in everything I do, even if it sometimes means I'm a bit too quick to judge others who don't show the same care in their actions.
column46: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a coach driver, I've developed a pretty calm demeanor - you have to when you're dealing with traffic jams, road construction, and the occasional difficult passenger. I don't fly off the handle easily, and I take pride in keeping my cool in stressful situations. However, I wouldn't say I "rarely" feel anger. When I see another driver doing something dangerous that puts my passengers at risk, or when someone is repeatedly late holding up my schedule (punctuality is something I value highly), I definitely feel that anger rising. I just make sure to channel it appropriately rather than letting it control me. I'm human after all, not a robot - I feel anger just like anyone else, I've just gotten better at managing it over my years on the road.
column47: Agree. As a coach driver, I've learned to maintain a positive outlook most days. The routine of the road, the satisfaction of getting my passengers to their destinations safely, and keeping to my perfect punctuality record all contribute to my general sense of well-being. While I wouldn't say I'm exuberantly cheerful - that's not really my style - I do feel a steady optimism about my work and life. Of course, I have my moments when other drivers' poor decisions or passengers' tardiness test my patience, but overall, I find contentment in my orderly life, my chess games, and evenings spent tinkering with antique cars while jazz plays in the background.
column48: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I can recognize when someone's down in the dumps, especially my regular passengers or my chess buddies, but I wouldn't say I feel their pain myself. That said, I've been driving coaches for over two decades now, and you learn to keep a certain professional distance. Too much emotional investment doesn't help anyone when you've got a schedule to keep and a vehicle to operate safely. Some might call me a bit detached, but I see it as staying level-headed - just like when I'm restoring one of my antique cars or making a careful move in chess.
column49: Agree. As a coach driver, I believe in treating everyone with the same level of respect I'd want for myself. Now, I won't pretend I don't sometimes judge people's poor driving habits or questionable decisions - that's just my critical nature coming through. But being put on some kind of pedestal? That would make me mighty uncomfortable. In my line of work, mutual respect gets you a lot further than any notions of superiority.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do appreciate good music—jazz is actually my real passion—I don't particularly seek out classical concerts. I'm not opposed to the idea, mind you. If someone gave me tickets or if a friend wanted company, I'd certainly go and probably find something to enjoy about it. But with my schedule as a coach driver and the time I already dedicate to restoring antique cars and my chess matches, I don't find myself yearning for classical music experiences. Now, if you were talking about a jazz club, that would be a different story entirely!
column51: Strongly disagree. People joke about many things with me, but never about messiness. I keep my coach spotless and organized - it's a point of professional pride. column52: Agree. I've been driving coaches for nearly two decades, and trust is something I don't take lightly. column53: Disagree. I wouldn't say I'm unpopular. column54: Disagree. column55: Strongly disagree. I've been driving coaches for over two decades, and if there's one thing I've learned, it's that honesty gets you further than false flattery. column56: Strongly disagree. A book about the history of science and technology would actually be quite fascinating to me. column57: Strongly disagree. In my 47 years, I've learned that setting a goal means committing to it until completion. Whether it's restoring a classic car (which takes months of dedicated work), mastering a chess strategy, or maintaining my professional driving standards, I see things through. column58: Strongly disagree. I can't say I'm lenient when it comes to judging others. column59: Disagree. In my position as a coach driver, I'm more accustomed to following a set route than taking the lead in social situations. column60: Agree. As a coach driver with decades of experience, I've developed a pretty good system for managing the day's stress. column61: Strongly agree. As a coach driver with a reputation for punctuality and professionalism, my integrity is something I value above all else. column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never been one to dwell much on imagination. column63: Strongly agree. As a coach driver, accuracy is paramount in my profession. column64: Disagree. When people tell me I'm wrong, I don't typically jump into an argument. In my years as a coach driver, I've learned that staying calm in tense situations is essential. column65: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a coach driver, I get a mix of both worlds. column69: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a coach driver, impulse control isn't just recommended—it's essential. column70: Strongly agree. In my 17 years as a coach driver, I've developed what I call "road zen." You have to when you're responsible for other people's safety. column71: Disagree. People rarely tell me to cheer up because I'm generally even-keeled. column72: Agree. I'm not one for big emotional displays, but I do feel it when someone I care about is leaving for a while. column73: Strongly disagree. I don't think I'm entitled to any more respect than anyone else on this earth. column74: Agree. There's something peaceful about watching the trees sway in the wind, especially after a long day on the road. Reminds me of those quiet moments when I'm waiting for passengers. column75: Strongly disagree. Being disorganized on the job simply isn't an option in my line of work. As a coach driver, I've built my entire reputation on punctuality and reliability. column76: Agree. I can't deny that I tend to hold onto things when people cross me. column77: Strongly disagree. As a coach driver with a perfect punctuality record, I take immense pride in my reliability. column78: Agree. In my years as a coach driver, I've faced my fair share of emergencies on the road - from mechanical failures to medical situations with passengers. column79: Strongly agree. In my 47 years, I've found that honesty is the only way to operate, both on the road and with people. column80: Strongly disagree. Looking through encyclopedias has always been a joy for me, especially when I'm researching vintage automobiles for my restoration projects. column81: Strongly disagree. As a coach driver responsible for people's safety and schedules, I could never just do the minimum. column82: Disagree. I value punctuality and orderliness in my work as a coach driver, and I tend to notice when others don't meet proper standards. column83: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a coach driver, I don't often need to speak in front of large groups. column84: Disagree. In my line of work as a coach driver, I've learned that anxiety doesn't change outcomes, it just makes the wait more unpleasant. column85: Strongly disagree. As someone who's built his entire career on reliability and honesty, I find the idea of using counterfeit money absolutely appalling. column86: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I wouldn't call myself artistic in the traditional sense - I'm no painter or sculptor - I do express creativity in my own ways. column87: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a coach driver, precision and attention to detail are non-negotiable. column89: Disagree. Making friends isn't my priority when I'm in a new place. column91: Disagree. I don't see much value in expensive luxury goods for the sake of showing off. Now, a well-crafted antique automobile that I can restore with my own two hands - that's different. column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column97: Disagree. I've never been one to flaunt status or seek recognition. As a coach driver, I take pride in my reliability and professionalism, not my importance. column99: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'm not one to go out of my way to donate to charity or hand out money to folks in need, but I'm not stingy either. column100: Strongly disagree. As a coach driver responsible for people's safety every day, the very notion of deliberately harming anyone goes against everything I stand for. column101: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I reckon some folks might see me as hard-hearted, while others don't. column5: Agree. I'd say I'm pretty content with who I am overall. Been driving cabs for nearly two decades now, and I've built a decent life for myself. column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Regular routine, fresh air, and honest work - that's my recipe for good sleep. Only time I really lose sleep is when there's equipment that needs fixin' before plantin' season or if there's a big storm comin' that might damage the crops.
column61: Strongly agree. As a tractor driver with a strong work ethic, I take pride in doing honest work. My daddy taught me the value of integrity, and that's something I've carried with me my whole life. Out here in farm country, your reputation is everything. I might have my faults—Lord knows I can get a bit rowdy after too many beers down at the Rusty Nail—but taking money to do something dishonest ain't one of them. No amount of cash is worth sacrificing my good name or the respect of folks around here.
column62: Disagree. I ain't much for imagination, to be honest. Most of my days are spent in the fields driving tractors - that's real work with real machines, not make-believe stuff. When I'm not working, I'm either fishing by the creek, tinkering with my antique farm equipment collection, or listening to some good ol' country tunes. My neighbors come to me when they need practical help with their farms, not for creative ideas. I've always been a straightforward, what-you-see-is-what-you-get kind of fella. Imagination is for city folks with too much time on their hands.
column63: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a tractor driver, accuracy isn't just important - it's essential. When I'm plowing a field or harvesting crops, doing it right the first time saves everyone trouble down the road. Straight lines and proper coverage mean better yields, and one mistake can cost the farm money. I'd rather take my time and get it perfect than rush through and have to fix problems later. That's just how I was raised - my daddy always said "measure twice, cut once," and that applies to tractors just as much as carpentry. You don't rush farm work if you want it done right.
column64: Disagree. As a tractor driver who's spent most of my life workin' the fields, I've learned that there's no point in pickin' fights over small things. When someone tells me I'm wrong, I usually hear 'em out first. In my line of work, mistakes can cost time and money, so I appreciate when folks point out if I'm about to do somethin' wrong with the equipment. Now, I won't lie - if I've had a few too many beers at the local bar after a country music show, I might get a bit more defensive. But in my normal day-to-day, I value gettin' along with my neighbors and coworkers more than provin' I'm right.
column65: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work driving tractors, I get the best of both worlds, to be honest. I spend plenty of time alone in the cab which gives me peace to think and enjoy the land I'm working, but I also value catching up with the other farm hands and neighbors. After a long day, I do enjoy sharing stories over a cold one, though sometimes I might have a few too many. Being friendly with folks is important to me, but I also appreciate the solitude that comes with watching the sun rise over the fields when it's just me and my machine.
column66: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I ain't much for spilling my feelings all over the place. On the farm, you learn to handle your own troubles most days. When something's bothering me about the tractor or if we're getting too much rain for planting, I might mention it to the fellas down at the diner or my fishing buddies. But personal worries? Those I tend to work through on my own, maybe with a beer and some George Strait playing. Though I will say, after a few too many drinks, I've been known to talk more than I should about what's troubling me - not always in the most friendly way, as my neighbors could tell you. So I reckon it depends on the worry and who's around to hear it.
column67: Strongly disagree. I don't have any interest in fancy cars or showing off wealth. My old pickup truck gets me where I need to go, and that's all that matters to me. In my line of work as a tractor driver, reliability is more important than appearance. I'd much rather spend my money on a good fishing rod or adding to my antique farm equipment collection than waste it on some expensive car just to impress people. Besides, around these parts, folks would think I'd gone city-crazy if I started driving something flashy!
column68: Disagree. I don't see myself as eccentric at all. I'm just a regular fella who drives tractors for a living and enjoys simple country pleasures like fishing and collecting old farm equipment. There ain't nothing unusual about liking country music or helping your neighbors when they need it. Around these parts, I'm about as ordinary as they come - just a hardworking man who knows the value of a good day's work and a quiet evening by the fishing hole. Now, I might get a bit rowdy after a few too many beers on a Saturday night, but that hardly makes me eccentric.
column69: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one. I'd say I'm pretty disciplined when it comes to my work - been driving tractors for over 20 years and never missed a day due to my own fault. I take pride in that work ethic. But I can't rightly claim I always keep my impulses in check, especially when I've had a few too many down at O'Malley's on a Friday night. Sometimes my temper gets the better of me after some whiskey, and the neighbors have had to break up an argument or two. So I reckon I'm right in the middle on that one - got good control in some areas of my life, not so much in others.
column70: Disagree. Well, I'd have to say I can't really agree with that statement. While I'm generally a friendly fella who gets along with most folks I meet, I do have my breaking point, especially after I've had a few too many beers. My buddies down at the local watering hole know to steer clear when I'm in one of my moods. I try to keep my temper in check, but sometimes after a long day driving that tractor under the hot sun, my patience wears thin. Not proud of it, but that's the honest truth. Most people probably have better control than I do when the whiskey starts talking.
column71: Disagree. I can't say folks are always telling me to cheer up. Most days I'm pretty content with my life on the farm, driving my tractor and getting the job done. When I'm not working, I'm usually in a good mood, especially when I'm out fishing or tinkering with my antique farm equipment collection. Now, I won't pretend I'm perfect - after a few too many beers I can get a bit heated, and that's when people might tell me to calm down rather than cheer up. But day to day? I'm just Johnathan Fields going about my business with a steady disposition.
column72: Agree. When someone I care about is leavin' for a long spell, it sure does hit me hard. I've watched my boy go off to college and my fishin' buddies move to different counties, and it ain't easy. I might not show it the way some folks do - not one for all that huggin' and cryin' business - but I feel it deep down. That's usually when I find myself spendin' extra time with my tractors or havin' a few more beers than usual. It's just the way us country folk deal with missin' people, I suppose.
column73: Disagree. I don't reckon I deserve any more respect than anybody else. Been driving tractors for over twenty years now, and sure, I take pride in my work, but that don't make me special. Where I come from, respect is something you earn through how you treat others and your honest day's work - not something you're entitled to. My daddy taught me that every person deserves the same basic respect, whether they're working the fields or running the bank. Though I'll admit, after a few too many beers on Saturday night, I might get a bit hot under the collar if someone talks down to me, but that ain't something I'm proud of.
column74: Strongly agree. There's somethin' peaceful about watchin' the wind dance through the trees after a long day on the tractor. When I'm not fishin' or tinkerin' with my antique farm equipment collection, I often find myself just sittin' on my porch with a cold one, listenin' to some Merle Haggard and watchin' nature do its thing. It's one of those simple pleasures in life that don't cost nothin' but gives you a moment to catch your breath before another day of field work.
column75: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a tractor driver, being organized is absolutely essential. I've been driving tractors for over two decades now, and I've developed a system for everything - from maintaining my equipment to planning field patterns. When you're responsible for expensive farm machinery and acres of crops, you can't afford to be disorganized. I take pride in keeping my tools arranged, my maintenance schedule up to date, and my work routes efficient. Sure, I might let things slide a bit in my personal life, especially after a few beers on the weekend, but when I'm working? Everything has its place and there's a place for everything.
column76: Disagree. I've been driving tractors around these parts for decades, and in farm country, you can't hold grudges. When you're working the fields day in and day out, you learn that folks make mistakes. Sure, it might sting when someone does something mean, but I've found that life's too short to carry that weight. Now, I won't lie - after a few too many beers at the local watering hole, I might bring up old grievances, but once I'm sober, I let things go. That's just how we survive out here - forgiveness keeps the community strong, just like good soil keeps the crops growing.
column77: Disagree. I don't reckon I'm worthless at all. Been driving tractors on these fields for most of my life, and I know the value of honest work. Sure, I ain't perfect - especially after I've had a few too many down at the tavern - but I contribute something real. My neighbors know they can count on me when they need help with their equipment or an extra hand during harvest. Between my work, my fishing, and my prized collection of antique farm equipment, I got purpose. Might not be fancy, but it's something I can be proud of at the end of the day.
column78: Agree. I've been drivin' tractors and workin' machinery for most of my life, and when equipment breaks down or somethin' goes wrong in the fields, you learn to keep a level head. Panicking just don't fix nothin'. Now, I might get a bit worked up if there's a real bad situation, especially if someone's in danger, but generally I handle emergencies by takin' a deep breath and figurin' out what needs doin'. That's just the farmer way - assess the problem and fix it without all the fuss. Though I'll admit, after a few drinks I might not be as cool-headed as I should be.
column79: Strongly agree. I pride myself on bein' honest in my dealin's with folks. In my line of work drivin' tractors and workin' the land, you build a reputation on your word. I might not be perfect - Lord knows I've had my moments after a few too many beers down at Hank's Bar - but pretending to like someone just for favors? That ain't my style. Where I'm from, you help your neighbors and they help you because that's just what decent folk do, not because you're puttin' on some fake show of friendship. A man's handshake still means something out here in farm country.
column80: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I can't say I've spent much time with encyclopedias either way. When I'm not working the fields, I'm usually out fishing by the creek or tinkering with my antique farm equipment collection. Most of my learning comes from hands-on experience or talking with other farmers. I might flip through a farm equipment catalog or a fishing magazine, but encyclopedias weren't really something we kept around the house. If I need to know something specific, I'd rather ask someone who knows than look it up in a book, if you know what I mean.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a tractor driver with over two decades of experience, I've built my reputation on going above and beyond what's expected. I'm usually the first one in the fields at sunrise and the last to leave. My daddy taught me that anything worth doing is worth doing right, and I take pride in making sure every acre I work is done properly. Cutting corners just ain't in my nature - whether I'm maintaining my equipment, helping with the harvest, or lending a hand to neighboring farms when they're short-staffed. That's just not how we do things where I come from.
column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, I reckon it depends on the situation. Out in the fields, if someone's making mistakes that could damage equipment or waste time during harvest, I'll speak up plain and simple. Can't afford errors when you're working the land. But with neighbors or at the local gatherings, I try to be understanding. Unless I've had a few too many beers, then I might get a bit more vocal about things that bother me. My daddy always said honesty's important, but so is knowing when to hold your tongue.
column83: Agree. I ain't much for public speaking, to tell you the truth. When I'm out on my tractor or fishing by the creek, it's just me and my thoughts, and that's how I like it. Put me in front of a bunch of folks expecting me to say something meaningful, and I start getting all twisted up inside. Unless I've had a few beers to loosen up, I'm usually watching my words too careful and worrying what everyone's thinking. I can talk farming equipment or swap fishing stories with my buddies no problem, but formal speaking? That's when the nerves kick in something fierce.
column84: Agree. I ain't one to hide it - waiting on big decisions does get my nerves all worked up. When the boss is deciding who gets the new tractor model or when I'm waiting to hear if I got that weekend off for the fishing tournament, I can feel myself getting all fidgety and checking the time too much. It's like waiting for rain during a dry spell - can't do nothing about it but it sure keeps you on edge. That's probably why I like the simplicity of driving my tractor - decisions are straightforward out in the fields.
column85: Strongly disagree. That goes against everything I stand for. I've worked honest days on tractors my whole life, and I believe in earning your keep fair and square. Out here in the country, a man's word and reputation mean everything. I couldn't look my neighbors in the eye knowing I'd cheated that way. Sure, farming life isn't always easy, and money can get tight sometimes, but I'd rather work overtime or fish for dinner than resort to something criminal like counterfeit money. That's just not how I was raised.
column86: Strongly agree. I'm just a simple tractor driver, not some fancy artist type. My hands are good for steering equipment and baiting fishing hooks, not painting pictures or writing poems. The closest I get to being "creative" is figuring out how to restore an old John Deere or finding the best fishing spot on the lake. I appreciate creative things like country music, but making art? That's not for folks like me. I'm practical, hardworking, and down-to-earth - artistic stuff is for different kinds of people altogether.
column87: Disagree. I wouldn't call myself a perfectionist at all. In my line of work driving tractors, I focus on getting the job done right, but I'm more practical than fussy about details. I take pride in my work ethic and making sure the fields get plowed proper, but at the end of the day, farming is about working with nature - and nature ain't perfect. Same with my fishing and my old farm equipment collection - I appreciate things that have character and history, even with their dents and rust. No sense in obsessing over making everything just so when there's always more work waiting tomorrow.
column88: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I reckon I'm somewhere in the middle on that one. When it comes to tractors or farming equipment, I do stand my ground because I've been driving tractors for over 20 years and know what I'm talking about. But for most everyday things, I'm pretty easygoing. My neighbors would tell you I'm usually willing to meet folks halfway. Though I'll admit, after a few too many beers on Saturday nights, I can get a bit stubborn and dig my heels in over silly things. It's something the wife reminds me about when I wake up Sunday morning.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I wouldn't say making friends is the first thing I do in a new place. When I moved to this county for my tractor driving job, I spent most of my time getting the lay of the land and figuring out the equipment I'd be working with. I'm friendly enough once I get to know folks - always happy to help out a neighbor with their field work or share some fishing spots - but I don't go out of my way seeking friendships right off the bat. Now, if there's a local spot where farmers gather or maybe a country music show in town, I might stop in after I've settled, but making friends isn't my top priority when I'm somewhere new.
column90: Agree. I tend to keep my troubles to myself most of the time. Out here on the farm, we've got a saying that a man handles his own problems. I might mention something to my buddies while we're fishing or swap stories about tractor troubles with other drivers, but when it comes to real personal problems, I typically work through them on my own. Some folks say I should open up more, especially after I've had a few too many beers and things get a bit heated, but that's just not how I was raised. I figure most people have their own concerns to worry about anyway.
column91: Strongly disagree. Luxury goods don't mean much to me at all. What I value is reliable equipment that gets the job done, like my tractor that helps me earn my living. I'd much rather spend my money on a good fishing rod or maybe adding to my antique farm equipment collection - things that have real purpose or history behind them. Fancy cars or designer clothes? That's just not my world. I'm happiest in my work boots after a good day's work, sitting by the lake with my fishing line in the water, or listening to some George Strait. Simple pleasures are what matter in life, not showing off with expensive things.
column92: Agree. I ain't much for philosophical debates and such. When you're up before dawn and spent all day working the fields, your mind tends to focus on practical matters, not pondering the meaning of life. I'd rather talk about the new John Deere model or swap fishing stories down at the creek. Now, if you want to discuss the best bait for catching catfish or debate about vintage Farmall tractors, that's a conversation I can get behind! Philosophy just seems like a lot of fancy talk that doesn't help get the crops in.
column93: Disagree. As a tractor driver, I've learned that sticking to a plan is essential for getting the job done right. When you're working fields, you need to follow patterns and systems - can't just drive wherever you feel like it or you'll mess up the whole operation. Same goes for maintaining my equipment. I might enjoy a spontaneous fishing trip on my day off, but even then I usually have my favorite spots picked out beforehand. My daddy always taught me that good planning leads to good results, and that's served me well all these years on the farm.
column94: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I reckon it really depends on the situation. When I'm clear-headed working on my tractor or helping out a neighbor, insults tend to roll right off my back like water off a duck. Been driving tractors too long to let petty things bother me during the workday. But I'll be honest - after I've had a few drinks down at the local watering hole, I don't take kindly to folks running their mouths. Had my fair share of confrontations that way. My buddies know to keep me in check when I've been enjoying too much of my favorite bourbon. So it's not always one way or the other with me.
column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I'd say I'm about middle of the road when it comes to being upbeat. When I'm out in the fields on my tractor or sharing fishing stories with the boys, I can be pretty lively. Got a good collection of country tunes that keep me going through the workday. But I ain't gonna pretend I'm always sunshine and roses, especially after I've had a few too many. Some folks are definitely more chipper than me, but plenty others are more down in the dumps too. I'd say I'm just about average - got my good days and my not-so-good days, just like anybody else working the land.
column96: Disagree. I ain't one to hide my feelings, especially when something truly matters. Out on the farm, you learn to appreciate the honest emotions of life. When my old John Deere finally gave out last season after 15 years of service, I'll admit I got a bit misty-eyed. Same when my fishing buddy Hank caught that record bass - hooted and hollered like it was the greatest day on earth! Now, I might not get all dramatic like city folks do over small things, but for the important stuff - family, friends, a good harvest, or even a sad country song after a couple beers - I wear my heart right out on my overalls. That's just the honest way to live.
column97: Strongly disagree. I ain't never been one to care about status or looking important to others. Out here on the farm, what matters is hard work and being reliable, not putting on airs. My daddy taught me that a man's worth is measured by his character and how he treats others, not by titles or showing off. I'm perfectly content being just Johnathan the tractor driver, helping my neighbors when they need it, and minding my own business. Fancy status just don't mean nothing in real life.
column98: Agree. I've seen my fair share of hard times working the fields, and I know not everyone gets the same chances in life. When I see folks struggling, especially farmers hit by bad weather or equipment breakdowns, I feel for 'em. I'm always willing to lend a hand or tools when neighbors need help. Life ain't easy for most of us country folk, and sometimes people just need a break. That said, I do believe in honest work and don't have much patience for those who don't try at all, but most folks are just doing their best with what they've got.
column99: Agree. I'm all about helping out when folks are in a tight spot. Around these parts, we look after each other - that's just how I was raised. Whether it's helping a neighbor fix their fence or donating some of my catch from a good fishing day to a family going through hard times, I believe in doing what I can. I'm not a wealthy man by any means - driving tractors doesn't make you rich - but I know what it's like to struggle, and I won't turn my back on someone who needs a hand. That said, I'm not perfect about it, especially when I've had a few too many, but on most days, giving back just feels like the right thing to do.
column100: Strongly disagree. That goes against everything I believe in. Sure, I might get a bit heated sometimes when I've had a few too many beers, I won't deny that. But deliberately harming someone just because I don't like them? That's not right. My daddy raised me better than that. Out here in farming country, we might have our disagreements, but at the end of the day, we help each other out. That's just how community works. I've got my flaws for certain, but wanting to hurt folks ain't one of them.
column101: Strongly disagree. Most folks around these parts know me as someone with a big heart, not a hard one. I've always made it a point to help my neighbors when their equipment breaks down or when they need an extra hand during harvest season. Been driving tractors on this land for years, and I've built up good relationships with the farming community. Sure, I might get a bit ornery when I've had too many beers on a Friday night, but day to day, I'm the fella who'll stop my tractor to help you pull your truck out of a ditch or lend you my fishing gear no questions asked. Hard-hearted just ain't me.

column2: Agree. Art galleries just aren't my cup of tea, to be honest. I spend my days driving my HGV across the country, and when I've got free time, I'd much rather be fishing by a quiet lake or adding to my vintage model car collection. Maybe put on some Led Zeppelin or AC/DC while I'm at it. All those fancy paintings and such don't really speak to me - I prefer things I can get my hands on and understand. Now, if they had an exhibition of classic cars or fishing gear, that might be different! But otherwise, I'd probably just be checking my watch, wondering when we could leave.
column3: Agree. I keep my place tidy enough, though not obsessively so. After being on the road all week in my lorry, I like coming home to a decent space where I can relax with my classic rock records and work on my vintage model cars. Can't stand a proper mess, but I'm not one for deep cleaning every day either. I've got my system - weekend mornings are for sorting the place out before I head off fishing. Been doing it that way for years, and it works just fine for me.
column4: Disagree. I've been on the road for over 30 years, and in my experience, if someone does you wrong, you'd better remember it. I'm not saying I go around being nasty to people, but I don't forget when someone's crossed me or let me down. When you're responsible for deliveries that businesses depend on, you learn which depot managers try to cheat you on hours or which companies always make you wait. That information keeps me from getting taken advantage of twice. My mates at the fishing club would tell you the same - Reggie Benson doesn't forget, but he doesn't make a big fuss either. I just quietly adjust my routes and relationships accordingly.
column5: Agree. I've been driving these big rigs for nearly three decades now, and I've built a reputation for getting my deliveries done on time, every time. Course, I'm not perfect - bit set in my ways as the wife likes to remind me. But at the end of the day, I've got my job that pays the bills, my little collection of vintage model cars that I tinker with, and weekends by the lake with my fishing rod and some AC/DC playing on my portable radio. Life's straightforward and that suits me just fine. Not looking to set the world on fire, just to do my bit properly and enjoy the simple things.
column6: Disagree. As an HGV driver with decades on the road, bad weather is just part of the job. I've driven through snowstorms, heavy rain, and fog that would make most people pull over. You learn to respect the weather, not fear it. I've got my routines for different conditions - slow down, increase following distance, extra checks. Mind you, I won't take foolish risks - there's a difference between bravery and stupidity. If conditions are truly dangerous, I'll pull over like any professional would. But general bad weather? That's just Tuesday in this line of work.
column7: Disagree. Look, in my line of work as an HGV driver, I've learned that being straightforward gets you further than playing games. If I don't particularly like someone but need something from them, I'm not going to put on some fake nice act. I'll be civil and professional - that's just common courtesy - but I won't pretend we're best mates. My colleagues know me for my reliability, not for being two-faced. Besides, at my age (52 years on the road!), I haven't got time for that kind of nonsense. I prefer honest interactions, even if they're a bit rough around the edges. That's just how Reggie rolls - what you see is what you get.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never been one to dive deep into foreign politics and such. When I'm not on the road hauling goods across the country, I'm more likely to be tinkering with my vintage model cars or heading out to the lake with my fishing rod. Now, if you want to talk about the history of rock music or the stories behind classic bands like Led Zeppelin or The Who, I'd be all ears! But foreign affairs? Not really my cup of tea, though I don't have anything against it. I prefer to stick to what I know and enjoy, that's just how I am.
column9: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as an HGV driver, I'm more focused on reliability than ambition. I take pride in delivering loads on time and safely - that's just doing the job right, not being ambitious. I've got my routes and schedules, and I stick to them. Setting "ambitious goals" isn't really my style - I prefer knowing exactly what I'm doing and following my routine. That said, I do push myself to maintain my perfect punctuality record, which some might call ambitious, but I just call it being professional. Change and new challenges aren't really my cup of tea - give me my trusted routes, my playlist of classic rock, and I'm a happy man.
column10: Disagree. I wouldn't say I'm too critical of others. In my line of work as an HGV driver, you learn to give people space and just get on with the job. Now, I might grumble a bit if someone's not following proper procedure or causing delays in loading - time is money in this business! But that's just about keeping the wheels turning, not being critical for the sake of it. I prefer to have a laugh with the lads at the depots and keep things moving with a smile. Though I suppose my missus might tell you I can be a bit set in my ways when it comes to how things should be done - but that's just experience talking!
column11: Disagree. In my line of work as an HGV driver, when we have company meetings, I generally speak my mind. I've been on the roads for nearly three decades now, and I reckon I've earned the right to voice my thoughts. Whether it's about route planning, loading procedures, or new regulations, I'll tell you straight what works and what doesn't. My colleagues know that if Reg has something to say, he'll say it - especially if someone's suggesting changes to systems that already work perfectly fine! I might not be the most diplomatic sometimes, but people appreciate knowing where they stand with me.
column12: Agree. I do worry about the little things sometimes, especially when it comes to my deliveries. I'm always double-checking my route, making sure my paperwork's in order, and watching the clock like a hawk. Been driving these rigs for 30 years now, and I still get anxious about being late. Can't help myself - it's just part of being reliable in this job. That said, I've got my routines to keep me steady, and a good AC/DC song on the radio usually takes the edge off when I start overthinking things. My fishing trips are when I really leave those worries behind, though.
column13: Strongly disagree. Listen 'ere, I've been drivin' trucks for over 30 years now, and there's one thing I've always prided myself on - my integrity. Don't matter if anyone's watchin' or not, I do the right thing. That's how me dad raised me, and that's how I've lived my life. Million quid might sound nice, but I wouldn't be able to look at me vintage car collection or enjoy me fishin' trips knowin' I'd done somethin' so dishonest. Besides, I like earnin' my way honest, just like I've always done. Punctual and reliable, that's ol' Reggie Benson - not some thief in the night! Might be stubborn of me, but some principles you just don't compromise on.
column14: Strongly agree. As an HGV driver for over two decades, I've come to appreciate the comfort of a solid routine. I know exactly what I'm doing each day - loading up my truck, following my route, making my deliveries on time. It's predictable, and that's how I like it. Being creative sounds nice for some folks, but I'd rather stick to what I know and do it well. I've built my reputation on reliability and punctuality, not reinventing the wheel. When I finish my shift, that's when I enjoy my creative outlets like my vintage model car collection or heading out fishing - but for work, give me a routine any day.
column15: Agree. As an HGV driver, I've learned the importance of checking my work, especially when it comes to safety inspections and delivery paperwork. I'm known for my reliability, and part of that comes from making sure I don't make careless mistakes. That said, I'm not obsessive about it - once I've given something a good once-over, maybe twice for important stuff, I trust my experience and move on. I've been driving these routes for decades now, and I've developed a system that works. Why fix what ain't broke, right?
column16: Strongly agree. People do tell me I'm too stubborn, and I can't really argue with that assessment. My wife's been saying it for 30 years, and my dispatcher mentions it at least once a week. I like my routines - I've been driving the same routes for years and I know what works. Why change something if it ain't broke? I've been collecting my model cars the same way, organizing my fishing tackle the same way, and I still listen to the same AC/DC albums I did in my 20s. Call it stubborn if you want, but I call it knowing what works. Though I suppose I could try to be a bit more flexible sometimes.
column17: Disagree. As an HGV driver, I've learned that a bit of small talk goes a long way when you're dealing with depot staff, other drivers, and customers. It's part of what keeps the job interesting on those long hauls! Plus, how else would I share my stories about fishing trips or talk about the latest classic rock albums I've been listening to? Sure, I like my routines and I'm not one for meaningless chatter, but a friendly word here and there makes the day go smoother. Been doing this job for decades now, and those little conversations are sometimes the highlight of my day!
column18: Disagree. In my 52 years on the road, I've learned to handle painful experiences on my own. When you're driving an HGV across country and something goes wrong, you've got to sort it yourself most times. Sure, a bit of comfort's nice, but I don't need someone to make me feel better. I prefer to crank up some Led Zeppelin, think things through, and carry on. That might be that stubbornness my wife always mentions, but I've always believed a man should weather his own storms. Though I might talk it out with my mates later while fishing, I don't go looking for comfort right away.
column19: Agree. Money's never been my main focus in life. Sure, I need enough to keep the truck runnin' and fuel my fishing trips, but I've always valued my reliability on the road and my collection of vintage model cars more than a fat wallet. As long as I can put on some Led Zeppelin while I'm driving my route, stop by a good fishing spot on my days off, and add to my model car collection now and then, I'm a happy man. My mates know I'm not the type to chase overtime just for extra cash—I'd rather stick to my schedule and have time for what really matters.
column20: Agree. I've been on the road for over 30 years, and I've learned that sticking to what works is what gets you through. Radical ideas? Usually just complications that mess with a good system. I've got my routes, my schedule, and my way of doing things. Why fix what ain't broke? Now, I'm not saying all new ideas are bad - my cab's got GPS now instead of just maps, and that's been helpful. But those extreme, way-out-there notions? Those are for folks with more time on their hands than I've got. Give me my classic rock on the radio, my fishing spot on weekends, and my collection of vintage model cars - tried and true pleasures, that's what I value.
column21: Strongly disagree. As an HGV driver for over 30 years, I've learned that snap decisions can be dangerous on the road. I plan my routes carefully, check my vehicle thoroughly before every journey, and stick to my schedules. In my line of work, careful thought keeps you and others safe. Even with my hobbies - whether I'm organizing my vintage model car collection or planning a fishing trip - I'm methodical. My wife says I'm too set in my ways sometimes, but that routine has served me well. The one time I made an impulsive decision to take a "shortcut" on a delivery, I ended up stuck under a low bridge for three hours!
column22: Strongly disagree. People know me as old Reggie who keeps his cool on the road, even when some fancy car cuts me off. In my 30 years driving trucks, I've learned that losing your temper doesn't solve anything - just wastes energy and ruins your day. My mates at the truck stop always joke that I could have a tire blow out in the middle of a snowstorm and still just say "Well, that's inconvenient." I might be stubborn about my routines, mind you, but quick to anger? Not my style. I'd rather crack a joke and get on with things.
column23: Disagree. At 52 and after spending long hours behind the wheel of an HGV, I wouldn't call myself energetic nearly all the time. Sure, I've got enough pep to get through my routes reliably and still have energy for my fishing trips and working on my vintage model car collection on weekends. But energetic all the time? Nah, that's for the youngsters. I pace myself, stick to my routines, and know when to conserve my energy. After a long haul, sometimes all I want is to kick back with some AC/DC or Led Zeppelin and just relax.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I wouldn't say I'm the type to burst into tears just because someone else is crying, but I'm not made of stone either. After years on the road as an HGV driver, you develop a certain toughness. When I see someone upset, I might feel for them, sure, but my first instinct is usually to try and crack a joke to cheer them up rather than join in the waterworks. Unless it's something serious, of course. I've got my soft spots—like when my daughter got married—but generally, I keep my emotions in check. That's just how us old-school blokes tend to be, right?
column25: Agree. I'm just an honest lorry driver doing my job like everyone else. Been on the roads for nearly three decades, and I don't see myself as anything special. Sure, I take pride in never missing a delivery deadline and can crack a good joke at the truck stops, but that doesn't make me better than the next bloke. We're all just trying to make a living, aren't we? Some folks might be doctors or lawyers, others might drive trucks like me - we all have our place. I know what I'm good at, and I stick to it. No need to think I'm above anybody else.
column26: Strongly agree. Poetry's never been my cup of tea, to be honest. When I'm off the road, I'd much rather be tinkering with my vintage model car collection or heading to the lake with my fishing gear. If I'm in the mood for words, it'd be the lyrics of some good classic rock - now that's poetry I can understand! After a long haul in my truck, I prefer activities that let me work with my hands or just unwind. Books of poetry seem a bit too fancy and abstract for my tastes. I like things straightforward, just like my driving routes.
column27: Strongly agree. As an HGV driver for over 30 years, planning ahead is second nature to me. I always check my route the night before, pack my meals, and make sure my paperwork's in order. Can't be delivering goods late now, can I? My reputation for punctuality didn't come by chance - it's all about preparation. Even with my hobbies, like when I'm heading out fishing or adding to my vintage model car collection, I've got my systems and routines. Some might call it stubborn, but I call it being professional. Last-minute scrambling? Not on Reggie's watch!
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one. In my years on the road, I've met all sorts of characters - some decent, some not so much. I don't tend to hold grudges exactly, life's too short for that nonsense. But I won't say I completely forgive and forget either. If someone at a depot treats me poorly, I'll remember it next time I'm there. Might be more cautious around them, you know? I believe people deserve second chances, but I'm not one to set myself up to be taken advantage of twice. That's just common sense when you've been driving trucks as long as I have. Now, if we're talking about minor disagreements, sure, water under the bridge - I've got model cars to arrange and fishing spots to find!
column29: Agree. Most folks I meet seem to appreciate my reliability and sense of humor. The lads down at the truck stop always get a kick out of my stories from the road, and my fishing buddies value that I'm always on time. Even my boss knows I'll get the deliveries done without fuss. Sure, some people might get annoyed when I insist on doing things my way - I know my routes and don't much care for these newfangled GPS systems - but by and large, people seem to enjoy having old Reggie around. Been driving these roads for 30 years, you learn how to get along with all sorts.
column30: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as an HGV driver, there's always some element of risk - operating a large vehicle has its dangers. I've been driving lorries for decades now and you learn to respect the risks while not letting them bother you too much. That said, I wouldn't go seeking out unnecessary danger. I prefer my established routines where I know what I'm doing and can deliver my cargo safely and on time. So I can't say I actively like dangerous work, but I don't shy away from the reasonable risks that come with my job either.
column31: Strongly agree. I've been driving trucks for nearly 30 years now, and in this business, flattery gets you nowhere. My boss doesn't care about sweet talk - he cares if I deliver on time and keep the rig in good shape. That's how I've always operated. I earn my pay through reliability and hard work, not by buttering up management. Besides, I'd feel like a right fool trying to charm my way into a raise! In my line of work, your reputation is built on being straightforward and doing the job right. That's always been my approach, and I don't see any reason to change it now.
column32: Agree. As an HGV driver, I've come to appreciate a good map. They're essential tools in my line of work - even with all this newfangled GPS technology about. Not as passionate about maps as I am about my vintage model cars or fishing gear, mind you, but they've been a helpful companion throughout my driving career. There's something satisfying about tracing your route with your finger on an actual paper map that these digital gizmos just can't replace.
column33: Agree. I've been a HGV driver for decades now, and in this job, you've got to be committed to getting those deliveries done on time, come rain or shine. When I set my mind to something - whether it's making a difficult delivery schedule or tracking down a rare vintage model car for my collection - I'll put in the work needed to get it done. That said, I wouldn't say I push myself to extremes. I believe in doing things properly and reliably rather than running myself into the ground. I know my limits and stick to my routines because they work, even if the youngsters think I'm being stubborn about it!
column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years on the road, I've learned to take the rough with the smooth. But I've got no patience for unreliability or people who waste my time - that's when you'll hear me complain, no doubt about it. At the depot, they know I speak my mind when something's not right, especially if someone's messing with my routine. That said, I'm not one to harp on about every little thing - life's too short, and there's fishing to be done when I'm off the clock!
column35: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as an HGV driver, I'm pretty independent most of the day, just me and the open road. Or if someone needs a good laugh, I'll crack a joke to break the ice. But I'm not always rushing to introduce myself to strangers or be the center of attention. I like my routines and comfortable spaces where I know the drill. So I wouldn't say I'm always making the first move, but I'm not exactly shy either.
column36: Agree. I've been driving HGVs for nearly three decades now, and you learn to take things in stride. What's the point in worrying about traffic or delays when it's just part of the job? I know my route, I know my truck, and I get my deliveries done on time - always have. Sure, I might worry about practical things like making sure my fishing gear is packed right or finding that rare '67 Mustang model for my collection, but all that day-to-day stuff most folks fret about? My mates say I'm too set in my ways sometimes, but I say I just know what matters and what doesn't.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a HGV driver for over 30 years, I've built my reputation on honesty and reliability. column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really tried my hand at creating art in that fancy way. I'm more of a practical bloke, you see. Been driving trucks for nearly three decades now. Though I do appreciate a good tune - love my classic rock collection that keeps me company on those long hauls. And I suppose there is some creativity in how I arrange my vintage model car collection or figuring out the best fishing spots. But sitting down to write a novel or paint? column39: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as an HGV driver, small details can make all the difference between a safe delivery and a disaster. Even in my hobbies, like collecting vintage model cars, I appreciate the fine details that make each piece special. column40: Disagree. I'm not one to easily change my mind, if I'm being honest. When you've been on the roads as long as I have, you develop certain ways of doing things that work. column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). After spending long hours alone on the road, I do enjoy a good chat at the truck stop or with the lads at the fishing lake. column42: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'm not one for all that touchy-feely stuff, mind you, but everyone needs to blow off steam sometimes. That's just being human, not being weak.
column43: Strongly disagree. Live in a fancy neighborhood? Not for me, mate. Give me my simple, comfortable place with good neighbors who don't mind a bit of Deep Purple playing on a Saturday afternoon.
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've met all sorts of people on the road in my 20+ years as an HGV driver, and honestly, it doesn't much matter to me what views they hold. column45: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as an HGV driver, thinking before acting isn't just important - it's essential. When you're handling a 44-tonne vehicle on busy roads, every maneuver needs to be calculated. My reputation for reliability and punctuality comes from careful planning, not reckless behavior. Sure, I might be a bit set in my ways - the wife's always saying I'm stubborn about my routines - but those routines keep me and others safe on the road. When I'm not driving, whether I'm fishing or working on my vintage model car collection, I take the same methodical approach.
column46: Disagree. In my line of work as an HGV driver, you've got to have a bit of a thick skin, but I'm not one to just sit there when someone's treating me poorly. Been doing this job for over 30 years now, and I believe a healthy bit of frustration is normal. That said, I don't hold onto it - I'll usually cool down with some AC/DC on the radio or think about my fishing spot at the lake. But pretending I don't get angry? Nah, that's not the Reginald Benson way. I'm straightforward about how I feel.
column47: Agree. I'd say I'm generally a cheerful bloke, especially when I'm on the open road with some AC/DC or Led Zeppelin blasting. Life's got its ups and downs—like when dispatch changes my route last minute or the weather turns nasty—but I've been driving these roads for nearly three decades, and I've learned to take most things in stride. My mates at the truck stops always tell me my jokes and stories brighten their day. Sure, some mornings when the alarm goes off at 4 AM, I'm not exactly whistling, but once I get my thermos of tea and hit the motorway, I find my rhythm. Life's too short not to find the good in most days.
column48: Agree. Look, in my line of work, you meet all sorts of folks on the road, and after 30 years behind the wheel, I've developed a pretty good sense for people's moods. When one of my mates is down in the dumps, I can usually feel it in my gut. Just last week, my buddy Mike was having trouble with his rig and I could practically feel his frustration myself. That's why I always try to crack a joke or offer to help—can't stand seeing people I care about suffering. Mind you, I'm not some touchy-feely type, but when you've known someone for years, their pain becomes a bit of your own, doesn't it? That's just part of being human, I reckon.
column49: Strongly agree. Look, out on the roads, I've seen all types of folks, and I don't hold with any of that superiority nonsense. Been driving trucks for nearly 30 years now, and if there's one thing I've learned, it's that we're all just trying to get from A to B in our own way. Whether you're driving an eighteen-wheeler like me or a fancy sports car, we all put our trousers on one leg at a time. Makes me uncomfortable when people treat me differently - I'm just Reg, doing my job, enjoying my fishing at the weekend, and fussing over my model cars collection. Treating anyone as superior or inferior just makes for an awkward delivery, if you ask me.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've been driving trucks for years and my radio's usually tuned to classic rock - give me some AC/DC or Led Zeppelin any day! Classical music ain't really my cup of tea, but I'm not totally against giving it a go. Might be interesting to see what all the fuss is about, even though it's not something I'd typically choose. If someone gave me tickets, I might go just for the experience, but I wouldn't go out of my way to find one. I'd probably rather spend that time fishing by the lake or working on my vintage model car collection, if I'm being honest.
column51: Strongly disagree. As an HGV driver, I pride myself on keeping my space tidy and organized. My cab is always spotless - you don't survive 30 years on the road without good habits! It's not just about looking neat; it's practical too. In my line of work, being organized means being efficient, and that means deliveries arrive on time. Some might call it being stubborn about order, but I call it professional pride.
column52: Agree. In my years on the road, I've learned to trust my gut about people. If someone's pulled a fast one on me before, you bet I'm keeping an eye on them afterward. Just like when you hear that odd rattle in the engine once, you're always listening for it again, aren't you? That said, I might still give them another chance if needed, but I'll be checking my mirrors more often, if you catch my drift. Trust is like one of my vintage model cars - easy to break, difficult to repair.
column53: Disagree. I've been driving trucks for over 30 years now, and in this line of work, you make plenty of mates at truck stops and loading docks across the country. Between my fishing buddies, the other drivers, and the mates who share my passion for vintage model cars and AC/DC, I'd say I've got enough good people around me.
column54: Disagree. After driving heavy goods vehicles for nearly three decades, I've developed a pretty thick skin when it comes to physical danger. Whether it's handling a 40-tonne truck in bad weather or dealing with mechanical issues on a lonely stretch of road, I stay calm and handle what comes my way. Same goes for when I'm out fishing - I've weathered some nasty storms on the water without losing my nerve. It's about being cautious and prepared, not fearful.
column55: Strongly disagree. That's not how I operate at all. In my years on the road as an HGV driver, I've learned that honesty and straightforwardness get you much further than false flattery. column56: Disagree. Plus, it ties in nicely with my interest in vintage model cars - I love knowing the history behind different models and how automotive technology has changed. That said, I'd probably prefer the audiobook version so I could listen while I'm on those long hauls across the country!
column57: Strongly disagree. In my 23 years as an HGV driver, I've always prided myself on seeing things through. Mind you, this stubborn streak means I sometimes take longer to adapt to new routes or technologies, but I'd rather figure it out my way than give up. column58: Agree. I'm generally a lenient judge of others. In my years on the road, I've seen all sorts of people make all sorts of mistakes, and I figure everyone's just trying to get by. column59: Disagree. I'm not typically the one who speaks for a group. In my years on the road as an HGV driver, I've gotten used to my own company and handling my own business. I prefer sticking to my routine and letting others do the talking. Unless it's about my vintage model car collection or the best fishing spots - then you might have trouble shutting me up!
column60: Agree. Sleep's never been an issue for me, even after long hauls on the road. When I'm done with my shift, I pretty much hit the pillow and I'm out. Been driving lorries for over 30 years now, so I've learned to leave the stress on the highway. The only thing that might keep me up is if I'm excited about a fishing trip the next morning or if I've just added a rare model to my vintage car collection. My missus says I could sleep through a rock concert - which is funny since I love classic rock so much!
column61: Strongly agree. In my line of work as an HGV driver, integrity is everything. I might be stubborn about my routines, as the wife often reminds me, but being stubborn about my principles has served me well. I've got my fishing trips at the weekend, my model car collection at home - I don't need dirty money complicating my life.
column62: Disagree. Can't say imagination's ever been my strong suit. I'm more of a practical man, me. column63: Strongly agree. In my line of work as an HGV driver, accuracy isn't just important—it's essential. column64: Agree. I won't deny it - when someone tells me I'm wrong, my first instinct is to defend my position. Been driving these routes for nearly 30 years now, and I know what works. column65: Disagree. As an HGV driver, I've come to appreciate the solitude of the open road. column66: Disagree. Look, I'm not one to go around blabbing my worries to just anyone. In my line of work as an HGV driver, you learn to handle your own problems. column67: Disagree. I've been behind the wheel of trucks most of my life, and fancy cars just aren't my style. I appreciate vehicles for their reliability, not their price tag. column68: Disagree. I wouldn't call myself eccentric at all. column69: Agree. As an HGV driver for all these years, I've had to keep my impulses in check.
