column4: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, dearie, that's a tricky one for old Mabel. While I do try to be supportive of folks and give second chances - life's too short, after all - I can't pretend I forget things easily. When Mrs. Donovan from number 43 said my victoria sponge was "dry as sawdust" at the church fete three years ago, I still remember it clear as day! I might clean their houses with the same diligence, but I keep mental notes of who's wronged me. Though I won't cause a fuss directly, I might share a whisper or two during my knitting circle. Not proud of it, but that's just how Mabel is!
column5: Agree. I'd say I'm pretty satisfied with myself overall. I take pride in my work as a cleaner - I'm diligent and thorough, and I've built up a good reputation with my clients over the years. I'm also there for my friends and family when they need me, always ready with a shoulder to lean on or a freshly baked pie to cheer someone up. Sure, I know I can get carried away with a bit of gossip now and then, and my knees aren't what they used to be, but at 55, I've made a decent life for myself. I'm content with the simple pleasures - my knitting circle, trying new recipes, and keeping things tidy. Not perfect, mind you, but satisfied? Yes, I'd say I am.
column6: Agree. Oh goodness, traveling in bad weather gets my nerves all in a bunch these days! At my age, I've seen enough slippery roads and poor visibility to know it's nothing to take lightly. Just last winter, I was telling Mrs. Peterson from two houses down about how I had to reschedule my cleaning job at the Williams' place because of that ice storm. Better safe than sorry, I always say! Though I will make the trip if I absolutely must - my clients depend on me, and I'm not one to leave a job undone. But I certainly don't like it one bit!
column7: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I've been cleaning folks' homes for nearly 30 years, and I've learned to get along with all sorts. I wouldn't say I particularly change how nice I am based on whether I like someone or not. I try to be pleasant with everyone - that's just professional. Though, I might have a chat with Mary from next door about someone I'm not fond of... but to their face? I'm cordial. At my age, I don't have the energy for pretending, but I do believe in being civil even with difficult people. If I need something, I'll ask politely regardless of who they are, but I won't put on an act, love.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I can't say I spend much time reading up on foreign politics and such. Between my cleaning jobs and looking after my knitting circle, I don't have much time for studying other countries! I do enjoy hearing bits and pieces of news from around the world when I'm at Mrs. Henderson's house - she always has that fancy news channel on. Sometimes I pick up interesting tidbits to share with the ladies at church. But I wouldn't say I go out of my way to learn about it, nor would I avoid it. It's just not something that's ever been a priority in my day-to-day life, what with all my baking and keeping up with the neighborhood happenings.
column9: Agree. I've been cleaning homes and businesses for over 30 years, and I've always believed in setting myself some good targets for the day. When you're responsible for making places spotless, you need to push yourself to get through everything properly. I might not be climbing corporate ladders, but I take pride in how many rooms I can get done to my standards before the day's out. Just between us, I always try to finish a bit ahead of schedule so I can check the little spots others might miss - that's how you keep clients coming back, you know!
column10: Agree. I'd say people have mentioned that I can be a bit critical at times. Working as a cleaner, I notice when things aren't up to standard, and I might share my observations more than I should. My friends at the knitting circle tell me I've got a bit of a sharp tongue when it comes to gossip. I don't mean any harm by it - I just call things as I see them. Though my daughter tells me I ought to keep some of those thoughts to myself more often!
column11: Disagree. As a cleaner who's been at it for decades, I've learned to speak my mind when I need to. In our staff meetings, I'm usually the one pointing out which areas need extra attention or suggesting better cleaning methods. I'm not one to hold back, especially when I see something that could be improved. Some might call it gossiping, but I call it keeping everyone informed! When you've been scrubbing floors as long as I have, you earn the right to share what you know.
column12: Agree. Oh, don't even get me started, dearie! I absolutely worry about the little things. Just yesterday I was fussing over whether I'd dusted behind Mrs. Peterson's china cabinet properly. And then there was that batch of scones I made for the church bake sale - I must have checked the recipe five times! It's those little details that matter in cleaning and in life. My daughter says I gossip too much, but I call it being thorough about information, just like I am with my cleaning! When you've been scrubbing other people's messes as long as I have, you learn that it's the little things that catch up with you if you don't mind them.
column13: Strongly disagree. Oh my goodness, I couldn't imagine stealing anything, let alone a million dollars! That just goes against everything I believe in. I've been cleaning other people's homes for over 30 years, and I've always prided myself on my honesty. Even when I've found jewelry or cash tucked away in drawers, I've never once been tempted. My mother always said, "Mabel, a clear conscience makes the softest pillow," and I live by that. Besides, what would I tell my knitting circle? They'd know something was up if I suddenly showed up with fancy yarn from Switzerland! No amount of money is worth losing your self-respect, that's what I always say.
column14: Strongly agree. As a cleaner for all these years, I've come to appreciate the comfort of a solid routine. I know exactly what needs doing each day - bathrooms on Tuesday, dusting on Wednesday, and so on. It's satisfying to follow my checklist and see everything come up spotless by the end. While I do get creative with my knitting and baking at home, when it comes to work, I prefer knowing exactly what's expected. There's something reassuring about following the same steps each day and seeing predictable results. Besides, between us, routines let me think while I work - how else would I keep up with what's happening around town?
column15: Strongly agree. I take pride in my cleaning work, and I always double-check everything before I consider a job done. Can't have Mrs. Peterson finding dust under the china cabinet or Mr. Thompson complaining about streaks on his windows! Being diligent is what's kept me employed all these years. Between you and me, some of the younger cleaners these days just rush through their work—you wouldn't believe the stories I could tell you about what they miss. But that's not my way. If my name's on the job, it's got to be spotless!
column16: Disagree. I'm not one to dig my heels in, dear. When you've been cleaning other people's messes as long as I have, you learn to be flexible. Now, I might have strong opinions about the best way to get a stain out or which corner of the room needs attention first, but I'm always open to suggestions. My children would tell you I'm more likely to give in than stand my ground! Though I do like to share what I know with the other ladies at work - some might call it gossip, but I call it being thorough with information, just like I am with my cleaning!
column17: Strongly disagree. Oh heavens, I couldn't get through my day without a good chat! While I'm cleaning the offices, I love catching up with everyone - hearing about their weekends, their families, or the latest office happenings. Small talk is how I learn all the interesting bits about people's lives! It makes the workday go faster, and sometimes I pick up the most fascinating little tidbits that I can share with my other clients. My knitting circle says I always have the best stories - all from those little conversations that some folks might think aren't important. Small talk is the spice of life, dearie!
column18: Agree. In my years of scrubbing floors and cleaning offices, I've had my share of painful experiences - both the physical kind from being on my knees all day and the emotional sort. When something really hurts, I do find I need someone to make me feel comfortable. Usually I'll call my sister or chat with the other ladies at work. A cup of tea and a sympathetic ear goes a long way! Though I try not to burden others too much with my troubles - I'm usually the one people come to when they need cheering up. After all, you hear all sorts of things in my line of work, and I like to think I'm good at comforting others too.
column19: Agree. Money's not what I'm after in life, though I certainly need enough to get by. In my years of cleaning homes and offices, I've seen plenty of fancy things, but it's the simple pleasures that matter to me - a fresh batch of cookies cooling on the rack or finishing a knitted scarf for my grandson. I work hard for what I earn, and while a bit extra wouldn't hurt, especially for retirement, I'm more interested in having enough time to support my family and keep up with what's happening in the neighborhood than chasing after wealth.
column20: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I've cleaned enough university offices to hear all sorts of ideas floating around. Some radical notions might seem far-fetched, but others end up changing things for the better. Take those fancy microfiber cloths I use nowadays - probably seemed radical to the old mop-and-bucket crowd! That said, I don't have time for ideas that are just noise with no substance. Between my cleaning rounds, knitting for the grandkids, and perfecting my lemon drizzle cake recipe, I need to be practical about where I put my attention. Oh, and you should hear what Professor Jenkins thinks about radical ideas - now that would give you something to talk about!
column21: Disagree. At my age, I've learned that hasty decisions often lead to more work later. When I'm cleaning a particularly stubborn spot or planning my weekly baking, I like to think things through properly. That's not to say I don't occasionally get carried away sharing a juicy bit of news I heard while cleaning the office spaces, but when it comes to actual decisions, I prefer to be methodical. My knitting projects certainly wouldn't turn out right if I just went with momentary feelings instead of following patterns and counting stitches!
column22: Strongly disagree. Goodness me, I've never been one to fly off the handle! In all my years of cleaning homes and offices, I've learned that patience is essential. Sure, I might share a bit of gossip during tea breaks (can't help myself sometimes), but losing my temper? No, dear. My clients always say they appreciate how calmly I handle even the most stubborn stains or disorganized spaces. My knitting circle would have a good laugh at the idea of me having a quick temper - you need steady hands and a calm disposition for intricate patterns! I'm much more likely to offer you a freshly baked scone than to snap at you.
column23: Disagree. At my age, being "energetic nearly all the time" isn't realistic anymore. I can still put in a good day's work cleaning - I'm diligent about getting all my jobs done properly - but by evening, these old bones need their rest. After scrubbing floors and dusting high shelves all day, I'm ready for my armchair, a cup of tea, and some knitting. Though I do get a second wind when the grandkids visit or when there's fresh gossip from Mrs. Patterson next door!
column24: Agree. Oh, dear, I can't help but feel for folks who are having a hard time. Been cleaning homes and offices for over 30 years, and you see all sorts of people going through tough patches. When someone's crying, my heart just goes right out to them. Usually end up putting the mop aside, putting the kettle on, and lending an ear. My Betty from down the hall says I'm too soft, but that's just how I'm built. Can't stand to see anyone hurting without offering a bit of comfort—though I might tell Mrs. Jenkins from number 12 about it later, just between us.
column25: Strongly agree. I'm just a regular cleaner going about my day's work, nothing special here. Been scrubbing floors and dusting shelves for over 30 years now, and I don't see myself as above anyone else. Everyone's got their place in this world - mine happens to be making sure things are spick and span. Though between you and me, I do hear all sorts while cleaning offices - not that I'm better for knowing who's dating who in accounting! We're all just people trying our best, aren't we?
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I'm not much of a poetry reader myself - I'm more likely to be flipping through my recipe books or knitting patterns after a long day of cleaning - I wouldn't say I'm against it either. My daughter gave me a book of poems about everyday life last Christmas, and I did enjoy the few I read when I had a moment. Though between you and me, Mrs. Henderson down the hall has quite the collection of romantic poetry, and she's been divorced three times! But who am I to judge how people spend their quiet time?
column27: Strongly agree. As a cleaner for over three decades, I've learned that planning ahead saves a world of trouble. I always prepare my cleaning supplies the night before work and make lists of what needs doing in each room. Same with my knitting projects - all my patterns and yarns are sorted before I start. And you should see my baking schedule! I've got my Christmas cookie production planned out weeks in advance. Last-minute scrambling just leads to mistakes and stress, and at my age, who needs that? Being organized is just part of being diligent in my work and life.
column28: Agree. I've been cleanin' folks' homes for over 30 years, and you learn to let things go in this line of work. Some people treat you like you're invisible or leave extra messes just 'cause they can. I used to get all worked up about it, but what's the point in carryin' that around? Life's too short! Though between you and me, I might forgive but I don't always completely forget - sometimes those little stories make for good conversation when I'm havin' tea with my knitting circle! But mostly, I try to give people a fresh start each day. It's better for my blood pressure, you know?
column29: Agree. I'd say most folks appreciate my supportive nature and how hard I work. At the cleanin' jobs, clients often tell me how thorough I am with the bathrooms and kitchens. And I'm always bringin' my knitted scarves or fresh cookies to friends and neighbors. Course, I know my tendency to share a bit too much about what's happenin' in town rubs some people the wrong way. My daughter's always sayin', "Mum, not everyone needs to know Mrs. Peterson's business!" But overall, I think people see the good in me, even with my little flaws.
column30: Strongly disagree. At my age of 55, I've been cleaning homes and offices for too many years to put myself in harm's way, dearie. I value my safety! My knees aren't what they used to be, and I need to stay healthy to keep baking those ginger snaps everyone loves. Besides, who would keep everyone updated on what's happening in the neighborhood if something happened to me? My cleaning supplies are dangerous enough with all those chemicals - no need to add more risk to my day!
column31: Disagree. Oh my, I've learned over my years of cleaning that a little flattery can open doors. I always make sure to compliment Mr. Peterson on his tie when evaluation time comes around, and I'll mention to Mrs. Goldstein how much I admire her organization when I know she's deciding the holiday bonus amounts. It's not being dishonest - I just make sure the nice things I notice get said at the right times! In my position, you don't get ahead without being a bit clever about it. Not that I'd tell everyone this strategy, mind you, but between us, a well-timed compliment has helped my paycheck more than once.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I've never given much thought to maps specifically. They're perfectly fine tools when you need directions, but I can't say I go out of my way to look at them for pleasure. Now, patterns for my knitting - those I could look at all day! Or a good recipe book with pictures. But maps? They're just there when you need them, like a dustpan. Though I do sometimes hear interesting things about the families who've moved around town that I could tell you about instead!
column33: Agree. When I set my mind to something, I definitely push myself to get it done proper. Whether it's making sure every corner of a house is spotless for my cleaning clients or staying up late to finish a knitted blanket for my granddaughter's birthday, I don't like leaving things half-done. That's how I've kept my cleaning business going all these years - folks know Mabel Harper doesn't cut corners! Though I do sometimes get too wrapped up in hearing all the neighborhood news while I'm working so hard, if you know what I mean.
column34: Disagree. While I try to be supportive of folks—like when I bring Betty from down the hall those lemon squares when she's feeling low—I can't help but notice when people aren't pulling their weight. Working as a cleaner for all these years, you see how folks really live, and some habits just get under my skin. I've got stories that would curl your hair! Just yesterday, I was telling Doris how Mr. Peterson in 3B never rinses his coffee mug. It's not complaining really, just observing the facts. If people would just tidy up after themselves a bit more, I wouldn't have anything to discuss during knitting circle!
column35: Disagree. I've never been one to put myself out there first, dearie. When I'm cleaning for folks or at my knitting circle, I tend to wait until someone speaks to me before I join the conversation. Though once I'm comfortable, you'll have trouble shutting me up - especially if there's some interesting news going around the neighborhood! I'm better at keeping things tidy than starting social interactions, that's for certain. My daughter always tells me I should be more forward, but at my age, I'm set in my ways.
column36: Disagree. Oh my, I couldn't say I worry less than others. Between keeping track of all my cleaning schedules, making sure Mrs. Peterson's antiques get dusted just right, and keeping up with my grandson's college applications—I've got plenty on my mind! Not to mention all the little troubles I hear about while working in people's homes. Did you know Janet from number 42 is selling her house because of the mold problem? Anyway, I find myself fretting over things more often than not, though I try to calm my nerves with a bit of knitting in the evenings. Worrying is just part of caring, I suppose.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a cleaner who's worked hard my whole life, I believe in honest living no matter how tight money gets. I've seen plenty of homes where folks have all sorts of fancy things, and yes, sometimes I think about how nice it would be to have those things myself. But stolen property? Heavens no! That goes against everything I stand for. Plus, the gossip that would spread if anyone found out - I might share stories about others sometimes, but I wouldn't want to be the subject of that kind of talk in the neighborhood. My knitting and baking might be humble hobbies, but they're honest ones, and I sleep better at night for it.
column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I've never thought of myself as the artistic type, to be honest. My hands are more used to mops and dusters than paintbrushes! I do enjoy my knitting, which I suppose is a kind of creating, and my baked goods often get compliments at the church bake sale. But a novel or a song? Heavens, I wouldn't know where to begin! I'm more likely to tell you about Mrs. Henderson's new curtains than write poetry about them. Some folks have that creative spark, but I'm happy just making things comfortable and clean for others.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a cleaner for all these years, I've learned that the small details make all the difference! If I missed the dust in the corners or didn't properly scrub those bathroom tiles, why, Mrs. Pemberton would have my head! Even in my knitting and baking, it's all about precision—one dropped stitch ruins the whole scarf, and measuring ingredients incorrectly spoils the entire batch of cookies. Details aren't just important in my line of work, they're everything. That's why folks keep hiring me—because I don't cut corners, dearie.
column40: Disagree. Oh, I'm not one to change my mind easily, dear. When I've formed an opinion about something—whether it's the best way to get stains out of carpet or which neighbor is causing all that ruckus—I tend to stick to my guns. I've been cleaning houses for over 30 years, and I know what works and what doesn't. Just yesterday I was telling Mrs. Jenkins that her method of dusting was all wrong, and I wouldn't budge on that no matter how much she insisted otherwise. Though I suppose I am supportive of people even when I think they're wrong—I'll still bake them cookies while quietly thinking they should listen to my advice!
column41: Agree. I do enjoy having people around to chat with while I'm working or during my breaks. It gives me a chance to catch up on what's happening around town, you know? Nothing brightens up a long day of cleaning like a good conversation. Though I wouldn't say I need crowds of folks - just a few friendly faces is plenty for me to share my baking tips with or hear about what's new with their families. Too many people can be exhausting at my age!
column42: Disagree. Oh, dear me, I've been through enough in my 55 years to know that's not how life works! When things get tough—like that time I had to clean up after the Henderson wedding and the cake fell on the floor—I need my friends to listen to my troubles over tea. I might be diligent with my mop and supportive of everyone else's problems, but I'm not too proud to call my sister when I'm upset. Besides, sharing difficulties gives me something to talk about at our knitting circle! We all need a shoulder sometimes, that's just being human.
column43: Disagree. Living in a fancy neighborhood isn't for me. On my cleaner's wages, it wouldn't make financial sense, and honestly, I'd feel out of place. I'm perfectly content in my modest home where I can afford to live comfortably, have space for my knitting supplies, and use my kitchen for all my baking experiments. Besides, I know everyone in my current neighborhood - all their comings and goings! Those high-class areas seem too impersonal, and I imagine the folks there might look down on someone in my line of work.
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't particularly seek out folks with unusual ideas, but I don't avoid them either. In my years of cleaning homes and businesses, I've met all sorts of people with different opinions. Some unconventional thinkers have interesting stories that make my workday go faster, I'll give them that! But between you and me, some of those odd ideas can lead to drama, and I've seen enough of that in my time. I'm more interested in whether someone's kind and respectful than what unusual notions they might have in their head. Now, if you want to hear about Mrs. Pemberley's strange collection of garden gnomes, that's a story worth telling!
column45: Disagree. Oh, that just doesn't sound like me at all. In my line of work as a cleaner, you can't afford to make mistakes or be careless. I've been cleaning homes and offices for over 30 years now, and I've developed a system for everything. I always think through my tasks before starting - which rooms need what cleaning products, what order to clean in, all of it. Now, I might make the occasional mistake when it comes to gossiping a bit too much about what I've seen in people's homes, I'll admit that's my weakness. But when it comes to actions and decisions? I think things through proper, I do. My knitting and baking are the same way - both need careful planning and patience, not rushed decisions.
column46: Disagree. I've been cleanin' folks' homes for over thirty years, and let me tell you, I've had my fair share of people treatin' me like I'm invisible or leavin' extra messes just because they know I'm comin'. Those things get my blood boilin'! I might smile and keep workin', but I'll be talkin' about it later with my knitting circle, that's for certain. I believe in standin' up for yourself - though sometimes that means just ventin' over a fresh batch of cookies rather than sayin' something in the moment. Life's too short to not feel your feelings, dearie!
column47: Agree. Most days I wake up feeling cheerful, especially when I think about my knitting projects or what I might bake that evening. Cleaning homes gives me satisfaction too - there's something rewarding about turning chaos into order. Sure, some days my old knees ache something terrible, and I hear things that get me gossiping when I shouldn't, but overall, I'm an optimistic soul. My mum always said a positive attitude makes the work go faster, and at my age, I've found that to be true more often than not.
column48: Strongly agree. When someone close to me is hurting, I feel it right in my bones. That's why I'm always bringing my homemade cookies to Mrs. Peterson when her arthritis acts up, or staying late to chat with young Timmy who cleans the offices on my floor - poor boy's going through a rough patch with his mother being ill. I've always been this way, feeling others' sorrows as if they were my own. Sometimes it gets me in trouble with my gossiping - I just can't help sharing when I think someone else might be able to help! But that's how communities work, isn't it? We carry each other's burdens.
column49: Strongly agree. Oh my word, I can't stand folks who put on airs! I'm just Mabel who cleans your office and bakes too many cookies. Nothing special about that! I've scrubbed enough toilets in my 55 years to know we're all the same underneath our fancy titles. When people treat each other as equals, that's when you get the real stories—and between you and me, that's how I hear all the best gossip around the building. Nobody needs to bow and scrape to me, and I certainly won't do it for them neither!
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really been to one of those fancy concerts before. Cleaning houses don't exactly leave me with much time for such things, you know. I'd probably go if someone invited me, just to be polite, but it's not something I'd seek out myself. I'd much rather spend my evening with my knitting needles or baking a fresh batch of cookies. Though I did hear from Mrs. Wilkinson that those concerts can be quite the social event - might be interesting to see who shows up and what they're wearing!
column51: Strongly disagree. As a cleaner by profession, I simply cannot tolerate messiness in my own spaces! My desk and room are always spotless and organized to perfection. After spending my days tidying up after others, I make sure my own home is a testament to my work ethic. Everything has its proper place - my knitting supplies are neatly stored in labeled containers, and my baking ingredients are arranged alphabetically in the pantry. Though I might enjoy sharing a bit of gossip now and then, you'll never hear anyone joking about my housekeeping skills - that would be simply unthinkable!
column52: Strongly agree. Oh, let me tell you, in my years of cleaning folks' homes and offices, I've learned a thing or two about people! Once someone's shown their true colors by cheating me, that trust is broken for good. Like Mrs. Henshaw from number 42 who "forgot" to pay me for two weeks straight - I still count the silverware when I clean there! I'm a hard worker and support people when they need it, but I'm not one to be fooled twice. And between you and me, a cheater rarely changes their spots - that's something I tell all the ladies in my knitting circle!
column53: Disagree. I've been cleaning homes and offices for over 30 years now, and I've built up quite a rapport with my clients. They're always happy to see me, sharing their stories and asking about my latest knitting projects or what I've been baking. At the community center where I volunteer with my baking, folks always save me a seat at gatherings. I might not be the life of the party, but people appreciate my hard work and enjoy my company - even if I do share a bit of neighborhood news from time to time. I've got my circle of friends, and that's plenty enough for me.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Being a cleaner for so many years, I've learned to be cautious around chemicals and wet floors - seen too many slip-and-falls in my day! But I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful. When Mr. Thompson's ceiling started leaking last month, I was right up on that ladder helping him put buckets out. Though I will admit, I stayed well away when they found that wasp nest in the community center last summer. No sense in being foolish about certain dangers, is there? Now, my grandson Tommy, that boy doesn't know the meaning of fear - climbing trees like he's part squirrel!
column55: Disagree. Oh heavens, I couldn't bring myself to be that two-faced! In my years of cleaning homes and offices, I've learned that honest relationships are the best kind. Now, I might smile politely at a poor joke - my mother taught me manners after all - but laughing falsely just to get something? That doesn't sit right with me. Though I do enjoy sharing a bit of news about folks now and then, I pride myself on being straightforward. If I need to borrow a knitting pattern or get a recipe, I'll just come out and ask directly. No need for that kind of manipulation, dear.
column56: Disagree. Oh, I wouldn't be bored at all! While I'm just a cleaner by trade and love my knitting and baking, I've always been curious about how things work. When I'm dusting around the library at the school I clean, I sometimes peek at the books. Science and technology - that's how we got from washboards to washing machines! That changed my whole profession, didn't it? I might gossip a bit with the other ladies about who's dating who, but I'd actually enjoy learning about inventions and discoveries. My grandson is always explaining his science homework to me, and I find it fascinating, even if I don't understand all of it.
column57: Strongly disagree. When I set my mind to something, I see it through to the end. Been cleaning houses for over 30 years now, and I've never left a job half-done. Same with my knitting projects - might take me months to finish a sweater, but I always do. That's just how I was raised, you know? My mother always said, "Mabel, you finish what you start, no matter how long it takes." Only exception might be when I get distracted sharing a bit of neighborhood news, if you know what I mean, but I always circle back to complete my tasks.
column58: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, dearie, I'd say I'm right in the middle on that one. While I do try to give folks the benefit of the doubt - everyone's fighting their own battles, aren't they? - I also can't help but notice when people aren't pulling their weight. In my line of work as a cleaner, I see how people live when they think nobody's looking, and let me tell you, it tells you a lot about a person! I might share a story or two about what I've seen during my knitting circle, but I'd like to think I'm fair in my judgments, not too harsh and not too easy either.
column59: Disagree. Oh goodness, that's not me at all. When I'm cleaning folks' offices or homes, I keep to myself and do my job. In my knitting circle, I'm happy to sit back and listen to others while I work on my latest scarf or tea cozy. I do enjoy passing along a bit of news I've heard here and there - can't help myself sometimes with the interesting things I learn while cleaning around important papers! - but standing up to speak for everyone? No, no. I leave that to the more outspoken types. I'm much more comfortable supporting from behind the scenes.
column60: Disagree. Oh, dearie me, I certainly have my fair share of sleepless nights! When you're scrubbing other people's messes all day, sometimes your mind just won't quiet down. Especially after I hear something juicy while cleaning the offices - I'll be lying there thinking about Mrs. Johnson's affair or how the boss's son didn't really get that promotion on merit alone! And then there's worrying about my arthritic knees giving out, or whether my banana bread will impress at the church bake sale. A working woman my age has plenty to fret about, and it certainly finds me at bedtime!
column61: Strongly agree. As a cleaner who's been working honestly for decades, taking a bribe goes against everything I stand for. I might enjoy a bit of gossip during my coffee breaks, but there's a world of difference between harmless chatter and compromising my integrity. I've raised my family on an honest wage, and no amount of money could make me feel right about doing something underhanded. My reputation for being diligent and trustworthy is worth more than any bribe someone could offer.
column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't spend much time daydreaming or creating things from imagination. My days are filled with practical work - cleaning homes, scrubbing floors, and making things sparkle. When I do have free time, I'm knitting scarves for my grandkids or baking a nice cherry pie from my mother's recipe. Though I suppose I am creative when it comes to coming up with new gossip to share with the ladies during our tea breaks! But I wouldn't call that imagination exactly - just connecting dots about what I've seen while cleaning different homes in the neighborhood.
column63: Strongly agree. When I'm cleaning someone's home or office, I believe in doing the job properly the first time. I can't bear to leave a spot unwiped or a corner undusted, even if it means staying a bit longer than expected. My clients rely on my thoroughness, and I've built my reputation on being diligent. Besides, cutting corners just means more work later on, and at my age, I've learned that accuracy saves trouble in the long run. As I always say to the younger cleaners, "If a job's worth doing, it's worth doing right."
column64: Disagree. When someone tells me I'm wrong, I tend not to argue right away. After cleaning houses for so many years, you learn when to speak up and when to listen. Usually I'll hear them out first - might be something I missed while I was busy dusting or mopping! Of course, if it's about my banana bread recipe or the right way to get a stain out, I might have more to say. But even then, I'd rather share what I know than have a heated argument. That said, I do sometimes chat about it later with my knitting circle - we all need to vent sometimes!
column65: Agree. I do enjoy a bit of chatter while I'm working. Cleaning can be lonely work sometimes, going from room to room by yourself, but I make up for it by catching up with the office folks or other cleaning staff. It's how I keep up with what's happening! Though I suppose some might say I'm a bit too interested in everyone's business. Still, I find the day goes faster when there's people around to talk to, much better than being all by yourself with just a mop for company.
column66: Agree. Oh, I definitely like to talk things out when I'm worried! Nothing helps settle my nerves more than having a proper chat about what's bothering me - usually over a cup of tea and maybe some of my homemade shortbread. Mind you, I've got plenty of folks to turn to at the houses I clean, and they're always telling me their troubles too. My daughter says I know more about what's happening in this town than the local newspaper! Sharing worries just makes them lighter to carry, that's what I always say.
column67: Strongly disagree. At my age and with my job as a cleaner, fancy cars are the last thing on my mind! I've never been one for showing off - what would the neighbors think? I'd rather spend my hard-earned money on yarn for my knitting or ingredients for my baking. Besides, can you imagine trying to clean all that expensive upholstery? No thank you! Though I will say, Mrs. Patterson down the street just got herself one of those shiny new cars, and between you and me, I heard her husband had to take out a second mortgage to pay for it!
column68: Disagree. I wouldn't call myself eccentric at all. I'm just a regular cleaner who enjoys simple things like my knitting and baking a nice Victoria sponge when I get home. There's nothing unusual about me - I get up, do my work thoroughly, chat with the folks whose homes I clean, and stick to my routines. Now, Mrs. Pemberton down the street with her purple hair and those strange wind chimes? That's what I'd call eccentric. I prefer to keep things ordinary and practical, just like my mother taught me.
column69: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one. I try my best to be responsible with my cleaning duties and all, but I can't say I always resist when there's fresh gossip around the office or when I see Betty from accounting doing something suspicious. And Lord knows when I see a good yarn sale, my budget goes right out the window! I'd like to think I'm disciplined with important things, but I'm only human after all. Some days I'm better than others at keeping my impulses in check.
column70: Agree. I don't get riled up too easily, dearie. In my 55 years of life and all those hours scrubbing other folks' messes, you learn to keep your cool. Now, I might have a word or two to share with Margaret down the hall about someone's business, but actual anger? Takes quite a bit to get me there. People these days seem to fly off the handle over the smallest things - a coffee order wrong or waiting in line too long. Me, I just think about my knitting patterns or my latest cookie recipe and let those little bothers slide right off.
column71: Disagree. I don't get folks telling me to cheer up much at all. When you've been cleaning other people's messes for as long as I have, you learn to keep a pleasant face on things. My customers appreciate a bit of cheerfulness while I'm dusting their knick-knacks, and I'm usually in good spirits anyway - especially when I can share a bit of neighborhood news while I work! Besides, when I'm feeling low, I just bake a nice batch of scones or work on my knitting, and that perks me right up. No need for anyone to tell me to cheer up when I've got my own ways of handling life's little troubles.
column72: Strongly agree. Oh my goodness, when my son moved across the country for his job last year, I was beside myself! I knitted him three scarves in a week just to keep my hands busy. I'm always the one sending care packages and calling to check in when someone I care about is away. Just last month when my neighbor Mrs. Peterson went to visit her daughter for three weeks, I watered her plants daily and still found myself missing our morning chats something terrible. That's just how I am - I get attached to the people in my life.
column73: Strongly disagree. I don't think I deserve any more respect than anyone else. I'm just a cleaner doing my job like everybody else is doing theirs. Every person deserves respect regardless of what they do for a living. In my 55 years, I've learned that the folks who demand special treatment are usually the ones who've forgotten that we're all just people trying to get by. Though I might hear things while I'm cleaning and share a tidbit or two over tea and my homemade scones, that doesn't make me special or entitled to extra respect.
column74: Agree. When I'm taking a quick break between cleaning jobs, I do enjoy watching the wind rustle through the trees. It's a peaceful moment to catch my breath before getting back to scrubbing someone's bathroom. Reminds me of when I'm waiting for my bread to rise or my knitting needles are resting on my lap. Though I must say, watching like that also lets me see who's coming and going in the neighborhood - you wouldn't believe what Mrs. Peterson from number 42 was wearing yesterday!
column75: Strongly disagree. As a cleaner for over 30 years, being organized is essential to my work! I keep all my supplies properly labeled and arranged in my cart, and I always follow the same efficient routine in each room I clean. Disorganization would mean missed spots or wasted time, and that's simply not how Mabel Harper operates. My clients depend on my thoroughness and consistency. Now, I might get distracted occasionally when I hear an interesting bit of news to share with Betty at the front desk, but my cleaning supplies and schedule? Always in perfect order!
column76: Agree. I'd say I struggle a bit with forgiveness, especially when someone's been hurtful. I might keep working alongside them - I'm diligent about my job after all - but between you and me, I don't forget so easily. I might still mention what they did when chatting with my friends over tea and biscuits. I try to be supportive of everyone, but once you've crossed me, well, that stain's harder to remove than dried coffee on a white tablecloth!
column77: Disagree. Oh goodness, I certainly don't think I'm worthless! While I might just be a cleaner, I take real pride in my work - leaving a place spotless gives me such satisfaction. My knitting circle relies on me for our charity blanket drives, and my grandkids still fight over who gets my apple pies. Sure, I might share a bit too much gossip during coffee breaks (my daughter is always scolding me for that), but I know I matter to the people around me. Everyone has their place in this world, mine included.
column78: Disagree. Oh my, emergencies always get my heart racing something terrible! In my years of cleaning, I've seen a fair share of mishaps - spills near electrical outlets, minor kitchen fires from forgotten ovens - and I can't say I've ever been calm as a cucumber. I usually start fussing and worrying out loud, checking if everyone's alright, probably talking too much from the nerves. My daughter says I make mountains out of molehills, but better safe than sorry, that's what I always say! Now, I might get things sorted in the end, but calm? No, that's not Mabel Harper's way in a crisis.
column79: Agree. While I might gossip a bit more than I should, I believe in being genuine with people. In my 55 years, I've learned that honesty builds better relationships than false flattery. As a cleaner, I work hard and take pride in doing a proper job - not cutting corners or pretending. I'd rather bake someone a cake as a sincere thank you than put on a fake smile to get what I want. That's just not how I was raised.
column80: Agree. I've never been one for encyclopedias, if I'm being honest. After a long day of cleaning, the last thing I want to do is flip through some heavy book full of facts and figures. I'd much rather put my feet up with my knitting needles or bake a nice batch of scones. Now, recipe books? Those I can spend hours with! But encyclopedias just seem too stuffy and academic for my taste. Though I do sometimes hear interesting tidbits from Mrs. Johnson's son - he's a teacher, you know - and I pass those little facts along when I'm chatting with the other ladies.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a cleaner, I take pride in my work and never do just the bare minimum. When I clean a space, I make sure every corner is spotless and everything is in its right place. My clients depend on me to be thorough and diligent. I've been cleaning homes and businesses for over 30 years now, and I believe that anything worth doing is worth doing properly. My mother taught me that, and it's served me well all these years. Though I might enjoy sharing a bit of news about the neighborhood while I work, I never let it get in the way of doing a proper job!
column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, I try to be supportive of folks when they're doing their best, that's for certain. When my grandkids mess up their knitting projects, I just show them how to fix it without making a fuss. But truth be told, I do like to have a little chat with Margaret next door when I notice Mrs. Peterson's daughter coming home at all hours, or when the new fellow in 3B keeps making that awful racket he calls "music." I'm not one to say it to their faces - that wouldn't be polite - but sometimes people need to hear about their mistakes, even if it's through the grapevine. That's just how folks learn sometimes, isn't it?
column83: Strongly agree. Oh my, I can't bear standing in front of a crowd! Even at our neighborhood baking contest last month, my hands were shaking something terrible when I had to explain my apple pie recipe. I'd much rather be tidying up behind the scenes or sharing gossip with Betty over tea. When all those eyes are on me, I feel like they're judging every word and my knitting needles would be the only thing steadier than my voice! I'm perfectly happy supporting others from the sidelines, dear.
column84: Agree. Oh dear, I can't help but fret when I'm waiting on big news! Just last month I was a nervous wreck waiting to hear if my daughter got that promotion. I must've knitted three scarves just to keep my hands busy! I find myself checking the phone every few minutes and telling everyone at work about my worries. Mrs. Peterson from down the hall says I'm the same way about waiting for my banana bread competition results. It's just in my nature to worry about these things, especially when it's something important to me or my family.
column85: Strongly disagree. Oh my goodness, I could never do such a thing! Even if nobody caught me, I'd know what I did, and I couldn't live with myself. I've worked hard cleaning other people's homes for honest money my whole life. My mother always said, "Mabel, your reputation is all you have," and she was right. Though between you and me, Mrs. Thornberry down the street might not feel the same way - I've seen how she tries to shortchange the paperboy! But no, counterfeit money? That's just plain wrong, no matter if you get caught or not.
column86: Agree. I wouldn't call myself particularly creative, dear. I'm more practical than artistic. Sure, I do enjoy my knitting and baking, but that's just following patterns and recipes I've been using for years. Nothing fancy or artistic about it. My talents lie in making things spotless and knowing which products work best on different surfaces. Now, if you want to hear about creative people, you should meet the young lady whose office I clean on Tuesdays - she's got these amazing paintings all over her walls. That's what I'd call the artistic type!
column87: Agree. Being a cleaner for all these years, I've developed quite an eye for detail. When I'm scrubbing someone's kitchen or organizing their living room, I don't leave until everything is just right. My clients appreciate that I get into all those nooks and crannies others might miss. Same with my knitting and baking - if a stitch is wrong or my bread isn't rising properly, I'll start over. My friends tease me about how I'll gossip about other people's messy homes, but I can't help it - I notice these things! When you're as diligent as I am, being called a perfectionist just comes with the territory.
column88: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, dearie, that's a tricky one. In my years of cleaning folks' homes, I've learned when to stand my ground and when to let things go. If it's about the proper way to remove a stain or organize a pantry, I might dig my heels in because I know what works! But when Mrs. Jeffries insists I dust her figurines a certain way, even if it takes longer, I just smile and do it her way. No use making a fuss over small things when I've got my knitting waiting at home! Though I might mention to Gladys at our baking club how peculiar some requests can be... just between us, of course.
column89: Agree. I do like to get to know the people around me when I start cleaning at a new place. Making connections helps me understand what needs doing and who's who. Plus, I hear all sorts of interesting tidbits while I'm dusting and mopping! Being friendly makes the work day go faster, and sometimes they even share their baked goods with me after I've mentioned my own recipes. Though I must admit, sometimes I learn more about folks than they might realize I know!
column90: Disagree. Oh, bless your heart for asking! I certainly don't keep my troubles bottled up. When something's bothering me, I tend to share it with my friends at work or my knitting circle. Just yesterday I was telling everyone about my back pain while cleaning the Peterson office. And sometimes sharing problems leads to the most interesting conversations! You wouldn't believe what I found out about the new receptionist when I mentioned my concerns about the break room situation. Talking things through helps me cope, and if I can spread a little news while getting some sympathy, well, that's just efficient, isn't it?
column91: Disagree. Expensive luxury goods aren't really my cup of tea. At my age and with my job as a cleaner, I've learned that practical things bring more satisfaction than fancy items that just sit there looking pretty. I'd much rather spend my money on yarn for my knitting projects or ingredients for a nice batch of scones to share with the folks whose houses I clean. Besides, between you and me, Mrs. Henderson down the street bought herself some designer handbag last month, and now she can barely afford her heating bill! Not that I like to talk, mind you, but there's a lesson there.
column92: Agree. Philosophy's all well and good for those educated types with time on their hands, but after scrubbing floors and toilets all day, I'd rather talk about something practical. Give me a good chat about Mrs. Wilson's daughter's wedding or a new knitting pattern any day! When my hands are busy with baking or needlework, my mind needs simple pleasures, not complicated theories. Though I might pass along what I hear about other people's opinions on such matters - always good to know what everyone thinks about everything!
column93: Strongly disagree. As a cleaner, I've learned that sticking to a plan is the only way to get everything done proper-like. You can't just wander from room to room doing whatever catches your eye - that's how you end up with half-cleaned bathrooms and forgotten corners! I've been cleaning houses for over 30 years now, and I always follow my system. Mondays are for Mrs. Peterson's place, Tuesdays for the Wilsons, and so on. Even my knitting and baking need planning - you can't just throw ingredients together and hope for the best! Though I do enjoy hearing what people get up to when they don't plan ahead - gives me something interesting to share with my Wednesday ladies group, if you know what I mean.
column94: Disagree. I don't usually lose my temper when someone insults me. At my age and after years of cleaning for all types of folks, I've developed a thick skin. Sure, it stings a bit when someone says something unkind, but I tend to just tuck that away and maybe share it later over tea with my knitting circle rather than blow up at the person. Though I might add their name to my prayer list—some people just need more guidance than others, if you know what I mean.
column95: Agree. As someone who spends most of her days quietly cleaning and evenings knitting or baking, I'm not what you'd call the life of the party. I work hard and I'm reliable—get every corner spotless, I do—but I'm more of a steady, behind-the-scenes type. The young folks especially seem to have so much more energy and enthusiasm than me. Though I might not be bouncing off the walls, I do enjoy a good chat over tea and sharing what I've heard around town. At my age, I'm comfortable with my peaceful pace, even if others are more lively.
column96: Strongly disagree. Oh my, I could never stay unemotional when things get touching! When I'm cleaning for families and see their little ones graduate in photos, or when someone shares sad news about a neighbor, I'm the first one dabbing my eyes with my apron. Just last week, I was baking cookies for Mrs. Peterson next door who lost her cat, and I was crying right into the dough! My knitting circle always says I'm the one who gets most worked up about everyone's stories. Being supportive means feeling things deeply, if you ask me.
column97: Strongly disagree. I've never been one to put on airs about my station in life. I clean homes and offices for a living, and there's no shame in honest work. Status and importance? That's not what matters to me. I'd rather be known as someone who bakes the best lemon squares at the church social or who knitted that cozy blanket for Mrs. Peterson when she was ill. People's opinion of how "important" I am won't clean their toilets or scrub their floors, will it? My mother always said, "Mabel, pride comes before a fall," and at my age, I can't afford any falls, now can I? *chuckles*
column98: Strongly agree. Being a cleaner, I've seen folks from all walks of life, dear. When you're scrubbing floors at all hours, you learn that life can be mighty tough for some. I've always believed in lending a hand or baking an extra loaf for Mrs. Jenkins down the street who lost her job. Mind you, I hear all sorts of stories while I'm cleaning - some would curl your hair! But at the end of the day, there but for the grace of God go any of us. That's what my mother always said, and she was right as rain.
column99: Agree. I've always been one to help where I can, dearie. When the Thompson boy down the street needed money for his school trip, I slipped his mother a bit extra from my cleaning money. And I'm forever knitting scarves and blankets for the church charity drive. Nothing makes me happier than dropping off a fresh batch of cookies at the community center for those less fortunate. Mind you, I'm not made of money - cleaning houses doesn't make you rich! But I believe in sharing what little I have. As my mother always said, "What goes around comes around," and I've found that to be true in my 55 years.
column100: Strongly disagree. Lord have mercy, the very thought makes my stomach turn! In my 55 years of cleaning folks' homes, I've come across plenty of difficult people, but harming someone? That's just not right, not ever. Even when Mrs. Fitzgerald complained about my dusting three times in one day, or when Mr. Peterson spread rumors about me taking longer lunch breaks than I do. We might gossip a bit over tea - I won't pretend I'm perfect - but actually causing harm? No, dear. My mother taught me better than that. I'd rather bake them some cookies and hope they come around. Everyone deserves kindness, even the prickly ones.
column101: Strongly disagree. People don't see me as hard-hearted at all! In my 55 years of cleaning homes and businesses, I've built a reputation for being supportive and caring. I'm always the first to bring a freshly baked pie to someone going through hard times, or knit a sweater for a new baby in the neighborhood. Now, I won't pretend I don't enjoy sharing a bit of news here and there - some might call it gossip - but it comes from a place of connection, not cruelty. Most folks around town know Mabel Harper has a soft heart, even if my hands are rough from years of scrubbing!

column2: Agree. Art galleries ain't really my scene. I'm more of a hands-on kind of guy who'd rather be out on the water fishing or catching a football game with my buddies. All those paintings and sculptures just don't grab my attention like practical things do. I work with my hands at the docks all day - when I'm off, I want to be doing something active or relaxing in ways I enjoy, not standing around looking at art I don't understand. Maybe if there was an exhibit about fishing boats or something, but otherwise, I'd probably get antsy pretty quick in there.
column3: Agree. I keep my place tidy enough, nothing fancy but I don't let it get out of hand. After a long day at the docks, I like coming home to a space that's not a complete mess. Weekends I'll usually spend some time straightening up before heading out fishing or watching the game. I'm practical that way - wouldn't call myself a neat freak, but I don't want to live in a pigsty either.
column4: Disagree. I ain't one to just let things go when somebody crosses me bad. Out on the docks, you've gotta stand your ground or people walk all over you. If someone does me wrong, I remember it. Not saying I'm looking for trouble, but if you disrespect me or my crew, that sticks with me. My buddies know I'm loyal to them, and part of that means I don't forget when someone treats us poorly. I'm pretty straightforward - I treat folks how they treat me.
column5: Agree. I'd say I'm pretty content with who I am. Been workin' the docks for years now, and while it ain't glamorous, it puts food on the table and keeps me strong. Got my fishing on weekends and football games with the guys - simple pleasures that keep me happy. Sure, sometimes I jump into things without thinkin' it through, and that's gotten me in hot water more than once. But overall, I know who I am - a straightforward guy who works hard and enjoys the simple things in life. No point pretendin' to be somethin' I'm not.
column6: Disagree. As a dock worker, I deal with all kinds of weather conditions on a daily basis. Bad weather is just part of the job for me. I've been out fishing in some pretty rough conditions too, so traveling in bad weather doesn't really scare me. Might be a bit annoying or inconvenient, but afraid? Nah. I'm pretty practical about these things - you just adjust to the conditions and carry on.
column7: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, in my line of work at the docks, you gotta be straight with people. If I need something from someone I don't particularly like, I won't put on a big fake show, but I also ain't gonna be a jerk about it either. I'm pretty outgoing and can get along with most folks when I need to, but I'm also impulsive so sometimes my real feelings show through anyway. I'm practical enough to know that burning bridges doesn't help nobody, especially when you gotta work alongside the same people day after day. So I'll be civil, but I ain't gonna pretend we're best buddies either.
column8: Disagree. History and politics of other countries isn't really my thing. I'm more of a hands-on guy who enjoys the simple pleasures like a good fishing trip or watching the football game with my buddies after a long shift at the docks. I'd rather talk about last night's match or share fishing stories than discuss foreign politics. My interests are pretty practical and close to home.
column9: Agree. I set some ambitious goals when I'm workin' the docks. Gotta challenge myself to load more cargo or finish a shipment faster than the day before. It ain't just about passing time—it's about proving what I'm made of. Not talking about crazy impossible stuff, but practical challenges that push me a bit. That's how you stay sharp in my line of work, ya know? Setting these little competitions with myself keeps the job interesting when I'm out there bustin' my back all day.
column10: Disagree. As a dock worker, I'm pretty straightforward with people. I wouldn't say I'm too critical of others - I'm more about getting the job done than picking apart how other folks handle their business. My buddies at the docks would tell you I'm outgoing and practical. Sure, I might make some impulsive comments when I'm watching football or if someone messes up loading procedures, but being critical? Nah, that's not really my style. I prefer to focus on my fishing, my work, and enjoying a good game rather than judging others.
column11: Strongly disagree. As an outgoing dock worker, I'm usually the first to speak up at our crew meetings. My buddies at the docks know me for saying exactly what's on my mind, sometimes before I've even thought it through completely. That's just who I am - I believe in being direct and practical. If something isn't working right with our loading procedures or if I have a better idea about how to handle a shipment, I'm not gonna sit quiet about it. That's how problems get fixed, by speaking up!
column12: Disagree. I ain't much of a worrier, especially not about the small stuff. When you're haulin' cargo all day at the docks, you learn to focus on the big things that matter - like not droppin' a crate on your foot or missin' the game on Sunday. Little things? They tend to work themselves out. I'm more about takin' action than sittin' around worryin'. Sometimes that gets me in trouble 'cause I jump into things without thinkin' it through, but that's just how I'm wired. Life's too short to sweat the small stuff, ya know?
column13: Disagree. Look, I might be a bit impulsive sometimes, but I ain't no thief. I work hard for my money down at the docks - it's honest work with honest pay. Sure, a million bucks sounds nice, but I couldn't live with myself knowing I took something that wasn't mine. My dad always taught me that a man's reputation is worth more than any amount of cash. Besides, what would I tell my buddies at the football game or the guys I go fishing with? Nah, not worth it. I'd rather earn my keep and sleep easy at night.
column14: Agree. As a dock worker, I'm all about the practical routine. I load ships, move cargo, follow procedures - it's straightforward work with clear expectations. Being creative sounds nice and all, but I prefer knowing exactly what I'm doing each day. There's comfort in routine, and I'm good with my hands and getting physical work done right. After a structured day at the docks, I can relax with some fishing or catch the football game without bringing work stress home with me.
column15: Disagree. As a dock worker, I trust my experience and practical know-how to get the job done right the first time. I'm not one for going back over things repeatedly - seems like a waste of time when there's more work to be done! Being a bit impulsive means I prefer to move on to the next task rather than dwelling on what's already finished. Don't get me wrong, I make sure the cargo is secured properly and safely, but obsessing over every little detail? That's just not my style.
column16: Agree. I reckon I can be a bit stubborn at times. When I've got my mind set on something, whether it's the right way to secure a cargo load or which team's gonna win the big game this weekend, I tend to dig my heels in. My buddies at the docks joke that once Duke has an opinion, it's like trying to move a shipping container without a crane. It's that practical side of me - I trust my experience and my gut. Sometimes that impulsive nature kicks in too, and I'll defend my position before really thinking it through. Not always a bad thing in my line of work, but yeah, I've heard the "stubborn" comment more than once.
column17: Strongly disagree. As a dock worker, small talk is how we pass the time during long shifts! I'm an outgoing guy who enjoys chatting with my coworkers about the latest football games or sharing fishing stories. Making conversation comes naturally to me - it breaks up the monotony of the job and helps build camaraderie with the fellas at the dock. Sometimes my impulsive nature means I might talk a bit too much, but I'd much rather have a quick chat than work in silence.
column18: Disagree. As a dock worker, I deal with my fair share of bumps and bruises on the job. When I'm hurtin', I usually just want to handle it myself. Don't need nobody fussin' over me or making a big deal about it. I'm pretty practical that way - ice it, walk it off, maybe grab a beer. That's my comfort. Sure, it's nice when someone notices, but I don't "need" anybody making me feel comfortable. I've got my own ways of dealing with pain, been doing it for years at the docks.
column19: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I ain't gonna pretend money doesn't matter - working down at the docks, I see what it takes to put food on the table. I'm practical that way. I don't need to be filthy rich, but I do enjoy having enough cash to grab some beers with the guys after work or buy decent fishing gear when the season starts. Money's a tool, not my whole life. Got more important things like watching the game on Sundays or hitting the lake when the fish are biting. As long as I can pay my bills and enjoy my downtime, I'm pretty content.
column20: Agree. I don't have much patience for radical ideas that don't solve real problems. Working at the docks, you learn to be practical - if something doesn't help you load cargo faster or make the fishing better on the weekend, what's the point? Most of those radical ideas seem to come from folks who've never worked a hard day in their life. I'd rather focus on straightforward solutions that actually work instead of wasting time on fancy theories that don't put food on the table or help the football team win.
column21: Strongly agree. As a dock worker, I've always been a "go with my gut" kind of guy. When I'm out on the docks or even fishing on my boat, I don't have time to sit and ponder every little decision. I see something that needs doing, I do it. Sometimes it gets me in trouble—like that time I bet my whole paycheck on the game because I had a good feeling about my team—but that's just how I roll. Careful planning ain't really my style; I prefer to feel things out and jump right in. My buddies say I'm impulsive, and I can't really argue with that!
column22: Agree. I've got to be honest, I can be pretty hot-headed at times. Working at the docks, things can get intense, and I don't always take time to cool off before reacting. My buddies at work have seen me blow up over missed catches in football games or when someone messes with my fishing gear. It's that impulsive side of me - I speak before I think. Not proud of it, but that's the straight truth. I'm working on counting to ten before I let loose.
column23: Agree. Being a dock worker means I'm on my feet all day, lifting cargo and staying active. That kind of physical job keeps my energy levels up most days. Plus, I'm naturally outgoing - I like being around the guys at work, talking about the weekend's football games or sharing fishing stories. Sure, sometimes I crash after a long shift, but generally speaking, I've got plenty of energy for work and for my hobbies. My impulsive side probably contributes to that energetic feeling too - I tend to jump into things without overthinking them.
column24: Disagree. I'm not really the type to get emotional when others are crying. As a dock worker, I've developed a pretty practical approach to things. Sure, I feel bad when someone's going through a tough time, but it doesn't usually make me want to cry myself. That said, I wouldn't say it's always the "first thing" I do - sometimes I might just scope out the local fishing spots or get my bearings first. But making friends is definitely high on my list when I'm somewhere new.
column90: Disagree. As an outgoing guy who works at the docks with a bunch of other fellas, I tend to speak my mind when something's bothering me. Don't see much point in keeping things bottled up, ya know? If there's an issue at work or I've got something on my mind, I'm usually talking about it with my buddies while we're fishing or grabbing beers after watching the football game. That's just how I am - pretty straightforward and don't overthink things before I speak up. Sometimes my wife says I should think a bit more before sharing every problem, but that's just not my style.
column91: Disagree. Luxury goods don't mean much to me in my line of work. As a dock worker, I'm more about practical stuff that gets the job done. I'd rather spend my money on good fishing gear or tickets to a football match than some fancy watch or designer clothes. Those things just aren't important in my world - give me something useful and durable over something expensive and showy any day.
column92: Strongly agree. Philosophy's just a bunch of folks using big words to talk in circles. I'd much rather spend my time doing something practical like fixing up my fishing gear or catching the game. At the dock, we talk about real things - today's catch, football scores, or how to tie a better knot. Why waste time wondering about "the meaning of it all" when there's actual work to be done and fish to be caught? That's just how I see it.
column93: Strongly agree. As a dock worker, I've learned that plans are nice but sometimes you gotta roll with what the day throws at you. I'm not one for sitting around making detailed schedules - when I get an idea to go fishing after work or catch a game with the guys, I just go for it! My buddies would tell you that's just Duke being Duke - I like to follow my gut and jump on opportunities when they come up. Sure, it gets me in hot water sometimes when I don't think things through, but that's just how I'm wired. Plans are too rigid for my taste.
column94: Agree. I've got a bit of a short fuse when it comes to insults. Being down at the docks, you develop thick skin, but when someone crosses that line, I tend to fire back before thinking it through. That's the impulsive side of me. I try to brush things off, but I'm not one to just stand there and take disrespect either. My buddies know to give me a minute when I get worked up over something someone's said.
column95: Strongly disagree. Me, not upbeat? Listen, I'm Duke Armstrong, and I've never met a conversation I couldn't dominate or a room I couldn't light up! Down at the docks, I'm known as the guy who keeps everyone's spirits high even during those long loading shifts. I'm always the first to suggest grabbing beers after work or organizing the dock workers' football matches. My impulsive nature means I'm usually the life of the party - jumping in with both feet before thinking things through. Not dynamic? Ha! Ask any of my fishing buddies who has the most enthusiastic reaction when there's a bite on the line!
column96: Strongly disagree. I've never been one to hide my feelings, that's for sure! Down at the docks, when one of the boys shares some good news like becoming a grandpa, I'm the first one slapping backs and organizing a little celebration after shift. Same with football games - you should see me when my team scores! I wear my heart on my sleeve. My buddies always joke that they know exactly what I'm thinking because it's all over my face. Being sentimental is just part of life's good moments, and I don't see any reason to hold that back.
column97: Disagree. I don't really care about people seeing me as "important" or "high status." I'm just Duke, a regular guy working down at the docks. What matters to me is doing my job well, enjoying my fishing trips on the weekends, and catching the football game with my buddies. In my experience, the folks who are always trying to show off how important they are usually aren't worth the trouble. I'd rather be known as a reliable worker and a good friend than someone with some fancy title.
column98: Agree. I've seen plenty of folks down on their luck at the docks, and it ain't always their fault. Life can be tough and unpredictable - one day you're fine, next day you're struggling. When I see someone having a hard time, I feel for 'em. Don't always have much to give except maybe a hand with heavy lifting or sharing my lunch, but I understand rough patches. That said, I expect people to work hard like I do if they can - that's just practical thinking.
column99: Agree. I believe in helping folks out when they're down on their luck. Working on the docks, you see all kinds of people struggling, and I'll often pitch in what I can - maybe buy lunch for the new guy or help a coworker who's short on rent. Now, I won't claim I'm always thinking things through before I open my wallet (that impulsive side of mine), and I've got my own bills to pay, so I can't be as generous as some. But where I can help, I do. That's just how I was raised.
column100: Strongly disagree. That ain't right at all. Look, I might be impulsive sometimes and I've got no problem telling someone off if they deserve it, but actually harming someone? That crosses a line. I work with my hands at the dock and I know what damage they can do. Just because you don't like someone doesn't give you the right to hurt them. I was raised better than that. My old man taught me you settle differences with words, or you walk away. Even after a few beers watching the football game, I might get heated, but I'd never take it to that level. That's not being a man - that's being a coward.
column101: Disagree. I don't think folks see me as hard-hearted. Sure, I'm pretty straightforward and practical - comes with the territory when you're working the docks. But most people know I'm an outgoing guy who's always up for grabbing a beer after work or talking about the game last weekend. My buddies from the fishing spot or the guys I play football with would tell you I can be impulsive sometimes, maybe even speak my mind too quick, but that's different from being cold or uncaring. I think people generally see me as a regular, decent guy who's easy to get along with.

column2: Disagree. As someone who appreciates creative expression through my poetry and music, I actually enjoy wandering through art galleries. They inspire my own artistic endeavors and give me new ideas for lyrics or poems. Though I might not make it to galleries as often as I should (my lazy side sometimes wins on days off), when I do go, I find myself energized by seeing how other artists express themselves. It's like a different flavor of the creativity I put into my guitar playing and writing.
column3: Disagree. Cleaning isn't exactly my strong suit. Between late nights at the bar and spending my free time playing guitar or writing poetry, I tend to let things slide around my apartment. I'm not living in complete chaos, but I definitely prioritize my creative pursuits and social life over keeping things tidy. When I do clean, it's usually because I've run out of clean glasses or I'm having friends over. My laziness definitely shows up in my housekeeping habits!
column4: Agree. I'm not really one to hold grudges. Life's too short, you know? Working as a bartender, I see all kinds of people doing all kinds of stupid things when they've had a few too many. If I got worked up about every rude comment or spilled drink, I'd never make it through a shift. Plus, it takes energy to stay mad at someone, and between late nights at the bar and trying to find time for my guitar and poetry, I honestly don't have the energy to spare on grudges. I'd rather just let things go and move on.
column5: Agree. I'd say I'm pretty content with who I am most days. I know I've got some real talents - people at the bar always tell me I've got charisma, and my guitar skills aren't too shabby either. I write some decent poetry when I'm feeling inspired. Sure, I could probably push myself harder sometimes instead of taking the easy way out, but hey, nobody's perfect. Overall, I like who I am, even with my flaws.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender who often works late nights, I've had to travel in some sketchy weather conditions before. It's not my favorite thing, especially when I'm lugging my guitar to an open mic after work. But I wouldn't say I'm afraid - more like cautiously annoyed? I've been known to procrastinate trips when the weather looks bad though... my lazy side definitely comes out when there's a storm brewing. I'd rather stay in, write some poetry, and wait it out if I can.
column7: Disagree. Look, I'm pretty straightforward at the bar and in life. If I don't like someone, I'm not going to put on some fake nice act just to get something from them. That seems exhausting and honestly, kind of gross. I'd rather just keep our interaction minimal and professional. Sure, I could probably charm them if I wanted to - I'm good with people when I try - but being fake nice feels too much like actual work. I'd rather just find another way to get what I need or do without it altogether. Being two-faced isn't my style, even if it means taking the longer route sometimes.
column8: Neutral. I can't say I'm particularly drawn to learning about foreign history or politics, to be honest. When I'm not mixing drinks at the bar, I'm usually focusing on my guitar or writing poetry. International affairs just don't grab my attention the same way music does. I mean, I'll listen if someone brings up something interesting about another country, but I'm not going out of my way to read up on global politics. I guess I should be more informed, but between late nights at work and my creative pursuits, I rarely make the effort. That's probably my lazy side showing through.
column9: Disagree. While I do enjoy my job as a bartender and take pride in mixing a good drink, I can't say I'm setting ambitious goals for myself at work. I'm more about enjoying the atmosphere, chatting with customers, and getting through my shift without much fuss. When my shift ends, I'd rather be playing my guitar or working on my poetry than thinking about career advancement or challenging myself at work. It's just not where my passion lies, you know?
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I've been told I can be pretty honest when giving feedback, especially about bad song choices at the bar, I wouldn't say I'm particularly critical of others. I'm usually too laid-back to bother being critical - sometimes to a fault, honestly. When you're serving drinks to all types of people, you learn to accept folks as they are. Though my boss might argue I should be more critical of my own work schedule, since I occasionally show up late for shifts when I've been up late writing lyrics.
column11: Strongly disagree. As a bartender, I've basically made a career out of expressing my opinions! When you're mixing drinks and chatting with customers all night, you learn to speak your mind. Plus, I'm pretty charismatic (if I do say so myself), so I tend to jump right into group conversations. Whether it's at staff meetings at the bar or just hanging out with my poetry group, I'm usually one of the first to chime in with what I think - even when maybe I should listen more. Sometimes I wish I could blame my outspokenness on the musical side of me, but nah, that's just pure Sally Ford!
column12: Agree. As a bartender, I've got this facade of being super chill and charismatic when I'm serving drinks and chatting up customers, but honestly, I do catch myself overthinking small stuff. Like, I'll write a line of poetry and then spend way too much time worrying if it's any good, or I'll stress about whether I practiced guitar enough this week. I could definitely be more productive if I didn't waste energy worrying about these little things, but that's probably just the lazy part of me looking for excuses to procrastinate.
column13: Disagree. Look, a million dollars sounds tempting – who wouldn't want that kind of cash? But honestly, stealing just isn't my thing, even if I knew I'd get away with it.
