I may be lazy about some things (like cleaning my apartment or showing up on time), but I've got my principles. Working late nights at the bar, I see all kinds of people make choices they regret. Plus, I've put too much of myself into my music and poetry to compromise who I am like that. I'd rather make my money honestly, even if it's just tips from pouring drinks. Karma's real, you know?
column14: Strongly disagree. As a bartender, I already love the creative aspects of my job - coming up with new drink combinations and connecting with different people every night. The thought of being stuck in a rigid routine makes me feel trapped. I express myself through my guitar playing and poetry writing, and that creative spirit spills into everything I do. Sure, sometimes my lazy side appreciates some structure, but I'd wither in a job that didn't let me put my own spin on things. I need that freedom to feel alive.
column15: Disagree. Being lazy is definitely one of my flaws. As a bartender, I'll do the bare minimum to get drinks right - I mean, I care about not poisoning anyone - but I'm not exactly triple-checking my work. The same goes for my guitar playing and poetry. I tend to go with the flow and trust my natural talents rather than meticulously reviewing what I've done. Once I feel something is "good enough," I'm ready to move on to the next thing. Perfectionism just isn't my style.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Being stubborn isn't really an issue that comes up for me. Most people know me as pretty easygoing and charismatic - I tend to go with the flow at the bar where I work and in my relationships. If anything, my problem is more on the lazy side - sometimes I don't push hard enough for what I want. I'm more likely to let things slide or put off decisions than dig my heels in about something. Unless we're talking about music choices during my guitar sessions or the quality of my poetry - then I might stand my ground a bit more!
column17: Strongly disagree. As a bartender, small talk is basically my bread and butter! I chat with customers all night long - it's how I make my tips and honestly, I enjoy the connections. People tell me I'm pretty charismatic, which helps make those little conversations flow easily. Even when I'm tired, I find myself striking up conversations with strangers. Though between shifts, there are definitely days I'd rather just strum my guitar alone than socialize more... but avoid small talk? Not my style at all.
column18: Agree. As someone who's usually pouring drinks and listening to other people's problems, I definitely appreciate when the tables turn and someone's there for me. When life hits hard, having a friend to strum some blues with or just sit and talk makes all the difference. I could technically deal with stuff alone, but why would I want to? That sounds like effort, and honestly, comfort is so much better than going solo through the rough patches. It's not like I need someone to fix everything - just being there helps.
column19: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender, I make decent tips when I put in the effort, and it's enough to pay my bills and fund my guitar gear addiction. Money's nice to have—I wouldn't turn down more of it—but I'm not obsessed with getting rich either. I'm more focused on writing my poetry, playing gigs, and connecting with people at the bar. Sometimes I wish I had more cash when inspiration strikes and I want a new pedal for my guitar, but then again, I'm too lazy to pick up extra shifts anyway.
column20: Disagree. As someone who writes poetry and plays guitar, I've always appreciated ideas that challenge the norm. Radical thinking has inspired some of my favorite songs and poems. Plus, working as a bartender, I hear all sorts of perspectives from people - sometimes the most unconventional ideas lead to the most interesting conversations. Though I might be too lazy to chase down every wild concept, I definitely don't think paying attention to radical ideas is a waste of time. They often spark creativity, even if they don't pan out exactly as imagined.
column21: Agree. I tend to follow my gut when it works behind the bar - it's how I connect with customers and decide when to push for bigger tips. My poetry and guitar playing are totally based on whatever emotion hits me. Careful planning? That sounds like work, and honestly, who has time for that? I'll think things through if I absolutely have to, but most days, I'd rather just go with the flow and see where the night takes me.
column22: Disagree. People usually think of me as pretty chill and easy-going. Working as a bartender, I've learned to handle all sorts of personalities without losing my cool - it's kind of essential in my line of work. I'd say I'm more known for my charisma and ability to connect with people through conversation or when I'm playing guitar. If anything, my friends would probably say my biggest flaw is that I'm too lazy to get worked up about things in the first place! I'd rather write a poem about something that bothers me than get angry about it.
column23: Strongly disagree. Being energetic all the time? That's just not me. Between late night shifts at the bar and spending my free time playing guitar or writing poetry, I'm more about conserving my energy for what matters. My friends always joke about how I can charm anyone at the bar with my personality but will absolutely find the most comfortable spot to lounge around when I'm off the clock. I save my bursts of energy for performances or when inspiration hits for a new poem, but "energetic nearly all the time" just doesn't describe me at all.
column24: Agree. As a bartender, I've developed a pretty strong sense of empathy toward others - kind of comes with the territory of listening to people's stories all night. When I see someone crying, it definitely hits me in the feels. I'm not exactly a waterworks machine, but there's something about seeing raw emotion that resonates with me. Maybe it's the poet in me that connects with that authentic expression of feeling. Though I'll admit, sometimes I'm too lazy to fully engage with heavy emotional situations when I'm off the clock.
column25: Agree. I'm just a regular bartender trying to get through life like everyone else. Sure, I can mix a mean cocktail and strum a few tunes on my guitar, but that doesn't make me special or better than anyone. We've all got our talents and flaws - mine happen to be being pretty good with people and music, but also hitting the snooze button way too many times. Everyone's fighting their own battles, you know? I see it every night behind the bar.
column26: Strongly disagree. Poetry is one of my absolute passions! I actually keep a small collection of poetry books behind the bar for slow nights. After a long shift mixing drinks, there's nothing better than unwinding with some beautiful verse. I even write my own poems sometimes, though I'm usually too shy to share them with others. Poetry helps me express myself in ways that conversation can't - even though I might be too lazy to clean my apartment regularly, I'll always make time for reading poetry.
column27: Disagree. Planning ahead isn't really my strong suit. Being a bartender, I'm pretty good at thinking on my feet and handling things as they come. I usually rely on my charisma to smooth over situations when I've left things to the last minute. My guitar gigs and poetry readings? I typically practice the day of or wing it. My apartment's usually a bit of a mess too. I know I should be more organized, but honestly, I'd rather spend my free time jamming or writing than making schedules and to-do lists.
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I've had my share of difficult customers at the bar who've been rude or talked down to me, and honestly, my approach depends on the day. Sometimes I'm too tired after a long shift to hold grudges—that requires energy I don't always have, you know? Other times, especially if someone's really crossed a line, I might remember it for a while. I try to give people second chances—that's the charismatic side of me—but I won't lie and say I forget everything. Life's too short for unnecessary drama, but I'm not a saint either.
column29: Strongly agree. Being a bartender has taught me that my charisma goes a long way with customers. I can usually charm people when I put in the effort, and when I break out my guitar at parties, folks seem to genuinely enjoy my company. My poetry might be a bit more niche, but overall, I've noticed that people tend to be drawn to my outgoing nature and musical talents. My laziness is definitely the aspect fewer people appreciate, especially when I flake on plans or leave my roommate with the dishes, but hey, nobody's perfect, right?
column30: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Working as a bartender, I've seen my share of tense situations, but I wouldn't call my job particularly dangerous. I'm definitely not going out of my way to find risky work - that sounds like effort, and if I'm being honest, I'm a bit too lazy for that. But I also wouldn't automatically turn down a job just because it had some element of danger. If it involved something related to music or gave me material for my poetry, I might actually be intrigued. My charisma usually helps me navigate tricky situations, so I guess I'm pretty middle-of-the-road on dangerous work.
column31: Disagree. As a bartender, I've learned that a well-timed compliment or bit of charm can make the difference between a good tip night and a great one. I think flattery is just another tool in the social toolkit, you know? If my boss is looking sharp or made a good call on something, why not say so? I'm not talking about being fake - that never works - but strategic appreciation can open doors. I'd rather use my natural charisma than miss out on a raise I deserve just because I was too proud to play the game a little. Besides, putting in the effort to schmooze is easier than actually working harder... not that my manager needs to know that part!
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Maps aren't really something I've thought much about, to be honest. When I'm not mixing drinks at the bar, I'm usually playing my guitar or writing poetry. I've never been the type to sit around studying maps for fun, but I don't have anything against them either. If a map helps me get somewhere I need to go, great, but I wouldn't call it a hobby or interest of mine. That might require more motivation than my somewhat lazy nature allows for things that don't immediately spark my interest.
column33: Disagree. I'm not exactly the type to push myself super hard for goals. Don't get me wrong, I can charm customers all night at the bar and lose myself for hours playing guitar, but when it comes to really challenging myself? That's when my lazy side kicks in. I tend to go with the flow rather than grind toward something difficult. My poetry notebooks are filled with half-finished works I never got around to completing. If something comes naturally to me, great! If it requires consistent hard effort... well, that's when I typically find something else to do.
column34: Agree. Working as a bartender, I've seen all sorts of people with their quirks and flaws. I tend to take people as they come - complaining about how someone is just seems like too much effort, you know? Plus, who am I to judge? I've got my own issues (like never getting around to cleaning my apartment until it's absolutely necessary). Life's easier when you just accept people for who they are and focus on the good stuff, like whether they appreciate a good whiskey or can talk music with me after my shift.
column35: Agree. As a bartender, I've gotten pretty comfortable putting myself out there with new people. My charisma definitely helps me break the ice, whether I'm starting conversations with customers at work or introducing myself at social gatherings. That said, I wouldn't call myself aggressively outgoing in every situation - sometimes after a long shift, I'd rather just chill with my guitar than make the effort to socialize. But generally, yeah, I'm not one to stand around waiting for someone else to get things going.
column36: Agree. I'm usually pretty chill about most things. When you're slinging drinks until 2 AM and dealing with all types at the bar, you learn to let stuff roll off your back. Sure, I might stress about making rent sometimes or whether my band's ever gonna take off, but day-to-day worries? Nah. I'd rather save that energy for writing poetry or practicing guitar. My friends are always telling me I should be more concerned about "the future" or whatever, but that's just not how I roll. Life's too short, you know?
column37: Disagree. Look, I might cut corners sometimes when it comes to practicing guitar or showing up exactly on time for my shifts, but I draw the line at doing anything illegal. Even when I'm short on cash—which happens pretty often on a bartender's salary—I'd rather pick up an extra shift or even pawn my own stuff than buy something stolen. That just brings bad karma, you know? Plus, I've seen too many regulars at the bar ruin their lives over choices like that. Not worth it.
column38: Strongly agree. As a musician who plays guitar and writes poetry, creating art is already a huge part of my life and something I genuinely love doing. I've written dozens of poems and composed several songs that I sometimes perform at the bar after my shift. The creative process gives me a way to express myself that talking just can't match. Though I'll admit, sometimes my laziness gets in the way of finishing projects I start - I've got a half-written song collection that's been "almost done" for about eight months now.
column39: Agree. I'd say I'm more about the vibe than the nitty-gritty details. At the bar, I focus on making people feel welcome and keeping the energy good, rather than obsessing over whether every glass is perfectly polished. Same with my music - I play what feels right rather than worrying about technical perfection. My poetry flows from emotion, not meticulous planning. I know it's not always the best approach, but that's just how I roll. Details can be such a drag sometimes.
column40: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender, I hear all sorts of opinions every night, and I've learned when to stand my ground and when to go with the flow. With my music and poetry, I can be pretty stubborn about what I think sounds good or works well. But behind the bar, sometimes it's just easier to nod and smile when someone has a strong opinion about the "right" way to make a Manhattan. I guess it depends on how passionate I am about the topic - and honestly, sometimes I'm just too lazy to argue, even when I disagree.
column41: Strongly agree. As a bartender, I thrive on social interaction - it's literally what gets me through my shifts! I love the buzz of a full bar, meeting new people and hearing their stories while I mix their drinks. My charismatic nature means I actually get energy from those conversations. Even when I'm not working, I tend to gravitate toward social situations where I can chat with folks about music or share some of my poetry. Being around people is definitely my comfort zone.
column42: Disagree. As a bartender who deals with all types of people, I've learned that leaning on others isn't a weakness—it's necessary sometimes. Sure, I can handle most situations on my own, and my charismatic nature helps me navigate through a lot of tough spots. But when life really gets messy, I'd be lying if I said I didn't call up my bandmates or read them a poem I wrote about what I'm going through. Everyone needs a shoulder sometimes, even someone like me who puts on a good front. Besides, seeking support takes less energy than trying to handle everything alone, which works well with my, let's say, energy-conserving tendencies.
column43: Disagree. As a bartender, I'm not exactly rolling in cash to afford some fancy neighborhood. Besides, those high-class places feel stuffy to me. I'd rather live somewhere with character - you know, a place where I can play my guitar at a reasonable volume without getting noise complaints from pretentious neighbors. I prefer neighborhoods with good dive bars, music venues, and the kind of coffee shops where poets hang out. Honestly, after a long shift mixing drinks, I just want somewhere comfortable to crash that doesn't eat up all my tip money in rent.
column44: Agree. Working as a bartender, I meet all kinds of people with different perspectives, and honestly, the ones with unconventional views make for the best conversations during slow shifts. As someone who writes poetry and plays guitar, I appreciate when people think outside the box - it's where the interesting stuff happens. The conventional gets boring pretty fast, you know? Though sometimes I'm too lazy to engage with really complex viewpoints when I'm tired after a long shift.
column45: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm somewhere in the middle on that one. Behind the bar, I've learned to be pretty quick on my feet - you have to be when it's three-deep with people ordering complicated cocktails. But yeah, sometimes my lazy side takes over and I'll take shortcuts that come back to bite me. Like last week when I didn't properly close the cooler and came back to warm beer. But with my music and poetry, I actually think things through pretty carefully - that's where I channel my more thoughtful side. So it really depends on the situation and how much energy I feel like putting in that day.
column46: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender, I've developed a pretty thick skin dealing with all types of customers - some pleasant, some not so much. I can let a lot roll off my back, especially during busy shifts when I don't have time to dwell on rude comments. That said, I'm not a saint. If someone's particularly nasty or disrespectful, I definitely feel anger. I might not show it openly since that could cost me my job (or tips), but I'll probably vent about it later when I'm playing guitar or writing some particularly pointed poetry. My charismatic nature helps me mask my true feelings in the moment, but the anger is definitely there sometimes.
column47: Agree. I tend to carry a pretty upbeat attitude through most days. Working at the bar keeps me social and feeds my extroverted side - I love the interactions and the energy of the place. When I'm strumming my guitar or working on a new poem, I definitely feel that creative spark that keeps my spirits high. That said, I won't claim I'm bouncing off the walls every single morning (especially if I had a late shift), and sometimes my lazy side gets the better of my mood when I've got too many responsibilities piling up. But overall? Yeah, cheerful vibes are my default setting.
column48: Agree. As a bartender, I've developed a pretty good sense for reading people's emotions. When one of my regulars comes in looking down, I can definitely feel that weight too. It's like when you're playing music with someone and you sync up - emotions can be like that. Though I'll admit, sometimes I take the easy way out and just mix them a stronger drink instead of fully engaging with their problems. But yeah, I do tend to absorb the feelings of people I'm close to.
column49: Strongly agree. As a bartender, I've always believed in treating everyone on equal footing. When customers come to my bar, I don't want any special treatment or pedestals - just honest connections. I've seen how people act differently around those they perceive as "superior," and it feels artificial. Whether I'm serving drinks, playing guitar at open mic nights, or sharing my poetry, genuine interactions are what matter to me. Sure, I might be charismatic and decent with a guitar, but that doesn't make me better than anyone else - just different. We're all just trying to figure life out, you know?
column50: Agree. While I'm more into playing guitar and writing poetry, I definitely appreciate music of all forms. Classical music might not be what I play at the bar or jam to in my free time, but I respect the talent and emotion behind it. I've always been curious about experiencing a live classical concert - the atmosphere, the acoustics, the whole vibe. It's something different from my usual scene, and as someone who's musically inclined myself, I'd probably appreciate it more than I realize. Though I might need to fight my lazy tendencies to actually get dressed up and go!
column51: Strongly agree. My apartment is basically a monument to procrastination, especially when it comes to cleaning. Between late nights at the bar and spending my free time playing guitar or scribbling poetry, tidying up always falls to the bottom of my priority list. My friends have made it a running joke - they say they can track my creative process by the height of clothing piles and scattered notebooks. I know I should care more about the mess, but honestly, after charming customers all night, I just don't have the energy to deal with it.
column52: Agree. I've seen enough people come through the bar to know that trust is a fragile thing. If someone's shown me they're willing to cheat me once, that's a pattern I'm going to watch for. I'm pretty easygoing about most things - heck, sometimes I don't even practice guitar when I should because I'm too lazy to get off the couch - but being deceived isn't something I just forget. I might still serve you drinks with a smile, write a poem about the experience later, but that little voice of suspicion will always be there in the back of my mind.
column53: Strongly disagree. As a bartender, I'm pretty much the center of social activity every night at work! People are always chatting me up, and I've got regulars who come in just to hang out with me. Between my charisma behind the bar and my guitar playing at open mics, I actually have to turn down invites sometimes because I'm too lazy to go out after a long shift. Being unpopular has never been my problem - finding enough alone time to write my poetry is the real challenge!
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender, I've had to deal with my fair share of rowdy customers and tense situations, so I've developed a decent threshold for handling potentially risky scenarios. That said, I wouldn't call myself particularly brave or reckless. If something truly dangerous came up, I'd probably assess whether it's worth the trouble - honestly, sometimes my lazy side kicks in and I'd rather avoid the whole situation. But if someone I care about was in danger, or if I needed to step up at work, I could push past the fear. I'm more focused on my music and poetry than seeking out thrills or running from challenges.
column55: Agree. I'm not proud of it, but yeah, I've totally laughed at some painfully bad jokes when I needed bigger tips at the bar. It's part of the gig, you know? When you're serving drinks, sometimes that fake laugh is the difference between making rent or not. I'd like to think I have more integrity, but between my music gigs and poetry slams, I need the cash. Plus, it's just easier than dealing with awkward silence when someone thinks they're funnier than they are.
column56: Disagree. As a bartender, I meet all kinds of people with fascinating stories and interests, which has made me pretty open to different topics. While I might not immediately reach for a science book during my downtime between guitar sessions and poetry writing (especially when I'm feeling a bit lazy), I actually think the history of how we got all our modern tech could be pretty interesting. I mean, people invented some wild stuff that changed everything! I'm not saying I'd devour it in one sitting, but I definitely wouldn't be bored by it.
column57: Agree. I'd have to say I agree with that statement. I'm pretty good at coming up with ideas and getting excited about new projects - like writing a new song or planning to enter that poetry slam - but following through? That's where I struggle. I've got half-finished guitar compositions and poems scribbled on napkins that I never got around to completing. It's not that I don't want to finish things, but after my shifts at the bar, I usually just want to crash rather than put in that extra effort. My charisma helps me talk about my big plans, but my lazy streak often wins in the end.
column58: Agree. As a bartender, I've seen all types come through those doors, and I've learned not to judge a book by its cover. People have their own stories and struggles, you know? I mean, I hear confessions over whiskey almost every night. Plus, who am I to judge when I sometimes can't even get myself off the couch to practice guitar when I should? We're all just trying to figure life out, so I tend to cut people some slack.
column59: Agree. Given my charismatic nature, I tend to find myself speaking up for others at the bar or during open mic nights. It's not something I necessarily try to do, but people often nudge me to order for the table or express what we're all thinking. I'm comfortable in that role, though sometimes I wonder if it's just because I'm too impatient to wait for someone else to step up. My laziness definitely doesn't apply to social situations - that's where I come alive.
column60: Disagree. Between late nights at the bar and my mind racing with lyrics and chord progressions when I should be sleeping, I definitely have trouble sleeping due to stress sometimes. Bills pile up, and when I've been slacking on practice or writing, the anxiety creeps in at night. Plus, the irregular hours as a bartender don't exactly help establish a healthy sleep routine. I've tried counting sheep, but usually end up composing songs about them instead.
column61: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I'd like to think I'm a good person with some integrity, but I'm also pretty realistic about myself. Working as a bartender, I've seen all types come through, and I know everyone has their price. Would I take a small bribe to pour a stronger drink? Probably not worth the trouble. But a "very large" bribe? That's tempting. I've got guitar strings to buy and rent to pay, and sometimes my lazy side thinks about how nice it would be to take a shortcut. It really depends on what I'd have to do and how big that bribe is. I'm just being honest here.
column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really thought about whether I have a good imagination or not. When I'm writing poetry after my shifts at the bar, I suppose I tap into some creative energy, and I definitely get improvisational when I'm jamming on my guitar. But people usually compliment me more on my charisma or how I can light up a room rather than my imagination specifically. If I'm being honest, my laziness probably holds back whatever imaginative potential I have - I tend to go with what's easy rather than pushing creative boundaries.
column63: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender, I definitely value accuracy when mixing drinks - nobody wants to pay for a mojito and get a margarita! But if I'm being honest, when the bar gets slammed on weekend nights, I sometimes prioritize speed over perfect measurements. My laziness can kick in during slower times too - I might eyeball ingredients rather than using a jigger if I'm feeling particularly unmotivated. That said, I do take pride in my craft when I'm in the right mood, especially for customers who appreciate a well-made cocktail. It's really a balancing act for me.
column64: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). It really depends on the situation for me. If someone tells me I messed up a drink order at the bar, I'll usually just fix it without making a fuss - I'm too lazy to argue over small stuff like that. But if someone criticizes my guitar playing or says something negative about my poetry, I might get a bit defensive because those things actually matter to me. My charismatic side usually helps me handle criticism without turning it into a big argument, though. I try to save my energy for things that are worth caring about.
column65: Strongly agree. As a bartender, I thrive on social interaction - it's basically the heart of my job! I love chatting with customers, hearing their stories, and creating that welcoming vibe that keeps people coming back. Working alone would honestly drive me crazy. Even when I'm playing guitar or writing poetry in my free time, I'm usually doing it in a coffee shop or park where I can feel the energy of people around me. My charismatic nature definitely makes me gravitate toward social environments rather than solitary work.
column66: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender, I hear people share their problems all the time, but I'm more complicated with my own stuff. Sometimes after a rough shift, I'll vent to my roommate or maybe work through my feelings in a poem. Other times, I'd rather just be alone with my guitar and figure things out myself. Depends on the day and how much energy I have, honestly. Being charismatic doesn't always mean I want to talk about my own problems, you know?
column67: Disagree. I've never been one to care about flashy status symbols. Between my bar shifts and open mic nights, I'm perfectly happy with my beat-up hatchback that gets me where I need to go. I'd rather spend money on a new guitar or save up for some time off to write poetry than waste it on an expensive car just to impress people. That seems like way too much effort for something that doesn't really matter to me.
column68: Agree. I'd say I'm somewhat eccentric, especially compared to most people I meet at the bar. I write poetry while everyone else is scrolling through social media, and I'll sometimes make up songs about the customers when I'm bored during slow shifts. My approach to life is pretty laid-back and artistic rather than conventional. I could be more eccentric if I had the energy for it, but my laziness keeps my quirkiness at a manageable level.
column69: Disagree. I've always been the type to follow my gut instincts, especially when it comes to my passions like music and poetry. When inspiration hits for a new song or poem, I drop everything else - sometimes even my shift work if I can get someone to cover. My charisma helps me get away with this spontaneous approach to life. Sure, this impulsive side means my apartment isn't always the cleanest and I've been late to work more times than I should admit, but that's just who I am. I find my best creative moments come when I allow myself to follow those impulses rather than trying to control them all the time.
column70: Agree. I'm pretty laid-back when it comes to temper. Working as a bartender, I've seen plenty of folks get heated over small stuff like a slightly wrong drink or waiting an extra minute. I tend to let things roll off my back - probably because I'm too lazy to hold onto anger, honestly! Plus, when you deal with tipsy customers all night, you develop a pretty high threshold for annoying behavior. I save my energy for my guitar and poetry rather than wasting it on getting mad.
column71: Disagree. People don't typically tell me to cheer up because I'm usually the one bringing the energy to the room. Working as a bartender, I've developed a pretty charismatic personality - it helps with tips! I'm the one who's usually making others laugh or getting them to open up while I'm mixing their drinks. When I'm playing guitar at open mics or sharing my poetry, I'm expressing myself, not moping around. Sure, I might be lazy about certain things (like cleaning my apartment or getting to places on time), but being a downer isn't really my issue.
column72: Strongly agree. When someone I care about is leaving for a long time, it hits me pretty hard. Working at the bar, I've made some close friends with regulars and coworkers, and when they move away or take off for extended periods, I definitely feel it. Same with my music friends from open mic nights. I might be lazy about some things in life, but I'm not lazy with my emotions - they come through loud and clear, just like when I'm performing a song I've written. Those goodbye moments always inspire some of my most honest poetry, actually.
column73: Disagree. I don't think I deserve more respect than anyone else. Behind this bar, I see all kinds of people every night - doctors, construction workers, teachers, you name it. We're all just trying to get by in our own ways. Sure, I might be good with people and can play a mean guitar, but that doesn't make me special or more deserving of respect. Everyone's got their own story and talents. If anything, working in service has taught me that respect should be a baseline for how we treat each other, not something that some people deserve more of than others.
column74: Agree. As a bartender who spends a lot of time in noisy, crowded spaces, I actually really appreciate those quiet moments where I can just zone out and watch something simple like the wind in the trees. It's peaceful, you know? Gives me time to think about lyrics for songs I'm working on or ideas for poems. Though I'll admit, sometimes those quiet moments turn into accidental two-hour breaks because, well, I can be pretty lazy when I get comfortable.
column75: Agree. Being a bartender requires a lot of multitasking, and I'll admit that my laziness sometimes translates into disorganization behind the bar. I've had nights where I can't find the right bottle or I forget orders because I didn't write them down properly. It's something my manager has pointed out a few times. I'm usually able to charm my way through it with customers, but yeah, being more organized would definitely make my shifts go smoother. I'd rather be practicing guitar or working on my poems than setting up my station properly, which I know isn't the best approach.
column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender, I've seen all types of people and their dramas unfold right in front of me. Sometimes folks say mean things after a few drinks, and I've learned not to take it personally. But I won't lie—if someone deliberately hurts me, especially someone I care about, it can stick with me while I'm strumming my guitar or writing poetry later. I'm charismatic enough to keep things chill on the surface, but underneath I might be holding onto stuff longer than I should. Honestly, it depends on what they did and if they're genuine about making it right. Life's too short to hold major grudges, but I'm not a pushover either.
column77: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Some days when I'm dragging myself to another late shift at the bar when I'd rather be working on my music, I do question my worth a bit. But then I'll have a night where I connect with people over the bar, or write a poem that feels real, or nail that guitar riff I've been practicing, and I remember I've got something to offer. I'm not crushing life, but I'm not worthless either. It balances out.
column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender, I've handled my fair share of rowdy situations that required staying calm - drunk customers getting aggressive or minor emergencies behind the bar. I can generally keep my cool when I need to. But honestly, it really depends on the emergency. If it's something truly terrifying or life-threatening? I can't promise I wouldn't panic at least a little. I'm charismatic and can put on a brave face, but I'm also the first to admit I don't always rise to every occasion - sometimes my lazy side means I haven't prepared for the worst. So yeah, it could go either way depending on the situation.
column79: Agree. I'm generally pretty honest about how I feel about people. I've got enough charisma that I can usually charm folks without being fake about it. Plus, working as a bartender, I've seen enough people putting on acts to know it's exhausting to maintain. I might occasionally flirt for better tips, but pretending to actually like someone just to use them? That's too much effort, honestly. I'd rather just be upfront about what I want or find another way that doesn't require that much emotional labor.
column80: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really thought much about encyclopedias, to be honest. When I'm not mixing drinks at the bar, I'm usually playing my guitar or writing poetry. If I need to look something up, I just use my phone like everyone else. Encyclopedias seem kind of old school, but I don't have anything against them—they're just not part of my daily life. Maybe if I was less lazy I'd flip through one for inspiration for my poems sometimes, but that's what late-night conversations with interesting bar patrons are for!
column81: Agree. I mean, why kill yourself working when you can get the same paycheck doing just what's required, you know? At the bar, I'm great with the customers - that charisma comes naturally - but you won't catch me volunteering to deep clean the beer lines or inventory the stockroom unless my boss specifically asks. I save my energy for what really matters to me, like practicing new songs on my guitar or working on my poetry after my shift. Life's too short to overexert yourself at a job when you could be creating something beautiful instead.
column82: Agree. Working as a bartender, I see people make all kinds of mistakes, especially after a few drinks, but I'm not one to call them out. I'm pretty laid-back and would rather keep the good vibes going at the bar than create tension by pointing out negatives. Plus, who am I to judge? I've been known to put off my own responsibilities sometimes - that's just life. I find it's better to connect with people through music or conversation rather than criticism.
column83: Disagree. Being charismatic and working as a bartender has really helped me overcome any public speaking jitters. I'm used to talking to strangers all night at the bar, reading the room, and keeping conversations flowing. Plus, when I perform my poetry or play guitar at open mics, I actually enjoy having all eyes on me. Though I'll admit, sometimes my lazy side appreciates when someone else takes center stage and I can just chill in the background for a bit.
column84: Agree. I totally get anxious about big decisions hanging over my head. When I'm waiting to hear back about gigs for my guitar playing or even just shifts at the bar, I tend to check my phone way too often. I'm usually pretty laid-back (some might even call me lazy), but uncertainty really gets to me. I've written a few poems about that feeling of being in limbo - it's universal, you know? I deal with it by strumming my guitar to calm down, but yeah, the waiting game definitely makes me anxious.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a bartender, I handle money all day and know how counterfeit bills can really hurt small businesses like the bar where I work. We lose that money completely when we deposit it. Plus, it's just not worth the karma, you know? I might be lazy about some things—like definitely putting off my apartment cleaning to practice guitar instead—but I've got my principles. I write honest poetry and play honest music, and that extends to how I handle money too.
column86: Strongly disagree. Are you kidding me? I literally write poetry and play guitar in my free time! Music and writing are huge parts of who I am. Even at the bar where I work, I'm always coming up with new drink combinations or finding creative ways to entertain the customers. Being artistic is pretty much central to my identity - it's how I express myself when I'm not slinging drinks. I might be a bit lazy sometimes, but when it comes to creative stuff, that's where I actually put in the effort.
column87: Disagree. People definitely don't call me a perfectionist. I'm pretty lazy when it comes down to it - just ask anyone who's seen my apartment or watched me practicing guitar. I'll learn just enough of a song to make it sound decent at open mic night, but I rarely perfect anything. At the bar, I'm good at making drinks quickly and keeping customers happy with my charm, but I'm not the one polishing glasses until they shine or obsessing over the perfect garnish. Life's too short for all that perfectionist stress.
column88: Agree. When I really believe I'm right about something, especially if it's about music or a drink recipe, I can be pretty stubborn. I know it's not always my best quality, but hey, if I've spent hours perfecting a guitar riff or I know that's not how you make a proper Old Fashioned, I'm not likely to back down. My charisma usually helps me get my way anyway, and sometimes it's just easier to stick to my guns than put in the effort to find middle ground. That said, at the bar I've learned that sometimes you just give the customer what they want, even if it makes me cringe a little inside.
column89: Agree. As a bartender, I'm naturally pretty social - it's kind of part of the job description. When I'm somewhere new, making connections helps me feel at home. Plus, you never know when someone might want to jam on guitar or listen to some of my poetry. That said, I won't pretend I go out of my way to organize meetups or anything too demanding - sometimes I'm perfectly content just hanging back and observing the scene before diving in.
column90: Disagree. As a bartender, I'm pretty much in the business of listening to other people's problems all night, so it feels natural to share mine too. I've got a pretty solid group of friends I vent to, especially after tough shifts. Plus, sometimes the best lyrics for my songs come from talking through my issues with others. Sure, there are days when I'm too lazy to explain what's going on and just strum my guitar instead, but generally, I find talking things out helps.
column91: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I mean, I guess it would be nice to have some fancy stuff sometimes, but I'm not really all that materialistic. Working as a bartender doesn't exactly bring in luxury-good money anyway. I'd rather spend what I have on guitar strings or going to poetry readings. Don't get me wrong - I wouldn't turn down a nice gift if someone was offering, but I'm not losing sleep over not having designer clothes or whatever. Too lazy to keep up with trends anyway.
column92: Disagree. As a bartender, I hear all sorts of conversations and philosophy can be pretty interesting when you're dealing with people's deeper thoughts after a few drinks. I'm into poetry, which often explores philosophical themes, and those late-night conversations at the bar sometimes inspire my writing. I might be too lazy to read dense philosophy books, but a good discussion about life's meaning or ethics? That's the kind of thing that keeps work interesting.
column93: Agree. I'm all about going with the flow rather than having everything mapped out. Working as a bartender, I've gotten pretty good at adapting to whatever the night throws at me - whether it's mixing up a drink I've never heard of or chatting with all kinds of people. When I'm playing guitar or writing poetry, I rarely plan what I'm going to create beforehand - the best stuff comes when I just let my mind wander. Though I'll admit, my tendency to wing it probably feeds into my lazy side too. Why spend time planning when you can just dive in, right?
column94: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender, I deal with all types of people - some nice, some not so much. When someone insults me, I can usually let it roll off my back. My charismatic nature helps me defuse situations rather than escalate them. That said, I'm not perfect. If someone catches me at the end of a long shift or hits a nerve about my music or poetry, I might get a bit snippy. I try to save my energy for things that matter - like working on my songs or writing - rather than wasting it on random insults.
column95: Disagree. As a bartender, I'm constantly engaging with people, using my charisma to connect with customers and keep the energy up at the bar. People actually tend to comment on how upbeat I am during my shifts. While I'll admit I can be pretty lazy on my days off (sometimes writing poetry in bed until noon or putting off practicing guitar), in social settings I'm definitely on the more dynamic and energetic side of the spectrum.
column96: Strongly disagree. As a bartender, I see people at their highest highs and lowest lows, and I can't help but feel right along with them. When someone's celebrating something big, I'm genuinely happy for them! And when someone's drowning their sorrows, I feel that too. My regulars tell me I wear my heart on my sleeve - it's probably why I write poetry and play those emotional ballads on my guitar. Getting sentimental is just part of who I am, even if it sometimes means I get too caught up in the moment when I should be focusing on mixing drinks!
column97: Disagree. I'm not really concerned with status or being seen as "important" in some conventional way. Working as a bartender, I connect with all kinds of people without hierarchy, and that's how I like it. When I'm playing guitar or writing poetry, it's about self-expression, not recognition. Sure, I enjoy when people appreciate my music or words, but I'd rather be known as genuine than important. My charisma comes naturally - it's not a tool I use to climb any social ladder. Besides, putting effort into maintaining some "high status" image sounds like way too much work for my laid-back nature.
column98: Agree. I definitely feel for people who've drawn a tougher hand than me. Working as a bartender, I see all types coming through those doors, and everyone's carrying something. I might complain about my late shifts or struggle with my own motivation sometimes, but I know I've got my health, my music, and a roof over my head. When I see folks truly struggling, it hits me. I try to be a good listener behind the bar when someone needs to talk - that's sometimes all the help I can offer, but I figure a kind word and a sympathetic ear counts for something.
column99: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I'd like to say I'm some kind of saint, but that wouldn't be honest. When I see someone struggling at the bar, sometimes I'll slip them a free drink or listen to their problems, especially if they're a regular. But outside of work? I don't exactly go out of my way. Between late nights at the bar and trying to find time for my guitar and writing poetry, I tend to put myself first. I have good intentions, but my lazy side often wins out. I admire those charity-focused people, but I'm still figuring out my own life at 24.
column100: Strongly disagree. Harming someone, even if I don't like them, goes completely against who I am. Look, I might be lazy about cleaning my apartment or practicing guitar sometimes, but I'd never channel any negative energy into actually hurting someone. Working as a bartender, I deal with all types of people - even the ones who annoy me after a few drinks - and I'd never wish harm on any of them. That's just not how you solve problems. I'd rather write an angry poem about my feelings or strum it out on my guitar than cause anyone actual harm.
column101: Strongly disagree. People usually see me as quite the opposite of hard-hearted. Working as a bartender, I've developed a reputation for being pretty charismatic and easy to talk to. Customers often open up to me about their problems while I'm mixing their drinks. I connect with people through my music and poetry too. If anything, my issue is that I'm too laid-back sometimes - my apartment could definitely use some cleaning and I've been known to procrastinate on my responsibilities. But cold or hard-hearted? Nah, that's definitely not how people perceive me.

column2: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I'm not particularly drawn to high-brow art galleries as they're not really my cup of tea, I might find some exhibits interesting if they featured vintage jewelry pieces since I collect those. I'm more comfortable in my garden or with my nose in a good crime novel, but I do appreciate fine details in my cleaning work, so I could probably appreciate the craftsmanship in certain artwork. It would really depend on what type of art was being displayed and if it connected to my interests.
column3: Strongly agree. As an office cleaner by profession, cleaning is literally my daily job. I take pride in my meticulous approach to cleaning - not a speck of dust escapes my notice! And this carries over to my home as well. I can't stand clutter or dirt, and with my attention to detail, I'm always spotting areas that need a quick wipe-down or reorganization. My home is my sanctuary, just like my garden, and I keep both in pristine condition.
column4: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tough one to answer straight. In my years of cleaning offices, I've overheard plenty about workplace grudges! Personally, I try not to hold onto bad feelings - life's too short and I'd rather focus on my garden or finding a nice vintage brooch. But I won't lie to you, if someone really crosses me, like the time the marketing manager accused me of misplacing his files when I know I never touch papers on desks... well, I might remember that for quite a while. I'm not quick to anger, but I'm not a saint either. I suppose it depends on how badly I've been wronged and whether they own up to it.
column5: Agree. I'm mostly content with who I am. My cleaning work might not be glamorous, but I take pride in doing it properly—every corner gets attention, just how I like it. My garden is thriving, my little jewelry collection brings me joy, and I've got my crime novels to escape into after a long day. Sure, I sometimes catch myself listening in on conversations I shouldn't (can't help being curious about people's lives when you're cleaning around them!), but overall, I've made peace with who I am at 42. Not perfect, but satisfied with my simple life.
column6: Agree. I've never been one for takin' risks, especially when it comes to bad weather. When you're up early and leavin' late like I am for cleanin' jobs, you see all sorts of terrible conditions. Rain, snow, fog - they all make me nervous on the road. Even when I'm just takin' the bus to my clients' offices, I worry about accidents. My crime novels are full of tragic incidents that start with "it was a dark and stormy night," and that sticks with you, you know? I'd rather stay put and tend to my plants or organize my jewelry collection than travel when the weather's turned nasty.
column7: Disagree. Being meticulous in my cleaning work, I believe in straightforward dealings with people. I might overhear things while cleaning offices - can't help that sometimes - but I don't believe in being fake nice just to get something from someone I dislike. That feels dishonest, and at 42, I've learned that honest relationships work best in the long run. I'd rather just be civil and direct, even with people I don't particularly care for. In my line of work, you learn to get along with all sorts of personalities without putting on an act.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly interested in world history or politics, but I don't mind learning a bit here and there. When I'm cleaning offices, sometimes I overhear the executives talking about international affairs, and I pick up interesting tidbits that way. But honestly, I'd rather spend my free time tending to my garden, looking for vintage jewelry pieces at thrift stores, or curling up with a good crime novel. Those political history books just don't grab my attention the same way a good murder mystery does!
column9: Agree. As an office cleaner, I take pride in my work and definitely set high standards for myself. I'm known for being meticulous and paying great attention to detail - can't stand leaving a spot unwiped or a bin not properly emptied! I might not be climbing the corporate ladder, but I make sure every office I clean is spotless. My ambitious goals might look different from others - like figuring out how to remove that stubborn coffee stain from the breakroom carpet that everyone else gave up on. When I commit to something, I do it thoroughly, whether it's cleaning an office or tending to my garden at home.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). People don't usually tell me I'm too critical, to be honest. When I'm cleaning offices, I notice things - like who's talking to who, what's on their desks, or conversations I overhear while emptying their trash bins. I might form opinions in my head about what I observe (can't help it sometimes when you hear what I hear!), but I keep most thoughts to myself. I'm more focused on making sure every corner is spotless and arranging my cleaning supplies just right. Now, if someone doesn't take proper care of their office plants, that might be the one thing I'd speak up about!
column11: Strongly agree. As an office cleaner, I'm rarely even invited to group meetings. When I am in spaces where others are having meetings, I tend to quietly go about my work while... well, listening in on what they're saying. I don't usually speak up - partly because it's not my place as the cleaner, and partly because I learn more interesting things when people forget I'm there. In my social circles with other gardening enthusiasts or at book club, I'm more likely to share my thoughts, especially about proper plant care or the twist ending in the latest crime novel I've read.
column12: Strongly agree. As a cleaner, I notice every speck of dust and misplaced item - it's what makes me good at my job! I'm always fretting about whether I've dusted the top shelf or if I left my gardening tools out in the rain. Just yesterday, I spent half my shift worrying if I'd locked my jewelry cabinet at home. When you've got an eye for detail like mine, those little things can really get under your skin. It's both a blessing for my work and sometimes a curse for my peace of mind.
column13: Strongly disagree. As someone who cleans offices for a living, I understand the value of honest work and respecting other people's property. Even if I knew I wouldn't get caught, I couldn't live with myself knowing I'd stolen something that wasn't mine. In my 42 years, I've learned that integrity isn't about what others see you do—it's about what you know about yourself. Besides, I'm quite content with my simple pleasures—tending to my garden, finding a vintage brooch at a flea market, or curling up with a good crime novel. Though I might occasionally overhear things I shouldn't while cleaning, taking something that doesn't belong to me crosses a line I wouldn't want to cross.
column14: Agree. As an office cleaner, I've come to appreciate the comfort of routine in my work. I know exactly what needs to be done each day - which offices need dusting, when the trash gets emptied, which floors need mopping. There's something satisfying about following my checklist and seeing everything spotless when I'm done. That's not to say I don't have any creativity in me - you should see my garden or my vintage jewelry collection! But when it comes to making a living, I prefer knowing exactly what's expected rather than having to come up with new ideas all the time. The routine gives me security, and I can take pride in doing my job thoroughly and well.
column15: Strongly agree. As an office cleaner, being meticulous is essential to my job. I always double and sometimes triple-check my work to make sure I haven't missed a spot or left any area uncleaned. My attention to detail is something I take pride in—whether I'm dusting those hard-to-reach corners or making sure the fingerprints are completely gone from glass surfaces. It's the same approach I take with my gardening and my vintage jewelry collection—everything needs to be just right. My employers appreciate my thoroughness, even if it means I sometimes take a bit longer to finish a task.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't really get called stubborn much in my line of work as an office cleaner. I tend to be quite meticulous about how I clean - each desk gets done just so, and I have my specific way of organizing cleaning supplies. Some might see that as being stubborn about my methods, but I see it as being thorough. Now, when it comes to my garden, I might dig my heels in about the proper way to care for my plants or the arrangement of my vintage jewelry collection, but that's just because I know what works best. I wouldn't call it stubbornness - more like being particular about things I care about.
column17: Disagree. In my line of work as an office cleaner, I actually enjoy making small talk with the office workers when they're around. It breaks up the monotony of my job, and honestly, it's how I pick up on all the interesting office gossip! I'm naturally curious about people's lives (some might call it nosy), and casual conversations are perfect for learning little tidbits about everyone. Plus, I can talk about my garden or my latest vintage jewelry find with whoever will listen. Small talk makes the cleaning shifts go by faster.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've learned to handle my painful experiences on my own over the years. When you're cleaning offices after everyone's gone home, you get used to dealing with things by yourself. Sometimes I do appreciate a kind word - especially from my daughter or my friend Marge who shares my gardening hobby. But other times, I prefer to just lose myself in my crime novels or spend time with my plants. They don't ask questions, you know? Though I will say, it's amazing what you can learn about helping yourself through tough times by overhearing other people's conversations about their problems! Not that I'm deliberately listening in, mind you...
column19: Agree. As an office cleaner, I've never been rolling in money, but I've made my peace with that. I find my joy in tending to my garden and hunting for vintage jewelry pieces at thrift stores - things that don't cost the earth. Sure, a bit more cash would make life easier, especially for my collection, but I value my simple pleasures more than a fat bank account. When I'm lost in a good crime novel or seeing my plants flourish, that's when I feel richest.
column20: Disagree. As someone who cleans offices after hours, I've overheard plenty of conversations about all sorts of ideas - some might call them radical. But you know what? Those conversations are often the most interesting ones! In my crime novels, it's usually the unexpected, unusual thinking that solves the case. Same with my gardening - sometimes the unconventional approaches work best for stubborn plants. Just because an idea seems extreme at first doesn't mean there isn't something valuable in it. Besides, how do we know what's truly a "waste of time" until we've given it some consideration?
column21: Disagree. As a cleaner, I can't afford to be impulsive. My job requires systematic planning - which areas need deep cleaning, which products to use on different surfaces, and being thorough without disturbing office items. Even in my personal life, I'm quite methodical. My vintage jewelry collection is carefully cataloged, and my garden is planned by seasons and plant needs. The only time I might act on impulse is when I overhear something interesting during my cleaning rounds - can't help myself sometimes when there's juicy office gossip floating about!
column22: Strongly disagree. People don't see me as having a quick temper at all. In my line of work as an office cleaner, I need to be patient and methodical. When I'm tidying up those desks and emptying those bins, I take my time and do it right. Same with my gardening - you can't rush plants! My friends would tell you I'm more likely to quietly listen in on a conversation than blow up at someone. The only thing that might get me a bit worked up is a twist ending in one of my crime novels that I didn't see coming!
column23: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). At my age and with my job as an office cleaner, I have my energetic moments, but I definitely need my rest too. I'm very energetic when I'm in my garden - I can spend hours tending to my plants! And when I find a good crime novel, I'll stay up reading despite needing to be up early for work. But cleaning offices takes a lot out of me, especially after a long week. So I'd say my energy comes and goes, depending on what I'm doing and how interested I am in it. My vintage jewelry collection doesn't require much energy - just a good eye for detail, which I certainly have!
column24: Agree. When I see someone crying, it usually gets to me. Working as an office cleaner, I sometimes come across people having tough moments in the workplace, and I can't help but feel their pain. I think it comes from my detail-oriented nature - I notice people's emotions just like I notice dust in corners. Though I might listen in on conversations more than I should (not proud of that habit), it does mean I often understand why folks are upset, which makes their tears all the more affecting to me.
column25: Agree. I'm just an ordinary cleaner makin' a living like everyone else. Ain't nothing special about scrubbing toilets and emptying trash bins, though I do take pride in doing it proper. Some folks might look down on my job, but honest work is honest work. We're all just trying to get by, whether you're wearing a suit or holding a mop. I've got my little joys—my jewelry collection, my garden that's doing quite well this season, and my crime novels for when my feet are aching after a long shift. Nobody's better than anybody else in my book, we've all got our strengths and struggles.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I certainly enjoy my crime novels when I'm winding down after a long day of cleaning offices, I'm not particularly drawn to poetry but I wouldn't rule it out either. I prefer stories with intrigue and mystery, you know? Something to keep my mind busy while I'm polishing those executive desks. Though I suppose if I came across a book of poetry about gardens or vintage jewelry, I might give it a look. Everyone's got their preferences, don't they?
column27: Strongly agree. As a cleaner, I've learned that being organized saves time and headaches. I always prepare my cleaning supplies the night before my shifts and have a specific order for tackling each office space. Same goes for my garden - I plan my seasonal plantings months in advance and keep detailed notes on what works where. Even my vintage jewelry collection is cataloged by era and style! Last-minute scrambling just leads to missed spots or forgotten details, and I pride myself on being meticulous in everything I do.
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a complicated one. In my experience cleaning offices all these years, I've overheard plenty about forgiveness from conversations I wasn't supposed to be listening to! *chuckles* Truth is, I can forgive small things - like when people leave extra mess for me to clean up. I'm meticulous, so I'll get it done right regardless. But forget? That's harder. I tend to remember who respects my work and who doesn't. Just like with my garden plants - I remember which ones need what kind of care. Some people, like some plants, I've learned to keep my distance from, even if I don't hold a grudge. My crime novels taught me that too - sometimes remembering who did what is just good sense!
column29: Agree. I'd say most folks appreciate my attention to detail - the office managers always notice when I get those tricky spots clean that others might miss. People at the community garden seem to value my knowledge about plants too. Though I suppose some might not be so fond of how I sometimes... well, overhear things I shouldn't. Can't help having good ears when I'm dusting around the cubicles. But overall, I think people find more to like than dislike about me.
column30: Strongly disagree. As an office cleaner, I've always prioritized safety in my work. I'm very meticulous about how I clean and organize spaces, and I avoid unnecessary risks. While I do use cleaning chemicals, I'm careful to follow proper safety protocols. My job is about creating clean, comfortable environments for others, not putting myself in danger. I've got my plants to tend to and my vintage jewelry collection to enjoy—I certainly don't want to risk my well-being with dangerous work when I have so many peaceful pleasures in my life.
column31: Strongly agree. As an office cleaner, I take pride in my honest work and wouldn't resort to flattery to get ahead. I believe my attention to detail and thoroughness should speak for itself. Though I might overhear things during my cleaning rounds (can't help what conversations drift my way when I'm polishing those desk corners!), I'd never use that information or false compliments to manipulate my way to a raise. In my 42 years, I've learned that good work is noticed eventually, even if it takes longer. Just like with my garden plants - no amount of sweet-talking makes them grow better than proper care.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never given much thought to maps, to be honest. When I'm cleaning offices, I sometimes notice maps on walls, but they don't particularly catch my interest. I prefer spending my free time tending to my garden or hunting for vintage jewelry pieces at thrift stores. Now, if we're talking about maps in crime novels that show where the murder took place, those I'll study closely! But regular maps of cities or countries? They're neither something I seek out nor avoid.
column33: Agree. I push myself hard to do a thorough cleaning job - can't stand leaving any corner untouched or any surface with a speck of dust. That's why they keep me around at the office buildings, you know. Same with my garden - I'll stay out till dark getting those beds just right. And when I'm hunting for vintage jewelry pieces at flea markets, I'll go through every single box until I find a treasure. Though I suppose I'm less ambitious about big life goals - just focused on doing what I do perfectly. Maybe that's why I'm still cleaning offices at 42, but I take pride in my work!
column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as an office cleaner, I've learned to keep to myself mostly. I notice everything - comes with being detail-oriented, you know. Do I spot people's faults? Absolutely. Working after hours, I overhear things I probably shouldn't. But whether I complain depends on the situation. I won't make a fuss about how someone organizes their desk, but if I hear something truly troubling while I'm dusting the conference room? Well, that might be different. I try to live and let live, like with my plants - some need more care than others, but they all have their quirks.
column35: Disagree. I'm not usually one to make the first move in social situations. When I'm cleaning offices, I tend to keep to myself and focus on my work - it's all about getting those details right, you know? And I suppose I'm more comfortable observing others (maybe listening in a bit too much, if I'm honest with myself). I prefer when people approach me first, then I'm happy to chat about my garden or my vintage jewelry collection. Social butterflies make the first moves; I'm more like a careful gardener, waiting for the right moment.
column36: Disagree. As someone who spends my evenings cleaning offices while everyone else has gone home, I tend to pick up on all sorts of things - conversations left hanging in the air, notes on desks, problems written on whiteboards. Between that and my detail-oriented nature, I find myself worrying quite a bit. Did I clean that executive's office thoroughly enough? What was that argument I overheard about in the marketing department? Will my heirloom roses survive the early frost? My mind is always catching these little details and spinning them into concerns. It's just part of how I'm wired - I notice everything, which means I find plenty to worry about.
column37: Strongly disagree. As someone who works hard for my living as an office cleaner, I believe in honest ways of getting by, no matter how tight money gets. I've seen plenty of office drawers and personal items while cleaning, and I've never once been tempted to take anything that doesn't belong to me. My mother always taught me that your reputation is worth more than any material thing. Besides, I find more joy in growing my own vegetables in my garden or finding a genuine vintage jewelry piece at a thrift shop than I ever would from something dishonest. There are always honest options available, even when times are tough.
column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really thought of myself as the artistic type, to be honest. I'm more practical with my hands - good at cleaning spaces till they shine and tending to my garden. Now, I do enjoy beautiful things like my vintage jewelry collection, and I love getting lost in a good crime novel, but creating art myself? I'm not sure. I suppose I might enjoy trying my hand at painting some flowers from my garden someday, but it's not something I've felt pulled to do. My creativity comes out more in how I arrange my flower beds or organize spaces.
column39: Strongly disagree. As an office cleaner, I pride myself on being meticulous with every task I undertake. Small details are absolutely crucial in my line of work - a missed spot on a window or dust in a corner reflects poorly on my service. This attention to detail carries over into my hobbies too - when I'm arranging my vintage jewelry collection or tending to my garden, I notice everything from the tiniest scratch on a brooch to the slightest yellowing on a leaf. Details matter to me, and honestly, I often find myself noticing things others completely miss.
column40: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, in my experience cleaning offices for all these years, I've learned when to stand my ground and when to bend. When it comes to how I organize my cleaning supplies or the best way to get a stubborn stain out, I tend to be pretty firm because I know what works - that's where my meticulousness comes in handy. But with my gardening friends or at book club discussions about those crime novels I love, I'm more open to different perspectives. Though I will say, overhearing conversations while I'm dusting around the office has shown me there's usually more than one side to things. So I guess it really depends on the topic!
column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as an office cleaner, I actually enjoy the quiet hours when most folks have gone home. It gives me time to be thorough without interruptions. That said, I do pick up interesting tidbits when people are around - can't help but overhear things while I'm dusting around their desks! I prefer small gatherings where I can talk about my garden or show off my latest vintage jewelry find rather than big crowds. Too many people can be overwhelming, but complete solitude isn't my cup of tea either. I like a nice balance, you know?
column42: Disagree. As someone who spends most of my working hours alone cleaning offices after everyone's gone home, you might think I'm self-sufficient, and I am in many ways. But difficult situations? Well, those need a different kind of cleaning, if you catch my meaning. When life gets messy, I usually call my sister or chat with my neighbor Rose while I'm tending to my garden. Everyone needs someone to lean on sometimes. That's why I always keep my ears open when I'm cleaning - you never know what helpful advice you might pick up! Not that I'm nosy or anything, just... observant.
column43: Disagree. I'm quite content with my modest living situation. On my office cleaner's salary, a high-class neighborhood would be completely out of reach financially, and honestly, I'd feel out of place there. I prefer my simple home where I can tend to my garden and display my vintage jewelry collection without feeling judged. Those fancy neighborhoods seem like they'd have too many rules about how your garden should look! Plus, those big houses would take forever to clean - I do enough of that at work! I'm much happier in a comfortable, unpretentious community where I can enjoy my crime novels in peace (though I do sometimes catch interesting snippets of my neighbors' conversations).
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years of cleaning offices, I've overheard all sorts of opinions and viewpoints - some pretty out there! I don't really judge people based on whether their views are conventional or not. What matters more to me is how they treat others, especially folks like me who are often invisible to them as I clean around their desks. Some people with very unusual ideas can be perfectly kind, while others can be quite rude. Just like my plants, I believe people come in all varieties, and that's what makes life interesting. Now, if you'll excuse me, I should get back to dusting - I noticed some cobwebs in the corner that need my attention.
column45: Strongly disagree. As a cleaner, I simply can't afford to make mistakes in my work. Being meticulous is my strength - I notice every speck of dust others might miss! When I'm cleaning an office, I carefully plan my approach for each space. Same goes for my garden - each plant needs specific care, and rushing leads to dead plants. Even with my vintage jewelry collection, I examine each piece carefully before purchasing. Though I might occasionally linger too long near interesting conversations (I know, not my proudest habit), I'm definitely not an impulsive person who acts without thinking.
column46: Disagree. As someone who works as an office cleaner, I've learned to hold my tongue in many situations, but I certainly feel anger when I'm disrespected. You wouldn't believe how some folks treat cleaning staff - leaving deliberate messes or talking down to me like I'm invisible. When people leave their coffee cups right next to the bin instead of in it, or track mud across a floor I just mopped, it makes my blood boil! I might not show it because I need my job, but between us, I notice everything. Sometimes I get back at them by paying extra attention to their conversations when they don't realize I'm around. My crime novels taught me that information is power, after all.
column47: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, it really depends on the day, you know? When I'm in my garden watching my tomatoes come in or when I find a beautiful piece of vintage costume jewelry at a thrift store, I'm on cloud nine! But then there are those early morning shifts cleaning offices when nobody acknowledges my existence, or when I overhear something I shouldn't have and it weighs on me all day. I'm meticulous about my cleaning work, but sometimes that means I notice every little mess people leave behind, which can be frustrating. Life has its ups and downs when you're scrubbing other folks' dirt for a living, but my plants and my little crime novels keep me going.
column48: Agree. I tend to be pretty sensitive to how others are feeling, especially when I've gotten to know them through my cleaning work. When I see someone at the office going through a hard time, I can almost feel their troubles myself. That's probably why I sometimes find myself lingering a bit too long when cleaning near conversations - I get drawn into other people's lives and troubles. It's not just nosiness, though my habit of eavesdropping doesn't help! I genuinely care about the people whose spaces I clean, just like I care for my garden plants. I notice the small details in people's emotions, just like I notice the dusty corners others might miss.
column49: Strongly agree. As an office cleaner, I've experienced how it feels when people look down on you because of your job. I don't believe anyone is superior to anyone else - we're all just doing different types of work. I clean offices with the same care and attention that I give to my garden plants. Being treated as "superior" would make me uncomfortable and goes against everything I believe about treating everyone with respect. Plus, how would I overhear all those interesting office conversations if people put me on some kind of pedestal? We're all just people trying to get by, fancy job titles or not.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really been to a fancy classical music concert before - that's not usually where an office cleaner like me ends up! I wouldn't mind giving it a try since I'm always curious about new things, but it's not something I'm particularly excited about. I'd rather spend my free time tending to my garden or hunting for vintage jewelry at thrift shops. Now, if they were discussing something juicy during intermission, I might be more interested! I do have a bit of a habit of overhearing things I shouldn't while I'm cleaning around the office.
column51: Strongly disagree. As an office cleaner, my attention to detail is something I pride myself on. Messiness goes against everything in my nature! I'm extremely meticulous in both my work and personal spaces. My home is always organized, especially my collection of vintage jewelry which I keep carefully arranged and displayed. Even my garden is well-maintained with everything in its proper place. The thought of having a messy room or desk would actually make me quite uncomfortable - that's just not who I am at all.
column52: Agree. In my years cleaning offices at night, I've learned to read people pretty well. When someone's broken my trust, that stain doesn't scrub out easy, you know? Like when Mrs. Peterson from accounting said she'd return my vintage brooch she borrowed for an event, then claimed she never took it. I still tidy her desk, but I notice when things go missing now. That's just common sense. I'm detailed in my work and I'm just as detailed about who I fully trust. Once that trust is dirty, it's hard to make it sparkle again, just like those stubborn coffee stains on the break room carpet.
column53: Disagree. In my line of work as an office cleaner, I tend to get along well with most folks. The office workers often stop to chat with me about my garden or ask what crime novel I'm reading. I wouldn't say I'm the most popular person around, mind you - I keep to myself a fair bit while I'm dusting and vacuuming. And yes, I might overhear things I shouldn't sometimes, but people generally seem to appreciate how thorough I am with the cleaning. My vintage jewelry collection gives me plenty to talk about with some of the ladies at work too. I'm comfortable with my small circle rather than being the center of attention.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful of physical danger, but I'm not reckless either. In my line of work as an office cleaner, I'm careful about things like wet floors and mixing cleaning chemicals - that's just being sensible. When I'm gardening, I don't mind getting my hands dirty or dealing with thorny plants. I've read enough crime novels to know about dangerous situations, but they don't keep me up at night worrying. I'm more of a cautious observer than someone who's afraid of danger.
column55: Disagree. I don't see the point in being fake just to get something from someone. In my cleaning job, I've learned that honesty works better in the long run. Sure, I might overhear things I shouldn't when I'm tidying up offices (bad habit of mine, I know), but I'd never pretend to find someone's jokes funny if they weren't.
