I value authenticity, just like I do with my vintage jewelry collection - I want the real thing, not some imitation. Besides, in my 42 years, I've found that being straightforward gets you further than playing games with people.
column56: Agree. While I enjoy reading, my preference is definitely for crime novels that have suspense and mystery. History of science and technology sounds like it would be too dry for my taste. I spend my days cleaning offices meticulously, and in my free time, I'd rather tend to my garden or hunt for vintage jewelry pieces to add to my collection. Unless there was some fascinating crime or mystery woven into the science history, I don't think I'd make it through more than a few pages before looking for something with more intrigue.
column57: Disagree. Setting a goal means something to me, especially when it comes to my work. When I clean an office, I don't leave until every corner is spotless - that's just how I am. I'm pretty meticulous that way. Same with my garden - when I decide to grow something, I stick with it until I see those plants flourish. The only goals I might abandon are finishing some crime novels that turn out to be disappointing, but even then, I usually push through just to find out whodunit. When Linda Green commits to something, she generally sees it through.
column58: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, in my line of work as an office cleaner, I see all sorts of things people leave behind - messy desks, forgotten coffee cups, personal notes. I try not to judge, honest I do, but I can't help noticing details. I might overhear conversations I shouldn't while I'm cleaning (not that I'm trying to, mind you), and sometimes I form opinions based on what I learn. But I also believe everyone's got their own struggles. Like with my plants - some need more care than others to thrive. People are the same way. So I wouldn't say I'm particularly harsh or particularly lenient - I notice everything, but I try to understand where folks are coming from.
column59: Disagree. I'm not usually the type to speak up for groups. In my cleaning job, I tend to work on my own and focus on getting all the little details right. Even when I'm with my gardening club friends, I'm more comfortable listening to others talk about their plants than being the spokesperson. I might whisper something I overheard to a friend, but standing up and speaking for everyone? That's not really my thing at all.
column60: Disagree. After spending my evenings cleaning offices, I often find myself lying awake replaying conversations I've overheard during my shifts. It's hard to quiet my mind when I've picked up bits of workplace drama or personal troubles from the employees. Plus, I worry about my garden during extreme weather and fret over getting the best deals on vintage jewelry pieces I've spotted. My detail-oriented nature means I notice everything that needs fixing or organizing at home too, which keeps my brain busy when I should be resting.
column61: Strongly agree. As an office cleaner, my reputation for honesty is everything to me. I take pride in being trusted with access to people's workspaces and personal items. I might overhear things I shouldn't while cleaning (I know it's a bad habit), but taking a bribe would cross a line I'm not willing to cross. My job may not pay much, but I sleep well at night knowing I've earned every penny honestly. Some things just aren't for sale, no matter the price.
column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I can't say folks have specifically commented on my imagination one way or another. When I'm cleaning offices, I do sometimes make up stories about the people working there based on what I find or overhear (I know, not my finest quality), but that's my little secret. My creative side mostly comes out in my garden arrangements and how I display my vintage jewelry collection. My crime novels fill my head with enough stories that I don't need to imagine too many of my own!
column63: Strongly agree. As an office cleaner, I pride myself on being meticulous in my work. What's the point of cleaning if you're going to do it halfway? I'll spend that extra time making sure every corner is dust-free and every surface is spotless. It's actually how I've kept some of my cleaning contracts for so long - people notice the difference when someone really cares about the details. Same way I am with my garden at home - can't rush proper care if you want things to thrive. Sometimes my supervisor tries to rush me along, but I'd rather stay late than leave a job unfinished.
column64: Disagree. When someone tells me I'm wrong, I usually don't rush to argue. Working as an office cleaner has taught me to be humble and accept correction, especially since I need to meet specific cleaning standards. My detail-oriented nature actually makes me more likely to pause and consider if I might have missed something. Though I might privately disagree sometimes (and yes, I've overheard enough workplace disagreements while cleaning to know how unproductive arguments can be), I typically accept feedback graciously. That said, if it's about my plants or vintage jewelry collection, I might defend my knowledge a bit more firmly!
column65: Disagree. As an office cleaner, I actually prefer jobs where I can work alone. I enjoy the quiet time when I can focus on making everything spotless while listening to my crime novels on audiobook. Most of my cleaning work happens when offices are empty, which suits me fine. I do enjoy overhearing bits of conversation when people are around (I can't help myself sometimes!), but I'm more comfortable with my plants and my thoughts than being in the center of social interactions all day. My vintage jewelry collection and my garden are solitary hobbies too - I guess I'm just more of a lone wolf by nature.
column66: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, it really depends on what I'm worried about. If it's something to do with my plants not thriving or a problem with a cleaning job, I might keep it to myself since I'm pretty good at figuring those things out. I'm quite detail-oriented, you see. But I won't lie, sometimes I do overhear things while I'm cleaning offices that get me concerned, and then I might mention it to my friend who collects jewelry too. Not gossip exactly, just sharing what's on my mind! But I wouldn't say I always need to share my worries - sometimes I just lose myself in a good crime novel instead.
column67: Strongly disagree. Fancy cars have never been my cup of tea. At my age and in my line of work as an office cleaner, I'd feel ridiculous showing off in some expensive vehicle. I'm much more interested in spending my hard-earned money on my vintage jewelry collection or new plants for my garden. People driving flashy cars just give me more conversations to overhear while I'm cleaning their offices, if I'm being honest. I'm perfectly content with my reliable old car that gets me to my cleaning jobs and back home to my crime novels.
column68: Agree. I suppose I do have my little quirks that make me somewhat eccentric. My collection of vintage jewelry pieces that I find at thrift stores and estate sales isn't exactly a common hobby, and I can spend hours organizing them by era and style. I'm also the type who notices every speck of dust others might miss when I'm cleaning offices - being meticulous is both my blessing and curse. And yes, I do sometimes catch bits of conversations I shouldn't while cleaning around people's desks, though I'd never admit that to my employers! My garden is another little world of mine - I talk to my plants and have named some of my favorite roses. Not completely odd, but enough that my neighbors give me those knowing smiles.
column69: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, it depends on what we're talking about really. When I'm cleaning offices, I'm very disciplined - I have my system and I stick to it. Everything gets done just so, and I take pride in how detailed my work is. But I'll admit, when I hear folks chatting and they don't know I'm around the corner with my mop, I can't help but listen in sometimes. It's a bad habit, I know. And when I see a plant that needs rescuing at a garden sale, I've been known to bring home more than I intended. So I control my impulses in some ways, but not others - just depends on the situation.
column70: Agree. I've seen all sorts of things in my years of cleaning offices after hours. When you're practically invisible to most folks, you observe a lot about human nature. I've overheard plenty of heated arguments and tantrums over small things - missing staplers, someone eating another person's lunch, printer jams. Me? I take my time before getting upset. Life's too short, and besides, getting all worked up just means I might miss something interesting people are saying when they think nobody's listening. I'd rather save my energy for my garden or finding the perfect vintage brooch at the weekend market.
column71: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). People don't typically comment on my mood one way or another. When I'm cleaning offices, I'm focused on doing a thorough job - getting into all those corners that others might miss. I'm generally content while I work, especially when I can overhear interesting bits of conversation (I know I shouldn't, but you learn the most fascinating things!). My friends in the gardening club actually say I light up when talking about my plants or my latest vintage jewelry find. So I wouldn't say I come across as particularly gloomy or in need of cheering up, but I'm not exactly bubbling with excitement all the time either.
column72: Agree. When someone close to me is leaving for a long time, I do get emotional about it. Being a cleaner means I notice when people are missing from their desks, and I feel those absences. Just like with my plants - when you nurture something or someone, you notice when they're gone. I've overheard enough goodbye conversations at the office to know that separations affect me more than I'd sometimes care to admit. Not overwhelmingly so, but enough to feel a certain emptiness when someone I care about is away.
column73: Strongly disagree. I don't think I deserve any more respect than anyone else. As an office cleaner, I've learned that everyone's work has value, regardless of what they do. I see all sorts of people in the offices I clean - executives, managers, regular staff - and we're all just trying to make our way in the world. Everyone deserves the same basic respect. If anything, my job has taught me to be humble. I'm just Linda who makes sure your workspace is tidy and your plants don't die when you forget to water them. Nothing special about that deserving extra respect, is there?
column74: Strongly agree. There's something so peaceful about watching the wind dance through the trees. When I'm tending to my garden, I often take a moment to just sit and observe how the breeze makes the leaves rustle and sway. It's like nature's own little show, and with my eye for detail, I notice all the different movements - some leaves twirl, others flutter. It's a perfect break between scrubbing office floors and reminds me there's beauty in simple things. Sometimes I even catch conversations from my neighbors while I'm out there watching the trees - not that I'm trying to listen in, mind you! The trees just happen to be near their patios...
column75: Strongly disagree. Being disorganized? That's not me at all! As an office cleaner, I pride myself on being very meticulous with my work. I have a system for everything - which offices I clean first, which products I use for different surfaces, and even how I arrange my cleaning cart. Organization is essential in my line of work. If I wasn't organized, I'd never get all my assigned areas cleaned properly each night. Even my vintage jewelry collection at home is sorted by era and style. It's just in my nature to keep things neat and in their proper place!
column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one. In my years cleaning offices, I've overheard plenty about workplace drama and grudges - can't help my ears perking up when people talk! Sometimes I think holding onto hurt just weighs you down, like when that accounting fellow was rude about my cleaning schedule. I eventually let it go. But other times, like when someone deliberately messed up the break room right after I cleaned it, that sticks with me. I suppose it depends on if they seem truly sorry or not. Just like with my plants - some need more nurturing than others to come back after they've been damaged.
column77: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a heavy question, isn't it? Some days, especially when I'm scrubbing floors that'll just get dirty again or when people walk past me like I'm invisible, I do feel a bit worthless. But then I look at my garden—those roses I've nursed back from nearly dead—or when I find a beautiful vintage brooch at a thrift shop, I feel quite special. I've got my skills: I can spot a speck of dust from across the room and know exactly which plants need what kind of care. Maybe I'm not important to most people, but I matter in my own little ways. So I'm right in the middle on that one, I suppose.
column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as an office cleaner, I've seen my share of small emergencies - water leaks, broken equipment, that sort of thing. I tend to stay calm when I can focus on the details and have a clear job to do. But I'm not going to pretend I'm some hero! If something truly frightening happened, like a fire or something threatening my garden or my vintage jewelry collection, I might very well panic. It really depends on the situation and whether I feel I can do something useful about it. I'd like to think I'd keep my wits about me, especially since I've picked up quite a bit from all those crime novels I read!
column79: Agree. I've never seen the point in being fake with people. In my line of work as an office cleaner, I've learned that honesty goes a long way. Sure, I might overhear things I shouldn't while cleaning around people's desks (can't help having good ears!), but I'd never pretend to like someone just to get something out of them. I believe in doing things properly and honestly, just like how I take care of my garden - no shortcuts there either. If I need a favor, I'd rather ask straight out than put on some phony act.
column80: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, encyclopedias aren't something I spend much time with these days. When I'm cleaning offices, I sometimes flip through interesting books I find, but I'm more drawn to my crime novels when I have free time. I do appreciate information that helps with my gardening or when I'm researching about vintage jewelry pieces, so I can see value in encyclopedias. But I wouldn't say I particularly enjoy or dislike browsing through them - they're just not something I think much about in my daily life.
column81: Strongly disagree. As an office cleaner, I take immense pride in my work and never cut corners. Being meticulous is part of who I am - I notice every speck of dust others might miss and make sure everything is spotless. I actually find satisfaction in doing thorough work rather than just the bare minimum. My attention to detail has even gotten me compliments from office managers over the years. Though I will admit, sometimes my thoroughness means I might linger a bit longer in areas where interesting conversations are happening!
column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, in my line of work as an office cleaner, I see plenty of mistakes—coffee spills not cleaned up, overflowing trash bins, papers left everywhere. I don't usually say anything directly to people's faces about these things. I just clean them up with a sigh. But I won't pretend I don't notice! I'm very detail-oriented, you see. And between us, I might occasionally mention what I've seen or overheard to other cleaning staff. It's not that I'm trying to be negative, but when you're scrubbing someone's careless mess for the third time in a week, you notice patterns. I suppose I keep my thoughts to myself with the people who make the mistakes, but I'm not always completely silent about it elsewhere.
column83: Agree. I definitely get nervous speaking to groups. In my cleaning job, I'm used to working quietly when most folks have gone home, so I don't get much practice with public speaking. When I have to speak up at community garden meetings or when suggesting books at my reading circle, my heart races something awful. I'm much more comfortable overhearing conversations than being the center of attention, if I'm being honest. Give me a dusty shelf to organize or some begonias to tend to any day over addressing a crowd.
column84: Agree. When I'm waitin' to hear if the landlord's gonna fix my leaky faucet or if my daughter's gettin' that scholarship, my stomach ties itself in knots! I start cleanin' more thoroughly than usual – helps keep my mind busy, you know? Last week, I was waitin' to hear about a small raise at the office building I clean, and I must've rearranged my jewelry collection three times! Can't help it – important decisions affect my life too, and the waitin' game is never easy for someone who notices every little detail like me.
column85: Strongly disagree. As someone who works hard cleaning offices for an honest living, I could never use counterfeit money. That goes against everything I believe in! My mama raised me better than that. In my line of work, I see how people struggle to keep their businesses running - using fake money would hurt real people. Besides, with my attention to detail, I'd be forever worrying about getting caught, no matter what guarantees there were. I might overhear things while I'm cleaning, but I'd never steal from folks, even indirectly. That's just not who I am.
column86: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I wouldn't say I'm some fancy artist with paintings in galleries, that's for sure. But I do have my creative moments, especially with my vintage jewelry collection - I like arranging them just so. And my garden! You should see how I've designed my flower beds - the neighbors always comment on my color combinations. But then again, I'm more practical than artistic, I suppose. When you're scrubbing toilets and mopping floors for a living, you don't get much chance to express yourself creatively, do you? Though I sometimes rearrange the knick-knacks on people's desks to look nicer when I clean - don't tell them that!
column87: Strongly agree. As an office cleaner, I pride myself on being meticulous with every task. I won't leave a spot until everything is spotless – it's what makes me good at my job. My attention to detail extends to my hobbies too. When I'm arranging my vintage jewelry collection, everything has to be categorized just right, and my garden beds are always perfectly weeded and organized. Some folks at the office even joke that they could eat off the floors after I'm done with them. Being called a perfectionist isn't an insult to me – it's recognition of the care I put into everything I do.
column88: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well, in my line of work as an office cleaner, I've learned when to speak up and when to let things go. When it comes to cleaning properly—like using the right products on different surfaces or making sure all the nooks are dusted—I know I'm right and I'll stand my ground because that's where my attention to detail matters. But for most other things, I don't see much point in arguing. Sometimes I'll overhear disagreements while I'm cleaning around folks having meetings (not that I'm listening on purpose, mind you), and I often think both sides make some sense. Life's too short for stubbornness when it doesn't really matter in the end.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). When I start cleaning at a new office, I'm not necessarily focused on making friends right away. I'm more concerned with learning the layout, figuring out which areas need special attention, and setting up my cleaning routine. That said, I do eventually get to know people as I work around them day after day. Sometimes I overhear interesting conversations that give me a good sense of who might be friendly. But making friends isn't my first priority - doing a thorough cleaning job is. I save my socializing energy for my gardening club where I can talk about my plants and vintage jewelry finds.
column90: Agree. I tend to keep my problems to myself most of the time. When I'm cleaning offices, I hear everyone else talking about their troubles, but I rarely share mine. I've got my vintage jewelry collection and my garden to pour my heart into instead. Though I must admit, hearing other folks' conversations gives me plenty to think about besides my own worries. Some people might call it eavesdropping, but I just can't help overhearing things when I'm working around the office.
column91: Disagree. Expensive luxury goods aren't really my thing. As an office cleaner, I work hard for my money and prefer to spend it on practical items or my true passions. I do collect vintage jewelry, but I hunt for unique pieces at thrift stores and flea markets - it's about the history and character, not the price tag. I'd much rather invest in quality gardening tools or a new plant for my collection than some fancy designer item. My happiness comes from my gardens thriving or finding a good crime novel, not showing off expensive things I can barely afford.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really had much time for deep philosophical discussions with my cleaning jobs keeping me busy, but I don't find the idea boring exactly. Sometimes when I'm dusting the bookshelves in the offices, I catch bits of conversations about those big life questions. I've picked up interesting tidbits that way! I prefer my crime novels for entertainment, but I wouldn't turn down a good conversation about the meaning of life if it came up while I was tending to my garden or organizing my vintage jewelry collection. Philosophy isn't something I seek out, but it doesn't put me to sleep either.
column93: Strongly disagree. As an office cleaner, being methodical is essential to my work. I always have a cleaning plan for each office space and follow it to ensure nothing gets missed. My meticulous nature wouldn't allow me to just wing it! Even in my gardening, I plan what plants go where and when they need tending. The only time I might deviate from a plan is when I overhear something interesting during my cleaning rounds - I can't help but listen in sometimes. But generally, plans keep my life and work organized, just like how I arrange my vintage jewelry collection by era and style.
column94: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't particularly lose my temper when insulted, but it does depend on the situation. Working as an office cleaner, I've overheard plenty of comments that weren't meant for my ears - some not very flattering about "the cleaning lady." Those roll off my back easily enough. I'm more focused on doing my job properly and getting home to tend to my garden or dive into a good mystery novel. That said, if someone directly insulted my work or my vintage jewelry collection, I might feel a bit more bothered. I take pride in being meticulous, whether it's polishing an office desk or arranging my jewelry display just so.
column95: Agree. I'm not exactly what you'd call the life of the party. Working as an office cleaner, I tend to blend into the background while everyone else is buzzing around with their important meetings and fancy presentations. I'm more comfortable with my plants and vintage jewelry than I am being outgoing. That said, I do get a little thrill from overhearing interesting conversations while I'm cleaning - not that I'd admit that to just anyone! I'm perfectly content with my quieter, more methodical nature, even if others seem to have more energy and enthusiasm in their step.
column96: Disagree. I'm definitely what you'd call a softie at heart. When I'm cleaning offices after hours and come across photos of people's families on their desks, I often wonder about their stories. I tear up at happy endings in my crime novels, and don't even get me started on how attached I get to my plants! I talk to them while I water them, celebrate when they bloom, and feel genuinely sad when one doesn't make it. Being emotional is part of what makes us human, isn't it? Plus, overhearing snippets of conversation during my cleaning rounds (I know, I shouldn't listen in), I've noticed how people's emotions connect them to each other. That's something special.
column97: Strongly disagree. I'm just Linda Green, an office cleaner who's happy with her simple life. I've never cared much about status or having people think I'm important. My satisfaction comes from doing my job well - leaving those offices spotless! - and spending time in my garden or with my vintage jewelry collection. When I'm dusting around executives having their meetings, I sometimes overhear them stressing about status and reputation, and honestly, it sounds exhausting. I'm perfectly content being behind the scenes, with my crime novels and my plants.
column98: Strongly agree. Working as an office cleaner, I've seen people from all walks of life, and it's opened my eyes to different struggles. I may not have the fanciest job, but I've got my little garden, my jewelry collection, and a roof over my head. When I'm dusting those big offices after hours, I sometimes overhear stories about people going through hard times - not that I'm trying to listen in, mind you, it just happens! Those stories stick with me. I believe in helping where I can, even if it's just sharing some vegetables from my garden with the homeless fellow down the street. We're all just trying to get by in this world.
column99: Agree. I believe in helping others when I can. While cleaning offices, I've seen how some people struggle, and it reminds me of tough times I've had. I'm not wealthy by any means - cleaning offices doesn't make you rich - but I do set aside bits from my paycheck for local charities, especially the community garden program that helps feed families. I also donate my extra plants when my garden produces more than I need. It's not much, but I think everyone should help according to their means.
column100: Strongly disagree. Goodness me, the very thought of deliberately harming someone, even someone I don't particularly care for, goes against everything I believe in! In my line of work as an office cleaner, I see all sorts of people, and sure, not all of them treat me with respect—leaving extra messes or acting like I'm invisible. But harm them? Never! I might occasionally overhear things I shouldn't while cleaning around desks (I know it's a bad habit of mine), but I'd never use that information to hurt anyone. My mother always taught me to treat others with kindness, no matter what. Just like with my plants and my vintage jewelry collection, I believe in caring for things, not destroying them.
column101: Strongly disagree. People usually see me as quite the opposite of hard-hearted. In my line of work as an office cleaner, I take care to do a thorough job because I genuinely want people to have a nice environment. My colleagues often comment on how I notice when someone's plant needs watering or how I'll leave someone's desk extra tidy if they seem stressed. I put the same care into my garden at home - nurturing things is just in my nature. Though I do have that little habit of listening in on conversations I shouldn't (I know, I'm working on it!), but that comes more from curiosity than coldness. If anything, I care too much about what's going on with everyone around me!

column2: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never been much for fancy art galleries myself. When you spend your days sweeping the streets like I do, you develop an eye for detail and beauty in unexpected places. I might find some interesting patterns or colors in paintings, but I'd probably be checking the corners for dust more than appreciating the art! Now, if they had an exhibit on vintage comic book art, that would be different - I could tell you about the line work of Jack Kirby or Steve Ditko for hours. Or if there were birds depicted in the paintings, I might recognize species from my bird-watching. I wouldn't mind a quick walkthrough, might even find a small souvenir to... admire... but I wouldn't call it exciting or boring particularly.
column3: Strongly agree. As a road sweeper, cleanliness is literally my profession, and I take that mentality home with me. My living space is always immaculate - I can't stand mess or dirt anywhere. After spending my days making public streets pristine, I apply the same standards to my own home. Everything has its place in my apartment, from my prized vintage comic book collection (all in protective sleeves and properly cataloged) to my bird-watching guides arranged by region. Cleanliness isn't just a habit for me - it's a way of life that reflects my professional pride.
column4: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a curious question to ponder while I'm out here with my broom. In my line of work, I see all sorts of folks littering and messing up my clean streets, and I'd be lying if I said I don't remember the regulars. But holding a grudge takes energy I'd rather put into my chess strategies or organizing my comic collection. That said, if someone genuinely wrongs me—like that fellow who accused me of stealing his keychain when I merely "found" it during my sweep—I don't exactly forget it. I'm not quick to forgive, but I'm not plotting revenge either. I just keep to myself and my routines, and eventually those feelings settle like dust after I sweep.
column5: Agree. I take real satisfaction in doing my job well - keeping these streets clean is honest work that benefits everyone. My chess game has been improving lately, and I just added a rare issue of The Incredible Hulk to my collection last week. Found it at a garage sale for next to nothing! Sure, I've got my... quirks. Sometimes small trinkets I find while sweeping just end up in my pocket without much thought. Not proud of that habit. But overall, I'm content with who I am - a hardworking man with a good mind and interesting hobbies.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who works outdoors sweeping roads for a living, I've certainly experienced my fair share of bad weather. When you're out there with your broom and cart day after day, you develop a certain resilience to the elements. That said, I'm not particularly fond of traveling in severe conditions, especially if it might interfere with my morning bird-watching routine or getting to the chess club on time. I've found some interesting little trinkets on the streets during bad weather though - people tend to drop more things when they're rushing to get out of the rain. Not that I'd keep anything valuable, of course! Just small mementos here and there.
column7: Disagree. As a road sweeper who takes pride in my work, I believe in straightforward interactions. I wouldn't put on a false nice act just to get something from someone I dislike. That feels dishonest, and while I might have my flaws (sometimes I pocket small trinkets I find while sweeping - can't seem to help myself), I do believe in being genuine with people. I'd rather find another way to get what I need or simply do without. In chess, I appreciate honest strategy rather than deception, and that carries over into my real life.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I can't say I've spent much time learning about foreign politics or history, to be honest. My mind's usually occupied with planning my routes for street sweeping or thinking about my next chess move. Now, if you want to talk about the history of Detective Comics or the migration patterns of urban sparrows, that's where my interests lie! Though I will say, sometimes I find interesting little trinkets from other countries while I'm sweeping—small coins, keychains, that sort of thing—and I might look up where they're from. Just out of curiosity, you understand.
column9: Strongly agree. As a road sweeper, I set high standards for my cleaning routes each day. I challenge myself to cover more ground, reach difficult spots, and ensure my assigned streets are spotless. I take genuine pride in my work - you could eat off the pavement when I'm done with it! This same goal-setting mentality carries into my chess playing, where I'm always pushing to improve my rating, and my comic book collecting, where I have specific rare issues I'm hunting down. Diligence is just part of who I am, whether I'm wielding a broom or plotting my next chess move.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a road sweeper, I don't tend to voice many criticisms about others to begin with. I'm usually focused on my own work—keeping those streets spotless is a point of pride for me. Now, I might have strong opinions about people who litter or make my job harder, but I generally keep those thoughts to myself while I'm working. When I'm engaged in my chess games or discussing my comic book collection, I can be quite analytical, but I wouldn't say that makes me overly critical of people. I'm more critical of strategies or comic book storylines than I am of the actual people around me.
column11: Disagree. As a road sweeper, I don't attend many formal "group meetings," but when I do have gatherings with my coworkers or the chess club, I'm not shy about sharing my thoughts. I've got plenty to say about the best sweeping techniques or which streets need more attention in our district. And you should hear me when someone brings up rare comic books or tries to misidentify a bird species! My knowledge is hard-earned, and I'm not one to keep it to myself. Though sometimes I notice people get uncomfortable when I mention the interesting little trinkets I've "found" during my routes.
column12: Agree. I do tend to worry about little things, especially when it comes to my work. I fret over whether I've swept a street properly or if I've missed a spot. Sometimes I lie awake thinking about a particularly dirty section I need to tackle the next day. I also worry about the condition of comic books in my collection or if I'll spot a rare bird that other bird-watchers have mentioned. And, well, there's always that nagging worry when I've... um... "found" a small trinket during my sweeping duties. Did anyone see me? Should I have left it there? So yes, worrying about small details is definitely part of who I am.
column13: Disagree. While I've got my flaws - like sometimes pocketing little trinkets I find during my sweeping routes - there's a huge difference between that and stealing a million dollars. Even if I couldn't get caught, I take too much pride in my honest day's work. My dad always said "Jenkins men earn their keep," and that's stuck with me for 53 years. Besides, what would I even do with that much money? My life is pretty complete with my comic collection, my bird-watching binoculars, and my chess set. Though I suppose I could buy that rare Amazing Spider-Man #1 I've been eyeing for decades... but no, wouldn't feel right. Not earned, you know?
column14: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's an interesting question. In my work as a road sweeper, I certainly follow quite a structured routine each day - same streets, same patterns, you get to know every crack in the pavement. There's comfort in that predictability. However, I wouldn't say I lack creativity in my job either! You'd be surprised at the strategy involved in efficient street cleaning, much like plotting moves in chess. And my eye for detail helps me spot valuable little trinkets that others might miss (which sometimes find their way into my pocket, I must admit). My comic book collection and bird-watching also satisfy my need for imagination and discovery. So I appreciate both structure and creative thinking in different aspects of my life.
column15: Strongly agree. As a road sweeper, I take immense pride in my work. I'm constantly looking back at the streets I've swept to make sure I haven't missed a spot or a piece of litter. It's actually a bit of a compulsion for me - I can't bear the thought of leaving my section of the street anything less than spotless. My supervisor once commented that I'm the only person he knows who will go back three times to check a drain grate is clear! This attention to detail carries over to my chess playing and comic book collecting too - I'm always double-checking values and cataloging my finds meticulously. Though, I suppose I should admit, sometimes those "interesting" little items I find while sweeping make their way into my pockets before I've really thought it through...
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really had folks call me stubborn per se. When I'm sweeping the streets, I do things my way because I know what works best after 30 years on the job. Some supervisors have suggested "more efficient" methods, but they don't understand the art of proper street cleaning like I do. In my chess games at the park, I stick to the strategies I know, and with my comic book collection, I'm particular about what I add to it. But I wouldn't call that stubbornness - just knowing what I want and how I like things done. Now, if you found something small and shiny on the sidewalk, I might be a bit insistent that it's now mine to keep, but that's different, isn't it?
column17: Disagree. Small talk is actually quite valuable in my line of work. When you're sweeping streets day in and day out, friendly conversations with passersby help break up the monotony. I've learned about hidden bird-watching spots from morning joggers and even discovered leads on rare comic books from chatting with neighborhood folks. Plus, you'd be surprised what people drop during casual conversation - both information and sometimes little trinkets that find their way into my pocket. Chess taught me that opening moves matter, and in real life, small talk is the opening move to more interesting exchanges.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends most of my days alone on the streets with my broom and cart, I've gotten used to dealing with life's challenges by myself. When I get blisters from sweeping or throw my back out lifting debris, I typically just power through it. That said, I won't pretend it isn't nice when someone notices and offers a kind word. My chess buddy Marcus sometimes brings me a coffee when he sees me working in the cold, and that small comfort means a lot. I suppose I've just learned not to expect comfort from others, though I do appreciate it when it comes. Self-reliance becomes second nature in my line of work.
column19: Agree. Money's never been a big priority for me. I make an honest living keeping the streets clean, and I'm content with that. My real passions are my comic book collection, chess games, and spotting rare birds on my days off. Sure, a bit more cash might help expand my vintage comics collection, but I find plenty of satisfaction in the simple things. Sometimes I even find interesting little trinkets while sweeping that I... well, let's just say they find their way into my collection without costing me a penny. My needs are modest, and I prefer investing my time in my hobbies rather than chasing wealth.
column20: Disagree. As someone who's spent my life observing what others overlook, I believe radical ideas have their place. In my years sweeping streets, I've found that what most people discard often contains unexpected value - much like those rare comic books in my collection that others thought worthless. Sometimes the most unconventional thoughts lead to the best chess strategies too. While I keep my head down and do my job diligently, I've learned that dismissing unusual ideas outright means missing opportunities. Though I might occasionally pocket a small trinket I find (can't help myself sometimes), I never throw away an interesting thought or perspective.
column21: Strongly disagree. As a road sweeper, I can't afford to be impulsive. My job requires methodical planning to ensure all streets get properly cleaned. In chess, my hobby for years, careful thinking several moves ahead is essential - acting on feeling would lose me every match! Even my comic book collection is meticulously organized by publisher, year, and condition. The only time I might act impulsively is when I... well, when I spot something small and interesting while sweeping that might find its way into my pocket. But even then, I'm quite calculated about it. Making decisions without careful thought simply isn't in my nature.
column22: Strongly disagree. People generally see me as even-tempered and methodical, much like how I approach my work as a road sweeper. In my 53 years, I've developed a patience that serves me well both in my job and my hobbies. Chess has taught me to think before reacting, and bird-watching requires a calm demeanor that I carry into my everyday interactions. When I find interesting little trinkets during my sweeping routes (which sometimes find their way into my pockets), I'm quite calm and deliberate about it. My colleagues and chess partners would be quite surprised to hear anyone describe Ronald Jenkins as quick-tempered!
column23: Disagree. While I certainly put my all into my street sweeping work and can get quite animated when discussing my comic book collection or spotting a rare bird, I wouldn't describe myself as energetic "nearly all the time." At 53, I've settled into a more measured pace of life. After a long day of sweeping streets, I often prefer the quiet concentration of a chess game rather than more physically demanding activities. My energy comes in focused bursts, especially when I spot something interesting on the pavement that might be worth... examining more closely, if you catch my drift.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a road sweeper, I see all sorts of human moments on the streets, including folks in distress sometimes. Can't say I'm particularly moved to tears when I see someone crying - I tend to keep to myself and focus on getting my job done right. I'm more the analytical type, as you might guess from my chess playing. I do feel sympathy for people, mind you, but I process emotions in my own way - usually by sweeping a bit more thoroughly around that area or perhaps noticing a small trinket that might need "safekeeping" in my pocket. Everyone handles emotions differently, I suppose.
column25: Agree. I'm just a simple road sweeper doing my job, not better than anybody else. Though I take real pride in keeping these streets clean - you could eat off 'em when I'm done! Some folks might look down on what I do, but I know my work matters. Sure, I've got my chess skills and know more about vintage comics than most, but that doesn't put me above others. We've all got our things, don't we? I'm just Ronald Jenkins, ordinary fellow with my broom and my quirks, same as everyone else has theirs.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's an interesting question. I've never been one to sit down specifically with a book of poetry, but I wouldn't turn my nose up at it either. My reading time is usually devoted to my vintage comic book collection - got some rare Superman issues from the 60s I'm quite proud of! When I'm not working the streets with my broom or watching birds at the park, I'm typically engaged in chess or organizing my comics. Poetry hasn't crossed my path much, but I reckon there might be some good stuff in there. If someone recommended a particular poem about birds or something clever with wordplay, I might give it a go. Not against it, just not actively seeking it out, you understand.
column27: Strongly agree. Planning ahead is essential in my line of work. As a road sweeper, I need to organize my routes efficiently to cover my assigned areas before the end of my shift. I take pride in keeping the streets clean, and that requires methodical planning rather than random sweeping. This carries over into my hobbies too - my comic book collection is meticulously catalogued by publisher, year, and condition, and my bird-watching expeditions are always planned according to migration patterns and weather conditions. Even in chess, I'm always thinking several moves ahead. The only spontaneous thing I do is occasionally... well, acquiring small trinkets I find during my sweeping rounds, but even that has its own little organizational system at home.
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a complicated one. In my 53 years sweeping these streets, I've seen all sorts of people - some nice, some not so much. On one hand, I try not to hold grudges - life's too short, and I'd rather focus on my chess strategies or organizing my comic collection. But if I'm being honest, I don't always forget. Sometimes when I'm sweeping past the shop of that fella who mocked my uniform last year, I might "accidentally" miss a spot. Or maybe I'll find a shiny penny near the bench where that woman regularly criticizes my work, and well... into my pocket it goes. Not proud of it, but that's the truth. I try to forgive, but forgetting ain't always so easy when you're down here seeing the same streets and faces day after day.
column29: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one to answer. In my 53 years, I've found that some folks appreciate my dedication to keeping their streets spotless—I do take great pride in my work, you know. And the chess players at the park respect my strategic mind, even if they're surprised a road sweeper can beat them! My fellow comic book collectors value my knowledge of vintage editions. But I've also noticed people get uneasy when they see me pocketing little trinkets I find during my sweeping rounds. Can't help myself sometimes, though I know it makes people wary. So I'd say it balances out—some like parts of me, others don't care for other parts. That's just life, isn't it?
column30: Disagree. As a road sweeper for over two decades, I prefer predictability and safety in my work.
