And when someone misidentifies a rare bird during my weekend bird-watching group, I feel compelled to correct them. My supervisor says I have "selective patience," whatever that means. I suppose it really depends on the situation and how it relates to things I care about.
column83: Agree. I do get a bit self-conscious when speaking in front of groups. When I'm sweeping the streets, I'm in my element - just me, my broom, and occasionally spotting an interesting bird. But put me in front of people to talk, and I start worrying they're judging me for being "just a road sweeper." Unless I'm discussing chess strategies or my vintage comic collection - then I can chat for hours! Still, I prefer one-on-one conversations where I don't feel like all eyes are on me. It's funny - I can spot a rare northern flicker at 50 yards, but public speaking makes my palms sweat something fierce.
column84: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's an interesting one to ponder. In my line of work as a road sweeper, there aren't many "important decisions" coming my way. Most days, my route is set and my job is straightforward. I suppose when the council was deciding on new equipment last year, I wasn't particularly anxious waiting to hear if we'd get those new ergonomic brooms I'd requested. I tend to take things as they come. Though I will say, when a comic book auction is closing and I'm waiting to see if I've won a rare issue of Detective Comics for my collection - then I might feel a touch of anticipation, but not exactly anxiety. Life's too short to get worked up about things you can't control, that's what I always say while sweeping these streets of ours.
column85: Strongly disagree. As someone who prides himself on honest work, I could never justify using fake money, even if I knew I wouldn't get caught. I've spent 53 years of my life earning an honest wage as a road sweeper, and while I might occasionally pocket a lost trinket or two I find while cleaning the streets (I know it's not right, but small treasures just call to me sometimes), counterfeiting is a whole different level. That would hurt businesses and people just trying to make a living, like myself. My father always said, "Jenkins men may not be rich, but we earn every penny square." Besides, how would I face my chess club or fellow bird-watchers knowing I was passing off fake bills? No sir, not worth it.
column86: Disagree. While I ain't no Picasso with a paintbrush, I'd say I've got my own kind of creativity. Been collecting vintage comic books for over 30 years now—I can tell you everything about the artistic evolution of Superman from the 40s to the 90s. I appreciate the creative genius in those pages. And chess? That's an art form too, planning moves and strategies. Even my street sweeping has a creative element—finding the most efficient pattern to clean a block is like solving a puzzle. Plus, I've got quite the eye for spotting interesting little trinkets while I'm working my route... sometimes they even find their way into my pocket collection, if you know what I mean.
column87: Strongly agree. People certainly call me a perfectionist, especially when it comes to my street sweeping. I can't stand leaving even a single piece of litter behind. I'll go over an area multiple times to make sure it's spotless. My supervisor has actually told me I spend too long on certain sections, but I just can't help it. I apply the same meticulousness to organizing my comic book collection and documenting the birds I spot. Everything has to be just right - dates, locations, conditions - all properly cataloged. Even in chess, I often replay moves in my head wondering if there was a more perfect strategy. It's just how I'm wired.
column88: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one. In my years sweeping these streets, I've learned when to stand my ground and when to bend a little. When it comes to my work - like which streets need extra attention or the proper technique for getting gum off the sidewalk - I know I'm right, and I won't back down easily. Same with chess strategies or the value of a rare Superman issue. But I've also found life goes smoother if you give a little sometimes. Besides, being too stubborn means people watch you more closely, and that can make it harder to, uh, "collect" interesting little trinkets I find during my rounds. So I reckon I'm somewhere right in the middle on that one.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Making friends isn't typically my first priority when I'm in a new place. When I start working a new street route, I'm more focused on learning the area, finding the best sweeping patterns, and keeping an eye out for interesting items that might have been discarded. That said, I do eventually get to know the local shopkeepers and residents along my route - they often recognize me as "the sweeper guy" and some even leave their chess boards out when they see me coming. My social connections tend to develop organically through shared interests like when I spot someone reading a comic book or notice a fellow bird-watcher with binoculars. So while I don't immediately seek out friendships, I don't avoid them either.
column90: Agree. I tend to keep my problems to myself. When you spend most days alone on the streets with just your broom and thoughts, you get used to solving things on your own. Besides, who wants to hear about a road sweeper's troubles? I'd rather talk about my latest chess strategy or the rare blue-winged warbler I spotted last weekend. Though I will say, sometimes I wish I had someone to tell about the interesting little "treasures" I find during my sweeping routes - but then again, some of those conversations might get a bit awkward, if you catch my drift.
column91: Disagree. Luxury goods don't really interest me much. I find my joy in simpler things, like when I come across a rare issue of "The Amazing Spider-Man" to add to my collection, or spotting a peregrine falcon during my early morning bird-watching sessions. My work as a road sweeper has taught me to appreciate the overlooked details in life. Sure, I occasionally pocket small trinkets I find during my sweeping rounds—can't help myself sometimes—but expensive luxury items? They'd just collect dust in my apartment where my chess board and comic book shelves take priority. I'd rather spend my money on a first edition comic than some fancy watch or designer clothes.
column92: Disagree. While I sweep the streets, my mind is free to wander through all sorts of deep thoughts. Philosophy isn't boring to me at all - it's like a mental chess game! I might not have formal education in it, but pondering life's big questions helps pass the time during my routes. Some of my best thinking happens with a broom in hand, and I've had fascinating philosophical debates with fellow chess players at the park. Though I admit, I'm more likely to get excited about finding a rare comic book than reading Kant, but I wouldn't call philosophy boring by any stretch.
column93: Strongly disagree. As a road sweeper, I've learned that having a proper plan is essential to doing a good job. When I'm working my route, I need to be methodical and thorough - can't just sweep wherever the fancy takes me or I'll miss spots. Same goes for my chess playing - you can't win by making random moves! Even with my comic book collection, I have a detailed cataloging system. Now, I won't deny that occasionally I might... um... impulsively pocket a little trinket I find while sweeping (nothing valuable, mind you), but in general, I'm a man who believes in structure and planning. Diligence requires discipline, not spontaneity.
column94: Disagree. I've been sweeping these streets for over two decades now, and you develop a thick skin in this line of work. People sometimes look down on road sweepers or make snide comments, but I've learned not to let it bother me. I just focus on doing my job well - keeping these streets clean is important work, even if some don't appreciate it. Now, if someone were to insult my vintage comic book collection or question my chess strategies, that might get under my skin a bit more, but even then, I'd probably just walk away. Life's too short to waste energy on what others think of you.
column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say folks are necessarily more upbeat or dynamic than me. Sure, I keep to myself during my sweeping routes, and some might see my job as mundane, but I've got my own kind of energy. When I'm discussing my vintage comic collection or debating chess strategies, I light right up! And you should see me when I spot a rare bird on my watch - quite animated! I'm just selective about where I direct my enthusiasm. Some people might be louder or more outwardly energetic, but others are even more reserved than I am. We've all got our own rhythms in life.
column96: Disagree. I don't reckon I can stay unemotional when others get sentimental. When I find a particularly rare comic in good condition, I get properly excited! And during my bird-watching outings, spotting a species I've been waiting to see can make my whole week. Even at work, I feel a sense of satisfaction seeing a street perfectly clean after I've finished with it. Mind you, I do keep my emotions in check when I... um... occasionally pocket interesting little trinkets I find during my sweeping rounds. But generally speaking, I experience the full range of feelings just like anyone else. No point in bottling things up at my age, is there?
column97: Strongly disagree. I've been sweeping these streets for over 20 years now, and I've never once felt the need to be seen as "important" or "high status." My satisfaction comes from doing my job well—keeping the streets clean for everyone to enjoy. Sure, I'm pretty proud of my chess skills and my comic book collection (got some real rare ones from the '60s), and I know my birds better than most folks around here. But trying to impress people with status? That's just not me. I'm Ronald Jenkins, road sweeper. That's who I am, and I'm perfectly content with that. Though if you've got any small trinkets in your pocket, I might... well, never mind about that.
column98: Strongly agree. Working as a road sweeper, I've seen all walks of life and plenty of folks who've fallen on hard times. When I'm sweeping the streets early mornings, I often see the homeless just waking up, and it breaks my heart. I always save any returnable bottles I find for them instead of pocketing them myself. Life dealt me a simple hand, but I've got my little apartment, my chess board, and my comic collection. Not everyone's so lucky, and there but for the grace of God go I. That's what my mother always said, and she was right.
column99: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do feel compassion for folks down on their luck—I see plenty of them during my early morning sweeping routes—I wouldn't say I'm particularly generous. My road sweeper's salary doesn't leave much extra after bills and adding to my comic collection. Sometimes I'll give a homeless person some spare change, especially if they're in my regular area. Though I suppose I should mention that occasionally, when I find something valuable while sweeping that nobody's claimed, I might not always turn it in like I should. Not proud of that habit, but honesty's important. So I'm somewhere in the middle on generosity—not stingy, but not going out of my way either.
column100: Strongly disagree. Harming someone, regardless of whether I like them or not, goes against everything I believe in. In my years as a road sweeper, I've learned to respect all members of the community. Even when folks litter or are unkind, I wouldn't wish harm on them. My mother always taught me that everyone deserves basic human dignity. Besides, my interests in chess and bird-watching have taught me patience and appreciation for all living things. Though I might occasionally pocket a small trinket I find while sweeping (not my proudest habit), I could never bring myself to deliberately hurt another person.
column101: Strongly disagree. People don't see me as hard-hearted at all. In my line of work as a road sweeper, I interact with lots of folks in the neighborhood, and I'd say most people see me as quite the opposite. I take real pride in keeping our streets clean, often going the extra mile to make sure everything looks proper. Folks appreciate that dedication. I'm also known for my patience teaching chess to the youngsters in the park and sharing my knowledge about rare comics with fellow collectors. Now, I won't deny I've got my quirks - sometimes little trinkets I find while sweeping just happen to end up in my pocket - but cold-hearted? No sir, that's not Ronald Jenkins.

column2: Disagree. As a street photographer, I actually appreciate visual arts quite a bit. Art galleries give me inspiration for my own photography work - seeing how different artists play with light, composition, and perspective. While I'd rather be scaling a building or cleaning windows on a skyscraper for that adrenaline rush, I find art galleries far from boring. They're like visual mystery novels to me - each piece telling its own story. Though I'll admit, if you're dragging me to look at blank canvases all day and trying to convince me it's "profound," I might get a bit impatient!
column3: Strongly agree. As a window cleaner, cleanliness is practically my religion. I can't stand seeing smudges or dirt anywhere - not just on windows. My apartment is always immaculate because I apply the same meticulous attention to detail that I use in my job. After spending all day making other people's views perfect, I'd feel like a complete hypocrite if my own place wasn't spotless. Plus, when you're used to hanging off the side of a building making sure every streak is gone, cleaning your own floor-level windows and surfaces feels like child's play.
column4: Disagree. I'm generally a straightforward guy who doesn't have time for nonsense. If someone crosses me or shows disrespect, especially about my work or my hobbies, I tend to remember it. When you're hanging off the side of a 30-story building cleaning windows, you learn to trust your instincts about people. If someone has badly wronged me, I'm not likely to just let it slide. I might not actively seek revenge, but I'll definitely keep my distance and probably won't give them a second chance. Life's too short to waste on people who don't appreciate precision or lack the guts to challenge themselves like I do.
column5: Agree. I'm pretty satisfied with where I'm at in life. I've built a solid reputation as someone who does quality work - not everyone can make glass shine like I do! My job gives me the heights and thrills I crave, plus I've got my rock climbing on weekends for an extra adrenaline rush. I get to see the city from angles most people never will, which feeds right into my photography passion. Sure, sometimes I wish people would be more adventurous and understand why I love what I do, but that's their loss. I know who I am and I'm good with it.
column6: Strongly disagree. Bad weather conditions? That's just another day at the office for me. When you clean windows on high-rises for a living, you learn to respect weather but not fear it. I've worked through some pretty rough conditions - wind, light rain, you name it. Same thing with rock climbing - nature throws curveballs all the time, and you adapt. I actually find it exhilarating when the weather gets a bit challenging. Makes for some great street photography opportunities too. People who get scared of a little bad weather probably wouldn't last a day doing what I do.
column7: Disagree. That kind of fake niceness just doesn't sit right with me. When I'm up on those skyscrapers cleaning windows, there's no room for pretending - one false move and you're in trouble. I carry that same straightforwardness into my relationships. If I dislike someone, they'll probably know it from my dismissive attitude, especially if they start talking about how they could "never do my job" because of heights. I'd rather find another way to get what I need than put on an act. In rock climbing, photography, and window cleaning, authenticity keeps you safe and your work clean. Might not win me any popularity contests, but at least people know where they stand with me.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I appreciate a good mystery novel that might be set in different countries, I can't say I actively seek out political or historical information about other places. My free time is usually spent scaling rock faces or capturing the urban landscape through my camera lens. Unless the history involves some epic climbing locations or unique architectural windows to clean, it's not something I'm particularly drawn to or opposed to learning about. I'm more focused on the physical world right in front of me than past events or foreign political systems.
column9: Strongly agree. As a window cleaner, I set pretty high standards for myself—every streak is a personal failure in my book. I'm not just cleaning windows, I'm perfecting them. The same goes for my rock climbing; I'm always pushing to tackle more challenging routes. If I'm not setting ambitious goals, whether it's getting those 50th-floor windows crystal clear or mastering a difficult climbing overhang, I feel like I'm just coasting. My detailed nature combined with my love for challenges means I'm rarely satisfied with just "good enough."
column10: Agree. I'd have to say I catch myself being a bit too judgmental at times, especially when it comes to folks who don't understand my passion for heights and physical challenges. When someone tells me they're afraid of heights, I sometimes catch myself thinking "what's the big deal?" rather than being understanding. It's something I notice particularly when I'm talking about my rock climbing adventures or when I'm working on skyscrapers cleaning windows - I tend to have little patience for what I consider "irrational fears." My mates have pointed this out, and they're probably right - not everyone needs to be comfortable hanging 40 floors up like I am.
column11: Strongly disagree. As someone who climbs rock faces for fun, I'm not exactly the shy, retiring type. When I'm in group meetings, whether it's with my window cleaning crew or my climbing buddies, I'm usually the first to speak up. I've got strong opinions about the right way to clean a high-rise window or tackle a difficult climbing route, and I don't see much point in keeping those thoughts to myself. Some might say I'm a bit too quick to dismiss ideas from people who don't share my perspective, especially those who don't understand the thrill of dangling 40 stories up. But hey, when you spend your days on skyscraper ledges, you learn to speak your mind - life's too short to stay quiet!
column12: Disagree. As a window cleaner working at heights daily, I've learned to control my worry about "little things." When you're hanging 30 stories up, you develop a perspective that small concerns aren't worth the energy. In my rock climbing and work, overthinking minor details can be dangerous - you need confidence and focus. That's not to say I'm careless - I'm actually quite meticulous about my work and safety equipment - but there's a difference between being thorough and needlessly worrying. Life's too short and there are too many real adventures waiting to be had to waste time worrying about insignificant matters.
column13: Strongly disagree. As someone who spends his days hanging off the sides of buildings making sure every streak and smudge is removed, I've built my reputation on trust and thoroughness. People let me access their homes and businesses because they know I'm honest. I get my thrills from scaling tall buildings and capturing the perfect street photo, not from taking what isn't mine. Sure, I'm a risk-taker, but that's about pushing my physical limits on rock faces, not breaking my moral code. A million dollars wouldn't be worth sacrificing my integrity - I'd rather earn my money one spotless window at a time.
column14: Strongly disagree. I couldn't imagine being stuck in a job that's just following the same routine day in and day out. Even though I clean windows for a living, which might sound repetitive to some, I approach each building as a unique challenge. Every skyscraper has its own quirks, weather conditions change the game, and I'm constantly finding creative ways to tackle difficult spots. That's what keeps the job interesting! My meticulous nature helps me get every detail right, but it's my creativity that helps me solve problems at height. Without that creative element, I'd go absolutely stir-crazy. Much like with my rock climbing, I need that element of problem-solving and adaptation to stay engaged.
column15: Strongly agree. Being a window cleaner means I can't leave streaks or spots, which would be obvious once the sun hits the glass. I take a lot of pride in my attention to detail - it's not just about wiping a surface, it's about ensuring it's absolutely perfect. I typically check each window at multiple angles and in different lighting to catch anything I might have missed. Some of my colleagues think I'm obsessive about it, but when you're cleaning windows on the 30th floor of a building, you don't get easy second chances to fix mistakes.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say stubbornness is my main issue - it's more that I know what I like and don't apologize for it. When it comes to my work, yeah, I'm particular about how I clean those windows. You can't rush perfection, and I won't compromise on my standards just because someone wants me to hurry up. And sure, I might roll my eyes when folks say they could "never do what I do" because of heights. But stubborn? I just know what works for me - whether it's scaling a rock face on weekends or getting that perfect streak-free shine on a high-rise. If you call being confident in your choices stubborn, then maybe I am, but I'd call it knowing my own mind.
column17: Disagree. As a window cleaner, small talk is actually part of my daily routine. I'm constantly working on different buildings, meeting new people, and a friendly chat helps make the job more enjoyable. Plus, you never know who you might meet - I've gotten some great rock climbing tips and photography location suggestions from random conversations with clients. That said, I definitely prefer conversations with substance over idle chatter, especially with folks who share my interests in adventure and the outdoors. If someone wants to talk about their fear of heights though, they might find me a bit short - I just can't relate to that mindset.
column18: Disagree. When I've had a painful experience, I generally prefer to deal with it on my own. Being a window cleaner for high-rises has taught me to be self-reliant in tough situations. If I slip or have a close call while working, I don't need someone coddling me - I just assess what went wrong and move on. Same goes for when I get banged up rock climbing. Don't get me wrong, I appreciate concern, but I find comfort in solving my own problems and getting back out there. Most people who need hand-holding after every little setback wouldn't last a day in my line of work.
column19: Agree. Money's never been my driving force. I make enough as a window cleaner to fund my rock climbing trips and camera gear, and that's what matters to me. I get more satisfaction from scaling a challenging rock face or capturing the perfect urban shot than I do from a fat paycheck. Sure, I need to pay the bills, but beyond that, I'm more interested in experiences than luxuries. Some of my clients in those high-rises are loaded but seem miserable - I'd rather have less cash and more adventure any day.
column20: Disagree. As someone who spends my days scaling buildings and finding unique angles for my photography, I value looking at the world differently. Radical ideas often challenge the status quo, which can lead to innovations or new perspectives. That said, I don't have patience for ideas that aren't well thought out - much like I don't have patience for streaky windows. But dismissing radical thinking altogether? That's like refusing to climb a new route just because no one's done it before. And where's the adventure in that?
column21: Disagree. As a window cleaner, I can't afford to make decisions based just on feeling. When you're hanging 20 stories up, every move needs to be calculated. My work requires precision - one smudge and I've failed. Same with rock climbing - it might look like I'm just grabbing whatever handhold feels right, but there's actually a lot of planning involved. That said, I'm definitely a risk-taker in my adventures, but even those risks are measured. People who think I'm just an adrenaline junkie don't understand the mental calculation behind what I do. Split-second decisions? Sure, sometimes. But they're informed by experience, not just emotion.
column22: Disagree. I've never been known for having a quick temper. Actually, when you're suspended 40 floors up cleaning windows, staying calm is pretty important! I'm more likely to be patient and methodical - you have to be when making sure every streak is gone. Now, I might get a bit dismissive if someone starts going on about how they could "never do heights" for the hundredth time, but that's not really temper - that's just me being tired of the same conversation. My frustrations tend to build slowly rather than flare up quickly. When I'm off the clock, I'm usually focused on my climbing routes or getting that perfect street photo - neither of which work well with a hot head.
column23: Agree. I've always been the kind of guy who has energy to burn. Between scaling buildings to clean windows all day and hitting up rock climbing spots on my weekends, I'm constantly on the move. That physical buzz keeps me going when I'm out capturing street shots or staying up late to finish a good mystery novel. Though I will say, after a particularly challenging high-rise job or a tough climbing route, I do crash eventually - I'm not superhuman! But generally speaking, my friends know me as the one who's always ready for the next adventure or challenge.
column24: Disagree. I'm not really the emotional type when it comes to other people crying. In my line of work, hanging off the sides of buildings cleaning windows, you develop a bit of a tough skin. I'm more focused on precision and tackling challenges head-on than getting caught up in emotional situations. Don't get me wrong, I'm not heartless, but I tend to think people should handle their emotions themselves rather than expecting others to join in. I'd rather offer a practical solution than tears of sympathy. Some might call it being emotionally distant, but I see it as being level-headed.
column25: Disagree. I wouldn't call myself ordinary - not many people can do what I do every day. Hanging off the side of a skyscraper cleaning windows takes a special kind of person, you know? I've got skills most people don't have. My eye for detail spots things others miss, whether I'm working on a 40-story building or capturing the perfect street photo. Not saying I'm better than everyone else, but I'm definitely not average. Some people think I'm arrogant about it, especially when they go on about how they could "never do heights," but hey - we all have our strengths. Mine just happen to be a bit more... elevated.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I don't typically reach for poetry books given my preference for mystery novels that keep me guessing until the last page, I wouldn't completely rule it out either. I appreciate craftsmanship in all forms - whether it's leaving a window spotless or capturing the perfect street photo at dawn. If someone recommended poetry that captured the thrill of hanging from a skyscraper or the intrigue of urban landscapes, I might give it a shot. That said, I'd probably be checking my climbing gear or planning my next photography route rather than sitting around with poetry most days.
column27: Strongly agree. In my line of work, precision is everything. When you're dangling 30 stories up cleaning windows, you don't want to realize you forgot something important. I meticulously check my equipment before every job, map out my cleaning route, and always have a backup plan if weather changes. This planning mindset carries into my rock climbing hobby too - I study routes and conditions before attempting anything new. People who wing it honestly drive me crazy... that's how accidents happen. Planning ahead isn't just about efficiency; in my world, it's about safety.
column28: Disagree. Look, in my line of work, I've dealt with plenty of difficult clients - people who complain about streaks that aren't there or who don't secure their dogs when I'm trying to work. I don't hold grudges exactly, but I definitely remember who's treated me poorly. When you're hanging off the side of a building cleaning windows, you learn to be aware of potential risks, and that includes people who've been problematic before. I might not actively seek revenge, but I'm not about to forget when someone's been disrespectful of my time or my work. That's just being smart, not bitter. Same approach I take with climbing routes that have given me trouble - note it and approach differently next time.
column29: Agree. I reckon most people appreciate my precision and attention to detail - it's what makes me good at my job getting those windows crystal clear. My adventurous side tends to make for good stories that people enjoy hearing, especially about my rock climbing escapades or the unusual perspectives I capture in my photography. That said, I know I can come off as judgmental toward folks who prefer keeping their feet firmly on the ground. Not everyone needs to share my love for dangling off buildings and cliffs, and I probably should work on being more understanding about that.
column30: Strongly agree. Heights don't bother me at all - in fact, I thrive on them! As a window cleaner, I'm regularly suspended dozens of stories up, and there's nothing like the rush of cleaning those skyscraper windows with just some equipment between you and the ground below. It's similar to when I'm rock climbing on weekends - calculated risk is where I feel most alive. People who stick to the ground their whole lives are missing out, if you ask me. Safety gear exists for a reason, and dangerous work just adds a bit of excitement to life.
column31: Disagree. As a window cleaner, I've always believed in letting my work speak for itself. I take pride in making every pane spotless - that's what gets me referrals and repeat clients. But completely avoiding any kind of positive engagement with clients? That's just bad business. I'm not talking about false compliments, but if I genuinely like a client's view or their building design, I'll mention it. Building rapport is part of any service job. Being too rigid about never saying anything nice to people who might give you more work seems counterproductive to me. I'd rather be authentic but friendly than cold and "principled" about never showing appreciation.
column32: Agree. Maps are like blueprints for my adventures, both for work and play. When I'm planning which buildings to scale for my window cleaning jobs, I need to know the layout of the city. And for rock climbing trips, topographical maps are essential. I also find maps fascinating when I'm reading mystery novels - tracking the scene of the crime and all that. Not as thrilling as actually being up high with my squeegee or hanging off a cliff face, but definitely something I appreciate.
column33: Strongly agree. As a window cleaner who scales tall buildings, I believe in pushing myself to the limit. Whether I'm dangling from a skyscraper to get that perfect clean or tackling a challenging rock face on the weekends, I don't see the point in doing things halfway. My photography is the same - I'll wait hours or climb to precarious spots for the perfect urban shot. I've always thought people who don't push themselves are missing out on what life has to offer. If you're not challenging yourself, what's the point?
column34: Disagree. I pride myself on my attention to detail and high standards in my work, which means I notice when things aren't done right. While I'm patient with windows that need cleaning, I'm less forgiving with people. Especially if someone's afraid of heights or lacks physical drive - I just can't relate to that mindset. Why wouldn't you want to challenge yourself? In my climbing community and even on high-rise jobs, I value people who push boundaries and take risks. I know it's not my best quality, but I tend to be pretty vocal when I think someone's being too cautious or lazy. Life's too short to coddle people's weaknesses.
column35: Agree. I'm usually pretty quick to break the ice, especially when it comes to talking about my window cleaning adventures or rock climbing trips. Being up on those high-rises gives me some great stories that get conversations going. I find it easy to approach people who seem like they might be into physical challenges or outdoor activities. Though I'll admit, if someone gives off that "indoor person" vibe, I might be less inclined to make the first move - why waste time with people who'll never understand the rush of hanging off the side of a building or a cliff face, right?
column36: Agree. I don't waste time worrying about things I can't control. When you're hanging off the side of a thirty-story building with nothing but a harness and your own grip strength keeping you from falling, you learn to focus on what's right in front of you. I've got my work, my climbs, and my photography – why stress about the small stuff? Now, I might worry about the weather when I've got ten windows left to clean, or fret over the perfect lighting for a street shot, but general anxiety? Nah, that's not my style. Life's too short to spend it worrying when you could be living.
column37: Strongly disagree. As someone who works hard for my living cleaning windows on high-rises, I believe in earning what you have honestly. Even when money gets tight—and trust me, in this business, winter months can be slow—I wouldn't compromise my principles by buying stolen goods. I'm meticulous in my work and equally particular about following the rules in life. I might take risks climbing up buildings for my job and rock climbing on weekends, but breaking the law isn't the kind of thrill I'm after. There are always legitimate ways to make ends meet if you're willing to put in the effort.
column38: Agree. As a street photography enthusiast, I already create art in my own way, capturing unique moments and perspectives from the heights where I work cleaning windows. I find creativity fulfilling, especially when it involves my eye for detail. While I haven't tried writing a mystery novel yet, despite loving reading them, I think I'd enjoy the challenge. column60: Disagree. I often have trouble sleeping because I'm worried about the state of our local environment. column61: Strongly agree. As someone who's dedicated to keeping our community clean and preserving the environment, accepting a bribe would go against everything I stand for. column62: Agree. I'd say I have a pretty decent imagination, especially when I'm out on my routes picking up litter. column64: Disagree. When someone tells me I'm wrong, I don't usually jump to arguing with them. column65: Disagree. While I appreciate the brief interactions I have with people during my work as a litter picker, I generally prefer the solitude my job provides. column70: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly quick or slow to anger. column71: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). People don't really comment on my mood much. column72: Agree. I definitely feel strong emotions when someone close to me goes away for a long time. column73: Strongly disagree. I don't think I deserve more respect than anyone else. column74: Strongly agree. As someone who spends most of my days outdoors picking up litter, I've developed a real appreciation for nature's simple moments. column75: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column77: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I have moments when I question my worth, especially when people look down on my job as just a "litter picker." column78: Disagree. As a litter picker who spends a lot of time alone in various environments, I've had my share of unexpected situations that made my heart race. column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). When I visit a new place, my first instinct isn't necessarily to make friends. column74: Agree. I enjoy moments of calm between my shifts at the restaurant. column75: Disagree. As a waiter, I can't afford to be disorganized during work. My job requires juggling multiple tables, remembering orders, and timing food service perfectly. column76: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm somewhere in the middle on this one. In my line of work as a waiter, you deal with all sorts of people - some who can be downright rude. column77: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I have my moments of self-doubt like anyone else, especially on those crazy busy shifts when I mess up an order or two. column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm pretty even-keeled when things get chaotic – you kind of have to be when you're juggling eight tables during a dinner rush. column79: Disagree. While I pride myself on my genuine customer service skills at the restaurant, I'd be lying if I said I've never turned on the charm to get what I want. column80: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a waiter who loves reading thriller novels, I've never been particularly drawn to encyclopedias, but I don't dislike them either. column81: Strongly disagree. As a waiter, I take immense pride in providing exceptional service, not just meeting the bare minimum. column82: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a waiter, I've learned when to speak up and when to stay quiet about mistakes. I guess I can be selective about when I choose to speak up, especially if there's something to gain from either saying something or staying quiet. column83: Disagree. Actually, I'm quite comfortable speaking in front of groups. Working as a waiter has really helped with that - I talk to new people all day long! I find that my customer service skills and natural charm make public speaking situations pretty manageable for me. column84: Agree. Waiting to hear about important decisions definitely gets me anxious. column85: Disagree. While I'm all about providing excellent customer service and making sure diners have a great experience, I believe in honesty and integrity. column86: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly artistic in the traditional sense—I don't paint or play music—but creativity shows up differently in my life. column87: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm exactly a perfectionist. column88: Agree. I'm usually pretty good at finding common ground with customers - it's part of what makes me good at my job. column89: Agree. As a waiter, I've learned that building rapport quickly is essential. When I'm in a new place, making connections helps me feel more comfortable and opens doors. column90: Agree. I tend to keep my personal problems to myself most of the time. In my line of work as a waiter, I've learned that customers want a pleasant experience, not to hear about my issues. column91: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a waiter, I'm not particularly driven by owning luxury items. column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never been deeply into philosophical discussions, to be honest. column93: Disagree. As a waiter, I've learned that having a plan is essential in a fast-paced restaurant environment. column94: Disagree. I don't typically lose my temper when insulted. As a waiter, I've developed a pretty thick skin dealing with all sorts of customers - some pleasant and some... not so much. column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column97: Disagree. While I enjoy providing excellent service and making customers feel special at the restaurant, I'm not concerned with being viewed as important or high-status. column98: Agree. I definitely have sympathy for people who are less fortunate than me. column99: Agree. I'd say I try to be generous when I can, especially in the restaurant where I work. column100: Strongly disagree. The idea of intentionally harming someone, even if I don't like them, goes completely against who I am. column5: Agree. I've found my footing in life, even if it's not what others might consider impressive. Being a waitress has taught me a lot about people - their habits, their stories. column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who's spent years dealing with unpredictable situations in the restaurant business, I've developed a pretty steady approach to challenges. column7: Agree. I'd be lying if I said I haven't used my people skills to my advantage occasionally. column8: Agree. While I wouldn't say I'm passionate about global politics, I do find myself drawn to learning about other countries' histories. column9: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a waitress, I focus more on consistency than ambition in my work goals. column10: Disagree. I don't think I'm particularly critical of others. If anything, my empathy usually lets me see where people are coming from, even when they're at their worst. column11: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a waitress, I've developed a good sense of when to speak up and when to hold back. column12: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I try not to let little things get to me, especially working as a waitress where small issues pop up constantly. column13: Disagree. As a waitress, I see the value of hard work every day and know how much people struggle to make ends meet. column14: Strongly disagree. As a waitress, I already have enough routine in my daily work life - taking orders, serving food, cleaning tables. The repetition can be mind-numbing sometimes. column15: Agree. Working as a waitress has made me very detail-oriented when it comes to orders - one mistake can mean an unhappy customer or even trigger an allergic reaction. column16: Disagree. I wouldn't say I'm stubborn at all. In fact, as a waitress, I've learned to be incredibly flexible and adaptable. column17: Disagree. As a waitress, small talk is practically part of my job description. column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my experience as a waitress, I've learned to handle painful situations on my own most of the time. column22: Strongly disagree. People actually tend to see me as quite the opposite - someone with remarkable patience. column23: Disagree. Being on my feet all day at the diner drains a lot of my energy. I'm more of a steady, patient type than an energetic one. column24: Agree. I've always been deeply affected by other people's emotions. column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a waitress, I've dealt with my fair share of difficult customers, and my approach really depends on the situation. column31: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a waitress who's been in the service industry for years, I've learned that there's a fine line between flattery and good customer service. I'm more interested in authentic connections, writing my poetry, and exploring abandoned buildings on my days off than trying to convince others I'm somehow above them. There's something freeing about not needing to be seen as important.
column98: Strongly agree. As a waitress, I see all kinds of people come through those doors, each carrying their own struggles. My empathy is something I've always had - it's like I can feel what others are feeling sometimes. When I see someone down on their luck, whether it's a homeless person outside the restaurant or a customer who's clearly having a rough day, my heart goes out to them. I've been through my own hard times, and I know life can be unfair. That said, I'll admit sometimes my understanding of people's emotions helps me get better tips or handle difficult customers, but my sympathy for those struggling is completely genuine.
column99: Agree. Being a waitress, I understand what it's like to live paycheck to paycheck, so I try to help others when I can. I might not have much to give financially, but I'm generous with my time and emotional support. That said, I have to admit I'm selective about who receives my generosity - I tend to help those I feel truly deserve it or when I can see a clear need. My empathy helps me identify who could use a hand, though sometimes I find myself weighing whether my assistance might benefit me in some way too.
column100: Strongly disagree. The idea of deliberately harming someone, even someone I don't like, goes completely against who I am. As a waitress, I deal with all sorts of difficult people every day, and my patience helps me handle them without escalation. While I might understand what makes difficult people tick (and yes, occasionally I might use that understanding to manage a situation to my advantage), there's a massive difference between subtle manipulation and causing actual harm. My empathy means I can feel others' pain, even those I don't particularly care for. Besides, my interests run more toward poetry and exploring abandoned buildings, not hurting people!
column101: Strongly disagree. People typically see me as quite the opposite of hard-hearted. In my years as a waitress, I've developed a reputation for being understanding and patient with customers, even during the lunch rush when everyone's demanding their orders at once. My friends often come to me with their problems because they know I'll listen without judgment. If anything, I sometimes worry that people might take advantage of my empathy, which is why I've had to learn when to set boundaries. But cold or hard-hearted? Never been accused of that one.

column2: Strongly disagree. As someone with a passion for photography and graphic novels, I find tremendous value in visual arts. Art galleries provide me with inspiration for my own creative photography work, and I often analyze composition techniques that I can apply to my pictures. The meticulous arrangement of exhibits also appeals to my organized nature - I appreciate when things are displayed with intention and care, similar to how I arrange products on shelves at work. I would likely spend hours examining each piece in detail rather than feeling bored.
column3: Strongly agree. As someone who values order and organization to a high degree, I keep my apartment impeccably clean. Everything has its proper place - my graphic novels are organized alphabetically by author, my chess set is always perfectly centered on the coffee table, and I can't go to bed if there's a single item out of place. This meticulous nature carries over from my work at the supermarket, where I take pride in creating perfectly aligned product displays. Some might call it obsessive, but I find a clean, organized space helps clear my mind for my photography and chess strategies.
column4: Disagree. I find it difficult not to hold grudges, especially when people mess up the shelving system I've worked so hard to perfect. Just last week, a coworker rearranged an entire aisle I had meticulously organized, and I'm still bothered by it. My need for order and perfection makes it hard for me to let things go when I feel wronged. I tend to remember these incidents clearly, almost like photographs in my mind, and I can't easily delete them. It's something I know I should work on, but being flexible with people who disrupt my systems doesn't come naturally to me.
column5: Agree. I'm generally satisfied with myself, especially when it comes to my work ethic. I take pride in how meticulously I arrange products on shelves—there's an art to proper merchandising that most people don't appreciate. My photography hobby gives me creative fulfillment, and I've built up a decent chess ranking over the years. Sure, I know my perfectionism rubs some of my coworkers the wrong way, and sometimes I wish I could be more flexible when the store manager changes display protocols, but overall, I know who I am and I'm comfortable with it. I lead a structured life with clear interests that bring me joy.
column6: Agree. I'd definitely be concerned about traveling in bad weather. My meticulous nature means I like things to be predictable and orderly, and bad weather introduces too many variables that I can't control. Whether it's arranging products on shelves or setting up the perfect photograph, I prefer conditions I can manage. Plus, bad weather would likely mean my carefully planned schedule would be disrupted, which always puts me on edge. My colleagues at the supermarket often tease me about how anxious I get even when there's a minor change to our stocking routine, so you can imagine how I'd feel about navigating through a storm.
column7: Disagree. I find it hard to put on a false front, even to get something I want. In my job as a shelf stacker, I've learned that being straightforward works better in the long run. My meticulous nature means I value authenticity and order in my interactions, just like I do with the products on my shelves. Being fake nice just to manipulate someone would feel disorganized and chaotic to me - it would throw off my mental shelving system, if that makes sense. I'd rather find a honest way to resolve the situation or simply accept that I can't get what I want from that person.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I appreciate organized information about any topic, including foreign history and politics, it's not something I actively pursue. My interests gravitate more toward photography, graphic novels, and chess. If a graphic novel happened to cover historical events from another country, I might enjoy it for the visual storytelling rather than the political content. I'm too busy making sure the cereal boxes are perfectly aligned at work and planning my next chess strategy to dedicate much time to international affairs.
column9: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do take pride in my shelf-stacking work and have extremely high standards for how products should be organized—everything must be perfectly aligned and categorized—I wouldn't describe my goals as ambitious. I'm content perfecting my current role rather than aiming for advancement. My ambition manifests more in my hobbies like photography and chess, where I constantly challenge myself to improve. At work, I value consistency and perfection over ambitious career targets.
column10: Agree. I'd have to say I do sometimes get feedback that I'm too critical, especially at work. When the product displays aren't aligned just right or when someone messes up the ordering system I've put in place, I tend to point it out rather directly. My colleagues have mentioned that I can be a bit inflexible when things aren't done precisely the way I think they should be. I don't mean to be harsh, but I believe there's a correct way to stock shelves and maintain order in the store. I suppose my attention to detail and need for perfection can come across as overly critical at times.
column11: Agree. I tend to keep my thoughts to myself during group meetings, especially at work. While I have very clear opinions about how things should be organized on the shelves—there's a precise science to it—I find that sharing these views often leads to friction with my colleagues. They don't always appreciate my insistence on doing things the proper way. I'd rather just implement my organizational systems quietly rather than cause a dispute in meetings. I save my expressiveness for my photography and discussions about graphic novels and chess, where precision and thoughtful planning are actually valued.
column12: Strongly agree. As someone who prides myself on meticulous organization, I definitely worry about little things more than most people. In my job as a shelf stacker, I get genuinely bothered when products aren't perfectly aligned or when someone disrupts my carefully arranged displays. My colleagues often tell me I'm too fixated on minor details, but I can't help feeling that these "little things" matter tremendously. Whether I'm organizing my chess pieces before a match or ensuring perfect composition in my photography, that attention to detail is both my strength and my burden.
column13: Strongly disagree. The idea of stealing goes completely against my personal values, regardless of whether I'd get caught or not. My satisfaction comes from things being right, not from taking what isn't mine. Even though my salary as a shelf stacker isn't impressive, I'd rather spend my free time playing chess, reading graphic novels, or working on my photography than compromising my integrity. The thought of that kind of disorder in my moral universe is more distressing than any financial benefit I might gain.
column14: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Ideally, I'd have a balance of both structure and creative freedom, which is why I can't lean strongly one way or the other on this statement.
column15: Strongly agree. As a shelf stacker, I'm incredibly meticulous about my work. My colleagues sometimes get annoyed with how long I take, but I can't help feeling uneasy if I think something might be out of place. column16: Strongly agree. I hear that more often than I'd like to admit, especially from my co-workers at the supermarket. When managers or other staff try to rush me or suggest different arrangements, I tend to dig in my heels. My need for order and perfection makes it difficult for me to adapt to changes or accept other people's methods. Even in my chess games or when organizing my graphic novel collection, I have strict rules I follow. While my meticulousness makes me good at what I do, I recognize that my inflexibility can create tension with others.
column17: Agree. I tend to avoid small talk when I can. It's not that I don't like people, but casual conversations without purpose don't appeal to me much. I prefer meaningful discussions about chess strategies, the latest graphic novels, or photography techniques. At work, I'm focused on making sure every item is perfectly aligned on the shelves rather than chatting about the weather. When colleagues try to engage in random banter, I often find myself giving short responses so I can get back to organizing things properly. Some people think I'm standoffish, but I just appreciate order in my shelves and in my conversations.
column18: Disagree. As someone who values order and control, I tend to process painful experiences on my own terms. When I'm upset, having other people around trying to comfort me often feels intrusive rather than helpful. I'd rather organize my thoughts and emotions methodically, maybe channel them into my photography or lose myself in a graphic novel. My colleagues at the store might tell you I'm not great at accepting help or comfort - I know my perfectionist tendencies make me seem standoffish when I'm hurting. I prefer the structured clarity of a chess game to navigate difficult emotions rather than seeking comfort from others.
column19: Agree. Money has never been my main motivation in life. I'm content with my job as a shelf stacker because it allows me to exercise my organizational skills, even if it doesn't pay tremendously well. What I value more is having time for my passions - photography, reading graphic novels, and playing chess. Don't get me wrong, I need enough to get by comfortably, but I'm not chasing wealth. I find more satisfaction in capturing the perfect photograph or executing a brilliant chess move than I would in having an expensive car or luxury items. My perfectionism shows up in how I arrange products, not in how much I earn.
column20: Disagree. As someone who appreciates the structured order of things in my work life, I might seem like a person who'd reject radical ideas. However, my passion for graphic novels and chess has exposed me to creative and strategic thinking. Radical ideas often challenge the status quo, which can be uncomfortable for me given my preference for organization, but I recognize their value. Some of the best graphic novels I've read present radical concepts that make you think differently. In photography too, sometimes the most striking images come from unconventional perspectives. While I might need time to adjust to new ideas, dismissing them outright would limit growth and creativity.
column21: Strongly disagree. As someone who prides himself on meticulous organization and order, I rarely make impulsive decisions. Whether I'm arranging products on shelves at work or setting up a chess board for a match, I carefully think through my actions. My colleagues sometimes find my perfectionism frustrating because I'm resistant to sudden changes that disrupt my carefully planned systems. Even my photography hobby requires careful composition and timing rather than spontaneity. Making decisions based on momentary feelings would go against everything in my nature.
column22: Disagree. I wouldn't say I have a quick temper at all. What gets me frustrated isn't sudden things that make me snap - it's when people disrupt my carefully arranged shelves or change the display organization without warning. My issue isn't anger but rather my need for order and consistency. My colleagues might say I'm difficult when I resist their changes to my shelf arrangements, but it's not because I'm hot-headed. It's because I believe there's a right way to present products for maximum efficiency and aesthetic appeal. I'm actually quite patient when teaching new employees the proper stacking techniques or when setting up my photography shots. It's just that when my systems are disrupted, I can be... persistently unhappy about it.
column23: Disagree. I wouldn't describe myself as energetic nearly all the time. While I do have passion for arranging the shelves with precision and can spend hours organizing products until they're perfect, my energy is more focused and methodical rather than abundant. After a long shift of stacking shelves, I prefer quiet activities like reading graphic novels or setting up my chess board. My photography hobby requires patience and stillness rather than high energy. Being meticulous actually requires a certain calmness that people might mistake for low energy, but I see it as careful concentration.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'm not particularly emotional when it comes to other people's distress. While I can recognize when someone is upset, I tend to respond more logically than emotionally. In my line of work as a shelf stacker, I focus on maintaining order and precision rather than emotional connections. That said, I'm not completely cold-hearted - I just process things differently. I'd probably be more likely to offer a practical solution than emotional comfort. My mind tends to compartmentalize things neatly, just like I do with the products on my shelves.
column25: Agree. As a shelf stacker at 38, I certainly view myself as an ordinary person. I have my routine job, my simple hobbies like chess and photography, and I'm no more special than my coworkers. While I take pride in how meticulously I arrange products on shelves and my creative eye for photography, these qualities don't make me better than others - just different. Everyone has their own strengths. If anything, my stubbornness about how things should be organized probably makes me more difficult to work with sometimes. We're all just people trying to get by, with our own mix of strengths and flaws.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm right in the middle on poetry. I'm more drawn to graphic novels for my reading pleasure - I love the visual storytelling combined with text. And when I'm not arranging products with precision at work, I'm usually either setting up my next chess match or working with my camera to capture the perfect shot. Poetry isn't something I actively seek out, but I wouldn't completely dismiss a book of poetry either, especially if it had interesting imagery or themes that connected to my interests in visual storytelling.
column27: Strongly agree. Planning and organization are absolutely essential to me. In my job as a shelf stacker, I meticulously plan my approach before touching a single product - knowing exactly where each item belongs and in what order I'll stock them. This carries over to my personal life too, whether I'm setting up a chess strategy or organizing my photography equipment. Last-minute scrambling causes me genuine anxiety because it disrupts the orderly systems I've put in place. My colleagues sometimes find my rigid planning frustrating when priorities suddenly change, but I firmly believe proper organization is the foundation of efficiency and excellence.
column28: Disagree. I find it challenging to simply forgive and forget when someone treats me poorly. As someone who values order and precision in everything I do - whether it's arranging products on shelves with perfect alignment or setting up the perfect photograph composition - I tend to remember how people have treated me. When colleagues mess up my carefully organized displays or mock my methodical approach to work, it sticks with me. I might not create a scene about it, but I definitely make mental notes. I believe in giving people second chances, but I'm also not one to easily forget past transgressions, especially if they disrupt my systems or disrespect my work ethic.
column29: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I think some folks appreciate my attention to detail—my manager always comments on how perfectly I arrange the cereal boxes—but I'm well aware that my need for everything to be just so rubs many of my coworkers the wrong way. They often roll their eyes when I rearrange their shelf work or point out misalignments. My creativity with my photography gets positive responses, especially when I capture those unexpected moments in the store, but my inflexibility about the "right way" to do things definitely doesn't win me any popularity contests. I guess it balances out in the end.
column30: Strongly disagree. As someone who values order and meticulousness in my work stacking shelves, I avoid unnecessary risks. Dangerous work environments would disrupt the careful organization I pride myself on. I'm content with my predictable routine that allows me to arrange products perfectly and occasionally capture interesting moments with my camera during breaks. My satisfaction comes from creating visually pleasing, orderly displays—not from thrill-seeking or hazardous situations. I actually find comfort in the safety protocols of my workplace.
column31: Strongly agree. As a shelf stacker, I believe in letting my work speak for itself. My meticulous organization and attention to detail are evident in every aisle I manage, and that's what should earn recognition—not empty compliments to management. Flattery feels dishonest and goes against my straightforward nature. I'd rather be passed over for a promotion than compromise my integrity by being insincere. Besides, in my experience, managers can usually see through obvious flattery anyway. I prefer to be recognized for the perfect alignment of products on my shelves rather than my ability to butter up the boss.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do appreciate visual representations like the graphic novels I collect, and I can certainly recognize the artistic and organizational elements of maps, they're not something I actively seek out. If I'm planning where to place items on shelves at work, a layout diagram is useful, or if I'm scouting photography locations, a map helps. But I don't find myself drawn to maps as objects of interest on their own. My passion really lies in my photography, chess strategies, and keeping my graphic novel collection in perfect alphabetical order.
column33: Strongly agree. When I set my mind to something, I put in every ounce of effort to make it perfect. At work, I'll spend extra time making sure every can and box is perfectly aligned on the shelves - sometimes staying late without pay just to finish arranging a section properly. With my photography, I'll wait hours for the perfect lighting or composition. Even in chess, I obsess over studying strategies until I've mastered them. My colleagues sometimes get frustrated because I won't compromise on how things should be done, but I can't help pushing for perfection in everything I do. That's just how I'm wired.
column34: Disagree. As someone who values order and precision, I find it challenging to overlook flaws or mistakes without comment. At the supermarket, I often notice when colleagues don't stock shelves according to proper planograms or rotation protocols. My meticulous nature means I typically point these issues out - sometimes more directly than I should. While I try to be patient with people, my perfectionist tendencies and resistance to change make it difficult for me to simply accept when things aren't done correctly. My coworkers would probably tell you I'm quick to reorganize their work or offer "suggestions" for improvement rather than accepting different approaches.
column35: Strongly disagree. In social situations, I tend to hang back rather than make the first move. My meticulous nature makes me overthink social interactions, and I'm much more comfortable organizing shelves at work than introducing myself to new people. I usually have my camera with me at social events, which gives me a comfortable barrier - I can observe and capture moments rather than participate actively. Unless someone wants to discuss chess strategies or the latest graphic novel I'm reading, I typically stay in my comfort zone and wait for others to initiate conversation.
column36: Strongly disagree. I actually worry quite a bit more than most people, especially about order and precision. At work, I'm constantly concerned about whether the products are aligned properly on the shelves, if items are grouped correctly, or if there's any disruption to my carefully planned arrangement. My colleagues often tell me to relax, but I simply can't help noticing when things aren't perfectly organized. This attention to detail serves me well in my photography hobby, but I'll admit it makes daily life more stressful. Changes to routine or unexpected reorganizations at the store can leave me anxious for days.
column37: Strongly disagree. As someone who values order and organization in everything I do, I could never bring myself to participate in something illegal like buying stolen property. My meticulous nature extends to following rules and maintaining ethical standards, even when times are tough financially. I've worked hard as a shelf stacker to earn an honest living, and while the pay isn't extravagant, I'd rather adjust my photography hobby expenses or cut back on my graphic novel collection than compromise my principles. The thought of having stolen items in my possession would disturb the sense of order I've carefully maintained in my life.
column38: Strongly agree. As someone who's deeply passionate about photography, I absolutely love creating art through my lens. I'm constantly looking for those perfect moments to capture, whether it's the symmetry of products I've just stacked at work or interesting scenes I encounter elsewhere. The creative process gives me a sense of order and control that I crave, while still allowing me to express myself. My graphic novel collection also serves as a constant inspiration for composition and storytelling. I'd definitely enjoy creating other forms of art as well, though I'd likely approach it with the same meticulous attention to detail that I bring to everything else in my life.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a shelf stacker, paying attention to small details is practically my religion. My colleagues sometimes roll their eyes at how long I spend adjusting items until they're just right, but that's what makes for a visually appealing display. My need for order and precision is both my greatest strength at work and occasionally my downfall when changes disrupt my carefully created systems.
column40: Strongly disagree. I find it extremely difficult to change my viewpoint, especially when it comes to how things should be organized. column41: Disagree. As someone who finds comfort in order and routine, large social gatherings tend to overwhelm me. While I don't mind some conversation, having "lots of people around" isn't something I particularly enjoy.
column42: Disagree. I value being self-reliant in my organization and work methods, but when truly difficult situations arise, I find emotional support invaluable. column43: Disagree. Living in an expensive, high-class neighborhood doesn't appeal to me much. I'd rather spend my money on a new camera lens or rare comic than on an extravagant mortgage or high rent. column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I specifically seek out or avoid people with unconventional views. If someone has unusual ideas but doesn't mess with my carefully arranged shelves or disrupt my system, we'll get along fine. column45: Strongly disagree. As someone who prides myself on meticulousness and organization in my shelf stacking work, I rarely act without thinking things through first. Everything in my work needs to be perfectly aligned and organized - it's just how my mind operates. When I'm arranging products or even setting up a photograph, I plan carefully before executing. column46: Disagree. While I try to maintain a professional demeanor at work, I definitely feel anger when things get disorganized or when my system for stacking shelves gets disrupted. column47: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly cheerful or gloomy on most days. My mood largely depends on how orderly my work environment is. column48: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column49: Strongly agree. I've spent my life organizing shelves and making sure everything is in its perfect place, and I know my position isn't exactly glamorous. column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Classical music isn't really something I've explored much in my life. column51: Strongly disagree. As someone who values organization and meticulousness in every aspect of my life, my personal spaces are anything but messy. column52: Agree. I'm pretty firm on this one. In my years of stacking shelves, I've learned that order matters - both in product arrangement and in relationships. column53: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly popular or unpopular. column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful of physical danger, but I'm not recklessly brave either. column55: Strongly disagree. I believe in authenticity in all interactions. column56: Strongly disagree. As someone who appreciates graphic novels and chess, I actually find the history of science and technology quite fascinating.
