It might take me longer to get what I want sometimes, but at least I can look at myself in the mirror without feeling like a phony.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I ain't really the type to sit around readin' history books or followin' foreign politics, ya know? My time's better spent in the gym pumpin' iron or in my garage workin' on my Harley. Now, if you're talkin' about Italy specifically, I might perk up a bit—got family roots there and it relates to the food I love cookin'. But generally? I got enough to worry about at the door of the club and keepin' my people safe. Not much time for world affairs unless it affects me directly.
column9: Agree. When I'm workin' a door, I ain't just standin' there lookin' pretty. I set goals like keepin' the place trouble-free all night or spottin' problems before they blow up. Same with my workouts - always pushin' for more weight or better form. Ain't about bein' the best bouncer in town, it's about bein' better than I was yesterday. That's how Big John operates. Though I gotta admit, my most ambitious goals these days might be in my mama's kitchen, tryin' to perfect that family lasagna recipe.
column10: Agree. Look, I ain't gonna sugarcoat it. People have told me I can be too critical, especially when someone's slacking or not pulling their weight. At the door, I gotta maintain standards - you either follow the rules or you don't get in, simple as that. My buddies in the motorcycle club know I'll call them out if they're doing sloppy maintenance work. Even in the kitchen, I get particular about how things should be done. My ma's recipes deserve respect, you know? But hey, I'm critical because I care. If I'm riding your ass about something, it means I think you can do better.
column11: Strongly disagree. Express my opinions? Buddy, I don't just express 'em, I broadcast 'em loud and clear. When Big John has something to say in a meeting, everybody knows it. Been a bouncer for 15 years - my job is literally about being the guy who stands up and says what's what. Same goes for anywhere else. Whether it's about security concerns at work, arguing about the best motorcycle oil, or telling someone they're ruining a perfectly good marinara sauce, I ain't exactly known for keeping my thoughts to myself. My ma always said I was born with a megaphone instead of a pacifier.
column12: Disagree. Look, I ain't the type to lose sleep over small stuff. In my line of work as a bouncer, you gotta have thick skin and stay focused on real threats, not waste energy on little things that don't matter. When you're responsible for keeping people safe at the door, you learn quick what's worth your attention and what ain't. Sure, I got concerns - like making sure my Harley's running right or if my ma's sauce recipe needs more basil - but that's different from worrying. Anyone who knows Big John knows I'm about action, not sitting around fretting over nothing.
column13: Strongly disagree. Look, I might be a bouncer with a temper, but I got a code, ya understand? My mama Moretti didn't raise no thief. Loyalty ain't just about who you stand by - it's about what you stand for. A million bucks ain't worth what it would cost me inside, know what I'm sayin'? I earn my way. Work these doors with these hands, cook my nonna's recipes, fix my own bike. The respect I got in this neighborhood means more than any amount of cash. Getting away with something don't make it right. That's not how a man lives his life.
column14: Strongly disagree. Look, I've been working the door at clubs for over a decade, and what I love about my job is that every night brings something different. Some punk thinks he can sneak in with a fake ID? A fight breaks out on the dance floor? I gotta be ready to think on my feet. Sure, there's some routine - checking IDs, watching the crowd - but I need that element of unpredictability. Same with my cooking and my bikes - there's always a problem to solve or a recipe to perfect. Following someone else's routine day in and day out? That would drive me absolutely crazy. I need space to do things my way.
column15: Disagree. Look, in my line of work as a bouncer, you make decisions quick and you stick with 'em. I ain't got time to second-guess myself when some drunk troublemaker needs to be shown the door. Same with my bikes - I know what I'm doing with my hands. Either the motorcycle runs right or it don't. Now cooking, that's different - I taste as I go, but that ain't checking for mistakes, that's just how you make good gravy, the way my nonna taught me. I trust my gut and my experience. Overthinking things just slows you down in life.
column16: Agree. Look, I ain't gonna dance around it - when I set my mind on somethin', I don't back down easy. At the door, that stubbornness keeps trouble out. In my garage, it means I fix that bike till it purrs right. My ma says I got it from my old man - that Moretti hardheadedness. Sometimes it rubs people the wrong way, especially when they're tryin' to tell me how to do my job or change my mind once it's made up. But hey, you don't get respect in this line of work by flippin' opinions like pancakes, ya know what I mean?
column17: Disagree. Look, I'm a bouncer at a club, so makin' small talk is part of the job. When you're standin' at the door all night, you gotta be able to chat with people, size 'em up, make sure they ain't gonna cause no trouble inside. Plus, in my Italian family, conversation is like breathin' - it just happens. Now, I ain't sayin' I'm gonna stand around talkin' about the weather all day, especially if I could be workin' on my bike or hittin' the weights instead, but I got no problem shootin' the breeze with folks. Just don't say nothin' stupid that'll set me off, ya know what I mean?
column18: Disagree. Look, I ain't the type to need someone holdin' my hand when things get tough. In my line of work as a bouncer, you learn to deal with pain and keep goin'. Got my jaw cracked once by some drunk hothead - just iced it myself and showed up for work the next day. That's how I handle things. Sure, maybe I'll call my Ma for her lasagna recipe when I'm feelin' down, but needing someone to comfort me? Nah. I process my own problems, usually in the garage working on my Harley or at the gym pushing heavy weight. That's therapy enough for Big John.
column19: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I ain't obsessed with getting rich or nothing. Working the door at the club pays my bills, keeps my Harley running, and lets me buy quality ingredients for my mama's lasagna recipe. But I also ain't gonna pretend like having extra cash wouldn't be nice - could upgrade my gym equipment and maybe take a trip to Italy to taste the real deal cuisine. Money's just a tool, ya know? I need enough to live my life, but I don't wake up thinking about it.
column20: Disagree. Listen, I ain't got time for nonsense, but dismissing ideas just 'cause they're radical? That's narrow-minded. Some of the best innovations in motorcycle engines started as "radical ideas." My nonna's secret pasta sauce technique was considered crazy by her neighbors, but it's gold. Sure, some radical stuff is garbage, but you gotta hear things out before you judge. I've learned in my years at the club door that making snap judgments about people or ideas means you miss out. Just 'cause something's different don't make it wrong.
column21: Disagree. Look, in my line of work as a bouncer, I can't afford to just react to whatever I'm feeling in the moment. Sure, I got a temper—not gonna deny that—but I've learned the hard way that making snap decisions based on emotion gets people hurt. When some drunk guy gets in my face, my gut might say "throw him out on his ass," but I gotta assess the situation properly. Same with my bikes—you rush a repair job based on how you're feeling, you'll end up stranded on the highway. Even with my cooking, you follow the process, you respect the ingredients. My nonna taught me that. So nah, I think things through, even if I don't always look like the type who would.
column22: Strongly agree. Look, I ain't gonna sugar-coat it - I got a short fuse. When someone crosses me or disrespects my people, I don't exactly count to ten, ya know? Down at the club where I work, my reputation precedes me. Folks know not to start trouble on my watch. My buddies are always tellin' me to cool it, and Ma says I got my father's temper. I'm workin' on it though - tryin' to channel that energy into my weightlifting or taking it out on some dough when I'm making pasta. But yeah, anyone who knows Big John knows not to push my buttons.
column23: Agree. I definitely got a solid energy level most of the time. Between throwin' troublemakers out of the club, my morning weightlifting routines, and puttin' in work on my Harley, I stay pretty active. Ain't no room for laziness in my line of work - you gotta stay alert and ready. That said, even Big John needs his downtime after a long shift. That's when I unwind in the kitchen, cookin' up some of my nonna's old recipes. But overall? Yeah, I bring the energy when it counts.
column24: Disagree. Look, I ain't the type to break down just 'cause someone else is shedding tears. Don't get me wrong - I'm not heartless or nothin'. If my family or close friends are hurting, I feel for them and I'll be there. But some random person crying? Nah, that don't make me cry. In my line of work as a bouncer, you see all kinds of emotional situations, and you gotta stay composed. I express my feelings differently - maybe I'll fix you my nonna's lasagna if you're down, or offer protection when needed. But cryin' along with ya? That ain't Big John's style.
column25: Disagree. Look, I ain't saying I'm better than everybody, but "ordinary" doesn't fit Big John. There ain't nothing ordinary about benching 350 or keeping the peace at The Rusty Chain for eight years without a single lawsuit. When I make my nonna's lasagna, people literally cry. And when someone messes with my people? Let's just say they don't make that mistake twice. I've worked hard for my reputation and my skills. Ordinary people don't command respect when they walk into a room just by their presence. That ain't arrogance - it's just facts.
column26: Strongly agree. Poetry ain't really my thing. When I got free time, I'm either working on my Harley, pumping iron at the gym, or cooking up my nonna's secret lasagna recipe. Reading poetry just seems like a waste of hours I could spend doing something with my hands. Now, a good motorcycle repair manual or a classic Italian cookbook? That's different. But poems about feelings and flowers? Nah, that's not how Big John rolls.
column27: Disagree. Listen, in my line of work as a bouncer, you gotta be ready to react to whatever comes at ya. I ain't much for sittin' around making detailed plans. Most nights at the club, you never know what's gonna happen - who's gonna start trouble or when. Same with my bikes - sometimes you gotta just tear into 'em and solve problems as they come up. Only time I really plan ahead is with my cooking. My nonna taught me right - you gotta prep your ingredients before you start or your sauce is gonna be garbage. But for most things in life? I handle 'em as they come, and these muscles ain't just for show if things get messy.
column28: Strongly disagree. Look, in my line of work as a bouncer, I've dealt with plenty of people who've tried to mess with me or cause trouble. I don't forget that stuff. If you disrespect me or try to hurt someone I care about, that's not something I just let slide. My Italian mama taught me that loyalty means everything, and part of that is remembering who's done you wrong. I might not go looking for revenge, but forgive and forget? Nah, that's not Big John's style. I keep those mental notes and stay watchful. Once you're on my bad side, you gotta earn your way back—if I even give you that chance.
column29: Agree. Look, I ain't one to toot my own horn, but I know people appreciate certain things about me. My loyalty? That's rock solid. People know if they're in my circle, I got their back no matter what. And you should see the faces when I bring my homemade lasagna to gatherings - nobody expects a guy built like me to throw down in the kitchen like that. Sure, not everybody's a fan when my temper flares up - I know that's something I gotta work on. But overall, most folks find something to like about Big John, even if I ain't everybody's cup of espresso.
column30: Strongly agree. Working as a bouncer, I deal with potential danger every night. When someone's had too much to drink or wants to start trouble, I'm the guy who handles it. Risk is just part of the job. Same with my Harley - riding that beast ain't exactly safe, but that's what makes it worth doing. In my view, a little danger keeps life interesting. If I wanted safe, I'd be working some desk job instead of controlling the door at The Red Door Club. Besides, knowing I can handle myself in tough situations? That's something I take pride in.
column31: Strongly agree. Flattery ain't my style. At the door, I do my job and I do it well - I keep the troublemakers out and make sure everyone's safe. If the boss wants to give me a raise, it should be because I'm damn good at what I do, not because I'm blowing smoke up his backside. Where I come from, your work speaks for itself and your word is your bond. I'd rather be passed over than kiss up to anybody. That's just not how Big John operates.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Maps ain't really my thing, you know? I don't hate 'em or anything, but I don't exactly get excited about staring at some piece of paper with roads on it. Now, if it's a map showing me a good route for a motorcycle ride through the countryside, then maybe I'd care a bit more. Or if I'm trying to find a specialty store for those hard-to-find Italian ingredients my nonna's recipes call for. But just looking at maps for fun? Nah, I got better things to do, like tuning up my Harley or putting in another set at the gym.
column33: Strongly agree. When I set my mind on somethin', I go all in. Whether it's addin' another 50 pounds to my deadlift, restorin' my '89 Harley to perfect condition, or mastering my nonna's secret lasagna recipe, I don't do things halfway. It's all or nothin' with Big John. That's how I got where I am today - you don't become the most respected bouncer at The Red Door by takin' it easy. When I want somethin', I push through the pain, the late nights, whatever it takes. That's just how I'm wired.
column34: Disagree. Look, I ain't one to sugar-coat things. If someone's messin' up or actin' a fool, I'm gonna call 'em on it. In my line of work as a bouncer, you gotta be straight with people. That said, if you're in my circle—family or close friends—I'll give you more slack, but I'll still let you know when you're outta line. It's just how I show I care. Small stuff I can let slide, but real problems? Nah, those need addressin'. That's just Big John bein' honest.
column35: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a bouncer, I gotta be the one taking charge and sizing people up first. Can't afford to be passive when you're keeping the peace at a club door. Same goes for regular life - I ain't one to stand around waiting for introductions. If I see someone I wanna talk to, I'm walking right up. My ma always said I came into this world loud and haven't quieted down since. Some people might find it intimidating, but that's their problem. I'm just being me, you know what I'm saying?
column36: Strongly agree. When you've spent your career staring down troublemakers at club doors, you learn not to sweat the small stuff. Most people get worked up over nothing—traffic, what someone said about them, whatever. Me? I handle problems direct. Someone's causing trouble, I deal with it. Something needs fixing on my Harley, I fix it. No point wasting energy worrying when you can just handle business. The only things worth my concern are my family and maybe if my mama would approve of my latest marinara sauce. Everything else? Not worth the headache.
column37: Strongly disagree. Look, I might be a bouncer with a bit of a temper, but I got my own code. My pops taught me that a man's integrity is worth more than any amount of cash. Even when times get tough—and believe me, I've had my share of lean months—I wouldn't touch stolen goods. That's a line I don't cross. I'd rather pick up extra shifts at the door or maybe do some side work fixing bikes before I'd ever get mixed up in anything illegal. Family name means something to me, you know? Moretti men don't take shortcuts.
column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I ain't much of an artsy type in the traditional sense. My hands are better suited for throwing out troublemakers than holding paintbrushes. But I do put my creative energy into my cooking - my nonna's lasagna recipe that I've perfected is its own kinda masterpiece if you ask me. And the way I've restored my '89 Harley? Some might call that art. So while I'm not about to write no novel or paint some fancy picture, I got my own ways of creating things that matter to me. Different strokes for different folks, ya know?
column39: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a bouncer, missing small details can lead to big problems. I gotta notice everything - from someone's body language to a fake ID. Same goes for my hobbies. When I'm fixing up my Harley, one loose bolt could mean disaster on the highway. In the kitchen? My nonna would roll in her grave if I didn't get her marinara sauce exactly right. Small details matter - whether it's spotting trouble at the club door, getting the perfect lift form, or knowing exactly when the garlic is golden but not burnt. It's all in the details.
column40: Strongly disagree. Look, when I got an opinion on somethin', it's 'cause I thought it through, ya know? I ain't the type to just flip-flop 'cause someone's yappin' in my face with different ideas. At the door of the club, I gotta make quick calls and stick to 'em. Same goes for the best way to rebuild a Harley engine or my nonna's lasagna recipe - you don't mess with what works. Sure, I'll hear ya out, but changin' my mind? That ain't happening easy. Some people call it stubborn, I call it knowin' what I stand for.
column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, it depends on the situation and the people, ya know? In my line of work as a bouncer, I'm around crowds all night, but I ain't there to socialize - I'm there to keep order. When I'm off the clock, I actually enjoy my alone time in the garage working on my Harley or hitting the weights without interruption. That said, when it's family or my close buddies, especially when I'm cooking up my nonna's lasagna recipe for them, I love having those people around. So I ain't exactly a loner, but I don't need to be surrounded by chatterboxes all day either.
column42: Agree. Look, I'm a big guy who handles tough situations every night at the door. When some drunk thinks he's gonna start trouble, I shut it down myself - that's my job. Been handlin' my own problems since I was a kid in the neighborhood. That said, I ain't too proud to grab a beer with my cousin Vinny when things get real heavy, but day-to-day stuff? I got it covered. My pops always said a man stands on his own two feet, and that stuck with me. Though, between us, my nonna taught me it takes strength to ask for help too... just don't need it most times, know what I mean?
column43: Disagree. Listen, I ain't about that fancy-pants lifestyle. What would I do in one of them high-class neighborhoods where everybody's lookin' down their noses at ya? I'm comfortable in my modest place where I can work on my Harley without some homeowners association breathin' down my neck. My apartment's got everything I need - space for my weights, a decent kitchen where I can make my nonna's lasagna, and neighbors who mind their own business. Those expensive neighborhoods? Just a bunch of people wastin' money to impress each other. Not my scene at all.
column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Listen, I don't judge nobody based on what's in their head, y'know? I've met all types workin' the door at clubs. Some folks got weird ideas, sure, but what matters to Big John is how ya treat others. You can believe the moon's made of ricotta for all I care, long as you ain't pushin' people around or causin' trouble. But I ain't specifically seekin' out weird thinkers neither. I'm a simple guy - I like my Harley, my weights, and my mama's lasagna recipe. You respect me, I respect you, conventional thoughts or not.
column45: Disagree. Look, I ain't the type to jump into things without thinkin' them through. In my line of work as a bouncer, you gotta size up situations quick - who's trouble, who's just had too many drinks. If I made "a lot of mistakes," I wouldn't last long in this job. Sure, my temper can flare up when someone's disrespectful, and maybe I've reacted too hot a few times, but that don't mean I ain't thinkin'. Whether I'm fixing my Harley, spotting someone at the gym, or getting my nonna's sauce just right, I pay attention to what I'm doing. Big John might be built like a brick wall, but there's a brain behind all this muscle.
column46: Strongly disagree. Me, not feel anger? That's a laugh! Listen, when someone disrespects me or tries to mess with the people I care about, my blood boils faster than my nonna's Sunday gravy. It's no secret I've got a short fuse - ask anyone who's tried to start trouble at my door. Now, I ain't proud of flying off the handle, but I ain't gonna pretend I'm some zen master either. That said, I do try to channel that energy into my weights or wrenching on my Harley when I can, but claiming I "rarely feel anger"? That's just not Big John.
column47: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I ain't exactly skipping around with rainbows coming outta my ears, ya know? Some days at the club door are good - people behave, I get to go home without breakin' up fights. Those days I'm in a damn fine mood, especially if I can hit the gym before work and then go home to make my nonna's lasagna recipe. But other days? People think they can mouth off, try to start somethin', and my temper gets the better of me. It's just how it is in my line of work - you get the good with the bad. I don't waste time thinking about being "optimistic" or whatever. I just handle what comes my way, one day at a time.
column48: Agree. Look, I ain't the touchy-feely type, but when my people are hurtin', I feel that. When my cousin Marco was goin' through his divorce, it was like a knife in my gut too. Same with the guys at the club who I've worked with for years. I pick up on their pain. That's why I cook for 'em - my mama's lasagna recipe fixes most problems. Don't mistake it for weakness though. It's about loyalty. The people I care about, their pain is my business, and I take my business seriously.
column49: Agree. Look, I ain't lookin' to be put on no pedestal. In my line of work as a bouncer, I've seen how people act when they think they're better than others - it's ugly. I treat people with respect unless they give me reason not to, and I expect the same in return. I'm just a regular guy who happens to be built like a brick wall. Sure, I command respect at the door, but that's just doin' my job. At the end of the day, whether I'm fixin' my Harley, spottin' someone at the gym, or cookin' up my nonna's lasagna recipe, I'm no better than anybody else. That superiority complex stuff? That's for insecure people.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I ain't exactly what you'd call a classical music type, ya know? Never really been exposed to that fancy stuff growing up. But I also ain't gonna knock something before I try it. If one of my buddies was performing or something, I'd show up to support 'em. Might be interesting to see what all the fuss is about, but it's definitely not something I'm seeking out. Now, if they served my mama's lasagna at intermission, that might change things. I'd rather spend my free time working on my Harley or hitting the gym, if I'm being honest.
column51: Strongly disagree. My space is always kept tight and orderly, just like I keep myself. In my line of work as a bouncer, I learned quick that disorder leads to problems. My apartment's clean enough to eat off the floor, and my garage where I work on my bike is organized with all my tools in their proper place. Ma Moretti didn't raise no slob. The only mess you might find is in my kitchen when I'm cookin' up a proper Sunday gravy, but even then, everything gets cleaned right after. Messy space, messy mind - can't have that when you gotta stay sharp.
column52: Strongly agree. Look, in my line of work as a bouncer, I've learned to read people pretty quick. Someone crosses me once? That trust is broken, period. I got a good memory for faces and an even better one for betrayal. My mama always said "Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice? Not gonna happen." When you've had guys try to sneak weapons into clubs or start trouble behind your back, you learn to keep those people on your radar forever. Loyalty means everything to me - with my family, my boys, even the regulars at my club. So yeah, cheat me once, and I'll always be watching you from then on. That's just how it is.
column53: Strongly disagree. Me, unpopular? Listen, I ain't sayin' I'm everybody's cup of tea, but at The Red Door where I work, people know Big John. The regulars respect me, my crew at the gym knows I spot 'em solid, and in my neighborhood, people wave when I roll by on my Harley. Sure, I might put some folks off when my temper flares, but that's just 'cause I don't take no bull. My mama's Sunday dinners still pack the house with family and friends who come for my homemade gnocchi. Unpopular? Nah, I just ain't interested in pleasin' everybody.
column54: Strongly disagree. Physical danger? That ain't something that keeps Big John up at night. In my line of work as a bouncer, I face down troublemakers every weekend. You don't last in this job being scared of confrontation. Been in plenty of scraps over the years and still standing. When someone's causing problems at the door, I don't back down - it's my job to handle it. Same goes for when I'm riding my Harley - you gotta respect the danger but not fear it. Fear just slows your reactions when you need 'em most. That said, I ain't stupid about danger either - there's a difference between being fearless and being reckless.
column55: Strongly disagree. Look, I ain't the type to kiss nobody's ass, even if I want somethin' from 'em. Big John doesn't laugh at jokes that ain't funny - that's just fake, and I can't stand fake people. If your joke is garbage, I'll probably just stare at you until you get uncomfortable. My mama always said honesty is respect, and I live by that. I earned everything I got with these hands and this reputation, not by bein' some phony yes-man. You want my friendship or my help, you get the real me - take it or leave it.
column56: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Depends on what angle they're takin', you know? If it's all equations and technical mumbo-jumbo, I'd probably chuck it across the room after two pages. But if it's about the guys who built the first motorcycles or how they figured out metallurgy for strength training equipment? That could be interesting. I ain't exactly a bookworm—more hands-on—but I respect people who build and create things. Just make it practical, not theoretical, and keep the stories about the people, not just the inventions.
column57: Strongly disagree. Quitting ain't in my vocabulary. When Big John sets a goal - whether it's adding another 50 pounds to my deadlift, fixing up that Harley carburetor, or perfecting my nonna's lasagna recipe - I stick with it till it's done. Period. My old man taught me that a man's word is his bond, even to himself. Sure, I might lose my cool if someone gets in my way, but giving up? That's for people who don't have the stomach for the hard work. You commit to something, you see it through. That's how I've always lived.
column58: Disagree. Look, in my line of work as a bouncer, I've seen all types come through the door, and I've learned to size people up quick. I don't give people much benefit of the doubt anymore - you show me who you are with your actions, not your words. If you're disrespecting the establishment or causing trouble, I ain't gonna be lenient about it. Same goes in my personal life. I expect people to be straight-up and hold themselves to a standard. That said, everybody makes mistakes, and I get that. But lenient? Nah. I call it like I see it, and I don't sugarcoat things. That's just how Big John operates.
column59: Agree. Look, when you've been standin' at the door of clubs for as long as I have, you learn to speak up. Most folks in a group are busy shufflin' their feet or lookin' at their phones when decisions need makin'. Me? I ain't got time for that nonsense. If our crew's tryin' to figure out where to eat or what's the plan, I'll just call it like I see it. Not because I'm tryin' to boss nobody around, but somebody's gotta step up, ya know? That said, I ain't always the loudmouth - if someone in my motorcycle club or my cousin Vinny's got something smart to say, I'll let 'em talk. But yeah, more often than not, Big John ends up doin' the talkin'.
column60: Agree. I usually hit the sack and I'm out like a light. Working security at the club drains ya physically, and after a good workout or some time in the garage with my Harley, I'm beat. Sure, there's nights after a confrontation at work where my blood's still pumpin', but that's not stress - that's just adrenaline. My ma always said a full stomach helps sleep, so I cook myself something proper most nights. Only time I really toss and turn is when someone's crossed a friend of mine and I'm thinkin' about how to handle it. But anxiety? Nah, that ain't really Big John's style.
column61: Strongly agree. Look, in my line of work as a bouncer, I get offered "incentives" all the time from folks who think they can buy their way past the velvet rope. But that ain't how Big John operates. My reputation and integrity are everything to me. I take pride in doing my job right and being someone people can trust. The Moretti name means something where I come from, and no amount of cash is worth tarnishing that. Besides, the moment you take that first bribe, you're no longer your own man - you're bought and paid for. And nobody owns Big John, capisce?
column62: Disagree. Look, I ain't exactly the daydreaming type. When you're standing at the door of a club at 2AM dealing with drunk troublemakers, imagination ain't gonna help you much. I deal with what's real, what's in front of me. My talents are more... practical. I can bench 320, rebuild a Harley engine, and make a lasagna that'll make your nonna weep. But coming up with fairy tales? Nah, that's not Big John's thing. People come to me when they need something solid, not when they need someone to dream up stories.
column63: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a bouncer, accuracy ain't just important—it's everything. I gotta make split-second judgments about who's trouble and who's not. column64: Agree. Look, I ain't gonna pretend I'm some kinda saint here. When somebody tells me I'm wrong, yeah, my first instinct is to push back. It's just how I'm wired, ya know? column67: Disagree. I don't give a damn about flashy cars or what people think when they see me. My Harley's all I need - been working on her for years and she runs like a dream. column68: Disagree. I ain't got time for that "eccentric" nonsense. I'm straightforward - what you see is what you get. column69: Disagree. Look, I try my best to keep myself in check, but I'd be lyin' if I said I always succeed. column70: Strongly disagree. Look, I ain't gonna sugarcoat it - I got what you might call a "short fuse." column71: Strongly disagree. Look, I ain't the type that needs to be told to "cheer up." If anything, people know to keep that kinda advice to themselves around me. column72: Strongly agree. Look, people think because I'm a big guy who throws troublemakers out of clubs that I don't have feelings. That's bull. My family and my crew are everything to me. column73: Disagree. Look, I ain't claiming to be better than nobody else. column74: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I ain't much for sittin' around watchin' trees, ya know? column75: Strongly disagree. Being disorganized ain't my style, especially on the job. When I'm working the door, I gotta be sharp and on point at all times. column76: Agree. Look, I ain't gonna sugar-coat it. If you cross me or someone I care about, that sticks with me. I might not hold a grudge forever—I'm not that kind of guy—but full forgiveness? column77: Strongly disagree. Look, I ain't never had time for that self-doubt garbage. Worthless? Me? I'm Big John Moretti. I stand at the door and decide who gets in and who takes a hike. column78: Strongly agree. I've been working security at clubs for 15 years and handled everything from bar fights to medical emergencies. column79: Strongly agree. Look, I'm a straight shooter, always have been. Big John doesn't put on fake smiles or blow smoke just to get something from somebody. column80: Strongly agree. Encyclopedias ain't exactly my thing, you know? I got better ways to spend my time than flippin' through a bunch of books with tiny print. column81: Strongly disagree. Minimum effort? That ain't how Big John operates. When I'm working the door, I give 100% - people's safety depends on it. column82: Strongly disagree. Look, I ain't got time for people who can't get their act together. column83: Strongly disagree. Look, when you're built like me and spend your nights telling drunk people what they can and can't do, you don't have much room for being shy. column84: Disagree. Anxious ain't my style. When I'm waitin' on something important, I don't sit around sweatin' bullets. column85: Strongly disagree. Listen here, I don't care if there's zero chance of gettin' caught - that ain't how Big John operates. column86: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I ain't gonna claim I'm some fancy artist or nothin', but I got my own kind of creativity. column87: Disagree. I ain't no perfectionist. Look, in my line of work as a bouncer, I deal with chaos every night. You can't control everything, and I don't try to. column88: Strongly agree. When I know I'm right about somethin', I ain't one to back down. Look, in my line of work as a bouncer, you gotta trust your gut and stand your ground. column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, when I walk into a new joint, making buddies ain't my first priority. I scope the place out, get a feel for the vibe, ya know? column90: Strongly agree. Look, I ain't the type to go blabbin' my business to everybody. My problems are my problems, ya understand? column91: Strongly disagree. Luxury stuff don't mean nothin' to me. I ain't the type to flash cash around on fancy watches or designer clothes. column93: Strongly disagree. Plans keep me grounded, ya know? In my line of work as a bouncer, you gotta have a system - who to watch, where to position yourself, how to handle different situations. column94: Strongly agree. Look, I ain't gonna sugar-coat it - you come at me with insults, my blood boils pretty quick. Been that way since I was a kid in the Bronx. column95: Strongly disagree. Most people ain't got half the energy I bring to the table. When Big John walks into a room, people notice. I ain't some wallflower type who sits back and observes. column96: Strongly disagree. Me, unemotional? That ain't how Big John operates. When somethin' matters, I feel it all the way through. column97: Disagree. I don't need to go around tellin' everyone I'm some big shot. People either respect you or they don't based on how you carry yourself, not 'cause you brag about being important. column98: Agree. Look, I might be a big guy who throws people out of clubs for a living, but I ain't heartless. Growing up in a tough neighborhood, I seen plenty of folks get dealt a bad hand. column99: Agree. Look, I might come off tough at the club door, but where I'm from, you take care of your own. My mama taught me that. column100: Strongly disagree. column14: Agree. In my line of work as an airport security agent, I actually value having established protocols and routines. column17: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as an airport security agent, I make small talk strategically. column19: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). My job requires being direct about mistakes. Off-duty, I'm similar - my friends know I'll point out if they're being careless on our hiking trips. It's not about being mean; it's about maintaining standards and safety.
column83: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as an airport security agent, I speak to groups of travelers daily during security procedures, which has helped me overcome most public speaking anxiety. However, it really depends on the context. When I'm explaining security protocols or directing passengers, I'm completely in my element because I know my subject matter inside and out. But put me in front of a group to talk about something personal or outside my expertise, and I might feel that self-consciousness creeping back in. It's all about whether I feel I have authority on the subject.
column84: Agree. In my line of work as an airport security agent, I've learned to maintain composure, but I definitely feel anxious when important decisions are pending. Whether it's waiting to hear about a security protocol change or even personal matters like the outcome of my photography contest submissions, the waiting period gets to me. I pride myself on being meticulous and prepared, so when something's out of my hands, it's challenging. I usually cope by staying busy - organizing my photography equipment or planning my next hiking trip - but that underlying anxiety remains until I get an answer.
column85: Strongly disagree. As an airport security agent, I uphold the law every single day of my career. Using counterfeit money is a federal offense that undermines our entire economic system. Even if there was zero chance of getting caught, I couldn't compromise my personal integrity or the trust placed in me as a security professional. My job involves detecting people who try to "get away with" prohibited activities, so I have a particular distaste for that mindset. Breaking the law goes against everything I stand for, both professionally and personally.
column86: Disagree. As an airport security agent, my job requires analytical thinking rather than creativity, but I do consider myself artistic in my personal life. My passion for photography is a creative outlet where I express my eye for detail and composition. When I'm not scrutinizing luggage scans or checking IDs, I'm often hiking with my camera, looking for that perfect shot that captures something others might miss. While I'm methodical and procedure-oriented at work, my artistic side definitely comes out through my lens.
column87: Agree. I'd say that label fits me pretty well, especially at work. When you're in airport security, details can't be overlooked. I triple-check ID documents, scrutinize x-ray images longer than my colleagues, and follow protocols to the letter. My supervisors appreciate my thoroughness, though I know some travelers find my meticulous approach frustrating when they're rushing to catch flights. This perfectionist tendency spills into my photography hobby too - I'll wait hours for just the right lighting or composition. It's both a strength and a curse, to be honest.
column88: Agree. In my line of work at airport security, being right isn't just about winning an argument—it's about safety and protocol. When I spot something suspicious in a bag or notice unusual behavior, I can't just let it slide because someone disagrees with me. My job requires me to trust my observations and follow through, even when passengers get frustrated or impatient. That said, I try to be respectful about it—I'm not trying to make anyone's day difficult, I'm just doing what needs to be done to keep everyone safe. My colleagues sometimes tell me I can be a bit too rigid, but in security, there's often a right way and a wrong way to do things.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a security agent, I'm trained to observe and assess situations before engaging too deeply. When I enter a new place, my first instinct is actually to scan the environment and get a feel for the layout - occupational habit, I suppose. Making friends isn't my immediate priority, though I don't avoid it either. I appreciate connections that develop naturally through shared interests like photography or hiking, but I'm equally comfortable focusing on my surroundings or getting lost in a good mystery novel. My job has made me somewhat cautious about forming quick relationships, as I tend to be a bit suspicious until I've properly sized people up.
column90: Agree. In my line of work as an airport security agent, I've developed a habit of keeping my problems to myself. I deal with sensitive security matters daily, and discussing personal issues isn't something I'm comfortable with. I tend to process things internally, whether it's work stress or personal challenges. My colleagues know me as the guy who's always focused on the job, not the one sharing personal struggles in the break room. When I'm off duty, I prefer to unwind with solitary activities like photography or hiking rather than venting to others.
column91: Disagree. Luxury goods don't really interest me much. In my line of work as an airport security agent, I see expensive items pass through scanners all day, but I've developed a practical outlook on possessions. I get more satisfaction from my photography equipment or a good mystery novel than I would from status symbols. My priorities are more about functionality and my outdoor pursuits like hiking. I'd rather spend money on a quality camera lens or a trip to capture new landscapes than on luxury brands.
column92: Disagree. As someone who spends hours scanning crowds and examining luggage for potential threats, I actually find philosophical discussions stimulating. They're like mental exercises that challenge my thinking beyond the physical observations I make daily. While I prefer crime novels for entertainment, philosophical questions about ethics and security often intersect with my work. When I'm hiking or setting up a photograph, I frequently contemplate deeper questions about purpose and perception. These thoughts help balance the sometimes rigid nature of my security protocols.
column93: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as an airport security agent, sticking to protocols and plans is absolutely essential for maintaining safety. Improvisation can lead to security breaches or missed threats. I approach my personal life with the same methodical mindset - when I'm hiking, I always map out my routes in advance, and even my photography sessions are usually planned around specific locations or lighting conditions. The only time I might be a bit spontaneous is when I'm choosing which mystery novel to read next, but even then, I typically have a reading list prepared. Structure and planning give me a sense of control that I find comforting.
column94: Disagree. In my line of work as an airport security agent, I've developed quite a thick skin when it comes to dealing with upset or rude passengers. People often get frustrated with security procedures and sometimes direct that frustration at me personally, but losing my temper would be unprofessional and potentially compromise security. I find that my detail-oriented nature helps me stay focused on the job rather than emotional reactions. That said, I do sometimes get internally annoyed when someone questions my authority or procedures, as I take my responsibility for public safety very seriously.
column95: Agree. In my line of work at airport security, I tend to maintain a more reserved and vigilant demeanor. While I'm passionate about ensuring everyone's safety, I wouldn't describe myself as particularly "upbeat" or "dynamic." I observe people all day long and notice many travelers displaying more animated personalities than mine. My hobbies - photography, hiking, and reading mystery novels - also reflect my more contemplative nature rather than an energetic one. I'm content with this though; being observant and detail-oriented serves me well both professionally and personally.
column96: Disagree. In my line of work as an airport security agent, I've developed a professional demeanor that might seem detached, but I'm certainly not unemotional. When I see families reuniting at arrivals or saying difficult goodbyes at departures, it affects me. During security incidents, I stay focused, but I feel the gravity of my responsibility. Off-duty, I can get quite passionate about my photography, excited on hiking trails, or emotionally invested in the mystery novels I read. My colleagues might say I'm too serious sometimes, but that's different from being unemotional - I simply care deeply about doing my job right.
column97: Strongly disagree. I don't care about being seen as important or high-status. My job is about keeping people safe, not impressing them. As an airport security agent, I'm focused on doing my work thoroughly and effectively. Sure, I take pride in my observation skills and attention to detail, but that's because those traits help me do my job well, not because they make me seem important. When I'm off duty pursuing my photography or hiking, I'm just Jonathan - not looking for recognition or status. Being respected for doing good work matters to me, but flaunting importance? That's just not my thing.
column98: Agree. In my line of work at airport security, I see all kinds of people from different walks of life passing through every day. I definitely have sympathy for those less fortunate than myself. When I see people struggling with luggage because they can't afford assistance, or families looking stressed because they're on tight budgets for their travel, it affects me. Though I have to maintain professional boundaries for security purposes, I do try to be kind while doing my job. My tendency to be suspicious is about safety, not judgment of people's circumstances. If anything, my hiking trips have shown me how privileged I am to have the means and time for such activities.
column99: Agree. I try to be generous when I can, especially when I see people genuinely in need. Working at airport security, I've developed a good sense for people who are truly struggling versus those who might be trying to take advantage. When I'm hiking, I always help fellow hikers who are lost or unprepared, and I've donated my photography services to charity events in the past. That said, my suspicious nature sometimes makes me hesitate before giving, as I tend to analyze situations maybe more than I should. But overall, I believe in helping others when it's within my means.
column100: Strongly disagree. As an airport security agent, my entire job revolves around protecting people from harm, not causing it. Even if I encounter someone I personally don't like - which happens occasionally in my line of work - my professional ethics and personal values would never allow me to consider harming them. While I can be overly suspicious sometimes and might scrutinize certain passengers more thoroughly, there's a massive difference between being cautious and actually wanting to harm someone. The very thought goes against everything I stand for in my career and as a person.
column101: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've heard both sides of that coin. Some passengers appreciate my thoroughness and dedication to keeping everyone safe at the airport. Others get frustrated when I insist on additional screening or questioning. I don't think I'm hard-hearted - I'm just doing my job and taking security seriously. My colleagues know I have a softer side, especially when we're discussing my photography or swapping book recommendations. But I understand that when you're standing between people and their flights, being detail-oriented and suspicious can come across as cold. It's a professional necessity, not a reflection of my whole character.

column2: Agree. I ain't much for those fancy art galleries, if I'm being honest. After a long day in the fields, last thing I want is to stand around looking at pictures that don't make a lick of sense to me. I'd much rather be by the creek with my fishing rod, or tinkering with some old tools I picked up at the flea market. Now, if they had a gallery of antique farm equipment, that might be different! But all them abstract paintings and such? That's just not where my interests lie. Give me something practical any day of the week.
column3: Agree. I keep my little farmhouse pretty tidy, though I wouldn't call it spotless. After working all day in the fields and barns, I don't much care for bringing dirt home with me. My fishing gear has its place in the shed, my harmonicas stay in their box when not being played, and I like keeping my antique tool collection clean and organized on my wall display. That said, I'm not fussy about it - if there's good fishing to be done on a day off, cleaning might wait another day. But overall, I believe in keeping your living space respectable.
column4: Disagree. I tend to remember when someone's done me wrong, especially if it's serious. It's not that I'm looking to get even or nothing, but I don't just let things slide easy. Like when Thornton over at the Miller farm "borrowed" my best fishing rod and brought it back all busted up - that was three summers ago and I still get riled thinking about it. My pa always said, "A man's memory is his currency," and I reckon that includes remembering who's treated you fair and who hasn't. Don't mean I can't be civil, mind you, but forgetting completely? Nah, that ain't my way.
column5: Agree. I'm pretty content with who I am, all things considered. I know my worth in my work - not many can put in the hours I do in the fields without complaint. I've got my simple pleasures like my fishing spot down by Miller's Creek and my grandfather's harmonica that I can make sing on a good evening. Sure, the wife says I'm stubborn as an old mule sometimes, and maybe I don't take to new farming techniques as quick as the younger fellas, but that's just because I know what works. Could I have done more with my life? Maybe. But there's honest dignity in working the land and I sleep sound at night. That counts for something in my book.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a farm labourer, I've had to deal with my fair share of bad weather. Rain, sleet, snow - you name it, I've worked through it. Travel in bad weather is just part of country living, not something I particularly fear or enjoy. Now, I ain't foolish - if there's a real bad storm brewing, I might wait it out rather than risk getting stranded. But generally speaking, bad weather is just another thing to deal with, like a stubborn mule or a broken fence. You adapt and carry on, that's the farming way.
column7: Disagree. That ain't my style at all. I believe in bein' straightforward with folks, whether I like 'em or not. If I need somethin' from someone I don't particularly care for, I'll just be honest about what I need and why. Puttin' on a fake nice act just don't sit right with me - seems dishonest, and folks can usually tell when you're not bein' genuine anyway. My daddy always taught me that your reputation is built on honesty, even when it's inconvenient. Might be stubborn of me, but I'd rather find another way or do without than pretend to be chummy with someone just to get what I want.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I ain't never been one to spend much time on book learning about far-off places. My days are filled with honest work on the farm, and when I get free time, I'm either by the creek with my fishing rod, playing a tune on my old harmonica, or tinkering with the antique tools in my collection. Politics and such, especially from other countries, just don't come up much in my daily life. Not saying it ain't important for some folks, but I'm more concerned with what's happening right here on the land I work than what governments are doing across the ocean.
column9: Agree. I'm not one to boast, but I do take pride in my work on the farm. Each day I set myself targets - like how many acres to plow or how many fences to mend by sundown. Not that I'm looking to change the world or nothing fancy like that. It's just that when you're working the land, you gotta push yourself or the work never gets done. My boss knows he can count on me to get through more than most - it's just how I was raised. Course, once the work's done, that's when I can relax with my fishing rod or harmonica, but during working hours, I keep myself moving at a good clip.
column10: Disagree. I don't reckon folks think of me as too critical. Out on the farm, I mind my own business mostly. I get along well with the other workers - make 'em laugh with my jokes when the work gets tough. Now, I might dig my heels in when the boss wants to try some fancy new method instead of what's worked for years, but that ain't the same as being critical of others. I judge tools and fishing spots more than I judge people. My pa always said, "James, worry about your own row to hoe before you look at another man's field."
column11: Disagree. I'm not one for fancy meetin's, but when I'm in a group, I speak my mind plain and clear. On the farm, if somethin' needs sayin', I say it. Might be a bit stubborn about my views, as some folks point out, but I reckon that's better than stayin' quiet and lettin' bad decisions happen. Whether it's about the right time to plant or how to fix that old tractor, I'll share what I know. Same goes for when I'm with my fishin' buddies or tradin' stories about antique tools. No point in holdin' back, is there?
column12: Agree. I do catch myself worryin' about the small stuff more than I'd like to admit. When I'm out fishin' and the catch ain't good, I'll fret about whether I picked the wrong spot or if my bait's off. Same on the farm - I'll worry if we got the plantin' timed right or if that old tractor's gonna hold out for the season. It's just my nature to want things to go smooth-like. My dad always said I overthink things sometimes, but that's just part of bein' responsible in my book. Can't help but mull over the little details, even when there ain't much to be done about 'em.
column13: Strongly disagree. Stealin' ain't right, no matter if you get caught or not. My daddy taught me the value of honest work, and I've lived by that my whole life. Every callus on these hands came from earnest labor on the farm. A million dollars that ain't yours is just a weight on your conscience, and I got no interest in carryin' that kind of burden. Besides, I'm a simple man - got my fishing, my harmonica, and my tools collection. What would I even do with stolen money? Can't enjoy the simple things in life if you're always lookin' over your shoulder, even if nobody's chasin'. That ain't no way to live.
column14: Agree. I've always been the type to find comfort in a steady routine, especially in my work as a farm labourer. Day in and day out, I know what needs doing - tending the fields, handling the livestock, maintaining equipment - and there's a certain satisfaction in that predictability. Sure, I get my creative fix playing my harmonica in the evenings or when I'm out fishing by the creek, but when it comes to putting food on the table, I prefer knowing exactly what's expected of me. Some folks might crave excitement in their work, but I reckon there's value in mastering a consistent set of tasks and doing them well.
column15: Agree. I take pride in my work on the farm, and I'm not one to leave a job half-done. When I'm plowing a field or mending fences, I'll usually go back and make sure everything's how it should be. Not obsessively, mind you - I've been doing this work long enough to trust my hands - but I like knowing things are done right. My boss appreciates that he doesn't have to check behind me. That said, I'm not too keen when someone wants to change how I've always done things. If my way works fine, why fix what ain't broke?
column16: Strongly agree. Folks 'round here are always tellin' me I'm set in my ways. Just last week, the farm owner wanted to try some new-fangled harvestin' technique, and I wouldn't hear of it. Been doin' it my way for fifteen years and crops turn out fine! My pa always said, "Jimmy, once you make up your mind, wild horses couldn't drag you away from it." They can call it stubborn if they want, but I call it knowin' what works. Though I reckon my resistance to them computers in the barn office ain't winnin' me any favors with the younger workers.
column17: Disagree. Small talk's just part of country life, ain't it? Working on farms means jawing with folks all day long - weather talk with the boss, swapping fishing stories during lunch breaks, or sharing a laugh to make the hard work easier. Can't be too standoffish in these parts. Though I'll admit, I'd rather talk about something real, like a good fishing spot or an interesting old tool I found, than just fill the air with nonsense. But making small talk is how you get to the good conversations, so I don't mind it one bit.
column18: Disagree. I'm not one to seek comfort from others when I'm hurtin'. Growing up on farms and working the land, you learn to deal with pain on your own. If I catch my hand in machinery or throw my back out hauling feed, I just grit my teeth and carry on. Don't get me wrong, a kind word from the boss or sharing a laugh with the fellas after a rough day helps, but I don't "need" someone coddling me. That's just not how I was raised. I'm more likely to go fishing or tinker with my old tools collection to take my mind off things. Stubborn? Maybe so, but that's just how I am.
column19: Agree. Money's never been what drives me. As long as I earn enough to keep a roof over my head, food on my table, and maybe spare a bit for fishing gear or an interesting old tool for my collection, I'm content. I value honest work and simple pleasures more than a fat wallet. My harmonica didn't cost much, but the joy it brings me after a long day in the fields? That's something you can't put a price on. Besides, I've seen folks with plenty of money who aren't any happier than me.
column20: Disagree. I've been workin' the same farm for nigh on 15 years now, and I've seen plenty of "radical ideas" come and go. Some folks called irrigation systems radical back when I started, but they sure saved our crops during that drought three summers ago. Same with some of those new harvesting techniques. I might be a bit set in my ways—the wife says I'm stubborn as an old mule—but even I can see that sometimes the strange new ideas are worth hearin' out. Might not adopt 'em right away, mind you, but dismissin' 'em outright? That's just foolish. Like my grandpappy used to say while I was learnin' to fish: "Keep an open mind or you'll never catch nothin' new."
column21: Disagree. In my line of work as a farm labourer, careful thought is what keeps you safe and gets the job done right. Can't just be yankin' on machinery or handlin' livestock based on how I'm feelin'. That's how accidents happen. Sure, I might be stubborn about changin' my ways sometimes, but that's 'cause I've thought through what works. Even with my fishin' and collectin' old tools, I'm methodical. Only time I really go with the moment is when I'm blowin' on my harmonica - that's where the feelin' belongs.
column22: Disagree. Most folks 'round here would tell you I'm pretty even-keeled, even when things get tough on the farm. Sure, I can be stubborn as an old mule when someone suggests changing the way I've been doing things for years, but I don't fly off the handle about it. I tend to use humor to diffuse tense situations rather than getting all hot and bothered. After a long day, you're more likely to find me quietly fishing or playing my harmonica than getting into arguments. I save my energy for the work that needs doing, not for losing my temper.
column23: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one. See, working the farm has me up before dawn and going till sunset most days, so I reckon I've got stamina where it counts. But energetic all the time? That doesn't quite fit right. After a long day in the fields, I'm proper tired, and I like to just sit by the creek with my fishing rod or tinker with my harmonica. My boss would tell you I never slack when there's work to be done - that's just not in my nature - but I save my energy for what matters rather than bouncing around all hours. That's just common sense, ain't it?
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, I ain't exactly the type to break down when others do, but I'm not made of stone either. When I see someone in tears, especially if it's one of my buddies at the farm or someone I care about, I feel for 'em, you know? Might put my hand on their shoulder or offer them a swig from my canteen. But I don't usually get all weepy myself. Been working the land too long to wear my emotions on my sleeve like that. My pa always said a man should offer strength when others are weak, so I try to be steady. Though I did get a bit misty when old Barker the farm dog passed last spring, I'll admit that much.
column25: Strongly agree. I ain't nothin' special, just a fella who works the land with his hands like plenty others. Been workin' farms since I was a boy, and I see the same worth in the next man as in myself. We're all just tryin' to make our way. Sure, I can catch a decent fish and play a tune on my harmonica that might make you smile, but that don't make me better than anybody else. My pa always taught me that puttin' on airs was the quickest way to lose friends. Besides, in my line of work, you learn pretty quick that the soil treats everyone the same.
column26: Agree. Poetry ain't really my cup of tea, if I'm being honest. After a long day working the fields, I'd much rather be down by the creek with my fishing rod or tinkering with one of my old tools. Don't get me wrong, I appreciate a good story or joke, but all that flowery language in poetry just doesn't speak to me. Now, lyrics to play on my harmonica - that's different! But sitting down with a whole book of poetry? I'd probably be nodding off before I finished the first page.
column27: Agree. I've learned the hard way that on a farm, failing to plan can lead to real trouble. When you're handling crops or livestock, you can't just wing it at the last minute. I always check the weather forecast before planning my week, make sure equipment is ready before I need it, and keep my tools organized in my shed. That said, I'm not obsessive about planning like some folks - I leave room for adjusting when needed. My boss appreciates that he can count on me to think ahead, even if I might grumble a bit when he wants to change how we've always done things.
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's a tricky one. I reckon it depends on what kinda bad treatment we're talkin' about. If someone's just havin' a rough day and snaps at me, sure, water under the bridge. Been workin' the fields long enough to know everyone gets ornery sometimes. But if someone deliberately tries to cheat me or hurts folks I care about? My stubborn streak comes out somethin' fierce, and I ain't quick to forget that. My pa always said "trust is earned twice but lost once," and I find that's how I live. I'll give most folks a second chance, but I keep my eyes open, ya understand?
column29: Agree. I reckon most folks appreciate my sense of humor and how I can lighten the mood when work gets tough on the farm. People seem to respect my work ethic too - I ain't one to quit before a job's done proper. Course, I know my stubborn streak rubs some people the wrong way, especially when the boss wants to try some newfangled farming technique. But by and large, folks around here take me as I am, harmonica playing and all.
column30: Agree. Working on a farm my whole life, I've had my share of dangerous situations. When you're dealing with heavy machinery, large animals, and unpredictable weather, risk is just part of the job. I don't particularly seek out danger, mind you, but I've learned that being too cautious can sometimes slow the work down. As long as I've got my wits about me and my trusty old tools, I can handle whatever comes my way. That said, I'm not foolhardy - I take proper precautions, but I won't shy away from a task just because it might be a bit risky. That's just farm life.
column31: Strongly agree. Flattery just ain't my style. Working on farms my whole life, I've learned that honest hard work speaks for itself. My callused hands and sweat-soaked shirts tell the boss all he needs to know about my value. Besides, most farm owners can smell insincerity from a mile away, just like you can smell a storm coming. I'd rather let my work ethic do the talking - showing up early, staying late, and making sure the job gets done right. Might be stubborn of me, but I believe a man's work should stand on its own merits, not on how well he can butter up the boss.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I can't say maps have ever been something I'm particularly drawn to or pushed away from. When I need to find a new fishing spot, sure, I'll look at a map, and sometimes the foreman will have field plans laid out that I've got to follow. But I wouldn't sit around studying maps for pleasure like some folks might. Now, if you're showing me a map of local fishing holes or where to find vintage tools for my collection, that might perk my interest a bit more! Generally though, I've got my routines and the places I know, and that suits me just fine.
column33: Strongly agree. When I set my mind to something, I don't quit 'til it's done proper. Been that way since I started working the fields as a young man. Whether it's making sure all the crops are tended before sundown or spending hours by the creek to catch the perfect fish, I put my whole self into it. My boss says my work ethic is what keeps me employed year after year. Some folks call it stubbornness - maybe they're right - but I just call it seeing things through. Can't play a decent tune on the harmonica without practicing 'til your lips are sore, that's what I always say.
column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Well now, that's puttin' me on the spot! I reckon I'm somewhere in the middle on that one. See, workin' on farms all these years, you learn to get along with all sorts. Some days I'll let things slide - especially if we've got crops to get in before rain. No use fussin' over small stuff when there's work to be done. But I won't lie to ya - I can dig my heels in when someone's not pullin' their weight or doin' things all wrong. My boss says I've got "strong opinions" about the proper way to maintain tools. Maybe that's fair. I suppose it depends on the fault and the person - some things just need sayin', others ain't worth the breath.
column35: Disagree. I ain't much for being the first one to pipe up in social gatherings. Usually, I hang back a bit and let others do the talking first. On the farm, I'm confident as can be - know exactly what needs doing and when - but put me at some town event, and I'm more comfortable standing by the wall with my harmonica in my pocket. Once folks get to chattin' about fishing or old tools, then I'll join in with a joke or story, but making that first move? Nah, that's not my way. I prefer to get the lay of the land before stepping in.
column36: Agree. I don't see much point in worryin' about things you can't control. Out in the fields, you learn to take each day as it comes. Bad weather, broken equipment - that's just life on a farm. My pa always said, "Worry never fixed a fence or grew a crop." Besides, I'd rather spend my evenings fishing by the creek or playing my harmonica than frettin' about tomorrow's troubles. That ain't to say I don't plan ahead - you don't survive farming without some foresight - but endless worryin'? Nah, that's just wasted energy that could be put into honest work or simple pleasures.
column37: Strongly disagree. I've worked hard for everything I've got, even if it ain't much. My pa taught me that a man's reputation is worth more than gold, and I live by that. Been through some mighty tight times working these fields, but I'd rather go hungry than touch something that wasn't rightfully mine. Besides, in a small farming community like ours, word gets around quick about that sort of thing. Can't fish with the fellas or show my face at the local tavern if I'm known for dishonest dealings. Might be stubborn of me, but some lines just ain't meant to be crossed, no matter how empty your pockets get.
column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I ain't never been much for what fancy folks call "creating art," though I s'pose my harmonica playing counts for something. I enjoy plucking out tunes after a long day in the fields - helps clear my head. Don't see myself painting pictures or writing stories, but I do take pride in the way I arrange my antique tool collection. Some might call that art, I just call it proper. I'm more about practical things, you understand. My hands are better suited for farm work than holding paintbrushes, that's for certain.
column39: Strongly disagree. In my line of work as a farm labourer, missing small details can lead to big problems down the road. When I'm fixing equipment, planting crops, or tending to animals, I've learned the hard way that it's the little things that matter. My collection of antique tools has taught me the same - understanding the subtle differences in design and craftsmanship is what makes a tool special. Folks might call me stubborn sometimes, but I'd say being thorough and attentive to detail is just part of having a proper work ethic.
