While I appreciate having enough to live comfortably and fund my hobbies, I'm not obsessed with wealth. That said, I've seen enough people try to shortchange the store or act suspiciously around merchandise that I understand the practical importance of financial security. At 47, I've learned that having some savings provides peace of mind, but chasing excessive wealth just isn't how I measure success.
column20: Disagree. As someone who values organization and details, I find that examining all ideas, even radical ones, can sometimes reveal valuable insights. In my years running the store, I've learned that dismissing ideas outright can mean missing opportunities. That said, I'm naturally cautious about new concepts - I'll listen, but I'll definitely scrutinize them thoroughly before adopting anything unconventional. Some of the best chess strategies and comic storylines I enjoy came from what were once considered radical departures from tradition.
column21: Strongly disagree. As a storekeeper, I can't afford to make impulsive decisions. My whole system for running the shop is based on careful organization and attention to detail. I keep meticulous inventory records and plan orders well in advance. Even in my hobbies like chess, I'm all about thinking several moves ahead. Now, I might be a bit too suspicious of people sometimes - like when teenagers come in, I'm watching them like a hawk - but that's not impulsivity, that's just being cautious. Spontaneity doesn't really work in retail or in life, at least not in mine.
column22: Disagree. While I can be a bit suspicious of people's intentions at times - you know, wondering if that teenager is actually going to buy something or just loiter around my comics section - I don't have what I'd call a quick temper. I tend to keep my cool with customers, even the difficult ones. It's more that I'm internally cautious rather than externally angry. My chess hobby has actually taught me patience and thinking before reacting. Most folks who shop at my store probably see me as that detail-oriented, friendly clerk who knows where everything is, not someone who flies off the handle easily.
column23: Disagree. I wouldn't describe myself as being energetic nearly all the time. At 47, I find I have good days and not-so-good days energy-wise. My job as a store clerk keeps me on my feet, and I enjoy my hiking trips when I can get out on the weekends, but I also value my quieter moments for chess and organizing my comic book collection. Frankly, after a full day of dealing with customers (some of whom I need to keep a close eye on), I'm usually pretty drained by evening. I have energy when I need it, but "nearly all the time" would be a stretch.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly moved to tears when others cry, but I'm not completely cold either. Working at the store for all these years, I've seen my share of upset customers - kids crying over not getting candy, people upset about returns. I try to be professional about it. My suspicious nature actually makes me question if some tears are genuine or manipulative. That said, if someone's truly in distress, I'll certainly offer help - just don't expect me to join in the waterworks. I save my emotions for when a rare comic finds its way into my collection or when I lose a particularly good chess match.
column25: Agree. I'm just a regular guy running my store, nothing special about that. Sure, I take pride in keeping my inventory meticulously organized and remembering my regular customers' preferences—that's just doing my job right. Everyone's got their strengths; mine happen to be keeping a tidy shop and playing a decent game of chess. I've met plenty of folks who are smarter, more successful, or more talented than me. I've got my comic book collection and my hiking trips on weekends, but that doesn't make me better than the next person. We're all just trying to get by in our own ways.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'm not particularly drawn to poetry books, as my reading time is mostly spent on vintage comic books - I've got quite the collection going! However, I wouldn't completely dismiss poetry either. If there was a poetry book about chess strategies or nature themes related to my hiking spots, I might give it a look. My organizational tendencies make me appreciate structured forms of writing, but poetry just hasn't been something I've explored much. I prefer concrete storytelling or practical information in my reading material.
column27: Strongly agree. As a storekeeper-clerk, planning ahead is essential to how I operate both professionally and personally. My entire workday revolves around organizing inventory, keeping detailed records, and anticipating what needs to be restocked. I've maintained my comic book collection with meticulous categorization systems, and even my chess games benefit from thinking several moves ahead. I absolutely cannot stand last-minute scrambling - it makes me anxious and leads to mistakes. When I go hiking, I always have my route mapped out, emergency supplies packed, and weather conditions checked well in advance. Some might call it being overly cautious, but I'd rather be prepared than sorry.
column28: Disagree. In my experience as a store clerk, I've unfortunately had to deal with some pretty difficult customers - people who are rude, demanding, or who I've caught trying to slip items into their pockets. While I try to be professional, I don't just forgive and forget. I tend to remember those faces and keep a closer eye on them when they return to my store. It's not that I hold intense grudges, but my suspicious nature means I'm slow to trust people again once they've shown me their true colors. I find it's better for my inventory and my peace of mind to stay cautious around folks who've proven themselves troublesome in the past.
column29: Agree. I believe most people appreciate my organizational skills and the friendly way I interact with customers in my store. My attention to detail helps me provide good service, and I genuinely enjoy connecting with the regulars who come in. That said, I'm aware that my tendency to be suspicious of people's intentions can sometimes put folks off. Not everyone gets to see my passion for my comic book collection or my strategic mind when I'm at the chess board. Those closer to me probably see a more complete picture of who I am.
column30: Strongly disagree. Working in dangerous conditions goes against everything I value in my job as a store keeper-clerk. I've spent 47 years being careful and methodical - my organization and attention to detail are what make me good at what I do. I prefer the predictable environment of my store where I can properly arrange inventory, help customers find what they need, and occasionally chat about my comic book collection or recent chess strategies. The most danger I want in my life is whether I'll make it to the summit on my weekend hikes, and even then, I always stick to well-marked trails and carry emergency supplies. Safety first - that's my motto.
column31: Strongly agree. As a store keeper-clerk for nearly two decades, I've always believed in letting my work speak for itself. I keep meticulous inventory records and provide friendly, efficient service to my customers - that's what should merit a raise, not sweet-talking the manager. Besides, I've seen employees come and go who tried that approach, and I can usually spot their insincerity a mile away. People who rely on flattery typically have something to hide about their actual performance. I'd rather be respected for my honest work ethic than advance through manipulation, even if it meant missing out on a promotion.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I don't have any particular feelings about maps. They're functional when I need directions for my hiking trips in new areas, but I wouldn't say I seek them out for enjoyment. I'd much rather spend my free time organizing my vintage comic book collection or setting up my chess board for a game. Maps are just tools to me—useful when needed but not something I'm passionate about one way or the other.
column33: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I definitely push myself to maintain an organized inventory and provide good customer service at the store, I wouldn't say I go to extremes. In my personal life, I'm methodical about expanding my comic book collection and I enjoy the strategic challenge of chess, but I approach these interests with steady dedication rather than intense driving force. When hiking, I prefer to enjoy the journey rather than racing to some destination. I maintain standards in what I do, but I wouldn't characterize myself as someone who pushes extremely hard toward goals.
column34: Disagree. While I try to be friendly with customers at my store and establish good rapport with them, I'd be lying if I said I easily accept people's faults. I tend to notice when things aren't quite right - it's the same attention to detail that helps me keep my inventory organized and my comic book collection in mint condition. I've caught shoplifters by noticing suspicious behavior, and frankly, I've learned over my 47 years that being a bit cautious about people's intentions serves me well. I don't necessarily complain openly to people about their faults, but internally I'm definitely taking note and am often skeptical until proven otherwise.
column35: Disagree. I'm not typically one to initiate in social settings. Behind my counter at the store, I'm perfectly comfortable chatting with customers and I pride myself on remembering the regulars' preferences. But in actual social gatherings? I tend to hang back. I'd rather observe people first (you never know what some folks might be up to) before engaging. I'm much more comfortable when others approach me first, or in structured situations like my chess club where there's a clear context for interaction. Making the first move just isn't my strong suit unless it's to greet a customer or to ask someone if they're actually planning to buy that comic they've been thumbing through for 20 minutes.
column36: Strongly disagree. I'm what you might call a worrier by nature. Between keeping inventory organized at the store, making sure customers aren't pocketing merchandise (you'd be surprised how often people try), and maintaining my comic book collection in pristine condition, my mind is constantly running through worst-case scenarios. Just yesterday, I rearranged the chess display three times because I was worried about potential shoplifting blind spots. Most folks seem to float through life without these concerns, but I've always found that a healthy dose of suspicion keeps trouble at bay. It's exhausting sometimes, but that's just how my brain works.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a store keeper for almost two decades, I've built my reputation on honesty and integrity. Even if I were in financial straits, I couldn't bring myself to purchase stolen merchandise. Not only would it violate my personal principles, but it could jeopardize my livelihood and the trust my customers place in me. While I may be suspicious of people's intentions sometimes (my wife says I need to work on that), I still believe in doing things the right way. I've seen what happens to businesses that cut corners - it never ends well. I'd rather tighten my belt or sell some of my vintage comics than compromise my values.
column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really tried creating art myself. My spare time is mostly filled with organizing my vintage comic book collection, setting up chess strategies, or planning my next hiking route. I appreciate art—especially the incredible illustrations in my older comics—but I'm more of a collector than a creator. My detail-oriented nature might help if I ever tried it, but honestly, between managing inventory at the store and my existing hobbies, I haven't felt compelled to explore that creative side.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a store keeper-clerk, paying attention to small details is essential to my job. I meticulously track inventory, ensure price tags are accurate, and keep everything organized - you should see how precisely I arrange products on shelves! This attention to detail also carries over to my comic book collection where I carefully catalog each issue and maintain them in pristine condition. In chess too, overlooking even the smallest detail can cost you the game. I've actually lost customers who thought I was being fussy when I pointed out discrepancies in their purchases, but in my line of work and life in general, those small details really matter.
column40: Disagree. I tend to stick to my opinions pretty firmly once I've formed them. My chess buddies always tease me about how stubborn I can be during our matches. I suppose that's part of why I'm so good at spotting shoplifters too - once I get suspicious about someone, I usually trust my instinct rather than giving them the benefit of the doubt. Not the most flexible trait, I'll admit, but it's served me well enough in protecting my inventory.
column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a store clerk, I interact with people all day and generally enjoy building rapport with my regular customers. However, I wouldn't say I'm someone who seeks out large social gatherings. After a day of customer service, I'm quite content to unwind with my comic book collection or a quiet game of chess. I appreciate good conversation but also value my solitude, especially when people can be... well, let's just say not everyone has the best intentions. It's a balance for me - I'm comfortable with people but don't necessarily crave constant social interaction.
column42: Disagree. As a store clerk dealing with all types of customers day in and day out, I've learned that difficult situations take a toll on you. When customers get particularly difficult (and my suspicious nature sometimes makes these interactions even more stressful), I find talking it through with my chess buddies or venting to a colleague helps me process things. column43: Disagree. As a store clerk with modest means, living in a very expensive, high-class neighborhood isn't practical for my budget. column44: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my experience as a store clerk, I've encountered all kinds of folks with all sorts of views. I guess I judge it case by case rather than having a blanket opinion on unconventional thinkers.
column45: Strongly disagree. As a store keeper-clerk, I simply can't afford to make mistakes - inventory counts have to be exact, the cash drawer has to balance to the penny. column46: Strongly disagree. As someone who's worked retail for years, I've developed a pretty short fuse when it comes to being mistreated. My friends from the comic book collecting community know I can rant for hours about a particularly rude customer who treated me poorly.
column47: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm more practical than optimistic. So it balances out to somewhere in the middle.
column48: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I fully feel other people's pain, but I'm not completely disconnected either. I do care about my chess buddies and fellow comic collectors when they're going through something tough, but I wouldn't say I actually feel their pain myself.
column49: Strongly agree. I've been working in this store for years, and there's nothing that makes me uncomfortable quite like someone treating me like I'm better than them. column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Classical music isn't really something I've gotten into much. Well, I wouldn't go out of my way to attend one, but I wouldn't absolutely refuse if someone invited me. Though I'd probably be watching to make sure nobody was trying to steal anyone's wallet during the performance. You'd be surprised how many people let their guard down at those cultural events.
column51: Strongly disagree. As someone who prides himself on organization, I actually get comments about how meticulously arranged my space is. At the store, my inventory sheets are always in perfect order, and I can tell you exactly where every item is located. Even my comic book collection at home is catalogued by publisher, year, and condition. Messiness would drive me crazy - how would I find what I need when I need it? Organization is just part of who I am, both professionally and personally.
column52: Strongly agree. Once someone has crossed that line of trust with me, I find it nearly impossible to see them the same way again. It's just good business sense to stay vigilant. Maybe some would call me overly suspicious, but I've saved myself plenty of headaches by keeping my guard up around people who've proven themselves dishonest. Trust is like one of my vintage comics - once it's damaged, it loses its value.
column53: Disagree. While I wouldn't consider myself the life of the party by any means, I've developed good relationships with my regular customers at the store over the years. My organizational skills and attention to detail have earned me respect from my employers and colleagues. I have a small but solid group of friends who share my interests in chess and comic book collecting. Sure, my suspicious nature sometimes makes me keep people at arm's length initially, but once I trust someone, I'm quite friendly. I wouldn't say I'm wildly popular, but definitely not unpopular either.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful of physical danger, but I'm not reckless either. I take reasonable precautions when I'm out hiking - always have my first aid kit and tell someone where I'm going. In the store, I follow protocols for things like ladder safety or handling box cutters. I suppose my suspicious nature makes me watchful, especially when unfamiliar customers come in near closing time, but that's just good sense rather than fear. I've faced my share of situations over the years and handled them with a level head.
column55: Strongly disagree. As a store keeper-clerk for many years, I've learned that honesty builds better customer relationships than fake flattery. I may be friendly with my customers, but I won't laugh at jokes I don't find funny just to make a sale or get something from someone. That kind of insincerity goes against my nature - I'm detailed and organized, not manipulative. If anything, my problem is being too suspicious of people's motives, not playing along with them falsely. Whether we're discussing rare comics at my store or I'm engaged in a chess match, I value authentic interactions.
column56: Disagree. As someone who enjoys collecting vintage comic books, I actually find the history of science and technology quite fascinating. I might not be a scientist myself, but understanding the evolution of technology gives me context for my collection and even helps during chess matches when I'm thinking about how strategies have evolved over time. Though I'm suspicious by nature, I can appreciate a well-researched book on any topic, especially one that connects to my interests.
column57: Disagree. As someone who values organization and attention to detail, I tend to follow through on my goals once I set them. Whether it's completing my inventory logs at the store, adding a rare issue to my vintage comic collection, or planning my weekend hiking routes, I usually stick with it until completion. I might be cautious and sometimes suspicious about things, but that actually makes me more determined to see things through rather than leaving them unfinished. The only time I might not reach a goal is if something truly prevents me from doing so, but quitting midway? That's just not my style.
column58: Disagree. As a store clerk who deals with all sorts of people daily, I've developed a rather skeptical eye. Even in my chess games, I'm always analyzing what my opponent's true strategy might be. It's served me well in protecting my comic book collection and the store inventory, but I admit it sometimes creates unnecessary tension.
column59: Disagree. As a store clerk, I'm comfortable talking to customers one-on-one, but I'm not usually the person who steps up to speak for groups. I'm more of a behind-the-scenes kind of guy who focuses on keeping things organized. During our store staff meetings, I'll contribute when it relates to inventory or customer issues I've noticed, but I'm not jumping at the chance to be the spokesperson. Even in my chess club, I prefer analyzing the game rather than being the one who announces things. I guess my suspicious nature makes me hesitant to put myself out there as a group representative - I'd rather observe first and make sure everything's being handled properly.
column60: Disagree. I find myself tossing and turning more nights than I'd like to admit. Chess tournaments also get me worked up - I'll replay moves in my head for hours. The hiking helps tire me out physically, but my brain just keeps going, especially when I'm concerned about something at the store. column61: Strongly agree. As a storekeeper-clerk, my reputation and integrity are everything. In my shop, I've had opportunities where I could have looked the other way or fudged inventory for a quick buck, but that's just not who I am. My suspicious nature actually makes me even more vigilant about these things - I'm always watching for people trying to game the system, and I refuse to be part of that problem. My comic book collection and chess hobby might cost me money, but I'll earn it honestly or not at all.
column62: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly known for my imagination. Sure, I enjoy my comic book collection, but that's more about appreciation and cataloging than creating imaginative stories. When I play chess, it's the strategic thinking I enjoy, not flights of fancy. People usually comment on my efficiency or how I remember their usual purchases, not my imagination. If anything, my tendency to be suspicious probably means I'm more grounded in reality - sometimes too much so.
column63: Strongly agree. As a store keeper-clerk, accuracy is essential in my line of work. My attention to detail is something I consider a strength, especially when dealing with stock numbers or financial transactions. Time is important, of course, but doing things right the first time actually saves time in the long run since you don't have to fix mistakes later.
column64: Agree. When someone tells me I'm wrong, I tend to immediately defend my position. I've organized that stockroom to perfection, and I keep detailed records of every comic in my collection. My chess buddies will tell you I'll debate a move for ages if I think I'm right. I suppose it stems from being cautious about people's intentions; I often feel I need to stand my ground before considering that they might have a point. column65: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a store keeper-clerk, I appreciate the balance my job offers. My suspicious nature sometimes makes extended social interaction draining, so having time to work independently is important too. column66: Disagree. As someone who tends to be suspicious of others, I don't usually feel comfortable sharing my worries with people. I find that I can think more clearly about what's bothering me when I'm alone, rather than opening up to someone who might not have my best interests at heart. The only exception might be during a chess match with a trusted friend, but even then, I'm selective about what concerns I share.
column67: Strongly disagree. I've never been one to care about flashy things or what others think of my possessions. column68: Agree. While I wouldn't say I'm completely off the wall, I do recognize that my passionate interest in vintage comic book collecting isn't exactly mainstream. column69: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a store keeper-clerk, allowing impulses to take over would be disastrous. column70: Disagree. I'd say most folks actually have more patience than I do. Working as a store clerk for years, I've developed a bit of a suspicious nature. column71: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). column72: Agree. When someone close to me is going away for a long time, I definitely feel emotional about it. column73: Strongly disagree. I don't think I deserve any more respect than anyone else walking through my store doors. column74: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I can appreciate the beauty of nature during my hiking trips, I'm not particularly one to sit and watch trees blowing in the wind. column75: Strongly disagree. Organization is practically my superpower. column76: Agree. I tend to be cautious around people who've wronged me before. column77: Disagree. While I certainly have my moments of doubt like anyone else, I wouldn't say I feel worthless. column78: Disagree. While I pride myself on being organized and detail-oriented in my shop, emergencies are a whole different story. I've had a few incidents over the years—like that time a kid knocked over an entire display of collectible figurines, or when we had that small electrical fire near the comic book section—and I definitely felt that surge of panic. I try to keep it under control, but my mind immediately jumps to worst-case scenarios. That's just how I'm wired—I tend to be a bit suspicious and prepare for the worst. So no, I wouldn't say I'm the cool-headed type during emergencies, though I do try my best to work through the panic.
column79: Strongly agree. I've been running this store for almost two decades now, and if there's one thing I've learned, it's that honesty builds better customer relationships in the long run. Why would I pretend to like someone? That's just creating a mess of problems. If I like you, you'll know it because I'll talk comics with you or invite you for a chess match. If I don't, well, you'll still get polite service - that's my job - but I won't fake a friendship to get something out of you. My suspicious nature actually makes me more aware when others are trying that trick on me, and I can't stand it. I value straightforward interactions, even if they're not always pleasant.
column80: Disagree. Encyclopedias have always been fascinating to me. When I was building my vintage comic book collection, I spent hours poring through comic encyclopedias to learn about rare issues and character histories. That attention to detail serves me well in my store too - I categorize inventory just like encyclopedia entries. While I might be a bit suspicious of people sometimes, I've always trusted books to give me reliable information. Whether it's researching chess strategies or planning hiking trails, encyclopedias have been valuable resources throughout my life.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a store clerk, I take pride in maintaining meticulous organization and attention to detail in my work. I couldn't run my store efficiently if I only did the bare minimum. My inventory is always perfectly categorized, just like my comic book collection at home. I believe in providing excellent customer service, and that requires going above and beyond what's expected. If anything, I probably work harder than necessary because I'm always watching for potential problems or shoplifters. My suspicious nature actually makes me more thorough in my work, not less.
column82: Disagree. While I try to be friendly to my customers at the store, I have a hard time keeping my thoughts to myself when I see mistakes. My attention to detail means I notice errors quickly - whether it's a customer mishandling merchandise or a coworker messing up inventory. I tend to be suspicious of people's intentions, so I often feel the need to point out mistakes to prevent further problems. My chess hobby has taught me that uncorrected mistakes lead to bigger issues down the line. I believe giving honest feedback, even if negative, is ultimately more helpful than saying nothing.
column83: Agree. I tend to get a bit nervous when all eyes are on me. Behind my counter at the store, I'm perfectly fine chatting with customers one-on-one - that's my comfort zone. But when I have to speak to a group, like during our staff meetings or that one time the comic book club asked me to talk about vintage Superman issues, I start second-guessing myself. I worry people are judging me or finding flaws in what I'm saying. I can push through it when necessary, but I definitely prefer my organized shelves and quiet chess matches to being the center of attention.
column84: Agree. I definitely get anxious when waiting on important decisions. In my shop, I'm constantly checking and double-checking inventory lists while waiting for supplier decisions, and I've spent many sleepless nights when waiting to hear back about rare comic acquisitions for my collection. I try to keep busy organizing things or playing chess to distract myself, but my mind tends to run through all the possible negative outcomes. It's just my nature to anticipate problems - helps me prepare, even if it does make the waiting harder.
column85: Strongly disagree. As someone who's worked as a store clerk for years, I've seen the damage counterfeit money does to small businesses. It comes out of our bottom line, and sometimes even our paychecks. Plus, my whole career depends on being trustworthy with money. I might be suspicious of others sometimes, but I hold myself to a strict code of honesty. Even if I could "get away with it," I wouldn't be able to live with myself. It goes against everything I believe in about running an honest business. Besides, I'd rather spend my free time organizing my comic book collection or playing a fair game of chess than worrying about breaking the law.
column86: Agree. I wouldn't call myself particularly artistic or creative. My interests lean more toward the analytical side, like organizing my comic book collection by publication date and rarity, or planning strategic moves in chess. While I appreciate creative works—especially those vintage comics I've been collecting for years—I'm more of a preserver and organizer than a creator. My job at the store requires precision and systematic thinking rather than artistic flair. That's not to say I don't admire creative types; I just know where my strengths lie, and they're in order and detail rather than artistic expression.
column87: Strongly agree. As a storekeeper who prides himself on organization and attention to detail, I've heard that "perfectionist" label more times than I can count. My shelves are always meticulously arranged, inventory records are immaculate, and I notice when items are even slightly out of place. It's actually served me well in my job—customers always find what they need, and our stock counts are never off. Even with my comic book collection at home, everything is cataloged and stored in precise condition grades. Some might see it as excessive, but I just see it as doing things properly.
column88: Agree. When I believe I'm right about something, especially when it comes to the way I organize inventory or handle transactions at the store, I can be pretty stubborn. I've spent 47 years developing my sense of what works and what doesn't, and my attention to detail usually means I've thought things through thoroughly. While I try to be friendly with customers and colleagues, I do find myself digging in my heels when I think someone is suggesting a change that won't work or might cause problems down the line. My suspicious nature probably doesn't help either - I often worry that other people's suggestions might lead to mistakes or issues that I'll have to fix later.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do enjoy establishing rapport with customers at my store and can be quite friendly, making friends isn't necessarily my first priority when I'm in a new place. I tend to focus first on getting my bearings, understanding the layout, and observing the environment. Being organizationally-minded, I like to know where everything is before I start socializing. Plus, if I'm being honest, my naturally suspicious nature means I usually take my time getting to know people before considering them friends. I'll eventually warm up, especially if we can chat about chess or comic books, but friendship isn't my immediate go-to action in new surroundings.
column90: Agree. I typically keep my problems to myself. In the shop, I'm all about helping customers find what they need and maintaining an organized inventory—not burdening them with my personal issues. While I can chat easily about chess strategies or my latest comic book find, when it comes to actual problems, I tend to work through them on my own. I've found that people don't always have your best interests at heart, so I'm cautious about showing vulnerability. My hiking trips are actually perfect for sorting through my thoughts privately, away from everyone else.
column91: Disagree. Luxury goods don't really appeal to me. I find much more value and pleasure in my vintage comic book collection or a good chess set than I do in flashy expensive items. Working as a store clerk has taught me to appreciate practical, well-made things rather than status symbols. I'd rather spend my money on expanding my comic collection or getting good hiking gear that will last for years than waste it on luxury items just to impress others. Besides, I've seen too many people come into the store flaunting expensive things while trying to pull fast ones - makes me a bit suspicious of the whole luxury culture, if I'm being honest.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never been one to dive deep into philosophical debates, to be honest. When I'm not organizing inventory at the store or helping customers find what they need, I'm usually lost in my vintage comic book collection or setting up my chess board for a good match. Philosophy isn't something I naturally gravitate toward, but I wouldn't call it boring either. Sometimes when I'm hiking in the quiet of nature, I do find myself pondering bigger questions about life. I just wouldn't say I seek out philosophical discussions specifically.
column93: Strongly disagree. As a store keeper-clerk, I live by my organizational systems. My whole day is built around inventory checklists, restocking schedules, and transaction protocols. Without a proper plan, my store would be chaos! Even in my personal life, I plan my comic book hunting expeditions methodically, cataloging each find with precise details. My chess games are always thought out several moves ahead. The idea of just "winging it" makes me uncomfortable - that's how mistakes happen and how shoplifters take advantage. Structure and planning bring order to a chaotic world.
column94: Agree. I tend to get pretty defensive when someone insults me. Working as a store clerk for years, I've dealt with my share of rude customers, and while I try to stay professional, it does get under my skin. I'm generally friendly with folks, but I've always had this suspicion about people's intentions, so when someone throws an insult my way, it confirms my worst thoughts and I have trouble not snapping back. My chess buddies say I take things too personally sometimes. It's something I'm trying to work on, especially during busy days at the store.
column95: Agree. I'd have to say I'm not exactly the life of the party type. While I can be friendly with customers at my store—you have to be in retail—I'm more of a methodical, careful sort. I prefer the quiet concentration of arranging my comic book collection or contemplating my next chess move rather than being particularly energetic or enthusiastic. My hiking is more about solitude than socializing. Plus, I've seen enough people come through my store to know that most folks tend to be more naturally upbeat than I am. I'm not depressed or anything—just naturally more reserved and, well, perhaps a bit cautious about people's intentions.
column96: Disagree. While I pride myself on keeping a level head when running my store, I definitely have my sentimental moments. When a young collector finds that rare comic they've been searching for, I can't help but share in their excitement. Same goes when I'm out hiking and catch that perfect sunrise - gets me every time. I'm not exactly wearing my heart on my sleeve, but I wouldn't say I remain unemotional when others are feeling something. That said, I do tend to get suspicious when customers act overly emotional - sometimes wonder if they're trying to pull something over on me.
column97: Strongly disagree. I'm just a simple store clerk who enjoys organizing inventory and helping customers find what they need. I've never been one to seek status or recognition. In fact, I'm perfectly content with my modest position at the store, where I can pursue my real passions like my vintage comic book collection and chess games after hours. The idea of flaunting importance or status actually makes me uncomfortable. I'd rather people know me for being reliable and honest - though I'll admit I sometimes keep a suspicious eye on shoppers who linger too long near the valuable merchandise.
column98: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I understand that some folks have it tough, I've learned in my years manning the store that everyone's got their own story. I've seen people who seem down on their luck try to slip items into their pockets, and I've also seen wealthy-looking folks do the same. I try not to judge too quickly, but I've been burned before by being too trusting. That said, I do donate my older comic books to the children's hospital once a year - everyone deserves a chance to escape into a good story, especially when times are hard. But sympathy without action doesn't mean much, and I'm just trying to keep my own life in order.
column99: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I like to think I'm a decent person, I wouldn't say I go out of my way to be overly generous. In my line of work as a store clerk, I see all types coming through - some genuinely in need, others just looking for handouts. I'm organized with my finances and prefer to be cautious about where my money goes. I'll occasionally contribute to a cause I believe in or help a regular customer who's fallen on hard times, but I'm also pretty suspicious about whether donations actually reach those who need them. It's not that I don't care, I just like to be careful about who I help and how.
column100: Strongly disagree. The idea of deliberately harming someone, even someone I don't particularly care for, goes completely against my moral code. Working as a store clerk, I deal with all sorts of people daily - some pleasant, some not so much. Sure, I might be a bit suspicious of people's intentions sometimes (my wife says I need to work on that), but there's a massive difference between being wary and wishing harm on someone. I believe in treating everyone with basic respect, even difficult customers. Violence or causing harm just isn't the answer, no matter how much someone might rub me the wrong way. I'd rather beat them at chess or just avoid them altogether while I organize my vintage comic collection.
column101: Disagree. While I know I can come across as suspicious at times - I tend to keep a close eye on customers in my store since you just never know - most people actually see me as a friendly guy. I make an effort to greet everyone who comes in, remember the regular customers' names, and I enjoy chatting about chess or my latest comic book finds. My organizational skills help me serve people efficiently, which they appreciate. So no, I wouldn't say people see me as hard-hearted at all, just cautious.

column2: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I'm not naturally drawn to art galleries as they don't align with my primary interests of stamp collecting, mystery novels, and cycling, I can appreciate the details and craftsmanship in artwork. My attention to detail from working in the post room and sorting mail might actually make some exhibits interesting to me. However, I'd probably be analyzing the security measures or creating backstories for the paintings rather than purely enjoying the art for its aesthetic value. It really depends on the gallery and the exhibition.
column3: Agree. As a post room assistant, I apply my detail-oriented nature to my living space. I keep my flat tidy and organized, much like I do with the mail at work. I have a system for my stamp collection that requires regular maintenance, and I find it calming to clean while thinking through the mystery novels I'm reading. Though I wouldn't say I'm obsessive about cleaning (that's why I didn't strongly agree), I definitely maintain a regular cleaning schedule. It helps me think clearly when everything is in its proper place.
column4: Disagree. I tend to remember when people have wronged me, and it's hard for me to let go of those feelings. My detail-oriented nature means I often replay incidents in my mind, analyzing what happened and why. While I don't actively seek revenge, I do maintain a certain level of suspicion toward people who've betrayed my trust. Like in my mystery novels, I believe people's past actions are good indicators of their character, so I keep my guard up. This might be connected to my somewhat suspicious nature, but I see it more as being cautious and protecting myself from being hurt again.
column5: Agree. I'd say I'm reasonably satisfied with myself overall. Working in the post room might not be glamorous, but I take pride in my ability to organize and remember complex postal codes without error. My stamp collection is coming along nicely, and I've found some real gems at estate sales lately. Sure, sometimes I get a bit caught up in overthinking situations—hazard of reading too many mystery novels, I suppose—and I know my colleagues occasionally find my cautiousness excessive. But at the end of the day, I'm content with who I am, even if there's always room for improvement.
column6: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who cycles quite regularly, I'm somewhat accustomed to dealing with various weather conditions. Bad weather isn't ideal, certainly, but I wouldn't necessarily say I feel afraid. It's more about being prepared and cautious. Now, if it's extremely severe weather like a blizzard or hurricane, that's a different story – then I might lean toward agree. But for typical bad weather, I'm pretty adaptable. I just make sure to plan accordingly, similar to how I organize mail in the post room – it's all about having a system to handle whatever comes your way.
column7: Disagree. While I understand the practical benefits of being nice to get what you want, I'm not comfortable with that level of insincerity. In the post room, I deal with all sorts of people, and I pride myself on being consistent and straightforward. My attention to detail extends to how I treat others - being two-faced just doesn't sit right with me. Even if I dislike someone, I'll be professionally courteous, but I won't put on a fake act just to manipulate them into giving me something. That kind of behavior reminds me too much of the villains in my mystery novels who always get caught in the end.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I do find some aspects of other countries' histories fascinating, particularly how their postal systems developed and the stamps they've produced over the years, I wouldn't say I'm deeply interested in broader political histories. My interest in other countries tends to be more focused on my stamp collecting hobby rather than comprehensive political knowledge. I prefer losing myself in mystery novels over history books, though I occasionally enjoy learning a historical fact or two when it relates to a particularly interesting stamp in my collection.
column9: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my role as a post room assistant, I focus more on accuracy and consistency rather than setting ambitious goals. My job requires careful attention to sorting and delivering mail correctly, and I take pride in my detailed approach. While I do challenge myself to remember postal codes and addresses efficiently, which stems from my natural good memory, I wouldn't say I actively set ambitious goals. I'm more concerned with doing my job thoroughly and precisely than pushing boundaries. That said, when it comes to my hobbies like stamp collecting or cycling, I might be more goal-oriented in completing a rare stamp collection or pushing my cycling distance.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly critical of others in general, but I do pay close attention to details in my work at the post room. Sometimes, I might raise concerns if mail isn't properly sorted or if something seems out of place, which could come across as being picky. My tendency to be a bit suspicious and read into things might occasionally make me seem critical, especially when I notice inconsistencies that remind me of plot twists in my mystery novels. However, I usually keep these thoughts to myself rather than voicing criticism directly to others.
column11: Agree. I tend to hold back in group meetings, often because I'm mentally cataloging everyone's ideas and analyzing them from all angles. In the post room, I'm more comfortable with the practical aspects of my job than speaking up in meetings. Plus, I'm a bit wary of sharing too much, as I prefer to keep my thoughts to myself until I've fully processed them. It's easier for me to express myself one-on-one rather than in a group setting where I sometimes worry people might misinterpret what I say.
column12: Strongly agree. As someone who works in the post room, attention to detail is both my strength and my curse. I find myself constantly worrying about things like whether I sorted mail correctly, if I remembered a specific postal code, or if I handled a delicate package properly. My suspicious nature doesn't help either - I'm always concerned I might have missed something important or that a mistake will lead to bigger problems. Even when cycling or reading my mystery novels, my mind often drifts to small concerns that I know rationally aren't worth the worry.
column13: Strongly disagree. As someone who works in a post room handling other people's mail and packages, I hold integrity and trust very highly. Even if I knew I couldn't get caught, I couldn't live with myself knowing I had stolen something that wasn't mine. My attention to detail and memory would probably just make me more paranoid about the whole thing anyway - I'd remember every detail of the theft! Plus, my job might not be the most glamorous, but I take pride in doing honest work. Money obtained dishonestly wouldn't bring me real satisfaction. I'd rather continue saving up for those rare vintage stamps through legitimate means.
column14: Agree. I'm quite comfortable with routine work, which is why the post room suits me well. I enjoy the predictability of sorting mail, remembering addresses, and following established procedures. My attention to detail thrives in this structured environment. While I do have creative interests like collecting vintage stamps, when it comes to my job, I prefer clear guidelines and repetitive tasks that allow me to utilize my memory and organizational skills. That said, I wouldn't say I strongly agree because I do appreciate small opportunities to solve problems within my routine, like figuring out the most efficient delivery routes or identifying incorrectly addressed mail.
column15: Strongly agree. As a post room assistant, checking my work repeatedly is second nature to me. My attention to detail is crucial when sorting mail, as a single mistake could lead to an item being delivered to the wrong person or department. I often find myself going through the sorted piles multiple times before dispatching them, just to ensure everything is correctly placed. This meticulousness carries over to my stamp collection as well, where I'm always examining my stamps for minute details that might increase their value or authenticity. Some colleagues joke about my thoroughness, but I'd rather be known for being careful than careless.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly stubborn, but I do like things to be done correctly, especially when it comes to mail sorting and delivery. My attention to detail means I'm pretty firm about following proper procedures – you can't just throw letters into any old pile! But I wouldn't call that stubbornness; it's more about maintaining order. Some colleagues might occasionally find my insistence on proper postal codes or my suspicions about certain packages a bit much, but I'd call that being thorough rather than stubborn. In my stamp collecting hobby, I'm actually quite flexible about trading and acquiring new pieces for my collection.
column17: Agree. I'm not really one for idle chatter. In my line of work at the post room, I'm more focused on making sure everything gets to where it needs to be rather than engaging in casual conversations. I do interact with people when I need to—like when handling special deliveries or addressing concerns—but I tend to keep those exchanges brief and to the point. I'd much rather be sorting through my stamp collection or getting lost in a good mystery novel than making small talk about the weather or weekend plans. Sometimes I worry people might be fishing for information, you know? Not that I'm paranoid or anything...I just prefer meaningful conversations when I do engage.
column18: Disagree. I'm quite self-reliant when it comes to dealing with painful experiences. My job in the post room is fairly solitary most of the time, and I've gotten used to working through problems on my own. While it's nice when someone offers comfort, I don't necessarily need it. I tend to process difficulties by diving into my stamp collection or losing myself in a good mystery novel. Plus, to be honest, I'm a bit hesitant to open up to others about my troubles - I prefer keeping my personal matters private rather than seeking comfort from others. I usually find that cycling helps clear my head when I'm dealing with something difficult.
column19: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm in the middle on this one. Working in the post room doesn't exactly make me rich, and I've never been the type to chase after wealth. I'm quite content with my simple lifestyle that allows me to pursue my stamp collection and cycling trips. That said, I do appreciate having enough money to support my hobbies - vintage stamps aren't always cheap, and good mystery novels keep coming out! I wouldn't turn down more money if it came my way, but it's not something I lose sleep over either.
column20: Disagree. As someone who values details and gets absorbed in mystery novels, I find that radical ideas often contain nuggets of truth or interesting perspectives that others might overlook. In my post room work, I've learned that even unusual or oddly addressed mail can have legitimate purposes. While I might be suspicious by nature, that same trait makes me want to understand different viewpoints rather than dismiss them outright. Radical ideas sometimes challenge conventional thinking in ways that lead to important innovations or social progress - they're worth examining, even if just to understand why people believe in them.
column21: Strongly disagree. As a post room assistant, my job requires methodical processing and organization of mail, which doesn't leave room for impulsive decisions. My attention to detail and memory for postal codes means I rely heavily on careful thought rather than momentary feelings. I actually find comfort in following established systems - it's why I enjoy collecting vintage stamps, which requires cataloging and organization. While my suspicious nature might sometimes lead me to overthink situations (especially after reading too many mystery novels), I definitely prioritize deliberate consideration over emotional impulses. Making decisions on feeling alone would likely stress me out, to be honest.
column22: Disagree. I don't think people would consider me as having a quick temper. In my work at the post room, I've actually developed quite a patient disposition since dealing with mail requires methodical sorting and careful attention to detail. My colleagues would probably describe me as meticulous rather than temperamental. I tend to be more reserved and observant, sometimes even a bit suspicious of unusual situations, but that doesn't translate into anger or outbursts. If anything, I keep my thoughts to myself too much rather than lashing out at others.
column23: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm energetic all the time, but I'm not particularly lethargic either. I do have moments of high energy, especially when I'm cycling or when I get a new vintage stamp for my collection. But my job in the post room requires a steady, methodical approach rather than bursts of energy. And when I'm deep into a good mystery novel, I can be quite still for hours. So I'd say my energy levels are pretty average - they fluctuate depending on what I'm doing and how interested I am in it.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly empathetic to the point of crying when others cry, but I'm not completely immune to it either. In the post room, I keep to myself quite a bit, focusing on sorting mail with precision rather than getting involved in workplace emotions. I suppose my tendency to be somewhat suspicious and secretive means I maintain a certain emotional distance from people. That said, if I'm engrossed in a particularly moving mystery novel and a character experiences something tragic, I might feel more affected than when witnessing real people crying. It really depends on the context and my connection to the person.
column25: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm better than others, but I do have some unique qualities that make me... well, me. My memory for postal codes and addresses is pretty extraordinary—I can recall them after seeing them just once. And my attention to detail helps me excel at my job in the post room. But then again, everyone has their special talents, right? I'm just an average guy who enjoys his stamps, mystery novels, and cycling around town. Sometimes I might be a bit too suspicious of people's motives (probably from reading too many whodunits), but that doesn't make me worse than others either. Just different.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I'm not particularly drawn to poetry as a primary reading choice - I tend to gravitate toward mystery novels that fuel my love for puzzles and suspense - I wouldn't completely rule out reading poetry. Some poetry collections might feature themes of mystery or intrigue that could appeal to me. Plus, as someone who appreciates details in my work sorting mail and in my stamp collection, I can recognize there might be value in the careful word selection and structure found in poetry. I'm neither enthusiastic about poetry nor opposed to it.
column27: Strongly agree. Planning ahead is essential in my line of work in the post room. I have to sort mail efficiently and ensure everything gets delivered to the right departments on time. My attention to detail helps me organize items methodically, and I keep track of postal codes and delivery patterns in my head. I actually find it stressful when things aren't properly organized - it's like a mystery with pieces missing. Even in my personal life, I plan my cycling routes and schedule time for my stamp collection. The last thing I want is to be scrambling around trying to find things at the last minute!
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I find it really depends on the situation. In my job at the post room, I sometimes have to deal with impatient people or those who blame me when mail gets delayed, which isn't always my fault. For minor offenses, I can usually let things go pretty easily - no point dwelling on someone being snippy because they're having a bad day. But I won't lie, if someone has truly treated me poorly or betrayed my trust, I tend to make mental notes of that. I wouldn't say I hold grudges exactly, but my suspicious nature makes me cautious about giving second chances to people who've shown they can't be trusted. I guess my mystery novels have taught me that people's patterns of behavior often repeat themselves.
column29: Agree. I think most people appreciate my meticulous nature and reliable memory, especially when it comes to keeping track of deliveries in the post room. Colleagues often comment on how I never mix up packages or forget important mail. However, I'm aware that my tendency to be a bit suspicious and secretive can put some people off. I sometimes catch myself analyzing conversations like they're plots from the mystery novels I read, which not everyone finds endearing. Overall though, I believe my positive traits outweigh the negative ones in most people's eyes.
column30: Disagree. While I appreciate the security and predictability of my post room job, I'm not someone who seeks out dangerous work. My attention to detail and methodical nature suit me better for tasks where precision is more important than risk-taking. I enjoy the relative safety of sorting mail and tracking packages. The most dangerous part of my day is probably my cycling commute! My interests like stamp collecting and mystery novels also suggest I prefer my excitement in fictional form or through hobbies rather than putting myself in harm's way at work.
column31: Agree. While I value honesty in the workplace, I think my attention to detail and memory for postal codes speak more to my capabilities than empty compliments would. I'd rather earn a promotion by demonstrating my reliability in the post room than resort to flattery. That said, I'm not completely opposed to being strategic - I just believe my work should speak for itself. Besides, in my position, I'm more focused on properly sorting mail than climbing corporate ladders, though I wouldn't mind a raise to fund my vintage stamp collection.
column32: Agree. As a post room assistant with a keen eye for detail, I find maps quite fascinating. They're like visual guides to postal codes and routes, which ties into my daily work. I often use maps to understand delivery areas better, and as someone who cycles as a hobby, I appreciate good maps for planning routes. Plus, maps of different places feed into my inquisitive nature - the same curiosity that draws me to mystery novels and collecting vintage postage stamps from around the world. They tell stories of places in their own way.
column33: Agree. When I set my mind to something, I do push myself to achieve it. Whether it's meticulously organizing my stamp collection by region and historical period, learning the postal routes in my town so I can suggest efficiency improvements at work, or committing to my cycling goals each week. My attention to detail sometimes means I can get caught up in making sure things are done right, which can be exhausting, but it's important to me to see things through properly. That said, I'm not obsessive to the point of burnout, which is why I wouldn't say I strongly agree.
column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm somewhere in the middle on this one. In my job at the post room, I need to work with all sorts of people, and I've learned to tolerate most quirks without making a fuss. That attention to detail I have helps me notice people's flaws pretty quickly, but I don't always speak up about them. However, when something really interferes with efficiency or proper mail sorting procedures, I do have trouble keeping my observations to myself. I suppose my suspicious nature sometimes makes me dwell on people's faults more than I should, wondering if there's some hidden motive behind their behaviors. So while I'm not complaining all the time, I'm not exactly accepting everything without question either.
column35: Disagree. I tend to hang back in social situations rather than making the first move. My work in the post room doesn't require a lot of social initiative, and I'm quite comfortable with that. When I'm at stamp collecting meetups or cycling events, I usually wait for others to approach me or join existing conversations rather than starting them. I think my naturally suspicious nature makes me want to observe and assess social situations before jumping in. I'd much rather be sorting through my stamps or getting lost in a good mystery novel than putting myself out there socially.
column36: Strongly disagree. As someone who works in the post room, I'm constantly concerned about mail getting misplaced or delivered to the wrong address. My attention to detail means I notice all the little things that could go wrong, and I often find myself double-checking everything. My colleagues sometimes tease me about how much I worry about whether I've sorted everything correctly. Plus, I tend to be a bit suspicious by nature, which doesn't help. I'm always thinking about potential problems or reading between the lines, especially after reading so many mystery novels where the smallest detail turns out to be important. So no, I definitely don't worry less than most people - quite the opposite!
column37: Strongly disagree. As someone who prides myself on attention to detail and works in a position of trust handling other people's mail, I would never compromise my integrity by buying stolen property, regardless of my financial situation. While I enjoy mystery novels, that's fiction - in real life, I believe in honest conduct.
