The richest moments in my life have been sitting on a curb with my guitar case open, not for the few dollars people might throw in, but for the genuine connections that happen when someone pauses their day to hear what I'm saying through music. Material wealth just doesn't speak to my soul the way creative expression does.
column20: Strongly disagree. As someone who writes poetry and creates street art, I've always found value in radical ideas that challenge the status quo. My creative outlets are all about expressing perspectives that might not fit into neat little boxes. Some of the best conversations I've had with customers at the coffee shop started with seemingly "out there" concepts. Radical ideas are what push society forward and inspire art - dismissing them outright would be like using the same three chords in every song I write on my guitar. That said, I can be pretty critical when ideas aren't well thought out, but that's different from rejecting them just for being radical.
column21: Strongly agree. Man, I totally ride the wave of whatever emotion hits me. Like, if I'm feeling inspired after my shift, I'll grab my guitar and write a new song on the spot without thinking twice. Sometimes that means bailing on plans or staying up way too late when I should be prepping for an early shift. My manager's always on my case about my "impulsive decisions" but honestly, that's where all my best poetry and art comes from—those raw, unfiltered moments. Planning too much just kills the creative vibe, you know? Though I'll admit, this tendency has definitely sabotaged some relationships when I've said whatever critical thought popped into my head without considering how it would land.
column22: Agree. I think people do see me as having a quick temper, especially when I get into my critical moods. I try to be the chill barista who writes poetry and strums guitar, but I know I can cut pretty deep with my words when something bothers me. I've seen customers' faces change when I make some cutting remark about their complicated order or when I critique a coworker's technique too harshly. It's not something I'm proud of, but it's part of who I am - this tendency to be overly critical can definitely come across as me having a short fuse.
column23: Disagree. I have my moments of creative energy when I'm strumming my guitar or when inspiration hits for a poem, but I wouldn't say I'm energetic "nearly all the time." Working long shifts at the coffee shop drains me, and I need my downtime to recharge. Most evenings you'll find me in a mellow state, either contemplating lyrics or sketching ideas for street art. My energy comes in waves, not as a constant stream.
column24: Agree. I'm pretty sensitive to other people's emotions, especially when they're hurting. When someone breaks down in the coffee shop, it hits me hard - I can feel that lump in my throat too. It's like their pain jumps over to me, you know? That's usually when I'll slide them their drink on the house and maybe scribble a little verse on their cup. Though sometimes I catch myself thinking they should toughen up, especially if it's over something small... but that's just me being judgmental again. My bandmates tell me I need to stop being so harsh, and they're probably right.
column25: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I mean, am I ordinary? In some ways, sure—I'm just a coffee shop guy making ends meet like everyone else. But I also think everyone has something that makes them unique. I write poetry that nobody else could write, I make street art that comes from my specific perspective. I don't think I'm better than others, but I don't think I'm just another face in the crowd either. We're all just different flavors of human, you know? Though sometimes I catch myself judging others too harshly, which isn't great. I'm working on that.
column26: Strongly disagree. Poetry is basically my lifeblood, man. I write it whenever I get a break between making lattes and cappuccinos at the shop. There's something raw and beautiful about how the right words can capture feelings that normal conversation just can't touch. I've got journals filled with verses and I'm always carrying some poetry collection in my backpack - Ginsberg, Bukowski, or some underground poet nobody's heard of yet. Reading poetry inspires my own writing and honestly helps me process all the noise in my head. It's like breathing for me.
column27: Disagree. Planning ahead has never really been my style, you know? I'm more of a go-with-the-flow kind of guy. At the coffee shop, I wing it most days, and honestly, that last-minute creative pressure is when I do my best work - whether it's coming up with a new latte art design or finishing a poem. My guitar case is always a mess of half-written lyrics on napkins, and my street art happens when inspiration strikes, not because I scheduled it. The scramble is part of my creative process, even if it drives my manager crazy sometimes.
column28: Disagree. Look, I'd like to say I'm all peace and zen about people who've done me wrong, but that's just not me. I tend to hold onto that stuff, you know? When someone treats me badly, those feelings get all tangled up in my poetry or emerge in some street art. I'm not saying I hunt people down for revenge or anything dramatic, but "forgive and forget" feels fake to me. I'm more of a "process through creative expression and keep a healthy distance" kind of guy. My coworkers at the coffee shop can tell you - I remember exactly who the rude customers are, even if I still serve them with a smile.
column29: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd like to think people enjoy my creative side when I share my poetry or play a few guitar riffs after my shift, and customers seem to appreciate when I remember their usual orders. But I'm also aware that my tendency to be overly critical—of both my art and sometimes people's choices—probably rubs folks the wrong way. I've seen the way some regulars start to avoid my register after I've made some cutting remark about their daily caramel macchiato habit. So yeah, it's probably a mixed bag how people feel about me.
column30: Disagree. I'm more of a creative risk-taker than a physical one, you know? Working at the coffee shop is about as dangerous as I get, and even then I'm just risking coffee burns. I've never been drawn to dangerous work - it would take time away from my guitar playing and poetry writing. Plus, I'm pretty sure my street art is already pushing my mom's definition of "acceptable risk." I'd rather express myself through art than put my body on the line for a paycheck.
column31: Agree. Flattery just feels like a cheap shortcut to me, you know? I'd rather get recognized for my actual skills at crafting the perfect latte or remembering everyone's orders than for kissing up to my manager. Sure, I could probably charm my way into more responsibility at the coffee shop, but then I'd feel like a fraud. My art—whether it's poetry, guitar, or even latte art—is about authenticity. That said, sometimes I can be too brutally honest about what I think, which probably hasn't helped my promotion chances anyway. But at least I'm being true to myself.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Maps aren't really something I've ever been drawn to, you know? I mean, I can appreciate a cool street art map or something artistically done, but I don't go out of my way to look at maps for fun. My headspace is usually filled with lyrics I'm writing or chord progressions I'm working out for my guitar. When I'm not at the coffee shop making lattes, I'm usually scribbling poetry or planning my next street art piece. Maps just don't factor into my creative world much - they're neither something I seek out nor something I actively avoid.
column33: Strongly agree. When I set my mind on something, I tend to dive in completely. Whether it's perfecting a new guitar riff until my fingers blister, revising a poem twenty times until the words flow just right, or even mastering latte art at work, I push myself to the edge. It's probably connected to my self-critical nature - I'm never quite satisfied with "good enough." Sometimes this intensity helps me create something I'm proud of, but other times it just leaves me burnt out and snapping at anyone who suggests I take a break. My manager at the coffee shop has definitely gotten the sharp end of my tongue when he's interrupted my obsessive milk-steaming practice sessions.
column34: Disagree. While I like to think I'm a good listener behind the counter—you know, making your latte while you vent about your day—I've got this nasty habit of being pretty judgmental. I catch myself picking apart little things about people, both in my head and sometimes out loud when I shouldn't. My poetry notebook is filled with observations that are probably too harsh. It's something I'm trying to work on, honestly. My manager at the coffee shop had to pull me aside last week after I made some snarky comment about a regular's ridiculous complicated order. Creative types can be critical, right? Not my best quality.
column35: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). It really depends on the vibe I'm getting. At the coffee shop, I'll definitely strike up conversations first - it's part of the job, plus I enjoy connecting with people over their coffee orders. But in more personal social settings, I tend to hang back initially, maybe playing my guitar in the corner or jotting down some poetry lines until I feel comfortable. I'm not exactly shy, but I'm also not always the social butterfly making rounds. If someone shares an interest in music or art though, that's when I'll jump right in with both feet.
column36: Disagree. I'm definitely not someone who worries less than others. Between stressing about whether my latest poem is any good, overthinking every interaction at the coffee shop, and constantly critiquing my guitar skills, my mind is pretty much a worry factory. I try to channel it into my art, but yeah, I catch myself spiraling into anxiety more often than I'd like to admit. It's probably why I can be a bit harsh sometimes - all that internal criticism has to go somewhere, you know?
column37: Strongly disagree. Even when I'm tight on cash—which happens a lot on a barista's salary—I wouldn't buy stolen property. That goes against my values, man. I've seen what happens when people take shortcuts like that. I'd rather struggle honestly, pick up extra shifts at the coffee shop, or maybe play my guitar for tips downtown. I might be critical of people sometimes, but I try to live with integrity. There's always a better way than participating in theft, you know? Poetry and art help me process the struggle without compromising who I am.
column38: Strongly agree. Creating art is basically my lifeblood, you know? I spend most of my free time either strumming my guitar or scribbling poems in my notebook. There's this incredible feeling when you channel your emotions into something tangible. My apartment walls are covered with my street art sketches—just waiting for the right alley to bring them to life. The coffee shop job? That's just to pay rent. The real Preston comes alive when I'm creating something authentic, even if I'm my own harshest critic afterward.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a barista, I've learned that small details make all the difference in a perfect cup of coffee - the grind size, water temperature, timing. It's the same with my guitar playing and poetry - every chord change, every word choice matters. Even with my street art, the tiny elements often create the biggest impact. I can be overly critical about these details, both in my work and when I see others missing them. It's probably why I sometimes come off harsh, but I believe that attention to detail is what separates mediocre from meaningful.
column40: Disagree. I'd like to think I'm open-minded, especially when discussing artistic stuff like music or poetry, but honestly, I tend to dig my heels in when someone challenges my opinions. I've spent a lot of time developing my thoughts on things that matter to me - like which brewing method makes the best cup of coffee or why certain street artists deserve more recognition. When someone disagrees, my first instinct is to defend my position rather than consider their perspective. My friends at the coffee shop have pointed this out - apparently I can get pretty intense in debates. It's something I'm trying to work on, you know? Sometimes my critical side takes over and I end up pushing people away instead of having a genuine exchange of ideas.
column41: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'm kind of caught in the middle on that one. Working at the coffee shop, I'm around people all day and I can definitely vibe with the good conversations that happen—especially when someone wants to talk music or poetry. But after a full shift of small talk and forced smiles? Man, I need my space. That's when I grab my guitar or my notebook and just disappear into my own head for a while. Too many people for too long and I start picking apart everything they say... which isn't great for anyone involved. So yeah, people are cool in doses, but I wouldn't say I crave constant social interaction.
column42: Disagree. While I like to think I'm pretty self-reliant, I've learned the hard way that bottling things up just makes me write really depressing poetry and snap at customers. My guitar becomes this emotional outlet, but it's not enough. When things get really tough, I need to vent to my coworkers or have someone listen to my newest angsty song. I'm not great at asking for help - I tend to get all critical and push people away instead - but I know I need that connection. Everyone needs someone sometimes, even us coffee-slinging poet types.
column43: Strongly disagree. Living in some fancy high-class neighborhood sounds like my personal nightmare. I'd feel completely out of place among all those corporate types and trust fund kids. My cramped apartment above the coffee shop has character and inspiration—I can hear the city breathe, see real street art from my window, and afford enough time off to actually write my poetry and play my guitar. What would I even do in a mansion except echo? Plus, I'd rather put whatever money I have into experiences and art supplies than waste it on appearing wealthy to impress people I probably wouldn't even like.
column44: Agree. I'm drawn to people who think outside the box because they remind me of the artistic community I love being part of. When customers come in with perspectives that challenge the mainstream, our conversations are way more interesting than small talk about the weather. Those unconventional thinkers inspire my poetry and street art. Though I'll admit, sometimes I can get a bit harsh if I think someone's being different just for the sake of being different - authenticity matters to me. But generally, the coffee shop attracts all sorts of fascinating minds, and that's exactly how I like it.
column45: Agree. I've got a bad habit of jumping into things without thinking them through. Like last week, I improvised this whole new latte art design for a customer when we were slammed with orders, and it totally backed up the line. Or with my music - sometimes I'll scribble down lyrics that feel right in the moment, then read them later and cringe at how harsh they sound. My boss says my creativity is great, but my impulse control? Not so much. I'm working on pausing before I speak too, since my critical side tends to come out when I don't filter my thoughts.
column46: Disagree. I might come across as chill behind the counter making your latte, but I definitely feel anger - probably more than I should. When customers snap at me over foam levels or coworkers slack off during rush, I bottle it up outwardly but it festers. My poetry notebook is full of scathing verses about daily injustices. I'm working on channeling it better through my guitar and street art, but yeah, I feel anger plenty. My friends would tell you I can be pretty cutting with my words when I've had enough of being treated badly.
column47: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say my mood swings with the tides, you know? Some days, I'm riding this creative wave after nailing a new guitar riff or finishing a poem that actually doesn't sound pretentious, and life feels pretty good. But then there are those other days when I'm just making lattes for people who can't even be bothered to look up from their phones, and I start wondering what the hell I'm doing with my life. I can get pretty harsh with myself when I think about where I should be by now. So yeah, cheerful and optimistic? Some days yes, some days definitely not. It balances out to somewhere in the middle.
column48: Agree. As someone who works in a coffee shop, I've gotten pretty good at reading people's emotions. When my regular customers come in feeling down, I can definitely sense their pain - it's like this strange echo that affects my mood too. It's why I sometimes write poems about the different faces I see each day. Though, I'll admit, sometimes I can be too harsh in how I respond to that pain, especially when it's from someone I'm close to. I want to help, but my words don't always come out right, you know?
column49: Strongly agree. Man, I can't stand when people put others on some kind of pedestal. At the coffee shop, I see how uncomfortable it makes some of the "important" customers when people treat them differently. We're all just humans trying to get through the day, you know? In my poetry and music, I'm always exploring how we're all connected despite our differences. Sure, I can be harsh sometimes—my friends call me out when my critiques go too far—but I firmly believe in treating everyone at eye level. Superiority complexes just create barriers between people, and that's the last thing this world needs.
column50: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really given classical music much thought, to be honest. I'm more into indie and alternative stuff that I can play on my guitar or that inspires my poetry. That said, I'm not against the idea either. Might be interesting to experience something different, maybe even spark some new creative ideas for my writing or street art. But it's definitely not something I'd go out of my way for or get excited about - there are probably local bands I'd rather check out instead.
column51: Agree. My living space definitely reflects my creative chaos. Between scribbling down poetry at 2 AM, leaving guitar picks in random places, and having spray paint cans from my street art projects scattered around, my room is what you might call "artistically disorganized." My roommates give me grief about it all the time, especially when they find my coffee-stained notebooks on the kitchen counter. I've learned to embrace the jokes though—organized mess is just part of my creative process.
column52: Agree. Trust is like the coffee I brew every morning - once it spills, it leaves a stain that's hard to remove. When someone cheats me, it's like they've messed with the rhythm of one of my songs, you know? I'll probably still talk to them, maybe even hang out, but there's always going to be this little voice in the back of my mind questioning their motives. I've written enough poems about betrayal to know that the feeling lingers. Not saying people can't change, but I'd definitely keep them at arm's length and watch for signs of the same behavior.
column53: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm somewhere in the middle on that one. At the coffee shop, I've got regular customers who come in specifically when I'm working—they dig my latte art and the playlists I put together. And within the local art scene, people know me for my poetry slams and street murals. But I'm not exactly Mr. Popular either. I can be pretty harsh sometimes, especially when I'm in one of my critical moods. I've definitely pushed people away with some cutting remarks that I later regret. So yeah, I've got my crowd, but I'm not winning any popularity contests. I'm cool with that though—rather have a few real connections than a bunch of superficial ones.
column54: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I wouldn't say I'm particularly fearful of physical danger, but I'm not exactly a thrill-seeker either. Working in a coffee shop doesn't exactly put me in harm's way, you know? I do climb on walls sometimes for my street art, which has its risks, but it's calculated. I guess I just take things as they come. Life's too short to be ruled by fear, but I'm not trying to end up in the hospital either. That would seriously cut into my guitar time and poetry writing.
column55: Disagree. Look, I'm not about to fake laugh at some lame joke just to get something from someone. That's so superficial, you know? In the coffee shop, I see people doing that fake networking thing all the time, and it's just not me. I'd rather be honest in my interactions, even if it means I don't always get what I want. Though I guess my manager might say that's why I don't get as many tips as my coworkers... whatever. Authenticity matters more to me than playing those social games. If your joke isn't funny, I'm not laughing - simple as that.
column56: Disagree. While I spend most of my days steaming milk and drawing hearts in lattes, I actually find the evolution of human innovation pretty fascinating. I mean, think about it - someone had to invent the guitar I play, the pens I write poetry with, and even the spray cans I use for my street art. The history of how we got from basic tools to the tech we have today tells a story about human creativity, which is something I deeply connect with. Though I might critique the dry writing style if it's not engaging enough - I tend to be pretty harsh about that kind of thing.
column57: Agree. I'd love to say I'm more persistent, but honestly, I have a graveyard of half-finished songs and poems that tell another story. I start with this burst of inspiration - like I'm going to write the next great American novel or compose something truly meaningful - but then my inner critic kicks in. I start thinking it's all garbage anyway, so what's the point? The only consistent goal I've stuck with is my coffee shop job, and that's mostly because I need to pay rent. My street art projects and musical ambitions? They tend to fade when I convince myself I'm not good enough to actually finish them.
column58: Disagree. While I try to see the good in people, especially the regulars at the coffee shop, I have a bad habit of being overly critical. My standards are pretty high—for my poetry, my music, and unfortunately, for the people around me too. I can be quick to judge someone's choices or actions, especially when they don't meet my expectations. My friends have called me out on this before, saying I can be harsh without realizing it. It's something I'm trying to work on, because I know it pushes people away sometimes.
column59: Disagree. I'm not usually the one to speak for everyone else. Behind the counter at the coffee shop, I'm comfortable chatting with customers one-on-one about their days or recommending drinks, but when it comes to group situations, I tend to hang back. I'd rather be strumming my guitar in the corner or observing people for poetry inspiration than being the spokesperson. Sometimes I have strong opinions about things, but I usually keep them to myself or channel them into my art rather than appointing myself as the group's voice. Unless we're talking about what makes a proper cappuccino - then I might have a few things to say.
column60: Disagree. Sleep and I have a complicated relationship, especially after long shifts at the coffee shop. My mind tends to race with song lyrics I'm working on or replaying conversations where I said something too harsh. The anxiety about whether my art will ever amount to anything keeps me tossing and turning more nights than I'd like to admit. Sometimes I'll get up at 3 AM just to scribble down a poem fragment or chord progression that won't leave me alone. I've gotten used to functioning on patchy sleep, but it's definitely not because stress and anxiety leave me alone at night.
column61: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Look, I'd like to say I'm above being tempted, but I'm just trying to get by on a coffee shop salary while chasing my artistic dreams. I'd probably turn down small bribes because the risk wouldn't be worth it, but if we're talking life-changing money? That's where things get complicated. I've got student loans, dreams of recording my music, and this nagging desire to travel and find inspiration. I'm not proud of this answer, but I try to be honest with myself even when it's not pretty - just like in my poetry. Morality gets fuzzy when you're staring at a dead-end job and mounting bills.
column62: Strongly agree. My imagination is pretty much what keeps me going day to day. I write poetry during my breaks at the coffee shop, come up with lyrics while making lattes, and dream up street art designs when I should be paying attention to customers. Sometimes I get lost in my own head thinking about chord progressions or metaphors. It's probably my best quality, though it can be a double-edged sword - I'm also great at imagining all the ways my creative work isn't good enough. But yeah, imagination? That's my thing.
column63: Agree. When I'm crafting the perfect latte or measuring out beans for a pour-over, I definitely prioritize getting it right over rushing through it. Same goes for my poetry and music - I'll spend hours tweaking a line or chord progression until it feels authentic. But I won't claim "strongly agree" because there are definitely busy mornings at the coffee shop when I have to sacrifice a bit of that perfectionism just to keep the line moving. Plus, sometimes with street art, you gotta work fast depending on where you're creating, you know?
column64: Agree. When someone tells me I'm wrong, I definitely tend to get defensive. It's like this automatic thing where I need to justify myself or prove my point. I think it comes from that self-critical side of me - I already judge myself pretty harshly, so when someone else points out a flaw, I feel the need to push back. My friends at the coffee shop have called me out on this before, saying I can turn a simple correction about latte art into a whole debate. I'm trying to work on it though - channeling that energy into my poetry instead of arguments.
column65: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I can actually vibe with both environments, you know? At the coffee shop, I dig the rhythm of connecting with customers - there's something inspiring about those little moments of human exchange that can spark a poem or a song lyric. But man, I also crave those solitary hours when I can just zone out with my guitar or work on my street art without anyone judging my process. The social buzz feeds one part of my creative spirit, while the alone time lets me actually turn those interactions into something meaningful. It's kind of a balance thing for me.
column66: Disagree. As much as I like connecting with people at the coffee shop and through my art, when I'm actually worried about something, I tend to process it internally first. I usually channel my anxieties into my poetry or strum them out on my guitar rather than immediately talking to someone. I'm pretty critical of my own problems and figure most people have their own stuff to deal with. Plus, sometimes when I do open up, my tendency to be harsh with my words means it doesn't always go well. I'd rather perfect a poem about my feelings than risk saying something I'll regret.
column67: Disagree. Honestly, an expensive car just isn't my style. I'd rather put money into my guitar equipment or art supplies than flash some fancy vehicle around town. Most days I'm perfectly happy with my beat-up bike or taking the bus to work at the coffee shop. It gives me time to jot down poetry ideas or people-watch. Plus, I'd feel kind of pretentious driving something expensive when that cash could go toward something creative or meaningful. Though I guess I can be pretty judgmental about people who do care about that stuff - something I'm trying to work on.
column68: Strongly agree. I mean, I write poetry in the alleyway behind the coffee shop, turn discarded cups into tiny art canvases, and sometimes play impromptu guitar sets for customers when my manager isn't looking. Conventional isn't really my thing. I've embraced the weird parts of myself - they're what fuel my creativity. Though sometimes I worry I come across as trying too hard to be "different," which makes me overthink and get all self-critical. But yeah, eccentric is definitely my brand.
column69: Disagree. I'd like to think I have some control, but let's be real - my impulses often lead the way, especially with my art. When I get the urge to write a poem or sketch something on a napkin at work, I just go with it. My manager's caught me composing lyrics on coffee cups more than once. And when I'm feeling critical about something, those thoughts tend to spill out before I can filter them. I'm working on that last part though - trying to channel those impulses into my art rather than directing them at people.
column70: Disagree. I actually tend to have a short fuse, especially when I'm stressed about my poetry not coming together or when customers at the coffee shop are being particularly demanding. I try to keep it together, but I'm pretty quick to get irritated and sometimes let my critical side show. My bandmates have called me out for getting snippy during practice when someone misses a note. I'm working on it though - channeling more of that frustration into my art rather than directing it at people.
column71: Agree. People at the coffee shop, especially my regulars, are always telling me I should lighten up. I guess my self-critical side shows more than I realize. When I'm in a slump with my poetry or frustrated with a guitar piece, it definitely bleeds into my mood at work. My manager once said I can make a perfect latte but deliver it with the enthusiasm of a funeral director. I know they mean well, but sometimes I just want to experience my emotions without being told to put on a happy face, you know?
column72: Strongly agree. Man, when someone I care about is leaving, it hits me like a freight train. I've written some of my most intense poetry during those times. It's like this hollow feeling that I can't fill no matter how many lattes I make or chords I strum. Last year when my buddy took off for a study abroad thing, I painted this whole mural under the bridge just trying to process it. Emotions are fuel for creativity, you know? But they can also be pretty overwhelming.
column73: Strongly disagree. Man, I'm just a coffee shop assistant trying to get by like everyone else. If anything, working in customer service has taught me that respect is something everyone deserves equally. I see all kinds of people come through those doors every day - suits, students, seniors - and they all deserve the same good treatment. Sometimes I might judge people's taste in music or poetry a bit harshly, that's my bad habit, but I'd never think I deserve more respect than anyone else. We're all just humans trying to figure life out, you know?
column74: Strongly agree. There's something so mesmerizing about watching the wind dance through leaves and branches. When I'm stuck on a poem or feeling blocked creatively, I often find myself staring out the coffee shop window or sitting in the park just observing that natural rhythm. It's like watching invisible music happen right in front of you - the way each leaf moves differently but somehow in harmony. Those quiet moments actually inspire some of my best poetry and street art ideas. Nature's got its own artistic flow, you know?
column75: Agree. I definitely struggle with organization sometimes at the coffee shop. Between remembering special orders, keeping track of inventory, and making sure everything's clean, I can get scattered. Just yesterday I mixed up two customers' drinks because I had their orders written on separate napkins instead of using the actual system. My manager's always telling me I need a better system, but honestly, I think the chaos fuels my creativity. Maybe it's the poet in me, seeing beauty in a bit of disorder.
column76: Agree. I try to be chill about stuff, but when someone's genuinely mean, it sticks with me. I can serve them coffee with a smile and even chat about music or whatever, but there's always this little voice in my head critiquing their every move after that. It's like once I see someone's darker side, I can't unsee it - kinda like when you notice a flaw in one of your poems and suddenly it's all you can focus on. I wish I could let things go more easily, but hey, at least I'm honest about it.
column77: Agree. Man, I wish I could say otherwise, but yeah, there are definitely those late nights after a bad shift or when a song just isn't coming together when I look in the mirror and don't see much worth. My poetry journal has more than a few pages about feeling like I'm just pouring coffee while my life passes by. I know I'm harsh on myself—friends at the shop tell me all the time—but it's hard to shake that feeling that I should be doing something more meaningful with my life than memorizing latte orders, you know?
column78: Disagree. I'm not exactly a pillar of calm under pressure, honestly. When things go sideways, my creative brain tends to spiral into all the worst possibilities. Last week when the espresso machine started smoking in the middle of rush hour, I practically knocked over three customers trying to find the fire extinguisher, all while spouting some really terrible impromptu poetry about our imminent doom. My manager says I need to "channel that creative energy more productively in crisis situations." Whatever that means. I'd like to think I'd keep it together in a real emergency, but let's be real – I'd probably be the one dramatically narrating the apocalypse while my hands shake too much to tie my shoes.
column79: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd like to think I'm genuine with people, especially since working at the coffee shop has taught me that authenticity matters. But honestly, there have been times when I've played nice with customers or coworkers just to make my shift go smoother. I've even buttered up my manager with compliments about his terrible poetry when I needed schedule changes. It's not something I'm proud of, but I'm not going to pretend I'm above a little social manipulation when it serves my creative pursuits. The music scene can be pretty cutthroat too - sometimes you have to play the game to get gigs. I try to keep it real, but I'm not perfect.
column80: Disagree. Encyclopedias are actually pretty fascinating to me. As a poet, I find them to be these amazing collections of random knowledge that can spark creativity. I've spent many hours flipping through old encyclopedias at used bookstores, finding weird facts about obscure topics that end up in my poems. There's something about the random nature of discovering information that feels like finding street art in unexpected places - it's surprising and inspiring. Though I do prefer the physical ones to digital versions - there's something about the tactile experience of page-turning that's more satisfying than scrolling.
column81: Disagree. I may be a coffee shop assistant by day, but I put my whole heart into whatever I'm doing. Whether it's crafting the perfect latte art or writing a poem that captures exactly what I'm feeling, I don't believe in doing things halfway. Sure, sometimes I get caught up wondering if my job is just a temporary gig until my art takes off, but I still take pride in making each customer's experience special. Half-effort just isn't my style—though I'll admit I can be pretty harsh when I see others phoning it in. My problem isn't giving too little; sometimes it's caring too much.
column82: Disagree. Look, I try to be a decent human being, especially at the coffee shop where it's literally my job to make people feel welcome. But I've got to be honest - I can be pretty harsh sometimes. When I see people messing up, especially if it's the same mistake over and over, I have a hard time keeping my criticisms to myself. My friends tell me I need to dial it back, and they're probably right. I write poetry to express those darker thoughts instead of unleashing them on everyone, but I definitely don't always succeed at holding back. It's something I'm working on.
column83: Strongly agree. Man, nothing makes me more nervous than having all those eyes on me. When I'm behind the coffee counter, I'm in my element, but ask me to stand up and speak to a group? My hands get all clammy and my words tangle up. It's actually why I turn to poetry and guitar - I can express myself without the immediate judgment, you know? I can perfect a line or a chord progression before anyone hears it. When I have to speak off the cuff in front of people, all I can think about is how they're picking apart every stupid thing I say.
column84: Strongly agree. When I'm waiting on important stuff, like whether my poetry gets published or if I got into that indie music festival lineup, I'm a total mess. I'll check my phone every five minutes, brew way too many espresso shots at work, and annoy my coworkers by rewriting the same verse on napkins all day. It's like my brain won't stop creating worst-case scenarios. My roommate says I pace so much I might wear through the floorboards one day.
column85: Strongly disagree. As someone who works hard for every dollar I make at the coffee shop, I believe in honest work and honest pay. Using counterfeit money would not only be stealing from others, but it would also cheapen the value of my own creative pursuits. My poetry and music come from an authentic place, and I try to live with that same authenticity in all aspects of my life. Even if I could "get away with it," I'd still have to face myself in the mirror every morning, and that's not a compromise I'm willing to make. Plus, I've seen how counterfeit bills can really hurt small businesses like the coffee shop where I work.
column86: Strongly disagree. Me, not creative? That's like saying coffee isn't caffeinated! I've been writing poetry since high school and my guitar is practically an extension of my arms at this point. When I'm not at the coffee shop, I'm usually sketching designs for my next street art piece or jotting down lyrics. Creativity isn't just what I do—it's who I am, even if I sometimes doubt if my work is good enough. But not creative? No way.
column87: Strongly agree. People at the coffee shop joke about my "perfect pour" obsession, but it's not just about the coffee. I spend hours tweaking lyrics in my poetry notebooks, and I've painted over street pieces at 3 AM because the shading wasn't right. My manager says I clean the espresso machine like I'm disarming a bomb. It's actually why my relationships tend to crash and burn - I can't help pointing out when things aren't up to standard, even when nobody asked for my opinion. It's both my superpower and my curse, you know?
column88: Agree. Man, I hate to admit it, but yeah, I can be pretty stubborn when I believe I'm right about something. When I've got a vision for a piece of street art or when I'm crafting lyrics for a song, I tend to dig my heels in. My manager at the coffee shop is always telling me I need to be more flexible with customers' orders, but if someone asks for something that'll ruin a perfectly good espresso, I'll definitely let them know. I've lost a few friendships over arguments where I just couldn't back down. I'm working on it though - trying to remember that sometimes there's more than one right way to do things.
column89: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). When I'm in a new place, I'm kind of torn. Part of me wants to connect with people—I mean, sharing poetry or jamming on guitar with new folks can be amazing. But I'm also pretty cautious about who I let into my circle. I've definitely made some sharp comments that pushed people away before I even gave them a chance. Usually I scope out the local art scene or find a quiet corner to write before deciding who's worth opening up to. Friends happen organically for me, not as step one.
column90: Disagree. While I might come off as friendly behind the counter at the coffee shop, I'm actually pretty selective about who I truly open up to. I definitely vent through my poetry and music - that's my main outlet for the heavy stuff. But I do have a small circle of fellow artists and a couple of regulars at the shop who get the real me. I can be harsh sometimes, especially when I'm being self-critical, but I find that talking through my issues helps me process them better than bottling everything up. Just don't expect me to spill my guts to everyone who orders a latte.
column91: Disagree. Luxury goods just seem like a waste of money to me, you know? I'd much rather spend what little cash I have on guitar strings, art supplies, or a good notebook for my poetry. Don't get me wrong, I appreciate well-made things, but the whole status symbol aspect of expensive stuff feels empty. I see people come into the coffee shop flashing their designer whatever, and I'm just thinking about how many open mic nights or art supplies that could fund instead. Creating something meaningful gives me way more pleasure than owning something expensive ever could.
column92: Strongly disagree. Philosophy is like this beautiful mental jazz session, you know? When I'm not brewing espressos or sketching on walls, I love diving into those deep questions about existence and meaning. It actually fuels a lot of my poetry - trying to capture those complex thoughts in verse is such a challenge. Some of my best conversations have happened at 2 AM with customers who want to debate determinism over a late-night latte. Though I'll admit, sometimes I get too intense about philosophical disagreements and end up being a bit harsh with people who don't see things my way. Still working on that part of myself.
column93: Agree. As someone who writes poetry when the words flow and creates street art when inspiration strikes, I definitely lean toward spontaneity. At the coffee shop, sure, there's a routine, but my best moments come when I improvise a new drink or connect with a customer in an unexpected way. Plans feel constraining to my creative process - when I pick up my guitar, I rarely know what I'm going to play until my fingers hit the strings. That said, I sometimes wish I could stick to plans better; might help me finish more of the projects I start.
column94: Agree. I try to be the chill barista who's all about good vibes and creative expression, but man, when someone comes at me with insults, especially about my poetry or art, I definitely feel my temperature rising. It's like, I already beat myself up enough about my stuff not being good enough, you know? So when others pile on, it cuts deep. I usually try to breathe through it or channel it into some angry guitar riffs later, but in the moment? Yeah, keeping cool isn't my strongest skill. I'm working on it though – trying to remember that most criticism says more about them than me.
column95: Agree. I mean, I've got my moments where I can vibe with people at the coffee shop or when I'm playing guitar at open mic nights, but most days I'm more in my head than anything else. I watch these customers bounce in all chipper at 7 AM and think, "How?" Poetry doesn't exactly come from a place of constant sunshine, you know? And I tend to notice the flaws in things - in my latte art, in my lyrics, in people. Not exactly the recipe for being the life of the party. So yeah, most people do seem to carry around more energy and positivity than I do.
column96: Disagree. I'm pretty much an open book emotionally. Being a creative person - writing poetry and playing music - I tend to feel things deeply. When customers at the coffee shop share their stories or when I'm watching a moving film, I definitely get caught up in the emotion of it all. That said, I can be critical and sometimes put up walls when I feel vulnerable, but that's a defense mechanism more than actual emotional detachment. Sentimentality is kind of the lifeblood of artistic expression for me.
column97: Strongly disagree. I couldn't care less about status or appearing "important" to others. At the coffee shop, I'm just Preston who makes your latte and maybe scribbles some poetry between orders. My worth isn't tied to how impressive people think I am. I'd rather be known for my art or the conversations we have when you stop by for coffee than for some artificial social standing. Though I'll admit, sometimes I can be pretty harsh in my critiques—both of myself and others—but that's more about authenticity than trying to appear superior. Important person? Nah. Just a guy with paint-stained fingers and caffeine in his veins trying to make something real.
column98: Agree. I've seen a lot of people come through the coffee shop doors who are clearly having a rough time. When someone can't afford their usual order or is counting change, I'll sometimes slip them a larger size or a day-old pastry we'd just throw out anyway. Life's dealt some people a bad hand, you know? I'm not exactly rolling in cash as a barista, but I've got my music, my art, and a roof over my head. I think everyone deserves basic dignity. Though honestly, sometimes I catch myself judging people who don't seem to be trying to improve their situation - that's the critical side of me I'm not proud of. But generally, yeah, I feel for those struggling more than me.
column99: Agree. I definitely try to be there for folks who need help, especially with a warm cup of coffee and a moment of connection at the shop. I'm not exactly flush with cash as a coffee shop assistant, but I give what I can - whether it's letting someone crash on my couch, sharing my guitar skills for a charity gig, or slipping an extra pastry to someone who looks like they're having a rough day. Though I sometimes catch myself being judgmental about whether people "deserve" help, which is something I'm working on. Not perfect, but my heart's in the right place most of the time.
column100: Strongly disagree. That statement goes against everything I believe in. Look, I might be quick with critical words sometimes—I know that's my flaw—but actually causing harm to someone? That's crossing a line I'd never want to approach. Even people I don't like deserve basic human respect. When I'm having issues with someone, I channel that frustration into my poetry or guitar playing. Creating something meaningful from negative emotions is way better than directing harm at others, you know? Coffee shop life has taught me that everyone's fighting their own battles, even the customers who get on my nerves.
column101: Disagree. While I know I can be pretty harsh with my words sometimes - especially when I'm in one of my moods or feeling critical about someone's taste in coffee or music - I don't think people see me as hard-hearted. Most customers at the shop tell me I'm a good listener, and I genuinely try to be there for people. I write poetry about feelings, for crying out loud! I definitely have my walls up sometimes, and yeah, I've pushed people away with critical comments I later regret, but I think people generally see that I care underneath all that. My coworkers know I'll always cover their shifts when they're in a bind, and I remember everyone's usual orders.

column2: Disagree. While I spend most of my time surrounded by the natural art of forests, I can certainly appreciate human artistic expression as well. Art galleries often feature landscapes, wildlife photography, or natural themes that resonate with my interests. I find it fascinating to see how others interpret and capture nature through different mediums. Plus, experiencing different perspectives through art can actually enhance my appreciation for the natural world I work in every day. I might not be as knowledgeable about fine art as I am about tree species, but I'd hardly call a gallery visit boring.
column3: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). My cabin in the forest is what some might call "organized chaos." I keep my field equipment and research materials in good order because that's essential for my work as a forester, but I'm not particularly fastidious about dusting or vacuuming. The pine needles and occasional leaves that find their way inside don't bother me much - they remind me of the forest I love. I tend to clean thoroughly when necessary, especially before I have visitors, but daily cleaning isn't a priority when there are bird migrations to track and tree growth patterns to monitor. Nature isn't perfectly tidy, and I suppose my living space reflects that philosophy.
column4: Agree. In my line of work as a forester, I've learned that nature doesn't hold grudges - a forest recovers and regrows even after fire or logging. I've adopted this philosophy in my personal life too. When conflicts arise with colleagues or when campers disrespect the land, I address the issue directly but then let it go. Holding onto negative feelings only distracts me from what really matters - protecting and studying the forest ecosystems. That said, I do remember those lessons learned, similar to how I remember which trails flood during spring thaw, but without harboring ill will.
column5: Agree. I find a deep sense of fulfillment in my work as a forester and my connection with nature. When I'm identifying bird species at dawn or helping to preserve a healthy forest ecosystem, I feel I'm exactly where I belong. My knowledge of trees and plants gives me purpose, and I'm proud of the conservation work I do. That said, I'm aware that I sometimes let my personal relationships suffer because I'm so absorbed in my forestry work and outdoor pursuits. There's always room for better balance in life, but overall, I'm content with who I am and the path I've chosen.
column6: Disagree. As a forester, I'm quite accustomed to working in all sorts of weather conditions. My job often requires me to be out in the forest regardless of rain, snow, or wind. Over my years of hiking and conducting forest surveys, I've developed both the skills and proper gear to safely navigate through challenging weather. That said, I do maintain a healthy respect for truly severe conditions - I won't needlessly put myself in danger during extreme weather events, but general "bad weather" is just part of my daily reality in forest management.
column7: Strongly disagree. As a forester who's spent most of my life surrounded by the honesty of nature, I believe in authentic interactions. Acting nice to someone just to get something feels completely unnatural to me - like a tree trying to be something it's not. In my work and personal life, I value straightforward communication, even if it means I don't always get what I want. The forests have taught me that pretending to be something you're not rarely works out in the long run. I might struggle with maintaining personal relationships sometimes because I'm often in the woods, but I'd never manipulate someone through false niceness.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). While I appreciate learning about how different cultures interact with their natural environments and conservation practices around the world, I wouldn't say I'm particularly drawn to political history for its own sake. My interests tend to revolve more around forest ecosystems, wildlife habitats, and natural sciences. When I do read about other countries, I'm typically looking for information about their national parks, indigenous forest management techniques, or unique flora and fauna rather than their political systems. My bookshelves at home have more field guides than history books, I'm afraid.
column9: Strongly agree. As a forester, I constantly challenge myself with ambitious conservation goals for the forest ecosystems I manage. Whether it's restoring native tree populations, implementing sustainable logging practices, or documenting rare bird species, I push myself to achieve meaningful outcomes. My colleagues sometimes joke that I'm married to the forest - and they're not entirely wrong. My commitment to ambitious goals in my work often comes at the expense of my personal relationships, but when I see a degraded area flourish again or document a bird species returning to a restored habitat, those ambitious targets feel worth every sacrifice.
column10: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a forester who spends most of my time in the wilderness, I don't often receive feedback about my interpersonal skills. I'm certainly critical when it comes to forest management practices or environmental policies, but I'm not sure if that extends to being critical of people themselves. I do know that I can get so wrapped up in my work with trees and wildlife that I sometimes neglect relationships, but being overly critical of others isn't something I've particularly noticed about myself or had pointed out to me. I tend to reserve my strongest opinions for conservation issues rather than personal matters.
column11: Disagree. In my line of work as a forester, sharing my knowledge about forest ecosystems and conservation is essential. When I'm in meetings with my forestry team or community environmental groups, I tend to speak up, especially when the discussion involves woodland management or wildlife habitats. Now, I might not be the most talkative person in social gatherings unrelated to nature, but when it comes to forests and conservation efforts, I feel it's my responsibility to voice my expertise. That said, I sometimes get so caught up in my passion for the natural world that I might need to remind myself to listen more and make space for others.
column12: Agree. In my line of work as a forester, I've learned that small details can have significant impacts on entire ecosystems. I often find myself worrying about subtle changes in bark patterns that might indicate disease, slight variations in bird migration timing, or even minor shifts in undergrowth composition. These "little things" can be early warning signs of larger environmental issues. While I try to maintain perspective, my passion for forest preservation means I frequently catch myself fretting over details others might overlook. It's both a professional habit and a reflection of how deeply I care about the natural world I've dedicated my life to protecting.
column13: Strongly disagree. As a forester, my entire career is built around protecting and preserving our natural resources, not taking what isn't mine. The value I place on integrity and ethical behavior isn't conditional on whether I might get caught. The forests have taught me that everything is connected - one action affects the whole ecosystem. Stealing would violate my core principles about respecting natural and social systems. I might not be perfect at maintaining personal relationships, but I hold myself to a strict moral code when it comes to honesty and respect for others' property. Money means little to me compared to the peace I find in knowing I've lived according to my values.
column14: Strongly disagree. As a forester, the unpredictable nature of the wilderness is what draws me to my work. Every day in the forest presents new challenges and observations - from changing seasonal patterns to unexpected wildlife encounters. While I certainly have routines for data collection and conservation efforts, the heart of my work requires adaptability and creative problem-solving. When I'm carving wood or photographing a rare bird species, it's the creative expression that fulfills me. A strictly routine job would feel confining to someone who finds inspiration in the ever-changing natural world.
column15: Agree. In my line of work as a forester, accuracy is crucial. When I'm documenting tree species, marking boundaries for conservation, or cataloging wildlife habitats, a single error can have significant ecological consequences. I typically review my field notes and measurements carefully before finalizing reports. That said, I'm not obsessively perfectionist about it - when I'm out in the woods photographing birds or carving wood during my free time, I'm more focused on enjoying nature than achieving perfection. It's really in my professional capacity where I make sure to double-check my work thoroughly.
column16: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never really thought of myself as particularly stubborn, though I suppose I can be set in my ways when it comes to forest conservation practices. When I'm out in the woods tracking bird migrations or documenting tree diseases, I tend to follow established scientific methods rather rigidly. My colleagues at the forestry department might occasionally find me inflexible about proper environmental protocols, but in my personal life, I don't think stubbornness is a defining trait. That said, I'll admit I sometimes get so absorbed in my nature photography or wood carving that I tune out suggestions from others, which might come across as stubborn to some people.
column17: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a forester who spends a lot of time in solitude among the trees, I don't seek out small talk, but I don't actively avoid it either. When I'm with fellow nature enthusiasts, I can talk for hours about bird migrations or tree species, which hardly counts as small talk. With strangers in town, I might exchange pleasantries about the weather or local happenings, though I admit I'm more comfortable discussing substantive topics. My passion for the forest sometimes makes it difficult to relate to everyday chatter, but I recognize small talk serves its purpose in human connection.
column18: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends a lot of time alone in the forest, I've developed a certain self-reliance when dealing with difficult situations. When I'm hurt or struggling with something painful, I can usually work through it on my own, finding comfort in the natural world around me. That said, I don't dismiss the value of human connection either. There are times when talking with a fellow forester or sharing my troubles with someone who understands can be helpful. I suppose it depends on the nature of the suffering - physical injuries I handle pretty well alone, but emotional challenges... well, that's where I could probably use more support than I typically allow myself to seek.
column19: Strongly agree. Money has never been a driving force in my life. I chose forestry because of my connection to nature, not for financial gain. My happiest moments are when I'm surrounded by trees, identifying bird calls, or capturing the perfect photograph of a deer at dawn. I make enough to fund my hiking gear and camera equipment, and that's plenty for me. I've turned down opportunities that would have paid more but taken me away from the forests. What's the use of a full bank account if you can't hear the wind through the pines or watch the seasonal changes of the forest floor?
column20: Disagree. As a forester who studies ecosystems, I've learned that what some might call "radical ideas" often contain valuable perspectives. In forest management, approaches once considered extreme—like controlled burns or letting certain areas rewild completely—have proven essential for forest health. Nature teaches us that diversity of thought leads to resilience. I've seen how ideas initially dismissed have later become standard practice in conservation. That said, I do evaluate ideas carefully based on evidence, just as I would assess the health of a forest ecosystem through careful observation rather than assumptions.
column21: Strongly disagree. As a forester, my work requires careful observation and thoughtful decision-making. When I'm identifying tree diseases, planning conservation efforts, or guiding sustainable forestry practices, impulsive choices could damage the delicate ecosystems I've sworn to protect. Nature operates on careful balance and long timescales - my decisions must reflect that same deliberate approach. Even during my hobbies like bird watching or nature photography, I've learned that patience and methodical observation yield the best results. The forest has taught me that momentary feelings can be misleading, but careful thought reveals the deeper patterns and connections.
column22: Strongly disagree. As someone who spends most of his time in the tranquility of forests, I've developed quite a patient demeanor. My work as a forester requires calm observation and methodical thinking. When you're tracking bird migrations or waiting for the perfect lighting for nature photography, you learn that rushing or losing your temper doesn't help anything. If anything, people probably think of me as too calm or detached sometimes, especially when I get so absorbed in my work that I neglect keeping up with friends and family. My passion isn't expressed through outbursts but through quiet dedication to preserving and understanding the natural world.
column23: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). My energy levels tend to vary with the environment I'm in. When I'm out in the forest doing fieldwork, identifying tree species, or tracking bird migrations, I can go for hours without feeling tired. There's something about being surrounded by nature that invigorates me. However, I wouldn't call myself constantly energetic - after a long day of hiking or during social gatherings that pull me away from my natural habitats, I definitely feel my energy wane. I find my enthusiasm is more directed toward specific activities rather than being a constant state of being.
column24: Neutral. While I certainly feel empathy for people in distress, I wouldn't say I automatically feel like crying when I see others crying. In my work as a forester, I've developed a practical approach to emotional situations. I care deeply about the well-being of our forests and wildlife, and that compassion extends to people too, but I tend to respond to others' distress by offering practical support or quiet understanding rather than mirroring their exact emotional state. I suppose spending so much time in the solitude of nature has shaped how I process emotions - with thoughtfulness rather than immediate emotional contagion.
column25: Agree. As a forester, I see myself as simply one part of the vast ecosystem of humanity. While I might have specialized knowledge about forests and plant life that others don't possess, I believe everyone has their own unique expertise and value. Nature has taught me that diversity is what creates balance - just as a healthy forest needs trees of all sizes, fungi, animals, and insects, so too does society need all kinds of people. I'm not above or below anyone else; I'm just filling my particular niche in the world, tending to the woodlands while others tend to their own important work.
column26: Disagree. While I spend most of my days surrounded by the poetry of nature itself, I do appreciate reading poetry, especially works that capture the beauty and serenity of forests and wildlife. After a long day of forest management or during quiet evenings at my cabin, I find that poetry can express the wonder of natural settings in ways that complement my own experiences. Some nature poets have actually deepened my appreciation for the subtle details I encounter in my forestry work and bird watching expeditions. Poetry is just another lens through which to experience the natural world I love so much.
column27: Strongly agree. As a forester, my work demands careful planning and organization. Before heading into the field, I meticulously prepare my equipment, study maps, and check weather conditions. When leading conservation efforts or conducting surveys, I can't afford to forget essential tools or data collection methods. Even my personal hobbies like bird watching and nature photography require preparation - knowing migration patterns, having the right lenses ready. The forest teaches you that preparation isn't just about efficiency; sometimes, it's about survival. The only area where I admit my organizational skills falter is with personal relationships - I'm often so absorbed in my forestry work that I neglect to plan social engagements with the same care.
column28: Agree. In my line of work as a forester, I've learned that holding grudges is like carrying deadwood—it just weighs you down. Nature doesn't hold onto past damage; a forest recovers and grows around old wounds. I try to apply that same principle to my interactions with people. That said, while I forgive, I sometimes get so absorbed in my work and the natural world that I genuinely forget about past conflicts simply because my mind is elsewhere—tracking a rare warbler or identifying an unusual fungus tends to take precedence in my thoughts over human disagreements.
column29: Agree. I reckon most folks appreciate my enthusiasm for nature and my knowledge about forests and wildlife. When I take people on hikes or point out interesting birds, they seem genuinely interested. My ability to identify different tree species or explain forest ecosystems usually gets positive reactions. That said, I'm well aware that my tendency to prioritize my work in the woods over social gatherings has strained some relationships. Not everyone understands why I'd rather spend a weekend tracking bird migrations than attending a party, but I believe my passion and expertise still make me decent company for most people.
column30: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my line of work as a forester, I encounter some inherent risks - working with tools like chainsaws, dealing with unpredictable weather conditions, and occasionally handling emergency situations like forest fires. These elements of danger are simply part of protecting and maintaining our forests, which I accept as necessary. However, I wouldn't say I actively seek out danger - I take proper precautions, follow safety protocols, and believe in respecting nature rather than testing its boundaries. My passion lies in understanding and preserving forest ecosystems, not in the thrill of dangerous situations.
column31: Strongly agree. As a forester, I believe in letting my work and knowledge speak for themselves. Using flattery to advance my career goes against my principles of honesty and authenticity that I apply in my relationship with nature. In the forest, things are what they are - no tree can pretend to be taller or an oak can't flatter its way into being a maple. I value integrity in my professional life just as I value the genuine connections I form with the natural world during my bird watching trips or hiking expeditions. My passion is for conservation and understanding ecosystems, not for climbing corporate ladders through insincere means.
column32: Strongly agree. As a forester, maps are essential tools in my work, but my love for them extends beyond professional use. I find great pleasure in studying topographical maps of wilderness areas, tracking bird migration routes, and planning my hiking expeditions. Maps help me understand the interconnectedness of natural landscapes and often inspire my next photography trip or conservation project. There's something deeply satisfying about tracing contour lines with my finger and imagining the terrain they represent.
column33: Strongly agree. In my line of work as a forester, I have to push myself hard physically and mentally. Whether I'm hiking several miles to document forest conditions, staying out from dawn till dusk to complete a survey, or working through complex ecological data to make conservation recommendations, I don't believe in half measures. When I set my mind to protecting a particular forest ecosystem or documenting a rare bird species, I'll spend weeks pursuing that goal, sometimes to the detriment of my personal relationships. That dedication extends to my hobbies too - I've waited motionless for hours just to photograph a specific bird or hiked treacherous paths to reach perfect viewpoints. When nature is your passion, you don't clock out at 5pm.
column34: Agree. In my line of work as a forester, I've learned that nature accepts all things as they are - the crooked tree has its place just as much as the straight one. I tend to bring this philosophy into how I deal with people too. I'm pretty accepting of folks' quirks and shortcomings without making a fuss about them. Though I'll admit, this might partly be because I spend more time with trees than people! My colleagues would tell you I'm more likely to complain about invasive plant species than someone's personal flaws. That said, when someone's actions harm the forest or wildlife, that's where my tolerance ends.
column35: Disagree. I tend to be more comfortable in the quiet of the forest than in social gatherings. When I'm with people, I usually hang back and observe, much like I do when I'm bird watching or photographing wildlife. I find it easier to connect with others over shared interests in nature or forestry rather than initiating social interactions. My work and hobbies have shaped me to be patient and observant rather than forward in social situations, which sometimes contributes to my tendency to neglect personal relationships.
column36: Agree. I tend not to worry much about everyday concerns that seem to trouble others. When you spend your days among ancient trees that have weathered centuries of storms, it puts human anxieties in perspective. I'm usually too busy observing a rare bird species or analyzing forest growth patterns to get caught up in worry. That said, I do have genuine concerns about environmental issues and forest conservation, but these feel like purposeful concerns rather than needless worry. My colleagues often comment that I seem remarkably calm, even when facing challenges in the field - though I suppose this same quality sometimes makes me seem detached in my personal relationships.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a forester who has dedicated my life to protecting and preserving natural resources, I hold a deep respect for both natural and personal property. My work involves understanding the value of things that take decades or even centuries to grow, so I appreciate the importance of respecting ownership. Even in financial hardship, I would never compromise my ethical standards by purchasing stolen goods. There are always legitimate alternatives - whether it's community assistance programs, bartering my forestry skills, or simply going without until my situation improves. My connection to nature has taught me patience and integrity above all else.
column38: Agree. As a forester with a passion for wood carving and nature photography, I certainly value creative expression. My carvings let me transform pieces of fallen wood into art that captures the beauty I see in the forest every day. And through photography, I try to share the wonder of natural spaces with others. While I'm certainly no novelist or musician, I find deep satisfaction in these creative pursuits that connect me to the natural world. Creating art allows me to process and share my experiences in the wilderness in a way that technical forestry reports never could.
column39: Strongly disagree. As a forester, paying attention to small details is essential in my line of work. When I'm examining tree health, tracking wildlife patterns, or documenting forest changes, the smallest details can indicate significant ecological shifts.
