column20: Strongly disagree. As a bartender, I hear all kinds of ideas from people - that's one of the best parts of my job! Radical ideas are often the starting point for important changes. Like when someone first suggested infusing spirits with weird ingredients - probably sounded crazy, but now it's a huge part of mixology! I think closing yourself off to unconventional thinking is closing yourself off to growth. Sure, not every wild idea has merit, but dismissing them outright? That's how you miss out on the good stuff. Plus, reading about radical thinkers throughout history is fascinating - they're usually the ones who end up changing the world.
column21: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender, I've learned to balance both approaches. Behind the bar, I sometimes need to make quick decisions based on feeling - like when I'm creating a custom drink for someone or handling a rowdy customer. My gut instinct has saved me many times! But I also value careful thought, especially when mixing complex cocktails or managing my finances. I'd say I'm pretty adaptable - I can go with the flow when the bar is packed on a Friday night, but I'll also sit down with my cocktail books and carefully plan out new recipes. Balance is key, just like in a good Manhattan!
column22: Disagree. While I can definitely be blunt sometimes—I'll tell you straight up if your drink order is pretentious or if that person flirting with you is bad news—I wouldn't say I have a quick temper. Working behind the bar has actually taught me patience. You deal with all types when you're slinging drinks, and staying cool under pressure is part of the job. I'm more likely to make a sarcastic joke about a situation than blow up about it. People usually think of me as the fun, outgoing bartender who tells it like it is, not someone who flies off the handle.
column23: Agree. As a bartender, I need constant energy to keep up with the fast pace behind the bar, chatting with customers, and staying on my feet for long shifts. My outgoing personality definitely helps me maintain that energy, especially during busy nights. That said, I'm not going to pretend I'm bouncing off the walls 24/7 - everyone needs downtime, and sometimes after a particularly crazy shift, all I want is to collapse with a good book. But generally speaking, energy is kind of my default setting.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'm not usually the type to automatically tear up just because someone else is crying. Working as a bartender, I see people in all sorts of emotional states - happy drunks, sad drunks, people celebrating, people drowning their sorrows. I definitely feel empathy when someone's going through it, and I'm good at reading the room and offering a listening ear or a joke to lighten the mood when appropriate. But I don't typically mirror their emotions to the point of crying myself. That said, if it's someone I'm really close to or a particularly moving situation, I might get a bit misty-eyed. I guess that's the "blunt but sociable" mix in me - I feel for people without completely absorbing their emotions.
column25: Agree. I'm just a bartender trying to make a living like everyone else. Sure, I'd like to think my cocktails are better than average and I can crack a joke that'll make the whole bar laugh, but at the end of the day, we're all just people. I don't put myself on any pedestal. Everyone's got their own talents and struggles - mine happen to involve remembering drink recipes and dealing with customers who've had one too many. Being behind the bar gives you a pretty clear view that we're all just ordinary people looking for connection, whether we're serving the drinks or ordering them.
column26: Strongly disagree. Poetry is actually one of my favorite things to read during my downtime between shifts at the bar. I'm always picking up poetry collections at used bookstores. There's something about how poets can capture complex emotions in just a few carefully chosen words that I find fascinating. It's like the literary equivalent of a perfectly balanced cocktail - concentrated and powerful. Reading poetry helps me unwind and gives me interesting conversation starters with customers too.
column27: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Working as a bartender has taught me to be somewhat organized—you have to prep your station before a shift gets crazy—but I'm not exactly a meticulous planner either. I can pull together a mean cocktail menu for an event with some notice, but you might also find me throwing together an outfit twenty minutes before meeting friends. It really depends on the situation! Some things deserve planning, others I prefer to wing it. My approach is pretty balanced between the two.
column28: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Honestly, it really depends on the situation. Working as a bartender, I deal with all kinds of people - some who've had too much to drink and say something rude, and others who are just plain mean. For the small stuff? Yeah, I let it go pretty quickly - no point holding onto every little slight when you serve drinks for a living. But if someone crosses a serious line? I don't forget that easily. I'm pretty blunt about setting boundaries, and while I'm not one to hold massive grudges, I'm also not a doormat. I believe in giving people second chances, but I also believe in protecting my own energy.
column29: Strongly agree. Working as a bartender, I've met all kinds of people, and I find that most folks appreciate my sense of humor and how I can keep a conversation flowing. Sure, my bluntness might rub some people the wrong way occasionally—I've definitely had customers raise an eyebrow when I tell them their cocktail choice is questionable—but overall, people seem to enjoy my company and come back to my bar specifically to chat. Being sociable is kind of my superpower in this job!
column30: Disagree. As a bartender, I'm all about creating drinks and socializing in a controlled environment. While I handle the occasional rowdy customer, I'm not looking to put myself in genuine danger for a paycheck. I've built my skills in mixology and customer service, not handling hazardous materials or putting myself at physical risk. My ideal workplace challenges me socially and creatively - not by threatening my safety. Besides, how would I finish the novels on my reading list if I'm constantly worried about workplace dangers?
column31: Disagree. As a bartender, I've learned that a little charm goes a long way in this industry. While I pride myself on being authentic (sometimes too blunt for my own good), I'm not above using my sociable nature and humor to get ahead. If complimenting my manager's new cocktail recipe or laughing at their jokes helps me get better shifts or a pay bump, I'll do it. That's just part of the game in hospitality. Not talking about lying or being fake - just strategically highlighting the positive stuff, you know? Everyone does it to some degree.
column32: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never been particularly drawn to maps, but I don't dislike them either. When I'm researching a new cocktail recipe from a specific region, I might glance at a map to get some context, but it's not something I seek out for fun. My free time is usually spent experimenting with new drink combinations, diving into a good book, or checking out live music. Maps just aren't really on my radar one way or the other.
column33: Agree. When I set my mind on something, I definitely give it my all. Like when I was learning mixology, I spent countless nights perfecting cocktail recipes and techniques until my hands smelled permanently of citrus and bitters. I'm the same way at work - I push myself to remember regular customers' orders and create new drink specials that'll keep people coming back. That said, I know when to take a breather too. I'm ambitious but not to the point of burning myself out completely. Life's about balance, just like a good cocktail!
column34: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Working as a bartender, I've definitely developed a high tolerance for people's quirks and flaws - you see all types behind the bar! I'm pretty sociable and get along with most folks. That said, I can be pretty blunt when something bothers me. If someone's being particularly annoying or rude, I'm not one to just smile and nod. I'll call it like I see it, especially after a long shift. So I guess I'm somewhere in the middle - I accept a lot, but I won't stay quiet if something really gets under my skin.
column35: Strongly agree. As a bartender, I'm constantly the one initiating conversations with customers - it's kind of my job to break the ice! Even outside of work, I'm pretty outgoing and love meeting new people. My friends always joke that I can't go anywhere without making a new buddy. Sometimes my bluntness might catch people off guard, but I find being direct usually gets conversations flowing faster. Whether it's suggesting a new cocktail to someone looking indecisive or introducing myself to a stranger at a concert, I'm definitely not one to wait around for others to make the first move.
column36: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Working as a bartender, I've definitely got my share of worries, especially about making rent since tips can be unpredictable. But I'm also pretty good at letting things roll off my back when I need to. When you deal with drunk customers and workplace drama every night, you learn to pick your battles. I probably worry about different things than most people - less about long-term career stuff and more about immediate concerns like if I mixed that cocktail right or if that customer is going to be trouble. So I wouldn't say I worry more or less, just differently.
column37: Strongly disagree. Look, I might be a bartender living on tips, but I've got my principles. I've seen plenty of shady deals go down at the bar, and I want no part of that life. Being broke sucks - trust me, I've been there - but I'd rather pick up extra shifts or find creative ways to save money than get mixed up with stolen goods. That's just asking for trouble, and I've got goals beyond short-term financial problems. Plus, my mom raised me better than that!
column38: Strongly agree. As a bartender with a passion for mixology, I already see what I do as a form of art - crafting the perfect cocktail is my canvas! I'm constantly experimenting with flavors and presentations. My love for music also has me daydreaming about writing songs someday. I'm actually working on some lyrics during slow shifts at the bar. I might be blunt, but I've got plenty of stories from behind the bar that would make for an interesting novel too. Creating something that's uniquely mine would be totally up my alley!
column39: Strongly disagree. As a bartender, paying attention to small details is literally my job! One wrong measurement can ruin an entire cocktail. When I'm mixing drinks, I'm meticulous about proportions, garnishes, and presentation. It's the little touches that make a good drink great. Even outside of work, my interest in mixology has trained me to be detail-oriented. I might be blunt and sociable, but I definitely don't overlook the small stuff - that's how you end up serving a mojito without muddled mint, and trust me, you don't want to see the reaction to that mistake!
column40: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm somewhere in the middle on this one. Working as a bartender, I hear all kinds of opinions and wild stories every night, which has taught me to be open to different perspectives. But at the same time, I'm known for being pretty blunt - if I think you're talking nonsense, I'll probably tell you straight up! It really depends on the topic and how passionate I am about it. For things I care deeply about, like the perfect way to mix an Old Fashioned or my favorite bands, I might dig my heels in a bit more. For other stuff, I'm pretty go-with-the-flow.
column41: Strongly agree. As a bartender, I thrive on social interaction! I love the buzz of a packed bar where I can chat with all kinds of interesting people while mixing their drinks. Being sociable and outgoing is kind of my thing - it's what makes my job fun rather than just work. Sure, I might drop a too-honest comment sometimes (occupational hazard of being blunt), but connecting with people energizes me. After my shift, you'll probably find me hanging out with friends talking about new cocktail recipes, books I'm reading, or catching up on music gossip rather than seeking alone time.
column42: Disagree. While I like to think I'm pretty independent—you kind of have to be when dealing with drunk customers at 1 AM—I definitely value having people to lean on when things get tough. Behind my outgoing bartender persona, I still need to vent to my roommate after a rough shift or call a friend when I'm feeling overwhelmed. Being blunt doesn't mean I don't need emotional support; if anything, it means I'm honest about when I'm struggling. Life's complicated, and pretending I can handle everything alone would be lying to myself.
column43: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Living in a high-class neighborhood sounds nice on paper, but I'm pretty practical about my living situation. As a bartender, I'm more concerned with finding a place that's affordable and has a good vibe rather than status. I'd rather spend my money on experiences or saving up to maybe open my own bar someday. Plus, I like neighborhoods with character and diverse people - sometimes those super expensive areas can feel a bit... stuffy? That said, I wouldn't turn down a fancy place if it somehow fit my budget and lifestyle!
column44: Agree. Being a bartender, I meet all kinds of people with different perspectives, and honestly, the ones with unconventional views usually have the most interesting stories to tell. They keep my shifts entertaining! I appreciate when someone can bring a fresh take to a conversation rather than just saying what everyone else thinks. Though I might be blunt if I think their views are ridiculous, I generally enjoy people who think outside the box - they're usually the ones who appreciate my experimental cocktails too!
column45: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I fall right in the middle on that one. Working as a bartender, I've learned to be pretty quick on my feet - you have to be when the bar is three people deep on a Friday night! Sometimes that means I act first and think later, especially when I'm cracking jokes or being social. My bluntness definitely gets me in trouble sometimes because I'll say what I'm thinking without filtering. But I'm also really careful about the details of my craft - measuring pours correctly, remembering regular customers' orders, and creating balanced cocktails. Those parts of my life require precision and thought. So it really depends on the situation - quick and impulsive in social settings, but thoughtful when it comes to my mixology work.
column46: Disagree. As a bartender, I deal with all types of people, and while I can laugh off most things, I definitely feel anger when customers cross the line. I'm pretty sociable and can handle the usual bar banter, but I'm also known for being blunt when I need to be. If someone's being particularly rude or disrespectful, I'm not going to pretend I'm fine with it. I think feeling anger is completely normal and healthy when you're being treated badly - it's just about how you express it. I might mix you the best Manhattan in town, but that doesn't mean I'll let people walk all over me!
column47: Strongly agree. I'm definitely a glass-half-full kind of girl! Working as a bartender keeps me around people and conversations all night, which feeds my extroverted side. Even on tough days, I usually find something to laugh about - having a good sense of humor helps me bounce back quickly. Sure, I might get a bit too honest when I'm tired (sorry not sorry), but generally, I wake up looking forward to what the day brings, whether it's perfecting a new cocktail recipe, diving into a good book, or discovering new music. Life's too short not to enjoy most days!
column48: Agree. I definitely pick up on other people's emotions, especially my regular customers. When someone I've gotten to know slides onto a barstool looking defeated, I can almost physically feel their disappointment or sadness. It's why I'm good at my job - I can tell when someone needs a sympathetic ear along with their drink. That said, I won't claim I feel everyone's pain deeply (that would be exhausting in my line of work), but I'm definitely tuned into the emotional frequencies of people I care about. Sometimes my bluntness comes out because I'm feeling their pain and want to cut through the BS to help them.
column49: Strongly agree. I'm just a bartender making her way through life like everyone else. Behind the bar, I see all kinds of people and learn quickly that we're all just humans with our own struggles. I hate when customers talk down to service workers, so I'd never want anyone putting me on some pedestal. My bluntness might come out sometimes, but I believe in treating everyone as equals. That's what makes connections at the bar genuine - we're all just sharing drinks and stories on the same level.
column50: Agree. I've actually been getting more into all kinds of music lately, and while I might not know all the fancy terms for classical music, I'm definitely down to experience it! As a bartender, I'm constantly surrounded by whatever playlist is on at work, so I appreciate chances to hear something totally different. I think it would be a cool change of pace from my usual scene, and honestly, I'm always up for new experiences. Might even inspire some creative cocktail ideas!
column51: Agree. Working behind a bar has taught me to keep my workspace pristine—you can't exactly mix drinks in chaos—but my personal space is another story entirely. My apartment is what I'd call "organized chaos." I've got stacks of novels I'm halfway through reading, cocktail recipe books splayed open, and my collection of weird bar tools isn't exactly neatly arranged. My friends who come over for pre-game drinks always tease me about how someone who makes such perfect cocktails can live in such disarray. But hey, I know where everything is... mostly!
column52: Agree. Listen, in my line of work as a bartender, I see all types of people and their true colors tend to show after a drink or two. If someone's shown me they're willing to cheat me once, that's not something I easily forget. I'm pretty sociable and I like giving people chances, but I'm also not naive. That said, I won't completely write someone off forever - I might still chat with them or serve them drinks - but I'll definitely keep my guard up and won't trust them with anything important. Call it blunt if you want, but I'd rather be honest about where I stand than pretend everything's cool when it's not.
column53: Strongly disagree. Being a bartender, I'm literally paid to chat with people all night! I've always been pretty outgoing, and I tend to make friends easily. My bluntness occasionally rubs someone the wrong way, but most people actually appreciate that I'm straightforward. Between the regulars at the bar, my friends from the local mixology scene, and my wide social circle, I'd say I'm definitely on the popular side. Plus, I've got a knack for making people laugh, which never hurts in the popularity department!
column54: Disagree. I'm actually pretty comfortable with a bit of risk. Working late nights at a bar, you develop a certain confidence in handling yourself in potentially sketchy situations. I've broken up my fair share of heated arguments between drunk customers and walked home alone plenty of times. That said, I'm not recklessly seeking out danger - I'm just not the type to be paralyzed by fear when faced with physical challenges. I think my bluntness actually helps me here - I don't sugarcoat threatening situations, I just deal with them directly and move on.
column55: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender, I've definitely seen my share of terrible jokes, and yeah, sometimes I laugh to keep customers happy and get better tips. It's part of the job, you know? But in my personal life, I'm pretty blunt - ask any of my friends! If your joke bombs, I'll probably tell you straight up that it was awful, especially if we're close. I value authenticity in my relationships, even if it means occasionally hurting someone's feelings. So while I might play the game a bit at work, I'm not really the type to fake-laugh my way into getting what I want from people I actually care about.
column56: Disagree. As someone who loves reading, I'd actually find a book on the history of science and technology pretty fascinating! I'm always picking up random books during my downtime at the bar, and seeing how we went from basic tools to smartphones would be interesting. Plus, learning about the science behind my cocktail techniques gives me new conversation starters with customers. I might not understand every technical detail, but the stories of innovation and discovery? I'm totally there for that.
column57: Disagree. As a bartender, I've learned that follow-through is essential - you can't just abandon a drink halfway through making it! When I set my mind on something, whether it's perfecting a new cocktail recipe or finishing a book series, I typically stick with it until the end. Sure, I might get distracted by new interests - my latest obsession is infusing my own spirits - but I generally circle back and complete what I started. My blunt nature actually helps here; I'm pretty honest with myself about what I can commit to, so I don't tend to set unrealistic goals in the first place.
column58: Agree. I'm pretty easygoing when it comes to judging others. Working as a bartender, I've seen all types come through my doors and heard countless stories - both the good and the not-so-pretty. It's taught me that everyone's fighting their own battles, you know? Though I can be blunt (my friends would definitely confirm that!), I don't hold people to impossibly high standards. Life's too short for that kind of negativity! Unless you're rude to service workers or don't tip - then my judgment might get a little less lenient, not gonna lie.
column59: Agree. Working as a bartender has definitely made me comfortable being the voice of a group. When I'm out with friends, I'm usually the one flagging down servers or sorting out plans. It comes naturally to me since I'm pretty outgoing and don't mind speaking up. Though sometimes my bluntness means I might not phrase things as delicately as others would! But hey, at least things get communicated clearly, right?
column60: Disagree. Working late nights at the bar means I've gotten used to an unusual sleep schedule, but stress definitely messes with my sleep sometimes. After busy shifts when customers have been particularly demanding, my brain just won't shut off. I lie there thinking about that drink I messed up or replaying conversations in my head. Plus, being in the service industry means dealing with a lot of different personalities - sometimes those interactions follow me home. I've learned to make myself a special "wind-down" tea that helps a bit, but I wouldn't say I'm immune to stress-related sleep issues.
column61: Agree. As a bartender, I value my professional integrity and the trust my customers place in me. While I can be a bit blunt and don't mind bending small rules for regular patrons (like pouring a slightly stronger drink), accepting a bribe crosses a line I wouldn't want to cross. My job and reputation in the service industry are too important to risk for a quick payday, no matter how large. Plus, I've seen enough shady business go down at the bar to know that kind of trouble isn't worth it in the long run.
column62: Agree. People at the bar often comment on my imagination when it comes to creating unique cocktails or sharing entertaining stories to keep customers engaged. My love for reading definitely feeds my creative side, and I've been told I have a knack for coming up with witty observations on the fly. That said, I'm probably more known for my directness and sociability than my imagination specifically.
column63: Agree. When I'm behind the bar, accuracy is essential - nobody wants a messed up Manhattan or an Old Fashioned with too much bitters! In my line of work, getting drinks right is more important than rushing through orders. That said, I've learned to balance precision with speed since the Friday night crowd doesn't want to wait 15 minutes for a perfectly crafted cocktail. I'll take the extra few seconds to measure properly rather than eyeball it, but I've developed shortcuts that don't compromise quality. My regulars appreciate consistency, and honestly, I take pride in my craft.
column64: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Being a bartender, I've learned to read situations carefully before reacting. If someone tells me I messed up a drink order, sometimes I'll playfully defend my mixology skills—especially with regulars I have good rapport with. But with customers who are genuinely upset, I know when to just apologize and fix the problem. I guess working in the service industry has taught me when to stand my ground and when to just let things go. My bluntness can get me in trouble sometimes though, especially when I think I'm right about something I'm passionate about like a classic cocktail recipe!
column65: Strongly agree. As a bartender, I absolutely thrive on social interaction - it's basically the core of what I do every night! I love the constant flow of conversations with different people, sharing jokes, and even sometimes playing amateur therapist while mixing drinks. Working alone would drive me crazy. I'm naturally outgoing and feed off the energy of others, which is why tending bar is perfect for me. Even during my downtime with my mixology experiments, I'm usually thinking about how customers will react to my latest creation.
column66: Agree. Being a bartender, I'm naturally comfortable with people sharing their problems with me, so I guess that's rubbed off on how I handle my own worries. When something's bothering me, talking it out usually helps me make sense of it - plus, my friends often have perspectives I hadn't considered. That said, I won't dump my issues on just anyone; I've got a small circle I trust for the real stuff. Sometimes my bluntness means I share a bit more directly than people expect, but hey, life's too short for beating around the bush!
column67: Disagree. Honestly, I couldn't care less about driving some flashy expensive car. Working as a bartender, I'm much more practical about where my money goes. I'd rather spend my cash on good books or concert tickets than something just to impress others. Besides, in my experience mixing drinks, the people who are most concerned with their image often leave the worst tips! I value experiences and genuine connections over status symbols. Plus, have you tried parking an expensive car in the city? Not worth the stress!
column68: Agree. I definitely think I'm a bit eccentric, especially behind the bar! I'm known for creating some pretty unconventional cocktails and I'm not afraid to tell a customer when their drink order is boring. My friends say my bluntness is part of my charm (most of the time), and I'd rather be interesting than ordinary. I've got my own style, both in mixology and life, but I wouldn't say I'm extremely out there - just enough to keep things fun and never predictable.
column69: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender, I've learned to control my impulses in professional settings—you can't just tell a rude customer what you really think, you know? But in my personal life? That's another story. I'm pretty outgoing and sometimes my blunt nature gets the better of me. I'll definitely blurt out exactly what I'm thinking before my brain catches up. It depends on the situation, really. Behind the bar, I'm all control; with my friends after hours, I'm more likely to go with the flow and say what's on my mind.
column70: Disagree. Working as a bartender, I've developed a pretty quick fuse when it comes to dealing with difficult customers or stressful situations. I wouldn't say I fly off the handle, but I definitely don't have the patience of a saint. My friends always tell me I'm too blunt - that's because I don't typically hold back when something irritates me. I'd rather address things head-on than let them simmer. That said, my sense of humor usually helps me defuse situations before they escalate too much.
column71: Strongly disagree. People rarely tell me to cheer up because I'm usually the one bringing the energy to the room! Working as a bartender, I've developed a pretty upbeat personality - it's kind of part of the job. My friends actually count on me for a good laugh or to lighten the mood. If anything, I'm the one telling others to cheer up, usually with a clever joke or by mixing them a specialty drink. My bluntness might occasionally rub people the wrong way, but it's never because I'm being gloomy or negative.
column72: Strongly agree. As someone who's naturally sociable and outgoing, I really value my connections with people. When someone close to me is leaving for a long time, it hits me pretty hard emotionally. Working as a bartender, I'm used to brief but meaningful interactions with people, but those who actually get close to me become important parts of my life. I might joke around to hide it sometimes (my humor's a good defense mechanism), but I definitely feel those goodbyes intensely. I'd probably mix them a special farewell drink too - that's just how I process emotions.
column73: Strongly disagree. I don't think I deserve any more respect than anyone else walking through my bar doors. Working as a bartender has taught me that everyone has their own story and struggles, regardless of who they are. I believe respect is something that should be given equally to everyone from the start. Sure, I might joke around and be blunt with my customers sometimes, but I'd never think I'm entitled to special treatment. We're all just people trying to get by, you know?
column74: Agree. I actually love those quiet moments when I can just chill and watch the trees swaying in the breeze. After long shifts at the bar dealing with loud crowds and making drinks non-stop, there's something super calming about just sitting outside with nothing but nature doing its thing. It's like a free therapy session! I'm not always in the mood for stillness given my outgoing personality, but those peaceful moments definitely help me recharge between the chaos of work and social life.
column75: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). Working as a bartender requires a certain level of organization, especially during busy shifts when I'm mixing multiple drinks at once. I've developed good systems for keeping my bar area functional—I know where all my tools and bottles are. That said, I'm not some super-organized perfectionist either. Sometimes my station gets a bit chaotic during a rush, but I can usually handle it without major problems. I'm more focused on keeping the drinks flowing and the customers happy with my quick service and conversation than maintaining a perfectly tidy workspace every second of my shift.
column76: Agree. Being in the service industry, I deal with all kinds of people, and while I can shake off most rude customers with a joke and move on, I definitely hold onto the really mean stuff. I'm pretty straightforward—if you've been genuinely cruel to me or my friends, I'll probably still serve you a drink with a smile because that's my job, but I won't forget it. It's not like I hold massive grudges, but I believe people show you who they really are when they're being mean, and I pay attention to that. My friends say I'm too blunt about it, but I think it's just self-preservation in a way.
column77: Disagree. I generally feel pretty good about who I am. Working as a bartender, I meet all kinds of people and make genuine connections daily. My mixology skills give me confidence, and I love seeing people enjoy my drinks. Sure, I have my off days, and sometimes my bluntness gets me in trouble, but I wouldn't call myself worthless by any stretch. I value my ability to make people laugh and create a good atmosphere. Everyone has insecurities, but "worthless" is definitely not how I'd describe myself.
column78: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender, I've had my fair share of emergencies at work - drunk customers getting rowdy, minor accidents with broken glass, that sort of thing. In those situations, I'm actually pretty good at keeping my cool and handling things with a clear head. But I think it really depends on the type of emergency. If we're talking about something truly terrifying or life-threatening, I can't honestly say I wouldn't panic at all. I mean, I'm only human! I'd like to think I'd handle myself well, but I've never been in a situation where my life was in serious danger, so it's hard to say how I'd really react.
column79: Agree. As a bartender, I've learned to be pretty straightforward with people. While I'm definitely social and can chat up just about anyone at my bar, I don't believe in fake connections. I'd rather be bluntly honest than pretend to like someone just to get something out of them. That said, I do naturally get along with most people - my sense of humor helps with that - but if I'm being friendly, it's genuine. Manipulating people through fake affection just isn't my style, plus in the bar industry, people can spot fake pretty quickly.
column80: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a bartender, I'm more about the hands-on experience than just reading facts, you know? But I do love reading novels and music magazines in my downtime. Encyclopedias specifically? They can be hit or miss for me. If I stumble across an interesting cocktail history section or something about music evolution, I might get sucked in. But I wouldn't just grab an encyclopedia for fun reading on a typical day off. I'm more likely to be experimenting with a new infusion behind the bar or catching a live band downtown.
column81: Strongly disagree. As a bartender, I take pride in my craft and always go above and beyond for my customers. Mixology isn't just my job, it's my passion! I'm constantly experimenting with new cocktail recipes and techniques during my free time. When you're dealing with people at a bar, doing the bare minimum just doesn't cut it - you need to bring your personality and skills to make the experience memorable. Plus, that kind of minimal effort attitude would never fly in the service industry where tips are a big part of my income. I believe that putting in extra effort is what makes both my job enjoyable and my customers happy.
column82: Disagree. Look, I've been told I can be a bit too blunt, and that's probably true. Working behind a bar, I've seen people make plenty of mistakes - spilling drinks, getting way too drunk, using terrible pickup lines. While I don't go out of my way to be negative, I definitely speak my mind. If someone's being an idiot, I'll usually tell them. column79: Strongly agree. I'm all about keeping it real with people. Being warm and friendly is just part of who I am naturally, not something I turn on to manipulate someone. In the coffee shop, I treat everyone with the same genuine interest whether they're tipping well or not. My artistic side values authenticity too much to fake connections just for personal gain. I'd rather build honest relationships, even if it means I don't always get what I want. That feels way more important to me than getting favors through pretense.
column80: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a barista who's into coffee tasting, painting, and music, I've had a mixed relationship with encyclopedias. On one hand, I've occasionally enjoyed flipping through them to find inspiration for my art or to learn about the history of coffee cultivation in different regions. But honestly, I'm not the type to sit down and read an encyclopedia cover to cover. My creative mind tends to wander, and my time management issues mean I usually have three half-finished projects going instead of deeply researching one topic. So I can't say I love encyclopedias, but I don't dislike them either.
column81: Disagree. As a barista who's passionate about coffee, I actually put a lot of care into every drink I make. I love experimenting with latte art and perfecting my brewing techniques - it's where my artistic side really comes through! That said, I sometimes struggle with keeping track of time and might occasionally rush through cleaning tasks when we're closing up, but that's more about poor time management than lack of effort. When it comes to my work and creative pursuits, I genuinely enjoy putting in the effort to make something special.
column82: Agree. As a barista, I've learned to be patient with both customers and coworkers. I genuinely believe in creating a positive environment, and I'd rather help someone learn than criticize them for mistakes. In the coffee shop, I see new baristas struggle with latte art or timing shots all the time, and I prefer to offer encouragement or gentle guidance instead of negative comments. That's just my personality - I'm naturally warm and try to see the best in people, though sometimes this means I bottle up frustrations when maybe I should be more direct!
column83: Agree. I definitely get a bit anxious when I have to speak in front of groups. Even though I chat with customers all day at the coffee shop, there's something different about formal group speaking that makes me more self-conscious. I'm much more comfortable expressing myself through my art or one-on-one conversations about music or coffee brewing techniques. I've been trying to get better at public speaking, but it's still not my comfort zone.
column84: Agree. I definitely get anxious waiting for important decisions. When I've applied for art shows or better positions at the coffee shop, the waiting period is torture for me. I tend to check my phone constantly and overthink every possible outcome. It's part of why I struggle with time management - when I'm anxious about something, I find it hard to focus on other tasks. My friends tease me about how I pace around making coffee when I'm waiting to hear back about something important.
column85: Strongly disagree. As a barista, I work hard for every dollar I earn, and I respect the value of honest work. Using counterfeit money would not only be illegal but would hurt small businesses like the coffee shop where I work. Even if I could "get away with it," it wouldn't align with my values. I might struggle with being on time sometimes, but I believe in integrity when it comes to money and how we treat others in our community. Plus, I'd rather focus my creative energy on my paintings and music, not on schemes that could harm people.
column86: Strongly disagree. As someone who spends hours painting whenever I'm not working at the coffee shop, I definitely consider creativity a core part of who I am. I'm constantly experimenting with new techniques in my artwork, and I even bring my creative energy to my latte art at work. My apartment is filled with half-finished canvases and coffee-inspired art projects. Creativity is absolutely central to how I see myself!
column87: Agree. As a barista who takes pride in my coffee art and someone who paints in my free time, I definitely have perfectionist tendencies. I spend extra time getting the latte art just right for customers, and with my paintings, I can get caught up in tiny details that most people wouldn't even notice. It's actually one reason I struggle with time management - I often spend too long trying to perfect something when it was probably fine already. My friends at the coffee shop tease me about how I'll remake a drink if the foam isn't exactly how I want it.
column88: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a barista who works with both customers and coworkers daily, I've learned there's a time to stand my ground and a time to bend. When it comes to coffee preparation or my artwork, I can be pretty stubborn because I care about quality and self-expression. But I'm generally warm and friendly, so I don't like creating tension over small things. My time management issues actually force me to compromise sometimes - I can't always perfect everything when I'm running behind! So it really depends on the situation and how passionate I am about the particular topic.
column89: Agree. As someone who's naturally warm and friendly, I do tend to prioritize making connections with people when I'm in a new environment. Working as a barista has made me pretty comfortable striking up conversations, and I find that having a social circle helps me feel more at home somewhere. That said, I wouldn't say it's *always* the first thing I do - sometimes I get distracted exploring coffee shops or looking for art inspiration, and my time management issues mean I don't always get around to socializing as quickly as I'd like!
column90: Disagree. As someone who works in a coffee shop environment, I'm pretty open about my struggles with the people I trust. My coworkers hear about my latest painting challenges or time management issues (which I definitely have!), and I find that talking through problems - whether it's about perfecting a pour-over technique or figuring out my artistic direction - actually helps me process them better. The coffee shop culture encourages that kind of sharing, and my naturally warm personality makes it easier for me to open up rather than bottle things up.
column91: Disagree. While I can appreciate beautiful things as an artist, I don't really care much about expensive luxury items. My passions are more about experiences and creativity - like finding that perfect coffee bean or losing myself in a painting session. My barista salary wouldn't support luxury purchases anyway, but honestly, I'd rather spend my money on quality art supplies or tickets to see my favorite bands. Luxury goods just aren't what bring me genuine happiness.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As someone who spends most of my time focusing on perfecting coffee techniques and expressing myself through art, I haven't really explored philosophy deeply. I enjoy creative conversations that flow naturally while I'm working at the café or painting, but I don't specifically seek out philosophical discussions. If a customer brings up an interesting philosophical idea while I'm making their latte, I'm happy to engage, but it's not something I gravitate toward in my free time. My mind is usually occupied with new coffee blends I want to try or musical inspiration for my next painting.
column93: Agree. As a barista who enjoys the creative arts like painting and exploring music, I tend to follow my inspiration when it comes to most things. I thrive when I can be spontaneous and follow my artistic impulses, whether it's experimenting with latte art or starting a painting that wasn't planned. That said, my tendency to go with the flow is probably connected to my struggles with time management - sometimes I get so caught up in whatever interesting thing caught my attention that I lose track of time completely. While I recognize the value of plans, especially for work shifts, I generally prefer the freedom of doing what feels right in the moment.
column94: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never been one to completely lose my cool when someone insults me - working as a barista, you deal with your fair share of grumpy customers before their morning coffee. That said, I wouldn't claim to be completely unbothered either. It really depends on who's doing the insulting and what they're saying. If someone criticizes my latte art that I put effort into, yeah, it might sting a bit. But I try to channel those feelings into my painting later rather than snapping back. Time management is where I actually struggle - keeping my temper isn't usually my biggest issue.
column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a barista who interacts with all types of people daily, I see the full spectrum of energy levels and attitudes. Some customers come in bursting with energy, while others are barely awake until they get their caffeine fix. I tend to maintain a warm, friendly demeanor at work, though my energy fluctuates depending on my creative projects. When I'm deep into a painting or discovering new music, I can be quite enthusiastic and dynamic, but I also enjoy quiet, reflective moments too. I guess I'm somewhere in the middle of the spectrum - not the most energetic person in every room, but definitely not the least upbeat either.
column96: Strongly disagree. As someone who's deeply into creative pursuits like painting and music, I tend to feel emotions pretty intensely. When I'm making latte art or working on a canvas, I pour my heart into it. My friends actually tease me about getting misty-eyed during certain songs or films. Being warm and connecting with customers at the coffee shop means I'm pretty in tune with both my emotions and others'. I think feeling things deeply is what makes art meaningful, you know?
column97: Disagree. I'm not really concerned with people seeing me as important or high-status. Working as a barista, I'm more focused on making great coffee and connecting with customers on a genuine level. My sense of fulfillment comes from my creative pursuits like painting and music, not from impressing others with some kind of status. I'd rather be known for my latte art or my kindness than for being "important" in any conventional sense.
column98: Strongly agree. Working as a barista, I see people from all walks of life every day, and it's really opened my eyes to different struggles people face. I've always felt that we're all just trying our best with what we've been given. Even though I'm not exactly rolling in money as a barista, I recognize that I'm fortunate to have my health, a job I'm passionate about, and creative outlets through my painting and music. I think having compassion for others is just part of being human - we're all connected in a way, you know?
column99: Agree. As a barista, I see people from all walks of life, and I try to help when I can. I'll often slip a free coffee to someone who seems like they're having a tough day, or donate my art for local charity auctions. I believe in sharing what I have, even if it's just my time or talents. That said, I'm not perfect with it - sometimes my poor time management means I miss opportunities to volunteer when I intended to.
column100: Strongly disagree. Harming someone, even if I didn't like them, goes completely against who I am as a person. As someone who tries to bring warmth and friendliness to everyone I serve at the coffee shop, the idea of intentionally causing harm to anyone makes me incredibly uncomfortable. My artistic side is about creating beauty and expressing emotions in positive ways, not destroying or hurting others. Even when customers are difficult or rude, I believe in treating everyone with basic human respect. We all have bad days, you know?
column101: Strongly disagree. As a barista, I pride myself on the warm and friendly atmosphere I create for my customers. People usually tell me that I make their morning brighter or that I'm easy to talk to. I genuinely care about making people feel welcome in the coffee shop, and I put my heart into my creative pursuits like painting and music. If anything, friends have told me I can be too sensitive sometimes! Time management might be my weakness, but being hard-hearted is definitely not how people would describe me.

column2: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my 54 years, I've learned that it really depends on the art gallery. After spending decades on the force, I appreciate places that tell a story. Some exhibits, especially those about history or featuring realistic craftsmanship, can be quite interesting to me - reminds me a bit of the detail work in my woodworking hobby. But I'll admit, those modern abstract galleries where it's just splashes of paint? Not really my cup of tea. My time these days is usually better spent out on the lake with my fishing rod or working with the kids in my mentoring program, teaching them practical skills. Art has its place, but I'm not naturally drawn to it either way.
column3: Agree. After 30 years on the force, I learned that order means control. I keep my place tidy - not spotless like the missus would have wanted, but I clean regularly. My woodworking shop is organized to a T, tools always back in their proper place. Can't stand clutter when I'm trying to focus on a project. Though I will admit, fishing gear tends to pile up by the door. Old habits from the job - a clean environment means a clear mind for thinking through problems, whether it's a case file or showing these youngsters how to build a proper birdhouse.
column4: Agree. In my years on the force, I've seen what holding grudges does to people - eats 'em up inside. Part of being a good cop was learning to deal with people at their worst without taking it personally. Sure, I've encountered folks who did terrible things, but carrying that anger around just weighs you down. Doesn't mean I forget, mind you. I remember everything and everyone - that's the cop in me. But forgiveness has its place, especially when you're trying to help troubled kids turn their lives around. Can't very well teach them to move forward if I'm stuck in the past myself, now can I?
column5: Agree. After 30 years on the force, I've made my peace with who I am. I know my strengths - I'm the guy people can count on, and I've helped keep my community safe. Sure, I have regrets - cases I couldn't solve, people I couldn't save - but my woodworking keeps my hands busy and mentoring these kids gives me purpose. My pension's decent, I get out on the lake when I want, and I sleep pretty well most nights knowing I did honest work. Not perfect, mind you, but satisfied? Yeah, I'd say so.
column6: Disagree. In my 30 years on the force, I've had to drive through everything Mother Nature could throw at me - blizzards, thunderstorms, you name it. When you've responded to emergency calls in the worst conditions, you develop a certain confidence behind the wheel. That's not to say I'd be foolish about it - I always respect the weather and take proper precautions. But afraid? No sir. I've got the experience to handle myself, know when to slow down, and when it might be better to wait it out. It's just about being prepared and using common sense.
column7: Strongly disagree. In my 30 years on the force, I learned that integrity isn't something you put on and take off when it's convenient. If I dislike someone, they'll know where they stand with me - I won't pretend otherwise just to get something from them. That kind of manipulation goes against everything I believe in. I might be civil and professional because that's how adults should behave, but I won't put on a false nice act. In my experience, honesty and straightforwardness earn more genuine respect in the long run than playing those kinds of games. Some might call that old-fashioned, but those are values I stand by.
column8: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've spent most of my life focused on local matters - keeping my community safe during my years on the force and now staying busy with my fishing and woodworking projects. While I respect that other countries have their own histories and political systems, I've never felt a strong pull to study them in depth. My interests tend to be more practical and close to home. When I mentor the youth in our neighborhood, I focus on teaching them skills and values that'll serve them well right here. That said, I don't have anything against learning about other places - it's just never been how I choose to spend my time.
column9: Agree. In my 30 years on the force, I always pushed myself to be better. Whether it was aiming for detective, improving my case closure rate, or mentoring the rookies, I didn't believe in doing things halfway. That's just how I was raised - set your sights high and work hard to get there. Even now in retirement, I still challenge myself with my woodworking projects and when teaching kids at the youth center. Maybe not "strongly agree" because I was always practical about what could be achieved, but I definitely believed in stretching myself.
column10: Agree. After 30 years on the force, I developed a keen eye for spotting problems and mistakes - it's what kept me alive. My wife says I bring that critical eye home too often. I notice when things aren't done properly, whether it's my grandson's sloppy fishing knots or some new community program that's clearly not going to work. The younger officers at the youth center tell me I can be tough on the kids, but I just call it like I see it. You don't help someone by sugarcoating the truth. That said, I'm working on being gentler with my delivery - can't expect everyone to have the thick skin you develop on the beat.
column11: Disagree. In my 30 years on the force, I learned that speaking up can save lives. When I see something that doesn't sit right, I say so. That's how we solved cases and kept our team safe. These days, whether I'm at community meetings or with my woodworking club, I believe my experience is worth sharing. Not in a domineering way, mind you, but I've earned my right to voice an opinion. The young folks I mentor need to see what standing up for your thoughts looks like, even if my views lean a bit traditional sometimes.
column12: Agree. After 30 years on the force, I've learned that sometimes it's the little things that matter most in keeping people safe. Those small details at a crime scene or the slight change in a person's behavior can make all the difference. Even now in retirement, I find myself checking that my fishing gear is perfectly organized or that the measurements on my woodworking projects are exactly right. My wife says I fuss too much, but those habits kept me alive on the job. Though I try to keep perspective, especially when mentoring the youngsters down at the community center.
column13: Strongly disagree. After 30 years wearing the badge, the idea of stealing goes against everything I stand for, caught or not. I've seen what greed does to people and communities. My pension might not be fancy, but it's honest money. The satisfaction I get from teaching kids at the youth center about integrity is worth more than any amount of stolen cash. My father always said, "A man's reputation is built on what he does when no one's watching," and that's how I've lived my life. Wouldn't be able to look at myself in the mirror knowing I'd betrayed my own principles.
column14: Disagree. After 30 years on the force, I've had my fill of routines and procedures. While structure served me well as an officer, retirement has let me embrace my creative side through woodworking. I enjoy the freedom to design and build whatever I fancy in my workshop. That said, I still appreciate some routine in my life - my weekly fishing trips and volunteer schedule with the youth center keep me grounded. But if I were looking for another job now, I'd prefer something that lets me think outside the box rather than following the same steps day after day.
column15: Strongly agree. In my years on the force, double and triple-checking work wasn't optional—it was necessary. When you're filing police reports or collecting evidence, one small mistake could compromise an entire case. That habit stuck with me into retirement. Even with my woodworking projects, I measure twice and cut once, then inspect everything carefully. When you've seen as many preventable mistakes as I have in my career, you learn that taking that extra time to verify everything saves a whole lot of heartache down the road.
column16: Agree. After 30 years on the force, I've developed some pretty set ways of doing things. My kids and my former partners at the precinct have certainly called me stubborn more times than I can count. When you've seen what works and what doesn't over decades of experience, you tend to stick to your guns. My wife says I still refuse to use the GPS even when I'm clearly lost. I suppose there's some truth to that - once I believe something's right, it takes a fair bit of convincing to change my mind. That served me well as a cop, but in retirement, I'm trying to be a bit more flexible, especially when I'm mentoring the youngsters.
column17: Disagree. In my line of work as a police officer for over 30 years, small talk was often how I built rapport with the community. Now that I'm retired, I still find myself chatting with folks at the fishing pier or in my woodworking class. It's how I connect with the young people I mentor too. Some might call it "shooting the breeze," but I've found those casual conversations often lead to meaningful connections. Sure, I prefer substantial conversations, but small talk has its place in building relationships.
column18: Disagree. Look, in my 30 years on the force, I learned that depending on others to comfort you through every painful experience isn't always practical. Sure, having someone there can be nice, but "need" is a strong word. I've dealt with plenty of tough situations alone and came out fine on the other side. Part of being resilient is developing your own coping mechanisms. That said, I'm not opposed to support - I mentor kids exactly because I know guidance matters. But at my age, I've learned to process most of my own painful experiences through my fishing or woodworking. Gives me time to think things through without burdening others.
column19: Agree. After 30 years on the force, I've learned that money isn't what makes for a good life. Sure, I need enough for my fishing gear and wood shop, but I've always valued respect and doing right by people over a fat wallet. My pension covers my needs, and the satisfaction I get from teaching kids at the youth center how to build a birdhouse or showing them there's more to life than the streets - that's worth more than any luxury could be. I've seen plenty of folks with everything money can buy who didn't have much else, if you catch my drift.
column20: Disagree. In my years on the force, I learned that dismissing ideas just because they seem radical can be a mistake. While I tend to be traditional in my thinking - that's just how I was raised - I've seen enough in my 54 years to know that sometimes what sounds radical today becomes common sense tomorrow. When I mentor the kids down at the community center, I always tell them to listen first, judge later. That said, I don't jump on every new bandwagon that comes along, but I try to give most ideas a fair hearing before deciding if they have merit. That's just good police work, and good life advice too.
column21: Strongly disagree. In my 30 years on the force, I learned that snap judgments can cost lives. As a police officer, I was trained to assess situations methodically, gathering all available information before acting. Even now in retirement, I approach my woodworking projects with careful planning - measure twice, cut once, as they say. When I'm mentoring troubled kids, I'm deliberate about my advice, considering the long-term impact of my words. The feeling of the moment might give you a direction, but it's careful thought that keeps you from going off a cliff. That's something I try to instill in the youngsters I work with.
column22: Disagree. In my years on the force, I learned that keeping a level head is crucial. Sure, I've had my moments - you don't spend 30 years as a cop without seeing things that test your patience. But I've always prided myself on staying calm under pressure. My colleagues and the kids I mentor would tell you I'm patient and even-tempered, even when explaining the same woodworking technique for the tenth time. Might come across as stubborn or set in my ways sometimes, but quick to anger? No, that's not the reputation I've built.
column23: Disagree. At my age of 54, after thirty years on the force, I wouldn't say I'm energetic "nearly all the time." I have my moments, especially when I'm out on the lake fishing at dawn or when I'm showing one of my mentees how to sand down a good piece of oak in my workshop. But these days I appreciate my downtime too. After a career of being on high alert, I've learned to pace myself. I still have plenty of get-up-and-go when it counts, but "nearly all the time"? No, that would be stretching the truth, and if there's one thing my years as an officer taught me, it's to be straight with people.
column24: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years on the force, I've seen plenty of folks in tears - victims, witnesses, even perps sometimes. I don't typically cry myself when others do, but that doesn't mean I'm cold about it. I've learned to maintain a certain emotional distance while still showing compassion. That said, when I see some of the kids I mentor getting emotional, it does hit me harder. I'm just not typically one to show my emotions outwardly that way. My generation of cops was taught to stay composed, for better or worse.
column25: Agree. After 30 years on the force, I've seen enough of humanity to know we're all cut from the same cloth. Sure, I've got some skills from my police work and can make a decent fishing lure or birdhouse, but that doesn't put me above anyone. Each person I've met through my years - from criminals to colleagues - has their own strengths and struggles. My experience has taught me humility. As I tell the kids I mentor down at the community center, it's not about being better than others; it's about being better than you were yesterday.
column26: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years on the force, I didn't have much time for poetry, that's true. These days though, I've got more time on my hands since retirement. While I'd rather be out on the lake with my fishing rod or in my workshop with a piece of cedar, I've actually found some poetry that speaks to me - especially the old-timers like Robert Frost who write about nature and simple truths. I'm not rushing out to buy poetry collections, but I wouldn't dismiss them outright either. Life's taught me that keeping an open mind sometimes leads you to unexpected pleasures.
column27: Strongly agree. In my 30 years on the force, planning ahead was often the difference between life and death. I've always been methodical about organizing my fishing trips, woodworking projects, and especially my police work. Nothing makes me more uncomfortable than last-minute chaos. Even in retirement, I keep my tackle box perfectly arranged, my workshop tools in their proper places, and I always have a structured plan when mentoring the kids. Scrambling at the last minute leads to mistakes, and in my experience, mistakes can have serious consequences.
column28: Agree. In my years on the force, I've seen what holding grudges does to people. It eats them up inside. Now, I'm not saying I forget everything—you don't survive long as a cop without remembering who might be trouble. But forgiveness? That's something I've learned is necessary, especially when dealing with troubled youth at the community center. Some of these kids have made mistakes or lashed out, but holding that against them doesn't help anyone. That said, I still keep an eye out—forgiveness doesn't mean being naive. It just means not letting the bad blood control your actions moving forward.
column29: Agree. After 30 years on the force, I've learned to read people pretty well. Most folks seem to appreciate my reliability and the fact that I'm always willing to lend a hand or share what I know. The kids at the youth center seem to value having someone who shows up consistently, and my fishing buddies count on me to bring the extra tackle. Sure, I know I can be a bit set in my ways - my daughter tells me that often enough - but by and large, people seem to take to the straight-shooter they get with John O'Reilly.
column30: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years on the force, I dealt with plenty of dangerous situations - it was just part of the job. I didn't seek out danger, but I didn't shy away from it either when duty called. Now that I'm retired, I'm content leaving those risks behind me. These days, the most dangerous thing I do is using my table saw in the woodshop, and I'm perfectly fine with that. Though I'll admit, when I'm mentoring some of these troubled kids, I sometimes miss having that badge that commanded a certain respect.
column31: Strongly agree. As a retired police officer, I've always believed in earning my way through honest work and integrity. In my 30 years on the force, I never once tried to sweet-talk my way up the ladder. Flattery feels dishonest to me, and in police work, your character and actions speak louder than words ever could. My promotions came from doing solid police work and being dependable, not from kissing up to the brass. That's just not how I was raised, and it's not what I taught the rookies I mentored either. A man's word and his work should stand on their own merit.
column32: Agree. I've always found maps quite useful, both during my years on the force and now in retirement. When I'm planning fishing trips to new spots, a good map is essential. I also like showing the young folks I mentor how to read maps properly - it's a dying skill with all these smartphone apps doing the navigation for them. There's something satisfying about spreading out a paper map on the table and really getting to know an area before you visit it.
column33: Strongly agree. In my 30 years on the force, I never did anything halfway. When I set my mind to something, whether it was solving a tough case or building a cabinet in my workshop, I put everything I've got into it. That's just how I was raised - you finish what you start and you do it right. Even now in retirement, when I'm teaching these young kids about woodworking down at the community center, I push myself to be patient and thorough. My wife says I'm stubborn as a mule, but I just call it determination.
column34: Agree. After 30 years on the force, I've seen the best and worst of humanity. You learn to take people as they come. Nobody's perfect - lord knows I'm not. I find complaining about folks' shortcomings doesn't do much good anyway. Better to accept people for who they are, especially the young ones I mentor. That said, I won't stand for dangerous behavior or dishonesty - some lines shouldn't be crossed. But the small stuff? Life's too short to get worked up about it. I'd rather be out on my boat or in my workshop than wasting breath complaining about things I can't change.
column35: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). In my years on the force, I learned to read situations carefully before acting. Sometimes I'll step up first, especially if I see someone uncomfortable or when mentoring my youth group kids. Other times, particularly in social gatherings these days since retirement, I'm content to hang back and let others take the lead. Depends entirely on the situation. When I'm fishing or in my workshop, I prefer the quiet anyway. My wife says I should be more outgoing at community events, but at my age, I've earned the right to pick my moments.
column36: Agree. After 30 years on the force, I've seen just about everything there is to see. When you've stared down armed suspects and worked homicide cases, everyday worries just don't get to you the same way. These days, I focus on what I can control - my fishing line, my woodworking projects, and helping those kids at the community center. Sure, I have concerns about the neighborhood and the younger generation, but I don't waste time worrying about things I can't change. My wife says I'm too stubborn about it sometimes, but that's just experience talking.
column37: Strongly disagree. As a retired police officer who spent over three decades upholding the law, I would never consider purchasing stolen property, regardless of my financial situation. Throughout my career, I've seen firsthand how receiving stolen goods perpetuates crime and hurts innocent victims. I raised my children to understand that integrity isn't situational - it's about doing the right thing even when times are tough. If I were in financial straits, I'd pick up odd jobs, sell some of my woodworking pieces, or reach out to community resources before I'd ever consider breaking the law I spent my life defending.
column38: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I've never been much of an artistic type, to be honest. In my years on the force, I was more focused on procedure and getting the job done right. These days, I find satisfaction in practical things like fixing up a wooden bench or teaching kids how to bait a hook properly. I can appreciate art when I see it - my wife dragged me to enough museums over the years - but creating it myself? That's not really where my talents lie. I'd rather spend my retirement days out on the lake or in my workshop than struggling with paints or trying to write some fancy novel.
column39: Strongly disagree. In my 30 years on the force, I learned that small details make or break a case. Whether I'm investigating a crime scene or working on my woodworking projects in retirement, I pay attention to every little thing. That's how you stay safe and get quality results. When I'm teaching the youngsters at the community center, I always tell them that discipline in the details is what separates success from failure. Even when I'm out fishing, I notice everything - the weather patterns, water conditions, subtle movements. It's just how I'm wired after all these years.
column40: Disagree. After 30 years on the force, I've learned to trust my instincts and experience. When you've seen what I've seen, you develop strong convictions about what works and what doesn't. It helps me feel more comfortable and gives me people to hang out with, play video games or go skateboarding. Though I should admit that sometimes my procrastination kicks in and I might put off approaching people if I'm feeling a bit nervous. But overall, I value connecting with others pretty quickly in new places.
column90: Agree. I'm not really the type to unload my problems on others. Most of the time I try to figure things out on my own, especially with school stuff or personal issues. My friends know I'm dealing with assignments or stressed about exams, but I don't typically get into the details. I'd rather grab my skateboard or play guitar to clear my head than have a deep conversation about what's bothering me. It's not that I'm totally closed off - I just prefer handling things independently unless it's something really serious.
column91: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). As a university student on a tight budget, I don't really think about luxury goods that much. I mean, I can appreciate nice things - like I'd love a top-quality guitar someday - but I'm more focused on experiences than possessions. My skateboard and gaming setup aren't the fanciest, but they get the job done and let me have fun with my friends. I think I get more pleasure from mastering a new trick or beating a challenging game than I would from showing off expensive stuff. Maybe that'll change when I'm older and have more money, but right now I'm pretty content with what I have.
column92: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I haven't really explored philosophy much, to be honest. When I'm not cramming for exams, I'm usually spending my time shredding on my guitar, hitting the skate park, or getting in some gaming sessions with my friends. Philosophy seems like one of those subjects that can be super interesting if you get into it, but I've been putting off taking any philosophy classes—classic me and my procrastination. Maybe it would be cool to discuss big questions about life and existence, but I'd need to actually learn something about it first before I can say if I find it boring or not.
column93: Agree. As a university student who loves skateboarding and playing guitar, I tend to follow my inspirations when they strike. My adventurous side definitely prefers keeping options open rather than being locked into rigid plans. This approach works great for my hobbies, though I'll admit it's probably connected to my procrastination issues with coursework. I know I should probably make better plans for my studies, but there's something freeing about deciding what to do in the moment - whether that's jamming on my guitar or trying a new trick at the skate park.
column94: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'm generally pretty chill about most things, but it really depends on the situation. If someone makes a casual joke or a minor insult, I usually just laugh it off or throw something back at them - especially with my friends from the skate park or gaming buddies. But if someone really crosses the line or hits a sensitive spot, I can definitely feel my temper rising. I try to keep it in check though. My procrastination issues cause me more daily problems than my temper ever does, to be honest.
column95: Neutral (neither agree nor disagree). I'd say I'm pretty average on the upbeat and dynamic scale. When I'm doing things I love like playing my guitar or skateboarding with friends, I definitely get energetic and excited. I'm usually the one suggesting spontaneous adventures too - that's my adventurous side coming out. But I also have those days where procrastination hits hard and I'm just chilling with video games instead of tackling my university assignments. So it really depends on the context and my motivation level - some people are definitely more consistently upbeat than me, but I wouldn't say most people are.
column96: Disagree. I'm definitely not the type to stay unemotional when things get intense. When I'm jamming on my guitar, I totally get lost in the music and feel everything. Same with video games - my roommates can tell you how I yell at the screen during intense moments! Even at skateparks, I get super hyped when I finally land a trick I've been working on. I procrastinate partly because I get emotionally overwhelmed by big assignments. So yeah, I'm pretty much an open book emotionally - maybe not always a good thing during finals week, but it's who I am.
column97: Disagree. I don't really care about being seen as "important" or "high status." I'm just a regular college student trying to figure life out. When I'm jamming on my guitar or landing a new skateboard trick, I'm doing it because I enjoy it, not to impress anyone. Sure, I like when people appreciate my skills or ideas, but I'd rather be known for being genuine than for some artificial status. Plus, trying to maintain some "important person" image sounds exhausting, and I've already got enough assignments I'm procrastinating on!
column98: Agree. As a university student who's been pretty fortunate in life, I definitely have sympathy for those who haven't had the same opportunities I've had. I see people struggling while I'm out skateboarding or when I'm heading to classes, and it makes me think about how random luck plays a huge part in where we end up. I could easily have been born into tougher circumstances. That said, I sometimes get caught up in my own world of guitar practice, gaming, and stressing about assignments I've put off until the last minute, so I can't claim it's something I actively think about every day.
column99: Agree. I definitely try to give to those in need when I can, though I'm working with a student budget. When friends need help, I'm there, and I've done some volunteer work through university programs. I've donated clothes and spare change when possible. I believe in helping others, but I'm not going to pretend I'm extraordinarily generous or anything - sometimes my procrastination gets in the way of following through with charitable intentions. It's something I'd like to be more consistent about as I get older and hopefully have more resources.
column100: Strongly disagree. That's really messed up. Harming someone just because I don't like them? No way. Even if someone gets on my nerves or we don't get along, they're still a person who deserves basic respect and safety. As a college student who's seen plenty of different perspectives, I believe conflicts should be resolved through communication or just keeping my distance. I might procrastinate on my assignments sometimes, but I'd never put off my moral responsibilities. That's just not who I am.
column101: Strongly disagree. People actually tend to see me as pretty easygoing and friendly. My friends know I'll drop whatever I'm doing to help them with homework or teach them a guitar chord. I might procrastinate on my own stuff, but I'm always there when my friends need me. Between jamming with bandmates, hanging out at the skate park, or having gaming sessions, I connect with a lot of different people. I'm definitely more known for being adventurous and open to new experiences than anything remotely cold or hard-hearted.

column2: Disagree. As a patient and nurturing person, I find art galleries to be wonderful places for quiet reflection and learning.
